_childDocuments_.review: Dome Keeper is a fun base defense and mining actioner. You are dropped on a hostile alien world to establish a base and dig beneath your dome for resources and artifacts; meanwhile you must build and use defenses to protect the dome from regular waves of various silhouetted alien monsters. The simple pixel graphics and animation and 8-bit style music and sound effects are cute and stylish. There are many nice little graphical touches; moss and plants grow in patches on the walls of your tunnels, and little native creatures poke shyly around the uncovered depths. The game plays like an old-school early console title; there is no save, so you have to win or die to end each 30-minute-or-so playthrough. Gameplay is designed for a console controller, which I recommend using.The gameplay has a decent amount of depth for such simple mechanics, but once you've played through a few times, there's not a lot of variety in further replays. There are about a dozen unlocks of different gadgets that you can choose from in subsequent replays, but for the most part the only variety past about 10 hours of play is in increasingly difficult settings and game modes. The developers have released new content since release, but thus far it seems to be limited to little bells and whistles for the same basic mode of play.Despite the atmospheric alien environments, there's no explanation of who you are or why you are here, nor any unfolding story over the course of multiple missions to reward additional replay. I think it could really benefit from some framework or context to the missions that allowed for some kind of progression... it could perhaps double or triple the amount of quality play time in the game. 10 hours is maybe a little bit light for the asking price.Overall, I found Dome Keeper to a fun and engaging action game. My main issue with it is that it left me wanting more, but that is not such a terrible thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Dome Keeper

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a bad game. I'm only giving negative, because I don't believe the game deserves such glowing ovations - this isn't a 9/10 game. Wish I could give a neutral for this one.The game looks, feels and sounds cool. It's an interesting spin on the rogue like formula, mixing resource gathering with sort of tower defense gameplay. There is no inventory, and physics play a big role here - if you're clumsy, you'll pay for it. You have some different game modes, some different abilities and you unlock things as you progress. You lose a game or two, start learning and progress. And here we come into problems.You mine resources as efficiently as you can, hoping to find as many upgrades/features for your dome that will make you even more efficient, and after a certain period of time (which starts short and becomes a bit longer as the run progresses), you need to go back to your dome to defend it against a wave of enemies. On paper, it sounds great, and for few hours, it is. If I rated the game just by first impressions, it would score highly.The hardest part of the run is the initial first half - usually, when you reach mid to late stage of a run, you are all set, and just go through motions. While you can up the difficulty to downright unfair, or add some obnoxious modifiers if you really hate yourself, the same issue applies, you still struggle at the beginning, the second half of a run is usually just part for the course. I've played the other mode, but the endless sandbox is sort of a bonus, not something I want to primarily play.After first few hours filled with addicting gameplay, I felt a bit deflated, as I've realized that core gameplay just isn't that engaging to me. Let me try to make a comparison, so it makes more sense.I always bring out Binding of Isaac as a perfect example of great value - it's a golden standard in rogue likes, because the game can change drastically each run. When it comes to the amount of content in a rogue like, there is a lots of it, and it's meaningful, it's not quantity over quality! Dome Keeper doesn't have this - there is a small selection, and most importantly, it doesn't change too much during each round, as you choose the main stuff yourself. You get additional support items, which are all sorts of active powerups, ranging from an automated turrets to lifts that help you carry resources. All of this is good, but it's just not enough, there are only like 10 additional items that you can find during each run.The game would function much better if it was multi-layered, if there were multiple things to strive for in a run, if you could switch the equipment you get, if you could buy additional things in a shop, I honestly would love to see a sequel that would borrow from BoI or similar rogue like games, because the core of this game is solid, but it's just not enough to keep me invested on it's own. The additional modes are fine, but clearly not something that can keep you occupied - if the core gameplay isn't good enough, obsessively chasing numbers does nothing for me. I also miss any kind of mystery or discovery - there isn't really anything like that. You can find few nice powerups in the mine, but they repeat in almost every run.There isn't necessarily a strong sense of progression, which I find it be really important in these rogue-likes. While the main equipment you unlock is very meaningful, as it can change how you play the game quite a bit, I think it also sort of works against it, because after switching my character for example, my initial impression was horrible, because the new character controlled very differently, and while I'm sure the experienced gamers might prefer this character, for me, it was just hellish. And that was the first thing I've unlocked! This is clearly very subjective, so if you like the idea of completely changing parts of the game around with different core abilities, you're going to love this, because the main abilities really change the gameplay significantly. You still do the same stuff (mining, defending), but a sword dome controlls very differently to laser dome etc., and you will feel that in your gameplay. There are some really cool additions, like a little dinosaur with a drill that helps you in the mines, an automated shotgun turret or a lift for the materials you carry. You can find a teleporter and there are many ways you can make your run easier and more convenient.Every game is repetitive to an extent, but here, it became mindless for me. There is no danger in the mines, your only concern is to be as efficient as possible, getting back in time and use additional gadgets when you can. Also I must say the back and forth dynamics didn't quite do it for me - it's fine, but just sort of irritating here. In other games like Kingdom, you also race with time, but you have plenty of quiet time to relax. Here, if I'm not digging or moving around, I'm wasting my time, and it's not like there is anything to really see in the mines.I've seen plenty of reviewers going for 30+ hours, so the game kept their interest for much longer than me - however, going by the achievements, I would be surprised if majority of players spent over 10 hours in this game.

name: Xuan-Yuan Sword: Mists Beyond the Mountains
detailed_description: The Journey of a Frankish Knight in the Tang Empire Xuan-Yuan Sword: Mists Beyond the Mountains is a classic turn-based RPG . Under the orders of Pepin III , the Frankish Knight Septem has embarked on a long journey to seek the Invincible Arts of War . Starting from the canals of beautiful Venice, the great knight's path has spanned the Middle East, Western Regions on his way to the mystical orient. In his adventures, Septem has drawn into the intricate power disputes between local powers, along with the decade-spanning ambitions of the dark lord, Satan . China enjoys peace and prosperity under the rule of the Tang Empire , Europe finds itself embroiled in the Dark Ages , the Arabian Empire is ascendant, and all the while, the march of progress brings these disparate cultures together. From ancient times, Chinese legends have spoken of the Xuan-Yuan Sword and Spirit Fusion Pot , along with the rise of great legends in the new era... A Symphony of Western and Eastern Culture The scope of Xuan-Yuan Sword: Mists Beyond the mountains covers a wide range, spanning all of Eurasia and covering the Arab World, Francia, and China. From the canals of Venice, Damascus to the beautiful Chang’an, the story introduces unique architectural styles, clothing, food, and customs. A Fusion of History and Fantasy The story of Xuan-Yuan Sword III takes place in an era of collision between East and West, covering a range of historical events that include the Battle of Talas, the Arabian Civil War, and An Lushan Rebellion interspersed through character dramas. Xuan-Yuan Sword III perfectly integrates history with Chinese and Western mythology. Players will encounter unique historical enemies such as Merovingian soldiers, the Venetian navy, the Abbasid Caliphate, Tang soldiers, and Taoists along with unique mythical creatures such as centaurs, Medusa, the Black and White Reapers, and the Xuannü of the Nine Heavens. Unique Spirit Fusion Pot System Players can use the Spirit Fusion Pot to capture enemies in battle. Items and monsters can be used to craft a new item or monster from the codex. Users can craft items and monsters from the Eastern or Western altars, which the resulting item differing based on the selected altar. Unique Ink Painting Artstyle The game features a beautiful traditional Chinese style, with the game map, battle backgrounds, and characters all painted in unique oriental ink. Improvements and changes 16:9 high-resolution graphic UI rework High-resolution item texture Controller support China Episode, originally added in mobile version

_childDocuments_.review: In Mists Beyond the Mountains, Knight Septem of the Frankish Kingdom takes us along on his spiritual and religious quest as he battles Satan, the ruler of the underworld. In the middle of a rebellion, the church's defenders intend to execute any heretics or atheists by being crucified or burned alive. Lords and nobles with immense authority don't dare to provoke them since they are able to commit crimes at will. It is up to us to put up a fight against this oppression, avert war, and uphold the honor of King Pepin III, Lord of the Palace and King of the Franks. We therefore travel to the Lombards in the South, the Saxons in the North, and even to the Muslim countries in the West in order to obtain the great secret of the Eastern Empire, who have the knowledge of winning any war. The addition of the Chinese continent in the east, which was previously only accessible on mobile devices, is also included here.In terms of gameplay, the whole thing is kept very simple. While running around in the open world, battles randomly appear within seconds. Once we are in a fight, we have the choice of attacking the desired opponent, using a special ability in exchange for "spiritual power", or select items. The abilities are different in nature, some of them allow us to cast spells to inflict magical damage on our target, and some of them increase our own stats. The ultimate bar fills up when we get hit or do damage, allowing us to use an ultimate attack that is unique to each character. As you play, more companions are automatically introduced, and they come in a wide variety. For example, Nicole is an underworld archer with magical abilities, while Li Jing is a spearman who deals a lot of physical damage. These characters all have a sense of importance and don't feel like afterthoughts.One of the most interesting features is that I can capture almost any type of enemy. The captured enemies can be equipped to increase the character's stats, or we can merge the captured monsters. What happens when you merge them depends on what you are merging them with. Whether we fuse a weapon and an enemy, two enemies, or maybe just two normal items is up to us. This adds a tremendous amount of variation and allows us to create new opponents, items, or equipment that you may not have seen before. In exchange for agility, the enemies in your collection can also be of assistance for the duration of the battle.It would be an incredibly beautiful and unique game if it weren't for the many technical problems and non-existent settings. I can somehow overlook the many spelling and translation errors (quite obviously machine translated), as well as the inability to change any of the graphical settings, but once the game started to crash, it was just too much. I was afraid the game would crash after every battle, and it was not uncommon to lose minutes of gameplay time that I had to catch up on. I'm glad to see that autosave is quite often, so progress loss is usually minimal, but still annoying. It makes it hard to focus on the game itself because you're always worried that it will be over soon. In addition, the spacing and tenses are inconsistent all the time, resulting in mixed messages. What I also noticed is that some of the abilities (Septem's ultimate attack, or even the shouts of battle victory) are so incredibly loud in comparison to the other effects.At least the games presentation doesn't have to disguise itself. The surroundings do a wonderful job of capturing the feel of the aforementioned nations. It's splendidly illustrated, the soundtrack fits each location, and it sometimes made me think of Chrono Cross. The transition between gameplay and cutscenes is also incredibly smooth. I'm not too angry about the fact that the cutscenes appears to be so "low-res" because they look like they were rendered as a 240p YouTube video and could definitely be of higher quality. I'm all the more saddened by the overall technical state of the game, because there are so many unique elements to it.I was actually looking forward to Xuan-Yuan Sword: Mists Beyond the Mountains. The historical and political adventure had a lot of potential because of its blend of turn-based combat, gorgeous background images, and dialog-heavy characters, and I was eager to start playing a game with such a rich history. But a terrible technological issue hides underneath the moving narrative. Xuan-Yuan III is easy to recommend once the issues have been resolved, especially for people who are simply interested in the main plot. Unfortunately, unnecessary issues like uneven fonts, unreadable dialogue, typos, and even a lack of sound in conjunction with a poor sound mix are the last nail in the coffin.

_childDocuments_.review: The unexpected has happened: a classic Chinese RPG has received a remastered release, and with it English subtitles.The game was originally released in 1999, and it is one of the most highly regarded installments in the franchise. Like most other games in the series, it’s historical fantasy, although this time, it is not just about Chinese history, as our protagonist, Septem, is a knight from the Frankish Kingdom. He is given an important mission by Pepin III: to travel to the distant East and obtain the secret method that can win all wars. On his adventurous journey, Septem travels to Venice, the Middle East, Central Asia, and finally to the Tang Empire.In terms of gameplay, it's basically a JRPG. You move around in isometric view with chibi style characters in the locations or on the world map, while the battles are team based and use Active Time Battle system. A wide variety of different items, equipment and character abilities add depth to the combat. One of the mechanics unique to the series is the Spirit Fusion Pot, which allows you to both capture enemies during combat (which you can then summon to help you) and to fuse not only items but also captured enemies too. Basically anything can be fused with anything. The game also shows what the outcome of the fusions will be, so there’s no trial and error, thankfully.This sort of crafting system is interesting, though you can do without it on a casual playthrough, since the game is not very difficult. The basic enemies and random encounters can be easily beaten using auto attack, it's only the bosses where you really have to pay attention to what you're doing. This also makes capturing enemies a bit more difficult, as you need them to be at low health, but they often die from a single hit. All things considered, I didn't mind that the game wasn't hard, and I also appreciated that there was no need for grinding or farming to finish it. It was only at the last boss where I had to turn back to stock up on healing items. By the way, apparently, this was not the case with the original game. That was harder than this release, which is based on an expanded mobile port.The visuals of the game are great, there was no need for a remaster here. The locations are beautiful and spectacular, and the backgrounds of the battles are done in the style of Chinese paintings. For most of the game we are looking at chibi style characters, but in combat we have nicely drawn and detailed sprites, not just for our teammates but the enemies as well. One thing that didn’t end up great are the cutscenes. It seems they tried to AI upscale them, but they just ended up being ugly. It would have been better to leave them pixelated. The audio is allright, there are some very nice music pieces, but the sound effects are mostly just doing their job.For me, the story was the most interesting part of the game. Septem's adventure begins in the 750’s and during his journey, which takes him through almost the whole known world, he meets many interesting and memorable characters, including of course historical figures (e.g. Pipin III, Emperor Xuanzong), and gets involved in political intrigues and historical events (Abbasid Revolution, Battle of Talas, etc.). Of course, it is a fantasy game too and this aspect is more pronounced. The story, rich in twists and turns, involves fantastical and mythological events, with the main antagonist being Lord Satan himself.I really liked this mixing of different cultural inspirations. I never thought I'd see a game world combine Christian lore with Chinese folklore, but this one did it. This was also good for the enemy variety, as we have everything from creatures inspired by European mythology to various genies and monsters of the Chinese fantasy genre. Interestingly, our hero is not even a believer at first, but a down-to-earth pragmatist who is as surprised as we are by the encounters with the divine and supernatural, but after what he experiences and learns about himself during his journey, he has to come to realize that 'there are more things in heaven and earth', if I may say so.The game is not short on dialogue. Not only do we talk a lot with our team members and the NPCs that join us, but almost every minor character and NPC has something to say about the situation. This adds a lot to the lore and the world, but talking to everyone is also ho we find side missions. Apart from the usual fetch quests these include, interestingly enough, math problems, which basically require you to put the game aside and start counting. There are also some NPCs who ask historical or religious questions, giving you a reward if you answer correctly. These also require some googling, but at least you can learn something from them.The remastered release isn’t flawless though. The biggest issue here, as with most Chinese games, is the English subtitles. It's noticeably machine translated, and you often come across odd phrases, typos or various stylistic errors that break immersion. This would be less of a problem in a game with dubbing, since the voice actors can establish the mood of the scene and present the characters, but here we only have the text, so sometimes it's hard to figure out what the original writer was thinking. Overall it's not that bad, you can follow the story and most of the stronger, dramatic moments come through, but it could have been a lot better. I also encountered a few cases of text disappearing from the screen too quickly and some crashes, which could be avoided by setting the game to Windows 7 compatibility. Apart from these, it was fine.Despite the translation problems, I had a lot of fun with the game, it was an amazing adventure. I would recommend it to those who are interested in Chinese fantasy games but also to those who have a passion for retro JRPGs, because in that category this game is a real gem, which was not available until now for those who don't speak Chinese. I hope to see more remasters of classic Chinese games in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I have beaten this game 4 times.  Once in 1999, once in the mid 2000s, once in the mid 2010s, and just now.  The first 3 times were the original CD versions (and subsequent expansion packs).  The most recent time was the current version (mobile remake).Classic sprite based art, unchanged from the 90s version (there's some upscaling, and upscaling up to 2K available for background and effects in the workshop), but it is mostly hand drawn water color style art, which still looks fantastic in 2024.  There were some additional animations added in the remake version to a few of the character avatars/sprites, but honestly I wouldn't have noticed them unless they were mentioned to me. The music is fantastic.  The first track you hear in Venice is one I've listened to at least a thousand times.  As you traverse the in game world, the music changes to fit the environment thematically.  The sound effects are sort of glitchy (inconsistent volume), but overall sound the same as the original.  There is no voice acting (same as original)There is a significant differentiation between the new/remake/mobile version vs the original, and that is enemies have their HP cut by about 70%.  For most of the first half of the game, every monster dies in 1 hit.  However you can play the DLC version of the original DVD copy which has the original damage values.  Keep in mind that these values were based around 90s game play, and they are tortuously hard to play with.  We're talking hundreds if not thousands of hours of grinding for certain "special rewards".  The remake vastly reduced the difficulty, to the point of it being almost boring to do fights because so many monsters are 5 to 10 second kills.  The final bosses (and the secret bosses) can be killed in a minute due to a special ability acquired from the expansion (that was released 20 years ago).  In the original version, this special ability while still overkill, would still not let you kill the bosses in a minute.  HOWEVER, I honestly preferred the vastly easier version of gameplay because I've already done the 100% completion on the older, much more difficult version.  So this time around I wanted to just cruise through the game.  This remake/mobile also includes additional China Campaign quests which extended the length of playthrough but the quests themselves were very easy (minus the trivia questions).  Many of the side quests are math or trivia questions, which may become tiresome and even unintelligible for some.The plot is great.  Perhaps it's nostalgia tinting my perspective but I really enjoyed learning and reading through the story once more.  I played this in Traditional Chinese all 4 times and cannot comment on the quality of the English Translation (which I hear is not good).  The story in Chinese is very intriguing and keeps the player guessing, learning, and understanding as the character develops.I loved it.  I loved it when it came out, and I loved it enough to do a full replay on the remake version, which I still loved.  I honestly feel this is one of my favorite games, it is not perfect but the story, character development, monster crafting capabilities were things I loved to spend time on when I were younger, and still hold true today.I wrote a guide and a post in the Community Hub for those trying to get the DVD version to work on the Deck.  Happy to answer any questions.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a 1999/2000 vibe in its purest form, it feels like a lost JRPG gem from the times of the original PlayStation that somehow made its way to modern times. Had it been released in English back then, and probably we would be talking about a renowned classic in the West.The pre-rendered backgrounds and the character sprites make this game beautiful, together with an excellent soundtrack and a storyline that keeps you hooked till the end. You actually get to learn some historical background of the 8th century and some details of the golden age of Chinese history during the Tang Dynasty.The QoL enhancements of this port address some of its original issues (not all) and make the game better than the original version. There are though some issues with the difficulty balance, from enemies too easy to enemies that will one-hit kill you, but these are minor grips. The English translation is not the best, but it is serviceable and good enough to play the game and understand it.I truly hope that someday we can see Xuan Yuan Sword: The Scar of Sky in English as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Ended up beating this game on Switch. I hope we get it's counter part one day. Great game.This game is a favorite of mine growing up and I had some Chinese friends help me get through it back in the early 2000s. It was a touching experience and this game was nothing like I had played at the time. This and it's counter part Scar of the Sky still remain in my top 50 favorite games. With that said, it is a little sad to see this English version get a mixed reception, so I will go ahead knock a few things out for anyone curious about this game. If I spot something new, I will edit my review accordingly. There are some math problems as part of minor side quests, but they are mostly optional and the rewards aren't anything too worthwhile. Some of the questions could be translated better.Haven't had the game crash yet on me. There are also recordings of the game that also show the crash isn't isn't happening for everyone. Text is a little funky in both it's engrish localization and text display. I haven't seen any invisible text yet, but there is an inner dialogue that flashes on the screen a little too quick for me.The original had controller support from the get go. This appears to be a port of the mobile version with extra content and some polarizing UI changes. I haven't tested game pad yet, but I get the impression gamepad is not fully supported. Keyboard is okay for a game like this though as the battles are turn based. There is one aspect that does really annoy me. Occasionally you will get a multiple choice question and I was unable to select the answer using the keyboard. I had to actually reach out and move the mouse over the desired answer. Customization options are very limited. You get windowed and full screen.. not much else from what I can see.So this is clearly a rush port of the mobile version which will work fine for some and not so fine for others. It just needs a little polish in its translation and UI. If you can look past it, the game is still a rewarding experience.As far as the game itself, it's still amazing in both it's presentation and simplicity. If you liked early PS1 and SNES rpgs, I would highly recommend it. I love the historical feel and the multicultural aspect of traveling from across the Eastern hemisphere.  The music is also incredible. Art and graphics still hold up if you are into the 2D look. I do want to suggest whoever published the English version of this game to strongly consider bringing over Scar of the Sky. That one is widely considered the best among fans of this series and they even made a (terrible) tv series based on it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good and the translation isn't too bad, considering it is done by an AI. The CG cutscenes are more so a mess as they appear blurry and stained due to a failed attempt to AI upscale them instead of reverting to the original resolution, making them near impossible to view comfortably.The story really drags once you arrive to China, and the final boss really punishes you for not completing missable questlines which are poorly detailed, some which require another playthrough once failed (I'm looking at you Salda merchant). Not the best in the series I feel but a very good RPG which will keep you engaged for hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this game for first time, so don't know how good the older version was when it came out, mentioned in few reviews etc gameplay is easy, only during boss fights player have to do something else will get killed unlike random encounters which are not challenging, so old players or those who are expecting persona or smt or other games in the series kind challenging encounters etc will be disappointed.So far the translation helps to understand the story, but for those who want to enjoy the story, see the story world and meet it's character it's good.Also find it interesting talking to every character in the city player visits each has something to say about the area, current situation, or give quests etc or riddles etc, lacking in challenging gameplay but interesting to search areas or talk to people in the story world or capture different demons etc and do fusion etc. But don't expect persona or smt level of demon capture and fusion etc. Using controller is very smooth no issues. _childDocuments_.review: It's an old  linear, turn-based RPG - if that is to your liking, then you've come to the right place. It's an old game, but this story of a young man's journey from the west to east is a kind of unique one whose like I don't think I've encountrered before - a kind of unique blend of elements from both East and West... I wouldn't quite call this a wuxia as such, but it has some elements from there. Either way, there's plenty of loot and weapons to find, secrets to uncover, bosses, both hidden and not to fight and creatures to capture as you follow the young protagonists journey from the west to east. A complaint you often see when it comes to these games is that the translation is found wanting to say the least. I shall not say that this one is perfect, but it does seem to be one of the better ones - it's seldom as strangely worded or full of half-gibberish as some such sometimes are... There are a few compaints of mine I have for the game though:- I feel that you level a bit too fast in this game - you can easily enough end up max levelled after going though only half of the game, which feels a bit unsatisfactory...- Some of the monsters are supposed to be different but look identical or very nearly so, which feels kinda lazy... doesn't help when you're trying to uncover every creature for the book either.- I wish you could do something to stop temporary party members from taking part in the fights, because often enough they end up kill-stealing or killing an opponent we want to keep alive for a bit longer (for purposes of taming, stealing or weapon levelling)...- It's good that there's an automode in the game, but it's not quite as fast as I wish it were. This is a very minor complaint of mine though.Don't worry about spending too much time on the game either, for unless you actively pour time into doing some extra stuff (as I did), playing the game from beginning to end should take no more than about 30-40 hours. It's also not too expensive a game and yet cheaper during sales so if games of this genre is your thing, give it a shot, I certainly do recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: If you like old j-rpg kind of, but one from China, get it, and celebrate that this one was traduced.About game itself, its about Knowledge of different cultures around centuries to countries, and tolerance and intolerance as well. It was happy to see a game with wisdom, and, paraphrasing Hayao Miyazaki's words: not just for immature otakus (even though he was referring to the way they lived rather than knowledge).Another point to remark is then 2D narrative, more like a tale, were charterers movements express them (who participates in the fight, for example, or, as happened in the FFVI, where the shy samurai interrupts the dialogue to ask us to bring him closer to the interlocutor).No crashing so far, and as a weak point, mention the 3D scenes.Kojima said that we get used of graphics sooner than later, and despite its graphics never left me indifferent at all (music either), talking about mechanics, we can collect monsters as well as some kindda cooking, some quests and riddles aside, further of story. Its story, well, reminds me of the great ancient epics. Kingcraft. Lambs. P. S.: Khawla bint al-Azwar.P. S.: As a personal suggestion, to figuratively show the 'knowledge' in it, I will say that its weapons have reminded me of what I felt when playing Baldur's Gate II, namely, weapons with a history behind them.PS: I wouldn't say that the game is particularly difficult, but I must add that in order to complete the main game I had to defeat an extra boss, which I don't know if it's common, nor if it's completely fair. In any case, I would say that to complete the main game then I would recommend exploring its environments (to get items and experience) as well as the menus (to discover skills).

_childDocuments_.review:
Under the orders of Pepin III, the Frankish Knight Septem has embarked on a long journey to seek the Invincible Arts of War. Starting from the canals of beautiful Venice, the great knight's path has spanned the Middle East, Western Regions on his way to the mystical orient. In his adventures, Septem has drawn into the intricate power disputes between local powers, along with the decade-spanning ambitions of the dark lord, Satan.

The game features a beautiful traditional Chinese style, with the game map, battle backgrounds, and characters all painted in unique oriental ink.

name: B.I.O.T.A.
detailed_description: MORE GAMES FROM RETROVIBE About the Game Pick your retro style and enjoy this ultimate run and gun throwback! You vs. monsters B.I.O.T.A. is an intense 2D action-platformer, in which you command a team of mercenaries and investigate a mining colony infected by an alien plague. Explore a pixel art world packed with mutant monsters and deadly traps. Try to survive using a multitude of guns and various crafts, including a mech, a sub, and a starship. The best of both worlds B.I.O.T.A. mixes the charm of retro games (including two-pixel breathing animations) with the modern-day convenience of full controller support, quick saves, customizing the visuals at any time, and a soundtrack so chippy that you'll want to record a cassette mixtape and listen to it on your Walkman. Pick your retro Craving for some old-school Game Boy esthetics? Looking for a neon-infused arcade style? B.I.O.T.A. has 54 unique 4-color palettes to unlock. Swap them anytime during your play to completely change the game’s 8-bit visuals. Uncover corporate secrets Take command of a team of 8 veteran mercenaries and switch between them to utilize their unique skills and weapons. Investigate the mining colony overrun by an alien plague and face 40+ horrific monsters that mutated out of the miners. Rescue the scientists, and uncover the truth about V-corp’s illegal activities. KEY FEATURES 54 unique 4-color palettes to swap 8 playable characters to unlock and upgrade Story campaign with two endings Arcade levels where you control a submarine, destroy enemies in a powerful mech and chase starships in outer space Additional time trials and target shooting game modes Retro fun with modern-day convenience 4 controller presets and 6 keyboard control presets to choose from Energizing chiptune-synthwave soundtrack

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic metroidvania action platformer where you are a group of mercenaries that were sent to an infected mining place to investigate the situationYou can watch some gameplay here: It's not so hard to learn the game, but i'd recommend a controller over a keyboard here.You'll have 4 available characters and 4 other ones that you can unlock, each unique in skills, stats and weapons.The story is also said to have two endings and there are levels where you also have to drive very special vehicles such as a Mech, spaceship or a submarine!Also in terms of enemies and bosses there is a nice variation that can avoid some monotonous gameplay.There is also a variety of upgrades that you can buy for your characters.Graphically the game is also very nice and a nice ode to the 8-bit era, the few colors that are in the game quickly give you a classic gameboy color impression and I think this is great.The retro inspired soundtrack is also present and every boss has his own music.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? This game looks like a Nintendo Gameboy release with 4 colors, but it uses a large screen. It also plays like a Gameboy classic - but this is not a bad thing. It's a run and gun game - jump and shoot (in 4 directions), avoid endless pits, other environemental dangers and enemies. Quite easy to understand, even for me. There are people to talk to, cutsequences to watch, weapons and other items to find - but simply shooting everything also works rather good (most of the time). Later in the game you have to use little vehicles, like a one-man submarine or a tiny mech. Furthermore, you don't play just one hero. You can switch between different characters with unique skills and weapons. The 4-color visuals look great (you unlock new color palettes to swap all the time) - but it does make dangers (or objects to pick up) sometimes hard to see. Save anytime and anywhere - but you have only one slot. My noname gamepad worked fine. So, is it a masterpiece? Probably not, but certainly a solid handiwork if you enjoy some retro action once in a while (like I do).Modern run'n gun in Gameboy visuals and with some exploring and backtracking required.
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately I can't recommend this game.  While the overall graphical, sound, and gameplay design meet and in many cases exceed expectations, there are too many problems with the controls and mechanics of the game which make it a chore to play.  The wall latch/jump mechanics, in particular, are completely broken: 1. When you jump normally, letting go of left/right will result in your momentum slowing to a stop, but out of a wall jump, your momentum is maintained.  It's tremendously non-intuitive and forces you to try and mentally keep track of things that should be muscle memory.2. You can't shoot while wall-latched (why?) but when trying to shoot, you will enter a glitched state where you alternate back and forth between trying to shoot and trying to de-latch.3. If you try to slide down the wall, after a couple of seconds you will de-latch and be completely unable to re-latch.4. Sometimes you'll wall-latch just trying to walk off a ledge.  And because of point 3, that will often result in you free-falling in a segment you were trying to do a controlled descent in.Plus the back half of the game is overloaded with tedious gimmick segments which tried my patience and put me in a bad mood and with no desire to try and post-game.It's not an awful game if you can get past the jank, but the reality is there are hundreds of more-competently made retro 2D Metroidvanias out there to play and this one mostly just frustrated me.
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s time to complain again about the lack of space in steam’s rating system for 3/5 games, as it does feel very mean spirited to give Biota a thumbs down. It’s a short, cute, polished metroidvania with no new ideas that is probably worth the asking price of £7.50. It reminds me a lot of Gatoroboto, another decent lo fi metroidvania that was a fun, if forgettable way to spend a lazy Sunday afternoon.Biota’s only real change to the formula is the ability to play a number of different characters, each with their own weapons and special attacks. It’s a neat idea that I’ve recently seen in the excellent Astalon, and like that game the class balance is definitely a bit wonky. Unlike Astalon there’s never any reason to change characters if you don’t want to, as there’s no real gating abilities – progress is determined by literal keycards (the laziest way to do it) and, slightly bafflingly, wallet size. All the key items can be bought from shops, and if your wallet doesn’t hold enough you can’t buy them so the bulk of exploration is based around finding these extra pockets to hold your change.There’s also a good few vehicle sections, including a mech and a submarine, and it’s here I think that Biota is at it’s weakest. If these had been used as a pace breaker or palette cleanser they could have been a neat diversion, but they all go on far, far too long and use none of the skills or abilities you have spent the rest of the game honing or upgrading. This even extends to the final boss, though I think that section is cool enough to get away with it.Biota is not a bad game by any means, and I honestly did enjoy my short time with it. But really, I find it tough to recommend over the dozens of superior games in the genre even for the low price.
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun science-fiction adventure with enough  two-tone palettes to satisfy the most demanding retro aesthete.  An evil energy corporation hires mercs to investigate reports of slimy tentacled aliens taking over their asteroid mining operation!  Kick-ass music and limited but effective (and grammatical!) dialogue carry the -on-a-modded-Gameboy mood!  Crunchy puffball sprites are notable for recognizability and even artistic value while somehow being one or two pixels away from jagged 8-bit boogers; use what you need, discard what you don't!It's a fun one, an adventuresome romp through a sci-fantasy land of cinematic and nostalgic imagination where the chunky pieces are usually a buzz to play with, but it's not perfect.  The alien grunts could make things more interesting by having minibosses among them and in general fighting harder; they just sort of mosey around like depressed and retarded cows, waiting to be laser-blasted by your band of interplanetary psychopaths.  The ability to save anywhere, while handy if you're on the run, somewhat trivializes the challenges.  And while I'm happy that  you don't have to collect all 30 samples to get the good ending, it's a little annoying that the devs keep moving the goalpost -- because I did indeed go through the trouble of shooting l the walls and looking everywhere for the things, even though I find this particular mode of  highly annoying, just to say I saved earth from a little of the ol' demographic replacement.But yes, it's fun!  I had plenty of fun, and I would have had even more fun had I known I didn't have to shoot all the walls and find all the whatsits to meet my psychological needs.  If this looks like your jam, that's because it is.  The trailer doesn't lie!

_childDocuments_.review: A nostalgic trip down the new-age metroidvania.After completing the tutorial level, you will be brought to a base located above the underground complex. You can use this area to heal, test your skills in a training facility, acquire upgrades on the black market, and switch between characters. Everyone has the ability to jump, shoot, and cling to the wall. Wall jumping, which is required to unlock in practically every metroidvania, is available right away.The only thing that distinguishes the characters is their weapon and special ability, which are listed on their ID cards among other information like age and nationality. At first, only four squad members are available; the others are discovered as you explore the complex and after you finish the game. Despite differences in speed and power, the shooting pattern is what you should be looking at. Some have a slower gun that fires stronger bullets, while others have a quick machinegun that fires weaker bullets. It all comes down to personal preference. You'll generally stick with one hero to the end, with the exception of a portion when a certain hero is required and vehicle stages. Special ability also doesn’t matter; the game can be finished without ever using it.You can buy ammo for special weapons and permanent boosts like health in the various black markets scattered around the map. The game’s currency viridium is dropped by enemies. However, until you discover a larger container, you can only carry a limited amount of viridium. I don't think I enjoy the training facility very much because it requires a recharge after each use. I get that the viridium-filled chest at the end of a training task may make obtaining upgrades a breeze, but foes drop the valuable material at a steady rate anyway.The complex is separated into various areas, each with its own set of enemies and aesthetics. It’s also very limited in terms of exploration. There are no permanent upgrades or special powers in hidden regions of the map, save from black marketplaces, which offer every key item you will need.  This necessitates a careful exploration of the map for the larger containers, as key items cost several hundred viridium bits, which you won't be able to stash in your starting container.Saving takes place at designated locations across the complex. For rapid travel around the base, some sites may contain an elevator. There's also the option of saving the game without having to find a safe room or base. Simply locate an area free of enemies or hazards and press a button on your gamepad. Oh, and respawning at these locations won't heal you; if you saved with one health point left, you'll have to continue in the same state. If you get yourself into a jam, you can use your teleport device to return to the surface.There are no checkpoints, so you'll want to save constantly. Death arrives quickly and in a variety of forms. The traps and natural threats are the ones that hurt the most. While weak enemies only take one health point from you, bombs and laser gates instantly kill you unless you have purchased an additional health point. The most common cause of death is being knocked into one of these by an enemy bullet. When navigating between rooms, I found it particularly fascinating that you only see the room layout and no objects. After the room is fully visible, enemies and destructible things appear instantly. It's difficult to explain, but it demonstrates that the developers are well-versed in the period; it's a minor element that complements the game's overall aesthetic.The enemy variety and design are both rather good. The presence of an entity known as "The Agent" can be seen throughout the base, and the black mold has taken possession of all lifeforms. Bosses are essential, and this game has a few. I like how these fights prioritize platforming patterns over shooting. However, they’re quite easy once you figure out their limited attack pattern.The color palette can be changed at any time from the pause menu. There’s a bunch of them and anyone will find the favorite that will stay with you from start to finish. Each option contains 4 colors. While the left and right are only different hues of white and black (or gray), it's the center two that actually make the difference. Obviously, not all colors work together. If you have a mild form of color blindness, like me, some settings may even make the experience uncomfortable. The Orion or Neptune palettes, for example, made my eyes hurt by making the screen pulsate. Wave is similar, but the colors are more subtle, and it quickly became one of my favorites. New palette options are unlocked by collecting specimen found in plain sight or hidden behind a breakable wall. A few notes here. The freshly acquired palettes, for starters, aren't marked. It's tough to keep track of which palettes are new when there are so many. It's also a pain to switch between them; you have to go through each one separately. And second, the breakable walls have no visual clue that there’s something behind them. Shooting at every wall section in the room is not fun.Music is great, it has that nostalgic ’80 feel with its synth beats. The intro, on the other hand, could benefit from a lower volume because the bass clashes with the narrator's deep voice. No big deal because that’s the only time you’ll be hearing it. The game relies solely on subtitles, which could require a minor tweak. All words are crammed into the upper portion of the large text box that displays during cutscenes, leaving the bottom part unused and making the text difficult to read. I believe that adding more space between lines would help.Achievements encourage you to replay the game and race against the clock. There's also a shooting gallery available right away, where you have to hit targets with a sniper, who is possibly the game's most underutilized character. The sniper is stationary; all you're doing is moving the crosshair and firing at targets. One final frustration for achievement hunters is that once you've completed the game, you can't go back and look for missing items. And the achievement for collecting 15 specimens did not unlock.

_childDocuments_.review: This game looks like it has a lot of potential but it actually shockingly mediocre. The game is piss easy in some parts and irritating in others. The level design is boring and extremely repetitive. The controls are slippery and unresponsive. You can essentially save scum for some reason. The main positive of the game is really just the music. _childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: The map design of B.I.O.T.A is amazing, I haven't played many Metroidvania, but the flow of the map feels really smooth, there wasn't a moment where the flow was broken, you get from one place to the next, always knowing what you need to do, even though there are some puzzle involved here and there.Sound track really fits the vibe of the game and changes accordingly to the level you're playing. The heroes that you can choose from are all specialists and each of them will feel better in each area of the map. You will have to try it yourself to understand this. Some are short range and defensive, others are offensive and long range.The aesthetic of the game is brilliant and since I love retro games, I enjoy a lot the game and the fact that the pallets will constantly rotate to always feel fresh. The pixel art is done very well and even though the color palette is just 4 colors, you will notice how rich the art actually is.Now about the downsides, wall jumping feels a bit clunky at times, while I understood how to use it properly, it feels a bit hard to use sometimes, but nothing to break the experience too much.Overall B.I.O.T.A is a good game that keeps me entertained, btw, I am playing it on the SteamDeck and it feels just right on a console.
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: Since I posted my First Impressions on BIOTA yesterday, I've now finished the game. _childDocuments_.review: I so rarely give negative reviews, but I feel like I have to in this case - the game looks great, and feels great most of the time, and then you get hard walled by dubious design decisions. 1) The game has two endings but you cannot go back to explore the map or get missed collectibles after reaching the final boss. There is a free roam mode that shortens a second playthrough but if you did the bad ending first you will be in for unnecessary extra hours.2) The map completion seems bugged and/or tied to rooms that are invisible on the map.3) The time attack mode has several screens where you can get stuck in platforms, ending your progress on the entire run.It's so close to greatness, but it misses so aggressively and pervasively that I want others to know about the downfalls before they would even think about playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a soft spot for both metroidvanias and the Alien franchise, which pretty much made B.I.O.T.A a surefire winner in my books. Having played the first few hours I can safely say that it won't win any GOTY awards, but if you're looking for a fun and undemanding romp that's heavy on nostalgia, you could do a lot worse. Gameplay is quick, fluid and varied. Sound, graphics and story are serviceable. Most importantly, you can tell that genuine care went into crafting the title. As I said, you could do a lot worse.
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool looking visuals and soundtrack. The controls are responsive and the exploration was decent. There are some annoying parts in the game, but overall its upsides outweigh them. NOT a metroidvania in my opinion. Getting the unlocks and the currency system tied to it was one of the annoying parts of the game, and it didn't feel too rewarding.Just make sure to look up a guide if you want to get both endings, because it's not obvious how to get the 2nd one, and also you can't backtrack to an earlier point of your save; so be aware.
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is, in my opinion, the definition of less is more. It features fairly simple platforming mechanics, enemies, and just overall gameplay, and it nails all of it. There are a few sections where it branches out and deviates from the main gameplay, and these sections can be pretty hit or miss. Either way, they are worth powering through, because the core of the game is very fun and creative. The ability to change palettes on the fly is a feature that does not affect the gameplay in any way, yet adds so much to the game for me. This game is worth it at full price, which is something that I rarely say.
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game, great music and art. It has problems, though.It's infuriating that you can't reload your save before stumbling into the last boss to find the remaining collectibles. You have to warn your players when there's no going back! I'm not playing it all over again just to see the good ending.Plus, being able to save anywhere is cool but it becomes a chore after a while. It's really punishing to forget to save after every screen, and it doesn't really add to the game. Could have had an option to save automatically whenever it becomes possible. On room transition, maybe.
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool little metroidvania. Jumping and shooting are tight and crunchy (which is a weird thing to type, but that's how it feels), you have various characters with differing weapons and abilities you can use, you can find simple upgrades and additional specials for each character, and there are quite a few secrets to find. If you've played a metroidvania before you'll know the drill, you tend to explore a modest-sized map, find a mission critical item, and then move onto the next area, but you can come and go between areas when you like, usually to find upgrades allowing you to access things you couldn't access before. Getting lost or forgetting where to go next isn't a problem in this game. There are also two endings, the latter demanding full exploration.There's some welcome variety in a few areas, controlling a stompy mech, or a submarine with slow missiles, a few bosses that rely more on problem solving than "gitting good", oh and the soundtrack is rockin'. I mean, it slaps. Good fun, good value, do it!
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.

_childDocuments_.review: B.I.O.T.A. is a retro metroidvania, similar in looks and tone to fellow indies 'Xeodrifter' and 'Gato Roboto'. The gorgeous pixel-art really pops on screen and the chiptune synth soundtrack perfectly accompanies the old-school Gameboy feel. The action takes place on a mining colony. There's been an alien infestation, and it's your job as a band of mercenaries to investigate and destroy the mutant scourge!Whilst BIOTA is labelled a metroidvania, it's is more linear than you'd expect. The map is fully outlined from the start, and most biomes need to be approached in a set order. There's an elevator fast travel mechanic, allowing you to quickly return back to HQ. As a result, backtracking is, refreshingly, kept to a minimum, with repeated visits to areas only needed for story items, or if you want to find all the secrets and get that magical 100% completion. To access many of the locked biomes, pass cards or other items are required, instead of new skills. Health and weapon upgrades are sold at the various Black Markets scattered across the map. To mix things up, there's arcade style areas where you take control of a giant mech, a submarine and a space ship. The story campaign should last you 5-7 hours, and features two endings. There's an additional four characters waiting to be unlocked, along with time trial levels and a target shooting mini game. The graphics are highly customizable, with 24 colour palettes available from the off, with a further 30 to unlock while playing. There's a lot to love here; I found the ability to manually save after any cleared room a real time saver.BIOTA is a super retro package, full of content and well worth the low asking price. If you're a child of the '80s like me, you've probably already clicked the purchase button!

_childDocuments_.review: Blast from the Past!Let me start by saying that the Sci-Fi atmosphere reminds me of Alien movies mixed with A-Team. The heroes of the game are real tough guys with huge weapons and... funny dialogues. It's like a trip to the 80's :)GAMPLEY is very SOLID. I like that game can be played with different characters.  Each character has a different weapon and special ability (for example grenade or sniper riffle). The design of the levels is great. Various areas in the game have distinctive graphics and enemies. You can teleport to the base at any time to heal yourself, replenish your supplies or change your character. There are stages in the game where you can control a Robot Mech or steer a submarine. And finally, there are epic boss fights!GRAPHICS are simply a work of ART. What really captivated me is that when you move between rooms, you can see the opponents appearing with a slight delay. This is what it used to be on old computers with memory limitations. Wow, the attention to detail is great. And one more cool thing: you can change the color palette during the game.I also like the MUSIC very much. Nostalgia pour out of the screen :) Ok, you already know that I like the game. I simply recommend it to all fans of retro games.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: yesHaven't finished it yet, but thoroughly enjoying it. First cons, then pros. CONS: - More of a platformer than a Metroidvania (MV): being tagged "MV" is the sole reason I bought it. The MV elements are bare bones. The whole point of an MV is exploration and backtracking with new abilities or equipment to open previously inaccessible areas. This game requires minimal backtracking to SOME areas, and none to the rest. Reminds me of Gato Roboto (not dissing either game. Gato Roboto was fantastic, but it's not a Metroidvania as it's also tagged like this)- No mystery: it being more of a platformer than an MV is further shown that the map is all already somewhat uncovered. Again, the whole point of an MV is exploration; this game shows you how the map of the entire game is laid out from the very beginning, which kills any and all mystery in what's to come. Also, none of the screens have any secrets, which is a staple for an MV. - I see no reason to play as any other character besides Flynt. It makes you play as another character where I'm up to, but Flynt has been unstoppable so far because of his ranged attacks. - Pretty easy. Each screen has 1-2 enemies which are easily taken care of. The combat feels like an afterthought. PROS:+ The soundtrack slaps.+ Handles great, tight controls. + Love the aesthetic. Looks and feels like a GameBoy game. + The cons above do not detract from any of the pros.

_childDocuments_.review: B.I.O.T.A. has left an indelible mark on my gaming experience, offering an unparalleled journey through a rich and immersive sci-fi world that captivates from the very first moment. As a passionate gamer, I've encountered many titles, but few have left me as deeply engaged and fulfilled as B.I.O.T.A.One of the most striking aspects of B.I.O.T.A. is its breathtaking visuals and world-building. From the sprawling landscapes of distant planets to the intricate designs of futuristic technology, every detail is meticulously crafted to create a world that feels both alien and familiar. The art direction is nothing short of stunning, drawing players into a visually stunning universe that begs to be explored.But B.I.O.T.A. isn't just about aesthetics; it's also about storytelling. The narrative is expertly woven, blending elements of mystery, intrigue, and discovery to create a compelling and immersive experience. As I delved deeper into the world of B.I.O.T.A., I found myself drawn into a captivating tale of scientific exploration, ethical dilemmas, and the mysteries of the universe.Of course, no sci-fi adventure would be complete without engaging gameplay, and B.I.O.T.A. delivers on that front as well. The mechanics are intuitive yet deep, allowing for satisfying exploration, strategic decision-making, and thrilling combat encounters. Whether navigating treacherous terrain, unraveling the secrets of ancient civilizations, or facing off against formidable adversaries, every moment feels exhilarating and meaningful.One aspect of B.I.O.T.A. that I particularly appreciate is its emphasis on player choice and consequence. Throughout my journey, I was faced with numerous decisions that had a tangible impact on the story and world around me. These choices made me feel truly invested in the outcome of the game, adding layers of depth and replayability that kept me coming back for more.In conclusion, B.I.O.T.A. is a masterpiece of sci-fi storytelling and gameplay. With its stunning visuals, compelling narrative, and engaging mechanics, it's a must-play for any fan of the genre. Whether you're exploring distant planets, uncovering ancient mysteries, or engaging in epic battles, B.I.O.T.A. offers an unforgettable journey that will leave you breathless until the very end.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: BIOTA is a 2d action-platformer with metroidvania elements. The many things BIOTA does right only make the few things it does poorly stand out more. Overall, the game is very good, and I enjoyed my time with the core gameplay enough to recommend it to anyone who isn't a completionist. Controls are generally tight/responsive. There's a small turn-animation that isn't intrusive. There was one edge case where you can be firing while sliding down a wall but if you then choose to jump off, the input gets dropped so you end up falling. This only ever mattered once in my playthrough but if you love perfect movement systems in your action platformer, you're going to stumble into it eventually. The enemy design is pretty diverse in both attack pattern and visual design. They also all have well-telegraphed attacks. Action platformers and metroidvanias live and die by their level design, but with the exception of some rooms feeling a little empty, the level design is excellent. The enemies are placed to encourage interesting action platforming, there's a new level mechanic in every region that keeps things feeling fresh for the entire playthrough, and each region's visual diversity is appealing. BIOTA autosaves whenever you pick up a floppy disk icon in game or whenever you manually push the save button. Because your manual save is only successful if all of the room's enemies are defeated, the excellent level design works with you to create organic difficulty spikes/valleys. Some rooms may have a few enemies that are difficult/time consuming to chase, but if you continue to the next room, you're forfeiting one (of many) chance(s) to save. One-hit kill obstacles that encourage clean platforming aren't problematic (*Cough* spikes in Megaman *cough*) because most of the time you can clear a neighboring room and save before/after your attempt. BIOTA also allows players to freely teleport back to base (in any room, at any time, except for mid-boss fight) with the tradeoff being that you can only teleport out of base to fixed, unlockable map locations (elevators). These two aspects of the save system add a lot of depth to the minute-to-minute decisions and can sometimes create that "I'll explore one more room" feeling that encourages players to gamble their progress on low hp without overly punishing players for doing so. In many metroidvanias, parts of the map are inaccessible to the player (a lock) until they explore and find a movement option that will allow them to progress (a key). In BIOTA, you have to buy all of the weapon upgrades/progression keys from vendors scattered across the map, usually in remote locations. Because you don't know the order to buy the keys when you find the vendors, it could be tedious to have to ensure you always have enough currency to buy whatever key you run into. BIOTA handles this elegantly by limiting the amount of currency you can have at once, greatly increasing the drop rate of currency from chests and enemies, and making "max currency increases" themselves exploration rewards. The vendors will often show you an upgrade/key that you can't possibly afford (because it costs more than your maximum) which can keep players engaged with the exploration to find those max currency upgrades (allowing them to form organic mid-term goals). This has the added benefit that if you ever find yourself short a small amount of currency before a purchase, any room transition can serve as an impromptu farming area (because chests/enemies respawn on screen transition and the currency drop rates are so high).This system is also justified by plot spoilers so it is ludonarratively consonant :)Many games feature alternate gameplay loops to break up difficult/continuous stretches of the core gameplay loop (See *why every RPG has a fishing minigame*). Many of BIOTA's alternate gameplay loops overstay their welcome, and are easily the worst part of the game, but there are enough of them that the novelty of each makes this a minor point. Depending on your tolerance for the lack of polish in these sections, this is either mid or bad. Not being able to continue playing on your "bad ending" save after getting the bad ending is pretty unfortunate but not a dealbreaker. Having to sit through another playthrough of the  bad alternate gameplay is enough to deter me. Completionists will likely struggle trying to 100% this game without a guide because a lot of the Specimen spawns are obtuse and there's a few  that I'm not sure how someone would find organically. For a game released in 2022, there's no reason this system should work this way (especially with how much else the game does wonderfully). Not even a fast forward...This is a cool idea to reward exploration but a lot of the color palettes make the game difficult to parse visually so I ended up only using a few of them. Having all of the unlocked characters available at the base means you get to pick the character that suits your playstyle, but outside of one section that's required as a particular character, there isn't a real incentive to switch between them. They have slightly better/worse matchups into some of the enemies in some of the regions but it isn't significant. Depending on your expectations this is either a good or a bad thing.BIOTA is really good when you're actually playing the game, really mid when you're not, and only worth starting if you trust yourself to know when to stop (even if that's the bad ending). I enjoyed my time with it, and at a little under 5 hours there are plenty of worse titles that cost more. Fans of action platformers should rejoice because BIOTA introduces many welcome, quality-of-life changes at the system level that I'm excited to see in more games.Also I'm still upset about the credits.

_childDocuments_.review: Conditional recommendation. I saw a lot of positive press about this game, and I don't necessarily think it deserves all of it. However, it definitely held my attention for the runtime and it has interesting gimmicks, so it's worth a go.The story barely exists. There are a couple lines that change depending on your character and a couple sequences that deliver exposition, but most of the game is just action. The metroidvania aspect is somewhat subdued as the actual progression is completely linear; you might find a dangerous area that only a specific character can access, or a vehicle that needs a component or key to operate, but usually you need to buy whatever that is from the black market shop and it will usually cost more than your current wallet size. The result is that progression is usually in order of item cost based on your wallet size since at times there are not enough wallet upgrades on the map for you to acquire an item without pursuing another route first. That said, combined with the frequent setpieces this keeps the pace nice and brisk. Add to that a feature which can swap your color palette every room and the game is constantly engaging for its runtime.You do need two playthroughs to get all achievements and you cannot return to the map once you start the ending sequence, so putting off map completion too long will bite you. The gimmicks are fun and the game is short so it's not a large time investment.

_childDocuments_.review: + The synth music is thumpin. There are a lot of tracks for this size of game, all of which fit in an 80s retro-future aesthetic. Likewise, the sound design is satisfyingly crunch.+ The graphics are cool and works well in most of the games palettes. All of the settings and creatures are conveyed well despite only using four colors, and some of the bigger sprites are lovely.+ The central gameplay is like 90% pretty satisfying. Running and gunning feels smooth, and most of the screens feel satisfying to move around and conquer.+ There are some fun gimmicky levels to add variety. There are a fair number of vehicle sections, all of which control slightly differently (though all of them are a bit too long).- Most environmental hazards are one-hit kills, which send you back to your last save. A lot are very easy to bump into, which leads to needless frustration. Now, technically you can save on any screen as long as there aren't any enemies around. So, the optimal way to play is a very awkward thing where you beat a room, then hit the quick-save button, then go to the next room, repeat. If you don't hit quick-save for a while because you forgot, you're punished by losing progress. - The playable characters don't feel that different to play. There are 4 available from the start, 1 (free) DLC character, and 2 unlockable ones. All but one of them have a gun that shoots about the same distance from their face and kills an enemy in about the same time. This is especially a problem because, even though the MAP is metroidvania-like, there is no actual progression of abilities (other than some optional unlockable special attacks). For example, you don't unlock a double jump that lets you get to a new area, you just get a key. So even though you unlock stuff, the game plays basically the same from beginning to end.- There are minor movement quirks that detract. 1) The wall jumping is awkward. You stick to the wall as soon as you touch it, and need to press down to get off, which doesn't feel good in this game. It would work better if you had to hold toward the wall to stick on. 2) You can't shoot down while jumping. Not all games need that, but this game feels incomplete without it. It makes fighting some enemies weirdly difficult.- This one is just me, but I'll die happy when I find a metroidvania that doesn't make me attack every unmarked wall on the 1% chance I break it and there's a collectable behind it.Overall, I do think this game is worth playing if you can get over some design flaws. There's some good 80s throwback pulpy action in there.

The map can mostly be explored in a linear fashion, with some backtracking for collectibles and tools that unlock new levels. _childDocuments_.review: My first impressions video: There's a lot of indie games with retro aesthetics these days, but it's still relatively rare to see one that aims to resemble something from the Game Boy Color era. B.I.O.T.A. does the look and feel very well, while also adding a lot of modern quality of life improvements that don't make it an easy game, but definitely make it a more appealing metroidvania.The story in B.I.O.T.A. is pretty simple, but it lays a good framework for the gameplay. You get to pick from a number of different characters, with different weapons, specials and stats. You can change these characters whenever you return to your hub space, but you can complete nearly the entire game with any of them. You'll face a variety of enemies, bosses and platforming challenges that aren't easy, but also aren't so hard that you'll be tearing your hair out. There are also arcade challenge modes that you can unlock.One of B.I.O.T.A.'s interesting modernizations is that you have the option to save almost anywhere with a single button press. You might think that would make the game extremely easy, but because of the way it flows, I found myself often forgetting to save and even when I did remember, it still didn't remove the challenges of newer rooms, especially later on. It's also completely optional so if you want the extra challenge of only being able to save at checkpoints, you have that freedom as well.I never found B.I.O.T.A. too easy, but I also never found myself getting frustrated with it, the way I often can with other metroidvanias. There's a great variety of environments to explore and some puzzles to solve, none of which will be too head scratching. In the end, it's a few hours long, but it felt like a well constructed, polished experience that I quite enjoyed.
_childDocuments_.name: B.I.O.T.A.
