_childDocuments_.review: This was a game that needed to be made, the developer supposedly had to even borrow money to make this artistic vision a reality and I'm glad they stuck through it. It's a game that show's that while the situations we're born into, whether it be our stifling political system or our own life induced traumas effect us, it doesn't have to DEFINE us. This game is about Freedom and meaning, and discovering what that means to you. Anyways lets get to the gameplay:If you're a fan of the old Road of the Dead Flash Games and of Road 96 you'll definitely like this game. The Roguelike nature of it as well as the fact that the narrative portrayed actually changes based off the questions you answer at the beginning of each run make it very replayable. It's a very different and very fun experience playing as a mean or well intentioned character with each playstyle being rewarded in different ways. There is no you're evil so you are automatically punished system in fact it's a lot harder to be good making both playstyles very viable and also I think fitting the narrative quite well. Please if this game looks at all interesting to you go ahead and buy it. It's super unique and very fresh in this stifling world and overly cluttered market and offers a breath of fresh air. Thank you for this game absolutely dripping with artistic creativity and love :)

_childDocuments_.review: Can you Double Jump in this Game? No.Heading out is a Rogue-like road trip across America, one man in a car. The thing is, you are being chased by your "fear" essentially working like rules from It Follows. Your goal is to get to some point in America to race "The Legendary Blue Racer". The main gameplay of this game is seeing your little dot drive across the map going from city to city, balancing how fast you go (will get you there faster/get further away from fear, but make up your wanted level/make higher fuel costs). There are little events at every city and sometimes on the roads. These are what I like about the game, I like the little events where I get to make a singular decision and then its done. There are also racing events where you actually drive the car and they are fine. I like the events stuff but everything else is pretty eh to me.Also it takes a lot for me to not want to listen to dialogue in a game, but this game has radio talk shows that feel aggressively trying to be "hip" with current events and its very groan worthy, especially the adult woman trying to voice a teenager.

_childDocuments_.review: The stakes are huge, but if we dare to take risks like our nameless hero, we will have an unforgettable 6-8 hour experience, after which we would love to jump back behind the wheel and the best part is that we can even do that. Due to the constantly changing events, the options offered and so many other factors, we will never have two playthroughs the same, and therefore, even if we know what the outcome of the game will be, it is worth running several times in the pursuit of our fear. Because the point is not necessarily the goal itself, but rather the series of decisions we make that form a bridge and take us from our initial rush until we finally dare to face the greatest threat we know, namely ourselves. Thanks to these great ideas, Heading Out is not only an excellent game, but much more than that, a perfect representation of a mental torture that everyone dreads, but will experience sooner or later, and the only thing that matters is when you make the right decision: the at the beginning of a journey or when you have already crossed all borders.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely owns. A rare 'WOW' game. I don't know what some people were expecting. You say "visual novel", I say "moody road movie where you make the choices and determine the outcome." It is a game of choices matter but the driving parts are not inconsequential - not at all. They pin the story you create together, and the choices you make are not limited to staged points, your decisions about where to go, what to do there and and what you do along the way all impact the outcome. The result is gripping, and there is an absolute ton of well-written scenarios to make that journey diverse, and add plenty of replayability. The art direction is noir comic meets Queens of the Stone Age's "Go With the Flow": The Music Video: The Game. It is striking, appropriate and very appealing. And that's not the only music reference you'll find, this game is packed full of the music knowledge of the devs, from intro to credits and even out of the game (check those achievement names!) The ingame music itself is understandably unlicensed but completely suits the feel of the game, just the right kind of desert rock, thrumming along with your tension. An outstanding game in its category, I love it.Bonus points to the devs for the Pick of Destiny reference - you know what I mean! It's time to blow doors down, boys and girls -best of luck with this excellent game

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad idea on paper but the narrative aspect is weak, shallow and loaded to the brim with blatant progressive malarkey. The racing is too simple to be fun for sustained periods of time and you may find yourself wanting to skip it as frequently as possible. The resource/time/travel management roguelike would be more fun if the story segments were longer, more frequent and your decisions had an actual impact the consequences of which you could see beyond a single line of text at the end and a change in resource values. It's not a good VN style game, it's not a good travel management game (80 Days this is not) and its not a good racing game. It reminds me of things like Night Call, but that game knew to fully lean into the story even if it was also politically loaded with bs. No part of the game is particularly good and in tandem they dont really mesh that well or amount to anything that interesting. Could have been so much better. Avoid.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel bad because this is definitely a case where my expectations didn't meet reality on this one; I saw the ads and figured what i was in for was a driving game, going road to road listening to the radio, clashing with cops and other racers, and all around soaking in this gloriously presented black and white slice of americana.... And what I got was a "resource management" visual novel with the occasional driving minigame attached to it where the roguelike aspects are very story-focused with no upgrading or changing how your car drives or any of that... And, while the atmosphere and general vibes are pretty great I just found it all to be, ultimately, really boring.Honestly, I think it's the amount this game doesn't want you driving on that open road for long; a lot of the "listening to the radio" stuff is done in a static menu, and when it does come in your car it's always predictably at the end of a race; it never feels dynamic or alive, and the way your car slows down too just means that it again feels like another cutscene rather then even having the basic joy of flooring it and seeing the miles pass behind you as the radio presenters do their monologues... And my god those roads get monotonous quick; the open setting meaning you'll be seeing a lot of fields and long turns, having done 2 acts all the driving just blurred together without the excitement of a desperate handbrake turn or any of that... That and the rubber banding is just bizarre with enemies happy to slow down to let you win, even on the hardest difficulty.Look if you like the visual novel stuff, good on you, you'll like this, but know that that's a lot of what your experience is going to be, a lot of sitting, looking at menus and texts and listening; and to me, I think it squandered some potential to really capture something, and sadly that's all I can personally say about it.

_childDocuments_.review: An unconventional genre of game, a rogue-like driving game. But, it works quite well. Having played many racing games form arcade, sim-cade and sim racing, this definitely brings a fresh experience.The handling of the game is good and you feel differences in terrain and the cars.  However, it goes beyond just driving, its a game that implores you to strategise, just driivng well wont win you the game, you have to make choices which can affect your experience and the relevant consequences.Throughout the game, the world adapts to your decisions and will again affect your personal experience in the game. However, the game aims to make a profound point, including various sensitive topics (Which in my opinion did not feel forced) and the way you decide to make choices can really make the game hit home towards your own real life but, this is your choice if you want the game to play in this way (The game gives you the option).I played through first time on balanced difficulty which proved to be no real problem, difficulty wise, therefore, I would probably pick a higher difficulty on my second play-through. Overall, I can easily recommend this game to anyone. Even if you are not big into driving games, I'm sure an enjoyable experience can come from the "story" difficulty option and the various encounters that appear throughout the game as you strategise to progress in the game. TL;DR: Fun driving game that requires strategy where your actions have consequences and aims to make a profound point to the player. It's worth a try even if you do not play racing games!
_childDocuments_.name: Heading Out

_childDocuments_.review: Rewriting my initial Review after i had some time to think about this Game.I feel mixed about this. I enjoyed my time with my first Run, but how most Reviews already say it could've been advertised better.This Game was advertised as a "Racing Rougelike" but It's more a Visual Novel with some Driving thrown in, i expected that you'd drive from State to State and not watch your Icon slowly move on the Map most of the time.The Story itself changes every time you play it and it's really enjoyable this way but the Radio Stations (which this Game heavily relies on) will get annoying pretty quick, they're a little too Unhinged and feel really out of place, they could've been cut and it wouldn't have made a big difference in how the Story goes. The Radio Stations are also very Political which is meh, would've been better if they just focused on your Journey as the "Interstate Jackalope". The Artstyle is great and fits together perfectly with the Visual Novel elements, this Game is Story first, Driving third, the Driving is locked behind Loading Screens and stops feeling meaningful after a while, all the Driving (Races, Police Chases, Fear-Races etc.) could be done on the map.The Character "Creator" where you can choose some options like your Relationship Status and such feel like they only make a minuscule difference in the Story.this Game looked like the spiritual successor to Driver: San Francisco ar a playable version of Vanishing Point but that is only case for roughly 20% of the game.This Game could've been so much more. As a Story Game it's great, as a Driving Game it is disappointing which is a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR A fascinating genre blend of VN, racing, and rougelike. Some rough spots but overall a fun, bite-sized time with a pretty interesting story. The writing is pretty sharp in most of the events that happen along the way. A little hard to parse at first, but trust me, it gets clearer in the second half. Genuinely pretty captivating and well-written. Some better than others, but overall good mix of humor, sadness, commentary, and reflection. I ended up in a "Softlock" situation ONCE, the rest of the times, my runs were a nice mix of getting close to failure, and then managing to get away at just the right moment. (Will also be in cons, see below). I love all of them. They provide a nice bit of humor and entertainment as they comment on some of your story choices or try to "figure you out". The comic-style coloring may get old to some, but i think it's a very jarring and attention grabbing style, and it helps make the bits of color in game (Which usually communicate obstacles) stand out better. Plus it looks rad af. Fits the tone and mood perfectly, well done to the VA. I don't. Here's the pattern i see: If you are someone who strongly opposes "the left" or despises their humor, these hosts will annoy you. I PROMISE the game itself ISNT POLITICAL. But the hosts are characters, with opinions, so if that sounds annoying, you will have a bad time. Car UNDERSTEERS LIKE HELL. It takes some practice to learn proper steering. Otherwise many races are bland af. This isn't NFS, it's not Forza, it's pretty linear sprints where there's a chance of crashing at just the wrong moment and you leading the rest of the race means nothing. I did one full run and honestly i think i say 95% of what there is to see. I AM HAPPY with what i got. Just dont expect endless replay value.-Your "goal" each run changes, so there can be roads on the map you never have the chance to see (tho environments are pretty hit or miss in terms of being interesting).Overall, rough around some edges, but if you're open to a really unique mix of genres, if you like the idea of a semi-randomly generated roadtrip where choices matter and you have quirky run-ins, I think you'll like this. Give it a shot, there's really nothing like it (not even Road 96).Tip btw: You do 4 runs, aka "Acts" to get the story ending. If you fail a run, you ONLY have to restart the act, which is merciful and I appreciate it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't perfect, but I loved it.There's a few things that I would consider before going in:This is not a game where you will be in control of a car the whole time, or even most of the time. Don't go in expecting this. Actually racing/driving amounts to around 40% of the game (at least in my playthroughs). The rest of it is resource management while driving on a map of the US, and visual-novel-style story beats.If, like me, you've played a lot of racing games and think when you start this "wow, this is kind of easy" - put the difficulty up to Challenge and set "Hide Consequences" to On. This makes it really feel like you're driving for your life and requires you to make smart use of every resource.Play in first person. It's a lot more immersive (and difficult) that way.Now for the actual review, starting with This is a driving game, but it's not really *about* driving. At its core it's an introspective narrative game, with driving and road trips through a stylized 70's America. If you want something that captures the vibe of driving down a highway far too fast while you listen to local radio, stewing in your thoughts about what the host is saying in between songs, this is that thing. It's the game I've wanted since I first played Need for Speed when I was a kid.The game not being 100% driving all the time is one of its strengths, not a weakness. This is not a racing sim and doesn't have incredibly deep and realistic physics, so it just would not be engaging enough if it was only that. Instead, it gives you plenty of downtime in between races (that you can even choose not to take, if you want) to think about what you've done, where you're going, and what you're driving for. This downtime also allows for different reasons for races/driving sequences to actually start, keeping things dynamic, especially on higher difficulties where tight resources can land you into a forced getaway situation fairly often. I was surprised how much I enjoyed this part, as I usually strongly dislike any sort of resource management as a core mechanic in roguelike games like this.The driving physics themselves are very well-tuned for what this game is. They're simple, fun, and easy to pick up and get a feel for. It gives you room to get really good at weaving through traffic as the game throws more and more obstacles at you, which is the game's primary mode of difficulty.The radio hosts you meet are really fun characters, and the narrator did an excellent job too. While it can lean into cheesy territory, the VO in the game fits the vibe overall and is mostly enjoyable. The fact that the hosts and drivers react to the actions you take is a great level of detail that I wish had been expanded upon more than it was.The visual novel segments are all interesting in their own ways. Little glimpses of your life and the lives of others give more meaning to the road trip you're taking, and allow you to better contextualize the radio host's messages. They also allow for good roleplay opportunities, as they often end in choices that let you build your version of the Interstate Jackalope.This is the only game that's truly captured the feel of speeding cross-country to escape something, making a name for yourself along the way. The music while you drive helps a lot and generally fit well. There's even lyrical tracks!That said, there are some things I would have preferred that the game  had done differently. The radio hosts are all great, and have interesting (caricatured, but fun) personalities. The racers you meet do not. There are only 3-4 voice variants, and they all say very similar things. I would have loved if they were able to give the racers more distinct personalities, especially since they . There was a lot more room for expanding on that side of the game and those characters that was not explored.The racers you meet and race against seem totally unable to handle themselves if two cars are side-by-side in front of them. They just kind of flail around and turn off the road. Even on the highest difficulty, the only time I lost a race in my entire playthrough was due to a bug. I ran into a few bugs - nothing major, but annoying as they happened. Once, the racer 200m behind me teleported 8000m in front of me, making it impossible for me to win the race. A few times, a dialogue line would start playing its subtitles but fail to play audio, leaving the mix very quiet until another line played and interrupted the previous "stuck" one.The environments, while nicely varied (unique environments for every state is a really nice touch), suffered from pretty bad pop-in even at max settings.I think the game's length is just about perfect for what it offers. I was starting to feel that I was getting the same scenarios I'd seen before by the end - but then the game ended, so it was fine.But like I said at the start - the game isn't perfect, but the whole is much greater than the sum of its parts. It vibes. It's fun. It's just right.I had a big smile on my face as I finished the game and let to the credits play out. I think this game is very unique, and well worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Full Gameplay Walkthrough - Heading Out is an intricate, compelling story that mixes modular storytelling and roguelike structure with deeply America-flavored media of the 1970s and on, particularly the “road” genre. I’m not a car guy but I do enjoy some crusty Americana, especially the kind that challenges authority and romanticizes the sheer scale and variety of this unhinged nation. Sometimes it may get a little too cute for its own good, but for the most part Heading Out captures its intended vibe with a shocking level of skill and accuracy, an academic level of cultural understanding through a lens of media and literature. That’s pretty darn cool. Between that and the intriguing, almost insincere roguelike structure, we have a game that doesn’t really feel like anything else in its own space.Go for It Rating - 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely write reviews but I just want to say that this game was EXACTLY the type of game I had been wanting without really knowing how to say that I wanted it. I LOVE driving and it's a very VERY important part of my life. A lot of my most memorable experiences and core memories of childhood happened on the road. This game feels like a trip into another world that I would love where I can simply exist, live fast, live kinda careless, and live free with a looming challenge over my head. I applied a lot of myself into this character provided and really enjoy the experience. The driving is a bit to get used to but it's fun and there is enough of it to not overtake the narrative but not enough for it to feel unimportant. Trips are fast enough to not get same-y and the radio chatter is the ABSOLUTE best. IF i had one thing I was upset about it would have had to be the fact the music wasn't filtered in a way that made it feel like an old school tape deck but I was too immersed after I got to driving to really notice anymore. I highly recommend anyone who wants a narrative that can ride shotgun to the gameplay. I find it actually odd how the choices you make don't come with extra scenes, they are there and then they are gone. It leave it open to really think about.I wouldn't recommend this game to anyone that's looking for more of a Forza, NFS, or GTA driving experience. There is more games like those but this isn't it.

_childDocuments_.review: Heading Out is a pretty unique blend of strategy and driving game, like if 80 Days let you speed (and take speed). The gameplay loop has the player travel between cities on the overworld map, encountering cops, races, etc. along the way in the form of markers on the road. These trigger driving segments that require the player to survive/win a race under the duration of a song from the game's soundtrack (which is all original music). There are also narrative events on the road/in cities where the player's choices influence their stats. The game is pretty well designed in that all of these segments interact with and influence each other. My preferred playstyle is choosing routes with races to earn more gas money, which covers my flagrant and unwavering disregard towards the speed limit and the additional police chases it invites.I also like the game aesthetically, and its minimal style is also very functional. The headlights of oncoming traffic and the red taillights tend to stand out against the road, and the occasional touches of colour are reserved for important details like road signage to help it stick out even while speeding by.The narrative is a weak point, as taking it in requires the player to slow down the game, so each story choice/radio broadcast doesn't get a lot of words or time devoted to it. The result is that when the writing often tries to explore more serious issues, it's too heavily constrained to explore them with proper nuance. Each radio broadcaster is prone to ardent expression of their flavour of politics, and they end up landing closer to stereotype than character. The obligatory Steam discussion for people who have never bought a game to argue about its politics has already been created, so the prospective buyer who takes issue with this should direct their concerns to the qualified experts therein.It took me ~7 hours to complete the four storied acts, each having a longer trip, a new car choice, and a few more elements on the overworld or in race. In this time I never encountered duplicate narrative events and did not fail a run, so I think it's a decent estimate for the absolute minimal hour count this game has to offer. It's not terribly difficult, so I'd say the best way to play it is with the difficulty set to challenging and with narrative consequences hidden. The developers also recommend a controller.

_childDocuments_.review: First to address what everyone's gonna inevitably comment about; this game is political. Most games are political. Some games choose more subtle ways, other games are more blunt about it. This game is blunt about it.But past that, I like the story, sort of mid 2010's "Life Is Strange" dialogue that'll turn you off if you're not into homegrown awkward characters or easy to hate authoritarian figures, but it scratches a certain punk-ish itch for me.The gameplay! Past a few bugs that might've ended up being on my end, the driving feels smooth - a bit simple, but not in a bad way? Moreso in service of letting the story take the reins, but cop pursuits and street races flex the muscles a bit more and make the obstacles ahead feel more in your face.Car choices are cool, but for the most part I just ended up settling on the 2nd one for its easy controls.And the actual map, the main roguelike element of it, feels really fun! Similar veins to something like slay the spire where you're progressing upwards to one big race, but the amount of side content and having to calculate your path on chance encounters or places with less "heat" from the police makes you take last minute detours.The fear system as well is a pretty good mechanic, where if your stats run low enough by not engaging with the map properly, your "fear" catches up to you, which then puts you in a race that you can still win! It's forgiving where it counts whilst making sure you're being challenged at the right points.And I LOVE the artistic choices here; black and white with Red/Yellow/Blue highlights just, works well, I can't really say much about it besides scratching a similar sort of itch, and making sure the obstacles are properly highlighted so you don't feel like you're taken out in a cheap shot.Overall, I'd recommend this, even if you don't like politics that much which, you do you babes, you can skip most of the dialogue and even replace story encounters with the in game radio.

_childDocuments_.review: Decent game. It's more of a choose your own adventure game, with good bit of fun driving. But it doesn't do any part of that spectacularly. The rougelite elements are not good. One wishes you could upgrade your car's speed or handling, none of that exists. As you progress through the acts, you will become frustrated with the gameplay rather than enthralled by it, as the races in the game have catchup features for both you and your enemies, as well as every race being a timer rather than a finish line. The entire overworld features are lackluster. You will lose 3 minutes of your life over and over again to 'failing' the rougelite part of the game, which is this weird form of economy management. If the developers switched this game to a finish line instead of an arbitrary clock the game would instantly go from not recommended to recommended, because the driving aspect is genuinely fun. Another thing they should have done is make the hard mode actually difficult. I played from the get go on the 'hard' version, and there's really nothing hard about it. It should have a much more car dense environment. You are mostly just driving by yourself, which makes the game feel less like GTA (which is the fun part of the game) and more like some random racing sim in mostly deserty offroady country-ish areas.Another bad aspect is the car's handling and top speed. The top speed feels kind of slow, and the handling is abysmal. That's honestly not that bad though, as neither are THAT off, and the drifting mechanic gives you a lot of leeway with turning that you would normally not have. So its not all bad, but the cars could top out a little faster and the turning on the base car could be slightly more forgiving. Speaking of cars, after each act you unlock new ones, but I could NOT get it to swap out. I assume then it's only accessible for a repeated playthrough of the campaign, but who would want to do that again??? Especially as you can't even play well to finish the game faster. That's another thing the forced timer system and not a flag point system fails at, is giving you any satisfaction for going quickly. I don't know if the devs understand that, that's kind of the appeal of a racing/driving game? I would have replay ability if you could perhaps time yourself and speed through all the races and finish the game quickly, but instead....Lastly the 'politics/story' element of the game is serviceable at best. The routes I like to take in video games are usually the good guy routes, and for this the game definitely has a left leaning political bias. There are many moments that kind of spell this out, but one notable one is picking up a guy with a swastika tatoo and then spray paining 'NAZI!' on him and leaving him in a dumpster. Nothing crazy, or even extremely objectionable but both choices for this were the same outcome. Just one was a little meaner! That is to say you get pidgeon holed into the 'right' decision quite a few times.In other words there is not that much in terms of 'risque' type content in terms of your decisions for shaping the charachter you've created, in a chose your own adventure game. That's a pretty bad. It ends up being a milqetoast center-left experience. Even though I picked mostly good guy answers, you can see all the options. It felt like the only times i was presented with a genuine selection of options was in situations where a milktoast liberal would say 'that's bad, but like forgive and forget' Like stealing, or looking a blind eye to malfesence. Or taking advantage of people. Something that makes the experience clear is there is no 'cop killing' or anything even close. There is an example of a policemen harassing black people for no reason, as the script says, and you can rev up your engine to lead him on a chase so the black kids wont get harassed. I mean, sure, but the game isn't provactive in any real manner at least that I was able to find. I would easily let a 13 year old play this game, with no doubt that they would not come across a subject matter in the game that they might misinterpret in a negative way. Which is kind of a betrayal of the type of game it 'should be' in my eyes. GTA is not meant to be a hugbox where noone could possibly come to a bad conclusion about the moral decisions based on the happenings of the game. That is to say, this game tows an unbelievably safe line when it should have been the exact opposite, leaving the game play as the only part of the game worth mentioning positively in any respect.

_childDocuments_.review: Back In 2011, Mayhem 3D released. A demolition derby racer with a comic art-style approach, which players didn’t appreciate much. Now in 2024, developers Serious Sim brings Heading Out with the similar art-direction & taking inspiration from the 1970s road movies giving a new taste in the driving scene like ever before & the adventure is astonishing.In Heading Out you play as Jackie, an Interstate Jackalope tagged by the media & everyone around you. Your mission is make your way across the country in order to chase down the world's greatest driver,your fear. There are several obstacles in your path of course, be it the police, car maintenance, managing money to refill the gas, eye focus & the stranger things type red cloud that spreads along the land & kills you. And once you finally catch up to this driver, the Interstate Jackalope has a mystery on their hands that they'll have to solve with each trip.Heading Out has 4 Acts to complete which makes you feel you are playing Red Dead Redemption on wheels. With each Strangers & Freaks you encounter, the decisions you create increase or decrease the Fame & Reputation bar as you progress & does effect the dialogue on the radio. Radio is crucial part which you can’t ignore, you can skip it if you want to but most of the radio shows are very balanced to listen too. Either be a good guy or a bad guy, choice is yours.Heading Out has a terrific resource management & provides a good challenge. You can progress at a steady 50 MPH avoiding the speed limit for each state, stopping only for the cop icon crossing by. You can also use gas to speed up, getting you to your destination quicker and putting more distance between you and the fear but would increase the wanted level for breaking the speed limit.Heading Out is like more of road racer, thanks to its emphasis on dodging traffic and construction barriers. Races are short and sweet, matching the length of the song choice from the radio, and the tie to music. There are 4 vehicles in total which you unlock each act. Each has been meticulously detailed to look like their real life counterparts, while they’re not licensed gearheads are sure to recognise a classic Dodge Challenger, a Ferrari 250 & a Nissan 2000 GTR when they see them. They all sound as cool as they look too. There are plenty of premade events in Heading Out but, while Serious Sim has been patient in rationing out its routes throughout the career races, the event types do get a little repetitive. Replayability is on hand to stretch out the lifespan, but I expect I’ll get more value out of the Updates it gets. The lack of Co-op or Split-Screen is disappointing but hey, it’s a great single-player experience.Heading Out is a unique blend of genres with visual novel that makes it worth checking out. Comic book style, killer soundtrack, funny radio host & a ton of interesting stories to explore. I have played plenty of serious racers, but sometimes it’s nice to experience a fresh idea into the genre & immerse into it.

_childDocuments_.review: A 70s Americana 'roadtrip' style game with a gameplay loop between segments of chases/races, boardgame/rpg strategization/management, and narrative 'choices matter' text adventure gameplay? brilliant! What is the vibe? What is the Game like?:Aside from those elements the point of each roguelite 'run' is to make it to a race against a 'special driver' at a random city on the American map hitting a series of node citys on the map in which can provide gas/shops/garage/story-beats etc. the goal of the run is ever present since fear is chasing you (in hours) across the board starting in one point and moving in every direction from that point (also there are different wanted levels per state) and a run takes an hour or two so even though there are cities where you might need to deliver something its near impossible to see everything this game has to offer in a single playthru. As There are a plethora of 'sidequests' meters to satisfy, different approaches, and the game really gets in the weeds about putting your personality into it, kind of like a personality quiz. All of this is set to goofy/cringe GTA style radio hosts (and music that I turned off for my playthru) and constant races/chases over the course of 4 acts (ending a run sets you back at the chapter you left off at but it takes awhile to complete a run so it's advised you value your time and plan accordingly.)How are the races?Which speaking of races I decided to pick this game up from Blackpanta's initial reaction. I can say it surely is a refreshing take on the racing genre especially since AAA has been fumbling the bag for awhile now turning racing games into FIFA style "service" games. This is anti-that obviously, but from a racing purists perspective it's like 50/50 a racing game and all the other influences, it's more a celebration of car/70s roadtrip culture. What I mean is playing on hardest difficulty is how you're going to get any enjoyment if you're looking for racing challenge. Most races are relatively straight with light traffic and some offroady bits or obstacles, but other than my focus meter (character gets sleepy over time can fix in a variety of ways) going low and some cool audio/visual falling asleep effects in the manual mode (sequential with gear shifts being A & B on xbox controller), and odd physics stopping me (random rollovers in what felt like random gusts of wind & unfair collisions/hit boxes from traffic, like trading paint swerves your car kind of stuff, or tapping the back of a car sending your car into a dead stop) it felt like the win-state was always guaranteed as long as you stayed in 5th and then downshifted around turns with only light braking involved. There are some curveball races like twistys or citys with narrow streets with OP sidewalks that flip your car, but those felt sparse and are state specific (that variation was fun). Should you buy it though?:I want to reiterate it's refreshing I'm so glad people are revisting the racing genre and getting creative with it. The story definitely takes the center stage here, but the gameplay loop was addicting with highstakes which carrys the story to be appreciated (but don't expect Asseto corsa level driving more like NFS the run/old arcade games.) Lots of replayability from a sidequest standpoint, and although I clocked in 10.5 hours and some have beat it in 6 hours I'd say it's worth it on sale, but supporting the devs at fullcost is cool too. Also would love if the devs made an artbook with all the dialogue stills since I'm sure there's many I missed <3.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: An art style that echoes Sin City, Outrun-esque driving segments, Faster Than Light influence, a fantastic soundtrack, and a narrative that flips the traditional indie game ideas on its head all make for a more than satisfying experience, though the lack of an endless mode is a bit of a bummer.Throughout nearly all of the gameplay, the screen is a comic book type style with colors ranging from black, white, gray, red, and rarely blue, but this is build up for something more, trust me. I've finished the game three times now, and every playthrough I notice more details. When you shift, a comic book cutaway showing your character's hand moving the shift knob appears next to the tachometer, when you work the pedals, a comic book cutaway shows your character's feet doing the motions. The timer for the driving segment is a cassette tape, and while it displays the time remaining in the center of it, I didn't notice until my third run that the tape in the cassette actually winds up on the other roller with how far along the timer is. There's plenty of detail to be found here, and I'm confident I'll discover at least a few more little tidbits.While the core of the gameplay is arguably the world map with it's FTL-like choices and decision-making, it is broken up by driving segments strongly reminiscent of the classic Outrun games. The driving isn't realistic, though it's not so arcadey that there are no consequences. Damage you incur to your car lasts until you can get it fixed. Winning or losing races determines whether or not you get the payout. The handling was initially different for me at first, what with my thing for sims, but I got a handle on it pretty quick - a controller is a strong recommendation. There are four different cars to unlock, and they all have their own characteristics and traits.As for the soundtrack, check it out on youtube, or discover it organically through the game. I don't want to write too much about it as I don't have the writing ability to fully encompass how much it works and how much I like it.While it's a meme that indie games are about the developer's parents' divorce or the like, Heading Out stands apart by making the arch fit  via questions that start off innocuous, but as you play through the game's multiple acts, they become more delving, and hit closer to home. This is revealed through the gameplay through various segments of narration, speaking portions from the various radio hosts, and what characters say to you, too. If you ask me, answer the questions honestly on your first run, and allow the game to speak to you.There are a few reviews going on and on about the game being overtly political, but because I go outside I can't say I share the same feeling. It's set in 70s America, one is to expect representations of the movements and beliefs there. Both sides of the American political spectrum are shown with the cast of radio hosts, and the player is not forced in either which way to do certain things. Personally, Heading Out is no more outright than Mafia 3 as far as representing the period goes.In my playthroughs I've never encountered a game or run ending bug, or anything that caused a crash to desktop. At most, I've ran into some clipping oddities in the driving segments, but so few that I can count them on one hand. My only real issue with this game is that I wish there was more, simply put. More cars to unlock, more ways to explore the game's map, more ways to experience what Serious Sim has put out for us. An endless mode where the player is seeing how long they can last whilst driving around the entire country would be awesome.All in all, this is one of the first games I've genuinely been sucked into to the point where I find myself staying up way too late to play it in a while, and I can easily recommend it to friends, family, and even you, reading this review, who had no idea I existed before I typed this all out for some reason.

_childDocuments_.review: Review after one full run on medium difficulty:Soundtrack 6/10 Some songs are good some are not, yet majority was on good/decent side for me.Gameplay "Race" 5/10 Decent ride, sometimes you end up spinning far too much when crashing and if you end up hitting non-participating cars, you end up on dead stop or lose almost all of your speed, costing sometimes race.Gameplay "Map/Stratigic" 7/10Rather interesting and forces in some to make choice between exploration or gunning for objective. Random events can eather aid or hinder you depending for your choice (some show what certain option will give you, some dont. There is option in keep reward/consequances hidden). You juggle a few resources: Reputation (Good or bad, can unlock, lock certain options in events and can be used to get stuff for free or access to illigal shop), Fame (Mostly impacts how NPC cars react to you, how much you get from races and what talk-show hosts say), Money (Buying stuff and in case of lacking money, you can be chased by police for "stealing" fuel or not paying for service), Focus (If too low you start to "black out" during race), Car condition (Can be lost during race or event, if at 0 you get game over), Wanted (Effects how often police chase you and what Talk-Show host say).Story 3.5-5/10 Rather decent but only if you have "regrets" of your own do ot option to choose why or hows of your run, which then effect talk-show hosts and narrator in certain moments. Otherwise it hovers at meh to bad. Some things that are said or scenerio in events are.. Very Weak (Or cringe, as folks say it now days) do to forcing you to writer/developer "political mind set" (FYI: Game leans hard on current time political "left" idiology. Its impossible to be neutral when game forces you to support only they way of thinking. Major failure for such game concept, do to game scolding you for not taking its option which in turn makes you unable to make your own story).Overall 5.5/10Decent but best to play it while under influence to "tank" bad writing in some parts. Concept it self is good for rouge-like (Not many driving rouge-like as far as I can tell) but held back by forcing political cool-aid. Yet if able to "ignore" those aspects it should be fun for spending a few hours on one run.

_childDocuments_.review: Heading Out is the perfect title for this unique road trip simulator that mixes psychological drama, fun arcade racing, and a narrative web that spreads across the USA just like our highway system.  The concept is simple.  You’ll be playing a troubled female driver fleeing her own personal demons, as you “head out” west to a randomized destination that changes with each of the four Acts in the story. What really blew my mind in Heading Out was the sheer amount of content.  It was nearly six hours before I had my first repeating story bite, and that was after I had to restart Act 4, so it was expected.  After finishing my first run I started a new game, and while the early radio broadcasts come at you in the same order, the story bits are randomized, so the passed-out Nazi I mugged in Gary, IN was the same one I mugged again in Dallas, TX in my new game.  There also seems to be content specific to regions or perhaps even states.  I know I heard a commercial that specifically called out "Arizona" while I was driving through Arizona, so the game knows where you are and curates the content based on your journey.Read the full review at More Steam reviews on our Curator page -

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really love it or hate it game. I'll go ahead and say, It's not focused on simply driving, as evidenced in the trailer. The driving is still a heavy part of the game and I found myself in races and other driving aspects such as pursuits at least every 5-10 minutes at most. The game honestly picks up after the first act as it's gently guiding you into the controls and the gameplay loop. Then adding more things like roadblocks, traffic races, etc. I recommend you start on challenging if you are familiar with racing games or you'll find yourself not coming across too much difficulty. As for the political aspect, it does exist. It's an alt-70s United states with the canadian civil war happening but still mentions real aspects such as the nixon impeachment and the space race. Think of it as strange real in a way if you know ace combat. Real ideas mixed with alt history stuff. The radio hosts I've seen people love or hate. As well as lots of people being offended by an alex jones parody in the game. Sorry man if that offends you I think you need help. The left leaning hosts aren't perfect charactures either. The game never calls these people "the good guys" and "voices of reason". I will say the game does lean left but the politics isn't the most important aspect. It's more about the "fears" we deal with and I like how the game handles these. If you can, answer them honestly and they can hit or miss. Mostly hit. I overall enjoyed the writing from the radio and the side stories. There is some awkward moments where a story just ends without any ending text which feels a bit unfinished. As well as some minor glitches like audio cutting out. Overall I recommend heading out if you're looking for a 7-10 hour experience. It's well written most of the time and I like the mental focus on the story about how we handle our fears, certain aspects we deal with and what we go through life experiencing.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game in terms of a mix between storytelling, ambience and gameplay. The storytelling has a melancholiac vibe to it which fits right with me and the art style it pursues. The game shines most in the small events on the road and in the towns, from those who actually moved me to others that are funny parodies to famous works. Although not all characters from the radio station were sympathetic (but I think that’s also the intend), they supported the travel well.The overall story guides the game well, but seems a bit lost in the whole scheme of things, unless you get some of the radio transmissions of the “antagonist”. The gameplay (racing and overworld) is alright, but the option for a higher difficulty level would have been nice, especially for the races. Although it is a rougelike and feels like one technically, it misses the genres usual unforgiveness and difficulty (I lost the game only once due to my own routing error).Overall, if you got the money to spare and are in the mood for a game that has a melancholic tone but won’t pull you down, this might be one for you. Just don’t expect a long playtime (I got through it in 7 hours) or a large challenge. It’s a rather satisfying experience crafted with creativity and heart (imo).

_childDocuments_.review: Strolling through the New & Trending page desperate for a racing game that had enough style to separate itself from the rest, this game immediately caught my eye. The Neo-Noir art style isn't a new idea for racing games with 2011's MAYHEM for Xbox and PS3, but Heading Out makes the art suit the gameplay - roads and obstacles are all easily readable from a distance, and probably make the highway racing segments easier for casual players who want a story.I used to think I hated roguelites because most of the greatest examples people celebrate have all the respect from me, but none of the playtime. Those games start to feel stale pretty quickly when you're running through the same boss fights over and over again. Maybe my biggest barrier was genre though, because I am obsessed with Heading Out.If you're expecting a lot of driving here, you might be a little disappointed; I went into the game expecting the narrative gameplay to come first, so the balance feels just as expected for me. If you want a driving-first game, the handling model will be satisfying but leave you wanting more of it. (EDIT: After another run and accepting a mission that took me way off course, it turns out if you throw your pedal to the floor with blatant disregard to cops you *can* get quite a lot of driving in. You can get some really exciting fun out of taking jobs that blow you way off course, getting back on track and racing down Fear.)Should you buy this game? YES. ABSOLUTELY.Regardless of whether or not you think the narrative concepts are relatable or engaging, this game sticks out like a gorgeous sunflower in the middle of nowhere. Other racing games look exactly the same and play exactly the same; pick a car, pick a track, drive. Heading Out dares to make bold artistic choices in a genre that has only just started to remember they're supposed to be entertainment. The driving feels forgiving and fun, with loads of grip but a requirement to occasionally manage your speed for the corners. The narrative implementation is short and sweet. The talk radio hosts are an eclectic dissection of current-day Americana, which really helped boost my immersion in the game's setting.Basically, it's a racing game that has a personality in the exact way racing games used to be.Get this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Heading Out

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first playthrough of this game. I presume each playthrough will only take 5 hours. Usually, I like to have a lot more hours in a game before reviewing it, but I doubt I'm going to get hundreds of hours out of this game. A close friend bought me this game recently, thinking I would like it, and now after playing it, I definitely know why he thought I would. Heading Out is a game that brings forth many interesting ideas, but honestly feels a little too short to pick itself off the ground. Heading out is a game about fear, regret, pain, and the feeling of just being lost or trapped. A feeling that I am honestly all too aware of. A lot of aspects of the game will also change from playthough to playthough. Person to person. That makes it very unique, especially for a racing game. That also adds some well-needed replayability. The story is very interesting and the ending is great, although I felt like it was spoiled long before the end of the game due to what many of the radio hosts said throughout the game. Some parts of the story I could easily figure out early on, such as the identity of the mysterious racer you're pursuing throughout the game. If you know these kinds stories about mental unrest, its easy to know who it is at the get go, and if you don't know who it is then, you'll likely figure it out at the end of act 1. Speaking of, Heading Out is divided into four acts. Throughout the game, you play as "The Interstate Jackalope", a name given by radio hosts after they hear of your escape from law enforcement in Detroit, Michigan. Your Mission is to drive as far as you can and to find and defeat the mysterious "Blue Racer". No need to find them though, because you already have an innate sense of direction telling you where they are. On your trek across the U.S. of A. you get mixed up in the lives of others trying to get by. The game gives you many options to be the good guy or the bad guy. The game has a reputation and fame system. Having a high reputation can grant you store discounts and more options in decision-based events. A high fame can also offer difference decisions and can get you more money when you race. Each act ends with you crashing and dying before coming to a major revelation. In the next act, You start back at the beginning and must travel across the country again, the portion you travel getting longer with each act.Eventually, word will spread and radio personalities will begin to hear about it. There are 4 main radio hosts you hear from throughout the game. One is a Libral who fittingly named their channel the "Rainbow Rebellion." One is heavily Conservative, taking direct inspiration from Alex Jones, the last two are more in a middle zone, both taken a beating from the system and on their last legs, one of which as taken their radio studio hostage. All four radio hosts will react to the actions of the Interstate Jackalope, some positive and some negative. For example, one time I ran out of money so I was forced to steal gas when I made it to a town. After this, the radio hosts kept lecturing me about how stealing is bad. Another time, I was having problems finding places to sleep and one of the radio hosts specifically called me out on my lack of sleeping. The radio hosts are an aspect of the game I really enjoyed. It really makes me feel like my choices has weight and people really do remember the things I do. However, due to the short runtime of the game, I'm sure there's much dialogue from the radio hosts I have yet to hear. It really does feel like this is the kind of game that will take multiple playthroughs to experience all it has to offer. Now, for the elephant and donkey in the room. Earlier I mentioned that one of the radio hosts was liberal and the other is conservative. I mostly bring it up because I know that its a touchy subject for many people. Most don't like politics in games because its just a large part of our own world and most people play games as an escape. Politics are a pretty big thing in this game, and can be brought up frequently. The game even asks you about what is your character's political view at one point.Now for the actual racing and style itself. Heading Out nailed an unique style for a racing game. The only colors you see the game is black, grey, white, yellow, and red. The game uses comic book visuals both in events and in racing. Other cars on the road will react to you and if your fame is high enough, they may even refer to you by your nickname. Sometimes, the player can get into police chases. Some of the chases are easy and just require the player to do a few special actions to get away from the police. As you continue through the acts, the races and police chases will get harder. When not racing, the player will spend most of the time looking at a map of the United States and planning a route to their destination. Throughout the game more and more of the map is being made inaccessible by "The Fear". The Fear is basically an all-consuming void that is slowly swallowing the entirety of America. Of course, it's just in the Jackelope's head, but they don't know that. The Fear is just there to pressure the player into continuing forward to their final destination. To be honest, the fear is an aspect of this game I'm not a huge fan of. There's so many areas you can go to and explore, but when the game puts you on a time-limit, especially in the form of an all-consuming void, it really takes away any desire to explore and be free, but maybe the absence of freedom is the point of it. The game also doesn't let you travel any east of Indiana, so some portions of America are entirely left out.Heading Out has a very interesting and fun story with a great ending, even if I could see it coming. I love the style and the actual driving itself is smooth and fun. I had a blast with the police chases. I appreciate this game for touching on sensitive topics of mental health and fear. However, I did feel like the game was too short and sometimes the story was predictable. I also know this isn't a game for everyone, especially due to its topics of politics. I'm giving Heading Out an 7/10, a stylish road trip with something important to say. It has a good story, some great music, fun driving, and new unique ideas, however the game is very short and feels linear with how limited you are due to the constant approaching Fear.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun racing focused narrative roguelike, you're in a loop of racing and death trying to reach and beat a legendary racerThe game is split into 4 sections, your overworld map- standard roguelike affair where you pick lanes (highways) to travel between cities with POIs along the way. The second part is the narrative choices section, a small vignette of an encounter you have where you choose your action in it, as shown in the screenshots for the game you have the choice to reveal the outcomes of your decisions but this can be turned off in the options if you want more difficulty and or realism- personally I leave them on as it helps with collections (as you can find various collectables from your choices sometimes) and some games if poorly worded or designed can bring about unwanted desires from the outcomes, however this has been fairly expected so far. The last part is of course, the driving- you start off with one car and gradually unlock others as you complete chapters each with a different handling model, the cars are fairly hefty and tend to magnetise forwards, some are built more for going flat out and staying true, some are better for drifts- you get the idea, if you've found this game you know how cars work in games- Beyond obviously beating your opponent in the races you're doing there's points you can gain to help boost your fame by doing tricks like driving close to other cars, getting airtime or drifting, the biggest thing to look out for are detour shortcuts- basically no downside to taking if you can hit them except some are slightly tricky. The last section I'll mention is actually the "Character Creation"- at the start of each chapter you'll be asked some questions to build the narrative of that chapter and your overall run- I cant say how much this will deviate between choices as is always the dreaded question when it comes to choose your own dialogue/adventure mechanics in games but if you're not here for the story aspects and just want the roguelite gameplay at least it spices up each run a bit.As a side note from reading the other reviews it is hilarious to me that the top negative ones are moaning about the "liberal leanings" of a game about being a racer outlaw speeding across america

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably going to come off more negative than positive even though I enjoyed the game overall, but there was just so much that was disappointing & could've made it so much more.Some spoilers ahead, mostly in the main story section. Will try to point them out.The game is at its best with the driving, resource management, & side stories. Since this is the majority of the gameplay, that carries the game & makes it worth it to me. The races are pretty easy even on Challenging (haven't played the final act on that difficulty yet, so maybe that's where it gets harder). I think I came second place once on Balanced difficulty largely due to wrecking the car one too many times. I was also never in danger of being caught by police. I didn't even see the arrest meter until the 3rd act, and I saw it for all of 3 seconds. That being said, I don't mind a game leaning towards too easy rather than too hard. With some games, I like just being able to continue to work towards the end. Resource management is really the one thing I found that can end your run, but even then, I only lost my first run before realizing the importance of time & then breezed through all acts in consecutive runs. Because of this, the roguelike aspects were really not relevant in my experience. The side stories (glimpses) are probably the highlight for me even though I have problems with them that I'll mention ahead.Repeated dialogue & content really started to wear on me in this game. For an indie game, I'm not going to complain too much about hearing the same lines repeated from NPC chatter, but I wish this chatter could be turned down/off without muting all SFX. The repeated radio recordings & glimpses were what actually frustrated me. I could tell I hadn't hit all the unique content because I would get new ones sprinkled here & there, but throughout one run of the game, I was hearing the same radio dialogues over and over. It doesn't even need more content. It seems like there needs to be a better system to avoid you hearing the exact same recordings multiple times in a single run unless you exhaust everything that fits your character's attributes. Glimpses didn't seem to repeat much throughout a run, but I was getting a lot of the same ones across acts. The glimpses themselves are kinda the best content the game has though. There are some difficult choices to be made, and it lets you develop an interesting character even if a lot of choices really are boiled down to good & evil in your reputation meter. If you play with hidden consequences, doing what you think is best may screw you in ways you don't expect. If you play with consequences visible though, you may feel forced into something you don't agree with just to squeeze your resources to the end of the run which was very engaging in my opinion.Another unfortunate aspect is that it seems like you get one major, 3-part story for each run. There's an achievement for each of these, so I can tell there are plenty more to see. However, with the lack of difficulty, I pretty much experienced one for each act & that was it. I may go back through a few more runs to see some new ones, but we'll see.Even with repetition aside, the radio dialogue & overall writing is probably the weakest part of the game for me. The radio hosts are largely one-dimensional & never seem to have anything too impactful to say (besides maybe Joy), The hosts are basically split into three camps. One is a generic news host that just gives the facts (don't have too much to add). Then there's the two it feels like you're supposed to be empathetic towards which are Joy & Riley. Joy is by far the better of the two for me because she felt the most real & the Riley dialogue was more annoying than anything. As another reviewer mentioned, very haha random angsty punk you knew in middle school. Joy on the other hand (minor spoiler but revealed pretty much at the start) , and listening to her trying to understand her shifting views of everything is the most interesting character development in the game. The last two, you're basically just supposed to see as irredeemable nutcases. One is portrayed as a dishonest, cheating man who locked himself in a radio station and has a mental breakdown on air. In some ways, this character was actually slightly interesting & seemed like more of a flawed character trying to grapple with a midlife crisis even though he's definitely written to be hated. The other character is literally just Alex Jones. There's zero nuance to it. He sounds & acts like Alex Jones at all times, and the game just constantly tells you that he's a douchebag & describes him as all the bigoted & phobic traits imaginable. I'm not a fan of Jones by any means, but I wish they'd tried to write a character with any depth rather than just being a POS alt-right man with 0 positive traits that you have to listen to scream about how much he hates you every once in a while.The main story is also extremely heavy-handed. They don't want you to miss anything & I wish it gave you more room to interpret. The "running away from your fears" metaphor doesn't have nearly the depth that it does in a game like Firewatch because it's so literal here. You drive away from a physical (or perceived to be physical) cloud of fear that closes off the map behind you. It's cool as a gameplay mechanic, but less so as a plot point. Vague comment about how you beat the game, but definitely spoils it:  There are a lot of not-so-subtle hints leading up to the end about what to do, but it still will tell you word for word just to make sure you can't miss it. I also didn't like how the entire backstory is revealed to you in a text/narrator dump. They do a decent job of giving you the pieces to see what happened for yourself, but 3/4 of the way through, you just get a text wall telling you what happened, so nothing is up to interpretation.One last way the writing is super heavy-handed is with the choices you make at the start of each act. You're asked to pick from a list of fears, relationship status, regrets, etc. so it can give dialogue that's supposed to feel personal. I don't mind when games do this even if it's hard for it to ever feel truly personal since they have to cast such a wide net. However, the game gives no illusion as to what these choices affect. Every time the dialogue is affected by this, you'll see your choice almost word for word highlighted in blue so you can't miss it. The way it uses them is also pretty surface level. Very minor spoiler, but when I picked "loss of loved ones" as a major fear, there was a scene where I effectively just heard "Your loved ones are going to die.", "Your loved ones are already gone.", & "You can't save your loved ones now." on repeat. Maybe other choices can have dialogue that hit home for some people, but they were so superficial to me that it had almost no effect which is a shame.A final suggestion that could already in the works for all I know: I wish there was anything you could do with your save after beating the game besides clearing it. A free-roam where you can race on each highway could be a nice addition so you can keep using the late-game cars.In conclusion, I enjoyed the game as a whole, and I think $20 is reasonable for a solid 8 hour game when having very few resets. That time could easily be extended with more deaths & subsequent runs. It falls short in a lot of ways, especially the writing of recurring characters which has a lot more misses than hits in my opinion. There are some interesting moments in here though, and I think it's worth the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: What an interesting and surprisingly fun game!Heading Out is a 30% Visual Novel,60% Racing game which style reminds me to the old school racing games like Road Rash was back in the day...We jump into a linear map where we need to react fast to the road's obstacles and the shortcuts.The other 10% is the rouglike elements...If we can call it like that. The game drops some random encounters into the map and the main cities like story elements - where we can get additional stuffs..... collectibles, money, focus (stamina) - , side quests and races .... Some quest encounters could escalade to a bigger stories if the RNG drop it to us, so the game calls you to explore and go bigger roads in one run or even replay the whole game again and again.This game not made to everyone , but those who bought by the trailer should give it a go...... because they will have a truly unique experience.It is short, but the rng system will make you to replay it again.At least to earn all the achievements. :D
_childDocuments_.name: Heading Out

_childDocuments_.review: There exists an echo, a roar in the bones and fuel in the nose. The need to escape your fears, the desire to drive to infinity and the despair of a better self that races you towards the void. The questions, they tug at you. Who are you? What are you? Why are you? What broke you? You wonder in the end if it even matters at all. This world, these roads and skies. They eat away at you like a cancer. Others who have taken this journey trapped themselves into a slow death. Floor it no matter what. Freedom waits for nobody but those at death's door. Good luck.
_childDocuments_.name: Heading Out

_childDocuments_.review: Every driver has their own stories of greatness as well as their failures. I was a bit emotionally attached to the story as it affects my actions towards the speaker on the radio. Your choices matter and it will cause a butterfly effect on the rest of the way, you can be the Most Wanted on the Interstate, but you can be a good person.Plan early on and decide carefully on where to go.Even fear will eventually get to you, don't stop and keep on driving.Drive forever, my friends.....drive forever.Just like the game says, "It's just you, your car, and the road."PS: Interstate Jackalope = Ryan Gosling confirmed

_childDocuments_.review: Sin City meets Driver meets Tarantino. This game surpassed expectations as you’re taken on this journey which you yourself write. All decisions you make have consequences but can also aid you to get to your destination. A fun twist on the genre with a mix of different gameplay so it feels really refreshing switching between the map and then into the drivers seat. A fun element of resource management and risk of choosing the wrong option as the story unfolds. Strong rogue like elements too which keeps you on your toes but extremely rewarding when it all clicks together. Can’t wait to get some more hours into the game, a really unique experience across both gameplay and storytelling! Would recommend to pick up!Note: also works really well on the steam deck too!

_childDocuments_.review: God I wish steam still featured the mixed review... remember that?If you're here for a clear answer as to if you should buy the game: Yes. Do it. It's a good time.The game is great. The writing is great, driving is solid, the random banter and radio stations are fun to listen to. Random events show a refreshing amount of creativity, only enhanced by the comments the mentioned radio stations make about those events.What's there is great... so I just wish there was more.Not just more content, mind you. I wish for what's there to be cranked up further. Each trip doesn't last long enough and you're practically forced to take the shortest route. Races and police chases are fun but don't really evolve after the first time and are soon trivialized - there's never a reason not to take a shortcut, after all. For the small events that trigger the most, radio shows seem to have one response each so once you run out of money again, expect to hear Wish Alex Jones call a manhunt on you again.Same for the music. What's there is generally good... just not good enough to not get repetitive. This seems like a game that could use a custom music folder... please give us a custom music folder.It's an amazing game that just... needs more of it. That's it. That's the only flaw. There's not enough. Go buy the game so we can get more.

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen a couple of reviews mention this, and as you can tell from my title, it is very much true. Heading Out doesn't present itself accurately on its front page : while the trailers make it look like a rogue-like racing game with narrative elements, what you get is actually the inverse : a narrative game with racing game elements. You wake up at the wheel, your fears are chasing you : Drive like hell, don't stop.What you will do most of the time is look at your point slowly moving onto a map, and answering choices or listening to the radio while on the road, going to your destination. Getting faster will cost you, literally : you CAN speed up to get by faster, but you'll guzzle more gas, which will cut into your money a tad more than expected. You also take more risks if a cop speeds by.You only actively take the wheel if something requiring it happens, and you only get control for the time of a song and a radio break - and I ALSO mean that literally. The song length is actually your timer for the driving sections, and you'll get a narrative part on the radio where you still get to drive, but all tension is off. Just... drive and listen.Also three things of note :- The rogue-like part game is , but it's truly not the focus. Events and races are randomized, sure, but you don't get like different builds or upgrades or stuff like that. You're as strong as you start as you will be later in a run. A successful run will get you to the following Act, with more distance to cover, some more dangers, and some more events.- A lot of resources management. You need money to buy gaz and stuff like that, you need to outrun your Fear encroaching on the world map so time is a factor, you need to actually sleep every once in a while to regenerate your Focus... And you can buy some items for future needs. It is possible to caffeine and drug your way to staying awake.- The game is... not hard by any metrics. I am playing in Balanced - the "Medium" difficulty - and considering pumping it up for my next run. There are a LOT of fail-safes in play. You get 5 Respawns  if you wrap up around another car. Despite a Car Condition gauge, you can take an incredible amount of punishment without losing much. Getting intercepted by the police launches you into a Chase. Letting your Fears catch up to you "just" puts you into a Fear Race to escape. You need to actually lose those to fail your run, and... Well, even with the constant pressure, I find that the game is more than generous when it comes down to it.Does a great deal to keep the tension up, but nothing else when it comes the time to actually strike. Like a movie monster turning into a wet fart.So yeah. The game is not really what you can think it is.Is it bad ?Absolutely not.The story is interesting and intriging enough to follow around, wanting you to get to the next Act. The stories you get on the road are a neat picture of the world, and as your place as a runaway drifter - you're involved into the lives of these people just long enough to make an impact. The presentation is . The voice acting and narration are really good. And the music, considering it's central part as a timer in gameplay, also does a good job of setting up an ambiance and pumping you up.And most of all, there's nothing quite like it out there. It is very unique in what it tries to achieve.If you know what you're getting into, that's a Recommend from me.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever watched Two Lane Blacktop or Vanishing Point and "Got the point" then this is the game for you.Triptikking, outrunning the law, being a vagabond.Game has a delightfully liberal agenda. Handling is very arcade-like. Cars feel heavy, but also the physics are pretty solid (like getting squirrely over a crest). The drift mechanic could be better.Excited to head out a few more times and see the other storylines.If you feel like you're not getting enough driving experience, SPEED THE WHOLE FRIGGIN WAY. The only thing you need to worry about is running out of money for gas.Make the cops chase you! Always engage in the chase. Always engage in the race. Just effing send it. Already onto my 3rd trip.
_childDocuments_.name: Heading Out

_childDocuments_.review: Pro's:While a Major fan of movies such as Death Proof and Drive, I was hoping to re-experience some of these moments that are seen in the movies. It does give a bit of that based on driving an Old Dodge Challenger, it certainly brings the feeling of living in the 70's with the unique art style and the cost of everything and for the price alone is worth it to me for Heading out.Cons:The downside though is that what other reviews are saying, that its blips of that experience due to most of it based on staring at a map and not really living the point A to B experience which is a major let down. And the difficulty is non-existent. I have made this the most challenging difficulty and I still easily beat all races and outrun cops. The rubbing banding is odd, but luckily not too predictable with vehicles but still doesn't give much of an exciting edge. Its either always in front most of the time or barely being behind. Some more personal takes:I have also maxed out the cars engine volume because I love to hear it rip and roar to life and lowering all other volumes except the master volume only to see feel its a bit muffled and tamer then it should be. I think for the price the game is ok so far and I plan to update my review as I progress further though. Steam Deck Experience: So far its been great on the steam Deck as far as play-ability, controls feel natural. But I get a lot of frame drops in the middle half of the game especially when a level is about to end several times. One was so bad my Steam Deck completely Froze. So I played another half hour on my PC and it has been flawless but its hard to beat a 4080.I hope this game may see more updates or patches for the various things I mention, I think it was released a bit early then it should have been as it can feel a bit bland at times and the menus are confusing at first. I think this game has so much potential. I do recommend the game still if you are a old school car junky like me wanting to get a taste of those experiences but if the game was more then $20.00 I would not recommend it.

Hop into a muscle car and drive through the American West in a game inspired by 1970s road movies. Enjoy the ride in this narrative-driven racing experience with a comic book aesthetic. Choose your own route across the USA in a game where every run is a personalized, unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The first Moving Out was arguably my best purchase I made on steam. This game is ok, even good in comparison to other games I've played, but comes nowhere close to what I liked about the first one. The game didn't have the same charm for me and I couldn't figure out why. I ultimately narrowed it down to the fact that the first game had fairly simple map design, but the progression of map obstacles through out the game made sense without over staying its welcome, This game seems to for the most part, focus on map design and not the gameplay. Even with this change in more complex map design, the game is actually easier because they don't give you medals. I Grinded out platinum medals for the base game and DLC in the first game. You had to learn how to improve by routing certain items first or improving your speed. That element is mostly lost, which is the element which was the best part for me. Most people probably don't care about this level of nuance for a game that is generally perceived as more casual fun, but the surprise of the depth of the first game is another element of why I loved the game so much, it was a beautiful surprise.

It's still fun to move things around but it feels a lot more chaotic, often not in a fun way. If you're looking for more games like overcooked I would still definitely recommend this, I just feel like moving out 1 felt more cohesive and something about the formula just clicked together more
