_childDocuments_.review: 20h without using a guide to know the level objectives before playing each level 3/10 met assist mode on, otherwise a whole lot higher 1 + replaying levels for level objectives and collectibles Yes,  and  No, can be done single-player with assist mode on.  No, there is level selection Not really, but doing all the objectives can feel as a grind No Yes, but within the assist options you can choose to have more time No No No, everything unlocks with assist mode on NoMoving Out 2 is a great sequel after the first game was already an awesome game. It plays a bit like Overcooked, with chaotic levels and so much fun in multiplayer. However, Moving Out 2 can be played in single-player because they have assist options in the game so you can carry items alone which you normally have to carry with 2 people. You can find 4 kinds of worlds in this game, the normal world and 3 worlds with a specific theme. It is amazing how much they added to the game and how creative they were with making each level. Don't just play the basic world and think this will become boring soon, as things will change in later levels. The craziness gets really crazy.One of the few downsides of Moving Out 2 is that it can become tedious if you play this game too much in a short amount of time. I became something annoyed with a level design or objective when playing for too long. When I took a break and came back later to the game, it didn't feel that tedious anymore and I could see the logic more clearly. So take your time playing through the 57 levels, so you don't burn out on the principle of the game. The achievements aren't hard, they are mostly for just finding all the collectibles and finishing every objective. Each level has 2 time objectives and 3 other objectives.  You can make the objectives easier by changing things in the assist settings. You can pick and choose which things you want to make easier and decided the right difficulty for you (and your friends) that way. which I highly appreciate. Another thing you can do to really speed up the completion time is to look at the objectives of each level beforehand using the guide by Powerpyx that I liked above. The game will only reveal them after finishing the level for the first time, but if you do them in your first try you will unlock them already and have less to do when replaying the levels for the second time, or maybe already have them all in one try. I really enjoyed my time with Moving Out 2 a lot and I'm very happy they don't have achievements this time for flushing all the toilets without having a way to track if you did that on each level. I'm also glad that it is totally possible to play Moving Out 2 as a singleplayer. This was already possible in the first entry but isn't always the case with this type of games.

_childDocuments_.review: A definite improvement on an already solid fun multiplayer game. Everything about it is charming and fun, and this sequel has so much more flexibility than the original. There's some weird quirks for sure. There'll be specific spawn points that always seem to be on an occupied space, and it takes a while to adjust even tho there's NOTHING around this one designated square they assigned. Nothing game breaking but it does get irritating when you fall off a cliff and the one object you have moved happen to be in the random spot they assigned as the spawn point. It's also rough when there's more time spent on puns than explaining how levels/things work. There's much more of a puzzle atmosphere which is great, but a lot of levels clearly expect you to run thru it once to even understand how it even functions.The weirdest quirk tho is the overuse of question marks? Half the sentences said end with that punctuation? And I don't even think it's poor translation or anything it's just always there? And I'm playing this game with my kid who likes to narrate characters so everything ends in an upward inflection? For normal sentences? The puns are bad enough (they're really really bad?) but honestly the frequent indecision is worse?

_childDocuments_.review: my sister and i bought this game because we're huge fans of Overcooked 2, and this game seemed like it'd be right up our alley... we were majorly disappointed.we like to play on our own PCs, but the online multiplayer is a laggy mess. combine that with how picky this game is and how intricate the physics are... it's not great. i really like the premise and think the game has potential; it's hilarious! but, it just seems unpolished and messy, especially if it's trying to promote online multiplayer.i will say, if playing this game, use a controller over keyboard. the controller better handles the physics the game is trying to achieve versus the WASD of the keyboard. however, this wouldn't be a problem if the game wasn't from a overhead, diagonal POV...basically, play at your own risk. i definitely wouldn't have gotten it if it wasn't 50% off.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent sequel to the first Moving Out. It takes what made the first game fun, and doubled down and added even more wacky things to work around.If this is your first time hearing of this game. All you need to know is that you are a worker in a moving company, and you must pack furniture in your moving van as fast as possible  The game will get chaotic very quick, and you'll be flinging furniture around at the speed of light through windows and walls to accomplish your goal. The first world is a tad slow, but its just to get you up to speed for the worlds to come. The 3 other worlds in the game really step up on the mechanics and every level adds a new unique feature to work around. You rarely get bored. There is also quite a bit of replay-ability with the level mission system. Each level has 3 extra missions that require you to do something different than just moving furniture. So you usually play the levels at the minimum 2 times or more depending on the missions.There is also some really nice accessibility options with assist mode. Longer timer, move 2 player furniture easier, removing obstacles, etc. So if you aren't as adept at this kind of game and would just like a chill experience, you can do so easily. Overall I recommend the game if you are looking for something similar to Overcooked 2, but more chaotic in energy.

The stages in the first game were better designed and more fun overall despite the few new level ideas in the second one. Difficulty balancing is all over the place(Only looking at it from the pro time perspective), most of them are either very easy or absurdly difficult.(The Dronies, Watt's house) Controls definitely needed some improvement from the first game, and unfortunately since it plays pretty much the same here, it's just as frustrating sometimes as it was before. Like how randomly my character's dropping an item as I'm holding it for no reason, how awkward it feels sometimes when the two of you try to move a single object together, how annoying it is when you try to rotate the character as you hold an item, and the tossing mechanic is just as frustrating. Still not a bad game, just kind of sad to see the lack of improvements here.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Moving Out 2 is very similar to the first iteration.  You pick up furniture through a maze of homes, fields, castles, and more.  Sometimes you have to do the reverse and put move furniture and items into the level.Here there are some varieties to the levels.  In the future levels, you use batteries to open up doors with limited time until the door closes or use robot to accomplish other changes to the levels to help maneuver to hard to reach furniture and items.  In the wizard levels you can use portals to find ways to areas that are not accessible by just walking and jumping.  In some levels you played games like a basketball game with furniture.  In other levels you had to place certain items into portals rather than moving them out or in, which meant going around the levels finding all the same items and bringing each item to their correct portals to finish the levels.As per usual, there are challenges in each levels to acquire stars.  The stars give you experience points towards higher levels which open up more portions of the maps you uncover.  I thought it was strange that this time around no achievement for getting all of the stars which kind of diminishes the purpose of having more stars than levels if there is not an incentive to get them all.Playing with others, especially couch co-op is the way to go.  While this game won't get you upset such as Overcooked, it will definitely test the durability of your relationship still.  The graphics are great for what you are playing, there is no need to be any more realistic, the art design works well.  The varying worlds offer varying backdrops to your levels and certain types of furniture and items to match.  The sounds are anything to write about, but they compliment the game quite well, especially the farts when you're trying to push furniture all by yourself exerting more energy than you should.While the game is not much different than the original, it's still a fun time and with enough new variations throw into the mix that it feels more like a full expansion (rather than a DLC) that adds to the original while not breaking the formula.  Pick this up if you haven't played the original, or pick it up if you enjoyed the original and are itching for more comic moving relief.

_childDocuments_.review: I embarked on the Moving Out 2 journey with two pals with the commitment to 100% the game as we had for the first game. Our couch co-op escapade was nothing short of chaotic joy. The camaraderie was tested during challenging optional missions, leading to blame games. It would be a crime to forget to mention the uproarious laughter and positive memories resulted from the game's funky and hilarious physics and events. Even if perfection isn't your aim, the experience is fantastic.Compared to its predecessor, Moving Out 2 introduces a plethora of characters, but not all are winners. Unlocking them adds a fun element, yet most lack the charm of the original cast. While not a groundbreaking sequel, the real star here is the abundance of brilliantly crafted levels with charming ideas and mini-games seamlessly integrated which were found in a separate mini-game sections.The subtle graphical upgrade and neutral changes in physics are noticeable, enhancing the overall experience. However, a definitive ending felt a bit underwhelming—missing the epic final boss vibe found in the original.Despite this, Moving Out 2 shines as one of the best co-op games, building on the success of its predecessor. Achievable goals and a few challenging levels keep you engaged, though the lacking grandeur in the final stage is a minor setback.Looking ahead, I eagerly await a DLC or Moving Out 3. Adding character abilities, one-time items, or special tools could inject fresh dynamics as these are some qualities that we expected from a sequel. More customization options for characters would be a welcome addition, maintaining the same lovable goofy charm.In conclusion, I highly recommend this gem. The unimaginably good level designs showcase meticulous attention to detail, ensuring a delightful gaming experience, overall.

_childDocuments_.review: Exactly this: "The first Moving Out was arguably my best purchase I made on steam. This game is ok, even good in comparison to other games I've played, but comes nowhere close to what I liked about the first one. The game didn't have the same charm for me and I couldn't figure out why. I ultimately narrowed it down to the fact that the first game had fairly simple map design, but the progression of map obstacles through out the game made sense without over staying its welcome, This game seems to for the most part, focus on map design and not the gameplay. Even with this change in more complex map design, the game is actually easier because they don't give you medals. I Grinded out platinum medals for the base game and DLC in the first game. You had to learn how to improve by routing certain items first or improving your speed. That element is mostly lost, which is the element which was the best part for me. Most people probably don't care about this level of nuance for a game that is generally perceived as more casual fun, but the surprise of the depth of the first game is another element of why I loved the game so much, it was a beautiful surprise."

_childDocuments_.review: The Steam Awards are coming up, and I want to progress the badge, so might as well kill two birds with one stone...Moving Out 2 is a physics-based co-op game developed by SMG Studio and Devm Games, published by Team17, where your goal is, you guessed it, helping people move out.If you're familiar with Moving Out's gameplay loop, consider this game as more Moving Out with new levels and a little bit of a twist. If not, don't worry, I got you.In Moving Out, you choose a character from a list of ridiculous creatures and start dragging objects from the house to the truck by holding the trigger on the controller. The task can't be completed alone: you need at least one comrade, and ideally more.Some items can be carried alone, while others require two people. Without cooperation, nothing is going to work. To meet the deadline, you need to work together, or a sofa might get stuck in the doorway, and the game will be over. Sometimes levels feature changing environments to make your job even harder. But most often, your main enemy will be the door, which I recommend knocking down at the very beginning of each level.The entire game gives off an arcade vibe where you need to plan your strategy, always fight for extra time, plan out an optimal route, sort the goods in the truck for extra room, and, of course, the most important and difficult part is coordinating with your teammates. The adrenaline is constantly pumping as you try to shave a few seconds off your record for that satisfying mark in your Journal and a precious achievement on your gamer profile. It's also fun to just mess around, and if you're not an idealist, there's an assist mode you can turn on to beat the entire game without any punishment.Overall, it can be a pretty chill game, finishing periodically with a few levels at a time, or your absolute nightmare if you're going for the lowest time possible because anything can happen in Moving Out. I also want to add that the optimization is pretty good, and I really enjoyed the overall visual style of the game—kind of minimalistic yet very readable level design. I beat the entire game on the Steam Deck and never encountered any issues. So, feel free to call your homies if you have any and hop on Moving Out 2 wherever you are because the cross-play option is also available no matter the platform.10/10

name: Dawn of the Monsters
detailed_description: The cataclysmic battle between giant monsters has begun in this manga-inspired, side-scrolling, kaiju beat-'em-up! Titanic creatures known as Nephilim have invaded Earth, and the only hope of stopping them is DAWN (Defense Alliance Worldwide Network), which unleashes its own colossal combatants to defend against the enemy hordes! Take control of four hulking behemoths - Megadon, Aegis Prime, Tempest Galahad, and Ganira - each with distinct abilities and play styles, and smash your way through destructible real-world environments spanning more than 35 missions! Power up with DNA augments, crush foes with devastating Rage moves and brutal finishers, and team up with a friend for 2-player co-op action! You are the planet's last line of defense...but will that be enough for mankind to survive the Dawn of the Monsters!? Key Features: -Four unique, monstrous playable characters: Megadon, Ganira, Aegis Prime, and Tempest Galahad -Earth-shattering monster-versus-monster one- or two-player co-op beat-'em-up action -Fully destructible cities based on real-world locations -Brutal Rage abilities, devastating Cataclysm Attacks, and merciless finishing moves -Fierce bosses and dozens of different enemy types -Customize your monsters with DNA augments!

_childDocuments_.review: - Great combat. 4 different characters to choose from, all with fun combo potential to play around with, and a nice amount of enemy variety.- Nice graphics, art, and animation- High refresh rate support, although it seems buggy. The camera snaps forward a lot on my 240hz monitor; this doesn't happen at 60hz.- Low difficulty- Limited replay value. There are a lot of unlockable colors, but there's just not much to do once you complete the story and get an S+ rank on every mission.I'm really hoping they expand on this game with an Arcade mode or survival mode, or even a higher difficulty mode (with remixed enemy placement?) after you finish the story, but it's still really good as-is. _childDocuments_.review: This is a really solid game, both for tokusatsu fans and beat-'em-up fans. The game looks great, has appropriate music and is mechanically deep. With four unique characters, large movesets and a fun gear system that works off the ranking system, the gameplay loop is solid. If you want a bit more in your modern beat-'em-up than an s-string and a jumpkick, you'll feel at home here. Parries, just dodges, animation cancels and juggles are a frequent part of every non-boss interaction. Outside of gameplay, the story, characters and their designs are a love letter to all tokusatsu subgenres, not just kaiju stuff.Sadly, the game has the major flaw of lacking any replay value. While the game is too long to boot up and play to completion in one sitting like SOR4 or Fight'N Rage, it's also too short to really make good use of the otherwise solid gear and build diversity given to the player. Gear drops in ascending tiers based on both the player's progress in the campaign and the ranking system. The scoring system is simple to understand and mostly just revolves around killing things quickly and using the overkill bonus to yield a lot of leeway in hitting the S+ threshold for each fight. However, most of the good gear only drops towards the end, and there is really nothing to use it on. The build diversity feels a bit hollow when you realize that the game is over by the time you feel like you've achieved your preferred playstyle, but that the gear also increases in stats, making the idea of putting the high tier stuff on characters you didn't use fall flat too. This game has a perfect foundation to be one of the best action roguelikes on the market, but right now this game's replay value pales in comparison to the recent greats in the genre (SOR4 and Fight'N Rage). At $30 the price is a bit steep for most, especially when the competitors are cheaper and better designed for replay value. I recommend this game, but I also hope it gets the extra content it deserves. While it would be relatively easy to fix the replay value issue with minimal need to create new assets, the developers have said they would like to expand on the game if it sells well. While this game is a labor of love to both tokusatsu and beat-'em-up players, it misses the mark on what has made people play games like Final Fight for decades. Hopefully with time this will be a better overall package, but it's still great for what it currently is.

_childDocuments_.review: Well time to give my thoughts on this game now that I've played through most of it except the very end.  The game's got really fun combat for a kaiju beat em up.  It reminds me a bit of King of the Monsters 2 with more focus on the mooks than the bosses.  The combo mechanics have got quite a bit of depth on them.  You have a bayonetta-like perfect dodge which stuns like a weaker witch time with the right upgrade and a just guard parry.  Most moves can be dodge cancelled to extend combos and the game is simple and fun.  Difficulty is just right for a casual audience with enough depth in combat for more seasoned fighting game players to style on the enemies.  Enemy variety is great, but I do dislike how many enemy types have super-armor or the inability to flinch.  I just want to combo everyone dang it.  I really think some of those enemies should just be launchable after being stunned by a perfect dodge or parry.  The default control layout feels a bit tough to get used to, but you can remap everything after the initial tutorial level.  The story is just a giant kaiju love letter and you just got all the tropes, telepathic children who are friend to monsters, an ultraman expy, a giant mech and a pretty good not-godzilla monster and not-ebirah monster who looks more like a rhinoceros beetle than a lobster, shady corporations, an earth defense force, and ancient prophecies.  All of it is here and the entire story is perfectly voice acted by an amazing cast.  The music fits well to this genre of game, and it is nothing too spectacular but also inoffensive.  Visually the game is pretty good, and subtle touches like very minor camera shakes really make everything feel sluggish and weighty like any good Kaiju game should.  I still can't believe the characters are all 2d sprites on a 3d backdrop, they mesh together really well.  The scenery gets samey and repetitive, but from the perspective of a giant monster, there really isn't much variety since everything is just a puny city to you.  The variety of walking through a rapid river or sandstorm provides a good variety.I do have complaints about the game though although they are minor.  The game definitely drags on too long for a beat em up which are supposed to be pick up and play for a full playthrough in 1 or 2 hours.  The power-up equipment you get by end game are amazing, but there isn't a survival mode or arcade mode to use them in.  Replaying the game from the beginning with them feel almost like cheating, and they really only have a use at the final chapter.  There needs to be more places to make use of them.  The only thing dragging this game down is the lack of replayability.  There needs to be more of a pick up and play for an hour mode.  Such as survival mode or rogue-lite mode with random augments after each wave. Pros:-Visually really nice to look at with many nice touches such as minor camera shakes-Voice acting really stands out and everyone involved did an amazing job.  I especially love Xander's portrayal of Dr. Ivakin.-Combat's got some pretty good depth to it for those who prefer more execution heavy beat em ups.  However the difficulty never gets too overwhelming, that a casual player can't just press buttons and spam special moves and still beat the game.-The story would not be out of place as a kaiju movie and follows the tropes perfectly.  If you love Kaiju, you will love this game.-Music is serviceable for the Kaiju genre.  Lots of dread and low brass!Cons:-It really lacks replayability and drags on way too long to replay the game from beginning to end.-The abilities you get near end game has no use outside of the final chapter, could use a survival or arcade mode that makes better use of them.  -Would be nice to have real online co-op.  Although we'll always have steam remote play and parsec.

_childDocuments_.review: My first impressions video: This is one of those games where I really wish Steam had a "thumbs sideways" button. I'm recommending this, but Ialso recommend you either watch my video or be prepared to try this and possibly refund it. This is definitely not a bad game, but I personally think it's let down by some pretty weak core combat.I love brawlers and one with Kaiju was instantly appealing. There is a story that explains why you can play not only as robots, but as Kaiju themselves. It sets things up well and while the various cutscenes are basic, they're well drawn, the characters are interesting, and everything is nicely voice acted. You have multiple characters you can play, all of which have different traits, and which you can upgrade and customize with items you earn from doing (and redoing) missions. It allows for a lot of different ways to play and influence how the levels progress.I admit to being the minority in this view, but I do think the combat itself is a major shortcoming here. I understand that you're playing as very large monsters fighting other very large monsters, but the movement and control response just feels laggy and clunky. There is a combo system, but it's basic and doesn't have a lot of variation. Button mashing won't win you the entire game, but it definitely can get you through a lot of it. Compared to other brawlers like Fight N' Rage or Streets of Rage 4, the fighting system in this just feels very limited and slow. This may be down to my preferred playstyle, but it's a major detraction to a game with a good framework around it, hence why I wish there was a "thumbs sideways" button.If you like brawlers, either check out my video or try this for yourself and see what you think. The combat may jive better with you than it did me. Even though I wish that part was batter, it still is super fun to beat our Kaiju while wrecking the city around you.

_childDocuments_.review: I would absolutely highly recommend. The fact that (at the time of me writing this anyway), only around 15% of players have even finished this game is beyond unfair.Sure, the roars are a bit meek and unsatisfying (seriously, amp up the fierceness of those roar animations, increase the volume and make the screen shake a little! These are MONSTERS, not your GRANDMA.), but the gameplay is satisfying. You can perform satisfying, vicious executions on low-health enemies, you can pick up buildings and smash your enemies in the face with them, and you can perform some nice meaty super attacks called Cataclysm Attacks.What at first appears to be simple, clunky movesets will become clearer to you as you learn how to use each move to perform ever-longer combo strings. In a way, there is a method and flow to it that feels a bit like learning to play Monster Hunter (although not quite as high a skill floor).Remote Play is a bit of a pain to get working. I would recommend resigning yourself to the idea that P2 will not be able to use a controller at all and you will likely need to give them keyboard access instead. Also, it seems as though you can only configure P2's controls from the option menu in-game before you select a mission. Furthermore, the default controls for P2 involve Confirm and Cancel being assigned to the number pad, so if their keyboard doesn't have one, too bad!That said, the game is plenty of fun solo but I hope they will work on online play at some point. Maybe even allow up to 4 players because it'd be a heck of a lot of fun to see.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really excited for this game, but quickly found myself dissapointed. The core mechanics are interesting enough, but this is a lousy pc port.The biggest issues is that the gamepad implementation is TERRIBLE. The game has an odd button layout (click the stick instead of start) that for whatever reason defaults to Playstation icons even if you're using an Xbox controller. You can change the controls in the options menu (the ui looks like an early 2000s game), but doing so doen't change the in-game prompts, this is really distracting because you see them every time you interact with an object or execute an enemy. Do not be fooled by that full controller support icon on the store page.Moving on to the gameplay properly, it's ok. It doesn't really play like a conventional Beat 'em up because you can't jump or grab enemies, but you have some unconventional options like blocking and dashing. You have some decent options when it comes to combos, you can cancel basic attacks into heavy attacks, cancel into dash attacks or special moves and even use some cinematic supers. Executing enemies to replenish your lifebar is pretty cool. Extra points for having a training mode, albeit not as robust as the ones you'd find on SOR4 or a fighting game.The art department is a mixed bag. The cutscenes and general art direction is good, but when you jump into the game you can see this game has a limited budget. The enviroments are very samey, low detailed and yet sometimes obstrusive because foreground elements can be pretty big. The main characters look decent enough, but NPCs have rather limited animation (even by guy in a rubber suit standards). The music is all white noise and there's strangely very little in the way of SFX, some good chunky sound effects would help making you feel you're controlling a heavy and powerful character. Also even though all custcenes have fll voice acting, the playable characters have little to no grunts or lines.All in all, I wish I could recommend this game because I like what it tries to do, but as of right now it's way too rough around the edges and not worth 30 dollars.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are in any way a kaiju fan, then this game is for you. And if you enjoy a fun beat-em-up, then this game is for you! Dawn of the Monsters is loaded with style and gameplay that's easy to approach but dynamic enough that you can master and grow with it in finding your style with the varied characters and the choice of augments. The grading system took some getting used to, since it's different from any other game I've played and it can be a touch unforgiving, but once you understand it better, you'll be able to work with it. The designs are great, feeling fresh while having nods to a variety of classic kaiju media and the story is a little predictable but still fun and the characters are charming. All around a solid game for fans of mecha and kaiju media and/or beat-em-ups, definitely worth picking up!

_childDocuments_.review: Don't think I would recommend this for full price, but for 10-15 bucks, sure. TL;DR: Slower beat-em up with lots of variety, tons of aggressive enemies on screen at once, cool graphics. Definitely a love letter to giant monster/sentai/ultraman/etc fans but has some drawbacks that definitely keep it from being as good as stuff like SOR4 and Fight'n Rage. It's a "modern" beat-em up. Basically what I mean by that is the weird standard that, as far as I remember, started with Castle Crashers where hits had weird feeling windups on heavy attacks. Also, the common gimmick of flashing enemy attacks that you choose to block or dodge. This has that stuff going on. Movement is pretty slow, but you could consider that thematic. It's a little weird not to have a run move, but then again, most of the Street of Rage 4 characters don't either. However, it gets a lot of things very, very right. The visuals are very Western "Anime" turned comic, something between Samurai Jack and a manga. I don't love this choice, but the actual aesthetics of the characters and monsters are fantastic. The heroes are recognizable tropes, and the enemies all have fun designs... the weird droopy faced guy with flexible horns, mimicking the rubber suit monsters of old films, is certainly my favorite, and their names just feel right. Combat itself is decent, too. At first it's just a few enemies, but very quickly in Arcade mode (a DLC with an extra character) you get absolutely swarmed. The story mode introduces enemies to you slowly, but you're constantly pushed to fight hard and smart to get the best rewards, with several elite enemies starting to crowd in with 6-8 minions being pretty common in solo play. I absolutely love a crowded screen, and when each enemy presents a unique threat, the combat math is fun. You start with basic dudes who collapse easy, but then green ones that take a few hits to stun start weaving in. Then you get the monster who launches bombs from a distance, and one that charges. Then, when you think you've got that handled, now the lizard monster spits water streams, the bomb guys shoot straight shots, the bull guys dive underground, and a buffing enemy comes into play. Chasing these dudes down and trying to group them around structures and stuff feels pretty good. Every character has different attacks aligned to the various attack chains, resulting in pretty wildly different playstyles. You'll pretty quickly learn optimal pathing for each situation, but basically, like Fight'n Rage, you do need to figure it out. Each player character starts with one rage attack unlocked, but over the campaign you get access to a couple more, the third by early Chapter 2, so plenty of time left with the base game. By using these you earn ultimate bar (called something else), which you use for, as you might guess, an ultimate-type move. These also help define what exactly the characters do. For example, the Ultraman ripoff is the quick guy, and he excels at movement, but has limited ranged options. His flying kick has good range but only hits one dude, while his Rage 1 attack inflicts a kind of "bomb" status at about a third of the screen, and his ultimate nukes a fairly small area in front of him. The giant crustacean, meanwhile, is kind of a weird stretchy tank; he's great at controlling groups, both sucking them in with the Heavy 1 Hold (hold Heavy) or wall bouncing them with the Heavy 2 Hold (Heavy, hold Heavy on hit), while also being able to summon a little crab minion for distraction. The Godzilla-like is your brute force monster, while the gun chick is all about ranged gimmicks, playing sorta similarly to the crab but having wildly different Rage stuff. The DLC character is a combiner type mech, and actually has three major styles depending on which Rage attack you recently did; 1 is the default sword, 2 is the axe, 3 is a hammer. Basically, lots of variety here, and the fact you can swap between characters between story mode missions is cool too. To add to the variety you earn abilities after missions. The base game gives you four abilities at the end of a level, with a power level based on how well you did. S+ earns you the 3 of the highest ranking stuff and one of the second highest, while S gives 2/2, A 1/3, and so on, weaker and weaker. Each of these abilities is restricted to one of three slots, and basically gives some kind of passive effect and sets your core stat boosts. The boosts are seemingly randomized, so you can have identical abilities and stat distribution but a +4% speed boost instead of +4% defense, etc. You can equip these to every character, no need to earn the same one multiple times, and that's cool, and you can also reroll the random elements while keeping the core ability. Each chapter you get access to higher ranked stuff. These can actually change up your playstyle quite a bit - perfect blocking (parrying) giving you two rage meters means you might be trying to block more, and spending more on rage attacks. If you gain ultimate bar by killing with a Hold 1, you may path into that more often, or equip it to someone who's got a really useful one for finishing, cuz remember, every character has different chains and not all attacks link intuitively into others. You gotta figure it out. Others do weirder stuff, like no longer letting you do rage attacks but focusing much more of raw damage and speed, and ability to earn ultimate bar without rage attacks. Suddenly you're playing a more basic beat-em up. It's weird. Sound quality overall is good. Weird warbles from the enemy monsters sounds correct. The voice acting is great, and sometimes the writing is a little funny, too. The story isn't amazing but then, if we're honest, giant monster movies are typically very contrived to start. It's presented straight, which is a pretty welcome departure from the super meta tongue-in-cheek everything else tries to be these days (Jitsu Squad as one such example within the genre), though you're not gonna get Hades level character development. Still, you get good reads on who these guys are, and that two of the team members are, in fact, very dangerous monsters held under tenuous control.  As far as critiques... it's a slower paced game, as mentioned already. If you don't like the kinda choppy "modern" style beat em ups, I'm not sure this one will change your mind unless you're a huuuge giant monster fan. It does some annoying things, like dramatic slowdown when displaying your rank after a section clear. The base game's story mode means going back to base between missions and doing some kind of unskippable dialogue option between characters, though this also serves as the hub where you spend in-game money to unlock new palettes for your characters, reroll your earned abilities, and equip what you want, and who you want, for the next mission. Not too many options besides controls and screen resolution, so feels like a console game that never got a proper PC option set. Music is pretty boring, typically just a buzzy drum and bass soundtrack that I'm sure is made to make you feel badass but it's very, very repetetive. Finally... I just don't think it's optimized well. The load screens are actually shockingly long for a game this simple. I'm running a Ryzen 9 7950X And Radeon RX6950 with 32GB DDR5-6000 from M.2NVMEs and we're talking like 10 seconds between transitions, which honestly feels like an eternity compared to pretty much everything else I've run on this. Doom Eternal loads in the same time at maxed out settings. There also may be some bugs. I noticed when I do the crab dude's ultimate, sometimes the game awards me with a rank even though enemies are still alive and need to be killed to progress. They just released a patch, so I'm not sure how long it'll be til the next one. Hopefully more playable characters make their way in.

_childDocuments_.review: A very mechanically solid and well executed beat em up. Played couch coop, campaign runtime about 8 hours with minimal revisiting of stages. Four playable characters with different playstyles, but even when you find the one you like the most you can still mix up your build/playstyle with the perks on the gear you'll accumulate, which is a very welcome touch. Mixing basic combos with resource spenders is immensely satisfying when it enables you to pull off a masterful juggle.  One of the bosses is pretty irritating to fight, and later stages can get pretty cluttered with actors but I enjoyed everything else.

_childDocuments_.review: [story]Titanic creatures known as Nephilim have invaded Earth, and the only hope of stopping them is (Defense Alliance Worldwide Network) aka DAWN. DAWN has its own monstrous combatants however, to defend Earth and defeat the enemy hordes! For 30 ish years earth's only defense against these Nephilim was a man named Eiji Murasame who could transform into a giant robot, much like Ultra Man, Aegis Prime. Now after all this time Earth has another combat ready robot suit and its pilot  Jameela . Lastly, science has advanced far enough that Earth now has 2 Nephilims on their side. Ganira, and Megadon.[Visuals]As previously stated, this game is heavily inspired by manga and graphic novels. This art style gives the game a nice, clear contrast with bright colors, deep shadows, and bold lines. The background buildings can look a bit muddy and under-textured, but honestly I think it works with the game’s visual style. Watching that intro video hits me hard with nostalgia. It reminds me of early 2000’s anime or the animated Teen Titans. I’m not exactly sure how else to describe it, but I like it.When you’re not controlling a humongous Kaiju destroying the city to save the world, the art style falls back to a more traditional manga/comic feel. Each scene is laid out as if it’s a comic book panel. Several other games have attempted this with varying levels of success, but I think 13AM Games nailed it on this one. [Audio]I don’t even know where to begin with the audio in this game. Let’s start with that soundtrack. =sample 10-15 seconds= It’s intense to say the least. At times I feel it gets lost in the battle noise as you claw and roar your way through the city fighting other Kaiju. At the points when it does come through, though, it fits perfectly with what’s happening on screen. The cinematic drama of this soundtrack really adds to the feel of this game, making you feel one with your character and the action around you.In addition to its soundtrack, this game is completely voice acted. While I think most of it is very well done I’ve encountered a few spots where it seems a bit lackluster, almost as if it was recorded in a restroom somewhere? =first Aegis example= I’m not saying it's awful by any means, there are just a couple odd spots that stuck out. Despite this, it's very apparent that 13AM Games cares deeply for this project and have done a phenomenal job.[Game-play]This is the real meat and potatoes of the game. Game-play in Dawn of the Monsters is solid. The attack controls feel like they have the right amount of weight to them. When initiating a light attack, it's fast and fluid. Opting for a heavy strike can do major damage, but it's slow and leaves  you open to enemy attacks. Even in these moments, though, I don’t feel the enemy Nephilim can just cheap-shot you repeatedly. And if you find yourself surrounded, you have tools at your disposal to clear the screen or make a path. It feels balanced, which is important when most of your game-play is based on attacking. The battles are challenging without feeling impossible, making for a fun experience.[Value]I’ve always been a fan of the beat ‘em up genre, playing games like Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Arcade Game, Guardian Heroes, River City Girls, etc. From what I’ve played thus far, Dawn of the Monsters is easily up there with my beat ‘em up favorites. At the game’s current price point of $29.99 you get over 35 missions with striking visuals, full voice acting, and an action-movie soundtrack. To me, it’s well worth it if you’re a fan of Kaiju and the beat ‘em genre![Final Thoughts]I think it's probably fairly obvious that I’m a fan of Dawn of the Monsters. While I haven’t beaten it (yet!) I am looking forward to completing the game and seeing how the story and game play evolve. I’ll admit I’ve gotten pretty sucked in by this game and hope to do a full review once I’ve finished the whole thing.

_childDocuments_.review: The cataclysmic battle between giant monsters has begun in this manga-inspired, side-scrolling, kaiju beat-'em-up! Titanic creatures known as Nephilim have invaded Earth, and the only hope of stopping them is DAWN (Defense Alliance Worldwide Network), which unleashes its own colossal combatants to defend against the enemy hordes! Take control of four hulking behemoths - Megadon, Aegis Prime, Tempest Galahad, and Ganira - each with distinct abilities and play styles, and smash your way through destructible real-world environments spanning more than 35 missions! Power up with DNA augments, crush foes with devastating Rage moves and brutal finishers, and team up with a friend for 2-player co-op action! You are the planet's last line of defense...but will that be enough for mankind to survive the Dawn of the Monsters!?

name: Dungeons 4
detailed_description: Digital Deluxe Edition About the Game Once upon a time in a realm far, far away, everything was lush and green. The unicorns mingled among the trees and the elves and humans lived peacefully in harmony with their surroundings. Yet somewhere at the edge of a clearing half-hidden among the trees, obscured by a rising veil of fog in the hazy half-darkness of a weather-beaten hut, a shape huddles over a large and ominously glowing crystal ball. A mumbling voice sings ancient formulae, urging the swirling glowing mists inside the crystal to part and give an insight into the future. “All is in flux, nothing seems certain. Come, oh vagaries of space and time, separate the veil and show us what is yet to come”, the voice grumbles with the hint of an eye faintly reflecting the glow in front of its hood. The shape’s audience, only barely visible in the dim light, leans in closer and listens intently. “Time ebbs and flows, forming pools and wrinkles… but when the mists part only vague images rise from beyond the veil. Shhhh—don’t come too close, you don’t want to disturb my delicate magical weavings do you?” The shape, still bent over the orb, mutters and shoos the other back a bit more into the shadows. “Ah, now it seems to be clearing a little. I can see… something… several somethings, hints of voices echoing in the haze. A baby, something happening on Hill Doom and the coming together of the Council of Snots – what could all this mean?” In a flash, the light reflected in the eye turns red and a distant evil laughter echoes through the woods. Stay tuned for the return of the Soothsaying Evil! The Absolute Evil and its trusted *cough* servant, the Dark Elf Thalya, return in Dungeons 4 after the events of its fabulous predecessor to bring about their triumph over the forces of good once more. Build a cozy and comfortable Dungeon to suit your creatures’ needs and rule over them, then send them out into the Overworld to kindly remind the good people living there that the Absolute Evil rules over their lands. Gather your Evilness in new and dynamic ways and unleash it upon the lush green forests and plains of the Overworld to turn them over to the dark side. But make sure that your Dungeon is well-secured by traps and defended by your creatures, for those pesky Overworlders won’t just twiddle their thumbs while you turn their land into the Absolute Evil’s most pleasurable holiday paradise . But what is that noise? “Gold, gold, gold and gems, gold and gems and gold!” The ancient song echoes throughout the underworld, accompanied by the clanging steel of hammers and axes. The Dwarves have arrived to claim their share of the abundant resources and together with the Elves and Humans of the Overworld, they send out their raiding parties to find the Dungeon’s heart. Dungeons 4 keeps the spirit of its predecessor, but everything is now bigger, better, and with even more dynamic Evilness™ . Everything is better with Dwarves™: The Dwarves have arrived to build their underground strongholds and the hardy little fellows (although they don’t like being called that) compete with the Ever-Expanding Evil for space and resources. It makes your Dungeon great again: Dungeons are up to four times larger than before and there are many more creatures who wait for the All-Commanding Evil’s orders to conquer the Overworld. Now the time has come for massive armies and truly sprawling dungeons! Ripe for the taking: The Overworld is bigger than ever before. Gain Evilness by beating Mini Bosses like the obsessively harmonious Unicorn and use it to transform the Overworld into stunning biomes of pure evil. New and shiny: An ability-based Perk system for Thalya, the Absolute Evil’s trusted *cough* and most loyal subordinate, grants her impressive new powers. The Absolute Evil can now enjoy taking over the world, governing the creatures and slapping subordinates even more with the customizable Evil Hand. Minions, everywhere: The Horde, the Undead and the Demons wait to do the Absolute Evil’s bidding, with more creatures than ever eagerly following the gesturing Evil’s orders, and Snots will play a much more prominent role this time. Many ways to tell the story: A long campaign, narrated by the beloved English Narrator from previous titles, as well as several skirmish maps all to challenge your rule as the Absolute Evil. Change the world: Spread your Evilness across the Overworld to bring lush and green environments over to the dark side, now shining even more vibrantly and beautifully evil as you spread your evilness across many new biomes. Work together, slay together: 2-player co-op multiplayer with both players managing one Dungeon together. All maps from the skirmish mode and the campaign are playable in co-op.

_childDocuments_.review: Realmforge studios have spent over a decade and 4 games painstakingly refining their approach to a modern Dungeon Keeper-inspired game, and this is without a doubt their best attempt yet. Looks great, runs smoothly, and has more depth and a larger scale than the previous games. I think it's gotten to a point where I can't imagine anything else that they can improve, apart from just adding more stuff. The game has a campaign of 20 missions, skirmish and co-op (with friends, no matchmaking). If you are a Dungeon Keeper fan, or a fan of RTS in general with an emphasis on base building, this is a must-buy. Hopefully they will release many more DLC campaigns, like they did with Dungeons 3.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons 4

_childDocuments_.review: Just got an updated eula notice (that I have to agree to) to continue playing. Says they collect and share personal information with third parties as per their privacy policy, but has no link to said policy. Contract is under the laws of Germany and they refuse any arbitration over disputes. Game supports multiple languages, but eula only comes in English and German. If you speak and read French, Spanish, or Italian...tough luck I guess. Hey Steam, I don't agree to having my personal information sold or given to third parties, can I get a refund?I know eulas like this are common, but their implementation is particularly odious. New eula showed up after installing and playing the game for several days. Being forced to agree after you have paid money just feels underhanded to me. Would really like to know how they collect that personal data and who exactly they are sharing it with.Game itself is pretty mediocre. Strategies are repetitive. Difficulty slider doesn't seem to have any real affect. Main campaign can be finished in a few days if you are a casual gamer, or a day if you are aggressive. Like other reviews have said, cost compared to length of play, would have been better to wait for a sale to feel like I got my monies worth.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed the last instalment then it's likely you'll find enough to enjoy in Dungeons 4. The formula is more or less the same, with a few UI changes that may or may not sit well with you.For anyone who hasn't played a Dungeons game before, there's still a lot here to enjoy. The game is a neat hybrid between Warcraft 3 and Dungeon Keeper. Despite the comparison, I wouldn't say the game manages to capture the depth of either of those titles, and most missions can be boiled down to maxing out the Undead unit tree and watching the chaos that unfolds afterwards. That's not to say that the gameplay is mindless; it's far from it. But if you're looking for complex strategy, then you won't find it here. At times, it feels more like a tower defence game than a traditional RTS. That isn't inherently a bad thing, but it's worth mentioning. Each game is split between two types of maps. An Overworld and the Dungeon layer. The former being played as an RTS, while the latter focuses on base building. The combination works without feeling completely disjointed, however, being only able to control creatures directly in the Overworld only can be jarring at times. It would have been nice if the developers focused on standardising the controls between the two.The graphics are nice, and clearly an upgrade from the last instalment, but the performance is okay at best. The game seems pretty taxing on the CPU, and busier maps can drop into the 30's depending on your setup/resolution used. I also suspect the game doesn't take advantage of shader caching, so expect a few stutters when loading assets/visual effects for the first time.The graphical settings are also lacking. Textures, Shadows, LOD etc are all missing from the in-game menu. Instead, you only have a few options to change post processing options so as AO and Bloom, which matter little in terms of scraping back performance. This isn't something that should be acceptable on a PC release, and I hope the devs can implement more options in a later patch.Arguably the most chalk and cheese talking point of the game is the writing and the humour. I have a guilty pleasure for goofy jokes, so I found myself smiling at a couple of the jokes. That being said, some of the lines are shamelessly eye-roll inducing, and are likely to be a complete turn off for a lot of players. The jokes are mostly self-aware, so I'd make the case that the writing isn't trying to be anything more than it already is.This seems to be a real deal-breaking sticking point for a lot of players, so I really recommend doing some research first before spending money. At the very least, the game is on Game Pass (as of writing), so you can at least try it out there first.I'd recommend watching a few videos online to figure out if the writing is for you. While the narrator can be dialled down in the settings, it's impossible to play the majority of the game without the best of the one-liners and dialogue being a part of it.If you're looking for a modern take on the Dungeon Keeper series, then this is it. If newer graphics aren't all that important to you, I'd recommend picking up Dungeons 3 instead. The gameplay is more or less the same, and you'll be able to pick it up for a lot cheaper, including all of the DLC's.If you've come from Dungeons 3 already, then I think you'll have a decent enough time in the follow-up. There aren't enough changes for me to recommend picking this up at full price, but there's enough content to play through, at least.That being said, if you're looking for a pure Dungeon Keeper experience without the hybrid RTS stuff, then I'd recommend checking out KeeperFX. It's an opensource fan remake of the OG game, and features a ton of bugfixes and QoL features, so it's worth looking into.If you're a score kind of person, then I'll include one below
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons 4

_childDocuments_.review: I played Dungeons 3 in Co-op and did the same for Dungeons 4. I usually take over the dungeon while my partner takes over the overworld. While in Dungeons 3 I found myself eventually running out of things to do, this game has scaled up so much. There is never a dull moment- the dungeons are bigger, there's more to do, you can build dungeons of a ridiculous size and scale and there are so many quality of life improvements especially if you get the good stuff from completing challenges. It feels both harder, more rewarding and more fun. There's so much more hidden in the walls of your dungeon and mining a glistening chunk of gold could ramp up the intensity quite quickly. And if you ever actually find a moment to breathe, you can become a little snot and view your dungeon from first person and do some mining yourself. We took on the last dungeon so hard and made it so ridiculous we were certain the game was going to crash it became so laggy, but it didn't. It was ridiculously fun and it's going to stay a fond memory. Slap the little snots. Stay for the funny humor and great game mechanics. Get revenge on heroes and live out your (very silly) evil life.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun if you enjoy the Dungeons series, but it's the same thing as 3. There is very little new content and does not feel worth the full price. The lack of new content can be addressed by selling DLC to players in the future, how convenient. I would suggest to wait and catch this on sale in the future if you enjoy the series, or just skip it all together.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the other ones, you'll probably like this. I only ever played solo and there have been no issues doing that in this one so far. New units, new traps, seems good so far.-edit-After playing many more hours, I can say that I really like the changes in Dungeons 4. People saying that this is just dungeons 3 clearly miss the point that it's the 4th entry in a beloved franchise. How much did they expect it to change? It's the same game with new stuff for each race and updated graphics. That's what I signed up for.I like:-New units per race-How much better undead feels, as a whole (I almost never went undead on hard in old games)-monsters don't need to work machines in the dungeon, snots do it-the new tech tree, makes it worth it to invest and focus on one race-skills on the hero help you focus on a build ahead of time-the emphasis on being active in the overworld to keep evilness flowing-moar traps-revive for orcs isn't locked behind undead tech, it's an orc tech now
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons 4

_childDocuments_.review: So dungeons 4 eh?Well my review of the game thus far is one of not recommending it.I should start by saying, I loved Dungeons 3. Played almost 300 hours worth. Bought and played through all the DLC, got all achievements.I really enjoyed the clunky beauty that was 3, was it perfect? no. But it was good.Dungeons 4 However, i cant say I am enjoying any where near as much as 3.The races feel unnecessarily cumbersome and the game runs terribly for seemingly no reason.The VA work just feels uninspired and Thayla feels more like an idiot then, the delightful delinquent I knew in 3. 3, I was playing to enjoy the game and the story.4, I am playing just to get through it. I even bought the DLC in the hopes that it would feel better. Unfortunately it doesn't and if anything the game lag got worse. I think the most annoying thing is the 3 slot for upgrades before a mission. Some of the skills are VASTLY stronger then others and the fact you have only 3 slots leaves little in the way of creating interesting combos. Half the abilities or skills I feel like should be in upgrade trees for the base dungeon or in unlocking high tier research in certain factions. Not trapped behind pre-mission buffs. IMO, i feel like they need to give you more slots or reevaluate what the pre-mission bonuses actually do. that or like i said before move some of them into layers or research.The amount of enemies seems ludicrous, especially the Dwarven strong holds in the DLC. My computer plays the game fine until one gets uncovered. Then it just CHUGS... but its like not even drawing on my PC, its almost like a visual memory leak or something. the FPS just plummets. While I do like somethings in 4, I don't really think the overall experience is worth it. Which pains me to say after falling in love with the series.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons 4

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of dungeon keeper 1 (yes i played the original^^) i was really surprised by checking out dungeons 4: this is actually pretty much fun! there's only one downside i wanna mention real quick: in comparison - dungeon keeper 1 was really bloody and brutal, which i loved. dungeons 4 is simply not like that, more comic-style based, nice battles with lots of creatures, good dark humour and lots of cool jokes IMHO. but for me, it really lacks a bit of brutality like blood flowing and some heads being cut off etc...but that's just my opinion, and under the line a really small complaint.and about the game itself? ... holy hell, it's so much fun! i absolutely love it! lots of spells, skills and research, creatures who can level up like a hero, and go even beyond maximum level by building certain structures - which takes a lot of time logically...and the 3 different research-trees offer a lot of variety from early- to late-game.some more skirmish-maps would be nice tho. ^^i totally recommend dungeons4 to anyone who liked the gamestyle of dungeon keeper 1, except when you wanna see blood & gore. XDgood job you developers! i really didn't think there would be an actual competition to dungeon keeper, but here it is... :)
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons 4

_childDocuments_.review: well hmmm. I don't really know what to say about this game. I liked dungeons 3 and i played the DLCs as well. I did not like the DLCs as much because instead of letting you build up your forces at your leisure many of the missions had "time limits" Why they would do that when the original game was a success is beyond me. But this is about dungeons 4Lets start with the good stuff. the new graphics look good and digging around in your dungeon and building it up is still just as fun as it was in 3. new creatures and abilities are cool. conquering the overworld is pretty similar to previous games.So on to the bad stuff. Something that drives me nuts about this game is trying to throw your creatures into a portal or get them to go back in the dungeon entrance. I've lost entire squads before because i got into a fight with high level mobs, created a portal and tried to instruct my creatures to go through only to have them stand on top of the portal and die. I've told my creatures to run back across the map into the dungeon as i try to defend against an enemy ambush with my dungeon stragglers, waiting for the calvary to arrive, only to finally notice that they are standing on the dungeon entrance and not entering. that is pure lazy programming. is there ever a time when someone would want to go near a portal or entrance without stepping in? why isn't the whole thing a hit box for enter and exit? this is infuriating!there are also overworld bosses you need to kill for evilness which are so broken and bugged i don't see how they ever QC'd this mess. almost every boss has a big running charge attack. if that charge attack takes them outside their arena they will  heal to full health, become invulnerable, and walk back to the center of the arena where you can do it all over again.Those are frustrations with what i would consider to be bugs. my next problem is a core game mechanic. the resource gathering is terrible. I have never been more frustrated with resources in a game. Virtually every upgrade in the game needs gold AND evilness. Evilness is not obtained as it was in dungeons 3. now you have to go into the overworld and slowly pick away at heroes and bases. killing boxes or barrels around their camps will yield a tiny amount of evilness. but when you need hundreds for each upgrade this is a terribly tedious process. special objectives like killing overworld bosses or intercepting caravans is the best source of evilness but even this will only gain you a couple upgrades when there are dozens and dozens of them that you NEED to get. and as mentioned before the overworld bosses are buggy as hell.In dungeons 3 i was able to kind of focus upgrades into certain areas and not focus on everything, in dungeons 4 many things are tied together. you need to get as many little snots as possible. but wait, now you need to upgrade them so they can dig through stone. and upgrade them even further so they can dig through greystone. if you don't upgrade them you won't be able to dig very far in your dungeon and gold will get locked behind terrain you can't dig in. so we need those upgrades, we need the dungeon upgrades for more imps. we need spells. so we need the demon tree so we can get a mana generator. in order to make a mana generator we need toolboxes, so we need the workshop. we need traps so we have to research those as well. and start building them which costs toolboxes and an insane amount of gold for no more damage than they do. then if we want our creatures to level up we need the higher level rooms, which involves higher level tree research. These are things we need which will cost thousands of evilness and you need them all at the same time. not to mention there are upgrades for ALL the rooms. more gold storage, more mana storage, more evilness storage, more toolbox storage, stronger dungeon heart. dozens and dozens more for the specialized rooms as well. It costs way too much to upgrade rooms, creatures, traps, spells, and then still deal with the mission at hand. ESPECIALLY when they put time limits on missions, which is the dumbest thing you could ever do with a game like dungeons.some of these missions are just plain not fun. I play something like this to have fun, and when i put an hour into a mission and find out that my decisions have lead to it being impossible to finish and that i will have to start over with a new strategy, well the game isn't fun anymore. I have had several rage quit moments in this game already, and part of me doesn't even want to go try it again because it is so frustrating. if i have to read a guide on how to do every mission in the game and follow a specific build (upgrade) order to get it done, well its not fun anymore. why put in so many upgrades if only a couple paths are viable. No... i guess i can't recommend dungeons 4. I want to like this game, but it really isn't all that fun. but if you want frustration, well its got that in spades.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons 4

_childDocuments_.review: I'm about 5 hours into the game and to be honest I feel dungeons 4 fall short of expectations, I dislike how evilness is obtained, I preferred the mechanic of dungeons 3, also the units don't work in any of the rooms anymore it's all done by snots, which has me questioning the need for some of the variety in the units, they are only used for combat now, which for me removes an element of the strategy that I used to quite like. Traps seems less effective than before, In particular my favour from Dungeons 3 the Ice Crusher has been removed. This game so far simply seems less about building and defending a dungeon then it does build up as big and army as possible and rush the enemy, you can train lot more creatures in this game. There are some good things, the voodoo potions was a good idea and the music is decent, but i dislike how the rooms all function with snots as oppose to units. If you like having a bigger army and not relying on dungeon building and defence so much, then this game may be for you, but if you prefer a more strategic dungeon building experience then I reckon you'd be better off starting a new save on Dungeons 3.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons 4

_childDocuments_.review: When I read Kalypso Media Group GmbH's End User License Agreement (EULA), I was very worried about its data privacy rules, especially in section 5. This part talks about how personal data is collected, stored, and sent to third parties, but it doesn't say who these third parties are or what their exact goals are for using the data. In a time when digital privacy is very important, this lack of clarity about how to handle user data is scary and feels like an invasion of privacy. This worry is made worse by the agreement's strict and broad limits on how their material can be used. For example, they don't allow changing, copying, or sharing software, which is normal in the business world but feels too controlling.In addition, the EULA allows changes to be made by one party only. This makes long-term agreement terms feel unpredictable and unstable. These things—the unclear handling of personal data, the strict usage limits, and the section that lets one person make changes—make it hard to trust and feel comfortable with the terms of service. Overall, Kalypso Media Group GmbH's method leaves a lot to be desired, especially when it comes to data privacy and giving users control over how they use their products. This makes me hesitant to fully connect with their goods and services.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons 4

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the Dungeons Series, you can go straight ahead and buy the game. It's great in Co-op and the humour is full with pop culture references, as usual. While the first missions feel like an overly long tutorial, starting with mission 12 the difficulty (on normal setting) ramped up quite steep and the game became challenging. You will find yourself trying to reach your mission goal while juggling with resources and decisions on what to unlock next in the research tree for the best outcome, while numerous threats lurking in the depths will make it hard for you to dig out a large dungeon early on. All that while glorious Heros and a new major antagonist try to conquer your dungeon from their outposts and fortresses on the overworld, which is also populated with mini-boss style good creatures. And because all of that is not enough, there also is the dwarf faction, who are now actively expanding in the underground to breach your Dungeon and go for your heart as well. It feels like it is very well balanced - always keeping you on your toes but, with the exception of a scripted event once or twice, never unfair. In the last missions, you will find yourself switching between Overworld and Dungeon several times a minute, casting spells, using potions, use other kinds of magic, manage combat and digging out more rooms while handling whatever you dug up, take care of your prisoners and use them for ... special purposes. It is then, that the game shows its full potential. Be aware that if you want a complex plot, great character development and well written surprises, you're not looking in the right place for that here. If you like a severly broken 4th wall, pop-culture references en masse and quite childish humour at times - especially when the great Narrator and Thalya are having an argument - you're spot on with Dungeons.It took me 42 hours to complete the campaign on normal difficulty, without unlocked all the perks that are available. I estimate another 20-40 hours if you plan on unlocking everything, which you probably need if you want to re-run the campaign on hard difficulty.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons 4

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr I'm having fun and that's what should matter. Some advice from my experience so far: don't spread your snots too thin or queue too many buildings as it can starve you of gold.Rambling:I tried the original Dungeons forever ago. It wasn't my vibe if I recall correctly.Then "War for the Overworld" by Subterranean Games scratched the itch for a bit but was too difficult for me. I bought DK1 and DK2 on GOG just for the memories.When I loaded up Dungeons 4 (having not played 2 or 3) I was surprised by how much humor there was compared to the serious tones of the DK series and WFTO. I didn't mind it as it got a few chuckles out of me so I kept playing the campaign.D4 felt slow at first, but then I realized that the missions were specializing in the different unit types and unfolding the complexity of the game one mission at a time. It gave me a chance to optimize my strategy for the limited tech tree I had on each mission. It allowed me to chase the achievements for each mission and unlock perks.I'm still not even close to finishing the Campaign but I'm having a lot of fun trying to 100% even though the Grogu mission seems impossible too reach 350 sacrifices in. The frustration just makes me want to try a different strategy that actually works.By the time the Campaign ends I should be a pro at managing a dungeon to level 10 of each tree, or at least I hope.Thanks for the fun, Realmforge.P.S. I blocked the Kalypso Launcher's domain  with my Pi-hole Ad Blocker and the game loads right up. ;)

_childDocuments_.review: From the trailer, I thought it would be a fun job to raise a baby while doing evil stuff but its just one-two missions with baby, the rest is just the new ability to nuke every good settlement.While I do like the previous titles a lot, this one feels more like a 20 map-pack. Not even a DLC since there are so few new assets or even probs compared to the previous title. Even the writing feels less. The references a just names from pop culture, the jokes are many but barely developed, there isn't even a new villian, and every map ends the same where the good you need to beat just escapes again and again and again.Overall, I wouldn't recommend it. _childDocuments_.review: So - whats new from the last game, gameplaywise? Essentially nothing, same troops, same buildings, same system, same format. Graphics must be better right? Not really. So, if theres no upgrade in quality, no addition of new minions, rooms, anything, then the campaign must be great right? No, again nothing new. In fact, we're repeating a lot of the previous game. We wiped out the entire landscape in the last game, and the Goddess in the DLC. Now given the entire premise of Dungeons is tongue in cheek humour it gets old, quickly. A new hero turns, up, raises the boss of the previous game from the dead, so you get to fight him all over again. Do you enjoy scripted defeats after a hard slog through a mission? We've got em! Do you enjoy the classic "I'll get you next time, but I'm running away now"? There's HEAPs of that. Again, I get that its trying to jam all the cliche tropes it can down your throat - there's even an infinity gauntlet with stones - it gets old, and boring very quickly. Only so many times you can hear "save the enemy, kill my troops, oops, the other way around" before it becomes cringe. At least its self aware enough to acknowledge its forcing material in for the sake of padding. Even the attempt at a lesson is the exact same as D3 - Good can go to far across the line in trying to fight evil. Just the same. And there are enough good survivors at the end to enable a sequel to bring back anyone who died anyway.Ultimately, not a terrible game, but not worth paying for if you have Dungeons 3 in your library.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Game has a few QOL gripes for me, nothing awful. All-in-all it stays true to the Dungeons franchise and if you enjoyed the previous ones you'll like this one. Probably not worth full price, wait for sale. Hopefully the Dev's plan to extend some features into the base game before they drop DLC's; doubtful though. I give it a soft-ish 7/10.I don't write many reviews, but I actually felt like this game needed one.I like the game and I would recommend it, but I don't think it's worth 49.99 in it's current state. Now I am a pessimist so I'm going to go all out on what I find to be wrong, but all in all for a Dungeons series game -- it's really not a game changer. The game is still enjoyable regardless of these thoughts.Here are my biggest issues:1. Traps are basically useless late game. Many of the elite units that enter your Dungeon take pretty much zero damage from traps after the game hits about the 30 - 40 min mark. This means that you have two options really. Either you build an insanely long series of trap based corridors or you divert your army from wherever it is which is usually in the over world trying to complete the mission and send it back into your dungeon to kill enemies. On some missions if doing specific challenges this can be... frustrating.2. The "Guard Room" is absolutely horribly designed. This in my opinion needs attention. I cannot fathom how the design of the "Guard Room" made it through Design and QA into production. I thought "Ok so if Traps suck maybe a Guard Room with some strong units stationed it it would be better." Nope, lets talk about why it sucks. When your units are in the Guard Room they still have needs. This means they will LITERALLY leave the room to going tend to those needs. This means 9/10 all of your units UNLESS you station so many it doesn't matter are not even in the Guard Room. If you wanted to fix this I think Guard Rooms should have build-able add-on's that can meet the needs of the units stationed there. Storage for food that Snorts can bring, beds, etc.3. The unit commanding options need a little work. In the over world it's not bad, it has some issues, but in your Dungeon you have 1 option... F2 to pick up ALL your units and dropping them close enough to enemies to kill them. A bonus problem is that it takes about 5 seconds for all your units to wake up from their dropped daze to attack the units and depending on how strong your army is... this can actually cost you a unit or even two.4. The first 15 - 20 minutes of every mission feels identical and it really sucks after you do it 10+ times. I'll also just say here that the game loop of finding the next gold vein can get old quick as well... but I don't really see how that could be improved.5. I've ran into a few glitches here and there. Nothing crazy, most of the time saving and reloading the save fixes it.6. This game would benefit from some QOL features for Snots. They could be present... but I don't know them. Primarily a priority system. Sometimes I want to queue up SEVERAL things for my Snots to do. Right now it appears they just do it in whatever order you assign it in, possibly some priority in a few things hard coded into them. But being able to set priorities on jobs would be HUGE.That's all I can think of right now.I plan to play the co-op with someone at some point.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very fun sequel to Dungeons 3! A lot of QOL improvements, like starting full of snots and getting to place tiles ahead of having the money for them. There's nothing more annoying than creating a large building plan of traps or tunnels and running out of money because every single snot abandoned their post.2) I can't for the life of my figure out why EVIL is the main resource now to revive demons. It's the least renewable of all the resources. It's the hardest to acquire, the least amount of any you'll have, and is needed for research! Really wish they'd change it back to arcana, because there's always tons of that to be unearthed AND a snot can generate it.

_childDocuments_.review: Things I love about Dungeons 4:-Amazing artwork, sound design, level design. The maps are absolutely gorgeous and take me into the fantasy world.-I love that you can plan out rooms even if you don't have the gold for it yet.-Thalya sitting on the throne. She just looks so badass!-In Dungeons 2, you were able to highlight areas of the dungeon in order to see where gold veins are before you have your snots start digging. I like that this feature is back in Dungeons 4, especially since the dungeons are so much larger.-The campaign is very well done. A lot more variability than previous entries. Scales from almost too easy, to very challenging (for this gamer at least). The achievements and new Thalya skills create really challenging levels when you're trying to do them all at once, which is great.-The thing that a lot of us missed the most from Dungeons 2 was the separation of the factions. Dungeons 4 strikes a great balance between 2 and 3. The factions are each very fleshed out, and it's definitely possibly to make an army solely from one faction, although you may want to dip into the powers/rooms of the others.-Optimized well, for my machine at least.-Hold right-click to attack move! (not sure if this was in previous entries??)Wishlist:-Something to show what buffs are on a creature-More skins for Thalya, for free, to give back to the community of fans-Ability to change Evil Hand skin in-game (rather than having to go back to the main menu) or at least some way to preview it when looking through the options-Ability to make Thalya sit on the throne after having removed herThank you to Realmforge for another excellent game that I'm sure will become one of my most-played. :)
