_childDocuments_.review: I have only played the first five missions of the campaign, as of writing this review, but I feel like I already got a good sense of this game’s core identity and can determine if I should recommend this to others.I recommend this to anyone that liked the previous two games, Dungeons 2 and three, and those who haven't tried the previous one, but think a more light-hearted dungeon management game with lots of fourth wall breaking and (bad) jokes could be fun.The game is very similar to the previous ones in its cartoony style and tone, so it obviously isn't for people, who wants a more serious and dark game. The reference-loving narrator returns from the previous title, along with the Dungeons 3s main character the Dark Elf Talia, who competes to see who can shatter the precious fourth wall the most.And yeah… for those who played Dungeons 3, this doesn’t feel like a new game. Sure, it has the campaign length, and variation, but its just not fresh enough in its style, story, or feel. For me though, it feels a bit off. Not sure why. On paper, it has all the same things as the previous ones, and I am certain if I play the campaign, it will have variety by introducing new mechanics in the different maps. Part of it, is having so many creatures from the start, rather than being slowly introduced to them over a campaign. It makes them all feel… sort of soulless. Like they don’t have an identity to them. And it often feels like you are just throwing groups of enemies at other groups of enemies, rather than every creature counts.But it also might be, that it doesn’t do enough to make itself its own thing. So, it feels like a movie sequel repeating what happened in the last one with diminishing returns.It isn’t that this game is bad, I just feel like I played it. And I’ve heard the jokes. (Of course, it didn’t help that over the first five maps, one of the jokes is literally that a character is repeating the same famous speech with a minor tweak. I don’t know if that is the game just really loving the joke or trying to be self-deprecating.) It is a solid game, certainly relaxing at the start and teaching everything before it ramps up the pace. And I can definitely see myself playing a few campaign missions every once in a while.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons 4 has traded the rpg aspects of the third game for more rts-like gameplay that asks the player to remain active and it's not the best. Passive evilness has been removed with the abscence of isles of good/evilness in trade for bursts of evilness with "bounties" such as good creatures and patrols on the overworld.To enable this bounty system all creature specific rooms have been reworked so the snots do everything in the dungeon. Problem with this is that there is no reason to have units of every faction to have a functioning dungeon, player preference aside. If I don't need horde for traps I will simply never use horde.The campaign feels passionless and repetetive, multiple times the subtitles don't match what the voice actor/actresses say. Repeating voice lines whenever you do things like destroying buildings, narrator KEEPS REMINDING YOU THAT THE SPEED STONE YOU CLICKED ON DOES IN FACT SPEED YOU UP, and then again when you click on another stone, looking at mission 19 and 20 here. You also pretty much unlock everything by mission 12~ so the latter half of the campaign is a massive slog to get through, and the constant commentary on how lame and stretched out everything is from the characters was tilting me towards the end. This is a meta game obviously but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if you ♥♥♥♥ talk your own product this much then I start to feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ moron for playing it.The story itself is literally "hey what if we bring back the main villain from d3 and have him be the main villain, again." When the opening missions conclude in all progress from the previous game being nulled then you know you're in for a lazy story.The new character Tristan was mundane and uninspired, simply a tool to bring back the funny racist paladin from the last game.Thalya felt stale in this game with the complete absence of "good Thalya" which in my opinion made the character fun and interesting in D3.The narrator was quite boring this time around, nothing more to add realy.My tinfoil theory is that the VA's saw how ♥♥♥♥ the writing was which lead to poor performance, I think the narrator did alright and Tristan's VA was the most impressive but all else just fell flat.One last tangent, there's a good creature that's a walking house and when he does a charge attack he moves out of his "home area" and becomes immune and heals to full, nice playtesting guys. Sloppiness like this and missmatched subtitles aswell as just wierd audio on some missons, mainly mission 1 with Thalya shows that this ♥♥♥♥ got rushed out.Some quick good points about the game are as follow.+Passive power unlocks from the campaign is fantastic and would be lovely to use in endless mode if I liked the game.+3D models are great and the 3d dungeon is really cool, running around as a snot is cool.+Undead minions are fun and I like the addition of blight as a resource.+Horde potions is a cool concept, but it mainly benefits horde heavy comps.If this is your first dungeons game then I think it's fine-ish as a game but it should be bought on sale, but if you're a previous fan you'll most likely be dissapointed.I am a big fan of Dungeons 3 and this sequel dissapointed me to no end.My feelings finishing d4 is that I did it out of courtesy for the product that is Dungeons 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Finished game. Review below still stands for the most part. The bug with the "dig" icon has not repeated. The main negatives in the game - evilness must be actively obtained and can take more focus and time to get enough for upgrades. Unfortunately, SO many of the missions have some type of "timer" or similar mechanic that you won't be able to get enough evilness. I absolutely hate "timer" based missions in any game so my bias is strong here.  Any lvl with a time I went full undead as it was the only manageable strategy.Massive positive; The missions are extremely varied and fun (besides the timer mechanic) and some are quite challenging. No more "build a big dungeon and steam roll this hero city" but actually unique missions with multiple, varied mechanics that require a level of multi tasking. The missions are really a big leap forward in the series and left me wanting to play more and replay some to get a better result. Achievement are doable but some are challenging.Zero regrets in buying and am looking forward to DLC's.-------------------------------------------------------------------12 hours in. Very few bugs. Had two noticeable bugs so far that were fixed by exiting and reloading and did not repeat. Sometimes the "dig" icon does not align with tiles but that has been rare. Does not require a reload to fix just move the cursor around.It's very similar to dungeons 3 so far. If you like that you will be happy with this game. Definitely foresee some DLC etc, as usual. If you like the devs, go ahead and get it now. If you want to save some money, wait for a some DLC to drop and a sale, then get your fix playing Dungeons 3 until then. _childDocuments_.review: Overall I say its fun, mostly an improvement over the previous game. However, there are some design choices that i find questionable:-Making evilness not just for research, but for demon resurrection and thalya's abilities, while at the same time making it a 'stockpile' resource (you store it in a room, thus limiting how much you can hold at a time), as well as there being minimal passive income-Making it difficult at times to set up defenses (traps). there is no way to deal with the underground lagoons and lava lakes except, well, suck it up and deal with it.-pathfinding AI can be... odd at times. also unit formations act weird, units on the back/side when hitting a turn wont hug the corner, but walk out into the intersection before turning. large formations get scattered as melee and ranged units separate, and dont automatically regroup on move all the time.-Hey in game help menu, whats the breakdown on unit abilities, scaling, role, needs, etc, like in the previous game? help menu: "Good question. idk"-separating jobs from creatures im kinda on the fence over. on the one hand, means i dont have to have diversify and can focus on one faction (given the tight evilness at times, mandatory). on the other, it eats up worker time, and sometimes doesnt get done in favor of other things, like...-Why is it when thalya dies, all the workers drop what theyre doing to revive her? In a run thats already going south, it can make it unsalvageable as any traps/doors that need rebuilding, resources collected, or machines operated dont get done, which can lead to creatures striking/not being revived/etc.I can probably think of some other issues/grumbles/etc, but these are the ones on my mind at the moment.devs, if you actually look through these...-Bridges, please. Even if its just a wooden bridge to cross water/stone for lava and cant be built on, having a way to bridge the gap would be such massive QoL...-more hotkeys. Ex, select only demons/horde/undead. great in coop, if you and your partner use one for defense and one for offence. Also an attack-move, so we can order a 'go here, kill everything along the way' would really help alleviate some of the unit control issues, like formations getting scattered all over because ranged units just stop once they start attacking and dont move up to attack nearby units, plus trying to go somewhere and fighting the small hero teams along the way-please improve the in game help. it explains barely even the minimum.-Hand of evil definitely needs some work. especially trying to pick up dead heroes for the crypt, it practically cant.-theres definitely some optimization to do, at higher unit counts (max creatures, plus a few freebies) the game starts to lag and get choppystill fun, still mostly the same formula, though at times feels more like a resource management game than a dungeon builder, trying to carefully balance your tight resources, especially evilness, until you hit a critical point and suddenly you snowball

_childDocuments_.review: Bottom in quotes for original thumbs down thoughts. After finishing the campaign and then taking my time to go through getting the achievements, I have to slightly lean toward recommending it. There's still loads of design decisions I don't agree with. I also really wish writers would stop thinking that pointing out the reason for a bad decision forgives it, which is a thing that's enjoyed a mainstream reawakening since Deadpool. Leave that to classic authors like Douglas Adams and Pratchett, who know how the technique works. The main reason for the change to to thumbs up is the art design and all the little details. I was grinding through some achievement and saw the little goblin wolf rider go back to his bed and hop off to take a nap, the wolf curling up in its bed next to him. I know a lot of these things are from the other Dungeons game, but I sort of relaxed and just had fun watching all the little animations and little touches that make the world pop. That, on top of the very few levels that are actually interestingly designed, and the fact I've played 60 more hours since the negative review, made me change my mind. Also, this latest update addressed a few big issues as well. The zoom thing wasn't game breaking, but it an excellent QoL thing. I kept trying to scroll out from time to time, feeling constrained on the map. So yeah, it seems to scratch that DK itch well enough for me, and I hate-played my way through the campaign. "If you like DK games, you will probably still enjoy this a bit. I was able to sneak some fun in on maybe 50% of the levels. There have been some really solid write ups on how this has been a downgrade to the franchise, comparing every little detail, but I won't get into that as they did it better than I would. Essentially, it feels like they're leaning too much into the RTS-Esports-micro-speed-run part of the game, over what makes the DK great. This was starting to become more apparent with each DLC from Dungeons 3, and this game just fully commits. It is tedious and frustrating and just not fun. I'm typically a slow player, and don't like to rush the overworld, so this is from that perspective. The volcano level was the point I decided I could not recommend this game anymore, unless you can get it for 50% off minimum. Full 20 squads of leveled and upgraded Undead immune to fire not being able to kill a single fire elemental started to make me think there might be a bug, but it doesn't seem so. The story is also the weakest so far. Thyala getting captured like that, and the over-reliance on spoof just got to be too much and added to the tedium. More Tanos...  Waiting on evil, with evil-generating tech being nearly worthless, and a tech tree that sucks the soul out of the game. Incredibly disappointed as someone who has played DK games since the first one came out. Guess it is back to War for the Overworld."

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons 4 feels like a raw improvement over the previous title, Dungeons 3. While this installment did indeed take a slight turn towards mobile graphics, do not let that fool you: Dungerons 4 sports a solid gameplay and can provide a challenging experience, especially in the second half of the campaign.While only a few new creatures and dungeons rooms have been introduced, what really stands out is that many of the pre-existing creatures and rooms have been improved. For example, undead in Dungeons 3 did not really justify their high research and production cost. In Dungeons 4, a full undead army is viable and strong due to minions, tanky frontline and combat healing. Faction levels (horde, demons, undead and dungeon) have been also re-addressed, with factions having now 10 levels and each level unlocking a new research tier. This makes leveling a faction more meaningful than what we had in Dungeons 3 (click button, get a little more damage and health). Titans are also gone, which is nice since they trivialized builiding a strong and functional army. In Dungeons 4 players also gain access to potions from the potions room - courtesy of War for the Overworld - which nicely complement spells. The UI for spellcasting was also improved.The writing of Dungeons 4 maintains the same style of Dungeons 3, with puns at every line of dialogue, consistent fourth wall breaks and a bit of self-deprecating humor from the developers. It's a very clear choice and it works. The story is, just like the previous title, a bit cliché and over the top but again, Dungeons 4 is not a game you play for the story, and it's not a game that tries to be what it's not.There are a few things of Dungeons 4 that I wish they were done differently. While the horde creatures can "evolve" with the champion research, this does not happen for the demon and undead creatures. I would love to see the champion succubus or the champion vampire. I was also sad to see the library room go. A few more traps would have been nice. Lastly, there are "good beings" in the game, but what about evil beings?In summary, Dungeons 4: very recommended if you like dungeon keeper games and are not put off by the cutesy style of graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons 3 is one of my favorite games, and I gladly purchased all the DLCs and enjoyed them. They were great.Dungeons 4 is a downgrade in nearly every way. Let's cover a few things that make the game obnoxious to play:1) Evilness, a resource needed to upgrade your dungeon and army, is a finite resource stingily doled out. No longer do you capture isles of evilness on the overworld to generate evilness, but rather you get evilness typically via a one-time payment when you destroy an army camp. That's fine, except there's a few problems with this. One, demons require evilness to resurrect. This means the 'horde meta' is alive and strong, which is a bitter disappointment. Second, Talia's spells require evilness, which is better-suited for research. Third, many missions become this weird chicken-and-egg problem. One example is a mission where you need to spend a boatload of evilness to allow your snots to mine through stone to reach objectives, except the overworld ALSO has mechanics keeping you underground because your army is shelled when on the overworld. I had to restart because I had spent evilness on army upgrades and couldn't reach objectives, and I couldn't resurrect my demonds because I also had no evilness. It's a poorly thought out resource, clunkily implemented. It's almost as if the Dungeons 3 team all left and they hired a new wave of amateurs for Dungeons 4 with little RTS experience. I believe some of this is somewhat mitigated later on with this weird unlock system they clumsily tried to add, but that's a whole other set of problems I won't go into.2) Combat is comparatively clunky. Units are floaty, unit movement is vague, assigning units to control groups doesn't seem to work right half the time, units don't always seem to attack-move correctly, sound effects are weak and nothing feels impactful, it just goes on and on. Select-all-units -> attack is alive and well, it's just easier to bulldoze all of your forces through areas and bring them home via demon portal. You still don't really need to build traps, though the process of doing so is easier since snots are now responsible for the entire process now.3) Art. Music-wise, they went for something new here, this grungy music with edgy guitar riffs. I for one think it's terrible, but that's entirely subjective. Unit art is also quite unattractive nearly across the board, or unchanged from 3. Art UX/UI is clunky. Unit names are tiny and blurry -- I think they're affected by AA graphics settings, which to me is pretty hilarious. It's like playing on a 480p monitor.4) Missions. I don't know how far along into the campaign I am -- probably not too far -- but the missions are either uninteresting or copy-pastes from D3.Overall I'm bitterly disappointed with not only this game, but the future of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: A Dungeon Delight: Dungeons 4 is a Triumph of Strategy and Humor!I recently had the pleasure of diving into the fantastical world of Dungeons 4, and what an absolute delight it turned out to be! As a longtime fan of strategy games, Dungeons 4 not only met but exceeded my expectations in terms of gameplay, humor, and overall enjoyment.First and foremost, the game's strategic depth is truly commendable. The combination of dungeon management and real-time strategy elements creates a unique and engaging experience. Managing my own dark and devious dungeon, complete with traps, minions, and resource management, was an absolute blast. The balance between building and expanding my underground lair and leading my army to conquer the surface world kept me on my toes throughout the entire game.The campaign itself is a rollercoaster of fun and challenges. The missions are well-designed, each introducing new elements and mechanics that keep the gameplay fresh and exciting. From defending my dungeon against invading heroes to launching epic overworld conquests, the variety in objectives ensures that boredom is never on the horizon.One standout feature of Dungeons 4 is the impeccable sense of humor woven into every aspect of the game. The witty and often tongue-in-cheek narration, along with the amusing banter between characters, adds a layer of charm that sets Dungeons 4 apart from other strategy games. I found myself chuckling at the clever dialogue and quirky interactions, creating a lighthearted atmosphere that perfectly complements the darker themes of the game.Visually, Dungeons 4 is a treat for the eyes. The art style is vibrant and detailed, capturing the essence of a dark fantasy world while maintaining a playful and cartoonish aesthetic. The animations are smooth, and the various creatures and heroes are creatively designed, adding to the overall immersive experience.The soundtrack deserves special mention, as it complements the game's atmosphere flawlessly. The epic tunes during intense battles and the subtle melodies during quieter moments enhance the overall gaming experience, making it a pleasure for both the ears and the soul.In conclusion, Dungeons 4 is a masterclass in strategy gaming with a generous sprinkling of humor. Whether you're a seasoned strategist or a newcomer to the genre, the game's accessible mechanics and engaging narrative make it a must-play. Kudos to the developers for crafting a game that not only challenges the mind but also tickles the funny bone. Dungeons 4 has earned its place as a standout title in the world of strategy gaming, and I eagerly await more adventures in the dark and delightful dungeons it has to offer!

_childDocuments_.review: Whenever I see the name Kalypso, I know I'm in for a boring, tedious, derivative experience. Dungeons 4 did not disappoint.This game simplifies the base building aspect, does away with a number of beloved features from the predecessor (for example, you can no longer corrupt heroes to your side and can only get lame ghosts now) and instead pushes a bootleg RTS experience on you. Most of the game is spent in the Overworld to the point you start to wonder why is there "Dungeons" in the title. And that is because every mission forces you to rush and your very progression is tied to attacking enemy bases. The story is constantly exploiting a few repetitive concepts, like your adversary escaping every single time. There is little variety between missions, and the content is unlocked at a very slow pace. The first three missions feel like an extended tutorial as you have to play Horde, Demons and Undead in order, with little meaningful difference between them.Allow me to give you an example of a typical Dungeons 4 mission. You have to break through a number of fortified enemy bases. In order to do that, you get a skill which summons an overpowered minion under your control for a brief period of time. And the skill has a cooldown of 5 minutes... And if that wasn't enough tedium, as soon as you're making progress, portals start spawning inside your dungeon, ignoring all the elaborate trap corridors you've set up and forcing you to abandon what you're doing and teleport back. And there's tons of padding like that. "Kill 250 heroes". "Make 250 barrels of beer". The overwhelming majority of the achievements boils down to "play the mission you already won a bit longer". It leads to the bs 2-hour long missions that overstay their welcome very quickly. I'll be honest with you, I only lasted for 11 missions out of 20 and I don't have it in me to continue.While Dungeons 3 was a parody of fantasy and popular culture, Dungeons 4 is a parody of Dungeons 3. Instead of an occassional witty reference you get those literal 2-hour long missions dedicated to unloading on you all the memes from a certain universe. Lord of the Rings mission, Game of Thrones mission, Warcraft mission... between that and the constant penetration of the 4th wall, Dungeons 4 tries so hard to be funny that it ends up exhausting you instead.If you insist on getting it regardless, I would advise to at least avoid the Deluxe edition. They chose an extremely weird distribution model for the artbook - in the game's "DLC" menu you get a download code that leads to a third-party site where you download the stuff. The code is one-time use only, and the link lasts for one hour. To make matters worse, in my case it led to downloading an archive that is corrupt and I can't unpack it. Sure, you also get a few Thalia skins, but her sex appeal is not enough to carry Dungeons 4 on its own.

_childDocuments_.review: i have mainly played the campaign and i think it fits quite well into the series, (whether one like thalia or not is up to each one but i like her) but, as much as the story fits, progression and balancing does not.balancing: in dungeons 3, the heroes had a clearly defined progression like; guard> stone guard> steel? guard> throne guardi think there were a few more steps but this made tracking enemy difficulty easy and helped with picking engagements. in D4 however, there are only two or three stages for heros; rgular and elites. in D3, elites would spawn fairly late on normal difficulty but in D4 they arrive way earlier and in force, overruning traps and desenses. it basically lacks a mid-game rank of heros that your minions kan kill to level up and pull even. as it stands, it is like a switch is flipped and your dungeon suddenly drowns in elites. the same goes for underground creatures like spiders and lava lumps. they too only arrive in two flavors, normal and elite. a few normal ones can be dealt with early on but each often comes with an elite that is a pain to kill early on. worse yet, the elites can pile up and you get the same problem as the heros. too many high level enemies but not enough minions in either quantity or strenght to keep them at bay.the other point is progression: it somewhat ties in with the balancing part. there are four research trees, one for each minion faction and one for the dungeon itself. this sounds nice on paper until one sees the costs. each tree has ten main levels which need to be completed to unlock the ability to research higher level rooms. this also appears to set the max level of minions of that faction. aka, if undead research is lvl 4, your undead can reach only lvl 4.combine that with the ♥♥♥ that minions have their own tiered research FOR EACH OF THE 12 MINIONS and it gets expensive fast. and expensive isnt something you can afford. regula gold veins give 4k gold each, a gold tile give 100gold and diamonds are infinite. again, nice on paper, not so mach in execution. some mid to late game research cost one or two K in gold and all undead minions need more than one K to be hired in the first place. (that is less than 4 undead for an entire gold vein btw) this is an issiue since we only get a handfull of gold veins out of the gat and digging up gold tiles runs the risk of unearthing nest; see balance ubove; making it rather risiky to expand early to mid game and at times even wors in late game when, again; see balance above; diamond veins are another issue, by the time one gets to them, the mission is almost over, making them less than useful. next up is evilness. in D3 detroying good locations gave islands of evil which passively generated the suff. that was perfectly alright in my book. the D4 version feels like a downgrade in comparison. destroying good locations/ creatures now gives a flat amount, a few hundred for locations, 1K+ for creatures. sure, locations can be rebuild now an creatures respawn but both always come back stronger, ironically, it doesent seem to scale as stupidly fast as hero attacks do but that isnt saying much. sure, ther is now a lot of other things that give small amounts of evilness too but that dosent tie you over if you run a lot of demons or work well because they need heros to work as fuel so to speak (prison, torture chamber see; balancing above) it often results in research stalemate where you have either a ton of gold or evilness but you cant research ways to expand to get gold or get better at collecting evilness, resulting in a stall that allows heros to scale right passed you; see balancing above. combine that with useful building being spread evenly between high level faction research and it is the perfect trainwreck. the best way to sum it up is that dungeons 4 has a decent early game, absolutly screwed up the mid game and the end game is only fun if you somehow get through the non existing mid game. i would recommend it for the story, in all fairness but otherwise, do not buy this game untill they gave it a ground up balance and progression overhaul.(ther first 8 ish missions are fine btw)

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first experience with this franchise, and I'm really torn about it. There are things I really like about this game, which is why I've spent so much time playing it. However, in the end, the negatives outweigh the positives for me and I can't recommend it. I've reached a point where easy mode is boring and the harder difficulties just feel too annoying and unfair if you want to experiment with more than one play style. This game is extremely slow paced while also being completely unforgiving.  Whether you're easily winning or completely losing, it's a grind. If you lose your army one time, you might well be on an unwinnable, tedious, and frustrating path to destruction and you just don't know it yet. Enemies grow more powerful and numerous over time, so once you start losing, it's hard to come back.Also, the game mechanics conflict with each other. The design clearly wants you to fight and the world map and also defend your dungeon at the same time. However, any resource you spend on one of these things takes way from the other and makes it more time consuming and difficult. It wants you to explore your dungeon in order to find gold, but if you explore too far, you'll uncover enemies and infinite enemy spawn points that make you regret exploring at all. It wants you to make traps, but then those enemies and infinite spawns you uncovered make those traps useless. (Traps aren't really effective in general unless you completely focus on them to the exclusion of all else). It wants you to take objectives on the overworld map, but if you do that, your army isn't available to help you in the dungeon. You can split your army up, but then they do neither job very well.No doubt some people will complain about "player skill," but the dirty secret of this game is that it encourages you to functionally cheat. There's a spell that allows you to teleport your army to and from the world map. This allows you to completely ignore traps and simply build the biggest most powerful army, which you can take to wherever they are needed in the moment. This works, but it's tedious to constantly teleport back and forth ever time an enemy appears in your base. It gets boring to always use the same play style. Also, it forces you to always tech up one of the factions instead of using the others. In short, it basically railroads you into always playing the game a certain way if you don't want to have to deal with all of the issues I mentioned above. To summarize, I can see why this franchise has been successful so far, but it has a lot of flaws that would have to be fixed before I would consider buying a Dungeons 5. Personally, I would recommend removing all of the discoverable enemies from the Dungeon and making sure that all enemies entering it come from the same entrances (no enemies teleporting to random locations, please). It's weird to have a tower defense game that is does everything it can to remove the impact of having static defenses.

_childDocuments_.review: Just a plain downgrade from 3. Visuals might maybe look slightly better, but it runs quite poorly. Everything is more annoying than 3. Resource gathering is a pain. Underground pods are a pain. Enemies scale way too fast compared to you. What was a funny, sometimes challenging game has become a grindey chore. I cannot understand the reasoning behind locking everything with evilness and then making it as annoying as possible to gather. Especially timing the resource. Thousands are needed all. the. time. And the game is here : "Nope! You'll have to wait for a random timer before you have a chance to get some. But be careful, the second you go out to get it, I'll throw everything at you." Which makes the game even less flexible, since you just have to commit to one race + dungeon. Don't even try to unlock 2 or 3 tech trees at once, you'll just end up with the lousiest army, unable to level past 2-3, unable to kill a single hero to get any precious evilness to bridge the gap. Which is just as well, why would anyone go for anything else than demons ? Orcs are plain bad and undead are so expensive, by the time you get the ball rolling, a demon army is level 23 and bulldozing the whole map.Also, no random maps. Granted, 3's random maps weren't that much random, but still. Here, there are none. Pretty short campaign, again with the fncking timed missions, and a whooping SEVEN maps. No titans either, those are gone, except the demon one as a summon spell with mana drain. And I really miss the randomness of the old sacrificial pit, the new one is just garbage disposal whenever I amass too many resources and it starts to mess up the Snots and storage. Not a fan at all of the revamp of skill books into potions, as it was much clearer with the books stored as treasure in vaults instead of potions with a glow that you have to pick up among the hundreds of useless pots laying on top (those go into garbage disposal pit too, just to empty the stocks). Haven't seen great effects like Horde Frenzy, Undead Poison or whatnot, dunno if removed or just unlucky.The one positive is the new goo ball trap, it is very funny to set those up in a way that sends heroes down three long corridors endlessly.Can't recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like while dungeons 3 was by no means perfect, that it came closer then this game does in terms of perfection. With D4 it feels closer to having to wait and / or grind evil now just to finish a mission. With the resource now much more limiting, it is a bother to branch out more then one path in terms of units in favor of instead maximizing one branch. Additionally the dungeon overall with the reduction of various traps, snots doing everything, and preference for one branch makes the whole dungeon aspect feel overall less ... interactive. I feel some changes they could make that might help would be:-Either revert evil back to islands aka passive gain, or add a 3rd resource for late game material that works as evilness does in D4 if the objective is to push players to be more offensive in the surface map. Being unable to advance the tech tree at all as it stands in D4 without evilness is painful. -Undead healer was much needed. Keep. -Bring back units that have functions in the dungeon. It gave reason to diversify rather then completely mono focus -Bring back old traps, and get rid of traps that consumes little snots I do hope they make a Dungeons 5. In short I feel like going back to the gameplay loop out of D3 and expanding upon that would do them more good then what is present in D4.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a downgrade in almost all aspects compared to its predecessor or maybe Kalyps just went and took the god awful aspects and made them worse / didn't improve them at all on purpose. It is nice to have Thalya back and seeing her story progress just for you to be introduced to new characters that should have been in the 3rd game but weren't even mentioned .Maybe after Kalypso has addressed some balancing issues and some of the bugs in the game it will be fun to play. As it is right now, I just can't recommend it.The good:+ Nice quality of life improvements+ some good room additions+ Nice UI overhaul. Took me some time to get used to, but now I can see the appeal+ All the good pop-culture stuff again. Nice.The bad:- The research tree(s). They are now 4 trees: Dungeon, Horde, Demon, Undead which need you to invest on two fronts. First you need to upgrade the main path to then upgrade the lower branches. Contrived and unnecessary. Expensive to research and just not fun because sometime really strong improvements are hidden behind a massive, MASSIVE paywall for no good reason other than "Hey look. We did a New. Its ♥♥♥♥, but we did it anyways". Should have stuck to the old system.- Keyboard commands not working like "Hold" or "Attack move" which makes at least one mission unnecessarily longer just because you can't attack the mission objective properly. You have to wait for enemy patrols to attack it. - Monsters are still as dumb as in D3. Dumber even at times (yes, that is possible). Be it pathing, attack priority in fights, etc. Just overall worse than in Dungeons 3. For example: Your melees start attacking back row enemies when you are still engaged with other melee units which then switch to YOUR back row instead of running after your melees. Same logic for AI and player controlled units. Fail.- Monster controls in general: Monsters rather attack ANYTHING that has a red health bar than follow a movement order, they stop for half a second if you rapidly give them movement orders (just like in C&C 1, all those DECADES ago), they keep being stuck behind crates, etc. - The encounters are just ... [insert any strong negative word you like]. In some missions you are starved for resources and barely 15 minutes in you are overrun by champion units that you can't hope to defend against without losing a good part of your army. And because you are resource starved, well good game. - Leveling up monsters is a pain in the ass and seems random. Some creatures level up naturally as they did in Dungeons 3, some don't seem to. Some seem to receive more Exp than others and you end up with a horde that has a mixture of Level 5 and Level 3 monsters just because.  - Traps are overall worse: Weaker, not all the good traps made it from D3 (mah HEATER T_T)- Spells are overall worse: Less damage, less shielding, mana cost too high, no charging up- Doors are worse: You now have to research different door levels to make them viable and even then they are not really good. Too little HP to be any obstacle at all even at highest research level.- Almost everything is done by Snots now which is OK once your dungeon is more or less finished. Not so good during the building and exploration phase and you are, lets say, trying to pool mana (yes, coming from Snots now) and the Snots are needed explore, farm gold, build rooms, pool mana, man traps (yes, that is a "feature" now) and you only have more Snots once you have higher Dungeon-Tree levels because you receive more of them per tree-level, which costs you more gold that can't be farmed because your Snots are otherwise busy and you still have to pay for your paydays which then again is just more garbage micromanagement, but you also have to level up your Snots to further explore the dungeon for more gold reserves because there are two new stone types which can only be dug out with higher level Snots (and yes. I wrote this as one big sentence, because this is how the ingame progression feels like).-  Evilness is no longer produced passively by Isles. You now have to go out of your way farming it or doing side missions and since some of the prices for later game research are incredibly high, that feels just bad. - The side missions: for extra evilness and some of them are just bs. Some have you spend hundreds of evilness on an objective to receive ... 50 evilness back. WTF?! Why would I go out of my way then to actually research something that is nice to have, but not necessarily needed, extremely expensive in the process, for 50 resources back? Even 500 would be a stretch. - Good creatures (the new Isles of evilness I suppose) are strange. Powerful early, reviving stronger, and just not fun. They feel more like necessities then extra encounters. They give you a bunch of evilness for too much time investment early and the amount received is barely enough to research more than 3 early game items and not nearly enough for later researches. Which then loops back to side missions which keep popping up to tell you to kill these things (and their re-incarnations) to then give you a greater amount of evilness. That is just Isles of evilness with extra steps. I'd rather have a passive income than to jump through so many hoops for sometimes quite underwhelming results.- The new progression system as a whole is one big mess. It is god awful and imo the biggest downgrade of all from the 3rd game. It rarely works in your favor, the upgrades are mostly not worth it, BUT mandatory to either enable more rooms, better abilities for your units, etc. and, of course, keep getting more and more expensive. The neutral:-/+ There are new passives from which you can pick 3 at the beginning of a mission and which vastly differ in usefulness. You can give Thalya 100% more experience (which is extremely powerful later in the game) or lower the cost of specific research paths (Horde, Undead, Demon, etc.) by 15%. Some should have been passives in the skill tree though imo. Make you choose between 3 (well actually two since Thalya's is mandatory after ) feels unnecessarily like "Here. Have a choice that isn't really one, because we couldn't case less about balancing.".

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has never played a Dungeons game, I would call this game a multitasking simulator.It combines elements of RTS games into a dungeon builder game. But there are multiple things to track all at the same time:1. Dungeon management: give orders to workers to clear areas of the dungeon, build structures to train units (units aren't trained, they are purchased with gold, but they need space to "live" in the dungeon). This can get really annoying because your worker units can't be assigned to a specific structure, they seem to go about it with some sort of predetermined priority list. There have been many times I've ran out of gold because workers weren't mining, yet they overproduced some other resource that I don't need. There seems to be some function of the code that makes the workers prioritize whatever you are looking at at the moment. But this is not reliable because 90% of the time you are busy with something else.2. Dungeon defense: your base gets constantly raided by incoming enemies ("Heroes") that you must prepare for by building traps. There is some variety to the types of traps you can build, but sometimes the maps start getting a bit cramped, and there's not a lot of space to get creative, particularly towards the later levels.3. The Overworld: in addition to your subterranean underground map, there is a simultaneously existing Overworld map, full of "Good" enemy units that you can kill for the hardest to obtain resource in the game, "Evilness." This resource is very hard to accumulate because you can only reliably do so in the Overworld, yet it's hard to focus on moving about your units there while trying to do everything else in the game. It's hard because your units do not have good AI, and it's not possible to micro them like in a traditional RTS game, so you kind of have to babysit them everywhere they go, or else they might get ambushed by passing by enemy units.4. Level objectives: in addition to everything above, there are objectives to completing each level of the campaign line, which are varied and interesting. But sometimes you wish you could just pause the game to focus on building your base, instead of running back and forth between four or five different things at once.As far as a story goes, there is none. I was introduced to all the characters having not played the previous game, but apparently they are all from Dungeons 3, and many of them have been miraculously revived to rehash their appearance in this game. The main storyline also revolves around obtaining pieces of an item what featured prominently in a popular Hollywood movie, but has since become quite old and overused.Despite all this, the game has a great sense of humor. I was laughing a lot. But you can't take the story seriously. And the gameplay is addictive enough to keep playing.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a fan of the franchise - I own every single title, DLC, etc. of every single title in the Dungeons franchise.  After having said that - and adding that I'm also very much enjoying Dungeons 4, more-or-less, I don't think I could or would recommend Dungeons 4 to anyone who has never played Dungeons before.  There are just too many little issues that I believe add-up to an mediocre to bad gaming experience (especially for first-time players.)  Let's pick on some of the hot-topic problems right-away: graphics, lag, & game performance.  When Dungeons 4 pretty much looks and plays like it's on the exact same engine as Dungeons 3, you would expect that Dungeons 4 would, more-or-less, run on the same (or similar) specs as Dungeons 3.  Dungeons 4, arguably, needs a computer with twice the performance and capability of Dungeons 3.  Honestly, the minimum system requirements really are the minimum - if you want to enjoy Dungeons 4 your system really should be closer to the recommended specs; the more RAM you have the better.  (Dungeons titles are always RAM eaters, and 16 IS the minimum for Dungeons 4, in my opinion.)  These are problems that Dungeons 3 suffered from too, but it seems amplified in Dungeons 4 (maybe because they are using the same engine.)  The UI, interface, and how you interact with the game is clunky and not intuitive (it's even worse if you're very used to previous Dungeons titles and have muscle memory.)  It feels like buttons and interface elements aren't where we've spent the last 3 titles learning; things are definitely moved around a bit.  Research is like they're trying to reinvent the wheel - there's no "tree", counter-intuitive to what everyone is expecting.  You have 4 main categories that have to be leveled-up in-order to upgrade the sub-items (and these items are further gated/blocked by needing a requisite level for the main item for each upgrade); would be more intuitive if the UI had a redesign if they're going to keep it the way it is.  As-is, you basically have 4 research items that HAVE to be independently upgraded before you can basically upgrade anything else.  Gold mining/income is way too slow and is a huge speed bump to most aspects of gameplay; could benefit from increased rates, otherwise it's a horrible time-gating mechanic to rely on to slow down people rushing through the campaign.  Traps cost way too much gold (especially when there's now more emphasis on traps); again gold being the horrible gating mechanic - compared to how easy it is to mass produce the trap-specific currency of toolboxes.  Trap diversity is worse (and not nearly as nice) as previous titles.  Traps & dungeons still suffer from the same cheese mechanic problem of previous titles - just make a nice, long winding 1 tile wide hallway around the map.  Snot AI is horrible compared to previous Dungeons titles - (before you attain the ability for snots to teleport) snots will often get themselves between a hero and an objective and just run back-and-forth doing nothing.  It's like the AI is running into an infinite loop and can't decide to just stop (previous titles snots would just stand if unable to reach or do a task.)  The snot AI problems probably contribute a bit to Dungeons 4's performance woes.  The new snot priority system is counter-intuitive - when you select a priority all the icons and symbols display indicating almost the exact opposite of the priority you've set.  It's like they originally meant for it to be an opt-out system but then changed it to an opt-in system but didn't update art assets to reflect the mechanic.  The UI has horrible lag issues - buttons needing to be clicked more than once to be responsive; buttons not quite working as expected; the hand of evil picking up the unexpected resource; the hand of evil not dropping or picking up things as quickly; F2 still has the Dungeons 3 lag spike; build/fill tile and demolish don't always respond the first click; etc.  There's a long list of the little things I could honestly write a lot about; and they all add up.  Honestly, in the current state - Dungeons 4 feels rushed and in Early Access.  It is not the title I would recommend to people new to the franchise - Dungeons 3 was marginally better.  There's been no graphical improvements; the story is basically a sequel; mechanic and gamplay "improvements" are clunky, counter-intuitive, buggy, laggy, and honestly not polished.  It just feels like Dungeons 4 really was shipped with a lot of (necessary) work canceled to meet a release deadline.  This game should have been held back for another 6 months.  We're the 4th title into the Franchise - Dungeons should be getting better, more polished, and improved - not taking steps backwards.  In the current state, Dungeons 4 feels like a 2000s remastered game.

_childDocuments_.review: Short Review: You like Dungeons 3? You want more Dungeons 3? Yeah get this game!!!Long Review: Dungeons 4 is a somewhat direct sequel to Dungeons 3 (previous 2 are almost standalone games albeit with a VERY loosely tied lore) which takes the foundations of Dungeons 3 and streamlines it for this game. Game plays somewhat like a dungeon keeper game but you get to choose your army lineup and tech progression. Unlike Dungeons 3, game allows for way more flexibility as resource producing rooms are no longer tied to any faction (Horde/Demons/Undead) units are are fully operated by snots (imps in DK) now. This means you are free to splash any combination of any faction units or focus independently on one as your unit's max level is tied to their faction research now. The addition of units with specific debuffs that buffs the damage of same faction units also means focusing on 1 faction set of units (like picking a faction in Dungeons 2) is also a lot more viable and potentially overall desirable.Also to break the whole turtle meta aka tower defence meta of the previous games, evilness (research resource) are now gained mostly by killing overworld units and resolving overworld events (killing certain escorts/boss units) making the game alot more active than passive now which is a huge plus imo. All in all, if you have the dungeon keeper itch, this game might be in your ballpark. If you played Dungeons 3 and enjoyed it, highly recommend you get it also since its more of the same.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons 4 developed by Realmforge Studios and published by Kalypso Media is a dungeon building RTS and the direct sequel to Dungeons 3. In this game we join Thalya and the Absolute Evil enjoying their success only for things to go wrong, at which point we will fight for evil an attempt to thwart the forces of good once again.     As always the first thing we ask is if this game is worth the 50$ price tag. The answer to that is yes. Whether you are a retuning a fan or a brand new player interested in this type of dungeon building RTS hybrid Dungeons 4 is a solid and enjoyable entry into the franchise.     The graphics are well done and expressive, with a simple glance it is very easy to distinguish units and rooms from each other. There are a plethora of tabs to give you information you need at any given time. The music is enjoyable and well done. The writing makes sense with in the universe and pushes the story forward at a reasonable pace. The tech tree is deep enough to provide options on play style while allowing experimentation. Finally there were no major game breaking bugs or glitches I experienced in my play through making it one of the most stable games I have played in recent memory.    However there are some issues with the game. It can be difficult to micro managing your units in an effective manor. While the tech tree is large, very often you will only ever get to use a fraction of it to complete a level in story mode. The biggest issue for me was the difficulty balance in the back half of the game. While the levels 1-11 felt reasonably balanced, levels 12-17 felt like the balance was a roll of the dice. On easy some of the levels felt closer to normal difficulty while others felt like they were on hard. Then when levels 18-20 rolled around they felt like they were back to being balanced accordingly. Finally the humor in the game is very 4th wall breaking and self referential. I can see this sense of humor getting annoying for some people, however as a long time player of the series and more importantly expecting this style of humor and writing. I felt they continued the humor of the series in an enjoyable way.     All in all for 50$ Dungeons 4 is a reasonable asking price if you’re a fan of the series. If you are not a fan of the series and are just curious give them some time to push out patches focused on fixing bugs and adjusting balance. Even then admittedly this a niche that it might be worth it to wait for a sale, unless you’re a die hard fan than it fully worth the 50$ asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: As a devoted fan of the Dungeons series, the fourth instalment has left me both exhilarated and deeply satisfied. With each iteration, the game has consistently raised the bar, and Dungeons 4 unquestionably lives up to its legacy, bringing forth remarkable improvements that significantly enhance the overall gaming experience.One of the most noteworthy enhancements in Dungeons 4 is the refined mechanics that drastically reduce the need for excessive micromanagement. The game introduces streamlined spells and traps construction, alleviating the burden of intricate management without compromising on strategic depth. This evolution allows players to focus more on the game's essence, fostering a more engaging and immersive gameplay experience.Moreover, the revamped mechanics have achieved a seamless balance, ensuring that the gameplay is intuitive and accessible without sacrificing its core complexities. The simplified spell and trap usage adds a layer of convenience that doesn't dilute the strategic depth, a feat that enhances the overall appeal for both veterans and newcomers to the series.Visually, Dungeons 4 is a treat for the eyes. The graphics are commendable, showcasing detailed environments and captivating visuals that effortlessly immerse players in the game's world. The attention to detail in character designs, landscapes, and spell effects contributes significantly to the overall aesthetic charm of the game.The storyline of Diungeos 4 is another highlight. As someone who cherishes the narrative depth of the series, I found myself captivated by the compelling storyline that seamlessly ties in with the game's mechanics. It beautifully continues the legacy set by its predecessors, offering a fulfilling and engaging narrative arc.For long-time enthusiasts of the Dungeons universe, investing in Dungeons 4 is a no-brainer. It successfully builds upon the series' foundation while introducing refreshing improvements. However, for those new to the series, I would recommend waiting for a sale unless enticed by the genre or intrigued by the positive feedback from established fans.In summary, Dungeons 4 is a testament to the evolution of the series, offering a fantastic blend of refined mechanics, captivating visuals, and an engrossing story-line. _childDocuments_.review: As others have said - if you liked the other instalments of the Dungeons series, Dungeon Keeper, War for the Overworld etc, you will like this game. I personally did not find it all that difficult, and I am by no means a skilled strategy gamer. Once you figure out a few basic tactics, they can be applied to most missions with likely-success. I stomped the last mission, and would have liked a bit more challenge there. The creatures you can bring into your dungeon are split into 3 factions, and I did like that you can use pretty much whichever you prefer for each mission. That said, some missions start you out with a great deal of research already unlocked in one faction, so it does steer you a little heavily in one direction. The later levels though are very open. I was perhaps a little disappointed that there is rarely any point investing in all 3 factions - by the time you advance enough in all 3 you will have either secured or let slip your chance at completing the mission.The price I would say is a little on the steep side. I would have liked a great deal more challenges and skirmishes, or for it to be about 30% cheaper. I would recommend others wait for a sale, unless in dire need of a Dungeon Keeper-esque fix. Overall - Kudos to the Devs. Dungeons 4 was a fun game, well planned and executed. A few tweaks to the difficulty and missions wouldn't have gone a miss, and more content is always appreciated, but a solid game none the less.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the game in Co-op recently so I wanted to give my full opinion.A lot of people say this is nearly the same gameplay as Dungeons 3, but I partially disagree. There are quite a few spins on the gameplay. Saying that this is "the same game" is on par with saying every Mario game is the same when each has different spins on things. Just like those games this this has differences too but similar overall concept. So in this series y, Dungeons, you build a dungeon, send your creatures to the overworld, etc. Read on for more.The main difference in this game is the research, and you can earn selectable 3 passives you can obtain through challenges..Gone is the tech tree, and now instead you have 4 categories: Dungeon, Horde, Demon, Undead. That you level up and then buy and level up the characters/rooms under. It's not a true tech tree because in 3, for example, you had to buy guard room before traps. In this one you just put enough levels into the category, and then you can level up the ability of your choice. The library is gone also, you level up the skill with the creature to get the upgrades now instead.This difference is huge because you will almost never in a regular campaign game unlock everything unless you avoid completing the level to farm gold and evilness. And the three passives you equip at the start of the game, you can specialize in something or go across the board and pick your favorites. Personally I think the snot/worker upgrade is overpowered regardless of the build I have.Also I feel that 4 has a more interesting system of getting evilness. Back in 3 you had to start with a small amount and you have to capture/hold points on the overworld to get more with a couple other things that could squeeze some extra points.In this one you get sidequests that come up during the campaign very often and a few repeating things like overworld minibosses that respawn and provide a good amount. Also you can slap gobblers/ (the turkeys) for 1 point of evilness each :D which is funny.Speaking of slapping you click and hold you can multislap workers in a group! And grabbing items is easier cause you can click and hold to vacuum up tons of gold or boxes.Gold and evilness are also both important.  In 3 I almost always had a gold surplus. This one feels a bit more balanced. Although be warned: creature costs are a bit higher.Also you have a lot more utility with this game. Spells are back, but now you have voodoo potions that do a bit more utility, like creating gold veins or destroying tiles.The room changes I REALLY like. Workers/snots do most of the things now. You no longer need horde to produce traps or demons to get mana. Doors can be built near immediately now, snots/workers do all the stuff while your creatures can guard things. The only thing is demons still need to use the torture chamber, but it's ANY demon now, not just the succubus. And I admit I still chuckle at the undead having the dance floor.The big unit for each race is gone Ogre/Grave Golem,etc. , but you now can use a ton of mana to summon a big demon for a bit or you can summon the dungeon lord (story based) using TaliaUndead have a currency for summoning their allies (zombies and skeleton archers are gone though) Horde can have champions when you max level their skill. Dwarves have underground bases... the list goes on.Seriously there's so much that I can name different that I can't say "this is the same game".Now I will say the downsides; there are way less skirmish maps. There are 4 and a sandbox mode. This they probably will be adding more over time. Dungeons 3 was the same way so hopefully it works out.There are less boss fights. This one is more or less a eh just how the campaign went.I'm also not keen on part of the story where it's a bit confusing if you are the absolute evil or if you were the dungeonmaster and uh... well it is PROBABLY a story thing but this game is supposed to be goofy as hell so it gets a pass.Either way I still recommend this game. At the very least, ignore the people who say this is basically dungeons 3 again.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Dungeons 2 & 3, you'll feel right at home. If you disliked them, I don't think there is a reason to check this on out either.The game feels very much like a re-mix of D3, a few mechanics got changed but nothing really "new" was added that would have had any significant impact on how you play the game. Sadly some things got "streamlined" that I actually liked in the last game, like how combat-units had "jobs" in the dungeon. Horde-Units had to build traps, Demons had to generate Mana, .... this was another tactical layer that gave a bit more personality. Or how some traps and spells got removed, which kind of sucks.The Research-tree is also still an annoyance. Not as bad as in the previous game (It's way more free-form), but having to re-unlock a nearl 90% of it every mission is exhausing. I really shouldn't need to unlock basic stuff and units every mission. Really feels like the devs need to check out Starcraft 2 again, a game that did the "Meta-Progression" between missions perfectly. There is some minor stuff like that, where you can unlock some bonus through optional challenges, but it's just not the same.The campaign is pretty fun (and probably the main reason one would buy it). The narrative isn't anyting impressive, mostly just pop-culture refferences that get you from one mission to the next. Can be a bit exhausting and I would probably like "more" then that, but it's fine. (Just please: No more Marvel Refferences. They were already dated 2 years ago)The missoins themselves are good, always different objectives and mechanics to handle. No complaints here.The campaing will likely take one between 20 - 30 hours, depeniding if there are any missions that one has to re-start, but this is a good length for a game like this.In a way, the game profits from RTS-games (in particular those with lengthy single-player campaigns) just aren't being made that often, it makes it much easier to handwave the grievances I have with it. It still fulfills that RTS-fix that I'm craving every now and then.For Dungeons 5 (or whatever else they are doing with the Dungeons-Brand) I'd still like a bit more inovation, it is a bit stale, Like new units/sub-factions (Lovecraft-Faction?), some more stuff to shake up gameplay ... or maybe go into a completly different direction, make a spin-off that is more about "managing" a dungeon and less about those ever re-starting RTS scenarios and more about building a single, well-working Dungeon. Think multiple layers, builidng up on the surface, managing units Rimworld-style and building an economiy like in an Anno game.

_childDocuments_.review: I had to do a double take when I realized that this series was running for over a decade at this point, the original dungeons having released back in 2011. If that just made you feel old, welcome to the club.Realmforge has spent basically the entire time putting the formula through the wringer repeatedtly. Starting from Dungeons 2, each game has been working off the same basic schematic, with only very slight changes, instead trying to refine the experience. This is very much a "Don't fix what ain't broke" kind of release, and if you liked Dungeons 2 or 3, you'll like 4 by extension, unless of course you already had your fill back in 3.If you're new, the game is 50/50 mix of Dungeon management ala Dungeon Keeper / War for the Overworld and a very simple RTS game. You build rooms and traps underground, recruiting an army that will want certain needs to be fulfilled with even more rooms, and then you send those armies above ground to break stuff and earn the research currency. All the while protecting your HQ in the basement. The primary gameplay loop is simple, and the difficulty mainly changes the amount of time spent on a map, rather than your actual chances of success. (At least, so far. I've played 11/20 missions).So what are the negatives? The game is overall incredibly simple, and lacks most forms of strategic depth. The RTS part is basically attack moving across the map and occasionally flinging a spell or a potion into the fray, which is fun, but not particularly engaging or challenging. Dungeon "design" is similarly basic. With the exception of the very basics (Keep rooms that fulfill needs central to cut down on travel time), the dungeons entire gameplay basically consists off waiting for gold to come in so you can place more stuff. The traps are equally simple to place and require little to no thought to be efficient.As a result of this, unless later campaign levels throw me for a particularly strong loop, the game is very much a McDonalds Meal of a game. Filling and tasty, but forgotten immediately after. There is little staying power, and I strongly believe Realmforge will have to start innovating if they plan to do Dungeons 5. The formula is getting tired and needs some new stuff to keep it fresh, or needs to deepen the mechanics to be more engaging in the mid to longterm.

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome back, naive gamer. You have just purchased a torture chamber for fifty gold.Enemies have entered the dungeon—from six different directions… all at once.Your snots have discovered a spider nest—six of them… all at once.You have unearthed some lava lumps—and the six million hit point nest is in the middle of an ass-frying lava lake.Your creatures are on strike—because you haven’t built them a six ton, gold-plated toilet to dump their gold-plated feces into.You have been surrounded by six elite healers who are circle-jerk healing themselves in a killing frenzy of invincibility.You can’t group and select your monsters properly.One of your creatures has died.One of your creatures has died.One of your creatures has died.One of your creatures has d…All of your creatures have died.You are no longer having fun!Your dungeon hole is being attacked! (you read that right)You have become livid with rage!You have just smashed your mouse into your keyboard!You have just smashed your keyboard into your computer case!You have just let out a howling screech Dungeons 3 players can hear on the opposite side of the Earth!Your neighbors have called the police!You are being arrested for setting fire to your neighbor’s car!  Ironically, I quit this game in the scenario where you could first purchase… you guessed it… a torture chamber. I was holding my own for almost forty hours up to this point, and thought I was on my way to certain, joyous victory on the medium difficulty level. But, by scenario eleven, I found myself drowning in attack waves I couldn’t manage, no matter how many times I changed my strategy and restarted the scenario. Switching to the easiest level did not help. I am now convinced—beyond doubt—Tanos the Insane took over as lead designer.  Play it if you must (like me, the third one prompted you to give it a go) but—be warned—if you manage to slog your way to the end of this unbalanced game (and grats if you did?), you’ll be blessed with the experience of stinging whiplash scars and red, swollen handcuff rings around your wrists. _childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game. Everything is present that would make me like it. The dungeon building is, in principle, fun. The faction options and build variety that can come from that are cool, as is the general humor and narrative in the story. I had good fun for the first 4 hours as I went through the first parts of the campaign. But then I tried the skirmish mode, which I believe to be instrumental in the game having any sort of longevity. The skirmishing also seemed cool, in principle, with a few unique scenarios to play with some slightly different parameters and objectives. However, economic balancing, and the unusual lack of micro-control over your troops in the dungeon (which you CAN individually control in the overworld for some reason), really make the gameplay frustrating. In addition, the economy seems largely fine since the enemies (at least in the earlier missions) appear relatively static. Later in games, having to pay your minions eventually becomes so expensive that you're often stuck at 0 gold until you happen to get lucky... which isn't particularly fun.  And then there's the enemy RNG... I can't tell you how many times I've had to restart a battle simply because enemy RNG decided to portal in troops into my base before I could even build any troops. Also not fun. So not fun that the last time this happened I just decided to put the game down and wait a few months (since I am well past the ability to refund it)And there's a few other things that I think should be included at this game's price point of 50 euros. I think it needs some more heroes, a few more troop types, and some more unique underground biomes to explore. As it stands, were the economy and micro control problems addressed, I'd pay 30 euros for this. There simply isn't quite enough variety, and certainly not enough polish for it to warrant the current price point.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game. Most of the 20 main campaign maps introduce a different mechanic to add variety and balance the difficulty. About 1/3 are win/loss mechanics that encourage you to finish the map asap, which can be disappointing. Some of them you can avoid triggering if you want to take your time, but some you can't, which forces you to rush the map and play it like a RTS. Skirmish mode has 5 more maps that don't have time limits. It also comes with a map editor (under "Extras" on the main menu). You can open up and edit all the campaign/skirmish maps in the editor. The editor is complex, it looks like the one the devs used. You probably can't whip up a simple map quickly, but I think a few time-limited campaign maps will be a non-issue in the future when we have lots of community maps.There is (was?) a free demo of the first 4 intro maps which is about 7 hours gameplay if you take your time.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an evolution of Dungeons 3, but fixed most of the things that I had an issue with in that game.  There's now four core creatures for each faction (up from three) and each faction is viable as a solo faction.  Research has been reorganized into more sensible sections - you no longer have to go horde for traps, or undead to upgrade horde creatures, etc.  Instead of the boring +damage/health research, research is now individual to creatures and a lot more interesting.  Most of all, it's just more of the fun of Dungeons 3.  An over the top plotline, self-aware 4th wall breaking, etc.  The gameplay is still tight - enough time that you can build a dungeon and get things going, but with enough pressure you have to go out on the map.  Overall I highly recommend it, and they've already added two new skirmish maps (with new abilities attached!).  Hopefully this is supported just as long as Dungeons 3 was, and I see no reason it wouldn't be.  Great developer, great game.

_childDocuments_.review: It really sucks to thumbs down this one. Amazing concept ruined by absurd expectations. Explanation:Playing the campaign is pretty fun and has lots of charm. It's odd how the game tries to mix G-rated dialogue with an occasional swear word. It's like it's for children, with G-rated humor, and then "Isn't that the same bullsh** you spouted earlier, Tristan?" I'm like wait... huh? I am confusion...It's dungeon management with endless interruptions. The first few chapters are endearing, and then you hit Heroes' Gorge.>:^(In the game, after demolishing a hero building, there will eventually be a team of heroes sent to rebuild it, and you can/should go make sure they don't make it there. That's both acceptable and expected. However...During that mission, you need to quickly make your way above ground and take their magic tower. Emphasis on quickly. If you take time to actually build rooms and summon minions, you'll be constantly insulted for not already having taken the tower. Meanwhile, "enemies have entered the dungeon" over n over. GFL taking that tower quickly. There are enemies galore in the overworld on this mission. Like twice as many as usual. But the tower is there to take them out. It aims at YOU until you take it out. So you'd think "Okay, take the tower, and it's easy street from then on." Holy crap would you be wrong.The moment you take it, the enemy sends for mana shipments for the wall protecting their city. You now have to go stop that shipment. Fine, no big deal. So you take one out, and Tristan says he'll now send 2 shipments at once "from now on" (once). Now, keep in mind that Thalya is capped at level 2 for the whole mission, for some stupid reason.Fine, it sucks, and there are enemies absolutely everywhere to basically make certain I don't make it there in time, and enemies are in my dungeon attacking the dungeon heart, but hey, let's risk it all to stop these shipments. Afterall, you don't get the new skill reward if you allow even 1 of them to make it, so it's more or less mandatory. I'm not playing this mission ever again.So I go to the dungeon to save the dungeon heart at the last second, go back above ground, and use the tower to take out a shipment, and fought my way through 4 mobs to get to the other at the last second. I got lucky, ngl.So there I am waiting for the next 2 shipments to be announced, only to hear "So you've taken both shipments. Very well. This time I shall send THREE shipm..." ALT+F4Enough. I don't ♥♥♥ think so. That's just ridiculous. I got lucky a lotta times in a row as it is, but now these devs actually expect me to somehow take 3 very separate locations at once, with a tower that shoots once every 2 minutes, with no less than twice the normal number of mobs in your way, within 2 minutes, while enemies are constantly entering the dungeon to attack the heart, with a small number of minions cuz the game kept telling me verbally to hurry and take the tower so I didn't have time to build properly.I suspect it woulda gone to 4 shipments at once if I somehow, some way managed to actually pull off that miracle, which had to happen on the first try and just wasn't gonna, so for the sake of sanity I got tf outta there immediately and played Skirmish instead. About Skirmish...Good ♥♥♥ luck winning a Skirmish. I died many times on the first one, on Easy, with benefits. In 77 hours I only managed to beat 1, and I only spent about 20 hours on the story.It's just a mode where you have to defeat all hero buildings, but you'll be invaded by heroes. Often. Like always. Sometimes enemies enter the dungeon while you're currently battling the ones who just entered. You have to clear pretty much the entire dungeon to get the gold you'll need to maintain, so get ready to hear "one of your little snots dug up a spider" while battling both hordes of suspiciously high-level heroes you're already dying to.Then you find out that "spider" is a nest, surrounded by spiders, who dig through rock to create a new nest. Now you have loads of legendary enemies (on easy) piling in, destroying your structures, costing you a lot of hard-limited gold, and crushing your level 6+ minions, sudden spider attacks, which also attack your dungeon heart, and more and more spider nests taking over. This means your first priority is to take out the spiders and nests as soon as you find them, before they become an unstoppable army. Speaking of armies...You generally have 2 hidden army bases of heroes in your own dungeon, who also randomly attack. So that's high-level invaders by the dozen, 2 enemy bases in your dungeon, a self-replicating spider nest (or 7... yes I counted 7), and limited gold, from the beginning of the first Skirmish, on Easy. Meanwhile, your actual goal is to stop mana shipments above ground, somehow.Did I mention Thalya SUCKS?! Cuz she DOES. She has noooooo types of talent, considering her All-powerful role in the game. In fact, she is so easy to kill, the narrator prepared lots of dialogue for all the consecutive deaths she will endure. But rest assured, she'll place herself directly in harm's way, since she's a short-range spellcaster (squishiest of all roles).I can still semi-Recommend this game, but only for someone who is either looking for hardcore challenges that take hours each and require save scumming (not what I'm looking for here), or to someone who just wants a dungeon management sim to casually chill to in Dream Dungeon. That is a Skirmish with zero threat. Just build anything you want, go to the overworld to fight and take buildings down if you want, or you can manually have a weak, moderate, or powerful horde sent into your dungeon for battle if you want. But, there is no "end", you just... screw around.I made a Harem of 32 Succubi and 4 Vampire Queens. So... just sayin'. There's fun to be had. :)You can build a cemetery, a temple (and sacrificial pit), a bar (only for Horde types like Orcs and Goblins, which sucks), a prison to starve enemies in (to death), a torture room... I mean this game's dark, man. Which only strengthens my confusion when I hear the oddly childish jokes and child-like dialogue, while a succubus whips a priestess and 5 people starve to death in my prison.Unfortunately, this game is really addictive. Good management games generally are, and this is a good management game. One that gets turned into an endless horde-wave war in your own house, while your main missions are always in the overworld. Then your minions go On Strike out of rebellion from being drastically overworked, right in the middle of battle. I would MUCH rather take a little time to enjoy the building and researching aspects, but it's just all fighting and tunneling through rock to scrounge for gold at all times.The thumbs down is  it's so addictive. I'm sucked into a game I don't wanna load, and Skirmishes can only entertain for so long. Maybe the story would be more interesting if the horde-wave annoyance, and mana shipment nightmare in Heroes' Gorge was toned way down, or if each chapter didn't always end in "Oh noes, Tristan ran away again. After himmm...", but as it is now, it's a deceptively painful wave-based horde game, where the researching and building are a thing you have to jump on quickly and rush through, just to have a chance of surviving the earliest attack. Then you spend all your time protecting your rooms and the Heart.I say Not Recommended, just barely, to maybe save people frustration. I'll still dive into my dream dungeon from time to time, but the campaign is just too damn annoying right now for me to even want to play it. To have a campaign I don't wanna continue, in a game with so very much going for it, is just a shame, and Dream Dungeon will not remain interesting forever on its own.In short, I love what the game can be, but not what it is. I love some things, and hate others.
