_childDocuments_.review: Its good but for me it doesn't bring that much new to the original Railway Empire, which I also own. If you are new to Railway Empire, it is worth a buy. If you played the predecessor, read on...I dislike the way the new gridirons are implemented; they are too long and you constantly have to rebuild your tracks into stations to accommodate the huge length of the gridiron required if you add tracks. There is no indication on how long parallel tracks into stations need to be to fit a 2/4/6/8 track gridiron. Gridirons are fussy - the tracks into stations have to be perfectly aligned and fairly straight to fit a gridiron.  In some places, the gridirons between stations are so long that there is little actual track between the stations.  My gridiron into London (UK) station on the British map is about the width of the M25 around London. A good chunk of my game time seems to be spent rebuilding tracks into stations to fit a bigger gridiron.  The new bigger maps are nice but they just make the scale of many things (platforms etc) feel wrong. And the journey times early in the game are measured in days, even in a small country like the UK. This is not realistic, but hey, in the end this is just a fun fancy game of managing networks and building your economy and not intended to accurately model a railway. I miss the dynamic presence of goods in the old Railway Empire, where goods would visibly build up in the goods stations indicating supply exceeds demand. Also, the number of passengers at passenger stations does not seem to vary much, so there is no visual clue as to passenger demand. The new signals system is ok, but you will still end up with congestion (train traffic jams)  even when using waypoints. Or maybe it is me? The trains always take the shortest route,  it is a shame the game could not have better AI control on the trains to reduce traffic jams. Its like all the railway signal engineers took the day off. Way points are apparently the answer but unpicking your routes to stop jams is a pain. Trying to work out why all your trains are backed up on a route, adding platform preferences, waypoints and redirecting each line quickly becomes a chore. The game seems to work best (for me) when I have a separate freight train network, so I end up with two or more stations per city.  Which is a shame because the stations accommodate both freight and passengers, and it shouldn't be necessary. But every attempt I have made to get freight and passengers to run on the same lines has not worked out (slow express trains, traffic jams, queues etc. The supply towers are a bit annoying. Placed on your main tracks, trains stops to refill/refuel etc and all the trains behind them patiently wait in a queue, even if they are a priority express. Breakdowns are also a pain. If your train breaks down it will hold up all the traffic behind it until fixed. Even if you have a maintenance depot at every stop, breakdowns still happen. I guess it is like real life but a bit frustrating at times.The pace of time can be too slow early game. There are lots of times when you are on fast forward to get more money, passively watching. Not a biggie, but you cannot leave your screen in case you miss an auction or other event.Having said all that, I am enjoying my play through. Railway Empire 2 runs well, has some nice new features, and it is not too easy to succeed. But if you already own Railway Empire 1, I would stick with that until this goes on sale.Now I must go and spend a few hours trying to unjam a jam outside Manchester...

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the first iteration, it is a (light) game about the age of steam. You decide on (painfully obvious) routes between cities and villages (that solely produce timber, for example). If you like the genre, it is a decent, if somewhat uninspired addition. A major improvement is that one doesn't have to put all the signs in manually, although in an upcoming update (see: roadmap) this feature will be returned for those who enjoy putting in the signs manually. Compared to Railroad Tycoon the game fails to really engage with the shenanigans of shares and mergers. The economy is a Potemkin village. However, unlike RRT, trains don't 'fade out' in order to allow passage. If your signs aren't properly placed, everything will grind to a halt until you fix things. However, with the automated signs this should never be an issue. The graphics are OK. Not brilliant, but not ugly, either. One thing that I enjoy is the ability to change the paint scheme of each and every available locomotive. I spent some time putting in historically accurate paint schemes for various companies. As always, check some YT action and decide for yourself. If you liked RE 1, you will probably like RE 2 as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty solid entry - it's generally an improvement over RE1, and represents reasonable progression in the genre. Most noticeable improvements involve quality of life updates, the overall scope of the game feeling meatier, and a welcome coat of realism polish. Maps feel more expansive as well.Par for the Railroad Tycoon genre, there are familiar gripes, almost all related to how 'micro' the management is to be successful... One example is laying tracks, considering the apparent encouragement to double track more that RE1. It would be nice to have a "lay double track" option, auto-including the junctions and direction settings. Another example is manually setting which goods can be stored at each warehouse... I personally don't see where the fun begins; isn't that what warehouse managers are for?(EDIT: The new auto-signaling does have some benefits, and once I got familiar with it, it's much less tedious now... They're also adding manual signaling in an upcoming update).The landscapes flirt with being awe-inspiring, yet are limited by the "always mid-day sunny" lighting... Some weather effects, day/night cycles would be huge (I haven't seen any yet, so I may be wrong).I got in after 1st patch and have had no technical issues, though I'd expect more patches for polish and balance.All said, it is very much the latest and greatest, and makes many steps (however small) in many right directions. If you're looking at this, you've probably already made up your mind; you're just calculating the value (sale or not?) I went in full price with intent to support the developer, but budget-minded Kalypso fans know some sales and expansions are inevitable.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. I'm playing my second save in 100 hours. Building large road systems across Europe. The process is very exciting. When the network of roads becomes large and you develop a couple of cities up to 200 - 300 thousand population, sometimes it is just interesting to sit and watch the trains arrive and depart at the station of a large city, supporting a huge flow of passengers and cargo. Special thanks to the developers for further developing the game. I liked the addition with electric locomotives. Only for atmospheric lack of power plants in cities. I don't understand the complaints of players who are unhappy with the “difficulty” of building routes. On the contrary, the ability to make the direction of the tracks manually, as well as fine-tuning the routes for each train and give the highlight of this game. I personally lack in the game:-seaports-ferry crossings-possible more types of production.What really upset me about this game is why couldn't the Balkan region be made into one map with Europe? It would have been very interesting to expand the road from Europe to Turkey and so on. As it turns out, I don't really need the Balkans supplement. I like to be able to choose as huge a map as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played the snot out of both.  The price yea a little on the high side but I think its what you do that matters, we didn't have multiplayer but now we do that is a hard thing to work out so overall the cost isn't the worse thing.  I heard some complaint about the gridiron, I love the gridiron in this game vs paying the 200k to auto setup rails to push them into the right lanes.  I love the fact I have 8 possible rail lines in a grand station.  I love the fact that you can make a full bridge with 8 rail lines vs the first one that had a limit of 2 that were able to be built together (hated that fact, had to build some weird railways that way in the first one). The rail line concept was one of the cleanest concepts that took me a moment to grasp probably because I don't remember it in the first one, the fact I can auto add trains to the same rail line and then i can toggle through them to see what was going on was great. The fact the utilization actually works is also great,  in the first game the loads would tell you you need x amount per week to keep things afloat but they never mathematically added up. So the utilization was great so I didn't have to overcompensate on the routes to make sure enough product for the factories worked. warehouse as an extension of the station was cool, didn't have to pay 200k to get a large warehouse just needed to target the right place.  The fact you can make any stop really a transfer stop with the hotels was cool.  the auto hiring of personnel was interesting. Some things I didn't necessarily like but were okay, the fact you now have to pay for the special freight cars to increase the overall haul of your loads. You got those Scott free in the first one but I never fully utilized them. The characters aren't as memorable I feel as the original ones.  The bond system may be broken in the sense that if you take a top tier bond vs taking the shorter tier bond you can technically start 2 of them when the higher value, longer period seems to only allow one.  The unlocking things as part of research such as steel and confectionery and stuff seems like why?  Do the cities need it if I don't research it, then why do I need to research it?  Extension limit of 2 for a grand station seems smol, it's a grand station maybe 3?Some wishes here the stock market bonds tell you little about anything, the documentation on the refrigerated car is kind of dated?  Why does it apply to vegetables but not corn? Thought it was just any food stuffs really in the old one.To the ones talking about you can't do things the way you want, you totally can they still have the waypoint system, used that multiple times in the campaign to make freight lines take the slower routes for my express trains.  The express trains now make actual sense on how to get them to express status, maintenance isn't counted into the metric anymore it never made sense to count it as part of the metric. All in all I think it was good, if you are torn on price maybe wait a little, yea it doesn't have  a ton in it yet but it'll get better.  That being said they're loading on platform 9, and I'm going to miss my train.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting challenge for those of us who like this type.Two major points: to players, make sure you have as little gradient as possible. Especially in early game. Weak trains don't do hills very well, taking up extra time you could be making money. This is a bigger issue than speed limits on turns. Don't do 2% when 1% will do. Don't do 1% when you can achieve 0%. Don't do 1% on the whole track when you can do 1% on just half the track. BUT ALSO don't push it right to the edge of where it changes between one % and the next. When you add multiple tracks the newer ones may not get the same gradients. Also don't worry about earthwork costs when adjusting gradients, you'll make that up over time with faster trains. But DO worry about bridges and tunnels. THOSE are expensive.To developers: *Bug report: something around 10% to 15% of the time a train will skip a destination.* Returning to the farm loaded with grain, for example. When it turns around there, it is considered as having made a full circuit, complete with weekly costs added. The only work-around I have for this is for one-off shipments, not regular loads. By making the destination listed first (origin) and the only other listed station one nearby, the wayward train will either head toward the original destination as intended, or sometimes redeploy(teleport) there.

The train AI's have some issues, but if this game gets as much post release attention as Port Royale 4 did then I don't doubt those will get ironed out. I think the release of this game is quite comparable to the release of Port Royale 4 which of course is another pick up and delivery economic game from Kalypso and has had similar mixed reviews. I know a lot of folks are finding the price disagreeable and frankly I'm inclined to agree that it's overpriced, but at the end of the day I do quite enjoy it and I'm glad I bought it. _childDocuments_.review: I have about 800 hours in RE1 and was both looking forward to and dreading RE2.  Dread because sequels often don't impress me.  I currently have about 24 hours in RE2 and I am really enjoying the game.  It's similar enough to RE1 that there was basically no learning curve, yet different enough to keep it interesting.  I'm not sure if I just used warehouses incorrectly in RE1, but the system here allows for really complex freight lines - They absolutely make my brain hurt when calculating what's going to end up where. Overwhelmingly I would recommend this game, especially if you like RE1 or RT2.  It will scratch that itch for sure!  The graphics are also really easy to look at.  Somethings to be warned about (Things I'd love to see improved). When laying parallel tracks, especially around bridges and curves, the game is buggier than RE1.  In RE1, maybe 1 out of a 100 track builds had a little red preventing the building of said track, but in RE2 I would say that happens 1 out of 5 track builds.  It's frustrating to have to go in and tweak what seemingly should be an easy task.  MP was a complete let down.  Currently you can only play cooperatively, there is no competing against other players.  Once my friend and I decided that, even though it was weird to share the same money and work on the same lines, we'd give it a shot... well, we were disappointed pretty quickly by the lag.  The lag eventually (before the first year is done) is so bad that it becomes unplayable.  It's annoying that you can only build so many buildings and extensions, but I suppose it just makes the game more challenging.  Those are really my only complaints thus far.  Overall, I was looking forward to this game.  The day it came out, I read the "mixed" reviews on steam.  I thought about the purchase for a couple of days and eventually was buzzed just enough that I decided to do it.  24 hours later, I'm glad I did.  Each chapter is a fun little puzzle that helps one settle after a long day at work.

_childDocuments_.review: After sinking a lot of time into the original RE1 plus all DLC's and can happily say this is a big improvement. Here are some pros and cons and what I'd like to see in an update:Pros:Graphics - The game is gorgeous. I find myself happily riding along a lot more with my new rail line to test it out that I did previously in RE1. I do, however, find myself missing the simple cartoon characters as the new animated 3D ones are a massive eyesore in my eyes and look pretty rough compared to the simple cartoon ones of RE1, an unnecessary addition.Stations - Up to 8 tracks that expand as you go. The gridirons can be a little finicky but so long as you keep them under 4 lines they seem to work smoother than signalled stations in RE1. The addition of station buildings to negate the need of separate warehouses and add another challenge to most efficiently setting up your lines is a huge plus for me.Contour building mode - Although we had contours in RE1 the contour screen mod is so much easier and clearer to build with. Manage trains as lines - Instead of individually making and remaking lines for every individual locomotive you now manage a route as a line and select how many trains you'd like to use that line. They even go as far spacing themselves out along the route, which can be an issue if they're idling in a busy station but I think it's a nice touch. No more snakes clogging up behind each other. Plus one change made to the line effects all the trains. Staffing - This bring me onto staffing which thankfully has been simplified. You now just control the general staffing for the whole company from one menu. Whilst I did kind of enjoy the mini-game of assigning people who got along to trains to improve output it got very tedious very quickly, big plus doing it this way.Cons:Signals -  I was the type of RE1 player that liked to place all my signals manually and often set up trains loading/unloading manually too. So I do understand the frustration with the new auto signalling in RE2. It's very convenient and for the most part works seamlessly and makes the game a lot more accessible to the average gamer. However I'd like the option to go back to manual signalling also, like in RE1 as there's certain situations this calls for. (I know everyone just wants engine queues back!) P.S. we have tunnel signals now!Game speed - I do enjoy the zoom function controlling game speed, to em it just makes sense. You want the game running realistic and slow when you're up close watching your trains but to speed up when you're up high watching the situation from afar. Essentially it's just automated what I did before. However, again would be nice to have the option. I know you can turn this off but it defaults to the faster setting which looks crazy up close. I used to play RE1 on 50% game speed for this reason which unfortunately is not an option currently with RE2. Slow down my trains please!Bugs - As with any new release these days there are a few bugs, like getting soft-locked in the tutorial because you closed a menu at the wrong time, or the refrigerator car just appearing as a 1st era passenger wagon (anyone else go that one?). However they proved with RE1 that they're attentive at patching and updating the game. (There was a time in RE1 before we even had diamond crossings or signalled stations!) So I'm confident we'll get these minor bugs fixed and manual signals back soon.All in, I can see why people think of RE2 as a re-skin, there's not any new trains from RE1 as far as I can see and the mechanics have been simplified somewhat. However the on the whole the game is better than RE1 in almost every other aspect. Managing routes is so much easier and can achieve much better efficiency than before, it's stunning to look at and I find myself just having more genuinely fun playtime than in RE1. I would like to see some more manual controlling back for the hardcore enthusiasts in the future and I'm keen for DLCs. But for now I will continue to enjoy RE2 as it is a fantastic successor to RE1.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the changes made in RE2.  I'm pleased to not have to micromanage all the track details and feel like there is control over everything I would like to customize with the tracks.  The wharehouses being able to be placed within every station really changes how freight exchanges and create so many more strategies for management.  Passengers changing at stations does the same thing.  Staff management is totally different and makes a lot more sense then the micromanagement of RE1.  If you are expecting a huge revamp then perhaps hold but for me there is enough change that this is fun and I'm looking forward to finishing the campaign.  The reviews that gave this a negative after 0.5 hours and refunded didn't give this enough time to even see how the new changes work.   I would only listen to negative reviews that gave the game at least 5 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: I have over 2000 hours in the first game, in less than four in the new game, but I can already tell I will likely play this game for thousands of hours. I don’t miss fussing around with the switches, or building the grid irons, and the separate warehouses. These have all been integrated into the new game so that you can worry about growing your company and building a railroad instead of troubleshooting switches or stuck merchandise in a warehouse. As a longtime gamer, who started on railroad tycoon, the Sid Meier classic from 1990 I can assure you that this game  is a worthy successor. The game has been out for less than a day. And as is typical on the Internet, the negative voices are heard first and it takes time for the positive voices to be heard. Bottom line is there are worse ways to spend $60, and I am glad the railroad Sim is still thing 30 years after Sid Meier made it a thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is not an arcade game; its a business sim and players will have to 'work' at it.  The tutorials are a must to enable a player to understand. It is here where I think the developers have scored an own goal in terms of marketing. The guides can be bought as an e book, which in itself is a bit cheeky. If I buy a game I expect it to come with instructions and not have to pay extra for them. There will be a hard copy set of books out in June apparently but by then players will have worked it all out or discarded the game. This is a poor bit of salesmanship.The game itself is quite absorbing and once you get the idea of track laying and management of your rail lines a lot of the rest of it can be worked out. If you just want to lay tracks and run locomotives then the sandbox scenario is for you. If you want to play the other scenarios you will need to be prepared to take an interest in the business side of things.There are a few quirks and I hope the developers put them right. For example there is no means of adjusting the speed of screen scrolling by moving the mouse side to side and its much too fast. There is an alternative of grabbing the screen with the mouse button and moving the map but it feels very unnatural.The interfaces of setting up tracks, lines and trains and editing lines is much easier than RE1.One issue I have is there are fewer cities than RE1. I play United Kingdom on RE1 yet RE2 has only a fraction of the RE1 cities. Considering that UK was the home of Railway development in the early 19th century I expected better.All in all its a very playable game and with a much improved interface than RE1 you can concentrate on game play rather than trying to puzzle out how to do things with the buttons that operate the lines, in cities and in business.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: The start of the game is a bit too slow to my taste. Once you start the game, the revenue starts to cumulate quite slow. Once you get things going, it easier.One annoying issue what I found out was that once you have activated the demolition mode and go to signal mode and try to setup the direction for rail, the demolition mode is still active and you end up deleting your rail.Other wise from the 10 hour experience I'm very happy with the game and recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR -- Quite a nice game on the whole but the price may be offputting . If you have not, I'm confident the game is worth its price, it has enough content to warrant it.The main complaint against the game seems to be that it's just a reskin of RE. While it's true that the main gameplay is the same, I would argue that there is enough new/revised content to warrant this game.The biggest ones are the (much) improved and changed graphics (I, for one, like these much more realistic-looking characters more than the over-the-top cartoon ones of RE) and larger maps, which allow for more flexibility in planning tracks. But this is not all that's new.For example, employee management is completely altered. Now you don't have to wait for a conductor/stoker/etc. to offer their services and assign them to one train so that they benefit that train (only to be snatched by a competitor later...), now you have an unseen pool of employees for all roles and you have to set the budget for their recruitment, training, welfare, etc. The more (or less!) money you spend on a category of workers, the more ALL trains will benefit/suffer from it.Then there is the new track laying system. This is, indeed, simpler than in RE, but I. for one, don't mind having to create all switches myself. (And you can still skip using grid irons if you want.) Also, I feel like the track laying system is considerably smarter and smoother now.That said, there ARE some features missing from the complete RE bundle (such as night mode) and the price may indeed be on the high side for what it offers compared to RE. If it is ever on sale for about 30-35 [whatever currency], it's a good deal then.You are in charge of a railway company in century between 1830-1930, the age of steam engines, and thus are tasked with connecting the cities and rural businesses of either North America or West- and Central Europe. Your main task is ensuring cities are supplied with whatever they need for progress.Rural stations produce raw materials for factories in the cities while cities produce passengers/mail and finished goods; the former are the more lucrative kind of "cargo" but the latter, along with many kinds of raw goods, are needed for cities to grow, hence producing more passengers and mail (and gaining new slots for different factories).The game offeres various ways to play. In campaign, you have to do a series of challenges in sequence, with a (pseudo-)narrative to tie them together; in scenario mode, you can play almost any of the 14 available scenarios (sets of mandatory tasks with preset settings on a given map) in any order; in custom game, you can customize your game and only have optional goals to achieve, doing which will increase your score and thus ranking, but can be ignored; and in sandbox, you can build any railway network on your selected map free of any worries for money, goals or score.As I wrote in the TLDR section, if you are a new player, the game is definitely worth its asking price.Personally, I, for one, find the game quite nice, with a good amount of content and am enjoying it so far quite a bit.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: hi all, i think its a great game, i dont understand the negative reviews, its fun, its relaxing, you will make mistakes but its fixable. great graffics and track laying is nice, the way you can adjust the tracks so it cost you less then the original settings by the game. its fun to adjust it to your likings. i play campain and its fun , dont listen to those haters this game made much improvements on track settings and more.for me this game is a 9/10 if you want a train simulation game ? this isn't your game, this is a tycoon and tycoon means your the manager, fun isn't it? yes its has its price but think about how much people need to be payed for making this game, it takes much time and efford to make such a game, so for me to the devs, great job, thnx for this game ;)
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: Really a genius recreation of Railway Empire.I used to play the Original Railway Empire on my PS4 with my parents watching, I really did get a lot of the stuff and scenarios done and it felt like the great endorsed version of all those train mobile games! Plus, they got me the deluxe version for the nostalgia! In game wise, great economic features, great rail planning, 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent and worth buying. Track laying has been simplified, but that's a good thing as now you can focus more on strategy and routes instead of grinding out track. You need to pick your stations well, and now passengers and cargo can connect so you don't have to build 15 routes between 5 different cities. Just make one of your stations a hub and let passengers, mail and cargo change trains as needed to get them to their final destination. Trains are much more realistic now vs Railway Empire 1. Now trains accel and decel based on weight and you really need to pay attention to the tractor force of your trains. Some engines you'll want for passengers and mail because of speed, but they won't be able to haul cargo due to weight, so those you'll need to select engines with more tractor force. All in all it's an awesome follow up to the original game.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's a very solid sequel to a great game. The core gameplay mechanics are heavily polished and there is a lot of content compared to RE1 on release. Some mechanics are streamlined, yes, and employees are removed which I will miss, but overall the things removed were not particularly important to my enjoyment of RE1. Track building, which could be an exercise in frustration in RE1 is extremely intuitive now, junctions, especially in parallel tracks were a huge pain - no more! The gridiron system makes signalled stations far more useful now too, as incoming tracks can be curved and sloped.The game looks great, lots of detail and the procedural cities are very charming.Station expansions are much more in-depth, the route system allowing multiple trains to follow one route is great.I have yet to encounter any bugs or technical problems.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not understanding the hate but maybe its because I didn't play the first one. Unbiased to that. If you used to play Sid Meier's Railroads, you will love this game, a lot of elements are identical, auctions, train planning, and few more things. Its great to waste time with a friend but I'd personally rather go head to head against my friend vs sharing a railroad and bank account. Hopefully that gets added in the future. Fun game if you seemingly haven't played the first. I'm enjoying. My friend is enjoying it, we're having fun and thats what matters. No crashing, pretty stableMultiplayer Pro's & Cons of just some things I noticed playing a few hours in. Pro's: StableUp to 4 playersCampaigns can be done with Co-opTrack laying planner helps plan across multiple friendsCan monitor and assist each others lines and upgrade themCon's:No PvP mode, only PvAihaving more than 1 friend in the lobby is definitely not fun early onNo color designation because youre on the same railroad, so its hard to tell whos trains are what later in gameYour rail road MUST connect, you can't just go off into another state and establish a separate railroad, the lines must connect
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: For me, multiplayer was the most important new feature of RE2. We had 2 crashes in 4h, which is pretty solid for a newly released game, especially from Kalypso :) Regarding the deepth of the game, I need to play a couple of more hours. We maxed our capital city in year 4, not sure if there is much more to come.As conclusion, my reason to buy the game is to play it coop, which works. It looks pretty beautiful, runs smooths and has a lot of things to discover (not played RE1 though).
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: + + Works well with Linux (via SteamPlay), tested with Arch Linux.+ + Graphics is better and uses less power(!) than v1.+ + New modes (warehouse-integration with stations)   + Play-strategy is slightly different compared to v1, but I like it   - price seems high, my guess: it won't stay at that levelEdit: the game also works with the beta of the upcoming next version macOS (Sonoma)using Apple's game-porting-toolkit [based on Wine/proton]. (Lots of configuration effort, not useful for endusers!)So it would be nice, if:a) Steam integrates the game-porting-toolkit drivers alongside with Wine/Proton/Linux support, since both are based on the same tech,b) Kalypso uses the game-porting-toolkit to generate an actual Apple silicon port :-)
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: Out of all the annoying and strange design choices in this game, blocking the placement of rail stations has to be the most frustrating. Let's say for instance you begin in Geneva--the game is unable to generate random objectives, so you will always have tasks to build two rail lines, paris-orleans and dresden-prague; however, you can't just purchase the region concessions for the areas and then build these two lines, no, they have to be connected directly to your HQ city through one continuous line. Why did the devs do this? To give the game scoring/leaderboards and clearly defined speedrun objectives that remain consistent through each playthrough. If you're someone who wants to just build logistics networks in the way that literally every other game in its genre allows for, this is not for you. It feels like transport fever but missing half the content and there's no mod support.There are so many other issues with this game, i'll list a couple of the more frustrating ones. The ridealong camera is completely laughable, I don't know how this made it into the game. Good luck learning about parallel tracks and gridirons, the tutorial is bugged. Gridirons must be placed on 0% graded tracks and stations cannot slope, so connecting mountain stations is absolute hell. There are only 13 levels of zoom from a nearly first person view to an almost full map view, there is no option to adjust this or pan speed. If your middle mouse button is broken tough luck, there's no option to rebind its functions. Track construction is janky, it feels like placing roads/paths in workers&resources in the sense that you constantly are blocked by proximity warnings. Building junctions looks ugly and asymmetrical out of necessity. The game automating signals is nice, but it also causes some issues and makes it impossible to fine-tune your junctions to know for sure they will work. From a game focused entirely on railways i expected more, it even manages to fail the people who just want to get zooted and watch little trains move around a map. At recommended settings you still might face performance issues, at least it performs nice on lower settings
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: Really don't understand all the hate. I'm a little over 30 minutes in and my initial impression is overall positive. The game looks beautiful, runs well and seems to be an overall improvement over the previous iteration, from which they've apparently learned a lot of lessons. My main gripe with the last game was the deconfliction of multiple trains on the same track, which would require a lot of tedious legwork from the player to sort out and would often be extremely confusing. But that's all been fixed in this one, as traffic control is a lot easier and the system is automated now. On a technical note, I haven't had any crashes or other issues, which seem to be reported by some players. I recommend Railway Empire 2 to anyone who loves trains or economy games in general. It's very streamlined and user friendly.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly don't understand all the negative reviews which people wrote after playing for less than 2 hours. The game is good, you can switch game speed change when you to zoom off in the options, graphics is good, and multiplayer is just an addition not the main goal of this new version of the game. Tutorial is a little bit clunky, but can be completed without any issues.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review: So I'm back...I originally preordered this and played launch day. I did not have good things to say about this game at the time so I refunded it. I guess I was used to how great RE1 was. I have since repurchased this game and gave it another shot. So far I'm liking it, good QOL updates, however I did enjoy the complexity of it all in RE1. The graphics are cool the trains are awesome. I will say and this is coming from someone who loves maps. They need to fix some geographical issues one example being the Columbia river is notably missing between Washington and Orgeon state.In closing this game has slight QOL updates, graphics are cool, gameplay is smooth, ehh...I like it so far. Hopefully they improve more with patches and DLC (eventually). As of now on a scale of 1-10 RE2 gets a solid 6.5. I'm hoping I can come back in the future and bump up that score, time will tell.
_childDocuments_.name: Railway Empire 2

_childDocuments_.review:
All aboard the express train to riches and fame in Railway Empire 2!

Don the coat of a clever entrepreneur, take over a small railway company in the early 1800s and turn your steam engines into the workhorses of the economy. Grow your company into the largest railway company of the continent and outsmart your competitors as you connect cities and companies with an ever-expanding network of rail lines, bridges, and tunnels.

60 famous steam engines are at your disposal, all pulling freight and passenger cars as they usher in an era of historic importance during the Industrial Revolution.

name: Loddlenaut
detailed_description: Loddlenaut is an ocean cleanup adventure set on a vibrant alien planet. Play as an interstellar custodian who is tasked with cleaning up the pollution left behind by a spacefaring mega-corporation. Befriend local axolotl-like creatures and explore sunken corporate ruins as you revive the planet’s lush ecosystems. 🚀 Explore an open-world alien planet 🐠 Raise aquatic critters called “loddles” that grow based on what they eat 🔫 Clean up icky goop and floating debris with your bubble gun 🌟 Unlock special gadgets to clean different types of ocean pollution 🛠️ Recycle collected trash to craft useful items and upgrades BRING GUP-14 BACK TO LIFE Your mission: Clean up the ocean planet of GUP-14 after it was abandoned by GUPPI, a mega-corporation that makes and sells everything from soda to spaceships. When you first arrive on the planet, you’ll find yourself amid murky waters, oil spills, and scattered junk. Within the polluted environments, you’ll find remnants of GUPPI’s buildings, ships, and machinery all sunken to the ocean floor. Discover clues about the planet’s past inhabitants as you clean up the mess they left behind using an assortment of high-tech gadgets. BEFRIEND ALL THE LODDLES As you clean up the planet, you’ll run into axolotl-like aliens known as “loddles.” Protect them from the polluted waters and feed them aquatic fruits while you make their planet habitable again. Depending on their diet, loddles will grow in different ways and develop unique traits and abilities that will further enable them to survive on this polluted planet. When the loddles are strong enough and the waters are cleaner, release them back into the wild and watch them thrive! Goddles Update Explore an expanded planet with three new caves that each contain a lost loddle with a new rare cosmetic mutation! Delve even deeper to discover Goddle Grotto, a secret sixth biome that is home to three mythical Goddles. Make use of the new gardening system to collect seedlings, grow your own flora, and increase each biome's resistance to pollution. Plus, track the positions of all pollutants with the new Global Pollution Tracker, expand your backpack with the new Inventory Capacity Module, and acquire gold versions of your tools by completing different milestones that will ultimately unlock a modified ending cutscene. Loddlepedia Update Track your loddle evolutions and see which ones you’ve yet to discover. Plus enjoy a new loddle ability, new loddle personality traits, new biome diversity ratings, and a new way to boost around the ocean! 0.05GBP per sale on Steam is donated to WDC, Whale and Dolphin Conservation. WDC is a UK registered charity no. 1014705.

_childDocuments_.review: The underwater is a very reassuring and happy place for me, but it's hard to find an underwater game that isn't about killing sharks or fishing.Loddlenaut is everything but that. You're here to clean and pet Loddles, that's it. It's the definition of "cozy".But while I adore the cleaning-feeding-petting, I also found myself enjoying everything around all of it. You're not a superhero cleaning after an evil corporation, you're a cleaner from a corporation sent by the corporation that trashed the ocean to erase their mistakes.You can ask yourself questions about their actions, why they lied about some stuff, why they ommited to inform us of others... Will it changes anything to the game? No. But it's called world building, and it's well done. The + : SOLVED Hehehe :
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: What do you mean that after all my satisfying hard work, I need to pack up and leave? Who would clean and maintain their biomes if I'm gone? Who would look after them when they get sick and infected? Who would feed them when they're too dumb (affectionate) to swim near the food and get all sad and mopey because they're starving? Who would make them toys for their own entertainment? And most of all, who would give them headpats 24/7? Glasses guy obviously doesn't get it, telling me not to get attached which is impossible the moment I saw those thoughtless, adorable creatures. 10/10 would be their garbage collector for life
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Super cute little game. Loddlenaut is stress-free despite having an oxygen timer as running out just resets you at home base with some lost inventory items floating in a circle where you last were. Within two hours your character can easily go on extended trips with a solid chunk of the map opened up, after another four hours the game world's open for you to clean at your leisure. Note there's also a Loddle breeding side-game of sorts at the same time as the main story with 13 different ones to create.Chill music and nice visuals barring the odd super bad lag spike seemingly unconnected to anything - these come and go but do not cause crashes so at least there's that.Completionists note you're looking at roughly 7.5 hours to finish at a moderate pace, most achievements unlock through playing but there are a few hidden ones.Easy recommend, surprised this was bundled so soon after initial release.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: I ended up 100%ing this game in just a couple of sittings because it's just too cute! Cleaning up every biome and recycling the materials is just soooo satisfying, and I love all of the different tools used to clean up the goop. And, of course, the loddles are the most adorable thing ever and I need a plushie of a Jumbo Loddle ASAP.The only thing I want to mention is that I feel like the game could've used a loddle compendium. It's possible there was one and I missed it, but I would've loved some way to track the different types of loddles I had already found (especially since it's an achievement you can get).
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: In the game Loddlenaut, you take on the role of an interstellar custodian who cleans up pollution left by a mega corporation on an alien planet.  Sounds familiar?  There is something really satisfying about cleaning up floating litter, microplastics and gloop in an underwater environment.  Plus watching the transformation caused by all your hard work.Along the way you encounter Loddles, simple cute creatures who help you to pollinate and cleanse the planets ecosystem.  You feed the baby Loddles, watch them through their metamorphosis into adults, entertain them and pat them.  Once a region is completely free of all pollution, you introduce the Loddles to the biome and they reproduce and fend for themselves.As you collect trash, you can convert it into usable bits which you can trade for more oxygen, lights, vacuum cleaner, new wetsuits etc etc.  There is bit of management to do here and being the first game I've played of this type, it took me a while to get the hang of it.  There is quite a bit of travelling around, but once you have portable oxygen rings, things become easier to manage.  Once you 100% a biome, fast travel is introduced between certain locations.I found the game quite addictive and time just whizzed by and twice I was up at 2am in the morning not having a clue how late it was!!  It is such a cute and wholesome game to play and absolutely suitable for children.  Nothing scary at all.Gameplay was WASD and both buttons on the mouse.  It can be repetitive, but you get rewarded for it.  There are no speedruns....just watch your oxygen levels.  You are taken back to the home cove when you die and lose all litter you were carrying.  I died many times as I'm an expert at it!!Music was lovely and gentle and non intrusive.  It really adds a peaceful vibe to the game.  Graphics are colourful and cute.I struck no bugs and managed to get all achievements bar 2 of them.  You continue to play for hours if you wish so you certainly get your money's worth.  There is communication between base and yourself and you get a pat on the back!I heartily recommend this delightful and charming game to those who want to make a difference.  A small percentage of this game goes towards the Whale and Dolphin Corporation.  Check out the demo!  9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Pleasant and short, though the side stuff that surrounds the cleaning activity is kind of weirdly laid out tbh. Ultimately I very much enjoyed my time with this game, despite it being a little on the expensive side to me personally for how much game there actually is. Definitely worth picking up, however, especially if you enjoy things like Powerwash Sim and such. I don't have any serious complaints but I do have a few annoyances and so...= DARE YE ENTER THE NITPICK ZONE =1) There's no real incentive to actually do anything with the creatures and the game never pushes you or makes you do anything with them either. To the point that you can just straight up leave them in a clean area and stuff with just passively happen in the background; I got three achievements related to their existence (growing up etc) without being anywhere near them, for example. It's very strange that it's laid out like this given the title and overall emphasis placed upon these critters in promo material. 2) I have some serious bones to pick with Dave, your...I guess "handler" would be the word? He pipes up to tell you whats going on, where to go, what to do etc. Except he's honestly kind of a jerk? Like the dude just comes off as very judgy and doesn't really get pleased with what you've done until well into the game. The most egregious one would probably be when you find the crates but haven't gotten the upgrade needed to get rid of them. Every time you hit the "use bubble gun" button in this scenario, he'll chime in with an unimpressed/annoyed looking face and a very derisive "As I said before" to explain you can't get rid of them until you get the upgrade...except the bubble gun is an automatically aiming device that quite literally moves around in erratic and unclear patterns and the crates are often positioned right next to floating trash or things that need cleaning. Back the hell off, dude, I'll get the bloody upgrade in a minute, christ. Thankfully you can turn his messages off entirely, but that then leaves you without what is effectively the thing that explains what the hell anything in the game is. Not a great move, tbh, and I think there should still be passively written info bubbles that show up when a new mechanic is introduced when he's turned off.3) There seems to be an oddity with the new mechanics where they're kind of only used Once and then not again? I haven't finished the last area but if the two new things that required entire new devices to clean are present there then that means they're literally only in two areas each, with four entire areas that don't have them. It's fairly clear that this game was probably scaled back somewhat from the original plans but hopefully if this sells decently then a whole new map as DLC will be in the cards where these tools will be more present. 3.5) Honestly the upgrade system could probably do with a bit of an overhaul in general; you'll get the majority of them very early on and they could probably do with being condensed. Up the default oxygen to 100, make it one single upgrade to 150, or something. There's also no real need for the "upgrade limits" on the other items, especially since you only really only need the one oxygen ring ever since you can dismantle them and take them around with you. An inventory upgrade would also be more appreciated as the storage mechanic is practically useless due to the fast travel ship only ever appearing until you've cleared 100% of the given area. 4) The crafting/cooking station, which requires actual items to make things with rather than the recycled bits you use for upgrades. Given that the upgrade station is literally creating brand new items out of these recycled bits, I'm a little confused as to why the things made in the crafting/cooking station are required to be the actual items intead. Okay, sure, the cooking one I can sort of understand for obvious reasons, but it doesn't quite make sense to me that we can't just materialise toys for the Loddles out of these bits as well; surely they would end up being of higher quality and better/safer for the environment in general instead of reusing and keeping literal trash in the ocean? 5) Really only £0.05 donated to charity per sale? 5 pence?? You may as well not bother.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Great little game! Simple, charming, relaxing. Sort of Subnautica meets Power Wash Simulator. I don't know if this is is worth the full $20, I'd put it more in the 10$ range. And it'd be nice if there was more to do with the loddles, like setting up farms to feed them, or ways to change forms as adults. But despite all that, it's still a good game!
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: I've waited for this game for quite some time, as I followed Moon Lagoon on TikTok. Loddlenaut is charming, well-meaning, and solidly-built on a mechanical level.Unfortunately, at least for me, it feels like the game runs of out ideas by 45 minutes and then you're left with linear progression in an "open" map. You collect SO MUCH trash that *can* be recycled after you've already bought every upgrade in the game. There's a whole Loddle breeding system that's not functionally necessary besides giving Moon Lagoon the abiltiy to make TikToks about it. I was waiting for something to pop up story or mechanic-wise where Loddles would be important. Such as needing X amount of a certain breed to accomplish Y task. Nope, entirely optional. I want to be explicitly clear: I did not expect a huge long-running campaign. That said, the ending still kind of just... shows up. You can tell the game wants you to be nostaglic for everything and bittersweet as you pack up your home cave to leave, but I'd just arrived 2 hours before. I thought I had like, an entire other "use all the techniques you've learned to defeat pollution" area left to clean. Nope. I recommend buying this, but I also worry that once the TikTok and content creator bump wears off the Recent Reviews will downshift into "Mixed" or "Negative" as randos who didn't have the outside context of relaxing lo-fi TikToks find the game and feel like they got a tech demo for a larger concept. Final criticism: for a game about cleaning up the ocean and sporting a Whale & Dolphin Conservation logo... they don't really talk about conservation in any meaningful way. The story kind of just acknowledges pollution exists, the company that did the pollution sucks for doing that polluting, and then we don't go to the natural follow-up of talking about the sci-fi company in a way that truly makes it an analogy for real-world corporate pollution. In the world of Loddlenauts, pollution has no real teeth. Nothing dies. Nothing is irredeemably changed, really. You just zap it with your goofy tools and boom: everything's fine again. I had fun with it, but it could've used a few more months in the oven to become a truly memorable title.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there was an option to give a game a neutral recommendation, because while this isn't a bad game, it has a lot of shortcomings that leave me pretty underwhelmed & disappointed.The first and main complaint that I have, is the the Loddles, the main staple of the game and what it is named after, offer practically nothing to the gameplay. Adult Loddles can have specific powers, but I never felt the need to bring them with me anywhere, especially since I didn't want them to spread goop around if I was attempting to clean someplace up. There really is no incentive to interact with the Loddles other than "hehehe cute little guy". My second issue is that the ending was just kind of... nothing. No interesting reveal, no twist, no nothing. You just finish cleaning the planet, and you leave. This especially felt like a slap in the face because some of the holobadges really felt like they were leading up to something. But there's just no payoff, just a bunch of little bits of dialogue that lead nowhere.My final issue is the inventory system. It's practically pointless. The only time you'll probably have to worry about having a full inventory is at the very end of the game, where there's the most diverse amount of trash. It just forces you to go all the way back o the closest fast travel point to dump your inventory, and they only show up in locations AFTER you've cleaned them, y'know, when you've already finished picking up all the items.It isn't a bad game, it just feels like it needs more.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good, but tedious!I was a kickstarter backer so I've been waiting patiently to get it, and it's just as cute and fun as I was expecting it to be!The only criticisms I really have for the game are small nitpicks that could probably be easily fixed.  Getting from place to place is *Very* slow.  You don't unlock fast-travel until you clean out an area, and especially later in the game once you get farther out from your base, that makes things *very* annoying to have to spend 2 minutes going back to your base and then going all the way out to where you were just to unload all your junk and continue cleaning.  I think I would have preferred either having the ship be drive-able, just having fast travel unlock the second you find an area, or even really just more boost upgrades??  It drains way too fast.Also things like the rate at which pollution goes back up in areas where you've already cleaned, and the fact that Lottles can over-populate which forces you to get rid of some (This one confuses me the most, I feel like there should just be a cap at which point they stop spawning, making it a thing where you have to pick and choose who can stay seems really strange)For a game that (as I understand it) is meant to be a fun cutesy meditative clean up type thing, the tedium and annoyance of certain aspects really seems to break the vibes it's set up.  I do recommend it, but I hope the devs can change some of these smaller aspects to make the game a bit more relaxing.

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenaut is a short (ca. 8h if you take your time, but it can be rushed through in less than half the time), very casual, relaxing, cute-looking, undersea clean-up game with additional, very basic mechanics for crafting and creature raisingYou're playing a custodian tasked with cleaning up an ocean planet after a big corporation left it. Unsurprisingly, you'll find out that the corporation was more interested in profit than in sustaining the planet's ecosystem. As such, there's a lot of pollution to clean up.That's pretty much all the story there is. There is no big secret or mystery to discover - your task is simply to clean up the planet and leave. While doing so, you can also raise cute little creatures called "loddles" (they seem to be mix of fish and axolotls), but they don't have much relevance for the story and don't affect the outcome.The game's main mechanic is the clean-up process. You start with a laser tool that can clean "goop" from plants and walls, which can be done very conveniently by just aiming and keeping the left mouse button pressed. You'll also find trash items floating around that you can collect and recycle into crafting materials at your base. As you explore the map, you'll encounter other forms of pollution that your laser tool cannot handle. For those, you need to craft new tools with the resources that you collected.The map isn't particularly large, but has enough room for diverse biomes and memorable landmarks. Exploration is rewarded with collectibles, but there are only 9 items to collect, and they don't have any effect on the gameplay - they just give you some background information as well as an achievement.While exploring, you need to watch your oxygen level - if it drops to zero, you get auto-returned to your base, but you'll use some of your inventory. You can craft upgrades for your suit that allow a bigger oxygen tank and faster movement, but their number is very limited. I crafted all upgrades (apart from a few story-locked ones) halfway through the game and was a bit disappointed that there wasn't more.You'll meet cute creatures called "loddles" that you can clean, feed, evolve into various mature forms, and release into the biomes you've discovered. The creatures are adorable and interacting with them is fun, but as a game mechanic, they feel very basic. You can evolve them into 13 different forms by hand-feeding them various plants, fruits, or crafted dishes, and you can craft toys for them - but that's it. They don't interact with each other, they have very little effect on their environment (though that may change with future updates), and they are completely optional for the game's story. This is not a creature-ranching game like (for example) Slime Rancher - you can't build corrals or feeders, the loddles don't produce anything, and different types of loddles share the same behavior. I suppose full-fledged ranching mechanics would have been misplaced in a game about restoring an ecosystem, but I would have appreciated more variety in the loddles' abilities and behavior.There are no enemies and there is no combat, in case that matters to you.I played this game while I wasn't feeling well, so that I couldn't focus on any complex tasks. Loddlenaut's zen-like clean-up routine worked pretty well for me in that state, and I didn't mind that the crafting and creature-raising mechanics were so basic. If I had been at full capacity, though, I would probably have gotten a little bored - I did experience that toward the end of the game, when I was feeling better. That said, the devs have announced that they will keep adding content and mechanics to the game, and some of their ideas sound like they would add a bit more complexity.The game uses stylized low-poly 3D graphics that you can also (if desired) pixelate to various degrees. I found the environments vibrant and beautiful, the colors capture the magic of a subaquatic environment. Plants sway mesmerizingly in the draft or periodically release air bubbles (which you can use to refill your oxygen tank). The textures are a bit plain, but I suppose that was a conscious decision to keep the production costs in check.The game's sound effects are evocative and fitting. The music contributes to the relaxed, meditative atmosphere - while the music of other cozy games is sometimes so repetitive that it gets on my nerves, I listened to this game's soundtrack throughout my entire playing time. The music doesn't stop when the game loses focus, though, which can be annoying if you need to concentrate on something else.The game does not feature any voice acting. You have a supervisor gives you tasks and advice from orbit, and that would have been a good candidate for voice acting, but it's far from necessary in a game like this (and may also explode the budget).The game provides basic screen settings such as a resolution selector, a screen mode toggle, an FPS limiter, but no other graphics options whatsoever apart from a pixelation setting with 3 stages (none, default, chunky). Four separate volume sliders let you finetune your acoustic experience.Controls can be fully remapped, you can assign 2 different keys plus one mouse function plus one controller function to any action. It's great to see that these indie developers implemented such comfortable rebind options when even triple-A publishers sometimes neglect them. The game also offers invert toggles for both axes, a camera sensitivity slider, and a toggle that switches between "hold" and "on/off" for your speed boost.The UI is intuitive and efficient. A "scan" function highlights pollution, loddles, and installations in your vicinity. Inventory stacks can be put into storage or machines with a single click. What's missing, is a) a way to scroll through the rows of your inventory (currently, only the top row is always visible, and while you can expand it to view your full inventory, it would be convenient to have a way to simply scroll through the rows one by one), and b) a way to set waypoints on the map and have them show up in your compass (as well as a permanent compass marker for your home base), because navigation in a 3D space can still be a bit confusing.You can save the game anytime, which is great. The game has room for three profiles, but each profile has only one save, and you cannot switch a game in progress to a different profile.I did not encounter any bugs. While the game doesn't have a lot of content, the existing content feels very polished.I recommend Loddlenaut to players who are looking for a relaxing clean-up experience in beautiful environments with charming creatures. Just don't expect the crafting options of Subnautica, the ranching mechanics of Slime Rancher, or the creature variety of either - this game is far more basic and casual in design. The price does seem a little high for the amount of content offered here, though, so you may want to wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, the game is mostly fine. However, it has a mechanic that really ruined the vibe for me. The areas you've already healed up re-contaminate overtime, which just makes me feel like my progress is completely pointless. I didn't want to engage with the pet sim side of the game because of how the little guys kept getting gooped up and it became a seriously repetitive task to un-goop them.The other thing that really irked me was the inventory management. I seriously went back and forth between the last area and the closest fast travel 5-6 times to drop off a full inventory and that's before mentioning the vacuum upgrade you get for clearing microplastics has a finite capacity, and I forgot to empty that half the time so then I just had to go back across a wide trench to clear it out, or just do without clearing microplastic that visit and clean as much goop as possible instead.Fast travel is unlocked at 100% decontamination of an area which will seem like a cool reward until you get to the later areas and then wish it unlocked at something closer to 70% just so you can beeline getting it and worry less about a full inventory.I wanted to give this game a recommend because I loved the demo and I enjoyed it, but it's seriously held back by things that made it feel tedious in the final third, without sufficient upgrades to "tech out" of some of the slog. You can't make yourself go faster, so crossing the trench from the campus to dump off goods was its own kind of slog.I think all the game's flaws would've been fine, though, if not for the recontamination part. I don't feel like I'm unlocking more of a garden to play with my pets in, I feel like I'm opting to play Power Wash simulator with a more appealing art style. I guess that's fine, but it's not entirely what I expected.I might return to this for achievements but I really would've liked to engage with the game's main draw more without being so annoyed by my work just being erased for the sake of padding.

_childDocuments_.review: A charming, cozy, relaxing exploration game with great progression and resource collecting!!Loddlenaut first captured me with its art style. _childDocuments_.review: In  you're an interstellar custodian tasked with cleaning up a heavily polluted planet after a megacorp has left it in shambles. You play as an interstellar custodian sent to clean up the planet of GUP-14 after a space-faring megacorp called GUPPI left it behind full of oil spills, pollution, junk and dirty murky waters. As you clean up the destroyed environment you will find remnants of GUPPI’s buildings left behind and their tech. Along the way you will meet alien-type fish called Loodles. Protect them, clean up their home and feed them to help them grow and develop unique traits to help them survive on their polluted planet while it heals. In this game you scoop up trash, zap clean gunk with your laser and recycle trash. The map is divided up into areas getting more complex as you go along until you ultimately get to GUPPI headquarters and the source of all the pollution and destruction. Along the way you will be able to upgrade your suit, tools and get new gadgets to help make cleaning up easier and more efficient. You do need to be aware of your oxygen levels (as all of your work is done underwater). Two ways you can replenish your oxygen is returning to your base or crafting a circular gate (bubble) you can make with easy to find crafting materials. This game is wholesome and geared towards a younger crowd but everyone can enjoy it for its relaxing pace. There is no combat or gore. The only thing you have to worry about is your oxygen running out on occasion. The game is polished and runs smoothly. I used a keyboard and mouse, although the game does say it supports controllers. Also you cannot remap the controls.In the beginning I did find it tedious to have to return to home base or get to an oxygen ring to replenish my oxygen (upgrades eventually help and crafting a reusable oxygen ring you can carry). I just wanted to explore without that hassle. It would be nice to have the ability in settings to turn off the oxygen meter for a more casual relaxed gameplay. I also wish we had more inventory space at times. You can store stuff in your ship inventory but your ship is not available at a new location for storage or fast travel until you 100% clean the area. Now visually the game is basic, with pixelated shapes of the main character and the Loodles that pop with color against the brown palette of the ocean bed. Depending on how pixelated you like your art you can choose between 3 styles, default, no pixels or a chunky look. The soundtrack for this game is so relaxing. Really serene and mellow as you go along and clean up the garbage around you. Once you get some upgrades and find your groove cleaning up the ocean it is a very relaxing game. Part of the game's proceeds go towards the WDC (Whale and Dolphin Conservation), so not only is it a game with a lot of meaning but you're doing good while having fun. Also the Loddles are adorable, do not forget to feed them and pet one. 🐟
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: In general, I will recommend this game, but only if it is on sale. The gameplay and music are very relaxing, and the loddles are very cute. The only drawback is that it is quite short, hence why getting it on sale is when it will be worth the money.That being said, the last two achievements, which is to get all the loddle evolution and to reach max loddle capacity, are not worth your sanity. Basically the summary of the last four hours I played today:1. Take loddles home2. come back to look for eggs. If I don't find the egg before it hatches (which was 100% of the time, as I don't think the scanner showed any unique sign for this), try to find the baby loddle (again, good luck with that, because all loddles have the same colour on the scanner)3. If successfully acquire baby loddle, take it home and feed it the food required to get the evolution4. deal with all the starving and depressed loddles5. Get more food coz you fed all the loddles and they're still hungry6. Release your least favourite loddles if you run out of spaceBasically this game loop was all I did for trying to accomplish those two goals, and I basically became the worst pet owner in the world to my beloved loddles, policing what they ate, starving them whenever I had to leave the house, and then kicking out the inferior evolutions to make space for the superior evolutions.Ultimately, I did enjoy this game, but the grinding near the end did expose some of the flaws in the game. If you just want to play it as a cleaning simulator, go for it, but I would still recommend to not try for those achievements. If I want to be a cruel god, I'll play Black And White

_childDocuments_.review: Very short but sweet game about cleaning up the ocean. Simple gameplay, no rush, all cozy. My only question is where those little devices from the demo went; they'd clean in a small radius around them. Perhaps they were deemed useless?My only negative about this game is that the boost is way too short, and you only get one upgrade for it. Perhaps a second or third tier to the upgrade could be implemented in the future? Another suggestion, for the perfectionists, is a device that helps keep the entire biome its in clean, kinda like a water filter that automatically collects garbage or microplastics. This would definitely help players who want to keep their biomes absolutely 100% clean.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a well-polished, calming, absolutely adorable game, I highly recommend Loddlenaut. The point of the game is to go around cleaning up areas of the ocean, and in the process you discover cute little Loddles that you can pet, feed, and play with. You can also upgrade your gear and build a few things around the areas to help make your clean-up job easier. A very cute, satisfying game!
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenaut is an adorable underwater cleaning sim where you play as a little diver guy cleaning the ocean after a major organization has left it in a sorry state. This was such a cute and relaxing experience. The soft visuals and sound design make for a sweet and cozy time, and I especially enjoyed meeting the different kinds of Loddles. I wish they had had more of a role in the game, as they feel more like background props that you could ignore if you wanted to, but I still loved breeding different traits onto them and caring for the different ones in each biome. There was lots to explore in this game and a lot of things to clean, and collecting the 100% was super satisfying. I might have liked the game to be longer, with more to clean up and especially more to do with the recycled bits, but I still loved this game and its cute creatures, and I would easily recommend it to anyone who likes cozy games with underlying messages of environmentalism.

_childDocuments_.review: It's almost good, some features are just tedious, especially later on when you have to spend time going back and forth between base and the objective+Power washing, garbage collection, lawn mowing, and pet maintenance. A great game for people who find casual housekeeping relaxing.+Suicide cuts down travel time in half, and your only punishment is dropping some items+/- Fast travel requires a biome to be fully clean. I think this is fine because it heavily motivates you to finish the job, but it does add a lot of padding by not coming in sooner+/- microplastics give you an insane amount of plastic material-boost doesn't get a speed upgrade, taking several minutes to return from an objective to a fast travel point even with rings dotting the path-boost upgrade is way too small, only adds a few seconds-vacuum upgrade is way too small, only a 3rd of an area gets cleaned before I need to return to base to dump microplastics-no backpack inventory upgrade. I have to spend huge chunks of the game ignoring pieces of trash because my inventory is full until I spend a lot of time returning to base-Loddles are locust puppies; they devour the land, overpopulate quickly, and whine for your help way too often. _childDocuments_.review: This is a simple and relaxing cleaning game! It is easy, and the story took me about 4 hours to finish, though the achievements are taking me a bit longer. The game is worth picking up on sale, as finishing 95% of what the game has to offer in about 4 hours for full price ($20) might be a turn off. I can see the replay potential, like speed running the story, or trying to create full biomes of specific types of loddles, but beyond that there isn't much to the game.Now some problems I had were the controls, and the loddles being a background/ambient element. The controls were weird, and hard to get used to (I am on mouse and keyboard fyi). As for the loddles, they are only really affected by the goop, and once you clean them they don't need any interaction from the player. They breed and grow all on their own, and it feels like they could be excluded and still have the game be fun, and enjoyable, if not a bit more empty.Overall its a nice game, and something easy to grind the achievements for, if you're a completionist. I'd give it a 7/10 it's really cute, and fun but there isn't much to the game overall.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so adorable!!! Very fun too, loved every second of it. It's a very chill underwater cleanup game! I adore underwater games/levels so this was a blast for me! _childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: I am in love!I've been in a game rut for a while and I think my tastes have changed, so it's been hard finding something that scratched the itch. I needed something engaging, but not overwhelming or stressful. Something that gave me a sense of achievement without having to work my butt off. Something aesthetically nice.Ohhhh man. I guess cleaning up goop and feeding fish was my niche here.I love the controls, and normally I don't like underwater feel in games, but this one is great. The controls are super duper intuitive and easy to learn, and I adore the Loddles! They're SO cute, and every time I think I'm getting bored with them, I get a new evolution of one that makes me squeal.I'm curious if there's any late game content outside of checking on your environments and making sure they stay as clean as possible, and I don't anticipate personally finding much enjoyment from that if that is all there is, but for now I love it and I'm very happy I gave it a try. Can't want to get back in it the next chance I can.EDIT: I have finished the game. It has a very logical finish and, I'll be honest, I was sobbing my way through the last little bit. I ran into my original Loddle and moved him from the first area I cleaned to the last and... WOW, that got me for some reason. You don't need to do a ton to help these babies along, but they really do leave a lasting impact on you. Maybe it's the pet mechanic? Or them singing along with your sensor?I'm happy where this left things. Normally I'm an "hour per dollar spent" kinda gamer but this game is a perfect exception.I hope we get DLC in the future or a sequel. More of this ocean to clean up or a whole new planet that needs help with their own unique creatures.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Super chill game, cleaning the biomas is very satisfying and relaxing. As a bonus, you'll befriend some cute creatures called loddles, which have different evolutions depending on what they eat. It's exciting when you find out that one of your loddles has evolved to a new, unknown type. Also, you can pet the loddle (very important).If you're looking for a comfy game, this is a really good choice!
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: 3-7+ hours to complete, Loddlenaut is an underwater open-world cleaning and pet sim. Restore biomes by removing oil and trash then replant native flora and re-introduce the wildlife, the Loddles. Depending on what they eat or what you feed them as they grow up, they can change into one of 13 different types! They can follow you around and help clean up areas, but they usually stay where you put them and can play with crafted toys.  Admittedly, there isn’t much of a story – the company that caused all the problems already got shut down, you’re just the guy hired to clean up the aftermath. No enemies, no puzzles, nothing time-sensitive, no quick time events, and nothing ridiculously grindy. It’s a colorful game with plenty of things to do, especially with the most recent update, and the only thing I can say it lacks is a photo mode.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for May 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before June 4th, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.I wish cleaning the ocean was this fun. Loddlenauts is just a chill game. You swim in the ocean, blast away pollutants, clean up microplastics, and find Loddle, essentially a cute fish friend who you can help out. There’s a large world with sunken ships, large reefs, and interesting locations to find, as well as challenges and a ton of stuff to clean up. However there’s not a lot of danger or challenge from what I have seen, it’s overall a pretty chill game. Even when I went the wrong way, the game pretty much says “Your goal is not that way, but go explore if you want”. The cleaning will be repetitive to some, but there are a lot of games like this that work in the same way. Think Powerwash simulator for something similar but this is far cuter.Pick this up if you want to just enjoy swimming in the water or exploring the deep. This will work great with young children, but even adults need a game to unwind with. Not everything can be about shooting baddies, sometimes just picking up a little plastic and turning it into a new device you’ve been needing is what works, and that’s what Loddlenauts has. _childDocuments_.review: It is a very cute game, around 6 hour completion for me but I plan to revisit to make more loddles in the future.
