_childDocuments_.review: This is a reluctant thumbs down - it's a very relaxing, cute, fun and in many ways well designed game, just too short and limited. The small amount of content present just doesn't justify the relatively high price.I'd give this a thumbs up if there was a bit more to the map, more things you could build, more plants, some random generation for replayability, etc. But although the game is at version 1.1 it feels like a well-polished early access game, still waiting to be filled out with more content.There are a lot of missed opportunities in the craftable items, most of which have minimal utility. The oxygen recharge ring is a major exception, being able to recharge your oxygen to full and clean loddles. However there is no need for more than one (you can just deconstruct it and redeploy it whenever you need). The light building is marginally useful in a few dark spots but not worth the effort of building. You can cook combined food items for the loddles, but there is no real benefit over just feeding them the raw fruit you can collect. You can build them toys, which you can watch them play with (and this will particularly boost the playful personality type) but like the food there is no real need to do so.Many buildings that would be typical of survival-ish games are absent -  you can't build a plant pot that lets you grow your own plants, which would be very useful for feeding loddles with fruit outside of where it grows natively. There is no furniture your Player Character can interact with, or homes for the loddles to chill in.In short, its a cute and fun game, but ironically it's not deep enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I was conflicted about this game because the core gameplay seems to work well for what it is and is very engaging. But given the short playtime, it's hard for me to recommend this game at full price.At its core, there are two parts to the game. The first part consists of cleaning up pollution, and the second is interacting with "loddles", fictional fish/axolotl creatures. I guess the idea is that you SHOULD be cleaning, but the devs are hoping you'll get distracted and play with the fish.The problem is that there's nothing useful you can do with the loddles, and I found it was way easier to just ditch them and clean solo because letting them follow you around while cleaning is detrimental. If they get too close to grime, they get dirty and you have to manually redirect them to swim into a device to clean them off, otherwise, they generate more pollution and work for you. I mean yes, I could play with the loddles and watch them grow into different shapes, but at the same time... what incentive do I have to do so other than "wow these are so cute"? It doesn't advance the game, and you have to progress the story to unlock most of the loddle interactions anyway.The cleaning can also be annoying at points due to the travel system. Some of the areas are quite large, but you don't gain the ability to fast travel to that area until AFTER you clear 100% of the pollution. With some of the later areas, there's a notably annoying amount of time wasted where you have to fast-travel across the map multiple times to fill up/drop off the items in your inventory.I will say that I appreciated the story not being too heavy-handed with the "corporation ruined the environment" plot. I get it, we all know corps are bad, I'm just a bit tired of seeing it used in these sorts of games. The good thing was that in this game, it was much more bearable. I appreciate this game taking a more restrained approach in that regard. I also thought the music was pretty cool in that it changed gradually as you cleaned up areas, with more layers and instrumentation being added as an area improved.I finished the game with most achievements unlocked in just over three and a half hours. The only achievements I didn't get were the ones that involved playing more with the loddles and one where you intentionally let your suit's oxygen deplete several times.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenaut is a frustrating game to me. I'm aware how silly that may sound on the store page of a cute little game like this, but let me explain. In Loddlenaut you clean up industrial pollution and raise little fish creatures that bond with you. This is all well and good, but the game never really goes anywhere beyond that premise. In almost every section of the game (story, creature collecting, exploration, etc) the game teases more complexity beyond the basic premise and then doesn't do anything with it.It almost feels like the game is too afraid to be anything more than a "cute indie game with small critters". I mean it's not even willing to fully stick with its eco-friendly message and basically says it's not for us to judge. It's a shame since I think there's a lot of potential here with Loddlenaut, but the game never followed up on it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: It's... inoffensive. Cute art style, cute critters, mediocre and bland gameplay, and a short and unengaging story. I saw so many reviews wishing for a "neutral" recommendation option, but defaulting to thumbs-up, so I'll balance it out with a thumbs-down. It's not worth full price, but if you can get it half-off, it's worth it purely for the cute factor. 4/7; mediocre, but of interest for game devs looking for unique aesthetics.One piece of advice for Moon Lagoon: get rid of the air requirement. It's trivial to bypass after the first excursion and doesn't really provide any tension. The main draw of your game is immersing oneself in the cute world, so forcing the player to regularly pay attention to a game mechanic is counter-productive.

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenaut is extremely charming and bug-free. It has fun visuals and great, crunchy sound effects, and it feels very rewarding to play. It's one of those games where you can go monkey mode and click to win which is  up my alley. The Loddles are extremely cute, but the game doesn't do much to explain how the Loddle evolution process or how reproduction works. I'm sure it's a very simple thing to figure out simply by feeding the Loddles, but they aren't interesting enough to be committed to when you consider the other part of the game:I picked this up for $15 on sale in January 2024, and then after playing it to completion I refunded it. The game is marketed at $19.99 regular price. Twenty dollars for a game that can be beaten in or around two hours (the length until the Steam refund window) is not value.I understand now that the Loddles are really there to be kind of like a pseudo-Tamagotchi: they are just an artificial time sink to occupy you past the refund window. Maybe that isn't how they were designed to be, but their functionality is very basic and to get all of the Steam achievements--particularly the one where you have to fill up every biome in Loddlenauts with Loddles--it is obvious that it is meant to take numerous hours to grow every Loddle and have them make plenty of Loddle babies which would no-doubt take time to do, and that component of gameplay just isn't interesting enough or rewarding enough to be worth the price tag of the game. The extent of making Loddle babies is literally just waiting for them to grow. You can feed them food yourself, but left to their own devices they will sustain themselves so long as they are in a clean biome. And that's it. That's how growing Loddles works: you just let the game idle. Player intervention is not needed. How is that even remotely a fun gameplay component? It isn't, which makes me believe this is only implemented to make you intentionally waste your time for a petty achievement. Maybe I'm pessimistic about this, but we are also talking about twenty dollars regular price.I would purchase this again in a heartbeat if it was half of the price as to what they are asking. For emphasis on this,  and it has over  times the amount of content. It's absolutely baffling to me that any publisher would think it is acceptable to slap a twenty dollar sticker on this. This is 100% where all of my problems lie, and while I implore anyone to play this cute little experiment, in this day and age 20 dollars can go a  way, and it should. And this game does  provide the value that they are asking from you.

_childDocuments_.review: 7 hours 1/10 1 Yes, for many achievements you don't need a guide, but I used  to mop up the last few achievements No No Not really, although getting all the different versions felt a bit like a grind No No No No No difficulty setting NoI have been looking at Loddlenaut since it was announced. Cleaning in video games is just so much fun and also having to take care of such cute critters, it sounded just like the game for me. And I wasn't wrong in my judgment, as the game is adorable! You play as this human whose job it is to clean up the ocean after some sort of company made a mess by doing some experiments or something like that. So you'll clean up all the litter that is left behind, but also some sort of purple goo. You'll go from region to region to clean up the mess, equipped with a handy scanner to tell you if there is any mess close by. While having an area clean enough, you'll see those little creatures start living there. All the items you pick up you'll recycle and build upgrades with them, like a bigger oxygen tank, or being able to suck up more plastic with your plastic vacuum. After cleaning an area for 100% there will also appear a hub that can store items for you and that allows you to transport you back and forth between the hobs. However, I wish that it wouldn't take 100% cleaning an area before the hub unlocks. So many times I just needed 1 more backspace to collect those last few items before 100% the area or just ran out of oxygen too early. Or you have to go back to the base to buy a new upgrade. In the beginning, I didn't mind the back and forth between a new area and the base area or an already unlocked hub, but after a while, it became a bit annoying. I'm so happy that none of the achievements are missable. This made it possible to just enjoy the game and not to worry about the achievements while playing through it. I'm a little unsure if this was the best strategy as it made the time to get all the different loddles a waiting game, instead of doing it while doing other things, but this way I only had to look that up after finishing the game. The hardest achievements are to maximize the population in each area and create all those different loddles types. A HUGE tip for that last one.. in the logs you can see which loddles you already have found. On the Steam forum, the developers said they were thinking about adding a way to easily see which ones you're missing, but for now, checking back the logs is doable. I had a lot of fun with Loddlenaut, and it shows an important message about how we litter our oceans and that it impacts not only the human race but all kinds of ecosystems. I give Loddlenaut 4.5 out of 5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: As a cozy game enthusiast, I wholeheartedly recommend Loddlenauts!  This is a short game, but a pleasure from start to finish!  It's simple, low pressure, very cute and relaxing.  The graphics are colorful and cute, the music very relaxing and pleasant.  The loddles are adorable!  This game really consists of 3 things - cleaning up the different areas and collecting trash to recycle, using the recycled goods to upgrade your cleaning abilities, and helping the little creatures called Loddles to evolve into their adult forms.  It's simple and obviously was very well thought out, because this game doesn't feel lacking in any area.  In fact, my only complaint is that the game isn't longer!I did get 8 hours out of this, at a very casual pace.  I did also 100% it.  This is a great choice for a cozy day in, or just something to hit up in short bursts when you have a little time to spare.  Excellent game devs, this is one wholesome, fun and relaxing good time!

If they update with more content, I'll update my review because it was enjoyable and very cute.Also, small but critical complaint - the fast travel mechanism should be adjusted. You should have fast travel access as soon as you discover a new area, not after you clean it. You're often required to go back to home base before being able to clean it completely and it leads to a lot of unnecessary swimming back and forth (probably to extend the already short game time). _childDocuments_.review: Swim around, clean some toxic waste, pet a loddle, feel better about everything. But also a little bit sad, because the work never ends. That's kind of the point. There's hints of a really interesting story and world building, but we never get the full story. The gameplay is extremely chill, with the oxygen system being the only nod to the "survival" genre, and easily and quickly overcome for most players, so it quickly gets out of the way of the cosy atmosphere.Accessibility notes: The game features a number of nice accessibility options, include settings for degree of pixelation of the art, control remapping (both mouse+keyboard and controller are natively supported), individual volume controls, screen resolution and framerate adjustments, camera adjustments, and even removing some of the in-game text. There’s a map to help orient the player, and a log book to keep track of current goals. The latter two features are well-integrated into the theme of the game, much like the multiple indicators for the oxygen and boost meters.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really cute and doesn't play terribly, but its just not enticing to play. _childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: I backed this on Kickstarter because it was such a cute looking game, but after finishing the storyline I find myself... underwhelmed. 3 hours of gameplay for $20? No thanks - and I paid even more for Beta access. Here are the things I liked and didn't like about it:Likes:-Adorable - Baby loddles are very cute, duh-Satisfying to clean - makes you feel like you're doing a good thing-Cute music and sound designDislikes:-Loddles feel like more of a burden than a reward - they follow you around when cleaning new biomes and ALWAYS get goopy again! You have to stop what you're doing and remove them or they'll spread the goop again and keep getting dirty-Length of play time - I played the game to completion in about 3 hours, and I was taking a pretty relaxed approach I think. There's really not much to do once the story is finished either. Sure you can reclean the biomes you've already finished, or play with the loddles I guess? They don't really seem to do much, even with the toys, and once they're no longer babies, they lose they cuteness.-Redundancy - I like that they made an effort to increase playtime, but at this point the goop and trash just slowly returns and you just clean the same things over and over again. A game like Powerwash Simulator is great because you get the satisfaction of having everything be completely squeaky clean all at once. But once you move on to the next area in Loddlenaut, the previous area is immediately back down to 99%TLDR: Overall, I'd give the game like a 5/10 - I wouldn't say it's worth it. Maybe pick it up on sale and enjoy it for a few hours. If they ever add more to the game, I'll amend my review.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: I had a great time with this game. Being able to return a planet to it's natural state and to be able to play around with the Loddles was so much fun!!! Lots of great little things in here. Will definitely be getting DLC and purchasing any sequels if/when they come out. The only thing that distressed me was the fact that the pollution returned really fast. Other comments on this game have mentioned that the pollution returning was a great mechanic for you to go back and check on old areas (and loddles!)For me, knowing the pollution was returning and not being able to ensure every area was at 100% before 'leaving the planet' left me without a sense of completion. Maybe in the end game, there should be a mechanic to spray the areas with a permanent pollution repellent to keep the areas from growing more pollution? That way, you can clean up any remaining pollution and have fun with the loddles before you leave, knowing the planet is going to STAY 100% clean once you're gone. This would help my 'end-game' anxiety- I literally just finished my first save file, and I am feeling antsy about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty short game. I finished it around the five hour mark.It's a very relaxed game about sucking up garbage in an ocean. _childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenaut is meant to be a casual, relaxing game, but it's actually quite boring and even though it took me less than 4 hours to complete I was glad when it was over.At first this looks like a simple, child-friendly version of Subnautica, but after a while you realize that what you do within the first 10 minutes of the game is all it has to offer. You clean up stuff and collect trash. And you use the trash to upgrade your equipment to clean up stuff and collect trash a bit more efficiently. There is no challenge, no variety in the tasks you do and the places you visit all look very similar to each other.The creatures that live in the ocean (so called 'loddles') are cute and there are a few different species, but ultimately they don't serve any purpose and you can't interact with them in any meaningful way.Even the ending was boring. You simply clean yet another part of the map and that's it.I honestly have no idea why this game has so many positive ratings. I like casual games, I don't need hardcore challenges to be happy, but this played like a very simple mobile game with very limited content.I got the game basically for free from the May Humble Bundle, so whatever, I played till the end, so I guess I've played worse games. But if I would have bought this on Steam I would have refunded it for sure, no matter the discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Metaphorically, this game is pure love and compassion expressed in digital formPlaying felt like a self-care ritual: venturing to a new area, cleaning the ocean blue bit by bit, and welcoming new friends• The animations are beautiful• Plant life is teeming with a cute, neon aesthetic• Audio and soundtrack blend to create a seamless, bubbly and immersive experience• Soooo many combinations of Loddles!• Different upgrades for cleaning and feedingTook me about 5 hours to complete, an extra 2 or so to unlock all achievementsHighly recommended to anyone looking for a chill game that carries a wonderful message!

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game, I would recommend it if it was less than 5 bucks.Game is very, very short. Few hours are far enough to finish it, even by taking all your time. But despite this, I don't even want it to be longer, because tasks are very repetitive and I don't think adding new levels on the same gameplay loop would be an improvement.Game feels very empty, fishes have no purpose, the light crafting system is forgettable, maps between levels are empty. _childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a cute little game. It's great for anyone who enjoys a menial-task-simulator: SnowRunner, Power Washing, etc, and wants to help the most adorable little friends.The gameplay is kind of repetitive, I think by design, but you can take it in little bits and have big breaks just to vibe out watching, petting, & feeding the loddles.There are some minor UX annoyances. Feed a loddle in a biome that has spare loddle-slots and they stop following you. Attempt to feed them in a full biome and they refuse to eat. Petting the loddles is a bit awkward and slow, and sometimes it feels like they just don't respond.As someone who plays a lot of games, I do feel the game suffers from being a bit easy: the oxygen is generous, and recharge rings are cheap, and you can build more of them than you'd ever need. I feel like the difficulty is perfect for a relative newcomer to 3d (especially jetpack-style 3d) controls, or to kids.Ultimately though, my love of cuteness and simple tasks (my job requires a lot of thinking, so games that aren't Too Thinky are often very appreciated for winding down!) means I overall love this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenaut is for sure an amazing game that can run on low-end PCs without any issues. The game is vivid with a lot to do and explore. Basically your goal is to clean the ocean while you befriend Axolotls that can evolve to help you on your journey as well as gearing up to make your work faster and more satisfying. This game is recommended for casual players as well as achievement hunters (like myself).Good points- The game is easy to understand, the missions are easy to pick-up and to get along with- Cute pets that you can evolve and change colors. very self-explanatory- 6 Biomes to clear and explore with each one habving a well-crafted enviroment and diversity- 30 Missions that don't require time to be completed- A somewhat very cute and sad ending but extremely rewarding oneBad points- The game absolutely lacks so many Quality of Life features. For example when you order an axolotl to follow you, if you feed it, they will stop following you, which can be extemely annoying when you're farming or cleaning and you accidentally drop a food. Trust me this will be extremely annoying if you are in the late game or hunting for achievements. I at least spend a good chunk of the game trying to work around it- The achievements, although easy, two of them stand out the most: *Loddle Possibilities- Encounter all loddle evolutions: this one is a massive grind that you absolutely CANNOT do without a guide because you have no damn clue on how to breed every one of them. I basically spent 3 hours to get this single achievement. *Loddles Rule the World- Reach the maximum loddle capacity in all biomes: This is absolutely time consuming along with the above. There's no single reliable information on how they breed, their time to hatch and how you can fill the world with the maximum capacity. I really don't know how I was able to achieve this....- The game has limited resources (except plants) so if you end up using it wrongly, you may not be able to 100% in a single save file if you did something wrong- The game lacks character & basecustomization, as well as a more comprehensive and open breeding axolotl guide, because they can help immensely on the game but its an overlooked feature that you'll just use on late game for achievement.- It would be better if we had more detailed axolotl information without scrolling back and forth on their information tab as well as adding easier features. One that could be added as example "whistle" so you can select nearby axolotls of certain types to follow you, example only calling cleaners, etc.- Craftable items are basically useless except the oxygen ring. I have never used them on my file and they didn't matter the slightest.- Limited upgrade tree Conclusion: is it a good game? Yes it is! Will I reccomend it? probrably not. The lack of QoL really drags the game down. Will I create a new save file? No i won't even if you pay me to do so. Will I play Loddlenauts 2 if it releases? Absolutely6.8/10 Very good game but there's a lot left to be desired and added
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Its a nice little game that's super relaxing and the creatures are adorable! If you just need a simple short game for some spare time or for something like a steam deck its perfect for that! It runs perfect on the steam deck. (I pretty much only played it there)I do wish it had a little more content, since its fairly addicting lol (as with most cleaning/cleaning adjacent games I assume) hopefully some more content will be released, but Its okay with what it has, Its still a very enjoyable and relaxing experience.I'd also say this is a perfect game to get for anyone you know who likes cute and simple relaxing games, or just likes shorter games. I think you could start and end this game in a week, or even a weekend if you wanted.I loved spending time with the loddles in game, they are so cute and they have many cool variations that also add to the gameplay a little. I felt a little melancholy at the ending of the game, I wasn't expecting that lol (especially with such a short playtime lol), I got attached I guess.Over all I would recommend this game to pretty much everyone I know lol, I'd definitely pick this up on sale, and I hope more gets added over time, but if not its still a very solid game, and is very fun and relaxing. I'll definitely do another playthrough. Thanks to the devs for making a pretty relaxing game, I'll definitely be looking forward to any other games they release!

_childDocuments_.review: is the first development effort of independent studio  and was published by  on the 16th November 2023. It is an adorable, laid-back experience, in a tiny open world. The game’s content will last you around 6-7 hours and they’re well worth the price of admission, especially on a sale (I personally got the game from a bundle, which made it even cheaper).The story, told through somewhat uninspired, but graciously brief and even somewhat humorous logs or “Holo-badges” as the game calls them, is one of GUPPY corporation. A company of which its efforts where chiefly concentrated on refining the various flora of the planet GUP-14. GUP-14 is home to a boundless oceanscape and colorful and quaint plants of various shapes, sizes and colors, as well as “Loddles” little creatures, somewhere in a liminal zone between amphibian and fish, who give the game its signature name.The name of the game is collecting plentiful kinds of trash and cleaning an assortment of “goop” – which is  stand-in for oceanic pollution – as well as disposing of the remnants of the GUPPY corporation’s energy research and other debris, of which you learn more of through some clever environmental storytelling and the aforementioned Holo-badges. smudgy, lo-fi aesthetic and soft, PS2-adjacent finish, along with its minimalist color pallete and sleek really help to define the game’s signature and ever-palpable identity. The stellar work on the score by  is nothing short of ambient brilliance and clearly shows a musical mind that understood what the game was and how to transplant that headspace from game to sheet music.Gathering trash in this game is as zen as gaming gets and the mechanical loop is simple, but iterative and short enough to not outstay its welcome. The subsequent vibrancy and spotless cleanliness of the little biosphere you end up purifying never fails to illicit the appropriate levels of satisfaction with your one-man environmentalist superheroics.Truly, the only two things I could criticize about Loddlenaut is how short it is, as I’ll definitely miss the brief time I’ve spent with it (an ultimately grand problem to have, I must say!) and secondly, and quite a ways more seriously: the Loddles.Where trash-cleaning and goop-swiping and -lasering are the mechanical name of the game, as stated before, loddles are the literal name of the game and they’re supposed to be its heart… but their implementation leaves me puzzled. They’re cute enough, not extremely descript, nor memorable, but cute enough and distinguished and varied enough in appearance from specimen to specimen, that they possess some level of cuteness and aura, but not too much of the latter for me, which is a damn shame. Truly though – and this is the biggest problem – maybe I wouldn’t have even made comment of their design, if it wasn’t for the fact, that they’re just kind of “there” they never become the focus of the main gameplay loop, their evolution mechanics, which are required for achievement hunting are never well explained and really, throughout the whole experience, they just feel at best like a cute afterthought, with some mechanical purpose for environmental purification and bio-diversity, and at worse, they feel like a nuisance, null-and-void in purpose, annoying to upkeep, manage and clean whenever you find a new one and accidentally swim too close to it while cleaning.You see, leaving a dirty, goopy Loddle uncleansed can make their goop spread onto nearby flora with staggering speed and efficiency, setting back a lot of your progress in cleaning a given area. This effectively means that any time a dirty Loddle starts following you (and they won’t let go until they’re clean again) you need to drop everything and look for the nearest oxygen ring to clean them off.At the end, I didn’t even bother to name most of them, so 95% of my Loddles ended up possessing the brilliant name of “Loddle” (no, really, that’s the default) and becoming frankly indistinguishable in my mind’s eye. They only really became more than extra pollution spread prevention at the end of the game, where I had the displeasure of switching between 2-3 incomplete Steam guides to make up for the lack of care put into explaining the game’s Loddle evolution/breeding system inside of the experience itself and swimming around Loddles like an idiot, testing out different food combinations and waiting for them to turn hungry and transform into cocoons and eventually adults. I did all of this just for one achievement and while it wasn’t horrible (I’ve done worse for achievements, believe me), it was definitely not a high note to end the otherwise great experience off on.Either way, even with these design hiccups,  is a game I wholeheartedly recommend for its aesthetic brilliance, tactful musical composition and chill vibes, along with a pretty killer, simple gameplay loop at the start, that will be right up your alley if you enjoy the strangely captivating genre of “games that are just gamified real world labor”. I also hope a qualm or two of mine will end up being remedied in future updates (as the game still receives them from time to time), such as a better in-game walkthrough of Loddle evolution being added.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really adorable game that caught my attention with its style and gameplay. Its premise is really nice and simple too, so if you'd like a little game that helps you relax with some cute little sea critters, then this is for you!You start off pretty simple by picking up trash inside what will be your Home Base for the rest of the game, and once you familiarize yourself with the controls and tools at your disposal, you're well on your way to cleaning the rest of the ocean around you by going to certain biomes and checking off tasks. As you explore the world and clean up more pollution, you'll come across these little guys called "Loddles", which are not only adorable but also need your help to clean themselves off so they can feel safe again. They can't eat or settle down anywhere unless you put them through a little Bubble Bath, so take them back to the Bubble Ring device at your home base to clean them off. There's many different types of Loddles depending on how you raise and feed them, so try out different things with them whenever you can.The upgrades you earn by recycling trash and using the recycled bits at your station are great too, although you'll still be using your Bubble Gun most of the time. There's just enough variety and quality stuff around to make this game just perfect for what it is. I'd highly recommend giving it a shot if you have the time to spare.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty chill cleanup simulator, with an OST I can only compare to Minecraft’s Aether mod. A few mechanics could use a little work, but for the most part, it’s pretty solid. The only thing I really didn’t like about it is that certain species of Loddle have no chance of spawning in the natural world as they require either crafted meals or combinations of fruits that don’t spawn in the same biome. This means waiting for an egg to randomly spawn so you can get a baby Loddle without a contaminated evolutionary diet and then waiting for them to get hungry so that you can feed them the required food items for that specific evolutionary tree. There’s also no way of knowing the dietary requirements for the evolution of an unknown species without looking up a guide, so you could be stuck repeating this process for hours on end if you decide to go off of trial and error. Good luck trying to evolve two different species of Loddle at the same time, because any hungry Loddle in the immediate vicinity will have a nibble on whatever you throw in front of them. It makes for a considerable amount of grinding not found anywhere else in the game and throws off the pace quite drastically. In fact, this facet of gameplay singlehandedly made up a third of my overall playtime.Edit: There is now a method of preventing this thanks to the 1.2.1 update.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Just a heads up on this review. I played Loddlenaut, exclusively, on Steam Deck when I played it because I was sick and it was a simple enough game that I could play it and enjoy it while not feeling well. So know that I have no comments on how the game controls in any other fashion.Anyways.Loddlenauts is a super cute little game. You swim around and suck up trash of varying kinds to clean up the various coves. Clean up messes such as growths on plants or oil on the ground. Use trash items to recycle and get stuff to then make upgrades. Such as longer oxygen, faster swimming, etc. You can also get a scanner that helps you see trash you might have missed. Which I have comments on, but let's do the good first. You'll clean up an area and unlock a new one till you've unlocked all the areas and you're goal is to clean them, breed loddles, and make things beautiful and clean again.The Good-Super super cute design. The whole game is very cozy and super adorable. It was very very good vibes while I was playing it.-It handles SUPER well on Steam Deck. I played it with very little effort and didn't have any problems playing-It's super satisfying to play. In the same way that other cleaning games are fun, this game is very fun and cleansing as you slowly clean up the trash.-There's different kinds of trash you will have to unlock new equipment for. Like oil spills and microplastic. So there's the satisfaction of having something you couldn't clean up, but then getting what you need to be able to go back and finish and unfinished job.-The loddles are so darn cute! They make me smile. They come in so many different shapes and colors and it's fun to try and collect them all... though I do have an issue with this one. We'll get to that later though.-The game is explained very very well other than one or two things. I was never confused about what I needed to do. I love it when a game makes sure I don't have to flounder for who knows how long just trying to figure out wtf I'm supposed to do.-Sound design! All the sound design is delightful! The sound of your jet bubbling. The water. The loddles. Everything just sounds great and the music is very very chill and cozy.-While this game can EASILY be enjoyed by adults... it would also be a good game for kids. This would be a great game to use as a spring board to talking about conservation and wildlife protection and water pollution with your kid. Like from a general perspective to more in depth, such as discussing what EXACTLY a microplastic is once you get to where you're cleaning clouds of microplastic. So if your kid likes that kind of thing or if you are homeschooling. Hell even if you are not and just want to supplement your kids education at home. This is a solid game for that kind of learning.-The price isn't bad. I got to the end of the story and then spent time trying to breed loddles and got a little over 10 hours in the game with still having a few achievements to get. I can't tell you how long just the story took to beat as I played the game months ago now (and just realized I forgot to review it). But if you are achievement hunting the playtime isn't bad for $20. Though I'd see if you can get it around $15.The Bad-I mentioned the different kinds of loddles and collecting them. This is genuinely the ONLY part of the game I didn't enjoy. Because you don't find the different kinds of loddles. You have to breed them by giving them different kinds of fruit. It's INCREDIBLY tedious. Especially going to different areas where you swear you had a certain kind of loddle and you have to back and search high and low for this one loddle you need to give this piece of fruit to. I wanted to like this part, but it was just frustrating and the only achievements I"m missing are in regards to the loddles (and leaving the planet cause I won't leave till I finish the loddle quests). At some point I'll go back in and try again... but it was frustrating enough that I gave up. Maybe others won't have the kind of problems I did. Maybe if you are breeding them sooner in the story it's less of an issue. But I didn't breed much and it resulted in me having beat the game and needing to spend time making new loddles.-Resources in this game are weird. I got SO many resources and I really just didn't need many. Saving up for upgrades felt like it didn't take that long and at a certain point I was cleaning but had nothing to spend my resources on. Part of this is because stuff continues to get polluted after you clean it which.... is another thing I'm not fond of. On one hand it's nice to know that I can go and clean something again for the satisfaction. But it's also frustrating because it insinuates that even when we leave the planet things are just going to get dirty again. It doesn't affect the game play, but from a story perspective it's frustrating that my characters work feels like it will be in vain. But going back to the excess of materials it just... I dunno feels like it makes the progression a bit weird when I can get things in abundance as easily as I can.-The scanner can be damn near pointless sometimes. There were a number of times where I was using the scanner and I was missing something. Why? because it was like a single can and it's just so small that I was missing it. Spending forever swimming around trying to figure out where this ONE piece of trash is that I'm missing. It got real frustrating.OverallThis is a decent game. There's some things that are a bit frustrating but honestly none of it overrides the overall cozy vibe of the game. It's also one of those games where if you enjoy it, it's easily replayable. Like once I finish breeding all these loddles -_- wish me luck.... I'll probably replay the game at some point. It's a relaxing game! There's no danger. No fighting. Just cleaning the ocean and feeding cute little axolotl type creatures. It's a game that is nice to play when you wanna wind down or as I said... very good to play when sick. So yeah. The length is a bit short... but if you like the r/satisfying nature of the game you can play it again. A comparision in that regard I could give is that a lot of people complain about the length of the game Unpacking. I love that game and have zero problems with the length because I've played through the game 4 times because it's so satisfying and relaxing to play. Loddlenauts has that same vibe. So if you think you'll be a one and done... maybe the price is a bit much for you. But if you just enjoy cozy simple clean up games, this game can be fun and easily be replayed.So if you can get past the frustrating loddle breeding.... this game is a really really good addition to your cozy gaming catalogue in your library.Side note: Please know that I have also not played the game since the update! So this review includes NOTHING on that update! I just saw there was an update regarding the loddle breeding. So it may have improved. I will update my review upon playing the update.

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenaut is a fun and simple ocean cleaner game. Save the planets sea life by removing garbage, goop and other forms of harmful waste left by the corporation you're cleaning up after. The gameplay loop is very simple - sometimes repetitive - but the game does a good job of making sure it introduces new and fun ways to clean the sea floor. The sea life present (the Loddles) are adorable little creatures that can evolve into other, more unique forms!  The game has a majority of straight forward and easy achievements to unlock. Most of them you'll get by just playing through the story of the game and exploring the ocean. A few though, have some annoying little qualities too them. Mainly achievements tied to filling up areas of the map with Loddles and waiting on breeding. This took me a while to get and probably added an extra hour  of game time for it. Not that that's a terrible thing to happen but I found myself majority of this time just waiting around or trying to manipulate the game by moving Loddles here, there and everywhere for best egg spawn chances. Whatever though, it didn't take anything away from my initial enjoyment of the game.Play the game if you'd like a couple hours of an evening to help ocean life thrive after a corporation laid waste to the environment. It's got a fun soundtrack that just suits the games under-water vibe really well and the graphics/visuals are fun and comforting. I'd give this game a 6.5  /10. The devs did a good job - it allowed me to have fun just some repetitive aspects of the game reduces the score slightly for me. Thank you dev team, was an enjoyable time!

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenaut is a charming underwater adventure that combines environmental stewardship with cozy gameplay mechanics. As a birthday gift from my partner, it proved to be a delightful surprise, offering a unique twist on cleaning simulators by setting it beneath the waves. The game's core mission of purifying the ocean to create a sanctuary for the adorable Loddles provides both purpose and satisfaction.The cleaning mechanics shine as the game's strongest feature, complemented by a creative crafting system that gives collected trash a second life. Exploring the ocean depths while restoring them to their natural beauty creates a zen-like experience that's both relaxing and rewarding. The attention to detail in the underwater environments and the charming Loddle characters adds layers of charm to each cleaning expedition.While the game excels in many areas, the cooking and toy-making systems feel somewhat underutilized. These features, though present, lack the integration and encouragement needed to make them feel essential to the experience. Despite this minor shortcoming, the core gameplay loop remains engaging enough to keep you diving back in for more.For those seeking a peaceful gaming experience that combines environmental consciousness with relaxing gameplay, this oceanic cleanup adventure delivers a refreshingly different take on the genre. _childDocuments_.review: Loddlenauts is a game that feels like two games collided with Loddlenauts being the outcome. Game one is a clean-em-up where you traverse an open world map, collecting garbage, cleaning up goo and detritus and cleansing the ocean. Game two is a creature keeping and breeding game where you collect fish, feed them various foods from the map and give them entertainment and such in order to grow different varieties. Both aspects feel quite independent of one another. Sure, you can't have loddles in dirty areas but once you're done in an area you don't really have a reason to return to it unless you're gathering resources or attempting to grow some loddles. I think that some of the biggest misses with the game come from the fact that loddles could have helped you clear areas or could collect resources for you or help you on your adventure in some way, making them more beneficial. In addition to this, more tools would have been nice such as gardens for your home base or hatcheries or a means of moving eggs or feeders that you could set up in the biomes in an attempt to produce certain types of Loddles. Overall both parts of the game are good in their respective areas but I really wish there was more that gelled the two together or more depth to the respective parts that led to the two providing some kind of support for one another in some way or another. All in all the game looks great, controls well and has some nice QoL such as fast travel once you've cleansed an area. There's some minor collectables scattered around the map and you have some easy to use tools that make the game less of a chore and more of a casual cathartic clean up. Overall it's a decent game that could have been better with a little more thought put into the major components.

_childDocuments_.review: A cleaning sim/pet-raising sim game that had a handful of issues on launch that made me not recommend it; but thanks to the developers listening to feedback, most (though not all) of my concerns have been addressed since then. The cleaning gameplay has seen small adjustments that made big improvements, but raising loddles is still a rather boring process that's lacking in some valuable tools to help players keep track of them all. Though I'm no longer hesitant to give it a positive score, whether I think you'll enjoy it depends on if you want a cleaning sim or a pet-raising sim, because it currently does the former much better than the latter.  is a game about cleaning up the ocean of the far-off planet GUP-14 after the megacorporation GUPPI polluted then abandoned it. As you start clearing the waters, you'll be treated to interactions with the planet's native species: the loddles, big tadpole-like aliens similar in appearance to axolotls. In time, you'll turn the freshly-cleaned landscapes into their home, where you can help them grow and reproduce before sending them back into the wild to thrive. I originally wrote a review of this game a few days after launch with Version 1.0.0, and despite loving the demo, I was a bit disappointed with it. There was nothing fundamentally wrong with the overall design, but it was in need of some tweaking across the board. The updates that followed made efforts to address the problems I and other players had back then, and with the Goddles update having launched just a few days ago, I wanted to give it another shot.The core gameplay involves cleaning up the ocean of litter, microplastics, and goop until each location is clean enough to accommodate loddles again. ; but when the game first launched, it was held back by your character's small inventory, as the constant need to backtrack home to storage caused this daisy-chain of annoyances that broke the overall flow of the game. Now, though, the base inventory size is increased and an upgrade was introduced to expand it even further, giving you enough space that backtracking is minimized if not outright unnecessary in some areas when it used to demand multiple trips. It might be a small change in the grand scheme of things, but it helped streamline the gameplay to finally become as relaxing as I had originally hoped it would be.Most of the changes made since release have been small, actually, but that's all it felt like it needed at the end of the day. Travel between locations was slow, so they added energy sprouts that let you zip along the roads in-between; the ocean felt empty aside from the Loddles, so they added little non-interactible critters that give a sense of ecological diversity; there wasn't much incentive to travel beyond the loddle habitats, so they added a global cleanliness tracker and some secret areas with unique loddles inside. While these may be small on their own, together they made a big difference for the better.One of the biggest changes besides the inventory addresses the biggest gripe I had with the game: recontamination, where litter and goop will slowly creep back into habitats you've already fully cleaned. In hindsight, I think I understand its purpose—there's a simple crafting system that requires litter, and if that resource is finite, you might get locked out of certain items/upgrades if you're not careful—but it was  on launch. Habitats would become contaminated just a few minutes after you'd stepped away from them, which once again daisy-chained into other issues by discouraging you from taking your time and interacting with the loddles. This has since been reduced significantly, and . It's even possible to slow the recontamination rate down further or prevent it entirely through the new Pollution Resistance system—assuming you can figure out how it works, which I'll get to in a moment. Polluted areas feature a discordant soundtrack combined with a dark purple haze that limits your vision, giving off a very unsettling vibe that only gets worse with each new, more polluted area. Each location tells a story with its pollution, using everything from the types of litter to the location and abundance of microplastics and goop to give you a sense of what exactly GUPPI was doing there along with the unintentional consequences that came with it. As you clean up, that haze will dissipate, the discord in each track washes away to reveal more tranquil and dreamlike tunes, and the dark purple color palette is slowly replaced with more vibrant colors, even going so far as to sparkle a little once you've hit 100% cleanliness. It really helps sell the impact of your efforts more than any NPC dialogue or mission log check mark ever could. There are still some small issues, like the fact that they still can't seem to feed themselves when placed in your home cave, but the big one is the lack of quickly-accessible information on the loddles you have in your habitats. The new Loddlepedia gives you some insight into the  by telling you which which ones you've unlocked and the foods used to trigger those evolutions; but there's still no way to see information on individual loddles, like their names/status/diets, without going into each habitat and tracking them down one by one. This information is more important now with the new habitat diversity score, which contributes to some degree to Pollution Resistance, another  that isn't properly explained. It's not necessary to maximize these two to reach the end of the game, but doing so unlocks an alternate ending that you'll miss out on if you can't figure them out, which can be a little frustrating., and although I could've spent just as long (if not longer) raising loddles to get that other ending, I stopped after about an hour because it just boils down to a lot of waiting around with nothing else to do. I'd argue that there's still room for improvement in some areas, especially in regards to caring for the loddles, but it's a big enough step up from before that I felt I needed to shift my review from negative to positive.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of A Short Hike, when I saw an upcoming game with a similar art style & premise, I knew I had to try it out. What followed was a sweet, but short, relaxing gaming experience.At its core, this is a relaxing ocean cleanup game. There’s no combat or thrilling moment-to-moment game play. Suit up, maybe throw on a podcast, and spend a few hours cleaning up the ocean to make it more liveable for your new axolotl friends. You gradually travel from biome to biome, unlocking more powerful upgrades for your suit and more powerful tools that allow you to clean up different types of pollution, from floating cans & bottles to micro plastic debris fields.There’s also a neat pet management side of the game with the axolotls, aquatic creatues you can befriend. You can raise them, have them follow you around, feed them, pet them, craft toys for them. It’s a fun side-activity to the main garbage collection side part of the game.The graphics are also very unique. If you’ve played A Short Hike, you’re familiar with this art style. It’s a 3D game, but the rendering and intentionally low resolution makes it look 2D.The game also has excellent controller support. I played using a Playstation DualSense controller and it was a great experience. All the controls and rumble worked flawlessly. The UI also changed depending on what input device I was usingOverall, it was a very enjoyable experience. At the end of the day, I do recommend the game. However, there’s a few issues that made it somewhat less enjoyable:It’s also somewhat expensive for the time played. Most players (including me) finished the game within 3-4 hours. For $22 CAD, that’s somewhat expensive, especially when you can frequently find triple-A, hundred-hour games on sale for that price. In conclusion, I’d highly recommend Loddlenaut for anybody who wants a peaceful gaming experience for a few hours. The game play is relaxing & fun, and the axolotl companions are adorable.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game! Found it on instagram and bought it almost immediately. I'm a big fan of slime rancher and this felt very much like the same genre. I got super invested in the story and got genuinely emotionally attached to my loddles in a way I didn't expect. The visuals and audio where beautifully done, hampered only by some small mechanical issues I had.Occasionally I had a bug with the bubble gun's laser. When I tried to deconstruct trash bags, sometimes the laser would randomly shoot way off screen into open ocean. However, it still destroyed the trash bag and stopped after I rebooted the game, so I wasn't too concerned.The movement mechanics were frustrating at times. It took a while to get used to the controls (more than halfway through my run)  I would have liked to be able to strafe or back up without disrupting the deconstruct laser. However, I was more frustrated with constantly finding myself right next to a piece of trash that I couldn't collect because it was too high/low. Something about the depth of field got really confusing up close. I think I would've liked to be able to zoom in or out to see my environment better. Maneuvering my character to pick up trash that was too close was maybe my biggest challenge in the game.I also found myself stuck after completing Tangle Bay. I was one electronic bit short of buying the depth module, so I had no choice but to wander around hoping to find the pieces I needed. Turns out I missed one right next to the ship, but it was still frustrating to feel like I was locked out of the story. I definitely liked the open world elements and exploring areas between the reefs, but I preferred to do it in small detours in between the story.Speaking of Tangle Bay - the microplastics mechanic definitely felt weird. I didn't dislike it, but it only felt relevant in Tangle Bay and the GUPPI Campus, with barely any in the open world. Something about it just felt off, and I kept forgetting to unload it, which I found a bit of a hassle. I liked the scrubber vehicle though! Its narrow path was frustrating at first, but with the upgrade it was a blast and extremely fun to use. While there was much less of it than the microplastics, I didn't mind since it was more of a late-game addition.By the endgame I had way too many materials and nothing to use them on. I was able to purchase all upgrades before stepping foot in GUPPI Headquarters, although that may be partially because I found the Goddle Grotto first (more on that later). I liked being able to set up oxygen rings at each location, and if there were more moveable structures I'm sure I would have used them. I didn't use the cleaning bombs because I found them tedious, and I liked cleaning by hand. If there were more loddle toys or even some cosmetics for my character, I absolutely would have gone out of my way to get them.As for Goddle Grotto, I was blown away by the design and loved it as a story element. The only thing that bugged me was... the size of the ancestral loddles. By the way Dave described them, you would think they were the size of whales. I didn't see them right away and I was actually a little scared entering this zone. While the ancestral loddles were definitely much bigger than the rest, I have to say I was a little disappointed. But as a story beat, I thought it was wonderful, and a great surprise location..Overall I really enjoyed this game. While I had some hiccups, I would absolutely play it again or continue my save to breed even cooler loddles. This beginning run I mostly focused on trash cleanup and the storyline, so caring for loddles took a bit of a backseat - I discovered all of the species except for the last, so I might continue to satiate the completionist in me. While I did want more story, I understand the game isn't meant to be a 150 hour campaign - it would get pretty repetitive and boring by the end. But if they added one or two more areas or even a DLC, I would definitely play again from start to finish.

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenaut is an absolute gem that every simulation and exploration enthusiast should experience. _childDocuments_.review: If you like Subnautica but the infinite darkness and dangers is too much for you or if you enjoy "cleaning" games this is a fun relaxing short underwater adventure. The majority of the game is cleaning, you'll spent the resources you gather to craft a couple upgrades or items but the list is short. There is no automation or anything more complex. Cleaning areas open them to the Loddles, hence the game's name, but they don't provide you with anything beside being cute. For fun or for achievements you can feed them different food to evolve them and keep their area clean but that's it.The story is very simple and is more of a tutorial to tell you what to do. The graphics are nice, you can even pick between three level of pixelation ( off, low, high ) if you don't like the look. The sounds and music are limited but quite fitting for being underwater. The controls are responsive, the only thing is that you don't aim where you look, it's your body that aim, and you can't strafe so you can't really move too much while cleaning, except forward and backward. It's not that much of a problem, it's not a fast action game.The only bad thing I can say is that there is an oxygen mechanic but it's so easy to fill up, because the map is not that big and you can craft oxygen "rings", that there is barely any point of it existing. Obviously I would like to be more content too considering the price, the game is about 5 hours and 1 or 2 more if you want all the achievements. There is not really any replayability either.

_childDocuments_.review: Clean the ocean, revive plants and befriend loddles in this cute underwater game. Loddlenaut's controls are smooth, and the limited oxygen levels kept me from doing everything at once (in a good way) without feeling too limited - which overall made for a good exploration experience. It's a relaxing game, one that works well spread out over a handful of sittings (with headphones on - always an important part of the underwater experience). I wish the "cleaning up after an exploitative company" angle were hit a little harder (I'm glad we're cleaning up, but it felt like companies could stop caring because we're there to help tidy afterwards?). But perhaps this milder messaging works better for other people.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenaut is a cozy relaxing game where you have to clean up the waters of an ocean planet, similar to something like No Place Like Home/Fresh Start. It's not too long either, take that as you will, but that's a plus for me because games in this genre can sometimes steal hundreds of hours of my life, so it was nice to play something more compact.------You have different tools for different types of waste and you can switch between them seamlessly, sort of how Animal Crossing New Horizons does it, but it felt even more intuitive. To swim up and down you use the top and bottom face buttons which felt strange at first but after a little while it became natural, I can't speak for M+K controls as I didn't try it.Once you've collected all the trash you can carry (your inventory is quite generous though) you have to return to your home base to recycle it and the byproducts then become currency to purchase upgrades, it's a rewarding and addictive gameplay loop.There are several different areas to clean but they are all seamlessly connected, it's a relatively small world, but an open one. Once you have cleaned an area fully you can then quick travel back there which was convenient.At first, you have to manage your oxygen so you can't stray too far from your home base which I didn't originally like, but after an upgrade, it becomes a non-issue. If you run out of air the only penalty is dropping some of the trash you had on you, but you can just go back and collect it again, there are no enemies to deal with, so it's pretty chill.You can locate parts you've missed easily with a radar that highlights the objects as well as eventually having an arrow that points you towards them, so there's no frustration in missing a tiny bit and being stuck for ages like there is in some similar games.Navigating was tricky at first since the map isn't great, but that's only because I didn't realize there was a compass at the bottom of the screen, that's on me, I'm telling you this to save any other potential idiots like me. There are little creatures called Loddles that are like little axolotls that you can find. When you first encounter them they are covered in muck so you have to rinse them off and then you can set a place for them to live either at your home base or one of the biomes you've cleaned.  After that, you can feed them various fruits that can be found on the plants that you've detoxified, and depending on what you feed them they can grow bigger and eventually evolve (is that the right word, metamorphize?) anyway they go into a cocoon like state and come out looking different. I'm going to be honest with you, I didn't mess around with the mechanic unless it was mandatory to do so, but I imagine there are some fun combinations you can make. You can also craft little toys for them, but again I didn't bother. They have happiness meters too but I starved them the whole game and I didn't have any repercussions, yes I'm a monster.--------The story is really minimal, this organization came and made a big mess of everything and we've been hired to clean it up. You find a little more lore in optional collectible holo-badges, but really the gameplay is the main focus. It didn't really try and convey any sort of message other than really subtly.------The soundtrack is relaxing and compliments the vibe of the game, it's not gonna blow your mind or anything but it wasn't intrusive. The sound effects are not the best I've heard, but they were satisfying enough.-------The art style reminds me of A Short Hike with that low-poly almost DS style, it looked nice.------I guess the only real criticism I have for the game is that cleaning just didn't feel that good, I felt more could have been done in that department, it's quite hard to verbalize but the feedback and feel of the tools didn't feel quite as satisfying as I'd hoped. I also wish it had been messier too, I know that's a weird thing to say, but the games I mentioned earlier did it better as you felt overwhelmed and that you would never get it all done, and that's something I enjoy in these games (I'm one of those people who loves the farms being a complete wreck at the start in farm sims) if only I enjoyed tidying as much in real life eh? but heck, it's probably a me thing so take it with a grain of salt.-------Overall I really enjoyed my time with it and would happily recommend it to anyone who likes these sorts of games.

_childDocuments_.review: Loddlenauts is a cute, relaxing cleaning sim type game, where you also get to befriend and help take care of alien ocean creatures called Loddles. If you enjoyed games like Power Wash Simulator or Fresh Cleaning Simulator, you should enjoy this game. The art style is very cute, and can be set as pixelated or non-pixelated through the settings. The soundtrack is very calm and soothing, and did not feel repetitive or annoying even when playing for long stretches of time. I play with a controller, and found the controls to be very intuitive and easy to remember. I also found them to be fairly accessible, as there is no need to repetitively press buttons, and there is a toggle option for the 'boost' in game. The actual story play time has been reported by the developers to be about 5 hours - but unless you're purposely trying to speed through the game, and ignoring the Loddles, you can easily spend 10-12 hours playing through the story. There is also the option to return to your save file after the credits, so you can continue to take care of your Loddles, experiment with new foods and Loddle forms, and more. The Loddles themselves are very cute. They start out as babies, and change into a permanent form later, based on their diet. It's very fun to try feeding baby loddles new food, and see how they evolve!  I haven't seen every form they can take yet, but they have very cool designs, and are more than just some minor differences. Some are quite different from the others! Also, you can pet the loddles. There are a few, very minor bugs, that the devs are working on patching soon. They have been extremely responsive (check out their Discord if you haven't yet!) and will also be adding a few small QoL updates to the game. Honestly, it's one of the best indie launches I've seen in a while, and it's also one of the most responsive dev teams I've encountered in a while. It's very refreshing, and I feel confident they will support this game for as long as it needs bug fixes or other support. Overall, 10/10, definitely lived up to, if not surpassed, my expectations from the demo. And definitely worth $20!

_childDocuments_.review: "Clever gamers curator review: 6/10"  This gives me serious Katamari vibes, despite being almost completely different in moment-to-moment gameplay.  I think this is due to the cute art style and a similar focus on obsessively collecting everything in an area. But the differences are much larger than the similarities; all you do in this game is move from oversized plant to oversized plant, vacuuming up trash until your storage is full, at which point you return to home base to recycle it all, and, occasionally, order upgrades like a faster vacuum or larger airtank. At first this mild gamification (don't run out of air, don't get lost, and don't miss any trash) makes for a moderately compelling game loop, if an exceedingly casual non-challenging one.  But as you collect upgrades it actually gets less fun, more trivial, and in no way less repetitive. 3 hours in I started to wonder if I could get paid to finish the game, because it was starting to feel a lot more like work than fun.  After 4.5 hours I uninstalled, with at least another hour of "gameplay" left, and no sign of anything new and interesting on the horizon. Katamari, by virtue of a time limit and a strict progression from smaller items to larger ones does a much better job of holding my attention from start to finish, and it's that lack of followthru that reduces this game from a 8/10 to a (somewhat generous) 6/10. However, I still recommend it for people who are happy play a game until it stops being fun, and can avoid dogged completionism. _childDocuments_.review: Really nice, visually, and the sound also complements it very well.Unfortuntately, the game design is pure busywork, with poor pacing - it tries to be a simple Subnautica, but the inventory size and oxygen limits force you to go back to base without the opportunity to upgrade anything, especially at the beginning.There is really nothing to it other than a compulsion to "collect every piece of trash". There are no interesting choices, no interesting experimentation. This was actually a big miss-step, in my view: the loddles, the little critters, could have been a great mechanic, if you could guide their evolution in the direction of surviving and even *thriving* or healing each different environment. But no, the evolutions are almost purely cosmetic, and you need to do the busywork of cleaning up the habitat before they move in. They are simply not part of the game, mechanically - I went through the whole game without interacting with the loddles at all, simply because I had no reason to. (I see this equally as my own failure as the game's; my own lack of curiosity, paired with the game's failure to encourage experimentation with its mechanics)Finally, I find the environmental theme completely backward. It's a wishy-washy setup where you were hired to clean up the ocean after some big bad company exploited and abandoned the planet.But, of course, it ignores all the details of who's doing the hiring, and how difficult it would be to solve any of these environmental problems (no, you don't just vaccuum up microplastics).It's uses environmentalism as a token of tribal belonging, without an inkling of critical thinking. This is not the way.Yeah, it's cute. The visual effects are really great, and it's a pleasant experience - if you want to numb your mind for a few hours. We should demand a bit more for our time.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: Five hours, perhaps closer to six. It was all it took to complete the game and get almost every achievement. However, despite the relatively short playtime, in a world where you can log hundreds of hours in a single game, those six hours were peaceful and fun. I really enjoyed Loddlenaut, and I plan to go back to get that final achievement later, and mark this as a 100% achieved game. The game's concept is rather simple; Collect trash, recycle trash, clean ocean, feed Loddles. Throughout the game, your "Supervisor" repeatedly checks in to give you tasks and tell you when you've completed them. Some things are not intuitive (It took me a while to figure out how to pet a Loddle) but most things are easy enough to figure out, if your Supervisor doesn't blatantly tell you. Considering how short the game is, though, the price feels a little high. If you see it on sale though, I would highly recommend snagging up. It was rather notable how quickly this cute game boosted my mood, between the pleasant feeling of cleaning the ocean, to singing with the Loddles. When I finished, it gave a sense that my time was well spent, I had completed a good game, and I was glad to play it. It doesn't have much replayability, but not every game needs that. Some games simply tell their story in the first go, and you get what you need from it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just kind of meh. I sat down and played through most of it in one sitting, so kind of short. I guess you could say it held my attention pretty good for 3 hours but that's basically the whole game. The loddles are neat but they are basically sea monkeys, you can feed them, they reproduce, they are fun to look at, but after 5 min you want to go do something else. The game just doesn't really have enough depth to justify a $20 price point. Clean up trash, clean up different trash, clean up gunk, feed loddles, give loddles toys... and that's the game. Unless I've missed some large part of the game I can't really recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: When I first started playing this game I was beside myself. It's cute, fun, has a wonderful graphical effect that makes it look all pixely, has cute little fishies and then after about 30 minutes of looking at things the novelty wore off. And that was it. The game just stopped. There is about 3-6 hours of cleaning the environment gameplay but I kept waiting for it to kick into gear and for something to happen or for there to be some kind of upset. It never came. Half of the game is cleaning up the environment and the other half is interacting with the fish things called Loddles. The Loddle portion of the game is completely pointless. It does not tie into the rest of the game and there is no requirement to interact with them. I was expecting there to be some kind of setup where you have to accomplish certain things with the loddles before you could progress to the next part of the game but there is no such setup. You can completely avoid them and the game will continue all the same.As for the cleaning portion, it is very theraputic .. for about 20 or 30 minutes and then it becomes a repetitive chore.I really want to give this game a thumbs up because I don't hate it, it's good for what it is it's just not fully realized. It's like a chef made a sample of a dish, let you try it, you loved it.. but then they never made the full meal, even after you gave them your money.The story is bland and the narrator guy just pops in to tell you that the biome is clean enough for loddle to live there or to randomly tell you something about the loddles .. without you ever interacting with them "That loddle seems to really like that food!", "What loddle mister narrator? What food? Who are you talking to? I'm cleaning a wall, what are you going on about?" Not to mention that he's constantly saying things like "You don't have to do this.. or It's not part of your job.. or There is nothing to actually do interaction-wise but hey why don't you randomly go look at a loddle that is in the same biome you are in, it's in a cacoon! Why don't you go check that out? Now it's out of the cacoon! Why don't you go check that out?" I mean.. what? The game clearly thinks I am much more invested in the little fish blobs than I am.. which I'm not, at all. I don't see the appeal at all. They are supposedly based on axolotls. I find axolotls to be obscenely adorable.. those blob things are not axolotls, not even close.So, I would say the game is worth about 2-4 USD, if you must have it, and that is solely for the cleaning portion. The blob fish portion is a nonfactor imo and that's sad seeing as it is the whole reason for it's namesake.
_childDocuments_.name: Loddlenaut

_childDocuments_.review: A big, resounding "eh".Cute, but extremely short and quite boring.Gameplay is an extremely simplified mix of Subnautica and PowerWash Simulator/Viscera Cleanup Detail.Go to a place, gather all the trash, scrub all the goop, move to the next place.Movement is incredibly slow and most of the time spent is wasted on backtracking. Even with the boost, you move very slowly, specially when ascending or descending, which also spends boost if you want to do a little faster.The only way to get a bit faster is to find special plants that basically serve as a "highway" and supercharges your boost for incredibles 3 seconds.The upgrades are incredibly limited and can be maxed 30 minutes into the game. They also don't do much, a bit more cleaning speed, a bit more boost capacity, a bit more oxygen capacity.I didn't even touch the crafting system other than making a portable oxygen dispenser/cleaner.This game also has a small problem with wasting your time.First, it asks you to go to a place. Then it says you have to get a new piece of equipment to suck the microplastics cloud, and so you must return to the base. After you craft the equipment, it only unlocks the capacity upgrade once you go back and use the vacuum once.Same happens with the upgrade for the scrubber, that you need to clean the floors, but at least this one you can craft before reaching the place you need it.Your inventory capacity seems to be JUST too small to not able to fit every different piece of trash you can find, requiring you to backtrack to your ship to store stuff, so you can collect the rest of the trash.You can unlock fast travel, but only after you completely clean a zone, so it doesn't helps much aside letting you save maybe 30 seconds of swimming to the area you have to finish.The portable air circle cuts a bit of the backtracking since you don't need to hunt for air that often or backtrack to your base to clean the Loodles, but sadly there is no portable storage.You can gather fruit and feed them to the local fauna, or mix the food into different dishes for the same purpose. Depending of what you feed them, they eventually evolve into different stuff, although I didn't notice any gameplay changes.What passes for story is the most basic thing they could create. Big company pollutes (alien) ocean, then moves on.Nothing is expanded or commented aside a few remarks and some joke cards.It might be a cute game, but its so slow, uninspired, mechanically shallow and short that it didn't grab me.If you want a simple cleaning game that won't last more than 3 hours, go for it, I guess.
