_childDocuments_.review: Neo TWEWY is an Action RPG but it's really a JRPG with individual battles where you can do some more actiony gameplay than just simple turn-based, don't expect Diablo, etc. You fight in battles against monsters called "noise" and gangs of people all in a forced upon you "game" that the main characters find themselves in.I enjoyed about the first 8 hours, after that it became quite the grind. I've gotten to the mid twenties in terms of hours in and can't keep on playing.  Combat is mostly wash, rinse, repeat with some slight variations in enemy type and then you collect different "pins" that give you different attacks in battle, but many of them can just be grouped into a few different attacks - light, heavy, damage, and support. However, there are "right" combinations to use for each enemy type so it limits the usefulness of many pins and you'll find yourself slogging through enemies with the same basic layout each time. Now, if the music and story were good, I'd probably slog on through as I've done in games like Persona (which combat is very similar and grindy but everything else I found superb).  However, the story and characters here were barebones. And for me, the music was not a good match. I ended up turning off the in-game music and listening to my itunes as it just didn't resonate for me after about 15 hours of hearing the same tracks over and over. It sounded like b-level artists from the nineties and early two-thousands.Gameplay - 2/5 - Grindy, repetitive battles that get really easy if you get overleveled, so the game wants you to bring your level down to receive more rewards for each battle, but pretty soon you find yourself having no need for the bonus pins. Quests are all the same structure, go out and fight more of these types of things. One of the story/game mechanics is an ability you'll get early on that has you go back in time to change some of the things you've seen as you've played, so you end up walking back and up down the same streets multiple times. I really, did not care for this, but I can see where some would so I give this a medium score. Buttons are responsive and battle has some flashy effects. There is strategy and not just button mashing, but again, it was not to my liking. No way I could get through another 40+ hours of this.Story - 2/5 - Started off interesting and then quickly came to not care for any of the characters. They're all given the anime tropes were they stick to whatever role they're assigned (annoying best friend, weird mysterious stranger who talks in math terms, which I found really lame, etc). You're forced to complete certain assignments each day, all of which involve battling other "players" or monsters and searching for points but the story is mostly linear so you are just along for the ride and it didn't feel like I really cared about the objectives.Music - 2/5 - I'm usually pretty forgiving of music. A 2/5 means either utterly forgettable or I actively began to dislike the songs. It's a bunch of pop tunes but by very b-level bands. Kind of alternative rock with some attempts at funky stuff but fell flat to me. Get used to the songs if you play, you'll hear them in your sleep.Fun-factor - 2/5 - That factor that some games have where you are always interested in one more round or one more battle. This game did not have that and I actively began to hate having to string together multiple battles just to get higher points (one of the additional grind mechanics). I tried to start just rushing through to get through and at the point I realized how much more of the game is left I couldn't get myself to even want to play. some people may dig these battles, but I grew very bored.overall - 2/5 - Not a game I would recommend. There are much better JRPGs out there for story AND gameplay, and there are much better Action games out there than this battle system. A forgettable experience in my book.

_childDocuments_.review: A great follow-up to the original The World Ends with You! The new combat system feels fitting both from a narrative and gameplay perspective, and it can really feel satisfying, fluid, and intuitive, especially the later in the game you get with more and more psychs (the attacks you use throughout the game) being unlocked. The art style and the music especially REALLY cement this game into a good place in my mind, and I'm thrilled that they managed to put a new spin on the stylistic choices the original game and its remakes made.The game definitely isn't without a couple issues, however. There are a few enemy types in the game that heavily tamper with the flow of combat, and end up putting the player in compromising situations that they can't really naturally counter, leading to enemies controlling the pace of the combat encounter entirely, one notorious example being the Chameleon Noises, the Mammoth Noises, or some late-game Wolf Noise that occasionally move too fast to be dodged. These, combined with the camera forcing you to focus on a single enemy at a time, can create more than a few growing pains as new players get used to the finer details of the game's combat, especially if a few lessons aren't learned by late-game.This game also has a few holes in its story (mostly in the threads between the first game and this one), but said holes are only found when taking a deeper look into the game's lore documents it gives you for completing endgame challenges. In addition, the game's pacing takes a massive hit during a specific point close to the halfway mark of the game, which unfortunately is right around the same time the Chameleon Noise is introduced as a boss encounter...Yet, while I've spent a while discussing the game's faults, I genuinely don't have too many other negative things to say! The game runs smoothly, has a well-thought out and satisfying combat system, a fantastic soundtrack, wonderful visuals, and a charming cast of characters, who each get their time to shine.All in all, I can only hope for more out of The World Ends with You, and I'm happy to say that NEO was a welcome sequel after all these years.
_childDocuments_.name: NEO: The World Ends with You

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Great original gameplay, and generally a great story, just don't set expectations too high if you played the first game.The first TWEWY, besides (subjectively) fun touch screen controls and two characters, had an underappreciated focus on mixing attacks, and NEO absolutely nailed it. In fact, it's even better, since while it was fun, the stylus control and multitasking didn't encourage me to try any combos, while in NEO, making your own combos is THE game. It's great. There's plenty of small problems with camera or some bosses though, that might drag it down if the combo system isn't doing it for you.It also generally had a great story, but, there were a few many annoyances, like pacing, or not doing enough with villains, and such that bothered me. It might be since I played the first TWEWY a few months earlier and it was a top tier, as well as being pretty original, even if on paper it's the usual anime JRPG.Also, you kind of need to play the original first. While the main story didn't really need most of them, the whole cast comes back anyway, which might be alienating by the endgame, and also spoils the big twists. If you're confident you won't play that one though, then go ahead, the plot should still be good.

_childDocuments_.review: +++ Incredible soundtrack.+++ Memorable art direction and character design.+++ Fluid, highly customizable combat.+++ Compelling plotline with next to no down times.--- Rough start with characterization.--- Can get grindy at times, especially in the endgame and postgame.Boating a whirlwind of a story in which every episode is rife with plot twists and turnabouts, this title pushes the pedal to the metal and never lets go for even one second.  There is plenty of action to be had — almost too much, in fact — but the main story is bound to keep one busy and entertained with both the plot and the dynamic fight mechanics.  The postgame, meanwhile, is more for completion purists who have no problem with sinking dozens of hours into minute improvements and rewards.

_childDocuments_.review: Put simply, if you want a great Story-Based Game, love a killer soundtrack or want something to introduce you to Party-Based Action RPG's, Neo TWEWY will be a VERY dense and decadent cake to bite~ A warning, though: This Game spoils a few details of TWEWY, and half-expects you to have poked at its Story Synopsis. It's enjoyable standalone, yeah, but if you feel lost or want extra story details, you know where to go.High Points:+VERY customizeable RPG, allowing for not just a lot of Equipment Loadouts, but also plenty of ways to bend the game to your favor. Need stronger Attacks? Evolve your Pins~ Need better Stats? Buy up food items and watch your Characters' Likes and Dislikes~ Still struggling with fights, or a Game Journalist wanting to complain about how the game's too hard? There's no shame, in lowering the Difficulty or modulaying your Level, though it does change Drops and Drop Rates a bit.+A powerful story, much like TWEWY, revolving around expanding your horizons, even if it looks scary~+Dat Post Game. My gods. There's a lot to the Post Game to enjoy.Tripping Points:-There's plenty of flexibility for all Play Styles, but you don't earn if you don't learn. Much like TWEWY, expect this Game to pretzel your fingers as your Party expands. I love the game, but I still fumble a button or three. There's no way around it, adjust (to the controls) or adjust (the difficulty) if you struggle.

The storyline harks back to the first game without leaning on it too heavily, and the gameplay maintains the iconic characteristic of using every feature on the controller, for a fast-paced and frenetic combat style.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most underrated games of all time, it's a shame square shadow drop this one of a kind game, this game oozes with charm and personality it's insane, the artstyle is soo stylish and the soundtrack is amazing, the new cast for neo are all great especially shoka and the old cast are great too and not just used for fanservice all the time. Gameplay is a great improvement from the first with the team combos I prefer over the og though it's because I played the remix version and that version made my fingers burnt. This game has some flaws however like some enemies being very irritating to fight against, the pacing can be quite slow at times especially during the middle but that's all my problems really. In conclusion please buy this game it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rollercoaster of emotions I want to see this game strive and be successful in the eyes of square so we can get a sequel to it but even if we don't the game's ending already left me satisfied, sooo yeah buy this game I recommend it and get the first game too if you can it's available on switch and mobile do be wary of your fingers tho.

_childDocuments_.review: Great soundtrack, I only wish there were more tracks as it feels like the music loops a bit too much. Gameplay is fast and fun, but I'd say the combat system in the original TWEWY was better. Hard to recreate the feeling of controlling two separate characters simultaneously like on the DS. Despite that, this game is worth picking up for fans of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed the original, you'll enjoy this one too. It's a great combination of story, music, gameplay, and then a neat set of features - a food system, a clothing "threads" system, and a pin evolution system. You might not need the first game to understand this one, but it's worth playing through the original anyways.
_childDocuments_.name: NEO: The World Ends with You

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a ton of style. The art, music, clothes, pins, food, characters, and locations are dripping with style. The gameplay can be good but can also be a lot of button mashing. Some of the pins are just head and shoulders more fun to use than others which can make the experience inconsistent. The story is alright. I feel that it's hampered by the main character. Other characters point out many times how bad he is at making decisions. It's not that he makes poor decisions, it's that he doesn't make any decisions. Overall this is a fun game with a ton of style and I recommend playing it. Especially if you played the first game.Finished the game and the plot really picked up. The main characters indecision is addressed and there's character growth across the party.
_childDocuments_.name: NEO: The World Ends with You

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal. PLEASE play this game! If you like Final Fantasy, Kingdom Hearts, and some Persona/Jet Set Radio and 2000's vibe stuff. This game is a must play. The story, music, characters and gameplay is really incredible. It's a shame Square Enix haven't really marketed this game because this series should be a lot bigger than it is. The characters are so real and imo they give Persona a run for their money here and in it's OST.The gameplay is simple, but very unique and addictive. This is a game where you don't have to grind, but with how fun the combat is, you could end up overleveled by accident just from experimenting. There's always a challenge still though as there's certain enemies you can't sleep on if you don't have the right equipment or time your dodges. For fans of TWEWY, this sequel is unreal. They somehow managed to make a sequel to an amazing game even better in every possible aspect. For newcomers, I will say if you can, you should watch anime of the first game if you don't have access to it. You'll appreciate parts of the story a lot more. But, it's still a good entry point for newcomers, especially again if you're into things like Final Fantasy, Kingdom Hearts or Persona.
_childDocuments_.name: NEO: The World Ends with You

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is incredibly fun and unique. You assign a pin to each party member that has a certain type of elemental damage, different reboot times, costs, and so on. Certainly you could mash your way through the end but where's the fun in that? By combining various pins against enemies who have their strengths and weakness and then using threads (clothing and accessories) to enhance some stats or pins just adds to the tremendous variety in gameplay. The key is to strategically boost your groove but it's hard to stop experimenting with so many pins at your disposal. The strongest pin doesn't necessarily have to be the best one. With that said, another great strength is the story writing and the characters. You can see the amount of love and dedication that went into this project. There are so many details to be found in the locations, the food, the visuals, even the side characters you meet have their own backstory which you can tie together if you care to. And last but not the least is the OST loaded with ear-worm melodies that will stick with you long after you've finished the game.I've already completed the game on PS and plan to do so on PC, well Steam Deck actually, as it plays perfectly and with no issues and I enjoy the experience even more so than I did on PS.
_childDocuments_.name: NEO: The World Ends with You

_childDocuments_.review: 15 month delay due to EGS exclusivity? Check.Square Enix doing next to no marketing for it so you'd barely know it even existed? Check.Releasing it at an absurd price when it's already pretty cult and niche? Check. Man, I loved the original TWEWY and was so excited that it finally got a sequel, but it feels like SE just want it to die and fail so they can go back to acting like the series doesn't exist. Which is such an enormous shame because its a brilliant little anime RPG with a great soundtrack. A bit too text and cutscene heavy at times, but so full of charm and style and the transition from the 2D original to 3D today feels more solid than I would have expected.I can't suggest buying it full price but if its on sale or a third party site like GMG is offering it cheaper, go for it
_childDocuments_.name: NEO: The World Ends with You

_childDocuments_.review: A love letter for The World Ends With You made with passion, too bad Square Enix is trying it's best to make the game flop because this game would be loved by a lot of people. Please give it a try, specially if you played the original TWEWY, Solo Remix or Final Remix. As a big big fan of the series, I am very much enjoying my time with this game and can confirm that I am indeed addicted.
_childDocuments_.name: NEO: The World Ends with You

_childDocuments_.review: I played the PS4 version before the PC version released, but lemme just say that the PC port is phenomenal. I was skeptical as a console gamer that I would like the controls, but they're much better suited to PC. I also really enjoy the camera angles and perspective view when walking around. It looks much more dynamic when viewed on a closer screen. The key bindings make combat with multiple characters very easy compared to the PS4 controls, where I was struggling to press every single button at once. Port and controls aside, the game is amazing and I enjoyed this much more than the original, which will always hold a very special place in my heart. The characters from NEO are fun, unique, and heartwarming, while the visuals are stunning and aesthetic. The story is exciting without being too cliche or predictable and the cut-scenes are a delight to watch. 10/10, I HIGHLY recommend picking up this game to show some support. Lord knows this game needs and deserves it after Square Enix did it dirty.
_childDocuments_.name: NEO: The World Ends with You

_childDocuments_.review: NEO Twewy is a great game and I highly recommend it! I'm someone who loves to 100% games and if you're one of those types of people then I'm sure you'll have a good time doing everything this game has to offer. Grinding in this game is slow and tedious but it's not something that's necessary to complete the game due to the fact you can switch your game difficulty at any time so you can make it easier on yourself if you just want to rush through the story. The game play is fun and there's constantly new elements being added in that keep it fresh and entertaining though some additions are much more useful then others. This game isn't perfect and it has flaws just like anything else but even with those flaws it's entertaining, charming and incredibly heart wrenching at times. So yeah...Even though Square Enix won't promote it I will by saying you should buy it!
_childDocuments_.name: NEO: The World Ends with You

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decent game with an incredibly flawed combat system. You could make hours of video essays just on what the combat does wrong, but perhaps also what it gets right; Although the combat system was frustrating, it still felt fun and lively. The narrative is enjoyable and without too many plot contrivances, though it didn't take me by storm. All in all, an enjoyable experience.Now with that being said, I cannot resist the urge to rant about the combat a little.It has poor camera controls, poor visual cues, allies that can get hit even when you're not controlling them and they're out of sight and at times get hit purely because of bad AI rather than you putting them in tough spots, attacks that move quickly from side to side in spite of poor camera controls, difficult to gauge hit boxes, spongy enemies especially towards the end, repetitive mob types, difficulty locking target on the target you want to attack, you've only a hint of an idea as to where characters will be when you take control of them, the dodge mechanic sometimes moves in the direction of your attack instead of your movement, some skills seemed to just not work as well as they should've because your characters don't aim right or move close enough to hit, skills that completely visually dominate an already messy battlefield, aaaand... I think that's enough to underline my point. It has been... Frustrating. Fun, but frustrating.

Oh yea and I wish I could change the cancel and confirm buttons I'm playing on an xbox controller and its just akward to cancel with A and confirm with B.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, what a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ great game. It's consistently causing me to stay up  later than I should be. I was reluctant to play it when it was first released, because I didn't really hear much raving about it, and I  liked the first TWEWY... and I didn't want the great time I had with it sullied by a mediocre sequel. Boy, was I missing out, and I'm incredibly glad to be playing it now. The gameplay is (in my opinion) a strict improvement from the original - TWEWY's combat was fun on the original DS release, but they just stripped out more and more of the personality with each re-release. NEO takes a new approach that feels great to play, the fully 3D areas are true to the original while looking better, and the storyline is every bit as compelling as it was in TWEWY. Add in plenty of throwbacks to the original and an  soundtrack, and it's just an utter joy to play. (They kept many of the songs from TWEWY, added a bunch of new ones, and some absolutely banging remixes.)If you played and enjoyed TWEWY, you owe it to yourself to play this. Square-Enix completely dropped the ball on advertising, but ♥♥♥♥, the game is good.

_childDocuments_.review: Final additions:Having finished the game, I can say that my opinion still stands. I'm left with some questions at the end of the game that I might have answered through secret reports, but IDK. Ending was satisfying, but I felt that a bit more tribute could have been paid to some of the characters. It was still full of great moments regardless(that final boss fight). As per usual, one I think I understand what's going on, I get hit with a curveball or 2. This game is fantastic. Give it a try. If you haven't played the first game, you should, as it ties back to the first game throughout. I didn't get the significance of a certain character that apparently appears in the remake of the first game, but I got most everything else. It can be enjoyed on its own, but the closer you get to the end, the less you'll understand. I suppose it does give you all the more reason to visit the first game, though. Easy recommendation. The best Square title you'll play in quite some time.By the way, you should avoid the Community section like the plague if you don't want to get spoiled.Updated Review:Rare instance of a sequel living up to its predecessor. This game is awesome and satisfied one of the main things I had been wanting more of since the first game: Team battles. It's not just awesome, it's one of the best JRPGs I've played in a while. It's interesting how different it is from the first game, yet still feels very familiar at the same time. I just started what I believe is the beginning of the endgame, so bear in mind this review comes with a lack of knowledge of the ending.Honestly, I'll keep it short. Cast is great, story has twists and turns, and having a group instead of a single partner allows for some great party dynamics to play out. There's tons of pins to play around with, and the combat makes for a more fluid coordination between your party members' attacks. It takes a bit of time to get a good selection of pins, but once you do, things get much more interesting. Beatdrop makes experimenting with different pins rewarding, and the greater variety of pins allows you to utilize enemy weaknesses more effectively. This game also doesn't suffer from the occasional missed input you'd get on a touch screen. OST's great, but that's to be expected. Characters are great(they gave me ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Minamimoto in the first hour of the game; I was STOKED). Honestly thrilled that this game came to be. I expect to enjoy the remainder of my playthrough. Top tier game right here. Even if you haven't played the first game, there is still more than enough to enjoy here. Strongly recommend.--Ignore my playtime; I own the Switch version. I had to support a PC release of NEO The World Ends With You. I never knew there was a Epic Games Store release, so this caught me completely by surprise. This can't be a Square port, because it's not broken(You still haven't fixed the FFXIII games, Square). It runs fantastically, even at higher resolutions and supports "unlimited" frame rates without breaking pacing.EDIT: That unlimited framerate is no BS. I'm averaging ~200FPS in the major overworld areas, packed with people, and I'm averaging ~300 FPS during random battles. 500+ during scenes, but that hardly matters, and I can't even see that lol. I'm running it at 1080p on a 5700XT, and even managed 4K ~90-100FPS average, only dropping to 60 during intense combat segments. You'll run it just fine on the average machine. I've encountered no bugs in the time I've played. It just works. And no Denuvo, either? Dude, get this game if you're even moderately interested. Would have been nice to include the demo, but ah well. Square negligence, I guess. I'll report back with game details when I finish it. I'll recommend it off of performance and being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ The World End With You.Obligatory "It Works On Linux" statement.

_childDocuments_.review: "Only the possibility of you can change our fate". A long-awaited new story in The World Ends with You series has arrived. Rindo comes to the grim realization that his life is on the line when he is forced to compete in the so-called "Reapers' Game." There's no telling how this tale will unfold—but it's up to you to find out! Put your psychic prowess to the test as you duke it out on the stylishly animated streets of Shibuya. Features:  Delve into a vividly illustrated Shibuya, animated with style, music and monsters. Collect and wield hundreds of Psych abilities to battle surreal threats. Investigate the world around you and beat the "Reapers' Game" to survive.

name: Zool Redimensioned
detailed_description: The Ninja of the Nth Dimension is back! Originally released by Gremlin Graphics in 1992 on the Amiga to critical acclaim, iconic gaming mascot Zool returns in Zool Redimensioned! This brand-new reimagining of the classic action platforming adventure has been rebuilt from the ground up for modern audiences. Help Zool jump, spin and shoot his way across eight alien worlds, taking down menacing bosses and saving the universe from the nefarious influence of Krool. Zool’s old school platforming action will challenge the most hardcore gamers, with modern enhancements that bring the game into the 21st century. Beat your speed run times, discover secrets hidden across every level, or go back in time and play the original classic game. Re-live the legend of the ninja that started it all! Features Over 28 retro platforming challenges, all enhanced for the best possible experience Choose between two main game modes: Redimensioned for a more accessible modern experience, or Ultimate Ninja to experience a true hardcore challenge Trade blows with the dimension's most dangerous creatures in seven completely redesigned boss fights Discover new secrets, challenges and extras across your adventure, with over 25 achievements to unlock Enhanced quality-of-life options, including a level select screen, checkpoints, accessibility options and more Play the original Mega Drive version for a truly authentic retro adventure Sumo Digital Academy Zool Redimensioned has been rebuilt from scratch by the Sumo Digital Academy, a talent development programme focused on creating new pathways into the games industry. With guidance from the developers of the 1992 original at Gremlin Graphics, we’ve retained the spirit that makes Zool a cult classic, while adding mechanics we’ve loved from the past 29 years of fantastic platforming games. The result is Zool Redimensioned, a game that transcends time and space - don’t miss out on this classic retro adventure!

I naturally played it old school.Trying to play the mega drive version from the emulator menu currently does nothing. Not that I am that interested in playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Zool is back! The (only) space-travelling, dimension-hopping goblin ninja has awoken from his 30-year old slumber for his first adventure’s retelling. The question is: how does this platform relic hold up today?The dev team team did an amazing job with this remaster. All the 2D sprites have been reworked and updated to work on today’s monitors. Zool I and II were visually the most impressive Commodore Amiga 500 games, and the graphics still hold up today.  The protracker-style music from Patrick Phelan has been untouched, and it delivers catchy 16-bit tunes that go nicely with the platforming action on screen.Controls remain very responsive and precise, so jumping around the level and avoiding obstacles is never a source of frustration. There are 36 levels in total and it’ll take you five minutes on average to finish a level. That means you’ll finish the game in 2-4 hours. Luckily, devs added a new game mode that has a double jump, and can be considered as a very-easy mode. The classic gameplay mode is here as well, and it’ll take you about 5 to 8 hours to finish the game completely, along with getting all the achievos.Now onto some less then stellar aspects: the levels are fine, but they are quite simple compared to modern retro platformers. The overall game is easy if you stack it to other platforming legends available on Steam. Out of seven worlds, only the last one ramps up the difficulty a bit, thanks to enemies that are more annoying then they are challenging.Zool Redimensioned is a faithful adaptation of the Commodore Amiga classic that is good fun which will impress the retro fans. As for the new players, it’s an alright game, but there are better retro platformer pickings out there.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up with an Amiga 500 which was eventually replaced by an Amiga 1200. Zool was the Amiga's answer to Sonic and Mario and while it doesn't get anywhere near those heights it was still a good platform game and a good mascot for the Amiga.I've had a lot of fun playing through it again and the devs have done a good job of creating this new version. Having the screen more zoomed out makes it much better to see where your going. It also comes with the original Megadrive version, which was a decent version. Its not perfect, the shoot em up bonus levels are almost unplayable for some reason, collision detection all over the place, but apart from that the core game is still a lot of fun. It was a wonderful nostalgia trip, and worth the 7.99 entrance fee.I hope Zool 2 and more Amiga classics get the remake treatment as I would buy them all. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Zool was the first game I ever played, but it's difficulty is something that has struggled to engage people nowadays. Not only that, but it's virtually inaccessible to most gamers given the release platforms it got. This game does so many things right, difficulty rebalancing, combines aspects from all ports, does new things incredibly well, encourages replayability, and is on the most accessible platform possible. Hands down, this is the best way to play the revived 1992 classic, and it is still both challenging and enjoyable in 2021. FANTASTIC GAME that I can wholeheartedly recommend to EVERYONE!
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Zool was among the first video games I ever played in the early '90s, along with Super Mario World and Donkey Kong. This reworked version is very well done and it's a huge improvement of how the game plays and feels. It's a lot smoother and more fluid than the original.Highly recommended, especially to anyone who used to play this as a kid. Sometimes nostalgia makes things from your childhood seem better than they really are, but that's not the case here. Zool is still cool.

Or the wheel you needed to activate the game when you had to match the correct Zool legs to the Zool head?) This is a different version where the levels are quite different from what I remember. I think there were only 3 levels in each world in the version I had where as this one has 4. I have only gotten to Fruit World at the moment- and I'm not sure if Toy World and Tool World are still in this game- but I am looking forward to meeting the "unmentionable indescribable two eyed thing" at the end of Funfair World! Definitely a nice dose of nostalgia from this blast from the past!

_childDocuments_.review: Zool Redimensioned is a remake of the popular 1990s platformer, Zool - Ninja of the Nth Dimension. Specifically it's apparently based on the level-designs from the Mega Drive version of the game, which I feel was a good choice as the stages in that version flowed quite nicely.The game offers multiple difficulty options: Redimensioned mode is a rebalanced remake where Zool has been given a fun new double-jump move and you can make a straight dash for the exit without worrying about collectibles, whereas Ultimate Ninja mode applies the original game's rules to the remake, removing the double-jump and requiring you to find the required number of collectibles before you can leave a level. You also get an emulated version of the Mega Drive game that the remake is based on, if you want a more challenging experience.I had a lot of fun with this one, as the modern niceties that have been applied to the game really help it - particularly the larger, wider viewport! I also appreciated the fact that the graphics have largely not been messed with, aside from adding some extra idle animations to let more of Zool's personality show through - I really liked these, as they're quite cute.Also, was that a hint at a sequel that I caught at the end, there? I certainly hope so, because I'd happily buy a Zool 3 in this style!I played this game on Linux, and it worked out of the box with Proton, running flawlessly throughout. It's a fun experience that you shouldn't hesitate to pick up if you liked the original.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Take notes Limited Run Games, THIS IS HOW YOU RE-RELEASE AN OLD GAME!This isn't just an emulator this is a ground up rebuild of the game based on the original, it plays fantastically with super fast response and perfect frame pacing, the only things I can knock are a lack of options, you can have perfectly sharp pixels if you change the viewport size but other than that you are stuck with a very ugly CRT filter and that's your lot, something like xBRZ would have been nice but overall this is a very high quality re-release all the more impressive when you find out this was done by interns at Sumo Digital.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Satisfying Retro Platformer, but only when you ninja through the levels, which the game is designed around anyway. Carefully scroll through the levels while aiming for collectibles and most of you will get bored, even with the fine (short) level length. However, my only complaint with this game is, that hazards & enemies blend in all too well with the environment, and so, most of the damage taken is to be considered 'cheap'. In the end, it doesn't really matter, as at least in the  mode, the game is quite forgiving with its checkpoints and ❣️-recovery! Furthermore, the game offers cool bosses and some more challenging ones near the end that are never unfair either. Last but not least, some appealing mysteries to uncover and fine challenges hidden within the achievements, which are make for an even more satisfying experience 🕵️‍♂️8/10 — 'Fast Platformer Food' in between

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to be so negative about a game I remember fondly from my childhood, but this is simply not very good. You might still want to buy it if you have nostalgic feelings about the original, but do so as an act of games preservation, not because you expect a great gaming experience.The remake is fine on a technical level. You can choose from three levels of widescreen zoom, all the way from original 1992 size-Zool where you have no chance to see what’s coming up as the screen starts scrolling, to a modern zoom level that really utilises the fact that modern screens are wide and high resolution.  There’s also an optional CRT-filter to mimic what the game might have looked like on a not super great CRT screen back in the day. The game looks fine either way, though, and I’ll always hold that I don’t remember games from this era looking blurry and scan-liney. I remember them being crisp and colourful. The music is catchy, although the tunes are short and loop far too quickly if you’re exploring a level fully. There’s also only one piece per world and four stages per world, so they do start to grate a bit. Of course, if you speedrun the levels, which is probably more fun than looking for rather meaningless secrets, this is a non-issue.No, the real issue is that the levels and gameplay are just sort of empty feeling. The stage layouts feel haphazard and simplistic, which makes platforming itself, as well as exploration, rather uninspired most of the time, and the enemies just have no variety, mostly just swapping out sprites between the worlds and then remixing a few different variations on how they move. To add insult to injury, interacting with them is not very satisfying either most of the time. The only exception is trying to shoot the drums in the music stages from the front! And this is a problem when the game’s only two modes of engagement are platforming and fighting enemies.To top it all off, the game is genuinely far too easy. I remember this being extremely difficult and never making it past the third world, if that, when I was nine years old. Now, admittedly, I was nine years old. But even today, I’m not a particularly skilled platform player. I muddle through mostly. But here, I made it to world five without even trying and was never close to getting a game over. (And that’s playing on the original difficulty setting, not the modern setting that gives you a double jump to smooth out the platforming.)I’m not saying that a game being easy makes it bad in and of itself, but when an action-platformer provides next to no challenge, to the point where you can mostly coast through it and mindlessly jump and shoot without hardly looking at the action in front of your character half the time, we have a fundamental problem with the design of the game.Again, I’m genuinely sad to have to say this. I’m glad Zool exists in an easily accessible version today, and perhaps people who enjoy chasing high-scores and speedruns will enjoy it more than I did. Perhaps the change to widescreen did something fundamental to the balance of the gameplay, or perhaps Zool was always more about attitude and style than about quality gameplay?(I also hate that I have to chose recommend/don't recommend. On the one hand, the game is kind of dull to me, on the other hand, I want people who remember the game and want to experience it again to play it).

_childDocuments_.review: As a child, I owned the SNES port of this game and could never get into it for one reason- the screen crunch. The former makes a *world* of difference and the game is actually fun to play and explore now. It still won't blow genre veterans away (then again, it didn't exactly set the world on fire back then either) but it's a pleasant enough romp. I will say that Redimensioned Mode can make the game a little too easy thanks to the double jump, but at least there's "Ultimate Ninja" mode which retains Zool's moveset from the original game. In either case, the physics and handling remain 1:1 to the original game...which is something I can applaud considering most of these retro remakes mess with these aspects just to add "extra difficulty". (Looking at you...Crash N Sane and Alex Kidd DX)For the purists who scoff at accessibility features and modern touch ups- don't worry. The Mega Drive game is also included if you want to relive those days of slamming into ♥♥♥♥ you couldn't see coming because of the screen being too zoomed in.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this expecting to go thru the original mode for a lil nostalgia & maybe play the reworked modern mode for the achievements tied to it. _childDocuments_.review: A great remaster, built from the ground up, of this classic platformer.I described this game on stream as "a fantastic remake of a troubled game" because the original versions of Zool have not aged well at all.  From the small viewport, to the floaty controls (exacerbated by the game being inherently designed for the 50 FPS Amiga and not optimised for its subsequent releases in the US), it doesn't play as nostalgia remembers it.The remaster, however, does a grand job of making the 60 FPS framework work by massively increasing the screen real estate, improving the once-slippery controls, and adding an absolute game-changer (at least in the Redimensioned mode) of the Double Jump.   These updates make Zool Redimensioned an absolute joy to play - everything feels tight, precise, and you almost always feel fully in control of every movement you make.Said Redimensioned mode also fundamentally changes the way the game is played - not just through the mode-exclusive Double Jump, but by changing the way the levels are completed.  Previously, Zool was a collection platformer - collect X amount of items dotted around the stage to unlock a collectable token, which finishes the stage upon completion.  The new mode ignores the collection requirements, which allows much more freedom to complete each stage.  Don't get me wrong - the game is still chock full of collectables, however now that they're not mandatory you can collect them with no stress nor pressure.Another quality of life improvement is how respawns are handled - with plenty of checkpoints and lives dotted through the stages, your momentum rarely gets interrupted as you storm through the levels.All the bosses have been reworked to fit with the remade gameplay - unfortunately most are a cakewalk, but some require patience and good reactions!100% worth your time and money

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I absolutely love, but I can't recommend to new players who haven't played the original.I grew up on this game, so I am biased in that respect. _childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor that I'd argue even surpasses the original (which is actually included as a bonus feature with this game), Zool Redimensioned is a fast-paced action platformer. It's pretty straightforward: just run, jump, defeat enemies, and collect goodies. This game features a "redimensioned" mode which is more focused on getting to the end, or a classic mode that plays more similar to the original Zool by restricting double jumps and requiring certain collectables to continue. The art style keeps the charm of the original, but updates it a bit as well. The music also rocks, especially the boss themes. One aspect of this game that I found really entertaining was the multi stage boss fights. Sometimes bosses just don't stay dead, and will have a second phase incorporating new tactics. Sometimes they'll even call upon their army to flood the playing field (which can actually work in the player's favour as enemies drop powerups!).All in all, this game is a great welcome back to Zool: a rather obscure mascot that, as the game is quick to remind us, hasn't been seen for about 30 years. Here's hoping they can make another one!

_childDocuments_.review: Zool isn't one I grew up with, although it's adjacent to a lot of the DOS games from my childhood. I've mainly heard this game mentioned for being released on every platform imaginable, with the consensus being that it was a pretty unremarkable platformer. I was drawn into Zool Redimensioned by the promise of a heavily modernized experience, and I feel like that update is extremely well done. While there are some control issues that result from the small sprites which couldn't really be resolved without turning it into a different game, the overall feel is impressively responsive and it's a lot of fun to play.The fact that the menus are copied nearly verbatim from Sonic Mania speaks volumes about developer intent. This was a labor of love, and it shows. Worth checking out if you're curious about a classic, especially on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing Zool for the Amiga when I was much younger so I was happy to see a remake of this game had been made and by a company that is giving experience to individuals aspiring to develop a career in the video games industry.Overall I really enjoyed the game, although the levels were based more around the Megadrive version which I am less familiar with, there have been some new features added which have really improved the overall experience.GAMEPLAYThe physics of the game are good and I like the way Zool controls in general. The modern mode allows you to double-jump which I have always enjoyed in some 2D platformers. I never thought though I had much use for the spinning attack and probably because for the location of the button in my controller I used it rarely. But otherwise this Zool controls much better than before and I love how you can also climb up the walls which was missing in the original.The game is challenging enough and it certainly feels each zone is more difficult than the last, I would say though that it feels a little too easy to grab enough collectibles before finding the exit whereas in the original you had to collect more.STORYLINEAs this is a 90s platformer there is not too much to say but I like how they mentioned Zooz who originally we didn't meet until Zool 2. Explains the story pretty well and towards the end makes a nod to the fact it has been around 30 years since there was a Zool adventure.MUSICThe Amiga soundtrack is there and it sounds really good, always loved Rave and Sonic Basher, I didn't recognise the track from the Tool levels but that it sounded great. The original game on the Amiga couldn't have music and sound effects at the same time so I am glad the team have fixed this. The only thing which is more nit picky is the music loop for some of the tracks don't feel so smooth but otherwise the sound is fine.BOSS BATTLESAlthough the boss battles are based on the Megadrive version it looks like the team made some very nice enhancements so even as you are close to defeating each boss it gets progressively harder. The difficulty curve is also just right so the last few boss battles certainly felt more challenging especially in the Toy zone. SUMMARYA very strong and good remake of a series that I enjoyed when I was a very young kid and very impressively done by a team at the start of their video game careers. I really hope that we will also see a remake of Zool 2 as I much preferred this game back in the day so it would be exciting to see what this team could do. 7.5 / 10

_childDocuments_.review: Video Review - Write Up - The original Zool came out in 1992 for the Amiga computer, with the game being ported to several home consoles and other computers of the time period. It's not exactly the most loved platformer ever made, so it's a little surprising to see it get a remaster.Zool Redimensioned intends to take the original Zool and remaster it for the modern age. This is quite definetly a remaster and not a remake or a reboot, it uses many of the games original assets, but increasing the field of view massively and the smoothness of the gameplay. It really makes a difference compared to the original, actually being able to see what's coming up helps out a lot.Zool Redimensioned features 28 levels, and as it's a traditional computer platformer, these levels are largely full of random stuff. One level is full of sweets, another is full of toys or of plants that have come to life, it's that sort of thing. There's no real coherence in the level design, but that's to be expected of an Amiga platformer from the UK. It also no longer features the chupa chups that were very prominent in the original, probably due to licensing. Redimensioned is actually quite a fun game. I wasn't expecting to like it too much as I wasn't a huge fan of the original, but the quality of life upgrades really do make a difference. It's made by Sumo Digital Academy, which is a group of developers within Sumo Digital mainly composed of young graduates, with this company intending to give them an introduction to actually releasing full games. I think they've done a good job with this remaster, they've managed to upgrade it in all the ways you might expect, but keep it faithful to the original, which is important in a remaster. Those looking for a complete remake should look elsewhere.That's not to say the game isn't without it's frustrations. They changed the scale of all the characters and enemies in order to fit modern HD displays, which brings with it some problems, as on some levels the hazards can be extremely tiny and difficult to see, especially at speed. Additionally, because the game is so full of random enemy designs, it can sometimes be tricky to know what is supposed to be an enemy and what is supposed to be a collectable, leading to some moments of annoyance. The game plays at a very smooth 60 fps, and the controls are extremely tight, so when you do die you don't often blame the game, which is exactly right for a platformer. Some of the later bosses can be a little difficult, but luckily the refined controls keep things moving. Having said that, I did enjoy my time playing this game. I beat the full Redimensioned mode in about an hour, which isn't too bad for a platformer of this age. I blasted through all the levels, so if you're someone who likes to collect everything it will take you a fair bit longer. There is also a classic mode which is a lot harder, and doesn't feature the modern niceities of being able to restart at the same level after you die, so if you're a hardcore gamer that level may inspire. It also features an emulated version of the Sega Megadrive port of the game, which is a somewhat strange inclusion and I think the Amiga version would have been a better include. It's currently sitting on steam at £7.99, which I think is a fair price overall, and I would recommend to anyone who is a fan of early 90's computer or amiga platformers, as the charm those games brought, this one still manages to retain. It has a lot of fun, nostalgic gameplay, and I think it's worth the cost of entry.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: I have now reached world 4, Toy World in Zool Redimensioned, and I can honestly say that this version of this game finally makes Zool an enjoyable game. I'm in my mid thirties now and was first exposed to the original Zool game on my brothers Amiga way back in the early 1990s. I remember playing Zool with an invulnerability cheat, just running through all the levels with the challenge being navigating through all those levels, collecting the required items and finally reach the exit.Playing without cheats back in the day made the game very hard, and not in a fair sense. The game was way to fast for the low screen resolution of something like 320x240 on the Amiga. The other issue (which was not that uncommon with games on the Amiga) with this game was that you would have to choose between the awesome soundtrack or sound effects on the original Amiga release, so the sound effects had to go. There was also a Sega Genesis- & an SNES release of this game, with the Genesis version having a not-so-great audio quality when you talk about the soundtrack, and the SNES version (although having better music quality) suffering from that cramped 8:7 aspect ratio (usually stretched to fit a 4:3 TV back in the day). Zool Redimensioned actually includes the Sega Genesis version of this game, which is a nice addition.This is the ultimate & only version one would need to play of Zool 1 in my humble opinion. The single greatest addition to this version of Zool 1 has to be the higher screen resolution compared to the original Amiga version; now you can actually see the enemies before smashing into them. Now Zool is no longer too fast for his own good, because there's no problems avoiding obstacles and enemies now with this upped screen resolution. Zool Redimensioned seems to be more inspired by the Sega Genesis version rather than the Amiga one if you compare art-styles, but at least now you have the excellent music quality from the Amiga version and sound effects as well.Quality of Life additions such as the three optional objectives like collecting the 3 big items in a stage, completing a stage within a set time limit & completing a stage without losing a single life surely adds a bit more replay value to the game. The game also saves your progress, making it possible to continue your progress and even replay previous levels if you would like to (like getting the bonus objectives on each stage). Achievments has also been added, achievments is always a good thing to include in any game in my opinion.This may not be a particulary long game to finish, or even one of the more revolutionary platforming games made in the early 90s, but playing this game once again with this enhanched Zool Redimensioned port actually makes this game a fun 2D platformer to play without using cheats for the first time ever in my opinion. If you're into 2D platforming games, and enjoy 2D platforming games like Sonic & Super Mario I'll guess you'll get your moneys worth playing this game. I'm having a blast with it.I wonder what's next? Maybe Zool 2 Redimensioned?

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot I could say about Zool but for this little review  I just want to focus on the graphically direction Zool chose. _childDocuments_.review: Zool Redimensioned is an ancient game from 1992.  It's a whopping 32 years old at the time of this review.  While the game has been updated to display in widescreen format, there's no support for modern gaming display resolutions.  The remaster does make the game playable and it runs okay on modern PCs, but the shallowness of the game and the fact the visuals and other aspects of the game haven't been addressed makes this just more abandonware, but slightly less abandoned.Despite this lack of modernisation, it carries a pretty high price tag for such an ancient game.  This seems to have been put on Steam as a nostalgia gouge.  Shouldn't developers be more concerned with making contemporary games rather than digging up stuff that the emulator crowd got tired of years ago?The game never really caught on with the millions of gamers on Steam, with a very low peak player count close to launch, and then just a handful of players launching this game every couple of days.  This is undoubtedly caused by factors such as those raised in this review.  It's always helpful with buying decisions to consider how popular and successful the product is, and unfortunately while this did accumulate a few participation trophy reviews, overall, people just aren't using it.  It's only appealed to a small handful of gamers. And frankly, Zool was the kind of game that went direct to the bargain bins at the front of the video game store, for gamers to walk right by on their way to pick up the latest AAA releases of the time.  Worth pointing out this is a contemporary of games like Wolfenstein 3D and Ultima Underworld.  This couldn't compare back then and it certainly doesn't now. Zool Redimensioned is relatively expensive for an abandonware nostalgia gouge, at $9 USD, and it's not worth it.  The game is just too old, hasn't been modernised.  And as the old saying goes, you can't go home again.

_childDocuments_.review: Just ran through this game on Single Player mode, it's very short, but it's a blast. It seems to have expanded a good deal from the original console games, though I don't know if it had all of the good charms of the original (such as that secret gag where Zool goes onto a giant arcade machine and press buttons to have his double jump obstacles to get extra lives, I think that's the amiga version). And there are multiplayer modes which I haven't got around to playing yet. I wish this remake had added maybe three more worlds and expanded the gameplay, but I very much enjoyed it anyway.Re: Oh, and the soundtrack is pretty cool as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly was a fan of Zool as a kid for some reason despite never being able to get past world 1 at my mate's house. Even borrowed one of the Zool books from the library. Loved the colourful world and crazy speed of the game, check out the 1992 MD version here and it's clear it's actually ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ terrible - huge levels with tons of hazards the zoomed-in perspective doesn't help at all with, every level is so slippy it feels like an ice level, tedious compulsory collectathon ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.Redimensioned does it amazing feat of taking a 1/10 turd and polishing it into a 6/10 1.5-2 hour long curio. Perspective is a thousand times better, collectibles are no longer compulsory, Zool moves quickly but not like every level is an ice level, and it's forgiving with lives and continues. It's main issues are it's faithfulness to the original - level design can be annoying, one of the bosses is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pain in the ass, and the final level/boss is random and unsatisfying. Turns out arch-villain Krool was never actually in any of the games. Still, the devs did a great job in making the game actually satisfying to play if you're not a hardcore oldschool amigahead who craves OTT difficulty.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Nostalgia plays a great role on how someone might review this game, my first and only contact before with zool was on the SNES and always thought the background music on this game was awesome and catchy the visual is very memorable, overall it is a game that appeals more for nostalgic fans, I was a little dissapointed that some levels WERE EXTREMELY EASY and POINTLESS mainly on WORLD 4, the Toy World BOSS was the only that posed some dificult.So the GOOD: Fans of the intergalatic Ninja will enjoy itThe music is greatoverall is a fun gameThe BAD:Many levels TOO EASYThe Ugly: you'll notice you're not in the nineties anymore when you close the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Fast and bouncy like the original but now in widescreen which makes the game much more playable and pretty easy. The cramped screen is what made the original so difficult but without that anyone can sit back and beat this in about an hour and that's not a bad thing in my opinion. There's a mode that replicates the original version by zooming in the screen and removing the extra features added for anyone that finds it too easy. The genesis version is included too which is nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Final 3 bosses are brutalZool is a perfectly fine game... For its time. Sorry. Its just there are so many better platformers today that Zool really feels its age. It reminds me of games like Aero the Acrobat and Super Adventure Island. B tier platformers behind Mario and Sonic in there day and with so many great Indy darlings like Celeste and Ori Zool feels antiquated by comparison. There are only 7 worlds and 4 levels per world each can be beat in under 1 minute 3-6 if your collectable hunting. Zool can scale walls, shoot, and double jump. (theres an old school mode where you only jump once) the levels arrange from linear and non linear design they aren't mazes thankfully and are easy enough to traverse. Beware this game has some sharp difficulty spikes not so much in the levels (except the final world where every enemy and bush have projectiles) but the final 3 bosses. The final 3 bosses are ridiculous I played this in one go and got through the first four with only 1 death or no deaths at all. I hit level 5 boss all my lives and 1 ups were drained. When I hit my last life I won't deny it I used cheats they were in the options menu however you won't earn achievements its also not a game I can see myself wanting to master. I turned them off when playing the levels and yeah this a game from late 80s early 90s very surreal worlds you think someone was high when designing them think earth worm jim only no level gimmicks. I still recommend this (but only during a sale its not worth 11.99CND) for anyone who wants to experience a little bit of gaming history just keep an open mind this game is old. Beware those final 3 bosses
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Classic game with some crutches to ease new players into it, feels like sonic the hedgehog mixed with a bit of ninja gaiden but in more of a comic style of zen the intergalactic ninja.  Graphics and gameplay are on par with jazz jackrabbit.  Very fun version of this ninja platformer that comes with emulated original as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: This one honestly surprised me. I never thought I'd see Zool returning in this day and age.Nevertheless it's a very welcomed remake. The controls are tighter, there are a lot of small QoL improvements that make the game less brutal, and the Mega Drive emulated game is also included! I really had a good time blazing through both Redimensioned and Ultra Ninja, although some fans of the original might find this remake a little bit too easy. Oh and if you owned Amiga as a kid, then it's definitely a must.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: mmmm I wish there was a mixed review button, not this yes or no thing.Zool Redimensioned is an interesting come back and, although I've heard about the game, I never played it myself.Simply put, a sort of sonic (more like Jazz Jackrabbit) clone, more slow paced and a little... confused? about level design (which are not bad..just... wow) and enemies type? like more than none, you are going to have trouble just distinguishing them from the background. Still, overall, it's a fun game... and while not holding the title of a masterpiece, it's definitely a cult classic. Plus, if it's your style, this game is full of that dank 90's juice (basically, that's the reason I bought the game in the first place).
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Like many retro game remakes before it, Zool Redimensioned proves platformers are better in wide screen. The original Zool always seemed unfair because enemies would just appear so quickly, but in wide screen that is never a problem. I really hope Zool 2 gets the same treatment, and if it does, do us all a solid and put the rest of the emulated titles in there too; Gameboy, Gamegear, SNES, Amiga. I appreciate the Megadrive/Genesis version here, but it'd be nice to have them all.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so my experience with Zool comes from the Amiga, so there may be some discrepancies with console versions etc.I have to thank Sumo for reviving this Platformer, this was "Sonic" for my childhood in the early 90s AND to add the quality of life enhancements as well; it's like they found all the flaws of the old game and ran the modern iron over it to clean it up:* Hi Res: no more leaps of faith* Double Jump* No more vicious respawns as soon as you leave the frame* Enhanced Boss fights with extra fighting features attached to each* Extra world?? I wasn't sure if Consoles had that last one after the Funfair)* Collectables are by quantity and not in percentage (for me that's a win)This is just a handful of what I spotted and remembered in comparison to the original.You can also play it just like the original game again as well if modernisation is not your thing.It's a short game: 2hrs by the time I completed Redimensioned Mode (modern mode) but keep in mind this was the average for platformers of the yesteryear; lives were limited, devs cared not for your skill level because they QA'd games so much that they just got too good at them (looking at you Psygnosis) and they were on a small pile of floppy disks.I know this game will appeal to those biased to it, but this feels like a mini-labour of love and not a phone-in, which is just great, so again, Thank You
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Zool as a game hits harder with its awful level design than any other I had the displeasure to play in recent years.There are just so many mistakes made, from the very inconvenient enemy placements that would give rage games a run for their money to some of the big collectibles being in unapproachable spots depending on which mode you are playing it. It also suffers from the "Sonic 2D syndrome" as in the character moves way too fast for the platforms or to make precise jumps which at times are required, specifically in tight spots or boss fights, more so with how close the camera is that you can't see more than a few steps ahead. To try to compensate for this, the original developers must have scattered around all those extra lives, to no avail though, especially for those not fond of the platformers from the past.That being said, this review is still positive mainly because of the redimensioned mode being more playable and enjoyable in general. A few big changes were added probably to skip all that level design and fill the retro lust to beginners. First and most importantly is the double jump which has saved me more times than hours I have played. Then there's the much wider camera angle that prevents leaps of faith as well as really helps with the collectible hunting. Lastly, the option to collect them as in some levels you just want to get to the end and skip all the nonsense the original developers were responsible for (on that note, screw the Toy ones).So overall, I'd say that this is a good attempt in bringing back a series that probably shouldn't have come back with those levels. The redimensioned mode is the one I recommend after completing it mainly for the mechanical side of things, and I didn't even mention the tweaked graphic designs, tracker masterful soundtrack and added cutscene by the end. It's also cheap.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up with Zool on Game Boy back in my days and enjoyed the gameplay and music. I remember the SNES version of the game and how awesome it was on the console, though I've never beaten it.Years later, I was under the radar when I found that Zool has been remastered and I knew I needed it.Gameplay felt faster than what it was back then. The big difference is that this remastered is much easier than the old school in collecting enough items before finishing a level. The gameplay is a breeze if you can get through a level without dying (at least) and fighting bosses is more widescreen and better. Just that for certain bosses such as the Toy Boss you'll run into some problems.The emulator brings the Sega Genesis version of Zool to light. After completing the game, I checked it out for a bit and it was the same retro feel that it was back in the 90s. I'll be sure to get through the original one day.Overall, I definitely recommend Zool if you are a fan of platformers. Whenever you grew up with the game back then or new, this game is definitely for everyone to give it a try (though it won't be for everyone).
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: The source material isn't as strong so if you don't have any nostalgic feelings for this, it might not appeal to you. It's a decent platformer but there are better ones. That said, I like what the developers did to update this. Zoomed out perspective, double jump, tight controls ... It's much more fun now than it ever was on the Amiga. Good job on their part. And thanks to DF for letting me know this exists. I hope more projects like this come along. James Pond 2 please.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: If like me you had Zool for your Amiga (or other classic system) back in the day you will enjoy this. This brings the game in the 2020's nicely with the same colourful graphics but enhanced, more screen space and updated controls. If you still want a challenge you can up the difficulty, want to breeze through just activate god mode.If you never played Zool before this may be interesting to see a window into 90 mascot platformers, or it may hold your attention for five mins before you head back to Celeste or whatever the kids play these days
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played the original back in 1990s I can confirm this is a brilliant remaster with lots of quality extras, such as cheats you can activate and a guide to the characters of the game. Well worth the price.My only criticism is that I wish they had included a port of the Amiga version rather than the weaker Genesis / Mega Drive version.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game as a kid growing up, having the little disc thing to prove you owned the game. Best form of drm ever. This is a brilliant update to the game making it playable on modern hardware. I particularly like the camera reveals more of the game. It does make it a bit easier, but it also makes it more visually appealing to me. I just wish they had the chup cup licence still.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: This remaster improves on many an issue of the original release while still giving more hardcore players the option to play on the game's original difficulty level. Also gotta love the removal of the OG's massive screen-crunch. This went from being a pretty decent platformer with its Amiga version to being one of my favorite platformers ever made with this remaster, so highly recommend.Edit: editing this with now over 40 hours in this game, as well as 100% achievements, and still gotta say, fantastic game and everything a remake should strive to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: What do I have to say? I never thought I would actually enjoy re-playing Zool and did a finish playthrough. It makes me wonder what Gremlin developers back then had to do to make it more playable. Noting the elephant in the room: the increased playing field makes a much needed difference - there's more breathing room to compensate for the fast-paced gameplay. The incredible thing is the original developers didn't have to do that much for playability, but I guess large sprites were all the rage (which they were) despite standard resolutions weren't as high as today. It does feel much better playing since the fear of not knowing what's ahead is more or less dissipated. Perhaps it's a game ahead of its time? Other small changes make the game feel streamlined. Heart and checkpoint behavior is straight-forward. And other "Assist" modes can be turned on to make easier playing, just to name a few.The graphics look as beautiful as before. Sounds and music are unique and interesting as before (glad they kept the AMIGA soundtrack). Controls are tight like before. It comes to show Zool was never a "bad" game - I never thought so either even in the past; it had lots of potential. It just had some unfortunate design flaws which made it difficult for players already used to Sonic or Mario to appreciate it as an equal.The "modern" and "classic" modes are a nice touch, and the included port of the MegaDrive version is always welcome.They should add the CD32 soundtrack as well as an option. A level editor would be really amazing for people to upload content! I can also see speedrunners jumping on this. I just see a lot of good things for this IP.I'm looking forward for the second part. The team did a solid release.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: A great little (by modern standards) platformer that lets you enjoy the speed of the main character without too many death traps (unlike Sonic). The larger playfield in this modern version greatly improves the feel of the game compared to the original Amiga version. The music and general look-and-feel stay close to the superior Amiga version instead of the limited Sega Mega Drive (Genesis) version. However, it would have been nice to have the comic book style intro sequence from the Mega Drive version included in the main game.Highly recommended for a quick, nostalgic platforming session!
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: Playing the original back in the day, I always found Zool 'fun', but attempting to go back to it these days has been hard with its slippery controls and generally unforgiving nature.Zool Redimensioned however, isn't just the original game slapped into an emulator. This game is tight and redesigned to play so much smoother, with I believe redesigned levels too and with a lot more quality of life improvements. For one, the screen is zoomed out more so you can see more of the level before you, and Zool handles now like a dream. The game plays wonderfully and it shows an expert use of nearly 30 years of hindsight to improve, yet keep the charm of the Ninja from Nth Dimension. And hey, if you prefer the original, it's here too!The ChuppaChups stuff and other product placement has been removed, likely for licensing, but that is a small thing. Only true Zool purists will mind too much.Highly recommended. Having a blast!
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review: I used to play this on my dad's Amiga when I was a kid. So glad to see it on a modern system. If you have a liking for retros and platformers, this is a real gem. Its faced paced, with some tricky boss battles. You really can't go wrong with it. There are 2 modes, classic and 'redimensioned' - which just makes it a little easier. There is also a filter you can activate to get a real 90's look to it. For those that played the original......a proper nostalgia trip.
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

_childDocuments_.review:
Originally released by Gremlin Graphics in 1992 on the Amiga to critical acclaim, iconic gaming mascot Zool returns in Zool Redimensioned!

This brand-new reimagining of the classic action platforming adventure has been rebuilt from the ground up for modern audiences. Help Zool jump, spin and shoot his way across eight alien worlds, taking down menacing bosses and saving the universe from the nefarious influence of Krool.

Zool's old school platforming action will challenge the most hardcore gamers, with modern enhancements that bring the game into the 21st century. Beat your speed run times, discover secrets hidden across every level, or go back in time and play the original classic game. Re-live the legend of the ninja that started it all!
_childDocuments_.name: Zool Redimensioned

name: Miasma Chronicles
detailed_description: AVAILABLE NOW FROM 505 GAMES CHECK OUT 'THE BLOODLINE' FROM OUR FRIENDS AT HOOK! FROM THE CREATORS OF MIASMA CHRONICLES About the Game In the not-too-distant future. America has been torn apart by a savage force known only as the ‘Miasma’. Meet Elvis, a young man brought to the mining town of Sedentary as a baby. Left by his mother in the care of a robotic older ‘brother’ and given a mysterious glove with which he can control the Miasma. Join the brothers on a quest across a post-apocalyptic wasteland to find the answers they crave. Answers which may change the course of human history forever. • Realtime exploration gameplay meets tactical, turn-based combat with RPG elements. • Explore rich beautiful environments meeting outlandish characters. • Upgradable weapons and abilities give your heroes the edge in combat. • An involving fantasy story through which you learn the truth behind the Miasma. From the creators of Mutant Year Zero: Road to Eden, comes a beautifully crafted tactical adventure you won’t forget.
