_childDocuments_.review: ONE OF THE MOST UNFAIR REVIEWS I'VE EVER READI am a turn-based strategy RPG buff. I've played dozens of X-COM likes, and I believe I can tell if a game is good or not. Miasma Chronicles is a good game. I would give it a 4/5. Solid gameplay, beautiful graphics, great setting, interesting characters and even a compelling story (which is something very rare in the genre - probably the best one I have seen so far, if we don't count The Banner Saga). Sure, it lacks some polish, and the main guy is not the most memorable, but I had a blast playing through it.So I was very surprised when I saw that Eurogamer gave Miasma Chronicles a baffling 1/5 rating. That's the rating you give to a completely broken game, with horrible gameplay and forgettable story - which Miasma Chronicles objectively is not.As I went through the review, it did not take me long to realise that the reviewer was clearly blinded by some kind of extremist "D&I" ideology ("wokeness", some would call it).The reviewer was particularly bothered by two things:1 - She considered the sidekick character to be a racist trope. That's because he is a tanky sassy/brash robot, voiced by a black actor, who is very loyal to his white friend (to the point that they consider themselves brothers), but does not get much credit for their feats. First of all, just because a robot uses black vernacular, it doesn't make that character black - it's a damn robot! Second, how is having a black sidekick racist? Sidekicks are omnipresent in fiction; it's not a crime if one happens to be black, as long as not all black characters are sidekicks. Plus, the supposedly "bigoted stereotype" robot sidekick at hand is easily the coolest character in the game. The reviewer also mentions that this robot descends from a slave race, but this parallel does not hold. Robots (obviously) used to serve humans in the early days, when they were not fully sentient. Some of these non-fully sentient robots can be spoken with in the game, but they don't have "black" accents or anything like that. Sure, the game's story revolves around political tensions between humans and robots, but so what? That is a very common trope in sci-fi, and actually works as social commentary. Plus, the game has plenty of human NPCs of colour (literally more than half of the protagonist's home town). Some of them also have very noble roles, such as the protagonist's mother, or the town militia leader. As for robots, they are voiced by a great number of different actors, presumably from all ethnicities.2 - Apparently there's a "throwaway transphobic line in a diary entry about the author not caring if drugs cause them to grow boobs". I haven't even read that line, as diaries are very secondary collectibles in a game that took me almost 40 hours to finish, with thousands of perfectly fine voice lines. codes entries and collectible diaries. Clearly, a single diary by a random NPC doesn't make the entire game or its message transphobic.That's it. Those are the reasons. The reviewer does go through gameplay, which she curiously considers much worse than the previous game by the same developer (which she liked). That's curious, because the two games are in fact very similar in terms of gameplay, as noted in practically every other review out there.It's so sad to see a game made with so much love fall victim to a reviewer (who describes herself as a "fat, disabled trans woman") fueled by some kind of rampaging self-righteous obsession with "inclusivity" that really had little to no role to play here.
_childDocuments_.name: Miasma Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: It runs perfectly fine on Steam Deck however in my case I needed to force compability to Proton Experimental as on default version game was not launching. Game has full controller support, no problem here, bindings are great. When it comes to graphic settings, better change some of them from ultra to high/mid - no worries, it still will be a top-notch experience compared to other tactics games! Only thing missing is that you cannot adjust size of in-game texts but it is a minor inconvenience.It’s like Mutant 2.0 so definetely yes :)
_childDocuments_.name: Miasma Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: The further into the game you get, the more you realise it's less of a tactical action RPG and more of a puzzle game - there's pretty much only one correct way to handle encounters and it's trial-and-error until you figure it out. Doing anything even slightly different to that will mean total failure. It just doesn't feel like there's much freedom or flexibility in the combat encounters, which is a fatal flaw in any tactical-action game.
_childDocuments_.name: Miasma Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to Mutant Year Zero, the story and depth of characters is bit flat. The world is intriguing, the characters have some wit, and the tactical fighting, focused on more silent ambushes is a good challenge. A fun 20 so hours, but buy it on a sale.***Update after 20+ hours: cannot put the controller down. The challenge of stealth/silent attack, and changing the combo of your skills, weapons, and consumables based on the enemy is addicting. Still not super bought in the the characters, but I want DLC, and I want more games from this team and developers!
_childDocuments_.name: Miasma Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: Art/Sound/VFX teams knocked it out of the park, looks and sounds great. The design/code teams not so much. Balancing is way off with the difficulty spiking pretty early on. As other reviews have commented; this isn't a strategy game where there are a few ways to approach any given encounter, it's a puzzle game with most encounters only having a single solution with little to no margin for error. If you survive an encounter it's usually with 1 or 2 team members incapacitated and the remaining one(s) on ~10 hp.It's a game that breaks its own rules: team members have little mobility/chance to attack each round, whereas enemies seemingly have limitless action points, some travelling across the map, up/down floors all the way to a team member in cover and still get to attack! Even the lowliest grunt enemies hit like a freight train on normal difficulty.I wouldn't mind the difficulty so much if I could grind other areas for xp/cash/items and return to an encounter stronger but the game is so stingy in this respect it's nigh on impossible.I'm sure there are people out there that will relish the hardcore aspect and have the time (and patience) to play the same encounter over and over, I'm not one of them.
_childDocuments_.name: Miasma Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: There seems to be quite a bit of drama about the balancing of this game. I'm writing this review to give a bit of a counter point to the negative voices that seem to be taking overhand from what I can see.The art and the world they created are stunning, I don't think anyone can dispute that. Let's focus only on the difficulty here.To put it into context, I'm playing on "Challenging" difficulty (that's difficulty 3 out of 4) in full tactical mode (RNG is fully in effect). The game is ball breakingly hard, at least in the beginning. You will have to restart encounters. You will have to get creative sometimes. But if you learn the game, everything can be overcome. And the feeling of accomplishment is all the greater for it when you do survive a battle. As you get more and more tools in the game, you will find it becoming more manageable. After 18 hours I'm reloading less and less. I can even do some encounters on the very first try. But it's still not a no-brain game. I'm getting better through the encounters because I'm making better decisions. Isn't that what a game should be about? I hear that the game is almost as hard even on normal difficulty. I agree that this must be changed. But the devs already said they will issue a balance patch next week already. If you are reading this a few months from now - that's the week after release. So they are listening and are going to adjust things. Please don't dismiss a great game because someone said it's too frustrating. It's very rewarding. I'm hoping they'll keep that feeling of reward while taking off the edge of the biggest frustration sources. 5 hours in, I was with the chorus of people who thought that things *needed* to change. Now I'm happy to try to beat the game before the balance patch.
_childDocuments_.name: Miasma Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: There is something wrong with this year. There were so many games i wanted to like. And so many times I wished for the option of a "Mid" rating. Here I am again. But now I realize, that the only reason stopping me from leaving a negative review here was sympathy for the devs; and the memory of good times spent in MYZ: RtE. I don't think this game deserves such good will.It is basically a glowed up version of Mutant Year Zero. With a stretch of imagination, one could even imagine it is a sequel, simply placed in a different part of world, where a different calamity has struck the society. The gameplay loop and mechanics are similar - story driven, small team, emphasis on the initial stealthy "trimming of the enemies' hedge", to finish the encounter with a strong coda of an ambush and mop up of the remaining baddies. I don't mind these mechanics - it might not be to everybody's taste, might get repetitive, but there is a certain satisfaction. There is also an incentive for savescumming, so there's that for the purists.Where the whole thing falls apart is the story, the setting, the feel. You have two main archetypes of your "XCOM-likes": a tactic driven one, where the story is just a pretext for you to lead a bunch of anonymous mooks into hundreds of smaller or bigger encounters, epitomized by XCOM itself, Phoenix Point, more recently Chaosgate. These usually are driven by some impending doom, some regular "reviews", are about base and resource management - and need to deliver super solid on the tactical part.And then you have your story driven ones, where your encounters follow the main story arc, there is little to none resource management, little to none base building, but your warriors have names, have stories to tell; and encounters are the pretext to tell a, hopefully, compelling stories. Expedition series is one good example. MYZ: Road to Eden was too - and it captured the player with its interesting tales and unique protagonists. It wasn't anything worth a Hugo or Nebula Awards, but kept one engaged and willing to see its end (shame we never got one, other than the mediocre wrap-up behind a DLC paywall). Miasma Chronicles fall short in this segment. The setting is as generic as clothes in H&M. World-building is merely drafted with a faint crayon. Story arc is unsatisfactory, with all the "twists" predictable by a country mile; and the last one really has awoken my PTSD after Game of Thrones Season 8 -.- The characters are either boring or outright vexing, with a notable exception of Diggs. The potential was there - to tell a good tale about transhumanism, about family, about environmentalism. Instead we got a knock-off about "99%" movement from back when, probably penned for a primary school writing competition.And if that is supposed to be the main engine pulling this game - then this game buckles, boggs down and fails. Im sorry Bearded Ladies - i really want to like your product, I really wish you the best. But this one here is a dud. Please keep your graphic department; and please hire some actual professional writer.
_childDocuments_.name: Miasma Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10This is not XCOM. This is a tactical stealth game. You will spend most of your time sneaking around sniping enemies one by one until you feel confident enough to engage them into proper "XCOM" battles. Low/high covers, RNG miss/hit chance, hiding mechanics, destructible objects, multiple skills are all present in this game. But this is not the focus. It is first a stealth game. With that in mind, it is a great game.I have beaten the game after 40h+ on the hardest difficulty, Alpha Editor (ironman). The most difficult part of the game is literally the first region. Only because you are low on resources like money, healing and distraction items. And this is one of the main complaints of many people. Not enough money and healing early on. In retrospective however, I believe it is correctly balanced because once you start the second region, you start swimming in money. I was able to buy all the best weapons and mods the game has to offer way before the end of the game.The story is pretty decent. Elvis, who is a teenager, is looking for his mother that is gone beyond a wall called "miasma". The only way to go through that wall is to use a tech glove that he carries with him at all times. It is your job to understand what miasma is and what that glove is. Anyway, I'll be honest. The story kinda s*cks in the first region. And what makes it worst is that the characters are meh. This is another complain from some people. What makes the characters meh is the way their dialogue is written. Lets just say the dialogues wasnt written by a proper writer. Diggs is annoying. Anyway, the story really picks up in the second region.Those are the two main complains that I have seen. The rest of the game is great in my opinion. Combat is fun, choosing builds is fun, graphics are fantastic, quests/side quests are well done and the stealth is great. So in my opinion, it is a solid 7/10. Just remember, this is not XCOM. This is a tactical stealth game.

_childDocuments_.review: Miasma Chronicles is an underrated gem of Tactical RPG genre. It deserves much better reception than it initially got. Its very similiar to Mutant Year Zero, which was a previous game from these devs. It merges elements of stealth, tactics and RPG in interesting ways.I actually think Miasma Chronicles is a better game than Mutant Year Zero, which makes the fact that its so underrated even more disappointing. Devs expanded all mechanics present in their previous game and managed to craft an interesting post-apocalyptic world. Characters and story are rather simple but likeable with enjoyably cheesy voice acting and fun twists along the way.Graphically Miasma Chronicles is quite a looker, for a game using isometric perspective. Environments are richly detailed and well designed, with many tactical options available. Particle effects are especially stunning! Performance wise its quite demanding and requires a decent rig or lowering of graphical settings.I was playing on Extreme difficulty and found gameplay to be pretty challenging. Every encounter required I "thin the herd" using stealth, before engaging in open combat. Fortunately, stealth has extra depth due to introduction of sound lures, used to separate enemies from groups. Stealth is well balanced as the number of silent weapons is very limited and you'll be only able to kill low tier enemies in stealth.When detected by enemies, combat switches to regular XCOM-style affair. Fortunately, its has more depth as each character is highly customizable via itemization and skill trees. I quite liked the skills available and the fact you could freely respec each character at any time. It made me micro-manage my squad depending on the type of enemies I was fighting.I had no expectations for Miasma Chronicles, but I'm happy to say that its a great tactical RPG and manages to stand out in the sea of XCOM clones. Its strange it was so under-marketed, considering the pedigree of the developers and high quality of the final product. I really hope it manages to find its audience and we get to see the sequel, as the story goes in interesting directions, but feels like just the beginning of a bigger saga.

_childDocuments_.review: A game set in a unique and immersive world and even the story is somewhat engaging. However, gameplay-wise it is your typical XCOM-Reboot TRPG with no innovation whatsoever and I feel like I have played this game for about 573 times by now. Oh, and unlike Mutant Year Zero, you can't even play with your mouse.  ++ mostly well written even down to the description of the loot++ coherent story...-- ...that lacks logic in the details: the protagonist lives in the same town for his whole life and fiddles around with his magical glove. And yet, a dear friend of his one day asks where he got that glove from?! Another example: You meet another friend and you tell her it is too dangerous for her to be here and she just laughs it off. You go literally 10 meters further and there are 5 devilish frogs that try to kill you. It just doesn't add up. There are numerous things like that. -- optimization seems pretty good first although there are some significant stutters during combat when someone gets killed or hit. They were endurable though. But optimization gets way worse further down the line. I went from 70 fps to 38 in certain zones.-- skills are easily refundable without any disadvantage. Which only shows that the devs KNEW that some skills were lacking and they didn't want you to get stuck on them. Hardly any build variety, half of the skills are just plus/minus things. -- VERY consoly. Unlike literally every other TRPG I have played so far, it is not possible to click on enemies, click on your skills etc. No, you actually have to cycle through targets with >Q< or >E< and press SPACE to trigger the skill. At other times though, when you've already committed to the keyboard only controls (begrudingly so), you HAVE TO use your mouse, for example when you use the gloves abilities. The more I played, the more outraged I became at how utterly stupid and unfriendly these controls are to PC players. -- looting is very boring. You loot scraps of plastic (the in-game currency) which are often times so low that it hardly pays to collect them. There are only a few unique items that you can sell like painted pictures or something like that but they are few and far between. What missed potential! The game could have actually made you feel like a junk collector, selling the stuff to buy new stuff. It would have made perfect sense in the gameworld. Oh, and a grenade is 100 plastics while a glass bottle is 200 plastics. Sure, glass bottles are very important in the stealth parts of the game to distract enemies but then again: why do you have to throw bottles? Couldn't you throw a stone, a piece of metal etc? It doesn't add up and the whole economy makes the game feel very game-y up to a point that you lose all immersion. -- VERY linear. I don't mind linear games and actually prefer them to some pseudo-open world. However, it is the combat that is painstakingly linear. Most of the times, there seems to be one and only one solution to make it through. -- as cinematic as the game is at times, it gets marred by a few oversights. E.g. when a cutscene triggers, suddenly a mouse cursor appears (you know, the same mouse cursor you don't need 80 percent of the game) and it just hangs there big and fat in the middle of the screen. Similarily, on the right bottom end there is a big and constant REMINDER that you can press right mouse button to skip the cutscene. We are in the year 2023 now, dear Bearded Ladies. Only show such a prompt when I actually move the mouse or tap SPACE or something. And don't prance it in my face when I simply want to enjoy the cutscene. -- there are dialogue options which doesn't make any sense because you have to click on all of them anyway. You just choose the chronological order (which doesn't affect anything). Just play the whole thing for Pete's Sake instead of nudging me into some pseudo-choices. -- you have to play the audiologs in the menu. When you close the menu, the audiolog stops. -- levels have very obvious "hidden" walls. -- unlike what people are telling you here, there are indeed bugs. And annoying ones at that. One time I carefully positioned my three characters which took about 5 minutes but when I started combat one of the characters had glitched from the roof of a house down to the ground so I had to do the thing all over again. Or: when there is bantering between your characters but a log about detected enemies shows up, it says "press X" to learn more about the enemy. When you do that it cuts off the voice over and it won't come back. So you are essentially missing story pieces.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really on the fence with giving this a negative review. I played through the entire game and, until the last hour or so, I would have given it a thumbs up. This game is a prime example of the developers making the last boss fight (and to a lesser extent the last few levels) a completely different game than the ~25 hours leading up to it.Additionally, there are some really odd decisions they made when making this game. Like making several of your characters really unlikeable, but treating them all like heroes. And the story gets really wonky towards the end, especially with some of your characters switching sides arbitrarily. And at one point in the game there is a massive ~40-minute battle where... the developers disabled saving. God forbid you are a human who may have something come up during that 40 minutes where you'd need to stop playing. (Note: I am one of those humans who had to stop playing about 30 minutes into that... so I had to start the entire slog of a battle again)And equally mysterious of a design decision, they made the Miasma Powers (ie. magic) such a rare resource in the game that it can't really be used. Even with the skills, equipment, and modifications to regenerate power, you'll still only be able to use a power once every 4 battles or so. Making it something that, by definition, can't be used as part of your general strategy. Indeed, powers aren't even powerful enough that they make a huge difference. You can do just fine without ever using them.All that said, most of the core mechanics are pretty solid. The stealth aspects are well done, the skill trees give decent utility, and it is satisfying to be able to crush encounters with careful planning. There are a few problematic bugs (most notably the teleporting and starting combat when leaving ambush mode), but the save-system means that you don't lose much progress when that happens.Overall this game is SO CLOSE to being great, but a few poor decisions put a damper on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Unbalanced fights with HP bloats making this anything but tactical.Pure copy paste Mutant Year Zero combat mechanics with worse implementation.As skills have no reset on a new encounter with just laughable 2-4 rounds reload times meaning in most fights you cannot even USE them to any effects.Fight areas are small and are just choke full of HP bloat mobs while your weapons deal virtually nothing.Example:Pretty early fight against a 200HP boss with armor supported by two 110 HP Snipers and 2 70HP goons.And you got 3 party members with each weapons doing 50 damage only.Mind you this on NORMAL.Also no healing between fights on normal, no rest points so you are broke from just buying overpriced healing pods or even worse reloads for your vaunted unique power glove as it also does not reload.Add a packed room and you get just kicked plus having no skills to "negate" a bit of this choke on cooldown because of some BS idiotic freeze from the last fight some 30 minutes ago while exploring the world.Skills are barebones and basic.When I need to be thankful to get even "Dash and fire", "overwatch" or meagre "1 bonus square movements" for precious skill points that does not feel "mighty" just choked off basics you have in any turn based tactical.Here you need to pay precious skill points for basics in other games.This is no tactical and frankly at the moment worse than Mutant Year Zero.Which I enjoyed despite the combat weakness.This game chokes off any enjoyment of the story by battles that are anything BUT tactical.There is no tactical fight fighting HP bloats with gimped weapons or skills.And the cred drops are a joke for the equipment costs when you are needing them to just heal buying heal pods.Avoid at the moment.As it is not enjoyable or worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: OK, but needed another 20 minutes in the oven. 3 out of 5 stars. If you liked Mutant Year Zero, you’ll like this. They obviously hit a budget wall and released before it was fully baked. Vote with your wallet and wait for a sale to buy. Show the executive that deciding to publish early without further play testing and improvements is ultimately not cost effective. I’m sure the developers told them it needed a few more weeks. Play Mutant Year Zero first if unsure if you like this type of game’s play-style as that game if fully baked.It has quirks but haven’t had any game breaking bugs at about 75% of the game. Weak PC port of controls to KB+mouse. It’s like the mouse sensitivity is set at minimum with no way to change it. You can max your Windows desktop pointer speed to help. Keys mapped to gamepad buttons without much thought and minimal options to change them. Interacting with a game object could be “E” or “Space” or “R” or “Y”… Or choose to play with a gamepad if you have the option and can tolerate slow point and click with a joystick for pointer icon movement. Character movement is thankfully OK with WASD or joystick. Another gameplay jank example is your team can often be forced to move to the focus character unreasonably. The game has a huge stealth gameplay importance. You may enter “ambush” mode only to find out your team is positioned wrong. Gun accuracy is range dependent, but it varies inconsistently (+/- 2 or 3%) for the same weapon. Sniper rifle is only 100% at max range and that accuracy can vary by only a movement square or two. Exit ambush mode to reposition and sometimes your other team members will move to you, breaking stealth. Deal with the too early botched ambush fight or reload from a save. A few other similar irritations. Not game breaking. How much are you willing to pay for often irritating functionality that could have been fixed?A great feature is the ability to change your skill point allocation and weapon modifications as needed when out of combat. You’re not locked into weapons attachment choices nor skills. You can change them before every battle. And you will need to as there is a good amount of enemy variety in weaknesses and capabilities. Go into most fights unprepared and you will suffer heavy losses.Half price was my threshold and I am happy with the game at that value point.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a good game in here somewhere, but it seems as its own systems are contradicting each other and ultimately limiting the whole experience. The game seems worried that it gave you too much power, so it locks abilities behind expensive costs and cool downs. Abilities like overwatch that are so long that sometimes battles are done before they're ready. That might be fine if the game didn't to swarm and outnumber you with enemies that even flanked and critted take multiple shots to take down. It's clear the game wants you to spend time in stealth, puzzling out how to cull the numbers, which it only allows you to do with 1 character for the first 10 hours at least. It turns a regularly enjoyable combat system into a slog. MC  wants to encourage exploration/scavenging so healing  (you don't heal out of combat) and energy (resource needed for glove powers) become outrageously expensive resources you'll need to scavenge currency for. A currency that seems to mostly exist as a reason to come back to town. Yes, it's the post apocalypse. No, interesting fight for survival and resources this ain't. I'm sure this eases overtime, but having to go back to the Pokemon center after every other combat and spend half your money on heals is more annoying than engaging resource management. MC also spends a lot of time being about story without the narrative design to back it up. I can forgive the bad dialogue (why is the robot Mr. T??), but some of these character decisions only make sense from a developer perspective. Need to create a sense of mystery and pull to go out into the world? Make the hero's mom's motivations unnecessarily cryptic and mysterious instead of having the confidence to develop the story and twists from a point of disclosure. Need to introduce level scaling and side quests? How about showing you a pressing emergency and then saying we'll come back later. Again this is a game at odds with itself.There are a ton of small decisions like this. Decisions that are trying to balance each other, but instead restrict what MC could be (gameplay-wise anyway). I'm hopeful that some balance tweaks or a major update can make this a recommend. Simply reducing the cool down times and significantly reducing miasma powers costs so they can pop off at least once per combat would do wonders. For now, you might be better off playing Mutant Year Zero instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Miasma Chronicles is The Bearded Ladies' third tactical rpg after Mutant Year Zero: Road to Eden. I had a lot of complaints with Mutant Year Zero's nearly unplayable gameplay and had doubts about Miasma Chronicles; but turned out it is much better. Story-wise both games are on par on the quality and delivery department. Gameplay-wise; let's dive in with positives then continue with negatives.+There were some well-put, funny easter eggs to the previous games.+Mutant Year Zero had square tiled turn-base fights but you weren't been able to see the squares until the fight starts. NPC area detection was made in circle form too. Miasma Chronicles have it all in squares now and I think it's way better. I can see the exact distance I should stay in and plan tactical approach depending on the tiles.+New knock back mechanic feels really good. If you topple the enemy on another enemy they both get knocked down. (Although you can't decide the direction you want to knock them down even with enough Action Point)+You can now auto-pick battle dropped items in fight when you walk over the drop.+There are puzzles in the game and they are in the keypad/passcode format. They are mostly fun to solve. Some of them are extremely hard for non-native speakers. Example: -There still is no quick save option.-Still no minimap and I don't think it helps with the "exploration vibe".-Can't register some keys like MB5~ (Side mouse buttons).-Quest rewards go like: "Pick one: Exocharger Alpha or Ultra Charger" and doesn't show you what they do when you hover over the curser.-Some interiors and covers are buggy. Characters stop following each other, refuse to move or attack. Shows full cover but doesn't apply etc.-Still auto regroups and cancels sneak after an ambush. Blows the carefully put positions and even sometimes put the team in danger. Those mechanics should be toggled on or off in options menu.-Some area designs are weird. Like there is a keypad which opens a door to a building but there is already a big hole on the wall which the characters would fit but they can't vault over it.-Too many NPC talks at the beginning of the game and newly discovered towns. Many trivia talks are fun but some of them are like 3 paragraphs long and doesn't contribute to the game or the story in any way.-You use "Glass Bottle" to throw and lure out an enemy in ambush mode. It's sold for 100 in game money. On par with a frag grenade or acid bottle. I think it should have been free in "throw rock" function. Buying an empty glass bottle for frag grenade price make no sense.-Girl in town says "Get lost" then make herself join the team 5 minute later in another zone. Also she can spawn a turret which deals area damage. If you target multiple enemies AND HER, she talks to herself: "What's your problem?" - "Sorry, my bad."-There is an enemy type that clones itself when drops below half hp. Clone starts with full hp and can also clone itself. Feels like a really bad design. I can say that it's a really good post-apocalyptic tactical RPG. I'd recommend If you are looking for a bit of tactics and a good story. Enjoy

_childDocuments_.review: Alright. **Miasma Chronicles** is done and dusted. I thought I had wrapped up all side quests but apparently I missed at least one. Anyway, I quite enjoyed this game. It was in my opinion, for *The Bearded Ladies*, a natural evolution in development from *Mutant Year Zero*. Not perfect, but a fun story set in a cool world with excellent gameplay. I played on the *Steam Deck*, and it functioned well at medium settings across the board with FPS locked at 30. It was however a battery hog, and at medium, you can expect to play for about 75 minutes before needing to charge back up. So, playing plugged into a charger is advisable. With that said:I want to start with the cons of this game, as they need to be considered before buying this. *Miasma Chronicles* hard crashes. A lot. Not in the middle of exploration or battle, but during area transitions, fast travel, and just generally using the in game menu (to access the map, inventory, party management, journals, etc...), it suffers a 'fatal UE4 engine failure'. This happened at least 50 times during my playthrough on a fully updated Deck. Probably closer to 80 times really. That was annoying AF. Additionally, the framerates drop significantly as you progress into the game and you can expect heavy stuttering. There were the occasional instances of clipping as well.With that out of the way, this game was visually stunning. The detail invested in everything from avatars to buildings and the general surroundings, combat effects, etc...was very well done. Additionally, the grid system in combat was easy to navigate as was the quest tracker. Despite all the detail, you never lose track of your party or where you are in the world. Detailed, but not cluttered.Gameplay is that mix of free roam exploration and turn based grid combat you should expect from TBL games. It's a pretty brilliant system I hope more devs in the tactical RPG genre will emulate.You have a good selection of weapons within four weapon archetypes. Each has clear advantages and disadvantages. You also find Miasma powers and have disposables in the form of grenades that are either buffs or combat depending on the specific one. Traversal is pretty seamless, both standard and vertical. There is a fair amount of exploration in most maps, and that never gets boring. You'll find useful items as well as journal entries and old robots that help with lore development.The story itself was okay. It won't blow your mind and is a heavy mix of pop culture and political statements which I enjoyed, but as I said, it wasn't top tier. Keeps you engaged however.The voice acting I particularly enjoyed. It was comical but also on point. Sort of a weird mix of over the top and yet restrained. A lot of journal entries were also voiced, which was a pleasant surprise.For me, this is a game to buy on sale given its technical issues which I really doubt will be fully fixed. Mutant Year Zero had the same persistent issues, so you know. I do think it is worth playing, and for $30 or less, it definitely matches value to price. Must play? No. Should consider? Yes. Took me about 26 hours to complete being pretty thorough overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Miasma Chronicles

_childDocuments_.review: 3 hours in. Don't get it twisted. This isn't so much of a "review" than it's what I've noticed and picked up so far. Created by the same team that brought us Mutant Year Zero. That game was fairly great. Short, but wonderfully done with character and flair by a new team. Fast forward to Miasma. Game oozes extremely capable dev work. Everything done in the graphics department is stellar. Character models, textures, set design and placement of real world items and materials. Just stellar work. It's like our world actually had something very bad go wrong. If you wished the Xcom games were a bit more "realistic" then this is right up your alley. Combat seems to be your basic "put guy here, then shoot or flank, etc" move set. There's verticality spread throughout, so, just like MYZ and the Xcom games, you get bonuses for going to high ground and shooting down. Cover is simplistic but works. Full cover gives you an 80% chance to negate damage. Partial cover only gives 50%. No random numbers just straight and to the point. I appreciate this. I haven't unlocked a whole lot yet but what I have unlocked and discovered so far leads me to believe there's a LOT MORE going to happen with my inventory, objects, powers, bullets, etc. Plenty of empty and open spaces I haven't gotten to yet that fill me with anticipation at what is around the bend in gameplay. Plenty of armament upgrade options seem possible as well as special powers and other items and skills. Sound is very well done as well. VOs are well done fitting each character sensibly. I've noticed some lip synch issues but nothing game breaking or terrible as of yet. Background music is nice. Combat music obviously ramps up when in, well, combat. Story seems to be coming along nicely and I'm looking forward to how far it's going to go. The two main characters seem to be well paired and there's none of that cringey back-and-forth that games like Forspoken or others have going for them. There's no 12 year old a$$ jokes so I appreciate that as well. If you're on the fence you can get a nice little discount over at GMG. So far, I'm happy with my purchase and will NOT seek any kind of refund. I'll edit this as I finish the game which I very much plan on doing. However, it's a fantastically well done game. No crashes, no freezes. I experienced one small hiccup in 3 hours of gameplay and it was due to a LOT going on screen at the same time. However, it happened and cleared up nicely. No more issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure, major Mutant Year Zero (MYZ) fan.I have 37 hours into the game and I am enjoying the storey immensely.  Some General Comments:Some people are slamming the accents ... uhm ... the story is set in Kentucky in the US of A ergo southern accents.  I quite like it because it gives the game a unique flavour.Mr funny shoes has it right this game is murderously hard.  I play MYZ on Hard and am able to complete with out getting my ass handed to me too many times.  This game I went on Standard and by level 4 found myself and my team surrounded by 4 or five 200 + life and 2 armour enemies with 2 to 3 lower levels but it would take shots form all of your characters to kill one of the lower levels.  With 2 weapons at 50 and one at 70 with no cover I could not find a solution to this.  Ready to quit but went on story mode and am thoroughly enjoying it.  Story mode here would be equivalent to standard in MYZ.  Once I play through and get used to the skill trees I will step up the difficulty.To the individual playing on hard mode.  Good lord you must be a dark souls masochist but more power to you.It is a very good game but you are going to have to like the mechanics and story.  You will have to learn the process and there is more than one way (despite some of the comments) to win a fightGood game particularly if you are a MYZ fanAddendumFinished game at 59 hours on story mode (as I have said equivalent to standard mode in MYZ).- Reasonable  to good challenge- deep story loved it- voice acting is better than most games I have played and quite enjoyed itNow that the new patch is out I will be doing another run through on Standard to start may step up to hard as I now have a feel for the game.  Definitely replayableThis is a very good game not only for its' genre but it is in my top five (I have been gaming since 1995).Highly recommendedFinal addendumI played through on standard roughly equivalent to hard in MYZ. Completed then went to extreme.What is the hate for the voice acting and the script.  It isn't academy award material but it carried the story along and the voice acting was of better quality than a number of AAA games out there.  Like I said above I quite enjoyed it.  Do agree with the running comment about the protagonist got a bit old for no relevance I could findFinal thoughts and some none spoiler suggestions:-  Play standard before you go extreme become comfortable with the system and the strategies.- it is a very good TBS.  Definitely one of the better ones out there.  You will be challenged but in a good way.  Take your time and scout all of the positions before committing.  They always hang some joker out in the back corner.-  Three things you need to buy;  one damage weapon mode (2 if the other one doesn't drop by mid game) for the silent weapons.; The big gun at the store in the DRC and the very expensive one that is offered later.  Trust me having these two heavy hitters make a huge difference in end game.-  At end game sell every weapon and scope and mod you are not going to use and load up on med pods emp grenades and energy cells.  You will use most of it.  Go into final game with at least 4 frag grenades and 4 poison bombs.  That extra hit can make the difference between taking a shot or not.  In extreme they hit a ton 1 to 3 shots even with armour and full health.I have done three run throughs now but it took me 5 tries to finish the end game.  Do not think I have the chops for the ultra over the top death march dead if you pass gas level.great game 8 or 9 out of ten (witcher 3 blood and wine being 10)

_childDocuments_.review: So, I stumbled into Miasma Chronicles, and let me tell ya, it's like a wild rerun of Mutant Year Zero – I half expected Dux and Bormin to pop up with their feathers and snouts. The story's got that Zone "complexity", but I swear journey of brothers is a déjà vu remix. Gameplay? It's Mutant Year Zero's lost twin, complete with the same XCOM combat (after stealth kill edge enemies) and scavenger hunt vibe.Graphics are snazzy, capturing the post-apocalyptic vibe. Soundtrack's like a rad mixtape, and yeah, there are a few glitches, but nothing you can't handle. Miasma Chronicles seems like Chronicle One is Mutant Year Zero's long-lost twin, while Part Two (67% of the game) is gearing up for another spin in the merry-go-round of Zone madness.

_childDocuments_.review: Earth has gone to hell because humans fiddled too much with technology - who would’ve thought! Despite this clichèd premise, MC introduces a world that feels and looks unique from any other in the realm of sci-fi. This tale is about Elvis and Diggs, a human-robot duo living in a ramshackle settlement called Sedentary, in what’s left of the former USA. Ruled by an allegedly immortal posse of tyrants dubbed “The First Family”, this setting couldn’t be farther from the Land of the Free it once… was? Pushed more by organically-created necessity than some ex-machina crap, the duo ventures out in the Miasme-infested lands and, incidentally, finds their true purpose.The situations and characters encountered by Elvis and his party, be them companions or NPCs, are all believable and plausible in a post-apocalyptic setting. Bearing in mind this isn’t a RPG with choices and skill-checks, but by all means a linear storyline, the way events unfold and how those involved react, is well-written and acted at all times. Despite getting a tad too dragged-out towards the end, the story is overall interesting and manages to keep player interest up without fail. The amount of optional dialogues, lore files and indirect narration are copious, there won’t be a shortage of interesting facts for the avid explorer.The world is divided in three main areas spanning the entirety of the USA, from coast to coast. Despite such an extension, there will be relatively few self-contained, linked locations to visit in each, so forget any sort of open-world exploring - that’s not happening. All stages are fairly large in extension, and house a number of optional locations that often contain resources, hidden weapons, key items, unique enemies and upgrades to collect. This makes exploration perhaps the most important source of character progression, far more so than quests - only by searching every nook and cranny can you hope to acquire enough skills, mods, weapons and additional XP to be strong enough for what’s ahead. The amount of secrets is generous, many of which hidden behind logic-based puzzles whose solution can be found by reading documents or using environmental hints. It can be said there are two types of combat in MC: Stealth and Loud. This title emphasizes stealth a lot, especially on higher difficulties, by providing you with silenced weapons and certain abilities that allow taking out enemies without being heard - but only if they aren’t seen by other foes, and only if you defeat them without raising alerts. The benefit of doing this is that, when things inevitably go “loud”, you’ll have to deal with fewer foes in a single encounter - and that is almost mandatory to pass many areas, especially on the hardest settings. It would be better if the stealth system wasn’t unreliable and bugged at times: that’s why I heavily suggest NOT trying “Ironman” mode, this game’s stealth system isn’t reliable enough for that to go well.On paper this system sounds fresh and interesting, but it’s actually a pain in the butt. While you have tools to pull enemies, like throwable bottles or static distractions, getting rid of single enemies is heavily-tied to critical hits - one bad roll and that enemy will have enough leftover HP to alert all their friends, ensuring your doom by sheer overwhelming numbers. You’ll have to reload, and a lot, if you want to do sections stealthily and save resources. This isn’t always possible, though, as some encounters start loud without a chance to use stealth at all - THOSE are the ones you should save up all your resources for.The loud combat plays out as any run-of-the-mill turn-based title, with a basic low/high cover system, 2AP per character to move, shoot and use skills, a rage system ensuring a crit once filled up by kills, and a swathe of consumables that expand tactical options considerably. You’ll always be underpowered compared to the full strength of enemy numbers and skills: there is no way to defeat any encounter without moving them down with stealth first.Bosses, in many cases, are named, amped-up versions of normal enemies that boast unique skills, better stats and even have their own lines or special behaviors. They’re always formidable, and can usually bolster their allies or summon new enemies to the field every couple turns. You’ll gain XP not only from combat and quests, but also by finding collectibles in the world, dubbed “treasures”. This will actually be an XP source on par with or better than quests. Leveling up gives a small Max HP boost to all characters, and also skill points to invest in one of the four separate trees each character has at their disposal. There’s no way to get all the skills; you’ll have to specialize - luckily, respec is free and can be performed at any time. Quests will usually entail finding a specific item or killing a particularly horrible monster, or rescuing someone in need.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, I really do--but the balance is such utter ♥♥♥♥. On normal difficulty, your own shots will miss easily half of the time, but your enemies' NEVER will, no matter what kind of cover you're in. At early levels, you can take *at most* three hits before you're down, and healing items are rare as radium enemas, so unless you do *everything perfectly* and luck is entirely with you, you're going to be replaying each encounter ten times before you hit the one AND ONLY ONE solution. And I'm sorry, but ♥♥♥♥ that. I don't have time for that kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.On the other hand, easy mode is Literally No Challenge Whatsoever mode. You have three times the health of even the strongest enemies. Healing items literally grow on trees. There's no effort or thought required whatsoever.No adequate middle ground exists between the two. Either you play on Good Luck Sorry About Your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mode, or you play Might As Well Just Read A Book mode. I can't recommend either: the former's too frustrating, and the latter is completely mindless. I wouldn't even purchase this on the deepest sale.

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to ultimately not recommend this game, because at first I really liked it, but it just overstays its welcome so hard ... and it reveals some serious flaws a few hours in. Add to that the relatively high price, and I'd say ... get this during a deep sale if you liked Mutant Year Zero and want more of that unique gameplay loop, because this game is pretty much that, just ... worse. But to explain that will lead to some spoilers, so read on at your own risk.- Out of combat gameplay:Once again you have a group of 3 individuals, which you lead around various maps to gather items (mostly plastic, the game's currency), find new weapons, and take out enemies, preferrably silently. You start off with Elvis and Diggs, "brothers", who complement each other quite well. Elvis can do some "magic" later on, strip enemies of armor, while Diggs is just a big meat shield with lots of armor and can also control the battlefield with not 1 but 2 abilities that stun enemies, which means you can basically chain stun an enemy. Later on you're joined by Jade, the sniper, who is the ONE AND ONLY character with which you can actually silently kill enemies. And that's the first BIG design flaw imho. In Mutant Year Zero (MYZ from now on) stealth gameplay was just as important as it is here, but that game gave every one of your characters options to do so. Here you are stuck with Jade at the beginning, and her sniper rifle quickly doesn't deal enough damage anymore to take out enemies on her own, which basically means you are forced to invest Elvis' first few skill points into his "shock glove", so you have another silent option. You will get ONE more silent weapon, an assault rifle, MUCH later in the game, which you HAVE to equip on any character other than Elvis. Why do I mention this? Because Elvis can also unlock a skill called Desperado, which let's you shoot at every enemy on a cone. Paired with a silent weapon this would be great, but then you deprive yourself of a 3rd option to silently kill enemies, and the AR just doesn't do enough damage to take out anything on its own, or paired with Jade's sniper. You NEED Elvis' shock glove ability. Even later you also get another character and then one more right before the end, however you can only sub them out FOR Jade, you know, the sniper lady who basically gets a guaranteed crit when she sneaks up on an anaware enemy, which is REQUIRED to actually finish anyone off. Without the crit, most enemies are just too strong to defeat in 1 turn. Funnily enough, the strongest enemies in the game are robots, which, guess what, your shock glove (and one other ability) can disable (most of them anyway), making them MUCH easier than anything else in the game. You basically get 3 full turns to finish off an enemy, instead of one.Another issue is that enemies are often grouped together, meaning you have to take out more than 1 enemy in 1 turn. Early on this works when you get a magazine upgrade for Jade's sniper rifle, because you get an extra turn if you "crit kill" an enemy. Later on, this becomes almost useless. And the ONLY way to separate enemies apart from very specifically placed noise makers are glass bottles. And guess what: glass bottles are a finite and very rare resource for some inexplicable reason. You can buy a few at shops (maybe 10 in total) and find like 10 more around the world. In the entire game. That's it. This should have been an infinitely buyable resource. It'd be a choice whether you want to save your money and take enemies head on, or avoid them, perhaps, or spend the money on them and kill enemies for resources and XP (and you kinda have to kill almost every enemy on the map anyway, because the game requires it).If you fail to kill any alerted enemy in 1 turn they will alert the rest of their squad, which can be like 10 enemies, leading to your quick and painful demise, at least at the start of the game.- In combat gameplay:This is the 2nd portion of the gameplay. You get your classic 2 AP per character per turn, using an item costs an AP, casting a spell usually costs an AP, shooting, reloading, running, you get the drill. Shooting also ends your turn automatically, unless you crit kill an enemy, which leads us to another big design flaw in my opinion. You are forced to use shotguns. There is just no way around it. I played this game on easy and with "True Tactical mode", which means you don't get guaranteed hits even when flanking (and neither do the enemies). Flanking is a big part of the strategy in most turn based tactical games. There are only 4 weapon categories in the game: Assault rifles, shotguns, launchers and snipers. The latter are supremely useless in most circumstances. They only have 1 shot, they only work at long ranges and funnily enough none of them are silenced, only Jade's special sniper, which makes her one and only great ability out of combat even less good later on, since you're stuck on a tier 2 weapon, instead of a tier 3... and she's STILL better than the other 2 characters I'd say. Launchers are even worse. Also just 1 shot, don't do a lot of damage, but can shoot around corners... still they pale in comparison to shotguns. As mentioned above shotguns get additional crit chance the more enemies you're targeting, killing an enemy this way gives you another AP to shoot and kill stuff with. I'd always use shotguns, since they do pretty much as much damage as an AR ... they also apply their respective status effects to ALL enemies hit. That includes STUNS! ARs on the other hand are single target only (apart from Desperado skill), and are only really better at range if you really want to stay in cover. So, since the latter half of the game is mostly against robots ... all you do is abuse the EMP stun abilities of your team to the max ... it's ridiculous, to be honest. In the final fight, I was chain stunning 3 to 4 enemies at once.The only other option you have are the Miasma powers, which I found to be pretty underwhelming. I only ended up using the Whisperer and Frog-Shaman in the final fight to put some bodies between me and the enemies. The issue with these powers is that they cost "energy" (mana), which doesn't automatically replenish after fights. Not even partially. The only way to get energy back is to use expensive consumables, which are also finite, or get weapon mods that give you energy back per shot, but that means you'll no longer be able to take far more interesting weapon mods ... Lastly, there's the "Rage" mechanic. After you've gained enough rage by shooting and killing enemies, you get a mighty increase to your crit chance for 1 hit only ... you can't choose NOT to waste this amazing ability on a weak enemy, though. At least, not in most circumstances... since any bonus above 100% is converted into extra damage this mechanic can be quite useful, but it's hard to control.Story and characters in the comment below.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for June 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before July 2nd, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.X-COM with stealth. The entire time I played Miasma Chronicles I thought “This feels like Mutant Year Zero.”  and it’s obvious why.  This is made by the same developer, likely the same engine.  This time you’re a loner who has a robot who is trying to figure out the secret of the Miasma and a special arm your mom left you.  The story sounds good enough to work, but I was more interested in the combat.  The combat heavily focuses on stealth and getting into position to execute surprise attacks on enemies and take them apart.  If you played Mutant Year Zero you might know what I’m talking about.While I did skip a couple of cutscenes, a lot of the story felt like stuff I had heard before, missing parents, giving strange items to their kid, and the kid having to learn how to use them. It’s all a bit cliche.  There’s a post-apocalyptic world where the focus is on a First Family of sorts that rules the land.   The gameplay was fun, but I also remember thinking the same on Mutant Year Zero and that wore off after a while.  This is a twenty-hour story, but I wonder if it can keep up the early momentum.Pick this up if you liked Mutant Year Zero, or want another X-COM title. Combined with Warhammer Battlesector, this is a good combination, but Miasma Chronicles does feel like the weaker of the pair.  Still, it’s trying something different and not a lot of strategy games try to include stealth like Miasma Chronicles does. _childDocuments_.review: I got suckered into buying this game just because i loved Mutant Year Zero. I will never buy a game from this developer as long as i live.I have never seen a team tactical game look so good graphically, but miss essential parts of the team tactical game. Let me explain:-overwatch has a cooldown-whenever you finish a battle the cooldowns don't reset so if you just used a skill with a 6 turn cooldown to kill the last enemy then bad luck you will take that cooldown into the next battle-too few customizations to be made in the game, i think there are 5-6 weapon attachment types with 2 versions (v1 and v2 with a bit better stats)-there are 4 weapons in the game, yep 4 weapons. The only difference you will find whenever picking up a new weapon is that it has a different skin on it compared to what you have.There is no way to heal in town besides using stimpacks from the backpack. Yeah you get the witch doctor miasma power later but that dude literally gets one shotted by the enemies on enemy turn even with good positioning.Store inventory does not restock so if you buy out an item you use, lets say the glass bottles for stealth then you are out of luck sucker.The story is a joke. You run around doing busy work type main quests and then suddenly you are at the end game. They changed the direction of the plot at the midway point of the game. First was find mama to take her back home then it changed to fight the first family. The big reveal at the end where  turns evil for 10 minutes then comes back around was a bad joke.The characters are so annoying, honestly i have never seen a worst cast of characters in a game where every single character is annoying.-Elvis kept saying 'Oh i miss mama, i want my mama' for half of the game until you meet her and then he switched the cassette to the other side and started saying 'You are not my real mama, i have no family'. Genius script right here guys, well done to the writing department 10/10 GOTY material.-Diggs was a racial stereotype with how they portrayed him like a brother from the hood that keeps on calling everybody brother.-Jade was boring and her so called  was so poorly done that i knew who she really is 10 minutes after seeing her -Bha Mahdi was the most cliche out of everyone with how indifferent she was towards Elvis when raising him-Mason just had written i will betray you but help you later all over his face, almost as cliche as The bugs where something else with this crap, i never had any crashes in Mutant Year Zero but here there were enough to almost make me quit the game.Had multiple UE4 crashes to desktop out of the blue, only had one where my character was still moving and i pressed the key 2 to shoot before the walking animation finished and boom the game crashed.Had a bug where my last save tells me i played for almost 300 hours even tho i only played 25 hours. Good job developers, you really know how to implement a counter.Had multiple bugs where secondary characters that are not in the party somehow occupy space on the map and become invisible walls that you can't go through, also had clothing floating in the air from them after putting outfits on.Had a nice bug where if you kill big bad boy cliche Elvis and then kill the 10 collectors the ending cinematic is bugged out. I have no idea how these people released this without putting some fail safes in case people do indeed kill that annoying mamas boy in the end fight.Stay away from this garbage and any future games these developers put out because it's not worth it. Definitely not worth 50 euros like i payed, but never again will i buy anything from these scam artists. Not even worth on sale since the story is cliche as they come, for a team tactical game is boring and lacks anything interesting about it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard for me to recommend this game, because although I found it to be a decent experience, the QoL and balancing issues cannot be overlooked.I played on Challenging difficulty (one below Alpha Editor), and after a certain point in the game every battle felt like it had to be done a certain way. I don't think I've ever save scummed as hard as I did here than in any other game. Enemies took little damage even with armor removed, while Diggs (who had 4 armor in my playthrough) was getting 2-3 shot by rank-and-file mobs. It also seemed like enemies had near-infinite AP, and were able to hit me every single time. Not to mention the obscene amount of consumables I had to use in every single encounter (why are they so expensive?).After a while I dropped the difficulty, and to my surprise, some characters were still getting one-shot (albeit it was definitely a lot easier to play the game).I really do hope that the difficulty and quality of life overall is addressed in future patches, because the game did have some enjoyable parts (and the graphics are pretty good I guess). All in all, I'd wait for a sale to buy this game in its current state, as it is definitely not worth the full price right now.

_childDocuments_.review: Miasma Chronicles: A Challenging but Rewarding Post-Apocalyptic AdventureJust finished my trek through the wastelands of Miasma Chronicles, and here's the honest scoop:Brutal Beauty: The world is a hauntingly beautiful mix of overgrown ruins and dangerous environments. It  creates a great atmosphere, but be prepared for some tough choices and tense encounters.Tactical Turn-Based Battles: Combat is all about strategy! You gotta position your characters wisely, use their unique abilities, and exploit enemy weaknesses. It's challenging, but mastering it feels very rewarding.More Than Just Shooting:  There's a surprising amount of stealth mechanics involved. You can sneak past enemies, set traps, and use the environment to your advantage. It adds a nice layer of depth to the gameplay.Not for the Faint of Heart:  This game is HARD. Enemies can be brutal, and mistakes are punished severely. But if you like a challenge and enjoy the feeling of overcoming it, Miasma Chronicles will be right up your alley.A Few Quirks:  The story can feel a bit generic at times, and the humor might not land for everyone.  Also, some of the missions outside the main story can be a bit repetitive.Overall Verdict:If you're looking for a deep, strategic, and challenging post-apocalyptic adventure, Miasma Chronicles is worth checking out. Just be prepared for some tough battles, some silly jokes, and a world that won't hold your hand. But if you can conquer the wasteland, the sense of accomplishment is fantastic!

_childDocuments_.review: I'll keep it short.- Good tactical RPG with some solid mechanics, if at time marginally marred by a couple of questionable choices when it comes to balance and fine tuning.- Solid production value, with pretty graphics and a nice (if not stellar) variety of visual assets, enemy types and so on.- Forgettable writing with a bunch of not-particularly-likable characters (to put it mildly).The story ends in something resembling a cliffhanger (which I doubt will ever see a follow up, since I don't think it sold particularly well) just when it feels it's just about to get interesting, but on a mechanical level I had blast with it (most of the time) and I don't regret the hours I spent playing.Overall I enjoyed my playthrough and I'd say that if bought on sale it's a very solid way to spend 20-30 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: My central issue is that in games your story should either be nonexistent so that your gameplay can shine through or it should be intelligent well acted and powerful.This is fully voice acted. The team who wrote the script was on a completely different page than the voice actors and the team who animated the game.So you will hear really bad southern accents bring the emotional severity of Saturday morning cartoons to scenes about cannibal frogs boiling your childhood girlfriend. It almost sounds like this could have been a comedy, but they are playing it for drama and the emotional thrust is human greed destroying the environment.Nothing fits together. Do yourself a favor if you -must- play it and unplug your speakers. Or listen to somebody play the game with your eyes closed. (This will still be bad, but at least not actively nauseating.)Then there is the game. 80% of which is running around being baffled by the design elements, but the rest of which is a very sloppy stealth infiltrator. Most combats are going to be luring enemies out of position so that your sniper character can thin the herd. You will do a lot of this, but the actual mechanics are based off of X-Com. So you will miss your stealth headshot, or it wont crit and you die to an obnoxious level of action economy difference OR you just save scum every shot until you are actually left with a reasonable tactical challenge... that you get less experience for because picking off enemies with crits awards double experience.You are mechanically -rewarded- for playing this game in the least fun way possible. To the level that later challenges can be frustrating if you haven't been maximizing your experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Miasma Chronicles begins by introducing Elvis a young man looking for his mom in a post-apocalyptic landscape while also being accompanied by a robot named Diggs. Elvis believes his mom is on the other side of this devastating wall of mist that he cannot get past or at least not yet as this is the main plot of the game. Miasma Chronicles world is fully explorable but in a linear fashion. Playing the game, you can easily see that the developers took aspects from other games like Mutant Year Zero and XCom and made a beautiful game that yearns to be explored by the player to search and loot, open those locked doors, and be as stealthy as possible. Not only does the game have an excellent story with excellent graphics but all of the conversations have been voiced. Combat is turn based and just like XCom the player and the enemies can hide behind some cover but be warned when you are wounded in combat then you will need to heal yourself afterwards with those resources you find.    Oh, for those that have ultra-wide monitors then yes, this game supports it!

_childDocuments_.review: This seems like a game I should like as a fan of turn-based tactical RPGs, but the pieces come together in a way that feels like less than the sum of their parts.My main issue is that the gameplay, while not as challenging as some other reviews make it out to be, just isn't that fun. The focus on critical hits and trying to increase crit chance bonuses also contributes to making the game feel overly punishing - I'd prefer for a crit to be a nice surprise or have just one character class that focuses on crit chance buffs rather than having it be an essential part of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love the game when it's at its best, hate the game when it's at its worst.The best: Sneaking around and learning patrols and sight-lines to set up ambushes. The capstone fight at the end of Act 1 is this in spades.The WORST: Ambushes you can't see coming where you're outnumbered 3/4:1 and the enemy acts first. It's so antithetical to the best parts of the tactical game design, and I can't fathom why they would do this. It's even worse since I'm playing on the highest difficulty, which means no manual saves. So the current ambush in the 3rd zone almost 20 hours in is just unwinnable, with no backup save.I really wish I could recommend this game, but I just can't. The bad parts of the design just ruin the game because they completely take me out of the experience. Or in this case, lock me out.

_childDocuments_.review: Miasma Chronicles is made by the same developers as Mutant Year Zero: Road to Eden. MYZ:RE was a surprise hit for me, fully utilizing the engrossing world of the Mutant Year Zero IP to craft a unique experience equal parts stealth,turn based strategy, and RPG (though a little light on the latter). I had high hopes for Miasma Chronicles since this was the developer's third game in the stealth/Turn based strategy genre, the second being Corruption 2029 which I haven't had a chance to play. Unfortunately, despite this being the third attempt Miasma Chronicles fails to improve or innovate upon any of the core design choices of the previous entries.The core gameplay loop consists of a few different actions:1. Enter a zone2. Explore the zone collecting plastic (this games version of scrap)3. Find enemies4. Pick enemies off in stealth ambushes to wittle down their numbers before fully engaging in turn based combat5. Engage in turn based combat6. Finish exploring the area for any loot like extra scopes, or relicsWhile the above is a bit reductionist, it does well to highlight how incredibly similar this is to MYZ:RTE. So similar in fact that the entire game I couldn't shake the been there, done that feeling. This feeling of familiarity runs deep in everything, from exploration, to stealth, to the turn based combat, to the perk system, to worse yet, the story. Steam has a pretty low character limit on reviews so I will limit discussion of some areas. In MYZ and Miasma Chronicles you MUST pick off enemies before engaging in full on combat. The game effectively becomes puzzle game for a few minutes between each encounter, where you must figure out exactly how to pick off isolated targets without alerting the entire camp. To do so you must use silenced weapons (there are only 2 in the entirety of Miasma chronicles), in conjunction with abilities to pick off targets. As the game goes on this doesn't necessarily get harder, but requires you use more resources to pick off higher health/armor targets. While this system was novel in MYZ:RTE it quickly wore out it's welcome in Miasma chronicles, partly because this game is longer, but also because the developers didn't add any new tools or mechanics to improve the stealth combat. In fact they went backwards in some areas like the removal of invisibility and many crowd control abilities from MYZ.  Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed this gameplay loop the first time around, but after a few attempts it would be great for improvements and additions added rather than a regression. There aren't really any additions to the formula that bring any new excitement to exploration, stealth, or combat, so the driving force behind exploration becomes the story. The story is told via conversations with NPC's when starting or completing a main quest, or through audio logs or journals littered throughout the world. Unfortunately, Miasma Chronicles fails to make any improvements in this department either. If you have played MYZ:RTE the story here retreads alot of the same themes, ideas, and plot points. As  just a single example that won't spoil anything- In MYZ:RTE you leave your home in a post-apocalyptic wasteland when your father figure goes missing. Throughout the game you learn about the ancients (humans as they existed prior to the apocalypse), and content with themes about figuring out one's place in the world. Miasma chronicles takes place in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, where Elvis (the protagonist) is in search of his mother figure who has gone missing, in the process learning about the Originals (human's prior to the apocalypse), all the while learning about who he is and his role in this world. While all stories can have similarities the retreading of MYZ was just too much to be coincidence. I frequently caught myself thinking, "they are doing this again, seriously"? Even without the retreading of old ground the story does't have much going for it besides being a passable heroes journey- boy leaves comfort of his home to cross a threshold into danger, ultimately becoming the hero. This game is good, and I recommend it, which is counter my entire review. I still recommend it if you enjoyed MYZ:RTE as it follows the exact same formula, for better or worse. If you liked the first game then more of the same should scratch that itch, just don't expect any improvements or changes whatsoever. I also recommend it if you have not played MYZ:RTE at all as everything presented here will be a fresh experience. But if that is the case and you haven't played MYZ:RTE go buy that one instead- the world and characters are more interesting, the combat and stealth has more variety, and it is cheaper.

_childDocuments_.review: This review will be spoiler free. You’ll probably still be able to infer some things however.I’m sorry to say I didn’t like this one.I’m going to be doing a lot of comparisons with Mutant Year Zero, the previous game by these Developers. They’re in different settings but the gameplay is very similar, and why I didn’t like this one will also be easier to explain with those comparisons.This game is okay but eventually enough things piled up and as a result I can’t really recommend it. I really enjoyed Mutant Year Zero. But it had its flaws and when I saw they had made another game with very similar gameplay I was very much hoping they had made improvements and perfected the formula. But this is not the case, in fact I think some things may be worse. A problem I found myself having with both games is that there is no replay value, unless you really want to replay the entire thing again on a higher difficulty. I’m the kind of guy that sees skill trees, party companions and itemization and my first thought is “Oh boy I can replay this and try different things!”. But alas, just as Mutant Year zero, this game is extremely linear, and has almost zero room for variance. Some examples.Every gear item is pre-set in the world, you get them from quests or find them, or buy them. You’ll always get the same weapons in the same order. And you’ll want to use the most powerful one you have, until you get the next level of it. So you’ll be built around what you have, which is always the same.You can respec at any time and you will be, your skill tree isn’t really about flavour, there is no real distinctly different build you can replay the game with(unless you’re forcing yourself to play poorly). Plus the skill trees are relatively short so you’ll see everything pretty fast. Mutant Year Zero actually did this better, not by much though. In having you get most of the companions available relatively early, so you could spice up your next playthrough by using different ones. You could also bring any combination of them you wanted. In Miasma you have two that are mandatory and 1 slot where you get a choice. However the optional slot will be occupied by the same person throughout 75% of the game, so no doing anything differently there. Except for the very last bit that is. Stealth gameplay is the same as Mutant, you sneak around and try to murder as many as you can before you’re forced to start the fight proper and alert the entire map(most of the time). This involves going “oh that guy has X HP points, I can do X from stealth, I kill him.” You have a sum total of 3 abilities to do damage from stealth, one comes with the third character, another you can select as a skill for the main guy. The third is a found weapon along the way. Making Stealth extremely inflexible and time consuming. It’ll literally always be the same, every playthrough, unless you choose to screw up. So for me, there’s zero replay value, which I guess isn’t bad for a 30 hour game. But urgh. The game is called Miasma Chronicles. Plural. When you start the game “Chronicle 1” fades in. 10 hours later “Chronicle 2” oh boy I think, this’ll be a long game and I may get to make interesting build decisions later. Then shortly after I look up at my EXP bar to find it saying “MAX LEVEL” Yeah I was near the end, there are two chronicles, two, the bare minimum to slap the plural on Chronicle. The voice acting and writing can be very fine sometimes, but then it flip flops weirdly in unexpected ways. And not in the plot twist way, characters are just oddly inconsistent, like the writer forgot who they were writing for at times, they’ll often contradict themselves and the character they’ve been established as previously. This gets much worse past the halfway point of the game, the story becomes a complete mess and any expectation of it being interesting you had in the beginning falls to bits and then dies. Which is probably what annoyed me the most, a lot was well written and acted, then it slowly dawns on me that it isn’t doing to have any pay-offs on those things, and I read too much into it, the characters start acting stupid, the plot gets dumb, and it’s just a bit nonsensical mess. Not nonsensical in the way you can’t follow what’s going on. Nonsensical in the way that what is happening is just so dumb and stands in such stark contrast to the earlier pacing and setup  that you’re left wondering if it’s trying to pull a fast one on you.Then it slowly dawns on you that it isn’t, and this is just how it’ll be. This gets worse and worse as the game nears the ending. The ending sequence is one of the most poorly thought out I’ve ever seen.Music is nice though.In conclusion. I still don’t know if I’m being overly critical on this because of how well it started out, and I’m bitter the quality of it just took a nosedive halfway through. Or if it’s because I enjoyed Mutant Year Zero so much and am annoyed this one didn’t do much to address any of the flaws in it. Again that expectation is on me, I guess.On a technical note, the controls can be quite garbage, they seem to be made for a controller, press Y to modify a weapon. Really? Just because an x-box controller has it you’ve one of the most awkward mappings possible for it? Right in the middle of the keyboard, where your hands will always be the furthest away from. Also you swap weapons with R, if you want to reload you have to press 3, then space. Wut?
