_childDocuments_.review: After months of silence (and over a year since the last update) the devs dropped another patch with a pretty impressive change log, however their complete and utter mishandling of the Kickstarter and lackluster communication is still a massive issue so my review score will stay the same.I did start a new game to see if anything stood out but after beating the first two bosses all I really noticed was the Noctilium drops have been boosted, enemies have a little less health, and you can animation cancel now. The changes might be more obvious if I put more time into it, but I don't really feel like bashing my head against this game anymore.For disclosure I did not try the new Prime Hunts mode, so I have no comment on that.• Falling into pits or bodies of liquid still warps you to the beginning of the room (or a previous room) instead of the last surface you were standing on• Cutscenes still replay after failing to defeat certain bosses, instead of skipping straight to the encounter• One-way trips still don't have a confirmation dialogue allowing you to back out• Enemy projectiles can still go through walls (even when your bullets can't)• Grenades are still essentially worthless because they do so little damage• Saving still causes the game to freeze for 5 seconds• Area transitions are still poorly signposted• There's still no map despite being a commonly-requested feature• Stats still cannot be upgraded by collecting feathers or spending Noctilium (despite the store page saying they can)• There's still no audiovisual feedback for your dark energy bar being full, only when it's depletedIf you're considering picking this up I'd recommend it on a  sale Nothing says "we're working on it" like radio silence and at this point they've lost a lot of people's trust that will be difficult to regain.Started a new game after the recent patch, the first two bosses are definitely easier and the load times are a little better, but unfortunately it seems most of the issues I listed remain. I've also confirmed by looking at the save files that Hunts do not increase your dark power bar nor do feathers increase your stats, both of which are listed on the store page. You also can't upgrade stats with Noctilium, which is again listed on the store page.I also didn't notice in my original playthrough that the glimmer of points of interest don't go away once you've picked up an item from them.Achievements seem to be working after they added a check to an NPC.If I had to describe  in it's current state, I would say it feels unfinished, almost like it should have been released in early access for some extra polish.Don't get me wrong, there's a lot going for the game: the pixel art, the music, the atmosphere, the world-building, the puzzles.But there's just so many bad and confusing design choices that, despite 100%ing the game, leave me not wanting to recommend it until the devs work on it a bit more.The biggest issue I have is with the combat: enemies have busted hitboxes, hit just a little too hard, and the combat is too clunky to allow you to handle encounters effectively. There's no animation-cancelling, no way to increase your dark energy pool, and no way beyond gear to permanently increase your attack or defense, just your HP. And beyond the 5 healing charges you can unlock and upgrade, life steal is your only way of getting health back despite not working on everything. You can also poison enemies, but the proc chance and damage are so low it's almost not worth it.The encounter design in particular is absolutely awful, with the game often swarming you with dozens of enemies, wall-piercing projectiles, or both that respawn between load screens despite the clunky combat not allowing you to handle multiple things going on at once very well. There are also quite a few enemies that, while they do telegraph their attacks, have such a short reaction window that you're almost guaranteed to take damage from them unless you pick them off using a ranged attack. And considering combat, the most tedious aspect of the game, is also the core focus of the game, I found myself opting to run past all of the enemies after a certain point because it was not worth the time it took to fight them, especially considering that they don't drop anything beyond the in-game currency, Noctilium.There's also a few small things I had issue with, such as:• The dash allowing you to fall off ledges or into bodies of liquid, only for the game to spawn you across the map or in another room entirely instead of the last surface you were standing on• Cutscenes replaying after failing to defeat certain bosses, instead of skipping straight to the encounter• One-way trips not having a confirmation before yeeting you into the abyss, resulting in needless backtracking• Area transitions that are poorly signposted save for some different lighting on the floor• No maps, although most areas aren't too difficult to navigate• • Hunt rewards not increasing your dark energy pool despite the store page saying they do• Broken objects loudly re-breaking in unison when re-entering a room• No audiovisual feedback when your dark energy is full or power cooldown is over• Not enough weapon, gear, and enemy variety• No bestiary or game stats menu• Jarring load-stutters after saving or when transitioning to a new areaAlso,  and some other bugs such as levers getting stuck, players not being able to attack or use dark powers, getting stuck in geometry, and  item pickup notifications not appearing or using the wrong window template. But with all that being said I definitely think the game is worth keeping an eye on, so give it a few months or wait for a sale if it looks interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Good. . . ish is probably the best way to describe my experience with Hunt the Night. On the surface it has a lot of things working for it that, in theory are fun, but it doesn't quite seem to know what do do with those mechanics. This game is sort of a shotgun scatter of different ideas that are loaded into it but never really seem to reach their true potential. The combat is sufficient, but the enemies don't really telegraph their moves so much as you learn the patterns and then just get the timing down. Enemies who shoot projectiles are almost easier to deal with than anything with a melee moveset. The exploration is fine, but the lack of a map means that a lot of the areas sort of just blend together and it's hard to get a sense of where you are at times. Power progression is strange in this game. It doesn't really exist. The weapons don't feel like they do enough to differentiate themselves from one another, the spells feel generally lacking, and the most direct upgrades are all to tertiary systems. Health is tied to optional hunts, finding sanguine altars, and your gear. It feels strange to have 3 direct ways of influencing your maximum health. It might have felt better if the altars increased your base strength or did something else other than just increase your max health because the optional hunts already do that too. Stats are all sort of okay. Hemostasis causes your attacks to heal you and Plagus is just a poison DoT. Those are the only two, and Hemostatis is objectively better because of the limited healing resources. Overall this game feels like a bite-sized version of a more full experience, and that has nothing to do with the actual length of the game. It's moreso that there's less nuance with the subsystems in the game than I expected. The campaign of the game is there, but the rest of it is still stuck in an early access stage. Some things should have been left out, while others should have been expanded. The traversal with Umbra is one of those things. It just doesn't feel fun, and it breaks the pacing of the exploration too much.The music and art are good. There's clearly a lot of passion put into the lore and world overall. The gameplay just leans into being  good enough, and so the game winds up feeling 'good-ish'. A very light recommendation from me. I think it's price point saves it in this regard.

_childDocuments_.review: I find myself in an oddly middling place with this review. I was left feeling ambivalent, yet want to call attention to the genuine talent on display.The soundtrack is pretty and atmospheric, but most tracks were fairly short, and there weren't enough to avoid repetition. It's a similar story for enemy design, as well. You'll see the same foes in every area with same powers each time (with a few area-exclusive exceptions). Worse yet are when said enemies' most common gimmick are damage-over-time debuffs. Poison-inflicters are everywhere, and you won't find a solution besides, "play super cautiously around them" for a while. If you're fast and observant, though, combat will be a fairly simple affair.This game features melee as your primary weapon, projectiles as your subweapon, and magic aoe attacks as an...existent feature. Melee is either fast and weak, strong and slow, or viable. It may just be down to my playstyle, but anything not a sword or a gauntlet never really felt right. Guns also had their own problem of being slow to draw and clunky to use. You have to stop dead in place to aim, and the draw/aiming is rather slow to wake up and actually point where you want it to, sometimes just...not doing it. I love shooting NOT where I point my joystick! Overall, combat is engaging but repetitive and finicky. With the right gear and playstyle, however, you'll practically melt through bosses. Which isn't really that satisfying?This game is listed as a souls-like, but once you know how to dodge a boss' attacks, they go down in barely more than a minute. At most. All of them (except for the minibosses that choose spawning minions as a secondary gimmick). It's a shame, since at least 2-3 of them have interesting fights. Or is that at most...?The pixel art is very well made, conveying a gothic aesthetic well enough to maintain the feel of the world the whole way through. Personally, I wish the game had more cutscenes and the like, as it would've given the artists even more chances to flex their skills. As it stands, this game's aesthetic and worldbuilding are my favorite parts about it. This place has a history to be learned of in the lore side of things, and though the main character interactions are thinner than paper, said paper has lot to say.I'd honestly rather see a novel or movie with this lore and aesthetic than a game. Both of the two endings were short and earned the exact same way, and one of them was far less interesting than the character dialogue hinted it would be. The player character has a solid motivation and an intriguing power, but the latter is barely explored at all.This is an indie game, so while I refuse to hold back on things that felt unengaging, I feel must praise genuine passion here. There's vision, there's imagination, there's an eye for lived-in worlds. They just needed a better way to engage with them than the player got. Keep creating, keep learning. With some refinement and expansion in mechanics and character interaction, something memorable has potential to be born. as it stands, I've been ready for this game to be finished for a while. I'm out!

_childDocuments_.review: From its charming 16-bit art style and sprawling dark fantasy world to its frantic Soulslike boss fights and intricate lore, Hunt the Night is a masterpiece... almost.   It is the 9th age of humanity and the Seal of Night has shattered. Night creatures, once held back by the Seal’s eternal daylight, now ravage the last vestiges of humanity. You are Vesper, the “traitorspawn” whose father—once a famed Stalker of the night—broke the Seal and doomed humanity to this extinction. You now walk the lonely, violent road of redemption as a Crow, a hunter of the night eager to restore the Seal—and, with it, your family’s name—one kill at a time. But this is not the only burden you carry: Umbra, a spectre of the Night and your dark doppleganger, grants you the ability to traverse the night’s corruption, but also makes you a target... a hybrid of Night and Day? Surely your ally Crows would destroy such an abomination, or so Umbra whispers. And so, together yet alone, you and Umbra carve your way through the endless night, but with each step your ghostly companion grows more powerful and more convinced she should be the one in charge. Hold up... An endless night? An order of hunters called Crows? A weird amount of cryptic lore about blood stuff? Plague doctors? Y’all... this is Bloodborne! True, Hunt the Night’s premise borrows heavily from its Soulsy predecessors, and the game’s story elements feel overly familiar as a consequence. That said, Hunt the Night’s story is easier to digest than were any of FromSoft’s incomprehensible narrative offerings. Not that it really matters, because you’re not here for the story, are you? •	Plot - 3/5•	Characters - 3/5•	Dialogue - 3/5 Hunt the Night sports a dodge-heavy, parry-free combat system that gives you access to a variety of armor types, stat-boosting moonstones, and—of course—melee and ranged weapons, the latter of which can be swapped on the fly. Each melee weapon comes in shades of green and red—that is to say, plagum and hemokinesis... which is to say poison and lifesteal—and melee blows will recharge your ranged ammunition. When you couple this with Vesper's beefy stamina bar, lack of a shield, and the fact that, unlike in most Soulslikes, bullets actually hurt enemies here, it becomes clear that Hunt the Night’s devs wanted to create an active style of play in which players empty their clip before dodging in to score hits, recharging ammo in the process, and then dodging out to finish the fight from afar.  I’m in love with this dynamic... in theory; in practice, I’m in like with it. It’s intoxicatingly frantic, yes, but without any aim assist, target-lock, or a means of customizing controller sensitivity (which is how Hunt the Night recommends you should play), lining up skillshots takes too damn long in Hunt the Night’s claustrophobic, enemy-packed rooms. And before you cry “skill issue!” know that some shots hit invisible walls and the aiming indicator will occasionally and inexplicably disappear. Also hampering Hunt the Night’s otherwise fluid combat system is the fact that Vesper—despite being able to aim guns in any direction—only melee attacks in four directions: up, down, left, and right.Now, if it sounds like I’m nitpicking... I am. But these tiny details compact to create combat that never feels as smooth as it should. Ditto that for the game’s non-combat platforming, as Hunt the Night’s rigid directional controls make the pinpoint precision required by these fairly frequent sections more frustrating than they are fun. The UI, meanwhile, is okay—just some minor gripes here and there like not being able to see the number of healing roses you have left on a white background. Oh, and the thumbnails directing you to hunts you can pick up from your home base to permanently increase your health are laughably unhelpful.Finally, consider me barely neutral on the game’s playability after seeing enemies (and myself) glitch through walls a couple of times. Worse, my ultimate ability or “Dark Power” wouldn’t trigger regardless of key binding, so if I made it to the end of the game without it, I’m sure you can with it! Other than that, nothing game-breaking, so let’s move on to what I do love about this game (because I swear this review's title isn’t clickbait). •	Combat - 3/5•	Non-Combat - 3/5•	U.I. - 3/5•	Playability - 3/5 Hunt the Night’s world-building is masterful. The game sports a wide variety of painstakingly handcrafted environments, from the maze-like Bowels of the Earth to the chemical hell of Ashdown Manor to the lava-soaked space vibes of Ipharis to the sanguine waterfalls of Bloodisfell. Each biome is a treat to explore and it’s a testament to Hunt the Night’s solid level design that, despite the lack of a map, I never got hopelessly lost. (Side note: if you do get lost, a lady in your home base will set you straight.)While the game’s objectives are straight-forward to a fault, they inevitably lead you to some truly breathtaking boss fights that build in complexity and difficulty as the game progresses. That said, they never felt hopeless to me, and I was able to get through each in an average of thirty minutes. Much less fun are the gated sequences dispersed throughout each level to prevent you from (I guess) dodge-spamming through everything. These usually unskippable sequences just gradually whittle down your health with wave after wave of trash, and they become almost impossible toward endgame. Puzzles, meanwhile, are overly simple if refreshing changes of pace. Though their answers are often obvious and easy to find if you just stop to look around a bit, I didn’t mind them and don’t consider them a weakness. That said, I do wish they used Umbra more creatively—this game gives you a supernatural phantom and all she ever amounts to is a paperweight.•	World - 5/5•	Objectives - 3/5•	Bosses - 5/5•	Puzzles - 3/5Oh well, on to style!  Hunt the Night sports a consistently wonderful visual variety that starts out simple and ends up insane, but some janky animations and an overreliance on fade-to-blacks to cover up missing animations holds HTN back from top marks here. Meanwhile, I was surprisingly underwhelmed by Hunt the Night’s soundtrack, considering it features legendary composer Hiroki Kikuta from Secret of Mana. Some moments are pretty tone deaf and the score as a whole feels a bit subdued; I rarely felt it elevated the moment. Ditto that for the game’s sound design, which can sound a bit clunky, but never stands out as annoying. •	Visuals - 4/5•	Music - 3/5•	Sound - 3/5 In the end, Hunt the Night comes painfully close to 16-bit Souls-like glory, but a lack of polish and some questionable design decisions hold it back from being the game I know it could be. That said, I very much enjoyed 90% of my 20 hours with the game and believe it presents strong value at $20 (Value - 4/5). I’m giving it an aggregate MEGA score of 3.4/5 and am happy to answer any questions you have about the game or my review. Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: Hunt the Night is the kind of game that is best described as a flawed gem. This review shall be a mixture of review for potential players and feedback to the developers. It will also be long.As a summary it is a game that does so many things right and clearly a lot of love was put into it, but also has some very baffling design choices. To try and explain this, I shall break it down into categories.- The graphics/style don't really require any explanation, if you see the screenshots/videos and such you will have already decided if it appeals (for me personally I think they are amazing). All I'd really say is that it has some incredibly designed areas in the game as it goes on (especially the final location).- Where things start to become less subjective is with the visual clarity. There are a lot of instances where this applies, so listing them all concisely is difficult. To name the most glaring, it can be unclear at a glance what you are selecting in the menu due to a lack of contrast, which also can apply to to status effects on Vesper and Enemies, or in some cases Enemy AOE effects. This can also be things such as doorways and paths not being easy to spot quickly (especially in the first two open areas after the starting castle. As such the game can often feel like it's working against you.In most cases the colours of certain things simply need tweaking to make them stand out a lot more, in others such as the levels, unfortunately I am not sure how they can be fixed except perhaps adding a map.- The music is really nice and fits well with the setting and style of the game.- The sound effects for the most part work really well, with clearly defined cue and with enough weight behind them.- The Rapier, however, sounds like rusty scissors and I found this incredibly grating to listen to. I really hope this gets changed at some point.- At it's core the game play isn't groundbreaking, but it works well and is pretty fun. You get a melee weapon, a choice of three ranged weapons, a special power and poison bombs. Combat feels quite fluid with the ability to mix these attacks up while dashing around (with a stamina system). It's also the kind of game that once things click it feels incredibly satisfying to pull off. - Where the game is let down slightly is an inconsistency with enemy spawning. In the starting area enemies stayed dead until you saved at a statue and a few other areas work like this as well, a la Souls games. Other areas on the other hand they respawn if you exit and return (for example going into and out of a house). While this isn't game breaking, it can be a little frustrating in the early game when health and healing is low, as these only come back once you save.- For the size of the game enemy variety isn't bad, though some enemies are not especially fun to face. Visually they are all pretty cool and they can keep you on your toes, with combat feeling very frantic at times, but you still feel powerful once you get the hang of it.- The bosses are pretty unique and the game makes good use of the various combat mechanics, with some having some pretty clever designs in them. The only downside I would say is that bizarrely they got easier as the game progresses. It took me about 15 attempts to beat the second boss and I beat the final one on my first try.- The Weapon/Armour/Powers/Moon Stones/Upgrades are possibly the weakest aspect of the game. There aren't as many as the game states: There's a Rapier, Twin Daggers, Great Sword, Spear and Gloves, but with each one having a version that provides healing/poison/higher damage.- While I found a few bosses worked well with mixing things up, for the most part I didn't see any reason to not stick to the same set up throughout the entire game. The Rapier seems like the best weapon and the Healing AOE the best power.- The Gun Upgrades are a neat idea, but have the same issue as the above, with some being clearly better and one actually being a downgrade despite being the higher tier (the twin bullets for the pistol I cannot see any reason to take and in some cases can soft lock you in an area).- With all of this said, I do like the way things such as healing/poisoning work, especially for bosses where it feels like you can approach them differently on preference.- The game has Hunts that you can embark on for rewards. While the fights themselves are pretty cool and a neat twist on existing enemies in the game, the rewards are pretty flat. You spend money to get the Hunt and after the fight you get 1HP increase, which is a little underwhelming. Especially as the game also has four hidden lore relevant areas, which provide the exact same thing.It's difficult to say what this could be changed to without a significant rework of certain things, but it's a part of a wider design choice that feels like it could have been pushed much further to feel rewarding.- The UI could do with some reworking, especially with the Key Items section. It throws everything together with no order and doesn't make it clear if something has been used yet. I still have no idea what the Bread or Bread Crumbs do and I've beaten the game with every achievement.- There's a fair few in the game which have been reported widely, this seems quite common with achievements which either don't activate or do so early (I got some where I'd done half the requirements).- If you drop of a ledge you lose 1HP and are put back on solid ground. Which piece of ground seems to vary wildly with the game seemingly selecting at random, and in some cases can be almost the entire length of an area. I am not sure if this is a bug, but it's very frustrating.- Sometimes certain things feel like they hit/don't activate when they ought to. It might be hitboxes, or it might go back to visual clarity.- The game sometimes got stuck on the Umbra sections, having to skip them and miss the dialogue.- The lore/world and idea is brilliant (am biased as I love Dark Fantasy and Gothic/Cosmic Horror). I enjoyed finding out more about the setting and what came before the present situation (and what may potentially come after). For how simplistic it was kept, it was portrayed very well and drew me in.- With that said, it's another area I felt could do with some fleshing out, given the most developed character we came across in the game was Beatrice (more Beatrice please). Most others had one or two lines and then either died or had nothing further. I hope if the game receives further development this aspect really gets more to it. There's no voice acting, so I feel this could be (relatively speaking) quite a straight forward area to expand.- For example more lines from people to respond as the game progresses, more NPC's out and about in the world and just general more characterisation from the ones standing about.Well first of all if you read all of this then thank you.Overall this is a game I enjoyed quite a lot and found I did more so as the game progressed. It has some amazing ideas, well thought out design choices and memorable moments, but falls short due to some unusual design choices and ideas.To be the kind of game that I'd rant and rave about, it needs a little more depth and fleshing out in certain areas and a little cleaning up in others.With that said, a big thank you to the developers, it's clear a lot of love went into this game and it was worth the wait.

_childDocuments_.review: I know what you're thinking based on that Target Audience:  “lol another bad comparison to Dark Souls because the game is probably difficult.” Well yes, the game is difficult, but the Dark Souls and Bloodborne comparisons go a lot deeper then a lot of comparisons that get thrown around now a days, and Hunt the Night mostly succeeds in what it set out to do, despite some hiccups along the way.The slower yet methodical combat that focuses on getting in and out is great, with a dodge that seems overpowered at first, until your realize that the level design has cleverly constrained you in a lot of cases. Each melee weapon has a good strength that makes it flexible to take down all type of good enemy variety, but specialized enough to really succeed in certain situations. The game has moments that really shine, like epic boss fights where you get through by the skin of your teeth; or sub-stories that pull on heartstrings and really reward those who pay attention. The atmosphere is dark and gritty without taking you out of it for the action, and really pushes you to see what's around the corner.Granted, the main plot is done alright and is what you've seen before, but a lack of punch in the main story especially with the connection of the main character does make the story slightly suffer. A lot of my complaints end up being small things that add up over time: like a lack of invincibility frames upon entering a room/spawning that could mean you're taking damage before you are even able to react. The game is also a game that for sure isn't for those new to the genre: it's a dark souls game without really any friendly elements for newer players, and some players will get really frustrated with certain sections lengths without save points or lack of tools to navigate in traditional senses.The thing is, the combat and strong set piece elements with some of the side stories are worth the price of admission here, as the game was enjoyable throughout my hours even when the game was frustrating me. Definitely worth a buy for any dark souls fan, or anyone who likes deliberate combat.

_childDocuments_.review: A dark, atmospheric title with fun level design, cinematic bosses, and a combat system that is engaging and rewarding to learn.  is awesome and definitely worth a play.   keyboard works well. Vesper is a member of the Stalkers, an Order dedicated to the protection of humankind and the defence of the Seal of Night, they are ruthless, and efficient. However, the Order was betrayed, the Seal is breaking, Night is encroaching, and humanity faces destruction once again. It is her duty to save the everlasting day and to confront the traitor, her very own father. Vesper is a mute, and so she can never defend herself, as a result every member of her Order sees her as damned, little better than her traitor father, and so they expect of her to take on the most dangerous assignments and generally fix things on her own. So, her quest is not only to save the day but also to clear her name and to make up for the sins of her father, this hostile attitude and her willingness to assist them is intriguing and is one of the major conflicts in . However, Vesper is not entirely mute, she can speak, just not in the real world, her only interlocutor is Umbra, a being that grows stronger and stronger as evening approaches. She constantly pressures Vesper, taunting her, and rightfully pointing out that the Order would kill her if they knew about Umbra, this duo, with their push and pull, their own wants and needs, are another central part of the narrative. These aspects are not only handled in a way that makes them interesting, but it also made me invested in the interpersonal struggles, it made me root for Vesper, and made me hope that she will get the recognition she deserves.A certain design choice can be considered a blessing or a curse and that is the game’s reliance on optional writing. Important dialogue is mandatory but hints about the next boss can be missed by simply not talking to certain NPCs, other important revelations such as those relating to Vesper’s family and her father’s motives are relegated to collectible notes. These are hard to miss if you explore thoroughly but a player can be fooled into thinking that all the notes are puzzle hints or simply background lore. I do like the worldbuilding, and I do think that people who get to that point are invested enough to actually read the lore, but it lacks gravitas, you would think Vesper or Umbra would acknowledge it in any way, but they simply do not. Presumably because certain players might have missed it, so they did not have time to make unique dialogue for it. Yet the narrative does suffer a bit and unfortunately it makes it feel like the ending is lacking certain resolutions.  is visually striking, they utilise stark contrasts to make stunning areas with reds and whites like Bloodisfell, drab colours to make suffocating undergrounds or unnatural hues to sell a mutated, wasted, Golden Meadow. The Cathedral is another stand out, a sprawling, and opulent location, it is beautiful and oppressive in equal measures. These areas have impressive designs, pixel art, but above all, atmosphere in common. It can be difficult for games to feel so immersive, and to make it seem so effortless, but  does just that and that is fantastic. We also get a number of horrible creatures of the Night, highlighting how dangerous it is and what it can do to unsuspecting humans. Some look like generic undead, but most—especially later on—do look disgusting, mutated and properly threatening with the bosses being the most impressive of all.  This is all certainly helped by the OST and the overall sound design, because they are equally impressive. Songs harmonise perfectly with the areas and makes the whole experience even more engrossing, they often have this sorrowful, oppressive air to them, while also nailing tracks that are more tense and anxiety inducing. Great soundtrack, I only wish all the songs were available for purchase or streaming.  is an action-adventure game and it does not like holding your hand. Its areas are often quite large, or feel large, on account of all the optional paths. It does not give you clear direction, and it also leaves a lot of things unexplained, so you are typically asked to find your own way and seek out what hints there are on your own. Not only are you hunting for keys, but you will also be doing a handful of puzzles, and a lot of dashing to avoid pits. It is fun, and there is often a clue or two hidden somewhere, but as long as you are observant you can figure things out on your own.However, I found the platforming puzzles to be a bit annoying, sometimes they are a very close shave, incentivising you to use Umbra’s powers. I do not mind but sometimes the game stacks your inputs even after you have fallen in a hole, so Vesper dashes as soon as she can, falling into another pit and taking out another heart. That does not feel good.     Yet, the somewhat meandering nature of exploration works especially well since it suits the level design, and it feels rewarding since there is always something to see, cool visuals, equipment, mini-bosses, or lore. It feels great, and because the game is short it is easy to keep track of all the places that are gated by abilities as well as those that are game long key hunts.This also gives you some time to familiarise yourself with the combat. It favours cautious aggression, enemies are individually weak but come at you in groups or waves so you should dissect encounters, prioritising targets, choosing when to use your gun, and using abilities when they are most beneficial. Out of bullets? Just attack in melee and you will scrounge up another bullet in no time. Getting hit is a bigger concern because your healing is limited, and enemies tend to wear you down as you explore large dungeons so, you need to be cautious, and you need to be aggressive. However, all these things are pretty easy, so easy that bosses can feel like a difficulty spike. You go from one or two attacks to combos, magic, whole hosts of adds, and fights that can be so visually busy that it gets overwhelming and difficult to parse. Yet it works so very well.  uses mechanics that I can find frustrating in other games, instant death attacks, bullet hells, endless adds, and more, but they make them fun, and satisfying to figure out. It feels very rewarding once you have nailed a gimmick, and understand perfectly what the boss is doing, and what that means for you and your tactics. It also makes you play like Vesper, a Stalker, this is a hunt, so you observe your prey figure out how they move, what abilities they have, if you can stop those abilities and the most efficient way to destroy them. However, there was one boss that got a bit annoying, it is otherwise an extremely fun but punishing boss, yet it has an unintuitive instant death attack right before it dies. I died to that attack, several times, because it is a field of instant death, and that field evaporates. I thought I was in the clear and could finish off the boss, but no, you are meant to chill in safety until you get a pop up. It feels weird, but it does not represent , because  is a great game with great bosses, and some really fun encounters.

_childDocuments_.review: Janky, buggy and over far too quick. The game has some solid fundamentals, the action combat is fine for the most part, but it misses the mark on actually having fun encounters. The paltry half a dozen bosses in the game barely wet your appetite, and the ordinary mobs are designed in such an hostile way they are not actually any fun at all to fight. The cherry on top is the final boss, an ugly, easy mess that feels like an ascended version of a kind of normal enemy you've killed dozens off by the end. Finishing this game i felt profoundly unfulfilled, and assumed it was due to not finding the true ending and true final boss or something, but after checking the achievements I'm forced to concluded that this is  all there is. Unsatisfying in the end, tho it started out well.

_childDocuments_.review: Zelda meets Bloodborne but more linear. There's some backtracking for a few upgrades.It's hard, but just keep dashing. Even basic monsters do a lot of damage so tanking anything won't work. Most bosses will take a few tries as you learn their attack patterns. A few I managed to beat on the first go. Others took many tries. A few late stage bosses have attacks that will one shot you, or kill you in a few rapid fire hits.The story I'm not thrilled about. There's some the good guys may be the bad guys, along with ambiguous dialogue and my most hated trope: the Player Character who doesn't remember their past. She also can't speak except in a mind-palace with a spirit.It outstays its welcome near the end with needlessly large areas to traverse. Many weapon/accessories felt superfluous once you find a groove.As a whole it's a good game and I can solidly recommend it. I'd like to see more like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Hunt the Night

_childDocuments_.review: It just doesn't feel good to play, really. The controls lack a certain snappiness that I'm going to demand if I'm playing a Soulslike and using dodge rolls, enemy attacks occasionally have weird hitboxes(hell, your OWN attacks have weird hitboxes), attacking has this weird laggy feeling to it, ranged enemies can shoot at you from off-screen and aiming your pistol with the controller is a bizarrely janky experience where the aim will suddenly default away from the direction you're aiming in to straight down.Note that all of this was with a controller, as recommended by the game.The game also delights in taking away your control for even the most basic things, like "oh no, an enemy exists" or blacking everything out for a loading screen, even though you're loading back into the exact same room you were already in, facing the exact same boss that was already there. It's baffling.About five minutes in I was already doing my best to just ignore all the generic enemies because there was something no purpose to fighting them nor any fun in fighting them, which I would personally say is a pretty bad sign.There's also the dashing mechanic, which fundamentally is a pretty nice dash, I will credit it with letting you dash cancel out of, as far as I can tell, just about any animation. On the downside... most of your dashing is across Evil Goop. The dash seems super unpredictable about whether it'll be generous in letting you cross a given volume of Evil Goop or if you were a centimeter off and whoops, into the goop you go. It also doesn't reset you to the nearest edge or the edge you started from when this happens, but seems to arbitrarily have one reset point in each room which can occasionally be a bit back.It doesn't even have a memorable soundtrack. It existed, I guess, but otherwise I couldn't tell you anything about it. Completely slipped off my gray matter.I could probably be a bit more generous if this game was trying to do anything of its own, but it's really just Bloodborne: We're Using Purple Instead Of Red, so no points even for trying.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay. This game is great. If you like Zelda or Bloodborne or even Dark souls or any 2D action adventure with well designed combat, this is an instant buy. Hunt the night does so many things right its an easy recommendation even at its full price. The combat is satisfying, the world overall is great and the zones are too. The music gets the job done, for what the game tries to achieve, so again.. the package is really great overall. It does have some flaws, that prevent it from being a masterpiece. Enemy variety, overwhelming and underwhelming narrative structure, and ultimately  a lack of meaningful secrets. Either way its a great game and its definitely worth your money. I hope these devs flesh the existing game out or make something new. Regardless, they do understand what is a good gaming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game loop, fluid combat, cool enemies and bosses, beautiful pixel art, story RICH and it's presentation kept drawing me forward deeper into the world. _childDocuments_.review: Hunt the Night - 8.5/10 This is a fantastic top-down Bloodborne meets Zelda-like! Not for the faint of heart, as the boss battles can be mind bendingly excruciating. Lots of neat little puzzles that actually trigger a cerebral response rather than just a paint by number puzzle system that could be cut and pasted into any dungeon in the game. Also a fair amount of collectibles like, weapons, armors, spells, gun upgrades, etc… to collect. The game’s achievements will actually steer you towards 100% the game if you’re so inclined. I love when achievements work like this instead of having weird requirements like kill 100 enemies with freeze or something silly like that. I would say this reminds me of something like Morbid and the Seven Acolytes meets Skautfold: Shrouded In Sanity or Ocean’s Heart and Tunic. There is definitely a strong Bloodborne vibe as well. I would love to see a sequel or another game in this style from the Team. It also worth noting that I did have a few technical difficulties but I believe those were day 1 issues that have already been patched. I also really have the keep the difficulty and don’t NERF it as it will be fun to replay down the line if it is still difficult in a year or two.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want my quick score, I give this game a 9/10. The setting was phenomenal, the pixel art was absolutely gorgeous, and the combat was really fun and challenging in some sections. All of the bosses felt unique and had their own thing going on, some of them were harder than others and some were super easy. I didn't focus 100% on the story, but from what I was able to gather through the lore spread out in the game it's a good story which ends with your choice on what to do with the world. The only reason I don't give this game a 10/10 is because of a few small issues. There were a few bugs that I encountered, mainly if you dash off of a platform upon respawn that momentum can be carried over and you fall in again, as well as just a few platform issues, but that was about it for bugs.  For the bosses, like I said I enjoyed them whether easy or hard, but I do wish that some of the melee attacks had better tell for when they are going to happen.Besides the few small issues I had, this was a really good game and I would recommend it 100%. If you like to follow the dollar per hour rule I would wait for it to go on sale as I got 100% achievements in about 10 hours (subtracting some afk time) but other than that please play this game it is amazing. 🐧

_childDocuments_.review: For a $20 game, it's fine. The game is very light on content, but the game is also took a day to 100% with the hardest boss being the second boss. I also found it fascinating that only 11% of the people that bought this got to an ending which might imply it's hard, but I'd say it's really just the second boss.Combat is fine when you can just dodge and outrun most hit boxes, however weapons feel pretty pointless over using great swords since its high damage and not horridly slow.Exploration on the other hand is rough since there is no map and dashing across platforms is inconsistent since you can miss the next platform and be sent all the way back to the beginning of the room or be sent to an entirely different room. The map is more of a nitpick due to getting a little turned around on some areas due to losing track of where I've been.Lastly the story is okay at best. A lot of the dialogue felt long-winded and the stalkers really never got to prove that you are a rookie and possibly weak since most get one-shot or die off-screen except for one late game. The endings are meh, with one feeling dull and the other not even showing the effect in the world after your choice.Honestly playing this after getting out of my rabbit hole of metrovanias felt refreshing, so that could be why I enjoyed this zelda-like style. Bonus points to this game for looking nice and having a good soundtrack too.

_childDocuments_.review: Temporary review which I'll edit later, but I want to give a positive review while this game is fresh. While not perfect, Hunt the Night is GOOD. The boss fights (I've just completed the third at the time of this review) feel great, the world looks nice visually, and exploration is pretty much always rewarded. There are some bugs that should get ironed out, but I'm sure that'll happen in the near future.EDIT: I've 100 percented the game so I feel qualified to leave a better review now. Overall quality is good though it feels the best during the prologue. I think the game could use more connective tissue for why you're doing what you're doing in the various zones, but on the whole exploration feels rewarded and the combat feels enjoyable. _childDocuments_.review: T.L.D.R:  Overall, it's a solid foundation of a game, with good combat bones and carried by the art and ambiance, but it's held back by some baffling design decisions, bad mechanics and buggy hitboxes (admittedly rare).This is all I can think of at the moment (also hit character limit, but I tend to ramble). I know my negatives list is longer and more in-depth, but I did overall enjoy the game. It desperately needs some polish though. Would buy again, but maybe only while on sale.I'll go with the positives first.* It feels pretty responsive, dodging into and away from enemies to land those hits before retreating from their counterattack feels good. * The enemy variety is good for how short the game is.* Hunts add a fun twist to some enemy types when you can find them, though I wish they were a bit more prominent.* The lore was fun to collect and the worldbuilding and ambience is really quite something. A bit cookie-cutter, but solidly executed. * There are a few builds you can go with throughout the game, not many, but the game is short so you can mix and match pretty frequently. If you don't like short games, that's on you, but I enjoyed exploring new builds every area or so.The negatives:* There are four types of weapons within the 5 subgroups of weapons that exist. Basically, starter weapon, poison weapon, lifesteal weapon and bigger damage number weapon. Poison and lifesteal are the more interesting of the four, but proc chances are usually low (lifesteal is like 5% for all/most of the lifesteal weapons), and some enemy types/bosses are just randomly immune to their effects. The final boss can't be poisoned (called Plagum in this game) or lifestealed. Other bosses and enemies seem to share this immunity apparently at random to one degree or another and it sucks to go into a boss fight with a loadout that prioritizes a mechanic the boss is just straight up immune to. It'd be fine, or at least more ok, if that was telegraphed in some way by NPC dialogue perhaps or anything really (Say, a plagum NPC dead outside the boss arena with a note saying "My weapons did nothing..."). Truly baffling design decision IMO, to make bosses occasionally immune to what little build diversity there is without any foreshadowing, or at least without any foreshadowing that I noticed.* Platforming and punishments can feel very inconsistent. Dashes sometimes feel like they need to be more precise than the game is willing to let you be. On top of that, dashing and falling can save your inputs after falling. For example, if you dash and miss your dash, hit dash again by accident, you'll fall from the first failed dash as the second dash fails to occur. You'll then experience a brief reload as your character gets placed somewhere randomly in the room (usually at the start of the room, but I've been sent back three rooms before, and also sometimes to the same platform I was just on, it's janky where it respawns you). After reloading, your saved input will immediately trigger, and you'll dash in whatever direction you tried to dash when you were falling. Which may cause you to dash into a pit and fall again. Hopefully you don't try to course correct mid-dash with another dash, save that input and repeat the cycle a third time. It saves movement and attack inputs too. I've tried to dash to platforms and immediately shoot the occupant of that platform, only to miss the dash for whatever reason, respawn a second or two later at the start of the room, and have my character immediately shoot the wall next to her.* Plagum grenades are probably the weakest stuff in existence. You get a grenade (three per respawn) mechanic where you throw out a bottle of Plagum that ruptures on enemies. It's good for the weakest enemies, but not much else. Near as I can tell, it ticks 3 times for 10 damage each and then stops. There's no upgrades for it that I can find (though the promo video on the steam page shows the upgrade vendor selling such things, it doesn't exist in the released version that I can see). It's almost not worth using at all. I went the vast majority of my playthrough without acknowledging their existence, and only used them when I was stuck waiting for the boss to let me hit them in melee again when I was out of bullets.* The occasional janky hitbox. Dodge behind an enemy as it's swinging and still get hit by the attack that's occurring somewhere else. Maybe it's a readability issue, where the damage should go through because you screwed up the dodge timing and got hit before the dodge, but the damage only comes in after the dodge? Idk, but it felt bad either way. Admittedly didn't happen much, maybe only a few times per area/boss, but it was noticeable and irritating considering how short the game is.* Hunts are another source of baffling game design. They don't really offer anything outside of health, which is lame. After a while, I stopped looking for them because my healthbar was big enough. I think I missed 3 or 4, but it's hard to tell what I missed or didn't miss, because there's no way to track completed hunts aside from by memory. You pick up hunts at the tavern, and they get crossed out as if you had completed them, and when you actually complete them, they don't change or differentiate at all from just buying them. So there's no way to track what you missed. Bizarre. And they're a bit difficult to find on top of that, you have to keep an eye out for a small orange eye on a wall. The design decor for the first half of the game is usually "spreading darkness corrupting the land and covering it with eyes and teeth and tendrils", so they don't stand out too much til later. They're also mostly just juiced up normal enemies, but I found them fun enough anyway. * No map or easy way to recall area layouts aside from just memorizing the area. They aren't that hard to puzzle out, but if you want to go back an hour later, unless you've got good memory, you're almost exploring from scratch again.* The final three bosses were kind of a let-down. I won't spoil anything significantly, but one was just a "summon boring adds" fight. Boss only had one move, but it one-shots you. So the fight was kill adds, refill gun, shoot boss, kill adds again to beat it safely. Another literally stands still while you wail on her and has pretty easy to dodge attacks, except for one move which covers the whole arena and one shots you at the very end of the fight, which you can only dodge by running to the far corner of the map and hiding for like 15 or so seconds. And the last boss is not only immune to lifesteal and plagum (build diversity straight up murdered), but also seems to have some inconsistent dodge timings and weird "immune to all damage while the lamest and easiest to dodge fire moves across the map" mechanic. Sometimes his main move is the easiest thing in the world to dodge, and sometimes it comes out with almost no telegraph and perfectly catches you at the end of each dodge to full health combo you to death. I killed him (twice for both endings) in maybe ten or fifteen minutes (half of that was a lifesteal build before I realized he was immune), because despite the janky full-health combos and immunity to all the status effects weapons, he's an easier boss than most. Basically a stronger version of the toughest trash mob in the game. Kind of a let down.* Enemies stay the same strength throughout the game, but so do you. There's no leveling or increasing stats (aside from health) outside of gear and runes, which you can only have one of each equipped at a time. So the very basic "tiny shadow child" is as tough to kill at the beginning of the game as it as at the end.  Which seems like a bit of a missed opportunity to explore increasing power level of the protagonist. Alternatively, it's a great way to have your own skill be the only thing keeping you from progressing, if you're stuck at a boss or enemy room.

_childDocuments_.review: Hunt The Night is a solid Zelda-like distinguished by its stunning 16-bit Victorian Gothic horror art design, which stands out as the game's greatest strength. Honestly, more games should embrace this art design. At this point, I'd even play a survival game in that style, despite it being my least favorite genre lol. Also how good looks that cover art?While its dungeon design follows a formulaic pattern, the boss fights are exceptional and well-crafted. One mid-game boss, in particular, requires your full attention, evoking the classic Souls-like challenge.The lore is there and has some great "aha" moments but is ultimately a bit cliché and flat when it comes to the story of the main character. Her sprite is very cute, though. I also like the light but nonetheless very satisfying environmental storytelling. There are even some visual clues in the environment that will guide you to your next objective, which I always appreciate, especially since the game has no map.Considering this is the studio's first "big" game, I'm genuinely impressed with what they've accomplished. Some aspects obviously need fine-tuning, but it's clear they had a strong creative vision. Hopefully, they will continue honing their craft despite the fact that it gone under the radar.

_childDocuments_.review: I personally quite liked it. While I hate using direct comparisons to other games, it felt like a 2D Zelda game with Bloodborne-esque bosses and areas.It was definitely a bit short (it took me just short of 11 hours to beat it with a good amount of extra exploration), but I found it was well worth the $20 I paid. The combat felt rewarding, especially dashing in and out to land hits with my greatsword and/or shotgun, although some enemies were a bit of a pain to fight. Also, while I never found any boss to be overly difficult, they all gave a decent enough challenge to be enjoyable, and they often had really great designs. I did notice a few odd performance/design issues, such as the music abruptly cutting at screen transitions or when resting at crow statues, and the hitboxes do occasionally seem a bit weird, but nothing seemed too bad. Enemies also respawn in most rooms upon re-entering, and I got hit once or twice upon entering a room, which isn't the best, but it wasn't terrible or frequent either. The story was nice, and I especially like how parts of it were told in pieces by picking up feathers containing lore. Also, the spritework was *really* good.Would recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: Hunt the Night is a souls inspired 2D action RPG with some platforming and shooting elements. It is a relatively short game that can be beaten in around 10 hours but can be further extended if you are going for 100% or new game+. below are some short pros and cons for the game.PROS:- The controls are responsive and dodge timings are tight but intuitive.- The shifting between melee and gun combat is pretty nice and the ammo system is not to punishing- Aside from 1 boss , I find them to be fun, have good auditory and visual cues, and have amazing designs.- The enemy scaling is pretty good, you can beat the game with the starting equipment on a first playthrough.- I know people are pretty mixed on this, but I really liked the puzzles as it doesn't hand hold you and 1 of them was down right cryptic.CONS:- I find most of the mechanics underdeveloped, I never use grenades as they are too clunky and deal little to no damage; the crossbow is inferior to the pistol and shotgun; and poison and burn don't deal enough damage or proc enough to warrant a build dedicated to them.- Exploration is a pain in the ass. You don't have map or a collectible checklist, and a good portion of the early game is a swamp that needed a special unlock to traverse through.- Story is pretty mediocre; I wasn't really invested, and the lore is pretty much all over the place.- Music is okay, I wasn't impressed nor disappointed.- Some bounty bosses are buggy; I bum rushed 2 of them and they died getting stun-locked by sword slashes.Overall, I find the game enjoyable, albeit unpolished for the most part. If you are looking for a short game to binge through, but still want a decent challenge, then I highly recommend playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: My impressions video: Hunt the Night is like if a Soulslike, a Metroidvania and pixel art had a baby, but it's also not like any of those genres traditionally are and takes these components to make something with its own identity. It's a Soulslike, but with faster and more agile combat and a lot more platforming. It's a Metroidvania, but there's no map and you have to find things on your own. And it's definitely a challenge, but also has just enough quality of life features to avoid being too frustrating.The story is somewhat esoteric and requires you to fill in the blanks, but the basics are that you are the daughter of a former monster hunter who turned traitor and are trying to earn back your family honour. The night is a dangerous time for the world, where demons come out and terrorize the population and things are getting worse, to where humanity might not survive and you have to try to stop the forces that are driving the night.There is a core quest to follow, but there are also many things in the world to find if you're willing to put in the time to find them. Everything from simple treasures to special monster hunts that yield potentiall big rewards. You'll find a wide selection of weapons and abilities, all of which you can switch to at any time. There is no inventory to manage, everything you find it just always with you. Things can get challenging, but checkpoints are not too badly spaced out and there's no penalty for dying beyond having to make your way past where you died and the enemies respawning.The pixel art and understated soundtrack do a great job of making the world feel both lived in and haunted. The game is never scary, but it always makes you feel that there's evil about.This is a game for people who like a story that leaves some things to your imagination and some tough 2D combat, but a lot of ways to approach it. I quite enjoyed it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is *fine*, but I've got a few gripes.  - Why is there no map? You made a pseudo-open-world game, but did not add a map.  - The dash is a little too OP. Tying the dash to the MP bar is a good idea, but the current consumption still gives you 8 consecutive dashes before a recharge. All the bosses are in big arenas - when in doubt, spam dodge.  - Also, the dash is a little uncontrollable when it comes to dashing between platforms. If I try to under-correct in any way I tend to crazily dive off the edge and get forced to respawn.  - Respawns feel a little random. Sometimes they'll put you right where you fell and other times you'll spawn somewhere way back. - Save points are a solid respawn point, but for some reason they take a good few seconds to pull off. Kind of feels like every time you save, the game is refreshing itself and then reloading its various progress flags. This is one of the few games where they somehow got Saving to be inefficient.   - The weapon and armor bonuses feel like someone bad at math is trying to scam me. 10% chance to block damage? That's a joke number, right? Guess that armor is just trash. Oh, there's a phantom that tricks enemies? I don't see it. Where is it? Does it exist?  - The story...I have no comment. Really wasn't paying attention much at this point. Something about day and night are broken, and the gods gave people a seal to turn day into night. Get the seal. Get some breakfast. That's the story. Definitely a 'sale if you're interested' game. There's fun to be had here, but its bogged down by technical issues, poor design, and crappy gear.

_childDocuments_.review: Only played for a couple of hours, but so far Hunt the Night seems like an absolute must-play for any fan of retro-style action-adventure games. With its pixel art and 'GIT GUD' difficulty, the game pays homage to the classics of the genre while bringing its own unique flair to the table.One of the most impressive aspects of Hunt the Night is the way it seamlessly blends elements of Dark Souls with its own unique style. The combat is challenging and unforgiving, requiring careful strategy and quick reflexes to survive. Yet, at the same time, the game never feels unfair or frustrating. Every fight with the vampires and eldritch horrors that populate the game world is a tense and thrilling experience, and the sense of accomplishment you feel when you finally emerge victorious is incredibly satisfying.The lore is intriguing and the environments are varied and atmospheric. The soundtrack is simply phenomenal, with haunting melodies and driving rhythms that perfectly capture the game's dark, Gothic aesthetic.10 out of 10, would hunt again.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I was really into the game, the first dungeon was challenging but not annoying, the bosses were the hardest part but the secret is using the biggest sword (sadly that'd become true for the rest of the game), the puzzles were meh, combat not really deep but ok, good art style and interesting story, at first I didn't care for the music but after a couple of hours I hate it, monotonous and earpiercing, here is an area I just don't want to explore anymore -the one immediate after you left the castle- just not to listen to that. Same with the tavern and that one is even worse, it's as if someone just saw Barry Lindon and decided the tone of that movie was needed to climate that area of the game. Anyways, after the first area the difficulty spikes, badly. Not in quality but in quantity. If you enjoy fighting against mobs that respawn the moment you leave an area you might find it good, I find it annoying. There are closed areas that enemies won't stop spawning and practically all of these are really small with other hazards like pitfalls that turn the dash ability -the dodge of this game- frustating to use.The game fails in the soulslike area, I've played it ds 1 and 3 and in those combat was difficult but at least you had an level/upgrade system that allowed you to balance it a little bit, but not here. From what I've seen you can only upgrade your guns (the weapon I use the less cause it has very limited ammo) and there's no level up or abilities upgrades to boost your damage other than some diminute percentages that some of the weapons may poison your enemies. Weapons are also varied but you'll end up using the big one cause the others are useless. You can get more hp by getting these blood drops that work more like heart containers. However that's too little, you start with only 8 of those and most enemies deal 3 of damage, some even 4, so you die in three hits, not even the ds games I've played are that unfair. To add insult to injury you only have 3 'estus flasks' type of healing and each heals only 2.5 drops, I think that even in the ds games you heal more and have more estus to begin with. You can buy more estus, the first one costs 15k and the second one 30k, considering most creatures give you between 40 and 80 money it's a slog.I don't know the technicalties of games but I believe Vesper doesn't have invincibility frames so there are parts where you get hit several times in a row without noticing, so there's also that.Sadly this game will have to go to the graveyard of games I've never finished which is a shame cause as I said I enjoyed the first dungeon. One last thing, the game doesn't have a map, I don't really have a problem with it but I know some people do

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10 - Absolutely loved this game!  While it has a lot of horror elements, it wasn't anything I would find too scary.The music/sound design in general is EXCELLENT, and I hope they will put the OST up on youtube. I loved the gothic horror art style in all it's pixelated glory. I was excited to see each new location, and honestly none of them disappointed. I loved that they really leaned into the fantasy element of environmental design and didn't just make 20 different generic elf forests maps like a lot of other fantasy games do.Enemy mechanics are not crazy complex given it's a pixel game, but each enemy type still has a completely unique move set. Boss battles can be spicy, but they are very skill-based, so as you learn their mechanics you will make steady progress further into the fight. They do sometimes have slightly wonky hit boxes, but nothing that makes them unclearable.Navigating without a map is a little frustrating at first, but as long as you pay attention to where you are and the information you get from NPCs it is completely feasible. It actually made me a little nostalgic for 90s gaming to have to actually pay attention rather than being hand held through quests.Overall, I would highly recommend this game, and if they ever make a sequel I'd be very interested in playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: 6-7/10 Hunt the Night combines Zelda like exploration and gated progression with more intricate and difficult boss battles of Dark Souls or Metroidvania. The combined effect is surprisingly pretty good. Sprite work and graphics are nice and weapon types do have there own unique ones. I would have liked to see more from the armor suits outside of a minor color change. Occasional puzzle elements add a bit more variety to the gameplay which was a nice touch.However, there is still plenty of areas where the devs could have used more consideration. A lot of the weapons & items are just not very impactful. I spent most of the game on a single heavy sword eventually getting a slightly more damaging one later. Also when your potions are fully upgraded and you have some specific skill you have so much access to healing its extremely hard to die to anything outside of one or two bosses. The "hunt" quest mechanic seems a bit of an underdeveloped idea. Lastly, the story lure was hard for me to follow outside of a few key themes.

_childDocuments_.review: While it doesn't do anything that we haven't seen before in this genera it's a fantastic entry and fun the whole way through without being repetitive. _childDocuments_.review: The game is ok.The combat is fun the puzzles are fun. Actually has a decent blend of puzzles and combat that i really liked. It kept both from getting stale.Exploration is encouraged and you can find items and stuff everywhere which is quiet nice.The boss fights were cool but a bit on the easy side. This is not a ultra hardcore game and actually gives you decent leeway, still some bosses will take multiple tries. Also ramps up really nice in the end.Most annoying thing is the amount of text. The hubs has like ~35+ NPCs and only 5 of them actuially do something for you.Then the game has a lot of lore but i did not really feel like getting into it, the bit i got from the regular cutscenes was enough so i could tell what was roughly going on.Apparently this was a Kickstarter game that might explain the Lore bloat. A lot of negative comments apparently come from unfullfilled promises like a physical edition.Took me 10 hours to complete without rushing the main story. Getting all items for 100% took 30 minutes more. It does not overstay its welcome.It is not really outstanding but if you want a topdown dodgy action rpg this might work for you.I don´t regret playing it but it definetly is not worth 20 €. _childDocuments_.review: Beautiful pixel art, responsive combat and a well-crafted spooky atmosphere makes Hunt the Night worth playing if you have an interest in Zelda-like and/or Souls-like games (though it is much more akin to Zelda than Souls).My favourite moments of combat were the bosses and the horde fights where you get locked in a room against waves of enemies, I find most of the weapon types to be very satisfying to use (though the spear weapon type has quiet attacking sounds). The progression is rather flat with most equipment (aside from the starter ones) being side grades of one another, and I actually enjoyed that a lot, with the main vertical progression being max health.I do wish that the Prime Hunt bosses were included in the main game so I could fight them without getting 2-shotted and use my full build against them, though.

_childDocuments_.review: Hunt the Night was much better than I expected.  Great mini souls like game.  I felt the bosses were challenging enough to be fun but not unforgiving to be annoyed.  I lost to most a few times, a couple maybe once, and a few like 10 times.  Near end boss ***her really was tricky, I appreciated the clever dodging required. It felt like the game was never too punishing, it balanced the save points and difficulty pretty well.  I didn't find the gun mechanic problematic. It is different, standing still, but honestly, it's part of the game, the trade off of shooting vs not.  I enjoyed the forced nature of having to melee to get ammo back, made for a good mix. Overall I really enjoyed it, well worth it. The only real CON was: I did get confused on where to go, especially in the 2nd and 3rd zone.  I don't know that a map is what I needed, like others have requested.  Once I figured it out, I realized the hints that I overlooked.  I think maybe early bolding some keywords might have had me realize those were really important words and not just lore.  I think it was well balanced where I had to be aware of the lore to solve some puzzles but not feel obligated to read everything and comprehend all it's detail. But the first couple zones I didn't realize that and got a little stuck.

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing the game, I feel some critiques have been too harsh on this title, which was fun and interesting enough to catch my attention until the end. The game has several good aspects, though it could improve in some others, I’ll try to sum both things as briefly as possible (I’ll try to mark down any potential spoilers):Gameplay: Character mechanics are fun and mostly responsive enough, and though I always wish there was more play style customisation in these sort of games, I believe the design team did a fairly good job at creating a set of engaging mechanics to carry the game forward in a fun way. That said, the dash needs some polishing, specially while loading the screen after falling, as any input can cause you to fall off again while your screen is black, this is not good.  Enemy design is also good, each enemy added different things to the game and in general the game never felt too repetitive, specially because encounter design was nice and always bringing a new challenge. This worked nicely in tandem with the game's great level design (which I think is one its strongest aspects), with nicely crafter dungeons and areas, and by the way, very fun puzzles.Story: I can see a lot of effort was put into trying to give it a meaningful story, however, I could never feel very invested in it, and I believe that is mostly due to the game not doing a good job at introducing players to it. Right from the start, too many names and events are thrown at you with little introduction, and the game expects you to read through the lore content it slowly provides in order to have a grasp of what’s going on; and while I can appreciate that “optional” lore mechanic, even though I read the content, most of the game I still felt like playing the sequel of an existing game, oftentimes confused about what was going on and who was who.  On the same note, a lot of the material, while well written, was sort of cryptic, and felt like added little value to the story; for instance, I wish ALL of the random notes you find in the floor always leaded to something, this happened sometimes but sometimes it didn’t at all. Likewise several NPC felt unnecessary, and also added nothing to the story, nor even gameplay tips, and I still don’t understand the point of having them in the game at all.(Spoilers in this paragraph)Boss design was alright too, though some of them could use more polishing: The second was very overwhelming for such an early appearance, and I could see a new player easily getting frustrated in it; The witches ability to remove your abilities lacks A LOT of clarity and probably disabling her big area attack while you can’t dash as it feels utterly unfair; And the mother needs some revisions, as fighting her was just too easy for one of the final bosses as you can simply hug her on melee and burn everything until she uses her ultimate ability, which by the way also lacks A LOT of clarity.Art: In general the Art of the game is good and befits the narrative nicely. Environment was beautiful, animations and VFX were very details and nice, and though character designs are cool as well, as some other reviewer mentioned already, I wish the player and human sprites in general had more level of detail (though I know that ship has sailed already). (Spoilers in this paragraph)Sound & Music: This is one of the aspects where the game excels the most. Both music and ambiences are spot on with the vibe of the game, and even in the busier moments, the mix never felt overwhelming or unclear. That said, there are a couple details that could still be added to even improve the experience further, such as more striking sounds on the few jump-scare/screamers the game has, and PLEASE a sound to inform the player that the witch has stolen your abilities; in general, sound could support a lot more Bosses clarity.Performance: Overall, the game ran smoothly in my steam deck, except for a few non-critical bugs here and there. That said, I wonder if the overall loading performance could be improved, as each screen took a few seconds to load for me, which felt odd for a pixel art game. This is not a deal breaking issue but is certainly a nuisance while exploring, specially considering the large amount of rooms/areas/instances it has.All said, it is very evident this game was made with a lot of care and love, and I wish sometimes players were more understanding of the difficulties and work that developing a game like these has. I applaud the team for undertaking the task of trying to create something meaningful and thank them for the fun 16 or so hours that it took me to complete it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game looks PHENOMENAL, amazing presentation, i loved the look and animations of the sprites of it, it has such an interesting idea for a story about Hunting the seal that prevents the forever night!HOWEVER.....While the game "Seems" difficult , it gets pretty easy as you get used to it, having a top down Zelda style to its game play, while borrowing some difficulty and other game play aspects from any sort of From Software/Soulsborne style game, but it's definitely not to difficult to discourage anyone tbhThe game definitely needs more polish. Graphical errors with lighting were persistent the entire time i played, when the lighting works, its amazing, but when it does, its still nice to see some of the detail in dungeonsThis game has ALOT of backtracking and NO MAP WHATSOEVER, which you could argue is to add to the difficulty, but for a game that doesn't really have a good sense of direction and requires you to find alot of things to finish out said quests for items crucial to completion of just the story alone? Not the best choice imo, not ONLY that, but like i stated, its lack of direction , even with the heavy dialogue to help the world building, which it does quite nicely, figuring out where you need to go and where not to go is all up to players first hand experience. I can understand this in games that allow you to do things out of order, but this is your Classic Zelda style's action adventure game, You need certain abilities and items in order to progress the story , you cant do it all out of order, nor is the game going to tell you where ANYTHING IS AT ALLThere was some game play hiccups too, nothing game breaking, though Steam Trophies are kinda bugged until you return to the church, which is like your main headquarters, but i was able to get them allThe options for weapons is fun, i will say, but there isn't much of an incentive to use anything besides the great sword up till the final dungeon, which then the final obtainable sword is honestly the best option for the last boss. Some of the "Builds" if you can call them that also don't leave enough of a lasting impression than just going full damage and beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of bosses. Though the bosses???? Topnotch, some will take you a few tries, but they were all super fun tbh, Overall, i can say i recommend this is you want a dark Zelda style game with difficulty that definitely bites back, but there are some things in the game that rather then making it seem "Difficult" is more Archaic game design to be honest.

_childDocuments_.review: Very impressed with Hunt the Night, quite a few nods to games of old and new.+Pixel art is fantastic, reminded me of Lamentum, a game i really enjoyed as well. +Environments are great and quite a variety. Might draw some similarities to 16 bit era RPGS from the SNES; and even some Bloodborne +OST and sound design was well done, from ambient sounds to creature sounds. And a somber soundtrack from Secret of Mana composer Hiroki Kikuta.+ Exploration was handled very well, lots of things to uncover, and platforming felt pretty good!+Boss designs were fantastic! Lots of variety, and a nice difficulty curve overall.+Lore!!! lots of story to uncover through NPC dialogue and 'feathers' you find throughout the environment. Fills in the backstory of everything quite nicely.+Weapons come in 3 varieties, melee, poison, life draining. and fist weapons, spears, 2 handed swords, rapiers/1 hand swords. Armour comes in a few different skins, with certain protections or bonuses. And there is a magic system (no dedicated class) just magic spells.+2 endings, New game +, Nightmare mode(1 health point), and Primal Hunts. -Only one negative i had, while dashing to a platform if you miss and get sent back, sometimes you get relocated a square in the other direction and might fall into another trap or lake or something that damages you. Then the game re adjusts you to actual land. Doesn't happen all the time, but just a small nitpick.Overall Hunt the Night was a joy to play. movement, exploration, looking at the beautiful environments. Fantastic gaming experience for the price. And if you enjoyed Bloodborne(thematically). This might be up your alley as well.
