_childDocuments_.review: I am pleasantly surprised by how much time put into this game! The graphics, mechanics, and dialog are a 10/10 for me and for an early access game, I experienced zero bugs. I will say that the mechanics are easy enough to understand and explain to kid through adult age range. I will say that i have unlocked all of the possible features of the game in just 8 hours of playtime, so if you are looking for a long term game right now, than i would wait to purchase after early access and follow the road maps, because once you unlock all that is allowed it becomes just you staring at your little creation. I am a bit disappointed in the fairy tale aspect of the game and would have really liked to have seen little dungeons your hero could have gone in to obtain more than just one item of loot. especially since the fairy tale rabbit holes are a one time use and they disappear off of your map for good. The only one that sticks is the giant bean stock which is cool to look at but serves no purpose after the one time use. I really loved decorating with all of the decor objects and spent most of my time after beating the game to the point i could no longer advance until they update the game. So In my opinion This game is a very nice demo version for what is to come for this games future. If you are looking to grow with a game in early access than  this will be a fantastic purchase for you. If you have high expectations of the game and what you think should be a finished version, than i would wait, watch and follow the road maps to get the game when you feel confident in the features.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game. Cute graphics. Adorable AF. However:Game is timegated based on new arrivals, which progressively gets slower. Your population can't organically grow. You can only accept immigrants. You also can't automatically accept new arrivals, which should be a QoL improvement.Labor I.E. population:jobs are extremely restricted. For every 3 new arrivals, only 2 will work because 1 is set to a "head of household" who will then waste their time grabbing supplies for the house. The early game is skewered because you have to sustain 1/3 of your population that isn't producing labor for your town.There isn't a lot of "fable" themed characters, buildings, or enemies, which is disappointing for a game called Fabledom. Where is my candy house? Where are my giant mushrooms? I was wondering if I could have elves and dwarves and talking animals as part of my citizen -- I could not. That alone is about 80% of the reason for "not recommended"Give me rabbitfolk to rule over, and I'll edit the review to a thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: On the first look, Fabledom seems to be a neat cozy game, hitting all the right notes. But after a while (in my case 5 hours in) you realize it's quite bland and lackluster.On first impression, it hits all the criteria for a building game, different civilian tiers, food, coal for the winter, several resources, and even production chains. But soon you notice, there aren't many grayed-out buildings, in fact, there are 4 different resource-gathering buildings corresponding to the 2 buildings that process the raw material. (to my disappointment iron doesn't even need to be processed, you just dig it as iron bars out)Reaching 'higher' tier buildings isn't an issue of resources but rather of time, and here is my main issue. This game is , extremely slow, idle game for your phone slow. And there is actually nothing cozy about waiting half to one hour for your lumber mill to finish its stupid boards so you can build something, I even built several lumber mills which kinda tank my economy so I can progress faster, playing it on the fastest speed wouldn't help either.Besides being a rather primitive and simple city-building game, there is also a hero and army system, about which I have nothing of value to say besides there is one. Can your hero and soldiers attack something? - yea maybe 3 different enemies per map. And you can send them out for missions, but the mission is just a text block with a probability value.There is also some sort of diplomacy, but as with the rest of the game it's also quite primitive, I admit I appreciate you can trade with them.So the last point, which I mistakenly thought was the unique selling point of this game, is that you can marry your neighbor. How does it work? - Do some MMORPG like quest and at the end you marry and you get a text that you are married, and also a buff.All in all it's a bland, uninspired game with some neat ideas which were never fully developed.

_childDocuments_.review: Simple city building premise, yet built in a gorgeous world.  Game is early access as of right now (April 2023) so there's about a good 5-10 hours of game play depending on how fast you play, without repeating things.  I would not recommend buying this at full price in its current state, however as long as promised features are released by the devs and game continues to grow out into what is promised, it will be well worth the price.I will be watching this one closely. There is tremendous potential here.Pros:- Beautiful dynamic world, looks amazing.- Simple city builder (for those who don't like the overly complex city sims)- Cosy, casual feel.- Unique take on the relationship sim.- Narration is well done, a lot of potential for story telling.Cons:- While the game is simple, there are some logistics involved which can quickly kill off your population if not managed. (There are currently no intuitive ways to manage food supplies for example, prior to winter).  Adding some adjustable limits for certain items in the stockpile would help.- There's also no way to see production or transport times, so a lot of it is guess work. (which does help to keep it simple though)- Currently very bare bones (April 2023). A lot of content has not released yet.

_childDocuments_.review: I grabbed Fabledom on sale for 35% off and just finished my first run, which took me about 16 hours. Honestly, I feel like I got my money’s worth. This game nails the balance between being engaging without being stressful. If you’re someone who enjoys a laid-back gaming experience, without needing to become an expert in city planning, then this game is surely for you.The fairytale vibe of the game is cozy and inviting, and I found myself really enjoying the simple pleasure of building up my little kingdom. It’s nice to play a game that takes some effort but isn’t frustrating. It was exactly what I needed for a more relaxed gaming session.That said, I do wish the hero quests had more to them. Having a hero character was a cool idea, but the quests felt a bit flat, and there’s definitely room to expand on that part of the game. More side quests and character development would have been great, especially when it comes to random encounters. I also find there is little replay value, unless I want to experience a higher difficulty setting or choosing another ruler to marry. Overall, though, Fabledom was a fun and chill experience that I’d recommend if you’re looking for something more relaxed. It’s definitely worth checking out if you’re in the mood for a cute city builder.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh Fabledom.. how I think of you fondly. (My first nation was a disaster. I didn't manage food production as well as I should have, and I watched in horror as a famine swept the nation. Luckily unlike in the real world, I could delete that save and start again. And pretend it never happened.)Anyways, my beautiful (2nd) city was a work of art. I had a variety of self-named districts that I was SO proud of, that I showed my relatively uninterested brother and girlfriend. They love me so they humored it, and I regaled them with tales of how this section here used to be lumber and iron until the necessity of a marketplace for better goods spread overwhelmed them. About how this section was new growth, and this section is the olddd town. About how carefully I plotted the castle area around my castle. (By the way devs, the system for building your own castle and government section is inspired, and I really hope future city builder games learn and push the boundaries of what you created here). My only wish is that there was even MORE content then the bountiful progression system offered, as I did eventually do pretty much everything there was, and alas thing did start to get rather repetitive. But this is a fault that no game can escape forever.Anyways, this is an absolute 10/10 city building game. Enjoy yourself, don't think too hard about it. (except for farmland), and if you don't like a mechanic, just don't engage with it. (I don't think I fought a single war?).

_childDocuments_.review: This is an early review (less than 2 hours currently) to give others some idea of the negatives. I've been thinking about a refund as there are things I heavily dislike. But I will give it a try and maybe I'll turn to like it.There are 3 main points I dislike about this game so far: two in resource management and one in city building aspects.. Each house takes necessities to their own storage - food, coal and other things. This results in hard to understand storage that would say something like "we have 0 food stored which would be enough for X days". This becomes even worse as there is no good way of understanding how much you produce vs how much you use vs how much is stored outside of your storage areas. There are some graphs, but they aren't easy to read and don't seem to portray actual situation.Another point is logistics. As far as I can tell, buildings don't quite use other nearby buildings for logistics. Let's say I have a forester (collects wood, has inner storage), a coal maker (turns wood into coal, has inner storage) and a general storage. Coal maker won't take the wood from the forester when there is some. Instead, wood will be delivered to general storage area from where your coal maker will take it back.. I can live with resource management. Through trial and error I will find better proportions of production to housing buildings. But I can't ignore the ugliness of city building. You create your village, you plan housing areas, separate it from production areas, maybe put some decorations in. You grow enough to start building second tier of population buildings... And you realize the horror. Instead of regular-to-genre housing updates you are required to build second tier buildings as if it's another village. On the same map. So your long living citizens within their village center would remain as peasants and new tier of population would be living on the outskirts or somewhere else completely. Otherwise you have to destroy your buildings and start planning again.---I was really close to refunding. This decision about city building tier separation is just wrong. Putting the game aside, will give it another chance after a long break. Disappointed, not what I was looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really on the fence about this one. It's a cozy city-builder with a charming style and a lot of good qualities. But it just didn't hold my interest the way I'd hoped it would. I think its biggest flaws are in the additional stuff that's sort of tangential to the colony sim, such as the hero, the missions, and the dating sim elements with "courting" other rulers. Most of this stuff feels really unbalanced and tacked-on, and really doesn't add to the experience. Some of the random encounters are cute, but for the most part it really just distracts from the core experience.I also found that it seemed to incentivize weird layouts; maybe it was just my play style, but I ended up with a city that sprawled in weird directions and really made very little sense. I think it's because the elements that you'd expect to be central, like the townhouses and especially the palace, you don't get at all until very late in the game. Demolishing structures doesn't return the resources, so it's very expensive and you try to avoid it. So unless you intentionally left huge holes in your city for some reason, you end up sticking what should be central things in weird non-central locations. Compare this to , obviously a direct competitor. The graphics and characters are substantially better in , but  seems to incentivize more sensible city layouts, with your city surrounding your keep, which upgrades over time---as opposed to in , where you don't have a palace at all until the endgame.It's probably worth getting on sale. But not at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: So far so good! One of the more stable early access experiences I've had. It's a charming city builder with a fantasy/fairy-tale vibe, and it sets itself apart by allowing you to form marriages, alliances, and invade other princes and princesses. There is also a split between peasants, commoners, nobles, and their quarters and needs, which is actually pretty charming.I look forward to seeing it grow. _childDocuments_.review: City builders are typically games I want to really love but struggle to do so thanks to a million different tiny issues. Fabledom initially looked to me like it could fix so many of these problems, but does it at least stick the landing, or is it nothing more than a fairytale?Fabledom doesn’t stray too far from its inspiration, but it adds enough unique quirks to comfortably stand out. As stated previously, it’s a city builder, similar to the Anno or The Settlers’ franchises, except with a heavy leaning into a fairytale-inspired world. This might give you the idea that it’s trying to be a more casual and cosy city builder, as it did me, but don’t let the visuals fool you: Fabledom regularly falls into the micromanagement pit that city builders often do, to its detriment.The game starts out with you naming and claiming a location for your new kingdom from randomly generated world maps. These have a variety of features, such as Hills, which have different resources and make it harder to build. There are a few things to pay attention to, but the game’s strongest suit is its innate simplicity, which is rare within the genre. The resources and location attributes are easy to understand, and you can avoid locations with fewer resources or decide to play in those locations for more of a challenge. Once your location is chosen, your kingdom is named, and you’ve made your coat of arms, you’ll be dropped into the game proper.Mechanically, it’s a few simple tasks to get you up and running: build some homes, a labourers camp, and some basic resource-gathering buildings, and you have yourself a relatively sustainable village. The starter resources you have are more than enough to become self-sustaining, but here is where you’ll need to start to think and begin actively planning your next steps. As time passes throughout the game, you’ll begin receiving more and more villagers, who require their own homes and jobs, and you’ll also progress through the seasons, which each have their own incredibly charming visuals. Building these homesteads and certain other buildings has modular attachments, allowing you to alter parts of them, which helps balance the beauty and desirability of parts of your city, making your villagers happier in the long run. This is absolutely one of its best features, as it stops each homestead from looking precisely the same, which is a trap many city builders fall into.Once you reach a certain size, you’ll need to purchase additional territory in the surrounding areas to allow yourself to build more while also finding interesting structures and items within these territories. This is a very basic decision; I found myself typically just building into the direction with the most needed resource or just whatever looked the nicest, but there are some interesting things hidden around, such as Ruins or some of the fairy tale-related structures. It’s pretty basic, and the game is incredibly generous with money on its base difficulty throughout the first few hours so expansion isn’t ever much of a concern.Fabledom has a Nobility system, which acts as a currency, often relating to how you interact with random events and other rulers (which I’ll touch more on shortly), which helps to make the world feel more in-depth and makes for some interesting if relatively binary, choices. The other rulers take control over the other locations on the world map. They each like a specific resource, and giving them said resources will increase their opinion of you. I do like that this allows you to entirely avoid conflict for the most part if managed well (along with a creative mode allowing you to build whatever you’d like with no costs or resource restrictions), yet it feels somewhat underbaked. I wish I had stronger feelings, but few of them felt interesting, and the mechanics surrounding them were a little uninteresting in practice. As previously stated, you can enter conflicts with other people, and the combat is also a perfectly fine system, but it was something I barely engaged with, opting for the non-aggressive options where possible.One of your best units for combat is your Hero, a special unit that can engage in combat and also explore certain structures found in the world, such as the Ruins mentioned previously. This fits incredibly well in the fairytale setting; every story needs its protagonist, after all. The fairytale setting it employs is absolutely its best trait, perfectly embracing the whimsy of the setting and connecting it with the gameplay, too. For example, I was given the option to buy some food for my villagers or some magic beans. Of course, I went for the beans, and slowly, a giant beanstalk grew, which my Hero was able to climb.Overall, Fabledom is a very solid addition to the city builder genre. It falls short in a few areas, being a little mechanically simple, despite struggling with micromanagement issues later on. Its setting is utterly fantastic, and this helps with one of the biggest issues I have with city builders: visual variety. Well that was fun, time for a real city builder. Frostpunk 2, here I come.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Dont, has basic issues, crashes on ultra settings (has since launch) and while shows great progress, and will probably be a great game. Not yet. I really wanted to love this game.. The magical creatures showcased, the fun chill management, and i loved seeing the progress they were posting in their logs- and now, after having "totally legally" tried it when it first came out, and whilst it was very flawed, i saw they had updated it a lot and i decided, now its time to give it a go! Bought it, now im refunding.. It has fundamental flaws, and ones unfixed - it isnt worth your time or money yet, if you are already on the fence about it.So first of all i found out, after only 15 min that apparently when i used winkey+prntscr for a screenshot of some funny text, that the game would hang (this isnt reliable, i couldnt replicate?) despite running smoothly, and then crash, and it took me another 10 min, trying to reload back into my auto save to get back, it would crash repeatedly, and then finally for no reason would let me back in - there was also some graphical glitches associated with it, like the ground texture being completely black. I eventually figured out that the ultra settings (im on a beefy system and it ran highest with very high fps) somehow the game would bug out graphically or crash. So was forced to play on medium settings..As for the actual gameplay itself, it has a cute gameplay loop and a lot of neat and fun ideas but it suffers from a few things - for a relatively chill looking casual game, it actually manages to put you in a perpetual under-powered state, leaving you constantly feeling struggles once you reach the "second act" or whatever you wanna call it. And it becomes kind of a dull repeated struggle, and limits your progression, it sort of went from "oh look we're having fun, and chilling" to banished like management of "your people are dying every winter!" and the fundamental issues in design really showed their face here, you get too little people, to manage your buildings, even when played perfectly & with prior knowledge. The problem isnt so much the difficulty though as it is that, it doesnt feel satisfying, being left with excess nothing, feeling like you didnt really progress. And meeting the "noble goals" is almost entirely imbalanced early game, being if your goal structure isnt already built (like if your goal is to catch fish, and you have just placed the building to be constructed, which happens often because you are progressing in the game and they pop up as you unlock them) theres 0 chance you can manage in time. It was kind of 50/50 if the goal was achievable or not. Again i think this game is suffering from a crisis of "am i a hard game, or a relaxed cute looking game" and being left in a position that constantly doesnt feel like "i could have done better with this" but instead "well this is just unfair and unreasonable with what i was able to do with the population i been given" And some other minor gripes, is that - theres no variation besides "skin color" in the people you get, everyone just looks like the same fat eggman dude or the same eggman looking woman, with only slight difference.. And they dont actually seem to have any level of life or soul in them, you cant really follow them around and name them and care about them, well.. you can if you try and make up your own story in your mind, but it doesnt come to play in game, which i feel is a lost opportunity, in many other management games, you have someone that you know what they do "oh john/jane doe here is a farmer, and he's been struggling with their tasks and making due and likes to go to the bar in the evening" or whatever, you end up with "another mindless eggman drone" - and i genuinely thought and hoped that this game would bring more life into the mix. And if you enter it thinking or hoping it will, you're be a bit let down im afraidThe Encounters are interesting and i love a lot of the mechanics, however, they also suffer a bit from "i dont know what i want to be as a game" be it hard, or relaxed, indept and following your "heroes" or just a "this is military unit #7" I think the game needs more identity and love in terms of "the people and personalities" and very much needs to ease up on the gas, or at least go harder and deeper on the petal. This in between life doesnt mesh well and isnt working out as a pleasant experience. I hope this has helped you. Ill leave some design suggestions- allow trading earlier and easier, so you can exchange resources - give more people, or increase effective output - give people more life and interaction, talking & going to have a meal or a drink, relationships!- give people variation and not just eggman#32... If they MUST have THE SAME body and face, at least give them hats/clothes? But id much rather be able to identify them. Make them people- when played "optimally" the game doesnt feel like you have much choice, id like to VIABLY be able to have more options.. Or focusing on a specific type of field like "this village is focusing on stonework and imports more food" or vice versa. The game feels too.. "closed loop"Good luck, and have a pleasant day.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Cute, laid back kingdom builder with some fantasy fairy tale elements tossed in that can keep you building for hours. But, be warned, the game loves to eat GPU resources for breakfast, so be prepared to play on lower settings if you still have a gtx1060 like me, and I recommend checking out the Discussions thread on continuing performance issues and turning GPUs into toaster ovens.Longer review: The gameplay loop: satisfying, and the randomly generated maps add to its replayability. Not only do you have a kingdom to build, but you can also expand your map and use a special Hero character to explore fairy-tale-esque encounters like witch huts, wishing wells, talking tress and dancing ogres. Different choices result in different rewards. On the world map, you must also garner favor with other kingdoms, send gifts, court a lord or lady, and eventually wed. I haven't gotten quite that far yet myself. resource management: There are a few balance issues you have to manage around, and I can't stress enough how important multiple lumber camps in early game is. Coal is king, so make sure you have enough for winter. As far as farms go, I always seem to have not quite enough or an overabundance of vegetables, while turning wheat into bread feels like more trouble than its worth. You will need to have multiple neighborhoods, as worker distance from job is a resource that matters, and some buildings affect desirability and worker happiness. You also have a resource called Nobility you can gain and lose through quests and choices you make. Gold is relatively easy to get once you have small population paying taxes. Graphics: I think they are a cute, storybook style with high detail even when you zoom way in, but they come at a cost to your GPU. I am not sure if they are poorly optimized, because I can play more graphically intense games with ease, but Fabledom loves to use 90-100% of my GPU on medium settings and Ultra is a non-starter. I do have an older card, gtx1060 6gb, but this is one of the first games I've played where it chugs, especially considering the art style. Maybe it's not as low-poly as it appears?  There are also only 3 graphic choices - Very Low, Medium and Ultra... which is disappointing. I am bottle necked at Very Low, but what they call Medium has my GPU over 85%. You must also use Vsync (I do), they recommend 60fps (I am) and 1920x1080 (I am) They are also not a recognized game by Nvdia Experience, which may be part of the issue? I feel the devs still have some issues to iron out here, but I think it is being worked on. Just, be aware of them and please check out the Discussions forum before buying. Bugs: I've only been playing for 7 hours at time of review, and aside from the graphics issue mentioned above, I haven't run into any bugs. The Discussions forum and Discord, however, have people talking about a few that the devs are working on. I think it's like a 2 person Dev Team, so patience is good.Is it fun?: This, of course, is subjective. I enjoy it. It's more laid back and casual than some kingdom building games, but this does come at a cost of depth. There is a long tech tree you slowly build up, but there doesn't seem to be a deep micro-management level to it like some builders. There are a few micro-management tools but so far I haven't needed to use them, there is no building upgrade system, I have yet to touch any type of combat, and making friends with your neighboring kingdoms is way easier than making them unhappy. Even the ruler who says he likes combat and dealing pain is easily made happy with a gift of coal. So, if you are looking for Sid-Civ level politics, this is not it. It's more oldschool Pharaoh level but instead of invading barbarians, it's orcs (I think...I haven't built a military yet)  Anyhoo, I recommend giving it a play if you enjoy city builders, are maybe turned off by the complexities of Sid-Civ, and don't mind that the devs are still ironing out some things.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a fan of most city builders, primarily because they're generally very complex and industrial in the sense that they're rustic and realistic, or space themed. I enjoyed things that were a little more colorful, such as The Wandering Village, and of course games like this, where you feel like you can simply take your time and enjoy what you're doing without feeling rushed or panicky as you create your ideal towns and cities while completing and taking on challenging objectives. It's neither too complicated nor too simple; as you fulfill your objectives, the game begins to open up, allowing you to meet other kingdoms and form rivalries and alliances and to take on much more challenging objectives in exchange for rewards.I enjoyed this game; there could be more music because it gets a little too quiet for lengthy periods of time when you're busy managing your kingdom's resources and commitments, but overall it's a very relaxing and casual experience.

_childDocuments_.review: "Embarking on the enchanting journey through Fabledom was a delightful experience, where the whimsical metropolis unfolds in the embrace of a fairytale world. As the overseer of my quaint village, the gentle rhythm of growth and prosperity resonated with the laid-back charm that sets Fabledom apart in the realm of city builders.The heartwarming essence of the fairytale setting infused every aspect of gameplay. From the quaint cottages to the bustling marketplaces, each building breathed life into the village, creating a tapestry of charm that made every moment a joy to behold. The meticulous attention to detail in the design and the gentle soundtrack transported me to a world where the magic of storytelling seamlessly intertwined with the mechanics of city building.One of the unique delights Fabledom presented was the element of diplomacy and trade, where interactions with neighboring settlements were more than just transactions. Navigating alliances and friendly competitions added a layer of strategy that balanced the serene pace of the game. The choices to either forge alliances or embark on friendly challenges provided a refreshing twist to the typical city-building experience, making each decision feel meaningful and impactful.The pursuit of a royal romance, a key element in Fabledom, added a fairy tale touch that warmed my heart. The delightful prospect of finding a prince or princess not only added a personal narrative to the game but also became a charming goal to aspire toward. The interpersonal dynamics and the ripple effect on the village's prosperity added a layer of emotional investment that made the journey all the more engaging.In the end, as my village flourished and the bonds with neighboring settlements grew, Fabledom became a haven of tranquility and joy. The harmony of city-building, diplomacy, and the pursuit of true love created an experience that felt like living within the pages of a storybook. Fabledom stands as a testament to the magic that can be woven when gameplay and fairy tales coalesce, providing a haven where players can immerse themselves in the art of crafting their own happily ever after."

_childDocuments_.review: I originally gave this game a thumbs down but ONLY because strange issue. I played the game for the first time for 10 hours then every single citizen began to starve for no apparent reason: food stocks over full; houses food stuff full; no witch in the area, etc. However, one thing I did notice was that a few of the fablings were stuck. Usually when a fabling becomes stuck (seems to be due to building placement) or their path fails you can click them and the game will transport them out of the jam. This didn't work for me on two that were stuck; then everyone began to rapidly die one after another after this. For anyone who has ever played the SIMS you may be familiar with the bug that causes a SIM to become stuck and it can then cause other SIMS to get stuck too until you use the console to RESET them. I believe what may have caused the issue in the first game play was this. Once the Fablings path failed, it sort of bottlenecked up the rest of them and really the game was failing at that point because of it.I decided to give it a go again and haven't noticed any issues; I just reached the point where the game failed last time (added the CONDOS) and everything seems to be running smoothly.So overall I would say, yeah you might run into a glitch or two which could very well be triggered by building placement, but otherwise the game is smooth, beautiful to look at, fun to interactive and an easy learning curve. _childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: No it’s not short for “domination”.It is a simpler city builder game, and while the ads want make you to believe it’s themed around the european fairy tales — it’s not. There are 3,5 cameos, 3,5 instances of generic fantasy things, the rest 97 is just a generic cartoony medieval city sim.The mechanics are very simple but are very poorly conveyed. And aren’t always working. There’s very little space for your big buildings. And since it’s a city builder game you take direct control of everything and have to babysit the citizens. They demand tons of stuff, but there is no space to provide all the necessary things in range. Each tier 1 house can generate its own food lowering the load on the system. But the game doesn’t explain it properly, and by default puts decorations into the allowed slots. The home decorations work only for one house and still cost resources. Instead you can put a global decoration in that plot of land which has a decent AoE. You personally assign a worker for every job, and the workers are not good. They suck at their jobs and are very slow and inefficient. The game is built around commuting, at least that’s what i think, because every workplace shows how far away the worker lives. But it never explains what that influences. And well, in real life a worker commutes for two hours, but spends the work day on the same spot, so it shouldn’t influence anything but happiness. You can have months worth of food, but your dummies can still die of starvation. There’s no automatic surplus trading deals, you have to sell // buy by hand every time.The game has negative pacing. Everything is already very slow at the fastest, and your goals only increase in scale. First you enlarge your city and buy neighbouring squares. Next you go to the global map. Then you do questing in foreign lands. Lastly you pick a neighbouring character to marry, you complete several bigger quests, build a giant palace and win.The GUI is pretty bad for this genre and the tutorial is not good either. There are no graphs, no list of problems, no income outcome balance sheets. And it’s not because this is a simple game with no those issues. You have all the issues and none of the feedback. Everything you can do or see is tied to each individual asset with no way to see the bigger picture or diagnose the problem. For example, to optimize the commuting, you literally have to write down everything on paper, and draw crazy-board graphs. All menus are cramped into a tiny window with miniscule FoV — barely a couple of rows fit there. And even that is unlocked only after you reach a way higher level. Even if it’s not your first city.You have 1000 wood in stock, 10 coal producers, and 0 coal, and no way to know why. How does the storage building work? In proper city-builders storage is mandatory and when you run out of storage you are notified with the place where it happened. Here you build one because the unskippable tutorial demands it, and forget about them. How do granaries work? In normal games they are tied to food distribution and are mandatory too. Here you can have tons of food and not care for granaries. How does decor work? It has AoE indicator, does that mean it’s not stacking even when it’s all different?You look at a damn magic black box, you scream numbers into it, and get an echo of other random numbers with absolutely no understanding of the math, and no way to disassemble the box and see how it works. This stupid iphone generation of devs doesn’t know how to make interfaces, because they think that users are stupid and everything works fine and automagically.In 4//3 half the global map is out of bounds.UngreatfulIt starts alright and it would be an alright simple and easy game, even with the terrible interfaces if they didn’t matter. I started off liking it, but then everything start to matter for no reason. The easy difficulty keeps you in purgatory allowing to ignore most of the problems until they go away. But under the hood everything is falling apart unrepairably, spiralling into abyss.The game punishes you for playing it. Even on the easiest difficulty citizens generate barely enough tax to go over the spendings. And then the game increases the developer tax — the money taken from you for nothing, for literally existing. And that reaches insane values.That terribleness is complemented by another terribleness. The combat is the worst. It literally doesn’t work. You invest into defensive structures, waste money for magic ammo, and then your towers deal no damage at all and can’t hit anything at all. I mean literally. Your forces are being annihilated by everything, and just like in real life not-dictatorial states each soldier is a citizen that required giant investment to be lured into the sexless kingdom, conscripted and trained. The hero gains levels once per 20 hours and those add nothing. The items barely exist and there’s no real choice. The hero dies from 1 hit and it can’t be healed. The regeneration takes hours of real time. To revive the hero you need absolute tons of gold.Most the random events just want to screw you over. And all the enemies lower the happiness. If a dragon spawns and you have 10 guns, they will waste all 600 stockpiled ammo (a giant number in the scale of this game) and will miss most of the shots.To offset the developer tax you build the gold generating cave, and in exchange for you finally getting 3 coins of income, it starts spawning trolls. The trolls are immune to all the cannons you have and they eat your conscripts with their gaze alone. They regenerate and kill the hero. In time it takes to wipe just one troll camp, two new appear.Now your happiness drops so much no one wants to migrate into your country, your citizen die, anyone you send into the army dies, tax was already bad but now it drops even more. There’s no GUI to see empty streets and shut down unnecessary buildings. You have no way out, even if you disable the gold cave, the present trolls will not go away.The additional problem is that no one plays this game. In popular broken games like AoE 2HD, KD:R etc, you can stumble upon a written or a video guide that has solved the game, and explains why and how these mechanics are busted and how you can play against them. But the only thing few people who are in the Steam forums say, is that to get cash you need to get happiness; to get happiness build inns; to build inns get peasants and more cash. Umadbruh? My initial problem is the lack of cash and peasants.The combat quests make you lose several thousands of gold investment into the troops, and you get 200 gold in return.And, well, for the quests and event quests you need to get X amount of a resource. But there’s no option to stockpile it. I sold all the things and bought some bread for the main quest. Despite me having a lot of veggies and fish, the citizens literally ate all of the bread in less than a minute. The only way i beat this crap is by kamikazying it. Each next step of the main wedding quest requires you to stockpile X. I was pressing pause, selling everything, then buying, while still on pause, the needed resource and finishing the quest. To fulfil the wedding requirements i had to sell absolutely everything i had and buy from everyone everything they had to finally finish this nonsense.Steamworld Build is literally everything this game is not. Literally launch Steamworld Build and see the resources balance tab, the working combat, the trading of surplus. And even a better story and stronger adherence to the advertised theme.

_childDocuments_.review: Fabledom is as relaxing as it can be, while still having all the mechanics you would expect from a city builder. The graphics, the music, the whole premise of the game make it a truly joyful experience. The idea of being able to befriend, court and then presumably marry one of the other rulers - while also being able to befriend and/or antagonize and go to war with the others - is a new concept for the genre, but a really welcome one.I'm mighty curious to see what will happen if you end up marrying one of the other rulers: will the kingdoms be united under one banner? Will they be permanently locked into an alliance? And how will the other rulers respond to the union? I can't wait to find out.TL;DR: if you want a city builder that is as relaxing as it is cute, with good graphics and an even better music score, then Fabledom is for you. The sandbox mode is perfect for those that wants to focus on building their city without worrying about unlocking buildings and managing resources, while the campaign mode lets you experience a more traditional city building trajectory, so to speak.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: I'm actually so excited to see what this game becomes, its the perfect mixture of a chill city builder with the fun aspects of other games such as Stardew valley. This is the first review I've ever felt I needed to leave on a game. Its so much fun and a perfect way to calm down or just do something by yourself. The narration is funny and unique, the music is calm and enchanting. Definitely worth the price. The only issue I have is that performance seems to be an issue right now. So read the discussion posts about how to work around that. It seems like they are aware and are working to fix it!!9.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: Once upon a time, in a land far, far away, there was a fairy-tale city-builder called Fabledom, created by "two villagers", one artist and one developer, a two-person team.- the fairy-tale premise adds charm- cutesy vibes and vibrant colors- solid mechanics, well-executed, well-connected, and well-designed- social interactions, build relationships, make choicesChill as you slowly build your own fairy tale kingdom, where it all ends happily ever after.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: This is easily one of my favourite games, I check periodically to see developments and get sooooo amped when I see an update coming. Finding just small additions to the game is so exciting like new mini quests or items, I genuinely gasp every time I notice them. I'm so in love with just existing in this game. Thank you so much for making Fabledom!!
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: It's a beautiful early access release that doesn't feel like early access.  UI is polished, the art style is unique and beautiful.  It tells a story and makes you feel like you're role playing in a fairy tale right from the first load screen!  Fabledom is a crowning achievement in the genre of chill, peaceful colony builders that diverges from the usual formula of Crisis Management, Traffic Management, Strategic Warfare and Complex Supply Chains to deliver something wholesomely unique that has not been done before.  It feels like a more aesthetically pleasing spiritual sibling to Foundation, while being different enough to have an identity all its own - and it has romance and flying pigs!  What more could you ask for?  Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: Chill game with cute artwork. Very calming yet addictive game play. Writing your own story and building your kingdom becomes personal. Love everything the game offers thus far and excited for it to get out of early access. Some improvements I would like to see:- Missions being a bit easier to do (the requirements sometimes are a bit much). Just have some easier missions via the Embassy before taking on bigger missions.- More options via the Messenger building.- More variety when it comes to other rulers in others kingdoms. Right now there are 4.- Combat isn't really a thing right now. Would love to feel a sense of danger even from the early - middle game.- More variety in creating your sigil- Multiplayer???
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: This is a cute game. I've played happily until year 30 (apx 40 hours) but it's now feeling a bit boring. The Witches/Dragons /Fairies "attacks" on he kingdom get a bit repetitive. Nobility points should be given for maintaining friendships with other kingdom leaders. Map feels small. When do I get to challenge my family to war or save nobility points to free my kingdom from taxes? Why don't bridges allow travel over rivers and lakes, why are they only working on land and streams? We need more quests and incentive. I could really get into this game if it kept evolving. Now that I've developed most of my land and money keeps pouring in I have no push to keep playing. Maybe I'll start over again, but how many times can that be fun?
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely game! Its well polished and there aren't many bugs. Most things are well balanced, and if you build too much into one resource you can easily readjust back to normal! The length of play is flexible to what you want, if you want to play for just an hour or for much longer it's still fun either way. I left mine idling on a second screen to build up resources and it was fine.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: One Line: Fun, well-themed, short, charming but a little slow fairy tale city builder.Details: Played on Standard Mode, Hardest Difficulty, Married Agnes.Pros:Very charming, looks great, strong theme.The ultimate objective (to marry your prince(ss)) and live happily ever after is a fun, themed goal that fits well with the tech tree & resource escalation.It's a competent resource management/city builder with light combat (think impressions city builders).It stands out because of a strong narrative theme and a lot of content for its length.Neutral:It's short - 11 hours for me on the hardest difficulty.Although the theme is great, it did often read more generic fantasy than necessarily fairy tale at times.There's a fair but of content but it's also simplistic - resource chains are 3 buildings long at most and there's not much you can do to improve production efficiency.Cons:As most other reviews point out, it's slow. I played the whole game at max speed and it's still got a bit of waiting around. The bottleneck on expansion is a drip-feed of new workers and there's effectively no way to speed this up, especially as every house (3 workers) requires a worker to stay at home, meaning 1/3 of your workforce is useless, further slowing down expansion. A way to upgrade capacity of your housing would help with this.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: Super cute and cozy little game. I put it on after a long day at work just to relax a littlePros:AMAZING soundtrackCute little villagers and overall great attention to detail! Sometimes i just zoom in on someone and follow him around and it does not get boring !great variety of things to doCons:I wish you could have some choice of heroes (like a ranger, magician, etc) and not just a default warrior brute (he is cute tho)Played on normal difficulty and it felt a little easy but all good for me!
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: With so many city builders out there, you would expect new ones to either excel on what have already been done, or have a good spin on it. This game lacks everything and then some. The devs clearly put 90% of their work on the great graphics but have no idea how to work around the city building or give it a spin:Cons- Clunky UI that requires 3 times more clicks than you would expect to make anything- Game is EXTREMELY SLOW, it looks as if it is playing on 'normal' speed if you select the fastest speed.- There is a hard-limit on where you can build which I had no patience to figure out how to increase, and you are tied to a tiny land when you start, no room to plan anything- Did I already mention 3 times more clicks to do ANYTHING?- The game plays as a tutorial to a 3 year old the whole time and there isn't a "turn tutorial mode off" anywhere- I didn't play much but for a game that parades on Fable / Magic things ... none to be seen at all. I expected this spin to be at the very start- Your "Fabledoms" (people) need to be assigned to everything. You built a farm? forget building it and expecting people to man it, you have to manually click on "assign" and add people to work there. No I did not count this as another click when you are building stuff, make it 4x more clicks to make anything.- Just too clunky and cubbersome. Pro- I won't really say the graphics are a pro, they are nice but all show and no content should be a PRO.Refunded. This was clearly rushed to 1.0 before being half-way finished, no saving this.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: Impressive for such an incredibly small team. Cute, relaxing, though sometimes perplexing game at this stage. Lacks content, but it's clearly in the works. Balancing resources, people, money, and employment can be a challenge at times. I thought peasants would leave if they were homeless for too long since that's what the writing implied, but they just straight up starved to death without a home and dropped dead at the 'plaza.' So I unintentionally euthanized a third of my people when trying to replace peasants with common folk from lack of space. Then my common folk also began starving too- I'm wondering if "They're more demanding" means they consume more food? I got confused there.Anyhow, after mass murdering dozens of people I made a new save and it's going great...Coal makers feel highly inefficient with little employment, slow production, low desirability, and high upkeep after so many of them- only for the game to not even react if my people don't have coal to heat their homes in the winter. So I opted to just let them freeze since it's easy to ignore with no consequence. Coal makers are definitely my least favorite building in the game.I hope the next neighboring ruler is a guy who looks... a touch more handsome than Giovanni... his character design is creative, funny, and unique- but I'm -not- that desperate. Oh dear.I'd love a preview of what royalty/nobility points could unlock for me in the future. For now, I didn't care too much- though the pop up quests not having an option to decline without penalty (especially early on in the game) stressed me out. It felt like time was rolling the dice as to whether I was punished or punished less harshly, especially when struggling with money and food already. Hell, an option to turn those off for a more relaxing experience would be great too. It reminded me of sim city's random destruction events.My least important peeve was the cake-like fog around the border edge of the map. Kinda kills my immersion when I view a map and the visual horizon from my camera doesn't match up, but I also have no idea how this could be fixed and I can see why the developers picked such a solution for now at least.This game is cute and fun though, I'd probably play it again alongside Dorfromantik whenever I want something less intense than the usual.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: Pick up on deep sale if you're really interested in playing this. The game is ok but doesn't have much depth. Devs abandoned it 2 months post launch. I don't think it needs more content, though some of the features could be fleshed out a bit more but the whole game lacks polish / performance optimization.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: I love everything about this game - from the quirky narrator, the depth of city planning, the attention to detail in buildings, and the overall game flow. The setting is cute but still challenging. It's exactly what I think qualifies as a chill strategy, settlement building game. I really like what I'm seeing with the diplomacy system, and this is the area I hope to see the most growth in. I think it has serious potential, and want to see new leaders and expanded interactions implemented to help add variety to games. Totally worth what I paid for it. Absolutely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: I dont recommend this game bc it has no day/night cycle. There is no sense of timing or pace, days go by in seconds and each season is just 30 days (or thereabouts) long... so seasons are like 10 minutes. Your people never walk home at the end of the day, since ther eis no end of day.  It's just always daytime as everyone constantly works, never going home, as the seasons race by around them. really dumb system, and it's about time they stop making city builders & park sims & tycoon games with no organic daily cycle, where you can pinpoint the income and costs of each day based on what was done. other than that it's the same as all other city builders, why bother. game is beautiful looking..... too bad it will never be fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed opinions.It is a chill and nice city builder. The learning curve is kinda gentle, even if sometimes it is not easy to understand why you are lacking resources.One of the main problems with the game is that even at maximum speed, it feels slow.The most annoying thing is the slowness of the expansion process. In the advanced part of the game, building new groups of buildings or the latest unlocked fancy building would take an enormous amount of time.So, I think it would need either a way to make it even faster or a way to scale better.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: I love and adore this game, it is a very chill game. I do wish it had mod support, to make things like bridges that can be longer etc. Also the game play content for me was mostly done about 15 hours in. All I have left to do is friend all my neighbors which I am close to doing and marrying another leader. Which is just on hold due to resources needing to be gathered. Otherwise the game has been beat and it saddens me. The balance is wonderful and makes me wish for more content. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: Simple, colorful, and one of the most laid back games I have played. I think one of the biggest things for me, which oddly is a positive is re-starting maps. As I keep running into layouts that just aren't perfect enough. The only negative is I feel like the end game just kind of fizzles out rather quickly and wish there was more content.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: there's a lot to this fantasy city-builder! Sometimes, it can be a bit overwhelming, especially if you're not a die-hard city-builder player. There's a lot to keep tabs on, but it isn't stressful, just keeps your brain busy. I do wish there was a bit more information on a few things in game, such as how to make more money, how to organize the city properly, or rearrange your city. Yes, you can figure things out by trial and error, but I know some people don't want to play the same game over and over and over to figure the game out. Maybe a "tips for beginners" website or something? Final thought.... I do love this game! I recommend it also, it's cute, good for problem solving, relaxing, and there is a lot of content!
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: If you find this game for $10 or less it is worth a bit of casual play. It is extremely unfinished. It is a good concept, it has cool elements that could be something but not in current form. A lot of content say coming soon but they have posted they are leaving EA without completing the game and raising the price to 25 bucks.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: Games these days use the excuse of being released in 'early access' to push out an incomplete product in order to start making revenue. This game, in particular, is not even ready for that. The content is so bare; I found my settlement unable to grow any further because we cannot cross rivers or mountains in the current state of the game. The artistic style is quite nice, despite the lack of content. TLDR: This game is not even close to ready, do not spend your money on it until 2024.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun to play. Played all the way until Year 18 when I ran into the starvation glitch of the game. Suddenly, the fablings will no longer work, they starve en masse even if I had ample food supplies and maxed out all my food and resource storage.I hope the devs fix this, my suggestion is that the starvation mechanic should only persist if there are no food being produced (especially during winter), or stored and that even if their work distance is far, it will not cause starvation since there are more than enough food being produced and stored.I haven't tried turning this game into a Total War game since the kingdom builder and the diplomacy features are quite fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great "realm building"-lite game. Unlike many other realm building games there isn't too much text, there's some humor, it's cute and not too many things to keep track on! Great for me with a bit of brainfog that still want to play this sort of games, and probably pretty practical for younger kids too(but just know the Fables can die).
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loving the game. The storybook/fairytale art style is adorable. I love the quests that are available in the game to help you move forward. I do hope the other content comes out soon though. A lot of content is unlocked especially compared to the demo but there are still many things that are locked behind early access which I could see hindering progression in the game. But the courting, curses, hero quests, city building element in the game are great. The only issue I've really had is the game taking up way more memory on my computer than it should. To the point that I can't do anything on my second monitor because it's lagging out. Considering the build of my computer this shouldn't be happening from a game like this. Hopefully, that is fixed soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review: Damn you, devs, any excuse to take royalty away. Broke and can't give food to passing beggars? -5 royalty per instance. Broke because you try to keep up with housing and can't buy territory to complete an Explorers' quest? -15 royalty. Over-building housing but no jobs for people. The people find any excuse to starve. Red fairies steal 25% of your crops if you're too broke to pay extortion. Too bad there's no market to unload excess things like stone for much needed cash. But then that's Early Access for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Fabledom

_childDocuments_.review:
Welcome, your Highness! A vast land awaits your settlers and is ready to be colonized.

name: En Garde!
detailed_description: From the forgotten pages of history, comes Adalia de Volador ! Legendary swashbuckler. Dashing adventurer. Hero of the people. Play as Adalia in her daring escapades full of sword-fighting, satire and shenanigans. Challenge the cruel Count-Duke and oppose tyranny with panache ! Beautifully painted locations, charismatic characters, and an astounding amount of battle banter will transport you to the golden age of swashbuckling comedy ! So, sharpen your sword, grab your boots and hat, and embark on a hilarious, action-packed spectacle! Fencing With Flair Parry, riposte and lunge your way to victory! Fight with style to fill your Panache Meter and unlock special skills! But you’ll need more than your sword to win the day… Adapt and Improvise Challenging, ever-changing fights push you to rely on your cunning and acrobatics to disturb your enemies. Learn their weaknesses to toy with them and express your fighting style. Experiment with the Environment Combat areas are playgrounds full of opportunities to create mischief and gain the upper hand. Surprise, stun, or evade enemies with a variety of objects - from rolling barrels to falling chandeliers. Arena Mode Unlock zany game-changing modifiers and new fight situations in the arena mode. Play and replay randomized scenarios to test your skill against waves of enemies! Theatrical Characters A flamboyant cast dazzles the screen! Adalia and her rivals react to each of your actions, exchanging witty one-liners during the flow of the fight. Story Episodes Discover the tales of Adalia, with unique challenges to complete and secrets to uncover. Fight through marketplaces, dungeons and palaces: the world's a stage for your epic duels! Award-winning Passion Project The game was first prototyped as an award-winning and much-loved student project. The original team has reformed and expanded as Fireplace Games to increase the scope, sweep and grandeur of En Garde! .
