_childDocuments_.review: YOU CAN PET THE CHICKEN!!!!!! 11/10Okay no, lets be a bit more real.Overall En Garde is a good game, but not without its flaws.The main combat is varied and more complex, than you'd think at first glance. I happen to suck at it, but i will not hold that against the game.What i WILL hold against the game is the leveldesign. While beautiful to look at, the game suffers from "Arena-Syndrome", meaning, that it is one arena, you advance into the next room, doors klock and welcome to the next arena, you advance into a jump-passage, to get into the next arena.The in-betweens are very empty. Still nicely designed from a looks perspective, but you just do not see anyone for the most part, until you get locked into the next arena.The looks and the fact, that there are A LOT of interactibles, you HAVE to use in case of some enemies, eleviate the issue a bit, but it cannot completely mask the fact, that you're just running from arena to arena.Also the jump-passages, for the most part, felt more like obstacles for the sake of having one. Not all! There are some, that manage to fit into the level more nicely, than others, so it is a bit hit and miss.Also, for the most part, you seem to fight the same enemies, though they are varied in the way you have to tackle them, so i'd put that into the neutral category. What is there, is indeed challenging and you have to pay attention to what the enemies are doing, in order to not get overwhelmed. So one could say, that the enemies do the job, they're supposed to do, there is just not much variety, especially towards the end.The core however, is rock solid and the things i pointed out are a pretty good task for a sequel.All in all, i like the game. It is very cheesy and the voice-lines give it a nice charme...quite litterally ^^If you're in a modd for a cheesy presented fencing game, with good combat, then this is for you.If you expect deep characters and challenging level-design, then this is not for you.It lives through the combat and if you cannot wrap your head around blocking, evading, attacking and using the environment to your advantage, to separate your enemies, you'll have a bad time.I guess it is a 7/10. It is decent and not bad for the first in its line. It "offers" a lot, a sequel can improve on, but that doesn't make it a bad game.I'd say: Get it on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: You can read my other reviews Video Review: En Garde! This rallying cry resonates throughout the swordplay featured in the thrilling exploits of Adalia Volador, the beloved champion of the people. With its incredibly satisfying learning curve, this title is sure to captivate players, leaving them eager to master its intricate mechanics while also underscores the enduring appeal of action games. Adalia stands as one of the stalwart individuals fighting against the oppressive Count-Duke regime, the primary adversary within this game's narrative. As players engage with the storyline, they will assume the role of this character, immersing themselves in the central role. While the setting remains relatively consistent throughout all the episodes, it functions as a cohesive thread, guiding players from the story's inception to its conclusion. Throughout the unfolding action, various characters will make appearances, allowing ample time for players to establish connections with Adalia, thereby embedding them in this universe and revealing their complete potential.At first glance, the graphics are the main point that caught my eye. The setting of each chapter introduces something new, from a dungeon, to sewers, all of them set with 3D models that appear to be painted in watercolor. In fact, there is an interesting detail of blur between the background and what is happening right next to the player’s view that makes the background look like a painting. There is also the inclusion of platforming elements, which serve as moments of pause between encounters with enemies, but without ever revealing that idea of filler content.Adalia is not only sharp with her quick sword movements, but her lines always feature some hilarious detail, whether in the cutscenes or in the moments of combat against the guards. Even the comments from the guards themselves denote small details from Adalia’s previous fights, creating a path for all the notoriety that an anti-hero carries.After finishing all the chapters of En Garde! (in Hard), I feel like I’m prepared to tackle a souls like or even Sifu and his extremely technical combat. In this case, although not being too technical, the combat system is fun and presents a very clear learning curve, especially during encounters against Bosses where it is possible to have the screen full of enemies. Adalia is equipped with her trusty sword, a dodge ability and special abilities that are unlocked over time, which consume the Panache bar and allow you to apply damage to a single enemy or area damage when surrounded by enemies.All objects present at the time of combat can be used to damage enemies or hinder their movement. It is interesting to understand the different attack patterns of enemies and what you have at hand to prevent them from inflicting damage. Throwing a roasted chicken, yes a roasted chicken, or a bucket at the enemy makes them passive without being able to attack for a brief moment. Boxes, tables, chairs are all elements that can be thrown at enemies with a simple kick. Enemies have a bar below their life bar, representing different types of protection. For the yellow one, for example, it is necessary to parry or attack the enemies until it reaches 0, and then yes, you can apply damage to them. The blue one is equivalent to the need to throw objects, such as boxes, until it reaches 0, so that, as before, it is possible to apply damage. The difficulty increases when there is a need to face several enemies, all of them with different attack patterns or different damage-taking mechanics.In addition to the story mode, there is the Arena mode. As the name suggests, the player will face waves of enemies in an arena, with small differences in combat, as there are positive and negative modifiers. Regarding the positive modifier, it is possible to choose one of 3 options at the beginning of each round. It’s an interesting addition to extend the playing time of this title, as I didn’t feel like repeating, at least for now, the chapters of the story mode.En Garde! It is an adventure that will generally take around 5 hours to complete. It will, of course, depend on each player’s finger dexterity. Adalia is a fun main character, who will try to mark her space in the player’s memory. The combat mechanics and confrontations against the different enemies keep the player attentive to all the details surrounding him, with the aim of surpassing himself with each movement. Recommended in its entirety for all players, even the most casual ones.

_childDocuments_.review: The Doom Eternal of swordfighting - Play by the rules and you will get a incredibly unique and satisfying swashbuckling experience.This game made me play like i was the hero in a action movie. It is one of the few games i have played that actually made the "use your environment" both effective and fun! The - think on your feet - strategy of isolating enemies for quick duels was thrilling and not something i have seen games execute this well before. It is definitely what makes En Garde! stand out from the crowd.Dueling felt so fun and fluid with super satisfying clings and clangs from clashing swords accompanied by cartoony sounds from enemies stumbling into walls and down stairs.  The voice acting is by far some of the most entertaining i have heard. The dialogue from enemies is on point - especially when i could hear them talking as i left the room after giving them an ass whooping. Fun and charming!The game is quite short, but the quality of time spent is well worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: En Garde! creates a really fun duelling system and fully uses its comparably short gametime to the fullest to explore every inch of its mechanics.In the end it left me wanting for more levels, but I guess this is better than a game having too many levels and stretching out its time.There is some replay value with certain level-specific challenges and there is also the arena mode for pure action.The story and dialogue is quippy and clichée on purpose. It's at times forgettable but that just gets you back to the action faster. Story for no other reason but to get you to the next arena is okay!I for one, love my lesbian zorro.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game.  The swordplay is simple to understand and very satisfying to master. The environments are vibrant and colorful. The characters are witty and enjoyable. The arena mode provides some fun changes to the basic game play. I was all smiles through the whole game. I only have two main complaints:1.) I wish the game was longer! The story is pretty short (took me about 3 hours to beat the game) and that was disappointing because I just wanted to keep playing. 2.) The game is pretty linear, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, they kept the game tight and straightforward which I can appreciate, but there were a good handful of times I thought I stumbled upon a diverging path to be greeted with a dead end, the movement in the game is fun and I just wish there was a little more to explore using the swinging and platforming mechanics.  With that said if you're in the mood for a short, fun, swashbuckling adventure then I can't recommend the game enough. What's here is fantastic, I just wish there was more of it.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is beautiful, the setting charming and the art style very pretty.The game sells itself as having quick and snappy combat that heavily relies on parry mechanics, unfortunately it completely fails in this regard.Almost the entirety of the game is spent fighting large groups of enemies, all doing different attacks and many of them not being parry-able, so in reality the combat is actually just dodge rolling away from huge groups of enemies and running around in a circle until you can pick off one guy.rinse and repeat until combat over.It's incredibly disappointing because this game has so much potential, and I hope the Devs continue to make games of this style and hopefully improve upon their formula.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a little gem with a super polished and well thought out combat system and it reminded me of Sifu in a lot of ways.The focus is not on combos and lightning reflexes (although you need to react quite often) but more on strategically separating your enemies so you can fight them one at a time and the way you do that is one of the most original I've ever seen: you need to use the environment a lot to stun and "surprise" enemies. Stunning them of course leaves them out of combat for a while so you can focus on the others, while surprising means doing something "unexpected" around them, like somersaulting from a table, swinging from a rope, or throwing a bucket on someone near them. This will stop them for a brief moment while leaving them open to attacks.Unfortunately it's not very long and leaves you wanting for more. One of the reasons is because unlike Sifu, it has a very forgiving checkpoint system, so you can quickly finish the main story in less than 5 hours, without the need to learn and master every level (That's why I recommend playing it on hard difficulty, even though it can be tough until you get the hang of the mechanics). But I'm pretty sure I'll replay the story a few more times just for how fun it is, while trying to find all the secrets hidden inside the levels. It also has an arena mode in case you want some more challenge.Still, I really hope the developers get the success they deserve and will work on a dlc, a sequel or another game where they can expand on the mechanics they created, there's a lot of yet untapped potential here
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game and a surprise (4/5). It should be promoted more. A good old third person action-adventure game, and well made. I recommend it if, like me, you're looking for fun single-player games that don't take fifty or hundreds of hours to play, and quick to play.+ The Zorro theme is refreshing and engaging+ The story is classic but effective+ Accessible and easy to learn (Quick to play)+ Fighting is challenging and technical+ 5-7 hours long only+ Can be played in short sessions+ Graphics are nice and frame rate is stable and fast+ Sounds and musics are good too. And voice acting is funny+ Price+ No bugs+ No micro-transactions- Last boss is really tough. I had to finish the game being invincible. Last arenas are crazy too- Can feel repetitive towards the end- The classic of a 3rd person view: The camera and the fighting that can get messy when there are too many enemies around you

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely fantastic, especially for their first game. The Artistic style, voice acting, and general charm of this game is breathtaking at best, I laughed many times throughout this, it has such a childish humour charm to it in terms of how "Not" seriously it takes itself. It'd be like Pixar making a swashbuckling game, and this is the result, the combat too is fun, though late game it gets frustrating due to the varied enemy types added into the game.The combat feels like something similar to Sifu, though there's no combos, there's special moves, a very heavy emphasis on enemy prioritisation and using the environment to your advantage, throwing things at them, kicking them off ledges, or into objects for an instant knockout becomes vital lategame.It took me 3 and a half hours to finish the game on normal in one sitting, there's also an arena mode, and hard difficulty too.The bossfights which are in the game, are all incredibly enjoyable. The only thing I find disappointing is its length, I wish it were just a bit longer, maybe 5-6 hours? There's not much replayability other than difficulty and small collectable notes you can find on each level of which there are five, each taking roughly 40 minutes to beat. Overall a solid experience. Totally recommend, and can't wait for what might come next.Sidenote: Whoever's complaining about the protagonist being female, and/or into women...get a life, it's a quirky little game that doesn't even take itself seriously, so why should you?
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: At first when started playing, this game feels like a good light hearted action adventure indie game set in post renaissance europe but in the later stages of the game it took a turn into become somewhat a souls like game for it's combat, although I never played any souls like gane before.Why do I feel that way? Because the combat devolved into evading and rolling from attacks where you're outnumbered and that higher level enemies attacks practically have to be evaded while you wait for the opportunity tunstrike back or using the environments to weaken them or to make them slip in funny ways or outright make red painted barrels and ammo crates went boom (as if this was a 90s shooter game)... But mostly you'd be expected to dodge alot to survive just like in souls like games...But I enjoyed it and the game doesn't overstay the welcome (unless you died a lot), it's a short game, a souls like veterans can probably beat all the main content (including a roguelike arena mode) in about 5 hours of play time... Or at maximum 10 hours I guess...Performance is acceptable, it has 21:9 display support and I like that it has TSR anti aliasing option and not forcing us with TAA solution only.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: For me, this is one of the best indie games released this year. The art style is really cool. I loved the final map. The combat is fun and satisfying. The combat reminds me of Sekiro's deflect mechanism. It's pretty cool that you can use environmental items to fight enemies, like throwing buckets on an enemy's head to blind them for a few seconds so you can fight the others, etc. The jokes are actually funny and not cringey. The voice actors did an amazing job. The story is short but good. It's like watching an old cartoon. However, I do have a couple of cons to talk about. One would be adds during boss fights. Instead of giving the boss more complex moves, they just added more adds to make it harder. The only 1v1 boss fight is in chapter 3; the rest have adds. I had the same issue with Remnant 1, but at least in that game, there's a reason for it. The ads give you ammo in Remnant 1, so it was understandable. The second con is the lock-on mechanism. Sometimes the game locks onto the wrong enemy, which is kind of frustrating. But overall, I enjoyed the game. From a student project to a full release on Steam, congratulations to Fireplace Games.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish we could get more swashbuckling games, this genre is sorely under-represented. There is basically... Well, only this one. Sadly, I can't recommend it. I really love the idea, the concept, the visuals, the humour, and it runs flawlessly. But the controls ? They are absolutely horrible.I've tried with a gamepad as they recommend it, but it's just masochism. The camera is controled, as you can assume, by the right stick. But in combat, you need to parry or dodge all the time, so your thumb is pretty busy frantically pressing the buttons, meaning you have to trust the camera to auto-position itself. The problem is, you can't. Auto-camera is absolute ♥♥♥♥. You get stabbed in the back without even seeing the enemy, or stuck into an obstacle that you can't see. Also, there seems to be some major input lag, because I couldn't for the life or me time parries properly with a gamepad, an issue that I didn't have with the mouse and keyboard.After dying 10 times in a row to the same 3 guards in the same fight on the market , I switched to keyboard and mouse, and won first try. Well, first try where I actually thought about checking what key was used for dodge (dodging is vital, even more so than parrying)... So second try. The game plays VASTLY better with a keyboard and mouse. You can actually control the camera by moving the mouse, which removes most camera issues. Most, not all.Unfortunately the controls issue isn't limited to the camera. It's pretty cumbersome to switch targets. Since your charater is always facing someone, you can't move about freely during combat phases to easily reposition yourself. More often than not I ended kicking a crate into the wrong target, or into none at all. One would think that in a game about fencing footwork would have been a priority...Also, that's an issue with my own hardware, but I couldn't rebind kick and dodge to my mouse thumb buttons. Granted, my mouse is finicky and those buttons aren't considered buttons proper, they just replicate keyboard keys. I usually set them to numpad 0 and 1 and pretty much every game plays along. Not this one. I tried to use the actual keyboard keys they replicate to no avail either. Somehow, this game doesn't recognize numpad buttons. Not an issue for most people but in my case it means alter my mouse profile for one game, while every other games are fine with it. No, thanks.As for the control issues proper, I could switch on the auto-parry on, or even the invulnerability. I have no issue in playing in easy mode, but there are limits. I don't buy games to let them play themselves, mind you. There is no point in having a game that looks good, runs nice, has funny dialogs, if you're fighting the game itself more than the enemies within it.I've been gaming for a long time and this might be the first game for which I couldn't even be bothered to complete the tutorial. The controls are so bad, I was annoyed enough before even getting there.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very challenging. I haven't played a combat game in a while. but this is glorious. Even on normal, if you don't use all the skills given to you, you're going to have a very tough time. You need to be smart and resourceful if you want to win. The checkpoints for The Old Fortress needs to be fixed. Having two annoying enemies be able to dodge the environmentals and cover each other means dying is expected. Especially when they throw out an unblockable while the other attacks. Dying means you have to do parkour all the way back up from the bottom, which makes it going from alright to frustrating. A bad checkpoint changes the attitude of the player and can make them want to put the game down for the day.That one section has soured the game for me. I wish it was placed earlier in game so I would've had enough time to refund it, but the next best thing is uninstalling and deleting from my game library.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very good, although a little short in my opinion; However, taking into account that I purchased it at a 55% discount, it is more than justified. The combat system is simple but complies; If the game were (paradoxically) longer, it would become tedious. The music can quickly become repetitive, although it is well composed. The game requires that you combine all the techniques that you learn, you have to think of it as if it were Zorro, but with a confusion between French and Spanish. The game's writing is intentionally ridiculous and the plot is just an excuse for things to happen; In fact, one can perfectly play without paying attention to the plot  and the game will continue. The characters may fall a bit into one-dimensionality, but once again, this is a game about dancing with enemies. The controls are quite responsive, with my only criticism of them being the recovery time after dodging. Ultimately I give it a 7.5 out of 10. I would play it again and introduce it even to someone who is not an expert player. Very good work.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: It's upbeat Sekiro meets 3rd-person Dark Messiah!> parry, dodge & posture-bar? - check!> "adrenaline" bar for special attacks - check!> kicking barrels into people - check!> kicking people down stairs, into fires & off ledges - check!> throwing buckets on people's heads - check!> corny dialogue - absolutely, unabashedly, check!The combat has some teeth too - you aren't gonna button mash your way through this.It's fun! Tough - like Dark Messiah - it often ends up being more of a furniture brawl than a swordfight.The only gripe I have is that you can reliably beat the campaign in under 4h.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: A light-hearted adventure with lovely cartoon action. Combat involves properly responding to enemy attacks with parries and dodges, while keeping groups of enemies split up and disorganised. You'll throw buckets on soldiers' heads, kick barrels down stairs, throw lanterns at chests full of gunpowder. Your character has a bunch of quippy dialogue with everyone, and even defeated enemies will taunt you from the ground. The campaign is fairly short but Arena Mode is very replayable.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: A souls-like if souls games had training wheels for the entire duration of the game.Like Sekiro, but instead you had loving parents.Graphics, sound, gameplay, comedy, everything about the game is in the "good" realm.The only major issue is the duration, since the game has only 4 missions, and even going for 100% achievements is more of a repeat / loop gameplay then new content.Takes less then 3 hours to do the main story, about 10-20 hours to 100%.Would still recommend this game if you can grab it for a good price and / or want a very simple and easier souls-like - but satisfying - combat.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: This is indeed, a very fun experience. Wholesome characters, crispy sword fighting and an okay parry system, that rewards creativity and patience. I played in medium difficulty but i still found a little bit of challenge. There are collectibles and secondary objectives that can make you play a second time. I recommend this game 100%, support indie developers, this is one real nice game!
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: I've just finished this game, and on the whole it's pretty nice, even if it is a bit short. The combat mechanics are easy to pick up, but still quite satisfying, and the soundtrack is pretty good. The only problem I had with the game was the final boss, which I found far too easy and unimpressive.a good 7.5/10 that offers replay value via its arena mode and challenges
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: Do I hate it? No, not really. It has character and style, and maybe a portion of my problem came from this being played through on Hard from the start.This plays a little like the Batman Arkam games, mash attack, hit parry, hit dodge, you have instead a meter that is accrued over a combo meter. You have environmental elements instead of a belt full of gadgets, and platforming in a classical sense instead of the set rails and grapple points.As someone who played through and platinumed a few of the mentioned batman games, I fell right in the rhythm, especially since even on hard you still see the visual indicators for En Garde!'s enemies, so it became a great fit for me for the most part. The only difference advertised is damage is higher, and being someone who grew up with a lot of beat em ups from teenage years on up this was a stepsister to it.It took me two whole hours to reach and clear the second episode, the majority of that being spent on the finale's boss fight.The second chapter introduces Grenadiers, a ranged enemy that is... funny. They throw some timed projectiles that have a set timer when they land on the ground, and will harm everyone not just you. That is fantastic, fair and balanced. Usually they are positioned somewhere that the main mob will not reach so you can pick between hit and run, or taking out the grenadier immediately. Also enemies by default regenerate their current hitpoint bar (all but the lowest enemies have multiple pips to refill their bar, and there are intricacies to that), so hit and run is less viable with the somewhat awkward autolock.Grenadiers also have a simple evasive maneuver, they smokebomb and run, knocking you down and fleeing when you get near either once or on a very long timer. Usually a nonissue, but in some cases they can be in the same area as the enemy mob.So, combine that with the a flat boss arena without an area for grenadiers, a lot of enemies, and few ways to force your movement like the table slides and other acrobat points shown in promotional material, the fight becomes a slog with limited environmental obstacles and again a poorly explained autolock system that makes using area of effect tricks harder to trigger, especially early on when you have a strong single use and a weaker repeatable in range at just the wrong camera angle.With only four hits to your name on hard with enemies that by design, and a good design as it does push you to use the environment, wanting to attack in unison with multiple attack types (dodge or parry response), and the game will be hard even on a normal difficulty for casual players unless it has more than just raw damage tweaks that the menus mention.The skill ceiling is weirdly high for such a cartoonishly presented game that has the hallmarks of a good outlaw game in the same vein as pop culture icons as Zoro and Puss in Boots, for all of the minor bugs you can encounter and the frustrating arenas you'll wind up in.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: Update: I knuckled down and beat the game. The review remains the same; weak thumbs up. The later fights can be frustrating as hell but overall its decent. Its a shame that the fights don't live up to their potential. A few of the later ones are so easy because they are duels. You can cheese the mechanics (kicking Zaida off the wall over and over). While later fights are just a terrible, mind-numbing slog (the final battle with the Count Duke). You can't really fight anytime there is a large number of enemies around. So, you run, hit them with something from the environment, pick off one real fast, start running again and repeat.Original review:Overall, I give this a weak thumbs up. The setting is nice, the humor is cheesy and entertaining, the voice acting is good, the story is decent, but the gameplay just isn't that fun for me. While the gameplay has merit, I just don't like it very much. The game is short and, while I didn't beat it, I'm half way through and just can't do it anymore. Its a Souls-like with a candy coating. If that is your thing, you will like it. If you hate spending half of every fight running away to better position yourself, you will hate it.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this game for 16 hours I am still hearing new lines of in-fight dialog. The game doesn't need a billion forgettable enemy types to be enjoyed when they play with the humour this well. The combat doesn't have a steep learning curve and is very enjoyable once you get the hang of it but don't expect souls-like fighting, it's more like Batman but instead you can throw a cooked chicken on someones head and then shoot them with a cannon.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is charming, the sheer amount of banter and reactions (especially in arena mode, with situations that don't exist in the story - basically characters react to everything) is incredible and gives even the nameless opponents a lot of personality. The combat system encourages tricks, parries and dodges in a way that's about perfect for the genre it represents (getting surrounded is bad).
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: ----- SMALL UPDATE AFTER STORY COMPLETION -----Story's a bit short and it's alright, but as I mentioned in the initial review, I think the combat system takes the leading role in this game. The later stages forces you to "cheese" enemies a lot more, running around tables, tossing pots at them, playing all kinds of dirty. This kind of gameplay actually fits in very well with Adalia's character and the overall world view - you are a vigilante of sorts, and you are in the lair of your enemy with no one to help you, so you need to use everything around you to win.I look forward to replaying it completing all the side objectives as well as the arena mode!----- Original Review -----This is one of the games I have been looking forward to the most recently, and it did not disappoint!Full disclosure - I have not completed the game yet. Just two chapters in. I also play on Hard straight away.Where do I even begin with the good things?The combat is silky smooth, which is vital for a game like this. Parrying and dodging looks effortless, fitting the character background of the master swordswoman herself. A lot of these type of games put in hyperarmor or staggers just for the sake of difficulty with no connection to the enemies you face at all. However, in this game the armored enemies looks and feels armored, and the process of fatiguing the enemy fits perfectly into the combat (kicking them down the stairs, hurling buckets at them etc.).I am a huge Soulsbourne fan and I have to be honest, I took on the wrong approach when I just started the game, trying to stand there and just parry everything. It worked for a while but being stuck in a few big fights (yes looking at you especially, Count Duke) made me realise that running around kiting and making use the environment IS how the game meant to be played. Don't get me wrong, gank fights in early game is still quite difficult even if you play this way in Hard mode because 4 hits will kill you already.I then tried the Arena Mode, which is the "challenge mode" basically. This is a test of everything you've learned in the game about the combos of the enemies, guardbreaking, kiting and making use of the environment. This surely gives me something to grind for.The music is so fun to listen as well, brilliantly crafted and enhanced that the setting of the game. One of the things I am most impressed with is the dialogues from the enemies. Even if you are just swinging and jumping around the enemies, they will react to the things you do like "Stop doing acrobatics!" This adds a ton to the immersion. The story is lighthearted with quirky dialogues. This reminds me a lot about Disney cartoons, especially when enemies you defeated (supposedly killed?) lies on the ground and whispers something funny along the lines of "Is it over yet?", "Don't make a sound! She can't see us.", or "I am not getting paid enough for this."The only complaint I have right now, is that monologues often get cut off because the distance between one area to another is quite short if you're running all the time. Sometimes I have to stand still in front of a door just to finish listening to the monologue. It does disrupt the story immersion and enjoyment a bit, but it is nothing major.Overall, great fun and I highly recommend anyone who is looking for a new game to play to try it out! Now time for me to hop back in the game :)
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: Really solid and fun indie game that is 100% worth getting! En Garde has so much personality and joy in it, and you can tell how much the developers love the classic swashbuckling literature and historical figures that helped inspire this game. The dialogue and voice acting is snappy and funny and campy (affectionate), the music could not be more perfect, and the gameplay itself is engaging. If you're a fan of swashbuckling stories like the Three Musketeers, Zorro, Puss in Boots etc then you'll almost definitely like En Garde. I would also say that it's very family-friendly (no killing, no swearing, lots of heroic shenanigans).The swordplay does feel similar to Sekiro, since Adalia is super mobile and has to parry or dodge fairly quickly to beat enemies. But En Garde is more generous with its timings, and you have a lot of interactivity with your environment to help turn the tables on baddies-- throwing a bucket on someone's head and kicking them down some stairs are my favorites. There are 3 difficulty modes and accessibility options too (e.g. auto parry), so I think anybody could play this game and enjoy it.The main story mode took about 4~ hours for me on the normal difficulty, but I didn't find all the secrets or do all the challenges on every level, so it'd probably take about twice as long to do all of that. There's also an arena mode that you can play indefinitely if you just want to swash some buckles. But if you just want to play the story mode, the game is definitely still worth it to me.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: The game lacks some gameplay mechanics... you dodge, but you have 30 around you, you dodge one... if you press dodge again and not at the right time, you get hit by all of them... same if you are parrying, you only parry one, and even if you press at the right time for another one, sometimes it does not register, like if she had a 0.5 or less seconds cooldown... ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ disgusting, raging, tilting and everything you can think about... massive trashThe ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ camera... sometimes it ges so close that you cannot see around you, so you get hit if you do not move the camera continuously... and the parries... my god... either parry or die... the game lacks something else...Playing this on the hardest difficulty since the first run and it is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ abussing you, even if you are quick, you MUST know each new enemy what they will do... lacks a lot around battle...
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: It's short, REALLY short for it's full asking price. But looking past that, it's an absolutely gem of a game. Strikes a great tone of whimsy and adventure, with non stop chatter that doesn't get grating and has an amazing flow to the game play that I haven't felt anywhere else. Definitely worth it on sale, and might even be worth the full price despite the play time being only a few hours.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: This game's sense of humor is a treasure.Even if the game was awful and torturous to play (which couldn't be farther from the truth), the fact that characters regularly reference stuff like Monty Python and the Princess Bride while actively getting their ass handed to them is a reason to buy this game all on it's own.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant game. A 3rd person swashbuckling adventure that feels great to play and has a heavy focus on using the environment to maintain the upper hand in fights. This game looks jaw-droppingly beautiful, has a wonderful Puss-in-Boots like style and vibe with great music, and is filled with genuinely funny dialogue. I only wish there was more story content, as there are only 4 missions.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: When I first beat the game, I though it was too short. Then I realised I thought that because I wanted to keep playing.Luckily that's what the arena mode is for. So I can safely say that this gmes combat system is so fun that you want to keep playing even if you have nothing left to unlock.Now i play it every so often just for the fun of it. This game gets more fun the better you get at it.- Intrinsicly fun gameplay- Not punishing- Funny- Feather hat, rapier, swashbuckling duelist aestethic10/10
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: En Garde! is just about everything I could have asked for in a lighthearted swashbuckling adventure.  The gameplay is engaging, the characters and story endearing, and the complaints of defeated henchmen delicious.  I do wish there were more than four episodes in the game, but I definitely got my money's worth.  I hope the team decides to continue work on the property!
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be, that knows exactly the kind of experience it wants its players to have, and it cuts to the chase and makes it happen.It's a swashbuckling game, and it has all the highlights and antics that you'd want from the genre -- flashy swordplay, corny banter, feats of acrobatics, slapstick action, duels with your rival/archenemy/love interest/partner in crime.  It's got it all.Where the game can falter a bit is how it manages the chaos. You'll find yourself going up against hordes of combatants, and, sometimes, you'll happen to forge a perfect path through the battlefield and use your environment in just the right ways to steamroll the encounter.  Other times, you get cornered, and, when you get cornered, it can be a huge pain to get out.  Enemies will *glue* themselves to you, hyper-extending their swings to make sure that you can't just get away and regain your footing.  It can drag down the fun in an otherwise delightful experience.I don't want the above point to undermine what a blast this game was.  It's fast-paced, it's exciting, and it's wonderfully silly.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: after reading a lot of the negative reviews I have come to the conclusion that there is a skill issue. you cant play this like dark souls. you need to throw objects, kick boxes and barrels, kite enemies into explosives, do acrobatics, and knock enemies into walls and objects, to stun them, knock them over, break their guard, etc. if you rely solely on attack/dodge/parry you WILL lose.*kicks an explosive barrel at you*
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game, took me under 4 hours but was a very enjoyable time. Not perfect though think my major gripe with it is that I wish they'd done more mechanically with the bosses most of them just send in waves of mobs which made them mostly feel samey.There is definitely replay value too with challenges and secrets in the levels to do/find and an arena mode
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting forever for someone to make a game like this!!!! Its a fantastic sword fighting game that makes references to all the greats like Zorro and Princess Bride, its super cheesy and funny too. Really great combat mechanics, slick animation, fantastic art direction. It amazes me that someone hasn't made a love letter to fencing like this until now. If you like sword fighting this game is for you. The combat has a bit more depth than most fighting games, which is fantastic considering its a 20 dollar game. It has a focus on getting enemies singled out in group combat so you can 'duel' them, using parries to break their guard, to get that to happen you've gotta use a lot of dodging, kicking, and environmental attacks. It reminds me a lot of the barracks fight in The Mask of Zorro! This is a unique and fantastic game, and I think anyone who likes swords should pick it up.
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review: Short, sweet and swashing buckles!Clearly made by people who love the swashbuckling genre, and the use of the environment makes it feel alive in a way that similar games don't. It lacks polish in a few areas and it's pretty short, but it's cute fun, and surprisingly tough in parts; I always felt like I had to really fight, not just rely on a few standard tactics.Come for the swordplay, stay for throwing buckets on enemy heads and kicking them into fountains, and laugh at finding references to favorite swashbuckling stories! (''States and Nations of the Moon' by Monsieur de Bergerac' made my night!)
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

_childDocuments_.review:
From the forgotten pages of history, comes Adalia de Volador! Legendary swashbuckler. Dashing adventurer. Hero of the people. Play as Adalia in her daring escapades full of sword-fighting, satire and shenanigans. Challenge the cruel Count-Duke and oppose tyranny with panache! Beautifully painted locations, charismatic characters, and an astounding amount of battle banter will transport you to the golden age of swashbuckling comedy!

So, sharpen your sword, grab your boots and hat, and embark on a hilarious, action-packed spectacle!
_childDocuments_.name: En Garde!

name: Hero's Hour
detailed_description: ➡️ Sweet home for strategy lovers About the Game Hero's Hour is an accessible, yet-deep and content-rich Strategy Roleplaying Game. Take control of your hero, explore the world, build up your town, fight fast-paced battles, level up your hero and amass an army large enough to take out the opponents - before they take you out. Turn Based + Real Time While exploring the overworld and developing your town and army are both turn-based, giving you time to think and plan out your next moves, in battles your units will do the best to fight for themselves in real time - all hundreds of them. Cast spells and give attack orders to swing the tide of battle - or just sit back and watch as your might unfolds. Procedural Generation Hero's Hour brings impactful procedural generation to the strategy game formula, ensuring that every time you play, there will be new areas to explore and strange buildings to enhance your hero or army. Seek out obelisks to start you on small procedural quests that send you around the world. You won't even be able to use the same build order each time you play the same faction. Features 11 factions with special mechanics, strengths and weaknesses 22 hero classes, with a special skill each 50 common hero skills 177 units (and 99 upgraded units) 80 unique unit abilities 166 artifacts 83 spells (+18 spells unlocked via skills) Dozens of impactful map buildings Local 'hotseat' multiplayer Co-op with other players or even with the AI Being on the faster side compared to other turn based strategy games, you may even be able to finish the hotseat games that you start!

It's a good recreation of what its trying to emulate and the only major downside aside from a few crashes has been the fair bit of imbalance of some factions. But that's pretty easily resolvable by not including those factions! There's tons so it's really a fun game for the price

It's a great concept and it does some things really well but it crashes, it lags, the combat is boring, the UI is not the best and many other things. _childDocuments_.review: It's fun. Surprisingly fun. The first time I grabbed the demo, I'd never played a Heroes of Might and Magic game, or any other games like it. Then, months later, I play HoMM3 and like it well enough. I come back to this and... oh. This is really good, actually. Now that I understand it, it's great.If you have never played a HoMMlike before, this might seem overly complex and confusing at first, but give it time and you'll have a really interesting game that rewards careful planning and strategy. It's fun! Now, if only there was real netplay...
_childDocuments_.name: Hero's Hour

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, similar to Heroes of Might and Magic. It has many pros, but also a few cons which are fairly major and make the game hard to play past ~10 hours. Overall verdict = 6/10. Pros:- Easy to get started and learn game mechanics- Fun/cute graphics- Lots of different factions, heroes, units and spells to discover- Many different skirmish maps to choose fromCons - the really bad ones:- The game lags and chokes hardcore - On medium+ map, if you have discovered > 50% of the map, everything starts to slow down- In late game, if you have large armies, fights will slow down and can take an excruciating long time to end==> The devs really need to upgrade the engine AND allow to skip / auto-resolve battlesCons - the not so bad ones:- No campaign mode- Game lacks an easy to consult info, such as character stats, unit stats, army strength (there are ways to get that info, but it's not intuitive and kind of painful to navigate; if you love tracking stats in games, then you'll be very disappointed)- Music is super repetitive and just not very goodOverall would recommend for a bit of fun, but all the add-ons are useless for now imo, given there is very little incentive to discover new maps and grow new armies considering everything will slow down and your game will basically become unplayable. If the devs fixed this massive engine issue, and added features to better track stats, I think it would make this game stellar and highly replayable. As-is, it just isn't.

_childDocuments_.review: Game has some fun features and is very clearly inspired by the Heroes of Might & Magic games.However after playing a single scenario for 4 hours there are definitely some issues that need to be addressed to make this game more fun for the players.1. It's clear that the AI blatantly cheats to artificially make the game harder, no matter what difficulty you set it on. I had numerous times where I would engage the enemy AI, and the game would tell me the battle against them would be "Easy", stating that my army power was much, much higher than theirs. And when in battle, the victory bar on the top would show my army at 80-90% win chance.Once the battle started my forces would start out strong against theirs. Then after killing most of them, the AI would pull out a handful of units from nowhere that proceed to blow through all my units. Even my strongest units that clearly should be able to handle them (things like my elite troops that were Power 25 or 30+ being decimated by their 10-15+ power units). I would then proceed to lose the battle, and the AI would run around claiming all my buildings before running back up to their base and INSTANTANEOUSLY refilling their army back to the same units they had before.2. How are the AI able to instantly refill all their lost units and add new units before the week is up? Again, there were multiple instances in my game where I would stomp through some of the smaller AI heroes (only had 20-50 small units), and within 1 turn they would already be back running around with the same, or even more units than what they had before. I get they probably had the Field Hospital upgrades for some units, but they usually always refill 100% of the missing units, or more. If the player is limited by the units they can acquire each week, why does it feel like the AI gets to "cheat" again and just buy units whenever it wants?The real-time auto combat is fun, however it's  barebones and needs some big QOL improvements to really make it shine.1. The ability to choose what units you add to the field needs to be tweaked. Having a limit to how many units you can have out before you throw some in the Reserves is nice, but it needs to be indicated clearer how many "points" each unit takes up on the field count. I found myself doing lots of guessing and trial and error when attempting to switch out units from what the game "auto picks".2. The UI needs to be updated to make it easier to select and choose what units you want to add to the field. Trying to add X amount of units from a group of 100+ is really time consuming when you have to split them individually on the troop UI and add them to the field ()3. Auto combat is nice, but there needs to be a way to target specific units. Currently you can tell units on the field an area you want them to go towards, but that's all they'll do. Say the enemy has a strong unit that you want your units to swarm and focus on to bring down. Currently you could select your units and move them over that way, however they'll just choose to fight whatever they feel like and ignore the unit you really want to bring down. Having a way to tell the units "hey, attack this please" would make it a bit more bearable during fights instead of watching your units ignore the strong one that's just ripping through them.Overall there's a lot here for a great game, but in its current state I'd suggest holding off until there's some Quality of Life changes to how the AI and combat functions. It currently gets too frustrating seeing how broken the AI gets, and how the game lets them cheat to win fights and come back from a loss so quickly when you're limited to restocking troops once a week.

_childDocuments_.review: An okay game but there is very little to no actual AI since it relies on being gifted free units around 100-200 that is impossible to build which is easy to see since if they were playing by the same rules as the player they wouldn't be able to gain 100+ archers plus several other units from just a single city with no outposts generating supplies. There are also issues with the map generation giving some players very weak starts that pretty much guarantee loses with 120+ units per stack while other players have weakly defended unit generation outposts and easy to beat neutrals overall (low tier, low quantity) allowing faster growth/boom. You are ultimately forced to focus on one unit stack waiting for the ai to leave its city undefended (which it frequently does) and take it causing it to become confused on priorities allowing you to use its suspiciously max developed city to destroy its retreating armies than after that you pretty much win the map.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR: Bought on sale . A fun turn-based/action HoMM3-like. Best for local multiplayer and quick games, as it's not without it's problems and a fair share of bugs. Loving 16 bit art style and super nice details. This is great product that needs some polish and redrafting still, With this low price it's a bargain and I will be grabbing the DLC too, but I also kinda feel like somethings could be better now or in a future sequel. Optional turn based combat style would be cool for example.Long story: Had the 1.6.0 Demo for two years on a HDD I loved to toy around from time to time but forgot to invest in. Surprisingly latest version that I bought remembered all the achievements I got. There are surprisingly many improvements and additions since that but even with added content the optimization issues.-  The game has some severe optimization issues with high unit and resource counts that drops the frame rate down and stuttering in both in over world and in combat which is the worst general thing about the game. Noticeably improved between old version and new. Usually this doesn't come into play on normal games but I like to test features and the games AI to see how it reacts. Still, I recommend Oligarchy skill and using anything that can drop unit and unit type counts in favor of Swarming and tactics, as well as fielding less than 10 heroes. I wish there was more options for the graphics and turning off idle animations. - The AI is kinda clever and dumb at the same time, it can for sure spot out a weak stronghold of yours half way across the map and aim at it but it can also get into non-accomplishing loops like sailing back and forth, sending a hero with less and less units every week on the same spot if it's naval access is locked. It can be unfair seeming even in Normal difficulty if it gets a optimal roll, usually with early diplomacy rush but most often it doesn't understand the value of protecting it's own base so they are generally easy to win on a war of attrition and sneaking bases from under them.-Skills are somewhat unbalanced and some are broken OP or just trash Bodyguards is the best all purpose skill, Imagination combined with Learning is the most powerful combo in the game if you are lucky, Devour is magnificently over powered with any skill combination that produces units. and for a HOMM3 type game that's expected, in the meanwhile..  Masonry is basically a complete waste of points and less useful than skills spawning in a rogue army like Dwarven guard or Wild fire - I don't see how sitting around any mount of turns would benefit the player if you block only square. Spatial rift is unreasonably UP for any normal game play as it's so its even more situational. - (edited out a segment regarding Hunting skill after I realized how much money you can make by selling the unwanted items from it, it's still tedious but unsatisfactory on high levels as it eats movement points but it's not exactly broken).As it is so long since the release these are unlikely to be fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: Hero's Hour is a surprisingly fun game ...with some room for improvement. It's been almost 20 years since I've really enjoyed a game like this. Heroes of Might and Magic III in 1999 and HOMM V Tribes of the East in 2007 were good... it's been a sad decline since then for this style of game, until now.The good:1. Variety: Many races, unique heroes, units with upgrades and variants, lots of spells, artifacts and builds to experience.2. Relatively simple real-time auto-battle combat:Small high-stakes battles where positioning, orders and terrain matters vs massive battles that fill the screen with hordes of units slamming into each other while you drop comets down on the enemy side (and sometimes your own) blasting huge holes in their formation and flinging units into the stratosphere (feels powerful).3. Game in active development, with a massive overhaul currently in the testing branch (both old and new versions are good)4. Stable (no crashes for me), has autosaves each turn if you make a big mistake.In games like this I always try necromancers first. if you want to raise an undead army you can:1. Use a might-based Decay hero that raises permanent undead with their weak attacks (meh), and some temporary skeletons whenever they die in battle (hero's respawn in battle after a while), 2. Use a magic-based Decay hero that marks enemy units for conversion after their death with every spell cast (super powerful if you cast the right spells and mark all enemy units), 3. Use a special conversion spell (with 2-day cooldown) to instantly kill and raise enemy units (weak at low spellpower, instant win at high enough spellpower), 4. Necromancy skill to spend mana after battle to raise specific units (actually the least impressive, but you can drain them for mana instead), this works differently for living heroes, 5. Take living units and convert them in a Decay city,6. Merge weaker undead into stronger forms, 7. Take a hero and their entire army and converting the hero via a special map building.8. Recruit undead units in a Decay town,9. Passively gain the undead units that each hero specialises in, with bodyguards of that unit type and skills to convert other units into that unit or make that unit stronger in some way (adds a bit of flavour to each hero)...plus temporary summons like skeleton archers in battle, spells to make corpses rise again or explode etc.I think that's a decent amount of variety... although necromancy is only one of about 6+ ways of ending each battle with more units than you started with, and not always the strongest of those options (there's also Creation, Elemental skills, Mind-control, Diplomacy, Demonology... and more).The Bad:1. Lack of balance (some spells, skills, buildings and artifacts are vastly stronger than others)Creation of units for free or with mana is powerful. e.g. Mesmer's artifact set makes temporary summons permanent (convert all your mana into units) while another artifact set only gives you an extra unit each week.Sacrificing unit power for hero stats is powerful. e.g. The Wizard's tower building sacrifices troops for spellpower, knowledge and experience (each week!) so you can have enough magical power you don't need the army you just sacrificed and the extra mana can be used in several different ways to get new units after every battle. Devour skill does the same but converting excess units into attack and defence instead....so the balance isn't perfect, but finding different ways making each hero powerful enough to beat what looks like a superior army is a large part of what makes the game fun. Some combinations are just a little too overpowered and easy to achieve.2. Needs more music tracks (The current music sticks in my head for hours after playing...)3. Battles slow down when too many units are on screen....Only some of your units enter battle while the rest is in reserves (game runs fine) but there's nothing stopping you from using spells to keep summoning hordes of temporary units that fill the screen and slow the battle to a crawl.TLDR:A good game, Lots of content.Would benefit from more work on balance (especially magic spells and summoning).Fun despite the balance issues.(Oh and if you read the negative review about troops standing still doing nothing... there's a defend button that makes your troops stand still instead of moving forwards... the reviewer probably pressed that and didn't know what they had done because combat is normally quite hands-off with units moving and attacking on their own.)

_childDocuments_.review: My review would be neutral, but more on the negative side of it, and here's why. I really just wanted to test this game out, because I'm more of a strategy game player myself. And looking into this game, showcasing some Heroes of Might and Magic tactical with some RTS features, I thought I needed to give it a try.I don't think 2h was enough to test it out, but here I am at 4h and :- I think it's a refreshing game by its design, new items, new factions, etc... it's a good change from old HOMM, even though the similarities are numerous..BUT- AI: It's clearly mentioned that the AI is cheating. I simply played a large map with 3 players (2AI). One was done by week 4, the other one, even though I'm currently stealing all of his resources generators, just popped up an "Impossible" army outside of his castle, although I have 2 heroes level 15+, and last time I checked, I could have taken his castle for easy- The RTS component is clearly gross. Besides macro actions such as Attack, Defend, Flee, there isn't much to actually do on the battlefield. You can move units, but only in chunks depending how close they are. You can't really move the units you want to move. - Moving those units will just make them move. _childDocuments_.review: Twenty-some years ago, I was in the right place at the right time to play the absolute hell out of the Heroes of Might and Magic III demo. Limited funds, lots of time, and a bright-eyed and endless hunger for what might lie around the next corner. "What if I really leaned into the ballista? Wow that's a huge stack of troglodytes... could I get one of those?"And now I am older and this is grounds for the very same. From town building to heroes, even down to the resources chosen, this is all quite familiar. But despite falling into some of the less-exciting patterns of its ancestor, it manages to inject just enough new spin to reignite my curiosity once again. Core to this is the choice to make the battle system real-time, with each individual unit acting for themselves. At first blush it seems chaotic— mash the guys into each other until the bigger stack wins— but the more time I spent with it the more I realized every unit was a specific piece I could set just so as to harness their unique properties, and lead my army into outperforming what simple numbers would suggest. It's a little like Total War in that way, though the unit abilities far outrange that series in terms of creativity.It's that creativity that takes this game above its shortcomings. Every time I feel the late game get a little bit rote, or tire of a particular style of army, I need only choose a new faction or just another hero to crack open the horizon yet again. I want more things like this. Familiar ideas taken and run off into the deep distance with wild abandon. The personal passion evident in handcrafting these hundreds of little digital figurines, now offered to me in a big ol' bag of possibilities? It feels good.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like Hero’s Hour. Hero's Hour is an Indie Love Letter to Heroes of Might & Magic.It is a Pixel Art Turn Based Strategy game, with a Real Time with Pause Battle System! It’s like Heroes of Might & Magic, but even Faster Playing, and with Procedural Generation! OMG Awesome!Hero’s Hour has 12 different Factions: Order, Arcane, Nature, Decay, Pyre (Inferno), Horde, Enclave, Earthen (Dwarfs), Lament, Tide, Pillar and the newest: Delirium! And they all play differently! 🤯 Wow! So many to pick! Which Shall You Choose!?Pick your FactionUpgrade your chosen townsLvl Up & Choose talents for your HeroesSpecialize to produce the Units & Resources you wantAdventure away!All will Taste the Terror of the Tides!Or the Oppression of Order, or the ironclad Earnestness of the Earthen! It’s your World, you choose!So Lvl Up your Heroes! Cast Spells in combat! Recruit your Troops, and direct them in battle to seize strategic control of resources on the map, like mines, mills, and enemy Towns. Take It All to establish the Dominance of your chosen faction! You Can Do This Hero!I should mention that Hero’s Hour even offers local Hotseat multiplayer for those so inclined! It’s a family friendly, party friendly, friend friendly co-op gaming experience! Awesome! The little ones will learn our ways!This may ruffle some feathers, but it must be said, as the amount of tactical depth present in the battlefield here deserves a callout; Hero’s Hour is no mere Heroes of Might and Magic 3 clone!I’d say Hero’s Hour has more tactical depth than HOMM 3, due to the fact that each individual unit is rendered and physically present on the battlefield.Unlike HOMM 3, there is no representing 100 units with 1 tier one unit, and another grouping of 1 represented as the same, and somehow taking up EXACTLY as much space.There is also no very game-ie and cheese-ie tactic of always filling all 7 army slots, and usually many of them with 1 stacks; taking advantage of the VERY non-tactical design decision of representing all units, regardless of how many there are, as equals on the board, with only their numbers and values being different.You can also group or separate units of non similar types in Hero’s Hour, something that is bluntly not possible in HOMM 3. So, I can mesh different groups of infantry in 1 block, setting up my own custom forces to handle a specific threat.And that is not even touching the massive roster of units available, and how each ability they have can radically change what you want to field against it, as I do NOT want my big, red, expensive dragon anywhere near a unit with slayer, which deal a % of an elite units hp each round. I instead, want my dragon held in reserve, after my arrow fodder, lower tier infantry tie up and distract the dragon slayers, letting me feel confident to unleash the red hell upon the enemy archers.Or I could try to nuke the slayers down with magic, or snare them. Or try to kite them around a bit. And that is 1 ability. I believe there are over 100! There are also the currently 77 hero skills, (probably even more now) which massively change things as well!And you do have control over your units in Hero’s Hour: they follow your standing orders to attack or stand ground and defend. And you can command specific groups to advance, while others hold, setting up a flanking maneuver to hit a group from both sides, or attempt to kite a slower group of units with ranged, or distract the enemy infantry, and rush down their archers, which tend to be trash in melee.I will not say Hero’s Hour is better than HOMM 3, as rose-colored glasses, and existing time investments can cloud both vision and perspective, but Hero’s Hour is an Extremely Tactical, fast playing Strategy game with Procedurally Generated Maps, that will EASILY give you hundreds of hours of enjoyment, maybe thousands.If a turn-based, retro indie Strategy Heroes like, with a Real Time with Pause Battle System appeals to you, get it; there’s even a free demo off the itch site if you want a bit of a try before you buy.If you have fond memories of Heroes of Might and Magic 2 or 3, get it now, seriously!Who shall Reign Supreme in this High Fantasy Turnbased, Tactical Adventure?! Shall I Reign Supreme in this High Fantasy World?Shall you Watch?

_childDocuments_.review: Hero's Hour is a ripoff of Heroes of Might and Magic that somehow has worse graphics despite being many years more recent.  There's a very basic rule in game development, a fundamental law... if you are going to rip off someone else's game, if you want people to take you seriously, you have to do  than the game you are ripping off.  Otherwise you're just polluting Steam and making the average quality of all games just a bit worse.  And the pricing... holy crap.  More on that later. There's some depth in the gameplay, lipstick most certainly has been applied to the pig here, but it's not notably superior to HOMM, and it's coupled with some really cringey, badly done pixel "art"... and again, you know, if a developer is trying to achieve a retro pixel look, it should actually resemble games of a specific era that they're ripping off.  Instead, the art here just looks bad, but also unlike old games where the developers didn't have a choice.  It looks badly done, almost on purpose, but we all know developers don't deliberately set out to fail, do they?  Ok, on with the stock set of other reasons this particular game isn't worth buying:From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.Some of the defects in the game can be attributed to the choice of using the GameMaker Studio construction kit/toolset.  This is a very poor quality toolset favoured by amateur developers as it's cheap and requires little in the way of development skill, but unfortunately has very limited capabilities.  Just as you can't make a silk purse out of a sows ear, you can't make a great video game if you use a terrible engine.  GameMaker Studio is most commonly used to make retro pixel shovelware and cash grabs.A strong argument can be made that construction kits like GameMaker Studio should never be used to make games for profit, as the "developer", Benjamin "ThingOnItsOwn" Hauer has done here.  These construction kits are intended to teach people some of the basic principles of game development, and to make small demos to pass around with friends.  They're not intended to replace to actual work of real, professional game developers.  So it's inappropriate when amateurs try to use these for profit, without any actual, real game development effort taking place.  This doesn't result in products that have any real meaningful value for gamers.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Hero's Hour has the eye watering price of $18 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  This is more expensive than any of the HOMM games that this is an inferior ripoff of!!!  You can get Red Dead Redemption 2, the Mass Effect Trilogy, The Witcher 3... those are all CHEAPER than this garbage!!!  Jesus wept.This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  Just play one of the Heroes of Might and Magic games instead, they're cheaper than this but also better in all respects.

In looking into the community, I found way more guides detailing how to exploit the game in order to win, rather than any effective strategy to overcome the odds. The game could almost be called a rouge-like (or lite), except it doesn't have the decency of including any progression outside the main game letting you slowly build in power as you slowly build skill in game play. If you don't mind buying a game and getting your ass kicked by an impossible size army out of no where, on easy, in a 4 player vs. map, before you can actually build enough strength to even leave your starting territory (game after game after game), then this might be for you, but i've never played a game so poorly balanced that you can literally be wiped out during the tutorial before you can even finish (not part of the tutorial, there's nothing to explain or teach about defeat built into the tutorial, it's not scripted, it's just that poorly built and unbalanced that you can be randomly wiped before the game FINISHES teaching you how to actually play it). Certainly not worth the price being asked for, or a second glance. Maybe if you got a bunch of mods to fair it up or make it fun to play, this might be ok, but at that point if you have load up a bunch of major mods to make it fun then you might as well just make your own game.

_childDocuments_.review: Heroes' Hour gives you all kinds of fun toys to play with: a dozenish factions, a few hundred units, all sorts of heroes, spells, talent trees, artifacts, faction mechanics, and more. You can get a few hours of fun just out of exploring each factions' binary choices - Might hero or Magic hero, unit upgrade 1 or 2 - and several more out of optimizing that.Unfortunately, you'll rapidly begin to notice some problems: The maps all seem  same-y, and the AI always seems to try to rush you. If you beat that rush and push back, you win. Most games are decided in 20-30 turns, with the rest being cleanup.Congratulations, you've found what's wrong with Heroes' Hour: while there's a wide variety of toys to play with, you'll mostly be doing so on a very familiar map against a mysteriously similar opponent you will use the same strategy to defeat. Every match ends up feeling the same, even if you play with different toys.Here's why that happens: the map generator does a terrible job generating variety in its nodes/biomes, and the AI cheats - just not in the way you think.The AI is accused of cheating quite a bit. The truth is, on Normal difficulty the AI is actually at an economic  compared to you. At Challenging, it's on equal footing. Higher and it starts to get bonuses. Where the AI cheats on every difficulty is : the AI is maphacking. It doesn't actually have to do any exploration whatsoever to find resources or your base. So you'll watch the AI level up a bit, flag many of its starter mines, then immediately beeline to the gold mine in the nearest neutral node and flag it. It repeats this until it happens to wander into a neutral node you're exploring, and suddenly it's week 3 and the AI is on your doorstep with an army that's fought a minimal number of combats.When this happens every game, there's only so much time before just playing with the toys isn't enough to hold your interest. This game  needs an AI rework. All AIs cheat - they're finite state machines versus a creative human - so "good AI" is just a matter of how obvious their cheating is and whether that cheating leads to a better or worse game. HH's is very, very obvious and leads to a worse game, thus it's really bad.After that, the node map generator needs a "complexity" setting. Nodes are very plain, basic, and predictable, mostly being guided tours along a road which almost everything can be seen from. Every node is connected via a road and a guard post. Where are the no-road connections, or no guard posts? Some of these options are buried in the cryptic editor, but few players are going to dive into that mess just to make a more interesting nodemap. These need to be options at match creation, not buried in nodemap editing.

_childDocuments_.review: Hero's Hour is a lot of fun. It plays like games such as Heroes Of Might And Magic with some differences.Firstly, the graphics are vastly toned down from the aforementioned game...not that that detracts from the experience, of course. The graphics make the game charming, in their own way.Secondly, the fights you come across take on an auto battler format. You can cast spells or choose whether to be attacking or defensive, but you are otherwise in the hands of the fates. You will get an easy, moderate, hard or impossible information tag at each battle site to help you. Chances are you'll win all the easy battles but they still do vary in strength. I have gone in to easy battles and lost way more troops than I expected to. I suspect it has much to do with the type of troops you face.And this is something I love about the game. There are so many different types of troop and this is mainly because there are so many race types to play. The depth of choice in this game really is fantastic.I love the amount of battles you can face. You'll start in an almost enclosed little area near your city where you'll battle to collect resource mines and to boost your armies. Then you'll slowly spread out to meet stronger enemies and eventually the AI opponents. The game is a sort of skirmish format with a set number of AI enemies. I've not actually met an AI yet (on smallest map size) but I've enjoyed the game so far still.I do love the amount of enemy types I've faced and I love the fact that new armies spawn across the map. There will always be something to fight.Each hero you own levels up and can pick from a good number of skills to improve their ability in battle. There are also spells and I'm dead impressed with the variety of skills and spells. I've had 5 or 6 heroes in my times so far playing this game and each has been so different. My first hero was able to recruit many new troop types after battles and my latest does a lot more damage whilst summoning elementals all over the fight maps. I'm really keen to see all the skills.There is one thing I've not liked so much up till now. In my first run I got so many troop types that it made it tough to organise things. When you have a lot of troops it squeezes the bar up. Add to this that the UI interface for your troops is not fullscreen and it can be a bit of a nuisance organising a lot of troops.What I do like in this regard is that when you do have a big army you don't go in to the battle with all your troops. Some will stay back as reserves that you can send in to battle at set intervals. I haven't done the tutorials (I'm gung ho, man) but I am sure there is a strategy to organising your armies and setting reserves so that you send just the right type of troop in to battle to change the course of war. I've had moments where my new troops arrive and I suddenly start destroying the enemy. I may be wrong. It is something I'll have to look in to.I just like the reserves mechanic though.Overall, I am just very impressed with the game. This is no early access title either. It's a full release and it's really rather cheap for the incredible amount of gameplay you get.Don't be put off by the graphics. It's really quite a pleasant experience to watch your troops battle it out in pixellated form.Thoroughly recommended game if you like your turn based strategy games.
