_childDocuments_.review: A very good strategy game. It asks you to not think too hard about the finer details, which is something I can appreciate. The autobattle system is a very welcome addition to the genre, battles are quick and fun to watch. Not to mention there's actually a great deal of strategy that goes into unit placement and movement. The fast paced nature of the game as a whole is a breath of fresh air for the genre and I believe it's the best one I've seen so far. People who enjoy a very calculated combat system where you control everything won't like this one though.The campaign map is very random, and runs almost feel like roguelikes at times with how much a lucky or unlucky streak can completely affect the game's outcome. Although it can be frustrating, it improves replayability. This is totally fine in a PvE game but it suffers in the PvP.The art is very cool and varied, I love this style of pixel art. It does exactly the job it needs to do, and it compliments well the craziness of creatures flying all over the place and dying in droves. The main draw for me is the variety in strategies and setups you can go for. Although some heroes, factions and strategies are WAY stronger than others, it's still fun to try out all kinds of different ways to play that actually have a different feel.As for improvements that need to be made, I hope they refine the quality of life side of things, it needs some work. For instance, placing units on the field at battle start is a real pain if you want a specific formation. It basically asks you to not care about it but some strategies rely a lot more on positioning than others, like Order's Rally ability which gives your hero an aura buff. The clunkiness of placement and unit control in combat is quite a detriment to the enjoyment of a strategy like that. So there's a sort of disconnect between the game's mechanics saying "Hey just sit back and enjoy the chaos" and "You need to have good positioning to be effective". Horde is a big offender of this and needs a lot of work for the faction to feel good as a whole. As stated before, the game is very unbalanced. They recently did an update that nerfed certain things like mysticism, but there is overall a big gap in power. I hope they keep introducing more updates in the future. However, the most recent update introduced crashes so I hope that gets fixed soon. This game is completely unsuited for serious PvP because of the unbalance, and the intense randomness. I think that's an issue because multiplayer is a big way I think this game could go further and get more playtime. If they wanted PvP to become good, they would need a lot of balancing as well as mirror maps, and probably some other adjustments to randomness and such.In addition, the hotseat function is pretty terrible. It would be nice to have some proper networking. Until then I can't see it taking off at all. Still, the singleplayer mode is good enough.In conclusion, it's a rather fun game. It still needs a lot of work, but I believe in it from the small time I spent playing it and I certainly got my 20$ worth. The Hardcore+ difficulty is a fun challenge, I like small duel maps where the games don't last long, because a longer game could see you waste time on an unlucky run. But as long as you know the way you enjoy the game, it can be a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: From my experience, Hero's Hour is an immensely enjoyable game. However, where it severely lacks is the finicky combat. Most of the time it runs rather smoothly and your units do exactly what they're told to do - But there's those times, often at very crucial parts, where they outright refuse to listen. They get stuck on terrain despite being placed nowhere near it, they stand in place doing absolutely nothing and sometimes they outright refuse to retreat, or do so at a snails pace.For example, I was besieging an enemies base after an absolute stomp of a match - It should have ended there and then, especially when my catapult took out their walls. I charged in and .. They refused to enter, they just stood there for, and I'm not exaggerating, five whole minutes getting picked off. At this point, I cast Swift Retreat which went about as well as you would think. Sure, they turned but that was about it. I spammed clicked FLEE FLEE FLEE .. But it was too late as half my army as already dead.Again, great game, but it's going to give me an aneurysm if it doesn't start making sense.

_childDocuments_.review: I can see how this game has a very positive review from the people that purchased it thus far. Pros:- It's got a huge number of units, lords and factions- It's colorful and cute and the graphics are pretty decent- It's ticking all the Heroes of Might and Magic / Disciples / Age of Wonders boxes, which is a painful genre to be a fan of at the moment. Age of Wonders, arguably the best on this list, came out years ago. The new Disciples is not well reviewed and Heroes hasn't released anything in yearsBut there are cons to the new things and issues with the bloat, call these lesser cons:- Autobattler is fine, and I think if I knew the (8 billion) units well enough it would be easier to control the battlefield, but that is exactly the problem. Rather than being a strategic battle where you direct troop and apply spells, really the only control you have is setting up where your troops start and spamming as many spells as you can at the enemy. All the choices you needed to make were on the strategic map with army composition and picking your fights. This feature is actually working against the other pros of the game at the moment and exacerbating the...- Balance issues. Honestly I don't care about this, I prefer the huge variety over the illusion (and often fleeting state) of parity. You don't get asymmetry without a little imbalance. I think this will get ironed out over time should the team continue working on it post launch, but this isn't early access and its sold very few copies, so buyer beware. I think this will turn off plenty of people who don't want to beta test factions.Then there is the absolutely WILDLY poor decisions (and things I will not change my review to positive until fixed):- 3 saves per game... Honestly I would say this smacks of "mobile" games, but with a 2 gig install size (for what exactly?) I can't imagine it's going on a phone- WAY TO MUCH reliance on RNG, and I would have never expected that. Yes Heroes had a map gen, but it really didn't create the best experience. I've had starts I just walk away from and that shouldn't happen. Additionally, and most confusing of all, it seems the building requirements have some RNG component? I've had a building required for another in one game for it to not be the next. There is absolutely no reason for this. It adds nothing. This game needs some premade level designed maps as well to offset the RNG of the mapsI can't see a lot of hours going into this game and I don't see a lot of hours in the reviews. At 20 dollars with balance issues and graphics like this I expect more from the game play. The fact of the matter is I can get like 3 different Heroes titles, Age of Magic, Disciples and probably other close ones likes King's Bounty for a similar price and I have put hundred plus hours in some of those.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like HOMM, but isn't quite there yet. I like all the stuff they took from HOMM and added some of their own ideas to it. Especially the little carts that move to your town is a very cool idea. The auto-battle is unfortunately a deal breaker here. It was one of the best points in HOMM and designed like a game of chess where you had to made strategic choices. Here there's an absence of an opportunity to influence the battle as you just wait for it to be over. And yes I know you can cast spells, but that's just isn't enough.I really like that someone wants to make a game that is inspired by the old HOMM series and want to encourage them, but this game is missing too much to be seen as an successor. Therefore it's a middle thumb for me that is rounded down because I doubt I'll play this over an old HOMM.

_childDocuments_.review: It's enjoyable, and I love the fact that so much of it is procedural generated content. You could definitely replay the matches as many times as you want. However, what I found most underwhelming was the editor -- it crashes all the time and feel very incomplete. I tried handcrafted a more asymmetrical map that might work for a more story driven player experience...and there were no options to customize player allegiances, factions, or colors. It doesn't even work when trying to customize those parameters when loading up the custom map. The node editor is ok, but unless you're making an incredibly simple map, it often creates a convoluted mess. The gameplay is fun and the graphics and music are unique, so I only have the one complaint -- if that were fixed, I'd be playing this game for hours instead of starting and restarting the editor for hours.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has sorted its initial difficulties, and has become a very enjoyable one.This is a kind of Master of Magic, or HoMM 4x game, with delightful pixel art and very entertaining auto battle which offers a spectacle of chaotic massive brawl that you can influence in just the right measure.I very much appreciate the variability of the game runs; with 12 unique and different factions and highly configurable game runs, there is ample replayability. _childDocuments_.review: 8-bit Lords of Magic/Might and Magic/Age of Wonders type game with a bunch of modern mechanics thrown in. There are a bunch of different races that definitely feel unique and different to play, and the AI will kick your ass until you start catching up with the 'meta' of the game.Balance between races is definitely a little inconsistent. I started out the game maining Arcane, and after losing dozens of times, finally came out as the victor in a 1v1v1v1 game. The next game, I played the cultist race and absolutely steamrolled the next highest difficulty opponents on the same map. After experimenting with both the openers and late games of all of the races, it seems like there's a decent amount of counterplay that you can do if your scouting is good.Combat can be as involved or as AFK as wanted. Mages will definitely require a lot more APM, but it gives you a lot more direct control of how a fight can go (with AOE cc's or powerful single target nukes for high-value targets, for example). I've seen some crazy dudes on Youtube that do a bunch of microing for each one of their units, and I can't say I have gotten to that point or have any desire to. It does seem like there is a big difference in fight outcomes when the super sweaty mechanics are utilized though.Great game, tons of replay value. Really wish there was online multiplayer (perhaps with 20 second turn timer limits or something).

_childDocuments_.review: Good:> Runs flawlessly on linux> Aesthetically pleasing> OST has some impressive tracksBad:> UX:    >> Event dialog boxes and other interactables are closed if you open other parts of the interface. This leads to frustrating encounters, e.g. you can't check your items/spells/other heroes/most things after a choice is presented without some penalty (since interacting uses a movement point). In some scenarios, you can't even interact a second time, losing the reward.    >> Massive lack of information (affects every aspect of the game).        >>> Example 1: Playing Pyre, picked the Samurai hero (Caprice). An apparently unique lv1 skill (Devour) reads: "Devours a group of friendly units. Doing so gives a temporary boost to all units in battle and gives permanent attack and defense bonuses to the hero. Devouring permanent units give the largest boost". NO MORE INFORMATION. No numbers, scaling info, level up bonus, units consumed count, nothing!        >>> Example 2: No battle information, except how many units each side lost. Unless you have several brains and pairs of eyes, there's no telling which unit did the most damage, tanked the most, cast spells, etc.    >> Minor UI bugs        >>> Example 1: in the lexicon, select a faction. Double click a hero to "stick" their skill tree, click another faction, go back to the first faction, the skilltree will be open until you restart the game. It doesn't go away if you reopen the lexicon. This blocks the information behind the skilltree, which is quite large.> Balance    >> I can't even... I know balancing is very hard. And I know players always want *more* variety/units/factions/... But the latter won't matter if things are completely imbalanced, *especially* in a strategy game. How many times are people going to play a match to the end if it feels like throwing dices around?> Performance    >> I have a 3900x (24 core ryzen 9). After playing the tutorial for a while, I started a single-player match in one of the biggest maps. Pressing 'end turn' on the THIRD TURN of a match that is supposed to last more than 100s-1000s took 20s. I just measured. It might sound like I'm being picky, but you press 'end turn' ALL THE TIME, and having to watch several progress bars for the other factions is so annoying. I would accept this if I had a weak machine, but that isn't the case. Yes, the actions are sequential, but I DOUBT this thing is properly optimized.> Combat / Simulation / Physics    >> During combat, the units walk around and collide with each other like they're all covered in soap. Do you remember those slippery levels of Super Mario World, or ice levels in other games? The entire battlefield feels like that, 100% of the time. If units have mass, it's neglected so much I didn't notice it was there in the first place.> AI and final rant    >> Take this point with a grain of salt, I haven't played enough to assess the AI as well as the topics above. Still, I had an unpleasant tutorial match in which at some point, the enemy hero just kept resurrecting and rushing to my town. He was able to reach me with a very high frequency (every few turns, never more than 5), and every time his army was VERY STRONG (est. difficulty: near impossible or impossible). Even though I won a couple times, I was losing units way faster than I could replace them, but this didn't seem to happen for the enemy faction. I still don't know what's to blame here, but I'd like to have something to look at. Maybe they had insane resource income at this point, with their power only limited by # of units available to recruit? It's impossible to know, there's no log. Maybe there will be some charts when the match ends, but that's just an optimistic guess.Current impression (with few hours post-launch and no playtime during early access): It *seems* the one(s) with relevant decision making power just went on adding features, but rarely stopped to polish them or even play the game. Many issues mentioned here or in other reviews don't require extensive playtime to notice, but impact the experience considerably.On the bright side, if the company decides to polish, balance, rework the interface, etc. - taking their time - they'll have an excellent title on their back. I hope they don't go greedy and jump to DLCs, change projects or disappear. Hero's Hour has lots of potential!

_childDocuments_.review: So since I liked HoMM3 I thought why not try this one too... And I have to say it has all the Charm of HORM plus a lot of fun engagement as well since the autobattler makes the fights much more enjoyable to look at and the whole thing just looks funny and cute. I have seen quite a lot of comments saying you are suppossed to play it on easy or cheese and exploit the game because the AI cheats too hard... That is not the case at all. The AI does cheat once you play at hard but untill then you do not need to worry especially if you played HOMM. First I have noticed people like to have only one army which DRASTICALLY reduces your weekly income. Since you can just have a hero or two running around and farming resources, SECOND you have, and I mean HAVE to use the Trading house CONSTANTLY to off set missing resources, and third, you have to play in the strengths of each Nation... All of them play differently so just spamming units does not work for all of them and once you encounter doomstacks you simply loose... For example:Earthen - SPIRITSThe Earthen mechanic of spirit summoning allows you to summon spirits with each of your units death... This sounds quite useless but it scales together with Destruction, which blows up every unit that dies (even the spirits) it also scales together with Bloodlust (Every unit that dies increases damage and attack speed of allies, which also works woth the spirits) and you can also combine spirits together to create earth elementals. This means you can litterally have 5 units die, they all explode and buff the summoned spirits, which upon death can all explode and create an Earthen elemental that gets buffed by Bloodlust... This means Earthen can pretty easely defeat Near Impossible enemies on regular basis. Arcane uses mostly magic, this means that ORE can be used to buy units and upgrades for your hearoes since no units need it, you also get bonuses for every spell you cast... Your Ranged units are also probably the best of all races. Lament has great AOE Crowd Controll in units as well as in magic.. Some units can Polymorph enemies and you can sue chaos in enemy ranks quickly. Pillar is a money machine, and is very powerfull with diplomacy skill. There are some races though that are less then Optimal, like TIDE. Which has great bonuses on watter battles, and the ability to dig for treasure all over the map... The issue is that the treasure allows you to increase weekly unit cap for units, but you wont have enough resources to buy them all... And the Sea battle advantage of course is quite random since not every map has water.. Still as you can see the game can be complex and is quite amazing, Just finding out what works for whome was funn in it on itself :3 I can only recomend this game, give it a shot and see for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is fantastic, but playing solo against the AI is frustrating and absurd due to IA cheating, this is the worst way to create an IA. It's disappointing that such a remarkable gameplay experience is marred by subpar AI programming. It's high time the developers address this issue by revamping the AI with more specialized human ressource.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended at sale price, but not at full with the current state of the game. I know it's still getting updates, so hopefully more balancing work will be done and single-player content added.The good:- Fresh take on the HoMM formula, accompanied by well thought-out game design choices. For instance, the realtime battles feel very different, and you'll take more losses than you're used to, but the game has skills and buildings for loss mitigation (e.g., infirmary, available early for all factions, rescues 50% of slain units). In general, the theme of sacrificing army for benefits, or compensating for army loss, is much more present here than any other HoMM-style game I've played.- Diverse factions and units. Despite most of the units feeling a little samey in combat across factions, unique faction buildings and hero abilities can make for very different gameplay and strategy. One faction has a super cool trait where you only have one real hero, but you can hire "avatars" that can have armies and engage in combat - but they have all the skills, stats, spells, and equipment of your main hero in a fight, as if your hero was there with that army.- Unit balance feels pretty good, and the "power" limitation on fielding units makes for interesting tactical choices when you have a large army.- Skills system is very fun and allows for a lot of different character builds. You can really focus in hard on stuff like making a hero amazing with swarms of weak units, having powerful and spammable spells of various sorts, permanent army unit creation over time or after battle, and so on. Really excellent variety even within some of these niches. The breadth of builds goes far beyond what would be allowed by any of the HoMM games for sure.- Great neutral enemy implementation - early start feels balanced, guarded buildings offer a variety of benefits that extend beyond what I've seen before in this sort of game.The bad:- Faction balance, aside from units themselves, has some standout issues. Some faction towns have incredibly powerful unique buildings, way beyond what others offer - I can't imagine losing with a pyre town in a game that goes more than 8 weeks; the demon portal requires a lot of investment but is patently absurd once you've paid into it. Some faction hero abilities are also way stronger than others (human faction casters are the biggest offender, as far as I've seen). However, take these issues of mine with a grain of salt as I've only played 20 hours. Perhaps balance is better at a more "professional" level of play.- Some skills feel very strong and others rather weak, or middling in a quick game, but absurd on a large map. Additionally, economic support skills are far too powerful on secondary heroes for how cheap additional heroes are. Even if I could only get 1 rank of a single support skill per hero, I think it would still be optimal to hire like 5 a week. That hiring one hero can bring you, say, 60% unit cost reduction and 20% increased unit production *in all towns* if you're lucky feels weird and bad. I have mixed feelings about bodyguards as well - a skill that gives free units to the hero in battle to fill some of the gap between it and your strongest hero army. They're highly disposable and fun to use, but it feels like cheating to get so much army out of such a tiny hero cost.- Content is limited, despite there being so many factions. You've got a good variety of preset map seeds for procedural generation, much in the same way you'd do HoMM3 map generation, but that's all you get. No campaign or scenarios. There's a handful of what seem to be player-created maps, both fully predetermined and procedurally generated, but it doesn't seem like there's much volume for user created content. This is honestly my biggest gripe with the game.- AI sometimes feels wonky and irrational. They can build up armies real nice on challenging and hardcore, and in a battle they cast spells effectively so they're a challenge within that context. But on the world map, it's hard to tell what their priorities are. Sometimes an "impossible" enemy will ignore one of my heroes in range, and do... not much with their turn. They'll often leave some guarded resources behind when they clear camps. It's not always bad and they're still pretty competent, but it surely doesn't feel anywhere close to playing against a person.

_childDocuments_.review: Hero's Hour is an incredibly charming game all the way through. The graphics seem very simple, but are incredibly clean and polished. The battlefield can be a bit of a mess on the endgame, but it's still a delight to see immense armies slug it out. Artifacts with different effects and set bonuses also add another layer of customization to your hero. A big diversity of interactives, maps, units, monsters and spells keep the game fresh for a good long time. About to hit 10 hours of play time and yet i still see different things here and there. The fact it has a workshop and incentive guides for modding tells me a lot, you can really feel the love poured into this game by author and it's community.Playing with different factions actually gives you a distinct experience, to the point that i've felt interest to try them all instead of sticking up with my favorite all the time like i usually do for these games. No copy and paste stuff with a different skin, they all do different things and excel at other areas.I see many complaints about the difficulty being obscene even at lower levels, and i personally disagree. Contrary to some reviews i've taken a look at, which have prior experience in similar games like Heroes of Might and Magic or even previous versions of Hero's Hour, i never played any of these. Jumped in on the Steam release, failed many times at first and eventually got around to understand it's mechanics. Normal is very casual for me at the moment and i have an enjoyable time.That being said, try playing against one opponent only at first until you understand the game better, then you can try climbing the steps. I feel like the amount of opponents has a way bigger impact than changing Easy, Normal or other difficulties. While you're learning how to play, it's also important to try different aproaches, like having more hero's or focusing on leveling up certain skills.I recommend it very much. Having lots of fun jumping into a few matches after work, and there's still many factions for me to try with.

_childDocuments_.review: Game looks charming and cute on the surface, but is rotting underneath. There are no controls for units in battle besides your spells and choices you make to build units are impossible to tell what's working and what isn't. Is unit A better than B? I have no idea since all battles are mosh pits that give you no information on what's going on. Are those spell you're using effective? No clue, just click the ones that seem useful and hope for the best.The AI is also hilariously unfair and needs serious rebalancing before I'm ever playing this again. The way the AI is set up literally forces you to play as cowardly and defensively as possible or you will get steamrolled. This is true even on the lowest difficulty. Want to ease into the game and set it to "easy" so you can learn what works and how to play? Want to try a new faction or make fun builds to actually have fun while playing? Too bad. Have fun getting obliterated for daring to not play the most meta garbage available. When the guides for the higher difficulties of the game are literally telling you to exploit the game, something is wrong.Stay far away from this unless you only want to play with friends or like repeatedly losing until you figure out the only way the game lets you play it. I figure I'd give this some time to grow on me, but now that I'm 5 hours in I regret not refunding this.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big HoMM3 fan so my opinion of this game will be largely biased. The comparisons aren't superficial, in many ways the Devs are riffing off of and making a parody game to HoMM3. That being said, it's a fun little game. Not very deep and doesn't really scratch that 'tactical management' itch that HoMM, TW, or other strategy games does, but it is entertaining. I'd say if you like those kinds of games and want something lighthearted that you don't have to take seriously, then pick this up. I think it's important to not expect a well balanced, strategic game out of this -- Think of it as an arcade version of a grand strategy game instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Its good. It Heroes 3 with a multiplayer focus, so things that made the game slow have been changed. They want you to be able to finish a game or two in a single night. The change to combat is the biggest example of this.Hero skill trees are more flexible and they fight in battle. You can have larger armies, but battles have a max amount you can field, you deploy reinforcements as units die. 6 creature tiers but more flexible choices. Only 5 resource types. Artifacts are less game breaking but more abundant. Better ship mechanics.The art style is what it is. I don't particularly care for it, or the music that much, but I don't hate it either, and it all fits together really well. Its very sure of what it wants to be, I just prefer a bit more detail.The biggest problem is the AI, It feels like they cheat. Even on normal, multiple times I've had the AI roll me before I can break out of my zone. In larger games one AI usually stomps the others by week 5 or 6 then its just me slowly chipping away at them.This game was clearly built with PVP in mind, which is where it excels. I'm hoping they can make a more balanced and enjoyable AI to fight against, then it will be a complete package.

_childDocuments_.review: Scratches that old school HoMM itch, but with an emphasis on chaos. Overland strategic choices matter a lot, as the battles are a cacophony of craziness. Unlike those old turn-based battlers, where you could outsmart the enemy with shrewd and calculated maneuvering, be prepared to just fight fist-to-face, as it were. Therefore, make sure you have plenty of fists, because the AI will throw face after face at you. Rough around the edges and a great deal of randomness to each game, so probably not for everyone, but overall I am enjoying it thus far, and am therefore giving it a tentative thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: A great, fast strategy game if you have an hour or two to kill, yet with enough depth and variety to replay many, many times.I have been playing since the early versions in itch.io (hence the low play time on Steam) and it has been amazing to see the rate at which TOIO has expanded the game and moved it away from the HoMM3 carbon copy it used to be.Definitely give it a try if you like Turn-Based strategy on the campaign map with asymmetrical factions. All factions play quite differently from one another and support multiple playstyles each. If you are looking for deep real time combat a la Total War, maybe pass on this though. Even though you can micro units in combat and interfere with spells, it still mostly plays itself. Though that is precisely why the game is so easy to pick :)
_childDocuments_.name: Hero's Hour

_childDocuments_.review: You can see and hear that a lot of love went into this. The townscapes, interface, unit designs, and musical compositions are all excellent. These are all so many peacock feathers sticking out of a very, very, very cooked goose of a game. This is beat-for-beat 1996 turn-based strategy nostalgia-bait gameplay, complete with abominable pacing, a deep burden of metagame knowledge, and a whole lot of clicking "Pass Turn" for resources to ripen. Benjamin Hauer has tried to dust off this old drumstick by throwing a bunch more RNG spices into the stuffing, but only serves to underline the fundamental flaws that make Heroes of Might and Magic games pretty much unplayable in Current Year. Apart from the *stellar* art, this retread shows all too clearly why turn-based strategy went the way of the dodo.

_childDocuments_.review: Hero's Hour is an incredibly well-written love letter to Heroes of Might and Magic. I've been looking for a game as good as HoMM 5 for so long I've lost count, and the much-beloved HoMM 3 just didn't do it for me. Hero's Hour, however, is a great time I recommend to all fans of strategic RPGs or RPGs in general. It's an easy 8/10 game for me.Positives: +Really nice pixel art+For the price, you get a huge amount of content, a map maker in case those in the game weren't enough, a mode for only battles, online multiplayer... Plus, the supporter pack costs practically nothing.+Said content also has great variety, featuring a whopping twelve factions, a gigantic variety of skills, creatures and artifacts and a spellbook the size of a bible.+Information about said things is also to-the-point and easily accessible.+Great, catchy music capturing the style of old-school games, but with modern quality and even the occasional vocals in a song.+Accessible, but challenging, featuring customizable difficulties and great quality-of-life changes you'll have to find a good use for.  For example: Buildings that spawn troops weekly don't actually charge you for the troops, and they're automatically turned into caravans that home into the nearest hero/town nearby. You can also decide where they go manually by turning them into Regiments, and you can turn your towns'/heroes' troops into caravans/regiments too. Regiments can also fight independently of their heroes.-Game tells you the name of the songs currently playing, THANK YOU! Negatives:-Unlike HoMM, where only the strongest units cost a certain resource along with gold, weaker units in HH also frequently cost resources AND gold. This can create some frustrating situations where you're constantly out of said resources if the map doesn't provide you with a source for a while. -Outside a few actions, battles play out automatically. This can be a major turnoff if you prefer moving your troops around carefully like chess. Not to mention big battles can drag on without being able to provide imput, and they can have performance issues too.-You can't load a save in a battle (yet)-Lore, but no actual stories/cutscenes. Very minor nitpick here, though.-Occasional crashes and inconsistensies with the autosave. When you save in the middle of a turn, loading it goes back to the beginning of the turn.-Supporter pack DLC content only available by browsing the game's local files, with the exception of the special sprites.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're like me and you love games like, Total War, Age of Mythology, Age of Wonders you'll probably like this game!I've played on a couple of different difficulties so far. Only made it through one of the more massive maps once on Challenging. Not sure if its because of the 'low' difficulty but the AI on water levels leaves much to be desired. Nonsensical movements all around. They ignore many different types of terrain like the saw mills and whatnot if there is an enemy presence. Favoring instead to run straight towards you. Leaving you free to pillage on the way to them. The city building is an important aspect in games like this, so I'm glad to say it is handled rather well. The game is turn based using a system of days and weeks. As you might expect you have seven turns till the next week starts and you can recruit more troops from your cities and monuments. You can build a city building once a day, which in my opinion is a little too fast and makes you notice each improvement a little less around city level 3/6. Each faction has an ability or a gimmick and the more fun ones are the undead. The ability to use mercury for your soul siphon on undead faction basically is the most downright broken element in the game. This allows you to make thousands of troops and all it costs to make more is mercury (which you can buy with a market) and attacking anything in sight. Pair this with a hero that has legion and swarming and you've got an unbeatable army on your hands. The spells are awesome in this game, as are the modifiers. The devs know this, so they make it so mana is scarce and regen is slow. There's plenty of options to choose from. Skills are much the same as spells, they scale to ridiculous heights. Occasionally you can get a hero after buying the tavern that has something stupid like bodyguard rank 9. That particular clown hero I'd send around without a single unit and he'd wipe the floor with anyone he came across as long as my main army was still going strong. This game is above all else an auto battler. If you play total war games with the skip feature on for most of the battles, this game has that. You do miss out on a lot of the fun though. all said and done7.5/10 for the gameplay (once you get to a large enough army the novelty of new units wears off)7/10 for the music (its original but there needs to be a few more tracks)9/10 hero rpg system8/10 city building5/10 AI10/10 pricing

_childDocuments_.review: If you've ever played Heroes of Might and Magic or even Age of Wonders to some extent, then you'll likely feel familiar with this game. The core mechanics of Hero's Hour are almost identical to HOMM series games with the exception of battles. In HOMM, battles are turn based, whereas in HH, battles are essentially real-time with minimal control over your actual units, other than to issue movement commands, order to defend (stand ground) vs attack, etc. The real control over battles comes in the form of magic, which is also quite similar to HOMM. Every single unit in each group of similar species will appear in the battle, which I find quite nice. It definitely simulates the feeling of a large scale battle, in a tiny space.A lot of people say that this game is quite difficult, and it is. This game is brutal at first until you learn a few key strategies early on to quickly develop an army and level up your hero faster than the AI can. After almost 60 hours on record, I still struggle on even normal difficulty unless I'm intentionally cheesing with a broken combination of spells or hero perks, such as making my hero an unstoppable force or having an army of nearly 100 red dragons.There are also a lot of complaints of performance issues - this is something I too can relate to, which surprises me for what this game is. Its all pixel graphics, yet my computer struggles on lengthy games and larger maps, with the largest pain point being the map "Patience", after several hours of playtime. I occasionally drop to less than 20 fps randomly until my next battle, which leads me to believe its something flawed in the game itself as opposed to actually being intensive.PC Specs: CPU: I9 13900KFGPU: RTX 4070TIRAM: 64GB @ 6400 HzOverall, I really enjoy this game and definitely feel that I've received my money's worth plus some. Here's to hoping for the possibility of more content and especially multiplayer.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun take on making a Heroes of Might and Magic with real time (mostly auto) battles and roguelike elements.If that doesn't mean much to you, the gameplay loop is basically: You get a procedural map set to certain parameters and randomly one of your faction's six hero to start. Each day you will move your hero and their army on the map to engage in battles, loot resources, claim buildings, ETC. You will also choose one improvement in town daily. Through the early game, you will mostly be fighting neutral mobs while you amass resources and power up your forces. Eventually you will break free from your starting zone, and begin to engage the other player characters - conquer them all to win.Frankly, for me, Hero's Hour scratches the same itch to build an army, explore a map, and feel dread that it could all come crashing down with every conflict if I misjudged my odds as Conquest of Elysium, but with a few key differences. For one, Hero's Hour takes much less time to play (not counting those games of CoE where either the bots or myself get demolished by random elephants by turn three). In a similar vein, it just feels more lightweight in a way I can't really explain - There are still hundreds of unit types, there are loads of abilities that you can and should try to synergize with your abilities and spells, and there's even the added elements of spellcasting during battle and needing to chose how you want to upgrade your town... but somehow the game still just feels like it takes less of my brainspace than CoE. It might just be because everything is more digestible and less obtuse, but still - it makes it more pleasant to play when I don't feel like burying myself into a game  hard.For negatives, there aren't many. The game doesn't really have a story or anything to that effect - this is a game for the sake of the game itself; it's to entertain the player. If you need some broader or grander goals than "win the game", you might not stick with this one - but if that's what you're looking for, you'll find loads of replayability here. Some of the balancing feels like it could have used some tuning - in particular, and I'm keeping the vague to avoid tainting any opinions, I found that one type of hero for one faction built around their base ability made their whole faction so grossly that I ended up walking into encounters with no units and leaving with armies... multiple times per turn. Finding busted strategies is part of the thrill of these games, but I think that one was a bit  busted, and too easy to build for at that.Overall, I do recommend Hero's Hour! I wholeheartedly recommend it to fans of Heroes of Might and Magic or fans of the Illwinter Games looking for someone a little less involved but still fairly deep. I'd also recommend it to folks who like a good autobattler, but want a little more engagement. It's a really fun way to while away a couple hours without needing to invest an entire afternoon. There's a ton of replayability if you like the game for itself - though you might find it lacking if you wanted more than achievements to strive for.

It's very fun and exciting to watch the armies clash, and it reminds me a lot of Warsong for SEGA Genesis. HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who loves strategy titles! :D

_childDocuments_.review: For a game released on steam only 3 months ago it's well put together and definitely worth the 20$ asking price. It is an auto battler, so don't expect real time strategy and tactics aside from positioning units on the battlefield and using a dizzying list of spells. The hero's you pick can also vary your playstyle, with unique artefacts, buildings and equipment that  drastically change your starting experience keeping the game fresh on the same maps which are also randomly generated.It also has a steam workshop page that's developing, with a comprehensive guide on how to add your own mods and sprites. A few downsides though, I wouldn't recommend higher difficulties for newbie players. Start at normal or easy even, get the hang of the game and the system, cause the harder difficulties follow Total War logic, giving the AI a boost in their economy, resulting in them fielding mass armies at hardcore while you only have a single hero.Another issue is the start of game. You wanna focus levelling a single hero as neutral armies can be pretty powerful to face. Resulting in a single overpowered army that can curb stomp anything in its path. With other hero's being delegated to collecting resources or basic chaff defence. This isn't too bad but it enforces a dominant strategy that goes against its replayablity. All in all I can recommend this game for what it is, a beautifully designed homage to Hero's of Might and Magic. Def deserves a spot in your library.

_childDocuments_.review: Hero's Hour is in my opinion a great execution of a strategy game. I had so many fun matches with this game and I still haven't played all the factions.The game can be easily described as "Heroes of Might and Magic but as Autobattler". The core gameplay is directly taken from the HoMM franchise and feels very close to HoMM3 (which many consider to be the best one in the franchise) but it also takes some inspirations from HoMM5. The combat here is however done as an Autobattler. You have some minor control over the battle, mainly through spells, but besides that you will watch your units and the enemy units fight it out by themselves. So the main strategic decisions are mostly done on a macro level, deciding what buildings to pick, what units to create and what structures you should take on the minimap. As you would expect from a HoMM clone, you have several factions, each with their own unique buildings, units and even special game mechanics. The creator of this game made sure that each faction feels very unique in their approach of playstyle and what strategies you could try. For example, Wyld is all about summoning small fairy-like "Anima" units, which are weak but come in big numbers, often replacing dead units. You can also gather many of them inside your town to recruit "grizzlies" over time and you can overgrow mines, which will have units to protect them and produce wood together with their usual resources. Another faction for example is Iczta Enclave, a sort of Mayan lizardmen faction. They create a lot of smaller units and ca either tame beasts as units or hunt them for artifacts. They also summon a hydra god over time, which they can speed up by sacrificing artifacts.There 11 of such factions in the game and I love that they are not just pure copies of the HoMM factions (although some come very close to it).Each faction has their own heroes, which are generally divided into two subclasses, which can be generally be considered a magical or physical class. The heroes in this game are actually the highlight of the gameplay. They have their own individual skill trees, which unlike the HoMM series, is not simply randomized. While skills overlap for heroes, they still are distinct enough in their playstyle, especially since each faction has access to faction-exclusive skills.Your hero levels up through battle or from resources and structures on the map. This increases their stats and lets you select one of their aviable skills. Each skill can also be leveled up but you need to have a higher level if you want to get higher skill levels. Building your hero correctly makes a major difference to your strategy and also gives you a good idea what you should aim for with your town.The game features also neutral heroes on the map, which provide resources and artifacts if killed but will never claim any structures or towns.Besides the faction units, there are also a ton of neutral units on the map, which provide you with XP if killes but mainly serve as a blockade for other structures or important pathways.To round things up, there are also a ton of different spells in the game. Some summon extra units, some deal damage or they buff or debuff units. There is a bit of variety here, although some spells might feel a little bit similiar. Spells are important to influence combat but have cooldowns and cost mana.Now about the graphics. As you can tell by the screenshots, the game isn't goodlooking. It uses a very simplified pixel-style, which makes it sometimes hard to distinguish units on the battlefield. Since this is an autobattler, it's not much of a big problem but it can be somewhat offputting at times. The Ui is also very basic, it serves it purpose and is at least not clunky or ugly but it could have been better. But it's easy to select your desired heroes and towns whenever you want, so it's good in that regard.The sound design is actually not that bad. The music is fitting for the fantasy setting, although slightly repetitive for a game with so many factions and heroes. Unit sounds are also pretty generic but shouldn't bother you too much.What could be however more of a bother would be the lack of online multiplayer. There is local multiplayer in the form of hotseat (players take alternate turns on the game) but nothing in regard of online functionaility and from what I've heard, there are no plans to ever do this. You can play online with Steam Remote Play Together, which is basically the most basic way of playing multiplayer. On the world map, this is less of a problem, but during combat it makes spells less appealing since both players have to take turns on casting (which is, I guess, closer to HoMM).In terms of Ai, it is also a bit lacking. The AI difficulty is simply defined by how many more units and resources the AI player gets, not actual intelligence. For people that hate "cheating AI", whis can be a real problem. Outside of cheating, the AI is lackluster, often ignoring structures and always going for the most basic strategy. I wish there was more here but there isn't.However, I have so much fun with the gameplay itself, that I don't even take notice from the Ai or how bad it is. I have mainly fun by trying out different builds and then steamrolling the Ai if possible.Overall, this game is very fun if you like a lot of content and want a game similiar to HoMM but not exactly like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly can't believe i hadn't recommended this sooner. I played a bit more on the non-steam version a while back, and my hours on steam do not reflect my enjoyment or praise for this game. I come from the old guard of Master of Magic lovers and somehow skipped over the Heroes M&M 3 era and went straight to games like Disciples 2. These sorts of "Hero based Strategy RPG" have always piqued my interest, but this one takes the cake and the crown. Ben "ThingOnItsOwn" Hauer has made something special here, granting endless replayability for (relatively) bite-sized adventures that give you just enough of everything you want out of this type of game. Town building, army raising, hero leveling, dungeon looting, rival bashing, map exploring, all the checkmarks are there. as with any game like this there is always some balancing issues here and there, but nothing that took away from my enjoyment at least. The combat being 90% automatic, basically just barring spells and pre-engagement setup, is such a huge plus because then every battle is just a thunderdome show for your enjoyment. over time you may increase the speed a bit to get to the point but it never actually gets old. and to make sure it never gets old, random map generation keeps things fresh and fun every playthrough, and even just got an update.TLDR: i like it, and if you like HoMM3 or other strategy/war games, you may like it too. the price also helps, and its constantly going on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: When I used to play Heroes 3 (and 4) a lot, I was always intrigued by the imagination of these massive battles playing out in real time with all individual units present and individually acting and fighting in front of the hero on the battlefield. Hero's Hour promises this exact idea. So, in theory I should absolutely be in love with this game, right? Unfortunately not: As is the case with many fantasies we have in life, they do not turn out to be as great in reality.First off there is some clear things not as good when compared to H3: childish pixel graphics style, the extremely basic animations, the mediocre soundtrack and basic level art. I am not a fan of the audio and visuals and especially H3 did really well on those, imo they were a huge part of the atmosphere and feeling of that game. Yet, if everything else is great in this game I would still give it a 10/10, and I have played and loved pixel-graphics games before.There are some things that are equally good: the town build-up, hero progression, spells, points-of-interests in the level,  generated random maps, unit roster and town roster are all well done, even in the cases when their design was changed from the almost perfect original H3 design. it is still great. The changes do offer some interesting new possibilities.Now to the bad part: The battles themselves just did not do it for me and they are a huge part of the game. They feel chaotic, hard to control and hard to understand and due to them now being real-time they lost a lot of tactical aspects too. The UX and UI could be much better in the entire game but at this part of the game the lack of good UX really irritated me. The units are clustered by type but also they are all individually moving. Ranged units block each other with the ones in the back not being able to shoot but there is nothing you can do about it because it is one big pile. Units attack each other with a lot of floating damage numbers but you get no real sense of what units are doing what, how effective each unit is or what you could do better next time. H3 is the exact opposite: you see cause and effect very transparently since each unit attacking each other and each spell cast is a discrete step of the battle that can be observed individually. To me that was part of the charme of H3. Amidst the chaos of Hero's Hour's battles I lost interest in the game very quickly, although it is clear a lot of love and work has been put into the game. It is just not a game for me unfortunately, although I would have loved to love it

Find a Tower of Mages to continually stack Knowledge. Then find a Brilliant Orb to do one big Spellcasting spec. In that instant you also become the most powerful mage possible.

_childDocuments_.review: Hero's Hour : By Triple F"Hero's Hour" is a genre-bending blend of turn-based strategy, city-building, and auto-battler elements, set in a captivating fantasy world. It takes inspiration from classics like Heroes of Might and Magic, while adding its own unique twist, offering a deep and engaging experience for strategy enthusiasts and casual players alike.The game throws you into the heart of a procedurally generated map, where you control a single hero representing your chosen faction. Each of the six playable factions, from the human Empire to the undead Necropolis, boasts distinct units, hero abilities, and play-styles, allowing for diverse strategic approaches.Your journey begins with a humble town, your base for expansion and dominance. You'll manage resources, construct buildings, and recruit diverse troops, from nimble archers to hulking ogres. Each building offers specific benefits, from boosting resource production to unlocking powerful spells for your hero. Resource management is crucial, as it fuels the growth of your town and army, making strategic decisions about building priorities a constant challenge.The map unfolds in a turn-based manner, with each turn representing an "hour" in the game world. During your turn, you explore the surrounding area, encountering various points of interest, including neutral settlements, enemy towns, resource mines, and hidden dungeons. These offer opportunities to expand your territory, gain resources, acquire powerful artifacts, and face thrilling challenges.Engaging in combat is inevitable, and here's where Hero's Hour takes a unique approach. Battles unfold in a real-time, auto-battler style. You position your hero and troops on a grid-based battlefield, but the actual combat is automated. However, your strategic decisions play a crucial role. You can choose from various formations, cast powerful spells, and activate hero skills to influence the tide of battle.This system lends itself to a mix of strategy and anticipation. You carefully plan your army composition and troop placement before the fight, then watch it unfold with a mix of excitement and strategic tweaks. While the lack of direct control during combat might initially surprise players accustomed to micromanagement, it allows for a faster pace and emphasizes strategic planning over tactical reflexes.As your hero gains experience through combat and exploration, they level up, unlocking new skills and abilities. These can enhance their combat prowess, improve their leadership abilities, or grant access to powerful magic. Investing in the right skill tree for your chosen play-style adds another layer of depth and personalization to your hero's journey.While conquering rival factions and ultimately defeating a powerful villain forms the core narrative, "Hero's Hour" offers replay-ability beyond a single playthrough. Procedural map generation ensures each game feels fresh, while additional difficulty settings and hidden challenges cater to both casual and hardcore strategy enthusiasts."Hero's Hour" utilizes a charming pixel art style, effectively conveying the fantasy setting. The soundtrack complements the world, creating an immersive atmosphere. However, the user interface can feel cluttered at times, and occasional technical hiccups might disrupt the gameplay flow.All in all, "Hero's Hour" offers a compelling blend of strategy, city-building, and auto-battler elements, catering to both casual and hardcore strategy players. The blend of turn-based exploration and real-time combat creates a unique and engaging experience, while the diverse factions, procedural generation, and character progression add depth and replay-ability. While a few technical issues and a cluttered UI might hinder the experience slightly, "Hero's Hour" is a gem for strategy enthusiasts looking for a captivating and accessible adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: When I first started playing it, I thought I was going to like it. After a few games of the same thing happening every time, I've found I'm not a fan and can't recommend it. If possible, I would refund because I'll probably never be touching it again. When the game is made to favor AI and gives them every advantage possible with fast troop spawn and infinite resources, it's not a challenge. It's just broken. I liked the concept. I liked the gameplay. I liked the different factions and powers. I HATED the unbalanced AI. Completely bogus. I shouldn't be getting out swarmed when I'm maximizing troop production from the start of the game. Yet somehow, the computer shows up with a twice my size army when it's possible to only recruit a certain number of troops each week. So how can they double my output of troops every game if I'm focusing on troop production and upgrade buildings? If it was a human player, they couldn't. But since it's AI and developers just love to give them some secret advantage on normal difficulty...they can.RE: Still not a fan after an additional 12 hours. Found that there's only one VIABLE way to play the game with every single faction. What's it matter to have different factions and units if they all still have to be played the exact same way to even stand a chance at winning a match? Unlike other strategy games which generally offer several different play styles or adaptive qualities to consider... Leaves it dull to have to play each game the same way to compete with broken ai. Not a good format for a strategy game.

Every faction has some exploits (at least the few of them i tried to work with) which allow them to snowball through the map.In combat, selection of units and positions may be crucial, even if you have not direct control of units, first times it looks like a chaotic mess, developers likely knew about this issue and put in the game a bunch of combat skirmish scenarios, in which you select a restricted number of units to face an enemy force, I highly recommend to try this mode if you want to increase your knowledge of units and their weaknesses and synergies.So, I had a dozen hour of play, I expect I will have at least a few dozens more, I had fun, I think it's enough for the price, but not enough for the potential this project could have had.Pro- There is a lot of content, in number of factions, maps, exploration- Maps are randomly generated thus increasing the longevity by a wide margin- Factions and heroes are extremely diverse from each others and require different play-styles- Matches last a few hours at mostCon- there's not single player campaign- the game screams for an online multiplayer mode, I hope they'll implement it in the near future.- please, change the autocombat musics, I dislike them! _childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome. It's a very well refined HoMM clone with a lot of its own spin on it. All the  HoMM stuff is there. You build up your towns, recruit heroes and creatures before marching them out to bash the snot out of the baddies while capturing resource generators and the like.  No campaign, which is a bit of a disappointment, I really enjoyed those in HoMM 3 in particular.  Bit of a steeper learning curve I'd say. At least in the early game, and there are a few key differences that seem to trip people up when they first start playing. It is a game that punishes you if you don't plan ahead and focus on using the strengths of your primary hero to amplify a particular strategy and I think that caused quite a few people to bounce off it pretty hard.The overworld has a lot in common with what you'd expect.  Early expansion can be quite challenging, and due to the random nature of the map, as well as even the random upgrade path within your starting town I did find myself with quite a few false starts in the beginning.  Ramping up a capable starting army within the first day or two is very important and I think this is the first thing that tends to trip new players up. Basically if you haven't got a significant chunk of your starting zone opened up and explored within the first week or you loose an early battle you should consider restarting. It's difficult to bounce back from a major early setback. There are a few nice QoL features like how in addition to being able to shuffle troops around without a hero and the various independent recruiting sites will automatically send their units to the nearest castle or hero. You can also garrison your surplus heroes by mines in order to boost their income and provide some defence. The maps themselves consist of zones to segregate the factions. The zones themselves are randomly generated, but their position relative to each other and any connections are preset. These will either be linked to a faction or labeled as 'neutral' depending on which map you pick. The faction zone is basically your starting area to get you access to the resources you need as well as a place to level up your primary hero. Neutral zones will have an independent castle in them as well as more advanced resource structures and is  where you will likely first encounter the enemy AI. It lulled me into a false sense of security in my first game and I expanded quite leisurely poking about with different units and skills to see how the pieces fit together. Ended up getting my teeth kicked in on like week 3 when the AI hero invaded. If there is an in-game encyclopedia or anything I wasn't able to find it, but besides, there is just so much stuff it would take ages to read through so expect to learn by failing, or reading/watching a bunch of guides.The battles are a ton of fun. Realtime, and very chaotic. Not as tactical as the hex based battles traditional to the genre, but again they reward preplanning and leveraging synergies between your hero (who is perfectly combat capable themselves) units, and spells. This is where your hero build really becomes important. Read the skill descriptions, figure out which units you have access to them that synergize with a particular skill and leverage that. Keep an eye pealed for anything that gives % increases to combat stats and/or HP. The mastery skills, legion and champion are three to really look out for.  Also look out for anything that will let you freespawn units. Bloodwarping, Mastery skills, and summoning are good examples. Also, as of this writing at least Bodyguard is a critical skill for your secondary heroes though you can get 1 rank of it for free from the Champions Statue though I have at least heard murmurings of a nerf, so if you want to exploit it do it soon. The battle UI is a bit awkward and could likely use some refinement... The edge scrolling with my dual monitor setup is a frustrating to say the least, shuffling units in and out of reserves particularly in the battle setup is a pain, the little pixel blood splatters and other particle effects can make it difficult to see how the battle is going at a glance and casting spells is rather finicky, but overall it works well enough and the fights are a joy to watch.Combat magic kinda deserves its own little mini section too. There are a ton of different spells, and other than a few of the dedicated caster heroes, exactly what spell you get is randomized so you need to adapt them to whatever strategy you plan on running. You can summon units mid fight, grant a wide variety of buffs and debuffs, do direct damage, and all that sort of stuff.Towns work pretty much as you'd expect from the genre. Each faction has unique units, and each faction plays very differently. Particularly since  every faction has access to their own unique hero pool each with different skill trees which opens quite a bit of variety within factions. Towns are upgraded as you'd expect. One building per day, one batch of recruits per week. I think all the recruitment buildings except for the Horde faction have at least one upgrade, and most of them also allow you to pick between two distinct recruit options each week as well. All the factions have at least a few unique buildings that do cool things, and they all have the markets and mage guilds and that sort of stuff that we're used to. That said, there are some different buildings available that can be easy to overlook, the Infirmary and Champions Statues are critical pieces of infrastructure and you'll eventually probably want hospitals as well. Pay attention to your units as well, particularly their abilities and again how you can synergize them with your hero skills. It will pay off. Leeches from the Enclave Lizardmen faction combined Legion can be terrifying for example.Heroes are probably the aspect of the game that differentiate it most from the traditional entries in the genre. Basically each hero has a unique skill tree. You'll find the same skill on different heroes, but it will usually be in a different location. The skills you have access to and the ones you choose to focus on are probably the most important part of the strategy gameplay loop. Get skills that boost your combat ability, leverage that to take harder fights with fewer casualties, gain XP, repeat. Planning out a build is quite important. Some skills will feed off of each other in terrifying ways. For example Liara from the Horde faction gets Archery, a skill that boosts the damage of her ranged units. She also gets Troll Mastery, which gives her free trolls which are a ranged unit. Finally she also gets Champion, which boosts the HP and Damage of all units with 9 or more power, which trolls... are you seeing where I am going here? They are all % based increases too so it can start stacking up like mad.Now as far as the AI goes, it seems... decent. It is very much based around the horde of troops philosophy, and this can make them quite challenging, particularly while on the defensive if they can get access to re-enforcement faster than you. It will likely win a war of attrition especially on higher difficulties with its resource bonus. Given the importance of hero builds though you start to see the limitations. I think the AI tends to pick skills randomly and mash together units into armies without much thought. As long as you aren't doing the same you can likely crush most enemy armies without too much trouble. The battle AI on the other hand is pretty smart. It seems to use spells effectively, recognize when it is likely outmatched and avoid the fight and that sort of stuff. It is a pity that there is no online multiplayer available, especially for asynchronous multiplayer but it would likely be a pretty tall order especially given the importance of the real time battles.Anyhow, if you are still with me, thank you for coming to my Ted Talk. Heroes Hour. Great fun. You should play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Basically HOMM with three differences:1. Graphics are much more basic2. Combat is real time based with less control (but some)3. Games are usually won or lost in the first 2-3 weeks and longer games are rare (about 15-20 minute games)If you are cool with these points, the game is fun and has potential.Personally my thumbs down comes from point 3: I dislike the rush gameplay and got sick of being forced into it. You have to do it, because the AI is doing it as well. You will die to impossibly strong armies, if you don't rush.Rush in this case does not only mean you need to rush buildings and army, but also bonus perks that somehow add to your army (like bodyguard, summons etc.). "Just" having the max possible army from towns is NOT enough to make it past week 3 on most maps.So not exxagerating here: You really need to rush hard to even beat normal AI.If you do however, even the hardest AI is too easy. I was unable to find a happy balance of challenge and fun gameplay. You either die horribly before even getting to level 7 heroes, or you dominate the game by week 3 and get bored.As a reference: There is even a guide for an achivement that shows how to win on max difficulty in 4 turns. Four. Turns.

_childDocuments_.review: I only recommend this game with much hesitation, because it's priced low, and because I think HoMM also had a lot of issues. I think it's great the devs attempted to reinvent HoMM in a more concentrated way, and the work on factions is great, they really feel and play differently. However I have some deep issues with some core components of this game.1) Difficulty: the AI seems to develop better than the player, no matter what (I think it cheats pretty significantly, even on normal difficulty), and you're essentially playing catch-up until you find one of the completely OP mechanics on the map, and then you can roll over the AI entirely. It does not feel like you get to apply your wits much, the gameplay basically goes from surviving through build and resource optimization (and taking what fights you can walk away from relatively unscathed), to beating the AI and the environment (fights rated impossible become a breeze) entirely and without any more challenge. Huge space for improvement here.2) Fighting system: you can rarely deploy your whole army, which makes a battle actually a string of small battles than one big fight. This makes for long and fairly passive/repetitive stretches of play, apart from spells and some direction you can give your army, as you're just watching variations of the same battle otherwise. This results in frustrating attrition levels even during "easy" battles (some of which can and will wipe out your army). Some unit and hero abilities can break this somewhat, by raising the number of troops you can field at once, or getting enemy units to fight for you, The tactical aspect, beyond unit mix and initial placement, is not very present. 3) Artifacts: in 25h of play, I think I maybe could get 3 pieces of an artifact set once. This feature just does not work. Even with the plunder hero ability that spawns artifacts after battles, you might get 10 copies of an "ultimate" level artifact during a playthrough, but you'll be stuck with 3 incomplete sets that you will never find the 3rd item for. Artifacts also become fairly anecdotal in power once you find an OP building to abuse.The city and resources management are ok, the special buildings on the map are also interesting, with a few that can be abused to deliver overpowered results. Abusing such buildings is the single most powerful mechanic to get a win in this game, and by far. I am pretty sure this isn't what the devs set out to achieve. It would be great if the core gameplay could provide opportunities to make meaningful decisions and get ahead rather than relying on what feels like exploiting a design loophole.

_childDocuments_.review: I've dropped a decent bit of time in now and think I've experienced a fair bit of the game. So far, after playing the Beta a bit and seeing the direction it's going, I like it. It's a fun game, with a lot of depth and the factions on the surface may seem similar, but with time to flesh out this will be a very fun game. Right now the issues I see are the lack of proper diversity with the cities, and only having a single city per region basically makes any bonuses to help defend the city are virtually useless. Complaints about the game being too hard are simply being made by people that are bad at video games. I've beaten a few games on easy and normal now and it's certainly not too hard. The complaint I will say is that there's virtually only one 'valid' play style, otherwise the game *is* impossible. In order to actually beat the game now, you basically have to throw all your units into a single doom-stack and run that around the map clearing out your starting area. If you don't do this, you'll capture everything in your area way too late and when you AI comes for you, you'll never stand a chance as they will simply doom-stack as well. There's virtually no viable way to make smaller armies useful right now because of the doom-stacks. If a lower unit cap was put on the generals, I think you'd greatly increase the play styles that were viable and allow people to actually think about their army comp beyond making their doom stack. Also, the inclusion of no proper multiplayer is baffling to me, why wasn't that out on release? You can steam play together with a friend and it actually works very well, but no proper multiplayer really should have been out on launch. So overall, a very good first impression, I do think it needs work and don't think it's 'complete' yet at all. I'm going to call it a 3.5/5 and with a few updates and a few small tweaks this will easily move up to 4.5 or 5 even. I don't regret the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the HoMM3 successor that ' New World Computing,/Contraband Entertainment' never quite managed.  Hero's Hour evolves the game-play by adding more choices with more depth, and having a real-time auto battle system.   It took me a couple of battles before i started enjoying the auto battle system, due to me: 1. expecting it to be a turn based battle (HoMM3 style) 2. Understanding what agency i had i had as a player during the battles.   However, 10 hours in and I believe this Auto-Battle system is a perfect choice to change up the (HoMM3) formula, reinventing it and keeping battles fun and engaging.Building up your settlements/armies and exploring the map is never dull.  Hero's Hour has a very fun world with tons of variety for replay-ability. This is a great game for those who enjoy HoMM3 style games, but want something new & interesting from the genre. A couple of things I wish were a little different are: 1. It took me a minute to adjust to the super low res pixel art, it is not bad by any standard, but the sprites could use more definition/clarity,2. Turn times for cpu players takes a while, it feels like they are taking their turn in real-time.  These are both minor issues when compared to whats on offer in Hero's Hour and I am sure I will get many more hours of fun out of this game.  Cheers G
