_childDocuments_.review: This game is really cute and relaxing to play. I haven't found card games interesting in the past, but the strength of this one is that you can just fumble your way through and learn more strategy as you go. The developer is really active and responds to things quickly. I'm fairly confident this game is only going to improve and grow. It would be a little more reassuring if it were in early access, as there are a few things that need a little more polish to really shine. Namely: More story content! I also hope in the future we'll have more to do with our Spirits than just walk around and feed them. Maybe they could help on the farm? Maybe wild spirits interfere with our crops or we have to deal with pests, blights, ect. The farming element is too easy to automate at the moment. I never use my watering can.The strength of the game really is in building your own little home and garden. I'm very carefully managing my trees so I don't cut them all down, which is something I appreciate. A lot of games respawn trees so fast you never have to worry, but this one requires a little more thought. It makes resources more finite which I hope has a solution down the track... maybe something you can unlock? A bit like the grow staff?Highly recommend. I've got a lot of hope for this turning out something super special, but in the meantime it is a joy to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island is a game that brings together several genres and mixes them into one fantastic experience, from its life-sim to its dungeon exploration, monster-catching and card battling. It aims for and revolves around inclusion and diversity, and the personalities of each cast member make you want to get to know them. Despite having a full plate of mechanics, the studio has managed to prove that they didn't bite off more than they can chew, and have left me in awe with this true gem of a game.The title follows the story of our character, a young girl (as I understand it has no defined gender, but for review purposes I'll use she) who is preparing to begin a journey away from her home and family, in pursuit of completing her alchemist training. In between some quick basic tutorials, we'll get a medallion that will allow us to store Spirits (I'll get to this), and after a touching farewell, the protagonist will set off on her flying broom; though it won't last long, as one thing will lead to another and she'll end up crashing on an unknown island. What a rocky start! Fortunately, the island where our character fell is inhabited, and together with the villagers who live there, we will begin our adventure.To begin with, we'll have to settle down. We can choose the outskirts of town or rent a room; but come on, who wouldn't want to set up their own little ranch in this kind of game!? As for me, I chose to stay in the vicinity, although the game hinted that I could go live on any of the many islands that make up the world, I thought it would be wise to be close to civilization; mostly because of the creatures that dwell in the unknown.These creatures are called Spirits, and they can be tamed to help us on our journey with different types of elements such as fire or darkness, and having their own strengths and weaknesses. To capture these Spirits, we'll have to feed them (instead of throwing balls or other stuff at them), and once in our team they'll be able to level up and get new abilities in the form of cards. Everyone has their own deck of cards, but we must be careful not to make it too big so that we don't draw bad hands.While we're on the subject of critters, I'll mention combat, which is turn-based and puts us in control of a maximum of three Spirits, which can be fed to get a buff; and we can also harm enemies with other types of plants or potions. All creatures have four stats: Vitality, Speed, Power and Armor. Armor is quite important, since it negates most of the attacks weaker than it’s value (that don’t target a creature's weakness), so I always tried to reduce that number with different cards to make fights easier. But if you are looking for more than just combat against fluffy, slimy, or burning beasts... you can also enjoy other aspects of the game, such as farming. Earlier I mentioned the food and potions, related mostly to crops that we can plant and harvest in the four seasons; and potions, which are the product of alchemy, resulting in various combined bonuses, both good and bad (for example, they can debuff Vitality or Power, making enemies weaker).In addition to growing our own veggies and fruits (and hands, and eyes; there are many rare and cool plants out there), we'll also be able to find wild flora and get their seeds to enrich our plantations, and I can't deny that I was very excited for a new season to arrive to go out and explore and collect new seeds. Now, in order to start our crop empire, we'll have to use stamina, with tools to plow the land and water the plants, and we can improve them with the village blacksmith.Let me take a step back and broaden our horizons, painting a bit of a picture of the world. The environment around us is made up of floating islands in the sky, and among these islands we can find materials, seeds, Spirits and various other little things. Now, each island has a hidden mine where you can collect minerals such as bronze and iron, which you can find by breaking rocks until you find the entrance.Apart from the mines, some islands have altars: mystical structures that will grant us one of three bonuses: remove, add, or improve a card from a Spirit's deck; and these altars felt crucial to me, because they facilitate the customization of each deck, and also, they reset in each season so we can reuse them. Speaking of seasons, I loved the colors used for each one, especially Fall with that soft cream palette, super pretty.Different islands also have their own biomes, plants and Spirits, varying from plains or beaches to volcanic areas, or corrupted by darkness. Some areas are more hostile than others, both because of the level of the Spirits and the hazards of the environment itself; for example, heat zones will constantly drain our energy. This can be partially, or even completely, mitigated with objects that we can craft to make exploration more enjoyable, fortunately.Something I also want to comment on are the dungeons: mazes with traps, puzzles, enemies, treasures and bosses, where fragments of the memories of a mysterious wizard are hidden. Finally, among all the islets scattered around the world, there are some mysterious temples that house artifacts inside, part of a parallel plot with a very cool outcome and a challenging final fight.Having mentioned the wizard, I'll take the opportunity to delve into the topic of townies. If we like to socialize, we'll be able to befriend a diverse cast of characters, chatting with them, completing quests, giving them gifts or asking them out. All characters can be asked out, no exception, including the wizard (no one is safe from us here). I guess that being stuck on an island seeing the same faces everyday can hit harder than I'd think, which is why they are all available; and the main character is adorable so I don't blame them.I really loved this section, as the variety and inclusion of characters was something newer to me than what I'm used to, and since I'm a big fan of the social aspect in games I feel they've done a great job. Conversing and learning about the characters, getting attached to them and growing fond of their personalities, are feelings that these types of mechanics convey very well, and on more than one occasion I found myself moved by a single speech bubble accompanied by a portrait; what else is there to say?While we're at it, I'll make a small mention of the visual section, which is exquisite, both the environments and the sprites of characters and Spirits. The portraits are charming, I adore them! Hand in hand with the art goes the audio, which is also very pretty, but left me wanting a bit more. I don't know if it was because of the early access or if it was intentional, but many times the music ended and I was left listening only to ambient sounds; which, for some may be relaxing, but personally I found myself looking for a playlist outside the game to fill in those gaps.In conclusion, Moonstone Island is a game that impressed and fascinated me with its mix of mechanics and how they were implemented. There are various things to entertain us such as going fishing, decorating the house, etc; there are crafting designs hidden in chests, a few transportation methods to liven up the journey, buried treasures, and more. It's full of cute details, like our little Spirits running after us adorably, and a sense of progression that feels very neat.Definitely one of the life-sim games I've enjoyed the most, and I've played from the early Harvest Moon and Rune Factory to the one that I think revitalized the genre contemporarily, Stardew Valley. I do feel that it lacks some things, but that's just me and because of comparisons that are not relevant. I really enjoyed the proposal, and the truth is that I see a lot of potential in the future, although that's for another time! I highly recommend it to genre lovers, and to those who are looking for an inclusive and extremely wholesome game.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun stardew alternative with plants used as battle items and pokeballs. Overall very surface-level game but entertaining enough to keep playing. My main issues are creature variety and direction. The creatures are basically the exact same besides their starting ability. Moves and stats are fully customizable which means getting new units doesn't have much impact. My other gripe is that there's almost no goal or direction. I'm getting to the point where I'm asking myself "why am I doing this"? It's almost exploration just for the sake of exploration. That said, the gameplay loop is fun enough that I can see myself continuing for awhile. Just wish there were more events and quests giving you goals and pushing you to do things differently.

I love the card game style play when you're in battles too. This brings together a lot of the elements of GAMES (video, card, board, etc.) that I enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun, it's cute, and it's all I could ever ask for in a game. It has multiple play styles to keep players coming back to it. Want to explore? It's got that! Want to battle little monsters? It's got that too! What to build and decorate? Say no more! The characters are fleshed out and diverse, with lots of charm and wit. The world is great, the music is bopping, and I cannot find a reason to not love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game, but with some caveats. If you like monster collection games, farming games, and card games, you will almost certainly get some fun out of this one. Game has heavy ghibli studio inspiration, good music, and a really relaxing game play atmosphere/loop - you will for sure get 20+ hours of enjoyment out of this game, no need to spoil your fun just go get it. Don't let the rest of the review sour playing the game for you.Now for some things that may turn people off the game if they are on the fence still:First off, it's impossible not to think of the phrase "an ocean a mile wide but only an inch deep" while playing this game. Sure, there are tons of islands, and ~70 monsters to explore and collect, but they are virtually all the same. Same thing with the dungeons, there is very little uniqueness to any of them. You've seen a few dungeons, you have seen them all. All of the monsters have extremely similar cards, the abilities on them don't change much - and even the different species of monsters all have fairly little difference between them. There is a little bit of nuance to some species, but even then it's all just kind of meh. If you play optimally most people would probably end up with pretty similar strategies I'd imagine - as there isn't really that much unique play styles between the monsters. Pretty simple to get a near infinite loop going for cheese, or later game you're really just stacking damage and ways to play more cards. There is a wide variety of plants, and lots are actually useful in their own ways, but the plants you get from the later seasons are quite a bit more powerful than earlier ones that you really should almost sleep speed run through your first year.  Then there are the characters - I will be honesty this was probably my least explored option. I didn't do any dates, and only got to ~4/10 hearts with most people. It is possible this is where a lot of the story get's developed, but aside from 1 or 2 characters, none really intrigued me that much. The whole year they all say pretty generic stuff for the most part - again, maybe the dating system REALLY fleshes them out, but I never was interested enough to engage much in it. Also, if your not really for the whole "woke" thing, that will be a huge turn off for you as nearly every character seems to be gender non-conforming or gay. I know technically this is the same thing as something like stardew valley, but gender ideology among the characters seems to be much more prevalent in this game (each character has gender and pronouns for themselves with lots of non-binary they/thems, most characters have dyed hair, strong female characters, feminine male characters ect). For me it's whatever, but there was a couple parts where I couldn't help but think "put a chick in it and make her gay and lame!". Lastly there is a swath of kind of poor coding things/minor annoyances. As an example, planting huge crops is a major pain because the clicking to place stuff is pretty inconsistent, and not smooth like it is in stardew valley. I have to really move my mouse around and character around all over to make sure everything plants properly. Harvesting you have to constantly move - stop - harvest. It's just not as smooth as most people would probably be used too from other farming games. There were a few crashes I had from entering/leaving dungeons while a monster attacked me resulting in some decent time loss. Getting around all the islands can be a bit of a slog - even with the max upgraded movement device it still takes a while to get around. Early game getting some resources is an absolute pain just to do things you need to do for the main game loop (like getting stalls that auto-feed, tool upgrades, buildings ect.). Some things also aren't explained in game very well, like for example resources on some islands need a stronger scythe to harvest - I had to look it up to know that. Lots of little things that just could have been smoothed out with maybe a teleport device or some easier acquisition of some resources. There are also temples - which are like little trials that you get a new item - the issue is the items you get basically are only used for that temple that can be ignored. Stuff like that just makes me think the game wasn't fully fleshed out or some ideas didn't get polished. And that is kind of where I see it now - good game, but a lot of features just didn't get that ending polish that would have made it a great game. Is it good to blow through a weekend or a few days to satisfy some game A.D.D.? Totally - is it a game I will likely keep coming back to and starting a new file like stardew valley, probably not. Just not enough depth, not much of an end game, and doing one thing of a certain type you have pretty well done all of it. So give it a go - but don't expect a mind blowing experience.

_childDocuments_.review: “Pokemon Stardew Valley” is… an inept description for Moonstone Island. This game isn’t particularly like either of them. It’s a collectible monster combat-focused deck builder that has cozy elements (such as farming and friendship) which support the combat. You farm to buff and heal your spirits, and villager quests encourage your engagement in the spirit related mechanics. This is the mindset with which this game should be viewed.The combat mechanics are great! Keep in mind, I’m not a massive deck builder person, and don’t have much to compare with other than my minimal experience with Pokemon, Digimon, and that one time my Dad tried to teach me Magic: the Gathering. I think the combat is fun, tricky, and allows for lots of versatility in terms of builds. Status conditions feel a bit overpowered, but maybe once I start using some on my team I’ll feel a bit differently. The armor and bash/dizzy mechanics are very fun though, and provide a layer beyond “most damage card.” I might choose Mind Spike over Memorize because it reduces armor, even if it’s weaker.On the other hand, the “cozy” mechanics are… In theory, very fun. I like the idea of farming to train and care for your spirits, rather than the typical “Fantasy Capitalism” of the cozy farming genre. (Not that fantasy capitalism is bad, but it’s nice to have a change of pace!) I like that you gather seeds by exploring, rather than by purchasing them. I really really like the EXP plants, and I’m excited to see how well they eliminate the end game grind.That said, I hate actually doing any farming, specifically because of how object placement works. I have the same issue with decorating and base building, but at the very least most objects can be picked up and moved around. Seeds? If you place them wrong, you’re stuck until they’re full grown, and it’s way too easy to misplace a seed. You can’t place seeds on the tile you’re on, and for whatever reason, aiming at which tile you want to place a seed on is… incredibly difficult? I have the same issue with decor/object/chest/building placement, and it’s even worse because of the limited range that your player character can actually reach. You have to be very close to the tile you want to place the item on, but can’t be standing on that tile. It’s… frustrating, and has led to me basically demolishing and resetting my fields for farming so that I can keep them more organized even when I misclick.A lot of people complain about the friendship mechanics in this game. Personally, I love them! I don’t typically engage in friendship mechanics (and when I do it’s because I’m getting something out of it), but I find them quite fun here! There’s a large element of rng, which is… probably the draw for me. You don’t really need to care about the characters, but when you interact with them, talk or joke a few times to raise those friendship points. I like that you can see the numeric increase or decrease on a success or failure. There aren’t a lot of characters either, which definitely helps too. My biggest issue with the game is the threat of finite resources. Specifically wood, stone, coal, copper, iron, and fiber… which are most of the resources in the game. Copper and Iron can be purchased directly, while wood, stone, coal, and fiber can be purchased indirectly (i.e. buy a sapling, grow a tree, chop it down, get wood). This technically makes these resources infinite, but there’s definitely frustration in the fact that you’ll eventually have to pay for them. Yes, every island has a mine, lots of trees, lots of stones, and massive plains of grass… but at no point do they ever respawn naturally. They’re so abundant it’s unlikely you’ll ever run out, but there’s the threat that they do, which deters long-term gameplay, as well as hesitance when crafting that can hinder progression.To add onto this, another frustrating progression hinderer is the Ando Acolyte skill in the skill tree. This requires at least two archaeology points, and at the end of each dungeon, gives you ten more max stamina. This means an extra 300 max stamina, total. If you clear the dungeon and claim your stamina before having this skill, however, you can’t go back and claim the extra stamina from the skill. You can potentially be locked out of an entire 300 stamina (For context, you start with 300). This is a massive issue, and one that made me debate resetting my save file. I will never have those 20 stamina I missed from clearing two dungeons, and it’s incredibly frustrating -- especially since you need to clear dungeons to get the points to get the skill. (A workaround for this, by the way, is to clear the temples first, and fight wilderness bosses that aren’t in dungeons. Or just don’t claim the stamina from the dungeons until you get the skill). There’s one or two other skills that make this offense, but nothing quite so egregious. With that out of the way, let’s talk about something I do like! Holos! Basically, this game’s equivalent of shiny pokemon. Like shiny pokemon, holographics are a visual difference, and that’s it. They’re way more common than shinies, but I have yet to encounter one. (Thankfully -- I really don’t wanna find one above my taming level limit!) Still, the concept of their existence is going to make me plug so many more hours into this game. To end us off, here’s some smaller points I don’t feel super positively or negatively about. Firstly is the number of spirits you can keep at once -- 120 (or technically 123, including your party). It’s enough to have one of every species (69), but not two, which is kind of a let down but also kind of fine. I like that you can have multiple bases, and decorate them however you like -- and I love that all of your houses link to the same interior, so you don’t have to shuffle resources around between bases. I wish fishing was explained better in game, because I currently have only ever fished to get a specific fish for a request. I wish there were more short term quests, or at least a help wanted board like in Stardew Valley because I often feel as though I have no direction and I’m just… waiting for things to happen.All in all, I definitely recommend giving it a try! It has its issues, but I find myself enjoying the game when I play it. I can binge it for hours on end and still be having fun. I may be slightly obsessed with it at the moment. I may be wishing the wiki page had more details. Still! Play it! Very fun! and worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: There's just too much going on in this game. While it's cute and can almost scratch the itch I needed scratched, I feel like it misses the mark.The game starts out promising but then it just.....introduces way too much. Between crafting, creature collecting, resource management, relationship building, exploring. There's just....way too much to do in too little of a day. _childDocuments_.review: Reminiscent of Stardew Valley, Rune Factory, and Pokémon, Moonstone Island gives a fresh take on the beloved farming / dating sim game. Complete with mysterious quests, a card-based battle system, the ability to go on actual dates, decorations galore, and your dream of becoming the best alchemist possible, this adorably stylized game has a little bit of something for everyone. A relaxing and low-pressure game (albeit with some challenging achievements for the go-getters out there), Moonstone Island has a charming allure that will have you coming back for more (even if it's just figuring out how to master that darn fishing minigame!).
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game. Combat feels fine; interacting with the villagers, for me, always bounced between mildly interesting and boring, its execution, especially when it comes to the "Talk", "Joke" and "Flirt" Options seemed a bit shallow, but it's fine; exploration is fun, more so in the beginnning (since it can get repetitive after some time); and the whole Stardew Valley-esque farming experience is ... servicable, though, for me, not really that interesting. Overall, intermixing all these different ideas, between the monster taming, floating island exploration and farming sim alongside the cute aesthetic of the game does lend itself well to developing its own identity. But what it does desperately lack, in my opinion (though this may of course change with later updates and patches), is polish and QoL:- Having to use your medaillon every time you want to interact with your team of monsters in ANY way (be that to heal, use items or level up) gets rather tedious quite fast. It doesn't take THAT long for a single time, but since you want to interact with your team in a game like this regularly, it quickly compounds to one giant annoyance. Having to go through an animation and a short loading/blackscreen TWICE every time i want to change something about my team, is discouraging to say the least, That admittedly wasnt so bad i stopped playing, but it does drag the experience of exploring and fighting for one long day down quite a bit. - I don't really understand why Furnaces are made to be so impractical to use. As of now, you can only have one ingot cooking per furnace at once, and you cannot put in more ore to queue up multiple ingots to be smelted at a singular furnace right after one another. This would do a lot to make smelting ingots FEEL a lot better. There are few things more satisfying in video games than returning home to slam all of your hard-earned ores into the oven. Here, you're kinda ♥♥♥♥-blocked out of that unless you want to completely spam your home or its surroundings with furnaces, which even then, would still not be as satisfying.- I feel like the game lets you overdose on quests just a bit. This is of course highly subjective: Having a lot of content can be a good thing, but I'm not the biggest fan of looking at my quest journal only to be bombarded with an entire encyclopedia of having stuff to do; it often leads to diluting the quality of the quest experience in games, since your attention is constantly split between eight different tasks, so each individual one loses a lot of importance to the player. - For some reason, you can't just hold your mouse button to quickly stash stuff into your chest, neither can you (i think) press any button combination like shift+rightclick or ctrl+rightclick or smth of the sort to immediately stash an entire stack of items into your chest; selling more than one item at once also requires you to press your way through arrows or use A/D buttons, instead of having a way to just sell an entire item stack on the spot, which you'd usually want to do in this sort of game.- You also cannot buy multiple items in any shop by holding down a mouse button as far as I've been able to discern, though honestly, that might be smth i simply missed.... and a bunch more nitpicks that ultimately come together to bring the whole experience down by just a bit, NONETHELESS, I have been enjoying my time with the game, I just feel it needs some more time in the oven, a bit more polish and QoL to tighten the whole game experience. It has interesting ideas, perhaps the execution falters at times, but all of this doesn't detract from the fact that love has been put into this game, and its fun!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun, it's a much simplified version of stardew valley IMO, the biggest problem is that there's a huge number of bugs. I crash to desktop several times an hour playing. I've posted bug reports and requested help but there doesn't seem to be any real understanding of what happening. Maybe in a few months they'll fix the issues and I'll give it another shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: It starts strong with a very solid card battling system and the familiar appeal of creature collection, but once I realized how shallow the farming/life sim aspect is I lost interest. There are very few crafting recipes that actually give you a gameplay advantage, so there isn't much to strive for like in other farming sims. The characters you can interact with are dull and flat, so I felt no incentive to get to know them (plus, the only way to do so is to go on cringey "dates" with them, which is a pretty restrictive way to frame your game's social system.)I'm sure you could min/max your farm for optimal yields, but there doesn't seem to be a reason to. Consumables are easy to hoard in mere days, and almost every craftable that serves any sort of purpose other than aesthetics is easy to obtain early on. This in turn makes it so the only real reason to make money is to make your house slightly bigger or put up a new wall hanging. I know this appeals to some people, but it's pretty much all there is aside from a few simple quests.This leaves us with the exploration and dungeoncrawilng, which is fun for a bit after you unlock the glider but quickly becomes same-y. Every dungeon feels the same, every battle feels like either a cakewalk or a level gate that you're not prepared for with little in-between. The spirits are cute, but combat is generally so easy to blitz through that there isn't much reason to put thought into your party composition (and swapping them out is an arbitrarily complicated mess of a process.)I know this game is perfect for some people, but if you're expecting complex mechanics or a game that will do much more than just give you a way to pass time, this probably isn't it.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who loves the cozy game genre but is feeling slightly burnt out from farming sims, this game is a breath of fresh air. It does feature farming and decorating, which I love, but the other aspects of the game, like the ability to discover new islands, travel by balloon or broom, and the turn based fighting with really uniquely designed spirits has me out of my gaming slump and really excited to progress in the game. I've played about two hours and I'm already obsessed. This is a really wholesome game that brought a lot of joy to my day.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game at the tail-end of 2023 and it very very quickly became a GOTY contender. As someone who appreciates the style of games like Pokemon, Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing but rarely feel like they suck me in for long, Moonstone Island is a perfect blend for me.Honestly, the fact that it let's you change the duration of the day to suit your playstyle is an absolute godsend. I'm very grateful I stumbled on this game and I'll forever be its champion! 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: 100% at 105 hours w. all current DLCs installed - the game was very enjoyable! At no point did it feel like it was dragging or grinding out days, relations, or exp. The cast of characters is diverse and there are lots of types of activities to complete.The deck building plays like Slay the Spire, the relationship and resources systems are similar to Stardew Valley, and a 'collect them all' creature research aspect gives it a slight Pokemon vibe; all of which are games I've thoroughly enjoyed as well. The way the play styles meld together in this game is very smooth and endearing, and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys those games.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game. I am inexperienced with classic games like OG Pokemon, Zelda, and other pixel games, but my husband says this game seems like a combination of those plus Stardew Valley. The color scheme of this game is lovely/distinct, so I can easily differentiate objects in this world. ( I struggle with Stardew Valley.) The character you play is gender neutral and uncustomizable. I love making my characters in games, but this character is unique/cute so I was not disappointed having to leave them be. The exploration is fun, as well as dungeon diving, spirit (pokemon) collecting, and being able to customize the inside of your home. <3 I also love that the characters are romancable! .Only 16 dates per character so keep that in mind- it can't last forever :'( . However, you can marry your chosen person and have an adorable wedding. Then the person will actually walk around your house when they are not working. I was thrilled by that given my last game (Fae Farm) your spouse only sat outside on a bench by your home. I have never played a deck building game, but I actually enjoyed that being the fighting style in this game. It was more strategic than just bashing enemies. Farming is actually useful as you/your spirits get unique stat boosts from the various seasonal crops. Plus you'll need specific crops for a several quests, so I'd recommend upgrading your scythe early and harvest all the crops' seeds within each season. (Or be like me and have to wait until year 2 to finish some of the earliest quests) Trust me, it'll be better to hop on those sooner than later. But all around I thought this game was very unique in its mixture of styles. The story line is a little vague, but I didn't mind that. So cozy and fun. Definitely will recommend to my friends.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! The only issue I really have with it is that compared to stardew valley or sun haven the controls feel clunkey(sp?) for lack of a better word. Also unlike those types of games u can't use tools on the tile ur character is on.It's such a minor issue and nothing a couple more hours playing can't fix I'm sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game. There is plenty to do and explore throughout the game and can keep you occupied for a long time doing various things. A few things I’d like to see changed is the time in the game seems to go to fast. Clearing out wood, stone or grass depletes the stamina pretty quick. You can eat things to recover this alittle but I’d rather be able to put my character to sleep to recover the stamina and have that count against time and then be able to wake up and explore whatever time it is. Sometimes I’ll be right out of stamina by 12 and then meander around or just put my character to bed the rest of the day. There seems to be plenty of things to do. I’f I go to buy something in a shop, it would be nice to have everything in your chests linked so you don’t have to go grab a bunch of stuff and put it in your backpack. What ever cost of wood for example would just be reduced right from the chests. But there is plenty of room in the chests to store stuff and it’s a minor thing. It’s great that the devs seem to be on top of the game, always working to patch things or improve the game and you really can’t ask for more. Totally worth the price of the game and totally worth buying the DLCs to help support these devs. Fun game and A++++ for the entire development of it. Thanks a bunch!
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: This game needs some love from the developer... It's in a rough state right now. The characters are charming on the surface level, and the art is nice... That's about where the positive things I have to say end. MOONSTONE IS A BLIGHT! Only getting 1-2 from each island is absolute abysmal. The ramping up from the early ores being available in excess to needing moonstone for damn near everything in large quantities is absurd. Also making the barn require 3 moonstone right off the bat to even start collecting creatures in a game where capturing a ton of these little/big guys is the main idea is asinine. There needs to be some sort of early game creature inventory and maybe another tier of ore to help make the early-mid-late game jumps not feel so soul crushing and grind-y. My other major complaint is that the writing and depth of the characters and interactions are abysmally shallow. It's not even a voiced game, there is room to have more dialogue, and it's an easy fix, but the characters all feel so shallow... For a life sim type game I want more depth please and thank you.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- The gameplay is exactly what I was looking for to pass the time. Even though I disliked Pokémon, I really liked the fighting mechanics here.- The overall visuals are cute!Cons:- The lack of a compelling storyline and narrative depth. There was an attempt, though.- Time management (a common complaint). Some trying to defend it compared it to Stardew Valley, but Moonstone Island has a significantly larger world with a Lot of islands to explore.- The NPCs are ones I couldn't care less about. Talking to them is minimalistic (they just mutter a single sentence), and lacks engagement (RNG-based, really?).While I did enjoy the gameplay in Moonstone Island, the game's expected duration of 40-50 hours doesn't compel me to continue playing beyond the 20 hours I've already invested.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love this game! Between the music, graphics, mechanics, and characters, this game is the cutest and scratched my itch for a new cozy sim game. I really love it and even got my boyfriend into it! It is a perfect mix of farm sim + 8-bit graphics + monster catcher + jammin' tunes. It's great for relaxation and I don't feel the rush to have to fit every single thing into the day and squeeze out all the time I need. Sometimes I pass out at 2am but don't really mind. _childDocuments_.review: I would recommend looking at this game more as a game about collecting monsters, building your deck, exploring, farming, crafting, and finding resources.The social aspect of the game at this point is a bit bare-bones, there is little to do after you get maximum hearts with someone. Sure you can go on dates to their house and get unique dialogue but besides that there isn't mush to do in terms of interacting with the characters at later stages. I wish different villagers could help you with different tasks, like Gaiana helping you farm or Ferra collecting and mining ores but there is no reward or progression earned when you choose a romantic partner.Besides that I really enjoy the game, there are lots of dungeons to explore, and creatures to catch, which makes exploring the wider world quite fun. After you explore you use the resources you got to farm different plants for different buffs, feed your spirits, and manage their combat decks/moves. The combat system is "Slay the Spire" style deck builder with each card using energy and only getting a certain amount of energy per turn, and can be surprisingly difficult when you are exploring new areas. The better you get and/or your spirits get, the more areas you can explore, completing the core gameplay loop.In Short:Explore for resources and spirits -> Farm/Craft items to aid in battle or exploration -> Manage your spirits (Your deck) -> Fight monsters -> Explore more areasI wish the social aspect of the game was more interesting and more rewarding, other than that I find fighting, farming, and exploring really fun and addicting. Good game!

I stopped interacting with the townspeople very early, and stopped talking to my partner after getting in a relationship since nothing really changed. • What is the point of a labyrinth when you have an item that let's you teleport to the end?• The bridges that I built at the start of the game to other islands were a big pain after I got a better mode of transportation. And there seemingly was no way to remove them quickly. _childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island is more of a decorating and monster battling game than a farming sim. Don't be too put off if the farming controls feel a little awkward; you might end up doing very little farming by hand. Even from early in the game, I had my plants watered with sprinklers and spent the time exploring the islands and dungeons instead, collecting spirits and setting up my home base. Island resources do not regenerate, but trees and rocks and grass can be obtained and replanted, and this gives the player a huge amount of control over their environment. You are not likely to run out of resources, as these too can be bought, and there are a huge number of islands, each with its own surface materials and mine. The town is populated entirely by young, cute people, all of them marriage candidates. Information is learned about them by inviting them on dates, which really should be done starting from early on, rather than waiting until you want to commit to someone. They're less flirty than the NPCs in Littlewood, but players averse to flirting will miss a considerable amount of character development, as well as information about the world. Hunting for the rare holographic spirits adds longevity to the game. Save files are nicely separated from each other and can even be named. which isn't apparent at first.

_childDocuments_.review: 6.5/10 Decent, but not quite on the level of Stardew Valley or Graveyard Keeper. A lot of small problems (examples below) create minor, but consistent frustrations that prevent the game from being truly great.1.) Poor Interface- Have to click sell good, press left to select max quantity, press down to move to 'yes', then click again to complete sale. For every, single, thing. Need an option to turn off confirm and another to default to max stacks. Or maybe you could make the sell box work like every other game like this in existence: put stuff in, and it sells at end of day.- Feeding spirits (to heal them) requires going into a Spirit Barn or taking a turn in-combat. If you try and use a potion from your menu, your character eats it instead.- Trying to place an item correctly is so annoying. There's like, a two-pixel window for the square I'm trying to hit, so I gotta inch up and down over and over to find the sweet spot to place that fence post in-between the other two fence posts instead of one up or one down from it.- Needing to swap to broom to fly over one-space gaps in dungeon. Glider doesn't work, even though it's better.- Flippers need to be selected as active tool to use. Just make them automatic, for god's sake.- Same for charms. Make a key item or equipment screen so I don't have to carry those things around in my inventory for the rest of the game.- Quest location markers would be... appreciated. So would the ability to add markers to maps, so I can keep track of which islands I've cleared so far this Season. Especially with, you know, the INVISIBLE but DESPERATELY NEEDED resource that respawns at a rate of ONE PER ISLAND every season.- For the love of all that is good, make it so crafting stations can pull from nearby chests. This is unforgivable for a crafting game these days.- FAST TRAVEL SYSTEM (and if there is one, but I haven't unlocked it in the first 25 hours of the game, then FAST TRAVEL SYSTEM AVAILABLE EARLIER)2.) Information is Unavailable- Skills menu is, as far as I can tell, ONLY viewable in-between days when you're levelling up.- No indicator for what levels each island is, which is a BIG frustration. Especially considering #3.- No functional status menu or HUD display for Spirits. Have to go into the Status menu to see their health. - No encyclopedia, of any kind. So no way to tell how long it takes a seed to grow, if the seed re-grows, what it'll sell for, what fish can be found on which island, how to unlock specific recipes. I'm 25 hours in, and the brush I need for my spirits is still greyed out, but I have no idea how to get it.- Some skills seem to be locked if you pick the other skill it's linked to. Can I switch these later? Does it cost an extra skill point? Is there a way to reset skills? I don't know, because the game doesn't tell me. Refer to the game's guide (AKA Google) for the 20th time.- Crafting stations need time indicators.3.) With Spirits each having their own abilities, you'd figure you'd want a group of levelled, deck-customized spirits ready to go for whatever challenge you're about to face, but the game makes this such a pain. There's no XP share or extra slots in your roster, and with swapping spirits between party, barn, and science centre, it's super annoying trying to find an island that your spirits can farm reliably but is also worth decent XP. I'm experimenting with using crops to level instead, but that's time-gated.4.) Balance issues. Poison and Burn are serious problems. If there's a way to heal them, I don't know what it is, and the game doesn't tell you. There's one dungeon where the guardian drops about 16-24 poison stacks on the very first round, which bypasses armor and will wipe my entire team in 2-3 turns.

_childDocuments_.review: Going into Moonstone Island I knew it was going to be a game For Me.  Creature collectors are the genre that brings me the most joy, and card battles are up there as well,  I've even been known to dabble in life-sims, so why not?  I came in expecting one of these aspects to fall short, they often do when a development team is juggling so many genres, but to my surprise and great excitement, that was not the case.The creature designs, the card mechanics, and the life-sim elements are all strong on their own and feed in to each-other in satisfying ways.  I found myself carefully juggling my time as I rushed out to find a new mine to harvest, constantly watching the clock to make sure I didn't miss my next date.  The world was wide and fun to explore, and it made the time constraints feel way more engaging than in this game's contemporaries. I always needed just ONE MORE HOUR to finish my list of goals for the day.  I really need to load up on Time Dilation Potions...The card battle system is comparable to something like Slay-the-Spire, with each element of spirit being a "class" with a shared draw pool.  All of the cards in a particular element have interesting identity and synergy, making each one feel like a unique playstyle.  On top of that, each spirit within an element has a special ability unique to their type that further tweaks how this base class plays, sort of like the more interesting relics within a run of Slay the Spire.  Every new creature I found tickled my brain as I wondered about their own specific synergies, except for the spirits who instead changed the way I operated on the overworld!  I was almost more excited for those ones!  Make sure you bring your Snorcko with you if you plan to spend the day fishing!Mechanics aside, special attention needs to be paid to the writing of the game.  All of the villagers on the eponymous Moonstone Island are diverse and interestingly characterised.  It is to my immense shame and regret that I waited until Summer of the first year to engage with the Date system.  At any time, you can ask one of the characters in town to spend a day with you, if you succeed in a dice role (with modifiers based on how much they already like you!) you can go out together at 20:00 and spend the rest of your evening with that character.  There'll you have an engaging conversation, followed by a question.  The correct choice is usually intuitive, but not immediately obvious.  After deliberation, I almost always came to the correct answer, except for one- I fumbled a date with Ferra because I engaged with her on the surface level interpretation of her character, but further conversations with her allowed me to understand the mistake I was making... I came out of the experience with a legitimately better understanding of the character on my screen.  Next time Ferra, we're gonna dig that big ol' hole!  Since you can start going on these dates right at the start of the game, and each of them is comparable to a "heart event" in something like Stardew, you can get right into the fantastic character writing as soon as your start your adventure.  And you should! The dates seem to be by far the fastest way to progress your relationships, and they should not be slept on.  Just make sure you don't die to a dungeon boss and miss the date!I've only played 17 hours so far (all on stream if you're doubting anything I've said so far) and I don't think I have it in me to play anything else until I've seen all the content there is to be found here.  With 84 spirits to collect, 30 dungeons to delve into, and 4 temples to conquer, this is a game that'll keep consuming my mind for many evenings to come.  I hope I helped you decide to give it a look for yourself, it's worthy of every bit of attention it gets!  Just make sure that if you're a completionist, you get yourself a glider and a moonstone scythe as quick as you can.  I'll never forgive myself for missing the dark islands' spring seeds in my first year... If I had just one more day...

_childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island provides many things to do: farming, crafting, spirit taming, dungeoning. I read a google article with just that description and bought the game 5 minutes later. All of it was appealing, entertaining and kept me hooked. I always found something else to do, but what kept me the most busy was exploring the map and spirit taming. I really enjoyed discovering the spirits and their deck themes, or exploring islands and seeing what they had to offer. Most of the time it was treasure, new crops to discover and add to the store's supply, and of course, new spirits! There was so much to uncover and that was a ton of fun.Using the deck-building format for monster taming battles is a fresh take on the genre and what drew me to Moonstone Island. It offers a different experience in each battle depending on how big your deck size is but it also slows down the leveling a bit if you're trying to grind to get your spirits' levels up. Overall though I loved the card system and the amount of customization and synergies available to mix & match spirits is huge. You could go an explosion build with a fire spirit and give it intangible from the psychic spirit deck, and just deal massive damage for 0 cost. Or go poison and burn, bypass shields altogether. The possibilities and theorycrafting are amazing, and adds another deep dimension of exploration.The spirits are cute, refreshing and unique. I do wish there were more ice spirits (since they have a whole separate element) and that they had their own island biome (i.e. frozen mountaintops) but since there are so few at the time of writing this review, I understand. I'm definitely looking forward to better documentation of all the spirits, such as a Dex, containing each elemental deck theme. Viewing card information + upgrades would also be very nice to have, so that I can properly compare which card to upgrade and see what exactly gets upgraded. It's a lot of going back and forth, upgrading, trial & error, removing, which is time-consuming and exhausting; could be a point of frustration for some.I didn't use the potion crafting much, so for me it was a forgotten system. I loved using crops to boost my spirits' stats though, that was nice. The villagers had cute personalities and each had their own thing (except Rowan, I've no idea what they like). I do hope the village gets events added or something to jumpstart the liveliness of the town. It often felt like nothing really happened in town; it was just where you go to chat with people, do commerce and that's it.All in all, Moonstone Island is a lovely developed game with charming soundtracks, beautiful pixel art, deep customization content in both decorations and spirit taming and just a great blend of systems.

_childDocuments_.review: Initially the sheer amount of stuff to do was overwhelming. Farming, crafting, monster collecting, deck building, world exploration, getting to know the villagers, most games would pick two or three of these and run with it. This is definitely not one of them and yet it manages to succeed for the most part.The game starts out with a brief tutorial, then tosses you in the deep end. Early game consists of short trips off the island, looking for mines that hold resources to upgrade your tools, figuring out the battle system and raising villager affection. Slowly you'll make your way farther and farther from your home island, until you unlock the last form of transportation, this is where the bulk of the game opens up. It took a while for me to make the connection, but progression feels very much like Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker.The randomly generated map is divided into a grid, and most squares on the map contain an island that has monsters and seasonally rotating plants to collect based on the island's biome. They can also have a dungeon or shrine that contains treasure and equipment that help you reach new areas or let you create your own shortcuts. There are dozens of islands and while not all of them have something exciting, there is still fun in wondering what the next island may have in store.Story progression is fairly open ended, and the game doesn't do much handholding at all actually, which may turn some players off. The farming and crafting systems are very light, I didn't interact with them much at all. You get access to sprinklers early on and there are far better ways to earn money than growing crops. You can find many of the potions you can brew in chests, most of which become obsolete once you craft items to reduce elemental damage from harsh biomes. The dating sim aspects are totally serviceable, though the decision to bury lore about the world's history unless you date a specific character was kind of strange.Honestly I could ramble on about more specific likes and dislikes, but overall the game's ambitious scope doesn't hold it back too much. No mechanic is truly useless or frustrating, visually it is vibrant and pleasant to look at (though some character customization would have been nice), and the music did not play very often during my game but I also have no complaints there. Again, this is primarily a deckbuilder with a focus on world exploration, if that unusual combo sounds even kind of interesting then I highly recommend you check this game out.

_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good. As of writing this review, farming games / cozy games and creature catchers are pretty stale but Moonstone Island manages bring a very welcome aspect to both, by intertwining these aspects and adding card battling / deck management. The sound design and soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal as well, you won't hear the music 24/7 which is honestly a good thing, because then I can hear the amazing ambience. You can really tell a lot of love went into this game, given the brilliant art design, worldbuilding, and thought that went into it.The game isn't too difficult, even for someone like me who's not overly familiar with card games. It requires some brain usage to maximise your success though, so don't expect a "shut my brain off" experience. There is no yellow paint. The game is a slow burn though, and that's not a bad thing at all. If anything, it works to the game's advantage given the sheer ~vibes~ this game gushes with.The only issues I have with the game are minor, and mostly QOL related. If I had to give any feedback, make it so spirits are semi transparent while atop items / farmland so it's easier to see what the player is doing or picking up.Overall I give Moonstone Island a 9/10, and I'm excited to see where the game goes in future and what future projects the devs are working on.

_childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island feels like a game that should be everything that I like in a game, but falls short on everything.Spirit Collection system feels like there's a lot missing, the combat is fun but often times feels hindered - there are type advantages but I found that this never mattered as much since I had Spirits that could bash, one-shot, and buff each other. The type advantage of breaking 1 single armour felt weak as a consistent mechanic since I could just bash, stun, then one-shot the following turn. You are able to feed and buff your spirits, this also works on wild spirits, but again this mechanic is overshadowed by mid-game because you are able to build spirits such that you can combo them in a single turn.In general the game deters players from collecting spirits, the mechanic of taming a creature is quick and uninteresting, and taming itself depends on the amount of resources you're willing to farm - and continue farming, as it costs a large amount of wood and vegetation to sustain the spirit collection aspect of the game. The lack of evolution's as well as card variety is disappointing.Farming System just feels very shallow, by around 8 hours in I had already unlocked a majority of the tool upgrades, and felt that there was little to no reason to farm (or invest into the tools) as you could easily craft a sprinkler that renders the watering can redundant. There is a wide variety in plants, however, collecting most of them is halted behind very expensive Moonstone crafting recipes. The only reason I was able to collect Fire and Lightning based plants is because I had gotten lucky and found consumables that would allow me to briefly visit these places.Romance/Social System is very underwhelming, NPC dialogue is basic and uninteresting, most NPC's lack any personality or character, and the RNG system of choosing Talk(75%), Joke(30%), and Flirt(15%) feels robotic at most. By the end of the first Season I had maximum affection with a majority (6/11) of the villagers. There is little to go off of with Gifting, and I found that the Gifting mechanic was completely unnecessary since you gain more affection exponentially from talking. Cutscenes give a little bit of personality and character but this is limited to a few lines of dialogue, and I don't enjoy having to ask every character to a date (always at 20:00) just to experience that. I haven't found any reason to enter any of the NPC's houses, the few that I have, had nothing to gain or explore as a player. Overall I just didn't care about the NPC's once I got max affection from them. The time system doesn't mesh well with this game as I found that I would have to cut my exploration short so I can watch a 10 second cutscene where a character talks about their one insecurity. The time system just often times feels so intrusive in a game that's trying to be wholesome.Exploration System was fun to start, but eventually became very tedious. Once I had realised that there are several islands that just house trees, plants, or the occasional Shrine - the exploration aspect became less fun and more work. Spirits will constantly follow you if you don't have a perk (low levels only) and collection animations last so long that the spirits can easily just camp over you and force you into combat. This becomes a problem especially later on when you're on an island that has hazards. Island exploration eventually became a monotonous job of collecting plants or resources, and hoping I could find a precious Moonstone so I can move forward in the game. There is a lack of platforming and methods of scaling the Z axis, which makes exploration often times frustrating, especially when spirits can traverse the Z axis for free. And since most islands lack a variety of uniqueness to them, I would often just tell myself to save the time and just go to a new island.Crafting System is completely redundant, I very rarely needed to craft anything other than bridges and sprinklers an hour into the game, eventually you will need to craft tables that have exclusive recipes, and EVERYTHING is locked behind the precious Moonstones, the game feels so tedious because everything is locked behind the acquisition of moonstones which you get very little of. I think the game visually is beautiful, however my experience playing the game felt shallow, most of the mechanics and systems just lack synchronicity and Moonstone Island falls short because of this. As of right now I do not think it is worth playing and further, I do hope that these systems feed into each other moving forward.

_childDocuments_.review: The core mechanic of this game is a card-based battle system.  As a result of that the game is going to sink or swim based on the core mechanics of that card system.  And..... the card system is very, very boring and lacks anything clever or interesting about it.  Basically either target an enemies armor or HP, and they're HP is nearly inaccessible until you wear down their armor.  Sound boring and lacking any decisions?  Yes, that's precisely correct.  You can tame multiple little critters to your side and each of them have a deck of cards that can be managed.  However, the cards among all critters are generic and boring.  Would have been a much better system to have your main human protagonist do most of the fighting and have the little helper critters just provide some unique benefits.  That way they could all have some unique and interesting reasons to exist.  Looks like they lacked any creative ideas on how to formulate the core systems of the game and just tried to do a bad ripoff of Pokemon instead of anything compelling.  Which is a shame because the rest of the game looks very cute and charming and compelling.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: This is THE comfiest of comfort games. Somehow they've managed to mix farming sim, dating sim, exploration, monster taming, and deck building and make it work. Admittedly, most of these features don't go fully in depth with its capabilities, but it doesn't really have to in this case. The cast of characters is so great and likable, I actually feel bad if I forget to chat to somebody (sorry Cleo!).  The Spirits designs can be quite typical monster designs or the wackiest things and I just love how they don't take themselves too seriously with these. I'm still learning the ropes with the deck building, but I like the possibilities behind them and the fact that each Spirit element has its niche to work with. Devs are so responsive and constantly releasing QOL updates, following player suggestions or feedback, and just making this an even more complete experience with every update. Love the DLCs and will continue to support by buying them. The decoration aspects are so cute. Ps. please more Dark Spirits <3
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, it has all the things i like in a life-sim. Bright, cute visuals, some combat elements, magical stuff, exploration, creature collecting, base building, but that is the problem right there. It feels like they tried to shove everything in this game without asking if it'll all mesh well, and it really doesnt.The combat is fun if you like card games, but gets repetitive very fast. The magic elements are barely utilized at all, sure you get a broom but it all feels very cosmetic. The exploration is based on procedual generation of islands and mines, and like most games that use procedural generation it all just kinda feels like same after a while with some cosmetic differences. Creature collecting is too easy, and there arent nearly enough varieties of spirit to make it worth it, and you dont do nearly enough with them. Base building is empty, theres about a bajillion useless cosmetics you can make in-game to make up for the fact that you only have 4 crafting stations and barely any farming. As well as the fact that crafting is also useless, you have a smelter, which can only make one bar at a time and you have to manually change it out for every bar, a magic station, which makes the only useful stuff in the game, a decoration station, a whole crafting station just for the useless cosmetics, and the anvil, which makes charms that you're probably going to forget about in 5 mins because they are only used on certain islands against certain enemies(Poison, Fire, and Darkness spirits) and you have to keep them in your inventory forever just to use them which makes me remember that YOU CANT INCREASE YOUR INVENTORY IN THIS GAME.I play lots of games with Stamina systems, they work decent in other life-sim games but the one here feels off, exploration feels like it was tuned for a game without a stamina system as you use massive chunks of stamina to travel between islands, which considering that travelling between islands is the only way to find dungeons and progress means that you feel like you never have enough to actually progress in the game without carrying around about 20 stonefruit everywhere you go.And i know this is going on a little long but one more thing, the Moonstone Island itself is very nice at first, everyone is nice and welcoming and the portraits are cute, then you realize how empty it all feels. Then you realize that theres only 11 npcs and all of them are age-appropriate romance options, no kids, no old people, no married couples, it makes the island feel empty and artificial, theres just not enough people to talk to here, and the ones you get are all just 'nice' in a very bland way. Apparently the 'diversity' is supposed to be some big thing in the game but they all feel super bland even if they wear neon colors and call themselves 'they'.Sorry for this massive rant but i just needed to get this all off my chest for a game i really wanted to like and just didnt.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island hits the sweet spot with its gorgeous pixel art and animation. The gameplay loop is addictive, offering a bunch of goals and battle mechanics that keep you hooked. The NPCs are really likeable and the mail system makes each of them stand out with their unique vibes. The best part to me is exploring—gliding around different islands, solving treasure maps, and stumbling on secrets. I feel like I did not get to know the NPC's enough, more interactive events with them would be nice, next to the short dates you can go on. As I got deeper into the game, the late stages felt a bit less shiny? There's just not as much going on, especially with limited farming automation. Also, for a game about alchemy, it could use more alchemy-centric quests, maybe some guild-related stuff? Moonstone Island is a visual treat with addictive gameplay. It could pump up the NPC interactions and late-game activities. And hey, more alchemy adventures would be nice. But even with these points, the game’s exploration and attention to detail make it a cozy and enjoyable journey.

_childDocuments_.review: I have fallen in love with this game so much. I intend to buy it when it comes out to Switch as well. It is a rather odd mix of farming sim, deckbuilder and monster tamer yet it works and combat is fun.The world is vibrant, beautiful and colorful. The NPCs are lovely and the Spirit designs are delightful. I am rather hooked on Poison types and Psychics are awesome. Though Octopup might be my number one atm because he is best boy. Combat takes very little time to get used to I think but I love how it's handled. Armor CAN be annoying but Burn and Poison are awesome. I adore that you can have your buddies follow you around. I'm working on more decorating to make my homestead look cozy. And I know this is kind of for a lot of games like this but I wish we could use the furniture. Just a minor gripe in the grand scheme of things.All in all I don't have very many problems with the game apart from the tiny RNG of Villager chatting. I'm greatly looking forward to the announced Valentine update and I think having sweets based Spirits would be awesome like an Earth type chocolate covered strawberry. This game is an easy buy for anyone looking for a new monster tamer game. It's well worth the asking price and it is being given regular updates and love from the team.EDIT: I am making a small edit with a few things I would love to see; maybe an option for spotting Moonstones easier. Even with Rablit I cannot for the life of me spot some of these things without maybe chopping down every single tree which just leaves sad looking islands. It's worst for me on the Electric biome. I don't know why it's so tough for me and it IS a minor gripe. And for decoration as things are being added with patches and free updates; maybe false walls! The basement is already huge with the second expansion. And false walls can lead to some nice ideas for room designs. And maybe some extra clothing options for the Alchemist. All in all these little things would be great to see for me. But the devs are already giving great updates and they're doing a great job with actual communication!

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore this game, before you think its just like stardew it is not. It has so many of its own charms, the gameplay is very endless. _childDocuments_.review: An original concept combining farming life sims, monster tamers, and card battlers. It draws you in with the farming, then motivates exploration to advance and build your farm, which then requires raising a strong team of creatures, which then motivates more farming and exploration to power your team up. Very addictive and immediately satisfying, not a painful slow burn that requires at least 10 hours to start seeing results.As with any new concept, there is tweaking that would improve the game's progression system, and I hope the devs read these comments for ideas in developing the sequel or DLC, which I am now excitedly anticipating. I find myself wanting to continue unlocking better modes of transportation and keep exploring wider maps or new worlds, and wish there was a level of procedural generation to dungeons that allowed me to keep delving. I spent a day just flying off the map to see if there was more to it and was disappointed there wasn't even an Easter egg. Farming is well executed, discovering new fruits, raising crops to craft stronger and stronger potions. I wish there was more to unlock, maybe some secrets that happen if you raise crops a certain way. I also wish stronger potions were more valuable. It would be interesting to have other NPCs as alchemists or monster tamers. The monsters are my favorite part. A fishbowl with legs, a newt with a snorkel, a beachball with sunglasses; when I first started playing I had a theory this game was a dream a child had and his toys had come to life. I don't necessarily think evolving the creatures in necessary, but it would be interesting to see a more rewarding leveling system, since it seems a change of seasons allows for more honing of a creature's ability than actually training and leveling them up. The battle system is cool and fun to play with, there are some clear winners as far as strongest types and creatures, identifying this had made the battles trivial but finding exploits is part of what makes card battlers fun. I'd like more types, more cards, more skill effects, varied abilities. The friendship system is fun because the artwork is gorgeous and my heart melts when I get the seed girl to smile, I've just been too distracted to actually learn her name.I haven't been able to lose myself in a game like I've lost myself in this in a long time. I want more.

_childDocuments_.review: I got it while it was on sale after getting hyped for it from some Tiktok reviews. I should have done more research before impulse buying. The game's art is great and the music is pretty good but that's about all I can say for it. It feels very much like an early access game. The world is very empty, all of the people in town are lifeless and not having actual dialogue when using any of the speech choices is mind-boggling. You can romance almost anyone but what's the point when there's no appeal to talking to people much less going on dates with them? There's three aspects to the game that it's a mashup of and it feels like it needs more time in the oven. The Stardew aspect of farming and having relationships is in the game but only at the surface level, there's no real need to farm at all and once again the communication of NPCs is lackluster.You have the pokemon collection aspect but seeing as how the spirits don't evolve or even really grow makes the appeal non-existant, you just collect a bunch of them to put into a barn to farm resources.The card battling aspect from Slay the Spire and other deck builders is decent but lacks depth. Everything revolves around knocking off armor and then doing damage. If you level up your spirits you gain too many cards and have to curate every spirit to be useful. If you lose a battle you lose out on the entire rest of your day so if you have one or two hands at the beginning where you can't take off armor, you're basically screwed.I'm glad to see the game gets updates frequently but due to the way the game was created there's no mod support so if there's anything you would like to change, good luck because every update will break them. It's so bad that the mod creators stop supporting their mods due to frustration.I'd give this game a 4.5-5/10; the foundation for a great game is there but it really needs work to shine.

_childDocuments_.review: 30 hours in 2 days, woops..It's a fun little exploration creature capture game. There's romance and friendship, but while the characters have fun personalities, it's not that deep. There's farming, but once again you'll only really do it to spam farm certain crops or when you're low on cash. There's some puzzles in dungeons, a low-story main mission, and you can build lots of useless decoration to make your house interior look pretty. The bosses and their skills range from cliche to pretty interesting, and the creatures you can use have skills to either boost your fighting style or playing style. Which basically means that any team composition is a good composition as long as you like it. If you've played Slay the Spire you know the combat, but while having three decks instead of one can seem fun and diverse in terms of building a team, it really sucks when you have a hand full of cards that can only be used by your one stunned character, meaning you're forced to end turn with no energy spent.In a nutshell. It's basically the Slay the Spire combat times three, worked into a fun, relaxing, and collection-focused game with exploration and plenty of surface level side-activities added.Definitely worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: What do you get if you mix Pokemon, Wizard101, and Stardew Valley? This game. :) There is a bit of eye-burning light-on-dark (dark mode) text, but none of it is essential to read. You can look away. The essential text is all disability-friendly (if your disability makes you sensitive to inverted contrast). The gameplay involves planting crops, watering them (or just place sprinklers, which you unlock pretty early in the game from a chest in an early mine shaft near town), and harvesting in a few days. You can sell the crops or use them to feed the spirits in your barn (which yields spirit resources you can use to craft other things). Spirits can be caught as long as they have a blue heart on their HP bar (spirits with a skull are bosses you can't catch but that give more EXP to your spirits and better rewards when defeated). There's a LOT to explore and, though some parts of the game play aren't explained terribly well, it's pretty easy to figure out. Overall, it's a lot of fun to play, and, if you're into games like this, then I highly recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island combines Creature Collecting, Card Battling, and Farming Simulation into a cozy experience for those looking to dabble into any one of those genres. That said, while it merges 3 great types of games into one, it hardly breaks the mold for any one genre type and might be a bit too shallow or simplistic for veterans of those genres.My only major complaints are that the game is quiet - not as in "just turn the volume up, silly" quiet, but the music drops out and you are left with extended periods of silence. This was okay for me as I have some playlists I enjoyed listening to while playing, but might be a turn off for some.  I also want to call it out for having a couple of really tedious achievements that weren't super fun to get - especially the fishing one.All that said, the price is certainly right especially when on a small sale, so 0 regrets and I enjoyed my time overall.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve never seen a game burying the lede as well as Moonstone Island does. On the surface it appears to do it all and scratch every itch:- Cute Vibrant pixel graphics and music? Check- farming/life sim with seasons, trading, and even character romancing? Check- Crafting and resource collection for that calming grind? Check- Building and decorating a house? Check- Pokémon-esque monsters you can collect and care for? Check- Deck building battles with customisation and seemingly endless combinations? Check - Huge world with different biomes to explore? Check- RPG elements with skills and items that can improve your gameplay or QoL? CheckOn paper this game does it all or at least something for everyone coming over from Stardew Valley, Pokémon games, or some sort of Zelda-inspired RPG. But the surface is where it stops. None of the above aspects have any depth and the game almost seems engineered to pass an initial litmus test making you think it has all you looked for and more but with each aspect being skin deep and lacking any real depth.Every aspect of the game becomes painfully repetitive and lengthy and truly does not spark joy. In addition despite the game being SteamDeck verified the controls on a controller are abhorrent and orienting the character to perform the most basic tasks, watering plants, feeding creatures, collecting resources is arduous and requires constant repositioning. So I’ll go ahead and recommend it. Some people may not be looking for much depth in games like this and will find plenty to keep them occupied but if you come into this looking to scratch a specific itch and depth in a particular genre you’ll likely end up disappointed.

I love it.
