_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game!! It feels so crazy that it’s released, it still hasn’t set in yet! I feel like I’m on cloud nine; this game is everything I’ve been waiting for and more.Now Moonstone Island is a cozy monster tamer/farm-sim, so if you're a player that enjoys the monster tamer genre, farm sims, home customization, and relationships, this game was literally made for you. I will not do this game injustice by comparing it to other titles.I'm a HUGE fan of monster tamers and farm sims, and this game is a wonderful marriage between the two. Seeing how well these genre's can work together, I only hope we can see more in the future as I am having literally the best time.Moonstone Island is, hands-down, my current all-time favorite game. You can enjoy the game as a casual player or player who wants a challenge. The battles are turn-based card battles, similar to Ooblets and other  indie titles yet-to-be-named in development. The game is easy to follow and immensely charming. I enjoy the writing and relationships much more than I thought I would. I really like how building relationships take a good amount of time (unless you're actively gifting and chatting everyday haha). I also appreciate that there's no real pressure and that it's a go-at-your-own-pace kind of game, that you're open to do as you like. The monsters are awesome, too. I love the designs, their move-sets, the battle mechanics, and sprites. It's been enjoyable to tame monsters and run into Holo Spirits (shiny-equivalent). I really love the idea of keeping Spirits in a barn to take care of and receive additional resources from for crafting. I really think the taming mechanic is refreshing, versus using a compact capture item. Makes the gameplay feel resourceful and puts every crop to use, whether for crafting, to tame, make potions or feed your monsters.I also love and appreciate all the work put into Moonstone Island, seeing as there is so much to look forward to. You can decorate your home with such a long list of furniture items! You can even build a greenhouse and build your own home (which there are recipes for different types of homes)!I highly recommend Moonstone Island; I hope that those who purchase the title enjoy it as much as I do.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: Super chill and relaxing. 10/10This is a card combat / creature collecting game, with 30 unique dungeons, dozens of creatures to collect, and an infinite variety of possible deck builds.The NPCs are boring, but when you take them on dates you learn a lot more about them. This isn't a social sim.Combat gets incredibly fun as you get more cards and start making combos. The combat is really where it shines - I've put in so many hours and I have the best team ever - but it's so fun to build decks that I'm excited to build more decks with a different team of spirits, just so I can use new combos. Farming gets more fun as you get into brewing, because the buffs your spirits get from plants just gets stronger each season; you haven't lived until you've brewed up 2 plants into a potion that gives your spirit +10 power and then gone on to destroy bosses that are 15 levels above you.And that's not even touching on the massive interior decorating options; hundreds of items that you can buy and craft to decorate your (massively expandable) home. People get SO creative with their designs.If you like gathering, creature collecting, and card based combat, this game is your dream. I absolutely love it.

Even if it was just a change of clothes, heck, a color swap would be great. But, I suppose that's a specific choice by the dev.Love the game, look forward to playing much more. Love the cooking update, just a game teeming with creativity and good vibes. Very fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm about 7 hours in so far, and I've kinda just been taking things at my own pace, which I think is a great part about this game. There are objectives and little side quests for progression, but you can get so much joy out of just exploring! I love the card based battle system, although I will say that it's VERY easy to overpack your deck with cards. I feel like maybe each spirit should have fewer starting cards, but it's not the biggest deal. This game has definitely become my go-to comfort game over the last few days. I'm a big fan of the types of games Moonstone Island seems to have pulled inspiration from (Pokemon, Stardew Valley, Slay the Spire) so seeing this game blend those elements together is awesome!It has some flaws that other people have mentioned. I already talked about deck bloat. So far, the NPC dialogue is pretty generic, but I'm also not very far yet, so that could definitely get better. And I have experienced some stuttering here and there, but not as bad as some people have reported.Overall, if you love cozy life-sim type games, but you've been looking for something different, this game is for you!

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★☆This game is a blast, and the little fellas are so cute! Mostly lol! Lots to do, and I LOVE the exploration aspect which I didn't even realize was a part of the game. You can really choose your favorite parts and focus on that without the game play seeming to suffer much, if at all, which I think is super cool. I have hardly used the social or farming features, which seem to be decently fleshed out, but that hasn't seemed to have held me back in progression.My ONLY issue with Moonstone Island so far is there is seriously no explanations for things. You need to figure it all out on your own or look it up online. Tutorials do not exist. So if you get lost or confused easily, or this is the first game you'd be playing of the genre, this might be a frustrating game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend it as long as you realize what you're getting. As it was fun to explore and build some things, and I enjoyed it more than similar games. The daytime clock gets a bit stressful at times. I get that they wanted to make things feel a bit more rewarding with the challenge and limited exploration time, but by the time you get a second house you have a choice between it and getting back to your resources where you need to visit almost daily. All of this makes exploration a bit stressful. A game like this can be extra epic if it's spread out a bit. I would have more enjoyed a three year campaign with more lands to visit. Also a lot of mechanics aren't obvious enough to plan for. The game overall suffers mostly from a lot of great buildup and neat tools, but by the time you get the tools you don't get a chance to use them. Give the game a couple additional years, incrrease the strength of mobs and challenge of dungeons each year, and add some more islands with a few more neat things to do. This way you can develop your relationships better and have more capped by the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely good farming sim/monster battler, with a larger focus on the monster battling, exploration, and deckbuilding overall. The main issue I have with the game is a lack of content overall, which I'll go into more in depth later, but what is present is polished to near-perfection. There's 60 total monsters, not that many cards for each to use. In fact, it seems like most monsters share the same set of cards, based on their elemental type. There's SOME variation, but it'd be nice if there was more. Their designs vary from decent to great, and each 'spirit' has a unique ability, which is nice. This ain't Cassette Beasts or anything, but it's got a decent amount of variety.There's 4 types of elemental islands plus beach islands (which don't have any unique plants), 5 creature types total as far as I can tell, and each have their own sort of gimmick except for Earth type which is pretty much the 'normal type' of this game, having no gimmick but overall higher damage. I actually like the low amount of types, it keeps things relatively simple and lets each type be more well-defined.The life sim stuff is nothing to write home about, at least from what I've seen. The characters are quite likeable though, and it was a fun surprise seeing they all had pronouns listed in the relationships tab in the menu (although it made me feel bad for having accidentally misgendered them, but oh well). I think this is the stronger part of the game, the quests are all interesting and provide good rewards, and I like how the quests for giving spirits to the NPCs actually result in them having that spirit around them every now and again, though honestly I'd like to see that more.Long story short though, there's just not that much to it? Collecting Moonstone is kind of annoying, and it's the main progression-gating item, aside from money (which incidentally is also somewhat tricky to get, though not nearly as much). You can get Moonstone from dungeons and chests, but mainly you'll get it from islands since there's 1 hidden in the grass on each island, re spawning in a new random spot every season. It's only visible during nighttime, which is a pain, since you only get so long before your character passes out, but whatever. The Warp Whistle exists for a reason.Mines being non-renewable is interesting but it's a pain having to fly further and further out for more resources as you expand. Would be nice if mines could show back up on a previously-mined island after 2 seasons or something.Also, the inventory wheel on controller, used to select your tools, is too small to fit all the tools you get access to, but only by like 3 spaces. For the different flight tools, it makes sense to only have 1 on the wheel and have you switch them out, but there's a fishing rod, the Warp Whistle... and so overall juggling your tool menu is kind of annoying. There's tons of inventory spots, couldn't you just let me put a tool or two in one of those to save time messing with the quick wheel? Aside from that though, the controls and inventory work pretty much flawlessly.Honestly, it feels like a late Early Access game to me, like it should be a version 0.8. It's good, don't get me wrong, but it desperately needs more meat on its bones, a little more polish. More sidequests, a bit more direction on the game's core progression to start with, and some quality-of-life features would make this game great. A little less waiting for things to happen, also, a lot of things are tied to game time but there's not a ton to do while waiting once you've got your bearings gameplay-wise. After ALL that, maybe some more spirits/monsters, I don't know.My last minor gripe with the game: the tutorial is completely inadequate. It teaches you mostly about farming, which is a SHOCKINGLY small part of this game, teaches you about battles, and leaves you on your own for the social aspect of the game, for crafting, for collecting Moonstones especially... it's not a BAD tutorial, but it's not a good one either. Dialogue doubles itself sometimes in the tutorial, it's really just a mess.So, tl;dr, this game is worth it for the price you pay, so long as the dev team doesn't abandon this for a newer project. Fingers crossed I guess?

_childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island is a fun game that has farming, mining, crafting, romance, magic, ... You can fly to many islands with different features generated randomly by a procedural algorithm. That means it has a lot of replayability. People tend to compare it with Stardew Valley. But it is different and it is unique. The main focus is to raise your spirits and to develop the cards that are used for dueling. You don't use weapons for combats; instead, you use cards. It is like many card games, except that you can farm and craft to make your spirits and their careds strong. If you like physical combats, this game is not for you. If you like card dueling, however, this game is taking it to a much higher level. I still have difficulties understanding the romance in this game. But this game is ok with or without the romance with the NPCs.

_childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island is a cute, fun, and fantastical game set in a post-apocalyptic world where “something” caused the world to shatter into many sky islands. It’s implied (but I don’t think explicitly stated) that this is Earth. There seems to be a lot of hidden lore to this game. A lot of lore bits I’ve gotten from going on dates with the characters. Now I beat the “main story” within the first year so the romancing aspect took a bit of back seat for a time and by the time I got to the last boss I wasn’t even entirely sure why I was fighting it other than it broke Waldo (the best character in the game). Which is enough reason for me to horribly murder it in my opinion. The main gist of the game is that you’re the most recent inheritor of a long lineage of spirit tamers called “Alchemists.” You primarily tame spirits and generally keep people safe with some alchemy on the side. The general drives of the game are:Complete Quests from townsfolk and parentsRomance townsfolkFinish your Pokédex… I mean spirit research…Beat the dungeons and templesBeat the last bossMake things pretty. (Lots of customization)-Con’s:The farming in the game is honestly tedious and boring without the greenhouse. I tried it for 2 seasons in the game then stopped.Some of the characters come off as pretty flat. I haven’t romanced every character in the game so I don’t know if those dialogues add more them but with some of the dates with a few of the characters I’m not really interested in further dialogue with them.The dungeons all have the same boss. They’re slightly different because depending on the island you find them on it changes their element but that’s it.From spirit to spirit there isn’t any difference other than passives and looks. That’s it that’s literally it. That’s all the bad things I have to say about the game.-ProsIt’s absurdly fun, I could not put this game down basically for the first week of owning it. I have a good bit of time invested into this game, and I’ve been playing since release (basically). It is so much fun and it feels so much like booting up Pokemon Emerald or Friends of Mineral Town for the first time. Those two games defined my childhood and this captures the feeling of both of those games while being unique and separating itself as a standalone that can hold its own.The spirit designs are great. They range from really silly, to really freaking cool, to…why?… So there’s something for everyone!The combat is probably my favorite card battler I’ve ever played. I generally am not a big fan of card battlers. There are far too many that I’ve played where building your deck feels grueling and difficult. This is up there with Slay the Spire with how fun and rewarding it is to build your deck in the early game and by late game building because very easy and you can really edit your decks to your liking once you’ve put in the time to get to the end game.The puzzles are simple but fun. This game is targeted towards almost all ages. So the puzzles can’t be too difficult but it still feels good to solve them. Honestly my least favorite dungeons are the ones that are just a gauntlet of battles back to back it’s much more fun to explore.The island exploration feels so cool. It’s so interesting going to see how all the islands work. There are a ton of island that all vary greatly and my biggest gripe with this is once I found them all I just wanted more!The creators are constantly engaging with the community to see what they want and what they’re looking for.The art style is very fun and cute. Honestly I’ve overall grown tired of the pixel-art style that’s everywhere nowadays, but this game really holds its own. Seriously the artists they have on this have done a great job and made so many good decisions with the direction they went.The characters on Moonstone Island are (for the most part) great. I know one of my cons was that some fell flat but others are absolutely incredible. I want you to find out for yourself but Ossono is probably my favorite with Gaiana being my least favorite (out of the ones I’ve romanced so far).I absolutely love this game and I want everyone to play it. My biggest hope for this game is that they release more islands and more towns with more NPC’s and more bosses. Just more of the same stuff and maybe another Element. If the devs do end up reading this, please release expanded content with all that asked for as paid DLC you’ve done great work and deserve to be paid for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely pixel-graphics. Fun characters. Chill vibes. Grow crops, craft stuff, make money, buy furniture, etc. Also collect monsters and make them fight for you. Sounds great, right?Sure. If you neglect to ask the central question: What about the actual, you know, GAMEPLAY? And that, unfortunately, is where it stumbles. Card-based combat that leaves you entirely at the whims of the RNG, exacerbated by the 'armor' system. The idea is to use ONE kind of card to break down the enemy's armor, then use a DIFFERENT kind of card to deal damage after inflicting armor-break, which leaves the enemy vulnerable for a turn. Do you get to CHOOSE what kind of card you draw? Of course not! So here, have a bunch of damage-dealing cards that will do 0 damage because of the enemy's high armor. Oh, did you just manage to inflict armor-break at long last? Then here, have an entire hand full of now-useless armor-reduction cards and low-damage/utility cards.I genuinely don't understand how these card-battle systems have become so frustratingly PERVASIVE in the indie-scene in recent years. Other than, perhaps, that they're just really easy to make?Anyway, the rest isn't much better. The pacing of the early game is just painfully off. At the start, you can only own 3 monsters, and have no way to store extras. Reaching the point where you have a Monster Barn for that purpose takes WAY too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ long - you'll come across loads of interesting monsters along the way, but can ya catch 'em? NOPE! The game doesn't even offer you the option of replacing one of your current critters with a newly-caught one, it just goes "No room, byeee!" and that's it. The actual catching is also extremely simplistic, lacking any of the strategy and nuance you'd expect from a dedicated monster-collecting game.There's also the way 'Mines' are absolutely key to your advancement, but - at least early on - the only way to find them is to break every large rock you can find, which is a slow, boring, and of course, RANDOM affair. Maybe you'll stumble on one pretty quick! Maybe you'll spend a whole day breaking rocks and have nothing to show for it 'cept several hundred useless pieces of stone. Do ya feel lucky, punk?I could go on. The game's beautiful to look at, sure, and with so many AAA-games coming out as hopeless lumps of bugs and copy-pasted features, it's tempting to just shower any halfway decent indie-game with praise. This one, however, unfortunately doesn't deserve it. It isn't TERRIBLE, and it's certainly in a far better technical state than anything the AAA industry seems capable of producing, but there's just way too many frustrating aspects, and the way the RNG is just constantly up in your face, making it perfectly clear that your success or failure has nothing to do with skill or strategy and everything to do with luck, earns it a thumbs-down from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island is game that makes me wish Steam had a "Neutral" rating option for review. But since the question is, "Would you recommend this game?" my current answer for Moonstone Island is a solid no at this current time which leads to my choice of giving the game a negative review.So now to answer the question of why I wouldn't recommend the game.I would describe Moonstone Island as very ambitious. Studio Supersoft clearly tried to include many different ideas into Moonstone Island but like with most Jack-of-All-Trades approaches they have failed to really find mastery with any particular element in their game.- The villagers aren't unlikable but they don't often really feel alive. It feels like a solid starting point for a game in this genre but doesn't execute past being the bare minimum most of the time. The date mechanic is nice and helps flesh out your chosen romantic partner's character. Some villagers are very forgettable like Cleo who I had to look up their name as part of writing this review.- Probably Moonstone Island's most fleshed out axis of gameplay. That being said "Creature Collector" is the wrong way to describe Moonstone Island. This game is fundamentally a deck builder. Do not go into this game expecting to catch "Pokemon" and each Pokemon feel like it's own individual unique entity. Each "Spirit" (This game's equivalent to a pokemon) has a deck of cards that they represent and when you are in battle with other spirits you draw from a combined deck of cards for each spirit you have active on your team, up to 3 spirits. There are only 3 things that make each spirit truly unique from other spirits; it's passive, it's type and it's weaknesses to cards of other types. The issue here is that most of the passives are inconsequential with eachother and, as far as I can tell, no spirit has any cards that are unique to that spirit. By this I mean, if you have an Earth type spirit, it has access to all the same cards as EVERY other earth type spirit, which makes all earth type spirit feel almost entirely the same outside of their appearance and passive. Moonstone island also somewhat punishes player for actively collecting spirits  due to the fact that unless you spend the tedious time to feed your excess collected spirits every day they will run away. There is an expensive recipe that you unlock early into the game that does ultimately remove that tax but it feels antithetical to a "Creature Collector" game to punish players for collecting creatures.- One of the other pillars of the game play loop in Moonstone Island that helps differentiate it from other farm-sim titles is Exploration. This feels relatively fresh for the first 5 hours of game play but eventually the vignette falls and the realization will set in that aside from their shape every island in the game is the same except for the biome they represent out of the 4-5 different types of biomes. That is unless have a randomly assigned dungeon on them.- Dungeons are just fine. They reward the player's exploration efforts with small amount loot but the main draw being a permanent stamina upgrade. I wish dungeons were more visually distinct from each other based on the biome that they are located in, it's mildly nonsensical to have to cross a river of magma in order to access a dungeon on a fire island only to be greeted by a grassy stone ruin once you enter it.- Moonstone Island's farming is just kinda . It's a feature that feels like it exists because there is an expectation for it for the genre but it really doesn't add much to the game play loop outside of generating income for the player or getting food buffs to feed your spirits. The clunky controls also contribute to it feeling like an under developed system. I feel like the devs recognized this because you start the game with access to sprinklers which automate that majority of effort required to farm in the game. There are some crops in the late game that give a lot of EXP to your spirits when you feed them but that feels more like an answer to the frustratingly low amount of EXP you get from actually battling other spirits.- The UX in this game is passable most of the time but occasionally is atrocious. You will run into this the most with the inventory management and any attempt to do larger scale farming efforts. Want to plant a large field of crops? Enjoy spamming right-click/space hundreds of times to buy each seed individually since there is no bulk purchasing option. Want to quickly move a stack of items into a chest? You have to drag and drop it, right clicking only puts in 1 at a time but thankfully you can hold down right click in this rare instance. - Fishing exists in this game but it feels like it's been tacked on solely due to genre expectations. - There are character level-up RPG-like elements in the game that really don't need to exist. Very few of the passives feel like anything other than a small incremental numbers boost and some exist just to slow down the game play loop. You cannot tame higher level spirits that you encounter in the wild until you unlock certain passives that let you tame those higher level spirits. - Progressing through the temples (the game's equivalent to a story/campaign/gyms) is blocked by progressing through the seasons. This forces the player to not rush through the game but in turn forces the player to pay attention to all of the other mediocre game play & game design. You'll eventually run out of things that feel worthwhile to do in the game so that the only way to feel like you are progressing is to sleep until the next season so that you can continue to progress the game.- The game occasionally really chugs when exploring certain islands. - I've had the occasional bug that would black screen the game and  force me to close out the game and lose some progress in order to resolve the issue.Moonstone Island feels like an early access game that had it's full release come preemptively. I suspect that with another year or two of development Studio Supersoft can make Moonstone Island a standout from other similar indie titles but currently just feels like it's trying to be nothing more than barely adequate to answer it's initial moonshot ambitions.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool concept but poor execution. You may think that 1.5 hours is too short of a time to make a judgement but I assure you it's not. This game isn't that deep and an arbitrary amount of time isn't necessary to engage with most of what's on offer here.The Good:- Good graphics and music.- Interesting concept where the game tries to combine elements of farm/life sims, creature collectors, card battlers, and Zelda-like dungeons.The Bad:- This game tries to be wholesome and cozy but it fails, in my opinion, do to the combination of a clock that moves too quickly and a stamina bar.  If you're going to have a fast moving clock, get rid of the stamina bar or reduce the number of actions that consume stamina. The clock is enough of a limitation. - The writing isn't great which makes the NPCs uninteresting. It's full of cookie cutter tropes. - The NPC interaction system boils down to choosing one of 3 interactions (chat, joke, or flirt) which rely on RNG. There's no dialog associated with any of these choices. It's just the number goes up or down. It feels robotic and not at all like human interaction.- Bugs exist that will soft lock your game thus forcing you to alt f4 and you lose the progress you made that day. Look at the bug reports if you're interested in what those bugs are.- Considering this game just came out two days ago and it's "sink or swim" time, you would think that the devs would be more responsive to bug reports and hot fixes would be happening multiple times a day or, at the very least, daily. Instead they seem to be more interested in celebrating Moonstone Island as if it's perfect and focusing on merchandising...for a two day old game. Worrying about a MakeShip collaboration instead of hot fixes feels grimy.- Released on day 1 with a paid DLC that's just a few cosmetic items. For a game that already costs more than SDV and offers far less in terms of customization, NPC interactions, and NPCs with complexity, it's not a good look.  Whether or not Moonstone Island is worth your money is up to you. I'm on the fence but leaning towards "no" unless some serious hot fixes come out quickly and options are added to either increase day length or disable the stamina bar. I could overlook the average writing (I'm being generous by calling it average), bugs, and shallow customization if hot fixes were incoming, customization options were being added, or the price was lower. As it stands, it very much looks like the developers are trying to cash in on the cuteness of this game before people realize the content is as deep as a puddle.Edit: They finally squashed some bugs two days after release, about an hour ago as of writing this edit. I still stand by my statements regarding this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I watched a couple people play the demo of this game a while back but was unable to play it myself at the time, so I obviously jumped at the chance to play it for myself when it finally came out and... I am completely obsessed.  No exaggeration, I've already completed every dungeon, every temple, collected almost every spirit (and two holographic ones!), and am in a very committed relationship with Waldo the magic man.  This game is literally everything I wanted and more, with very simple and easy-to-understand overworld mechanics, but with complex and exciting battles mixed in to keep you on your toes.  The pacing is great, the characters and story as a whole is delightful and fun, and 80 hours in, I'm still not bored!  After beating the main story, I am now spending my time decorating my wizard tower, filling my spirit barn, and getting full hearts with all the villagers, and I'm having a blast!  I do have a few complaints relating to small bugs (such as an invisible wall in one of the dungeons that prevents you from accessing an optional chest, and a treasure map that didn't lead to anything) but while I do think that a few quality of life changes here and there would help with a lot of the smaller issues I have, I largely I have nothing but love for this game, and absolutely recommend it to anyone who enjoys this genre!  Super excited for the Halloween update as well :)

_childDocuments_.review: I'd give this game a sideways thumb if I could. I enjoyed it but it did disappoint me in a several ways. The game is a lot shallower than it appears at first. Sure there's a hundred handcrafted Islands but they're all pretty much the same. if you thought this game might scratch an itch that you have for exploration, look elsewhere. (FYI, I did finish the game, but did not 100% it.)GAMEPLAY SPOILERS AHEAD.…The islands all have one moonstone,  often a dungeon, and sometimes a teleporter thingy.  Really there are just five types of islands corresponding to five different elements. Also, the islands are laid out on a giant, predictable, square grid, which looks pretty silly when looked at from above.Once you've seen a few of each island type, you've pretty much seen them all.  The same goes for the spirits.  As far as their stats and moves go, I found very little difference between each of the fire spirits, each of the poison spirits, and so on. If you're comparing this to Pokémon, I'd say that Pokemon in general are about 10 times more complex (and interesting) than these spirits. I leveled one of my guys all the way up to 50 and got no new moves for the last 25 levels. The optimal strategy that I found was to just catch Spirits at as high a level as possible, then use those to battle others to level up my ability to catch even higher level spirits, etc. This means that I had to abandon my few starting Spirits which I had grown quite attached to but they were simply too weak to continue on.  Unfortunately, these high-level Spirits have tons and tons of junk cards in their deck which you have to spend a lot of cleanse talismans to remove, though it was worth doing. However, I shouldn't have bothered. It turns out that you can grow plants in the greenhouse that provide experience to your spirits directly. And quite a lot of it, too. And they can be picked over and over again. (I'm talking about Willowisp. Spoilers!)  So, there's no need to even battle anymore. Combine that with a tool that directly turns stamina into growth for plants, and you'll find there's no reason to even try to battle anyone anymore. Later, you got a staff that lets you teleport over enemies, even dungeon bosses,  meaning you don't have to battle a single Spirit to complete  dungeons anymore. (This might be a bug/oversight, since I didn’t get an achievement for beating all the dungeons, even though the game says I did)The battle system is actually quite fun, and it's the best part of the game… well, until you discover overpowered cards like “Blind Blow +”, costing only 1 energy, with the description “Draw the top two cards from your deck and reduce their energy costs to zero.”  …and it's easy to get, too.  This might as well be called the “win the game card.”That's the main problem with Moonstone Island. For most of the mechanics that it has to offer, it also offers a convenient way to skip right over them… leaving you with little game left in your game. You certainly could choose to play the game without “abusing” these mechanics, but it's not the player's job to balance a game like this.  And frankly, the game has very little replay value. It's just shallow.Oh, and there's a boss that works differently from everything else in the entire game. This boss has a power that will randomly increase the energy costs of the cards in your hand by 1, every 3 real-time seconds. And it never stops. This is absolutely insane in a game that is otherwise completely turn-based.  I could hardly believe it. I ended up pausing the game every time I looked at a card just to give myself some time to think, as usual. I was able to beat it easily by doing this, so I think they made that boss easier to compensate for this bizarre power, but it just goes to show that I don't think the game designers knew what they were doing. I'm sure that many others will be complaining about this as well. I'm also sure that some people loved it.  But it definitely has no place in a turn-based game like this, though I really can't properly articulate the exact reason why. It just felt so wrong.There are other bizarre small issues and oversights, like the fact that trees never regrow, but you're never told this.  So if you clear-cut an island thinking you can just plant a bunch of trees later, you're out of luck.  Permanently. I didn't even know that talismans regenerate each season, so I started hoarding them until the next season came around and they all, mercifully, came back.There are a lot of ideas here, and I don't think any of them are particularly fully thought out, other than the battling, which again is pretty good except for the few cards that break the game.This game was clearly made with a lot of love and passion, but it has a lot of rough edges on it.  Like, I couldn't even level up my spirits because the only islands/dungeons available were fire islands and the team I had selected was mostly weak against fire.  On top of that, I couldn't find an island that was at the same level as me; it was just much higher or much lower than I could handle.  That is, until I figured out that you can just grow crops to earn experience and then the game was a breeze from that point on.Again, the game designers put in a lot of things that let you just skip over parts of the game,  possibly due to a lack of confidence in the systems they have created.Oh, and I absolutely hated the way that the game handles tools.  They are all independent from your inventory and on a giant wheel with awful fiddly little arrow buttons that let you swap individual tools for something else, but you have to hold down a button to get to it. I'm on a PC so this wasn't necessary at all since I have plenty of keys to choose from, and I absolutely never got used to it.  For a tool like the warp whistle it makes sense to have to hold it down because you want to make sure that the player actually wants to warp home.  For the tool wheel, having to hold down a button was just frustrating.  Also, using the rest of the inventory hot bar was clunky and annoying. It was just slow to scroll through. I admire them for trying something different from Stardew /Minecraft/etc, but it just fell short.A lot of people say that this game is Stardew Valley + Pokemon, But frankly, those games are better than this one. It's not that it's impossible to combine those two ideas.  They've done a decent job.  But there is a clear lack of experience showing through here, and some deep structural problems with the game that I'm not sure are able to be solved.  Will they just completely get rid of the crops that provide experience?  Probably not. They seem to be a big part of the game. But they shouldn't be here at all. I felt like I had to use them because leveling up the traditional way was getting to be quite tedious. Well, that’s all I can think of for now. Sideways thumb. Had some fun. But won’t be back.

_childDocuments_.review: The game fails to deliver on everything it has to offer. _childDocuments_.review: 9.5/10: Highly Recommend!One of the best things about the game is that as a player, I have a lot of control on how I play it.Unlike other monster taming or farm sim games, there is not a linear story playthrough. Islands are generated uniquely first time you create the save file, and you can:- explore new islands- decorate islands... ALL the islands.- socialise and romance (Hi Ferra!)- add and upgrade cards, and trim down decks- find holo (shiny) spirits- hatch spirit eggs and collect resources in the spirit barn- fish (it's fun, I promise)- battle dungeon bosses- complete quests- find seasonal plants and plant them ANYWHERE, but mostly, your greenhouse- create potions from plantsYou don't have to do all that. I like that socialising never felt overwhelming or necessary.You can also create strong potions that can help you in battles, making it much easier for those who are not as comfortable.And above all that, the devs have consistently published free updates, including new spirits, and much-welcomed Quality of Life improvements (like auto-collecting Spirit Resources without clicking).At face value, the game seems like it does a lot, but it never got to a point where it felt too much!Thank you Studio Supersoft, your love for the game makes me Superhard. Oop-

_childDocuments_.review: This game is everything I’ve wanted in a modern life sim game. On a surface first impression, I was constantly thinking, “oh that’s a neat way to implement that mechanic.” It’s not just a regurgitated copy of every dated mechanic from games released in 2010. This game has fresh and new ideas and makes small tweaks to everything from the farming to the mining and combat. Speaking of combat, thank the lord there’s finally a game where I don’t just smash A on a monster in a mine. In this game, you get a simplified version of a deck builder similar to Slay the Spire, as well as dungeons that will remind you of the classic legend of Zelda games with their puzzles and layouts. Combat actually has a rewarding value to it and is captivating rather than a half-assed thought out addition that was put in because “well every other farm game has it.”The soundtrack slaps and is also reminiscent of LoZ. The graphics are vibrant with colors that make me happy just looking at the game. And then there’s the Pokémon aspect, because this game just kept delivering on making a FUN sim game. You get to capture creatures which all come with their own set of decks that you’ll be able to customize as well. The NPC art is incredible and everyone in this game is hot. I want to marry everyone. You get to build friendship via a dialogue option that has 3 different levels (chat, joke, flirt) and different chances of raising or lowering friendship. It makes it feel less like a recycled chore and more of a game, because this is a game and every feature should actually be fun. All in all, get this game. If you like turn based RPGs, or creature captures, or just farm/life sims in general—get this game. You won’t regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so good it's tempting me to start a youtube channel because I want to talk about how nice it is and walk people through it a bit, etc.Somehow the creator has pinpointed every way in which other games in this genre/vein (Stardew of course included) are or become stressful, and just decided to remove EVERY SINGLE POTENTIAL BIT OF STRESS that games like this have - and I love them for it!  It makes this game truly a place of peace and fun and zero stress.  A few examples of this:-when you pass out from not going to bed on time, you DON'T lose any items (something that made me wonder, for the first time, WHO IN STARDEW VALLEY IS ROBBING ME WHEN I'M PASSED OUT?! 😂)-if your inventory is full and you have to leave items behind, they will just BE THERE whenever you go back to that location, even if its days or seasons later -if a creature faints during combat, you don't have to go somewhere or use a special item to revive them, they just have 1HP so you can feed them enough and they'll be ready to go again right away, no special "revive" items needed-talismans respawn every season, so you never won't have enough for what you're doing/wanting to do-materials are easy enough to come by that you don't run into things like the "sprinkler stress" (and beyond) that you find in Stardew, etc, like I had more sprinklers than I needed literally as soon as I decided, "oh yeah, lemme go mine so I can make some sprinklers" like it is never a chore, burden, or stress the way it can be in other games, to get to where you need to be production-wise; it's chill and easy and I LOVE THAT ABOUT IT and appreciate it so much-you can stretch the day length with settings like "default, slow, slowest" and wow did putting it on slowest make me enjoy the game even more-moonstones on each island also respawn every season, guaranteeing you enough to do whatever you want as the game progresses-leveling monsters up is also not a huge stress, you just need to learn the system and the crops (some give experience points) and go from there; it's not as arduous, grueling, repetitive, and/or time consuming as similar games in similar genres imo, they make it very smooth, efficient, and again - stress free-the list goes on & on!This is truly the epitome of a stress-free game.  It is the most relaxed I've ever felt while playing in these genres, period, and it makes the game a safe haven for me honestly.  A game I can come to and enjoy without ever having to feel stress at all/in any moment.Also, the Ghibli nods/inspirations as well as the Stardew & Pokemon nods/inspirations just coalesce into a universe and aesthetic that I adore and appreciate in every way.Now for my one and only critique (which, let me say in advance, has NOT negatively impacted my enjoyment of this game AT ALL or in any way lol.)I don't love the townsfolk in the same way I do/did with most of the Stardew NPCs (though that could just be because I played Stardew first and it was the first game I ever played that was like that - dating/life sim mixed in), but I do love the diversity of the characters in Moonstone Island and feel it makes up for my not really romantically vibing with any of them in the same ways that I/my character did with the NPCs in Stardew.  In Moonstone I'm in the Spring of my second year, have max hearts with everyone, and feel no pull towards having my character actually become boyfriend/girlfriend of any of them whereas in Stardew I knew pretty early on that my character would wind up with Abigail or Seb because they just drew me in and I related to them and/or they reminded me of my friends/partners in real life, etc.  Whereas these characters I do relate to and/or see some traits of friends in them, etc. - but somehow they just don't hit the same for me. They are great in their own ways for sure and again I LOVE the representation here a ton and think it's very well done on that front.  I'm not even sure how this could be fixed, I just personally was not grabbed by the townsfolk as much despite really liking them and the vision of diversity/representation overall.  I'm a writer myself yet still can't really pinpoint why exactly they fall a bit flat for me.  Maybe the creator can look at this and tweak them a bit down the line, idk.  I definitely don't expect them to do that just off one comment, lol, I just did think it was worth noting if giving a full review.  This is the only area I think needs some tweaking, and I don't even know exactly how, I just know that for me none of the townsfolk really drew me in to the point where I ever had a clear thought of who my character would go for.  I lean towards Gaiana or Cleo, but have to get to know Cleo a bit more first.  I also kinda like Zed?  Sort of?  Lol.  I haven't gone on all the dates with all the townsfolk yet, I maxed hearts with gifts and a few dates here and there, and then flirting once the hearts were high enough; so maybe I just need to actually go on all the dates to really feel them out more, idk.  If my opinion changes after I eventually do that, I will update this review!Regardless of that, I still enjoy this game to the max.  I haven't found the love interest aspect to be something that hinders me from playing or that stresses/bums me out at all, I've just been enjoying the game and seeing how it flows.  I'm currently at a point where I'm leveling up my creatures to go to Dark type islands, and I haven't even done any of the Temples yet at all, so I'm focusing more on those things and on Dungeons at the moment.  So yeah, maybe I'll dive deeper into the townsfolk later on and have different opinions - but even if not, it doesn't diminish my enjoyment of this game at all.  It's my safe haven game and I love Studio Supersoft for making it and taking such care to have it be enjoyable, wholly stress free, and with endless Ghibli nods that I greatly appreciate.Thanks, Studio Supersoft!  Can't wait to see what you do with this game moving forward, and to see what else you do in the future as well!  Excellent work with this game, I applaud you!  🙏💜

_childDocuments_.review: I am a little bit stoned but I am going to tell you exactly what I like about this game and you are going to listen to me if you want to.This game really has a lot of potential for VERY unique experiences each playthrough. Since there are 100 islands and you can set up your home wherever you want and decorate the space both indoors and outdoors, you could live a pretty different daily routine on a distant island dungeoneering than someone who lives very close to town on moonstone island  to farm or be social. You could even build houses on every single island, if you wanted to and you could get enough moonstones. It feels like the whole world could be your home. Home has a lot of impact on the experience for me.Also, the characters work for me. I love Stardew Valley, but only for the gameplay. The characters in Moonstone are actually unique and interesting to me. Living on the beach with Tobin and fishing together and going on dates with him has made me feel like doki doki for the first time in a game with romance in a very very long time. Maybe it's because I'm high idk. He's just so cheerful and his smile is so bright. Coming home after a long several days or so of exploring and just chilling out on the beach with my pretty fisherman wife and his radiant smile makes my soul feel like it's healing.The spirits are adorable and I'm pogging all the time at the cute designs. The deck-based battles are interesting and fun, even if the system is not as deep as deck building fans want it to be, but also not what creature battling fans want it to be. In fact, it seems to be a major theme in negative reviews that the game is trying to bring too many disparate elements together and not doing any of them particularly well, but I think that's a pretty negative way of looking at it. I have ADHD, and games where there are lots and lots of things you CAN do but don't HAVE to do are my absolute jam. Fantasy Life for the 3DS comes to mind similarly. This game is great. It's the closest thing I can get to living my actual fantasy. I played it for 13 hours straight yesterday. My greatest hope for this game is that it will continue to be developed for a very, very long time. If it had the support that SDV has, it could be something game-changing. I hope it becomes that. And I also hope it gets multiplayer.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has great potential but feels very much like an early-access game. I enjoyed travelling to new islands and collecting new spirits but everything got boring fairly quickly. There's no real incentive to doing much in this game. The islands and dungeons all become sort of the same. Rewards, if any, are just new furniture to craft that you can just buy at the store anyway. Decorating anything is also insanely tedious and not worth the effort as you can't interact with anything anyways. The controls are very annoying to get used to, and I never crafted potions or used most things that were unlocked. You'll never use most of the tools beyond the temple you get them in. Not sure what the spirit brush even does. Do the hearts raise it's level or mean it will drop items more frequently the more the spirit likes you? Who knows, not much is explained. There's really not much of a story either. After the big boss battle at the end, which I didn't even know about until the end, everyone congratulated me and threw me a party where I just danced by myself, and that was it. None of the townspeople have much for dialogue or personality. You can kind of get to know them if you go out on dates but I don't want to date everyone. Once they like you enough, you get to enter their house, but there's no diary or anything even in it. If you're a straight female the only option for a romanceable character is the crazy guy with cards glued to his face. It's great to have LGBTQ representation but not all gay men are into fem guys either. A brooding loner lumberjack you can just throw in the back of the island somewhere would be nice, just saying. I'm pretty disappointed because I enjoyed the idea behind this. I don't get why so many people are in love with all these half-baked games, giving them amazing reviews. I swear I'll never trust any cozy game reviewer off YouTube again. Somewhere down the line they might add updates but there's just so much they need to work on that I doubt it will ever be everything it should. They really just should've made it early access and worked on things because this could've been amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: To start this off on a positive note: I love the design of the game, the music, and the overall concept of the game. Unfortunately.. that isn't enough for me to recommend. _childDocuments_.review: Hi! I'm a looong time Stardew Valley super-fan and wowie; this game is sooo close to being like SV (although no game can ever amount to that gem, tbh). I would be so happy if the devs would take some inspo from SV on story/character development. It absolutely feels like a half-baked game, especially since they JUST announced an update in which you can marry? HUH?? Why is that JUST NOW happening?? Do they expect us to replay the game after every major update?Please, devs, take the game, finish it, then give it to us.It also bugs me to NO END how the devs keep giving us new furniture. I don't want to keep having to change my house's decor every update because there's new furniture ;v; this might seem like a good problem for some but for others...please just give it to us now so we don't have anxiety when decorating, knowing this is only temporary. (Also, before you come for me, there's a difference between what's happening here and just simply being able to unlock furniture while IN-GAME.)Another point that a top review had is WALDO. I understand he's disabled/has mental issues but why is his story so anti-climatic and after you get together...just weird? :( All he does is sit in his home, praise you, and no one acknowledges him! LIKE AS IF HE'S NOT A LONG LOST HERO!?!? Like come on dude that could be AMAZING. Although, I guess every character's story is like that ;v; We need the characters to have some depth, please, it's killing us. Heart events, drama, history, relationships, etc. anything lmao! As for the combat-side of the game, it's ok, nothing to write home about. It's also confusing as to how the spirits and I have a relationship, what their role is, why they'd want to fight alongside me, how to level them up (without cheesing it), and more. I am comparing this aspect a lot to Pokemon but I think these are simple mechanics and stories you can bang out in a week or two (I'm saying this as someone who's been in game/character development for 10+ years and has a BFA). Lastly, the farming aspect is next to abysmal. It's JUST so you can grow certain plants that have status effects. That's it :( To sum it up, this game feels half-baked as you can tell from these major (GAME PLAY) updates dude :'( It's great that Steam can allow for game devs to continue working on their games after they've released it but this is taking it too far lmao! So, unfortunately, while this seems like THE PERFECT game for us cozy-gamers, it has left a bad (and confusing) taste in my mouth, one that'll be hard to remove if I ever want to try to finish/continue the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't review games so early in, but seeing as I spent a good many hours in the demo before the full release, and Indies have a hard time getting out there without reviews, I'll share my thoughts.The game is a pleasant mix of Stardew Valley, Pokemon, and Megaman Battle Network. (I say MMBN rather than something like slay the spire because it's not roguelike, meaning the deck you build is permanent and persists, which makes a very large difference gameplay wise.) The game elements can be a bit shallow in terms of the Stardew side, but it covers a broad enough area to be satisfying.Where the gameplay really hits home is the other gameplay aspects. Each creature you tame has access to a unique ability and a cardpool depending on its element. This lets you mix and match your team to achieve a wide variety of strategies in combat, and it knits together in a very satisfying way. Don't expect the element system from Pokemon here, either. Individual spirits (the creatures you tame in this game) can have varying stats and weaknesses, such that even two of the same type of creature might be weak to differing things.Alongside that system is the fact that *you* control where the stats per level are distributed, and the stats are all meaningful in terms of gameplay effect. Different cards scale with different stats, and stuff like how much HP you'll gain etc is listed outright when you level up. Further, you can augment these stats by feeding some of the crops you grow to those creatures, allowing for a wide degree of customization, and helping to tie the farming and combat sides of the game together nicely.As it stands, I am happy to recommend the game at any price you can pick it up at. The devs did a fantastic job and deserve the support.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: 9 cute little spirits/10. Manages to take games like Stardew and Pokemon and not only fuse them together, but in some ways surpass them. Easily worth the price.I remember like, a year or two ago, I was telling my partner how much I wished there was a Stardew-style game where instead of just having random barn animals, you had Pokemon-style creatures you could collect and who served various farm functions. In my head, it had the flavor of Howl's Moving Castle and a warm, cozy vibe where you co-existed with these monsters in the way that Pokemon always claims its universe inhabitants do, but rarely ever shows. I only mention this because it's SO bizarre that the exact dream of a game that I wanted is THIS game. Sub out Howl's Moving Castle for a charming pixel-art version of something closer to Kiki's Delivery Service, and you have the exact game I had always dreamed of playing but despaired anyone ever making.This game is FANTASTIC. I'm surprised I haven't heard any hype about it. It's such a fun, clever blend of Pokemon/creature-collector style games and farming sims like Stardew Valley, but honestly, I think it improves upon both genres. You don't have to spend an eternity like in most farming sims grinding to automation, stuck toiling away on your farm waiting spending whatever energy you have left to hopefully level up your gear so you can eventually make coveted sprinklers. Instead, all you can farm is also forage-able, meaning you can turn a few into seeds to keep that engine started, but you can spend most of your day pursuing your other passions: talking to a cast of delightful villagers, mining in dungeons for resources, battling your spirits in fun card-based combat, fishing, or sailing the expanses of the sky with your balloon/broom discovering strange new biomes in neighboring floating islands. There's skill trees that feel thought-out and impactful, with every node that I've seen seeming like a valid option depending on how you want to play. I was worried the spirit battling would feel clunky, or that the pet designs would be uninteresting and uninspired, like the majority of attempts to translate Pokemon end up being. But this is honestly one of the coolest pantheons of monsters I've seen in a game like this. You can tell there's genuine love towards the original titan of the genre, with spirits like the cute fire/earth fox Fluffox or the hilarious pseudo-wood-o long log simply titled Longlog. But there's also fun spirits that are more original, like the totally rad Coolslime, which is just a cool looking slime in a backwards baseball cap but MAN does he make me laugh every time I fight him. Combat is a deck-builder, where leveling up your pets alters things like power and health, but also drafts new cards into your team deck, allowing you to create really cool combinations between your three spirit teammates. It's easy to pick up but I can already see the potential for great depth in higher level combat.The story itself is fairly bare-bones, but not in a bad way, with the premise being that you are a young Alchemist apprentice who's leaving their home to do their mandatory year abroad to become a full-fledged Alchemist. The vibes are VERY Kiki's Delivery Service, both in terms of premise and in terms of overall ambiance. The music has that Miyazaki wistfulness in 8-bit, and the aesthetic matches it to a T. You can't create your own character, which initially I was worried about, but honestly I think the game works better with  a set appearance (you even get to see your character in beautiful hand-drawn loading screens), as the designers were able to really tighten up the aesthetic choices for maximum impact. You do still have say in customizing your world, between choosing what characters you elect to talk to, certain dialogue choices, and a fully-customizable home. The economy is also balanced enough that, unlike Stardew or Sun Valley or other games in the genre, I don't feel overwhelmingly pressured to save every scrap of money I make for farming equipment. I already have a nice little cozy spirit-communing nook/library in my home that I created! You can also decorate the world around you, and even move your home to settle on different islands!Long-winded, but I wanted to really spend time writing this review because I haven't seen like, any advertising for it, and this game is an absolute GEM. If you're thinking of trying it out, take the chance like I did. It's not that expensive (cup of coffee to a dinner depending on when you buy it), and it's absolutely a game you can lose yourself in if you like any of the genres it flirts with. The developers should be VERY proud of this game, it exceeded my own expectations and quite frankly is a phenomenal entry compared to other games in these genres.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, let me start by saying this is an absolutely gorgeous game. The art and the animation are both some of the most beautiful out there.Now, when it comes to gameplay... I was really excited about the "magical path/career" aspect of the game.. To the point where I am wondering if it was designed as is with tje purpose to extend the longevity of the game, as it lacks proper substance. For instance, when trying to upgrade/improve one's creatures, it is impossible to simply navigate from one creature to the next, to compare their status. Nothing in that process is smooth. Even getting to the upgrade/improve your creatures "menu" is a bit of a quest.. You first have to open a radial menu, then select the right tool (medalion), then click or press E to open the "medalion".. and THEN the "medalion" screen opens, where you have to WALK to each creature, click on it, select on a list what you want to do.. _childDocuments_.review: Fist off lets give a shout out to Studio Supersoft and Raw Fury for this delightful Gem!I haven't written a review in a long time not since Little Wood I believe. but this game definitely deserves mentioning.First off it's only $20 should be $60 (it's that good).Take Zelda, Pokemon, Farming with new seeds you discover on islands that change to new ones during the 4 seasons, Crafting, Turn Basted Card Battles, Skill trees, Open world games, exploring and new island loads every new game like Minecraft, and adorable art, music, and graphics and you've got Moonstone Island. It takes the best parts of everything you love in a game and rolls it into this one.I've found myself so engaged that I'm missing out on sleep. there's so much to discover, do, and never a dull moment. There's quests, discovering new islands, plants and seeds, Spirits to collect and discover (Pokemon), finding Caves from smashing large rocks with treasure chests that give new recipes and discover new potions to brew in your cauldron. Spirits to battle to collect or level your own Spirits in your team. There's a Spirit Barn where you keep all your Spirits. You can switch them out at anytime.  You can feed found items or plants you harvested. To boost your Spirits stats or tame/level them up like Pokemon berries. There's also a really sweet new twist to Spirit battles instead of attacks you have cards to battle with and it's random so it spices things up and gives you more strategic thought into your battling. there's quirky villagers to meet and you can romance and even date too. You can decorate your really cool Alchemy Tent and you can make more tents and place them anywhere on the islands. Every tent will have all that you created and your stations in it so you don't have to make them over and over for each island you wish to stay at the moment. You only have to make the tent and place it where you want. How awesome is that talk about a time saver. There's also fishing too! Get lucky and fish a treasure chest! collect different fish from different island Biomes Fire, Earth, Water, Poison, Electric, and Physic. That's what I got so far from only playing 20 hours and there's still more to do like the Main Quest, Side quests (collecting a spirit for every villager) Discovering all the different Biomes and collect resources from them and deliver them to the Researcher Zed to name a few, and just random quests you get in the mail.Starter Suggestions to help you:When you find a whistle on the island try to place your tent and Spirit Barn as close to that. So you can use this whistle to recall to town once a day. Where you can feed you Spirits, collect resources, check on your crops, and talk to the towns people to boost friendliness, collect daily freebies, turn in quests, or go on dates.  In my world it's East of Paolo the Carpenter in town. My mistake I liked the beach and fishing. So I placed my tent there first and had to hoof it into town or to my crops the first season of Spring wasting a lot of time.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of monster taming games, Stardew Valley and Slay the Spire, this scratches every itch imaginable. The developers have taken the core mechanics and refined them into a player friendly experience. You have Stardew Valley farming and social/dating simulation, Pokemon monster collecting and raising, and Slay the Spire deck battling. The result is a cozy amalgam that doesn't force you too hard into any one aspect.I disagree with the many comments about the days being too short or asking for adjustable time speeds. The days are a similar length to Stardew Valley's, and that mild pressure is central to the time management aspect. If anything it is more forgiving than Stardew Valley - you don't get penalised for falling asleep outside and don't lose stamina for sleeping late. Farming is not the focus. You get sprinklers very early on, and a warp item (which Stardew Valley doesn't give you till the very end!). This immediately frees you up for other aspects of the game, which includes exploration and monster taming. The map is procedurally generated, adding significant replayability. Combining the Slay the Spire card mechanic with a Pokemon-lite experience keeps things fresh. You carry three monsters (or in this game, Spirits) at a time with their own cards which forms the basis of your "deck." You vary your deck by using different Spirits or levelling up your Spirits which allows you to add cards to their set. In battle, being given a random hand each turn forces you to improvise, rather than repetitively selecting the same moves. You can also upgrade, add or remove cards with talismans, which are relatively uncommon.My only gripe with the above is the game doesn't make it obvious that you can "skip" adding cards. If you're not familiar with Slay the Spire mechanics, you can easily end up with a very bloated and ineffective deck. All in all, this is a wonderful game that streamlines and takes the most important bits of some very good games. Here's hoping there will be DLCs to really flesh it out!tldr:Pros:- Unashamedly uses main mechanics of Stardew Valley, monster taming and Slay the Spire, but streamlines it into a more user friendly experience- Adorable monster design and general visual feel - the Octopup is my favourite- Procedurally generated map makes it very replayable- Music is great!- One of those "has a bit of everything" gamesCons (mostly minor):- Slight lags here and there. Hopefully can be optimised out- Most Spirits of the same element seem to have similar "cards", may only differ in passive ability and initial stat distribution- Difficulty level is mild- Finding mines is a bit random. Probably similar mechanic to finding ladders in Stardew Valley mine.- Needs to make it clearer to new players how to streamline deckScore: 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: As a farming game, it is very generous. As a creature catcher, it's a little flat. I didn't expect it to be a deckbuilder-- I only came for the other two parts-- but somehow that was the part that I enjoyed best.This is a good fit for:- People who found Stardew Valley stressful- People who play creature catchers mostly to see cool designs- Serial interior decorators- People who can't get enough of deckbuilding gameplayI still very much enjoyed the game, and I was tickled to see that they are still adding new creatures (and qol) even during my playtime. That was delightful. As of February 2024, this feels like a very solid version 1.0 or 1.1-- worth your money and worth its promises. Plenty of decorations to find and make, plenty of exploration... but it is not yet exceptional. It is a wonderful base that I hope they continue to add to and polish for years to come.The above is my general summary. Below, I'll broach some specific points less for the benefit of prospective players and more on the presumption that perhaps some feedback will be heard.- Not all starters are created equal. With a wider pool, that might be fine. These choices felt strange.- I completed what appears to be the 'main story' within a year, and I don't feel the need to continue past. It feels like I have already accomplished the foremost goals. If that is intentional, the inclusion of years is odd. If it is not, then the pace is too fast.Seasons are novel and a farming staple, but most farm games don't feature exploration so heavily. Each season's crops invalidate the previous, and some spirits are only available in certain seasons. So it feels to me like the best way to 'progress' was actually just to wait. I would rather leave the season mechanic in other farming games and focus on the exploration of the flying islands-- spring islands, autumn islands, winter islands... Make the better crops relegated to further islands rather than time-based. Maybe they can only be planted in certain environments rather than times-- the game already seems set up to let you establish bases on outer islands. This is a ghibli-esque game, let's have a color wheel door like in Howl's Moving Castle. I'm just saying...Ultimately the reason I am not continuing is because I know Spring Year 2 holds nothing for me, and if I don't find every Ice Spirit by the end of the winter, that's going to be a long time to wait. - This might be an unpopular take, but the farming side of the game is -too- generous right now. Money stopped being an object for me by the end of the second season, so I no longer felt compelled to engage with the farming beyond harvesting EXP-- and with how easy the greenhouse was to upgrade and fill with reharvestable plants, that stopped being much of an engagement too.- The glider is wonderful. Love for the glider, love for Nausicaa. But I would still love to be able to craft an expensive end-game even faster version of it for QoL. There are many end-game automation QoLs that I can imagine-- boomerang for harvesting rather than cutting, incubator for quick egg hatching, a way to remotely access the science center... so on.- As a creature catcher, my biggest lament is that while types feel varied from each other, I do not feel like there is much meaningful difference within types. One water creature is as good as another-- maybe there are slight differences in what decks they get, but I can't really tell... but it's especially true for farming.As an example, early in the game I found a big bricky spirit. I caught it, thinking "oh, this will probably be a good way to get bricks!" Fool that I am, bricks are not a resource. The bricky boi will produce exactly the same clay as every other earth spirit. And I am only fighting with three spirits at a time (and I am obviously going to use the cutest ones)... and the big brick buddy's collision eclipses the food trough so he's annoying to feed.... so he is goin' in the science center jail 4 ever.But I would love if there were a reason to collect specific spirits for specific resources. bricks from the brickman. goop from the goop girl. heated wool from the fireysheep. The crafting could become a lot more in depth with more of that and more components/ingredients... In general, I would love more reasons to hunt and engage with specific spirits (matchmaking was fun) and intertwine the two main halves of the game more and more.Plus, the fact that spirits are only ever found in groups by their also does a lot to contribute to them feeling homogenous. Give us bee in flowery areas! Give us water spirits from fishing! So on!!!The devs are still adding new creatures, but what I'm really hoping for is depth over breadth.In all, I hope to play this again someday-- in a lot of years, with a much deeper, fleshed out system of the same concepts. But even as is, the game is easy to enjoy for a short while.

_childDocuments_.review: I am one of those who felt into a trap of: Oh look, it's like pokemon-stardew-zelda in open world and with card battles!Well, maybe it's just me, yet the concept above sounds better than it actually works when put together. I love the art and atmosphere of this game, I love that there is  a ton of things in this cute world, but my main problem is - none of the features advertised work that good to keep your attention. We have  a mash-up of mechanics and features that are stapled together to form a perfect working ecosystem, yet as a result: - this is not a good farming game;- this is not a good creature collector game;- this is not a good exploration game;- this is not a good card battler;Yes, all the things are in and everything works with minimum amount of bugs, yet do you know the difference between a good feature and just feature? It's excitement. It should be exciting to find new spirits, it should be exciting to get and use rare cards. or find and grow new seeds, explore dungeons, all of that. That should reward you with interest, progression, whatever. To my taste - most of the things feel like a routine in this game. Wanna go there? You can't, your level is too low, kill 240+ mobs to level up to be able to bypass this dungeon guard. Want to have a better tool? You can't. Run around and destroy 200+ stones to discover a randomly generated mine, that will (or will not) allow you to mine out 10-30 iron ore within couple of days of game time to craft a better tier pickaxe. What? You got only 11/12 iron bars? That's a shame. Go buy some. Don't have that much gold? Repeat the 200+ stones step. Yeah, you find recipes and new stuff pretty often, I must say, yet still the game feels like completing a dozen daily quests in a MMORPG, or filling in a Battle Pass goals. Anyways, that's just my complaints for this game, Maybe it's the exact opposite for you. Give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: So what exactly is this game about? It's a bit of the following:1) A pokemon like card game.2) An open world exploration game.3) A farming and ranching simulator.4) A dating simulator.In that order. If you don't wan't to play a lot of pokemon card game, you aren't going to have a good timePros.-* The card game is simple, intuitive, and fairly fun, but late in the story you will be spending a lot of hours grinding experience. Many hours.* I like the world building.* I like being able to explore about 100 islands, each of which has at least 1 point of interest, but usually more.* I like most of the spirits themselves. They do start out with some stat variance between individuals, but not between species. Early game spirits and late game spirits will have the same attributes, so don't worry about having to get the best for stats. Now each does have passive ability and some are super powerful, while others are worthless, but you can get through the game with your favorite spirits without having to use the most powerful.* Also some pets give out of combat effects to you, such as +% to walk speed, bonuses on charisma checks with the villagers, a loot magnet.* I like the art style, and vibrancy of the world, with one really off-putting exception. One of the early game earth spirits is straight up the coal spirits from Spirited Away. Also seems to be inspired by Castle in the Sky, and Howls Moving Castle.* Like the food mechanics in this. Food heals, recruits spirits, and gives huge stat buffs. You'll be eating lots of your own crops and feeding them to your spirits. Seriously, food bonuses last all day and make a big difference at a low cost. Feed your pets often.* The game seems really stable. Only soft crashed once in 95 hours.Cons-* The farming is really simplified compared to Stardew Valley, but then again you are expected to be putting the majority of your time into exploration.* Not many NPCs. The village is tiny; 11 romance-able npcs and thats it. No families, no kids, no elderly.* Alright, officially in game, you are the minimum legal age to be emancipated in this world. Whatever that is exactly.  But you look like 10 year old girl. Maybe you suffer from symmetrical dwarfism like that girl on TLC. But all the rest of the villagers normal. Kinda. Like normal for Portland Oregon, but adults in a stardew like art style. Then you look like a little girl. Why??* Also no character customization in any way. Your a little girl. Not that it ever matters in the story.* A matter of personal taste, but I really wasn't interested in many of the villagers. As a little girl I wasn't exited to romance any of them, but I went with the pink haired, lesbian, tom boy, blacksmith, because she was the most normal.* The romance scenes were really disappointing. Seriously the entire scenes are only 5 or 6 text boxes long then done and over in a matter of seconds.* The islands have a lot of M. C. Escher physics. Sometimes you can use this to your advantage, but the physics really seams to struggle with the concept of height.* Trees, grass, and weeds never regrow. Neither do ore nodes. It's not a big deal, but in a game where you are trying to fix the environment, I feel bad about stripping island after island of ever tree and metal ore. That will never regrown again. Ends up feeling like a dying world as the islands become more and more bare of resources the longer you play. A multi year farming simulator where plants don't grow seems really weird.* Not the game maker's problem, but the game is very new, many of the elements of the game are not yet documented and some YouTube guides are giving out mechanically incorrect information. Generally a pretty decent game. But again this is a card game with some farming and romance in it.
