_childDocuments_.review: I just beat Moonstone Island in 23 hrs and 59 minutes (according to my save file, not sure why it says I have 28.1 hrs on record...). While I enjoyed the game and would suggest it if you're a fan of the genre, I do have some feedback that I hope the devs consider in any  future titles. Keep in mind I fully support indie dev teams and totally understand there are practical limitations involved in game dev without a AAA budget. For the small team that made it, I think the team did great. It's also worth noting I don't recall running into any bugs in my time spent playing, which is highly commendable. It's also obvious, but the visuals are also stylized and come together great (except the pixelated character portraits when talking are a bit odd, I think cartoon portraits may have been a better fit if there were enough resources to make them happen). Overall rating: 6/101. Lack of cohesion in character design - I've seen this feedback floating around, but the character design does not seem cohesive across the different types of media. The character's outfit seems to have slight differences between the into movie and the title screen and appears completely different in the splash art when you fall asleep in the field / lose a battle. The game also apparently has a separate outfit for when the player goes to bed, but you can never wear this while you have control of your character. It does not make sense why this second outfit was even added to the game / had art made for it.2. Lack of character identity - You are an "alchemist" in the game, but I never once felt compelled to make any potions (or "concoctions"). While the option is there, concoctions only provide an additive sum of the two ingredients used to brew it, so there is no special reason to use them. Combat / training spirits is also fairly easy so you can just get by feeding the ingredients to spirits directly. Making concoctions is also cumbersome. First, making a potion-making table is locked behind rare resources and first even needs another crafting table (which is also locked behind rare resources) to even make it. Then in order to make potions, you need to first make glass bottles which relies on uncommon drops which you can only get if you have water-type spirits in your spirit barn. This incentives the mass hoarding of water spirits, taking up precious space in your spirit barn. And then once you get a potion brewing, each table can only make 1 concoction at a time and it takes a few minutes of waiting to do so. The overall story of the game also starts as you leave home to take part in your alchemist training (spoilers: you eventually "pass" your training), but there is no obvious connection between your daily activities and this broader goal. I can't help but compare this concept to Potion Permit which actually made you feel like you were applying alchemy knowledge to meet specific milestones in your training. 3. A parallel aspect to the story is that you need to close some evil rift by collecting 4 magical tokens. However, this story is never introduced. Instead, you stumble across a single temple and are given the quest to collect the tokens, but the reason why is never fully explained until the very end of the overall quest. And even then, closing the portal is said to have saved the world, but there is essentially no impact on the world to have known it was in danger in the first place. Sure, spooky dark-themed islands might indicate something is wrong, but their representation within the game is almost no different from the fire-themed islands (ex: you take hazard damage over time, enemies on them are highest level in the game). 4. From a user interaction perspective, I found my fingers getting tired from spamming inputs while navigating menus. Need to buy some seeds? Good luck mashing A over a hundred times to buy them individually. Did you just load materials into a furnace for smelting? You literally need to move your cursor over to a start button - why not map it to some keybinding? 5. Mining is critical for early-game progression but discovering mines is locked behind randomly mining large rocks and hoping to find an entrance. I don't see why they couldn't just assign mine entrances and have them be discoverable like any other landmarks. 6. Not being able to track skill level progression was irritating. Yes, we can craft a magic mirror to look at the skill tree, but even then its not clear to me how my actions translate into exp earned. And why even hide the skill tree to begin with?

_childDocuments_.review: This game is Stardew Valley meets Pokemon meets Magic The Gathering. If that sounds like something you would like then play this game. I enjoyed it equally as much as I did Stardew Valley. But they are a bit different in some way. My playtime ran me through an entire year. I completed almost all quests within that year. Just a few gathering quests left over that would be near impossible to complete on your first year through. I did what I wanted in that first year and feel no need to be a completionist. That said, I got almost 50 hours out of this game, and it was pretty cheap. _childDocuments_.review: I've been hyped for this game since months prior to release and having played a fair bit now, I've got one big take-away: SOOO MUCH POTENTIAL!The start of my play-through was extremely exciting - no clue what I was doing, floating on a balloon into the absolute unknown, when I found a very nifty (and rare!) spirit early on but failed to catch it. I thus spent several in-game months hunting it down and although this personal quest dominated my early playing, with me spending every single night doing the same thing, I didn't feel like I had missed too much in the meantime.Which brings me to my next point: there's a lot this game still needs to remain engaging and long-term in comparison to something like Stardew Valley (which, credit where due, has been years in the works by now).I do agree with other reviews that there are some flat dimensions, chiefly the NPCs (I personally don't like any of them except maybe one, they are not only flat but kind of annoying/too caricature), the farming (good beginnings to it but feels a bit tacked on), the skills (particularly going from 5% to 10% in some skill affect, very underwhelming), and just the overall aim of what to do on a regular basis. The game is lacking any strong lore to help bind the various concepts together, so outside of personal goals (exploring the whole map, hunting the same damn spirit night-after-night), there's not a huge amount of meaning or intent behind the things you can do in it.Also - and this may be seen as an odd critique - but a month or so into the game... That being said, there's a very serviceable amount so far, and a lot of back-end concepts are well structured (the gift system for example having all items categorized into shapes or types; gift somebody that lump of coal, they may even like it!), the spirits so far and element types associated are beat, card system is simple enough and fun to pick up, the actual just exploring from island to island is honestly BOMB! but most importantly the dev is already actively creating updates and new content!So, all in all, I have great hopes for this game and I'm along for the ride!

_childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island is exactly what it advertises itself to be. And it is exactly what you expect it to be. And while there are a lot of negative reviews that criticize the game for lacking in a lot of areas, I am not going to give it a thumbs down. I agree that it is strongly lacking in some regards and there are a lot of things that can be worked on to improve the overall experience and longevity of the game, but those are not points in and of themselves to warrant a thumbs down or a bad review.The game tries to do many many things, and while it succeeds in having those many many things, it falls flat on almost all of them in terms of engagement and length of play - but it is not without its fun. I do think the game is worth its price for what is currently offered and I do think that you should give it a shot if "Cozy" games are your cup of tea, the community is friendly and inviting and the discord is always active. The team takes feedback and suggestions and answers questions pretty quickly and they seem to be really passionate about the project as a whole.I do think that maybe the game should have been marketed as "Early Access", but I do understand why they didn't go that route. But, sadly as Steam only allows for an 8000 character maximum review, there is not enough room for me to give my full thoughts on the game. If you are interested and would like to read a full detailed dive into the game as well as my own thoughts and opinions on it, then I have begun writing a rather lengthy review/guide on the game over on Medium. Feel free to drop by and give it a read sometime and see if this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty great. It has good farming and good creature collecting, and since those are at the core of the game it ends up being a fun experience.I particularly liked the dungeons, which are the core of the game's story - there are 30 dungeons of varying difficulty, but the main story only needs you to complete 15 of them, letting you choose to leave some dungeons behind without penalizing you.The game's only real flaw is that it feels very front-loaded. It feels like 75% of the game's quests are dumped on you as soon as the tutorial ends, creating an illusion of urgency that's at odds with the slower-paced play where the game really shines.As a final note: If you're a completionist, beware that the fishing achievement sucks.

_childDocuments_.review: Card combat system can feel a bit flawed early game since if you have a lower level spirit with your decently leveled spirit, it just feels like youre mixing your good cards with trash ones from the low level spirit. I recommend leveling up everyone somewhat evenly if you can to mitigate this cause once you have an even team, the synergies between spirits feel really good to use which makes combat fun.I wish animations was juuust a touch faster, 1.1x maybe? I also wish when you fish you dont automatically face down cause I sometimes waste stamina by using the fishing rod on the ground.Story is very light hearted and starts off really cute. NPCs dialogue start off a bit too flirty even when you just met them and they barely even have half a heart in romance.First 2 hours of the game is somewhat slow but I like how you can immediately do your own thing right after the tutorial and the game doesnt hold your hand anymore after it. It makes it feel more immersive and adventure feels more rewarding.Highly recommend if you want a chill game that has combat like pokemon mixed with some card RNG with gameplay loop of farming, romancing, and adventure.My only cons about the game maybe is the art of the NPCs. I wish it was a bit more cute and anime. Less western-retro-ish.  I also wish there was a character creator too.

_childDocuments_.review: I am only 11 hours in and this game feels super grindy. I don't really have any "Direction" being given on what to do or where to really go. What is this game about? What am I working towards? What is the point? This is the problem I have with a lot of "cozy" type games is there is nothing for you to even put as a goal. You're just given free reign and sometimes a quest or two that doesn't really mean anything other than character friendship.You can tell this creator was heavily ( and by heavily I mean use the exact same story but change 1 or 2 details) inspired by Hayao Miyazaki films. Which I don't have a problem with, I love those movies and it is fun to see the little bits and pieces of their take on the films in the game.... Also the battle music is almost a direct replica of Zelda gameplay music... I have no problem when creators use inspiration from other amazing games/movies but also seems like they could have put more effort into making it their own.Befriending townspeople seems extremely redundant and very unfulfilling. They have Hearts at the bottom of their chat window, You can "Chat"  "Joke" or "flirt" with them but it creates no dialog, just either hearts or broken hearts upon success/failure.... So there is no real interaction. Also I have talked to the same people for a month now and have barely reached a full heart... I am sure gifts would speed this along but also... why?I do like the battle system, although I have encountered one too many times where all I get are non attack/attack cards and no armor breaking cards and can pretty much do nothing but waste my turn.Leveling in the game is weird. There seems to be a huge jump in wild creature levels from level 1-5 and then all the sudden the next island is level 13s in a trio that can all just add afflictions and take out your armor in 2 turns even with a full team that is in similar level ranges. Oh,  get this element type it'll make this area easier!Cool, that level element type is like 3x higher than the area I need to be in so I can't even use them if I tame one since I have a tame level cap?They claim a material is super rare in the game and that only one material exists per island but then require 9 of them per building craft...so far, I've only just hit summer, I know most farming games don't pick up til later on, but this seems like they added farming just to say it has a farming element... Its a "Oh get seeds and grow these 3 plants per season that all do the same thing except this ONE plant you will use relentlessly."I am hoping I change my review later on, but so far it's very grindy for no reason, there is no real direction in the game that makes me want to continue.I know a lot of people like those laid back cozy games like Animal crossing, and don't get me wrong I do too on occasion when they are well done and give atleast some reason to play it day by day. But you're not even told your character has the desire to see all the creatures, or gather badges to beat a final boss. You're literally just told to go "live on your own" by your weeping parents. Stardew was atleast escaping your old life and defeating the evil corporation, harvest moon games are saving the homeland, Animal crossing is a collection game that still gives you goals and achievements to work towards. Rune Factory you're trying to save Something and have a plot to  go along at your own pace.  Sunhaven is super cozy game but has better story telling and an end goal. Serin fate is an amazing farming/creature collection game that has a direction.All in all. I might give it a few more hours... but I don't even really want to, which is a shame because I expected to really like this one.

This game has a lot of things to offer to always keep you engaged for many hours and I personally recommend this game to those who enjoy creature collection like Pokemon, those who enjoy farming sims, and those who enjoy deck building combat games :3! Not only is the game enjoyable but the devs are very hardworking and have many updates planned and I am very excited to see what they will add or change about this game! The only issue I think I have is we need some sort of teleportation device. I know we have the flute to return back to town but I think we need some sort of device to place on an island to teleport there to finish a dungeon or to go to our outer island bases/ homes. _childDocuments_.review: This game has great music, cute graphics, overall has just been a delight. The battling, monster collecting, and deck building mechanics are all very fun to interact with. Traveling around from island to island, digging up treasure, mining, dungeon diving and getting to know the large world map feels very fulfilling. I'd like to give a second shout out to the great sound design. Music makes or breaks games, and this one has a soundtrack that makes it very easy to lose yourself in this big little world. Secondary sound designs are on point too. Picking up materials has a very satisfying noise, activating your magic broom, etc.I've only completed the first season and a half, so I haven't seen everything the game has to offer yet. That being said, I have two minor complaints so far:The first is that though the mechanics of combat are fun, and the design of the monsters are cute and interesting, the attacks lack graphical pizzazz. Many attacks have lackluster animations (Avalanche is a 3-energy attack that is very fun to use as a finisher, and it's especially underwhelming), and there's no extra dopamine fix like a screen shake or achievement if you deal massive amounts of damage (or maybe there is, and I just haven't gotten my numbers high enough yet). The second complaint I have is that I love all these villagers so much. I really wish I could see more of them, maybe celebrate some holidays with them. Like I mentioned earlier, I've only played through spring and half of summer, but so far the only things to celebrate with them have been birthdays and dates. I love their designs. I've gotten one character to maximum hearts, and didn't get any extra scenes with her yet. Though it's been really fun doing other side quests for the villagers.I'm having lots of fun with this game. I know there's more left for me to find.

_childDocuments_.review: Really a quite wonderful and charming game with a lot to be said about it. Mostly positive things to say from here. It's marrying of Farming Sim and Creature Collecting was executed in a way such that you could focus on either aspect at your leisure, without the sense of urgency the former usually comes with and the grinding of the latter.For a detailed rundown--Likes:- The art. It's very simple, readable, and polished. Reminiscent of GBA pokemon games or LoZ Minish Cap. Nothing feels cluttered. It could have maybe benefited from having a bit more variety in the environment, but what is there delivers.- The designs of the spirits. The majority of the spirits are wonderfully designed. With the exception of a couple "everyday objects with humanoid features slapped on them" designs that make me sigh, they all have a very unique feel to them with their own charm to offer. There's enough variety to their designs and enough similarity between their gameplay (we'll get to that later) that I'm confident in saying there's a few for pretty much anyone to love.- The balance of the spirits. This game forced me a bit out of my comfort zone that pokemon instilled in me of just grinding my starter and using it to plow through everything. That distinctly will not work in this game. Going into midgame the wild spirits will always show up in groups of three, and there's no real forced targeting system to keep them from attacking the one they're strongest against. And they -will- attack the one they're strongest against, potentially wiping out a type disadvantage party member in the first turn. Holding onto your starter all the time is impractical at best, and you will be punished for it. Having one favorite of each type and swapping them out depending on where you plan to explore is greatly rewarded.- "Go your own way". Something I especially appreciated about this game was that the only really necessary point of focus was battling with the spirits. Everything available in the game benefits you to some degree: Farming gives you extra stamina to do more material collection and improve the stats of your spirits, mining can improve your tools, fishing can nab you some extra cash, relationships can give you extra goodies, etc. The greenhouse to grow things in any season is easy enough to unlock early on, removing the sense of urgency of getting crops done by a certain deadline.Generally, it feels like there's a lot available for you with meaningful benefits, but fairly little forced on you if you just want to focus on exploring and training your spirits.- Decoration Options: Exploration frequently awards you with crafting recipes for your decoration table, and boy is there a lot of them. Compared to the somewhat bare-bones feel of the decoration in the overworld, the decoration options you have for inside your house feel rather robust, including the ability to make custom wall and floor tiles.Now, let's get to the games few less-than stellar qualities--Dislikes:- Lack of character customization: I don't think the game is in need of an elaborate character creation with dozens of options. But in a game that is clearly friendly towards the LGBT+ and recognizing of ninbinary individuals, it feels rather out of place to lock the player into a distinctly femme presenting player character. They feel very "up to viewer interpretation" most of the time, and are never referred to by gender, but when you go to bed and change into night outfit it feels pretty apparent what the MC's presentation is supposed to be.Gender presentation aside, it'd just be nice to have a few outfit options (unlockable, maybe?) or the ability to dye your outfit so you can match with your favorite spirit. Beardini supremacy is all I'll say on that last matter.- Bare bones overworld design. The world is procedurally generated, and I imagine part of how they managed being able to do this in such a simple game is having rather limited assets. Not counting the few objects (spirits, chests, two plants), basically every island has sprites for a big tree, a little tree, a big rock, a little rock, and grass. The sprites change depending on the element of the island you're on, but islands of the same element tend to feel very...same-y. The mines have three sprites, a rock, a copper rock, and a silver rock.The temples are the most egregious, though. They're very designed-up and neat looking compared to the rest of the game, but ultimately all have the same format of "put object on pedestal, walk forward with x item, fight thing, rinse and repeat."-Lack of resource restoration: There is no returning of resources in this game from what I've seen. If you clear the trees on an island, they're gone for good. There's no planting seeds for new ones, no having some come back next season or next year. My understanding is that, as it stands, if you clear all the resources off of every island, they're gone for good and you can no longer acquire wood, stone, ore, or fiber.- Spirits of the same element are basically all reskins: Aside from having their own unique ability, spirits of the same element functionally all get access to the same skills and are subject to the same "you choose their stats" mechanic. This leads to feeling like there's not really much of a sense of discovery with getting to use a new spirit you've found. You level up that new fire spirit and the cards given to it look exactly like the cards of your previous fire spirit. There's a positive to this, in that you're never really gonna run into "well crap, this spirit I really like sucks compared to the others", but a negative in that there's little sense of individuality when it comes to these spirits in a combat context.- Lack of information: There's really not a ton of hand-holding, for better or worse. There's no sort of tips menu to explain various mechanics of the game, and some things are just...false? For example, a letter you get in the beginning of the game explains mechanics around collecting the game's most precious resource: Moonstones. It says that every island only has one -per season-. But if you loot a moonstone and go back to the island once a new season has begun, there is none to be found. As far as I know, once you've collected a moonstone, the island will not make another.They've made updates to fix some of these communication issues, but there is still broadly rather poor communication.- Controls. The updates are showing they've been patching this and...honestly it's still pretty bad. Walking up to things and having it select something behind what you want to select is a frequent occurrence and sometimes it's so bad you just have to play the "get in the right pixel for positioning" game just to select something. Hopefully this one gets remedied with time.---Ultimately, none of those cons break the game for me. I've gotten a good chunk of hours out of it and will be going out it for more. There's a simple charm to it that's easy to appreciate and laid back. Perfect for winding down at night.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll summarise my thoughts at the start and tell you that I think Moonstone Island is a really good game with a lot of potential. Importantly, the world setting, art style and music are all irresistibly charming and reminds me of Stardew Valley, my favourite chill farming sim and one of my favourite games of all time. On top of that, they get a lot of the core features right but manages a surprisingly fresh take of it with the exploration, deck building combat and Pokemon-esque collecting of team members called spirits. In a genre filled with SV clones, I'm quite impressed and this has been one of my favourite new finds of 2023.The game is not without it's issues but the dev team seem quite proactive and are implementing fixes and bugs. There's some nitpicks and gripes I have with certain game mechanics such as the cards not being clear on how they scale with stats, nor how much of an improvement they are when upgraded which can be quite key as combat is a significant part of the game. The game can also feel a bit grindy and stall as you're often limited by Moonstone and spending it sub-optimally can really slow the progress of your early game.Moonstone Island is really a jack of all trades. The farming and variety of crops is plentiful but intentionally not a key part of your economy as you are generally better rewarded for exploration. The romancing mechanics are just adequate but outside of dates, daily conversation is limited to a greeting and roll checks which removes some of the charm and personality of village NPCs. Given adequate time and perhaps some mods, it could turn the game from good into something great. For now it's still a solid recommendation and at the relatively reasonable entry fee, I've more than got my moneys worth.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: ***Update 10/27*** The devs came through and fixed all my nitpicks, so am happy to fully endorse this game and recommend it as a must-play for fans of cozy games.A promising little game that still needs polishing. Mostly it needs small quality-of-life stuff, such as better UI and easier ways to transport items around. However, there's on major issue: resources don't respawn.That tree you cut down? Gone forever. And no, you don't get a seed from it to replant, it's just gone.That mine you cleared of resources? Empty forever.That grass you cut? Never going to regrow.This is genuinely a vibe-killer. I don't want to be clearcutting forests and stripmining for ore in a cozy sim game. Give us the ability to replant trees, make trees able to spawn on their own as the seasons change, make grass regrow over time, and give us some way to close old mines and have a chance of finding new ones, and I'll be much happier with the overall experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island is by far the most fun, interesting, goofy, and enjoyable game that I've played. It's hard to say that it's an entry into a specific genre, as it combines farming sim, creature collecting, crafting, adventuring, and dungeon diving all into one, but if you're a fan of classic farming sim series such as Harvest Moon, creature battling (Pokemon), and generally like to have fun discovering new things - this is most definitely the game for you. I have put in nearly 60 hours on my first play through and I've been seriously addicted to it. I've played nearly every game of this type as I find them enthralling most of the time, but to date this game takes the cake for the most fun. The farming is fun but also not obnoxious, the townsfolk are funny and different than most similar games, and flying around on your glider is a blast! easy to control, easy to pick up and learn, enough quests to keep you working hard but not too many to overwhelm you... just fantastic game design through and through. Keep up the great work Studio Supersoft!

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty solid. Felt like a card battler with passable dungeons crawling and farming sim attached. It does not excel at any of those, but if you do want to play all of them its good. My main complaint is that I feel like the characters are a bit flat. Some even seem redundant. It feels like there was a decision to make everyone romanceable, but that means there are no non romanceable characters to make the town feel more like a town. But then they also ran out of "roles" for characters, so some had to double up. Like 2 people selling house plants. Overall, I do like it, but I am a card battler + farming sim addict.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to be honest, it takes a lot of aspects from different games, tries to combine them into one, and doesn't really nail it. _childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to rate this positively. Overall, Moonstone Island is a great idea whose execution is diminished by a surface-level design of its features and a clear lack of game balance.As a fan of Pokemon, Zelda, Slay the Spire and Stardew Valley, you'll find that Moonstone Island offers familiar settings do what brought you to these games but without any of their depths. While there are a lot of spirits, they all share their elemental decks (meaning you really have half a dozen unique decks). While there are a LOT of dungeons, they are all solved by stepping on buttons, building bridges and beating bosses. While the deck-building aspect can seem interesting at first, you quickly realize that not focusing on bash cards is a waste of time. Bashing stuns enemies, so you can take your time defeating them.And finally, farming. You get seasonal crops and you'll mostly farm for alchemical reasons. Shame the tables and cauldrons you need are gate-locked behind quests that require items that force you to be on higher tier islands which will kill you unless you craft items made of moonstones, a finite resource that you can find once per island, also forcing you to explore before you're ready! The temples are this game's Community Center, asking for offerings of seasonal crops and forageables. Shame those temples are also located on islands you'll likely not have the time to visit before their respective season is over! Better luck next year! Gating things through quest lines and moonstones seem to be the game's attempt to pad things so you'll play more than a year.Which is weird because even if I play with day length in the settings and set it to the longest, I don't have enough time during the day to do all the exploring and farming and socialising I need to do to keep the game going and not have to wait for the next year to finish quests I'm getting on year 1 spring. It can be a bit frustrating.You'll read reviews mentioning that NPCs are one-dimension and bland and at first glance, it's true. Haven't had the time to max their hearts because even that mechanic is a skill check with a percentage chance of failure and for some reason, I've been incredibly unlucky. Yes, this means that even if you talk to everyone all the time, they can theoretically hate you for it. Which, with the sheer amount of stuff one needs to do to avoid missing any seasonal seed / fail to complete quests, is not optimal.So at surface level, it's a beautiful game with tons of exploration, funny-looking creatures and farming. When you dig deeper, you realize the spirits don't really matter, the dungeons are all the same and the game features HAVE to be used with near omniscience if you don't want to get stuck waiting a whole game year to finish quests. I'm just looking at my quest log grow and grow and grow and I grow depressed.I'd say wait and see what the developers do to balance the game but it seems they're already at the stage where they're selling DLCs so I'm pretty sure we won't see any core improvements.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: I hopped into this game expecting to enjoy it right from the start. It matched a ton of my interests and the art style was adorable, so I had to try it out. What I was not expecting was the insane similarities between it an the movie "Kiki's Delivery Service" from the main character starting off by leaving home to fulfill their training, to the shop keeper you first meet having the same name as the baker from the movie! I absolutely love that movie so I immediately fell in love with this game. Personally I almost want to meet the developer myself to congratulate them and thank them for making such an amazing game! Heck, I rarely make reviews in the first place so that already shows how much I enjoyed this game in the first 20 minutes of playing it!

_childDocuments_.review: I am the exact target audience for a game like this (cozy, wholesome, etc.).  I'm a huge fan of games like Stardew, Littlewood, and Slay the Spire.  This game is not really a farming sim, even though you can (and probably should) farm to get crops that will help you recover HP and tame spirits in combat.  Rather than a cross of Stardew and Slay the Spire, to me it's more like a cross between Animal Crossing New Horizons and Slay the Spire.  I mean that it's more focused on the card game combat, adventuring to different islands, and completing quests than it is on farming or earning gold.  You can also ignore the quests that don't resonate with you without much (if any) repercussions.  For example, I ignored all but the very first alchemy brewing quests in my first year and no one expressed disappointment at the end of the year (no <4 candle type situation for those who know Stardew).  I've heard comparisons of this game to Pokemon, but I don't know how accurate that is since I've never played one of those games.  I can say though that the combat is fun, the spirits are cute, the villagers are charming and diverse, and the fishing is now more accessible than it used to be.  The game is regularly upgraded with improvements and I've had a fun time so far playing a couple of hours here and there over the months since release.It's of course, not a perfect game.  The RNG on the fish, for example, caused me to delay completing the temples for so long that they became comically easy.  I would have liked to see those more scripted encounters scale up with my party's increased level.  I also understand that the art was hand drawn etc. etc. but I would have appreciated the ability to change my character's physical appearance.  Even just a slider to change the skin tone and hair color to more closely reflect who I am would have been nice.  I also believe there are supposed to be holo spirits, but I've yet to encounter one, and some quests I want to do remain unfulfilled because it is so difficult to find the right spirit (I'm really sorry Ferra!).  Things like this are not dealbreakers for me though, and I hope they won't be for you.  The game has been a lot of fun for the past 60 hours I've played of it, so it's still incredibly worth the money even at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Moonstone Island

_childDocuments_.review: To start, I have not beaten the game. TLDR; The game feels underbaked. It has all the right ideas. However, it doesn't quite commit to nor develop any of them fully.The main issue and why only about 7% of people that own the game have tamed 10 spirits (which is basically the equivalent of going on route 1 and catching 9 pidgey for a total of 10 pokemon.....really simple and easy) is because the game is not intuitive nor set up in a way that is accessible.In order to tame more spirits than the 3 you can carry in your medallion, you have to LET GO on one of them, tame a level 5 spirit, turn that research into Zed, and the next day by mail he will send you a blueprint for a spirit barn where you can house more spirits. But there's a catch! It costs rare materials to make AND you have to farm out MORE materials in order to even use it once you have made it. You have to craft individual stalls within the barn to even get more spirits despite....spending a good chunk of materials to craft it in the first place? From what I have seen, this is one of the biggest qualms from the playerbase. It is why people put the game down after taming 3 spirits.Essentially, the process of the....basis of the entire game....is clunky and not welcoming. There's also big imbalance in typings. I believe there are at least more than 10 earth type spirits and water type spirits...but 3 ice type.... For whatever reason!The characters are alright and easy to interact with. But the system in which you gain affection is...underwhelming. You have 4 options to interact with everyone: Chat, Joke, Flirt, and Gift. While gifting follows the traditional standard of games like Stardew Valley, the others are disappointing. Rather than having dialogue for the first three options, it is just an action that you perform with a chance of succession. For example, let's say you want to chat. Instead of any dialogue popping up, which feels natural, you gain affection points if the chat is successful. Have you, this is an immediate process as soon as you click the option. It just feels like the romancing/social building aspect was shoehorned in to make the game seem more desirable. You don't get any real personality from the characters other than Tavern Owner LOVES to drink, Scientist is a Nerd, Carpenter LOVES Wood, Plant Lady loves grass....etc. You don't actually get to interact with the people in this game. You just click buttons to farm points with them.Even after giving your lovely, special character of choice a moonstone bracelet, that is it. That is all that happens. Ever. There is no point in dating.The animations take forever and you spend more than half the day on your farm if you need to harvest/plant. Crops do not sell for much unless you choose to make a massive farm and spend your ENTIRE day farming. Options like fishing take up much less stamina and ends up being more lucrative. Upgrading tools make things easier but when you have the maxed out version, it still, for some reason, takes multiple hits to harvest something. For example, a small rock normally takes 4 hits with the standard hammer, 3 hits with the copper hammer, 2 hits with the iron hammer, and 2 hits with the moonstone hammer..... The fact that moonstones are also quite rare, makes this frustrating. While I haven't upgraded to a moonstone scythe, I believe it still also takes multiple swings to harvest crop seeds with it where it should only be....1 swing.All in all, this feels okay. I do not have any qualms. To be fair, I barely have engaged in much of it since I have spent most of my time farming and really unable to have any time to do much else? The game, for whatever reason, loves to lock recipes behind feats. It does not makes sense. The fact that you also have to put points in your medallion in order to tame low level spirits is....another block in the road for most people. Oddly enough, there is none. There will never be and this is....so dividing for many. You don't even get to give yourself a name.There are many QoL issues that you'll notice as soon as you get into the game.- Not being able to sell stacks at shops, you have to individually sell every item.- Trees, rocks, and grass (all essential resources) are limited and NONRENEWABLE. Once you chop a tree, smash a rock, and cut some grass, they are gone forever.- Mines that are uncovered, and once fully cleared out, remain a gaping hole despite having nothing in it. There is no way to cover up these mines and there are a limited number of mines throughout the map.- Having to individually load furnaces rather than putting your stacks in and coming back when they are all done...... Also 3 iron ores making 1 iron ingot is crazy.....especially when each island has 1 mine and materials are non renewable.There is many more issues that tons of people in the official discord bring up. But the sheer number of issues makes me feel like this game should have absolutely been early access and not fully launched.Do not buy this game right now. The whole game needs a rework.THAT ALL SAID!!!!I loved all the ideas Moonstone Island brought to the table. It just feels like I'm drinking a la croix....It's like I'm trying to play a game but the game is in the other room. It's not quite there. Hopefully with future updates, it'll be MUCH better and fleshed out. But as of right now, it is not quite there.

_childDocuments_.review: does not work with my 8bitdo pro2 ,somehow adding extra inputs and doesnt seem to be respecting the steam controller settings.Edit. It's slow and lacks quite a bit of the polish from other games. Moving from island to island is painfully boring at first. The main items to be crafted all require moonstones/moonstone ingots. _childDocuments_.review: I've been playing games on and off all my life. As we age, we have priorities that doesn't allow us to spend too many hours on our hobbies at home. This game was perfect for me, because it's not overly complicated and gets you straight into playing. It's a mix of stardew, pokemon, and a deckbuilder. _childDocuments_.review: Moonstone Island has me in a choke-hold. I have almost 19 hours at time of review, and I bought the game not even 5 days ago. Yes, I know. I need to touch grass.All jokes aside, this game is addicting. As everyone describes, it's a Stardew Valley x Pokemon x Slay the Spire game, which came across strange to me at first. See, I LOVE Pokemon and Slay the Spire, but Stardew never caught my interest. I own it on switch, sure, but I played maybe an hour. Something about it didn't click with me. So, when I saw this game streamed by a friend of mine on twitch, subsequently seeing those 3 games named in numerous reviews, I was halfway hesitant. That was a week ago. It only took me 2 day to gave and buy the game, and I'm so glad I did. Moonstone has a ton more than one may realize off the bat, and it's definitely a slowly paced game. Recipe unlocks are behind quest walls and dungeon chest RNG for the most part, and resources are definitely a time grind. But for me, I think it's the music, sound effects, and overall atmosphere that make it feel not as grindy as other games. The pixel art is super cute, and while the OST overall is great, there's a couple songs in there that have me wanting to buy the soundtrack soon. Both of those make breaking rocks and chopping trees less boring than it could be.Spirits are definitely interesting. As far as I can tell, they have no evolutions, and I haven't seen any cards 100% unique to a spirit yet. They do have varying base stats but, overall, I think you could make a viable team with whichever spirits you like if you're just a casual player like me! That's my thought so far, at least. I was concerned at first at the low number of Spirits overall, but it seems like they are adding a few more with each update so, I have faith that they will continue to be expanded upon. Not to mention, there is a shiny mechanic just like Pokemon. The base chance is .2%, which is higher than Pokemon and much preferred. I like being able to have a chance to find something rare, but without it being astronomical. I mean, I've already found 2, which just makes me want to play more to find more! My only negative point at this time is just the number of mechanics - or pieces of mechanics - that aren't really obvious. I've found myself asking a lot in the Discord, which has been extremely helpful, but isn't perfect for anyone who may not use Discord. For example, the fact that you can move a little while on the Balloon isn't really clear, or the fact that the ring at the top left changes color based on the Spirits levels on the island compared to your party's. Overall, this game is definitely a time sucker, but well worth it if it's even relatively up your alley.

Following your village's tradition for Alchemy training, you've moved to an island in the sky to spend a year away from home. Armed with simple tools, Alchemical recipes, and the ability to tame nature spirits, you set out to start your new life. 

Make new friends, explore the world, and build a home for yourself in a land stifled by wild spirits and dark forces.

detailed_description: CRIME BOSS REVIEWS AND ACCOLADES Digital Deluxe Edition Get the most out of your adventure with the Digital Deluxe Edition, which includes the following content: • Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes full game • 1x Easy Journey Pack: (6x Healing Herb, 4x Healing Incense, 2x Revive Medicine. 3x Runeshard of Return, 1x Gold Coin) • 1x Headquarters Custom Object • Season Pass: [3x Original Wallpapers by Junko Kawano, Story Expansion: The Chapter of Seign, Story Expansion: The Chapter of Marisa, Story Expansion: The Chapter of Markus and HQ Makeover Pack (Golden & Pink Headquarters Exterior Paint)] • Digital Mini Artbook • Digital Soundtrack Join the community on Discord About the Game Our story begins in one corner of Allraan, a tapestry of nations with diverse cultures and values. By dint of sword, and by way of magical objects known as “rune-lenses,” the land’s history has been shaped by the alliances and aggressions of the humans, beastmen, elves, and desert people who live there. The Galdean Empire has edged out other nations and discovered a technology that amplifies the rune-lenses’ magic. Now, the Empire is scouring the continent for an artifact that will expand their power even further. It is on one such expedition that Seign Kesling, a young and gifted imperial officer, and Nowa, a boy from a remote village, meet each other and become friends. However, a twist of fate will soon drag them into the fires of war, and force them both to reexamine everything they believe to be right and true. Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes became the #1 funded Kickstarter video game of 2020 thanks to phenomenal support from the community. 505 Games is truly honored to publish Eiyuden Chronicle and work with Rabbit & Bear to help deliver a memorable gaming experience to fans. The goal of Rabbit & Bear and 505 Games is to make sure Eiyuden Chronicle reaches its true potential and delivers a worthwhile JRPG the community will enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game but could be improved greatly by a single adjustment. Make the map movement bonus permanent once you get the related follower.You do a lot of running in this game. _childDocuments_.review: This is mostly spoiler free - I won't be mentioning specific plot points or character names, but will have some commentary on the overarching theme/feel of the story, and some of the side content.Like many others I've been here since Suikoden 1. Honestly, although there's lots this game left me wanting for, I was prepared to give it a recommendation - as while nothing really lived up to my expectations and hopes, I acknowledge my hopes were high to begin with.It's hard for me to find major faults with the game. On the whole, it was fine, okay, good enough, passing grade. If that were it, it'd be fine, but one bit stops me from giving it the thumbs up. I'll put that at the end, but first, the other main features of the game:The story is probably the worst offender here for failing to live up, as things just don't really feel...built up enough to me. Some have theorized this is from the game being E for everyone instead of T for Teen, and I could see it. The stakes of war are never really felt, the investments of the characters for their fights, their backgrounds, it all feels a bit too Saturday-Morning Cartoon. Villains don't get expanded upon enough to feel compelling. Attempted epic, scenic moments don't feel as impactful as they could. I think one reason may be because we're told who's good, who's bad - but we're not really shown it through story events. Why is this person good? Why should I get the feeling they're a bad character? It's relatively surface level, and very repetitive. There are no real "reveals" in the story. There is a hint at something grandiose going on in the background, but we never get anything from it or learn even the littlest about it. That's a far cry removed from everything with the True Runes in Suikoden that they were trying to follow suit with in this game.But again, it's...okay. It's serviceable. There's just nothing that stands out to me storywise. I was driving 30mph down a road with no real traffic and nothing interesting to look at for 40-50 hours or so. Not bad. Got me from point A to B. Just with nothing to really remember.Heck I don't think there was even a single significant storyline twist?But let's move on.Combat is 'fine' - there are issues with the balance, tuning, and timing that will lead many people to a lot of auto battling rather than using unique character setups for the team combos, as the team combos just really aren't worth the hassle and setup, or magic for the majority of the main game is useless aside from healing due to high MP costs with limited restoration methods for, again, the majority of the main game. While late game combat starts shifting things up a bit, I feel your first 20-35 hours are going to leave more an impact on most players. This leads to it being pretty stale and uninteresting for much of the game, but it works. Again, it's fine.The war battles are pretty bad. They're mostly glorified cutscenes that drag on due to some abysmal pacing of the actual fight once you say "go." These were never ridiculously amazing in Suikodens, but I still made more choices and felt like I had more agency in most of the other titles. There's a lot of "turn 1, turn 2....okay cutscene time something unexpected is happening aaand battle is basically over" here.Music ranges from fine to good, with one piece that stands HIGH above all the others that you luckily get to hear pretty early on. If there's ONE thing I'm taking away from this game, it's that track.I really enjoyed most of the voice acting. It is clear the voice actors gave it a lot of attention, and it especially shows in some of the side content dialogue. Things could sound deadpan or as comedic as they wanted, and sprinkled throughout the voice acting gave me a lot of fun moments to remember. The voices alone probably saved this game for me due to the memories I'll have of them. Not all are amazing, some of the localization I don't...love and the direction made it fall flat, but by and large I loved the lines from everyone.Some of the side content is good - there's so much voice acting for one of them that it's almost worth getting the game alone to play around with, but alas, here comes the bit that makes me give the thumbs down.Two of the characters (needed for the true ending) in the game are locked behind obscenely long minigame stories, one of which includes 160 minutes of idling around waiting for challengers to spawn in between progress. It is probably better if you do this as soon as you can so you can poke at it here or there - but if you wait until later to finally do the minigame, you're in for a boring hell of waiting, then mashing a, then waiting. The other is a beyblade minigame story that, again, is needlessly padded by requiring you to go demolish NPCs who have no chance just so you can progress the story of it.These two minigames alone stopped me from progressing for almost a week - not because they took THAT long (They did take at least 5 hours, probably 6-7 since I didn't spend the whole time being "ultra efficient" with them), but because the sheer droll of these very badly made minigames plus the ridiculous time grind of them had me dreading starting the game up when I could be doing other things. I had to force myself through to get these two characters. They dragged this game from, say...maybe a 7/10 experience for me down to a 6 or possibly a 5.It's a shame, too, as the stories for those minigame stories are perfectly fine, cut from the same cloth as afternoon anime and humorous in the same ways with over the top voice acting to boot, but they were simply so long and the games themselves so lackluster that the sheer tedium of it all made me just want to skip all the dialogue.All in all this is a standard, okay JRPG that evokes a fair bit of the feelings of the PS1 era. It falls short from achieving the highs of its predecessors, but I would say it doesn't fall short in any super egregious ways. I enjoyed most of my time with it, I wish the story, characters, and villains had more going on for them, and I really really really wish the two aforementioned minigames weren't such a miserable experience and speedbump in an otherwise pretty okay title.

_childDocuments_.review: Some thoughts after playing Eiyuden after 25 hrs:Summary: All in all, I think they played it too safe in creating this game. Honestly I would have liked if they made bolder or riskier decisions and more mature storyline but I kinda understand because of what’s on the line with this first game and new studio. Expecting more if there’s a sequel. And still a decent game all things considered. With Murayama gone (RIP), really curious what’s the future of the series will look like.Detailed thoughts:Background: I played Suikoden 1-5 a lot and know it like the back of my hand. Can recruit 108 characters and do the true ending without looking a guided even after all these years. So with that out of the way, here are my thoughts.This is a decent JRPG game. But falls short since it’s supposed to be a Suikoden successor. Might be better than Suikoden 1 (arguable) but can’t live up to Suikoden 2 and 5.Some gameplay thoughts:1. Changes the Suikoden rune system to Rune Lenses. Kinda nice. MP and system are nice too but the random SP during encounters make me rage. Why is it random?2. I love that there are at least various weapon types and it’s not all physical damage. Kudos to this. 3. I don’t like that they removed the party formation system from Suikoden 5. And only 1 support member? And can’t freely move party in entourage. Changing party members in inns are nice tho.4. Teleport system is way better. I miss Viki tho. :(5. I hate the war gameplay so much specially when I compare it to 2 and even to 5.6. I hate the treasure chest gimmick battles as a completionist.7. World map seems way smaller? Since they’re segmented to smaller areas.8. Almost third person POV is still throwing me off, I still prefer top down.

_childDocuments_.review: The main issues i've seen people post about this game and why they seem negligible.1 - localisation. This seems fine for anyone that hasn't gone out of their way to realise some lines are changed compared to their Japanese counterparts. Yes some are a bit cringey, but hell, it's a suikoden spiritual successor and a cheese fest jrpg, it's to be expected.2. A lack of encounters. This can be modified with accessories, I feel if it were higher it would become aggravating for people exploring the world, also you can build a dungeon underneath your castle that provides battles with high exp and gold. 3. A lack of fast travel. This is redundant as after about 10 hours of in game time you unlock a character that provides fast travel, save a majority of exploration until you've recruited them. 4. Objective markers. So, if you're actually reading the text, the only times there isn't a marker the next goal is explained to you, or visible on your map. One complaint details one of the first quests "It says to recruit heroes but not how many", which is potentially the dumbest complaint as you only have 5 areas unlocked at this point, go through them, recruit everyone, and come back to check progress, the complaint just seems a bit brain-dead and wanting hand holding. The only real issue I have with this game is the army battles, they feel underdeveloped as they don't even show the characters you're using, just generic sprites. I feel a fire emblem inspired system would have been amazing here. Other than that i'm enjoying the time i'm sinking into this game, the heroes all feel unique to some degree, they all have different points they excel at, and the amounts of anime and other game references always makes me smile. Also if you ever get overwhelmed by the text heavy story, just take a break with one of the numerous side activities that seamlessly fit into the game and allow you to recruit more characters. There's racing / breeding, cooking, fishing, Beyblades and card games.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the rare games I backed on Kickstarter some time ago is a the spiritual successor to the cult classic Suikoden games, made by their original designer. In Eiyuden, we play as Nova, a newcomer in the local law-keeping organization/mercenary guild. Soon, events rapidly escalate, intertwining ancient magical (or perhaps not-so-magical) technologies, political intrigues, and war. Unintentionally, we find ourselves leading this guild, responsible for recruiting new members, developing our base, and planning operations. It would have been a bit more believable if Nova had any kind of charisma, but he usually comes across as an awkward and rather compliant young man.However, the game isn’t just about Nova—there’s no shortage of characters of all kinds, each with their own quirk. They say that if you gather them all, you can unlock a happier ending, but I didn’t make it that far. The characters are quite appealing, though I would’ve preferred if instead of 120 of them, there were half as many, with each getting twice as much screen time. Still, they have enough charm to make you care about them and see them as real people rather than nameless units.The combat system is moderately interesting, combining tactical planning with auto-battle. We select 6 characters who stand in two rows—front and back—just like the enemies (except for bosses). Then, we choose actions for all the fighters at once, and the round plays out automatically. Different actions/skills can move our fighters up or down on the initiative scale. On one hand, this system allows for planning, but often the lack of direct control makes it impossible to efficiently use healing (since enemy targets are unknown) or area attacks, leading to wasted actions. The game has a full auto-battle option, and honestly, on normal difficulty, most fights are easy to get through without any commands from me.Base building is fun, but more because of the satisfaction of upgrading than the actual gameplay—gather resources, choose an upgrade, done. The game has many mini-games, but none of them turned out to be particularly interesting—at least for me. On top of that, some of them require random drops just to play.So, what’s the verdict? Unfortunately, the attempt to create a serious political story didn’t work, but I wasn’t really expecting it to. It’s a missed opportunity, but one that's easy to overlook. Ultimately, it’s impossible not to see the soul and love with which this game was made, and it’s hard not to feel warm feelings toward the characters, so the game succeeds in its goal.

_childDocuments_.review: Now hold on there, before you get all angry, it's important to note that, like you (probably) as someone who has played Suikoden, Breath of Fire, and so many other fantastic classics of the past where video games were created with limited space, massive leaps in creativity, and genuinely fun mini-games, story, music, and characters that even without dialogue, voice acting or any eye candy visual effects were able to keep you engaged for hundreds of hours and often times on the edge of your seat crying out in response, this game lacks all of that. Lian and Nowa are portrayed so heavily as Nanami and Riou to the point where it is sickening that they are butchering my image of them both, I keep confusing them as Suikoden.I haven't even finished this game yet, and I'm literally at my limit of patience. The localization is 50/50; it's not bad, but it's far from optimal if you speak or understand any Japanese. Something as simple as a character saying "..." (Gasp) in Japanese only to have it translated to "We should probably get going" or completely ignoring specific lines of dialogue like "Yes! We did it!" (Yatta) to something more basic and bland like "It's done." and putting in whatever they feel they should to give each character some personality like Lians obnoxious "Ayup!" or really stupid dialogue like "You fartfaces!" The voice actors rarely feel like they bring the characters to life, instead ruining every single moment in every cut scene, with the exception of Garr or Francesca, who are mostly good, and Lian and Nowa, who are both annoying as hell and sound like they found some dude outside their studio and said "Hey, want to voice this character in our game?" with no background in voice acting. I wouldn't be surprised if it was one of the kick starter benefits. I hate them so much.Yes, there are a hundred heroes, as the title implies, but everyone you bring with you on your journey outside of the main core team (Nowa, Lian, Seign and the others) all provide empty worded dialogue to make it appear as if they are contributing, but they aren't; the main characters will respond with the same dialogue regardless of who is with you, bringing to life their lifeless design. Consider games like Breath of Fire, Suikoden, and anything else you played as a kid or in recent years. What was the most enjoyable aspect of these games? It was generally the mini-games, particularly fishing, the music, the thrill, the action, the fear of missing out on that treasured catch, and the desire to be rewarded for your efforts with just exploring the world. Eiyuden Chronicles makes everything as bland as possible. Fishing is just sitting there watching the bait get chewed on till it goes under, with no music and Nowa repeating the same phrases over and over. "Nnng...! Hnnng" "Alright!" Repeat 5-7 times until the fishing spot is expired, with each cast taking around 1-2 minutes to complete the animations, some rare fish take 0.5 seconds to react to catching them or you lose that chance and have to leave and come back in 5 minutes for the area to refresh, they also kindly made it so the rate of catching specific fish is very low so you waste even more time. Eggfoot races? Watch and listen to the narrator make bad egg-related puns at you for 2 minutes straight while you watch your bred eggfoot race 9 times before breeding it with another eggfoot you raced 9 times to produce something that is more or less inferior to the originals in every aspect never really guaranteeing you get your times worth farming them.Shi'Arc desert races were alright, though it appears that many people complained about how difficult they were, and 99% of the playerbase has yet to complete them all, which is strange given that they only took 10 minutes and none of them were particularly difficult. The benefits were quite mediocre, as they were quickly surpassed by the upgrades you received in the next town.Joey Wheeler Yugioh looking character portraying "Baigoma" (Beyblade) mini-games is just weird. Why not have him doing the card mini-game it just feels so off. The castle is a literal motivational pressure to locate heroes. Instead of wanting to go out and get them yourself, the game limits many features that do nothing for you directly behind all of them, with the exception of about three, such as the Hot Spring and Shops / Inn and most of the time they are forcing the main characters into your party meaning you're never going to be able to run with the same crew all throughout the game, because they want and will force you with the lower level heroes who you forgot to give items to and to level up, or in rare cases you enter a fight with a team of heroes that have no place in formation so they just sit their defending since you can't change their formation in combat. Did I mention that Combat has an automatic feature? Why? The entire game is basically a cutscene where you're only there to guide the player characters through them by watching them fight, or watching the "tactical" not tactical War Battles where it's 99% cut scene 0% strategy and 1% you moving your battalion to a square watch a cutscene only for the fight to be over and the next scene to begin or for the next long unskippable battle cutscene to start. Oh and if you somehow lose, you load right back to your previous save file, rather than a auto save before the fight. Good luck with that.I'm not lying when I say this. Eiyuden Chronicles is an extremely boring game. It may have brief moments of being truly decent enough not to make me want to rip out my hair, but it is nowhere near the level or magnitude I expected from this game. I want to say so much more, but the more I think about it, the worse my headache becomes surrounding this. I have no emotional connection with any character, I didn't think this to even be remotely possible. The English voice acting/translation ruins everything. The mini-games will put you to sleep. The entire game is one lengthy cut scene after another, with the exception of occasionally moving the joystick in the direction to the next location while the game is playing itself. Save for the specific boss fights where you are more of less needed to play the gimmick to win unless you're overleveled. (Gimmick) a mechanic that helps you defeat the boss by disabling their ultimate or dealing massive damage to them. If you have time to waste and nothing better to do, go ahead, give it a try. But I'm done with this.That's a passionate game. There's plenty of character and emotion, exploration, mini-games, and a genuine studio of brilliant nostalgic Developers of old games like Suikoden, Breath of Fire, and Chrono Trigger. They even got Yasunori Mitsuda to do a lot of the music, how amazing is that!? The original composer for Chrono Trigger. Probably the only indie game in recent years to even scrape the surface of what it should feel like to play a game built around everything being fun, emotional and engaging. Even if the combat was a little repetitive.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most boring JRPGs I have played in a long time; The movement speed combined with the large, open areas really just drives home how much time is being wasted, a majority of random battles can just be won via the auto-battle option, boss battles drag on way too long as well, and not in a challenging way, but in a "we just wanted to make it last long" way. What praise I have for this game are all superficial; the visuals are pretty. the sprites are nice to look at, and the music does a good job at hitting that nostalgic JRPG feel. Navigating the menus feel laggy, even playing on PC, I dread to think what it's like on the Switch and PS4 versions. The game is riddled with baffling design choices - screen transitions for tiny areas containing a single treasure chest, the game being constantly interrupted by cutscenes where two characters say something, followed by a gameplay section where you walk two steps, then you get interrupted again by either a battle, or another worthless cutscene. The duel and war sections feel time-wasting and tedious, and they feel like they were put in not because they're fun or enjoyable, but because they were in Suikoden as well. The story is nothing to write home about either, events happen just for them to resolve off-screen immediately. The very first duel in the game was built up to be this inevitable, epic clash between two former friends, when in reality, these two wooden planks disguised as characters shared about 5 to 10 minutes of dialogue with each other. The scene was built on matchsticks, and was not earned whatsoever. Basic concepts in the world are either not explained, or barely touched upon at all. The recruitment of characters just feels like a chore, the characters themselves don't feel integrated into the main story, or part of the world naturally either - they could be crossover characters from other franchises for all that it matters. People who say that this is meant to be a love letter, a successor to the Suikoden series as a justification to all the flaws and issues; Is Suikoden supposed to be boring, tedious, frustrating to navigate and play at almost all times?

_childDocuments_.review: 20 hrs in...Nostalgic, yesBeautiful characters, yesGood writing, mostly yes though I wish the MC was a little more fleshed out in motivations and relationshipsStill get a castle and I like the new expansion system for it's developmentDisappointments...MAPS... I don't know who designed these maps, but they are my biggest peeve. It's 3d graphics, which is fine, but this is not particularly well done. Sometimes, I'm walking in/out the side of a building and suddenly standing in front (so the outside perspective doesn't match the inside) I'm annoyed with not being able to rotate the screen on most maps AND I am really bothered by the fading. For example, the panorama in the backgrounds are faded and the back quarter of the screen is faded in ways that make me think I'm staring through part of my glasses where it's crisp, but not another part where it's aggravatingly blurry. WHY?!?!?!A few too many coincidences in the writing. The characters are colorful, the dialogues are good, but I feel that it's a back step from most stories in the series as far as how the main character is positioned to take charge (the WHY) and also why other people are choosing said character to be the leader. Also, I liked the former games having main characters with special "true" runes. In this game, nothing like that so far and I suspect there won't be. A couple of other minor disappointments for game play...1. is the way inventory is handled and the limitations (I keep picking up things, but for awhile had no easy way to go back to town and store them). In Suikoden, you'd at least see how many "slots" an item took up (e.g. 6 healing herbs takes 1 slot). 2. more complex rune systems that are harder to see which rune is equipped/unlocked. It's more convoluted, harder to navigate UI, and not an improvement.3. not fond of the new way they do war. It's another regression compared to all of the Suikoden war mini-games. The movement feels more constricted, again UI not as good, and a less clear tactical advantage for pitting different fighting styles against one another (arrows vs. infantry for example).Overall, if you were a fan of the first ones (as I was) then it's still worth the buy. It's very much like a Suikoden, but I don't feel it quite lives up to them from what I've seen so far. Still, you can recruit more than 100 beautiful characters, you get a castle, and the story is interesting enough.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game overall, but some things I want to point out first.First, some positives: - The gameplay and art direction is very reminiscent of Suikoden II (with some bits and pieces of other Suikodens thrown in)- The music is fairly pleasant, Motoi Sakuraba was in his element here.- Plenty of things to do outside of the main plot, arguably my favorite version of Suikoden's "Build Your Castle"- Lots of party customization, there are 120 recruits but around 70 of them are actually playable and can really change up your party dynamics. One update to this I enjoyed was if you are forced to take characters you didn't really want to use for whatever reason, you could shove them into your Entourage and use a different party (you can even do it to Nowa if you want)Now for the negatives:- The first, and biggest one, is the localization. The quality of it is all over the place, and a lot of the characters have been changed in some pretty stupid ways (we all know the "rub-a-dub-dub don't be a flub", but Momo also lectures you on assuming genders and talks like a "quirky girl" instead of his "old man" matter of speaking in Japanese, among other changes). I do not blame this on Rabbit & Bear, I just blame the localizer in question. There is currently a translation fix patch in the works, I recommend.- The rest are smaller complaints that didn't impact my enjoyment nearly as much. Magic seems a bit underpowered most of the time compared to just hitting the enemies with a Hero Combo or physical attack.- The Rune system is hit and miss, I like the idea they were going for, but (at least early game) it feels very limiting. An example of what I mean would be some characters cannot equip Magic Runes until the late to mid-game because each slot only allows for certain types of Runes to be used. It also feels like there aren't that many Physical Skill Runes to compensate for not being able to equip Magic Runes.All in all, I think it's a great game that is just marred by a crummy localization and some minor gameplay nitpicks. Hopefully these are things that can be improved going forward with the franchise. R.I.P. Murayama-san, bless you for your wonderful work with this game, and thank you for continuing Suikoden in spirit.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all: This is not Suikoden. It is a spiritual successor to that series, and it does follow it very closely - sometimes, even a bit too closely, maybe - but it is its own thing. That said, comparing the two is inevitable. And here, Eiyuden does go toe-to-toe with some games on the series, but never reaches the highs of Suikoden II, in my opinion. However, those are big shoes to fill.First of all, the plot: It's about what you'd expect from a Suikoden game, but there's a certain innocence and light-heartness to so much of it. It's the same thing but on a different tone. Not that there aren't darker moments - or that Suikoden didn't have lighter ones - but it is pending a bit to that side here. This can be a good or a bad thing to you, but in my opinion, it worked, and it's not that detrimental to the overall plot as some people would expect.Characters are overall good, and the voice acting in particular suprised me, both in quality and quantity. Not every line and character is perfect, but most of them work really well. The recruitments and plot progression themselves had a bit of a Suikoden I feel to it - it's a bit rushed, and a lot of people join just because they join, but again, it's not a bad thing, just something to be improved on sequels.This a good base for something great, but some things need a bit more polish. At launch, there were some pretty big bugs, and some minigames needed more balancing. Some things felt a bit rushed, some things needed more work, but... this is a really solid start, and I can't wait to see what's next.EDIT 1: After finishing the game, I can say: This sure feels like we have Suikoden back. It's not the same, if all you care about is the lore, but it does fill that same void and it hits all the exact same beats. It's amazing how much I loved this.

_childDocuments_.review: I like JRPG but I'm going to give this a thumb down for now.The Limited Inventory is really annoying. You can only hold 30 type of items. Consumable, gears, runes all under the SAME category, not only that, you can only hold up to certain amount for some items (eg: basic healing potion x6 / revival potion x 2, holding more than that will take up another spot). Limited inventory is not new but it just feels weird to me that this is in a turn-based JRPG, this feature is frequently seen in action game as to encourage player to dodge and limit incoming damage, but when put in turn-based JRPG, it is unreasonable as there are tons of unavoidable damage, and it really discourages dungeon exploring, my inventory is constantly packed and I have to throw away something every time I open a chest. To make it worst, the game won't tell you what is in the chest when you open it, it simply says your inventory is full, imagine throwing away a gear hoping to get something good from the chest, but it give potion.I read some reviews say that it will eventually be expanded, but I'm 12 hours in and haven't reach that point, and it irritated enough to make me spend time writing this complain. I know this game is kickstarted but a lot of indie game have done much better at some of the basic feature of an JRPG.

_childDocuments_.review: This game brings me straight back to the good old days of Suikoden 1&2! So far, I am having tons of fun playing the story and while I can recommend buying the game, here are some details for pros and cons:Pros:-beautiful art style-voice acting is surprisingly good, even the English ones (the THEATHER MODE is genius. Try it out, do it Anakin!)-well known & entertaining battle mechanics with tons of interesting combos (party members, hero combos, runes, etc.)-beautiful music-interesting characters / personalities & story (while being a bit similar to Suikoden 2 in particular)-low running speed can be dealt with via items and/or support-slot heroesCons:-a bit slow at the start with many mini-cutcenes that can get a bit annoying at times-the sudden running animations while everything moves at normal speed (e.g. fire in background) are disturbing any immersion and are quite silly/ distracting-grinding is a bit slow since monster encounters are taking a bit of time until they spawn (good for exploring, bad for targeted leveling)-some illogical things, e.g. a mine cart blocking a way... climb in it/ over it? Or how running straight next to a soldier makes him not spot you during stealth missions. Or... being wanted and running around freely, even talking to enemy soldiers in cities.-the running animation when you walk feels weightless. There are no foot prints, no sounds, no dust, nothing. It feels like you would figure skate / slide over the ground.-cooking minigame is bugged-magic is too weak and MP costs are too high to use it regularly-routes are linear & open world feels EXTREMELY empty-yeah yeah, translation issues are well-known by now but I am not talking about that woke/ anti-woke nonsense. Some translations are outrageously wrong (I play with Japanese voices and English texts). I get it that some Japanese expressions cannot be properly translated since there is no equivalent, but the interpreters went into completely different directions for no reason. One example: In Japanese, they say 'uh, sou da ne' which means 'uh, right' but the English text reads as (paraphrasing since I didn't take a screenshot) 'yes, the three of us will have our backs!'. Makes general sense in the context the scene is presented in but very liberally translated... not the only one but the most recent I remember. Nothing game breaking but irritating and ruining immersion when you hear and read two completely different things.
