_childDocuments_.review: This is all very bittersweet for me.I've waited for a successor to Suiko for a LONG LONG time. I backed the Harmonius Knight package.(Which needless to say, not receiving any of the physical items of my backing at launch was kind of a big let down).I'm 10 hours in so far and here are my first impressions. For a game that got backed WELL above it's initial goal and was pushed back it still feels rushed. It feels like there's plot lines and situations pulled STRAIGHT out of the suiko's without much creativity. Recruiting many of the characters seems....fruitless. Too much of the early recruiting is straight up just talking to someone and vibing for 2 seconds then "let's be in an army together". It seems like there's not much of the initial interactions that speaks anything at all the these characters backgrounds or personalities. OR the drastic decision of joining and ARMY and what the upcomming war means. This Beigoma game has the be the poorest introduction to a mini-game I've ever come across in a game. Not only does it NOT go into much of the history or why the game exists or why pieces are unique, it gives you a pokemon style choice of first top which is more or less useless THEN it gives you 2 other tops which ARE actually useless against ANY SINGLE PERSON IN ANY OF THE STARTING TOWNS. Not a single person was touchable with 2 "Practice Tops" doing 2 and 3 dmg to the 1 star tops 9-11. It makes ABSOLUTELY NO SENSE. I'm really disheartened with this. I want to love it. RIP Murayama, I'm so happy you got to create one last world before you left this one. I'm even happier you didn't get to witness how disastrous of a launch this game had. Again. The game seems very plot basic, very rushed, almost RUSHING you and pushing you into the gameplay that we loved from the suiko's as side hustles to the main story that was happening that had real intrigue and REAL emotion. This game keeps yanking the suiko tropes in very copycat fashion and not well at all. The story has been extremely predictable up to this point and I can't say this game is currently worth the backing I paid for it. Including, again, the fact that I don't even have a timeline for when I might receive the physical backer items. I fear this game has now not only suffered from a very cliche and forced story, rushed design but an also very very poorly planned launch. I would say spend your money on game-pass and give it a try there....I'll update as I go along.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit mixed on this game. I think it is worth checking out for Suikoden fans as it does have the same vibe from those games. However, I feel like for most it won't click. Personally I did enjoy parts of the game, but it has some major issues. From story issues to poor balancing there are enough frustrating aspects that I can't really recommend this to most.First of all the story is terribly paced. I understand they are doing the whole "collect over 100 characters" thing which is difficult to balance, but the main story and cast needed more focus. From the beginning they want to push Nowa and Seign's friendship but they never flesh it out properly and it's very forced. The guardians are an interesting group that feel half fleshed out. The elves are barely there at all. The dragons are under utilized. Basically no group really gets enough time to shine. Really the only character they gave enough time to was Perrielle who IMO came off odd - almost like what a Twitter warrior thinks they would do in medieval times. Nowa is bland and uninteresting which works as the self insert character but not so good on his own. Seign gets a few moments but he's mostly in the background. Marissa was boring and generic - I was expecting more from all 3 cover characters.The gameplay is okay. They needed a 2x and 3x speed imo as the battles are very repetitive. Auto battle is nice on easier fights. Fleeing is worthless as it fails more often than not and puts you in a bad spot if you aren't careful. The characters are not balanced well at all. I understand it's impossible to balance everyone perfectly but some are terrible and others are amazing. Most of the mini games are poorly balanced and overly easy or difficult. There's just enough frustrating aspects that it pulled me out of the game one too many times and I gave up on getting every character because of the cooking mini game that never ended and the bayblade rip off that was terribly implemented.Despite my negativity here, I will say I did still have fun and I did beat the story. The core gameplay mechanics of building up a castle and collecting characters worked for me and was enjoyable. The characters I used in battle were fun - although swapping out ruin lenses was a pain because of limited inventory and limited places you can change them and limited slots per character. I feel like the process to swap characters, equipment and runes needs to be streamlined if they want more people to experiment. I felt the MP system was a bit off as you'd use a large amount of MP and get very little damage/healing. They did release a patch half way through my playthrough and it was a bit better. The overall story does work well enough even if the characters feel generic. The voice acting was pretty decent. I would say if you have GamePass to try it there but full price will be too much for most people IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: This game succeeds in emulating the 90s era of JRPGs which includes many of its strengths but also a fair number of its weaknesses. That being said, if you have a tolerance or experience with these types of JRPGs, you're likely to enjoy this game a lot more. This game has random encounters and an upgrade-able inventory limit which are fair things for people to be bothered about, but I'm fairly accustomed to these kinds of mechanics so it kind of just rolled off me. Positives:- 120 characters to recruit many of which have unique exclusive skills allowing for a wide variety of team compositions. Additionally, getting these characters is either a very simple item/dialogue/stat check or involves an enjoyable side quest/boss/dungeon, so it never felt like a chore getting these characters. Even if you don't end up using or liking the character, getting them was either effortless or gave you a reason to explore side content and optional areas so you still gain money & EXP from it. The game also has an EXP catch-up mechanic to quickly level late joiners.- A common complaint is the lack of a quest log which is fair but I never felt it was necessary. There's an NPC you unlock around the mid-game who gives you hints about the location of recruitable characters and shows how many you have left among those currently available to you. Also, a lot of the character quests aren't super long or difficult so you can mostly just finish them as you encounter them rather than needing to come back to them.- Character designs are great and the main story is easy enough that you can mostly just use whoever you want regardless of their stats.- I played on Hard difficulty and some of the boss fights early on posed a fair challenge. I also personally don't mind that auto combat or spamming regular attacks can deal with most trash mobs. The game doesn't have healing points aside from Inns so I feel as though the sap on resources from your encounters leading up to the bosses is supposed to be the challenge rather than the standard fights themselves. - Base building feels rewarding with the broad diversity of features you can unlock and aside from a few of the end-tier materials, you get a lot of these resources passively so it never feels like a chore to upgrade your base. - The rune system is fairly easy to understand and allows for a bit of customizability in that you can either make characters have a diverse set of abilities or you can load them with stat boosting runes to make them good at once specific thing.- The game almost always allows you to use whoever you want thanks to the attendant system. There are a few protagonist splits where you play as Marisa or Seign with fixed parties, but generally, you only have to bring along 2-3 story relevant characters who you can put in the attendant slot rather than actually placing them in your combat party. Attendants will tag along and comment on story events and will appear in cutscenes while allowing you to keep your ideal party of 6 for actual combat. You can even shove Nowa in the attendant slot if there's space and avoid using the protagonist if you feel like doing so.  Negatives:- The localization isn't great and undercuts a lot of the tense or dramatic moments in the game. However, it's also worth noting that even with the minute-to-minute dialogue not being great, it doesn't seem as though there was a super deep or complex story under the game's hood to begin with so this became less of an issue the more I accepted that I was playing for the gameplay. The story is still a serviceable vehicle to move along the plot but for anyone who has played a fair number of JRPGs, it is nothing you haven't already seen. - The game is weirdly clunky and slow. Every time you fast travel, the character that facilitates this brings up a dialogue prompt that disappears with a weird lag which is followed by an overly long loading screen and then another witty remark about teleportation. The menus in combat also have a delay before you can start scrolling through options which becomes especially annoying when you have 6 party members to control. There's also no turbo option for combat which makes trash encounters particularly annoying. - The character balance is utterly nonsensical. Some characters are completely unusable from the get-go, some have weird stat spurts way too late (around lv 60 for some), and some just stop experiencing stat growths after a certain level (like Hagukin and Yusuke's attack just ceasing to grow around the late game). On the other hand, some characters just consistently grow throughout the entire game and are just objectively the best options to have on your party because in addition to insanely high stats, they also have really good rune set-ups. I don't mind all characters not being balanced in a game with I believe 71 combat-playable characters, but it's less of a gap and more of a canyon between certain characters. The game also ends around Lv 50 - 60 so characters that don't hit their major stat growths until around 60 just make no sense for this game especially considering there's not much post-game exclusive content to use them on. - The characters are all kind of bland. The three protagonists are fairly typical JRPG trope characters and because so much of the rest of the cast is optional, they say 3 or 4 one-liners sporadically throughout the game MAX. The result is that there's not a lot of cohesion between the cast.- Unexplained mechanics and behaviors. Some of the item descriptions are sort of unclear in what they do like the armband accessory states that it increases attack range which I assumed meant it would allow short range characters to have mid-range, but it instead refers to the actual damage range they inflict. After completely upgrading the base, I still have no idea what the population does, what is affecting my HQ funds gain, and how my passive resources are being calculated or distributed. This stuff just randomly showed up in my inventory after playing for a certain period of time and I'm sure that in the future, a wiki will make all of this clear but the game itself should explain these mechanics.- The War mechanic. It is slow, the animations are excessively long, and there's actually not much strategy involved or it's just super easy because I felt like every other turn there was some scripted event that massively shifted the tide of the battle or ended it prematurely. I don't know if these were tied to certain health percentages, but I think there's only about one or two war battles near the end of the game where you actually get to deplete the enemy's health to zero without something interrupting the battle. - The game likes to use a duel mechanic for the more dramatic 1v1 fights where the only options are attack, counter, and break when the enemy hits a certain HP %. These are cool to look at but playing them is a bit of a pain. The logic is that the enemy will say something which then prompts you to either specifically attack or counter. There's no real strategy involved you just have to note these down because what they say doesn't pertain to what they're about to do, and they also only have about 3-4 things that they'll say so it becomes a bit goofy when the characters just repeat dialogue for 10 minutes.- General lack of polish. The game is stacked with these minor oddities like certain skills just not showing the visual effect randomly, oddly long loading screens, random 5 second delays after selecting your moves where no one moves, grammatical errors, and one instance where a dialogue box said "Nowa" but had a totally different character speaking and it showed their picture instead. Also, in the final dungeon, I wore the accessory that reduces the encounter rate but it would appear that a room transition also resets your encounter rate because I came across less than 10 random encounters in the massive final dungeon.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfaithful localization full of cringey words/sayings, weird unfunny jokes and to make it worse, changing a character from the original work to the point it's basically a different person. I supported this game for the japanese developers vision, not a rogue localizer's reinterpretation of it.I'm an European Player who always chose english in every game I played, I never had any problems understanding these same games, this includes more recently, Baldurs Gate 3, which is heavy with dialogue and story.Yet with EC, even the first minutes present terminologies specific to the American Culture and does a poor job, in fact, detracts player connection to the game's dialogue and story.Chub - apparently, this refers to a political side in America, and I ask, is english only meant for Americans? Why would this word be appropriate in the EC world in any context? "Rub a dub dont be a flub" - is apparently a rick and morty joke, why would anyone assume non-american but fluent english speakers would understand, relate or connect with this sort of joke?Incidences like this keep happening in the game and makes the entire gameplay experience bad. I tried giving it another try after the closed beta - but the way they changed the Lian character, that appears to have a significant portion of the script is just too much - I am aware the character is supposed to be a vocal, silly comc relief - but the way the EN localization portrays her is not the same as how the author did,Shame on you all that support this sort of behavior and devalue the original work - this is what allows this sort of shenanigans to persist in every other game.

_childDocuments_.review: Eiyuden Chronicle Hundred Heroes is a great game with some flaws, but it deserves a good review, despite what some people are saying. This will be spoiler free. I'll talk about some mechanics, but that's all.The good :¤The game is visually attractive. You've got the retro feel thanks to the sprites, the overworld, and so on, with a modern touch. The sprites are dynamic, the character arts are gorgeous. They kept the kind of "barren" overworld from old games, but it's still enough that it doesn't look bad.¤The music is flawless.¤The japanese voice actors did an awesome job.¤The castle system is really on point.¤There's a ton, and I mean A TON of mini-games and activities to do besides fighting. Some are better than others, but you won't get bored.¤The story is pretty good. The world building is also quite interesting.¤The characters are great. You'll find enough character you want to play and some more.¤You have 3 spots in your team for characters you have to bring with you (due to the story) but don't want to play. This is really clever.¤99% of the characters can't be missed.¤The exploration part is fun, especially after you unlock a specific character.¤The game is really funny, full of easter eggs, and fun things to discover.Neutral : The combat system. It has really good and really bad points. Overall, it's interesting, some characters posses special actions or abilities that make the battles more dynamic. The range system works well.Now, some characters are just bad from beginning to end. They have bad stats and you'll feel bad playing them. That being said, a lot of them become really good later on ! For all of those that cry because Mio is bad. She is... until level 50-60, then she's quite good.The magic seems really bad at first, and it is. Magic is mostly for buffs and heals at first, then in end game, it becomed better than physical attacks. The Hero comboes aren't working properly. If I'm not mistaken, there's an issue in the damage calculation, so for now, it's usually not that good. Maybe it'll get fixed.Some defensive actions aren't really intuitive, like defending other characters or counter-attacks. These are luck based, and since the targeting system is mostly random, it can feel like a waste to use them.¤The english translation is.... weird. I didn't think it was bad, but if you understand japanese and set the game in english, you'll find the translation to be somewhat off at some point, and I don't mean "not a literal translation", just not matching what's going on or whoever is currently speaking. There's so weird bias on the translators' end. It's not that bad, and is mostly good enough, but I understand that some people didn't like it. What I don't understand is going on and on about political stuff and giving this game a bad review only because of that. That's nonsense and that's denying the hardwork of everyone else involved in this project. If you don't like it, don't read it and move on. If you only understand english (well then please go learn something else), then put the english voices on and don't read the dialogues, and if you understand another language, don't put the english translation if you don't like it, and move on.The bad :¤A few characters are locked behind hours of unfun grinding. One of them being worst than all the others. I won't say who it is, but there's a spin on it...¤Some characters are also locked behind really unintuitive stuff. Hopefully a character gives you hint regarding recruitment, buuuuut they're also locked behind some unintuitive stuff and the hints don't solve some recruitment issues that are luck based.¤A few mini-games are just bad and poorly made. It wouldn't be an issue if you didn't have to play them, but you have to. One in particular is just the worst. Your introduction to it is bad, it is impossible to win it at first (and there's no "getting gud", you just can't) and have to farm in endgame to gather the tools to win it. And the gameplay of it is non-existent, you just have to press a button. It's visually appealing, but that's the only "good" part of it.

_childDocuments_.review: After all the excellent reviews, I've read, I'll make it short: "shut up and take my money!"As a long time Suikoden fan, this game took me a while back. Allthough the beginning seems very promising, it soon muddles down and you're expecting some thing that never happen. Why? Because the plot leans too close to Suikoden II, without beeing able to reproduce it's unique personal little magic.Let's face it: the game is a bit too childish, while the fanbase of Suikoden are around 30-40 years old by now.Is it bad? No, quite on the contrary: it's very good. This is Eiyuden Chronicle, not Suikoden VI. It's a heartwarming hommage to a game series that was itself referencing classical chinese litterature. Do I miss some unexpected and crippling moments like Pahn's duel and his conflict between his task as a tutor and his fealty to the Empire? Absolutely. Do I miss the subtle hint that Annabelle is the protagonist's mother? Yes. Do I miss the option to brutally execute your ennemies, while you also can forgive unforgicable people for the greater good? Yes.However, people need to understand the Zeitgeist. To any younger players: if you like this game let it be a gateway towards older Zeitgeister. Learn to enjoy works of fiction from other Eras: be it wideogames, animes, films, novels or plays. It will considerably expand your worldview. One day, you will be at the forefront of the World which is to come.In the meantime enjoy the nice story and grind those eggs!!!

_childDocuments_.review: If you can play it in japanese or don't at all care about story or dialogue I'd reccomend it. If not, Id wait for a fan translation or a retranslation of the game if the company does one. Now on to the rating.I find this one hard to rate accurately. Its an overall good game, but the localization kills it for me. You can argue its bad writing and not the localization choices, but the issue still stands. A large portion of the dialogue comes off as overly childish or jarring. Along with quite a lot of repetitive phrases. It frequently pulled me out of the experiece due to how odd or just bad it was. Another argument I've heard a lot is  "all JRPGs have cringe", and while I disagree sure there have been several JRPGs that had odd or hammy/cringe lines but not as frequently or in some cases as bad. The English voice acting cycles between being good for some character to either sounding exceptionally bored or just downright awfull I cant tell if thats due to direction or what. Japanese voicing sounded solid for all the lines I've heard so far.Ignoring the dialogue, the games pretty good. There are the normal mechanics you would expect with a JRPG, along with many minigames, etc. Getting more and more heros is intersting it gives a solid amount of choices for party comp. There are some oddities with some mechanics like the lack of info on exactly how far the range of chars attacks were but it looks like there is a short medium or long identifier now at least that seems  clear enough. As well the length it takes to get random encounters in some areas being very long. Nice when you want to get from a to b, but terrible when grinding. Plus you unlock teleportimg later so it seems even more odd to lower the encounters that much. There are supposedly some issues with recruitment, but I haven't ran into any yet I don't think they also seem to be getting fixed with patches. As well as there are some text mistakes for names in the bestiary and menus. The minigames aren't exactly complex, but are they're fun enough and are a nice add to the game. The story is alright. Mind you I haven't finished the game yet so I can't give a complete review of the story. Its pretty standard jrpg territory, though so far the story isn't really that complex. There are bits of lore to look for as well so world building is pretty solid. The design is phenomenal, some may disagree, but I really liked most of the areas Ive seen so far as well as many if the character designs. I also just have a soft spot for 2.5d games. Overall its a decent game. It does somethings better than other JRPGs even. It just seems to be held by the terrible localization. If I totally discount the localization I could probably reason giving it a 7.5 or an 8 out of 10. Pretty good but definitely not perfect and shows the designers put in effort. With the localization it drops down to roughly a 4 out of 10. It just really ruins the flow and overall feel of the game. As someone who focuses on story and dialogue that just kills the game for me. As for not rating it higher i almoat never rate games higher than a 7 or lower than a 3. On a 1-10 5 is just a normal fine game 9 and 10s are exceptional to literally perfect and anything less than 4 is terrible to basically unplayable at 1. So yea to be generous a 4.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Hmmm...after browsing some of the user reviews, what else can be said, especially when I haven't beaten the game yet? Well, I like it quite a bit and certainly recommend it as exactly what it's store blurb says it is ("a modern take on a classic JRPG experience"). And yes it is, through-and-through; those who didn't play ED Rising won't be lost at all, and anyone who played Rising and liked the setting and characters enough will want to keep going. Rising of course wasn't a prequel, it was a Metroidvania spin-off that came out before this main big game did. I like this universe and hope this franchise sticks around with other instalments and genre spin-offs set within it (let Final Fantasy keep starting from scratch with its settings). So the only stuff I can add is that there's a few things haven't been mentioned in the reviews I've seen that ought to be: 1) It has a bit of a slow start. I'd say it doesn't get going until about 8-10 hours in and I'm all for letting a story breathe and not be rushed, you will have to wait a bit before it shifts gears. There's some padding at the start that I haven't found too bad later on(or "so far since then"), but that abandoned mineshaft that leads to the abandoned fortress is a DRAG and could've been cut in half with nothing lost.   2) If you liked the cast from EC: Rising and are anticipating that they come along ASAP, alter your expectations. I'm 32 hours in and I still haven't run into CJ, Garoo has popped up a couple times and just re-joined the party for the next big quest, etc. On that note...3) With a cast that large, some of them you'll want to hang around, most are fine, and there'll be some you can't stand. Pick and choose who you like, they aren't all winners. Pretty much everyone loves the shi'arcs, of course, but Mellore shows up relatively early on, before the others from Rising (for some reason), and she's just as much of a blabbery bubblehead as she was in that game. Which leads to:4) As you can probably tell from the art style and presentation, this is whimsy galore instead of grimdark. Depending on your liking of that sort of thing, some or even most of it lands, such as the aforementioned desert-dwelling sharks with their pirate-y speech patterns and hardcore scepticism that they ever had anything to do with water in their people's entire existence, and parts of it...really doesn't. Actual quote after a boss battle: "How could you defeat my monsters?!" "We have the power of JUSTICE on our side!" (UGH.) Thankfully I'd say it's more good than groan-worthy but YMMV. 5) You WILL have to play a mini-game or two to progress the plot; one review on here went negative over the desert race. The controls are a bit wonky and it took a few tries more than I'd have liked, but it can be done. It did bring things to a halt though and I think most of us hate it when that happens.6) The story (so far) is only slightly-epic. Quality wise, it's fine; not the worst at all, but you can sort of see how it could be more grand. On the other hand they can't all be, let's say, FF6, and that one got rather dark at points, and EC really doesn't seem to want to go too far in that direction. Probably just as well, going too epic and dark can bring about its own faults and failings too.Thankfully, classic-style inspiration aside the grind part isn't that bad; just fight most of your random battles as they pop up and you'll be fine. The devs were wise enough to have auto-saves and recruit-able characters who take out the tedium (one allows you to teleport to previously visited locations, one allows you to change your party at save points, etc.), and sometimes you won't actually have to get into a huge boss fight after getting smoked en route to the encounter with decimated party members (I'm strongly referring to the part with Seign infiltrating the rune-lens lab with the rune-tank). Yes, recommended, and here's hoping the DLC and future stuff is legit good too!

_childDocuments_.review: Eiyuden Chronicles has two major problems that existed in the backer beta and do not seem to have been fixed so far. The first is the very poor translation; not only are there some questionable localization changes which alter the personality of some of the characters and inject modern day lingo into a non-modern setting, but I've noticed quite a few grammatical and spelling errors as well as some nonsensical dialogue lines from town NPCs ("You're not on my level yet." from an NPC I've never spoken to, with no context given as to why they're making such a comment) and un-capitalized names on some animal npcs. I assume those are backer rewards or something (pay x and get your pet in game), and maybe the backers told them to include the name in lowercase, but proper nouns are capitalized in English, so this is an error. These errors are notably present in the party chat and the NPC discussions, but is usually not seen during quests, mostly because it's nearly all voiced dialogue in quests.The second major problem I've noticed is the pace of combat and the menus. In regards to combat, attack animations take far too long for a game where you have 6 party members on screen. There's a neat thing they do (which Suikoden did too) where if every character and enemy are only using basic attacks, some of the characters will strike at the same time, but I feel like this should have been the standard for every action. I don't care how much work was put into an attack animation when I have to wait 10 seconds for said animation to finish. An easy solution to this is to have an option to speed up skill and spell animations, where a shorter animation plays after seeing it for the first time, with a toggle in combat for this option. The menus are also weirdly slow, with a long fade out and fade in when you go from menu to menu, and a delay after you select something. It makes navigating through the menus a chore, especially since it could have taken a fraction of a second to slide between menu screens, but instead it feels like a labor to go from the backpack menu to the party formation menu.These problems are very amateur issues that should have been ironed out early, and shows a lack of care for the presentation of the product.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface this by saying that like many players, I'm also a Suikoden alum so I did come into this game with certain Expectations and preconceptions. But I've tried to write this review with as objective a view as possible. The good: - In as far as traditional JRPGs go, this is a very solid addition. So if you're looking for a JRPG fix that's not a remake and are tired of digging through RPGmaker-based games or giving in to KEMCO... this is a good way to go. - This is a fairly pretty game. I won't go so far as to say it's perfect or gorgeous, but it has some moments where you look at your screen and think 'that's beautiful'... provided you disable the subpar depth perception setting. - The soundtrack has some absolute bangers, especially the main theme.- I won't say the story is particularly complex, but sometimes the characters display unexpected depth considering we're dealing with such a large cast of characters (120+ just on our side alone!). - Speaking of which, 120+ characters, fully voiced? That is a huge addition to a kickstarter game. Huge. Even if you complain about the quality of the voice acting, the fact that it's available in two languages is a remarkable investment. - The rune slot system has a lot of potential. I think there's room for improvement, but I think it's a good system in general.- I for one enjoy the optional auto-battle system. It's not as in-depth as say... FFXII's gambit system, but it does the job for the most part. Compared to Suikoden's original basic 'everyone just does their regular attack' auto-battle, this gives you some control over the party's actions and with some tweaks, you can breeze through most random battles just fine.- Most of the gimmick battles are interesting, I just wish we had more outside of the boss fights.The bad:- Despite the fact that this game is a spiritual successor to an existing franchise and the team working on it were experienced in the genre, this game feels very much a proof of concept. I feel like it shouldn't be. We've had five similar games to show us what did or didn't work, and yet Eiyuden doesn't seem to have taken any of those lessons to heart so it feels... raw and half-baked in ways that it shouldn't.- The UI is trash. There I said it. I think this is symptomatic of a lot of games these days that attempt simultaneous cross-platform releases, but in particular when a handheld system like the Switch is involved. The idea that 'we have to design this with a potentially smaller screen in mind' has resulted in horribly nested layouts and ugly mobile game-esque menus. And yet... ironically, there's also a weird amount of unnecessary info being given to us. My eye is frequently swimming through irrelevant info when trying to make the simplest of choices. - There's a curious lack of documentation in many aspects of the game. Whenever you encounter a new feature or mini-game, you get a perfunctory 2-3 short page explanation which... honestly only barely explains what the heck is going on. Equipment and combat-wise, most items and abilities are described in unquantifiable terms. Something 'boosts your counter rate significantly', a spell 'causes minor elemental damage'. You can't really tell how much is much actually significant, in fact, you're not even sure if the item is working at all so you don't know if you're wasting your accessory slot. - The game could do with many QoL additions that are already available in many newer RPGs or remakes of older RPGs. Among which are battle and movement speed options, auto-run, a more reliable quick-save. More efficient management of my huge cast of characters would also be appreciated. Trying to buy equipment for your party from the HQ armory is... An Experience. - While the towns are pretty and the dungeons are pretty interesting with some puzzles, the winding spaces and generally slow-paced traversal speed of your main character (you either have to equip an accessory or add a certain character to your party to get a bearable movement speed) make wandering around an exercise in extreme patience. In addition to that, there's a ton of wasted exploration potential because the only things you can pick up or interact with are only puzzle-related, treasure chests, or shiny resource points, most of which are immediately visible on the field, more on this point later. - There are mini-games, most of them aren't anything to write home about. Even the ones that are sort of fun begin to outstay their welcome before they can become remotely rewarding. I'm pretty sure I could write a thesis on everything I would've liked to improve about the game and most of it would be about the mini-games.- One of the key features in the Suikoden games are the 1v1 duels and the big war strategy battles. These are included in Eiyuden as well but... a lot of effort has been put into making these as cinematic as possible, especially the 1v1 duels. But the price for doing so is that gameplay wise, we can barely tell what's working and what's not. The big war strategy battles were sort of fun, but one of its key features is that there's an ongoing 'stream' of faceless NPCs (made up of Backer names) dying the whole time, so you can't really see what's really important like actual impactful things going on during the battle. It again circles back to my complaint that there's a lot of information being given to you, but very little of it is helpful or explained meaningfully. The ugly:- So many bugs. So. Many. Bugs. Most of the game-breaking ones have been patched by now, but it puts a bad taste in your mouth when you realise how many there were on release despite beta testing. - So many things in this game are reliant on RNG that it becomes tiring. There are characters and accessories you can equip to mitigate some of the pain of being reliant on random item drops from battles, but there are other times when I think to myself 'these items could've just as easily been found slotted into a bookcase in the environment, or hidden in this corridor that apparently has absolutely nothing in it, and just exists to make you waste 30 seconds hugging the walls to find... nothing. - With the exception of story-relevant characters, most of your recruits don't feel like they live in the world. With few exceptions, only the characters who are immediately recruitable (maybe with some minor requirement that's easily achieved) are visible on the field. Most of the others don't seem to exist until you can. This forces you to backtrack through towns repeatedly 'just in case' someone new appears. That's not only detrimental to engagement, but just plain disrespectul of the player's time. A recruitable character later provides a service to provide 'hints' of potential new recruits, but this doesn't change the fact that the world doesn't feel 'lived in', or that the people in your army really have a stake in what you're fighting for.- If I'm to be perfectly honest, you'll get a lot of playtime out of this game if you just want to mess around with the mini-games and finish the achievements,  but I'm not sure you'll get much replayability out of it. The game forces you to invest way too much time into some of these mini-games to recruit certain characters. Replaying JRPGs is about reliving the magic, but being forced to slog through a not-so-fun mini-game for the best ending... isn't really my idea of that. All in all. if you really really like JRPGs or are a Suikoden fan still feeling kicked in the nuts by Konami, then this is the game for you. Despite my complaints, there is plenty of magic and potential here... it's just... more unpolished than I thought it would be.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Stop comparing it to Suikoden. This is a great game on its own with excellent combat expression through its wide cast of party members, unique skills, magic, runes, and hero combos. The story is slow but overall great once it picks up. Must try for JRPG loversI will start by saying that I have never played the Suikoden series and I hadn't even heard of it until I read reviews of this game. I (believe) I am half way done with the main story line at the time of this review. With that being said I feel like this game is getting a bad wrap bc most of the negative reviews are comparisons to suikoden 2. Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes is a fantastic game! It very much feels like old school jrpgs but with modern QoL features and mechanics. Not having played Suikoden 2 I will say that the gameplay of ECHH feels very fresh and fast paced with a WIDE variety of characters to build the perfect team you feel works for you. The world feels very vast and backtracking is rewarded with new discoveries that are worth the extra time. Combat expression feels wonderful with magic, skills, and runes that make most characters feel very unique. The story does take a little while to get going as this is most definitely a story focused on the main character and cast. There is the classic backdrop of a medieval fantasy opera but the story is more about the growth of Nowa and his rise to power and his relationships with the people he meets along his journey.  The few gripes I have with ECHH is that it did take about 20hrs before fast travel was unlocked but after that the game REALLY opens up. There are also basic features that the game fails to explain or makes difficult to understand. (Basic stat attributes are never explained anywhere in the game and you will have to look up what each one does)Lastly while there are roughly ~120 playable party members, the wide cast does leave VERY little room to get to know each one of them. Most are forget about outside of their introduction (outside of the main cast) and how they can help run things around your base. All in all ECHH is a wonderful game and is a must try by any JRPG lover

_childDocuments_.review: In a gaming landscape saturated with titles vying for attention, Eiyuden Chronicles: Hundred Heroes emerges as a beacon of excellence, a masterpiece that not only captivates but also pays homage to the beloved Suikoden series. As a fervent admirer of both Suikoden and the RPG genre, stepping into the world of Eiyuden Chronicles was akin to revisiting a cherished memory, yet with an exciting and fresh perspective.From the moment the game begins, it's abundantly clear that Eiyuden Chronicles isn't just another RPG—it's an immersive journey that resonates deeply with the essence of what made Suikoden so beloved. Developed by a team of industry veterans who were integral to the creation of Suikoden, Eiyuden Chronicles exudes a sense of reverence for its predecessor while forging its own identity.At its core, Eiyuden Chronicles is a tale of camaraderie, political intrigue, and the pursuit of justice. Much like Suikoden, it places a strong emphasis on character-driven storytelling, where every hero you recruit has their own unique backstory, motivations, and role to play in the grand tapestry of the narrative. Building your army isn't just about assembling a formidable force; it's about forging bonds with diverse characters, each contributing their skills and personalities to your cause.Visually, Eiyuden Chronicles is a feast for the eyes, with meticulously crafted pixel art that evokes a sense of nostalgia while boasting modern flourishes. Every environment is brimming with detail, from bustling cities to lush forests and treacherous dungeons. The character sprites are imbued with personality, their animations bringing them to life in a way that's both charming and expressive.But perhaps the most impressive aspect of Eiyuden Chronicles is its gameplay. Drawing inspiration from Suikoden's signature features, such as the expansive recruitment system and large-scale battles, Eiyuden Chronicles refines and expands upon these mechanics, offering a deeply satisfying experience for both newcomers and seasoned veterans of the genre. Whether you're engaging in strategic turn-based combat, managing your growing army, or uncovering hidden secrets scattered throughout the world, there's always something new and exciting to discover.What truly sets Eiyuden Chronicles apart, however, is its soul—the intangible essence that permeates every aspect of the game. It's evident in the heartfelt writing, the evocative music, and the genuine passion poured into its creation. Playing Eiyuden Chronicles isn't just about completing a series of tasks; it's about embarking on an unforgettable odyssey that leaves a lasting impression on the soul.In conclusion, Eiyuden Chronicles: Hundred Heroes isn't just the best game in the world—it's a testament to the enduring legacy of Suikoden and a shining example of what can be achieved when creativity, passion, and talent converge. For fans of the RPG genre, it's an absolute must-play, offering an experience that's as enriching as it is unforgettable. If you're looking for a game that captures the magic of classic RPGs while pushing the boundaries of what's possible, look no further than Eiyuden Chronicles.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this game? Definitely not at full MSRP ($49.99). This is a $19.99 game, tops. I backed this during the kickstarter campaign and was hoping for something similar to Suikoden 2 but definitely did not get that. Story is, meh. Mini-games are extremely generic with very little to no strategy needed. The fishing "mini-game" is literally just pushing a button to reel the fish in when you see/hear a bite. It's pretty pathetic, honestly. I would've been happy with a fishing mini-game similar to Stardew Valley or anything else....not just pushing a single button and you instantly catch it. Recruiting feels very shallow - with only a very few characters that need certain requirements to be met for recruiting. I did not find any compelling stories with any of these recruit-able characters. Combat can mostly be won with just using Auto battle. Magic is pretty useless and doing combos with your different character combinations is also not very needed. Sad.All in all, it could use another 2 - 3 years of development for more polish and to find its soul. In its current state, it feels very lifeless and generic. Again, the best I can describe it is, it just does not have a soul.Overall, would not recommend, especially at $50....

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like Eiyuden Chronicle and recommend it, because on the surface this is a Suikoden sequel in all but name. But also its 2024, where is the Suikoden vibes, gameplay mechanics, and pacing, but with QoL features and a better UI than what we got? So much of this game is confusing, even coming from a background of having played Suikoden 1 - 4. So many things also don't work, Eiyuden is really buggy and broken. For example, the cooking contests; you can only win them with two different recipes and that's it, use anything else and the judges will rate your meals a 0/10. The PC version has a broken frame rate that is tied to your encounter rate, so if you play above 60fps, you'll just never get a random enemy encounter. There is also a bug that will prevent you from getting a recruit as well which can lock you out of getting some endings. Then there is the god awful english localization, and how bored the english voice actors all sound when delivering their lines. The combat animations are great at least! The combat is a joy to watch, and R&B Studios really nailed this aspect of the game. Its the one thing that took what looked and worked great with Suikoden and improved upon it, even if everything else is outdated. Balance though can feel completely out of whack, and some mechanics are pointless or make no sense. There is front and back lines for your characters. Some characters cant fight or do certain attacks if they are behind the other characters in your party. This is fine on paper! But the game never tells you about this, you just have to experiment and hope you get it right, and then remember who can be placed where. There is no saving anywhere you want. Come on now, this is a gigantic RPG releasing in 2024, there is no excuse for this. Especially since you'll have long stretches of story followed by multiple combat encounters, and you won't be able to save. In one instance the Inn was right there, but an NPC prevented me from going over to it to save. I had to just continue on and hope for the best, when all I really wanted to do at that point was take a break from playing. The rest of the game though just feels lifeless and devoid of any personality. Pacing can be really bad and a huge chore. You will be backtracking a lot because new recruits become available to find in previous locations as you advance through the story. And you have to be careful with this because some of them could become unavailable later on. So you're kinda forced to do all of this backtracking.Inventory space is also very limited, and items can only stack a few times. Like healing herbs can be in stacks of 6 only, and then take up another inventory slot. Later on you get expanded inventory though, but its still a huge inconvenience for no reason until you get there. Why even have limited inventory space to begin with if you're going to just arbitrarily expand it later on anyways? I really want to recommend this game a lot, but its held back, and is missing so many Quality of Life features, and has a lot of outdated design, that it's a really tough game to enjoy. I love Suikoden, but I was hoping we would be getting that experience in something a bit more modern, not to mention vastly more polished then what we got.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of those occasions where I would love a mix recommendation, but I incline more for the no and here are the reasons.This game is... unremarkable and bland across the board. The story so far is nothing to bring home about, very generic in general, which isn't bad in itself, but it's boring and bland.Characters are at best mediocre, and usually extremely generic JRPG tropes, most of them barely have any kind of interactions (which is normal for 100 characters) in conversations or beyond their initial presentation. They say some things here and there but nothing reacts to them. Also, there is not even one character that isnt shallow af. There is nothing interesting going on with any of them, so you will generally choose just based on looks.The combat is very hard to describe. It looks good, but 95% of the fights its better to just hit auto and see all the animations play on. Over and over and over and over and over and over. I know this happens generally in JRPGs, but the thing here is that you cannot speed up anything, so every combat is rather slow, and even fleeing is not fast. Then added to this, character builds are extremely simplistic, which is also understandable because, again, there are 100 of them, but this doesn't imply that is fun to use most of them, it isn't.Also related with combat there is an extremely fake difficulty. In one fight you could be lvl 15 and receive 40 hp from enemies. Suddenly, you go up one level, just one, and the same exact enemy starts doing 18-20 hp to you. It's kinda hilarious how it is so extremely tied to level, its normal than when you level up, you become stronger, but not to the point of halving damage received in just one level. It reminded me a lot to Triangle Strategy, which has the exact same type of difficulty.Then the open-worldish that you are when travelling between locations. It's empty. Completely barren. There is absolutely nothing to discover in it except locations that you see on the map, and fishing spots. That is it. I love this kind of world maps, I love them, but they need to have something to discover. Anything.EDIT: To add that exploration in general is awful, you will barely find interesting things in cities, but it is true that some companions are locked behinh NPCs conversations, and those NPCs are not generally recognizable. But no items, no secrets, nothing, either in cities or dungeons.Then we move on to the blocked zones due to story. There are sooooooooooooo many of them. Like I can understand a few, but you constantly see soldiers blocking your path, or a location, that is clearly going to be accessible, non-accesible. Way too many of them, feels like there is 0 freedom in any regard in this game.Finally, I do really like how the game looks, and the soundtrack is good. If you don't play this game, you are not missing in anything. It brings nothing new or interesting at the table. If you reallly like old-school JRPGs and want to play a game that, while it does improve in a few things, it's generally worst in what matters (story, characters, combat, builds). It's not a terrible game, but you can spend your time better elsewhere quite easily. I saw that I was going to need at least 40-50 hours to finish this game so not even ignoring the sunk cost fallacy will make me play this game

_childDocuments_.review: I was a kickstarter backer for this game. Supported it from right when the campaign began because I believed in the creators and the product. Unfortunately I had no way of knowing at that time that they would hand the game to a truly, and I mean truly, awful localization team. But look I'm gonna break this down as fair as I can so lets go.Mechanically: the game is fine. I have no issues with performance personally although I have heard there is some kind of frame rate bug tied to the random encounter rate. Hasn't affected me so its moot. The core gameplay is good. It feels very much like a Suikoden game. Which is what they were going for and what the supporters wanted. Some of the boss fights drag on a touch if I had to be real nitpicky but it's not a big deal.The art style: the game is visually appealing. Its good looking in many respects from character design to set pieces. You can tell a lot of love went into this games visuals. Pair that up with a generally solid soundtrack and yeah what you have is good all around product in terms of presentation. All good.However..... the gameplay, the visual appeal, the soundtrack...... none of those things matter if the writing is terrible, if the characters are grating, if the voice overs make you want to turn the game off and play something else. And thats the deal breaker here. And its heartbreaking. Even more so because it seems to be an issue stemming from localization. They re-wrote dialog, and I don't just mean a few throwaway lines, nah, more like entire characters personality sets from the Japanese and it shows through inconsistencies in the writing. And everything is worse for it. It got to the point where I muted the voiceovers because I just wanted to grind through the game in silence rather than hear anymore dialogue from certain characters. Certain characters that you are stuck with for 6-8 hours minimum at the start of the game and can't swap out. I don't blame the voice actors for the most part I'm sure they just did their best with what they were given but the writers really screwed them over.So yeah. Theres a gem in here. Unfortunately because the localization team massacred the main storytelling mechanism you have to go through to reach that gem..... It isn't worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: This is a mid game review.Eiyuden Chronicle is a love letter towards Suikoden series, specifically Suikoden 2 looking at Nowa, the main character, in fact they both have the same creative director (Yoshitaka Murayama), however I think the game doesn't quite live up to its predecessor.I'm not sure how much I have progressed into this so I will refrain from giving my opinion at this point but mostly it's about politics and kingdom invasion caused by some individuals pulling the strings from the shadow.As the title of the game says, it has over than a hundred playable characters that you can recruit over the course of the game which a good amount of them will join you automatically as you progress the story. A good number of them will join you without any requirements, they would just require you to find and talk to them but lots of them will require you to deliver some items or monster elimination after you talk to the characters.Eiyuden Chronicle has basically the same gameplay as its predecessor, turn based combat with up to 6 characters participating in the combat. There are some addition to the game that do add more flavor compared to the older games but it all boils down to the same thing. Most of the game, you'll be spending exploring and listening/reading the story, having played a lot of other JRPGs, Eiyuden feels weird for having the random encounter being scarce or rather, you could almost go in an area without any random encounter.  Luckily, the amount experience you get from the battle is quite generous and would give more to underleveled character so you don't need to grind as much when you're trying out new characters.In addition to those the combat, you'll have several minigames which would be something like a beyblade but much simpler, card games which is basically like trump card, fishing game and kingdom building (not sure if we'll have some more)The exploration is mostly linear and will give you a trivial rewards, occasionally you'll get a good accessories but that's about it, I don't think I've had a moment where I'd be thrilled getting rewards from a chest that gives me a good piece of equipment. There would be a lot of closed off path that will be unlocked gradually.Some village/town is definitely a bit too big for its own good and the lack of fast travel can be a little bit annoying sometimes, especially in your own headquarters.Overall, 15 hours into the game, I will have to say that the hype that I have after waiting since the kickstarter have died down a lot, I don't think it's that much better than the original, I'm not even sure if it's better than Suikoden 2, if you're unsure wherether to buy it or not, either wait for sale or wait a little bit more for Suikoden 1 and 2 remaster.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't play a lot of traditional RPG's anymore. I grew up playing FF7, 9, Wild Arms, Fire Emblem, and Pokemon. Eiyuden Chronicle does a great job of capturing that "Gotta Catch Em All" feel. I love that each side quest in this game matters and you know you're very likely to find a new companion for your efforts.Auto battle is a god send! I dread going back to having to choose each and every attack for my characters. Even so auto attack isn't perfect. I would love to see it have more options and specifically let's you pick a few options for pre planned attack strategy's "macro's" such as letting your whole party play it more safe, or spent some resources without having to change it within the menu between battles.Battle is fun through and it's fun to sit back and watch my character go to town on a mob of enemies. Gear doesn't seem to be super impactful early on, which is fine I suppose. I would like the addition of actual weapons though. The scaling however is kind of wonky. Mage's just aren't worth the hassle of running in your party until much later in the game. Kind of a bummer to see such variety in allies but not all of them filling a role even in a unique tangible way. Sorry but some characters meant for combat are likely only to be use in some sort of challenge run.Rebuilding your castle is awesome. Even though forging for material isn't the coolest idea it's alright. I would like the see the Guild system expanded upon and let you send our far more groups of your collected allies to gather resources and bring your back treasure. The story is kind of just stock tropes 101. I didn't expect much tbh but there were still some legit cool moments and the overall vibe was fun and light hearted. I wish some of the dialogue went faster though. The voice acting is a bit drawn out.Duel are pretty cool. I hope we see more of them.The army battles were also fun but there weren't a ton of them and I would like to see some with more challenge.The card game is fun and I kind of hope it returns but expanded on a bit more with more locations to buy or even trade/earn cards. I hope the ground work layed in this first instalment makes the already announced sequel even better. This game may have rekindled my love of JRPG's I'm going to check out FF6 next :) They all but have my money for a sequel but I'm not totally sure I will buy the DLC

_childDocuments_.review: Let's deal with the elephant in the room: The localization.It really is very bad. Whoever did it should be ashamed of themselves; and the voice acting is absolutelly horrendous. It's like someone told the voice actors to speak as if they were in some zany morning kids anime. My advice if you don't speak japanses, is to play with english subs and japanese voices. At least then you get the -tone- of the voice actor, and can try to read the text in that tone to help you out. It's not always possible, such as that time the person whose daughter's life is on the line, decides to call the one threatening his daughter "farthead". It's jarring, it's utter nonsense, but these truly jarring moments, are few and far between.Okay, with that out of the way; here are some MORE criticisms:So why am i giving it a recommended? Well... because it's a lot of fun! I love gathering companions like they are pokemon, i love testing out zany party combinations that don't really work well, but is fun to watch. I love the old school jrpg feel, and I like the often over-dramatic storytelling. I love that your enemy is called Mighty Dux.This certainly feels like a Suikoden game, and while it struggles to live up to those; it does do some things better. Voice acting is a great addition (again, avoid the english voice acting). It gives a touch of flair to the characters that were missing in the past.The greatest thing it does though, is it gives you 3 "attendant" slots in your party. These slots can be filled with "story-critical" characters that you may not want to use in your active party. This was one of my main gripes with the old games. So often you are forced to bring certain characters on certain quests, and you have little control over your party; this is not a thing in Eiyuden. You can always bring whoever you want! You don't even have to use the main character!If you like Suikoden, you'll like this. If you loved Suikoden, you may be a little disappointed in places, but should still like this. The translation is fine for the vast majority of the game, just do not use the english voice acting, my goodness...

_childDocuments_.review: Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes (EC:HH), is touted as the spiritual successor to the Suikoden series, and I'm going to be blunt, it lived up to that spirit wonderfully, and then some. Since it is a JRPG, I will be reviewing under that genre.Combat is your traditional turn based JRPG. Like a lot JRPGs, there are minimum information about mechanics, and they are meant to be solved by the players in-game, like a mini puzzle. Newer generations of players are going to find this annoying, but people who like to not be handheld with endless tutorials will find the experience of experimenting with the mechanics enjoyable. Like a lot of JRPGs, minigames are galore. The quality of some of these minigames can be iffy, but JRPGs are often designed with minigames to break up the tedium, not as a main component. Having so many options to choose from is great when you need a break from farming. I spent about 40 of my 160 hours of game on minigames, which I feel is a good balance.The base building is really satisfying if you're into seeing your headquarters grow. Visually, it really scratches an itch. The hero recruitment also scratch that same itch. Some people might not enjoy the tedium of the search, but that's more a tastebud than a flavor issue. The heroes are not all directly connected to the story, but still feel like they play their part. Enough of them interact regularly that I don't find it underwhelming or overwhelming. The story is about a solid 7/10. It's nothing outstanding, but it's serviceable and enjoyable. The greatest downside though is the 3rd act, which felt a little rush towards the end. It felt like the developers wanted to push in 1 arc into the game, but was forced to end early due to deadlines. My favorite moments are the quiet interactions between characters that you can dig up at rest, when entering new areas, reading the lore, combo attacks, and sometimes in cutscenes. There's a solid character writing team behind this game that carries inter-character interactions well.A 2D pixel art on a single-camera 3D world. You'd think that'd be jarring, but it ended being a really beautiful and simplistic art direction that combined the beautiful animations of retro pixel art and details of 3D. The art style reminds me of games in the late 1990s, where we were just transitioning to the 3D world and developers had to do a lot with very little. But now, we have access to far better resolutions and processing to truly push that same spirit of "making it work" to its limit. You can tell the developers chose this style due to budget reason, but they really pulled it off. It's really beautiful, and the battle cutscenes done in the same style are amazing. HOLY RUNES! The audio! It's amazing!The amount of voice acting done for this game is insane. Almost every line in every quest and side quest are FULLY VOICED. The optional dialogues, the cutscene interactions, the theater! I cannot stress enough that the amount and quality of the voice acting in a game of this scale from is absolutely BONKERS!The music is really pumping it too. They get a lot of mileage out of it's main theme, "Flag of the Brave", with it being the primary key to a lot of the music. Reminds me a lot of the music direction of HALO:CE. And all the other compositions really stand strong in their own scenes. There's a little something missing from the directorial usage of the music that stops my score from going to a perfect 10. Like some scenes just feels a little bit out of sync from the music required. But other than that, I have no complaints. I really enjoyed the difficulty. The game has a normal and hard mode, with multiple optional modifiers for the hard mode. I maxed everything out to give myself the hardcore experience, and it really delivered. On hard mode, you really have to manage your SPs and MPs, and know when to deal, heal, and take damage. Fights are balanced, more or less. There is 1 difficulty spike in the early game that is not that hard to overcome once you click with the basic mechanics. Because of the location the spike is in the story, I think it might be on purpose to weed out the people who may not enjoy the rest of the game, which is a sort of old school kindness. It's just after the prologue, so you should still be able to get a refund if you don't gel well with the gameplay. A solid JRPG that does what it says on the tin and delivers a fun experience. From a studio of this size, they definitely made a game of this scale the best they could, and that deserves a hearty clap. You know what I'm talking about. You probably saw some of it while scrolling through the reviews. I'm talking about the "controversy". There's a group of terminally online, politically obsessed, and borderline racists that are angry that the English localization is "too woke", "too political", and "mistranslated". First off, my credential. I'm an English language professional writer (18 years) and game designer (11 years) IRL. I also work with translations as a hobby (8 years). Suikoden as a series, and the original novel, Water Margin, that it was based on, are the first literary works that I performed analysis on. So I know what I'm talking about when I say those types of negatives reviews are full of sh*t. The game does have some legitimate areas worth giving a bad review for, but the translation is not one of them. Firstly, localization is not the same as translation. A translation is usually direct, and requires the readers to have an understanding of the culture to pick up on nuances. Honorifics like "sama" and "senpai" are usually kept under this context, and words with no direct translations are sometimes left to it. It can be simplifed as "DIRECT TRANSLATION"A localization is usually for a general audience. Everything is translated to an English equivalent or nearest. The cultural context like honorifics and no direct translation words are given a cultural equivalent. For example, a character in the game calls the protagonist "aniki", which is an honorific for "brother". But in context, it is said in the same tone as a mafia calling someone their family, so the English localization turned it into "cousin". Like, "Ey~ Cousin Tony!" Basically, it is "EQUIVALENT TRANSLATION".The localization in the game is not only correct, but actually went above and beyond to fully translate cultural contexts. Jokes and puns that only work in Japanese are brought over with equivalents, even sound effects and gags are done. The localizer is a veteran in their craft, and from what I know of their works (Kingdom Hearts/Fire Emblem/Gotta Protectors etc), they are top notch. One of the best in world, let alone the industry. Here's the REAL reason why these detractors are making noise. The game is "too woke" and "too political"? We're talking about the spiritual successor to freaking Suikoden! SUIKODEN! A game series particularly about war and political intrigue being too political? Is this a freaking joke? "Too woke"? Are you talking about Suikoden III, which is a game about segregation that has a large ethnic cast? Or Suikoden IV & Tactics, which are about the horrors of unregulated weapons leading to gun (cannon) violence? Or Suikoden V, which is a game about FEMINISM?! Some of the most iconic cast in the series are DRAG QUEENS! Tierkreis is anti-fatalism, Suikoden I is anti-oligarchy, and Suikoden II is anti-nationalism! Hell, Water Margin, the original novel the games are based on, has a mythical prologue about PRISON REFORM! The Suikoden series, and by extension, Eiyuden, HAS ALWAYS BEEN WOKE AND POLITCAL! These people don't know what they're talking about and are clearly using this game as an excuse to push a warped ideology.

_childDocuments_.review: One day, 505 Games was celebrating their Kickstarter success with Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night. Shortly afterward, they looked at Octopath Traveler and thought two things: “Hey, that looks nice but I think we can do that better” and “I remember Suikoden and I wonder if we can hire some of the original Suikoden staff and make our own Suikoden game.” And that’s how Eiyuden Chronicle was conceived. And it’s been very well conceived. A huge cast of 100+ characters, voiceovers, and animations? And in a turn-based RPG? Balancing for a 6-party team? Furthermore building a separate war battle and duel functions along with several minigames? And at the same time making the game look great and sound incredible? That’s a team that is really sticking their necks out to revive Suikoden, and no other studio in the world would ever dare to sign off on it. The fact that the game is actually good despite the above risks is its own feat.I haven’t finished the game yet, but I’m currectly 50 hrs in, including some of the minigames. I think this game is a solid 8/10. There’s a few choices that I think are questionable mechanically, but the Rabbit & Bear studio has wildly succeeded in making a good template to passing off the torch from Suikoden and I trust the studio with continuing with this series.

_childDocuments_.review: I should have waited and buy Suikoden Remaster instead - those are  the thoughts that I've been having for at least the last 5 hours of my Eiyuden Chronicle playthrough (and I have 20 hours in total, at the time of this review).I know this may be harsh, but this game has so many flaws, that rather than a "spiritual successor", I would rather call it a "cheap imitation". It is definitely partly my fault for expecting too much, but considering who created it and how long it was in development, I think that my expectations for a better game were at least a little bit justified.What is wrong with it, you may ask? Well, I will try to describe everything that peeves me in this game, although there are many things to list here so be prepared for a wall of text:First of all, this truly feels like a game from a bygone era, and not in a postive, nostalgia inducing way. I also am not speaking about graphics, because honestly that is one of the things that are fairly tolerable in this game. No, I'm talking about assortment of small, little things that simply annoy the player for the sake of being annoying:Unfortunately, there are also far more serious issues. The one that annoys me the most at the moment is an absolute lack of any balancing whatsover. I mean, I've played and love Suikoden and god knows that there were mediocre characters there as well (and quite a few of them). Thing is, not only  characters in this game are like that, they aren't  mediocre. For the most part they are completely awful and useless. Frontline characters with abyssmal defense and equally bad strength (Mio), a character with very high magic and nearly non-existent MP that also does not have any other stats that could redeem him (Leon), and many, many, many others. Then, there is a story itself which so far is not engaging in the slightest. I can't come to care about any of the characters so far, especially that after 20 hours, I still have access to only one of the three "main characters" around whom I thought the story of the game would revolve. Not so much. Aside from two very short segments, I didn't interact with two other main characters at all. The fact that the story feels extremely slugish is not helping either.Terrible english voice acting (and from what I know, translation itself) certainly does not help either, because rather than getting attached to some of the more important story characters, I'm hoping they will get killed off as soon as possible (yes Lian, I'm talking about you!).Even further amplifying this issue is terrible art style of this game. Suikoden had a plethora of characters from different races and representing different tropes, but here it is taken up to eleven. I have a feeling that 1/3rd of the cast is some sort of dog / tree stump / talking bag, while the next 1/3rd of the cast is some sort of beyblade protagonist / magical girl wannabie / anime character expy that fits the game's setting like pineapple fits a pizza. However, I could even live with ignoring a 2/3rd of the cast, if not for the fact that the remaining 1/3rd of cast is compromised of the most unbalanced / terrible characters in battles...Now, as for the battles themselves, they feel fun only for a few hours. Once the Suikoden's nostalgia wills stop clouding your mind, you will start to get more and more annoyed by the exceedingly long animations of every attack. Auto-battle does not help to alleviate the issue at all, since you still have to watch it fully. Not to mention that auto-battle has its own issues, where the control of what the character can actually do should be much bigger.Lastly, there is a music which is actually the smallest of the issues of the game. It is simply... forgettable. Which is a shame, considering that I still remember how great was the music in Suikodens, but it definitely is not as bad as other parts of the game.Now, this got so much longer than I expected. I apologise for what to most must seem like a rant, but I just had to get it off from my chest. However, if it will save at least one person from buying this game, I think it is a job done well. Unfortunately, I've expected so much from this game, and got so dissapointed that I can't recommend it to anyone, even the most starved for Suikoden-like experience players. I actually think that this may be the straw that broke the camel's back and I won't ever try to play again any "spiritual successor" type of game that relies on a nostalgia toward one of the 90s games. Not a single title like that in the last decade has proven to be worthy of my time and probably none will ever do. I would rather stuck to (usually) mediocre quality remasters where at least I know what I can expect, rather than to get my hopes high and then get dissapointed every time with those "spiritual successor" games.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives: + You get your own castle town and army.   + Fun base building with upgrades available for resource buildings, blacksmith, runes (allow you to do magic), armor shops, renovating buildings (at first the castle town looks ugly and old but gets some nice revonations as you progress the story).+ Over 100 characters to recruit ( I think 120?) that perform various functions/roles for your base and A LOT of them that participate in battle (there aren't too many games out there that let you recruit 120 characters along with the option to use many of them in battle.+ Interesting storyline with some branching paths depending on your actions+ Fun unite combos that involve using 2 or possibly more characters to perform powerful combos.+ Interesting story with compelling villains and heroes+ Big overworld+Beautiful artistic style+ A ton of fun mini gamesNegatives:- A bit on the short side for my taste  (should be 100 plus hours for this epic) but about 60 hours if you dont rush through it so not too bad.- The combat system is a bit basic but I hear magic becomes more powerful towards the end game.- War battles are fun but too simplified.  I'd like to see more complexity for Eiyuden Chronicle 2.- The English localization is a bit wierd but not a huge deal.- It would be nice to be able to explore the interiors of more buildings in towns.Overall rating: 10/10.  If you're a fan of Suikoden, you will love this.  If you're a JRPG fan, you will love this.  It's probably unlike any game you have ever played.  Do yourself a favor and go buy this and tell everyone you know about it. It's that amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who grew up with Suikoden, I am extremely happy with how this game came to be. Sure, it's not perfect--there are bugs and glitches from time to time--but it checks all of the things I love about JRPGs and Suikoden. It also works really well with the Steam Deck, which is a bonus.The dialogue, although light at times, does not take away from the heart and soul of the story. The characters are all very diverse, each with their own personalities that the voice acting breathes life into. The artwork is nice as well and there are a bunch of characters that reminded me of the others I've encountered at having played all the Suikoden games. There are moments I actually burst out laughing and moments when I was somber and angered on behalf of the characters I am journeying with. I particularly like Francesca, Ymir, and Perry--from the new roster. But my faves will always be the OG trio: Garoo, CJ, and Isha because they introduced me to the lore and the adventures to be had in this world.The battles can drag a bit, though. And the teleportation can get a bit annoying with the added dialogue every time you warp someplace. The minigames are all so fun, albeit a bunch of them requires farming for things that can help you through--like the money needed to purchase cards, finding the recipes, and farming enemy drops for beigoma. There's something about the overworld music that makes me remember Wild Arms, though, but I don't really know why that is.I really do love everything there is in the game, and I feel like I would be replaying Suikoden again (for the umpteenth time) right after I beat this game, and the NG+.
