_childDocuments_.review: RIP Yoshitaka Murayama! Head writer for Eiyuden Chronicles and my favorite games of all time, Suikoden I and II.Review Summary:Eiyuden Chronicles is a must-play for fans of Suikoden I and II, and classic JRPGs will likely love this too. It has a nostalgic appeal and a mix of old and new mechanics. Despite many old mechanics and some roughness (that was common in that era of video games), and the modern updates like introducing new mechanics, 2d pixel art in a 3d world, the game overall retains the charm and challenges of 90s-era JRPGs that I grew up on.Pros:Richly nostalgic for fans of classic JRPGs, a real spiritual successor to Suikoden I and II.Beautiful visuals blending pixel, 2D, and 3D art.Great soundtrack.Familiar yet updated turn-based combat.Somewhat new spin on mechanics to the rune system.Well-defined objectives with room for exploration.Over 100 unique characters (even if some are unimportant or 1 dimentional)Mini-games and other special mechanics! (Sadly no iron chef competition :'( ... )Fully voiced storyline.Cons:Pacing and scene transitions can be awkward.Reliance on old-style save points without autosave...Difficulty can be inconsistent at times Camera controls aren't always available, but when they are they feel clunky.Some poor voice acting (looking at you Lian) Inventory space feels too limitingTutorials leave you wanting more, while simultaneously feeling cluttered Outdated menu design and navigationMixed Feelings:Battle mechanics are deliberately retro, which can be both charming and frustrating.The combination of pixel art characters in a smoothly rendered 3D world creates a strange, albeit intriguing, visual contrast.Translations and wording choices are generally good, but occasionally the phrasing feels more like conversational speech rather than well-crafted text.If you're a fan of Suikoden I and II, or old school JRPGs in general (think story-driven adventures, turn-based combat, random encounters, deep world-building, and plenty of character development with a healthy dose of grinding), then this game is definitely for you. I backed this project on Kickstarter four years ago and have participated in both the closed and early access betas. Despite some mixed feelings about certain aspects, I've been swept up in the same nostalgic joy I felt playing Suikoden II as a kid.In the first few hours, you might find yourself conflicted. There's an initial surge of nostalgia followed by frustration with dated mechanics like fixed save points, excessive button pressing if you opt out of auto-combat, and random battles.Save points are a quintessential element of classic JRPGs, but you don't realize how inconvenient they are until you're in a rush and can't find one—echoing those childhood memories and feelings of desperation to save before you could leave the house all while your mother is screaming at from the front door for you to get of your game and get in the damn car because we're going to be late. (Love you and miss you mom!)   Despite these annoyances, true fans of the genre will find these issues minor and enjoy the game's overall charm.The combat system will feel familiar to Suikoden fans, offering traditional turn-based battles with the option for auto-fighting, which allows for different tactical approaches such as conserving items or MP. Boss battles and character-specific combos add variety and depth to the combat.Interactions between characters are dynamic and can change depending on your party composition, adding layers of replayability and engagement. The main character, Nowa, could use more development, but the game provides interesting choices that affect conversations, enhancing the experience for those who enjoy multiple playthroughs.The game's settings, from villages to cities, are beautifully rendered, bustling with NPCs, artwork, and wildlife, though they can sometimes feel sparse with few interactive elements. Eltisweiss, the first major city you encounter, illustrates this with its distant base location and one exit which feels like an eternity of running away after youv'e done it a few times.Difficulty can be inconsistent, particularly when entering new areas with stronger enemies. Such encounters can be punishing, for example I had a random encounter with 6 heavy hitting enemies that punished my party and forced me to use many of my limited health potions to keep exploring to the next story point. This is especially difficult when resources like health potions and money are scarce at the begining of the game. Pacing generally varies, with periods of inactivity or awkward transitions where it should be a single cut scene but its split up by a simple walk a few steps, before the next one comes in.I'm looking forward to seeing the rest of the story unfold, I remain optimistic despite some hitches with the Kickstarter campaign, which, while my experience was better than many, still had its downsides. Yeetee who facilitied many of the interactions with backers were terrible, though the Devs were usually great. The 'physical copy' is an incredible disappointment, a waste of money for everyone involved, and a waste of plastic for what is essentially art you've seen before in a cheap case with a cardboard cutout in the shape of a CD with a Steam key on it. Hopefully the other physical backer rewards will be great.In summary, I can't stress it enough that for fans of Suikoden I and II, this game is a must-try. Despite some rough edges and questionable development choices, it's an invitation to step back into a simpler era of gaming. It's worth picking up to let the modern gaming world fade and revisit a time fondly remembered.

_childDocuments_.review: It hurts me to my core not to reccomend this. The game itself is fantastic and Rabbit & Bear did a great job at not only catching the spirit of classic JRPG's but also the series Eiyuden evolved from. The issue is, as many others also pointed out, the localization. The English localization is already quite lackluster, taking a lot of liberties, rewriting large parts of the script, inserting contemporary jokes and quips etc.It gets problematic when further localizations are then based, verbatim, on the english script.Not only does this further dilute the original authors intent, it also has to deal with the above mentioned inserted quips and jokes that more often than not only work in English and the cultural anglosphere.For instance, there is a prominent example going around about a quip regarding proper pronoun usage.Said quip only works in non-genrered languages such as English, yet is still translated 1:1 into gendered languages such as German and Spanish.So as much as it hurts me, and it does so a lot, i simply can't recommend the game like this.The localization job is lazy and, in parts, downright broken, especially if you're looking to play it in languages other than English. I wish the game all the best in its original language and hope that it enables Rabbit & Bear to continue creating fantastic games such as this, hopefully under a more competent publisher.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start off by saying I am a huge fan of the Suikoden franchise, and when I heard about this game I was ecstatic. If you are a fan of that style of game you will enjoy this game to a degree. In fact, for the first half of the game, you will be deeply invested in the gameplay, the characters, and the story. The developers do a very good job of setting up a high stakes, there is no winner in war scenario that grabs you by the collar and will have you playing for hours on end and not even notice the time. Where things start to take a turn is when the game opens up and gives you free rein of the world to go recruit, train, gather resources to build your base, etc. There is just TOO MUCH going on in this game. The Devs packed the back half of this game with SO many different mini-games, side quests that don't feel like they have any meaningful impact on the world-building, and a war games mechanic similar to the Suikoden franchise that is so easy it is painful. They try to make this easier on you by giving you two functions;1) Quick travel.2) A deus ex machina boss rush mini-game mechanic that can level up any character in the game at the snap of a finger. (Important for when certain characters are required for the story or for you completionists out there)It just feels like the back half of the game was a smorgasbord of meh ideas instead of polishing a couple of really good ideas to give it a nice clean feel. Even though the game ran out of steam at the end it did still scratch that itch and I did feel the love for a franchise that hasn't been touched since I was in high school. It's out of love for the kind of game it strives to be that I do still recommend it, but only if you have a deep love for JRPGs and a love for the Suikoden franchise. If you can't check both of those boxes then I recommend staying away or waiting for a Steam sale to give it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: : You can play this game without having played the prequel and still understand it. It’s really a matter of preference. Rising is a lighthearted, quest-a-thon, action JRPG. I would’ve liked if both games were Suikoden-like, but that’s because I like more serious stories and turn-based JRPG combat. A lot of people found the prequel’s battle system and gameplay fun, so if that appeals to you, then you should play the prequel. You can read  for more perspective.     • The Eiyuden Chronicle games are intended to be a spiritual successor to the Suikoden series.     • The battle system of Hundred Heroes is very much like Suikoden. Turn-based. Up to 6 party members in battle, two rows. Characters that have some kind of relationship can do combo attacks that are known as Hero Combos. Those with runes can do special, magical attacks or healing/buffs. Random enemy encounters.     • Difficulty settings: Normal Mode or Hard Mode. This game’s Normal Mode seems built more for experienced JRPG players.    • Player can freely roam on the world map.     • Fast travel is unlocked after recruiting Carrie, a character who knows how to teleport.     • Gameplay involves War Battles and Duels, similar to Suikoden’s.     • The HQ is a large castle. Upon improving it, the player can add several shops and services after acquiring materials for building  the correct character recruit to operate it.     • Fishing mini-game is simple. Player presses X (or its equivalent) when an exclamation point appears over Nowa’s head.     • Cook off mini-game involves choosing an appetizer, main course, and dessert for random recruited characters of the castle as judges. Getting to know what characters like is the key to winning. It also involves smashing X to fill a timed gauge.     • It’s too annoying to describe the card game in detail. Please just watch a video somewhere, if you’re interested in knowing about it. The player can build a better deck of cards to increase chances of winning.    • The beigome (spinning top battles) mini-game is fairly simple. Collect better tops to increase chances of winning. Press X at the right time to do a good spin, then smash X when the tops battle.    • There are two different racing mini-games. One involves breeding egg creatures to improve their stats, then they automatically race each other. The other racing mini-game involves manually guiding a sand ship in the desert.    • Theater mini-game. The player casts characters for roles in various plays. If the acting is good, one can receive an S rank and a special item. If the acting is bad, it’s good for a laugh.     • The POV is highly focused on Nowa, only occasionally showing Seign or Marisa’s POV. (Thus, it isn’t like Suikoden III, which equally shared POV with three protagonists.)    • Please be aware that . My PS5 (DualSense) controller worked perfectly for it.    • Ten languages available for interface and subtitles (though, for some reason, Latin America Spanish isn’t available like it was in the prequel).     • The English voice acting was good. Some better than others, but overall, I was happy with it! I like the different accents. There is American (with variations), British (with variations), Scottish, Spanish, Australian, and a few I’m not sure about. Also, stereotypical pirate. (I don’t know if Japanese voice actors ever attempt other accents that aren’t just different Japanese accents.)    • The story is much more interesting and serious than the prequel. It is also reminiscent of Suikoden story plots, as they always revolve around war. My favorite part of such stories is getting people to realize that the only people that ever benefit from war are the rich and powerful.     • Great character development of characters central to the story. Similar to the Suikoden games, this story shows that “enemies” in war are people just like anyone else and that many people can be changed by war.     • Decent humor. We can’t just have the doom and gloom of war; there are spots of humor all throughout the story. The duel between Nowa and El Alicanto is over-the-top and hilarious.    • The music is good (again). They got Motoi Sakuraba!    • The backgrounds are even more elaborate than the prequel’s were. I’m grateful that they allow the player to disable Depth of Field, because that blurry stuff messes with my head.     • The castle (Alliance HQ) is plenty big, with several improvements to be made over the course of the game. Nowa can decorate his room and the castle.     •  Suikoden,  in this game. (In Suikoden, it was super easy to f*ck up one’s file and have to start over again, because for a lot of recruits, there were small windows of opportunity to get them.)    • One of my favorite mini-games in Suikoden was the theater plays. They did a fairly good job replicating the experience in HH. I find it addicting to see all the different outcomes.    • Femboy character unapologetically wears feminine clothing and aspires to be .      • An achievement for talking to animals. Lots of cats, dogs, and other cute creatures can be found roaming around each town. :3    • A capybara humanoid character runs the hot springs. THAT IS SO F*CKING CUTE!    • Pressing  key on the keyboard skips the cinematic intro to the game, so I was unable to get screenshots of it.     • While recruiting Douglas, it’s really unnecessary to make the player get “fresh” iron ore. He asks for 10 iron ore and even if Nowa currently has it in his inventory bag, Douglas won’t take it. You have to get it after talking to him.     • The sand ship racing mini-game is terrible. The track boundaries aren’t visible. The only guidance the player has is to go for these blue orbs that boost speed, but if you hit a boundary it forces you to  turn around; sometimes, in the  direction.     • Some theater plays don’t have voice acting.    • The game doesn’t autosave frequently enough. Lost an hour’s worth of progress, because during all that time, there was no autosaving.     • Teases possible romance between Nowa and , but nothing comes of it.     • What few romantic pairings or confessions there are, they’re all heterosexual.     • Tokenism. Are there dark-skinned people? Yes,  there are 120+ characters and only a handful are dark-skinned. Are they as important or have the same amount of power? No. While Marisa is a main character, she is not on the same level as Nowa or even Seign. This is a marginal improvement from Rising, which had no dark-skinned characters at all.     • Overpriced, cash-grab DLC content. Story segments as DLC, which is the ultimate offense for a JRPG. Story-related stuff should always be included in the game. Could be the greed of the publisher though.     • Several typos. Mainly, the names of cats and dogs. Were these backer names, and people were derps, and didn’t capitalize their names? Pfft, I would’ve capitalized them for the game anyway. I’ve missed the Suikoden games for years. I played and completed the main five games in chronological order of the series’ story (for funsies), back-to-back, in 2011. (Never got a chance to play Suikoden Tactics.) Konami has abandoned the series after the DS game Suikoden Tierkreis didn’t sell particularly well. (I haven’t played that game either.) Thus, I am  to say that this game filled some of that void. It might not be as good as what it aspires to be, but it was a damn good attempt. I highly recommend it to Suikoden fans and JRPG fans who still like turn-based combat.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, thank you and rest in peace, Yoshitaka Murayama. Your dedication towards continuing the Suikoden legacy, if only in spirit, is greatly appreciated and I'm saddened at the thought that you don't get to see people enjoy it.To give some background behind my review, I am a longtime Suikoden fan that played through the original series and even Tierkreis. I have long been a vocal supporter of the series, for what it has accomplished and what important lessons I have taken from the series. It has always been near and dear to my heart, and it is clear that Eiyuden hoped to remind me of that.For fans of the Suikoden series, this game will bring about a sense of nostalgic familiarity, particularly with regards to Suikoden 1 and 2. In many ways, this is exactly what I wanted, a brand new Suikoden experience to revel in all over again. It is both very new and very familiar at the same time.I am loving building a base all over again, filling it with a wide variety of interesting and unique characters. The music by Motoi Sakuraba and Michiko Naruke are absolutely fantastic, and while I had to adjust a little since I'm not used to hearing their styles in an experience like Suikoden, they have quickly grown to feel truly natural and wonderful to listen to. The games' aesthetic is impeccable, and the 2D pixel art is beautiful especially when overlaid onto the 3D environments. This couldn't be truer than during the duel segments, which are eye-poppingly gorgeous.The game is not perfect, however, and while I have greatly enjoyed my time playing it, its flaws were hard to ignore. I take no umbrage with the localization specifically (it's pretty standard JRPG dialogue, as far as I'm concerned), and I feel like the general complaints regarding it are overblown and highly dramatic. There are errors, to be sure, but to suggest that alone can ruin the game is sheer hyperbole. My bigger concern is less the localization and more the actual game's story. While enjoyable, it carries a much more light-hearted and optimistic tone than the Suikoden series, and I feel that it loses a drastic amount of emotional tension and weight as a result. The Suikoden games were often always bittersweet and had left me with serious considerations about war's impacts on humanity. This game had no such impact on me, and I'm saddened by that. There were no real stakes in this war at any point in the game, and I just felt like it was hard to get behind the characters motivations.The game also had a plethora of questionable design choices that led to less efficient gameplay than I'd expected from the Suikoden titles. They weren't gamebreakers for me, but they did take some teeth grinding until I'd gotten used to them as quirks of the game.Aside from all that, I did genuinely really enjoy playing the game. While it wasn't quite the game I wanted it to be, it did a great job of nailing a lot of the core Suikoden experience and was a lot of fun if not particularly impactful. I don't regret backing it, and I sincerely hope the devs continue to give it some TLC over the next while to soften some of those rough edges.

_childDocuments_.review: This is more of an early impressions sort of review -- if you're a fan of Suikoden and have been languishing in despair as Konami allows yet another fantastic and storied series to rot in obscurity, you absolutely owe it to yourself to play this game. It is a spiritual successor in every sense of the term, and while there are some gameplay elements I would have liked to have seen go in a slightly different direction, I've been having an absolute blast playing this.The story is pretty typical fare for Suikoden -- lots of intrigue, betrayal, revenge, and star-crossed bonds of friendship. I'm sure it hasn't developed all of its threads at this point, but it's been serviceable enough that I haven't wanted to put it down in 10 or so hours of playtime. Nowa and Seign's relationship is clearly attempting to evoke Riou and Jowy's friendship from Suikoden II, which is a smart choice.  It's also largely been succeeding, owing in no small part to a great and convincingly sympathetic performance by Seign's voice actor.The roster of characters is appropriately boisterous and colorful... not a lot of subtlety in the supporting cast, but that's to be expected when you're competing for lines with a hundred other characters. One neat thing I will point out as a veteran of the Suikoden series is that non-story critical characters seem to interject in cutscenes more than I would have expected, which is a nice touch. I can't remember how much of that there was in later Suikoden titles, but it makes them feel like meaningful additions to the party long after recruitment.As far as the gameplay is concerned... it's new Suikoden, and it's quite good so far. I don't have a whole lot more to say than that at this point and I'll probably update my "review" when I finish the game. In the meantime, if you miss the days of scouring the map for new characters to recruit to your cause and occasionally forgoing the usual adventuring party in favor of grand, pitched battles alongside your comrades, Eiyuden Chronicle is a must play.UPDATE: The war is won, and I have a lot of thoughts about this game.I just finished it, and while the 124 hours of playtime I have on it is somewhat inflated due to idling, I put a LOT of time into playing this. I threw myself wholeheartedly into the minigames, successfully recruited every character, and had an all in all great time. My early impressions review remains true, but I definitely see a lot more about the game as missed opportunities.First off, the mainstay of Suikoden that similarly makes this game what it is is still the character recruitment, and I really enjoyed it. The base building aspects were also fun and satisfying, and I spent an insane amount of time wandering around home base and exploring every nook and cranny of what was on offer. It's quite good, and with that in mind, it was a lot of fun to play.However, I do have some gripes with the way some of the game systems played out. When I wrote my earlier review, I believe I had just participated in the first of the game's army battles, and seen the first of its duels. Both of these aspects of the game felt lackluster to me, and that's probably the thing I'm most regretful about. Most of the army battles lock you into a predetermined set of commanders, and there isn't much to do in terms of customizing their units. The exception to this comes in the form of a couple of the mock battles you're able to undertake at the base with the help of a certain character, the last of which was fairly challenging and required some actual strategic thought. In fact, I think that's where I learned that you could move a unit two spaces at a time if they were composed entirely of cavalry... which is a weird place to learn something like that. The mock battles were more like what I wanted the army battles to be like, but unfortunately, during the story they play out more like cinematics and are basically over before they begin. I hope they take another look at the mechanics for the sequel and consider overhauling them completely, and they'd be in good company to do so, considering Suikoden changed its army battles substantially with every entry.The duels are disappointing for a similar reason. First of all, they are very few and far between. Even at times where duels with recruitable characters seemed appropriate, most of the time they just led to normal battles, with a single exception towards the end of the game. If memory serves, there are a total of five duels in the game, and two of them are essentially just cinematics that can't really be won or lost (though I have heard reports its possible to "win" the first duel, I don't think it would change anything, other than possibly one interaction later in the game). I can easily think of at least twice as many spots where a duel would have been appropriate and satisfying. I also feel like the impact of your actions in the duels isn't as readable or satisfying as the duels in the Suikoden games, though they certainly look much cooler and feel much grander here.I was really excited for the Beigoma minigame, but it was not really fun to play in execution. It felt entirely too random and luck based for the amount of time it required to complete. Similarly, the cooking competitions were theoretically fun, but the entire system seemed to be completely broken for the entirety of my playthrough. I made the same three things every time, and any time I tried branching out, everyone started puking and trying to close my restaurant. The Eggfoot races turned out to be pretty fun, and I'm guessing at least 10-15 hours of my playtime was the result of trying to breed one with perfect terrain adaptivity. However, the most enjoyble minigame is probably the card game, and it was neat that it gave you some pretty decent recovery items early on.Last but not least, the game was extremely uneven in difficulty. There were some fights I really struggled through on hard mode, especially because I was trying to play with parties appropriate to the situation as opposed to just putting the clear best choices in for every fight. However, others were... questionable. I actually think the final boss encounter might be bugged at the time I completed it. Granted, the boss did do some massive, concerning damage to my party with its opening attack... but, that's literally the only one it got. I killed the final boss of the game inside of two turns. I'm legitimately wondering if there's a zero missing from the end of its HP count.Gripes aside, the game was a lot of fun, and I still wholeheartedly recommend it. I think there's still more content to be completed and I'll probably stick around with it and try to clear every achievement. I also hope they'll take another look at some of their game systems and patch them up... surely, the most talented chefs in the world can't all be this bad at cooking.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a backer of the Kickstarter campaign.And Eiyuden Chronicles is not a bad game and deserves a positive recommendation.But, it's a Mixed/Mostly Positive game that I would rate as a good 6/10, as there are many flagrant flaws in its: game design and combat stats, User experience and user interface, lack of polish in many places, absent sounds and glitched audio, very generic and unequal writing.The team bit much more than they could chew, that's for sure. Yet, for the nostalgic factor of old rpg on the snes/ps1 era I believe it does scratch the itch; if only it could be at the height of stellar games of thoses eras... A full run-through took me 60h before I see the end credits. I'm quite a completionist in general so I try to complete all activities, but there are evident gating of some achievements behind an end-game (post-credits). The game can take you maybe a 100h to fully platinum; it needs to be said that those last 40 hours are a real pain and slog that I found completely unappealing and made me drop the game flat-out.The main story follow a thread that is very generic and shounen. It has many tropes and has (unlike it's inspired predeccessors Suikoden I & II) a very one-sided villain that is seen from a mile away. There are, in the side-quests, funny moments and some texts and characters that made me giggle either of cringe or cuteness, which is fine by me. Alas, there are aboslutely no "real meshing" in the main protagonists the justify their camaraderie. There is, overall, a overload of quantity of everything and a lack a quality as a whole,Combat is nice, has a good flow and plays out in a very classic manner for a turn based RPG. Effects are nice and characters have impact. But, again, its marred by absurdly high mana costs that devoids all mages and healers for items until level 50-60's and upwards. A non-sensical limited inventory management that becomes more and more aggregious the further you progress, and bosses gimmicks that are very unequal in interests/fun factor.Also, many of the 100's of characters have very limited kits of skills they can equip; which is fine, until you realize about 10 of them are actual very good and the rest is bottom barrel garbage that are useless... some protagonists included. It feels like this game was designed to not be fun, and not give players any agency and interesting "builds"; if only those they could control with the small team they had.I have very few words for the Art Direction.I found the monsters sprites to be very nicely done, as much as the character sprites. The issue lies in the environment and, more precisely, after we had the Star Ocean 2nd Story R remake not so long ago. It thought the environments and level designs lacked in cohesiveness if only to support puzzles that are sometimes very janky and old-fashioned. i think in a straight-line without participating in activities and side-quests or finding everyone the game takes about roughly 30-40 hours or so, give or take. A full completionists run though might take you about an 100 hours or more. The end game consists of boss rush battles and a secret hidden dungeon at the moment; all other content are tedious side activities not related to combat: fishing, egg races, cooking, cards collection, beigomas battles (beyblade) and the likes.Okay. Why is there no audio for footsteps?The very basic sound that grounds the character(s) in the universe are non-existant. Also, when defeating multiple ennemies at once with AoEs, they sounds all adds up cranking up their volume twice or thrice. Sometimes voices are loud and the music is not, other times its the opposite, why? Please devs play with your headphones on your heads! This is ridiculous.The OST though, is very good although very repetitive, there are variants of the battle theme, and enough thematics per countries/dungeons/biomes to have a nice grasp of the soundscape of each seperate nation.As for the Localisation issues others brought, I,m no Japanese expert so I won't mention if it's bad or not; but I'll say some english actors/actresses were very nicely coached and others were very unaware of what they were doing; to the point of hitting the cringe ceilling levels very often. The worst is that it's sometimes at very touching moments and it just makes every ounce of tension falls down the drain.I never encountered any crashes, few dips here and there but overall very stable.Had excellent FPS, I locked at 144 fps at DLSS 4K constantly.No crash whatsoever.On a good rig here:4K 43" MonitorRTX4090AMD RYZEN 5950X128GB DDR4 3600Mhz980Pro Samsung 2tb NVME DriveIt's a shame. And I know I bashed the game for a 6 million budget game, but the reality is this game is sold at64.99 CDN$ if not on sale. I have to rate it like a "semi high budget game" it tries to sell itself at.The tedious back and forth in menus to manage items and all it's bloat, the audio glitches, the very toned-down and barebone stats limitations and poor classes choices concerning mana and defenses makes this game a very bizarre take on what could've been a very enjoyable experience. Add to that a story without much cohesion and overall meshing that you wonder what all those kickstarter goals meant in the end if the foundation wasn't so good after all.I wish Rabbit & Bear all the best, but now that we seee DLC's, packages, Raodmaps and ♥♥♥♥♥ that were supposed to be handed out to backers and we actually never got after months, I will not be backing the follow-up the studio plans to make in the future.Honestly, go try it on Gamepass if it's there! But don't buy this at full price, regardless of small studio or not. I'd fully heartedly recommend this game at 30$ or less, else it's not worth the shot in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: 4/10 - Weak.Steam has a character limit, so my full review is here;In summary though;A juvenile game that is afraid to allow the world to suffer consequences, everything bad that happens is eventually handwaved away, there are few repercussions, deaths and injuries are limited, if they ever exist at all. Characters quip in modern lingo, with childish jokes at inopportune times, leading to a set of characters that don't take the situations unfolding seriously. It is a political story that fails to kick on, where odd illogical decisions are made. The game rides on the coattails of Suikoden but does little to refine the systems of those past games, duels are poor, the war system is uninspiring, and about the only mechanic that genuinely does improve on is the castle (HQ) building.I do not agree with commentators suggesting this is a political translation/localisation ~ I never got that vibe at all, however, the localisation/tone is a complete mismatch for the type of story that it is supposed to going for. If you're after a serious political drama, with consequences and issues (a la Suikoden series) this isn't it. This is baby's first JRPG, where all the bad stuff isn't so bad, and everything will be absolute sweet and roses. If that's what you want, you'll be right at home here.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is about scratching that pesky Suikoden VI itch. Ok, it does scratch that itch. That is why I recommend this game, but only IF YOU HAVE THAT ITCH.This game is supposed to be a nostalgia trip, and that's fine. But gameplay from the late 90s / early 200s without any kind of effort put into improving it, however, is NOT.It has it all: Ditzy teleporting magic girl, red and blue knights, the elven trio, you name what Suikoden had, this game has it.THAT SAID, there are a few things to talk about.Point 1: It's crazy to me that this game is published in 2024, and 90% of the characters you can put in your team are subpar. That was ok in the 90s, but this is NOT ok now. Either reduce the playable character pool or spend more time balancing the characters you choose to make playable.Point 2: Game balance - a certain character whose name starts with an M basically trivializes all the content that comes after you obtain said character.Point 3: Pick better translators. I don't care about the whole woke debate, but seriously, the English translation is at points too poor. At least you can easily patch that though (using a mod though).Point 4: The cooking battles are a tradition, but you do not need something that feels like 20+ battles. Moreover, I won every single one by using poached egg / fried eggs and OMELETTE AS A DESSERT. That literally makes no sense, and again, it's just laziness on the programmers' part.Point 5: At stage 4, building everything in the castle is gated behind getting items for construction that only appear each in ONE dungeon, and you can only get 6 per dungeon (with the support who increases the yield...) or through missions in the mission guild that, you guessed it, require those elements to actually be unblocked first.And on top of that, you then have buildings which require an element that can ONLY be obtained through clearing missions. And missions last 30 minutes, with no way to speed them up.Anyone saying "This is optional" obviously does not play JRPGs. It's not REALLY optional, unless you do not plan on finishing the game.Again, this is 90s gameplay. Not ok in 2024.Point 6: Tbh, the story itself is bland as hell, and that is because (I realized it at the end of the game), it does not have that true rune driving it Suikoden had. This is just a war story. The justification is mildly mystical, but in the end there is no real driving force. You talk about the empire, but you never do see an emperor, either.If you take all this into account, I have two conclusions:1. Are you a Suikoden fan? Buy it and enjoy it.2. Are you a hardcore JRPG fan, and are used to this kind of formulaic gameplay? You might enjoy it.3. If you are neither, then this game is a HARD pass.

_childDocuments_.review: So there's a lot to say, but I'm going to break it up into three parts: The localization controversy, the comparison to Suikoden, and the actual game.Localization:So I spent some time in the forums for another issue only to see a large percentage of the people in there genuinely angered by the localization.  Same for the reviews.  I was genuinely confused by this, because all my time in the forums, not a single person mentioned they played the game through in both English and Japanese to definitively make the statement that the localization is bad.  And what I'm lead to believe is that there are just a handful of cherry-picked instances of genuinely odd or unfavorable translations and used those to dismiss the entire game.  I played with both English subtitles and dubs, and the VAST majority of the dialog was just fine.  Like 99%.  And I can say that because I was even trying NOT to think about the localization while playing through, but because of the reception, it was subconsciously thinking about it the whole time.  Some people in the forums claim that there was some right-wing political push to review-bomb the game because there was LGBTQ+ representation in the game.  I'm unsure if this is actually the case, but it would explain things.  Ultimately, to discredit the game over a few terms is the best example of throwing the baby out with the bathwater that I have ever experienced.  I loved the story, and the writing is absolutely fine the vast majority of the time.  It saddens me that a fun game that should be celebrated was dragged through this mess.Comparison to Suikoden:The only other negative reviews/threads that I've seen are about how much the game isn't like Suikoden.  But here's the deal: the game isn't Suikoden.  It never claimed to BE Suikoden.  Was it inspired by it?  Absolutely, is it BETTER than Suikoden?  That's going to be subjective from person to person.  But again, the devs never claimed or promised it to be better than Suikoden.  And just for argument's sake, let's say that the game is, in fact, worse in every way to Suikoden.  That does not change the fact it's still a fantastic RPG that celebrates the era of gaming's past.  Hating this game because it is not like (or better than) Suikoden is a bad faith argument.  It was inspired by it, and it's very clear that goal was achieved.The actual game:So the funny thing is, I generally don't like games with a vast roster in a story driven genre.  Because there's absolutely no way they are all going to get the screen time they need to be developed, fleshed out characters.  So you end up with a bunch of throw away, forgettable characters, again, in a genre who's leading feature is story telling.  And that's still true even in Hundred Heroes.  And despite this, I still loved this game.  The overall story and the events as they unfold were absolutely compelling, and it was a great ride from beginning to end.  And I imagine that those who don't have the hang up that I do will love it even more.  Though something that genuinely impressed me was how your less story related characters would actually speak up and say something about what was happening, relevant to them.  Like, we're not talking Chrono Cross here, where your tag-along characters say the literal exact same thing.  They are unique to that character, and that goes a long way to make those characters feel more real.The battle system was really good, and I enjoyed putting together parties that have different play styles.  One mechanic I pretty much used all game was having a charge-up character with some ways to buff them just to see how big of numbers I could get.  The combination of gear and rune lenses allowed for some pretty cool player expression.  Though I do feel that the combination Hero Attacks were mostly not worth it.  Like you have to give up multiple character's turns and SP, and the damage was never higher than what I could do with those characters just attack independently.  Like, they are super flashy and cool, but the utility they provide feels a little lacking.  But what wasn't lacking were the boss gimmicks.  Actually having something to do or interact with outside of normal battle mechanics was super cool, and I hope to see something like this in future games.  And the duels.  Holy hell.  They were so cinematic and cool.  Like there was always a big dumb smile on my face after the building up Break. The mini-games, while vast were kind of hit and miss.  I like how a few of them had legitimate story beats to experience as you went through, particularly the Beigoma stuff.  But while things like Beigoma and the card game are really fun, you have some things like fishing or the cooking which have very little input from the actual player.  And actually, the cooking mini-game really felt bad.  Like, I was struggling with the second battle for a long time, until I found someone who said if you just use these three things, you always win, and that is still the case.  I played it for the story beats, and that's it.  But overall, the amount of content you get is mostly great.  You always can have something to do outside of progressing the story.  Even if not mini-games.  Like recruiting characters, upgrading your base, etc.The graphics and the music are also both worth mentioning.  I mean, you can see by the trailer what you are getting into, but it's still just a beautiful world to be in.  And the boss battles were always a spectacle.  But there was something that actually bugged me about the game.  Despite promises that you wouldn't be locked out of any character, this is at least one (due to a bug).  And I happened to miss them.  I found this very disappointing.  I missed out on the recruit all characters achievement, and it kind of killed my interest in making an effort to achievement hunt.Overall, the game was an amazing experience.  I think that you're really missing out on something great if you allow yourself to be taken in by all the drama over localization or the fact the game is not Suikoden.  As a huge old school RPG fan, I really can't stress enough how much of a good experience this was overall.

_childDocuments_.review: A very flawed gem suffering from way too many technical issues.I wish I could recommend this game; I truly do. There are so many things to like here, but the flaws, bugs, and non-functional features make it hard to recommend.The developers have left multiple progress-breaking bugs in the game and are very slow to address them. Loading screens are everywhere, and there is no frame cap in the game, except for half refresh rate V-sync or full refresh rate V-sync (aptly named as 30fps and 60fps caps in the game settings). Thus, one needs to use RTSS or another frame-limiting software to cap the fps. Otherwise, if you play in windowed mode, you will see 1000 fps. You know something is missing when both the opening intro and credits are bugged and unfinished.Many game systems do not work as intended or are bugged or even outright broken.The game's core revolves around collecting multiple heroes. Unfortunately, quite a few recruitment events are bugged and require either a workaround, a mod, or a patch to complete. There are also quite a few recruitment quests that are time-gated, so prepare to spend hours recruiting just a single character.The game does not explain anything, so be prepared to check the game's help menu to understand what is going on.Localization has received a lot of criticism from others. It's passable, but the English script differs from the Japanese script. The English script contains many typos, even with something as basic as "your" vs. "you're." The English voice acting is horrible. I do recommend switching to Japanese voice acting, which is better but suffers from a really bad audio mix, as does the rest of the game.When the game is good, it really is enjoyable. Collecting a vast array of characters and building your own city feels rewarding. The story is pretty mediocre—it’s not bad, but it’s so forgettable that it’s a shame the characters aren’t utilized better. Almost all of the characters are underused, and even if you want to build your own party, most of the game restricts you to a few specific characters. It seems many elements were cut from the final product, leading to some odd dialogue both early and very late in the game.Wait until the developer, if ever, fixes most of the issues, and this game could be much better. At this point, it's a solid 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Skip this hollow shell of the amazing Suikoden series. It is full of bad design (see inventory system critique that I guarantee no other review found this intentional bad design)For those that want more of a breakdown, I changed my review from recommended to not once I have completed the game. This is a game that is shallow in every aspect but let's break it down by category.Story: Let's get the obvious out of the way. The story is a paint by numbers, dollar store knockoff of Suikoden 1 & 2. Main characters have no arcs whatsoever. Their entire personality is a flat line throughout the story. There are no greater depth of characters like Viktor, softening of Filk, sacrifice of Mathiu, or tough choices of Jowy. Of course there are tons more characters that have amazing moments in Suikoden series but the point is all the characters in Eiyuden Chronicle is a parody of the well written characters. Localization is abysmal. You'll hear a lot of current day words that suck you right out of the world. Deus Ex Machina rules the story with no smart writing. Main characters are bland and you can tell that splitting it to three characters galvanizes a lot of much needed payoffs. Gameplay: Tons of bugs with gameplay balance where physical damage is king, mana is weaker and cost too much, and hero combos are weaker than just attacking individually. INVENTORY is purposely designed to annoy you and I found that out recently playing today. If your inventory is full, you'll get a message that you cannot add the item till you make room. HOWEVER, IF YOU GET AN ITEM FROM THE BAYBLADES MINIGAME AND YOUR INVENTORY IS FULL IT AUTOMATICALLY SENDS IT TO THE WAREHOUSE. Why on earth they didn't implement that feature for the entire game is maddening.  EVERYTHING is SLOW. From conversations, to walking, to battle, they're all about .5 the speed it should be. These are some massive problems considering finding all the characters and seeing what combos you can create was a major appeal of gameplay for Suikoden. Bosses have cool gimmick mechanics but they aren't enough to save the gameplay. Auto battle mechanic is archaic compared to Unicorn Overlord. You'll find auto battle either wasting MP or not using the preferred attack. Recruiting feels meaningless with someone that will give you hints and massive gameplay imbalance. There is even a character that you find that requires you to barter $50,000 PROFIT to recruit. You'll find yourself wasting 1-2 hours of your day just bartering and waiting for items to refresh.This game needed a lot more QA.Music:Probably the best part of the game. Battle music is solid and for the most part I have no issues with it. Mini Games:All the mini games are designed to WASTE YOUR TIME.They are not balanced, well thought out, and REQUIRED for characters.- Duels are only about like 4 or so and they're story related. You feel no challenge, agency, or satisfaction from them. - War Battles are also story driven, require no strategy, and are always 100% anti-climatic. - Bayblades knockoff you'll be excited by first until you realize you cannot get them without fighting monsters which means you need to progress the story to even play.- Card Game is the best of the mini games in my opinion but instead of walking up to people to challenge you can only do it in a static menu. The balance and thought of the card game is great but it's sad that Bayblades trash mini game got the love. - Fishing is wasting your time to just press a button at the right time- Cooking is heavily bugged and you will realize that all the rules set don't actually apply. I beat it using 3 appetizers every time. No challenge or preference of characters needed. Time waster. Summary: This game makes me appreciate of the storytelling of JRPG's in the mid 90's and early 00's. You don't realize you had it so good until something is gone but if you haven't played Suikoden 1 or 2 i'd highly recommend it even with all the flaws.

I'd recommend trying it out for yourself before passing judgment based on some reactionary comments.

_childDocuments_.review: Eiyuden Hundred Heroes is a game crafted with love and passion by early genre pioneers, reflecting their expertise in storytelling and character development. While it isn't perfect, it offers a mostly enjoyable experience and worth playing for fans of the genre.Nostalgia plays a significant role in the game, balancing old-school elements with modern expectations. While some 90s and 2000s mechanics may feel outdated, the developers' commitment to their vision deserves credit.The game's strengths lie in its world-building and graphics. The HD-2D visuals are stunning, with detailed backgrounds and impressive effects. The storyline, focused on empires, rebellions, and political intrigue, unfolds believably and avoids gratuitous twists.Characters are another highlight, with strong voice acting and engaging personalities. However, the large cast can lead to some characters fading into the background post-recruitment. I always want more of certain characters and less of others, but that's the way the wheel spins when you have over 100 characters in your troop.A major issue for me is the game's unbalanced experience. Combat difficulty spikes early but becomes routine later. The turn-based system, while nostalgic, can feel tedious, although the auto-battle feature helps. The inability to grind beyond a point and random battles offering little reward are also drawbacks.Pacing problems emerge about a quarter in, making the game feel slow and aimless. However, I found for myself that playing on handheld devices can alleviate some of this frustration with multitasking. The music, mini-games, and base-building mechanics are adequate but not exceptional.Overall, I'm glad I backed this project despite some mixed feelings. As a fan of JRPGs, supporting pioneers in the genre is important. I look forward to their next title, hoping they learn from Hundred Heroes and Rising to create something truly special.*[Footnote: I did not address the English localization controversy, as it seemed rooted in bigotry and did not impact my experience during 70+ hours of gameplay.]*

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't perfect. In fact, there are several issues, and, if you're paying attention, it becomes painfully clear when they started running out of time and money. This was developed through Kickstarter promising a spiritual successor to a series of games that are revered and near-mythical. Many are upset because, in several respects, this failed to reach those heights.But speaking as someone who plays roughly 50-100 JRPGs in a year: This is something special and it's most definitely worth your time.I'll get my two biggest complaints out of the way right off: The game is rated E for everyone, meaning a lot of the darker and more intense elements are completely offscreen. This feels rather inappropriate, and provides something of a tonal dissonance.Additionally, the modern disdain for "missable content" had so impacted the development that there is a near-comical lack of consequences for various story developments, further undermining the tone and the sense that the world politics are a big deal in the grand scheme of things.Both these decisions are somewhat reasonable in the goal of reaching a broad audience, but they do somewhat cheapen the final product.Additionally, tying in to the previous comments of budget and time constraints, there are several design elements which feel poorly calibrated. Not enough to ruin the experience, but enough to elicit a sigh of regret.All the complaints out of the way, what makes it good, even special?The visuals speak for themselves, as the designers have accomplished a pleasing blend of hand-drawn pixel art characters on rendered backgrounds.I consider myself a poor judge of music quality, but this is a rare game where I chose to play unmuted, granted that this was in no small part due to an excellent case of voice actors. And the voice acting is definitely a place where you can clearly see a dedicated budget, as nearly every interaction beyond conversing with random NPCs is fully voiced, to include "peanut gallery comments" from party members otherwise uninvolved in the event.Character customisation is a generally pleasing blend of limited freedom with enough restrictions to give each character their own distinct identity. A particularly nice touch is the unique skills held by some characters, as well as "union attacks" performed by characters who have some special relationship. Even when such skills aren't especially useful, they serve to convey a lot of personality, to the point where you begin to love and care for a significant portion of your loads and loads of characters.Which brings up the roster. You recruit over 100 special people to contribute in your effort, be they farmers, merchants, or soldiers. Around 80 of them can serve some sort of combat role, as well. Not all fighters are created equally, but the game is generous enough that you can probably have a viable team by choosing the folks you like the most (no one likes a game where you have 100 options, but 95 are unusable).You gather people to your side. You build a town. Your people spend down time together, playing card games or discussing beard grooming. It's a wonderfully cozy environment where you won't think twice about spending hours making your most socially awkward friends perform a train wreck of "Romeo and Juliet".It's not the best game I've ever played, or even the best game I've played this year. But I can guarantee that it's one I'll remember for a long time, and likely revisit.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a love letter to the JRPGs of the PS1/PS2 era. If Suikoden was amongst your list of favourite games, buying this game is a no-brainer since it's essentially a spiritual successor from the same team, made with so much love and attention. I feel like I've been transported to my childhood bedroom without a care in the world.The story beats might seem reminiscent of Suikoden II at first with the Nowa/Seign and Riou/Jowy parallels, but I promise you'll quickly see that isn't the case as the game progresses. The game, overall, isn't as serious as Suikoden II, but it definitely treads into the world of political intrigue and has passionate tactical battles and very cinematic duels. It starts off on rails, but once you make it past the first big military battle, the game opens up in a big, big way. By the end of the second military battle, the world is your oyster. I haven't progressed the main storyline in about six hours with how much other stuff I've been obsessed with!Eiyuden Chronicles feels like a warm hug from an old friend. There are so many wonderful familiar mechanics and fun inclusions (hot spring scenes, cooking contests, art collecting, minigames that you can sink hours and hours into), and even if you aren't a Suikoden veteran, you'll no doubt be delighted by the sheer mind-boggling variety that can be found in this game.Pros:- There is SO much to do. It's so easy to spend hours on end playing the game because if you get sick of progressing the story, there are minigames galore to sink your teeth into- It's very well-paced -- I never felt like something was getting tedious (save for the Proving Grounds which I would absolutely recommend a guide for because it's literally a moving labyrinth -- every game has a portion that a player dreads and this was Eiyuden's)- The battles are short and snappy, and the "Auto" function and the various rules you can set for the AI behaviour make random encounters a breeze- It's a beautiful game that still captures the essence of PS1 spritework- The voiced dialogues make the game absolutely vibrant- The variety of characters is absolutely hilarious and I'm always looking forward to my next recruit- The castle expansion system is delightful and the castle in general is so much fun to engage with!Cons:- The menus are strangely slow and can get annoying at times. Would love to see a QoL update addressing this- I both hate and like the inventory limit. It makes it so that you have to strategise in regards to what items you can keep for battles, but I hate that trading post items/equipment count towards that limit. This ceases to become a deal when you upgrade your inventory space, but you definitely notice it early on- I'd love to be able to save my game on the overworld! I don't mind only being able to save at save points/inns in dungeons and in towns, but it'd be a nice QoL to be able to pop a save on the overworld map, too- The vehicle controls make me want to drop dead at the worst of times

_childDocuments_.review: I've really been enjoying my time with hundred heroes.I didn't have the highest expectations, I knew it was a small Kickstarter and was hoping to get something kind of like Octopath Traveler but with a more cohesive story, and I feel like thats exactly what I got.  don't recommend going into this expecting to relive your first play through of Suikoden II. Those are big boots to fill, even for Suikoden II (Nostalgia goggles and all that).I am a Suikoden fan, but I am also just a general JRPG fan, and as a general JRPG fan, I'm really digging this game. I like the characters and the story, it is a little on the lighthearted side, not that it doesn't touch on some mature themes, it certainly does, but they aren't really in your face. Its not super dark is what I'm trying to say.Anyway, there's full voice acting here, which I'm really glad for, because I can handle a lot of classic JRPG design decisions ( of which there are many in this game) but the things I really need to have in the modern day to stay engaged, is voice acting, interesting characters, and a good story. And this checks all the boxes.Combat is also a thing. Mostly you'll be a party of 6, dungeons, fighting monsters, finding loot, you know the drill. One thing I will say is, MP is a valuable resource, especially early game, so bring lots of healing herbs with you. Enemies can hit pretty hard but I wouldn't say its a hard game overall, with six characters its pretty easy to get some heals off when you're in a tough fight. If you do want more of a challenge, there are options for that, a hard mode and few other toggles like double MP consumption or hyperinflation. Not really my thing, but its there if you want it I guess. You can also calibrate the difficulty by the party you choose to bring.The graphics look really nice. The pixel art is well done. One thing that bothers me though is the LOD transitions, which can be rather distracting at times. You might not notice if you sit far away from your monitor/tv but if you sit close, they are easily spotted. I do wish there was a slider for this, I understand why its needed on switch or a low end pc but I have 4090, I don't need the detail phasing out 2 feet from the camera. Shadow resolution is another thing, its pretty low. However there is a mod to fix that if it bothers you. Overall, good graphics, but could use some improvement.Now, I haven't run into any personally, but I am aware of some bugs in this game, even a game breaking bug. So I do recommend saving whenever you get the opportunity, and use all the slots available incase you need to fall back even further than your last save. A good habit to get into with all games really.So, if you are classic JRPG fan, you'll probably like this game. However, you may not like this game if you are unable to play without some QOL features we have become accustomed to. For example, your bag space is limited, mana is limited as I mentioned before and running speed is kind of on the slow side. Luckily you will get some tools a bit later in the game help out (like fast travel, bag upgrades etc). I personally found the return of resource management in a jrpg kind of refreshing, but I understand if not everybody feels that way.Guess I better address the Elephant in the room, the localization..... its fine! Its actually pretty good. I can't believe its become such a big deal. Its really just like any other jrpg.There was only a couple words that stuck out as odd choices. And it seems like the original Japanese script wasn't exactly Shakespeare to begin with (for example, Japanese steam scores are massively lower than English review scores, at this moment Japanese in 40s, english in the 80s). So idk if a more literal translation would have made this any better. I like how they give the game some personality. One might even look at the numbers and walk away thinking this game was saved by the localization.As long as you don't expect 1:1 and as long as you aren't easily offended by a couple out of place words, its good and you probably never would have noticed, especially if you play a lot jrpgs.Anyway its quite amazing what this small Kickstater team was able to deliver and I highly recommend it. Just - take it as its own thing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough sell. I am personally quite mixed on the game, even if I mark this review as recommended. If I put this many hours into it, it kinda has to be that way. I am a kickstarter backer, and Suikoden 2 is one of my favourite games of all time. Suikoden 2 is essentially a masterclass on how to convey an epic story with a minimalist approach, and could be studied in writing classes.(I am also quite fond of 3, 5 and 1, in that order).For simplicitys sake, and because this is essentially a suikoden title, I rank them thusly: 2-3-5-1-Eiyuden-tierkreis-4.If you are a fan of jrpgs, you might want to consider this game. There is an insane amount of stuff to do, the characters are overall charming and the game does have difficult moments and some interesting dungeon designs. The duels are top notch as well.If you are not a jrpg-lover, this is probably one of the harder ones to get into.Basically, I like a large part of the game design. Some aspects are underbaked, and way too many characters are mid to bad, magic is mostly for support, and I am not certain if certain abilities and hero combos work the way the designers intended them to. This might be patched later, so I will revisit this review in a year or so.Also, If you've read this far. I loved the suikoden series primarily for the story, and while there are hints to a larger narrative and so on, large parts of the story does not land, and way too many characters are paper thin, superfluous or both. Suikoden was a quite edgy series at times and this game does not have that.

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts out incredible and exciting, but then it nosedives so hard for me personally.The story isn't great, it's not bad either. Generic bad guy hellbent on becoming powerful and conquering every nation. There's a LOT of characters, but they're all actually pretty unique in terms of dialogue and presentation. The pacing isn't too bad either. Traveling around and backtracking to check on new characters is a chore and a pain until you unlock fast travel halfway into the game.The music is AMAZING and I absolutely love it, which is to be expected with Motoi Sakuraba and Michiko Naruke. They really set the mood for each town, dungeon, fight and scene.My biggest gripe with the game comes in two forms. There's so many characters: some are great, some are terrible, and the rest are mediocre. Some characters are literally a pain in the ass to recruit, and they turn out to be the most terrible characters so the pay off isn't there at all. Some characters are good when you first recruit them, but fall off later. Some are terrible, but really spike in performance *much* later. The others are either mediocre, or just flat out terrible.My other gripe with the game is magic. It's useless for 2/3 of the game, existing only to heal and buff your allies. My casters do triple the damage their spells would inflict, which is incredibly hefty in MP cost as well. There's not a lot of variety in magic either, with most of them being buffs or heals. AoE tickles the enemies, and single targets just isn't worth the MP cost when your auto attack can do triple its damage. From what I've gathered, magic doesn't become useful until late game and seeing how I'm nearing the end of the game and magic is only just starting to become useful, it just leaves a really poor taste in my mouth. I love magic, and it's an afterthought in this game.Also I really, really hate the mini-games in this. They're either buggy and incredibly frustrating, or just a button masher which tires me out in my old age. None of them are fun at all, yet you need to push through a lot of them to recruit some characters.If you don't mind spending the majority of your battles simply auto attacking and healing, occasionally using skills, with a generic story, a plethora of characters where some are good, some are terrible, and the rest are mediocre, and great music, then this game is for you. If you enjoy having variety in your party like magic and a lot of characters that have their uses, I'm sorry to say this game isn't going to do much for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I actually bought this game to pay off my debt to Suikoden and was happy that the series would come back to life.My first impression is enough to make me nostalgic. Exploring the world to recruit lots of characters before continue the main quest. Experience the Suikoden feature in a new game.The first problem I felt in Eiyuden was the story, it wasn't memorable enough or maybe it would be better if an important character died and could come back later or something like that I guess. The root problems of each character are not related to each other or are not strong enough to make them come together in the first place and so on. I'm just comparing the story to Suikoden III where each "main character" also has their own team, but Suikoden III is still good at bringing them together.Nowa - Seign's duel is also less constructed to make it more dramatic like Suikoden II. The one that helps this duel is the background music, it is awesome. The 1-on-1 duel mechanic is also not good that you have to rely on the one success rate in the final action, I just like the Suikoden version which is really rock paper scissors.But I like the voice act which has lots of accents, it's just that there are some intonations that sometimes bother me, especially from Nowa.And I just love the card battle mini games, even though the others are boring or just too simple and too much to get through. Like why do I have to fight all the beybladers in the world with just pressing one button in three rounds, it's so repetitive. And I have to know what food is best for all the characters in order to win the entire cooking competition, and so on.Despite all of that, the combat is cool to me, the visual effects, character animations, unique positions, and gimmicks in boss fights, and all of that running together feels cool. In my opinion, the pixel art for the characters doesn't feel like pixel art, just like 2D art in general. I think it would be better to reduce the dimensions to be more pixelated.Eiyuden Chronicle is already cool but not cool enough because of the label as successor of Suikoden, which the players already have very high expectations. I think the developer still could do much better in Eiyuden Chronicle 2 considering Suikoden also utilizes the cameos and character relations in each series, etc.Still waiting the next Eiyuden Chronicle.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a Suikoden fan, then you'll feel right at home with this. Everything about this game seems meant to carry the Suikoden DNA and they pull it off quite well. All of the staples are here with 120 heroes, your own alliance headquarters and some mini-games to boot. (Things like a Yu-Gi-Oh! styled card game, a Beyblade knock-off and some eggfoot monster racing!) The art direction mixes a simple yet charming 3D world with 2D sprites. It almost gave me Ragnarok Online vibes at times. The story might not be quite as deep as something like Suikoden II, but it's decent enough to provide you with reasons to build your army. As with any game that throws a million characters your way, you won't find yourself connecting with the majority of heroes you'll collect as there's simply not enough time or story for each of them. The game provides you with some backstory on each character that you can read if you're willing to grind the money required to unlock their backgrounds, but you'll most likely find a small team you prefer and stick with them throughout all the story beats. The game will force specific characters on you at times, but it also provides you with a method of bringing those heroes along as "attendants" without forcing them in your fighting group. Overall, I really enjoyed the throwback nostalgia that Eiyuden Chronicle provided here and would easily recommend this to any classic JRPG or Suikoden fan. Full disclosure, I did not play Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising before this despite some of the characters crossing over into this game. That game did not hold the same appeal to me. Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review:
Our story begins in one corner of Allraan, a tapestry of nations with diverse cultures and values. By dint of sword, and by way of magical objects known as "rune-lenses," the land's history has been shaped by the alliances and aggressions of the humans, beastmen, elves, and desert people who live there.

The Galdean Empire has edged out other nations and discovered a technology that amplifies the rune-lenses' magic. Now, the Empire is scouring the continent for an artifact that will expand their power even further.

It is on one such expedition that Seign Kesling, a young and gifted imperial officer, and Nowa, a boy from a remote village, meet each other and become friends. However, a twist of fate will soon drag them into the fires of war, and force them both to reexamine everything they believe to be right and true.

Eiyuden Chronicles: Hundred Heroes is designed to bring players a modern take on a classic JRPG experience. Get ready to lead 100+ playable characters through a war-torn world only you can save.

name: Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising
detailed_description: CRIME BOSS Available Now! About the Game Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising combines a thrilling adventure through ancient ruins with the tale of one town’s rise from the ashes. Drawn by lenses and other treasures in the nearby Runebarrows, our heroes learn that the town is struggling to rebuild after an earthquake and decide to help. Along the way, they’ll resolve disputes between eager adventurers and wary locals who don’t think the Barrows should be disturbed. And they’ll learn more about each other’s reasons for seeking treasure, deepening their bonds in the process. As you will learn, these Runebarrows hide a great secret that has fateful implications for one of the characters. What begins as a simple treasure hunt turns into a dark conspiracy that will shake the world and plant seeds that carry over into the main story of Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes. The game will introduce a portion of Eiyuden Chronicle’s cast of characters in an original story with thrilling action and engaging town-upgrading elements. There will be some perks for players that link the game with Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes . *The name of one character from the Eiyuden Chronicle franchise has been changed from JB to CJ.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say this game is for everyone. The gameplay loop is a very repetitive, but sometimes I just really enjoy checking all the boxes and doing the "Go get me 3 of this resource" or "Go find this person who wandered into the Quarry". Going through cancer treatment, playing something with a predictable gameplay loop is just what I need. The great fast travel system makes it all way less annoying than it could have been. And watching the town expand as you help the townspeople rebuild and upgrade their stores is very satisfying. The combat is pretty basic and simple, but once you get your companions there are some cool (but still very simple) link attacks that just light up the screen and are a blast to trigger. The potentially annoying gameplay loop aside (it didn't get old for me until I was reaching the final mission at around 18 hours), the game looks incredible. I'm a sucker for the kind of beautiful 3D backgrounds in this game. They're full of detail (and I took A TON of screenshots). You visit all the usual biomes (forest, underground ruins, snowy mountain, lava field, etc.) over and over again, but I never got tired of it.So your mileage may vary. A few hours may be enough for you until the repetitive gameplay gets boring. But I thoroughly enjoyed my 18 hours with it (which included completing over 100 side quests for the town) was a loop that I really enjoyed.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as i would have liked to recommend this game, sadly i cannot do that, due to its many flaws and repetitiveness of the mechanics. Now, don't get me wrong, i love metroidvania and jrpg games and while being in anticipation for Eiyuden: Hundred Heroes sadly this one is in a league on its own. Even though it has nice backgrounds, good music and a feel of Suikoden with its town management and upgrade, the cons are outnumbering the pros in a big way. Skip to the bottom of the review for TL:DR. - The games boast about fast paced combat but with clanky mechanics, link attacks that hit the air instead of the enemy, hitting trees or ores, being stun locked by enemies or being hit repeatedly without even a single second to recover or to recuperate the battle is pretty much over before it has even started and even though i haven't seen the game over screen yet, all of the above lead to frustration instead of having fun while playing the game. If you are a fun of super Mario games then you are in heaven because enemies also damage you even if they touch you. - Another big problem is the grind in this game, where you have to revisit the same places again and again and again, uncovering a small percentage of the area every time -even for starting areas- in order to pass through blocked area for measly reward, which you could do without them, in order to progress the game in completely different areas way ahead in the story. Even the thousands of side quests will make you do repeated visits, which probably by the end of the game, you would remember every area by heart so much that you could navigate to them even being blindfolded. "Yes, that how metroidvania games work" you would say, but I'm talking about the same place, not places close to them, not places near them, but exactly the same areas again and again. You also need a huge number of resources and money to upgrade things in this game (and believe me there are many things to upgrade, from food, to farms, to tools, to weapons, armors, runes, stores etc etc) while the resources and money being scarce to say the least. You can probably do it if you farm for hours and hours on end. - The enemies in every area are just exactly the same (same bats, same trees, same minotaur etc.) in every single area, the exact same models but with different color and element attack variations. That's it. The only thing different is the bosses of the area and nothing more. They could have change that to give a different feel in each pap but probably even the creators were aware of the repetitiveness so they just copy/pasted the models and got over with it. - The story... Story... is pretty stale and shallow, with boring dialogues where character repeat the same things every now and again, and when you are about to follow a lead to actually see what is about to happen, you get locked behind blocked paths, many side-quest and revisiting the same previous areas again and again to search blindly for the missing link or item needed to –not progress the story- but to get a lead for the lead which will lead to the lead. Misleading. I wish the game had at least voice overs but I guess beggars can’t be choosers. Either way, I'll try to 100% game like every other Jrpg and metroidvania I played and maybe I will come back to update the review after. TL:DR: Clanky, grindy, repetitive and pretty much shallow story but with nice background and average music, sadly I cannot recommend this game at all. Thanks for reading and I hope I have helped even a handful of people.

_childDocuments_.review: So bad, that it's actually good! :DLet's set this straight - this is NOT a RPG/Action RPG/JRPG in any sense that you would be expecting of it. I mean - yeah, the game mechanics are there and you could probably try to nudge it towards "hey, you also could not influence the plot or char progression in classical SNES, JRPG! Besides, this one has active battle system, so yeah  - that's an Action JRPG!".Ok, ok. Let's assume that. Yet what this game really is when you give it a try is a massive grindfest with really primitive quest system and story development. You see, there's a town that you have to rebuild. Why? Constructing the blacksmith allows you to lvl up your weapon, Inn allows to cook/buy food to boost your stats and so on.What do you have to do to make it happen? Do quests, of course. By collecting certain amount of materials for each. Let's say you need 10 lumber - go to that place run through this room and get them. Put some amulets to increase drop rate. Done? Cool. Now go for 10 stones, another location.And that's basically all the game out there. But the paradox of it - it feels fun to grind. One of those competitionist type of games where you sit down and convince yourself that these three quests will be the last for today, finding later that you had to be in bed for couple of hours already. Yes, grindy, boring, bosses are joke, was there even a plot?, just three more times and were good - that type of game.Yet somehow magically it just keeps you going, hunting for those achievements/stamps and unlocking everything. Probably because the goals are clear and you understand that it's bearable. Also - movement system is quite nice. :)Won't recommend at full price, but at 75% discount - why not? Give it a try.
