_childDocuments_.review: I'm one of those guys that have Suikoden 2 as their best games of all time. So please bear with me if I get too sentimental or nostalgic while giving this review.So for me Eiyuden Chronicles: Rising is not a perfect game. It has it's flaws on some of it's controls and the sidequest/crafting/town building cycle is bare bones. There are times that it gets tiring to play, but what made me continue playing this game is the story. The world building elements is really good and you know that feeling that this game is made to build before the release of the main game. Did it succeed in doing so? I would say yes! I have a strong feeling that the main game is going to be a definite banger because it would not take time to explain a lot of things in its world because Rising already gave us a taste of what the lore is of the world. It introduced us to the concept of rune lenses, characters that would be vital in the story and much more. CJ, Garoo and Isha are some of my favorite characters in the story and I can imagine them being on my main party on my playthrough of the main game. They've succeeded in making me attached to them as well as other potential characters (well it's too obvious because of their portrait avatars). I'm definitely excited to have the Rising advantage when it comes to recruiting them :DThe HD-2D presentation is so good. It's vibrant and alive. You do not feel that you are playing in a lifeless world.The upgrading, crafting to purchase, swap chaining mechanics are really good. It's definitely a must play for suikoden fans if you want to squeeze every bit of lore from the game.I highly recommend it if you like metroidvania games with jrpg elements.I do not recommend this game if you do not like grinding and repetative side-questing.Oh and yes there is a hard mode of the game when you complete the game for the first time. _childDocuments_.review: Disclosure: I am a kickstarter backer and had no problems redeeming my code.I have been a Suikoden fan for a long time, and that's largely why I own this game. Honestly, I'm not sure if I would have even played this if it wasn't for that.Before I forget, I played the majority of the game on Steam Deck and it ran like a dream. The game ran at a consistent 60 frames per second with all settings set to maximum. There are occasional dips in a couple of areas.Once I got to the meat of the game, I had a really enjoyable experience. The script was quite light and easy going, the characters were all likeable, and the game was quite accessible for pick-up and play, which is ideal for me. The art style is lovely and although the game operates essentially as a 2D side scroller, it's beautiful and a delight for the eyes.The negatives would be the side quests. They're really lazy for the most part and 60% or so of the content here should be cut. But then again, the game would be wafer thin if they did that as the story is very light and more of an introduction to the world before 100 Heroes next year. The ending was abrupt and the final boss outside of the fight was a bit underwhelming.There really aren't many similarities to Suikoden aside from building up a community of rag tag losers who help with an armoury, runes etc. However, the rune powers and return of magic in this format have me excited for 1H.But all in all, it's one of the few games I bothered to 100% and I had a fun time throughout. It's not Suikoden - far from it

_childDocuments_.review: As a Steam Curator I must say: Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising presents itself with such ease, heartfelt, welcoming and light adventure that owns its charm completely. Suitable for both veterans who are fond of the genre and for newbies who never got involved with this project but are still curious to play it, in all its forms. The whole experience is centered around its tale, finally introducing Eiyuden's world for the first time and its gorgeous artistic direction and wonderfully written characters. The game offers an Action RPG style game that winks at the metroidvania genre, with very simple Town Building mechanics, which leans further in being a cozy relaxing game, where basically all its charms naturally lands. I was pleasantly surprised by the attention to detail: several times I stopped myself from going further to admire the beauty of the backgrounds and the strange but functional contrast between a cartoonish but semi-realistic environment and the Pixel Art of the characters. It is really engaging and one will feel easily hooked to it, wanting to play some more. The only downside aspect of it is that the Hard Mode is locked, forcing one to complete the game once to be able to play it, but there isn't really a reason to replay the game itself rather than the new difficulty. The community hopes it will be patched to be unlocked from the very first start of the game.Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising is a fantastic light hearted prequel that sets the base of a world that will become more serious and definitely of higher quality in its twin sequel project that goes by the name of Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes. Really excited to see where Eiyuden franchise and its world will evolve next![If you find my reviews interesting, follow me as a Steam Curator and join my group: I go by KureinInSight]

_childDocuments_.review: Eiyuden Rising is definitely an important introduction for Eiyuden: Hundred heroes to establish not only the lore, but the quality of product (even though it is developed by a partner studio) that the developers are aiming for this new IP - a spiritual sucessor for Murayama's Suikoden, which personally I don't have a lot of emotional investment since Suikoden is perhaps the most important game of all time for some people but this is my first "experience" with it. Even though Murayama is doing the Hundred Heroes game, he actually supervised this game and the whole scenario creation is his.At its core, Eiyuden Rising is actually pretty simple (gotta remind that this game was developed and released in pretty much a year): A very straightforward town building system based on NPC quests to gather resources, bring back to the town and finish the buildings to unlock more gameplay options. The gathering resources per say is a metroidvania dungeon crawling with a very tight combat system that is definitely inspired by some of the best side-scrolling JRPGs from the early 2000 like Valkyrie Profile - which actually made it more action based with its linking attack mechanics mapped at different buttons. And the simplicity aforementioned is not a bad thing at all, the game is consistent and very solid focusing on what it does best.One of the most amazing aspects of the game is it's art style, a blend of carefully animated 3D environments with very detailed pixel art characters is simply gorgeous. The game has a "feel good" direction reminding me once again of those great JRPGs from the 90's and early 2000.I have to mention once again that this is a companion game for the Eiyuden Hundred Heroes game developed in a year with a fair price tag for what it delivers, so content wise don't expect a full blown JRPG with 100+ hours, this is not the goal with this game, it is NOT a JRPG - and doesn't sell itself as one, but it delivers what it promised: A nice prequel introduction for Eiyuden Hundred Heroes in form of a more simple companion ARPG. Oh and the Soundtrack is absolutely lovely especially in the Quarry / The Forest.I have never experienced anything so bare-bones as this. In order to upgrade the village you have to gather materials and gather stamps in order to fullfill the townfolks requirements and do level up your houses and village overall. The System isn't changing much and nearly every quest is forgetable. I lost all interest in doing sidequests for stamps after my 100th stamp because it was so mediocreThe Writing is god-awful mediocre. The main Story is kinda neat but also nothing special and the sidequests are absolutely forgetable. The Writing could also come off of a high-school / student and I would've accepted it as: "Wow thats neat for a student" but I really hope they improve the writing in the main game + quests variety overall because if they don't I'll definitely downvote the main game if its as bad as this one.Don't get me wrong I really enjoyed my time in this Game but I can't force myself to 100% this game. I saw everything, unlocked hard mode and also discovered 100% of all the Dungeons / maps. Grinding for stamps / quests? No thanks. Don't see the appeal in doing so because its so mediocre in writing and variety. Main Game coming for 2023:

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay, very grindy and with tons of hollow repetitive side quests ( primarily of the go fetch or carry my letter variety ). The game is supposed to be an action side scrolling game, but fails hard on the action part. Combat is different - anytime you preform an action, there's a slight pause in the game ( like maybe a whole second or less )... meaning you can't change directions or perform a different action until that first combat action has done it's animation. So if you have multiple enemies on screen attacking your character from both sides... you are going to take damage no matter what. There's dodging, but like the action animations, there is a slight pause between dodge attempts, because the game has to finish animating each dodge action. You can't do multiple dodges in row fluidly without stuttering pauses in between. Some monsters are wider then the dodging animation action, so preforming multiple dodges is useless. You could switch characters to try and guard, but again there's that ever so slight pause in the game for it to do it's character switching animation. Then there's monsters... touching them hurts your character and their attacks as well. Monsters can overlap each other and don't suffer the same fate as you do when attacking in combat. They are free to fluidly attack in any direction as they please without pause or delay. As I'm playing this game I kept thinking that there's potential here, but it falls short on the action part of what it's supposed to be, and plays more like a grinding go fetch game. Your resource bag is small. You're constantly needing to go back to town to off load, and or you could throw everything away. But not have any materials needed for the various quests and necessary weapon upgrades. Kill, grind, fetch and repeat.Why is this game trying to slow and hamper my progress with silly game mechanics? Garoo has a bottemless magic bag and I kept thinking - why isn't this guy letting me use his bag to store all the goodies I pick up from each dungeon run?I got to a point in the game at the snowy ice peaks and I was being ejected from the current zone from a monster attack knock back damage animation. Every time I re-enter the zone I was booted from, the monster was back to full health. Monster was too big to jump over and too wide to dodge through without taking damage - again, if you get hurt there's a slight pause in the game for your character's damage animation to finish doing it's thing. I eventually got lucky and killed it. Then after that there's the boss fight with 2 wolves and white foxes falling from the sky. I was basically stunned locked the whole time until all 3 of my health bars got depleted to zero.Rage quit and write bad review time... lol. Almost 10 hours of silly side quests and grinding just to get stun locked because of weird combat mechanic in this game. I really hope the developer changes combat mechanics and make the game fighting feel more fluid. I hate leaving games unfinished in my library.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend the game with a big caveat: the game is worth your time *IF* you're excited about Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes and want to get to know the world and characters a bit more. I doubt there is much of interest here to anyone else.You might be looking for a casual, straightforward and easy game to play just to ward off boredom and sure, this game checks all those boxes. However, be warned that there is a lot—and I do mean a *LOT*—of fetch questing and backtracking. Even if you're used to this in other JRPGs, this game is really all about busywork. You'll be sent to fetch the same materials and trudge through the same handful of areas over and over and over again, and the majority of townspeople quests are literally just "Go talk to this person on another street, then run back to first area to report to questgiver". Best played in short bursts, like a mobile game.Positive aspects: the graphics are charming (especially the backgrounds), the music is nice, and there is a lot of heart in the characters and dialogue. One nice little detail is being allowed to name a few things like our weapons. It would be great if those names carried over into Hundred Heroes.I was initially excited when I heard this small side game was much longer than I anticipated. However, in this case less is more. The game could have easily cut -50% of its content and not been any worse for it. Fans of Suikoden may enjoy glimpses into the shared DNA found in Eiyuden's world and characters. If that's what you're looking for, it's a cute and harmless time-waster. Just be sure to keep your expectations in check.

_childDocuments_.review: OK, finally 100% it. Now my honest opinion: The game is fun if you like grinding. I think playing casually you might be able to get through if you avoid _some_ side quests, but you'll be missing out on some stuff. I had fun with the dialog between the characters as you do their quests, I had fun becoming stronger because I had resources to get better equipment, and I had fun becoming a bit too strong eating the food that gives permanent stats (never found the cap). I was definitely overlevel because money is short through the entire game (even when I was getting the last few I was always short on money), and my money grind spot was also a good exp grind spot.I see why some people wouldn't like the quests considering they're usually "go to x spot in y map and kill some enemy that'll drop that thing I need", though there's also some "bring me so much of so and so material" and you might already have enough to hand it in. I didn't super like the "go talk to this dude across the street" ones but at least the dialog was funny. There are some animations that slow down gameplay I wish I could speed up (quest complete! or when you view what you looted in the dungeon), but the combat got sooooo satisfying with the upgrades to the movement set.The elements were also a bit annoying because you need to go into a slightly slow menu to swap them out but it wasn't a deal breaker for me.Overall I had fun figuring out the enemies and the bosses. Would definitely recommend, I feel like I got my money's worth. I'd say the negative reviews aren't "wrong" but you might be more or less sensible to some of the "problems". I got my fill of side scrolling rpg goodness where I can level up, grind for better equipment and enjoy some characters. Oh, and also, the game looks beautiful in my personal opinion, but that's just a plus.

_childDocuments_.review: So this is one of those times I wish I could leave a neutral review rating rather than just Yea or Nay. I'm going to lay out what I liked and disliked and you can decide for yourself.Liked:- The artwork, especially the character designs are just delightful.- The party characters are well understood, their motivations and personalities come through nicely. I do think CJ (ostensibly the main character) is a little one-dimensional, but the other two are actually quite nice.- It's short. I'll get more in to this later.Disliked:- This is Fetch Quests - The Game. If you aren't interested in revisiting the same handful of areas over and over again to farm resources and complete just the most basic fetch quests in the universe, this is not going to be the game for you as that is like 80% of it.- Difficulty... this is easy as hell. I'm not one of those people who beats off to Souls-like difficulty, but this feels like the polar opposite of that. The bosses, while nice set pieces in their own right, are never any kind of threat. The normal monsters have one attack pattern that they just do over and over, so once you've seen it once, you're good.- Controls. I'm not even sure how to describe this exactly, but the game feels unresponsive when trying to execute the combat maneuvers it gives you. This really came up and punched me right in the face when I got the upward and downward attacks for CJ (happens fairly early on). The game has a very particular idea of how and when you should be pushing those buttons and it feels inconsistent and unresponsive. Since nothing is really a threat it isn't THAT big a deal, but it makes what combat there is feel somehow worse.Neutral:- The town building aspect. It's not bad per se, but it's also not particularly interesting. At no point are you ever making any decisions. If you just do all the side quests when they open up, the town just sort of builds itself and your input is largely meaningless. You have to build the town to get better weapons and armor, so you end up feeling kinda railroaded into this feature that's just kind of "meh."- The story. It's there, but by the middle-end of the game you kind of stop caring about it. They don't really give you any reason to get invested in the story or the characters beyond the little interactions between party members that are kind of fun to watch. And the side quest stories are just the blandest things you can imagine. I feel like the story here is trying to set up for Hundred Heroes and it does supply a little bit of background and world building, but it doesn't do it well and you end up not caring about it by the end.Personally, I'm walking away from this game unimpressed. I appreciate the groundwork they've tried to lay for Hundred Heroes, but I also feel like everything I'm doing is just to pad out the game so it's not like 4 hours long. I didn't care for the story presented here. I'm still looking forward to Hundred Heroes. I genuinely hope this game isn't an indication of the quality I should expect from that game.

_childDocuments_.review: + Art and design+ Town visually improve by your actions+/- Simple but enjoyable gameplay- Too Easy with no option of harder difficulty ( except in the endgame. )A good introduction into the Eiyuden universe before the main game. _childDocuments_.review: As a long time fan of the Suikoden RPGs, I've been a bit reserved on Eiyuden Chronicles, uncertain if the new art-style and game-play would really capture that nostalgia. _childDocuments_.review: A lighthearted prequel to . : If you’re more interested in a Suikoden-like game, that would be Hundred Heroes. Rising, on the other hand, is not too much like it, except visually. It sets up some characters’ backstories, mainly CJ, Garoo, and Isha, who all appear in Hundred Heroes. However, if you’re not interested in a lighthearted, quest-a-thon, action JRPG, you  skip the prequel and still understand Hundred Heroes perfectly well. CJ arrives at New Nevaeh as part of a Rite of Passage for her family of scavengers, as she seeks a treasure even greater than what her father found before her in the town’s quarry. Unfortunately, the town is in bad shape, and her conscience just won’t allow her to say “no” to the people’s plights.     • The Eiyuden Chronicle games are intended to be a spiritual successor to the Suikoden series.    • Despite the point of above, the battle system of Rising is nothing like the Suikoden series. (There’s a clip of the game’s battle system on the store page. There are probably plenty of videos on YouTube of Suikoden’s. Explaining in text the difference between the two would be lengthy.)    • There is no difficulty setting (except for post-game when “Hard Mode” becomes available for re-fighting bosses). However, from my perspective, the game is beginner-friendly. While the boss battles are a bit challenging, as long as the player knows when to dodge and when to strike, they should be able to get through them.     • A very quest-heavy game. Countless sidequests, along with the main quests. Sidequests are almost exclusively fetch quests (“go get this item for me” quests).     • There is a fishing mini-game. The player must hit a sequence of buttons without making a mistake. The timer is fairly generous, so most people should be able to do this without issue.     • Don’t know if there’s a more official name for this type of puzzle, but I’d call them “complete the line” puzzles. The player has to rotate tiles to complete a line for magic to flow from one point to another. I’m pretty bad at puzzles, but I found these to be quite easy, so people who like puzzles will probably think they’re not at all challenging enough.     • The game worked perfectly with my PS5 (DualSense) controller. I didn’t need to use mouse/keyboard whatsoever.     • Available in ten different languages with two variations of a language. Spain Spanish  Latin America Spanish? Well, isn’t that fancy.     • Good music. Definitely JRPG-style sound effects.     • Decent humor. The relationship between CJ and her reluctant spelunking partner Garoo is quite amusing; she wants to help everyone and he just wants to help himself.     • Lovely anime art. Character designs have been inspired by Suikoden.     • I really like the backgrounds to areas; some are pretty. There are even objects in the foreground to give it a more 3D feeling.     • There are three sidequests involving procuring a cat.    • Most sidequests are uninteresting, which makes doing a lot of them tedious and boring. My main motivation for doing them all was the Steam achievements and baqua (money).     • I wish there was a way to more easily avoid enemies, because a lot of the sidequests have the player revisiting areas with super weak enemies and they’re really just not worth the time.     • Platforming is frustrating at times. Getting the characters to jump just right seems flawed.     • Not a single dark-skinned character in the whole game. I know they’re trying to make it like Suikoden, but that’s one of the things they shouldn’t be striving for.     • Several achievements for Hard Mode, which makes 100%-ing the game less accessible to JRPG beginners. I definitely didn’t feel like fighting all the bosses again either.The story didn’t actually get all that interesting until toward the end, when more serious story plots and subplots are revealed. Overall, I feel mostly neutral about this game. It is just supposed to be an intro for the main game: Hundred Heroes, so I’m not taking it too seriously. I didn’t hate it, so it’s getting a positive review.

_childDocuments_.review: This was an unexpected find, and I heartily recommend it.If you are allergic to sidequests or reading, you may want to skip it.The game's focus is very apparent:  Simulate an entire town's population as you resurrect said town from the ashes.  It has a friendly tone and a leisurely pace.  This is the sort of game you can pick up for half an hour at a time without losing your place, since every objective is pretty straightforward.Preparation is the watch-word here.  If you are going out of your way to complete all the sidequests as they become available to you, you are going to demolish the standard (only) difficulty setting.  I can't fault the game for this; rebuilding the town is the initial stated goal of the game, and in that sense, the raw power of gear upgrades feels extremely validating and worthwhile.That said, I can see the criticism about locking the higher difficulty as post-game content.  At the same time though, all that switch really does is stack ~20 levels on every monster/boss.  This would render the player insta-dead from the slightest breeze without mid to end-game defenses, so the argument falls a bit flat.The visuals are beautiful and have a certain charm to them.  ARPGs of this style tend to be a visual mess in combat; by contrast this game's presentation is exceptionally clean and well ordered.  Very rare occasions in which I lost track of where my characters were.  Hit boxes were well proportioned; there is contact damage with enemies, but it happens so rarely, it's easily recognizable as player error.The music was pleasant.  Nothing especially notable that I can recall, but it does its job of generating atmosphere.The main characters were well written and enjoyable.  NPC dialogue starts off strong and never lets up.  Even post game has a surprising amount of writing effort to it.The story is a bit of a slow burn, but that's to be expected with the initial focus of helping to rebuild a town.  There are larger stories at work, both for the town and the neighboring regions.  I appreciated how even with foreshadowing, they still provided strong twists and turns in the plot.  It's strong foreshadowing for what they plan to do with Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes.I'm glad we're finally getting a spiritual successor to Suikoden, and this does a pretty good job of inviting people into that new world.  These devs have some big shoes to fill, but I'm excited to see what they can do.

_childDocuments_.review: I had such a great time playing Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising. Relatively simple combat (though not always easy), side-scrolling dungeon exploration, town improvement, and (sometimes grindy) questing/resource collection are paired with gorgeous HD-2D graphics and a lovable cast of characters. I frequently found myself admiring the vibrant colors and quality of the backgrounds in town and the movements of the character sprites, both during action and idle animations. I particularly loved Isha's floaty, ethereal style of walking and the way her blue braids swished around her when she moved.Story-wise, it's a feel-good tale of friendship, overcoming obstacles, and reconciling with the past. CJ, Garoo, and Isha became such a lovable trio to me. At one point, they put their hands together in a huddle as if to say, "GO, team!"—and I was cheering right along with them. CJ's unwavering optimism and sense of adventure, Garoo's gruff sarcasm that hides a big heart, and Isha's courteous, if abrupt, practicality made them all come to life so wonderfully. Even the NPCs in the town all had distinctly enjoyable personalities.To me, the combat was very unique. You start with only one playable character (CJ), but later have two and eventually three. Each party member has their own distinct weapon, movement style, and special skill. These weapons and skills also each have their own unique upgrade paths that unlock new and interesting ways of traversing the terrain and fighting enemies. Each character is controlled by a single button (e.g., X, Y, or B on a controller), which is used to switch to that character and also for attacking. The special skill button triggers the skill of the character that is currently active. These mechanics allowed me to strategize and experiment with different ways of approaching certain platforming challenges or exploiting enemy weaknesses. It was fantastic! I found the game to be quite addictive and powered through most of it during the course of a weekend. It was fun and straightforward to achieve 100% and I wholeheartedly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you can accept that this game is really just bonus content, an appetizer before the main course of Eiyuden Chronicles, then you may be able to adjust your expectations accordingly. However, on its own merits Eiyuden Chronicles Rising is an otherwise average 2D action RPG that is undermined by its overreliance on uninteresting, repetitive sidequests and resource gathering. It reminds me of the worst Ubisoft open world games, filled with busy work that inflates the playtime at the cost of making the player slog through boring drudgery to get to the interesting parts.In the long run, the reputation of this side project will likely rise or fall depending on how people come to feel about the main game. As things currently are however, there's very little here that makes this a game worth remembering or recommending. That is, unless you've really been pining for a game in which you can play a kangaroo with a big stupid anime sword. In that case, the game delivers in spades. GOTY.Not Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: So, to preface this- I was already invested in Eiyuden Chronicle going into this. The Suikoden series is my all-time favorite video game series, so when Murayama, Kawano and co. announced their spiritual successor, I was immediately on-board. This game is, to be clear, NOT that successor, but all the same, I wasn't going into this with a blank slate. I feel that's important to get out of the way before the review.First, it's probably a good call to clarify what this game IS. Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising is a companion game and prequel to the (as of the time of writing) upcoming JRPG Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes. This game is meant to be a little teaser of what's to come in terms of characters, setting and tone, while carrying with it an entirely different mode of gameplay. It is not reflective of the entirety of Hundred Heroes. It was made by a separate studio (Natsume Atari) on a small budget, with an intentionally limited scope.Even with all that said, I honestly didn't expect this to be as fun as it was. It's very, very simple metroidvania that's very much on the easy side, but there's a few more layers of complexity than I expected it to have. It never blew me away, but I was never bored, either. The gameplay starts out a little slow and clunky, but as you acquire various upgrades it becomes surprisingly intricate. No real complaints, I enjoyed it.The part that I (and most people like me, who are eagerly awaiting Hundred Heroes) was more interested in, though, was the characters. I'm very glad to say that I found the characters showcased in Rising to show a lot of the charm and uniqueness that the best Suikoden characters did. The plotline was nothing amazing, but I grew to really enjoy CJ, Garoo and Isha, as well as the supporting cast who'll be returning for Hundred Heroes like Hogan the crocodile-man and Squash the bird-man. With the limited scope and simple plotline still being able to put on a good showcase for these characters, I'm very much looking forward to what Murayama and the other writers on Hundred Heroes will be bringing to the table.All in all, for $15, this is a very enjoyable little experience. If you've any love for Suikoden and are interested in Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes, you should absolutely get this (you'll even be able to transfer your save game into Hundred Heroes to get some bonuses!). Even if you aren't, if you're in the market for some lite metroidvania fare, you could do a lot worse than this for $15.

_childDocuments_.review: The companion game for Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes, Rising was initially announced as a minigame collection where you could help rebuilding a town. What we got, instead, is a platformer RPG that follows the initial idea in spirit: Explore the world, complete villager requests, and the town will grow.Taking that into account, this game is, yes, more than what was expected by fans. There is a main plot, with good writing that we came to expect from the Suikoden team - even if the main scenario was actually written by Tadashi Satomi, and not Yoshitaka Murayama. The dialog is, most of times, of the humorous kind, and the characters - even the NPCs - have a lot of personality.The gameplay itself is pretty simple, with three possible characters that can be switched by the press of a button, each having their own unique skills for combat and exploration. There is a good variety of places to be explored, and a humongous amount of side-quests.Speaking of them, the side-quests may be the weakness of this game for many people - most of them are simple fetch quests or kill X enemies types of quests. However, most of those are actually pretty simple to complete, and many can be completed at the same time, on a single run. Personally, they never felt like too much for me.There are also some things that may cheapen the experience, like the character animations - 2D Skeleton based animations, that makes the game looks a bit cheap at times - but the art and backgrounds are, in general, great. The game also feels a bit too short - maybe padded by the subquests - but again, it was always supposed to be just something to show a bit of the world before the main game was released.Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising is a fun experience, that in my opinion is well worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: , formed by Yoshitaka Murayama and Junko Kawano, creators of the Suikoden series have given us a taste of what they are capable of with a surprise release of Eiyuden Chronicles Rising. And I can honestly say it is a solid modern classical JRPG that will appeal to old and new fans of the genre. With gorgeous 2.5D graphics, cute anime-style artwork, a fully-realized cast of characters and world-building as well as excellent soundtrack will give you a thoroughly enjoyable experience. The gameplay mechanics are interesting, where the bulk of it is based around a simple but addictive town-building and the combat mechanic is also a new spin of an old concept that works well enough but is wanting a bit more depth. It’s not perfect, but I’m guessing EC Rising was meant to be a buffer for the upcoming  which is the Rabbit & Bear Studios flagship product. For what it is, EC Rising is accomplishes what it set out to do, which is to entice you and give a positive expectation of what is to come. Recommended 8/10This game is a looker no doubt about it. If you’re familiar with the original Suikoden 1 and 2 on the Playstation, the art style of Eiyuden Chronicles is a modern interpretation of that and it looks stunning. CJ and Isha both look cute and dynamic, while I think Garoo could have used a bit more detail. Regardless though, the in-game animation and graphics is beautiful to look at with vibrant and lively background and foreground with parallax scrolling that gives you an immersive level of perspective and depth. The world of Eiyuden Chronicles is also effectively told, with interesting flora, fauna, people and politics. CJ is a great protagonist, tomboyish with a lot of heart and enthusiasm and Isha has a great backstory that serves as the backbone of the main plot. All in all, these 3 factors are the main drivers of the game that will keep you glued to the very end. The bulk of your gameplay consists of fetch quests. Over 100 fetch quest to be more accurate. These fetch quests tie-in directly to the town-building mechanic. Fortunately, these Fetch Quests aren’t long or inconvenient, in fact, they’re pretty simple and most of them are completed naturally as you progress through the main quests. This really respect your time and effort as you don’t need to needlessly grind for materials or levels to complete a certain quest. Moreover, you can visibly see your progress as being represented by the building of the town. Each time you complete a stamp card, the town gets upgraded and more stores and gears get unlocked. The game-loop of fetch quest and town building is a simple but effective game loop that lasts all 17 hours of gameplay. The combat is an interesting take on the old Castlevania 3 hero swap mechanic, where instead of swapping heroes with different abilites with the select button, you assign each member and their attack on a dedicated face-button. This leads to  where you can chain each members attacks immediately and without pause. You’re also able to chain each members unique skill which adds to more sophistication in platforming. While good enough for a simple game, I cannot help but feel that the combat and platforming mechanic was begging for more depth. There could’ve been a number of ways to push the link attacks and link skills to be more dynamic. As it stands, the mechanics are there and aren’t being utilized to it’s full potential. I do hope if there is a EC Rising 2, that these mechanics get flesh out.This is a great appetizer for what Rabbit & Bear Studios can achieve. If you like JRPG, these will definitely appeal to you. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising, it's a fairly simple game, 2D-action game that may not be for everyone.The combat is basic but a lot of fun, which is lucky because if you're going to be doing a lot of it. The quests are pretty much all fetch quests but if you enjoy the base gameplay loop that's okay.The game, however, is intriguing, especially if you're looking forward to the follow-up Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes. It sets up an interesting world for the sequel, introduces compelling characters and I found myself even more excited for Hundred Heroes after playing, than I was before (I was already very excited).If you're looking for a deep RPG with hundreds of hours of content; you're not going to find that here, you'll be better of waiting for the follow-up game.However, if you're looking for an easy to play fairly simple side-scrolling action-RPG that sets up an interesting world for the main game and is great for playing on Steam Deck, then I highly recommend checking out Eiyuden Chronicles: Rising.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really serves only one purpose:  A lead in to the main game. The gameplay itself is largely full of fetch quests and talk to people around town quests which is boring as hell as most of the characters you interact with don't have any real personality and only exist for the single quest outside of like the shop owner.  You mostly get rewarded with "Stamps" and a middling amount of experience, rarely do you get money for your quests or special materials.The characters are sadly rather poor, only Isha really stands out and the game is really about her despite how the game starts.  CJ's quest is just to get the biggerest treasure evar, and turns out to be a bust in the end, personality wise she's just a character who "wants to do the right thing" with little in the way of personality besides that.  Garoo is unfortunately lacking in backstory till the very end of the game, and even after learning it all it's very very basic and simplistic which really isn't a good send off.  The only one with a personality that can be described as compelling is Isha, who has a strongly defined character, she's just sadly held back by how bland CJ and Garoo are.The combat's really basic as well, you only have one main attack with each character and swap between them rather than having multiple different attacks for each character.  Largely you're going to use CJ and maybe occasionally Isha for her ability to hit things at distance.  Garoo, again, feels rather tacked on here lacking a strong defined role as his only notable ability is the ability to break physical shields more easily but those are few and far in between.  Besides for that, his damage is not any better than CJ's despite lacking a massive amount of mobility.  The fight with the Bandit Leader towards the end of the game was honestly harder than the final boss itself, which is also not a great thing to say about the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun side-scrolling RPG. The story is based around a team of three people exploring a place called the rune barrows for treasure, and each one of them has their own reasons for doing so. The game world is fairly small, with just 5 main areas. Make no mistake, it's grindy as hell, you have to keep clearing out the same areas over and over again to find crafting components and quest items, especially if you want to complete all the side quests (which are mainly fetch quests). Despite the grind it's a lot of fun. The art style is pretty and the music is nice. The fast travel system is great and you can move around the world easily. The story is okay, it's not that deep but the characters are fun and have some good dialogue, although there is no voice acting.The game is fairly easy, but you can unlock hard mode on completion, and can then play new game+.I recommend this game for a simple, relaxing and fairly short rpg experience.

_childDocuments_.review: After having 100%'d the game, here are my thoughts:- Story was enjoyable, even if the main character had a one-note syndrome- Gameplay was smooth, even if simple. Link attacks are great feel to use, too.- Isha felt a bit awkward to use at times, but she gets much better after some upgrades.- There were a ton of backtracking to be done, needing to go through the same places over and over again. It gets boring pretty fast given the little amount there is to actually explore- The game was too easy for a veteran metroidvania player- 16 hours for a metroidvania is... fair. I kind of would've wished for more post-game content though.I think this could be a good place to start for people enjoying the metroidvanias if they are not wanting to go to Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.  I kind of were wishing more from the game though at the end, since fetch quests get boring after a good while.Still, not a bad game at all. I can recommend it for a good 10-15 hour trip. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get the first, most obvious criticism out of the way: The opening fifteen minutes of the game will not give you a good impression of the writing or the combat. The first fight feels incredibly stiff, and afterwards you are dropped in a series of long, text-heavy cutscenes. This is *not* an accurate impression. I'll talk about the writing later, but as far as the combat goes, here's the issue: Once you unlock the full movesets of the characters, the combat feels *good*. Not Hollow Knight levels of good, but good enough that I was looking forward to fighting the same enemies over and over again. It's like if you took a character action game and squashed it into a 2D platformer: You have freeflowing combos, character switches, and a wide array of moves. You can juggle the bodies of enemies. You can cancel animations. All of it feels GREAT; I just wish it was available from the begining of the game.Now it's time for the other, more difficult elephant in the room: Fetch quests. This game is almost entirely fetch quests. A lot of people are not going to like that, and that's totally fair. I was very leery of the gameplay loop going in, and I don't blame anyone for being completely turned off by it. Here's the weird thing, though: I ended up enjoying it. The structure of Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising ends up feeling as relaxed as it's story, and I think that's actually a good thing. It's a game that you can pop in for an hour and just chill out with, getting thanked by townsfolk for finding lost cats and helping them build their houses. This repetitive structure mirrors the lives of our main characters, and I personally found it helped me fall in love with the town and the inhabitants. Do I think that there are way too many fetch quests? Absolutely, positively, one hundred percent yes. At the same time, though, I think the quests feel like an intentional design choice, and they help the game rather than hurting it.Here we go: The good stuff.The writing and localization absolutely shine in this game. It's a pretty standard fantasy tale, so don't expect anything revolutionary, but by God are these characters charming. CJ, Garoo, and Isha are an incredibly endearing group of protagonists, and it's very easy to get caught up cheering for them. CJ's optimism, Garoo's gruffness, and Isha's scheming makes the way the characters bounce of one another endlessly entertaining. I went from looking at the game with a critical eye to believing in our three leads, and genuinely hoping they would accomplish their goals.All of this is driven home by the final chapters of the story, in which town-building gives way to  This kind of writing is what makes me so hopeful about the upcoming Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes. Suikoden is a seres that is known for its player punches, and its willingness to showcase the horrors of war through the eyes of children in a colorful fantasy world. Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising demonstrates this same inclination, and that more than anything else makes me excited. This feels like Suikoden, but written 20 years later, by people who are not under horrific levels of crunch and are not bound by character limits.Does Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising have an overreliance on fetch quests? Almost certainly. Does it give a very bad first impression? Definitely. But it has heart, and that's what makes the difference. This isn't a soulless mobile game or a blatant cash grab, it's an introduction to the world of Eiyuden, created by people who very clearly care about what they are doing. If you're in the mood for a relaxing fantasy jaunt, or are a big Suikoden fan in general, I recommend it. See you in a year when Hundred Heroes comes out, friends.Also, this game has a grumpy kangaroo uncle with a greatsword and a magic pouch. Why are you even reading this review? Just buy it already.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm extremely excited for the main Eiyuden Chronicles, but honestly I wasn't expecting much from this. I'm excited to say I was wrong! _childDocuments_.review: Embracing 2D HD visuals, Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising is a Metroidvania-lite and meant to serve as appetizer for developer's upcoming JRPG. Step into the shoes of our intrepid trio lead by a noble Scavanger CJ as they embark to not only find the Giant Lense, treasure above all treasures, but also restore a troubled village of New Nevaeh along the way. Restore? Well, as you repeatedly go to same few dungeons over and over again people will also open up shops in the village, and CJ is there to facilitate. Side action combat with one attack button per-character, basic statistics alterable by upgradeable gear and Rune Lenses to spice up your attacks elementally form the basics of a game that well overstays its welcome due to numerous side missions. Still, I can't say I disliked it.We step into the shoes of the intrepid Scavenger CJ embarking on a quest from her home town with a simple goal in mind – don't return until you've found a treasure more impressive than the one your father brought home. So CJ comes to New Nevaeh, village with a peculiar situation where locals are allowing adventurers, mercenaries, and the like to take their chances with dangerous nearby locales like the Great Forest... as long as they pay for the license and taxes, as enforced by Acting Major Isha. It doesn't take long for our heroine to realize she doesn't have the money to outright buy the license so she settles for a stamp system where every assistance to locals means she's one step closer to getting approved. Along the way she comes across beastfolk called Garoo as they go after mysterious rumors of a Giant Lens, more potent version of a device letting people cast magic. Perhaps there is more to discover in this waylaid village, though.I'll cut the usual preamble short and outright tell you story isn't Rising's strong suit. Yes, it eventually goes beyond just a treasure hunt as personal stakes get involved, certain developments hint at a bigger picture involving the League of Nations and their rival Galdean Empire, but I think where the most personality stems from are characters. It's kinda jarring to see couple of definitive sideshows or glorified shopkeeps get a dedicated “whoa, this character matters” info screen, but you have to keep in mind this is laying down the groundwork for the upcoming Hundred Heroes set to be a JRPG taking after its spiritual predecessor – Suikoden.Even though you don't unlock all three characters at once I'd say it's not really a spoiler since they're plastered over promo art. CJ is your GOTTA GO FAST Scavenger with an easy going personality primarily driven by need to find treasure and willingness to help with people's small problems out of pure goodness. In comparison our mercenary Garoo is probably the most complex one as he slowly reveals there's more to him than “gruff merc barely tolerating everyone's nonsense” given it's him of all people who diffuses tense situations. And lastly, Isha. Acting Major of the village capable of casting magic without a Lens, making her an oddity, she goes from being an aloof bureaucratic obstacle to discovering her own past and working for the benefit of New Nevaeh even as it sometimes puts her at odds with village elders.Beyond those three playable characters there's also named villagers, some with portraits marking them as important, who bring their own antics to play as you interact with their missions. I'll get into those below, but as far as fluff goes it was nice to see most of these background characters get some semblance of personality and even tiny stories of their own. Like the on-going gambling matter between two characters, or an old geezer constantly challenging CJ to see who can catch higher quality fish, etc. It's the small touches that make the game come to life provided you care about such things.Like I hinted at in the opening this is an action adventure game with some rudimentary platforming. There are no special abilities to buy in traditional sense, though. Our trio's advancement primarily comes from upgrading gear, conferring both statistical upgrades and few ability-equivalents like longer float time, double jump, improved dashing, etc. Why I'd say there's only traces of Metroidvania design here is because those abilities aren't really vital for progression. In fact, your way is barred only by obstacles in the form of elemental pillars cordoning sections of levels until you've found the appropriate Rune and slotted it to proceed forward. Naturally, this is mandated by the plot as you trek to five distinct locales in linear fashion. And believe me, you will be revisiting them often from the central hub of New Nevaeh.CJ, Garoo and Isha each bring their own style of gameplay; fast-attacker, heavy tank and spellcaster, thus covering all the archetype bases. In practice you only need Garoo to bust some rock walls... and parry.. and deflect projectiles back at enemies. I'm sure you'll find your own favorite, but CJ's mad criticals as she hits enemies with her pickaxes are hard to dislike. Isha is your ranged attacker with charged ability AND projectiles changing type depending on slotted Rune. Rising adheres to an interesting control scheme where each character is keyed to one button effectively making switching between a breeze. On the flip-side there's little nuance here to speak of beyond switching characters mid-attack for a combo chain. DMC this is not.Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising is Chores: the Game. I refuse to call them quests or missions because, in the attempt to get those aforementioned stamps, villagers will send you on your merry way to do their bidding. In most cases this means revising the same locations over and over and over again to gather resources or kill something. Just to give you context for my complaining: keeping in mind some main scenario objectives will also net you a stamp, there's a total of 160 stamps to get your hands on. Let me just say you'll be praying for the uninspired “character X wants you to talk to character Y” because at least that won't take you to the Great Forest for the hundredth time. I'm not even taking into account all the post-game chores game showers you with because you clearly wanted more recycled content.In essence the real issue is that Rising is simply too long for how little [unique] content it has to offer. Looking at my total playtime having finished the game, completed the adventurer's card with all the stamps, and beaten the bosses on hard mode, I'd say probably good five hours could be shaved off if devs chose depth over breadth. However, they couldn't because there's a village development aspect at work aka various shopkeepers open up stores and have missions taking you out into the world to expand those stores, hence offering improved stock. It's a cycle that makes sense in a vacuum, but not in an inherently short title like Rising should be. Did we really need a dedicated store to get new mining/fishing/hunting tools, or a store that just sells better backpacks to increase your carry capacity when dungeon delving, or an Inn that lets you take a bath for stat bonuses? That's really up to you, but I have a feeling this was also a test run for Hundred Heroes like some other features in the game.Lets end this with a production overview. Which is good because we're looking at another 2D HD project subscribing to an art style that's become all the rage recently. Combining 2D character sprites with 3D levels. I don't mind it as Rising doesn't revel in its pixels, but rather has pretty spruced up sprites and background assets edging more into PS2 era of geometry. If you ask me it looks better in motion with snow levels in particular being standouts. Due to how the game re-uses areas you'll sadly be subjected to same few tracks constantly further hampering an already limited soundtrack. Notable tunes end up being used almost too sparingly for my taste.

_childDocuments_.review: The ugly: Side quests are extremely tedious and maxing out your equipment is even more tedious. Most of the side quests are dull and boring, which is unfortunate because you need to progress through a lot of them if you want decent equipment. Some of the animations are disgustingly bad, especially on the main character. You legit look like the QWOP guy while you're running. The game is a cakewalk, I haven't died once and I'm close to 100%ing the game. I would have played on a higher difficulty, but I wasn't given that option until after I had beaten the game. I'm keeping the game on hard mode now while I level up my characters and the difficulty increase is noticeable, but I've been button-mashing and haven't died yet so I guess it isn't that much more difficult.The good: The characters are interesting and unique, their designs are cool and give me Suikoden vibes. The artwork is stunning and beautiful, I really adore it. I like the upgrading system, it reminded me of alchemy in the Atelier games. _childDocuments_.review: Full context - I'm a huge Suikoden fan, and backed the full game on Kickstarter, getting this game as a (cheaper) addon.That said, I highly anticipated this game, even as a side-scrolling spinoff.PROSThe platforming and combat is...fine. Nothing to write home about, and gets better as you get the 3 different characters, and upgrade their weapons and armour.The character designs are pretty nice, and the backgrounds are close to gorgeousCONSThe story is pretty bland and generic. Treasure hunter discovers her real treasure was the friends she found along the way. This is also the same lesson that the other 2 characters learn. That's it.Some plot points are introduced within 30 minutes of the ending that serve either as plot twists that IMMEDIATELY get resolved, or as set up for the Real Eiyuden Chronicles game (Evil empire names, etc.)The gameplay loop is so tedious:The main questline is Forest, Mine, Magic Mine, Ice Cliffs, Same Magic Mine, Volcano, Same Magic Mine, Final Boss, doing the same thing over and overThe sidequests are the main bulk of the game. There are 3 flavours: - Talk to someone else in town, and then talk to me again (maybe with multiple people to talk to) - Gather X amount of some item(s), or just talk to me again if you already have the items - "Find this item", aka go to a dungeon, fight an enemy that drops the item, or walk past an enemy maybe to pick up a sparkleEven as I slogged through this game, trying my hardest to have fun, I thought "Oh well, maybe it's an easy game to 100% the achievements on". Frankly, it is. But after the credits rolled, and I got ready for the post game, I realised I didn't WANT to finish grinding a character to level 50 (I finished with all the quests up to that point complete, at level 36). I didn't want to refight the bosses at a higher level, buy all the weapon and armour upgrades, the accessories, etc. and I certainly didn't want to do the remaining post-game sidequests.CONCLUSIONA disappointment, maybe give it a go if it's super cheap, for a short game, but I recommend blitzing through and ignoring the sidequests unless you really want to do them for shop upgrades, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite my initial impressions Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising is an enjoyable game to play, even if bogged down a little bit.Combat is a core pillar of the experience and, despite my initial impressions, has a good amount of options that kept me engaged from beginning to end. Assists add a lot to fighting some of the tougher enemies, especially with the new attack moves acquired with upgrades, and are satisfying to utilize for big combos.Story is nothing that will "wow" you but establishes a world that will no doubt be much more fleshed out in Hundred Heroes. Most of my enjoyment from the story came from the character writing which was spot on and had a nice amount of charm.My biggest gripe with the game is the abundance of side missions that bog the game's pacing down in the early game stages, as well as in the later parts of the story when you need more money and materials to upgrade your weapons/armor.I personally found the game, while having some merit, is not something I want to necessarily play again or even go back to for the sake of 100% completion.As a whole, Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising is not a bad, mediocre, or even great game, in the end I found it to just be good.

_childDocuments_.review: How do I start with this? First of all, if you are a fan of Yoshitaka Murayama's work on Suikoden, then this game is right up your alley.Since this game is a collaboration between Natsume Atari and a small Rabbit & Bear Studios team, don't expect much. Especially this game got announced a few months after Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes' Kickstarter.===========================================This game is right up on my alley since it's a straightforward action RPG that RNG doesn't exist. There's some grinding right here and there, but the RNG doesn't punish you for grinding countless hours to get a rare material. Funny enough, some accessories can boost your luck chance of dropping some rare materials.I love and hate the "Stamp" feature of this game. I love this feature because it makes you revisit some places you have already explored. However, I wouldn't say I like it since you need to complete those Stamps for more powerful weapons, armor,  accessories, etc. Also, I'm not too fond of the repetitiveness of this feature. This feature is also troubling, especially if you are an achievement hunter. My tips for "Stamp":- Collect all of the quests first until you exhaust all of them.- Sort them based on where they are. If it's on the first area, do it on one run.- Rinse and repeat.The next one is the story, and I must say that I skipped almost all of the story on this game. I will blame those things on the developers since they added the "Skip" button on the side quests and main missions. I can understand if that button is only on side quests; what if it's on main tasks? You can blame me if I use it to skip all of the important stories. I'm not saying that the story is boring, but it's their mistake to add that into the main missions. I hear from my friends that are still playing this game that the story is fascinating and endearing but that the "Skip" button is a letdown for me. I  recommend the developers erase that on main missions and stick the "Skip" button just for side quests.The next one is the gameplay. I must say that I like the gameplay since it's addicting to see those excellent combos for thousand times. But, I must commend the Normal option of this game. In the "Normal" option, especially on the controller, you need to press a specific button to use that character. It's pretty okay in the first half of the game, but the end game? I must skip those. I prefer their "Simple" option even though the changing character will be automatic. If the developer sees my review, I suggest you change those "Normal" options and make the button more accessible to access. I mean, L1 and L2 buttons don't get used at all. Or maybe add a key bind feature?Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising's performance is very optimized for an action RPG game. No dipping FPS whenever I make combo moves with lots of monsters.Boss monster is too easy, and the mechanics are too simple. I play it on "Hard" difficulty after completing the "Normal" one, and I can still close my eyes while spamming the attack button on bosses.=================================================That's all of my complaints, but where's the good thing?Since it's a bias that I like Murayama's work on Suikoden, I find all of those problems are a lesson for his team to make better games. Do I like Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising? Yes, I do, but I need to point out those problems for people to get the real expectations. I like RPG/JRPG games with grinding on them, but this one is still easier than most, and I recommend you try it. Do you like collecting things?Do you like maxing out everything after grinding countless hours?Do you like interesting stories, especially if this one is a prequel? Do you want to spend 24 hours grinding on this game?If you can answer those, then I suggest you buy this game. I already spent 24 hours completing this game down to tea, even with those "hard" achievements that look impossible to get. You can find the proof by visiting my Steam profile.I will rate this game 85/100. It's not perfect, but it's still good. I understand why the game reviewers give this game low scores since I'm a journalist working in the same industry. But it's rather sad if they only played it for 6 hours since the actual content unlocks after 10 hours. I'm still excited to see Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes in 2023. I hope they don't delay it.

_childDocuments_.review: Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising is a pretty fun and satisfying sidescrolling 2.5D Action RPG. You play as treasure hunter CJ and companions Garoo and Isha on the search for a lens that CJ can take back home to prove herself worthy to her family. Using a town as a central base, you venture out into a few different locations, slay enemies in active combat, get materials and use it to complete quests that upgrade the town's facilities further.It's a pretty engaging gameplay loop overall, and the game isn't too long. It only gets a bit grindy if you want all achievements, which takes about 15 hours or so. The game definitely doesn't overstay its welcome. Combat is pretty simple, with each button corresponding to a characters attacks. There are a few special abilities, like dodging or charge up attacks, and later on you can equip runelenses to grant offensive and defensive elements to your characters. It's a pretty simple system and I feel there could have been done more with it, as overall the impact of the runes is negligible. The game is definitely on the easier side until you finish the main story, which unlocks a hard mode; but even that just raises the levels of enemies and makes boss patterns a bit different. The game never gets super hard, but it doesn't need to be.Overall, Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising is definitely an engaging game and worth the time. It's got a good soundtrack, a nice artstyle, some metroidvania-like progression elements and has the "one more quest" feeling. I exclusively played it on the deck and it plays fantastically there on max graphics if you lock the fps to 40 or 45, or 60 if you lower them some. My only negative is that the game could have been a bit "more" overall: combat is a bit simplistic, the element system is negligible and it gets a bit repetitive after a while, but since it isn't too long, that's just fine. I hope that the sequel will flesh out the combat and accompanying systems slightly more, but even so, this is a great game worth your time and money, and an absolute steal even at full price. Looking forward to Hundred Heroes!

_childDocuments_.review: Good game! A bit on the short side, with very little difficulty to speak of as the game gives you a lot of tools to get strong fast. You can 100% this game in 10 to 20 hours depending on your dedication.One major gripe is the backtracking. Though you would expect some backtracking in a Castlevania-style game, this game handles it pretty poorly, as there are only 4 different levels with about a dozen rooms each, and you'll be revisiting them all upwards of 10 times for fetch quests. You can save yourself time and headaches by making sure to select sidequests in the quest menu to see where they are on the map, at least.The way the world gates parts of its stages off is also very bland. Rather than pick up exploration powers, at X Y Z moment in the story you are basically given a new colored keycard that lets you bypass colored obstacles. Don't come in here expecting to sequence break or to do clever parkour tricks, the story will tell you exactly when you can go past the colored doors.The game also LOVES enemies that either stun you for 2-3 seconds, lock you in a damage loop, or inflict status effects that stun you for 2-3 seconds or otherwise cripple you, like disabling character switching. By the time you reach the end of the game you will be sick of those. First two stages aren't too bad about it but the last couple are awful.Those complaints aside, still an excellent game. Easily a 7.5/10. Visually very pretty with good character designs.

More importantly, this game serves as an appetizer for Eiyuden Chronicles: Hundred Heroes, a full JRPG experience coming out in 2023 (hopefully) and spiritual successor to the Suikoden series. Buy Rising to support its development and hopefully this franchise will become a long running series!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to give Eiyuden Chronicles: Rising a temporary positive review until "Hundred Heroes" releases and I have a moment to dig into that (the true game) and find out how "Rising" affects it.So, I'm the type that played through the entire Suikogaiden series (Suikoden), beginning in the mid-1990s with the original title on PS1. I even suffered through Suikoden: Tactics and Suikoden: Tierkreis. Not having enough of the franchise or the formula, I also chewed my way through "Exit Fate" (it's excellent, check it out). So, when I heard of the Kickstarter that was going to be another one "those" spiritual successors with one or some of the original auteurs/leads/staff, I was on board!"Rising" sort of reminds me of what Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes was pejoratively labeled after it's release: a $40 demo (though Rising is only fifteen bucks). This title feels, looks, and plays like *another* Unity-gussied, quasi-mobile trash port being hawked on every platform. It's essentially one very large drawn-out series of fetch quests to collect stamps and inadvertently complete a town full of motley interlopers.I give this title a (tentative) positive review because, if you're like myself and have seriously been yearning for more Suikoden due to Konami being utterly worthless, then you can see as you play all of the cameos and potential tangential, self-referential nods to the greater gestalt. You can clearly walk past character sprites that are obviously not Bob or Sally the NPCs, but are (yet) named and portraited characters. *Some* characters obviously do make an appearance to a variety of magnitudes. All of this is tantalizingly agitating because you know it *has to* have some kind of profound tie-in to "Hundred Hearoes."Nevertheless, we'll see. This could be pure bait 'n' switch pandering for folks like myself. Until Hundred Heroes releases, this review hinges on how Rising alters it. Just saying, it better not be some trivial bullshiite like when porting Suikoden 2 to Suikoden 3 was. Fingers crossed.

_childDocuments_.review: No chance of changing my mind. I would never recommend it to anyone. The game doesn't deserve your time, guys, and has HUGE problems.First and foremost is the quest system. The cancer mechanics here. About 200 quests if you want to finish the game and get all the upgrades. And you can ask, is that wrong? Probably it could be great to have so many missions in the game. It could be, but not the way it is done here. Most of them are like "go find 10 twigs or 5 rocks", "go tell him I want to talk to him and go back and tell me what he told you". You have to do about 200 laps (or more) around the town before you complete all your tasks. There was a moment when I had a task to talk to Lugo from a civilian, and after completing it I got a new task to talk to Lugo from another civilian. And speaking of rewards, I get a stamp in a stamp card every time. Have you brought the mayor's daughter's clothes back from the laundry? Get a stamp. Fed the cat? Take another stamp. Saved the town? Take a stamp! STAMP! STAMP again and again.And the character has no motivation to do it. Funny thing is, according to the story at the beginning, it was a necessity. And CJ (our protagonist) didn't want to do it. After the 10th stamp, the story went in a direction where we didn't have to fill in the stamp card at all. But CJ was unstoppable. She was hooked, addicted. Don't do drugs, kids. Drugs are bad!Grind. Here you have to replay the same dungeons over and over again. Because of the rocks and twigs, because of the endless quests, because of the limited inventory you have, and because of the sick fetus of the Metroidvania element.The pacing is terrible. It's as if the game couldn't decide whether it wanted to be a 2.5D action platformer or a visual novel. Tons of useless and boring lines made me tired extremely fast. Especially the side quests. Even the ChatGPT AI could do better with dialogue. We can spend 20 minutes adventuring in dungeons and the same amount of time talking to someone. After each completed quest, you'll see a token with your reward, then a token about completing that quest, and an achievement animation. Sometimes this may be accompanied by a level-up message. Each pop up is about 2-3 seconds long one after the other as you complete your mission. Every ~200 missions. And it is so annoying.In summary, the game with the name that I always forget doesn't deserve your attention. It's got a lot of problems and nothing to make you love it. A waste of time.P.s. You can find all my short reviews .

_childDocuments_.review: I will allow that this game is good, if you're the type who loves to run errands in an RPG.The game serves as a prelude to the newer and much more ambitious Eiyuden Chronicles : Hundred Heroes. Many of the heroes in the new game appear in this, however only 3 of them are playable characters, and the story is a much more contained and small-scaled narrative about rebuilding a small destitute village into a booming adventuring town, and uncovering the mysteries of its ancient past. Unlike Hundred Heroes which is a turn-based spiritual succesor to the Suikoden games, this game is a side-scrolling action RPG where you eventually get to juggle 3 characters archtypes : Fast melee speedster who can dodge and abuse i-frames, Big Tanky Heavy who hits hard and can parry, and a mage who can abuse the power of ranged attacks and modify her attack patterns by equipping various elemental lenses, and also teleport and hover, which is neat. The game encourages you to switch between these 3 characters regularly via a "link in" system where upon delivering a successful hit, one can activate the attack button of another character to switch character, dash to the last hit enemy, slow down time and execute a powerful blow. These linked attacks can be chained up to a degree that increase as you reach milestones in town development (and by the end of the game, you can acquire an artefact that allows you to chain those suckers infinitely, as long as you can keep hitting enemies in a chain) which will make most fights a rather trivial affair.I should warn you however, the game has a very slow start. Initially you have access to a single character with a lackluster set of moves. As you go through the motions of the intro sequence, the building of modest shops, and the introduction of the major characters and narrative, you will eventually unlock all three characters and upgrade their moves to a point where the game's combat finally begins to shine. This took me 4-5 hours. No joke. It took 4-5 hours of a roughly 25 hours playthrough before I got to actually enjoy the core pillar of this game known as combat. I am not going to defend this decision by the developers to limit what you can do in battle for such a ridiculous length of time. It is a drag, but it does get good when you finally get the mage character to join and have at least a couple major upgrades done on each character's defense and offense capabilities.The journey to get there however, will involve a lot of side quests. To upgrade the town and unlock more features and make progress both mechanically and story-wise, the game regularly unleashes a bunch of fetch quests at you, which involve talking to people, gathering materials in the world, or killing a specific pack of monsters to retrieve a specific quest drop. There's over 160 of these in total for those who want to fully upgrade the town and acquire the most powerful artefacts in the game, and YET MORE await you in the post game if you haven't had enough.That sounds like a lot, and it is, but once you know what you're doing and have unlocked all the fast travel points, you can cruise through these quests rather quickly. Consider the fact I have completed over 180 of these quests in just over 25 hours of total play time which included completing the 31 much more elaborate main quests, grinding all achievements of the post game, and even did a bit of free roaming in between it all, and I'd say in hindsight it's less daunting than I initially imagined.Speaking of the Main Quest Line, this is where the game shines. It's a simple story, but told well, with a few twists and turns. It begins with a rather cozy vibe, but slowly escalates the stakes, and by the end does not pull its punches, and it does an excellent job at building anticipation for the next title, Hundred Heroes. The main trio has good chemistry, the support characters are memorable, and the village of New Nevaeh itself could be considered a well fleshed-out character. They've put a decent amount of effort into showing through subtle background scenes and interaction with common villagers the transition and growth from a decrepit backwater into a neat and prosperous little town you'd love to live in.The music is neat too, I dig it. The pixel art style is lovely yet modern.Overall I'd say the game was more than worth the 7 bucks it cost me, and I am pumped to dive into Hundred Heroes next. I give it a 7/10, -2 points for those sluggish first few hours, and another point deducted for cramming way more fetch quests in there than was entirely necessary. Can't wait to see what CJ, Garoo, and Isha and all the rest of the Hundred will get up to!

_childDocuments_.review: From the moment I saw the game, I was excited by the potential. Something akin to Steamworld Dig, with a town-building aspect and way more upgradeables. Surely a recipe for success. Well, I got  of what I'd been hoping for. I can't quite call it a "bad game," but I can't really recommend it either.Pretty much immediately, it felt like everything was drawn out. The town does indeed get built and upgraded because of your character's actions... But it's all incidental to your questing. Town residents ask for crap, you bring it to them, and occasionally construction happens. There's no sense of agency, accomplishment or satisfaction.What's left is the presumably "fun" part. And the dungeon-crawling and combat was indeed more-or-less what I expected. The problem is there's so little of it, both in terms of space-- when viewed as a whole, the four "maps" provided really aren't that large-- and in terms of time-- as the town's annoying messenger quests keep you away far more than they ever should have.With that, the note I would end on is that the game could've been good, and indeed still could be made good, but it's focus at the moment is the completely wrong direction.

_childDocuments_.review: I've recently noticed that, with so many games available with even games from over ten years ago running decently well on current hardware, we're really spoiled for choice.  It becomes easy to have no attention span when you've gotten a bunch of games in a bundle.  Many games I end up reviewing in the hopes that other people will enjoy them don't actually get a huge amount of playtime...  And then there's this gameThe difficulty is rather easy, and I tend to suck at real-time, non turn based style of games.  For many, this might be a dealbreaker, and, to make things less appealing, the soundtrack is rather mediocre.  But this game has *nailed* atmosphere, vibe, the sense of wonder that truly good games provide!Each character has a specific moveset.  You really get the feeling that while they might survive if they were on their own, they work well as a team and complement each other's strengths and weaknesses.  I love that about various games with varied rosters: no character feels like dead weight.  The resource management is still not that annoying, though I'm one of those weirdos who loved Koudelka, a 20+ year old game where weapons broke and you could only get supplies through enemy drops and finding them, so I might be biased :PThere are other nuances to this game like combo attacks, slightly varied elemental loadouts, a horde of sidequests that distinctly reminded me of running errands for people as a member of the Bracer Guild in Trails in the Sky, but it was a really enjoyable experience.  I suspect this game will be a lot shorter than Trails in the Sky too, so if doing too many sidequests gets annoying you might prefer this game.  You'll also notice the town slowly grow because of your efforts!So in the end, there are a lot of games you could spend your time on.  Eiyuden Chronicle's gameplay is a bit too easy for people used to more challenging platformers, but it excels in the secondary factors like narrative, like character interaction and dialogue, like establishing a world and the people in it that might tug at the heartstrings of the sort of people who like story based games.  You should give this a tryEdit: Finished my first playthrough.  I honestly don't want to grind for achievements, ironically because the game is easy and I'd rather spend my time on other games.  But if you want a relatively smooth 100% completionist experience, go for it.  It's a good game for narrative and worldbuilding, probably what it was intended to do.  As a platformer there are many others who are more challenging.  The genre is probably known for grinding out upgrades, needed materials from enemy drops etc. so this game is just like the others in that way
