_childDocuments_.review: As a major fan of the Suikoden series, I just had to play this game, and I wasn't disappointed. This is a love letter to the series and a great intro into what the full game will have to offer. A lot of the things that made Suikoden what it was is trickled throughout the gameplay. There's still town building, although I do miss getting to decorate things like the bath house. The story plays out with the same type of formula. Runes are very different, now adding to your physical attacks and defense. The graphics and environments are gorgeous. The battle system is a bit simplistic, but being the spiritual successor to Suikoden, the full game will have MANY more characters to play around with so I imagine the fights will have much more to offer that way. There was much more to the game than I expected for $15. 5 types of dungeons, 3 playable characters, and 132 quests. My only real complaint is with Ishas targeting. It's very hit or miss. Sometimes I would stand directly in front of an enemy and her bolts would go right past them, hitting nothing. This could get frustrating when dealing with the mini boss battles. Over all Im very happy with this intro into the Eiyuden Chronicles. Well worth the money, and left me feeling excited for the full game release.

_childDocuments_.review: As a backer of Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes (the larger JRPG this game is a prequel to) and a longtime fan of Suikoden (the classic game of which Hundred Heroes is a spiritual successor made by the same creator), I had fairly low expectations for this game. Since it is not made by the same studio as Hundred Heroes, and does not have the same turn-based gameplay, I was expecting it just to be a fun time-waster, but also a proof-of-concept for the Eiyuden setting. Would the visuals, music, dialogue, and characters live up to the legacy set by Suikoden, demonstrating that the full game has the potential to capture the magic of Suikoden? My answer to that question is certainly yes. But this game has also demonstrated to be extremely enjoyable in its own right, occupying most of my free time as I approach 100% completion. This is a game for those who enjoy grinding, and I use that term lovingly. The game makes no bones about this: even the characters themselves reference how much of your time is spent completing errands. When executed well, grinding can be an enjoyable and relaxing experience. In this game, you will revisit the same areas, completing lots of side quests, gathering materials, running back and forth across town to talk to people, and fighting the same monsters and even the same bosses multiple times. For this to work, the world has to be an enjoyable place to be. The town that you improve and assist with your quests needs to be pleasant, and the people have to be interesting. The combat and movement have to be fast, fluid, and satisfying. And all of these are true.The setting is extremely reminiscent of Suikoden, both in appearance and in the cast of characters who are colorful, but typically not over-the-top. The world is gorgeous, with decent sprites for characters and breathtaking backgrounds. The music is good, and certainly gives vibes of Suikoden 2. Dialog is energetic without being cartoonish, and addresses serious topics in mature ways without seeming out-of-place or preachy. The main characters are likable and play off each other well. And you are given just enough hints about the broader story to be interested in how it will be expanded in Hundred Heroes, without feeling like you are only being given part of the story. The story of this game is straightforward and interesting enough, and tells a complete tale even if you don’t plan to continue to the larger game. My expectation was to enjoy the story and endure the combat, playing the game off and on until I was finished or got bored. At first, the movement felt slow (you have a dash but cannot use it in the air, for instance) and the combat was clunky (the attack animation had a long downtime and you couldn’t attack in multiple directions). This changes quickly, and made the combat so much fun that I played for several hours at a time and always had to watch the clock as the time got away from me. When you upgrade weapons and armor in this game, it doesn’t merely increase your damage dealt or reduce damage taken. Upgrading weapons unlocks things like directional attacks and longer combos, and upgrading armor unlocks double jumps, mid-air dashes, and more. This make the combat get increasingly smooth as you go on, and makes finding materials to upgrade your gear actually exciting. This has an interesting effect on exploring the dungeons, too. The game ends up being a “Metroidvania-lite”, with areas being unlocked as you upgrade and get new movement abilities and the power to break elemental barriers. Since these upgrades are tied to crafting instead of preset locations or story occurrences, you don’t feel gated to progress in a certain order, and improving your character feels truly rewarding as you unlock whole new areas with the purchase of a rune or upgrade. The result is a game which is relaxing and makes you want to keep coming back, running one more dungeon to complete a sidequest or gather some more loot. Even the sidequests have just enough interesting dialogue to provide context to even mundane fetch quests. Having the combat start out a little clunky may have been a mistake, potentially turning people off before it starts getting smoother. But in the end, this game is well worth the low asking price.

_childDocuments_.review: *WARNING MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD* A really fun game, but it is a companion game so it won't be anything big or scratch the itch that the main game hopes to scratch when it releases next year. The combos are fun, the characters are neat and the presentation is pretty damn neat. Though, my biggest complaints about the game are the side-quests and a very minor issue with the character animations when moving. The character's arms look so weird when moving or when animating and it reminds me of those paper dolls where you would attach their limbs to them with a thumbtack or small nail to simulate their joints and again it's very minor but it does throw me off every time I see it. The side-quests are a bigger complaint. I would say it's probably about 60-70% of the game and there are an annoying amount of them that are like "Go talk to this person in the Residential Area who will tell you to talk to someone in Outlander Lane, then from there you have to go to the Quarry and then go back to the Residential Area to finish the quest" or "Hey, I need this totally rare and unique item that will only spawn after you've accepted my quest so even if you decided to grind out areas for materials, you won't be able to easily complete my quest and will need to come back after going back to the area you probably just came back from to complete my quest." There are thankfully a lot of quests that are basically "Just grab 5 of these items that you probably have in your storehouse if you grind in areas" but for someone who may not grind, they might find themselves revisiting areas multiple times to complete said quests which might be annoying for them. I didn't feel I needed to grind for materials for quests but mostly just to upgrade my equipment and the like. Heck, the game even tries to acknowledge that material gathering isn't a problem because there is a shop where you can sell your excess items because it's much harder to get Baqua (money) in this game than getting rarer materials and some end-game(?) upgrades require quite a bit of money for one upgrade (I've seen it at about 2-3K Baqua) out of the 5 you can get (for one character mind you) and each quest is "nice" enough to give you 500 baqua for each quest making money the hardest thing to get in this game and you'll end up grinding for money then you will grinding for mats or for exp. On that note, combat is relatively easy and it would be rather easy for me to become OP and one-shot most mobs upon my first encounter with them. They do have a rock, paper, and scissor system (kind of) with the combat where shields and some projectiles it recommends you use Garoo to one-shot the shields or deflect the projectiles or you'll run into mages with magical shields that can be one-shotted by Isha but if you're stubborn, you can still break their shields with the other two characters but it will take a few more hits than the 1. I would say that's as difficult as the combat gets as enemies are very one-note and there is no real variety to their attacks (Unless you're refighting the bosses which add one additional thing and then it's a very minor thing you can generally easily dispatch or ignore) or behavior and makes it super simple to beat any enemies that come your way. Another thing I would say is a bit. . . annoying would be the resource bag. They start you off with a 50 slot bag which sounds like a lot but when going through dungeons you can easily fill up that bag and if you decide (like me) to beat each side quest before moving on to the next story section, it can take quite a bit of time to get to the point where you can unlock the 100 slot bag which is a blessing, but I'm also finding myself filling it up rather quickly in the Barrows/Snowpeak dungeon and might end up being that way for the Lava Ruins Dungeon too. Though, I will say despite what seems like big complaints I am loving the game a lot and the QOL features they have (free and quick instant fast travel once you've been to a location) make it a great time and an easy amount. I backed the original game and managed to pick this up for 7 USD, but I easily recommend it even at the 15 USD price point because there is a good game here and if you're interested to see some of the characters you'll get to meet again next year in Hundred Heroes, Rising will definitely help get you hyped for Hundred Heroes especially if you enjoy ARPGs.
_childDocuments_.name: Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising

_childDocuments_.review: This was a fun simple game where the grind did not feel grindy, a bit wordy and long in the cutscenes, but a solid game.It did give off some suikoden vibes, since that why I am here, why most of us are here. Again, it's only the vibes, it does not quite pull of the same charm, at least in regards to the first Suikoden games.But the game itself had plenty of charm of it's own, the music was great, the art was great, the 64bit character art really sells it, it's kinda unfortunate it's just a 2.5d side scroller, since it does limit the game in certain way, combat is kinda clunky in the start but gets better as you get better, along with convenient skill upgrades.It's a fairly short game, but it is a prequel, which did make grinding out all the achivements less grindy, and more fun, in fact there was not a single 'bad' part that reduced my experiences of it, sure there was a few typos, and some awkward scene changes, but thats just how it is, and does not really count against them.It's a cute lil' game i hope will be outmatched and destroyed by it's successor, with this being a short prequel and all.
_childDocuments_.name: Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising

_childDocuments_.review: I love being able to help advance the towns. I also like that you can choose between the simple mechanic or not for the battle system. The simple one makes it where the party members change automatically when in battle. The game isn't too hard if you are not use to games like this, like me. You revisit dungeons quite a bit for materials but is to be expected with a game that mostly focuses on upgrading everything.

Overall, a pretty fun experience -- contains some base building and questing as you repeatedly make your way through a handful of locales. I'd probably be more critical of it if it weren't intended to be a companion title, but going in with that knowledge has set my expectations a bit lower, and as a result I think I'm enjoying it more than if I were expecting it to be a fuller fledged metroidvania. _childDocuments_.review: If you plan to play Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes then this small game will act as a good preface to get the taste of the world and various characters in it. Technically speaking, the combat animation is kinda clanky but the combat itself is fun (though a bit later when you have complete party and can switch runes) it remind me to the first Valkyrie Profile. _childDocuments_.review: To summarize at the front end: If you even remotely like sidescroller gameplay and are interested because of Eiyuden Chronicle, this game is probably worth it for you but if you're at all hesitant check out somebody's gameplay first. With that out of the way, I'll continue with my overall thoughts.Eiyuden Chronicle Rising is a decent-to-good sidescroller with light RPG elements, serving as an introduction to the Eiyuden Chronicle franchise. As a sort of spiritual successor to Suikoden I think that the overall tone and sense of humor is captured well, and CJ in particular serves as a decent "classic Suikoden protagonist".Garoo and Isha have more interesting stories underneath the surface than CJ does however, and I'd consider her to be a weak character by comparison. The set-up for Eiyuden Chronicle overall is pretty good though, and what backstory CJ doesn't have is well-established for the next game by this one.Gameplay-wise Rising is relatively light on the mechanics of both genres it comes from; you can see the influence of games like Castlevania, but although your abilities expand they're proportionately fixed. Your overall abilities are comparable to a Megaman X character, with double jumps, dashes, "power jumps", short-range teleport, and a temporary hover. RPG elements (apart from broad RPG-like story structure) are mostly down to the upgrading of armor and weapons as well as the usage of accessories which can modify various aspects of how combat (or other combat-adjacent things like drop rate) plays out. Runes are similar, mostly modifying the elemental powers and resistances available to the player characters.The items you can carry into battle are limited by your stash's current level, which is neat and can be upgraded across the game. Your ability to get item pick-ups is also limited per "run", beginning at around 50 items and then escalating to around 200. This, I find, is mostly annoying busywork to get around-- it's not fun to upgrade it, just less inconvenient.You do some village building, which is nice. It's neat to see buildings go up and get upgraded over time, and by the end of the game New Nevaeh looks like a proper village that's had a "gold rush".Although there is no lack of things to do in theory, the actual quests you're given are fetch quests. There are around 160 you "need" to do in order to get pertinent achievements and high-end equipment, but the game cycles the quests back in case you'd like to do them again.Personally, this game got me pretty fired up for Hundred Heroes and I'll probably go through clearing achievements later.On its own merits, I'd say it's a 7/10 and worth its price tag. It's cute, entertaining, has charming enough characters, and I wanted to know what happened in the story next. But it's by no means revolutionary and there's certainly a reasonable argument that its gameplay becomes monotonous.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little game and denser than I expected. Took me 16 hours to 100%. Takes a little bit to warm up but once Garoo joins the cast is very likable, A good little story building up to something much greater. The game is ridiculously easy, but the mechanics are satisfying and I enjoyed the gameplay loop of fetch quests town building and upgrades. It's somewhat repetitive but I found it very cathartic. The presentation, visuals, exploration and feeling of the combat prevented me from getting bored, except for some of the post game grinding which didn't even take that long. If you're looking forward to the main game and don't mind something a bit mindless but satisfying, I'd recommend giving this a go. Was expecting basically nothing out of this prequel and came out quite happy

_childDocuments_.review: While I have mixed feelings about Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising, I can at least say that it comes with some merits. As a fan of the Suikoden series, I can honestly say that I was looking forward to digging into Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising. Serving as a prequel to the traditional Japanese Role Playing Game Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes, Rising has around 15 to 20 hours worth of content. It's a relatively short experience by RPG standards. That, however, isn't Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising's main issue. In Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising, you play as "CJ". Her story involves searching for Rune Lens. Along the way, CJ befriends two other characters who join her on her journey. Garoo, a kangeroo looking guy who wields a giant sword, and Isha, a mage with the ability to float across gaps. In the game, you have multiple bosses. A giant tree, a big rock golem, a fire worm are just a few of the encounters in the game. None of them are particularly difficult. However, I will say that the first time fighting them was sort of fun. Beyond that, you also have the option of playing on a Hard Mode after completing the main story. This allows you to re-challenge powered-up versions of every boss in the game. However, if you spend any amount of time upgrading the town, none of these bosses should be of any particular challenge.  Further explaining the gameplay, it's relatively simplistic. You can combo with your party members and use them to help you traverse the metroidvania-esque world. There are lots of monsters to farm across the game and also many materials that can be used to craft weapons, armor, accessories, and various consumables. Unfortunately, the game suffers from severe repetition. This comes from the questing system. With the quests in Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising, you are tasked with hunting monsters, mining, logging, and even fishing. The key issue is that you repeatedly perform these tasks over and over and over and over and over and over and over again to the point where it becomes grossly sickening. I spent around 17 hours actually playing Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising to get 100% and I can say that it felt like 10 of those hours were wasted gathering random nonsense. It's insanely boring. If the game wasn't so easy, I probably would have dropped it after completing the story. Other things worth mentioning are the graphics and music. I did like Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising's visual style. It looks nice. Stepping into a new area was always the most exciting part of the game. I wasn't entirely sure what to expect from the world, but I did leave the game feeling satisfied enough to say that the visuals were nice. The music was alright too. However, nothing really stood out. It's not like I'm going to go to YouTube and listen to the game's soundtrack or anything. It served it's purpose and I'll probably forget about it in a week. Overall, Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising is a decent game. It's short, but does enough to provide a sufficient amount of content to the player. Unfortunately, this time padding comes mostly from repetitive fetch quests. However, the game's pricing makes it hard to complain about. $14.99 USD isn't so bad. I've paid more for far worse games. That being said, if someone was to pick it up for even cheaper, it's certainly worth trying out. It's not a bad game, but has issues with the side content. I never once had an issue with focusing on the main story, which is why I'm recommending this game. It's just that I highly recommend being weary because the game's side quests are really boring and take up a lot of the time that the player will spend playing.

_childDocuments_.review: This IS NOT the upcoming Eiyuden Chronicles main game - this is a 15 dollar COMPANION game, made by an entirely different studio. This is like buying a side dish to go with your main course, and the side dish is going to be entirely different from your main meal.I love it.I love this game. It's a bit slow at the start, a bit wordy, but you can skip that stuff if you want - so far, there's no REQUIRED reading (although I have done so to give myself the opportunity of an immersive experience.)This game (at the time of this writing) is only 15 bucks. I have already put 8 hours into it, and I can tell I have at least another 8-16 hours to go. For a return on investment that is a gigantic bang for your buck.The entertainment factor is here, too. It's colorful, fresh, the controls aren't awful, and they aren't overly complicated.It's been just released (again at the time of this writing) so like all new games, there are some bugs to work out, but they're working on it and I think they're doing a great job.I would easily pay twice as much money for a sequel to this game if they were to ever make one.Based on my experience so far, I am also now MORE excited to the main Eiyuden Chronicle game as well.Fingers crossed. Here's hoping this post ages well. Thank you, devs, for all your hard work thus far! And if you are a player on the fence - buy the game, play it for 2 hours, and if you dont love it, return it. Or not....give it a few more hours, see if you fall in love with it. Are you really going to miss 15 bucks that badly? It's the general price of a movie ticket with a much better bang for your buck!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun romp. The game is very easy and is mostly a series of fetch quests with fetch side quests. The game is generous with it's drops, so it feels rewarding to run around even when you have already been to an area. The three character party has an interesting mechanic to switch between them and a fun combo system that gets pretty absurd when you unlock unlimited combos. The dialog is enjoyable and the main character is good at reminding you who someone is, sometime with a bit of snark for the fetch quest she knows is incoming. There are a bunch of characters and the town does feel like a town. It is a tad clunky in certain areas, but this mostly causes a bit of frustration at having to wait for a transition or checking a second menu for information.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a long time Suikoden fan, and a backer for Hundred Heroes. I wasn't sure if i would like this game as side scrolling fighting games are not usually my cup of tea. I prefer RPGs with turn based combat, but I was pleasantly surprised by how much i like this game. It does start slow, and combat feels stiff at the start. However, once you are able to upgrade weapons/equipment it start to pick up, becoming more fluid. _childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty-looking game with modern pixel art for the characters with great 3D background. As the companion game of the anticipated Eiyuden Chronicles Hundred Heroes, which hopefully released in 2023, I feel that this served as a good lore introduction for the series. The characters are quirky with some genuine comedic moment from time to time, but so far the storyline is pretty generic as there is nothing important at stake. The gameplay and quest are average -- but since you are able to teleport/take shortcut, the mostly fetch quests are barely bearable, the reused enemy models doesn't help either but at least they have different move sets. As for combat it certainly feels responsive with the three main characters able to combo with each others and they get more combat moves as they upgrade their gears, although it is not quite as challenging as I though it would be.All in all this game gets a solid 6.5/10 from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics: Clean and crisp, the characters are 2D and although slightly pixelated, I know they are going for the whole Suikoden (JRPG series from the PS1 to PS3 era) look.Music: Really nice soundtrack, it's very appropriate for the scenes you're in and very relaxing. I only wished the Boss music was a bit more epic.Controls: If you're playing with a controller, the responses are smooth. It does tend to feel a bit sluggish with certain combat situations if you're used to more fast-paced games like Skull: The Hero Slayer and Hollow Knight (although this is not the same type of game).Gameplay: When I started playing, I was quite excited. This game is developed by a team that also worked on my favorite JPRG series of all time: Suikoden. And even though this is a warm-up game until Hundred Heroes arrives, I love the look and feel. In the hours that I played it, I was enjoying myself, but soon there were a few things that started to bother me:1. Quests - After about 15 side-quests I started to notice a horrible trend that all games are suffering from: that repetitive feel of sub-par and boring fetch quests.... Why can't rpg's be as dynamic as they used to be in the old days? I don't need endless quest to be force-fed. Too much handholding too. It tends to slow the pace of the story too.2. Completion Notification - Oh god, this started to annoy me very quickly. You complete a quest, you get a message saying "QUEST COMPLETED", followed by a message that says WHICH quest you completed, FOLLOWED by a text of the NEXT quest. You can't move while all this happend so all these notifications slow things down.. and at some point I was like "OK!! THANK YOU!! I'D LIKE TO MOVE ON NOW!" I know it's just a minor thing, but this could've been done much better.Story: As much as you can expect from any adventure / rpg. It doesn't pull you in right away and after 5 hours you're wondering if anything interesting will happen. I think it's important to have that sense of intrigue and wonder early on. But this game starts out quite mildly.All in all - I do recommend this game as I support the developers and I think they created something worth your time. The price is right for what you are getting. Hope this helps.

_childDocuments_.review: Backstory: I was a backer of the main game and bought this as the companion game so I only payed the 7, not the 15. That said I would have paid the 15 for this if I had missed the backer window.It has a slow start. A very slow start. Once you start getting the town going and getting more shops opened then it starts opening up. Things like crafting items, accessories, weapons/armor, food, etc. The weapon and armor upgrades have both a numerical upgrade at the smith for more damage and an upgraded version from the Weapon/Armor shops that give you bonuses. Things like a higher hit combo for a weapon, double jump being unlocked for an armor. The good thing on the weapon and armor upgrades is that crafting the new version just gives upgrades it. So previous upgrades are not wasted on a piece of equipment you might no longer be using as you cannot "equip" weapons and armor, just accessories and some other type of equipment later on that is used for exploration and enemy weaknesses.The gameplay is simple. It's a 2D walk around and upgraded your town, explore dungeons, kill monsters and get materials. Very reminiscent of a non-time restricted Atelier game in its material gathering to produce more items in town. Once you create an item, say a food for the tavern or an accessory, you can then purchase that item for money if you don't want to craft it again. The food restores health and gives a permanent, but small, stat buff to whichever character eats it. Exploring the dungeons has you returning back to places quite a bit due to them always having some area you cannot explore yet. You might need another characters ability, upgraded movement from a new armor, or special accessories that let you break certain colored rocks. A very light Metroid-vania aspect in its exploration I felt. The maps are kind enough to show you a linked room so you know at least where you need to come back to.Side quests are the main content of the game. Side quests are everything to get stamps. Stamps in tiered quantities (like 10/20/30) will get you a one-time specific item and collecting a lot or all of them can get you some busted accessories. Note that stamps are not taken when redeeming them so your total is always the same. Side quests upgrade your buildings to offer better items to create, higher upgrades for equipment, or better Inn options for day buffs. The day only ends when you rest at your base to regain health, which you rarely need to do once you get the tavern open and can create/buy food. However resting for the day does not progress anything so there's nothing really to lose by doing that.The one nitpick I would have would be the animations for certain characters seem doll-like in their movement. Once you see the MC moving her arms around swinging to and fro you'll understand. However that is a minor complaint to an otherwise fine game that you can just zone out and play, killing mobs and getting new and rarer materials to create stuff for the town.Overall though, a very solid game done by a separate company to introduce us to the world we'll find ourselves in when Hundred Heroes releases sometime in the future._____________________________________________________Edited after finishing: So now that I have 100% completed the game, in terms of story and achievements anyway, my thoughts are still the same. I actually enjoyed the story more as it went on with the characters becoming more fleshed out and finding out about their pasts. It ends in a flash in the pan, but its set up in such a way that we may be introduced to these very characters in Hundred Heroes. There is a "post-game" which is right before you enter the last little dungeon that you can explore the towns again and get the last few stamps to fill out your card and even then there are (seemingly at least, I did not do a lot of them) repeatable quests for money and items after you can no longer get stamps. A hard mode is unlocked and there is an achievement for beating each area boss and the final boss on hard. Hard mode is not a joke at times so fair warning.

_childDocuments_.review: Eiyuden Chronicles: Rising.So we have a game that is trying to be multiple things at the same time. Some of them it achieves, some of them it could use a little more polish on. Some of the, it doesn't meet expectations in my eyes.First some context on the game:This is the "companion game" that was announced at the end of the Kickstarter for Eiyuden Chronicles: Hundred Heroes.  That game is supposed to be a spiritual successor to the jrpg franchise Suikoden.For those who hear "spiritual successor" to "beloved old game franchise" in the same breath as "kickstarter" might be getting some Mighty No 9 flashbacks, but stay with me here.This companion game was sales pitched as this little aperitif. Something to wet your whistle. Get you excited for the main game coming out a year after. There were some indications on completing this game will influence some events in the main game (as of writing this, the specifics are unclear...but as it's the same folks who did Suikoden there are things to speculate on if the importing of saves between games in that franchise are anything to go on).The Game Itself:What we have here is a blend of action-rpg and metroid-vania with some of the grind a jrpg fan might remember. Fans of either of the two main genres listed should enjoy this game as it does it's job well. It's not soul-crushingly difficult, even on hard mode, rewards system mastery by making the game fairly trivial when you master the mechanics involved.The art style is going to be something you either love, or hate which is purely subjective. If you enjoy what you see in the preview videos or the images in the slideshows on the store page: That's what you get.  Things feel mostly smooth, a few of the cuts to conversation screens could be polished a little more but nothing super jarring. The story, while not complex, is an enjoyable one. It's a save the world/town type feel while still keeping it down to earth and small scale. This is good as it allows itself to also worldbuild and develop characters besides the three player controlled ones (albeit in very small fashions for the other 'important' NPCs).One thing I would like to bring up as a big plus for me is the sound design. While most people focus on the soundtrack, and the songs are fun, the EFFECTS are what make me smile. Striking something while doesn't sound impactful it has an iconic feel to hit like the early beat-em-up games or even marvel vs capcom which fits SO WELL here.Price Point:So I usually measure a game based on price to enjoyment ratio. With a "good" or "great" game being 1 hour of enjoyment per dollar spent on the game with being a little more critical on the game if it suffers from continuous delays (such as FF7 Remake, or the upcoming VtM Bloodlines 2) and a little more generous if it comes out ahead of schedule on any meaningful level (as that usually means they're trying to beat a timetable so not compete with another game).I also backed the kickstarter, so I only paid the kickstarter price of this for roughly $7 USD. For the kickstarter price I would say this is a GREAT game, getting roughly 20 hours of enjoyment out of the game for a full completion (and that's with me moving quick through text windows and the like instead of slowly savoring each scene). For the normal price of roughly $15 USD? Good game. Still getting your money's worth.Conclusions and Rating:We'll use an X out of 10 system here where 10 is what I would consider a perfect game and 1 is what I would consider Superman 64.I'd consider this game a solid 7.5 or 8 out of 10.It's a fun little game, gives you a nice self-contained story that also expands into a larger plot. This could've expanded into sequels if it wasn't a precursor to a bigger game already (and depending on how that game plays out, this could still have sequels).If you're a fan of Metroid-vania games: It's worth picking up full price if you enjoy the genre, like the art style, and don't mind a little of a JRPG grind for items. If you're not a fan or the art or JRPG item grind isn't a bit of a turn-off: Wait for it to go on sale and snag it then (25% to 33% is when I'd start eyeballing it), the story is still fun, the art is nice, the execution of mechanics is there.If you're a fan of Suikoden games: Pick it up. This scratched the itch I had for the Suikoden storytelling and has left me chomping at the bit for the main game knowing I have to wait another year or so. If you're not a fan of Metroid-vania games: Still pick it up, it is worth it for the worldbuilding. Maybe the same 25% to 33% sale price point if you absolutely LOATHE the Metroid-vania genre but I would still encourage it.Left comments on if somebody has questions. Toodles.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interesting game. It is quite unlike a lot of the other platformers that have been released recently, and instead it feels about as close as you could get to an RPG turned into a platformer. It is not particularly difficult, and the action is just okay, but nonetheless it is very satisfying to play. I enjoy building up the town and improving my characters, and I am satisfied each time I expand or get stronger.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent game that has a lot of room for improvement.Things that could've been better:- The option to directly take/turn-in side missions from the board located in the plaza "which btw already lists side missions" instead of having to walk allover town searching for side missions on every visit.- The unbroken elemental stones blocking dungeon paths should appear on the map after being discovered, this skips having to re-discover every dungeon every time I'm able to break a stone type.- Teleportation inside dungeons should use the dungeon map instead of the world map, I often teleport to the wrong check-point because of this.- Auto item pick-up should be an option, having to stand still for every monster drop greatly slows the flow of the game.- Difficulty option, this game is extremely easy, I Have beaten the game without using a single potion or seeing a single gameover screen.In conclusion, I do like the game but unfortunately its so far from being its perfect self.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall Score: 8/10Cute anime graphicsfunny storygood musicGetting point reduction from some issues with Mechanics and keeping track of rare resource vein spawnsI can't for the love of all thats holy find the Chunk of Ice vein, so I have to search the entire mountian zone by zone for where it is. If their Main/side quest on the sector map also had "Search for material" that you have already found then it would have gotten 10 of 10 from me. But alas, the whole fact of searching previous zones for a rare resource node because you forgot where you got it, then yeah, unnessecary time sink, which you already have because you need to do the maps over and over again for materials.anyhow, onto the meat of the review.A Metroidvania like gamewhere you use your characters special abilities, elemental runes and so on to advance while fighting monsters and bosses.You also build up a frontier town that has been ruined by monsters, bandits and earthquakes.You grind monsters for materials to improve your weapon, armor, make potions to heal or buff yourself, make magical elemental runes that improve your weapon and function as "keys" to destroy elemental pillars.Building up the town and solving the adventure "Stamp card" will yield you many bonuses like chain combo attacks between the various heros. You will end up with a party of 3, and you switch between these characters during combat, linking these attacks will deal massive damage and can easily turn higher level enemies into minced meat if done correctly.All side quests are thus important to solve even if most of them are go to person A, go talk to B, return to Awith a few items from monsters or resource nodes to turn in, and if that person is a shop owner it is a good chance it will give you access to better armor, weapon, food and potions.Food: very important in this game as it give your character permanent attribute bonuses, but they are expensive unless you have the materials needed. So if you can afford 1500 coins you can get 1.5 permanent luck increase that will also give you better drop rates, so I suggest go for luck in the start, will make things a ton easier for you in the long run. Later on you will need Physical and Magical Defense food and attack power and critical hit chance food to build up your character. On average when you level up you get 3-5 attribute points to attack, defense and some HP. So food is super important, trust me, you will not regret it.Do not sleep unless you are forced to as it will cancel out Inn hot spring buffs like XP boost or Luck Boost effects. Instead go to the tavern and buy some cheap food that will also give you permanent stat boosts.This game will carry over its savefile to another Eiyuden game in the making that is more likeSuikoden from PSone to PS2 era. Suikoden is an RPG where you build up an army of heros, build a Base with these heros and civilians that will give you shops and so on. Which alone is a good reason to get this game if you plan to play the next Eiyuden, but as the next Eiyuden is compleatly different in mechanics I feel I have to warn that it will not be an Action RPG/metroidvania game like this Eiyuden it will be more of a traditional JRPG.In short this game is an Action RPG, with minor managment aspects and metroidvaniaish qualities, learning double jump, air dash, levitation, super jump and more to advance and explore for hidden treasure. You build up a town and gather materials to improve your equipment rather than replace it.Again, Food is totally OP if you do it right. Enjoy. This is a fun prelude of the "Real" Eiyuden game that is a spiritual successor to the Suikoden franchise, which these developers was originally a part of making it for Konami. If you like metroidvania games and JRPGs this title will be a ton of fun for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising offers itself as a fun companion title to the main game, Eiyuden Chronicles: Hundred Heroes which is slated for a 2023 release. You play as CJ, a "Scavenger" coming into a town with the dream of striking it rich by treasure hunting. She soon begins to help develop the town as a suitable adventurer's destination and help bring prosperity to the inhabitants of New Neveah.The game mixes town building with fast paced Action RPG elements. A core part of the game is taking on quests from the townsfolk and dungeon crawling to either grab materials that they need for building new structures or other various reasons, or defeating monsters that lay deep in the wilderness. There is a monumental amount of backtracking, but this is mostly remedied by having the ability to fast travel to just about any location that you've already been to, saving you loads of travel time. As you progress you will gain access to new features in New Neveah, including the ability to upgrade your party's equipment to gain new combat abilities.On the surface, this game is a lot of fun and is sure to scratch the itch of fans of both genres. However, it is extremely repetitive, and could turn some people off. You will find yourself going to the same areas multiple times to grab more of a specific item that a quest asks of you to collect. On the flip side, you will gain new abilities that allow you to go into different areas of previous locations that were blocked off initially, breathing more fresh air to areas that previously felt stale. The art style is charming and features a somewhat "Octopath Traveler-esque" feeling with vibrant and colorful backgrounds with sprite-like character models, and the music overall has been great for each different location I've been to thus far.For $15 this is a solid game. While it doesn't have the intricacies or content of games like Hollow Knight, it is still enjoyable and a neat little bridge to Hundred Heroes, especially for fans of the Suikoden series that eagerly await the main game's release. If you plan on getting Hundred Heroes, I recommend checking this game out to get some more backstory on the world and the characters. If you're still on the fence, watch some gameplay footage to see if this is for you. What you see is what you get with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: To be blunt, the game itself is subpar to other side-scrolling game (ex: Rogue Legacy). The visual presentation is okay and the animation a little bit clunky. The sound/music is charming and comfy. But, the only reason I bought this game is the nostalgic purpose of playing Suikoden. Which mean, the story, the characters, and the vibes that make me attached to this game. I DO NOT recommend this game if you seek gameplay/challenges (the HARD difficulty only available after your beat the game once).  If you plan to play Eiyuden Chronocle: Hundred Heroes, finishing Rising will give you a reward to carry over to the main title (Hundred Heroes). That's also the another reason to play this game. Oh yah, lastly, I'm surprised that this game run okayish (22-30fps) on my old GT 940 M laptop. Hope the Hundred Heroes is the same.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really easy going game and old school-like, with a lot of personality, If you're feeling nostalgic about AJRPG's from the past, you'll surely like Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising and if you haven't played any, this is the perfect game to start with, but if you're a Suikoden fan or just waiting for Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes to release, this is a MUST. Natsume Atari did a pretty good job.

_childDocuments_.review:
Eiyuden Chronicle: Rising combines a thrilling adventure through ancient ruins with the tale of one town’s rise from the ashes. Drawn by lenses and other treasure in the nearby Runebarrows, our heroes learn that the town is struggling to rebuild after an earthquake and decide to help. Along the way, they’ll resolve disputes between eager adventurers and wary locals who don’t think the Barrows should be disturbed. And they’ll learn more about each other’s reasons for seeking treasure, deepening their bonds in the process. As you will learn, these Runebarrows hide a great secret that has fateful implications for one of the characters. What begins as a simple treasure hunt turns into a dark conspiracy that will shake the world and plant seeds that carry over into the main story of Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes. The game will introduce a portion of Eiyuden Chronicle’s cast of characters in an original story with thrilling action and engaging town-upgrading elements.



There will be some perks for players that link the game with Eiyuden Chronicle: Hundred Heroes.

short_description: The War of Crowns rages on. Knights and brigands run rampant throughout the land, sowing destruction. From your castle base, rise to become the lord who leads the battle against the forces of evil in this turn-based tactics and strategy game.

_childDocuments_.review: Timers, timers everywhere.You have a timer for travel, Fine.You have a timer for healing after combat, Understandable.You have a timer for research, Makes sense.You have a timer for Doomsday, hate it but I get it..You have a timer in most missions where you auto lose if you don't kill all of the enemies in the area AND they are hidden around the Tactical games are supposed to be fun and strategic. They're not supposed to force you into terrible situations over and over just to beat a timer. How is that fun?It wouldn't be so bad if you were heroic, but more often than not, the enemy has better skills than you do and they have ZERO problem popping poison in large areas over and over again. I had really high hopes for this game. Now I'm patiently waiting for a modder to fix this cluster-fart so I can actually enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: As the developer of a very similar game, Zodiac Legion, you should take my opinion with a grain of salt:Crown Wars follows the XCOM 2 formula to the letter:You have a castle to manage, where you upgrade buildings, recruit soldiers, and research "blueprints" to make your weapons and potions better.Your characters have a simple progression system (1 skill to pick among 2 at each level, for each of the 6 classes).You send your soldiers on missions on the campaign map. There are several mission types, like capturing an enemy, freeing a prisonner, defending a position...Several "pods" (ie, enemy groups) are present on a map waiting for you to engage them one at a time in turn-based fashion.The pods are even less reactive than in XCOM 2 (they will remain in position with 1 of their member patrolling a little around), and you can see further than them, so you can usually engage on your terms, but all missions have a turn limit (the countdown starts as soon as you engage the first group).As it is a medieval game, it has a much stronger focus on melee, with 2/3rd of the classes being either melee centric, or having a melee option. Cover is also much less of an issue when the main mode of operation is putting large pointy steel objects into opponent skulls.Another big change is that you have 2 actions and 1 move in Crown Wars instead of 1 action+ 1 move in XCOM. It makes misses a bit less critical than in XCOM 1/2, as you can usually attack a second time.Many have complained about the turn limits, but I think it is really out of place: If anything, they are pretty lenient and have been an issue exactly 0 time for me (while I usually had to extract on the last turn in XCOM 2, here, I typically end missions with half of the turns remaining, at the highest difficulty settings).The core combat is quite enjoyable IMO. And some missions feature siege engines for you or the opponent to play with, which is pretty cool. You have 2 elements to advance: your base and your "research":Progression is mostly numbers going up.You improve weapons and armors (improving all greatswords once the technology is researched), then upgrade the forge to improve weapons and armor even further.Potions need to be paid on top of the research cost (classes can equip between 0 and 2), but they get filled up for free.Upgrading buildings lets you research better weapons/armors and potions, or recruiting higher level characters, ...It works, even though it is a bit barebone (and strongly gives incentive to rely on as few weapons as possible, as you upgrade each weapon type separately).There are a few weird choices in combat:Archers can still operate at 100% in melee, and melee characters can usually just eat your attack of opportunity to murder your backline, so you have to use taunt a lot, making Crusaders (aka knights) a must have.As in XCOM, it is mostly about unleashing as much damage as possible before the opponent gets a turn (hint, improve your main weapons before anything else!):Being focused will get your archer or alchemist killed in a single turn.There are some weird balance issues: It is cheaper to recruit a competent character than to train one of your own (ie, recruiting a level 4 knight will be cheaper than training your own knight from level 1 to 4, but combat XP is "free").Your characters have some kind of fate points (they lose one everytime their HP drop to 0, and are gone for good when the last one is used up). It is a weird system, as it gives an even stronger incentive to skip using or leveling them.Regarding level ups, you have very few occasions to get conditional extra actions(like counterattacking an opponent, or refunding the action if your backstab kills the target), which are the strongest options in this kind of games, while some skills waste a precious action to get a situational effect, so it is not balanced very well, but some classes can have choices that support a pretty different playstyle (your ranger can specialize in melee or range, your alchemist can be a healer or a grenadier, but your knights will all be sturdy warriors that taunt opponents while inflicting a lot of damage under the right conditions...).The Hundred Year Wars settings is also a bit weird, as you end up fighting everyone. You also meet 50% of women among every faction soldiers (how is murdering women with warhammers a progress to begin with?), and no one except your characters (if you wish) puts helmets on.Actually, armor cosmetic customization is rather cool: you unlock new options as you improve each armor type, and can put heraldy on some parts. As for bugs, I have encountered quite a few, but nothing game breaking (and no crash, nor GPU melting), but your mileage may vary, but animations can be a bit slowish, and you cannot issue orders while waiting for a move to complete.The worst one has been parties teleporting back home and going to the mission site again on some missions (corruption removal), but fortunately, it has not caused much damage to my game (the party becomes immediately available again upon reaching its destination a second time).TLDR: A competent medieval XCOM, that may become great with some more patches and minor QoL/balance reworks.
_childDocuments_.name: Crown Wars: The Black Prince

_childDocuments_.review: I have to admit there may be a good game here, but it is marred by some (in my opinion) poor design choices.The most egregious one is time limits in most missions. It's a hard limit too, as in defeat if you don't finish the mission in X turns. This just isn't fun and it doesn't even have balancing reasons.There is also the weapon upgrade system, which urges one to not diversify the weapons (Why upgrade a greatsword which only one class can use, when you can upgrade a bow which 3 classes can use?).I'll be waiting for a change to make the time limits go away or at least optional.

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect game that lands the MEDIEVAL-TACTICS theme, all while pulling from obvious inspirations; "xcom", "battle brothers", "darkest dungeon", "othercide", etc; especially... the difficulty.** Game is quite unbalanced, and favors the A.I heavily.** Clearly an unfinished product with the SHEER AMOUNT OF BUGS/PROBLEMS.** Re-used/skinned assets from Nacons "War Hospital".* MISSIONS ARE A COIN-TOSS- "Easy", "Normal", "Hard"; all this means is [# of Enemy Units per Group] x [How hard they'll out-stat you]. The unbalance here is this scale is on an exponential curve the further you progress. Well into mid-late game, even those "Easy" missions become a burden because of how hard the Enemy out-paces you in terms of "HP"/"Abilities"/"Stats", where it might be few, but you're still drowning in Poison/Bleed/Crits. Early Game, its a test of patience to get over this face-smashing-wall so you can get Units that aren't entirely useless, but even after that remain useless because of the sheer powercreep.- Mission TYPES, are what makes the Game actually HARD, regardless of the Difficulty; "Hard Assassination"(Escort/Rescue/Capture) Missions are all the same, and are actually Easy. Because you enter, kill a group of 8-10 Units, then flee for the Extract before the next groups of 6-8 Spawn; "Hard Skirmish" is only Hard because you're racing against a clock/Turn-Timer; "Hard Defend" Missions are stupid impossible - You land in a random location,(usually with a Ballista staring you down), and need to hold for 10 Turns while absurd groups spawn directly ontop of you every Turn.- The A.I is BRUTALLY SMART. They will always take the most convenient and affordable pathing for them to maneuver around your flank. They have ZERO Self-Preservation, in that they will always move out of an Attack of Opportunity(AOP) just to Single-Out the Lowest HP/Armor Unit nearby(e.g -ALWAYS- TARGETING YOUR ANIMAL), and Poison Bomb their own people. Additionally, the A.I inherently knows where an OBSERVATION outline is or an Artillery Line of Sight, and will always deadstop exactly outside despite having a clear path and target to approach. Intentionally wasting the "Timed-Turned-Limit".* POWERCREEP-The Enemy blatantly outpaces you; which adds another layer to the artificial difficulty. Every time you upgrade, the A.I Units do as well - so you never really "get stronger". Upgrades and levels feel like you're scrapping by at higher difficulties, meanwhile the enemy "upgrades" are about 2-3 steps further ahead in comparison; via, HP and Abilities. The Turn-Economy violently shifts from focusing on DMG/Kills to "My Unit DIES next". Especially because now they CRIT far more than you, cheat Mechanics with +ACC, and given more utility to play "Debuff-The-Game" =  PoisonCritPoisonGunnerBleedShivPoisonCritHeadshotCrit. -*SPOILER* Upgrading the Domain, and unlocking Companion Slots for Missions? The Enemy does as well. Which automatically adds more layers behind "Missions", as its [Your Baseline #]+[Difficulty Modifier]. So getting that extra 1 or 2 Units, then means you've got to deal with another 1-2 multiplier. Easy? It's still 16-22 Enemies. Hard? Yeah, 24-32; not including potential Animals.-Isn't that GameDesign101? "Let the Player feel like they're getting stronger as they progress", but instead, its just "I'm being matched with the same odds, and the A.I is rigged, so it's still getting harder".* POSITIONING BE DAMNED- Okay. THIS. Is the BIG NOTE. "Positioning in a Turn-Based-Tactics-RPG" should matter, but falls flat in this Game.- First, Attacks of Opportunity(AOP), are inconsistent AF; There is no point in locking down a Group of Enemy Units with a Single-Tank, because the AOP is; 1 Unit, per, 1 Unit. Literally, your Unit's will only have a single AOP proc per turn, regardless of positioning. Other times, it doesn't proc entirely; I've had Enemy Units WALK A TILE AWAY to flank someone else, or they dance around to stab my back; yet, YOU'll get an AOP for doing the same maneuver. So, why even bother?- Second, Enemy Units DO NOT receive the same Mechanics treatment - I've had an Archer posted on the second floor, INSIDE, of a barn while an OUTSIDE, enemy Flayer, on the far other end, sent their Falcon inside to Mark me. NO Line of Sight; Then, having enemy Archers/Alchemist land shots/bombs around the most questionable of angles with absolute ACC/aim. The AI gets a blatant pass on some mechanics.- Lastly, the "Positioning Bonus" is only for the A.I to exploit - You can have an Archer/Xbow in a Tower? Enemy will more often than not land a shot UPWARDS and CRIT, more than you will DOWNWARDS; Flanking Bonus is shifty at best - Enemy can be surrounded by a Flank and a Sword @95%ACC will still miss both Actions.(CANT STRESS THE AMOUNT OF TIMES A 95% MISSES. LIKE BRUH. ITS A BEAR, HIT IT), and they only need 1v1, while landing crits; Axe-Flayers have walked up to the Tile adjacent to an Archer that's a FULL Story/Elevation above them and still land BOTH Actions despite Cover+Elevation. Meanwhile, if you block a path that leads to an elevation (e.g, stacked boxes, etc), it DOES NOT provide any increase to ACC - I've had a Crusader block a Flayer trying to climb a half-elevation, and still miss @80%ACC; Also, Halberds CANNOT attack down ladders.* THE TIMERS ARE TIMED. **Patch Note 31/05/2024**- The Dev's updated the Game by providing 5 more Turns to Skirmish/Capture Missions; having these extra 5 turns does help. - Keep in Mind; it's less PvE and more YOU vs TIME; Fighting HARDER, more STURDY, with MUCH MORE HP type Enemy Units, spending a Single Turn to either Advance or Reposition literally means the difference between Winning/Losing some Missions. Which, creates a game-play loop of cherry-picking missions.- Research, Time: Forge, Time: Recruit, Time: Broke, Time: Mission, Time; Some of that makes sense, some of that has me catching myself wondering "Oh ♥♥♥♥, am I playing a Moblie Game? Where are the Pay to Win MTX Menus? Is there a "Watch this AD now to Skip Waiting" button?"** Speaking of MTX... 7$ Cosmetic on Launch? Damn, that's ballsy. Dev's better be buying some fine wine with that bread.* Prison Concept is neat, but poorly executed.- The Perk's don't stack//doesn't allow multiples of the same capture. Fair, they could get out of hand very easily. However the system was a last second add with how unpolished it is; with things like having a "Duelist Tough" not being allowed with "Crusader Tough" despite being different; or, "Mentor" NOT actually giving any extra XP.*The Forge, and "I understand".- Yeah, I know, I understand you finished that thing I told you to start a Month ago. Please. I'd like an easier way to "dismiss notifications" inside of the Forge. It's unnecessary to drag a scroll bar ALL THE WAY TO THE BACK of the "Completed Forges" every time, just to remove the " ! ".*30 HOUR UPDATE- I've had several Crashes now, usually when loading into a Mission. It's also a very common occurrence for Animations to trip over themselves to a point it backs up the Game. Sometimes, the AI/Game will initiate an attack, the Game will try and get ahead of itself and calculate either the DMG or Animation necessary and instead applies it all at the same time resulting in a messy-lag. The worst I've seen is when a turn starts, no one does anything during "Enemy Turn", then 3-minutes later combat catches up; and that's not a joke - I've had to force close the game at times because it lingers on "Enemy Turn" without anything happening.- Poor Optimization.The Game CAN be Enjoyable, and I will absolutely continue playing after this mild "I'm kinda tilted" type rant - but the "artificial" difficulty of just having RNG/Stats be in favor of the A.I doesn't make it actually difficult, or fun to play against. It's like playing Dice Poker against rigged dice.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I like the game, but it has some really weird and annoying aspects.- Each new start you are forced to play the tutorial. Having a "skip tutorial" option should be standard.- Difficulty is largely created by implementing turn restrictions, which I personally find annoying. - Inexhaustable enemy reinforcements. - Unskippable animations during combat, you can only deactivate the killcam. - Everything has a timer on it, all the time. - Sometimes horrible game mechanics. I.e. enemies who were floored can still dodge attacks. There's a bunch of things to do from a Quality of Life perspective, too many for me to play the game right now. Will look at the game again when it got more polish.

_childDocuments_.review: At the moment I can not recommend this game. I was super excited for this game, instantly wishlisted and bought it when able. From what I have played I do enjoy the game but the timers to find enemies on the battlefield does not feel tactical at all, more often than not you end up losing people to try and beat the clock. You have 15 turns there are 4 of you and anywhere from 10-15 enemies that you have to kill, and then look for others (which usually wastes a few of your turns because you are running around blind as a bat trying to find them. NO tactical repositioning because you just killed 11 enemies and you have 3 turns left to kill the other 4. I hope the devs get rid of the time constraints on the battlefield, because last I checked in medieval times the enemies didn't attack each other and run out of turns. It is just super difficult when you are trying to survive the more than double enemies on the field and you only have 3 turns left. I think I killed the last dudes on my last turn and lost 2 of my people while doing it.

_childDocuments_.review: I might come back and edit this to be a more detailed review later, but the amount of people whining and downvoting this game because of mission-timers and the difficulty curve is CRAZY - and actually really unfair to the game!If you're a mature, adult gamer who loved the fact that XCOM was BRUTAL until you understood the mechanics and how to manage the early-game, then honestly I think you'll enjoy this.Sure, it will certainly improve with some added love and patches but really, as someone who loved XCOM (all the way back to UFO: Enemy Unknown!) and who also really enjoyed WarTales - I am REALLY enjoying this game.Strategy "layer" is a bit light, sure - but it serves (I'd like to see them expand on it in future) - but the battlefields are all amazing and varied, character progression and skill trees fun and interesting (including levelling up skills in individual weapons alongside class skills, which is a great mechanic for a ton of variety), and I just thoroughly enjoy all the battles - especially as your mercs start developing their skill-sets and finding synergies between them.So if you can deal with the initial difficulty curve (which, much like XCOM, is primarily managed by unlocking the 5th - and later 6th - slot in your squads as quickly as possible), then there's a LOT to enjoy here. Negatives reviews based purely on difficulty and timers are totally unfair and largely unfounded.Also worth noting that the devs are listening and rolled out a couple of very quick early patches to address the biggest issues, which I hope bodes well for the future of the game. I'm very hopeful it'll be a success, because I'd really love for the devs to build on what they've created here.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure you understand by reading other reviews this is a lot like a 100 years war era X-Com. The problem is the graphics are not nearly as good as X-COM 2 and though there are many weapons options and career paths for your champions none of them except expertise with hammers and armor removal will allow you to defeat the final boss. I played through several times on different levels making the mistake of using other weapons that worked well all the way through until the final boss and could never win the battle. I did eventually finish the campaign on Baron Level with Hero option chosen. Steam advised only 2.6% of people completed campaign (at any level apparently) and only 0,2% in Hero mode. I would think this alone would indicate there is a problem with the game if only 2.6% of players finish it. You can modify your champions looks, voice, name and sex, but there is an element missing that made it so I did not care at all about them, how they looked or sounded. The game is not really engaging and I did not complete the campaign on highest level, because I enjoyed the game, but rather because it made me angry I was unable to do so on lower levels. The game needs lots of work, fine tuning and the final boss should be beatable with most weapon options not just expertise with hammers and armor removal. Perhaps after graphics improvements and mods I might come back to play it some more. Final thoughts. I wouldn't repeat my purchase of this game in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you play and love King Arthur: Knights Tale? Are you an XCOM 2 fanatic, but also love the medieval setting? Then this game was made for you!!  ##### :REVIEW: ######1) The interface is fantastic. The game play is fluid and solid! 2) Setting and plot is great, the writing is decent, nothing cheesy, and a believable story.  3) Sounds and Voice acting aren't anything to write home about; I could have honestly voiced over many of the characters much better. lol ;-)4) Combat is fun and enjoyable. 5) Camera is very nice and easy to use. I like how I can zoom way out and get almost a straight top down view. ++++++++: DEVS PLEASE ADD AND FIX: +++++++++1) Why can't you fight on stairs? You can't even stand on them, either gotta be at the top or the bottom. This is lazy mechanic. Needs to be fixed! 2) Why can you attack people behind walls or crates. this should be cover and you should have to destroy the cover before attacking someone that is hiding behind it. Makes no sense that you can just slash away when their is clearly something blocking/protecting me! Needs to be fixed! 3) Castle Management has some nice depth, BUT I wish there was a separate interface page just dedicated to the upgrades, rather than having to go to each page to see what the current level is and upgrade cost will be. It's annoying to keep going through them to see what I can afford to upgrade. It's tedious and could be done better! You could use the empty space on the LEFT of the screen in the Great Hall. This would be a perfect place for this!! 4) Unique weapon missions: You need to show us what weapon we are trying to unlock? Is it worth it... This needs to be displayed on the map and somewhere in the top right or left of the screen, what weapon we are trying to unlock. Maybe have the weapon in a spot we have to collect on the map. Make it more interesting and more definable please! 5) Prisoner idea is great! HOWEVER, you need to either make it very clear as to what benefit a prisoner is going to offer and if you already have a prisoner with that bonus in your jailhouse. It was super stupid and discouraging when I captured my second prisoner only to find out i already had the same guy with the same bonus so it wasn't worth anything but gold? If I would have known that I might have not even wasting my shackles and saved it for another prisoner. How about you just have random perks for each guy you capture! At least show on the screen under details of a enemy as to what perk i'll get for capturing them.  =====: QOL / Non-Xcom Clone ideas: ======1) Why is the extraction point just a box in the middle of the field? Just because XCOM did it this way doesn't mean you have to copy it to a T? Lazy..... you mean to tell me not one person on your development team couldn't come up with an original idea for this game?  I'll give you an original idea for free----->>>> How about you have horses at the area where you want us to extract, then when you get to the area you click on a horse for your character to get on, then once all characters are on their horses you hit extract and they ride away. Otherwise it's pretty dumb when I get all my characters in the extraction zone to hit extract when there are enemies breathing down my throat. It would be more believable if I got to my horses and rode off with a short cut scene of enemies firing arrows at my party but I miraculously ride away into the sunset to complete the mission. Be original.. not a clone. This will set you aside from the tired XCOM clones out there. Unless this is just a practice project for something completely original in the future and you don't care to make money on this game? 2) You made beautiful maps and environments. Why nothing around to pick up or interact with on any of them, other then some stationary weapons like catapults, crossbows, etc. (which was a nice touch btw) You should have items, resources, etc scattered on the map and have pockets on the characters that allow for items to be held. Maybe each character can carry one  item unless you upgrade them somehow, where you can carry 2 or 3 items. This would be separate from the healing items perhaps. Everyone loves loot... why not reward the player for finding loot littered around the map. It could be gold, wood, leather, bars, maybe cosmetic items to change the look of your characters. 3) We need more outfits, gear, weapons, skins!!! After 17+ hours... I finally got to a point where it's getting overly difficult. Complete party wipes with 0 chance of winning due to my characters not being leveled up enough. And if you work on leveling up with side quests then you pass time that makes the enemies even harder. The worst missions I have the most difficulty with are the defense/protect area missions. Enemies just keep coming and there is absolutely no chance to win. :-(  So going to put them game on the shelve and let it brew a bit more. Hoping they will make some changes to make it more enjoyable and less annoying. It's still a fun game tho... just don't have the patience or time to keep repeating missions and trying to balance the leveling of my characters is very challenging as the game has too many timers and I feel rushed and stressed out playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: I love TBS games. I love medieval or antic themed games. I love games where you have a home base where you can upgrade and build up. So I really hoped this game will be something just right! Alas.. It falls just short in almost every aspect of what it tries to do. Because potential is definitely there!1. Fighting. First of all it's slow. I feel weird saying it about TBS game but I don't know how else to put it. For example: if I move a unit - I must wait until it finishes to move before I can order another unit even thou I can already select a new unit I will act with. Maybe it just me but I feel like I should be allowed to order two separate unit at the same time right? When it comes to actually hitting someone: I was frustrated on several occasions and the worst was how having 75% hit chance I missed 3 of 4 hits with a sword standing next to the opponent (its exact opposite of 3/4). And that theme repeated itself several times in different capacities. It feels like you miss 80-90% shots way more than you should. I remember playing XCOM and being frustrated if that happens, but it was quite rare. Something is definitely off with settings on this one.Secondly: I am not a fan of games there you HAVE to use Turn Based move even thou enemies are so far away that you need at least 2 turns to reach them. There are so many examples how to do it better. Wasteland 3, Mutant Year Zero, Expeditions: Rome - comes to mind from the top of my head. Thirdly - I am not sure how LOS works in this game but sometimes feels that enemies spot you even if you are behind cover. It begs for simple (hide behind cover) feature to actually be able to hide behind it and be able not to get spotted unless enemy actually comes really close.2. Home base. I liked the idea of having a castle with up-gradable features and its quite nice. It feels a bit lacking as well thou.. I mean we have a chapel to cure our wounded for example. At 1 level we can treat 3 units. Next upgrade: 4 units. And that's it. It kind of lacks in content a bit. For Barracks. Training takes so long that you can take same unit to different missions and get that level much faster.. so was not sure why should I use it. 3. Story. It's there but that's it. And to be honest if gameplay would be great - I wouldn't bother with it (like I mostly do with WarTales), but then one aspect is lacking you want to at least cover that gap with different aspect of the game. But that's definitely not a story. One nice thing I can say is that I liked the idea of travelling to your missions and seeing your progress on the map. I would however would like to suggest that you could incorporate a feature from Last Train Home where you can diverge squad from one mission to another, or for example if return home path goes close to next mission - give me an option to send the same squad there. Maybe with small nerff for stamina or something. Overall this game is not a garbage game or the worst game. No no no. It's just not that good at the moment. There is a lot of small things that can be improved or changed a lit bit. But until that or similar outcome - I cannot recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: After spending several hours with the demo of "Crown Wars: The Black Prince," I would like to share my initial impressions. A comprehensive update to this review will follow as I spend more time in the game.War of the Crowns: A Grim Medieval Atmosphere"Crown Wars: The Black Prince" takes us to 14th century France, where knights and bandits roam the land while dark forces scheme in the shadows. The game's grim atmosphere is enhanced by its accurate depiction of the historical period and the introduction of occultism and dark arts. This unique element adds depth to the game, presenting the Hundred Years' War in a new and fascinating light.Challenging Turn-Based StrategyAs a fan of tactical and strategy games, I was eager to try out the turn-based battles and management elements of the game. The challenges presented are varied and require both strategic thinking and good resource management. Assembling troops for each mission and the necessity to manage resources wisely create an intense and satisfying gameplay experience.Diverse Soldier Classes and Tactical DepthOne of the game's greatest strengths is the variety of soldier classes and their unique abilities. With classes such as Crusaders, Alchemists, and Beastmasters, the game offers numerous possibilities for strategic troop combinations and synergy utilization. The ability to upgrade soldiers and customize their abilities adds depth to the game, allowing for personalized and effective troop formations.Building and Managing Your DomainThe aspect of base-building and domain management is also well executed. Upgrading buildings and crafting new items for combat provide a meaningful addition to the tactical battles. This management part of the game requires strategic thinking and long-term planning, adding another layer of complexity to the game.Atmosphere and DesignThe game's atmosphere is captivating, and the graphics are impressive, especially the detailed recreations of historical weapons and characters such as Nicolas Flamel and Edward of Woodstock. The design of the dark arts and occult elements adds an eerie and exciting touch to the game.Conclusion: A Promising Start"Crown Wars: The Black Prince" has captivated and convinced me so far. The blend of historical accuracy, tactical depth, and dark fantasy creates a unique and engaging gaming experience. The first few hours have shown that the game has great potential to appeal to fans of turn-based strategy games and lovers of dark medieval settings alike. I look forward to spending more time with the game and sharing further impressions in a future update of this review.After several hours with the full versionNow that I've spent several hours with the finished game, I can say this: I'm pleased that the developers have released an update that fixes some issues with the controls and tactical depth of the archers on the wall. This update significantly improved the gaming experience and expanded strategic options, making the game even more challenging. The optimizations show that the developers are listening to player feedback and continually improving the game. One improvement I would like to see is that if one of my units is spotted by an enemy fighter, not all of my units should become visible to the enemy. Instead, the other units should remain hidden. This would add more tactical depth to the game.
