_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, but it is still a way off from being great. I'd prefer a neutral thumb than up or down, but I went with UP because I want the score to be better, for more people to play it, and thus the developers to continue to improve it. I see so much potential with this title and I hope they stick with it because it could legitimately be a medieval rival to X-COM in replayability.  TLDR: The game is fun, I'm almost 40 hours in on my long weekend and I'm still enjoying it.Now let me bash on it a bit.Right now even the good parts seem a little bare bones, or lazily implemented. Even the strategy guide that comes with the Sacred Edition is full of typos, incorrect images for some abilities, and incorrect descriptions for abilities that must have had their mechanics changed before launch and the guide wasn't updated. Leading to a seemingly overall lack of quality control and perhaps even rushed or lazily implemented features. My biggest complaint is along the lines of the people complaining about the turn limit on most fights. I think this can be an interesting feature for some specific fights, or for portions of fights maybe, like at the beginning you have a certain number of turns to rescue someone from execution, but after they are saved the timer should be removed. Sure some of your companions can heal themselves and others with skills on a cooldown but there are much better ways to prevent your troop for sitting back and healing up before the second engagement, which again makes this seem lazy.There is character customization, but its minimal. The animals can have their fur customized, but it seems like an afterthought. For example, I chose for the dog to be white with an accent color based on the 3 fur options, but when you click for both colors to be white it turns the dog into a grey-green sludge color.There are unique weapons in the game, 5 according to the strategy guide, which is pretty neat. Only your companions get EXP for using specific weapons to unlock higher level skills with those weapons. So by the time you get your first one, which I believe is at the start of Act 3, if you've done any grinding at all your companions will be at rank 3 or even maxed at 4 with their weapons and have to take a substantial power hit to start gaining EXP all over again on the new weapon, even when the weapons are virtually identical to the basic weapons they replace. Example: a Flamberge instead of a greatsword, or a repeating crossbow vs. a crossbowThey have released a notification about addressing the crashes. I've experienced crashes several times. The crash is usually preceded by graphical glitches, for example the status bar that shows how many days remain until a companion is healed will be blank, only showing the green symbol that they are still healing. Speaking of healing, the time it takes a character to recover is a bit too long in my opinion. It seems that around 10-20% health lost takes about a week or more to recover, and upwards of a month if the companion barely escapes with their life. My problem with this, is that with healing skills and items you can recover that companion back to full health right before you extract them and then they have no delay at all before they can redeploy. Either let companions deploy while still injured, make them have to recover based on how much health they lost rather than ended the engagement with, or shorten how long it takes to recover once back at the Domain.The extraction zones are also *ALWAYS* immediately next to where the enemy reinforcements are coming from, and it is always timed so that they will intercept you as you are attempting to escape. This is absolute silliness, only because it is every single mission that is a rescue or assassination. In the Skirmish you win as soon as you kill everyone, why not these two, why are there infinite reinforcements on those two mission types, and again ALWAYS reinforcing right next to your extraction?The awareness of the enemy units is also 360* which I think really hinders the gameplay. Maybe a crusader in full plate and mail would be too noisy to sneak up behind someone but the duelists have skill trees for backstabbing etc, allow them to ambush units with their backs turned. Or at least make it so they cant see you when youre behind half cover or something. The AI can at times be really awesome, I've seen some really clever sequences pulled off by the enemies and have been out maneuvered a couple times. However, it can also be completely imbecilic. The enemy prioritizes attacking your squishy units above all else. I've thrown down poison caltrops, set the ground on fire underneath them, and surrounded an enemy heavy unit only to watch the heavy suffer 3 opportunity attacks and run through the full length of poisoned/flaming caltrops, easily removing 90% of its health to make a single attack on an archer, dealing maybe 10-25% of the archer's health in damage. (This is a heavy unit with very high armor designed to be a damage sponge and it takes itself out). When against enemies that swarm like the Zerg this is an understandable tactic, but with humans (that arent WW2 Soviets) it seems stupid. Of course in most battles they have infinite reinforcements so maybe it is practical after all.Also the enemies seem to scale in power as you do, I dont know if its based on your companions levels or if its based on the in-game calendar, but it doesn't seem to apply to the story missions. For example, you can grind your troops to max level and fully upgrade all of your castle in Act I, and all of the enemies will improve right along with you. However once you jump into the story missions they are still designed for low level and you'll steamroll through it.If you've read this far you'll see I've done nothing but seemingly bash the game, but I'm just hoping the developers add this review to their list when they are making future changes.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: A surprisingly and pleasantly strong entry in the tactical turn-based genre with very solid combat and eco management fundamentals and a host of rare (but very welcome) extras -- like full customization of colors, heraldry, voiceset, and appearance of the companions and unique family lineages to shape the main story. Interesting, challenging, and above-all fun -- Who wouldn't want to shoot a medieval peasant in the knee with a crossbow before mauling him to death with a bear? Long version: I'd had this game on my radar since before launch -- but hesitated to buy when that launch was rocky. I finally bought the game after reading from the devs how they have seriously patched the game up in the last six months. That kind of dev commitment inspires confidence -- especially when the vast majority of the game's negative reviews are in response to launch-era issues that have (apparently) been patched out. So I decided to jump in.I've been extremely happy with that decision. Tactical combat is thoughtful and challenging, but not overly complex. As your companions grow in skill, they grow in complexity -- so the difficulty curve is quite nice and the game is accessible from the get-go. Combat itself FEELS punchy and impactful, with a nice but not overwhelming variety of weapons to choose from for your different companions. There are six classes, and each class can use different combinations of weapons -- some use Crossbows, some use Axes and Swords, some use Bows and Throwing Axes and melee axes. Etc. Weapon variety adds a fun layer of customization to your squad, as well as extra tactical richness. Graphics are very pleasant, kind of cozy -- very much not AAA mega wowie eye-bleedingly detailed. But again: nice to look at. Animations are generally excellent, especially the kill animations -- your macemen will pulverize enemies, twisting legs and breaking spines. Your axemen will chop an enemy while he's down. Dagger users will slit throats. Your war dog will rip out an enemy's throat. Etc. Really cool to watch, and fun.Eco-management is complex -- loads of resources with many different ways to spend them, from research to building upgrades to improved gear to new consumables. Resource management intersects with the game's time management and companion management systems -- you need to go on missions, which means maintaining enough squads for travel time while accounting for injuries/healing, training, etc. The different systems interact nicely to create the most important thing here: a feeling that you are making strategic decisions often and that these decisions shape your playthrough. Story is very B-movie, action-jackson pow and wow. A mysterious Brotherhood during the 100 years war is attacked by an even more mysterious Order at the start, your family scion (whose lineage you pick after the opening tutorial) dies in the attack, leaving you destitute and on the run. So you retreat to an old domain, and start building up strength again. Story missions then involve rescuing kidnapped noblewomen, killing bandits, showing up for meetings that go haywire and spilling blood, etc. An extremely solid 6 or 7 out of 10 on story -- I love B-movies, I like simple plotlines, I want to be given some nice framing for mauling people with a bear. It's just fun. I've watched loads of medieval movies like this (King Arthur, Black Death, Kingdom of Heaven, to name a few). English language voice acting is hit or miss -- while the narration of the campaign is great, the very first cutscene ratchets up the corny to 11. But it hardly matters at all for the vast majority of the gameplay. The most important thing is this: the actual unit barks during combat are fun (sometimes funny) and often quirky and endearing.SOME of the voicesets are truly not my cup of tea -- painful. But the voice and appearance customization is just such a blessing in that regard! I simply make all my companions into people who have voicesets I like. It rocks. Performance-wise: It runs great on my mid-range AM4 PC. No notes.All in all, a good game, with a unique feel and vibe -- perhaps in part because it's not just another piece of AAA turbo slop. Being not-AAA means there is some jankiness -- sometimes unintuitive UI elements, sometimes unclear interactions or ability descriptions, animations sometimes not triggering correctly (happens most often on Attacks of Opportunity) etc. But that's all easily overlooked or even adapted to and embraced -- because the game is really cool and fun.I admire the devs for listening to feedback and clearly polishing, refining, and rebalancing this game to where it can really shine. But I also have to imagine the game deserved a fairer shake at launch -- minimally, I can say with confidence it deserves one now. I've sunk thousands of hours in tactical turn-based RPGs like this, and this is a game I'm grateful was made and happy to play. Good stuff. Glad I bought it.Update: I've played the game a few dozen hours more since my initial review -- I continue to enjoy the game. Difficulty ramps up, but becomes more tough and exciting, around Chapter III. I've experienced one crash.I will likely get another 50 hours out of the game -- Can't recommend enough just giving it a go. The story, of course, is all over the place -- like National Treasure had a baby with The Messenger and John Wick -- pretty bonkers. The game throws characters at me as if I know who they are -- my cousin Roland, apparently, betrayed me! But I didn't know I had a cousin Roland. Etc. And the English-language story voice-acting remains wooden and oofy.But I increasingly think there's something kind of mentally deranged about criticizing a tactical turn-based game because it doesn't have "good story" and "strong voice acting." This isn't cinema after all -- it's a video game. And the gameplay is all there -- as is the music, sound design, and visual design.

_childDocuments_.review: At this time I can not recommend this game.Even after cancelling the release for 2 months 2 days before it was due out, the game is still full of bugs.*Bears can't run across buildings (they just freeze the screen.*When enemies are killed with arrows they just rag doll across the screen for 15-20 seconds.*When an enemy uses a skill to attack your own squad, the camera is focused on that enemy, you don't get to see who is being attacked or what damage they have taken.*Game freezes for 20 seconds or so when you've finished your turn before the computer will take it's turn.Let's not mention how unfair the game is, extremely difficult on the easy missions and how easy the difficult missions are.This game needs to be put back into the oven and let cook for a few more months before being released again

_childDocuments_.review: The mechanics of this game are wildly out of balance. I am playing on medium.All missions have a 'Time till defeat' timer which forces you to push hard and take chances on movement when you should not have to. Enemies ALWAYS get attacks of opportunity even if they use all their action points, while your troops only get them if you have left over AP which you never do. This forces you to engage troops in melee range to deal with them or risk taking an insane amount of damage trying to move away (This really SUCKS on the modes where enemies spawn forever until you get to the extraction point).Assassination and Capture missions not only have turn to defeat timers but enemies spawn in waves every 3-4 turns forever which means you are overrun and almost always have one or two troops that fall in combat. Your troops can only fall in combat three times before they die and you lose them. In a game where you level up not only the troops but the weapons they use for increased weapon skills... this mechanic combo is absolute trash. Enemies also ALWAYS know where you are when they spawn in, so they literally never stop attacking you. Skirmish missions on the castle walls give you 18 turns to win... but you use over half the turns running around the walls and you cannot split your troops up since enemy patrols are 4-5 troops. Troops that get animal companions add free controllable troops (Bears and Dogs) but the AI targets them instantly and they are dead by the time you fight two patrols. Moving troops/troop pathing is clunky as all hell and with the non-removable sticky selection of your troops half the time I accidentally move someone and lose a turn with them, or they move themselves into AOE traps you set (Caltrops or fire) and take stupid amounts of DOT. Devs need to remove these arbitrary countdowns for turns till defeat AND/OR limit the number of reinforcement waves. I could see this combo being on the hardest setting or the iron man mode but on medium it makes no sense.

_childDocuments_.review: ► Play takes place on a WORLD MAP, of the territory where the Hundred Year war took place. Filled with tokens representing story-driven missions and supporting quests which pop-up and disappear with regular vigour throughout the game. Only a limited number of squads can be sent out.► The actual CAMPAIGN would be short if only story missions were counted, despite taking place over five acts. Gameplay is puffed out with filler battles required for the resources to build up the infrastructure of the castle, the soldiers under the player's command.► The HUB/CASTLE (base of operations) is the focal point needed to beat the game. It provides an uncomplicated strategy layer that doesn't detract from the TBT combat and remains relevant throughout the campaign.► CHARACTERS are limited to set classes. Starting off pretty lame, it is only once they reach level 3 newly gained abilities begin to distinguish their potential capabilities in combat. Standout is the beastmaster who has a companion animal to control.► SQUAD MANAGEMENT errs on the side of less is more, embodying a number of choices from soldier appearance and set of voice responses, to the items carried in individual mini-inventories. The selection of armour they may wear; shields and ranged or melee weapons is fixed by their class..► The fixed-style INVENTORY removes the need for much micromanagement. Though there is some provision giving players the scope to equip characters with their preferences. With classes also limited in the amount of consumables they can carry.► The scope of ENCOUNTERS is thankfully wider than usual in this genre, given the emphasis on battles. While story-driven encounters propel the campaign forwards, filler battles are vital to ensure soldiers and the castle are upgraded to required levels.► COMBAT is brutal, yet frustrating. Right now unbalanced as it is, it only demonstrates its promise. It gets better once characters have gained 3+ abilities. Even then battlefield decision-making requires the painstaking deliberation akin to puzzle-solving. The use of a one point move/two point action system gives players great flexibility to determine their tactics. ► The AI is okay. It does sure likes to focus on killing one target, which it can do in a single turn if left unchecked. As if there weren't already enough issues arrayed against the player! This gets worse if the player has the misfortune of having one bad round mid-game.► AUDIOVISUALS are decent. Animations are clunky, but perhaps only because of a lack of optimisation (or my opted for framerate.) Voice acting of the narrator is better than in-game and cutscenes, whose voices lack weight and conviction.🔶 ACCESSIBILITY - The first act is essentially an unofficial tutorial, but the information offered is on the lean side. Each act thereafter introduces at least one new strategic concept to the campaign so the learning curve is about right.🔶 DIFFICULTY - x3 options are available to the player to set their preferred challenge. This review was made using medium. As such the first act was much tougher than those that followed.🔶 BALANCE - The first act starts slow as battles are tougher than they should be for a party without consumables and many combat abilities.🔶 PACING - The acquisition of upgrades needed versus the amount of filler battles needed to acquire resources, is pretty good. 🔶 SCALING - Strategic elements align with the rate of PACING. Across acts research and building upgrades match those required to progress.🟨 REPLAY VALUE - The story and their associated battles may be scripted, but random battles can make prospective playthroughs different. By then the player will also be in a position to be more choosey in the classes that compose their army.🟨 LONGEVITY - There is not much to keep playing beyond 100%ing achievements. For those inclined, the game can be replayed a few times, perhaps once per difficulty.🟣 QUALITY - With only a few bugs caught during play the game already has a fair amount of polish. Other seemed to have experienced more. It could certainly use some QoL on several features, even if already the basic game is very playable. Keys can be remapped.🟣 STABILITY - No crashes or freezing occurred during play. However, a small number of gamers have reported issues.🟣 STEAM - Achievements. Cloud saving. Overlay screenshot capture. Mostly compatible controller support.🟣 OPTIMISATION - The framerate can be limited to between 30 and 120fps or disabled. The game was played at 30fps. Low end specs like mine will run loud if not using a lower resolution.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a mix of good and bad here, play at your own risk. I would have given it a positive review but a bug has killed my save file (no mods) and I'm simply not going to restart at 60 hours in.[the Good]-The game plays like new era x-com with medieval combat with custom difficulty options. -There is a good selection of interesting low fantasy appearances, armors, and weapons to customize your troops as armor tiers level up.-A wound system is in place to prevent characters from being killed out right, something a kin to ttrpgs like Mordhiem or kill team games.-Different team compositions are required to get through the different factions, particularly once they start corrupting.-The prisoner system is a pretty interesting idea for tweaking your army to your play style but needs some more time in the oven before it can be fully digested. [the Mid]-Resource types cannot be sold or exchanged for one type to another making the trade post critical for getting the resources you actually need. Resource missions seem somewhat RNG.-The classes are all fairly interesting but some skill choices are really lacking compared to their counterpart.-The story and dialogue.. I waffled between subtitles with French or English. The voice acting is fine but the actual dialogue is nothing to write home about.[the Bad]-I personally can't stand the overly holy crusader dialogue but the class is critical and all around pretty awesome for any party.-There has been various bugs that have wounded troops outright, thrown outlandish RNG numbers or situations where you complete all the objectives and the the missions still fails (one being a story mission). Some other players including myself have reported these on the forums and they have yet to be fixed. I personally reported some light debugging testing and took a two month break in hopes of a fix. Came back to reload the save once again making sure that all objectives and surviving members were within zone.. still broken. With looking over the patch notes my recommendation is to find developers that value your time. This game has/had some promise.

_childDocuments_.review: Having to constantly move your units around out-of-combat in turn-based mode while making no tactical decisions is the death of this and any other game that decides to structure itself this way (or at least it should be). It's the anti-"just one more turn" of ta turn based game. I don't want to do one more turn, because the next turn is just going to be watching animations of my units moving all-too-slowly around the inactive battlefield. These interludes where all you do is groan in frustration as you slowly move your units around one-at-a-time, doing movements that never interest or excite you but are just tedious busywork, while struggling against yet another isometric game's typically unwieldy camera.This gameplay kind of worked in XCOM for a whole bunch of reasons, not the least of which is the fog of war and satisfication of setting up a perfect ambush in that game (and the controls being less annoying to struggle with, so the act of moving units around isn't as frustrating). But it doesn't work in most games. In most games it's just *boring*.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this 'Mixed' reviews feels crazy to me. For my taste this is exactly the kind of tactics game I wanted (graphics style, medieval/fantasy, customisation) and so I want to support it by leaving my review to try and encourage others. Personally speaking I've had no crashes or issues and have been playing this 60fps on my laptop plugged into my ulta wide (yes it supports 5120x1440!) and about 30fps on the Steam Deck (though it does draw a lot of power). Play overview: Maintain a roster of characters with a good amount of customisation including static upgrades of armour and weapons (and there are many different weapon styles to equip your characters with e.g. mace, halberd, dirk and so on) mixed with binary skills choices per level. There are set story missions that you can choose to tackle whenever you want (and it tells you what the recommended unit level is for these) and in between that you do as many optional side missions as you want. These side missions level up your characters and grant resources which are used for the aforementioned upgrades. Ranging from normal to hard ratings the side missions have different types e.g. assassination where you have as many turns as you want to set up your ambush, but once you engage combat you have X number of turns to get the target down and exfil to a set location all the while re-reinforcements will appear at set intervals. On most levels there is some siege weaponry you can use to cull enemy numbers quickly. There are also assassination graphics which I think are really cool, especially the one that the war bear does, so satisfying.So called 'issues': -There isn't a hyper speed mode but I hadn't thought that a problem because enemy squads seem to be about 4-6 at a time meaning enemy turns are snappy.-Time difficulty I think is on point, the game puts you under pressure in line with the objective (e.g. the assassination mentioned above) so you're not always under timer during missions just at a certain trigger point and I think it's good because it adds a very light puzzle mechanic to some missions where you need to think about where you are going to exit as well as make the most of the environmental benefits (could be a barn that funnels enemies or a cannon that does huge damage etc.)-Roaming to find enemies I think is being blown our of proportion. I think the idea is that on these missions you should bring the right troops and one of the unit types has a 'scout' ability that is designed specifically for this mission type so I think some people are missing that point. You also get auto saves every turn so if you found where the enemies were but ran out of time you can always wind it back a few saves and 'cheat' it.My feedback to the devs:-Unless I've missed this somehow, show where the exfil is at the start of the mission, I feel like in real life the soldiers would know this so it's not immersion breaking and it makes it easier to plan your assassination and feel like a bad ass getting in and out with minimal kills/damage-I think the scenario where you've 90% accuracy with your sword standing next to the enemy that ends up as a miss is a bit silly. I'd rather it be that in such situations you do a glancing blow or something so it's reduced damage-It's not clear to me if there is height bonus for the ranged units?

_childDocuments_.review: Overall Impressions"Crown Wars: The Black Prince" stands out as a solid tactical RPG with many strong points, particularly in terms of its graphic design and animation. The fluid combat system and reasonable RNG (Random Number Generation) make the gameplay enjoyable, and the tactical depth is comparable to well-regarded titles like "King Arthur" and "Final Fantasy Tactics." The voice-acted story and enticing cinematics add to the immersive experience.For the XCOM VeteransGame Pace: The game is slower compared to XCOM. You must wait for each unit to complete their movement before moving another, which can be frustrating.Over-watch Feature: The melee character's over-watch feature is underwhelming due to AI's ability to avoid it, even when concealed by line of sight.Enemy Behavior: Enemies do not patrol the map dynamically. They stick to fixed locations and only move towards the player when engaged. Reinforcements always head directly for player activity, making encounters predictable.Mission Structure: Non-slay missions often feel repetitive. The strategy involves moving in one direction to complete objectives and then extracting, with little variation.Geoscape Strategy: Optimal strategy involves prioritizing nearby missions and ignoring others unless they're critical. The research tree is basic, and consumable items are costly.Customization and Difficulty: Character customization is adequate, and the game offers a challenging experience with customizable difficulty settings. However, the game currently has bugs that can disrupt the experience, making Iron Man mode risky.For General PlayersValue: The game is worth the investment. It's enjoyable and refreshing, especially for those with limited experience in tactical games.Developer Engagement: The development team is responsive to community feedback, indicating a promising future for the game with potential bug fixes and quality-of-life improvements.Suggestions for DevelopersSpeed Up Unit Movements: Allow free-er movement for player units to improve the game's pacing.Fix Animation Bugs: Address bugs that force players to use ALT+F4 to reset the game.Enhance Prisoner Buffs: Implement dynamic changes to each playthrough using the prisoner buff feature.Improve Mastercrafter Buffs: Many buffs are currently not useful; rework these to add more value.Expand Geoscape Activities: Introduce additional mission types, like runner or scavenger missions, for variety.Increase Mission Variability: Diversify mission objectives and layouts to keep the gameplay fresh.Enable Roaming Enemies: Allow enemy units to move freely around the map for a more dynamic experience.Add New Classes: Continuously introduce new classes to keep the game engaging.In summary, "Crown Wars: The Black Prince" has a solid foundation and shows great potential. While there are areas needing improvement, especially for seasoned tactical game players, the overall experience is positive and worth exploring. The developers' commitment to addressing feedback is encouraging, suggesting that the game will continue to improve over time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fine game if you look at it as a budget title. Strategy layer is kind of pointless; mostly just take closer missions to reduce down time other than that idk, more of just 'pick the next battle from the list' as opposed to a strategy layer.    There is meaningful choice on what upgrades to take when so there is that.  Sadly consumables are too expensive when compared to the opportunity cost of doing a weapon upgrade.Combat can be repetitive though the maps can spice it up a bit and meaningfully change game play.  I love the use of siege weapons.  In response to other reviews - I see some hate about combat or balance and I disagree.  While not perfect it isn't bad.  Each class can work although each class has useless talents too so you can build a useless character but that isn't really a class problem.  Some talents are just a must take.  What is more important than class are upgrades.  An archer with a base bow is kind of useless. An archer with upgraded weapon, and expertise in that weapon, is a terror.   You need to adjust to these mechanics and not complain tricks you used in other games don't work here.  For example, have a heavily armored crusader take the Opportunity Attack to get better positioning.  Then anyone else can run by for free.  So instead of receiving an attack on an archer for 50% of its hit points you take 4 on a armored meat shield. Final thoughts now that I've finished - There are some rough animations, bear can be odd and slow.  It crash twice.  As mentioned earlier Balance around research is off so I never felt I could spend on consumables.  Boss mechanic was neat the first time, but not much changed when you get to the next boss.    Some of the hover over is finicky, I was 1/2 through before I saw a % chance with restraints.  Times with a polearm clicking "1" wouldn't work so I'd have to hit icon on the UI.   Special weapon pacing is off, I got one piece when I was grinding out some research and past the point I could have finished the game already.I loved some maps, hated others but that shows it had variety and the maps made a difference.   Probably for the first time ever I would choose the escort quest.  (They could be done fast like assassination and free the prisoner)   Defend the point I avoided, while interesting the strategy layer of trying to avoid damage taken back to base made it the least efficient mission.All in all, if you like turn based tactics this is worth playing if you keep in mind it is a budget title.  It is still being updated as I write this review so some of these little issues will likely be resolved by the time your read this.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wanted to play X-Com but you wanted it to be in medieval and with only 1/3 of the production value?Then here ya go!Cuz that's it. That's this. Right here. That's what you get.It's a medieval strategy turn based rpg set during the hundred years war between France and England. You play as a young lord whose families estate was sacked and now you've returned to bring it back to its former glory all while trying to figure out who attacked your family and get your vengeance.It has a big map you can send squads to and fight random thieves and bandits and eventually some evil organization.You can customize your units and level them up. You can upgrade your castle, build healing powders and upgrade weapons. You can customize your game with difficulty settings, it's own version of Ironman Mode, custom banner, pick a family to belong to each with their own back story and buffs.And then you've got the combat which is turn based and very very similar to the old X-Com games. The game looks okay I guess but it sounds even better. And despite everything here it still feels like it's missing production value. The cutscenes aren't as big or as fancy as other games over 10 years old. And once you get into the game it's pretty much just go here and complete a mission. Return home and see that you're castle was renovated while you were gone. Rinse and repeat.Now maybe the game'll pick up the further you play with more stuff included but I doubt it. It needs diplomacy. It needs espionage. It needs a side mini-game which would consist of large battles. It could even be similar to the fighter fights in X-Com where you just kinda watch a little clip of two armies fighting and you can buff them with things you unlock later. Kinda like how you're jet would take off to fight alien ships and you could buff it back in X-Com Enemy Unknown. But I doubt that's in this game and thats what I mean with lacking in production value.I just don't think it's worth 40 dollars. It's a decent game. Hell maybe even a bit above average but that might just be my proclivity to enjoy these kind of turn based tactical games. My recommendation would be to wait for a discount. But overall it's not a bad game. Just a bit pricey for whats there.If you'd like a more in-depth look at the game with video then please check out my review on my YouTube channel (link below).Otherwise, thanks so much for reading and I hope I managed to help some of you out there spend your money wisely.

_childDocuments_.review: The premise of the game is very promising, medieval squad based XCOM like game. We have some faction based mechanics (I've yet to experience) and a base building aspect. As I haven't fully progressed full the story I will not comment on that piece so far.My main problem is combat and level generation. As other commentators have said, you face a lot of enemies in certain zones on a map and you have to find and clear them out in most battles (despite the mission objectives being different). My main problem with this is the time limit, I have just completed a easy skirmish that have 4 squadrons based around ramparts of a castle which I was easily clearing out but takes time to run between each group of enemies thus in the last squadron i ran out of time. Rather than being a challenge/race against the clock puzzle it was a chore and not engaging. My guess is the level generated and worked out there should be enough time to get between units as the crow flies but didn't consider boundaries of the walls.I have also spawned into a map where I've had unit trapped under building assets that have no entrance but tiles open inside so I start a mission minus one character, without an option to cancel mission so I had to play it (luckily I won).The domain building reminds me very much of a mobile game screen where you just build up building chains with resources. There is no depth or customisation here.The character creation is okay, I do like the weapon specialisation and customisation of appearances for each character but I feel we are missing character traits, custom weapons (currently it is a upgrade weapon research) and just general care for characters. If my beast-master's dog dies in combat there should be something that happens rather than they lose 1-2 attack points and a couple of skills and then finds a new lifelong companion in the castle.I think there are some solid bones to a game here and my issues can easily be addressed with some tweaks to game-play. If this was an early access game I would be really hopefully for the future of the game and I really hope the developers quickly address mine and others issues but currently at the price i wouldn't recommend

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Turn Based Tactics games, I've really enjoyed Crown Wars. If you are a veteran of XCOM, Wartales etc then you'll find a lot to love here. You can build up your crew of highly customizable companions, and send them to fight in whatever creative way you want. Kit them up with all kinds of consumables, gear, and skills. The boxes get checked.However, the mistake is that this is not XCOM. It has multiple nuanced systems that are throwing casual players off because they likely haven't taken the time to understand them, learn them, and exploit them. It is one of the harder Turn Based Tactics out there sure, but has fantastic depth once you understand how it plays. You're not meant to perfectly win every battle, where your crew is untouchable, but that is possible if you get familiar with the systems within the game. But if you try to brute force 'XCOM it' as a lot are doing, then you'll get frustrated. It looks like it plays that way, but it doesn't. It is its own beast. Is there room for tweaking? Yes, a few of the timers and missions need a fix ,which the devs are actively working on, but if you craft the right crew and consider the playstyle of the faction you face then you can still come away with success. Graphically it does well, the customization all looks nice and you can go into significant detail. The battle fields have catapults, ballistas and all kinds of toys to mess with your enemy. And the finishing move cinematics are brutal and satisfying. Storywise it does the job, pretty cutscenes and well voiced. The plot is enjoyable and moves at a challenging pace. Overall, a really well built title with some room for improvement. If you are an impatient casual, then drop it on easy. If you have beat some of the giants of the genre, then go normal and dig into the system.

_childDocuments_.review: Had to jump in to help what I think is a pretty good game.Yes I've had the occasional crash, but the save system (on ironman or otherwise) is excellent. If you're sending a group of guys somewhere, and the game crashes as you click to load into the game, the game starts you off right as the group arrives - No extra time spent beyond the short time to boot the game up again.Yes, it's not as advanced as Xcom 2 though they share many similarities. I haven't found the timer to be -much- of a problem, it's just what it is. I like there being some haste. My absolute favourite part of this game is the setting. I'm a big fan of medieval ♥♥♥♥, and love the more darker themes added to an otherwise realistic setting. Magic is extremely specific, and not something you get to partake in. You're a noble heir-turned-lord leading a holy Crusade-like organisation against satanic-but-not-really enemies that are infiltratring the five factions.Customization is really nice, I'm a huge fan of armour upgrades leading to more helmets, shoulderpads, kneepads, etc etc. More of this please, shame about the standard weapons aren't the same.English vocalization is kinda weak, but a friend told me to switch it to French speak with english subtitles - And it completely sold it, I love the french voice actors. Wish they had English with french accents, but hey, French with Parisian accents are excellent too. Gameplay loop can be pretty satisfying if you love execution animations, I always love going through them discovering what weapons have what. In a world where AAA games have excellent animations and QoL but ♥♥♥♥♥♥ gameplay loops and stories, and none AAA have ♥♥♥♥♥♥ animations and QoL but great gameplay loops, taking risks and stories - I gotta say this is very comfortably in the middle. It doesn't take as many risks as it could've with its combat system to make it a little more interesting, but I love the animations, the French voice actors and the game in general. I couldn't get 1000's hours in it, but I'll probably end up on a comfortable 100+.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Medieval X-Com is good in concept and fair in execution.  The kill scenes are very satisfying. I enjoy the blood and grown-up look and feel to the whole thing.  Its very flawed though and you have to overlook that to appreciate this game. While others may fall for it's quirky charms, It's mostly for people who like the genre and setting.It needs some significant love though.  The UI has problems and it's been discussed. As a controller user I made several unintentional mistakes.  With no "undo" action and the clunkiness of controls, I actually lost missions over this which was frustrating.  And this game NEEDS better tooltips.  At least the option of it in the gameplay settings to have more details on tooltips versus a more simplistic rustic approach on harder difficulties maybe.  Because some of it is wild.  While random RNG nonsense is no stranger to these games, this game has maddening concepts that I'm sure go beyond randomness.  And could easily alleviate frustration if I just knew what was going on.  For example, I had a scenario where my archer (flayer) was two spaces away from his target and on top of a table for higher ground. And STILL had a 45% hit chance against his opponent who wasnt in any cover and I simply didnt get it.  Highlighting "more info" gave me no indication on why this would be the case. There was no explanation.  Just... a problem I had to deal with.  I'm not claiming unfairness against me personally or anything.  The opponent probably had some special stat that made him harder to hit or SOMETHING that made sense, but since it wasnt explained its more like "heres a problem, screw you deal with it".  And you can! With save scumming but thats not how we want to win these things. I also hate hate hate round timers in these games in general.  Now with an "assassination" type mission... ok the devs got me here it makes sense.  You kill your target theres a set amount of turns to get out before youre caught. That tracks.  Still dont love the mechanic and never will.  But I love the focus on combat.So why recommend? I just like it lol.  Thats all there is.  With only 4 different resources to worry about it's base building part isnt overly complex nor is it too simple.  Thats the thing that keeps me coming back to this style of game and theres just the right amount of customization.  Because I do NOT want to micoromanage my sqquads too much in the overlord campaign type thing but I still want them to feel unique and special.  The missions I played were very COMBAT focused.  I love this in these game. I HATE when I have to traverse all the way over across the map to find some tiny item only to have to run all the way back.  These missions generally (so far anyway) arent really like that.  I'd like a better indicator when there IS a specific place to go... but otherwise I do appreciate the focus on combat and mission objectives rather than things that waste my time like many of this game's genre mates tend to do.

_childDocuments_.review: From what I have played with this game, this is a really poor execution for a game in the user interface, design, and pacing categories.I will not be able to judge any of the deep content in the game, it was impressed upon me very early that the nuts and bolts of the game were not meeting my expectation.This game gives the player extremely limited information. Important pieces of information about the qualities of abilities are just simply missing and you cannot adequately examine things in the combat environment.For example, you have a defensive stance you can take that raises your defensive attribute. All you get is a buff indicator saying it is raised, you have no idea by how much. Are we talking about a 5% increase or a 50% increase? Is this a valuable use of an action point?You have a "chance" to incur status effects on enemies. Is this 90%? 70%? 50%? I have no idea, and I don't know how much of a benefit or malus most of these status affects incur. The information is absent. I must concede, I only played for an hour. I scouted the tooltips and hotkeys and found no way to ascertain any of this information. If it is there, I am sorry, but it is not evident to a player who has a lot of experience with tactical RPGs.I even tried to pull up my character sheet during battle to see if I could get an update there, but it doesn't appear you can bring up a character sheet during combat.Enemy capabilities are equally opaque. You can get some sense of their movement radius, but outside of that, you'll have to guess what they are capable of.I did not make it deep into the game obviously, but the design of the game feels like a worse version of all of its predecessors that it seems to be borrowing from. The class design seems a bit odd at first glance, but I did not have enough time to vet that thought.There is some really interesting ideas with the variety of weapons that you can use in the classes though -this looked interesting but I don't believe I can tolerate my other problems to explore this.The pacing of this game is really painful for the time I spent in combat. The entire levels are spent in turn-based movements and this really makes the pacing of the levels agonizing and clunky.You cannot queue up movements of your units and you cannot accelerate the animations of the units while they move. There is an unforgivable amount of time watching units slowly move into position one-by-one both by the player and the AI. I know that this was XCOM's style, but I just do not feel that it works for this game. A better approach would have been to borrow the combat style that King Arthur: Knight's Tale uses and package combats into bites instead of having the player agonizingly move slowly through the levels on the turn-based platform.Different players could take it or leave it - but I did not enjoy what I was experiencing.In my opinion, the overall polish is not there for this game. Too many quality of life features missing, a lack of information, and poor pacing just aren't acceptable when so many competitors have a much better product available. If you're interested in a Medieval Tactical RPG - look at King Arthur: Knight's Tale instead. It's not perfect, but it looks really good by comparison to what is going on here.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, I have been dying for something like this to come out but of course it was too good to be true. I have found the maps to be buggy; I have found a few spots where there is something like an open door in a building that is impassable and treated like a wall while also the opposite has happened to me where I have been attacked by an enemy at a much lower elevation and through a wall and the combat is completely unbalanced. The only tactic the AI knows is to rush you and they have no problems using grenades on friendlies if it hits you too leaving literally no counter-play to the abundance of enemies armed with poison grenades, you just have to eat it. Every Enemy you encounter is at least an equal to every character you have and that can be fine when you can take them on in small groups and use positioning to your advantage but that barely works The straw that broke the camel's back and compelled me to write this review and delete my game was sending a squad of level 1 Characters to a mission marked as "easy" and when I got to the mission it would've been completely impossible for even my highest level characters to win. The map was a mostly open field so there is no position that has any advantage over any other and alerting any enemy always alerted the entire map, (which has never been the case on any other mission) so I was expected to fight 14 enemies (all of whom are, again, at least equals to or better than each of mine) at once with 4 characters in a straight up slugging match which is the antithesis of tactical gameplay. I cannot in good faith recommend this game in it's current state. Go replay X-Com with only rangers or something like that and you will have a better medieval tactical experience.

_childDocuments_.review: So, even after the beta the game still lacks polish.  Not surprising, but disappointing.  I very much looked forward to this game.Some side notes:No combat or map movement speed up options and you also have to watch the same slow finishers each.and.every.time.Arrows can go through cinder walls (this I actually laughed at) - if these were futuristic weapons, I could forgive it (not really).Graphics are pretty mid for a 2024 game - they probably should have just gone for a stylized look instead to cover up the models and animation.You manage your domain, which is like your camp/base.  You can recruit, select classes, manage inventory, and do some appearance customization.Turn limits exist - I dislike this arbitrary mechanicRight click acts as a back button (nice!) - ESC is also back (not so nice considering you sometimes have to go back 4-5 screens just to save).Enemies can see around corners - this borks some strategy as sometimes you have to position yourself even further away.Enemies always seem to be placed outside your ranged units, so you're never out of the enemies range considering how far you and enemies can move.   And, it looks like you do less damage the further away you are making these units less than desired.Some enemy units are super tanky requiring your full team and multiple turns to kill one of them.Opportunities of attack! _childDocuments_.review: I came in expecting medieval XCOM, but I got medieval Xenonauts.If you know the difference between those two games, you'll get the gist of what to expect here, and "medieval XCOM" can build up a lot of hype unfairly against this game. Xenonauts has less production value, less mainstream appeal, but I'd argue it has more heart and you can really enjoy it if you don't just compare it to XCOM and give it a chance on its own. It feels the same with Crown Wars.You will probably want to start with Squire difficulty (and this can be changed at any time outside a tactical battle, thankfully!) and then work your way up from there to your comfort zone. The difficulty feels like it leans on the hard side due to timers, "stronger?" combatants, incoming reinforcements, and other factors, but also seems true to its intent of requiring planning, tactics, and foresight. It can get a little tedious to have to do that over and over and over (and I like upgrading, so I need all the resources!) if that's not for you, but a lot of missions can be really fun when you discover how to effectively use interactable map items like ballistae, trebuchets, and even bombards.  I had to discover these things on my own just by randomly bumping into them, and sometimes I wish there was an undo button to fix a mistaken movement, but I definitely think there could be a more informative tutorial. It does well to inform you of the basics, but I don't remember it saying anything about map interactables, and those felt essential to any difficulty above Squire.The AI seems very competent. So much so that it can feel unfair how good they are, especially if luck is not on your side, but if you imagine your group as ragtag underdogs it makes more sense (I don't know if that's really what you're supposed to be, but it sure felt like it). If you really take all of the options available to you, (e.g., taking wounds by exiting the map with people outside the area, not killing every enemy in your path, using items, sometimes just booking it for the exit and taking attacks of opportunity) it really does seem like the whole game is very fair and true to its intent--being a bit of a Hobbesian nightmare in the wake of a devastating war. I feel like getting injured and losing companions is part of the game cycle. I'll never, ever leave anyone behind (!) but I can see the elements that support your fighters dying and having to replenish them, definitely.Alchemist grenades feel very powerful, and I wish there weren't so freaking many of them in certain fights. I know they are a core class and they should be on both sides, but it can get frustrating when you have to fight several waves in a row, all with grenadiers punishing you harshly for even thinking about having people less than 4 squares apart. Overwatch is also something that can feel very underwhelming when you approach it like a gun-focused game like XCOM. It took a while to unlearn those instincts and use it more as a zone-of-control tactic for short range fighting--focusing on chokepoints and boxing enemy combatants in. The AI is good about not rushing headlong into it, but that doesn't feel unrealistic to me at all since the system also warns the player about rushing in. It feels like an even playing field that way. I would love to see a way to predict enemy movement/action ranges, kind of like Fire Emblem-style games. With the tactical chess match that higher difficulties can feel like, that could make a huge impact for the player. Sometimes it seemed like this might already be implemented, but I was never sure and it was never obvious to me. The preview system for targets available when moving is okay and maybe very fitting but having a simple indicator like a simple gradient to show how effective the shot might be at the new position would also be helpful. It was frustrating to discover that you couldn't set up ranged overwatch from behind full cover with the same range as a regular shot, but this also seemed very related to the "facing system", which I don't think got any explanation or introduction, leaving the player to figure it out for themselves. Once you do, you discover just how powerfully it can work both for and against you, and is one of the contrary-to-XCOM mechanics to re-learn.I'm enjoying it a lot so far now that I've got my head wrapped around it. I really appreciate the work!

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game that demands only a few updates to make it more pleasant to play.First, you need to play with the french audio, the voices are fun.The AI is good at normal level and manages to use its skills, environment, and focus on easier targets.Reviewers complaining about the difficulty rating of missions might not take into account that the different factions in the game have their strengths and weaknesses, so you have to adapt a bit to each of them. The type of missions and the flavor text coming with them also give you information to help you try to optimize your group. Being reckless can turn an easy mission into a nightmare, that's why it's a tactical game and not a slaughter party...Doom timers are what they are, you either like them, dislike them or accept them.The battleground generator gives nice maps that manage to bring variability (not like in some other games where you can see it's a simple different angle of the same battleground for instance). So it's definitely a great positive.To me the negative so far would be a lack of certain information regarding bonus/malus and stats.It would be useful to be able to see a sum up of the stats of your units during combat, and bring a bit more clarity regarding the % you win/loose with buffs/debuffs (a quick pop up window on key words for instance, without the need to go to the help section).The animation of bears needs to be fixed as it lags with the movement+positioning and can result in unwanted opportunity attacks sometimes.A randomizer button for looks and names would help a lot in the customisation of the characters since you end up rapidly with a bunch of soldiers.And i think artisans should give better bonuses in some buildings to make them more attractive.All-in-all it's a solid game that will become great with a few fixes and the hope of future content/addons with the success it should meet.

_childDocuments_.review: A medieval XCOM with a small touch of magic in what is otherwise steel and leather combat. You recruit knights, soldiers, alchemists and archers, and send them off to missions which earn you resources. You then turn those resources into a better base, which allows you to improve your equipment and recruit more squads. There are two main mission trees, but most of your time will be spent in side missions, which exist solely for the purpose of gathering resources and gaining experience for your troops. There's nothing hugely original here, but if you like squad-based, turn-based combat with a bit of base-building, then it's here. More detail:The Good- Graphics are good- Weapon options and troop variety keep things reasonably fresh- Can be genuinely quite challenging, and even on normal difficulty you'd be well advised to plan your moves ahead- Decent sense of progression as you train troops, research new and better gear, and build your baseThe Bad- You can't move multiple pieces at once, and move animation is quite slow, so you'll spend a lot of time, particularly on first moves, doing nothing but watching your characters and their pets move individually towards where the fight will take place. It's wasted time in every battle.- Although in theory each faction you fight has differences (heavy armour specialists, ranged specialists etc), in actual fact the only difference you'll notice is their coat of arms, so you'll end up using the same squad makeup all the time, which reduces variety.- The grind is fairly serious. If you want to upgrade all your armours and weapons, you'll have to complete a *lot* of side missions, and there are only a limited number of types and maps, so you do repeat a lot.- My pet hate is games which say your hit chance is 90% and then you miss that hit 75% of the time, meaning you need to resort to save scumming. This is one of those!The Ugly- Some serious bugs. The occasional crash is to be expected in an EA game. This has a few.

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen a lot of negative reviews complaining about big bugs and issues, but I honestly have not had that experience.In many ways this plays like a budget version of Fire Emblem and I found the overall gameplay solid, if maybe a bit inconsistent in difficulty. The number of classes is limited but they are fun to use, the historical context is informative and enhances the experience. The game doesn't knock my socks off with its visuals, but they're still pretty decent. The difficulty levels offer the tension weight of decision making like Fire Emblem but offer more leeway, with the option to have allies die after falling battle twice or three times instead of just once. The latter is still an option as well.There are two things from Fire Emblem I wish the game had though. First being the undo feature newer games in the series have. The game does mitigate this somewhat by automatically making auto saves for your last few turns in battle. This also, for me at least, mitigates some of the technical issues others have discussed. Generally very little progress is lost if the game does crash, which only happened to me once. The other thing I would wish for is interaction between allies, like FE's support system. The only problem is currently, the allies you get are random and also customizable; for these reasons  it would be difficult to implement as you can't really get attached to your companions. Overall I found the game to be very enjoyable with not too many issues. I was rather surprised to see the low Steam review score after playing. I did run into some bugs and one crash; but nothing terribly bad or unusual.I write game reviews for . A link will be provided when its available.

As the fighting rages in the Hundred Years' War, you are the head of a noble family seeking glory in this tactical turn-based strategy game. Fight enemy factions and battle an evil force that has corrupted the highest echelons of power and is exploiting the conflict for its own gain through a violent and mysterious cult.

From your castle - your seat of operations - recruit, equip and train your soldiers to fight your enemies and protect the population. Build your squads to suit your needs as you set out to find the source of the Evil and thwart the malevolent plot.

This collection provides a unique opportunity for gamers to experience these immensely popular and very influential games on Steam and includes a fantastic set of new quality of life features: Added Online Play* for certain games and Local Couch Play Save Anytime and Rewind Eleven Japanese Regional Version Releases Button Mapping Unique Development Art & Sketches Historic TMNT Media Content The games are based on the characters and themes from on the 80's children's cartoon and comic book series, The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. _childDocuments_.review: It's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunbga Collection, of courseYeah. But this is not a new game, but rather a new collection of old titles. Hence the word "collection".13 games in total per region. You can play each game in a US and Japanese version. You've got an assortment of titles ranging from platforming action, to arcade beat em ups, a trio of fighting games, and even a very rare metroidvania style game in the mix.  The platforms these originally appeared on were the Arcade, NES, Super Nintendo, Genesis, Gameboy, and their Japanese counterparts. I know it might look like this, but in the case of doubles (or even triples) the games are different enough to really justify them as different entries. There might be added levels in one version, better music and audio in the other, different bosses in both versions, and more. In the case of the 3 Tournament Fighters games, let's just say we have 3 very different fighting games that all happen to share the same name. Basically each entry in this collection offers something unique. No worries. Digital Eclipse brought over a great feature they also used in the SNK 40th Anniversary Collection. A "watch" mode. This essentially lets you watch the entire game in a sort of speed run of sorts from beginning to end. This can be used as either a tool to help you learn some stuff about the game, perhaps a strategy on how to beat a boss maybe, or just to learn the layout of enemies through a level, or maybe just to watch. The other thing it can be used for is to allow you to skip to a certain part of the game, as you can jump in any take over at any time during the watch mode. Yeah, that's right, you can skip right past that DAM water section in the first TMNT game. Keep in mind, you can not earn achievements for beating any games using this feature however. The other tool to help out is something that is being used in more and more retro compilations these days: The rewind feature. This allows you to rewind up to 10 seconds of gameplay. Really handy when you want to learn through trial and error on how to overcome something, or just a nice little cheat to help you out in a jam.These mixed with the fact that some games (not all) have some options to enable unlimited lives, level skips, god mode and other useful tools will make even some of the more difficult TMNT games a mere walk in the park. And of course anyone who does want a challenge, everything is optional, and it's really up to how you want to play. It does. But only for a few games unfortunately. And more unfortunate, the online is not that great. Hopefully this is something that Digital Eclipse or Konami addresses and works on fixing. And hopefully if enough people voice their feedback maybe we'll see them adding multiplayer to some of the other games. Well, aside from the games this collection offers one of the biggest museum modes I have ever seen in a compilation. You have high res flattened box scans for all of the console and handheld games, instruction manuals, comic book covers from the Eastman & Laird run up to the newer IDW stuff, magazine ads, old design documents and concept art, and more scans. You also have soundtracks for all of the games, and more goodies. The oddest thing is the inclusion of screenshots of various episodes of the TMNT cartoons. I guess that might appeal to some people, but the rest of the museum for me is where it's at! I literally spent an hour day 1 just going through exploring the various things, and I go nowhere near seeing it all.There's also a very handy strategy guide that covers all of the games, and is styled like the old game magazine guides we used to read through back in the day. I think it's both cleverly done, and also extremely useful at the same time. Aside from that, each game comes with a special menu to enhance the selected games features. For some games this might mean enabling additional characters, for others it might mean adding in god mode or unlimited lives. My favorite though is the ability to remove the flickering from the old NES games. You don't get the same options for each game sadly.Each game does also have a universal set of options that you can typically find in most retro compilations that allow you to add various filters to the games, and also to change the size of the game window (or even stretch it to fill the screen). Sadly because they used this as a shared universal set of screen options they overlooked 1 important thing... No Gameboy filters. Instead you have TV, Monitor and LCD screen filters, and this reflects on all of the games, including the Gameboy entries. So far this is my biggest gripe. I'd love to be able to play these classic Gameboy titles with better filter enabled, and ones that actually are representative of the hardware these were originally played on. Why yes. Yes it is! Well, it depends. If you only wanted this for the online play, that might be the biggest downside in general, as it is only limited to 4 of the 13 titles And even then, the online component is not all that it could have been. Aside from that one detractor, the rest of this compilation is bar none one of the better entries I've seen in ages. Digital Eclipse took great care to bring over one of the best retro museum modes I've ever seen in a compilation before. On top of that the games are extremely fun. And even if you're not a long time TMNT fan (who will have bought this regardless), and instead a new turtle in training, or just someone curious, there is bound to be something here that catches your interest.

This is about the eternal struggle of man against this ruthless life.It's about a whole generation, the youth of the late 80's, who engulfed a staggering amount of cash in arcade and large chunks of his soul, for games with glittering colors but mean, unfair, crushing difficulty. _childDocuments_.review: Not too long ago, , developed by M2 and published by Konami. While I enjoyed the small, but fun and exciting collection of games, I was disappointed by the uninspired presentation and scant collection of archival materials. Believing M2 could have done a better job in updating classic games for modern systems and preserving gaming history, I was relieved to see Digital Eclipse was the studio that handled the development of .Digital Eclipse is known for doing great work in classic game modernization and preservation, so I was not surprised to see  being a fantastic compilation of games and archival materials that memorializes the  media franchise. Every element of this collection, including the colourful menu backdrops, dynamic game selection screen, and comprehensive digital exhibits of memorabilia, celebrates the fun of Turtlemania of the late 1980s to early 1990s.Of the 13 games in , the 1989  arcade game and its NES port (), as well as both arcade and SNES versions of , are particular standouts. Sadly, the PC-exclusive  wasn’t included. I get that its omission was (largely) due to it requiring a keyboard to play, making it inaccessible to home console gamers. Yet, it would have been nice for us PC gamers to have it as a bonus title on our Steam version of this game compilation.I never got to play all the  arcade and console games as a kid, so to be able to play all of them now is a treat. Many games in this collection don’t hold up well, and  for the NES and Genesis just weren’t good to begin with. The truth is many beat ’em ups and action-platformers in this compilation have rather repetitive gameplay. As a result,  (a Metroidvania) and SNES version of  are comparatively refreshing titles. Also unsurprisingly then, online multiplayer is only added to a handful of games:  arcade, , arcade and SNES versions of , , and SNES version of .If it weren’t for nostalgia or historical importance/interest that we have for these games, it’s be hard to convince someone new to this game franchise to get . This is especially when , which was coincidentally released around the same time. Thus, my praise for  doesn’t lie in the quality of the original games, but in the excellence in emulation, the impeccable presentation and preservation of the classic games, the thoughtful inclusion of quality-of-life play enhancement features (e.g., rewind, save states), and the care with which the archival materials are curated.The museum of  game boxes and manuals, ads and catalogues, comic book covers, animated cartoon stills, original game artwork and style guides, and game music is simply astounding. Digital Eclipse even created strategy guides for each game, similar to those found in Nintendo Power. The amount of materials the developers have gathered and meticulously catalogued shows their love for this media franchise and their dedication to preserving gaming history. Digital Eclipse truly sets the bar for how classic game remastering, preservation, and archival should be done. is made for  fans and gamers of the Turtlemania era, and supporters of game preservation. There may not be many of us out there who fall into these categories for this compilation to make a big splash, but this is an important collection. If these 13 TMNT games aren’t enough to convince you to check out , then the impressive gallery of archival material may just change your mind. Digital Eclipse has done a fantastic job in celebrating Turtlemania and furthering game preservation with his compilation, and they deserve your attention, if not support, for their efforts.

_childDocuments_.review: Back in the early ninties, i was a huge Ninja Turtles fan. I got up on saturdays early in the morning to watch the cartoon, had the first two movies on VHS to watch them over and over (even bought them again on DVD a couple of years back and re-watching them now and again ;)), had some of the action figures and of course I played every Turtles videogame I could get my hands on, so there was no doubt I would sooner or later fall for this collection and I don't regret it at all.Overall, there are 13 games in this collection. Three were released for the Nintendo Game Boy, four for the NES, two each for the SNES and Sega Genesis and finally there are the two original arcade machine games.Let's start with the Game Boy games. The second one called "Back from the Sewers" was the one Turtle game I actually owned myself back in the day, and I played it so often that I still can breeze through it on easy and even beat it on hard. I still have all the tricks and strategies implanted in my brain. "Fall of the Foot Clan" was the one I occasionally borrowed from a classmate back in first or second grade, and while that game is p*ss-easy and can be completed in less than half an hour, it is still a quite enjoyable action-sidescroller. The third Game Boy Title "Radical Rescue" deviates a bit from the simple sidescrolling formula of the previous two games and is actually more like a Metroidvania game. I haven't played it back in the day, but even for today's standards it is a pretty good game, except for the absolutely bs boss run at the very end, where you have to beat all four bosses of the game again plus two forms of Shredder, and you have to do it with two life bars. It's insanely difficult and puts some of the Castlevania games to shame. But overall, all the three Game Boy games are consistently good.This also counts for the SNES titles "Turtles in Time" and "Tournament Fighters". "Turtles in Time" especially is probably the best game of the whole collection: I didn't own it back in the day, but I remember that whenever I was in a store that sold SNES games, I would immedately scan the shelf for "Turtles in Time" and just stare at the box, thinking that this must be the coolest game ever made. And if I would've played it back in the day, it most likely would have blown my mind: It is basically the best Beat'em Up ever released for a 16bit console, and while it definitely has its flaws, it is still very fun today. Furthermore I dare say that despite being way too hard on anything higher than the default difficulty setting, "Tournament Fighters" might be the second best Fighting game on the SNES, only topped by Street Fighter II Turbo.Then there is also "The Hyperstone Heist", originally released for the Sega Genesis. It is basically the Sega-Version of "Turtles in Time" and plays very similar, but in some areas it is distinct enough to stand on its own. It has slightly weaker grafics, but on the other hand, I found it to be less difficult and more fair than Turtles in Time, so that it is at least as enjoyable, if not more so.Now we hit the "Meh"-part of the collection: The two original Arcade games (The SNES-Version of "Turtles in Time" is actually just an arcade port with a few minor differences) play just fine, but since you don't have to pay for each try like you had to on the original arcade machines, you can start with hundreds of lives, which makes the games way too easy, no matter the choosen difficulty level, and ultimately renders them a bit obsolete and out of place.As mentioned, "Turtles in Time" for the SNES is just a port of the second original arcade. The second game released on the NES, called "Turtles 2: The Arcade Game" is just a port of the first arcade. It seems okay, but I only tried it for a few minutes, because why would I play a watered down and much harder version of the arcade with massively inferior visuals?Then there is "Turtles 3: The Manhattan Project". It seems similar to "Turtles 2: The Arcade Game" and according to the internet, it is good and the best Turtles game released for the NES, but it is also the one game in the collection, that i haven't tried out yet.Unfortunately, there is also a couple of very weak games in this collection, namely the first NES game and the NES- and Sega Genesis-Versions of "Tournament Fighters". Basically there is no need to talk about that first NES game. All that is to say about it: Everything the Angry Video Game Nerd said in his famous review for this game is actually true. I couldn't believe that there is a game about my beloved Turtles that is bad, until I played this game myself. Finally, the Genesis-, and NES-Versions of "Tournament Fighters" are not only inferior to the SNES-Version, and thus kind of redundant, they are actually pretty bad and completely devoid of fun, even if they wouldn't be overshadowed by the vastly superior SNES-Version.But overall we have a pretty good average here: Six good games, four games that are at least decent and that I'm just a bit indifferent about personally, and only 3 stinkers. Sure, almost every game has it's flaws and occasional spots full of b*llsh*t-difficulty, but all the different difficulty settings plus the modern convenience factors and quality-of-life improvements (savestates, rewind function etc.) still make this collection a fair, fun and highly enjoyable TMNT gaming experience. All of this is accompanied by an overall great presentation and tons of bonus content (stills from the comics and TV show, concept art, galleries with the original boxes of all the games, the original manuals, etc.).Admittedly, in the time of emulators 40 Euros is a little bit too expensive, even for devoted Turtle lovers, but when you see this on 25% or even 50% off, I can definitely recommend the Cowabunga Collection to every TMNT fan and 80s or 90s kid who is looking for that bittersweet taste of nostalgia.   __________________________________________________________________________TEENAGE MUTANT NINJA TURTLES THE COWABUNGA COLLECTIONGenre: Fighting / Beat'em Up / Platformer / Arcade-ActionRelease: Q3 2022( ) 0/8 Simply one of the worst games ever made. Don't waste any money on this.( ) 1/8 Bad. Seriously flawed with barely any redeeming qualities. Worth a couple of Cents at best, if at all.( ) 2/8 Sub-par. Only for hardcore-fans of respective genre / series. Don't pay more than 5 bucks.( ) 3/8 Meh-diocre. It‘s okay. Don't pay more than 10 bucks.( ) 4/8 Decent, but not for everybody. Don't pay more than 15 bucks.(X) 5/8 Good game, Must-play for genre- / series-fans. Worth 20 to 25 bucks max, if you are not a fan.( ) 6/8 Great game, universal recommendation. 30 bucks would be a steal for this.( ) 7/8 Outstanding game, a milestone of it‘s respective genre. Definitely worth its full prize.( ) 8/8 Simply one of the best games ever made. Get this, the prize doesn't matter.
