_childDocuments_.review: I am 41 years old.  The original TMNT NES game was one of the first games I had to play on my new NES and boy was it a disappointment. The game is legendary for how difficult and poorly targeted it was to the age-group the TMNT cartoons attracted.   In  typical Konami fashion, it was extremely challenging, and extremely punishing if you didn’t memorize it enough to master it. It was easy to get killed, because the game demanded you develop a certain set of skills. They demand you learn to manage your 4 turtles per each individual situation in the same manner MEGA MAN demands you manage weapons per situation. They demand you learn to master twitch reflexes and your jump timing. They demand you play to near-perfection or else suffer a humiliating and frustrating demise. That's classic game design.Modern game design has no consequences and is designed for casual sit down and play. Modern game design forces you forward instead of attempting to hold you back. Modern game design is like giving trophies to the losing team. TMNT  polarizes  reviewers then and now because the game itself suffers from poor game design.  Enemies respawn (or disappear) as you move from frame to frame.  Sometimes they respawn in your immediate path and you can’t avoid them, which causes you to take damage.  Running out of health causes you to lose a turtle and because Pizza (energy refills) are sparse, you’ll find yourself running out of health when you need it most. To make matters worse, if you lose a turtle, you’ll have to search for their respawn point so you can rescue them which leaves you open for more damage and more loss of life.    Further increasing the difficulty is that some levels have paths that lead to dead ends and simply entering an area may cause you to take more damage than you want to take. The Technodrome level is infamous for this.  When the game starts, the Technodrome spawns in one of five areas randomly leaving you to search for it.  You’ll have to fight through waves of enemies (that respawn) and are horribly balanced.  They ignore chip damage and invade your personal space causing you to lose health rapidly with almost no invulnerability period whatsoever. After playing through the first MEGA MAN games, I recognize that part of TMNT's difficulty being so poorly balanced is the fact that the respawning enemies DO NOT OFFER HEALTH.  In Mega Man, the respawning enemies can give you health boosts, energy boosts and even extra lives.   It's tolerable to have respawning enemies so long as repetitive killing of them gives you some reward.  Here: the most you can hope for is throwable weapons like ninja stars or boomerangs.   The game also features an array of enemies unrecognizable from the cartoon.  Bizarre  aliens and mutants who have odd methods of attack and generally present a nuisance as you try to make unfair timed jumps or avoid environmental hazards that either send you back to the beginning of the level or kill you outright. The COWABUNGA COLLECTION helps solve this by offering you a short rewind feature that allows you to rewind a few seconds to reverse a bad situation, giving you the Groundhog Day advantage.  Unfortunately, the game has input lag and many unfair jumps are even more unfair because your timing never seems right.   OVERALLY, I still give it a 7/10 for being a memorable staple in gaming history and the feeling of achievement once you are able to finish it.  I don't mind taking an hour to play through it when I have nothing to do. I've beaten it several times.What is truly needed is a COMPLETE REMASTER OF THIS GAME. The TMNT games that followed this game all addressed its shortcomings either by being created to be 2 or 4 player beat-em-ups (arcade style) which is exactly what the target group wanted in the first place (and very fun at parties) or they became side-scrolling singleplayer action games far easier than the original.   The feeling of adventure and backtracking is mostly gone in the sequels which is why the original remains so lauded. There are three Game Boy games included in Cowabunga Collection.  I still have “Fall of the Foot Clan” but I never played the other two:  “Back from the Sewers” and “Radical Rescue”.  They are easy enough for anyone to play through on their Nintendo Switch or console/PC.   Very simple, straightforward and with the exception of great music, they are otherwise forgettable and nowhere near as impactful (mentally scarring) as the original NES game. "Back From the Sewers" is a side scrolling action game with slightly upgraded graphics and visuals, but it's extremely hard for the young target audience.  Konami makes these games far too difficult for no good reason by reducing lives, continues and opportunities for power regains."Radical Rescue" is a "Metroidvania" style adventure game where you must use each of the turtles and their special ability to make your way through an enemy base.  You start with just Michelangelo, fight your way to a boss, defeat the boss, get a key and then unlock a cell to rescue your next turtle brother.  Then you must use your new abilities to move deeper into the maze-like base.  It's an interesting adventure, but it's very difficult and difficult to beat in a single sitting.  Furthermore, the replay value is questionable.  Once you've finished it, you probably will not want to play through it again. It's no wonder why TMNT games will be remembered most for the Arcade ports. In the 80’s and 90’s you would have needed the system, multitap (4 controller adapter) and 4 friends to get the full intimate experience of playing the ARCADE GAME ports.  I never had the latter two requirements. I played through the original TMNT ARCADE GAME in the Cowabunga Collection last night.  It was extremely difficult as a single player but because you have virtually unlimited virtual quarters, it’s easily finished in time.  Had I played it in the arcade,  it would have cost me nearly $13 to play through it in quarters as I died over 50 times.TMNT 2, I feel is more of what kids of the time wanted, but even it suffers from balancing issues.  The game is excessively difficult. It only supports 2 players, doesn't offer online multiplayer and the enemies are overly buffed. Your slow movement speed and slow animations allow the enemies to wail on your poor turtle in ways they can't in the newer games that addressed these issues (Turtles in Time).  Without cheats, it's impossible.    The game is designed to suck your allowance away in a Saturday visit to the arcade. It's not designed for young kids to simply "have fun".  The Cowabunga Collection’s online play allows for 4 players of each of the arcade games - which is a tremendous selling point.  Unfortunately, you are limited to just 2-players for the Genesis version, 'Hyperstone Heist' and the SNES version, 'Turtles in Time' (which are both basically clones of the “TURTLES IN TIME” Arcade Game) They are welcomed additions to the collection, but once again, they are mindless beat em ups rather than action adventures. Genesis’ Tournament Fighters is also included and 2 players online is supported. UNFORTUNATELY, in the case of the few games with 4-player online, the ONLINE NET CODE NEEDS SERIOUS WORK.  Playing with 2 players online was smooth, but the 3rd player brought so much lag the game slowed to a crawl.  Short of local play with 4 players and one machine in a room, multiplayer is very problematic.  If you have a Laptop/ Desktop, Console or Switch, I absolutely recommend THE COWABUNGA COLLECTION. It's everything I hoped it would be (minus the online lag) and well worth my $40 for years to come.  The original NES game  sells the entire package as the sequels are less memorable simply because they are mindless beat-em-up fun and relatively short. Considering that none of the classic console releases or the Nintendo Wii offer any TMNT games, this is a MUST BUY for TMNT fans young or old.

_childDocuments_.review: The collection is amazing with an entire room of extras including manuals, stills from various TMNT shows, snippets of advertisements from the 90's, various extra sound clips, and even TMNT style guides that the developers had to work with. The online and local co-up are both seamless with the only hiccups coming from 3-4 player co-op.You all know the games however, Tournament fighters is a janky if lovable street fighter rip off, the beat'um'ups are all gold and the various differences between platforms make them all worth a go, the NES original being a lesson in frustration, but there's an outlier among these classics.The third gameboy game, radical rescue, is an actually amazing metroidvania game where you rescue the other turtles. Each turtle acts as a power up with mikey hovering with his nunchucks, donny wallclimbing, raph going into his shell to become a morphball, and leo drilling through certain floors. It's an actually amazing game that caught me by surprise. Deeper than even Nintendos own efforts on the gameboy.

_childDocuments_.review: A well put together package, done with a lot of TLC...but it's not for me. My hats off to the developers for doing such a great job with this collection. I was a big turtles fan in the 80's and 90's. In fact, the best comic-themed movie to this day, is still in my opinion: the original teenage mutant Ninja turtles from 1990. Many hours were spent playing these games when I was younger, with friends, on the couch and in front of the television; or at the arcade, This is the problem I have with "retro"--which is a marketing term, somebody repurposed, in order to cash in on nostalgic memories, which has become an industry and a genre all unto itself. I sat down to play this, as somebody who is in now in their 40's and maybe it's the lack of sleep; but I just can't seem to enjoy them, the way I used to.  It's just a reminder of days gone by and no matter how much we may wish we could sometimes--we can't turn back the clock. I am a middle-aged cynic :D If it didn't force me to vote: I say the package is neither good nor bad; but it's a love letter to fans and should definitely be enjoyed with friends. The presentation is nice and there are a lot of extra features, magazines, box art, cover art, trivial bits; even stuff from the T.V. show and comics. The games themselves are what you'd expect; though a couple of them do feature online play. I don't really know what I can say about the package that hasn't already been said. There are multiple versions of every  game, regional differences-but the games themselves are largely intact, as they were back then. I will say that I think the price for this is a bit steep; the only reason I got it, is because it was for my birthday--otherwise, I would not have been able to afford it. for a collection of 8 and 16-bit games; it costs a bit too much I think. That's my major complaint about it: the price. What was really intriguing to me; was all the documentation: the booklets, the art, the behind the scenes stuff; even the design documents--I really wanted to look at those.If you're a turtles fan--it's a must have. Otherwise, I'd wait for the price to drop before you pick this up

_childDocuments_.review: I should preface that despite listing this review as "not recommended," I do recommend this game for any Turtles fan looking to pick up the collection during a sale. At full price I would not suggest it, but at even half price the value (and convenience) you get from having 13 games, alongside their Japanese region counterparts, is a great deal.Now going into my personal issues with this bundle, it has to do specifically with how you interact with the collection. Those 3 reasons being:1. ) As often stated, the online function is a ghost town. If you do get it, be sure you plan on either playing by yourself, locally, or you also have friends who plan on buying the collection as well. If you just search for lobbies, you will not find anything. The quality of netcode is also quite middling, I'm not sure whether this game has rollback or not, but it does stutter. Your mileage will vary on that front.2. ) This game, much like other emulation collections, is filled to the brim with manuals and strategy guides and artwork and all kinds of digital novelties. This game in fact goes above and beyond with it, there's even high quality boxart scans for every game. This is very fun, but unfortunately the issue I have is that the scans are so high res that it takes every page about one second or less to actually the load the assets, which are blurry at first. This doesn't sound like that big of a deal on paper, but it's very annoying when you're scrolling through the features, and especially so when you're playing the fighting games and have to keep cross checking strategy guides for movelists and other information. What would be a fun novelty became something I specifically avoid just because the asset loading turns it into an exhausting eyesore.3.) The collection does offer button mapping, but seemingly from the games I've played, you cannot remap the buttons attached to the emulator overlay screen and the rewind button. The reason this would be an issue is because when I played the Tournament Fighter games, I specifically used a fight stick controller, and I would accidentally press the overlay button in the middle of a match while I was playing. So for a collection of games that are frankly either arcade games or ports of, this seems like a very bizarre oversight to not test and optimize the emulator mappings for controllers that feature all-front button layouts akin to arcade cabinets.With this said, as mentioned earlier, the bundle of games itself is quite impressive and interesting. Personally I dislike setting up MAME/Arcade emulation, so having all the arcade versions available in one practical set is already reason enough for me to own it, but what's even more fun is that you have access to the Japanese regional versions of each game that can be switched with one press of a button, so really it's like having 26 games, and quite a few games in this collection have subtle enough (or even noticeable) differences to justify checking them out. Another incredibly useful feature of this collection is that you can activate all the "enhancements" (which are really just the original cheat codes/secrets) of each individual game from the selection menu, without having to go through the older process of plugging a 2nd controller or memorizing an intricate button code.The value you get out of owning this bundle is definitely worth it, however the premium features do not quite match the premium price of the product.

_childDocuments_.review: Konami certainly has been on a role with re-releasing their classic series these past few years.  Not gonna lie, I was surprised that they made The Cowabunga Collection, but I'm so thankful they did.  TMNT was the first interest I had as a kid and this collection has my childhood favorites as well as the games I didn't get around to playing.  Let's tackle this 13 game collection:  Always a fun game to revisit.  Yeah, the underwater level with disarming bombs is frustrating, but living in the age of the internet we have now, there are plenty of resources for tackling this bad boy (as well as save states and rewind features).  What stands out most to me is the devs based most of the game off the og comics since the 1987 series was so new when they were making this game.  Even 30+ years later I let the intro rock on this one because it gets me hyped up.  Probably a hot take, but this game is superior to the The Arcade Game its based on.  The stages are longer and have a better balance to them since the game isn't designed to keep eating your quarters.  Solid game all around.  This is the GOAT right here for me.  It was the first game I beat as a kid with my older brother.  I still remember so vividly.  A Saturday morning living way out in the boonies, my parents were out doing yard work and left us kids alone.  With Black Cherry Kool-aid and leftover pizza to fuel us my brother and I tackled this bad boy one faithful morning.  What stands out most to me out this game is it isn't based on a pre-existing arcade game.  Easily my favorite TMNT game (next to Shredder's Revenge).  I love the extra challenge added to the game where your special moves takeaway health, really makes you think about how to approach and engage the enemies in each game.  Also, this one has some of my favorite affects when the Turtles are hit with various objects.  As fun as it is to go for No Damage strats, getting flattened by a wrecking ball is pretty silly.  Similar to TMNT2 on the NES, Turtles in Time on the SNES is vastly superior to it's Arcade counterpart since it isn't designed to eat your quarters.  Also, Slash the boss of Prehistoric Turtlesaurus replacing Cement Man and offers the player a real challenge.  The game expands the Turtles move sets from TMNT3 and allows for more creativity in the game.  This is definitely the strongest game in the collection.  Really strange how incredibly different each version of this game are.  The SNES game is clearly riding Street Fighter II's coattails, but unlike most fighters from the 90's trying to ride that wave, TF on the SNES does is a remarkable imitation with depth to it.  I don't know what was going on with the Genesis version.  My guess is they were trying to cash in on the Power Ranger or Primal Rage crowd.  Not a fan of this version at all.  I didn't know there was an NES Tournament Fighter for most of life, but I absolutely love it.  The devs were clearly inspired by the og movie from 1990 and that's always a good thing in my book.  Really wish there was a GameBoy TF game so we could've had a version with Mikey on the cover.  Oh well Speaking of the GameBoy, FotFC is a charming little game.  With some basic knowledge and routing, you could definitely get a No Damage run on this game in a short amount of time.    Technically a more impressive game than FotFC, but there wasn't anything special about this game for me.  Definitely a one and done experience  Not gonna lie, I gave up trying to play this game in my younger days.  It's incredibly rare, and buying a copy on eBay is ridiculously expensive.  I'm glad it's in the collection and after some time with it, I really want to see what a modern TMNT Metroidvania.  I had always heard of how amazing this game was.  I grew up in a small town with no arcade, so I never got the chance to play this one.  It wasn't until my 20's when I experimented with MAME that I finally played it.  Wasn't impressed with it.  I decided to give it another shot with TCC since it has online support.  Even with 4 players, this game doesn't have anything going for it.  It's definitely a game where you had to experience it in when it first released as a kid with tons of quarters to have a good time.    Definitely a step up from TAG, but inferior to it's SNES version.    Let's end the review on a high note.  I really wish I had played this game as a kid when I got a Sega Genesis for Xmas instead of the Super Nintendo.  Maybe then I'd have some fond memories of the console.  I'm thankful that we got online support for this game because it's definitely the unsung hero.  And there's a reason for that since it feels like an incomplete game.  Just as you get into the meat of the game, you're already doing the final boss rush to Shredder.  I'm fine with it now since it makes for a short and sweet experience.  Also, it's the only time Tatsu from 1990 movie and Secret of the Ooze appears in a video game.  That's pretty sweet.I know Konami made video games for the 2003 TMNT series on PS2, Xbox, and GameCube.  If they do release a collection of those, I hope they give the games some QoL updates because all I remember from those games are loading screens.  They're solid games and need another chance to shine.

_childDocuments_.review: You either grew up on these games or you didn't, all there is to it really. This was my childhood, both the cartoon and most of these games. Had all the nes/snes games and must have played the two arcade machines 1000s of times at various pizza places and other arcades. Just mindless fun really, it essentially was some of the happiest times of my childhood. $40 is steep if you this wasn't your childhood, but anyone who grew up on these games 40 is a fair price when you break it all down. You are getting 13 games all ported perfectly, box art scans, instruction manual scans, and a bunch of other extras as well. Local coop play even tho that isn't really much of a thing these days as an adult and online play for some of the titles as well. Online seems to be hit or miss, but even if it was perfect, it's not why I bought this collection. I just wanted to experience my childhood again and have all the games in one legal and easy place. They put a lot of work into this collection not to mention the legal hurdles they had to deal with for all the various licenses, I really wish more companies would release high quality collections like this. Mortal kombat, metal gear solid, original resident evil trilogy, just a few games off the top of my head would be great, but that is for another day. Anyway a review isn't going to convince you to buy this collection or not, when you first saw the trailer for this collection and the announcement, you knew you were going to buy it or you were not, this is simply a love letter to turtle fans. Any younger people wanting to check these games out, I'd honestly say wait for a sale unless you just have $40 burning a hole in your pocket atm. I just want to end it by saying thank you to the devs who worked so hard on this project and konami for being on board with getting this collection out, you have delighted the young child that died in my heart years ago and if even for a short while, it was fun to get to relive some of those precious memories once more.

_childDocuments_.review: A good collection of games that sadly only includes the 13 arcade and console games released before 1995 and nothing in the years after that.Online play is added for a few games which is good, assuming you already have someone to play with.Presentation is nice, although they apparently don't have rights to have some of the proper music to play with the games even though they are part of the original games.Some games have additional mod settings you can use to change how they are play, though somewhat limited and vary between each game.The 'digital bonuses' are ok, although you will not ever look at them for more than a couple minutes, unless you really want to read through the old manuals. They also include a lot of comics, but they're literally only showing you the cover art; you can't read any of them, which is very disappointing. In addition, some of the bonus ads and magazine articles included are heavily censored in an attempt to hide anything non-turtle related.All in all, it's a good purchase for any turtles fan, but honestly, even though you're getting 13 games with this, it's simply not worth the full price. Only buy it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection is a nostalgic compilation that brings together a selection of classic TMNT games from the late 1980s and early 1990s. Released by Konami, this collection is a treasure trove for fans of the franchise, offering both gameplay and historical context for each title included.The collection features 13 titles, including fan favorites like Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles IV: Turtles in Time and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Arcade Game. Each game has been carefully preserved, allowing players to experience the original gameplay while also benefiting from modern enhancements such as save states and rewind functionality. This makes it accessible for both newcomers and seasoned veterans who may want to relive their childhood memories.While the graphics remain true to their original pixel art style, they have been upscaled to fit modern screens without losing their charm. The audio retains its iconic soundtracks, which are instantly recognizable to fans. The combination of retro visuals with enhanced clarity creates an engaging experience that feels both nostalgic and fresh.The user interface is intuitive, making it easy to navigate between titles. Additionally, the inclusion of a comprehensive museum section provides insights into the development of each game, featuring artwork, design documents, and interviews with key creators. This aspect not only enriches the gaming experience but also serves as an educational resource for those interested in video game history.Many titles in the collection support local multiplayer, allowing friends to join in on the fun just like in arcades of yore. This feature enhances the social aspect of gaming, making it a perfect choice for gatherings or family game nights.Overall, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection is a well-executed homage to one of gaming’s beloved franchises. It successfully balances nostalgia with modern conveniences, making it a must-have for TMNT fans and retro gaming enthusiasts alike.Highly recommend this game 10/10   , thank u for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: What you need to know is that all of the games are Ninja Turtle nostalgia for 80s and 90s kids. When I was young I remember playing the vast majority of these titles. And as a grown up, I now see just how ruthless Konami could be as a brand, 'cause they straight-up repackaged some of the games over and over again for the profit. Perspective and time sure is one hell of a way to see some hard truths.Either way, I still loved the Cowabunga Collection, not just for the games but for all the extras that come with it. Seeing the old ADs from magazines and all of the different era of comic covers, along with stills from the animated series up until the more recent revised Ninja Turtle series are perfect. The catalog of character and game design pages are great insight into how to build up the content you want to create if you desire to become a video game creator, which should be done more by companies. I mean, they used some of the original drawings to show all of this -- super cool behind the scenes look in my eyes.If you are on the fence on buying The Cowabunga Collection remember, these are classic games with all the classic feels and more. Take a trip down memory lane to a simpler time if you are of the age, and if you are young, dive into the realm of retro gaming and see what paved the way for where we are now.

_childDocuments_.review: A ton of fun, solid action games that take between 20 minutes and an hour (mostly around an hour each). _childDocuments_.review: TBH, it's overpriced and the online is dead. Those are really the only two criticisms I would have. Absolutely not worth $40, but the $20 I paid on sale wasn't terrible.That said, I still had a great time playing through all of the games again. I feel like I was able to get a really good sense of comparison for things like Turtles in Time (SNES) vs Turtles in Time (Arcade) vs Hyperstone Heist. Also the original arcade game vs the NES port. I made it a point to practice the NES games with help from save states and rewind so that I could then go to my real NES and beat the original games without help. One interesting thing I feel like I learned in all this is that the arcade games may be prettier, but ultimately the console versions are more fun to play because they have tighter controls and actually forced you to play well to win. Arcade games were a little more mindless when you just add more coins to win. Also, I would say the first NES TMNT game is actually the most fun to replay once you've got the hardest parts down. There's a lot more depth to it and some random elements that keep you on your toes. The one game in the collection I had never touched before was the third gameboy game, which I had no idea was a metroidvania style game. The bosses were tough mofos, but it was a very fun game.If you love the old turtles games and want to give them a deeper dive or if you never played them before, then I think you'll have a lot of fun with this. The NES and GB games in particular though require a bit of determination to get through, but honestly worth the effort.You could just as well emulate these games too though and I certainly have. From a game standpoint, there's nothing extra here. The collection is probably better for fans that like the extras or like the simplicity of pulling this up and picking a TMNT game.
_childDocuments_.name: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection

_childDocuments_.review: If you love TMNT, and especially love the classic games Konami did back in the day, this is a major win. All the additional stuff featured like strategy guides and tips designed by the current devs to help you out, the original game manuals and boxes recreated here, all kinds of behind the scenes stuff, and online play for a few of the key games (sadly not all of them, but at least we've got other options to get around that), there's a lot to like about this package.Considering you're getting 13 games with various enhancements and cheats enabled right from the start, plus a save feature the original games didn't have, and all the tips and hints laid out for you at your disposal, it's worthy of the price. The fact they did more than just throw the roms together and sell it back to us is worth applauding them for, there's a lot of effort put into this that makes it really cool to have. Definitely recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Holy cow, this is an amazing collection. 95/100EXTRAS: Filled with game boxes and manuals from all the games, comic book covers from the last thirty years, screenshots of each seasons of the four TV series, music from each game. And of course notes from the designs and behind the scenes documents. The EXTRAS section is full of a massive amount of stuff. GAMES: Near perfect and perfect emulation. The music from the original arcade game beginning is different due to licensing (Arcade1up encountered this as well), and I think one or two sound effects sounded different from what I remember, but otherwise a truly masterful collection of the old TMNT games. Growing up in the 80's, I was able to play nearly every game in this collection, except for any of the three Tournament Fighters (SNES, Genesis, or NES) since I wasn't a fan of those games, although I was a fan of Street Fighter 2. I played every game in the 80's and early 90's a ton of times, and finished them as well multiple times. This collection is perfect. CONTROLLER: I use a Google Stadia controller, and I setup a Turbo button for attack in Steam so I don't have to keep pressing the attack button. It's lazy gaming but so satisfying. I also tested and used my Xbox 36 controller, and no problems. It works perfectly, although I did have to reconfigure my controller settings and setup Turbo attack for the Xbox360 controller. When I first started the game, the keyboard and controller were not recognized but then I just clicked my mouse a few times on the screen and then I was able to press ENTER on the keyboard and my Google Stadia controller was recognized as well. SAVE/LOAD: There's only one save slot, but the ability to save and load is awesome. Also the Left shoulder allows the ability to rewind.  I originally thought having a single SAVE slot was fine, but now I think having three to five SAVE slots with screenshot of each SAVE (so I know where in the game that I saved) would be perfect. See notes at bottom in "things to improve" section. SAVING NOTE:  Saving your game in the US version of a game is a separate SAVE file from the JAPAN version of the game (but not all games have a Japan version), so you don't have to worry about your SAVE file overwriting when switching between US and JAPAN versions.  The Turtles in Time Arcade game only has a US version. Even though it says JP at the bottom, it hasn't switched, since there is no JP version of Turtles in Time Arcade.  You can tell when you do switch betwen US and JAPAN versions when the title of the game switches or the cover switches. If there is no change in either of the two, then there's no JAPAN version.  I tested and verified it using a run with MIKE in the US version and RAPH in the Japan version on TMNT Arcade, TMNT Turtles in Time Arcade, and TMNT Turtles in Time SNES.SETTINGS: I set the filter to TV FILTER, do a FULL SIZE screen, and remove the border so its black borders. To me, this is perfect. Love playing these game so much. I own the TMNT arcade machine from Arcade1up with the two arcade games, but I had to buy this collection. This collection is a must own since I can play on a bigger monitor and with an Xbox  controller or arcade controller and I'm 100% satisfied with my purchase. Highly recommended.THINGS TO IMPROVE: Now that I play it more, i guess just having a few more save slots instead of one, especially with a screenshot of the save point so I know the location in the game where I saved it. Even having the screenshot of the location in the game right now with a single SAVE point would be extremely useful. Each game does allow you to choose the starting level through the Enhancements, but sometime I want to start right at Shredder and not have to worry about fighting through the level. It doesn't take more than a few minutes, but it would be nice to have a few more save slots.

_childDocuments_.review: A good collection of games, a bad selection of video options. I don't consider myself too picky but there are no interpolation options leaving you stuck with hard edge nearest neighbour pixels. This would be fine except for the games not having consistent pixel sizes resulting in shimmering with motion.There are several filters to choose from but they're not filters so much as overlays. One adds scanlines, which is nicely implemented and the only one I find usable, your other choices are an uneven shadowmask or an equally uneven pixel grid that both look like a mess.For the asking price the lack of basic options here is a cowabummer.

_childDocuments_.review: For a single player experience, this package is the real deal - and I couldn't recommend it enough. There's so many great games bundled into one package, and a TON of extra content that Turtles fans will really enjoy.However, the reason I don't recommend this game is that the online experience - a major selling point, and the main reason I wanted this in the first place - is currently a mess. Two player co-op on any of the arcade-like titles has bizarre audio issues that results from emulation being slowed down to compensate for connectivity issues, and playing with three to four players has such poor performance that I'd classify it as utterly unplayable. For $40, the online experience being how it is currently is a MAJOR issue. I'm hoping Digital Eclipse fixes this soon. I'm really disappointed. There's clearly a lot of work and love that went into compiling this, so a flaw as bad as this is surprising. Once online play has been fixed and works well (or at least, works passably), I will reconsider purchasing. But right now, I can't recommend it at this price.
_childDocuments_.name: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this to play online with other people. I was actually really looking forward to that experience.Unfortunately the online feature is a bust. There are no servers. You connect to people's computers directly, resulting in a very broken, laggy, glitchy experience. There's no way of knowing what your ping distances are, etc. You can't pick and choose lobbies.  You'd have to invite -local- friends to play it with you if you want to have a smoother experience. But hardly anyone plays online. So it's basically dead on that front. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯While the included games do play quite well and the extra content is fairly vast (and some, rather redundant), with helpful maps and tips,  I still feel that paying upwards of 40 dollars is simply not worth it to me. Maybe when it's on sale.I was just really hoping the online feature would be as great as Shredder's Revenge, which provides a more robust experience, though not always perfect either. SR is a lot of fun. They added a set of ...well, not the best CRT overlays and one decent LCD filter (for the Gameboy titles). But I would rather use Reshade for this. It's simply more efficient than the overlays provided (which have no bilinear filter).You can play these games fullscreen without borders or smaller aspect ratio with borders. I always go full screen no borders. The borders, while nice, I find to be a visual distraction and I wish there was a dimming option for each one. With that said, I sadly can't recommend this unless you're a huge fan of the library and never emulated before in your life and don't care about online play. All games ran really well. The extra content is pretty rad. Full high res game manuals, etc.  Also, not all games have the option to run multiplayer online. Only like 5 games are available for that. The first two arcade games and their console ports and I believe the Tourney fighters are now available. Here's hoping they continue to update the game and help with the online feature along the way.. But, since it is peer-to-peer, I can't imagine them doing more on that front. It really depends on the amount of activity from people playing online, which there isn't much of at this moment.:(I wish I could rate this a "maybe" or "eh", because its not a bad collection,  but because online is really what I wanted the most from this collection, I have to say no.

_childDocuments_.review: Full Steam Deck Performance Preview Here: I was definitely looking forward to jumping on the Cowabunga Collection early to play some of the Arcade games that really was a part of my Arcade experience as a child. The home console titles in the collection are great, but the Arcade titles really were the draw for me. My disappointment in the game started with the lack of games available to networked multiplayer. Only 4 titles in the collection let you play online. In some ways this is not surprising, but it shows how little was done to really turn these titles into a quality release. That was the first issue...then I tried playing an online session...wow. The idea of drop-in, drop-out was amazing. How could you go wrong with random people being able to leave and someone ready to fill their spot? Well, the impact to the game when someone enters is almost game breaking. It basically causes the game to choke and stall. The lag is horrible and you essentially end up with an unplayable mess. I actually thought that it can't be that bad, and maybe it was my wireless connection via the Steam Deck, so I tried on my hardlined PC Rig and had the exact same experience...How can you release this?!If you are only looking to relive the experiences locally on your couch with friends, then I think the game is okay, but for me, I moved far away from the friends that used to play the game with me and I don't think the game is up to par to pay the asking price. Hopefully they fix the online play and I'll try once again, but for now, it is a refund.Want to just see the online play? _childDocuments_.review: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection is the avid fan's dream collection. Finally, a singular source to play all the old classics without having to rely on old consoles, ROM's, emulators, or any other hi-tech jazz (old man alert!). Having acquired the game for ~$20 USD (on sale), I'd consider the Cowabunga Collection to be an incredible value - especially when you consider how many titles you get. Granted, there are some console-specific redundancies in the list but it's still a lot of unique games nonetheless.The inclusion of various screen filters and the ability to rewind live play or add credits at will are excellent QOL features that mix both nostalgia and modernity.All positivity aside, there are some elements of this collection that aren't so great. For starters, the UI/menus for a lot of the titles seem clunky and unintuitive. Some titles force you to pick your player count and turtles before even launching your chosen TMNT game but still navigate you through the normal in-game character selection screen (albeit unable to cycle through characters at this point). I don't know enough about the porting process or the logistics for allowing these older games to have online play but the pre-game selection menu feels mildly annoying and needlessly cumbersome when encountered. Additionally, some of the 'extra features' artwork feels a bit tacked on. The manner in which you can browse and view the content is tedious and makes the effort of looking through the extra materials off-putting. A large majority of the included material is just untranslated box art, concept drawings, and other art from Japan. I wasn't aware that TMNT was such a big deal over there but all of the in-game artwork makes it seem like it was HUGE! Some extra history snippets or translations of the included images would have been a nice addition to contextualize all of the Japan-specific artwork but I suppose what we got is better than nothing (or so the developer/publisher probably thought). All-in-all, a great purchase for big-time TMNT fans. However, if you're not enchanted by nostalgia or are newer to the world of TMNT games, I highly recommend you consider skipping this collection and instead starting off with 'Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge.' It is the newest TMNT game and is absolutely phenomenal - perfectly blending all of the best elements of the older arcade titles/cartoon media and utilizing more modern mechanics and QOL features that breath new life into the series. Having played them all (and as blasphemous as this may seem), TMNT: Shredder's Revenge is so good that it makes the older titles look way worse in comparison....but hey, if you're ballin'-shot-callin' you could always just get both! ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

_childDocuments_.review: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection is a collection of almost all the TMNT games released in the 1980's cartoon's run.  The games all play exactly as one would expect on classic hardware.  Where this is both good & bad, it leans much more toward the good side of things.  Each game comes with a variety of options, though more were given to the more robust titles.  It also has the standards of newer compilation, that being the ability to save, as well as rewind a few seconds back to correct mistakes. Though an extensive list, it is lacking a few titles for obvious reasons (Manhattan Missions is a DOS game with an inability for controller layouts & Pinball is owned by Data East).  The only real hiccup is that a good number of the titles, while positively here for preservation, are just not very good.  The Game Boy titles are pretty much just there, the NES titles are still punishingly difficult, & the Tournament Fighters all feel incredibly basic, even for their time. One just needs to clear every title in order to complete this list.  Though difficult, there are plenty of ways to cheese them.  The biggest thing to note it that some of the games cannot be completed on Easy, due to the need to achieve the harder ending.  The rewind feature can be your best friend in those regards. Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection is another standout retro collection from Konami, with the best TMNT games (arguably best beat 'em ups) of their time, as well as the other titles for ease of accessibility & preservation.  It's flaws are minor at best, making this a must have for TMNT fans, beat 'em up enthusiasts, or just those wanting a few hours of retro play.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a compilation of all classic Konami developed titles with the license of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles from the late 80s to the mid 90s, across several platforms and with different regions presented. If you’ve had experience with similar official collections before, you might know that it is basically a set of game ROMs running in hopefully perfect emulation with little to no changes to how games used to be, unless specifically enabled. There’s one slot save state per game and all games have some sorts of “enhancements”, ranging from just reducing slowdown and sprite flicker that the original hardware running these games would have, to enabling invincibility or special debug abilities. Apart from the save state, you can also rewind, which is another typical ability in modern emulation.Unfortunately, the collection has some rather frustrating limitations in terms of button rebinding, so if you would want to play a select title with a platform-correct controller, it might be tough to make things work as intended. But as a nice bonus, the collection features not only games, but also scans of box art, covers of the comic books, stills from the animated series, design documents for the games and other cool behind the scenes elements. They are rather limited, but are still a welcome addition. Plus, given that a lot of the games in the collection are best played in coop, several titles (mostly best ones) support playing them online with friends.But are the games worth revisiting, especially now that Shredder’s Revenge exists?Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles for the NES is conceptually really cool and has wonderful music, but the “difficulty” is unreasonable and you can die in seconds or get locked into an unwinnable situation without even realizing it.Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (Arcade) still looks good, has plenty of fine stages and cool tunes. But it’s also pretty rough and it also has a lot of the “quirks” typical for arcade games that were meant to be somewhat unfair. Whereas the NES version of the game, due to hardware limitations and its attempts to mimic the arcade game, is pretty frustrating. The combat and movement feels stiff, turtles are very slow, most hits send you flying across the screen, enemies are tougher and faster than you and have plenty of invincibility frames. There are a few unique levels and all, but it’s very much not worth and I’d rather they’d make a completely unique game for the hardware…Which they did with Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III: The Manhattan Project - the “best of” collection of all ideas that existed with the series, perfectly adapted for an 8-bit system. Yes, the difficulty is still somewhat unreasonable and the gameplay is considerably slower than the arcade titles or the later 16-bit titles, but it’s so full of creativity and fun that I like it about as much as Turtles in Time.Speaking of, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Turtles in Time was the direct sequel to the first Arcade game and this game (or its port) is the most likely reason people buy this collection. The original arcade version is still a bit cheap with its trickery, but it feels far more balanced and fun than the first title. Plus, it’s full of cool animations, sound bites, wonderfully creative stages, awesome soundtrack… It’s really good even if the bosses get quite unreasonable.The SNES port of Turtles in Time is, in my opinion, an almost straight up improvement over the original arcade version. Sure, due to hardware being more limited, it does less fancy stuff and there’s less action happening on screen. But it’s better balanced, bosses are better (apart from the final boss) and there are additional levels that are actually good. That’s on top of recreating most of what the arcade version already has. The only annoyance, apart from the final boss fight, is probably the classic approach of “beat the game on hardest difficulty to deserve the credits”.But Turtles in Time was also released on the Mega Drive/Genesis… Sort of. Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Hyperstone Heist is not a straight port of the original game, but rather a complete reinterpretation of it, reusing huge chunks of levels from it and the original arcade game, but shuffling them up and also adding new levels and other stuff. The big issue with this game, apart from reusing the worst boss from the original arcade game, is probably how painfully long each level is. All of the beat em up titles preceding this game have a very good pace and levels always end before you get bored. But in Hyperstone Heist they just keep going on and on and on way past the point of being fun. And while it’s not a terrible game, it’s somewhat boring and is the least interesting interpretation of Turtles in Time.While even on NES, Konami could find a way to implement a beat em up gameplay, GameBoy wasn’t the best platform to do it. So the TMNT games released for that platform had to adapt. Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Fall of the Foot Clan was just primitive. It’s a simple side scrolling game where enemies spawn from the left or the right of you, so all you have to do is aim in the correct direction and hit them. It’s just a very boring game. For Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: Back from the Sewers things were made to be more complicated. But in a terrible way. Now the game had endless enemy spawns, terrible auto-scrolling and isometric sections and everything is put just perfectly to hit you to the point where I don’t think it’s actually possible to finish the game without taking damage. Honestly, this easily competes with the first NES game in terms of terrible design and the only thing it has over that title is that here you can’t screw yourself over without realizing it.Thankfully, for Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III: Radical Rescue the developers decided to take Metroid II: Return of Samus as a reference and make an exploration focused action platformer. Unfortunately, they didn’t make it good. While there are a couple of optional upgrades, each turtle gets a unique ability and the world is interconnected, the exploration is usually unrewarding and at times punishing. Plus, the bosses are extremely frustrating to deal with and action in general isn’t good. So unlike Metroid 2, replaying this game in modern age is not very fun.And finally, there were three fighting games all named Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Tournament Fighters released on three different platforms that I can’t say much about as I’m especially bad at fighting titles. It seems like the games had positive reviews, at least the SNES version did, so maybe you’d still find these titles fun today. But I have no opinion.So, is there a reason for anyone who didn’t grow up on any of these titles to get the collection? Or are they better served with Shredder’s Revenge?.. Oof. I think there will be a huge chunk of potential players who will get everything they want out of this kind of game with Shredder’s Revenge, if I’m completely honest. But, that doesn’t mean that this new game completely overwrites the coolness of Turtles in Time (arcade and SNES versions) and The Manhattan Project. I think that while difficulty wise these games might’ve not aged as gracefully as I hoped, they’re still absolutely worth playing even today. And the rest of the collection? Well, it’s nice to have. And even the worst games at least have a really good soundtrack. …apart from Back from the Sewers, that one’s just bad.

_childDocuments_.review: The Cowabunga Collection is a wonderful compilation of many of the Turtles' most iconic and memorable games.I grew up with many of these (the NES original, which I had never passed, the arcade original, the NES arcade port, Turtles in Time on SNES and the GameBoy original), and I love that I can easily play them on Steam now, along with plenty of other games I had previously only played a little or not at all. While I have heard criticism about the emulation, I found all the games played great. Save states (one per game) and a rewind feature are present and are very welcome. There are a ton of extras, too, including box and manual scans, guides with tips and maps for the games, promotional art/ads, a thorough music test, and much more. You even get to play the Japanese versions of these games if you are so inclined!I find most of the games hold up pretty well, although the beat-em-ups (though great) tend to feel a little same-y. I find several of the other games to be more interesting conceptually and mechanically, like the NES original being a mix of overworld exploration and brutally unforgiving platforming/action, or the third GameBoy game being a compact and charming Metroidvania. Even though I wasn't a fan when they released, I'm really glad all three versions of Tournament Fighters are included. They each have unique rosters, stages and mechanics, and I was surprised at how much I enjoyed the NES one (particularly considering how few 1-on-1 fighters the console has).A particularly useful feature is that you can access the "strategy guide" for any of the games easily while you're playing them. This came in handy to check the moves lists for the fighting games and the overworld maps for the NES original. I did think it was strange that the compilation includes scans of the games' manuals, but you can't access them while playing the games (you have to quit back to the main menu then choose "Turtles' Lair"). The achievements are relatively straightforward (just beat every game, but be sure to play the genesis Tournament Fighters in a high difficulty to trigger the "real" ending) and the rewind feature goes a long way in making the more difficult parts of these games manageable.I adore compilations of classic console/arcade games like this and the Cowabunga Collection is up there with the Mega Man Collections and the Konami Anniversary compilations. While these games have high nostalgic value, they're also a fascinating insight into the video game evolution of a well-loved franchise. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been quite a year for fans of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. We've already had Tribute Games' outstanding Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge, a game we called a "lovingly crafted and supremely entertaining return to the glory days of early 1990s Turtles action" in our 9/10 review, and now the heroes in a half-shell return in a compilation collection that serves up some of the best of the pizza-loving pugilist's back-catalogue alongside an expansive selection of extras for aficionados to dig into.Yes, where we've sometimes been left a little disappointed with the variety/quality of games and extra bits and bobs included in some retro compilations of late, Digital Eclipse's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection absolutely delivers the goods, with a generous selection of 13 titles that cover the glory years of 1989 through to 1993, alongside an exhaustive museum mode that's stuffed full of bonus goodies.Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection Review - Screenshot 2 of 4And we're not just talking about a throwaway selection of goodies here. Oh no, my most radical party dudes, we're talking about a deep dive right down into the very sewers of turtle history. We've got never-before-seen concept art, fully remastered soundtracks to browse through, the original video game boxes and manuals to pore over, design documents, stills from the original tv show, advertising and promo material and wonderfully stylised new guides for each game that you can dip into for tips, tricks, boss battle help and even a bunch of good old-fashioned cheat codes. Far out!You've got rewind and save state functionality, online multiplayer, couch co-op support, a choice of original, full and full-screen views, a selection of screen filters, custom button mapping and US and Japanese versions for 11 of the 13 games included. Further to all of this, you can also choose to watch a real-time playthrough of each game in the collection, checking out how the computer does things before taking over with a simple button press and jumping into the action when you're ready. This is a huge addition when you consider how hard some of the earlier titles in this compilation are (we've never beaten the original arcade or the first NES game) as it gives you the opportunity to see how tricky areas and tough enemies play out and get defeated, giving you the knowledge required to get stuck in and beat some of these hard as nails oldies for yourself.Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection Review - Screenshot 3 of 4Honestly, there's so much extra content included here it's quite difficult to concentrate on the games themselves, but concentrate we must! The 13 titles on offer are as comprehensive a collection of the glory years of side-scrolling Turtles beat 'em ups as we could really have asked for. Yes, if we're being super picky, it might have been nice to see some more recent games just for balance, but those new-fangled efforts aren't really what the Cowabunga Collection is all about, this is a selection that's laser-focused on the classic beat 'em ups and, as you blast through them, it pays to remember that these weren't just throwaway licensed efforts, they weren't secondary to any other beat 'em up franchise at the time. Konami and the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles were a big deal in the genre, these were super popular and wonderfully well-made games that drew lots of new gamers into the hobby. If an arcade didn't have a four player Turtles machine in it back in the day, was it really even a place you wanted to hang out?Further to this, some of the console classics included here were among the first games to really nail the transition from the arcade to your home, a real holy grail at the time, serving up the exact same graphical prowess and gameplay speed in the comfort of your own sitting room. It may seem quaint now, but boy-oh-boy was it exciting as all heck back in the day to get in from school and boot straight into arcade quality action instead of some dreadfully slowed down, graphically inferior mess, as was most often the case at the time.In terms of the games themselves, there are some real standouts here that folk will immediately zero in on. Turtles in Time, The Hyperstone Heist and Tournament Fighters are our own personal highlights, but dig into the Game Boy efforts and earlier NES games and you'll find surprisingly solid fare with Back From The Sewers and The Manhattan Project in particular still holding up really, really well.Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection Review - Screenshot 4 of 4With regards to performance, there's a little bit of sprite flickering and slow-down in places with some of the NES games in particular (we've even managed to capture it in one of our screenshots) but, overall, Digital Eclipse has done a fantastic job in presenting this stuff in a wonderfully well-rounded package that doesn't skimp on the extras and delivers a fact-filled and thorough journey through Turtles history that fans of the heroes four, and beat 'em ups in general, will get a lot of satisfaction from.If you played Shredder's Revenge this year and enjoyed it, this really is a properly fascinating trip down memory lane that gives a nice bit of insight into how these games developed and grew into what Tribute Games served us up just a few months ago.ConclusionTeenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection is lean, green and totally not mean. This is a wonderfully thorough compilation of the glory days of 8 and 16-bit Turtles beat 'em ups. There's thirteen games here, covering everything you could possibly want from the glory days of TMNT side-scrolling action, alongside an exhaustive array of extras that goes above and beyond what we've seen from most retro compilations of late. Turtles fans and beat 'em aficionados, get that pepperoni pizza order in, kick back and prepare to relive some of the true greats of the late 80s/early 90s era. Over 30 years on and, as it turns out, we still love being a turtle!A generous helping of 13 classic Turtles beat 'em upsTons of never-before-seen extras to dig intoPlenty of options with custom button mapping, screen filters and ratios to muck about withRemastered soundtracks, bespoke strategy guides and online/local MP actionYou get to do the Konami cheat codeA few stutters and glitches here and there in the older titles8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection is truly such a blast from the past, it totally rocks! I grew up playing those classic TMNT arcade games and my goodness, they play perfectly on here and truly brought me back to those golden days. You know, whenever you went to an arcade or a movie theater to play arcade games there before a movie, you’d stand next to the most popular arcade machines and hope you got a turn to play.Almost everyone huddled in front of those TMNT arcade machines for hours on end waiting to put their quarters into action and game on. I cherish those memories and still do to this very day as BOTH Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles Arcade AND Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Turtles in Time are both here and that alone is worth the $40 since it plays so seamlessly on PC.Digital Eclipse did a wonderful job with this collection as it has all the classic games I remember playing as a kid on Nintendo, Super Nintendo, and even those Sega Genesis TMNT games. They even have the Gameboy TMNT games as well that I remembered borrowing from friends to play many moons ago.Besides all that, the additional content you can see and relive from the entire history of this legendary franchise in gaming is all here. You can head to the Turtles’ Lair to see all the old-school gaming boxes, manuals, listen to all the songs in every game’s soundtrack, check out the TMNT comic book covers, and even images from all those awesome TV shows from the late 80s all the way to the 10s. You don’t have to unlock anything, it’s all there ready to check out. They even have strategy guides for every game from way back in the day.There are thousands of things to go through and enjoy in the Turtles’ Lair, especially all the behind-the-scenes original artwork for every game featured in this collection. It’s all just so incredible and a lot to take in as you go through all these great games and everything in the Turtles’ Lair. I also very much enjoyed the Rewind option to go back in time if I made a mistake or died as it makes going through all these games a breeze.When it comes to the multiplayer options of this game, unfortunately, not many people are playing this these days on Steam. There is no cross-platform so needless to say, you won’t find random gamers to join your games to do some co-op. I’d recommend using the Steam Forum for this game and see who is available to join. Either that or if you have a group of friends to fill up a four-player co-op game for those legendary Arcade games, that would be a ton of fun together.I give Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection a perfect 5/5 and would highly recommend this to anyone that wants to remember those incredible days when these TMNT video games were the most popular anywhere. Whether you grew up playing these games in the arcade or on a console, you’ll enjoy this and then some. Even if you just want to take a trip down memory lane to listen to all the soundtracks, see artwork from every game, or go through the best stills from the comics from this legendary franchise, that’s all in here. It’s worth sitting back after you finish each game and going through the entire Turtles’ Lair while enjoying some pizza and remembering a golden age in gaming thanks to the TMNT!

If it doesn't, maybe send it back and hope the game gets cleaned up further. Darn shame. :xI've been looking forward to this for weeks. It's so close to being amazing.Two major problems:- no audio options at all, including basic volume, so good luck listening to anything else while running this- controller support issue: my controller's detected as both players 1 and 3 simultaneously, which means any game with multiplayer has me running two turtles at once off the same inputs—no ability to play just one turtle normally. Distracting, kinda game-breaking, and just overall weird issue.If those get fixed, or at least the controller problem, I'll probably repurchase and cowabunga all over the place. _childDocuments_.review: (I received a review key for this game.)I had TMNT and TMNT2 on the NES, so I mainly focused on those.In short: TMNT is pretty bad, in the sense that the original was pretty bad and buggy and they reproduced it all. TMNT2 has some sprite alteration to remove the Pizza Hut branding; not much else to note of there.Unfortunately, TMNT is a black sheep here in that this is not a complete reproduction of the original game. The original NES game was not ported correctly in PAL Regions and Australia, so owners of the original (like myself) will have played it at 83.33% speed and fondly remember the music at a lower tempo and pitch. This collection concentrates on having two versions for each game: Japan and North America. While this is mostly okay, NES TMNT is the one exception I take.(Some European countries also had 'Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles' branding at the time, so there was both a slow version of TMNT and TMHT.)Aside from that, the bonus material is a goldmine of historical design material that you can study.

_childDocuments_.review: So the games themselves are great: a bit jankey by today’s standards, but that is to be expected.  (In fact I was quite impressed by Radical Rescue: rather than being a sub-par devolve as many GB games are, it was a unique little metroidvania.) It is the presentation that I have a problem with.First of all, there is no reason this collection of old retro games should take up 8GB of disk space.  Clearly, this is due to the UI which nobody asked for.  As much as the cartoon show was part of many or our childhoods, I did not purchase this for a guide to the seasons: you could find this information on a dozen different websites; I purchased it for the games.  The same could be said for the “strategy guides” that are accessed through the pause menu: no doubt the devs are trying to justify the price-tag!  On the other hand, something that was also part of my childhood was the fact that there were tie-ins between Pizza Hut and TMNT (which if memory serves, was going on with the new TMNT cartoon movie), yet they erased the product placement in the games, leaving nothing in its place.  Are we going to go back and edit out every product placement in old movies because the contract expired or whatever?  As least put something clever in its place if you are going to edit stuff... mater of fact, just stop trying to rewrite history: 1984 was a CAUTIONARY TALE!But the most maddening thing about this collection--and apologies in advance that this game is getting the brunt of my rage, but it has been building in me for some time and it needs to be said--is the REWIND FEATURE!  I am so goram sick of devs putting this feature into games!  If you can rewind the game until you get the outcome you want, you make the achievements completely meaningless!  As least some games that offer this feature give you additional achievements for NOT rewinding and that is what should have been done for these games.  But I think it is really telling that this feature is only being put in collections of retro games: it shows that the devs have no respect for these games or their place in history, relegating them to the curiosity cabinet of backwards nostalgia!  For shame!!  CHECK YOUR PRESENTISM!!!Anyway, while I do not expect this review to override the nostalgia that will certainly influence you into buying this offering (as it did me, unfortunately), I hope I have given you (and the devs if they deign to listen) something to think about before you go chasing another retro-game cash-grab.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m a first time player of these games, but a fan of retro gaming in general and love it when companies release these big collections of older titles. The Cowabunga Collection seemed right up my alley, but now that I’ve played it, I can’t help but feel a little bit of disappointment despite the goods on offer.The games themselves are all there and I have no doubt fans may be happy with them, but so many of them are just reskins and nearly all of them have some sort of technical issue bringing down the experience. I played both solo and local co-op with a friend and noticed a variety of issues including input delay, audio glitches, and the gameplay generally just feeling “off”, particularly with things like hitboxes that don’t feel right even as someone that has played a lot of similar games on the original hardware that these come from.I also wasn’t a fan of the cumbersome UI and the bare minimum quality of life additions for what should be THE definitive collection of these games. We get the ability to save anywhere, filters, and a rewind feature, but miss out on things like per-game settings, speed-up options, and actually having more than one save slot...Otherwise, the games themselves are fine. I don’t have nostalgia for these, so they play like any other side-scrolling beat ‘em up from the era for the most part. Not bad, not particularly good, just fine. If anything, I’m glad to finally have the ability to play them on a modern platform, but I also cannot deny I kinda expected a bit more.So that’s kinda where I’m at with this collection and I unfortunately cannot see myself getting any further than I already have. Decent collection, plenty of issues, standard gameplay, expensive pricing - that’s pretty much it.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: As a kid TMNT: Tournament Fighters use to punish me, as an adult it still does. Nevertheless this collection was a great way to replay some of my favorites and try some others.Games/Gameplay/Maps: This collection comes with thirteen games that various from Game Boy to SNES and few arcade style types. The older the game the simple and less features you have but surprisingly still fun and engaging. They have a nice variety of gameplay from side-scrolling action platforms, fighting and beat 'em up. They all allow you to select one of the four turtles or even some villains (In TMNT Fighters). The maps are well designed and good looking for its time. Online play seems to be very slow to dead. I only manage to jump into 1 party and everything was working fine until the host left. Feel free to add me if you want to play online. _childDocuments_.review: A quality collection of some great games. For the longest time, I'd wanted a TMNT collection just like this, but never did I actually expect to see it release. I've seldom been as happy to be proven wrong.Having both JP and US region versions of each game is a very welcome inclusion. I was naïvely also hoping for the EU "Hero Turtle" versions, but I also understand that the differences were likely too minor to warrant the effort. The Turtles' Lair gallery is an amazing addition, it was a joy to go through all the concept art and stuff. Can't comment on the online play portion of the collection, since I don't really do that, but it's awesome that the option is there.So far, the games have played great, with the only exception of the game randomly freezing for a second or two, but that might just be my PC. You're given various enhancements (cheats, basically) for each title on the game select screen, allowing you to select a level, adjust starting lives, et cetera. Things that let you adjust the difficulty to your liking. Each game also has a rewind feature and the ability to do one "save state" per game. The only thing I've noticed was how in stage 2 of TMNT II: The Arcade Game (NES), the vertical scrolling segment looks much rougher than I remember it being, with the entire street quaking.So, do I recommend this? Yes. Absolutely. A great deal in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: (completed every game at time of review obtaining all achievements)As far as a collection goes, this is very well put together. Looks cool scrolling through the games as the preview is fit between comic panels. Nice scans of all game manuals and boxes. Nice amount of behind the scenes things to look at (sketches, comic covers, ect.)In game stuff is reasonable: graphics look crisp and you can rebind keys/buttons (wouldn't read my PS4 controller properly even when I had DS4 launched. Xbone controller worked fine). Emulation wise, you can save wherever (limited to one save state per game), rewind 30 seconds, and given adjustment options for borders and turning off/on sprite flicker/slowdown and the like.The games are what they are, and ultimately probably only half are still fun/interesting to play. But all are interesting in a kind of game historic sense. If you are looking for just gameplay fun and fluidity with ninja turtles, I would suggest Shredder's revenge instead (I played it on the PS4/PS5 so can't 100% know everything about the PC version). This is a good showcase of the history of turtles that inspired many of the elements within that game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been having a blast with this collection. Haven't tried the online multiplayer features so I can't speak for them. _childDocuments_.review: I guess I was expecting more given these are classics but I suppose you realize that they released the same game almost 4 times when we were growing up. This seems to be a culmination of emulator versions of the game, shoved in an easy to access repository with some menus and paint splattered on top. Unlike one of the very prominent negative posts I see at the time of this writing by another user, I feel they did put a decent amount of effort into this. Some people clearly haven't viewed all the information available. They have high quality scans of the original artwork and storyboarding used for the games. Pretty cool.One thing that's nice that is in this is a sort of 'strategy' quickstart guide that is different from the manuals that came with the games. There's some tidbits in there that I do not recall, at least when playing Turtles in Time. I suppose now I understand why the game was called TMNT IV when I was a kid.Unlike others I experience no issues, but I haven't played online. That's a technical issue on that person's end and I don't think a game should be penalized for that. What's awkward to me is that they have some 'enhancements' you can enable for some games and not others. For example, the original Turtles in Time (e.g. NES version?), you can increase the amount of enemies, and/or enable God Mode. That's a lot of fun -- but why can't I do this in the SNES version? Super frustrating. I dislike consistently like this and get annoyed. Give us all the options for all the games or set the game up in such a way we can modify it to our heart's content.The game files look to all be stored in some binary blob in the user directory, assets.pie. I haven't looked closely at this, but it sort of looks like each emulated is just stacked on top of each other, one after another and selected accordingly at play time. If you want to be literal, you could say this is sort of a great way to make a lot of money off of people given the cost difference.I haven't played through all the games. But all and all, I enjoyed this for what it is. I suppose you just have to really love Turtles, or have never played any of the games for hours on end like some of may have done as a kid.

_childDocuments_.review:
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Cowabunga Collection assembles thirteen classic TMNT games by KONAMI in one incredible package. This collection provides a unique opportunity for gamers to experience these immensely popular and very influential games on modern consoles and includes a fantastic set of new quality of life features:

* Added Online Play for certain games and Local Couch Play
* Save Anytime and Rewind
* Eleven Japanese Regional Versions
* Button Mapping
* Unique Development Art & Sketches

name: Wild Bastards
detailed_description: Grab The Original Bastards About the Game From the veteran team behind Void Bastards and Card Hunter, Wild Bastards has you travel from planet to planet to recruit, manage and gun sling with a team of 13 outlaws, each of whom has their own weaponry, special power, and growth tree. On planets, you’ll wrangle loot and start showdowns that are then played out in intense, bite-sized shootouts. The Wild Bastards were the most deadly gang in the galaxy until a posse from the puritanical magnate Jebediah Chaste eliminated one outlaw after another. Faced with their own mortality, the two remaining members have teamed up with the Drifter, a mysterious sentient spacecraft, to find and resurrect the dead gang members as they flee to the mythical Homestead. Intense Showdowns Prove you’re the ultimate gunslinger by blasting an array of enemies in bullet-flying shootouts. Tactical FPS Combat Use your wits to overcome crafty enemies that utilize cover, flank you, and employ a huge variety of special moves from teleportation to homing poisonous quills. 13 Outlaws to Play Rebuild a gang of 13 outlaws, each with their own unique weapon, stunt, personality, relationships, and ability tree. Build & Maintain Relationships The gang know each other well, but that doesn’t mean they like each other. It’s your job to manage their dynamic relationships, but good luck getting feuding outlaws to ride together. Keep The Gang Thriving Accumulate resources to heal injured gang members, level up characters, improve relationships, and more. Strategize for Victory Evaluate each planet’s terrain, enemies, and traits before selecting which gang members you want to land there. Collect items, level up, and use special locations carefully to turn the odds in your favor! An Ever-Changing, Lawless Galaxy Roam the procedurally-generated galactic sectors and planets with varying parameters such as gravity, terrain features, weather, and more. Challenge Mode After completing the main campaign, a challenge mode unlocks to offer a sequence of challenge sectors with increasingly difficult levels and mutators to modify the play experience.
