short_description: The spiritual successor to the award-winning game Void Bastards, Wild Bastards is a roguelike strategy shooter with heart-pounding FPS action, mod management, and a tactical campaign. Saddle up and lead the most notorious outlaws in the galaxy.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: While it may not be for everyone, to me this is a fantastic strategy game with engaging showdowns peppered throughout.Two things that you should be aware of before you play this game:To address point 1, while the screenshots and trailers seems to suggest that this is a First Person Shooter first and foremost, it is not. The real meat and potatoes of gameplay is the strategic movement across two kinds of procedurally-generated maps (planetary and interplanetary) and the management and careful application of your crewmates and resources. While the gunplay that you participate in can be fun, engaging and challenging, you're actually better off avoiding fights when you can so that you can be best prepared for the fights you can't avoid.To address point 2, no really, this is NOT Void Bastards. While it shares its DNA in terms of its writing, visuals, personality, charm and Challenge, this is a very different game when you're actually controlling the player characters. While in Void Bastards, you are crawling around in cramped, maze-like ships laying traps and sneaking past enemies in a timed scenario to find the most loot, in Wild Bastards you are often placed in wide open areas with the sole objective of finding the most survivable way of killing every enemy in the encounter, strategically locating enemies and dispatching them with the tools at the disposal of the two Bastards you chose to fight with. If you are expecting Void Bastards 2, you may want to give this one a miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of Void Bastards, I was excited when I heard about Wild Bastards. I eagerly awaited its release, but after two hours of gameplay, I’m left disappointed. While it's a well-made game, it lacks the fun I enjoyed in Void Bastards.Let’s start with the levels—especially the night stages. This might be a personal learning curve, but the thrill of navigating through tight spaces on a ship in Void Bastards was far more enjoyable than roaming around the open maps of Wild Bastards. Instead of scavenging for loot, you're limited to picking up ability tokens. It feels like the real action is happening on the overworld maps, not in the FPS segments.Wild Bastards uses two overworld maps. One lets you choose your path between planets, allowing you to target specific types of loot, and the other, which is more tactical, comes into play when you land on a planet. This planetary overworld feels like the true heart of the game, where you strategize your movement and make decisions based on guard positions, loot spots, teleporters, stores, and exits. Unfortunately, it detracts from the more hands-on FPS gameplay that I was looking forward to.Speaking of FPS, the firefights aren't terrible, and I imagine unlocking more characters would make the game more engaging. You don’t get a variety of weapons; instead, you control two characters that you can switch between, almost like weapons themselves. You can choose your pair or split them to suit your strategy. Navigating this second overworld with its tactical map ends up being the most critical part of the game. It's about planning when, how, and with whom to move through these maps. Unfortunately, that becomes the primary focus of the game, not the firefights themselves.Nighttime levels are a particular slog. You’re essentially shooting at shadows, relying on enemy banter and noise effects to figure out where they are before firing blindly in their direction. It’s frustrating, and I'm not a fan of these segments at all.Lastly, the showdowns in the FPS stages lack variety. Unlike Void Bastards, where you had to search for items or avoid certain dangers, Wild Bastards just has you clearing out enemies. There's no deeper objective during these fights.Maybe the game gets better later, but after my initial two hours, I decided to return it. I’d rather replay Void Bastards or finally check out the DLC. Perhaps I’ll revisit Wild Bastards when it goes on sale, but for now, I’m passing.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Void bastards was fun, but intensely frustrating, had a horrible fail loop and often left you scrambling to just try to get one stage done in a new area.Wild Bastards? Holy hell, WB Shows what happens when a dev team goes "Yeah that was a good idea with some bad parts but we can fix it." Frustration is gone, loss protection is in. Smart leveling, unique weapons for each character to avoid loot traps. Loot itself just being temporary so you don't base an entire run on it, level ups being permanent so you can't fail spiral.Great spread of characters to choose from too, even if the whole bean thing is a little creepy. Well worth the time and money. I still can't believe Blue Manchu started with a freaking cardboard cutout board game/card game sim and ended up here.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Many reviews compare it to Void Bastards, which is essentially a wrong approach. While the rouge-like nature and graphical style of the two games are similar, apart from a few basic elements, the similarities end there.It's a game where you're constantly gathering your team, upgrading your existing members, and progressing through small board game-like planets with super-rapid FPS showdowns. Some of these showdowns can last 5-10 minutes, but the majority of them will last just 1-2 mins (or sometimes 10-30 secs) instead. This is not a fault, but a core element of the game and one of the main reasons it is so frickin' addictive. The "just one more round" type of game if you want. In many ways, it's a much simpler and more basic game than its spiritual predecessor, and exploration as such is completely absent. The strategic factor here comes down to which team members you take to which situation (or more like opponent composition), what upgrade you equip them with, and how you upgrade them during your full campaign. That's it, that's all, but that's also all you need.It seems almost too simple a formula at first, but the 13 heroes, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of upgrades offer just enough variation. Each hero is very, very different from the others. For me, there were more sympathetic and less sympathetic characters in the first hours, but in the end, I realized that all 13 were really useful and some were actually way better suited to certain situations than others. (not you, Sarge, sorry, but you need a serious buff) It looks like that the game has been subjected to a huge amount of balance testing, and it shows. No filler characters, which is an epic win!The story and dialogue are unfortunately more forgettable than the characters themselves. Not bad, but nothing to write home about. Honestly, it feels as if the characters and their design were invented much before the actual story itself, into which they were forced. This is palpable and the story as such has unfortunately become very forgettable and bland. The humor is there, but it lacks any satirical tone or deeper depth, rather it has a kind of Saturday-morning cartoon vibe. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but for me, it was a tad disappointing.Biggest con (for me): Unfortunately, the creators have once again fallen into the same mistake they made with their previous game. There is no closure or catharsis at the end of the game, no final big confrontation, no final boss planet, and not even a simple boss fight. The game just ends - almost in a blink of an eye. It's like there's a final chapter that we didn't get. I hope that's the case and that we can take down the game's main villain in a DLC, or something because although I enjoyed the game throughout, the ending left a bit of a sour taste in my mouth. Of course, that didn't stop me from starting it again immediately on a harder level!But overall: It's almost impossible not to compare it to Void Bastards, I know, but we have to, because this game deserves to be treated as a unique entity of its own! It's crazy addictive and fast-paced, infinitely stylish, and very easy to just pick up for 10-20 minutes, even on a lunch break or before bed. That is if you can actually stop after that short time because the game will do everything in its power to make sure you don't. You know the drill:"Just one more planet, just one more showdown..."(PS: I need a whole game with Billy the Squid on the lead role!)

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of the negativity for this game stems around "Well it's no Void Bastards". And yeah they're right: this is Wild Bastards.Half Life 2 wasn't exactly like Half Life 1 either, instead of being confined to Black mesa and surroundings you are met with way bigger levels and new mechanics like physics. People need to stop with this whole "new = bad" trend as it's starting to ruin our very world, as people don't allow themselves to have fun anymore or to give something new a shot anymore. Now I got to level with you: I'm not a fan of Action Roguelites, I'm not a fan of finite lives with lots of strategical and tactical play involved. But I am a fan of this game. Blue Manchu is a master of their craft: Their enemies are funny, their style is great and yeah even the gameplay is solid here.

_childDocuments_.review: Im so torn on this one, but I think overall my thoughts lean slightly south of positive. I want to like this game so badly, and broadly I do, but there are certain aspects that hold it back from its full potential, IMO. But the TLDR is game is good, but not as good as id hope. I dont think youll necessarily regret your purchase, but if youre like me you might not get as many hours out of it as you'd hope given the genre. IF youre interested in my more detailed thoughts read on. First off the things I am a fan of. Love the art style. The music (when present) is thematic and good. The voice acting is phenomenal and does a lot to characterize the different outlaws. The outlaws themselves are varied and interesting with unique playstyles, personalities and use cases that make assembling a team feel engaging. Now on to the negatives/areas for improvement. -The shooting feels...off to me. Its certainly not bad, but certain characters just dont feel as good to shoot with as others. For example, the dual revolver wielding spider woman has such insane bullet drop on her pistols that it feels like youre shooting nerf darts. Trying to fight at range feels like youre playing sniper elite when it really shouldnt at the ranges we're dealing with on these small encounter stages. Other characters like the sniper feel great.-Damage feels hard to mitigate in a game where healing is often limited and expensive to come by. You have to make effective use of cover to avoid attacks from some of the enemy types. Thats okay, but at times enemies will camp behind an object and refuse to peek, forcing you to push their position and shooting you as soon as you come into view. Certain characters like the explosives expert can deal with this thru splash damage, but others cannot. Also nothing feels worse than sitting in cover listening for the enemy to shoot before popping your head up, waiting and waiting, hearing nothing, then taking damage the second you decide to peek. Or maybe youre pinned down by snipers and get rushed by critter melee enemies (thats fine btw and good you should pressure the player. I'm just saying it makes it hard to avoid damage). Overall I just found myself taking so much of what FELT like unavoidable damage, regardless of whether it actually was or not. -That brings me to my next point which is injuries and feuds. You are often limited (at least where I am in the game) to 2-4 outlaws per mission, with 2 being able to be grouped together at a time once youre on planet. My roster currently has like 8 people. So losing an outlaw to injury can be quite punishing when you factor in that half your roster can be feuding with each other preventing you from bringing them into a mission at the same time. I have had cases where one or two injuries combined with the various feuds left me only able to take 3 out of 7 available outlaws into a mission due to all the conflicts. That feels bad. Especially when the feuds appear to be purely RNG. It reminds me of the (quite divisive among players) relationship mechanics in darkest dungeon 2 that were so annoying. But at least there you could directly manage and impact the relationships to mitigate it significantly thru smart gameplay. Here it just happens. And the resource needed to resolve it is so incredibly rare in my experience that it feels impossible to effectively keep your crew in check. In one starmap you might endure 5-6 feuds and only receive one can of beans to clear one of them. Its just not enough and I expect it will be changed in the future cuz this is insane. It would be one thing if you could still bring two feuding party members but they just couldnt be teamed up on the planet, or maybe they just got a debuff or something. But completely locking them out is super annoying.-The strategic gameplay feels a bit shallow to me so far. Once youre on a planet you decide how to group up or split your party and can move them independently around the map nodes. There are various roadblocks, loot, roving packs of enemies, POI's etc to explore. And there is the looming threat of the arrival of a bounty hunter if you stay on the planet too long. The game presents the bounty hunter as a big threat, but the first time one caught me I killed him without even taking damage. They likely get more threatening but it was a bit anticlimactic. But yeah each level feels a bit like a puzzle trying to figure out how to maximize resource gain while managing your parties health and avoiding injury. Except often I was able to easily get everything with minimal planning/efficiency and get out before the bounty hunter arrives. Once again, likely the maps get larger and more complicated later, but I am over 6 hrs in and still feel like the strategy component is lacking. So long as you are generally proficient at shooting mechanics and skip unnecessary fights, its pretty easy to fully clear a map. It feels like there is a lack of meaningful choice/consequence. -The upgrades have not felt super impactful so far. The "Aces" you pick up for each outlaw enhance their abilities in some way and "Mods" are equipment you wear with varying effects only active for that star system before you warp. without exception, everything I have found so far is just some variation of a stat increase (more health, more armor, lower bullet spread etc.) which, while useful, is also boring. Where is the ace that turns smokeys fireballs into a flamethrower? Where is the mod that allows me to lasso an enemy and pull them towards me or makes the lizard character invisible while sprinting and low to the ground? Something that actually changes the way the outlaw plays instead of just making them more effective at the thing they already do? Maybe it exists just later in the game. But once again im 6 hours in. Most players wont even give you that long if theyre bored. I want something to grab me and make me go "oh thats cool. How can i build around that with mods? I wonder what aces exist for X character I enjoy" etc.Overall im just struggling to see what will make me want to play this for 20, 50 or 100 hrs like other rouge-likes I enjoy. Not every game needs 100's of hours of replayability to be good. This is a competently made game. But sometimes a decent game with unrealized potential feels worse than a subpar game with little potential beyond that if that makes sense. I love this genre so much and have logged hundreds of hours across various games, but im struggling to find the hook with this one to keep me coming back for more runs. And especially at $35 this game is a bit on the expensive side compared to its contemporaries. Maybe with future updates/content ill be able to update this review. I sincerely hope so!

_childDocuments_.review: I am surprised at how much Wild Bastards didn't land for me. I liked Void Bastards so I figured this would be a similar win, but there are a few issues Controls feel bad. If you are crouching you cannot go from crouching to sprinting by pressing the sprint button, you have to uncrouch be in the upright position which makes you more vulnerable and then you can sprint. I do not like this game desing and think that it adds unnecessary tedium to the game . On top of that while you are sprinting you cannot shoot, which means if you are repositioning you have to stop running, get into walking mode and then shoot. There are no animation interrupts which feels both bad and clunkyThe bastards are interesting but they seem really poorly designed. They hit like wet noodles even with mods and later on in levels it feels like even with damage mods and damage aces you still have to 2-3 tap enemies at minimum. This would be fine if there were 3-6 of them but sometimes there are 10-20 and it makes fights turn into a slog  and not a showdown. Enemies range from fun and well designed to outright infuriating. The designs run into this issue where they are anti synergistic and in some cases punish you for playing the game. A lot of strategy revolves around ducking behind cover and taking pot shots whittling down enemies as you traverse the battlefield. The problem is enemies with poison do so much damage to you that if you play cautiously you take more damage as you give the poison time to deal damage to you. I was playing in normal mode and by later levels was getting two to three tapped by enemies.  The ladder system is frustrating. There are these enemies that release glowing orbs which have very little in the way of audio cues and they can stack up and outright kill your character. If you get to high ground to avoid them the orbs can climb up the ladders and teleport right next to you and explode. Same thing with some of the 4 legged creatures, you get  to high ground to get a better position and they just teleport up with you. Maybe I am being nit picky but that seems like bizarre design to me and I didn't much like it. Accuracy is weird both for the player and the enemies. sometimes when I am running enemies miss me and sometimes they don't like it is random. Character accuracy is odd. Sometimes it is pinpoint where the cursor and reticle are and sometimes it fires slightly off.Character range from really well made to horrible. the snake character with the whip literally only has one purpose and that is boss killing. You pair him up with Smokey the chef and Smokey takes out all the mobs and then you just bum rush the boss, permastun them and they die after about 7 seconds. Snake boy has no other discernible purpose outside of that. He does one thing and one thing well but there is not other reason to play him. Preach would be fun but she does so little damage and the fact that she has to wind up her shots means you have to waste ammo, which she goes through like a fat kid through candy, or you have to get in front of enemies and tank damage which hasn't worked out to well for me so far.  I am not sure on this game, it's new and I think the devs will continue to refine it but until then I is a no from me. I think a bandaid solution would be to increase player damage and decrease enemy damage so that I feel more incline to take risks and explore more of the map. Right now I only really grab loot that is on the way to the exit beacon and maybe an emergency beacon. I can spare any more HP or supplies otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: Opinions are funny. People love Void Bastards. And why wouldn't they? It's a great game. Charming visual style with the thrilling gameplay of salvaging derelict ships. On paper, it's exactly the kind of thing I'd like. But I'm afraid it just didn't click with me. I liked the idea, but I disliked the execution. It's nothing to do with the developer. I'm happy that people love it.Now take Wild Bastards. I hated the idea, but I loved the execution. I wasn't too thrilled about it. I think my impressions were that it was a singleplayer Overwatch...A hero shooter, but without the crowds. Watching the videos didn't really do it justice, either. But then I picked it up, and I tried it..And I love it. It's a different experience than Void Bastards, with an emphasis on FPS combat whereas Void Bastards was more about avoiding combat. And at the end of the day, I think that's why it didn't click with me? It's like I can craft these weapons, but they're not something I should rely on. Wild Bastards is different from that, and I love it. And what's more, I love the characters. I wasn't too crazy about playing as multiple characters. Just let me collect different guns. But I'm glad they went this route. Each character is charming, demanding different playstyles depending on their weapons and their set of skills.The visual style is phenomenal, and exactly why I was drawn to give this game a shot in the first place.. And the guns feel so good to use. The sounds to them are satisfying, as well as the visual flair. It makes each combat encounter fun, and when you plan accordingly and perfectly execute it, you feel like a gunslinger.Imagine.. This game gave me more of an outlaw experience than Star Wars Outlaws. This game is money well  spent, and extremely addictive to play on the Steam Deck. I swear, I better start seeing this game in lists of "Best Games For The Steam Deck"
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Wild Bastards is the game for people (like me) who wanted to like Void Bastards, but didn't. Everything about this game fixes what I didn't like about VB and then some. I barely managed to slog through 4 hours of VB, and 5 hours into WB the only reason I'm stopping myself from playing more is because of work. It's really fantastic, on desktop and Steam Deck. Tons of variety, good strategy, fun characters, and really tense shootouts, especially in the dark. Absolutely get this if you can!
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: It's an experience that never fully comes together, so to speak.Earlygame in the first/narrative campaign is great, you've only got two characters and have to play carefully, making due with their abilities and semi-stealth in shorter warp-maps, but... that unfortunately doesn't stay too long, as by the time you get 4 characters, the game starts to fall apart. Warp maps expand out to basically 3x7 Slay-the-spire-map type choices, with other, typically larger grids on the planets, and you're encouraged to fully explore to get cards and resources, except you have the Prince timer breathing down your neck and have to get through multiple repetitive shootouts in order to get that loot, and you're encouraged to get infamy by doing all the shootouts and packs/patrols, but that ends up being exhausting and not really worth it most of the time... Guess what, there's like 15 characters and THIS is the unchanging loop you get for the entire game.With that said, that's where the cracks show up. As more enemies get introduced, and you start building characters in a more-roguelike manner (levelups have a random draw of 3 cards, some generic, some specific to the character, this might also apply to the Core cards because I did see a different core card during the first Challenge run on a character that I had three core cards on in the Narrative Campaign...) , and enemies get introduced that are meant to be countered in certain ways, but... You WILL be forced to use characters that don't necessarially counter those enemies, including not being able to use characters that WOULD be perfect for the situation if they weren't randomly feuding, so those cards and intents become retroactively useless and gimmicky, cause everyone can do everything with varying degrees of efficacy and play style. On that note, feuding is just a bad system. The characters never decide that they're going to be pals even if you just slayed through 6 encounters with both characters competently and barely took damage, no, instead that causes "oh I hate you now and won't let you recreate that success until you find more beans!" for no damn reason. It seems to happen more if the playstyles clash or you lose 50 hp on both characters... Or just exist as my favorite example, Preach and Ros, who have pal skills that complement eachother, Preach giving 3 healthkits on Ros being hit three times, Ros giving 3 armor after Preach gets 3 times, allowing for a loop of recovery- they even immediately pal up when you revive Ros, but then immediately after using them on one planet, they instantly split, so you can't even make use of the gimmick. Better yet is when you repeatedly use beans to make a pair that works well happen, then they repeatedly fall out. The ONLY times I have seen pal-ups is when a character gets rescued from Jail or Scattering, otherwise it seems to happen between characters it's useless for, like, say, Billy and Kaboom or Billy and Judge, where Billy sets 3 enemies HP to 1, but Judge and Kaboom do so much damage that that's hardly ever necessary.So you'd think that means Beans are super common, right? Nope. There's like 1 can every 5 planets. In the same vein, the whole Charge mechanic applies at the same rate, a character will be charged and have their buff only the first time you use them in a system, then you need Tonics to get that buff back, but they're also rare, which then loops back into the cards feeling like unnecessary gimmicks, and since some characters are just better than others, you'll make those characters perpetually tired, and......This all comes crashing down. The whole thing just sort of feels irritating by midgame, especially since you'll make most of the characters pals until Ros arrives, then he just turns most everyone against eachother and immediately causes multiple feuds, which then force certain character combinations, then you get into the repetitive loop, leading you to possibly try to get beans more rather than cards just because Ros pisses everyone off constantly, then you go and rescue Spike, who technically starting the endgame by making everyone but Smoky and Billy leave, and then... Then you have to do extra showdowns to get one character back per warp map, if you choose to go for them, then you make it to Fletch, who then basically reserves 4 characters three times to make you play certain characters and not others, so none of it's really your choice, your builds don't really matter, and the game just feels like it's not right.Then there's the ending. For all that repetition, for all that grind, for all that work, you get a "Oh, sorry, the entire goal of getting to homestead was a lie, it was for these three children we made you rescue for no big reason, k thanks byeeeee" and then it. Just. Ends. You unlock Procedural mode and Challenges, but all that work you did, the builds you made, it's all just vanished despite the post-credits saying "oh hey, we're going to make this go on forever, you're here to stay". Dear. God. This is where I went "Yeah, the devs clearly wanted to make a different game and then changed it into this one."Challenges aren't challenges, they're deceptions with annoying modifiers and RNG reliance. You start them with certain characters at certain levels with certain gimmicks, and since you didn't build them, you're relying on enemy RNG and auto-chosen-card RNG to be kind to get them done. Bleh.Procedural seemingly leans more into the Roguelike nature, but it still ends at some point and you still don't really get much control over what happens anyway so it's just more of the Campaign but with a lot more randomness.All this and without mentioning Cramm. Cramm's the "gold" of this game, but you LITERALLY NEVER RECEIVE IT DESPITE SHOPS APPEARING ON NEARLY EVERY PLANET, so I just ignored them most of the time.Tldr, I'm expecting some kind of massive changes to occur because the state of the game right now is just.... Abrasive and chaotic.PS: The robots can be poisioned, the literal Ghost can take damage, and the flaming skeleton can take fire damage. Only two of three of those get somewhat solved by core cards. Also, the loudest thing in the game is the showdown intro tracks, which isn't controlled by Music volume, no, it's on Main volume and turning that down makes everything else basically inaudible.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Loved Void Bastards and while this does share some of its DNA, Wild Bastards does a lot quite different, and so far most of it works quite well.The different characters all play very differently in shootouts, and bringing different characters that can cover different types of combat feels pretty important.Speaking of, I know opinions seem a bit mixed so far, but personally the combat itself feels a lot better than in VB.Anyway, early days, but keen to put some more time into this and see how it progresses.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Really sad to say this game did not hit the mark for me. I adore Void Bastards and still like the art and vibe of this title, but find myself very confused by the design here. The game also feels like exactly the title its devs set out to make, so it could very easily just be subjective taste at play.This game has none of the friction and serendipity of Void bastards. Runs are extremely linear, with no loot really affecting how I played in any meaningful way. There's rarely a meaningful risk-reward element at play and no real push pull in the resources or in the choices I found myself making planetside or in the solar system map. The feeling in Void Bastards of risking it all on an insanely dangerous situation to get one piece of loot that'd let you craft an upgrade is totally absent. The rewards are impotent, the lack of stealth means there's no strategic options to how you approach an encounter, and the lack of maps a la ships means there isn't even interesting frictionin how you navigate an encounter spatially.Combat is fine-to-good. Weightless but satisfying nonetheless. I think the game takes its time way too long doling out the characters as I only felt like I had meaningful tactical choices to make once I had 5-6 characters unlocked. The combat arenas function as intended, though skirmishes have an unfortunate habit of petering out. Most fights end with a single enemy left somewhere in the map shouting combat taunts at me as I hunt him down for minutes at a time as the momentum bleeds out of the action. My major disappointment is in the individual heroes feeling not all that distinct to play. They have slightly different move speeds or some fun qquirks like the snake man going to crouch height when he runs ie slithers, but their weapons all work more or less as well as each other at different ranges, have broadly similar reload times etc. The feeling I expected of a dozen odd shaped keys you have to fit to their proper holes else get really creative with them is not present. Maybe I have yet to unlock the quirkier characters.I very strongly feel the lack of the chapter break story cutscenes and little dialogues from the ship computer from VB. With such a strong focus on the motley cast of characters this game feels oddly quiet and sedate. There's no story events during a run and the events that happen at the end of each chapter feel somehow rushed and overwritten at the same time. The villains are fine, McNeil's voice actor puts in a fantastic comedic performance, but I found the way they appear (random single threatening messages at the end of each chapter that go completely unacknowledged by your crew) very abrupt.Darn! I was really really looking forward to this game and probably will continue to play hoping it reveals more complexity as I go, but I am so sad to say I would not recommend this game in its current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Anyone coming into this game expecting Void Bastards in the Wild West, you're setting yourself up for disappointment. What you instead have is the perfect bite-sized game. As someone who is often jumping into and out of play sessions, I can say there is definitely an audience for this (and I'm it). Managing the overworld map is picking one point at a time, and beaming down. Once on a planet, you manage your team of Bastards a few squares at a time, trying to min/max getting as much loot as you can while picking as many fights as safely possible, with an eye on a timer that says it's time to GTFO. Firefights occur on a wide variety of biomes, with several modifiers and enemy types to keep things interesting, but the longest I have had one last would have been 5 minutes. Even gear management and relationship management for the outlaws is bite sized, with no more than 3 gear and a simple "Are they pals, meh, or nope?" that can be altered in the press of a button - provided you have the magical beans. Beans, beans, the magical fruit, the more you eat the less you feud. I'm leaving that in. Bonus points for the writing, the humour is for a specific type of person (this is where being the spiritual successor to VB comes in, imo, along with the constant sense of forward motion while being a loot goblin) but the dialogue feels very authentic - the actors definitely enjoyed themselves and it shows. All the Bastards play differently, and as you get more Aces for them you can really start to feel less like just a gun with a voice attached to it, and more like an entire unit/character that you can plan around. Seriously though, this might be the epitome of Steam Deck play - pick the game up, spend 10 minutes taking 3 turns on a planet and winning (hopefully) 3 showdowns and then you put it down, and it'll be there waiting for you to come back like a Bushwhacker behind a door. If polished jump-in, jump-out action with a side of usin' yer noggin is your thing, give this a try. You won't be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Void bastards was more of a randomized bioshock experience. You enter a complex environment, have complex objectives, escape. There is light resource management and stealth is important for certain encounters.This is more of an arena shooter. The enemy chatter reminds me of outlaws. It's a fun arena shooter. Don't go into it with expectations set by void bastards.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: After...a LOT of play, I have to say I wouldn't recommend this game. If it went on sale, it might be worth it.There's just not a lot of variety in the game. The original gameplay loop is nice and interesting, with cool aesthetics and gunplay, but you end up doing the same thing for the rest of the campaign.The rogue-lite aspect of this game is not well-executed, and helped me to put into words how roguelikes in general can really aggravate me. In theory, there's a lot of variety to your equipment, characters, and enemies/encounters, but in practice, a combination of randomness and difficulty keep this entirely out of your control. You can't control what items are granted at start or drop as loot, and you're often prevented from accessing shops by princes, enemy encounters, or a lack of money (I almost never had the Cramm I needed to buy items.) Then, at the end, all of that effort goes to waste when I end a sector and all of my items disappear. The challenges do a good job of giving you unique items and circumstances that allow you to explore specific circumstances, but they're only a small part of the game. The plot seems half-finished. It would be fine if the game were a great gameplay experience held together by a plot that just explains why we're doing this, but, as above, the gameplay is a bit lacking.Some stuff I would do to fix the game:1) Allow players to keep an extremely small amount of stuff upon warp. 1 or 2 equipped mods, a small amount of Cramm. 2) Change the Infamy system so that players can buy randomized packages of different things, rather than having a completely random, tier-based package. So, for example, I can ask for armaments to help out my low-damage outlaws, but I can't choose which specific armaments I get.3) More of the cool, funny items that add pickups or change the environment or impact enemies, less of the number changers. Change how I play the game beyond 'my gun is better, so now I am better at damaging people'. 4) Larger swarms of lower-tiered enemies, later into the game. It's more fun to take out a bunch of weaker guys, and a larger number of weaker enemies will present a more forgiving and dynamic challenge vs. a few of the strongest enemies.5) An option to skip some of the repetitive animations and notices: infamy meter, princes coming down to fight you, 'are you sure?' when you end a turn without moving a bunch, etc. These can get annoying when you have to do them over and over.6) Please buff Casino's gun. It is really bad.7) A post-campaign mode that allows you to play a little bit with the characters that you spent the campaign developing.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: While Void Bastards put emphasis on avoiding combat, Wild Bastards puts it front and center. Combat takes the stage, but it's not all guns blazing. You still need to think strategically and plan ahead. Different enemies require different tactics and this allows for some creative combos utilizing the different strengths and weaknesses of the 13 outlaws, each with their own unique abilities and weapons. Wild Bastards still exudes that Void Bastards style, but this is its own game and it's a rootin' tootin' good time!
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Would give this a "meh" option if I could.It oozes style. The outlaws are all distinct in their appearances and manners. Definitely love the space cowboy overarching theme. But the gameplay feels clunky, and there isn't enough to set the outlaws apart IMO. I don't really understand the point of the turn-based map movement between battles. The constant entering and exiting battles feels very jarring for the pace of the game... at least with Void Bastards you had a lot more to explore during each "battle."It has potential. Just not sure if it's for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: You can see where they thought to expand the areas of Void Bastards that proved engaging and successful, but this loop is far less interesting than that game, and for all the effort put into character design and production, I'm just not having any fun. Grindy, bad pacing, floaty and unimpactful shooting. Like you're playing a complicated board game at someone's house who keeps telling you every five minutes, "now THIS is where it gets good," except that it doesn't.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who loved Void Bastards, this is a miss for me.Roguelike shooter set in the wild west. There are two unique gimmicks for this one. First, you can swap character in the middle of play to change weapon & health/armour. Second, there are two turn-based tactical layers, choosing which planet to land on and then choosing where to go on each planet.The positives - the art style is fantastic, the sound design is good, and for me the guns all feel nice and kinetic. The vibe is good.But this falls down relative to Void Bastards, the spaceship-hopping prequel. Each level in Void Bastards was fun because you had a limited supply of oxygen on each ship, and had to therefore make quick decisions of where to go and what to try to do. Different parts of the ship typically held different kinds of items, and could be blocked off with some ludicrously powerful tanks. So you felt pressured to make interesting decisions. You might leave early. You might push your luck. And you needed some of that food, fuel and oxygen in order to sustain your ship on the tactical map.Wild bastards has none of this. In standard levels you can take as long as you like to pick enemies off, and the level ends when you kill every enemy. All of those interesting decisions are removed.There is a decent turn-based tactical layer, with you deciding which levels to fight on and being chased down. But none of the levels match the sweaty feeling of danger of the original space ships. Return to the Void.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Wish I could give a neutral rating.They took the gunplay of Void Bastards, improved it but made the surrounding gameplay loop worse.It's trying a WH40K Mechanicus overworld gameplay, but there's just nothing to do in the overworld. No crafting or upgrading, everything for your characters is just random loot and upgrades you find down on the planets. Encounters feel like they have less variety as in Void Bastards. Maps are just randomly generated chunks to hide behind. I'm 8 hours in, I don't know if there's an actual gameplay loop that comes once you resurrected all characters, but if this is what it takes, I'm not going to find out.For me at least it missed the mark.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Wild Bastards is a roguelike hero shooter where you control a gang of outlaws tasked with resurrecting their fellow gang members. A ship called The Drifter helps you find them and the outlaws have a belief that it is trying to reunite them and help them go to a place called The Homestead so they can stop running from The Chastes who are chasing them all around the galaxy.The gameplay loop is rather simple and the layers that surround it don't take too long to grasp. You basically go from one solar system to the next and beaming down planets to find Helixes that will resurrect your fellow gang members, all the while having showdowns with a variety of monsters and other cowboys. Each fight is rather short, and while I didn't like that at first, I started to appreciate how it's more about strategic positioning and hide and seek than it is drawn out and crazy action like all the other FPS games I play.On top of the gunplay where you see yourself controlling 13 different characters, each with their own unique weapons and abilities, you will also need to manage their relationships with each other and the abilities they accrue as you venture out on your mission. Outlaw relationships are fickle and if you have two feuding against each other, then that means you can be put at a disadvantage in certain showdowns because each character has their advantages and disadvantages against certain enemy types. It may start off simple, but later into the campaign, you will find yourself having to choose your teams carefully and learn how they synergize together.Last thing I'll say is that for a roguelike, the story is deceptively good. In my first run I didn't care for it and I just wanted to shoot stuff, but upon restarting, I realize that this is a game where you need to take it as a full package. The story heavily gives you the context for your actions, and helps the emergent storytelling that happens when you beam down on planets with your selected outlaws. Modding them with equipment, upgrading their unique skills, as well as finding how they can assist each other in showdowns makes for a damn good game and I highly recommend it.Despite the long main campaign, it is still highly replayable considering how remixed each solar system can be and how you might not appreciate certain outlaw pairings until you experiment even further than you do on your first run.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game, I absolutely LOVED Void Bastards and this one is just dripping with the same awesomeness. The story, Characters, and overall Vibes are a MASSIVE improvement over Void Bastards IMO. I would definitely recommend playing the demo beforehand as it may not be for everyone but definitely worth a shot. I do wish there was actual randomization in aces and core aces, because it really feels like that on the first playthrough. If it were there, it would really up replay value. In any case, good gaem.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: While Wild Bastards is labeled as a roguelite, it doesn’t fully feel that way during the main game. Sure, it has procedural generation, unlocks, and different paths, but it’s not run-based—unless you consider a 10+ hour, story-driven experience to be a “run.” You do unlock a true roguelike mode after beating the story, but only if you’re willing to complete it first.Thankfully, the writing is excellent, and the choice to unlock new characters as you go keeps things engaging. Each character has unique skills and playstyles, though some are more effective than others (hello Sarge). However, you don’t get to just stick with your favorites. The game forces you to rotate characters due to mechanics like exhaustion and feuds, which can be tough if you’re not comfortable with a particular character’s playstyle.There’s also a big difficulty spike when you first encounter the porcupines. I died a few times before realizing that collecting aces is key, as it’s the only way to upgrade your team over time. All the other power-ups are temporary, so you’re constantly learning new mechanics.Once you get the hang of navigating the planets, the difficulty is pretty manageable. The arena shooter gameplay is solid, though enemies can blend into the background at times, making them hard to spot (luckily, there are some visual cues).I’d recommend Wild Bastards to anyone looking for a fun, story-driven adventure with great voice acting and interesting mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: This game has lots of quirks and things going for it, but unfortunately the gameplay loop is a bit long and overdone. The combat is fun but you can easily learn to manipulate certain AIs, especially the princes'. You can easily turn all the prince fights into really easy/mundane tasks and farm Infamy from jump to jump pretty early on. I wish there were some other quality of life improvements as well: -PLEASE add a button to function in the same way as clicking "Continue". Especially when the cursor position resets when loading a fight, PLEASE just allow us to press Space or Enter or F or ANYTHING to pass by the "Continue" prompts.-On this note, it would be nice to be able to press that same button to also skip certain animations like the end screen results after showdowns.-It would be nice if you could wait for more days at a time. When farming infamy, clicking wait and then yes to the double-dare like 3-5 times per prince gets really, really boring. It would be cool to have a "Challenge" button that would wait X days until the next prince arrives.As a general gripe, the gear system feels a lot like Cube World's leveling system: lose everything except maybe the one or two upgrades you earned for a few characters per jump. It feels like it could've been done different because you feel so powerless after every jump until late game, where you're practically one-shotting people depending on the character. And once you're confident enough, you realize you don't even need the Charged Aces because you're strong enough as is so there's no real incentive to diversify your roster. Find your favorites and just drop. I got to the point where I just set out to planets dropping 2 Bastards for a 4-max planet just because I knew it wouldn't be a problem. The Charged Aces mainly ended up being defensive bonuses, so if you don't care for defense you don't have to care about an entire core mechanic of the game.Also, I found a few typos. Nothing big, but come on.I loved the art style. The music is great too. The dialogue is sharp and some people have some fun lines among each other, it kept me wanting more! I just couldn't get over some pretty glaring problems about the main gameplay loop.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Never seen anything like it, a minimalistic Sci-Fi-Wild-West Hero-Shooter Rogue-Like. But it definitely works in every aspect!This one is even better than Void Bastards cause it has a real voice acted story, likeable characters and funny over the top enemies.Also, I wonder if The Drifter's (Destiny 2) voice actor found it funny to say Drifter that often.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't aiming to be an imsim, so don't expect Void Bastards 2. It's attempting something altogether different. But I'm a weirdo who liked Void Bastard's shooting more than its stealth, so this is almost tailor-made for me. Big fan of the cast, too. Each one of them really comes to life with their voice acting, art, and abilities.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Loved Void Bastards, and Wild Bastards has a lot of the same appeal, but I found the game play and encounters a bit lacking.I hate to compare the two so literally but I found myself doing it constantly throughout my playtime so far.With Void Bastards you dropped into a ship or station and planned your actions and equipment based on the environment and enemies. And then you had sort of a dungeon run to play through.Wild Bastards drops all of this in exchange for these very short sort of game play interactions. I think they were going for a sort of wild west shootout style, but I don't think it's enough to really keep me interested. The strategy and planning is sort of just gone and somehow the stakes feel lower. The smaller in size but more open feeling maps also make it feel like there is less risk if that makes sense. The claustrophobic corridors of Void Bastards really upped the tension I found and WB just didn't seem to have that same level of tension for me.The outlaws are fleshed out nicely. The relationships between them, their interactions, voice acting etc. all feels great. The style and personality of each is well done. But then it just feels like you don't do a whole lot with them and most of the time I just end up using the same 3 characters for almost every situation.I like the turn-based overmap gameplay, but it really needs some extended gunplay/encounters with some more variety to really shine.Overall still enjoying my playtime with this game, but finding I'm not enjoying the actual actionable time in game as much as I was with Void Bastards.Still a thumbs up from me though as it's a quality game from a quality developer.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Its not void bastards 2 and honestly thats ok, its got alot of the same strong style and unique choices as void bastards but a different game overall, alot more fighting in this game compared to void bastards which was more of a stealth game for alot of it. It also shares void bastards "grab what you can an run" style of choices.Its a game where you play as a group of space outlaws on the run, You move across short slay the spire type maps to pick planets, then you pick as many of the wild bastards as you're able to to beam down to the planet,  you're then given another map where you move around the planet grabbing what loot you can before leaving, on the planet you can get into fights where 2 of your characters are put up against a number of enemies having to fight them off in first person.On these ground battles you can't run and gun, if you do you'll get gunned down as quick as any of the enemies get gunned down by you. Instead you need to play it careful, wait and listen to the enemies, they'll check on eachother and give themselves away.Every outlaw has different abilities, they tend to be very different and each has its own way of going about things. From straight up gun slingers like spider rosa to a snake that slithers on the ground at high speeds lassoing people he can get close to with hopalong, miniguns, space blasters, dynamite, ect ect.You move from short slay the spire map to short slay the spire map, at the end of each one you unlock a character, each time you lose most of what you gained besides aces. Aces are your permanent level ups and they range from simple stat increases to more interesting things, you also gain equipment that has even great affects but those are lost when you jump to the next map.There are more mechanics I haven't gone over but honestly I really like this game. Its fun, its more strategic than a standard shooter and it has alot going for it once it really picks up. It is slow to start as you start with only 2 characters, but once you get about 5 characters unlocked or so the game really starts to get into a good and fun groove.Its just a good game to me
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay loop is fun, but there comes a point where you are facing a lot of very annoying enemies who hide behind shields that require you to use specific characters and it kind of defeats the purpose of the character system in my opinion.It makes the game exponentially harder and it's not an enjoyable obstacle to overcome, I would recommend if it wasn't for that.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Dang, I really really want to recommend this game. The structural progression bones and character differentiation is there... but the combat (which all the great surrounding systems are supporting) just feels... incredibly clunky? Slow? And the kind of clunky that ends up feeling unfair? Ex: The snakes popping out of the ground in a frame and spitting poison on you. Perhaps if incredibly mousy cat and mouse combat is your style, you'll enjoy it, but I'd watch a gameplay video before you buy is all.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: It's a yes but only so long as you don't think of it as a shooter. It's not an action roguelike! Instead, it leans much more into resource-management and movement planning side of gameplay. The shooting is almost like a mini-game to apply those resources and strategic planning. Which I think is fun. But definitely have the right expectations.I think the "roster" gameplay, and the "switching weapons is switching characters" is a fun twist.But it's a bit less shoot-y than I was hoping for, and the main thing for me is the pricing. It just feels really expensive for what feels like an experimental roguelike.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: I was worried initially, since combat was so quick and there were so many characters. However, this does a good job of following up Void Bastards with something a bit different! It's not as immersive-sim/exploratory heavy, but it feels like a proper FPS version of FTL(one of the great rogue-lite games). Bigger outer space map to advance through, pick a location, then outrun a chasing super enemy on the smaller map nested inside. Combat encounters are quick-paced "find and kill all enemies on each small map" type of thing, and it works for what this game is going for. Tl:dr Don't expect Void Bastards, but it's good!
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very targeted experience and is definitely not for everyone.At the start I liked the game a-lot, however the game just drags on and on with me doing very few of the parts I was interested in. Whilst the other stuff just turned into a grating feeling that I wanted to get over with. I haven't played the game for a while now, and on reflection I surmised it as this:TLDR: Wild Bastards is like an old school final fantasy game (think 8). You take 5 steps and your in a random battle, your trying to get to your parts of the game that you like (character progression), but you having to do 20-30 battles to do so and you just want them to f*** off.  I find this very fun to think about. Essentially you have 1 active party member and one inactive member. However the inactive member's passive abilities still trigger in the backline. This creates interesting combos, where you may keep a party member for his passive abilities whilst using a primary character for the shooting that you like more. This means that even the characters you don't like may have no use as your backliner. New abilities for your guys only come very seldom. These seem to be evenly distributed for your characters so you never have one guy too far ahead of the others. This is the bad part, because it takes so long to come across the new stuff that (may or may not and just be a stats) add interesting dynamics to the shooting gameplay. However it might be for a character you don't want to use so your stuck having to RNG wait another 30m through another 40 gunfights that you MAY get an ability for a character you are interested in.The board game ends up being something that hasn't got that much decision making to it. It ends up being somewhat obvious what the move is on each map so it ends up [EDIT} not really adding much to the game in the long run.The shooting is what the entire game is made of and sure it's fun, for a while. However like I said before, after a while it becomes extremely samey as around 5hrs in there aren't really any new enemies just harder versions of what's already there. New abilities that might end up giving variance to the combat doesn't come often, may be for a character you dislike or might just be a stats upgrade that doesn't add any dynamic to what you've been doing for the whole game. The shooting part of the game isn't strong enough to carry this for me. Halfway through the game also the story just deletes the party. Your stuck with some guys you don't like playing and the ones you actually like you don't get to see for another 5hrs.I haven't finished the campaign but i'm finding it hard to continue. An easy win for me would just to have a mode where I can pick 6/8 characters of the whole roster and just endless run until I die or something.

_childDocuments_.review: The most common comment I see is that this game is not Void Bastards, and I highly support that. However, it does share an important quality with Void Bastards; namely, it's not exactly fun but resembles fun. The game can be broken up into two distinct parts. Moving outside of FPS combat scenarios called showdowns, and showdowns. The movement outside of the main action sequences is just plain boring. After the first three rounds you end up waiting impatiently for enemy units to move along a set path. To its benefit, there is some strategy here. You can avoid some enemy types or prioritize going for some buff, but the risk/reward factor just seemed so bland. Conversely, showdowns are FPS sequences where you are dispatched with two characters to kill five or so enemies. It's what the game is arguably centered around seeing as how upgrades in the movement section directly support the FPS section. Yet, the FPS section boils down to picking two weapons in the form of characters that may have certain buffs depending on what you have given them. I think this is where the game resembles Void Bastards in the way I mentioned above. The gunplay is kind of fun, and that's where it peaks. I never felt like the FPS sequences were pulling me in. It was just a click-till-thing-dies event where maybe it started tickling that desire to experience more. You can talk tactics -- limited to crouching behind a piece of environment to block damage-- but it's just so narrow in scope. It's a shame because the game is so stylized, and it feels like it was made with love. Yet, it is a chore to play. I don't know what happens to the Wild Bastards by the end, but I hope their existence thereafter is far less tedious than what I experienced.Maybe worth a look on heavy discount, but I'm sad to say that this needed more polish before reveal.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game despite having some issue with it that are largely incidental to actually playing the game along with some points that are maybe me specific but i cant be sure.apologies up front as this is gonna be a little all over the place.Going into this game i was very hesitant as it looked a lot slower than void bastards, a game a really enjoyed, but after playing it recently, its not that much slower really, tho you can certainly play both pretty fast and loose once you know what your doing. Wild bastards also plays extremely similarly to how void bastards plays, insofar as moving around a map and shooting guys goes, if you played void bastards you'll feel at home with this, the differences come from the layer outside of the shooting, while in void it was a pretty simple screen of ships you moved along and jumped into, while managing your upgrades, here you travel from planet to planet in a similar style to void, once you choose one, you beam down to another grid that you work through to get upgrades and escape.This is somewhat where my first quibble comes in, while i like this, it does eventually get kinda tiring traversing these planet maps, in part due to the constant going in and out of fights. It might work out to be a similar time spent with exploring to combat ratio in void, but constantly going into tons of small fights that all last 10-60 seconds and going back to the map gets very draining, this isn't helped by the limited maps that are nice enough, but after the 30th time you beam down to the fort or mountain canyon map it does get tired.The next issue is tied together with something I really like, and is more if a disappointment of missing potential than anything else. I really enjoy the characterisation, there isn't a ton of writing in this game, but what is there is well done it gets across the character well, which is also achieved in how every bastard plays, it all comes together in a really fun way making all 13 feeling more or less different. unfortunately this leads into the thing i find disappointing with the characterisation, each character has 6 semi random level up slots, 3 core unlockable abilities, and one special ability that levels up and can only be used occasionally, the first group is mostly fine, but it did lead me feeling like I made poor choices with early abilities since the later ones with include upgraded versions of potential earlier ones but whatever. The second set is mostly very good with making each bastard distinct, sadly tho some character feel like they got stuck in a role that feels rarely useful like preach, who is designed to be a tank/healer, that seems nice but i rarely if ever needed it and some abilities don't scale well with the game like her medkit ability, some others are just boring like the last character just getting the same ability but upgraded again. But my biggest issue here is the charged aces, these are all, in there entirety boring, as they are all just basic stuff like more damage or health or armour. This feels like a big missed opportunity, since you only get to use it every now and then i was hoping for some cool unique stuff but it ends up just being a buff, that while nice to have, I never cared about and certainly never planned around it.This leads into more missed potential, I feel, with the pal/feud system, a small handful of things can cause characters to become pals, granting a minor buff in combat, or start a feud, meaning they cant descend to a planet together. maybe half of this is that, outside of one scripted moment, but i never had any feuding going, almost everyone was pals due to how i played, but that inst the real issue here for me, I understand you need or might want a system to force people to mix up teams by limiting them. What I find lacking is that when you are pal, the benefit you get is, after taking three hits in game, if you have a buddy, they do a small helpful thing, like using there juice ability (ult effectively) or giving you health and armour, but i really wish this was some cool unique thing that was unique for all the different combinations of teams you can have, like maybe if sarge is your second character, when you use a juice ability, you reflect the next one attack or something, maybe if its casino, when you juice, you deal 30% damage to two different enemies, I dunno. I understand that might be asking to much for how many combinations there are, but as is it just feels like a mostly ignorable vestigial system.This leads into my last disappointment with the characterisation, the balance of the characters. While certainly every character plays differently for the most part (a lot of them have guns that shoot, but how they shoot is whats important) and they all have certain enemies they are better or worse against, due to there being 13 characters this does lead to some overlap. Now I also understand everyone will have a different fav/worst character, i for one really like rawhide, but i struggle to think of someone who loves playing as kaboom, yes his dynamite is very strong and he can arc it everything else about him is lackluster, his invis, while nice feels wasted on him and billy has a more useful version and characters like smoky or casino have much more useful juice abilities, his core aces are lackluster to, he becomes immune to his blasts and doesn't take fall damage but this isn't much of an issue ever. kaboom isn't the only problem character here, i fell preach is pigeon holed into being a healer/tank and it isn't very useful most of the time, spider rosa is a good initial character but she falls of quick in usefulness. when compared to characters like hopalong, who is pretty niche sure, but through his core aces and upgrades feels like a cool assassin character who excels at picking of any single target in a way one one else can, Its just a bummer. and maybe they are better at higher difficulties but to that i cant say.The final real problem i have with the game is a lack of a good tutorial and a useful glossary. for instance, the game says smoky does 100* damage, obviously the * means something but the game doesn't tell you if you want to find that out, and while yes i did realise what it means after using him a couple time, it is an example of multiple different problems that all could be solved by a better tutorial or a glossary. how is fire damage different from poison? its in a tool tip but nowhere else. what is radiation damage? i have no idea. why doesn't it tell me sarge can see every enemy he has line of sight on. there a many things the game never tells you and you are left to figure out. Now i don't think this is inherently a bad thing, I'm fine with discovering things in games i like souls games, but considering the game tells you what a characters weapon and juice ability is when you first play as them, the least it could do is let me look at more detail on what characters can do and have access to.After reading all that above you may be thinking, "sounds like they hate this game why is it a positive review" because despite everything above, they are ultimately minor problems i have, with a game i enjoyed as much as i did, these small pain points felt extra painful when i thought about what the game would be without them. I like planing my teams for each planet, looking at its size and enemies, I loved sneaking around as hopalong or building an army or critters with rawhide. I enjoy the banter the characters have when you have a falling out with each other, the shooting is good, its feels good to learn how to take out a porcupine without taking any damage. I liked learning how to demolish to bosses that show up. While I might not like Wild Bastards as much as I like Void bastards on the whole, Wild takes a lot of the things in void and makes them better, expands them in cool ways. This game leaves me excited for whatever they do next.The game is just good.

_childDocuments_.review: "Just one more planet.... just one more solar system" - this is what I've kept telling myself throughout my nearly 60 hours of utmost fun I've had with this game. It was a hard purchase initially, seeing as the price is pretty steep for something that looked pretty convoluted/uninteresting from the gameplay videos I caught glimpse of on Youtube, but man - once you get into the saddle and learn the ropes, the game keeps you glued well into the night with its tight FPS arena showdowns and light strategizing on the overmap.The main star of the show are (of course) tense showdowns (played on Very Hard difficulty, both normal and a repeated run on Super Ironman, back to back) where you will sprint, shoot, try to outflank enemies and use many of the different outlaws' weapons and abilities (powered by Wild Bastards' version of whiskey/booze called "the Juice", which you can find throughout the arena) to be the last mutant/xeno/robot standing once the dust finally settles. The showdowns can also be quite underwhelming (when you use many of the overmap sites to reduce initial opponent count to basically 1,2 or zero), but most of the time prove to be extremely satisfaction-inducing once the adrenaline starts pumping as the enemy peppers you with lead, lasers, exploding ordinances, rockets and everything in-between. Should you survive through sheer will, cunning wit and keen aim, you will most assuredly feel like king of the world at that moment. The narrative presented in the main campaign also hooked me from the get-go - all characters had interesting personalities, and paced the otherwise pretty standard roguelite runs nicely, forming a coherent whole of some 15 interconnected, consecutive runs until you reach the end credits. I liked their petty squabbles and bond forming, while the language used throughout the game was very much in the spirit of Wild West genre and speech of that era, thoughtfully and cleverly written by someone who apparently lives and breathes Western flicks.The music, while quite atmospheric and therefore not too high key, managed to present a few themes that stuck to my ear even after a week from finishing the game - namely, the "Forest" (ear worm, this one), "Outlaw Sortie", "Posse is Coming", "Moon" and "Wild Bastards Titles" tracks stood above the rest.The artstyle made me wish this was a Cartoon Network Toonami series aimed for older crowds, with lots of cussing, brutal showdowns and overall somber tone full of both camaraderie and resentment. All characters were designed in such a way that you could easily discern each and every one from their outline alone, and much though was evidently put into how they look and play (on a personal note, Roswell and Spike stood out as not-so-Wild West-ish, but there are kinda lore/personality reasons for such design). The enemies (of which my favorite personality-wise and looks-wise was the first Prince, the half-witted McNeil) were also designed with heavy Wild West inspiration behind, with some even tiered (and their design slightly changing to reflect this). Overall, great visual presentation!Should Blue Manchu find success with this second "Bastards" game (Wild Bastards being sort of spiritual successor to their first outing - Void Bastards), I would urge them to cease experimenting with universes and stick with making a direct sequel (or DLC) for Wild Bastards - I am not the one to do a re-run of a game back-to-back once I've beaten the campaign (and have done so on maybe 2-3 occasions in my 30+ years of gaming), yet Wild Bastards made me do it! Not only that, but I had even MORE fun the second time around, knowing how the game flows, who works best in tandems and who plays better solo for those 3-man beam-downs, all the while staying on my toes with Super Ironman defeat conditions looming over my head ominously. If there ever was a game to simulate an entire Spaghetti Western Epic with all that it offers, it is, without a doubt, Wild Bastards. Here's to riding towards a distant sunset, somewhere in another galaxy far, far away...

_childDocuments_.review: and now onto the short review//intro//Hello, MF Kraven here- and welcome to a less than 10 mins review. A YouTube series where I take a look at niche titles, hidden gems & often overlooked games & tell you whether or not you should buy it, in less than 10 mins. So if that is the type of content that you like, consider subscribing, & liking this video.Today I take a look at Wild Bastards, an FPS Action Roguelike where you manage a gang of 13 space cowboys going from system to system, getting into showdowns, looting what they can all while being chased across the galaxy by the powers that may be. Can you keep your team well equipped & off each others necks? Or is it high noon for the bastards? Lets find out.//Graphics, Sound & Artstyle//Being a spiritual successor to 2019's Void Bastards, Wild Bastards brings a lot of that graphic novel charm to the game with an old western aesthetic that is just absolute kino. The voice acting is great at times & the ambiance music brings everything all together.//Gameplay//FPS Action Roguelike sound a lot like buzz words, and to label Wild Bastards just that is a disservice. The game starts you off with two members, and you go from system to system trying to revive your old crew. Upon arrival in a system you acquire loot (that you will only be able to use in this particular solar system). Each system has a few planets/events all with individual loot, you must go through them to get to your fallen comrade. Upon moving your ship to one of said planets, you must then beam a specific amount of your crew (can range from 2-4) down & there you will enter the procedurally generated map where you must reach a teleporter to "recharge" your ship to go to the next planet in the system. Like i said planets all have loot anywhere from Ace Cards, that work as a leveling up token, Mods (equipment you can use), Beans that you can use to mend feuds or create friendships with, Tonics that will revive a fallen team member or heal their fatigue, Cram (the in game currency). Each planet will also come enemies & "roadblocks" with a danger level & a specific amount of enemies you must defeat. You will be launched into a small map with said enemies & a showdown will occur, each Bastard comes with a weapon, HP bar, Shields & an ability. Abilities can be activated by acquiring "Juice" a floating canteen in each showdown. If you are traveling with a solo character you're on your own however the Bastards will travel in pairs of two, you may switch between them in a Showdown. Mixing weapons, abilities & synergy between the 13 characters is one of the wonders of this game. Upon reaching the teleporter on the map you will beam up & only Ace Cards will carry over from system to system all other loot will be disassembled upon completion. Which begs you to choose carefully what you think you may need going forward. The first playthrough is narrative driven & will have you collect all 13 members before going on specific missions to end the game. Upon completion you will unlock a challenge mode & a procedural generated run. //Price// 34.99 USD//How many hours estimated//It took me about 10 hours to beat the game, I rushed a lot of it to get the review in order & I sort of regret it cause I couldn't enjoy the game as much but now that I've unlocked the procedurally generated mode- I feel I can now just cozy up to it. //Is it Playable on Steamdeck?//Yes it is, however I truly do believe because the AI is just spectacular- you really do need the edge of mouse + keyboard. Especially if your Bastard happens to be Judge.//Final Thoughts//What can I say other than "WOW" there were so many moments where I felt like all hope was lost, there were moments I JUST got out of a showdown by a hair & 4HP left. One of the key words in the marketing is "Heart Pounding FPS Combat" & I didn't know how true it would be. Granted I suck at FPS games. Upon seeing the selection of characters I thought, theres no damn way this will work. There are 78 different combinations of teams you can make not to mention the equipment that will affect each character in a distinct way. And at first there were characters I said, Oh i don't think ill use them going forward & was thrusted to use them- then ended up really loving them like Hoparound, with a useless lasso but sprinting with him he'll slither along the map, & using his ability will render the enemies stunned for a few seconds, pairing him with Billy as I slither through the map with all stunned opponents, switch over to Billy & light their asses with lead or alternatively with Smoky & literally light their asses on fire. Using Judge to snipe all enemies & pairing him with Preach to switch over to in case enemies get to close- BAAM. Sarge has sort of X-Ray vision so I pair him with Spike & use them to assassinate from close to far in alternating forms. What I'm getting at is, this game is tons of fun.Picking up Ace cards for your guys will not only level them up but give them a buff too, some may just be extra HP or more shields, some may include "Takeout" where after a showdown they get HP recovered or adding more ammo to your weapon, more damage, adding an immunity to poison, spawning to a showdown with a hired gunman, etc etc. For a AA game it sure does feel like there's a LOT of replayability to offer but this may be where some are discouraged because the game relies a lot on RNG. I know people who wont even touch a game because of RNG. However to me, it adds that extra bit of randomness each time I pick it up.So I've told you the good, what about to bad & the ugly?I really wish we could have multiple saves, I want to try a Iron Man mode, a Very Hard & a normal one I can play on my SteamDeck when I'm on the go. Unfortunately it only has ONE Save file.I wish we could choose our starting two Bastards in a new run, or the very least try & go for a certain one in a playthrough. I know that Neil & his siblings are there so you wont cheese a level too much & get all the loot but sometimes it discourages me from battling an extra roadblock or two for the sake of just getting tf out of a planet. Sometimes I feel like the AI is TOO GOOD. Like they have xray vision, I can understand if the more elite enemies can do this but a simple hunter sniping me across the field is just frustrating at times. Also I would love a melee attack for all characters damage based on their physicality/weapon. The whole team synergy system is just too random, there are times I think- man I'm glad I choose these two to go to this planet just for them to start talking dookie to each other upon being beamed up- then I gotta spend a can of beans just so they don't beef anymore. And the last complaint I have, is often times a fellow bastard can be extremely annoying, like Spider Rosa will straight just be talking DOODOO if I miss my shot, unbeknownst to her I am clearing up covers to flank an enemy. Other than that, I have no real complaints- the game looks amazing, the gameplay feels intense and fluid, the roguelike elements, team management, inventory management, thinking about sending what team to retrieve what on a planet & choosing the best exit strategy when the inevitable Neal & Family come to try to clap your cheeks. Initially I didn't think I'd like the game as much as I do but here we are. Do I think Wild Bastards is worth the full entry price of 34.99 USD? Absolutely. Buy it Now!
