_childDocuments_.review: Extremely fun. No clue why this game isn't getting a fair rub. From what I can tell, it's because people expected this to be a completely different game. People are calling it a sequel to Void Bastards which is completely unfair. This is a cross between a strategy game and a roguelike, with a dozen characters, all with wildly different kits. There's a ton of variety here, really fun encounter design, excuses and builds to either play slow and carefully, or to stack invuln on kill with a teenager with two revolvers that fire at the speed of a machinegun. It's fantastic.Considering I didn't even hear it had come out, I blame marketing more than anything, but I'm very glad I picked it up and am always going to be excited to see what Blue Manchu puts out next.

You can switch between a few each fight which makes for some great tactical decision making.Overall I like this game a lot. Really unique and fun. I love how each of the mini games interact with each other and make your decisions in each one matter.

_childDocuments_.review: (Update after finishing it at the bottom)I've not finished it yet but after a relatively lukewarm impression of the demo there was something about it that made me want to check out the full game. Well I'm glad I picked it up because after about 8 hours (as of the time of writing), with about 7 sectors under my belt, this is shaping up to be better than Void Bastards.It takes some time to reveal its subtleties and clever mechanics and layers, but once you've got a few characters unlocked and you're hot-swapping them, popping off abilities during showdowns while enemies bark, flank and flee, it all starts to click and feel great. And that's just the showdowns. The turn-based overworld and space-hopping make it very difficult to put down. Just one more planet... or roadblock.The presentation across the board is gorgeous and super smooth, the user interface and access to information is nice and clear, the characters and enemies are really entertaining and full of personality with some stellar voice work and distinct AI. This has been such a pleasant surprise and it gets more exciting with each new bit of gear, biome, modifier, character and enemy that gets thrown into the mix. Some showdowns are real slow burns and tense after a botched beam-down, others are fast, chaotic and action-packed. Just tremendous stuff, so far.Update: well, I enjoyed this more than Void Bastards. It perhaps needed another ace up its sleeve towards the end, but overall a really surprising and satisfying strategy shooter. I recommend playing on the hardest difficulty you can stomach just because it forces you to carefully consider your options more. It makes your route through each sector a lot more interesting, tense and exciting. Wild Bastards is at its best when you're really having to think on your feet and fight for your life to get off each rock.

There is a LOT more strategy than void bastards or most other roguelikes, the art style takes some getting used too but can be absolutely gorgeous. It is a wonderfully made, beautiful, unique game. Thank you Blue Manchu for making great games

_childDocuments_.review: This has to be my GOTY 2024What a nice surprise! You can tell it was the same guys as Void Bastards and a lot of reviews mention that, but there's not much similar in gameplay. This for me is a plus as I gave up quite early on VBOn VB you can quickly go on a downward spiral as all your resources get eaten up each run. So a bad level where you have to run away early means you'll have even less resources for the next trip.With WB you have unlimited bullets, amazing special moves for each character. Characters to switch out if you get a bit stuck. Honestly sometimes even in the most dire of circumstances, you can totally 180 and come back on top. Even if you lose on the planet, you still get to keep the core pickups, with the ability to heal your character, or switch out to other characters to pick yourself up and try again.With VB you had a random, voiceless, dispensable  character. Now in WB you get handcrafted, upgradable, fully voiced characters with some truly unique special skills and weapons, with bonus interchangeable collectables for each zone. The pal/feud and energy mechanic is so good as well. This way you get gently encouraged to switch out your characters each run so the gameplay never gets stale. I'm 11.5 hours in now, and I still have a bunch of characters to unlock. Each one seems to help me out in their own way.VB had good, but repetitive ship environments. WB has totally different levels. Maybe I'm fighting in the treetops, or a toxic swamp, or a classic western, or frozen wastes, or low G planet. It's awesome! Having different equipment each run, so perhaps I can leapfrog over entire buildings, or have a hired gun with me. Switching a character mid battle is so cool as well. Pick off cowboys from a distance with the Judge, but then there's a fire-spewing grizzly behind a big tree? No problem, I switch to Kaboom and launch a stick of dynamite at them! I have so many memorably battle scenarios in my head I could blather on for ages!VB had a time limit as your oxygen ran out slowly, so I always felt rushed. WB you can either camp out as long as you want, or go all guns a-blazin' invoking panic in the enemy. You can be really sneaky if you like. The enemies can't help shouting at each other and give their position away on your compass. At the same time, of you make a noise, they know where you are. They don't always hit you straight away either. Many times I've had a bullet whizz past my head and thought "phew that was close!". The combat just feels fair and balanced. Sure they outnumber you, but you can have so many tricks up your sleeve to overcome them.The map system lets you split up your groups if you like and either get pickups or significantly cripple various enemies on the map, such as chow time, runaway buffalos, reduce their heath to 1, fight with a pack of helpful grizzlies, or destroy them altogether. This tactical play just works so well with the arenas. One injured party member can scour the planet and hoover up valuable resources, whilst your healthy pals can take on the enemies in another direction.The only negative thing for me is the 'rage mode'. For me it restricts the vision a bit too much with a red filter, which really gets obstructive in the night levels. Sometimes I just avoid collecting these altogether. Perhaps if the devs switch the screen to have a flaming border instead, or even enhance your vision? I dunno, maybe it's just me?I can only imagine just how much work went into character development and balancing in this game.Well worth your money and well worth your time. I can't wait to see what these devs are working on next.Oh and remember, beans fix everything

_childDocuments_.review: Void Bastards is a game that almost instantly climbed its way onto my Top 10 all-time favorites list, and that's not a list I update very often. So when its spiritual successor, Wild Bastards, was announced, I was excited but also wary. I could tell just from the description that it was a bit of a departure from the VB formula and themes. However, while I admit the game had a bit of a slower start with me before I really 'got it,' I'm happy to report that while Wild Bastards is in many ways a very different game, it shares the unmistakable DNA of its predecessor which made it so addicting and so fiendishly fun.There are a LOT of mechanics at play in this game and I'm not going to try and describe them all, but I will try and cover the key features throughout this review. You'll have to play the game for yourself to truly get a sense of the depth of its gameplay loop.The main idea of the game is that you travel from planet to planet, weighing its pros and cons, enemy types, and potential loot when deciding your route. Once you fly to a planet, you choose which of your outlaws to send down, between 2 and 4 of them depending on the planet's limit. Outlaws each have unique weapons and abilities so you want to choose a posse that best compliments each other. Once you're on the planet, the game shifts to perhaps its most unique element, the board game-like planet map. Here, you have a limited number of moves per turn to get your outlaws to where you want them to be, either over loot, character buffs, or the roadblocks of enemies you must defeat in order to move on. Your outlaws can be paired together in 'bunches' where they share moves and can fight together during a showdown (think of it as like switching weapons, except you're also switching characters and health bars as well). After so many turns, a dangerous Prince enemy lands on the planet to pursue you, at which point you're encouraged to grab what you can and get to the stairs to beam back up to your ship before the Prince reaches you, forcing you into a much more challenging showdown. The map also offers services like a shop to buy or sell items, chowhouses which lure away half of the enemies from all Roadblocks for a turn, vaults which can be opened for valuable loot at the cost of adding a very dangerous posse to the map, enemy debuffs which can make roadblocks easier such as weakening enemies or subverting their loyalty, and much more. The planet map is overwhelmingly the source of loot in the game, a peculiar departure from Void Bastards, where most looting was done during direct gameplay/combat. The nature of this element makes the overworld a strategy game unto itself though possibly at the cost of combat segments, which, as a result, offers little other than shooting and dodging.The game's combat segments take place primarily at roadblocks where a Showdown occurs. The combat of the game is fairly simple, perhaps to a fault at times, and could be considered the weakest element of the game although it does get more compelling as time goes on. Your basic movement is limited to walking, sprinting, crouching, and jumping. Since the early goings if the game will have you relying more on shootout-style shooting from cover, a lean function would be appreciated but alas, you'll have to settle for crouching and strafing. The weapons at your disposal depend on which Outlaws you brought into the fight with you. Your starting pair are Casino and Spider Rosa, who offer a fairly standard pair of pistols in the case of Rosa, and a Shotgun for Casino. But as with all outlaws, their weapons come with unique benefits. For instance, Spider Rosa's extra arms allow her to reload one pistol while firing the other, so she's rarely defenseless, even though her damage output is low. Casino meanwhile has a shotgun with a very short effective range but, true to his name, it rolls a random chance of one of 3 extra benefits, or none at all, during each fight. Outlaws also come with Stunts, or powerful, special abilities that can give you the edge when you need it most. Spider Rosa, for instance, throws out a decoy which is guaranteed to distract the enemy for about 10 seconds. Casino's Stunt is simpler, instantly killing one random enemy. You'll collect more outlaws with more unique stunts as you go. Learning to pair outlaws together in ways which best compliment their abilities is the key to success in combat and helps make the otherwise basic mechanics of fighting a bit more interesting.One of the strongest points of the game would be the Outlaws themselves. The characters have distinct personalities and motivations and it makes you care much more about individual outlaws and might ultimately cause you to favor some over the others for reasons other than their combat characteristics. Smoky, for instance, is a devoted cook who is deeply sensitive about his bean cooking and does not take kindly to criticisms (or sometimes even praise!) of his beans. Sarge is the 'old war dog' type of character...except he's a horse. Hopalong is an incredibly charming snake-man rancher who seems to want nothing more than to settle down with a nice farm, somewhere. An interesting mechanic to the game is that you have to maintain the relationships of your Outlaws as you go. If outlaws having a Falling Out, either through scripted or random events, they will be unable to beam down to the same planet together. To fix this, you have to find the rare-ish cans of beans found throughout the universe and have the feuding outlaws share a can together. Additionally, if you do this with outlaws who aren't already feuding, they will instead become Pals, and help each other out during showdowns with powerful abilities that can be a literal lifesaver when your back's against the wall.Wild Bastards is more story-driven than Void Bastards. While VB mostly focused on somewhat random protagonists who never said a word, Wild Bastards' story takes the specific characters into account when crafting the narrative, and features unique interactions between then, either during scripted events or during Showdowns. A small but appreciated detail is how even your enemies will call out your character by name, making everything feel just a bit more 'personal.' The story itself is predictably silly but also a bit dark in a way, as it sees you traveling the universe, resurrecting your dead allies who were systematically hunted down and murdered by the Chaste family for reasons that appear to be purely racist in nature, with humans having some kind of deep disdain for Xenos. Indeed, all other robots or alien creatures you see are subjugated as servants or attack dogs for the enemy, and human enemies shout out condescending insults at your outlaws as you fight, making it just that much more satisfying to cap them, especially when the final enemy realizes he's all alone and offers to 'talk it out.' The game's ending may seem a bit sudden and leaves a myriad of questions unanswered and situations unaddressed. Not sure if this is in preparation for a sequel or DLC but those looking for more of a concrete finale might be left wanting.All in all, while Wild Bastards was, at first, a bit slow on the draw so to speak in terms of getting me on board with what it offers, after a sector or two I found I had really gelled with its gameplay and find it to be similarly as addicting as Void Bastards. The games themselves are quite different and its possible Wild Bastards might be too much of a departure for people looking for more of the same as what VB offered. But as I said before, they share enough unmistakable DNA in their core mechanics of planning, strategy, and luck for Wild Bastards to be a more than worthy successor to what remains one of my favorite games of all time.

_childDocuments_.review: I dig it. The fights are tense. Tough decisions must be made. It's a nice mix of elements. Sound design and voice acting are top-notch and add to the tension (and fun) of the showdowns. "Them boys done ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up" TLDR: Wild Bastards is much more than I expected, and it's got at least one foot in the circle of 'greatness.' Equal parts tense action and satisfying strategy- and it only gets more fun as the mechanics get deeper with each successive Sector.A Hearty Recommend---I see some whinging about 'unfairness' and ' lack of balance' in the user reviews. With over 30 hrs under my belt, I don't see the 'major balance issues.' Learn the mechanics, plan well, and you'll be okay.  For my part- there were a few mechanics that I disliked when I first came across them- only to discover that they are very well placed in the full-scheme of the game. At the risk of being long-winded: I went back and played Void Bastards as well, which is a 'sibling' to WB, and there is a common theme to the negative reviews in both games: It's folks who can't be bothered to learn the mechanics. Certain dangers have 'counters' that you're meant to employ. If you don't counter the danger, they'll F you up. If you don't plan well,  or get very unlucky, you may not have a counter on-hand. It's okay- death is not the end of the world in these games- it's just a lesson.Give it time, and don't go throwing a Thumbs Down before you give this game a good chance. Wild Bastards was very thoughtfully designed. It's a rogue-like (although not a traditional one)- You will get caught out from time to time, and if you learn your lesson, hopefully it won't happen quite like that again. Usually, you made a mistake. Rarely, you just got unlucky.There are different difficulty levels, and playing on normal is challenging but not overly punishing. A good place to learn. Hard is a stiff challenge, and you'll likely lose a few showdowns, and possibly a few maps. I think this is the sweet spot for me. Very Hard is on offer- as is Easy, for the cowards among us.Now, I can't say for sure whether this has the legs to last for dozens of hours (EDIT- it does. Lots of content). There is a solid bucket of maps for each planet/biome type, so I have no complaints there. Each map is different each time based on what you're fighting. Plenty of different enemies- and you'll learn to hate a few of them, but they certainly keep things interesting!I've gotten some great mileage out of this, and I'm looking forward to playing plenty more- I have not exhausted the content by any stretch.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a really great chunk-based FPS rogue-like where you jump from sector to sector in a large galaxy, losing all your material possessions between each jump, but keeping any and all stat upgrades you get for your characters in the form of "ace" cards that help you specialize your crew of misfits to your exact liking.There's also 13 different characters you can get in the game during your journey (and I love them all except the stupid pink crystal guy, but even he's pretty fun to play as). You get them in a specific order in the main, more story driven campaign, but the order can be randomized on a followup playthrough, and they can all be paired with each other so that you can freely swap between them like holstered weapons in combat. So you can bring in the funny shotgun robot in one hand, but then freely swap into the the long range sniper robot if you paired them up.Some characters also sport unique movement powers along with a unique weapon such as the martian having a better jump, or the horse-man having a highly empowered sprint who can act as powerful aids to whoever your main carry is, and each character has an ability that ranges from a mildly useful buff to game breaking "set everyone on the enemy team on fire" effects, all of which combining to make really interesting combos and synergies between all the different cowboys/cowgirls.If none of that appeals to you, there's also a busty dummy thicc nun woman in a skintight black bodysuit who kinda looks like Caleb from Blood and uses a crank-gun who wants to kiss the martian man, and a milf-mommy fish archer. I was sold on just the fact I could play as a robot with a slot-machine eyes and a 4 armed Spanish spider woman, and you better believe, I would have bought it twice as fast if I knew those two were in the game too.

_childDocuments_.review: Regretfully and thankfully, this game isn't Void bastards.The structure of Wild bastards is very similar to Void bastards, but with a much greater emphasis on the turn-based strategy part. While in Void bastards the turn-based parts only served as a way to get to new (and more dangerous) areas, Wild bastards heavily commits to it and makes it much more important than the actual FPS segments in between. Void bastards was an FPS with turn-based strategy segments, Wild bastards is (almost) a turn-based strategy with FPS segments. Both parts of the game are very intricately linked, and that makes the gameplay very addictive. The roster of bastards is varied and with some really creative gameplay mechanics to add variance (eg. a bastard who sprints very close to the ground, being able to move from cover to cover more safely). Environments are very well made as well, with a really stunning high-tech wild west art direction that fits the game really well. Bugs are very rare, during my 60 hours of playtime I only found about 4-5, most of which resulted from the characters accumulating velocity while getting stuck, and then taking a lot of fall damage. This game is well worth the asking price, if only to support the devs who did a stellar job with making this one. Hopefully they'll make some more content for the game, including at least a DLC or two.

_childDocuments_.review: I was expecting something akin to Void Bastards. Wild Bastards is nothing like it. But even on its own merits, I thought it was a mediocre game to play. Wild Bastards is essentially a rogue-style arena shooter. You select different rooms on a map and complete somewhat annoying arena encounters with enemies, defeat them, and move on to the next room. Most resources collected decay once you move onto the next galaxy, and any permanent upgrades found are weak, like +10% damage. The only unique aspect of the game is dealing with your guns deciding they don't want to work with that other gun because he made fun of their mother, and the only way to fix their relationship is to feed them a can of BEANS 🙄. The worst part of this game is the arena shooter aspect. You move too slowly, enemies blend in really well with the environment, and it's very difficult to tell where or who's shooting you. Paired with certain enemies invalidating certain weapons, and whose counter you couldn't bring because your guns were arguing over who's the best Beetles member or something. Wild Bastards is a game whose genres are arguing with each other as much as the guns.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you ever play paintball? When you're hiding in the bushes hoping not to get spotted and startled by every sound in case you're gonna get shot? This game gives you that feeling of being outnumbered and outgunned, but trying to pull off a win against overwhelming odds. This is not a standard FPS, or even a standard rogue-like. This is a strategy game where the encounters are each a semi-randomized arena shooter. Each fight is a quick-draw cowboy duel where both you and your enemies are surprised to see each other around cover and you get a (brief) window to get the first shot off - or hide on a roof and snipe with a bow - or mow down all the cover on the map with a gatling gun - or burn the place down with fireballs or dynamite - or summon a pack of wild animals to flush out the bad guys. You play your characters out like a board game and the strategic loop is optimizing their strengths with the enemies you're up against, or sometimes just making do with a non-optimal encounter - limitations breed creativity! Also the writing and voice-acting are great, and actually quite funny!

_childDocuments_.review: Wild Bastards is the latest cell-shaded, strategic, single-player, first-person shooter from gaming studio, Blue Manchu.It's touted as the "spiritual successor" to 2019's Void Bastards, a charming, rogue-lite, FPS that saw you travelling through space and looting parts to build new equipment and repair key instruments on your space craft. It still holds up today and I highly recommend it.I'm sure there are some ways in which Wild Bastards could have been better but I also don't think Blue Manchu left anything out because of constraints, they had a clear vision of what they wanted to deliver and given the level of polish of their finished product, I think they can pat themselves on the back for having delivered it.I am still enjoying it. I would say that it's not the type of game that you play through in one sitting but given how quickly it gets going from launching the game to being in a showdown, it's great for pick-up-and-play.If you can stomach the random swings in difficulty then I can definitely recommend Wild Bastards.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted this to be leaning more into being an immersive sim; that's on me.  It  an immersive sim in the slightest.This is an obscenely shallow game: it's basically just 'showdowns', which are spit-and-it'd-reach-the-other-side arenas full of hit-scan/homing shots that force you to spend most of your time trying to re-locate shouting at your monitor screen in disbelief due to all the bullet spam coming from the tiniest angles, heat-seeking the pixel you've got overhanging.  ...and that's it: that's the whole game.The 'roguelike' elements amount to barely anything.  You don't feel like you're in control or that you're actually 'getting somewhere'.  The crew 'feud' system gets into a death spiral, and there's never enough beans.  ...and  it's fricken annoying being blasted by heat-seeking shots you  avoid without having terrain in your face.  ...but you can't even do that because there's a load of mechanics in play to  you to move...right out of your safety spot where you're trying to hide from the deadliest goons you've ever known whilst  character's shots make you second guess if the characters drunk.And no, it isn't 'too difficult for me' - the game is lacking a 'dodge' mechanic.  If you couldn't dodge attacks in DOOM Eternal or Dark Souls it'd be brutal.   is just bad game design.I honestly - and I hate to say this - wish I could refund this.  The base idea is sound, but it's so badly executed.  I guess I have to hope they, y'know, see sense and buff this up slightly?

_childDocuments_.review: Never played Void Bastards, so no references on that one.The game is good, though I did see some flaws that made the hunts rather trivial to deal with like with spamming the teleporters and making them bug out and stand in the acid, dying very fast without you having to do much. I wouldn't call it a heart-pounding or particularly engaging FPS; rather, it's a straightforward survival game in which you must complete objectives while selecting powerups and character compositions to cycle through while taking risks to acquire more wealth or be captured by powerful bounty hunters that keep coming even if you manage to kill the previous ones.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the visual style, but I found the voice acting to be really hit or miss. Some characters were downright bad, others were tolerable-decent. You choose two characters to warp down to a planet with, but while you're using one, the other constantly yells at you to switch to them, which is really annoying. If I'm at a long distance sniping guys I'm not going to switch to the shotgunner or pistol user... stop yelling at me to use the other character. I'm not a big fan of the structure of the game. Moving around the "game board" style map doesn't feel fully fleshed out. It's turn based with a certain amount of moves per turn, but early on at least, it feels entirely pointless. The basic enemies who move around the map aren't a threat whatsoever so it doesn't really matter if you run into them, then when the big baddie shows up I'm told to avoid it entirely. So you'll maybe hit two "turns" where they actually matter at the end of a map run, since the enemies turns don't matter until the big baddie shows up. I also found the moment to moment gameplay to be pretty boring and lacking. You can basically take as much time as you need to move through an arena and it pays to go more slowly and pick enemies off, who basically just wander around yelling for each other, giving away their positions the whole time, making the whole thing really easy. The gunplay itself doesn't feel terrible, but also not very satisfying or meaty, so just kind of mediocre. Progression for the characters seems mostly non-interactive too. You find cards on the playing field and they get slotted in automatically, leaving very little up to choice. You do get to choose your cards for level-ups, but that's also limited to a few upgrade slots per character. Items disappear between warp areas and are only temporary, making buying them at shops seem pointless since they are only temporary buffs. I only played my 2 hours and returned it, but I just don't think it was engaging enough for me to continue playing past 2 hours. It seemed relatively glitch free, at least.

_childDocuments_.review: Full Gameplay Walkthrough - Wild Bastards has a lot of charm and style, and that's enough of a hook to want to dive in and see what the game has to offer. Using a sizable roster of characters who are the major differentiators for gameplay as the main motivator to keep going is effective as well. But once you've got the Bastards roster filled out and you have combat figured out well enough, that's about where the buck stops in this sci-fi western. It's a chaotic and challenging experience, but promises a lot of complexity and nuance that seems bountiful at first, but fizzles a bit given time. Some balancing issues hold it back the most from being truly fulfilling, but there's a little bit of genre fatigue talking on my part as well. On its own merits, Wild Bastards is ambitious and kinetic, and will definitely put FPS fans' skills to the test.Overall its Wacky , Funny and all the right mixture of things Rating - 8.5/10Go For It

_childDocuments_.review: Overall Rating - 7.8/10I beat this game in a two-day streaming marathon on release (shameless self-promotion hehe).  I played it on Hard difficulty and with Ironman mode enabled. Playing this way definitely made the stakes higher and the whole experience feel way more tense.  The threat of losing my progress once all my outlaws were injured (Ironman mode's core feature) made every combat and gear decision matter a whole lot more. I mostly enjoyed my experience with this game. I went into it not knowing too much about it and was pleasantly surprised.  The roguelite and RPG elements work well.  Each outlaw character has their own unique personality, abilities, weapons, and play styles.  This keeps gameplay fresh throughout the play through, especially when you're forced to use characters you're not familiar with.  The modifications and class cards (which give characters extra abilities and stats) give you something to strive for as the game goes on.  Enemy variety is definitely a plus, although the boss Princes are a bit lackluster and grew stale after I fought them a dozen times to grind Infamy (the game's roguelite currency).  More boss variety definitely would've been nice.  Some areas are a bit difficult to fight in.  It can definitely feel a little cheap when you have minimal cover and enemies that can easily see and hit you.  Tracking down the last enemy in the map can sometimes be annoying, but it's not too big of a deal.  I also had to reload my game twice after enemies got stuck within the map itself.  I feel like the map design and enemy AI/accuracy could be tweaked a little bit, but overall I didn't find this too big of an issue. Enemies are challenging and mostly fun to fight.I think this is a cool game, one that is definitely worth playing, primarily if you like the RPG, Roguelite, and FPS mash up concept.  I think Ironman mode makes this game more appealing and rewarding, but to each their own. The initial price point is a tad steep, but it's definitely worth picking up if you're interested in it or when it eventually gets a better sale. Once I started this game it was hard to stop playing. Honestly though, I don't know if the endgame challenge mode brings too much more to the table for me personally.  I don't see myself going back to it now that the main campaign is done, but I really enjoyed almost all of my 27 hours with it. GG

_childDocuments_.review: It's a braindead arena shooter with almost no mechanics to speak of. Unlike their previous games which had RPG mechanics, looting, etc all of that is gone here, you have 12 generic outlaw characters going to generic outlaw planet being chased by generic outlaw hunters. All of them use generic shooter guns, you fight generic enemies, all of which is done on generic planets. There's zero progression too. The game bathes you in money, items, etc and then yanks them away from you ALL THE TIME. You very quickly learn never to explore or take risks because the only thing you get to keep is aces; everything else is pretty much worthless. Your character start weak and more or less stay weak the entire game, as you cannot just upgrade your guns to make them better. The theme of the game is "Lazy design", a lot of really safe choices were made because it was easy. Stairs and ladders just teleport you from side to side lazily, enemies can you see you from across the map and just bombard you with hitscan attacks, and pretty much the entire game is composed of those really lazy arena shootouts. The number one thing I am seeing from the reviews is that everybody is confused why they chose such a rediculous soup of mechanics and dressed it around these shootouts. Why is the game obsessed with stealing all my items? Why are all of the character names so bad? Who in their right mind thought that being bombarded from all sides all of the time was a good idea?

_childDocuments_.review: Having finished this game, I highly recommend it. Great writing, great action, and a cool strategic overland game. If you've played Void Bastards, some things will feel familiar, but it doesn't have the immersive sim elements or sprawling levels of that game.The structure goes like this: you navigate through a sector comprised of nodes like a typical roguelike map. Some of these are planets you choose a few outlaws to beam down to. On the planet, you've got another node-based map, but this one's less linear and requires more planning, and you've got a turn limit before the big bads show up. Some of the nodes are showdowns, which are your first-person segments.In these segments, you've typically got two outlaws you can hotswap between, and you have to kill all the bad guys before they kill you. Sounds simple, but it also requires a lot of thought and careful planning, and these segments can be very tense games cat-and-mouse. I thoroughly enjoyed them.The Bastards themselves are wildly (heh) different from each other. You've got a guy with a shotgun, a guy with a sniper rifle, a lady with a minigun. You've also got a snake man with a lasso, a ghost with dynamite, a fish lady with a homing bow, and some other cool stuff. Each outlaw has an active ability and a variety of passives you can pick up that make them feel even more different from each other. The character design is top-tier; I found each of the Bastards a lot of fun to play with, and finding fun synergies between them was also great.Anyway, highly recommended. I super like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant to purchase this game at first. I watched a ton of reviews and still didn't really have my mind made up.I like the aesthetic of Wild Bastards, but not as much as Void Bastards (never played VB though). Void Bastards also has a reputation for being very good so, I felt that this game would be quite good even with the sizable departure from VB.I purchased the game taking advantage of the two hour Steam "trial." After hitting that two hour mark I felt a little worried as I was having fun, but didn't know if the repetition and Hopalong (lowest tier character) would grate as things progressed. I did a little reading on Reddit and that helped quite a bit. The professional reviews are pretty poorly written in my opinion and Reddit has some pretty positive energy around this title even if not sizable (I am also very curious how this game is doing). So, diving back in, I've found myself having even more fun and this game very much has that, "one more time" energy. The learning curve is still there and I don't have all of the bastards yet. I'm still very much engaged and don't know why I worried at all. It also functions really nicely as a jump in and jump out kind of game which I needed. I have enough time-consuming rpgs and don't play online games all that often. This fits very nicely I would recommend it at the current full price.As far as price is concerned, there are so may things that cost close to $40 that I get far less out of. _childDocuments_.review: Some levels are great.  Some not so much.  The gameplay loop is pretty simple to pick up, and overall it's a fairly fun shooter.  Once you've unlocked all of the bastards you have more variety in how you approach each zone, but I found myself mostly sticking to the same ones whenever possible.That being said, I really hate the whole falling out system.  It just feels like this incredibly annoying factor that's designed to make you switch up characters.  I get it, you want us to play as all of the bastards.  But I don't want to.  Because I don't like all of them.  Just let me have fun and stop making them always fight.The maps aren't really all that varied and you'll start to remember the best ways to handle them as you play.  This does make the game feel a bit repetitive fairly early on, and perhaps it is because none of the characters really truly feel like they're designed for fast paced combat.  Maybe it's just the way I played.  I don't know.In any case, I've played the game before, elsewhere away from Steam.  I finished it, and I'm slowly and casually playing it again here.. It's a decent roguelike shooter.  If you liked Void Bastards this might be a solid follow-up of sorts for you to try out.

_childDocuments_.review: Although Wild bastards has flaws, over all it is a good game. More like middle of the road. The encounters feel samey as there doesn't seem to be much enemy variety. My biggest gripe is that I don't feel like there is any danger. If you die with all of your characters, you don't start over. You go back to the beginning of the section.        I wouldn't call this a roguelite/roguelike game, either. There are only a couple of changes to each run. There are not any extra items/abilities/guns to pick up along the way. Don't get me wrong, each character uses a different gun and has different abilities. However, these don't change and they are always available. The equipment that you get doesn't seem to matter much, either. I found myself just mindlessly installing them on whichever character I would send out to fight.        Overall, this game is entertaining. I do not think it has the legs to keep me coming back over and over like other Roguelites, but I enjoyed most of the time I spent playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been looking forward to this game for a hot minute. I was a huge fan of Void Bastards and had beaten the game a few times, and when I learned about Wild Bastards I knew I was gonna love it. The best way I can describe this game is that it's FTL with the Darkest Dungeon 2 relationship mechanic. The loop is simple, you arrive to a sector, go between various planets, choosing which characters get beamed down. You fight through the planet, looting anything and everything you can, then bail. Rinse, repeat until you get to the end, where you can spend any resource you didn't for Infamy (which is also rewarded from killing enemies). There are one big issue with the gameplay loop, and that's any mods (weapon mods, armor mods, etc) and normal cash (called Cramm) are lost, along with your resources. I feel like it's a step too far, it makes grabbing anything that isn't character upgrades feel useless by the end, even with how powerful some mods are. This isn't a deal breaker, but it feels like a lot of the unlocks in the game are Mods, and some mods are "character specific", where they either give an extra buff to specific characters or they debuff the character its equipped unless it's one specific character. The worse part about these mods, you can get those types of mods even if you don't have the character. I've gotten Sarge's weapon mod numerous times way before I got Sarge, and every time it went unused. Now granted, that complaint is ultimately minor compared to how much good this gameplay has. A lot of people say the gunplay is "weak", but if you play Void Bastards, you know the Gunplay involves less mechanical skills and more tactical. And let me tell you, this game is BRIMMING with it. Some characters completely counter specific types of enemies (Smoky and Kaboom get 75% and 100% Fire Resistance for example, making them a hard counter to any character that deals Fire damage, which is a lot of extremely powerful enemies.) The looting on planets is fantastic, the only complaint I have about it is not being able to tell how long you have until a Prince arrives. So sometimes you have a big planet with the Prince arriving in one turn. But it also adds a level of Risk versus Reward. You keep anything you loot on the planet, even if your characters 'die', so you could risk it even with a Prince on the board.TLDR: Lot of depth, if you enjoy FTL/Void Bastards, you'll love this game. a solid 8.5/10 in my book.

_childDocuments_.review: Wild Bastards is a uniquely fresh experience in the roguelike shooter genre, it has one of the most entertaining and addicting gameplay loops I have seen in a while. It combines the board game genre with first person shooter and some light roguelike elements to create this unique mixture unlike anything I played in a while.Throughout the game you will unlock 13 unique characters, each of them very different from the rest. At first I was playing favorites, but once I started experimenting with all characters I discovered they aren't just different sets of weapons. For example: Hopalong is a snake-man that uses a lasso to choke out enemies and slithers low to the ground when sprinting making him perfect for taking out isolated targets. Since he needs to stay still when choking enemies, he is an easy target for groups like Cyotes. Thankfully you can take two characters into every encounter and you are encouraged to mix and match their strengths and weaknesses.Each character can level up by finding more aces for them which serve as a passive bonuses that persist throughout the playthrough. Over time these bonuses accumulate and in combination with equippable items can lead to some broken combinations that rip through most encounters in game.However, your enemies are just as varied as your heroes and require a variety of tactics to overcome. Mortitians hide in the environment and send out homing orbs of energy to hunt you, so you need to locate them and rush them asap to avoid being swarmed. Yellowbellies hide behind energy barrier that is hard to flank without getting hit, but they can be easily countered by Rawhide character who fires projectiles that go through their shields.Whole game is this balancing act of choosing best characters for the job but not over-using them, as they get tired and lose some of their passive bonuses until rested. You constantly balance risk vs reward, especially when moving on the board between combat encounters. If you take too much time to accomplish your goals one of the Princes will land on the planet and start chasing you. They can be beaten once they catch up to you, but they are challenging enemies and its better to avoid the confrontation.Wild Bastard just like previous game from Blue Manchu has beautiful, timeless artstyle that is unlike any other. This game looks amazing and will look amazing in 20 years, its such a unique look. Voice acting and music are very catchy and there are many funny dialogues in the narrative campaign.Anyone who is even remotely interested in shooter-rogulites should give Wild Bastards a try. Its a unique experience that offers solid amount of content over multiple modes and difficulty levels, all of that at much lower price than we usually see.  I really hope this game finds its audience as it seems its misunderstood by many players.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is Void Bastards, but instead of playing cat and mouse on space ships, it's shootouts in mini arenas.During shootouts you can pair up combinations of two distinct characters, all of which has their own unique weapons/playstyle, and you can quickly swap between the two characters. In that sense you can find some effective pairing.Just like Void Bastards, you can either sneak around the enemies as you take them out and get character unique abilities, and use audio and visual cues to find enemies in each stage.There's a slight learning curve as you figure out the mechanics and each characters unique playstyle but once you get the hang of it it plays real quick and fun like Void Bastards. There's also a lot of funny quips and dialogue throughout the gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: A deceptively familiar rejigging of the Void Bastards formula - which unleashes the true potential of the strategy-roguelite-FPS hybrid Blue Manchu had been working towards. While it may not seem like it at first, this remix offers more varied situations and rewards experimentation a lot more. Be warned, however: the environmental interactions, level exploration, and immersive-sim touches from Void are pretty much gone - an acceptable trade-off imho, given that those were a bit shallow and the source of much of the repetitiveness.The added characterization (through weapons, basically - each being tied to a character) also adds a lot of personality to the game, thanks to some sharp writing, terrific voice-acting, and a feud system fueling the banter between the characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game! It’s a thoughtful and rewarding fps for people who have played fps for most of their life. Each character is a play style and pairing them on outings becomes strategic with how to approach encounters and gain resources to upgrade and outfit the team. Every scenario feels rewardingly difficult and is a blast to overcome. You’ll discover builds and tactics for each character and come to appreciate their individual play styles. Enemies are fun, the art unique, the sound design satisfying (every click is a visceral audio reward), gameplay top notch. I really only have one complaint is that I wished the narrative was a little longer, and the ending more satisfying! You’re exposed to a roster of ‘bad guys’ and you never really have a final confrontation with them, which felt like an opportunity missed sadly. Still, easily worth the money, and plays amazing on steam deck!

_childDocuments_.review: The joy of this game is picking your tools (items, heroes, buffs, upgrades) and figuring out how to use different combinations of them to beat a variety of enemies in a variety of locales. Each character plays differently, each enemy poses a different threat, and each environment causes a different level of discomfort. I wouldn't say it's a masterpiece, but I'd say it's 12 hours of campaign-time that I sure will remember as being fun.Look it  an fps at heart. It's just one where you have to constantly learn and switch tools to take advantage of the enemy and situation. There's a light strategy element in the overworld, but it's very hard to screw up on that. There are stealth elements, and some characters heavily benefit from them (to the point of being able to solo otherwise-impossible encounters). It's just not the "crabwalk and quickload" kind of stealth. And, it thankfully omits any survival elements.Some complained about the length (12hr for me on first playthrough). But the pacing isn't far off the mark. There's a mid-campaign beat where your characters change, and it acts as a test to see if you're able to work with a limited set of tools after having such a wide set of tools.But, really, let's be honest, the impressive thing here is that half a dozen guys can come together and make titles that are stylish, innovative, engaging and fun. Sure, they've got industry-defining titles like Bioshock, shock 2, terra nova, captain forever, and thief under their belt, so they're a stacked deck; but it's a different world when there's only like, 6 of you.I hope whatever they come up with next is just as different as WB is from VB.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a slow burn, it took a few hours for me to really start clicking with its systems and loop. But once it got its hooks into me, I really started to love it. I don't think Wild Bastards is for everybody, but if you enjoyed the excellent Void Bastards, you will probably like this roguey-er, gamey-er sequel.

Only thing I would change is add an extended campaign mode or more to do after beating the game cause I some really good op mods and  level up all my outlaws only to start from fresh all over after the campaign.Hope their be more content in thee future

_childDocuments_.review: can't recommend this atm. The random generated elements of the game are often unbalanced. I'm playing the hardest difficulty. and have reached a point where progress is viciously slow. The progression you make to your squad over time is still no match for 9 ironclads, who will decimate you, if you aren't willing to cheese them, which is no fun. The feud system seems busted on this difficulty. Why you would ever want to create 'pals' instead of stopping crew from feuding alludes me on this difficulty. The more feuding takes place the more i notice how poorly implemented this system is. - two of them feuding because of trite reason, you give them beans, immediately feud is over. nice one. Feud takes place over 'bean' related disagreement?....give them beans. feud is over. Shame they didn't take these character interactions as an opportunity to develop them all more. it's beans this, beans that. gets old fast. Also...what do i care if my crew are 'tired' or how 'tired' they are? on this difficulty it's all hands on deck, it doesn't mean anything to me.Update. Gave it a lil break out of frustration, jumped back on and same problems persist. You end up in battles that are just unwinnable. Just doesn't make any sense to keep on with it. Really wanted to enjoy this game, it does have a lot to enjoy but the balance on the highest difficulty is simply broken.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: I've thoroughly enjoyed my time with Wild Bastards so far, and I was a big fan of Void Bastards. It's been the perfect Steam Deck game. Like Void Bastards, you make strategic decisions as you navigate a map and duke it out in small arenas. Also like Void Bastards, the world building here is really lush, despite the game moving quickly and not taking much time to explain itself. The maps are varied and interesting, and sometimes downright pretty in a way that makes you wish this was an open-world adventure game. I love the cast of characters. The style is lovely. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who loves his fair share of boomer shooters and rogue-likes (roboquest my beloved), this game is very different from anything I've played before. And honestly, it's a lot of fun. I think one thing that helped me wrap my head atound the combat is that its primarily meant to be played rather slowly, since enemies can drop you faster than you can drop them (on a count of how often you find yourself outnumbered). There were so many times where I found myself getting into perilous situations because I tried to run around like I was playing DOOM and lost a run.In the early hours of the game, I had a lot of success (and fun) playing it like something more akin to a tactical shooter, listening to enemy footsteps and voices, and waiting for the perfect opportunity to strike.This felt off to me at first since it seems like a typical boomer/arena shooter. But if you treat it like that, you will get demolished, especially as the game introduces more difficult enemies and environments.That's not to say that the game can't be played more aggressively, especially as you unlock more Bastards whose abilities may make these kinds of approaches easier to pull off, but you may find yourself dead in the dirt before you've even managed to drop a single enemy if you aren't prepared. The real shine of the game comes from the mods that you pick up as you play and level up your Bastards that can change up your play style. They range from increasing your health and giving you extra bullets, or augmenting your weapons with homing rounds, to being able to run faster, jump higher, and outlining enemies to make it easier to target them. And with so many different Bastards, and their own unique synergies, the game continues to capture my interest by encouraging experimentation. Even as you get powerful mods, the game reigns you in by adding limiting factors like the relationship system that can keep you from bringing your favorite Bastards on a run if they are feuding (solved by using a precious comoddity of beans), or having your Bastards health drop to 0, making them unavailable in future runs unless you heal them (using healing Tonics, another precious commodity). Overall, I am genuinely enjoying this game many hours in, and having unlocked half of the Bastards. Oh, and the art style is *chefs kiss*.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Void Bastards seems to be a bit of a cult game - I don't see much about it online, but now and then I'll find a fervent defender on Reddit or Youtube, who's found the same something special in the game that I have, that's kept them playing the game over and over. If you're one of these folks, I think this game will speak to you in the same way, even though the gameplay is entirely different. There's a lot going on, and a lot of moving parts as far as the strategy elements between battles... but when you are actually in the maps, this game is about shooting and killing everything before it kills you. Also, if you didn't play Void Bastards at all, or didn't care for it, you still might enjoy this game. The writing is funny, the design is fantastic, the art style is gorgeous, and the gunplay and battle mechanics are spot-on.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: This game is honestly amazing. Saw it was coming out not too long ago and knew I had to get it after incessantly playing Void Bastards. I was a big fan of that game so I figured this would be like it. Well its not entirely like Void bastards at all but rather snippets of void bastards with invisible inc, fist full of frags, call of Juarez and Oregon trail thrown in the mix. Overall 10/10 high replay-ability and a good story line that changes based on decisions you make & actions along the way. Highly enjoyable and your skill level only takes you so far, strategy and game comprehension is huge!
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic space western romp.When i first saw Wild Bastards i worried it might play alot like Void Bastards which while it wouldn't have been a bad thing it would have limited my interest in the game as it really loses its flair after only a few runs. Wild Bastards however, has a more cohesive narrative and a borderline obscene amount of gameplay variety with its assorted cast of outlaws, villains and enviroments.Almost every encounter can be unique, sometimes you'll end up in the same or very similar arena when you fight a group but at least the enemy diversity and numbers will be different.Each time you go planetside you can choose from different outlaws to mix up your game, some outlaws can get friendships going which add another layer of options on the table, not to mention pickups, buffs and allies you can rope in on a encounter. It all adds up to keep things really fresh.I was worried the game would pigeonhole gameplay by forcing your hand with certain characters but it rarely actually does this and the few times it does you'll have more outlaws around the next bend to unlock and keep playing with.Some characters feel more powerful than others, others seem to have unique advantages but no one so far is truly worse than another, i feel though like a few could use some adjustments (Like Roswell's special ability and how its not useful 90% of the time)I feel like the only thing some people may get tired of is the Space Western themes which are laid on THICK. if you don't like cowboys, westerns or people talking like its 1887 you'll grow tired of it quickly as the game never lets up with it much like how Void Bastards as almost comically British.Visuals are mostly fantastic, some enemies seem to have duller pallets but they still stand out among the scenery most times the biomes you encounter are mostly vibrant affairs even the swamps with their purple goo lakes. Sound design is AMAZING, each character even has different walk sounds, enemies will regularly make noise to ping their location for you so no encounter draws on unfairly due to simply not knowing where they are.Wild Bastards is really really well made and very fun, ive encountered only a single bug dealing with the Kyotes getting stuck on ladders and being immune to any damage that wasn't AOE, a distinct problem but has only happened twice.5 Stars, Joe Bob says check it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: I've played two sessions so far and I'm enjoying it, and will keep playing, so I figured it's time for a review. As others have said it's not Void Bastards (which I loved), so I went into this at peace with that fact, but was happy that the art, humour, and even gunplay feel familiar enough.The arena-style engagements initially felt a bit strange to me, but I quickly got the intention of how everything fits together. Some maps are a whack-a-mole sneakfest, others are over in a minute of hellfire - most are a blood-pumping mix that compels me to keep playing. The RNG feels well balanced and creates some intense situations that I'm surprised I managed to get through.Wild Bastards is a mix of so many different things that I love in games, and I'm impressed that it actually works together. Hard thumbs up from me, and a recommendation for anyone willing to go in with an open mind.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes most of what made the original good and expands upon it. Rather than a collection of mostly generic weirdos, here we have a gang of specific weirdos, each of which does something interesting. The exploration is less immersive-sim interesting and more tactical decision-making. Story's great, characters are great, and it's rare to find a "rogue" game that so consistently makes you deal with unforeseen consequences. In terms of being sequel, it's an obvious improvement over Void Bastards and a damn good game besides.Personally, Hard Ironman's the way to go after you finish the story. Once you get good, normal with no permadeath kinda becomes too easy by the end of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Grateful for the roguelite FPS spiritual successor of Void Bastards. Beat it, was fun, sometimes feels unbalanced but the game lets you retry enough times that you learn the enemies' attack patterns enough. Satisfying mechanics throughout, devoured in about 20 hours and had a good time. Might go back and try on Hard.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Wild Bastards. Its a fun, often tense, rouge-like with overlapping strategic systems that are very engaging. The gameplay feels really good, especially with how unique each Bastard plays. The character designs are great and are full of personality, and the art style works even better here than it did in Void Bastards.I would highly recommend this game for a first playthough (play on hard, feels way better than normal) but don't expect a ton of replay value, the systems are there to facility replays but I dont think the game is varied enough to warrant them. I might change my mind on that as I play more though. Either way, a very good game that I greatly enjoyed.Edit: Yeah ok, I was wrong. I've beaten the game on the hardest difficulty and done everything besides the ironman runs but I keep coming back to it (might even attempt an ironman run), this game is great.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Don't expect it to be Void Bastards 2.0. It's a different game with a different focus, despite both being roguelikes. Wild Bastards focuses on bite-sized but challenging shootouts, and the more focused approach may seem limiting, but allows for a very satifying gameplay loop. The story has a greater focus than Void Bastards, and the main campaign goes in directions you might not expect. The characters are fun and shooting racist space cowboys never gets old.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: I like this! It's got a good sense of humor and it's doing a minimalist thing with the gameplay that I really like. A lot of games would be tempted to give every character three guns and two special abilities like it's Overwatch... Wild Bastards said no, the shotgun guy only does shotgun, so find a way to make shotgun work or play as somebody else for a bit.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Great game so far, am not disappointed in the slightest. I really like the cast of characters and their personalities, its fun to watch them bicker or give call-outs. I also like the strategy you can put into the game on all layers. Planning out which planets you want to hit, planning out where to send your groups on the planet, and planning out where you need to go in the actual shootouts, its really fun. It also has a lot of replay value between each sector since you can't keep any items, forcing you to build up different characters with certain items for the zone ahead. Overall, great game, excited to see how it grows.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: With hopes to get a Void Bastards 2, Wild bastards does justice of being its spiritual Successor. Different formula, but it works well and i just love the design. don't need the best graphics for a game to be good. my only thing in the game is that if one of the wild Bastards dies, you have to Relocate there Helix Again, but if you do you gotta get it while its in some Morgue with a Revive check. if you do a successful revive you get a buff, but if you don't you get a temporary Debuff. other than that straight aces
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: This is not void bastards and that’s alright.I’m loving this game, the variety of enemies mixed with the variety of bastards and maps makes each showdown a different beast to explore many are tense cover focused  outs listening for audio cues from your enemies others are frantic twitchy dashes as flankers swam you out into the open. All are fun and the progression/ temporary progression systems keep you moving forward while varying how each bastards plays from sector to sector
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Like many others here, I come from playing Void Bastards. But, while this game is a "spiritual successor" of it, it's surprisingly different.Let me try and differentiate them (it's been a while since I've played VB):> WB's characters and their weapons are preset, unlike VB where characters are randomly generated and any gun can be equipped by any character.> Instead, WB has mods and abilities that get reset at the start of every "sector", regardless of death or progress.> There's also levels now, which grant both permanent and temporary abilities and buffs.> WB has 13 preset characters - the main campaign is all about collecting them all, one in each sector - and there's a "feud" system that lets you manage the relationships between these characters. Characters in a feud won't be working together while characters that are pals can help each other out.> Characters drop down onto planets where there's paths lined with pickups, enemies and other loot in "bunches". The amount of characters that can be dropped down depends on each planet.> Enemies should be defeated in order to unlock more paths. They can be defeated by participating in "showdowns", which is where the shooting happens.> Something to note, VB's gunplay is much better than WB's, which is floaty and if it weren't for the damage numbers, you'll never know if you even hit an enemy. It's really sub-par.> VB consists of British people while WB consists of American Cowboys who speak weird.> Some "Outlaws" are pretty much garbage - there's no way someone got through a level only by playing as the snake guy.If you liked VB, there's a good chance you'll like WB. I'm personally conflicted but I *do* find WB fun. Just know that technically, there are just 13 sectors, for each character (I think, so far) which means that the game could be very short.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: It's really good. I legitimately do not know why it has mostly positive rating atm. It's a fantastic game and deserves success. Absolutely worth the money.Don't go in expecting void bastards 2. This is a 'spiritual' successor. It's a different game at the end of the day with some of the same DNA as VB, yet still has it's own identity. Especially given the state of the rest of the industry, games like this deserve our support.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: Great Action Roguelike, very similar to their previous game Void Bastards. Combat and level design hasn't improved greatly, but many of the other aspects seem to. You travel a tactical map that determines what you encounter. I've only just started playing, and tried the demo earlier, This game might really open up once you have access to more heroes and enemies to fight.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: "The spiritual successor to the award-winning game Void Bastards, Wild Bastards is a roguelike strategy shooter with heart-pounding FPS action, mod management, and a tactical campaign. Saddle up and lead the most notorious outlaws in the galaxy."Exactly what it says on the tin. I think they do a great job of having the strategy and action work in equilibrium and feed into each other, which makes this stand out against a lot of other 'roguelite shooters'. Good strategic play can make up for bad action segments and agile FPS skills can make up for poor planning. I find myself making many tough and considered choices on the ship and overworld map, which is an important metric in such a game. There are a lot of systems here and it all feels very well thought out and designed. My favourite moments have been when my best laid plans go to ♥♥♥♥ (usually as result of being unable to execute in the combat) and I'm forced to react and come up with something new that works: a compromise, but still escaping with the loot and my life in the nick of time. That feels like a good example of the gameplay tying into the games' aesthetics too. Beyond all that, I wasn't expecting the writing and voice acting to be so entertaining. Let me keep this short by giving obligatory praise to the art and sound an' all (I should speak more to the shooting part of the game but I grow weary and require more dextroamphetamines (OK, so just real quick, you start off with a couple outlaws and as you play through you unlock more and more and they each have a unique weapon and ability and some other stuff you can take so many down to the planets' overworld and they further get split into groups of two that traverse independently of each other and you control one outlaw at a time in combat but can instantaneously switch between them as if switching weapons if that weapon had a corresponding ability and stats and mods and its own health in this way you're limited to two in a combat encounter actually maybe that's a little piece of where the Halo mentions are coming from I've seen the enemies are varied and have their own AI quirks which are important to exploit appropriately to be successful in combat so it actually makes the enemy intel you gather that describes them genuinely useful to refer back to in turn you will find certain outlaws will work better given the makeup of enemy forces given their innate abilities, your personal skill/preference for the character and how you've built them through the course of your run additionally the shooting takes place in randomised arenas not literal arenas but these small open areas different planets have different 'biomes' you might be fighting among a saloon and scattering of smaller buildings like a space western or a forested area with a damaging swamp or a snowy peak with good vantage points for sniping and to be sniped from also a lot of the enemies have the ability to teleport (if not most?) very much keeps you on your toes the whole time either keeps you on the move dashing about cover constantly looking out for signs of the enemy sound is very important in this game they have made good use of it you will have an easier time with the sound up headphones are even better I had to pause The Simpsons during the combat portions which is not something I do lightly no this game almost demands it which is cool actually oh they do this really cool thing where your secondary character the one in reserve will shout out the direction you're being flanked from the teleporting enemies would have been frustrating without such a feature but it totally works and is a cool feeling when you react to the AI calling out "behind you!" and you spin around and waste the guy before he gets ya I was going to say the enemies can feel a little tough sometimes like to avoid damage I mean but seems part of the point they give you lots of tools and opportunities to balance this out in the strategic layer and I don't mean to say the enemies feel unfair again knowledge, planning, skill and/or caution are rewarded well I suppose I did talk about the shooting huh)).Really glad someone made this game (and Void Bastards). They really speak my specific sensibilities.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: You have an interesting rouge-like, that allows you to play with many different play-styles. its complexity ramps up as you travel deeper into the vortex of space. Its definitely worth the price tag as it can easily sink in double digits of time into this game experiencing a different pathway but similar story along the way.  Thanks for creating it and good luck with the release
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

_childDocuments_.review: I was a pretty big fan of Void Bastards. I know the game has some quirks people didn't like though. This game has the same awesome comic book 2.5D visual style to it and I'm all for it, absolutely love the visual style. Gameplay is really fun in this one, similar to how Void Bastards worked, this game has a sector travel based system, with each node in the sector you drop down at having a little traversable area in a turn based style packed with various loot, special items for you characters. enemy road blocks where you go in and experience the real game play, varied 1st person arenas you have to dual various amounts of and different types of enemies in.Game honestly feels relatively challenging while also feeling fair at the same time. I can't really properly explain the game well enough so go check out some gameplay and you'll see what it's like. I definitely recommend it though!

_childDocuments_.review: Another absolute belter IMO, different to void bastards so i think a lot of people wont be happy, but the core loop is satisfying and the combat is hard but fun to learn. The upgrade systems and mods give enough to adjust playstyle. Also think because the core of the game is solid theres a lot more room to expand on this compared to void bastards so expecting great things ahead <3

_childDocuments_.review: its been good so far, storys fun and the banter between the characters keeps the game fresh.kinda gets a little repetitive mabye wait for a little sale i feel like 40 is a little to much but saying that i have payed more to have alot less fun all in all solid game and i much prefer this over void bastards :D super fun on the steam deck i feel it shines of there!

_childDocuments_.review: A bit 'mid' right now:Yay* fun writing, characters and voice acting* stylish (though lo-fi) visuals* diverse character styles with interesting power progressions (eventually)* the character hotswapping turns out to be quite innovative, can be used very strategically during gunfights - I expect to see more games copy this neat mechanicNay* the actual gunplay and movement feels bad, floaty and imprecise (like Void Bastards but somehow worse)* level 'design' for half the game is kinda non-existent - most biomes are just piles of themed assets to hide behind or climb* takes a while to get going; the best mechanics, upgrades and biomes happen later on - can be offputting to begin

_childDocuments_.review:
From the veteran team behind Void Bastards and Card Hunter, Wild Bastards has you travel from planet to planet to recruit, manage and gun sling with a team of 13 outlaws, each of whom has their own weaponry, special power, and growth tree. On planets, you’ll wrangle loot and start showdowns that are then played out in intense, bite-sized shootouts.

The Wild Bastards were the most deadly gang in the galaxy until a posse from the puritanical magnate Jebediah Chaste eliminated one outlaw after another. Faced with their own mortality, the two remaining members have teamed up with the Drifter, a mysterious sentient spacecraft, to find and resurrect the dead gang members as they flee to the mythical Homestead.
_childDocuments_.name: Wild Bastards

name: KarmaZoo
detailed_description: KarmaZoo is about helping people, working together, and finding bliss in cooperation — especially when things go wrong. Make meaningful connections with completely random players online as they are all striving alongside you to earn the most precious resource of all: Karma. A NEVER-ENDING CHALLENGE The Loop is where you’ll join a team of up to 10 random players around the world. Together, you’ll tackle a series of increasingly challenging levels that adapt to the size of your team, the characters you play and the perks you pick together. No two runs are quite the same when the players and the game itself are changing! THE POWER OF KARMA Doing good earns Karma! Stick together, use your character’s strengths, and even sacrifice yourself because helping one another is essential in the Loop’s deadly challenges. Every good thing you do, one way or another, earns you the sweet Karma you’ll use to unlock new characters and abilities for future Loops. LOCAL MULTIPLAYER Welcoming friends or family at home? Compete to reach the top of the Totem on a single screen. Challenge up to 8 players in frantic quick-fire mini games that bring a new spirit to abilities that were designed for doing good. TAILORED FOR YOU Anyone can help their team earn Karma! Whether you’re new to games or a seasoned veteran, you’ll find a community reaching for a common goal. Available in 22 languages, cross-platform play between PC and console, and private lobbies to play exclusively with friends, we invite all of you to the KarmaZoo!

_childDocuments_.review: The cohesion in this game is so strong that it actually is very touching to me. It reminds me of a time, when I actually had friends and social interactions in reallife. I don't know why, but this game actually just keeps making me cry like a little baby. I mean... you don't even know the other people, but just seeing how everyone keeps caring for each other just hits me on a real deep level. No one is left behind, even if that might be the death of the whole team. People are coming back and helping me when I'm stuck... they actually care about me. Deep down from the bottom of my heart I really, really wish that people all around the world would just treat each other a little more respectfully and equally.Thank you  for making me feel a bit less invisible.11/10 would cry till dehydration again...
_childDocuments_.name: KarmaZoo

_childDocuments_.review: There was a short period of time where this game was fantastic. You'd hop in and a handful of folks were your new best friends for the next 20 minutes or so, trying to work out how to get through challenges without being able to talk directly. The game was doing exactly what it promised.However, a lot of the game actively worked against that ideal. Each character has secret side-quests, many of which required rushing ahead selfishly and couldn't be communicated to your friends. The cost of new unlocks quickly became prohibitive, and only a few of the characters' abilities actually make a significant difference in how to approach challenges (usually when challenges were designed so a particular ability was required.)Adding onto this, there just aren't that many different levels, so as players got more experienced, the best strategy was to just try and rush through the same old levels as efficiently as possible to farm more unlocks. There became less and less for new players to do, as well, as experienced players would often choose the required characters if they'd already completed the side missions.I'm not entirely sure why I wrote this all out, because while all these decisions, individually, I think, in the end are solvable, the result now is that there's basically no one playing. As of writing this, according to the charts, there are exactly two people in game. Maybe you could get in a game with them, but more than likely, the game is now totally unusable. There's nothing you can do in this game on your own.I'd love to swap this to a recommend, if KarmaZoo is somehow revitalized, but I'm not holding my breath. It was a decent attempt, Pastagames.
_childDocuments_.name: KarmaZoo

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great vibe of a game, I wish I found the time to play more of when it released and it had an active player base. The whole point of the game is coop with strangers, but everyone that played has gotten their fix and moved on to other games. Less people play, so it takes longer for a lobby to fill up. Players have to wait to long, so they give up and go play something else. Now there's even less players. This game was always going to be a short lived thing. I would give it a positive review if the developers would figure out an approach to expand to a new wave of players and to give the player base a reason to return at specific times in the year. Maybe free weekends, followed by new content then a holiday themed event. Halloween into Christmas period. For now, unless you got friends to play with, you gotta just check when the game has it peak daily and weekly traffic on SteamDB and try playing at those times.

_childDocuments_.review: During the initial demo you could invite friends through steam to play in public matches with you, but that's not the case in the full game. Bought this to play with a friend based off of that and now trying to play together is frustrating. It's overly pessimistic to assume people are going to go out of their way to troll and grief others by enabling the option to play with your friends, and it probably hurts the game way more than it helps.
