_childDocuments_.review: I want to start this review off by saying that this a great game and I would recommend it to anyone who simply just wants to relax from work or school and enjoy a great story.The one thing I really enjoyed about this game was that it was not trying to be a new and improved game, but it was just episode 2 of the first game (episode 1). Of course they did add some new ingredients and some new additions to the game, like having to give items to certain characters and adding stories and update posts on the social media service. That being said, they kept to the original story and characters, only having a few more people. A part of me wants to say, " Oh I wish there were more new characters and more ingredients..." but I feel like that would take away from it being episode 2. It is not supposed to be a remaking, but just what it says 'Episode 2'. I also love the idea of more episodes in the future and expanding more on the characters and their stories/relationships.This game feels like I am really interacting with these people, they have genuine relatability. They do not have 2D personalities. Some of them are stereotypical like 'the shy girl' and the 'mean girl' but they add on to those personality traits, like showing aqua's confident side and myrtle's soft side. I enjoy that. This game is a beautiful story and the lore is AMAZING. The newspaper articles and the history told by the characters is so well developed. There is politics, racism, and more. It is amazing. I really do feel immersed and with story novels I feel that is very important. I also like that there is not over the top quirky comedy and fourth wall breaks. A lot of visual novels try to be 'meta' and it just comes off as suffocating and hard to read. The writing in this is realistic, the characters struggles are realistic. The conversations are realistic. The developers literally put their own emotions into this story and it works.The art style is beautiful, the pixel art, the color schemes, the way the drinks are designed! Everything is so aesthetically pleasing. Some people think pixel art is overused but it works so well for this game. Its unique, the characters look 3D and well fleshed out. Everyone has their own design without being over the top and flashy just to appease the public. There is a couple more things I want to mention. As someone who is a perfectionist and LOVES fully completing games, I appreciate that the achievements are not unachievable. A lot of games put in 20 different achievements for one task that are super impossible to achieve. They could have easily put a '10 hour Latte Art achievement' its a small thing but one I tend to look out for in games. I also love the latte art mechanic, it is hard to use but when you make something pretty it is very satisfying. However, I really wish there was an undo button. ;-;Overall this game is beautiful, has great writing, and will make you cry. (At least it made me cry but I am an emotional baby).I am hopeful and excited for an episode 3.(Please have more of Freya and Riona, I LOVE their stories).

_childDocuments_.review: A missed opportunity. But, if you liked the original, you'll like this one as well.Great graphics and sound, just like its predecessor. Once again, bonus points for ultrawide support. No complaints about the presentation, but some of the characters definitely rub me the wrong way. YMMV in that department. I had read that the original writer passed away. I see this left the team with a difficult choice. To their credit, I could not tell the difference between the two. It emulates the same style and tone, and I imagine this is intentional to honor the spirit of the original author's intent. Unfortunately, I think the writing was the worst part of the original by far, and I see this as a missed opportunity to move on from that. All of the supernatural elements in this story are but the thinnest of veils for what is ultimately a collection of modern day social media discourse. There is rampant virtue signaling, and every character speaks about the world around them as if they live inside Twitter. There are a scant few genuine moments, and I can appreciate the fact that the writer(s?) clearly feel a lot of angst about putting themselves out there and the creative process in general. There is a complete lack of subtlety in the writing regarding this, but I see it and I get it. It feels a lot more disappointing than the first one, as we're familiar with much of the cast already, and there's not a lot of progress or poignancy in their respective narratives. I genuinely came away from this game feeling like I spent a few hours reading Twitter threads. It's nothing but surface level social commentary.Given that the intent here was probably to honor the original writer, I'd still be in for a Coffee Talk 3 in the hopes that they show some growth and try something different. If that one also ends up being the same, I'd definitely call it quits. FWIW, this is certainly a worthy tribute for those who do not find fault with the original.

_childDocuments_.review: Sequels to games don’t always hold up to the original. With coffee-based, visual novel games, sometimes the sequels don’t even come out at all. When Coffee Talk released its second episode, I was thrilled, as I greatly enjoyed the atmosphere and character stories in the first. I played it only shortly before starting this game- by like a day- which made the initial stories fresh in my memory. This game re-captures the spirit of the first, despite taking place in 2023. The writing and characterization is consistent with what was written initially, and I found myself enjoying the new characters as quickly as I liked the first set. There’s a variety of new personalities to meet, as well as old characters you may be fond of from the first game who have had three years to grow, learn, and also struggle.Let’s start here: You do not technically need to have played the first game to enjoy Coffee Talk Episode 2, but I would recommend it. The story has new characters present, but also has characters you meet and spend ample time with in the first game. It resumes about three years after the end of the first, but callbacks are made frequently, including drinks that may have been served during the first episode’s playthrough.The protagonist is the same in the sequel, and is the owner of a cafe called Coffee Talk, which is only open in the evenings. All sorts of wayward wanderers find their way to the cafe, and it’s the barista’s job to listen to their stories, offer them items they may have forgotten or intend for other recipients, and to give them what they want- even if they don’t know what that is.The patrons are people that either already care about each other, or are seeking some form of connection. Plenty of the characters in this game are in some sort of tailspin, and the cafe can become their home and place for guidance- or a place that they abandon in the event that you offend them enough with your mistakes and terrible memory. Themes in the game include loss, grieving, love, societal oppression, listlessness within a job, family ties, and more. While the writing can be a bit on the nose when it comes to issues echoing our real world, I don’t think it loses any heart in the narrative for it. A lot of this is real stuff that happens to real people, and sometimes only community can aid folks through some of these major problems. Community and family are things that get built up and emphasized in the game, and it warmed my heart to experience.Yet again, the visuals are beautiful. Pixel sprites show different range of emotions for the characters that will visit. The background outside the coffee shop shifts, keeping things rhythmically moving while drinks are made. Ingredients are all easily differentiated to make drinks quickly, and the drink sprites are all different as well. The new drink ingredients make some of the most lovely beverages in the game, and discovering them and the new sprites was one of my favourite parts of my playthrough.At its core, Coffee Talk is a visual novel. Main gameplay will always involve reading through dialogue and committing it to memory for each character, and then making them a drink. Sometimes, they tell you precisely what they want, sometimes they’re a bit vague, and other times they give little direction at all. There are multiple endings, and in order to get the best one, serving proper drinks to your patron is of the utmost importance. Drinks are made by combining three ingredients. It’s a simple process, and you’ve got the option to make latte art for latte drinks once the beverage is completed. A gameplay mechanic unique to episode 2 of Coffee Talk involves item management. That’s not to say managing the ingredients for drinks- though that’s also important. Instead, NPC’s in the game will sometimes leave items at the cafe, or give you items to provide to someone else. It’s important once a drink is made to be sure to hand the item over before serving them, or you can lock yourself out of some endings/achievements. Though, sometimes forgetting is what you need to do for certain endings and achiements as well. It's as easy as clicking the item and dragging it to the tray to serve one your drink is finished, or holding the trigger of your controller and moving it manually and then confirming. Admittedly, I wish the item management was used even more often in episode 2 than it is, but it’s a nice addition so the gameplay offers more than just two new ingredients.Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly is a faithful sequel that expands on the first game without losing the heart, love, and intimate moments that made the first game one to remember fondly. Only one new character grated on me even a small amount, and I found him to be likable by the end, he simply took more time to grow on me than the others. Characterization is done well over time, and there were multiple emotional moments present that made me want to tear up- especially one of the endings. No spoilers, but if you enjoyed the first game, you should definitely consider playing this one, as it’s a sequel that improves on the first game in every way.

_childDocuments_.review: The game was overall an enjoyable, relaxing game. The first game was better, though, in my opinion. I do appreciate how a majority of the game play has upgraded since then, such as the inclusion of items throughout the story, as well as more characters, more drink combinations/ingredients, and more endings. But, they didn't do anything new to the base system of making beverages, or latte art (still the exact same system). Yet, the game wasn't full polished, story-wise, anyways.(there may be some spoilers, as I have 100% the game): I found Lucas annoying, feeling like he was a replacement for Freya from the first game (albeit a bad one). I understand the "influencer" thing, but it felt like it was too much the focus of the story (minus Jorji's story) and then that affected Riona, who was a bit underwhelming. I felt like her story didn't feel rewarding, even in the good path.  She is literally the face of this game on the promotional pictures, and yet doesn't have the same level of story as Freya from the first game, who was the face of that one. And her content is not even really written as good. She's tied to Lucas completely, and I think that's unnecessary. It's not like Hyde and Gala from the first game,  or even Bailey and Lua. And I am not saying the story needs to repeat the duo that is going on, but first of all, it doesn't have to, and second of all, it disappointing that it does in the way that it did. Also, always calling her "Lady" was aggravating and disrespectful. (More on Riona  and Lucas later). Speaking of Hyde and Gala: What's up with Gala? He got the Riona treatment. He is only tied to Hyde in this game, but in a different, arguably worse way, in which he has no story?  Jorji's character line was the on most interesting but still lacked, as it focused on an ongoing mystery in the city that teamed into the supernatural, as well as a conversation on mortality and the memory of mortality... but that conversation was left largely unexplored, or didn't really make me think at all. I have a degree in philosophy, so I perked up at the mentions of this, however, was left disappointed at how shallow it was. I much prefer the more direct political conversations in conjunction with people from everyday life from the first game. But generally, it was the coolest, despite being shallow. It felt patchy, trying to connect the mortality theme with a history less, as well as as crime, his own fears, and his family life (which got forgotten?). Pinning those all in one story caused depth in any of them to be lost, despite feeling like there could be all these plausible conversations occurring with appropriate depth. Also, Silver/Amanda's story was not particularly fleshed out either.  I feel like their story was written to be a set up for the next game, and that's it...which bothers me. I didn't feel that way at the end of the first game about  Which, wholly, was better. The stakes felt higher this game, which was a highlight of the game!Rachel was in the game to maybe help Lucas and Riona's story, and to add 4(?) more achievements, but that was it. That's annoying. Hendry didn't need to be in the game, but he was. They could have built off the first game to have issues beyond  but they didn't. It was pointless. Aqua and Myrtle's story was underwhelming. I don't even know what to say. The two outcomes to the very short, underdeveloped conflict, didn't matter either way.   On that very specific note, Baileys and Lua  Hell,  I would love to know why a visual novel like this has such shallow writing? Freya  was wonderful, as it reminded me of the first game and why I loved it. She was that character that they tried to recreate with Lucas-- a brash, seemingly irresponsible, nosy, career driven person, who means well. But with Lucas, he didn't have the charisma, his story felt shallow, his ideas felt like a super forced life lesson to make him look well-intended. The most interesting thing I learned about him was from the bad ending of the game, where he explained  Finally, I felt like the characters had less defined personalities than the first one, which directly seemed to lend to my problem with the lack of consequences in the game. The tone and mood of the game remained largely the same throughout, and I resent that about it. I also want to reiterate that removing the mystery of the character in the first game, and doing nothing with it in the second, cause me to dislike/not care about my character. I wished there was better dialogue, or dialogue at all, if you kept handing out wrong drinks to customers. I feel like they would all notice, sitting like ducks in a row, if you gave them all three espresso and none of them ordered that. This game franchise also scratches the itch of the long missing public, community brick-and-mortar place that has plenty of lively conversation and a friendly atmosphere. That's what I miss about the first one, and what I hoped this one would do even better. It still *does* it, but not as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Just like a good cuppa joe, this game gives you an instant energy boost with its zen gameplay loop, savory art style, chill soundtrack as well as diverse cast of engaging characters and story arcs. _childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: The first Coffee Talk is my favorite game of all time, it just was so beautifully done and hit me at just the right time in my life to truly speak to me so i was ecstatic when i heard that the second episode was in production. I bought the second game on release date but put off playing it cause i was worried that the game might not have the same magic that the first one had for me. Boy was i wrong, Hibiscus and Butterfly might just be the greatest visual novel game i have ever played, it builds off the first game well and adds new characters and stories that are just as magical and fun as the first. Earning the trust of new and old customers alike by serving them the drinks they need is more rewarding and interesting then in the first game. By the end of the game you really feel that these characters are an important part of your life and you cant wait to see their faces in your shop again. I truly love this series and am very happy i got the chance to experience these games. Rest in Peace Mohammad Fahmi, your game and the world you created are an important part of my life and i will be forever grateful.

_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: Time to open the Cafè again!I played and loved the first one so I had to play the next one as well. It brings back some beloved characters from the last game, their stories, and how they changed over time, while it also introduces new characters along the way.You open your little Cafè every night and have your loyal customers come to enjoy their coffee while they tell you about their lives, and during your time with them discover interesting stories about the town and world you live in.It is all filled with fantasy citizens and each of them has their unique problems and taste in coffee of course.I do miss one character that didn't get a lot of time spent in the Cafè, but I hope if it continues that they give her a well-deserved coffee break in the future.The things you can do to influence the stories are limited. You get to brew the coffee according to what the customer described with a well-rounded stock of ingredients (that looks absolutely delicious). It is a bit of experimenting to hit the flavor they wanted, but it is not too hard.A new mechanic seems to be that customers forget things in your cafè, or entrust you with an item that you are supposed to give to another character or keep(forget about) it.The music and art is great and lets you dive deep into the whole setting.All in all I enjoyed the vibe of the game as I did with the last one, so I can recommend it to everyone that wants to sit down and relax to listen to some interesting stories while serving delicious coffee and tea.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best sequels I have ever played to an already amazing game.To me, the original Coffee Talk felt so far ahead of its visual novel contemporaries in terms of story and character development. It was hard to imagine that I could get as invested, or let alone more invested, in what followed from the first game. And I won't lie, part of that doubt did come from the untimely passing away of the beloved series' creator, Mohammad Fahmi. His design and writing, as far as I'm aware, played an enormous role in why Coffee Talk looked and felt so unique in the first place. So going into this sequel, I was hoping that what he brought to the original game creatively, in both the design and writing departments, would be preserved.I got more that what I bargained for with this release.Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly is an amazing continuation that fluidly builds on stories from the old game while also weaving new ones with novel characters and fantastic designs for them, to boot. The new mechanics introduced for coffee-making AND storytelling are one-of-a-kind, something that I didn't even think of as a possibility yet felt so incredibly seamless and natural upon my first impressions of them.I can't say much more without spoiling this game for anyone reading. This is a masterpiece, and everyone who worked on this game should feel immensely proud for what they've accomplished. Somehow, despite the odds, Hibiscus & Butterfly not only preserved what made the original Coffee Talk so great, but dare I say, /improved/ on the original product.I have never felt more happy to give a release a positive review. Recommended 100 times out of 10.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful return to my favorite fictional coffee shop (❁´◡`❁)  This title has a wonderful understanding of what made the first installment so incredibly special, and has polished many existing features, as well as adding stellar new game mechanics that add even more enjoyment.  Wonderful world building and stunning design all around makes this a must-play for any coffee and storytelling enjoyers ☕

_childDocuments_.review: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly is a continuation and concluding message to Mohammad Fahmi. Some of the stories might seem boring and the game less diverse, but new characters, drink ingredients, and features are added to make Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly more enjoyable and appealing to new players.Ultimately, Coffee Talk is about the cafe's atmosphere, listening to customers' life stories and complaints. Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly is a great game to play after work and enjoy the unique stories from Toge Productions.

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty much a continuation of the first game. There's some added replayability which is interesting, and it allows for branching in the storyline that allows for "good" and "bad" endings for each of the characters. Compared with the first entry, I think its definitely an improvement, but I'm still somewhat put off by the game's writing. I like the idea behind the main character, where it feels like they're just making a small contribution - subtly inspiring people towards different choices (or not). But, I also think the fantasy elements of the story are not really used. The identities of the characters are meaningless in your interactions with them. There's all this talk of the clashing of cultures, but all of these characters act like fairly pleasant humans. There are no villains, no antagonists, not even an snobbish jerk. You're just helping nice people sort through their baggage. Its very sterile.

_childDocuments_.review: Steam deck compatibility + comfy: yes (of course, PC, but SD is much comfier)Rating: 7/ 10 (consider this a neutral rating)I played through Coffee Talk 1 and enjoyed it. While I admittedly enjoyed tackling through the first good route for this sequel, this game overstayed its welcome too long, the further I replayed for the achievements. Most of the achievements were easy to get, except for some that needed a much longer playthrough, in order to acquire such as . Especially the last three mentioned were a huge pain in the ass.It was much more tedious when you factor in the long splurge of dialogue throughout each day (you have a total of 14 days including the 15th addition just like in the first game), which has both its pros and cons. It's kind of nice, since the the days were shorter in the first game. And FYI, I've played a good amount of visual novels and I also love to read, so I normally like and can handle lots of text.  However, for replay-ability purposes, once you've seen it all, pressing down on the skip button for long sessions becomes tedious and monotonous. Plus, it kind of puts pressure on your mouse or R1 button. While I understand that the story's central theme revolves around , it would have been better had they cut down on a lot of the unnecessary fluff and preachy allegories that kept being reiterated throughout the story. Or they could have changed the skip function to be a one tap button, so all the dialogue could actually be skipped entirely and much faster than holding down on it (I'm surprised this one hasn't been changed/ improved since the first game). Moreover, possibly changing a lot of the dialogue for every new route you enter (since there's three routes total--normal, bad, good).Speaking of dialogue, due to how similar a lot of the dialogues are from all three routes, the story's outcomes were very predictable. Basically, you get into a good route and then you enter the bad route, which is the total opposite of that route and the normal ending could easily have been neutral/ leaning over to the bad route depending on the character you helped/ screwed over honestly.As I reflect on the character development, I realized I was quite indifferent with it. I just couldn't find myself caring enough about the characters and the next big chapters of their lives, even when  As stated before, a lot of it has to do with the unnecessary dialogue bogging down on it.I will say that I did enjoy the secret ending. It was very heartwarming and sweet of the devs to have created that ending. Additionally, the new character designs for the two new character additions, Lucas and Riona, were my favorite and were mainly what got me to playing the sequel. I also really liked the butterfly pea and hibiscus drink designs, they were very beautiful and a big improvement from the first game's drink designs. The soundtrack as well was a major plus. If you do plan on purchasing this game anyway, please do check out these guides. They saved me so much headache when achievement hunting! Also, be advised that if you don't want to spend hours pressing down on the skip function, just auto play the dialogue and run the game in the background while doing something else.Guides for your sanity:♥︎ ♥︎ ♥︎ ♥︎

_childDocuments_.review: coffee talk extends beyond being just a game. i first picked up coffee talk in the summer of 2020 and i never knew that it would leave such a lasting impact, almost 3 years later.i work as a barista part time and i actually had what i described as my first "coffee talk" experience in real life only a couple days ago with this woman that ordered a chai. i like to think that was incredibly divine timing, considering this sequels release.she asked me something along these lines, "what do i do when i am vulnerable with someone and they mistreat me for being emotional?" of course i was taken back by this question as i have never been asked such an introspective and openly vulnerable question by a customer before. we have a beautiful conversation, and for a couple hours i am stuck in my head wondering how i may have given off an energy that she could feel that she could confide personal feelings with a barista, a stranger she's never met before.in the same day, she comes back. she thanks me for listening and giving her advice and explains that there was a situation where she was refused accommodation for an unseen disability she has. i tell her that it wasn't her fault and that when someone has the ability to be accommodating & kind and chooses not to be, it isn't a fault or something that she did and this leads into what i want to say about coffee talk. coffee talk is just a game really. but its a bit more than that, at least for me personally. you might know a person, you see them all the time walking around, doing typical human person things but there are stories and so many memories attached to each person you see. i don't think i will forget the conversation i had with her, she reminded me that we are complex & to comfortably express being vulnerable, something i need to practice myself sometimes. why not listen to our friends and provide a safe space for them when we can, rather than refusing outright when we have capability to be warm & loving people. we can absolutely practice being more vulnerable & more accommodating to someone being vulnerable. which includes writing this sappy review of one of my favourite games i have ever played. thanks coffee talk for being such a comforting game & that teaching me that humans were made to connect <3

_childDocuments_.review: If you played the first Coffee Talk, you'll know what to expect here - and if you haven't, I recommend you do, since it's a continuation of that game's story. _childDocuments_.review: I'm two and a half hours in, and I'm bored. It's my own fault - I've never been much for visual novels, which must be read a line at a time as they flash past in front of me. And I played the original Coffee Talk to completion, even giving it a positive review. So I should have known what I was getting into.This is basically the same game as the first installment. I'm on Day 4 and I believe I've only had a total of eight customers so far (how does this place stay in business?), six of whom are repeats from the first game (most of them with the same art, even). Once or twice a day someone will ask for a drink. "I'd like to try Hibiscus tea with milk and warm spice!" they say, so you click Hibiscus, milk, and cinnamon. Done. Later I know I'll have to guess at their more vague descriptions, and if I get them wrong they'll be disappointed and I'll miss a chance at an achievement, and that's all. The story progresses anyway.And the story, so far, isn't very engaging. The characters are dealing with various challenges in life, and as the friendly barista I listen and offer some suggestions. It just all happens at a leisurely pace, which some people might enjoy, but I'm getting antsy. The music is repetitive and unremarkable, changing occasionally to fit the mood. The only gameplay difference from the first game is that the characters sometimes ask the barista to pass along small items for them, so it's a matter of waiting for another character to show up and then hoping you remember to give it.This story would have made a wonderful book. Toss in a couple of recipes for various kinds of tea and coffee that the characters like, sell it with an attached package of a few of the blends and spices they use, and market it as a story that you can read while you sip the tea or coffee that's being served in that chapter. Now that would be cozy!_Edit:_ Because I'm an achievement hunter, I pushed through and I finished the game after a total of 7.7 hours. For the first half of the game I had it on 'Auto On' with text speed 'Fast', so I could watch it without needing to click. For the second half, I set 'Auto Off' and text speed 'Instant' so that I could click through it quickly. The characters are _so chatty_.There's a mystery about cars being vandalized that takes shape close to the end of the game, The relationships between the characters also wrap up nicely. But still, the heart of the game is that you're just listening to people talk about their lives, and I really didn't find that very interesting.After I finished, I went into the 'Free Brew' mode so that I could brew the rest of the drinks that I hadn't brewed yet ... but even that became dull, so I gave up on that as well as the rest of the achievements, which involved going back and replaying specific days to get different outcomes. I just got tired of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey there, everyone! I recently had the pleasure of diving into a delightful sequel, "Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly." Now, let me tell you, it's a gaming experience that's both comforting and utterly heartwarming.Picture this: a cozy café tucked away on a rainy Seattle side street. It only opens in the late hours and caters to the night owls of the city. As you might guess, the key ingredient here isn't just the coffee; it's the people. But these aren't your average folks. In this version of Seattle, mythical creatures like satyrs, banshees, and vampires coexist with humans. It's like a dreamy blend of fantasy and reality.Now, before we dive in, let's pour one out for the creator and writer of "Coffee Talk," Mohammad Fahmi. He left us way too soon, but his legacy lives on in this game. It's apparent from the start that this game is crafted with love and care, a tribute to his brilliant narrative skills.So, what's this sequel all about? It picks up three years after the first game, and if you haven't played that one, I strongly recommend you do. See, "Coffee Talk" is all about relationships, and the sequel leans heavily on your knowledge of the characters and their histories. It's not newcomer-friendly, but that's okay because it's like catching up with old friends.The heart of this game is in its stories. You're the owner of the café, a sort of mix between a barista and a bartender, listening to the tales of Seattleites from all walks of life. It's not just about serving coffee; it's about being a shoulder to lean on, a sympathetic ear when the world outside gets too loud.The characters and their arcs in Episode 2 are simply fantastic. The writing is mature, grounded, and universally relatable. You'll find pieces of your own life reflected in these characters' struggles. Whether it's identity issues, creative blocks, or the complexities of friendship, this game delves into it all.Now, here's where the game gets interactive. The bulk of the gameplay revolves around crafting drinks for your customers, taking into account their preferences and mood. It's a bit like solving a puzzle, and getting their orders right can influence their decisions and, ultimately, their lives. The addition of new ingredients keeps things fresh, and the latte art mini-game adds a charming touch.But there's a catch. Failing to deliver the right item to a customer can lead to less-than-optimal outcomes. In fact, it's surprisingly easy to "fail" the game's few challenges, which can be mildly frustrating. A little guidance would have been nice here.Overall, "Coffee Talk Episode 2" is a heartwarming sequel that continues the tradition of meaningful storytelling over a cup of coffee. It's like catching up with old friends, listening to their stories, and being reminded of the beauty in shared connections. If you played the first game, this one's a must-try. If you haven't, well, it's the perfect reason to start.In the end, this game serves up a warm, comforting experience that's perfect for a cozy night in. So, grab a cup, pull up a stool, and lose yourself in the rich, relatable narratives of this wonderful creation. It's a gaming experience that's not to be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, I love the game. And I'm sure most other positive reviews will talk about why the game is great.I'm instead going to highlight 2 points that I think people should know before buying this game:1. There are failure achievements.As of this writing, the game is on version 1.05 on steam. There are in-game achievements, but no steam achievements.The first time I booted up the game and looked at the potential achievements, I said "Oh, no". because I like to go for all the achievements, especially for the games I love. And in a game focused on chill vibes, deliberately screwing up orders for customers while going for the "Not So Hot Business" achievement just felt bad. This definitely wasn't in the first game.Now, the game actually surprised me with how good it is about screwing up. There are only normal and good endings: The customers might get in a bad mood, but screwing up their drink order doesn't ruin their lives. Life still goes on, and even in the normal endings, the customers still strive to do their best, and you even get to discover new things about them. But Riona specifically... oh boy. To deliberately screw up and make them unwelcome, to someone who's a victim of cyber-bullying and racism, to drive away a person looking for a place of warmth and comfort... just made me feel like a bully and racist, and made me feel all gross and disgusted inside. That was rough.It won't matter if you're not going for those achievements, but if you're a completionist like me, just know that there are in-game failure achievements, and those routes might be upsetting to certain people.2. There are less new regulars.If you're looking at this game because you've played Coffee Talk (and let's be honest, you really should play it before starting Episode 2), you might remember that only 3/11 customers were regulars at the start of the original game: Freya, Jorji & Gala. Everyone else was a newcomer.In Ep2, that number is flipped: There are only 3 new regulars. Everyone else is a returning face, or a guest character. I loved the focus on expanding the stories from the first game, and the new stories we got are great. But I kinda wished there were more new folks who became regulars. The world is so interesting: I wish they explored more stories, especially since everyone's in a good place in the best ending.That's the 2 things I feel people should know when buying this game.1 last personal gripe: I did not really enjoy Silvers & Amanda's storyline.Most of the storylines are fantastical beings in everyday situations: An elf and a succubus, but family issues interfere with their romance. A werewolf, who's a veteran recovering from PTSD and trying to be better. An alien, but he's just looking for love and finding out more about himself. Amanda's storyline is a lot more... dramatic and less grounded? Agent Saitama walks in, and tension just skyrockets. Their ending, too, is the least joyful and most mixed. In the normal route, even Baileys lampshades how his problems just pale in comparison to Amanda & Silvers' situation. I'm sure their storyline has an audience to whom it is relevant, but personally, the vibe clashed with the rest of the game for me. Just my personal experience.I definitely recommend the game, especially if you liked the original. This is one of the few games I bought full price on day 1: I really loved the uniquely calm and mature atmosphere of the series.  Sure the "Not So Hot" route was rough, but I was surprised at how much it revealed about the characters. The characters are all good-natured and have the best intentions, the music is great, learning more about old friends was wonderful, a couple of guest characters look a lot healthier than their gaunt, faceless original sprites. and there were moments of real emotion.Oh, and if you're somehow reading this without playing the original game, GO PLAY IT! This series is truly a unique masterpiece of art, music and storytelling.

_childDocuments_.review: Coffee Talk episode 2 is a sequel to the original game, but does not require much of the first game's context for enjoyment. This game is what I expected, in that the coffee shop vibe is nice, but much of the story is a bit underwhelming. I think the best characters in terms of development continue to be Gala and Hyde. The added characters, Lucas and Riona, have their interesting moments, but not enough of them to have me really root for them as characters.On a technical level, my biggest issue comes from the way the game handles its multiple endings. Taking a note out of Japanese VNs would be a great thing for this game, especially in its read text function. This game makes you hold to skip, which drove me nuts while trying to do achievements, because the dialogue, even on skip mode, was so slow. The lack of clear route paths also made the secret ending difficult to achieve, and for the time spent I did not find it worthwhile or much of a secret.I was hoping for some lore, and a better deep dive into the world of Coffee Talk, which this game just didn't cut for me. Once again, I still recommend it to casual players for the music and drink options, but if you are looking for a deeper story, you may be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Tl;dr: a relaxing 6 or 7 out of 10 game worth it if you are into visual novels.First: actual gameplay is limited. There are no dialog options, so all you do is guess a drink 3 times per ingame day and try to remember passing a few items along. That's not what you come for.Secondly: Music and art are great, fitting and expressive. I love it.Now, the meat of it: The characters are actual characters and feel alive and genuine. That's great.The dialog, however, is very "American Metropolis". It's believable enough but the issues are far removed from what I can relate to. I also feel there were some boxes to be checked and it reeks of allegory.If you are not as sensitive to that feeling and relate more to city folk than I do, you'll probably have a great time.Still a recommendation, but check first that I'm recommending it to YOU.

_childDocuments_.review: Visual novel does not begin to explain the experience that is Coffee Talk.Through the pandemic, Coffee Talk one was there to ground me and make me feel like I had a little collection of friends I could pop in and see whenever I wanted. In a time of isolation, it helped me get a little bit of normalcy. Hibiscus & Butterfly was like seeing old friends. The game is warm and inviting and definitely worth the price. It tells so many stories in such little time and somehow manages to make you feel close to every character in them. You become a part of their world, and when you're done with the game you take a little part of them away with you.My only complaint is that we won't get to have another one. I'd love to see the characters again, but I understand why it has to be the way it is. Thank you to everyone who worked on this for making me feel a little less alone. Thank you to Fahmi for sharing your beautiful vision with the world. I hope you rest well.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Coffee Talk 1, Coffee Talk 2 is a wonderful elaboration on the original. Double the playtime, more drinks, and a whole new item-gifting system that puts an extra breath of life onto some of your interactions. What's not to like? Much like its predecessor, it's a very cozy game that offers a lovely visual novel experience for someone looking to kill some time. The core story itself further deepens the lore of Coffee Talk in subtle touches of worldbuilding, fleshing out the series overall. Both of the new main characters are charming and have a beautiful story to tell, while other old characters that were left behind in the previous game such as Hyde get some much-needed development. At the same time, Coffee Talk 2 isn't a totally perfect game. Some characters which received more development in the first game are more just cameo appearances in this game, having smaller or otherwise nonexistant arcs. New drinks are mostly limited to hibiscus and butterfly pea beverages where I would have liked to see more inventive coffee drinks (as I loved a lot of the references in the first game to different coffees around the world). The stories from The Evening Whispers app are just not worth reading. Looking back on the ending, as well, I find myself wishing there was more there to wrap up the series in an epilogue. While each character had their ending, I do hope there might be talks of a future Coffee Talk 3, maybe focusing instead on the barista themself rather than their friends.All in all, I highly recommend this game for visual novel enthusiasts and Coffee Talk 1 fans. A solid 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Although this is the sequel to , I want to note that I have yet to play the first game (but I have plans to do so XD). is a visual novel developed and published by Toge Productions.  It is the sequel/next episode to .  However, I feel that it isn't necessary to have played the first game although there are a few returning characters and such.  Nevertheless,  can be played on its own.  Anyway, you take on the role of a barista (you can choose whatever name you wish) at Coffee Talk, a coffee shop in Seattle.  There is a brief introductory narrative which details how life is in the city and the troubling times that its citizens are enduring.  However, they can always drop by for a cup of coffee (or tea or any alternative beverage) and tell their burdens to a friendly barista who's willing to listen.  (Think of the coffee shop as being the equivalent of a bar, but the patrons don't get drunk. XD) You are that barista, and various patrons drop by for a warm drink and to tell their troubles (and maybe they'll find a way to resolve them).  That's the basic story premise, and I'll stop my synopsis here to avoid spoilers and all that.As for the gameplay, there are no traditional choices, despite that this is a visual novel.  In lieu of choices, the customers order various drinks.  Now, depending on how accurately you make the drinks and such, you'll end up getting either the best, normal, or worst endings (and there's a secret ending after you obtain the other endings).  As I just mentioned, the main gameplay consists of brewing drinks for customers, and the drinks can range from traditional coffee to the more eclectic tea and such.  Also, you can give items to customers, which may be necessary to advance certain storylines.  This is the gameplay for the main story.  In addition, there is endless mode in which (as the name implies) you serve as many correct beverages to customers before either the time limit runs out or too many customers are dissatisfied.  Also, there is a varied soundtrack as well as lots of pixelated CGs.  Of course, there are Steam achievements, too, although no Steam trading cards at the time of this review.Now that I've gone over the story and gameplay, I'll move onto my critique.  I won't make this a secret.  I enjoy a warm, soothing cup of coffee, and what better way to simulate that experience (or get close to it) than to play a game that revolves around coffee and other warm beverages?  Anyway, I'll first comment on the story.  I enjoyed the premise of taking on the barista role, listening to patrons' worries while making them a beverage that would (hopefully) help soothe them.  There are definitely quite a few stories to tell.  For example, Officer Jorji is dealing with some vandalism in the neighborhood, and he has no clue who the perpetrators are or why they're engaging in such activities.  Also, there's Riona, the banshee who wants to be a soprano.  However, opera highly favors sirens (since sirens have beautiful singing voices), so Riona (being a banshee) is more of an outlier.  Of course, there are plenty of other stories, but it would take way too long to go over all of them. XD  The characters who are owners of these stories are great as well, with varying personalities and such.  Some are clearly more tsundere-like (such as Hyde, the modeling vampire) while others are more upbeat and cheery.  Honestly, I liked all of the patrons who entered the coffee shop and enjoyed listening to their stories (while trying to help them out). ^^As for the writing, I found it well-paced, with the story expanding over the course of 15 days (in game time, of course).  I noticed a couple of grammatical errors, but because the narration is excellent, I could overlook them.  In regards to the art, it has a pixelated style.  This style is occasionally used in visual novels, and it really works for .  The art is very well done, and I liked looking at the beautiful CGs and noticed how detailed the animations of sprites were.  Even the coffee art is done well, making me really want to try a hibiscus tea. XD  Regarding the music, there are a lot of tracks with plenty of variety.  While some tracks are traditionally more relaxing and soothing, others are a bit more upbeat (and there's even one that makes you feel like you're in a bit of a dangerous situation, but I won't reveal which story has that XD).  There are some tracks which can only be unlocked if you follow a certain character's story, which I liked.  I enjoyed getting to explore and unlock as much of this game as possible.Overall, would I recommend ?  If you enjoy visual novels, like those with life simulation, and want a warm, relaxing story, then without a doubt, I totally recommend giving this a try.  No amount of gushing would be enough to convey how much I truly enjoyed this visual novel, making me want to play .  Also, it goes without saying that it's worth the full price.  The story is warm and soothing, and perhaps there might be another episode in the series.  Of course, that's totally up to the devs.Finally, I want to give a major thanks to the devs for the review copy. ^^

_childDocuments_.review: A vampire, a werewolf, and a banshee walk into a bar.That's not the start of a joke. It's the premise of the Coffee Talk series. You play as the Barista, the owner of a coffee shop that's only open at night and largely serves a clientele of supernatural beings, in this narrative heavy game where you serve warm drinks as you lend a ear to your patrons' problems. Episode 2 is pretty much more of the same thing as the original Coffee Talk. The pixel graphics are amazing. The soundtrack of lo-fi beats is soothing, and the conversations are interesting. You'll encounter new characters as well as get continuations of the characters from the first episode's stories. I believe the entire cast returns with the exception of Henry, Rachel's father in some capacity (some characters only get cameos). Oh, and there are new drinks, Blue (Butterfly) Pea and Hibiscus which give the game it's subtitle. Correction: Henry does appear for one night toward the end of the story, but he contributes very little to the ongoing plotlines. Not that I'm complaining. I enjoyed him very much in the first game so I am glad they found a way to utilize him the second episode. You influence the story subtly with the drinks you serve. Give your guests what they want, and you will steer the story toward a good outcome. Unwanted drinks will take you to a bad ending. Just pay attention to the dialogue and you should be able to get the drinks correct. Sometimes at the end of the night, you'll find an item someone has left behind and you need to return it to the owner the next time they come into the shop. To get the perfect ending, you have to give the correct drinks and remember to give people their items back.I honestly did not like this new mechanic. Due to the story's rather placid/ slice of life nature, I never read more than a chapter or two in a sitting. This is my wind down story that I play late at night before bed when my brain it already a bit tired. Honestly, I pretty much missed the majority of the instances when I was supposed to give the items back because I forgot I even had them in my drawer since a day or two would have passed between when I booted it up. Adding something like this kind of betrays the chill nature of the series since I know some people really stress over not getting the best ending.The story takes place over fifteen nights, which I believe is the same length as the first game (in number of chapters), but this one is about twice as long. The final couple of nights felt a bit padded out, and the narrative would have been a bit stronger had they trimmed some of the fat. The plot for new characters Riona and Lucas went on way too long for a story that went somewhere but not far enough to justify it taking over the latter half of the story. Worse, Myrtle and Aqua, my favorite storyline from the first episode, got positively snubbed for how little they appeared. When I reached the end, I was ready to see those end credits roll if I'm honest. Despite the late game pacing issues, I am looking forward to Coffe Talk: Tokyo.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid sequel to the original Coffee Talk. The game takes place a few years after the first one. Each character from the original Coffee Talk makes an appearance at least once, and there are a few new characters too. Each character's story line is distinct and helps keep things fresh and interesting. Game play is similar to the first game, except there are two new ingredients, hibiscus and blue pea. The specialty drinks you make with those two are especially unique and pretty. I've never had a hibiscus or blue pea based drink but might have to try after playing! One new feature is added: items. Characters will sometimes drop items or tell you to give items to other characters. Your decision to return or not return these items impacts the story. The only nitpick I have with this game is that making the correct drink can be a pain. Characters can be very vague about what they want, "Make me something based off a Pumpkin Spice Latte," one character says, knowing you don't have pumpkin. Messing up orders affects your relationship with characters, and the story. It's a cool mechanic but getting all the orders right is difficult without a guide. Still, this game is worth checking out. If you liked the slow-paced, character-focused nature of the first game with a cozy atmosphere to boot, you'll find more of the same in Coffee Talk Episode 2.

_childDocuments_.review: Brewing Up More Love in Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly If Coffee Talk was your favorite cozy corner café, Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly is like discovering they’ve added your favorite dessert to the menu—just when you thought it couldn’t get any better. This sequel serves up more of what made the first game a hit: heartwarming stories, endearing characters, and a dash of caffeinated magic.Characters and StoriesReturning to this café feels like meeting up with old friends—and maybe some new ones who have equally interesting backstories and questionable life choices. The characters in Coffee Talk 2 are as lovable as ever, with their quirks, dramas, and late-night dilemmas. The game offers deeper glimpses into their lives, making you feel like the world’s most empathetic barista-slash-therapist. Who knew serving coffee could be this emotionally rewarding?Atmosphere and StyleThe game’s pixel art remains a visual delight, continuing to evoke that warm, inviting atmosphere that makes you wish this café existed in real life. The blend of modern and mystical, with the ever-present Seattle rain, sets the perfect stage for introspective conversations and the occasional werewolf rant about societal expectations. SoundtrackIf you thought the first game’s soundtrack was as chill as a snowman on vacation, Coffee Talk 2  kicks it up a notch with even more relaxing lo-fi beats. It’s like your ears are getting a gentle massage while you whip up a triple-shot espresso for an insomniac vampire. The music keeps the vibe mellow, perfect for late-night gaming sessions or pretending you're productive while sipping your own cup of joe.GameplayThe drink-making mechanic is back and better than ever. With new ingredients like hibiscus and butterfly pea flower, you can now pretend you’re a mixologist in addition to being an amateur psychologist. Experimenting with these new additions not only keeps things fresh but also lets you subtly meddle in your customers' lives. Want to see how a mermaid handles a spicy latte? Now’s your chance.ConclusionCoffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly is a delightful return to a world where your biggest worry is getting the milk-to-coffee ratio just right. It’s a game that feels like a warm hug—if that hug also came with witty banter and occasional life advice from an orc. If you loved the first game, you’ll fall head over heels for this sequel. It’s a perfect blend of heartfelt storytelling, charming visuals, and a calming atmosphere that makes you wish you could actually tip your barista.Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5)

_childDocuments_.review: This along with the Coffee Talk 1 is my favourite visual novel. It is just so well written! The characters are all interesting and unique (old and new ones alike) and you are (or at least I were) really invested in their stories. It is emotional (in the best way possible) and cozy and it is a great tribute to the original game with little additions that contribute to more complexity and add a little more challenge (you're not only trying to find correct drinks for everyone, but also to give right items to the right customers). Even after playing it two times I still have things/outcomes I'd like to explore. But what I like the most about Coffe Talk Episode two (but one too!) is how this fantasy world full of nice werewolfs, cool rude vampires, loving and lovable elfs and sucubbuses and all the other fairies and lifeforms just depicts troubles of our own world so much better than any realistical drama could. It truly is The game with a soul!
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: Coffee Talk Episode 2 is just as enjoyable as the first game with a bite more to it! We learn and see more of our original characters- their continued stories and growth. Along with new teas added to our Brewpad's we meet new characters who are just as delightful as the regulars we're familiar with.Helping people through coffee and teas still goes on with an added element of giving items to customers as well. Be it an item lost or contact info in hopes for someone to connect to another new face, it adds to the experience of helping out people who come to the cafe.I enjoy that there are more play-throughs to be had to get even more story by giving everyone their proper drink or item. Coffee Talk is cozy, warm and perfect for a rainy day.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: Coffee Talk 2 is literally everything you might expect it to be: Exactly every bit as good as its predecessor, but somehow even better. There is nothing I could say in this review that could account for how this game made me feel when playing it. Sure, it might seem like a "safe" move to rely on its predecessor's structure and success, but it is actually incredible to me that this game managed to do even better in those fields. Coffee Talk 2 isn't just some upgrade for the base game, it is a proper comeback to a place of wondrous stories and characters with that extra little pinch of salt that really makes you sink into their world. I will miss the rainy nights I spent chatting with those characters and preparing them warm drinks to soothe their woes. I could not recommend this game enough, especially if you liked the first one.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: This is how you make a VN! Puas hati sangat. Happy to see everyone achieved great things in their lives. Somehow I can't get enough of this game. I want to lepak with them more than that. I feel attached to them and it's so hard to let go because I can feel our friendships are getting strong and I don't want to say goodbye... again :')
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I was not sure what to expect in this game. I was expecting something new and something familiar since I have already played the first game a while back. At the same time, I did not hold high hopes to see all our favorite faces from the first game. This game, however, exceeded my expectations by bringing back basically EVERYONE from the first game and introducing new patrons to our mysterious barista.How this game differs from the first one is that emotion expressions seem a little more explicit and fun this time. Old characters have all grown a little and it is nice to see them again, sharing their new conflicts in life. I simply adore how the new characters interact with some of our old faces, which is what brings the two games together cohesively.The game has also introduced some new features, which can drastically alter the endings for some characters, and I love it. It gives you more reasons to deviate from trying to reach the perfect ending unlike the last game, of course with the help of achievements.Overall, lovely game that makes me want to look forward to another episode in the future, though the endings in both games are satisfying enough to call it a day. In fact, I would say the second game (this one) did even better than the last one.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not finished with Episode Two yet, but I can tell that the conflicts, dialog, and character interactions are a quite a bit deeper, touching and more heartfelt here than in Episode One. That's not to say that Episode One was bad by any means, but it seemed like some of the interactions in Episode One were more cliche or superficial before (especially Rachel's "I'm an adult!" bit) by comparison, whereas here you really get to enjoy some ambiguity and compelling narratives where both people have valid points to make coming from different views.It's been enjoyable so far, but one complaint I have to make is that I wish that the Tomodachill friends notifications didn't update at the beginning at each day since it tends to spoil a new face that will be coming later on during a given day. Also, Toge could really use an editor to check over their scripts. There's been several typos and grammatical errors between Episode One and Two that can take the player out of their immersion in a mostly-visual novel experience. These are clearly not stylistic choices, but rather plain and simple writing errors.Apart from that, I've been enjoying the ride so far and look forward to an Episode Three!
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: Ahhh yes finally my tri-yearly dose of happiness.The game brings back a lot of the same characters with a few new ones whilst also enriching the existing characters story. I already knew the story will be a banger to be honest and i half expected the same formula since i bought into this just to read a bit more story but the introduction of new mechanics (The lost & found stuff) was a very nice touch. Something to keep things a bit interesting and at the same time provoke a bit more thought into your decisions such as .Overall, love the game. Love the characters. Love the story. Can't wait for my next dose in year 2026.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very nice game. It says I have 103 hours but most of that is me falling asleep before getting back to the game while leaving it on, though it is a game worth your time. I recommend playing the first game before this one, though it may not be absolutely required.My main complaint with this game is how long it can take to get all the endings. Depending on drinks you give and the items you decide to give and not give, you can get different endings. You can skip through days to give specific characters the required drinks to get other endings, but even with that it still feels like it takes a while with the amount of dialogue there is. But, the amount of dialogue makes first time playthroughs good, so I can't fault it too much on that.Overall I'd recommend the game, it was very fun and as someone who loved the first game, I can say it is a great sequel. New drinks, new characters, old characters, and new scenarios. Please support the devs and buy the game!!!!!!!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love the Coffee Talk series and this sequel was very...emotional/sentimental. I feel like we got to see different sides to all of our beloved characters and we got introduced to Lucas and Riona whom are great additions to the story. I also enjoy Amanda, albeit we didn't see them very much. There were a lot of sweet moments in the story that tugged at my heart. If you enjoyed the first Coffee Talk, you'll definitely love this one. Pros (for me): Freya is basically nonexistent in the story-line (sorry Freya lovers), , the addition of objects being able to be given to certain characters, and like I said above...I feel like this sequel is a bit more heartwarming. I also love the incorporation of new drinks and I love the butterfly pea and hibiscus drink options. The colors are lovely and were a great addition!Cons (for me): not very many cons, but I find the soundtrack from the first game to be more memorable. I still loved the soundtrack for this one, but the first game had something that stuck out to me more. Also, I would love for the next game to be a bit longer in terms of gameplay! I know a lot of hardwork goes into making this, so it's really just a personal wish. I enjoy playing it regardless of the length, but since I love it so much I'd enjoy even more gameplay lol. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: So glad to finish the entire story on the same day as designed in the game... I saw my own mentality via Riona's and Lucas' perspectives, and their conversations with other characters were quite encouraging and comforting towards my real situations. Thanks for making this game, and, Mr. Fahmi especially, I wish you best of luck on your journey.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: The first one was great, but I found this one was so-so. The extra ingredients and item system was a nice little expansion to the base game, but it didn't hit as hard on the story side which was the main pull for me.Compared to the first one, this felt like a chore to get through because the general writing didn't really seem to be all that interesting unfortunately. For example, it touches on and covers the same kinda fantasy themes and such from the first, but it felt shallow this time around, so I never really cared for the new characters and such.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: I played & enjoyed the first Coffee Talk, but this one not so much. The "new" features are now you have a drawer and can hand over items along side drinks, and you have a social media feed on your phone (which doesn't affect gameplay). I almost want to be snarky and include "blackouts" as a new feature, as the number of times lightning affects the power is comical. It rains every... single... day...Much of the game is the same, just with two new characters and continuing storylines. The first game introduced the world to you. I don't give this game as much slack because it didn't really move the narrative forward for me - it felt more like small chit-chat, no longer about race relations or whatnot.The aspect that most disappointed me was the previously mentioned item drawer. For example, I knew I had to give X to Y character, but you "lose" the item somehow (it's scripted and unavoidable). This was done to  I hate it when the game sabotages you like this. I'm not doing another playthrough, no matter how many 4th wall breaking hints you dropped at the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adored the first game and this is a worthy sequel. While I was sad that some characters only appeared briefly (my beloved Aqua where are you :<) it made space for new characters to shine. And they were equally delightful as the old cast. My first run was obviously good, as I want to see all of these people prosper, but the bad run also brought something to the table in form of giving more depth to some characters. So it was intriguing to keep messing up to see where the story will go and what stories these characters have to tell. Overall it was a great experience accompanied by wonderful soundtrack. I recommend this game with my whole heart.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, I understand is a tad mean to leave a "don't recommend" review with only 2 hours of gameplay, but...this is as much as I felt I could play. I never played the first one, I heard this one is a sequel but can work as a standalone, so I wanted to give it a go. I played visual novels before, I had been a big fan of the genre, and I value more characters than plot in a story, so this wound like my kind of game, right?Sadly, that wasn't the case.The conversations are extremely slow, I understand that you are trying to built a connection with these people, and realistic dialogue, but a lot of times it boils to a lot of small talk where I am pushed to move forward just to see if something interesting will happen. I liked the mini game to make drinks, but that's not the main focus of the game, so it can only do so much.Every time I would play this game, I would tell myself to play more than just one day (gameplay-wise, not real time,) just to go through that day, felt numb after reading so much dialogue where with some luck, something mildly interesting will pop up, but not enough to compensate for the small talk and awkward dialogue lines.It doesn't help that I feel I am not doing much; I understand the gameplay isn't the focus of a visual novel, but when that aspect is not doing enough for you, this lack of options truly starts weighing you down. Maybe at some point I may try to give it another go, I had heard so many good things about this game and its characters, that I want to believe all of it; but for now? No, pick something else.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to start by saying that the producers did an excellent job. Although it is not a complex game, its story gives important messages from society. It is a game that I think can appeal to everyone, and what makes me think about this is the differences between the characters in the game and the things they represent, just like real people. I also loved the music and the artwork we could access in-game. I think I've fallen in love with this game series. Thanks for reading my review <3

_childDocuments_.review: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly - A Familiar ComfortCoffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly delivers a comforting cup of the same brew as the original.  Returning to the late-night Seattle cafe, you'll listen to the stories of a new cast of fantastical creatures facing everyday struggles. Most of the core gameplay remains unchanged save the fact that you now have the ability to give items, which can leave a lot of impact on the. While the narrative is charming, it doesn't quite reach the emotion heights of the first gameDespite the slight dip, Coffee Talk 2 provides a relaxing and familiar experience. The lo-fi beats and calming visuals return, alongside new lore tidbits and cultural references.  For fans of the original, or those seeking a heartwarming escape, Coffee Talk 2 offers a delightful return to the cafe.

_childDocuments_.review: The first game has a lot of charm to it. I recently played it again just to see what it was like in anticipation for the sequel.If you are asking if this game delivers, I would say yes and no. the game is a lot like the first one, built upon it, like a 1.5, which is probably why it is titled Episode 2 instead of a straight up sequel. The story takes place about 3 years after the first one, and you end up catching up with everyone and seeing how things have changed. If you like the first game for the atmosphere and characters, then this game will definitely be something you'll enjoy. If you're looking for expansion on the game-play however, you'll probably be disappointed, as the game does very little to change it up. given it's a "don't fix what's not broke" approach, it makes sense, but still a fair warning. the good of the game is a lot of what the first game had, but it also is the downside of it as you're getting more of the same, just slightly expanded upon.Story wise, it felt either too fast, or too slow at times. some moments will go by quickly, and you'll be wondering what happened, while other times it feels like they're dragging on a bit, exploring the world but given how you don't have as much direct input, it doesn't feel quite as impactful(stop forgetting your lighter Jorgi). Freya isn't around this time, so when the days are over, you'll be talking to yourself, and most of the time won't really have a moment to reflect on everything that happened. Still, you do get your happy endings, but some of the story weren't explored as much, such as with Aqua and Myrtle, so it isn't as impactful.gameplay wise, it's the same, just with 2 new ingredients and an item giving mechanic that really is underutilized in my opinion. it does affect what endings you get, but honestly the items you get are a small selection and it's fairly easy to figure out the right item to give, and moreso of knowing who to give it to(hint: you sometimes give an item not to the person directly, but someone related to them). aside from the small changes, they aren't really as big to where the gameplay evolved, but given the kind of game it is, it's not as big of an issue. as for the length, it took me roughly less than 7 hours to beat(beaten within 2 days) not counting the reloading I had to do, so it is a short game if you know what to do or look up a guide.I'm a fan of the this series, so I am slightly biased when i say I give this game a 8/10, given how long I've been wanting to play this. However, if your'e someone new, and only recently played the first one, this will probably be more of a 6 or 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Coffee Talk Episode 2: Hibiscus & Butterfly

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked the first game; surprise, there's more!It's pretty much more of the same tbh, which is nice if you loved the first game, but tbh, the novelty was lost on me after a whileThe new characters are interesting and their stories/outcomes are fun, but to get the "ultra-most-secret-ending" you need to play through the game many times and get all of the available endings, which... Gets exhausting after some point - especially since the "fast forward" button frequently gets stuck on character animationsCouple that with the fact that the achievements are broken and support doesn't reply to any emails about it, I'd recommend ppl sit this one out.

_childDocuments_.review: *spoilers ahead*Eh.... I liked the first game better. This is not bad nor lazy in the slightest, but this is not as compelling as the first game. The dialogue has this 'wattpad' style writing to me. I could not care less for the 'fairies' subplot. Jorji is not as interesting as Freya. He isn't witty, funny nor charming like she is, so having him as the main focus this time around is honestly a drag. As a matter of fact, Aqua and Myrtle's subplot had me the most invested. Too bad they got the least screen time. The new characters are okay, nothing special.Literally besides the characters, everything else improved. The UI itself, new stuff being added to the social media apps, the attempt at world building,  the new ingredients, the music, tasks that you have to remember to fulfill - like giving certain characters items that belong to them, etc. This is why i am recommending this game for those who completed the first one. Cheers.   For a heavy-dialogue game, the characters and the various sub-plots NEEDS to be near perfect. This was alright. 6/10.
