_childDocuments_.review: Good selection of games, a lot more loving than the previous Pac-Man Museum (which not only was kinda cheaply done, every museum aspect was in service to the Ghostly Adventures cartoon which barely has anything to do with the actual games, not to mention the 720p lock that also meant it didn't scale to a higher resolution.) And it has my favorite game, Pac-Man Arrangement Arcade, which was oddly absent in the previous version.I do have a few gripes that I hope will get fixed, mainly some minor control delay (which is absolutely killer in Pac-Mania due to the isometric viewpoint and more aggressive ghosts) but also the lack of DIP switch options, which even the previous game had.The same games (minus the single DLC game) from the previous Museum (Pac-Man, Super Pac, Pac-Land, Pac&Pal, Pac-Mania, Pac-Attack, Championship Edition, Arrangement PSP and Battle Royale) are all still back, though Attack has switched from the Genesis version to the SNES version, maybe would have been preferred had they included the Namco Anthology version of the game that was featured in Pac-Man World 2 but it works fine enough i guess (though honestly I suck at attack). Otherwise, these games are the same as before except minus DIP switch options and having new borders (no integer scaling though)The new games (Pac-Man Arrangement Arcade, Pac-and-Roll Remix, Pac-Motos, Pac-Man 256, Pac-in-Time) are sort of a mixed bag. Arrangement Arcade is a welcome addition at any time since its probably the best version of the original game's formula with the additions of power-ups and the "Kinky" ghost that modifies the other ghosts into more difficult versions of themselves) Pac-And-Roll and Pac-Motos feel like they were part of the exact same game cut into two seperate ones (same menus, same models, i would not be surprised if these are modified from the Pac-And-Roll DS game to play without needing a touch screen) They're fun but Motos especially is extremely basic and feels like a side-game in a bigger game.256 is literally the exact same as the PC version that already exists, did they even take that off sale? The only difference is the museum tracks your scores and how many times you play, making it a good way to rack up tokens.Pac-In-Time is a bizzare game that is strange to play and honestly not that great. Of note is they used the more difficult Super Famicom version of the game rather than the SNES version. Its a shame that none of the Pac-Man World games were included, but I guarantee that's because of the FMV sequences and how much of a hassle it would be to remove Ms. Pac-Man from those to continue to spite AtGames. A true shame but it could also be that they didn't want to have like five extra copies of original pac-man playable as well (and World 2 would also have to remove the Ms. Pac-Man ROM too or block people out of the arcade entirely).Great collection, few minor gripes but I hope those will be fixed in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was kinda just announced out of nowhere, and I'm a little surprised to see little people talking about it. Pac-Man Museum+ reminds me of the Pac-Man Museum game that used to be on Steam, but was taken off, likely due to the unsuccessful Ghostly Adventures brand slapped onto it. Well this game is very much the style of Pac-Man I like. It has a number of old and obscure games that make for a fun package. It isn't the best collection ever or anything, but it's solid for what you get. The 14 games offered are decent picks, ranging from arcade games that are both popular and underrated to the popular mobile game that is Pac-Man 256 (though this collection thankfully includes the console re-release), and fascinating console releases like Pac-In-Time, Pac-Man Championship Edition, Pac-Motos, and Pac-In-Roll Remix. Glad that they brought in some of the 3D stuff too. They play as you'd expect, though as a user of VSync, I did have to manually mess with graphics settings outside of the game, since while this game does have graphics options, they only apply to the game's arcade hub and not the games themselves. But other than having to boot up NVIDIA Control Panel for this one, the emulation quality of the games are fine. (Edit: The emulation is pretty middle of the road. The games play just fine, with maybe a bit of input lag which is unfortunate, but the pixel scaling from what I heard is pretty off. Like some pixels are larger than others because the resolution isn't scaled properly. It's hard to notice, but once you do you can't really unsee it. But if that doesn't bother you, you'll be fine.)The arcade customizer is pretty cool, I sort of wish there were more things to do with it like increase the size of the arcade or interact with some of the furniture and objects you get, but it's a pretty neat system nonetheless. There's also some neat figures and other collectibles you can collect for the arcade by spending tokens in a machine, they pull from lots of various Pac-Man media, so it's pretty fascinating. It would have been pretty cool to have some sort of online functionality where you can visit other people's arcade online or even play the games in VR inside your arcade, but oh well.If you like the games offered here, you'll likely enjoy this collection, it's pretty odd to see that Pac-Man 256 is here despite being a fully released $5 game on Steam separately, so that version is pretty obsolete now, but it's nice to have. I'd say buy it if you wanna see more Pac-Man games in the future, it's a solid collection that thankfully isn't too expensive. Hopefully good sales of this will lead to new Pac-Man games, or a collection of the Pac-Man World games, which is what I personally really want. So... get it if you're interested, it's pretty good.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid collection of many games throughout Pac-Man's history. There are some exclusions such as Ms. Pac-Man and some games that could see a return such as Pac-Man: Adventures in Time. Nonetheless, the games present here all have their place and offer a variety of experiences, from the old to new.All the games in my experience run and play well, there's some input lag issues in games such as Pac-Land and Pac-Man: Championship Edition, but for the most part the games play well. Games are played in their correction aspect ratios, controls work fine on most games, and all the arcade games are their actual arcade versions.The addition of the Arcade adds a lot of charm to the collection, being able to decorate your own Arcade room however you wish. You start off with a basic room, but you can earn more decorations by completing missions in the games, which can include missions such as eating a set number of ghosts or completing a certain level. These missions can earn you rewards to use in the Arcade room such as new decorations, more arcade cabinets, and background music to play.As you play games, you can earn coins to use in the Arcade. The amount of coins you can earn from the games can depend on your performance in a game session, mainly your high score for most games. Normally you would use these coins to insert them into the arcade games such as the original Pac-Man (like a real arcade), but you can also use these coins to buy more decorations from the Vending Machine and figures from the Gashapon. Figures in the Gashapon can consist of characters and items, including the fruits and the ghosts. These figures can also come in silver or gold, though they are rarer to obtain.Pac-Man: Museum+ is a nice collection of Pac-Man games at an affordable price, it is a nice way to get back into Pac-Man and explore some of his familiar and even unknown titles over the years. It has a nice amount of replay value and getting better at Pac-Man is always a fun time. Looking forward to Pac-Man World Re-Pac!

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a video game compilation actually worth money, skip out on Sonic Origins and get this collection. It has tons of obscure games from Pac-Man's library along with a really cool customizable hub where you can create your own arcade and unlock items as you play games. The game selection isn't the greatest but it's absolutely solid, with games such as Pac-Mania, Pac-Man Championship Edition, Pac-Man Battle Royale, the Super Pac-Man, both versions of Pac-Man Arrangement, Pac-Attack, Pac-in-Time, Pac-Man 256, and who could forget good ol' classic Pac-Man. The emulation is decent aside from some input delay that varies from game to game. With that said however there are some drawbacks to this release. For one thing there is no way to change the arcade dip switch settings. Dip switches were physical switches that would be in the inside of a real arcade cabinet which would allow you to change the settings of the game, for example you could change the amount of lives you start with in Pac-Man as low as one to as high as five. This isn't really a big deal for most of these games but for one game in particular, which is also my favorite Pac-Man game: "Pac-Mania," its a real issue. Pac-Mania is already a pretty challenging game on it's own, but the current dip switch configuration for this game is so unforgiving that it makes the game extremely frustrating to play. Setting the game to "Rank A" (easy difficulty) and increasing the lives to five balances the game considerably and makes it much more enjoyable to run through. Other collections in the past allowed you to configure the dip switch settings, so to not have the option here is honestly inexcusable. Another problem is the lack of options in general. You can only remap specific buttons for games and there aren't enough filtering options. Another downside is that you can't change a game's region. The reason why this is a big deal is because some of these games actually have significant regional changes, so you don't get the option to experience whatever region you grew up with or just like better. And the last downside (which in all honesty doesn't really affect the collection too much) is the Mrs. Pac-man censoring, but hopefully one day those legal issues will be resolved. Overall this is indeed a great collection, but if you're not interested in the exclusive stuff and only interested in the 80s arcade games then you'd probably be better off with M.A.M.E.

_childDocuments_.review: What does NAMCO Bandai have against save states? You'd think the latest collection in the long line of NAMCO collections there'd at least be save states. If there's any consolation, NAMCO included a suspend save feature that can be exploited, effectively making it possible to beat games like Pac-Land which would prove difficult to do otherwise. Instead of a proper quick save/load feature to load a save, you have to back out to the arcade after having died, and then when you go back into the game, it'll ask if you wish to start where you last left off. What this does is load the gamestate from the last level you were on as if you didn't lose a life. The game doesn't tell you this, you either have to figure it out yourself or find instruction elsewhere.It should be noted that this is clearly a straight port of the Switch version, which you can tell with the "swap A/B for confirmation button" setting that only affects the menus and not the emulated games themselves. The game defaults the action button in-game to the right face button, which WOULD be A on Switch, as opposed to the bottom one. Kinda disappointing that a PC game released today doesn't have proper key mapping settings, but I digress. This annoyance can be overcome with SteamDeck's nifty system level button remapping feature which should make menu navigation AND primary button prompts in-game to work with the Xbox controller's A button.Additionally, the game supports a limited credits system with no free play option. This credits system is global across all relevant arcade games, and they can be acquired by completing optional objectives provided for each game as well as through general gameplay. Not sure what happens if you decide to use up all your coins on the gacha machine, though, so I can imagine it becoming problematic in the end if you run out of coins to play the arcade games with.While there's a great selection and variety of titles, this release is missing so many quality of life features, such as proper saves states and free play for the arcade games. Additionally, enabling VSync doesn't appear to work because there's screen tearing whether you have it enabled or not, and enabling the FPS cap doesn't appear to help either.All said, the game works perfectly fine on SteamDeck, if not arguably better, because you can remap the buttons at the system level, though if you're gonna play Pac-Land it's best to play it with a keyboard, because mashing a key to move is far easier than busting an analog stick on a controller.I'm down voting this collection, purely on principle, because save states aren't easily accessible, forcing the player to go through multiple (6!) key presses EVERY TIME they need to reload their game after frequent unfortunate deaths.

_childDocuments_.review: PAC-MAN MUSEUM+:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ My first-ever meeting with Mr PAC-MAN was in the 80' on a family summer holiday in Cattolica, a popular destination located on Italy's Adriatic coast. The daily schedule was very basic; sunbake to lobster tone from 10 am to 3 pm, then from 4 pm until dinner time, walk down the main strip and visit all the gaming lounges! And everything single one of them had at least one of the super-popular, the one and only PAC-MAN Arcade game! I kid you not. And we had to wait our turn in those days; sometimes, it could take up to an hour. Aahhhh, the good all days! After a few years, Pac-Man games started to be released on consoles, and I am so glad to have the opportunity to revisit them with PAC-MAN MUSEUM+.PAC-MAN MUSEUM+ is a compilation of 14 PAC-MAN games developed by NOW PRODUCTION and Published by Bandai Namco Entertainment on the 28th of June 2022 on the Steam platform. This compilation is only available on PS4, Nintendo Switch and Xbox One.I love these types of compilations where you can see the evolution of a classic game, and it’s also interesting to see how they can morph into different genres of gameplay. In PAC-MAN MUSEUM+, you'll have seven games where you need to insert a coin to play a game, just like an Arcade game machine, and seven other games which do not need a coin. However, you must play at least two games to unlock another PAC-MAN game. And as you probably guessed, you'll start with the original PAC-MAN, followed by SUPER PAC-MAN, and so on, until you unlock all the games. Don't worry about the coins, as you'll start with 500 in hand, and it is very easy to accumulate more coins. Each time you play any of the games, you'll receive a minimum of two coins, and if you do complete one of the game missions, such as eating a certain number of ghosts, completing a certain number of rounds, passing a specific score or beating your last best score, you'll be rewarded with more coins. You’ll also receive items by completing missions which you can use to customise your own gaming lounge, which is a lot of fun. It’s nostalgic and so enjoyable to replay some of these originals; I loved some and disliked others, and also played new ones that I hadn’t experienced before. I can hear from my desktop, coming from the four corners of the globe . . . How can you dislike a PAC-MAN game? In fact, I disliked a couple of them. As much as I enjoy good platformers these days, I couldn’t get into PAC-LAND and PAC-IN-TIME. Even the nostalgic aspect of these games couldn’t stop me from cringing; I know it’s harsh, but PAC-MAN almighty, playing these two games took a lot of courage and positivity to get through. PAC-ATTACK was better, but yeah, a Tetris genre with a PAC-MAN twist didn’t do it for me. The other big NO NO for me is the PAC-MAN BATTLE ROYALE, I just don’t get it! A lot of people may like this battle royal genre of game, but it’s not my thing.The original PAC-MAN is still my favourite followed closely by PAC-MANIA, PAC-MAN ARRANGEMENT CS Ver and PAC-MAN CHAMPIONSHIP EDITION. The big surprise for me was the PAC-MAN 256 which I hadn’t played before, and I went back for more!You’ll appreciate all the graphics and the controls work well, except for the few platformer games (cringe, cringe). Plenty of items to unlock to customise your gaming lounge. You’ll have plenty of fun and nostalgia playing PAC-MAN MUSEUM+, especially if you experienced the original game back in the 80s. You’ll be back for more each time you have a few minutes to spare.Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Nice graphics as well as nostalgic+	14 PAC-MAN games+	Plenty of items to unlock for customising your gaming lounge+	A good boost of nostalgia+	AchievementsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	Platformer games have terrible controls-	No trading cards as yetRunning away and eating ghosts is so nostalgic and so much fun! PAC-MAN MUSEUM+ is a beautiful compilation, thank you Bandai Namco for the past and upcoming hours of gameplay!8/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: For the TL;DR: Great collection at a price point steal, mediocre presentation quality, fair game selection (popular and obscure) and nice customizable extras albeit a lot feels missing from making it the essential package.There's a lot to break down for this collection so I wanted to break it down to a pros and cons list:PROS:- Amazing game selection across Pac-Man's history, from the well known to the more obscure. This is the first time the Wii Pac-Man games from Namco Museum Remix/Megamix are included in a collection outside of the original- Pac-Man Arrangement (1996) included. best pac-man ever with pac-man CE DX- Alternating 2-player modes from the original arcade games retained- Save feature for continuing later across most games- Arcade HUB is fun to customize, is presented very well- Online leaderboards and in-game missions add replayability to all the gamesCONS:- Game emulation/porting quality is poor:--- Classic games have audio latency, audio splicing--- Input lag (most notable in some games like Pac-Mania and Pac-Man CE)--- Modern games like Pac-Man CE are missing visual effects or have awkward sound mixing--- Classic games are not pixel perfect/use interger scaling, games use bilinear filter with cheap video settings- Ms. Pac-Man's complete erasure. Not only is the Ms. Pac-Man game notably missing, but the character has been edited out of all the games she was previously featured in; the character is replaced by a stand-in design, which ALSO effects Jr. Pac-Man and Baby Pac-Man. these changes make the collection's presentation inaccurate to Pac-Man's history in various ways. what the hell are you doing bandai namco- Arcade games are missing game options from their original releases- All arcade/SNES games (sans Pac-Man and Pac-Attack) are based on their Japanese releases instead of the international versions. While it may not seem much, games like Pac-Mania are lengthier than usual. Pac-In-Time is especially notorious for this, considering the Super Famicom version is much harder to finish compared to the international version. Another factor to Pac-In-Time is that it features Japanese text with translated subtitles overlaying them, despite the international versions having already existed with a translation.- Some missions require excessive grinding, most especially Pac-Man 256- No online playOverall a fair collection with some oddities! I would recommend this if you're a Pac-Maniac like me; but if you're nitpicky over detail, I'd otherwise recommend to Pac-Away for the next collection or settle with the Arcade Archives releases on PS4/Switch.

_childDocuments_.review: REVIEW #80PAC-MAN MUSEUM+----------I've known the PAC-MAN series to get packaged and REpackaged many times over, especially since the explosion of optical media-based game consoles in the 1990s, and as much as I do love a good PAC-MAN game, Bandai Namco hasn't always done these packagings with apparent love. I believe it's safe to say that it isn't the case here.PAC-MAN MUSEUM+ features a pretty solid list of 14 games, and not all of them are mazed-based dot muncher titles. For the players here primarily for the classics, there's plenty of those present. Included in the bundle are the original PAC-MAN, PAC-MAN CHAMPIONSHIP EDITION, PAC & PAL, PAC-MANIA, and even 2 versions of PAC-MAN ARRANGEMENT. If you're ever in the mood for something different, there's plenty of unique and interesting PAC-MAN titles in this bundle as well. For example, there's the classic action/adventure arcade oddity that is PAC-LAND, the Tetris-like PAC-ATTACK, and a newfound favorite of mine, PAC'N ROLL REMIX, a surprising adventure game that lets the player literally roll our spherical hero around different areas while munching dots that he rolls into.While on the subject of the included games, I wish to point out what I feel are 2 glaring omissions, those being MS. PAC-MAN and PAC-MAN JR. As the series has aged, I've noted the former getting added to PAC-MAN bundles as paid DLC only, and JR. has been getting left out of recent PAC-MAN collections completely. I feel that both are very solid entries in the series, and watching each game's different cut-scenes in between levels is always a joy, so to see that these 2 classics are absent is a mark against MUSEUM+ for me. Additionally, some games have to be unlocked by completing goals in other games. This isn't really a problem if implemented properly, and for the most part, it is done well in PMM+. However, one headache that I had involved the atrocious and ugly PAC-IN-TIME, since there's an unlock quest which is only completed by playing that horrid game. If there was no unlock quest tied to that game, it would be easy to ignore. However, not only having to play it to unlock the full game roster in PMM+ but also having 2 games that I really wanted to be included completely missing from this bundle is a double-insult for me.Back to what MUSEUM+ is doing right, all games here look and control beautifully (or in PAC-IN-TIME's case, as they should.) What's definitely worth mentioning, though, is that the main platform of the game is an interactive arcade that you can decorate and fill with arcade games as you wish, letting you later control PAC-MAN himself and have him interact with his surroundings. Features include a jukebox with unlockable tracks, a Gashapon toy-dispensing machine with collectible PAC-MAN figurines, and other characters from the series to roam around your arcade creation. My only complaint is that the arcade space is a little small, and I'm unsure if it ever expands. Regardless, it's fun to have PAC-MAN run around your own design of an arcade with a giant smile on his face. While an actual menu with the list of available games is in PMM+, this arcade platform essentially works as a menu itself, and I think that they did a great job in implementing it and making it appropriately customizable.So, if you have any love of classic PAC-MAN games (or even recent ones like PAC-MAN 256), PAC-MAN MUSEUM+ is a great way to enjoy them. On a personal note, I'm happy to have finished this review, as I'm quite fed up with having to type so many game titles in all caps. Ugh.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to the original Pac-Man Museum, this is not perfect but it's a big improvement over the original. It could be better though.This collection has almost all the original arcade games-the first one of course, Pac & Pal, Super Pac-Man (my personal favorite), Pac-Land, Pac-Mania, Arrangement, Battle Royale, Championship Edition and a handful of console/mobile games including the star of that bunch: Pac-Man 256, a Crossy Road-inspired take. It's a sightly earlier version of the previously released standalone game also available separately.All the games are arcade-perfect ports and, against what was in the first Museum, the controls have been improved (namely analog stick responsiveness), but it's still best played with a D-Pad. There are only 2 real complaints: No Ms. Pac-Man here and what really hurts Battle Royale and 256-no multiplayer. Battle Royale is a great party game that allows up to 4 people to play against each other in arcades, so not having that here is a huge loss. Same with the multiplayer in 256. The console/mobile games are a mixed bag, Pac-Attack is the Genesis version of the unique puzzle game, I like the Motos-inspired Pac-Motos, while Pac-in-Time (again seems to be the Genesis version) and Pac-N-Roll are okay.This game also allows you to earn items you can use to decorate the main room to look like your own personal Pac-Man arcade, a clever touch along with being able to have the ghosts and family from Pac-Man World as guests. It's only cosmetic but a nice touch.If you didn't buy them separately already, Championship Edition and 256 here are more than enough to warrant a purchase. Battle Royale is a lot of fun but is killed by lack of multiplayer. Even if you have the original Museum, there are enough improvements and new additions here to warrant buying this one despite the lack of Ms. Pac-Man and multiplayer. Maybe they'll get added in someday but I wouldn't count on it.

_childDocuments_.review: For anyone who wants to take a trip down memory lane with the Pac, this collection comes highly recommended. While the loss of and censoring of Ms. Pac Man is unfortunate thanks to the legal snarls, the 14 games here are all noteworthy in their own right, including the first rerelease of Pac-In-Time, and the first home console port of my favorite Pac-game, Pac-Man Arrangement 1996, since 2002. While I would've preferred having the Genesis version of Pac-Attack due to sound preference, and the sound emulation problems crop up here and there, I'd still suggest that anyone with even a passing interest in Namco's mascot give this collection a shot. There's a little something for everyone, and here's to hoping DLC eventually becomes possible in the future. Maybe give us a little section on Pac-Man's history and merch like the PS1 Namco Museums, and options to control game settings like lives and extend scores?

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty solid collection of Pac-Man titles, and I'd highly recommend it if you like Pac-Man and want a convenient way to play a crash course of Pac-Man history. That being said, some of the emulation can be weird since it's Unity handling the emulation, there's a surprisingly lack of screen filters(minus an okay at best CRT filter) and a lack of titles like Ms. Pac-Man or the NES versions of these games make me a bit hesitant to call this the "Definitive" Pac-Man collection.When all is said in done, if you think this is for you, it probably is. I already had it on the Switch, so I waited for a price cut and I was fine parting with the $10 I ended up paying for it. If you're on the fence, I'd recommend doing the same, but if you absolutely need to play it now, $20 is not a bad price tag. Just be aware of the minor issues I mentioned above.If I were to give Pac-Man Museum+ a number rating it would 8/10, which is pretty damn good, but I do seriously wish that Ms. Pac-Man was here, I'd even be willing to shell out $5 as DLC to have her in the collection.

_childDocuments_.review: This could very well be the most complete collection of Pac-Man games you can play on modern platforms. Many "Namco Museum" titles have existed throughout the years, which usually include Pac-Man, but a Museum entry focused exclusively on Pac-Man is a much welcome addition. Many Pac-Man titles are mostly arcade games, or obscure entries on older consoles; barely any have even gotten ports.As for the games themselves, you'll have a lot of different opinions. The variations of the original arcade game are a "love it or hate it" kind of thing, but I think all are quite interesting in their own way, and are worth at least trying out every one of them. I was pleasantly surprised as I've hardly played any of the games in this collection besides the original, 256, and Championship Edition. I ended up having an appreciations for Super Pac-Man, Pac & Pal, Pac Land, and numerous other entries as their own take on the original, even if I didn't love every single game. If you want a crash course on Pac-Man's history, this is the game to get. You may be surprised at how much you may potentially like the games you've never played.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is a wonderful game where you can play many old pacman games. I was surprised by how they didn't make the customer have to grind to play each cabinet and just gave them 500 coins right off the bat. And to play the games, it only costed 1 coin; some games were free to play. I guess they were going for the feeling.Kinda dumb to have insert key be the button to use coins. Never have I ever used “insert.” Because the game says "insert coin" like an arcade doesn't mean we should on keyboard. It's insane, especially when there's no key config.When you open the game for the first time, the screen is quiet, waiting for you to press the spacebar. So you press it and then the agreement shows up and a ton of  absolute garbage noise hurts your ears like they want you to just accept it and move on.  Like wow, man... Luckily there's a jukebox and you can change the background music. My fav was "world 0 bgm - toy boxes world."It was interesting to see how much the games have changed as time went on. What I really liked was the section where you can read a little bit about the game and when it was released.I think the interface and ui for the game was really good.The whole customization of your arcade is okay but I don't think it was really needed cause it just makes everything a clutter to navigate through. The ai people who show up just get in your way and do nothing! I kind of expected them to at least use the benches but they didn't.The items that you can buy from the vendor is kind of dumb. Just a couple of items and 10 of each of them. Like seriously, who's going to use 10 of the same flags? I bought out the entire vendor and no new items showed up.The gachapon thing is alright. I liked the models but I think having a figure just be silver or gold is a coppout of not putting in more work. It's really just a simple material change to the model. Something like the witch from that snes pacman game would have meant more to me than another baby pacman but he's gold now. I gave up trying to collect all the figures cause I felt like it wasn't a good use of my time. Too much tapping the spacebar and seeing the same figures.For some reason, this game screentears and stutters when I'm not using my better 60 fps monitor (my main one is capped at 48). I'm not sure why it's happening. I guess it's just unity or programming?I think this game could have been better in some ways but it's good enough and I had fun. I will leave my reviews of each pacman game below.Pac-man (1980) is a classic game. Simple but good, though a bit too hard. Not enough change in gameplay the longer you play.Super Pac-man (1982) is a more complex game. You need keys to open pink doors. The level design and the pink doors locking other paths make the game feel more restrictive. I think it hurts the game. You can power up into giant pacman now but it's so much harder to control. You'll be running into walls at every turn. The bonus stages were a nice add. I think they added some great things but also took a couple steps back. Pac&Pal (1983) I like this version of pacman. There's a new character who walks around taking your items. I just wish she would bring you them instead. The new item where you can shoot is so great. It really makes life easier when playing the game. The bonus stages are back and they are done a little differently and I like that. Even though I like the game, the game is kinda hard. This would be one of my fav old pacman games for sure.   Pac Land (1984) is great. It's just that it's hard and it's controls are questionable. At round 6, you'll be met with a springboard and water that you need to jump across. No one playing would understand that you can hover over it by repeatedly tapping "right" to keep going, and you also need to press "jump" at the right moment to get the best height. The game looks so great and I made it to the medieval castle place but the game is just too hard. With only 3 lives and no way to continue progress, I had to stop. No way I'm going back and forth just to make little progress, you must be mad. Pac Mania (1987) is an easier pacman game. It looks 3d and isometric. The problem is, is that there's just not enough change to formula. You can jump now and that's cool but by the time you are at level 3 and the game is getting hard, it's just the speed of the enemies that change. The music is nice though.Pac Attack (1994) is like tetris. It's cool that pacman shows up and can help you but I don't like the game.Pac in Time (1995) is a game from the snes. The controls are just awful. It's so crazy to think that they did it that way. I guess that's why this game is translated now, because it was so bad, it stayed in japan. One thing to note is that I died by a log (it only goes up and down) that was on top of me and squished me. Why?Pac-man Arrangement (1996) is the better pac-man game that I've played yet. It controls really good and there's some new gameplay changes from the drugs that you can take, such as; running faster, making a copy of yourself, and putting enemies in a bag for a couple seconds. Enemies can also make a copy of themselves and make themselves bigger and stronger, the bigger ones can teleport to you. The problem with the game is that, the game doesn't feel that fun to play. There's just so much going on that it makes me feel lost. The music was nice, though. Also, one thing to note, is that you can continue playing from where you left off. I believe that they cut whatever points you get from your new run in half and add it to your old one. Personally, I don't see a point to continue playing if that happens. I guess I could continue but with no story other than small random cutcenes, there's no point to.Pac-man Arrangement (2005) A new 3d version of pacman that's just slower. It was putting me to sleep. The cutscenes were nice and the world seemed nice but it's all so emotionless and so gamey. Later on in the game, the game gets really difficult and just confusing to navigate through with warp points. The game isn't great. The boss part was neat.Pac-man Championship Edition (2007) One of the better pacman games. And you can date it's age just by looking at it. A lot of games on the xbox store during this time had this neon look. Anyways, it's a pretty great pacman game as it's easy to play, the controls are great, and the music is soothing. It's just, now that I'm not playing the game, I have no rush to want to play it again.Pac and Roll Remix (2007) Don't know what's so remix about the game but it sucks. It's one of the worst games I've played and it's crazy how bad they messed up. It could have been an enjoyable game but it's so bad. The ghosts look horrid, pacman sounds like a little japanese cartoon kid, the levels suck to navigate through, and the camera fights with you. Do not play this game.Pac Moto (2007) I'm going to be honest. The game sucks and it's a game game. Judging from the history of it, they just copied some other game. Neat idea but a waste of time. Also, online multiplayer doesn't work.Pac-Man 256 (2015) The best and most addicting game that I've played in this pacman museum game. It feels and looks like a phone game, and I could have sworn I've seen it on the app store. It has a lot of items you can use but most don't appear often. Only ones that show are your loadout ones and the next item that you are unlocking. You can choose 3 for your loadout and they will appear randomly on the board as you play. What I enjoyed the most from this game was upgrading your items and seeing how far you could go in the game. Only problem that I really had with the game is that there is no music. I think this game is a rogue-like. This game has potential to be something great. Anyways, this is the game that gave me the most money for buying stuff in the overworld. It may be the best game to farm money.Pac-Man Battle Royale (2011) The worst game. Do not play.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, this is  on Steam Deck. I'm pretty particular about  / Namco collections and while I do have some small gripes here and there, this is probably the best and most complete Pac-Man release yet with an incredible level of care put in and some truly obscure cuts along with the hits you love. The glaring omission many will note is the absence of  which isn't really this collection's fault, there's some legal weirdness going on with the character and game, and there  a current Ms. Pac-Man release on Steam under the "Arcade Game Series" banner that also works well on the Deck if you want the whole Pac-Family in your Steam library. I do hope they'll cut a deal to release it as a DLC like they did with the 2014 Pac-Man museum, but I don't mind switching over either.That said, they more than make up for it by including the  version of  which has long been a fan-favorite but was last included in the PS2 era . The 2014  had a different game also called  which is enjoyable in its own right (and is also included here) but that version is a bit slow and easy, real Pac-Fans know the 1997  is the real deal and it's here in its full glory.Emulation quality seems pretty decent, there does appear to be  of a bilinear filter applied to most of the arcade games, but it's very mild and most of them still look fairly sharp even if it's not razor-crisp like I usually prefer. The only game that looks straight-up  is  which is noticeably much blurrier than the other games and that's an issue I seem to recall with the 2014  as well, so I'm not sure what the deal with that game is. Personally I wish they would let you choose the scaling filter you want to use, but the release is mostly fine. Purists should know that some of the games have had Ms. Pac-Man's sprite altered into a new design because of the lawsuits which is noticeable in both  and  but otherwise I think these are as accurate of releases as can be done given the circumstances.Also included are several more modern Pac-Man games, some of which are newer arcade games, some were made and remixed for earlier Namco/Pac-Man museum titles, and others such as  and  had full-blown home releases (256 is even still available as a standalone here on Steam!). These all play how they should and add a lot of value, putting in some of the more exclusive or otherwise hard-to-get titles that are nonetheless part of the character's more recent history.Rounding out the package is the hub world and progression system. Certain games have to be unlocked by playing other games twice, and simply opening and closing the game like in  won't do. You actually have to play to a game over. With compilations I generally prefer to have every game available at the start, but it is an interesting way to get attention on some of the lesser known games here as those are what you have to play to unlock some of the more well known ones.  is an extremely obscure platformer that I had actually forgotten about and you have to play it twice to unlock the more popular , and while I do appreciate the sentiment,  is frankly  so having to suffer through it to get the better game is a bit annoying. Don't get me wrong, I'm  it's here and that people can see such an obscure part of Pac-history, frankly  the kind of stuff that really needs a re-release moreso than the stuff everyone already knows, but it's gonna take a while before I figure out beating the first level.More charming however, is the hub. Each game has little missions and sub-oibjectives you can do, and completing these gives you more decor for the arcade. Characters gradually filter in and you can use the coins you earn to unlock more decoration. I imagine this will appeal to people who enjoy Animal Crossing type games and while I probably won't put a ton of time into my arcade, I do enjoy seeing all the things I keep unlocking and it gives you good motivation to actually try each game in-depth. The coins are also used to play the arcade games, and while that  like the setup for a horrifying microtransactions system, I don't think it's actually possible to run out given how many they give you at the end of each game, it's just a fun way to keep with the theme adn give players some reason to invest time into each title.My only other potential gripe is I do wish they did more with the  aspect of the collection. That's really a complaint I've had about every post PS1 Pac-Man/Namco Museum but the PS1 games had such love put into showing all the different advertisement flyers, merchandise, artwork and  of these games. This release  have a "history" tab on each one, but it really reads more like a general synopsis/advertisement for the game and the only real historical info is the actual release date. As much as people make fun of Konami for barely making games anymore, their recent collections have had entire books about the franchises in them, so some kind of deeper retrospective would have been neat.Overall though, this is a stellar collection, the only other games I think I would want to see are Pac-Man 2, Pac-Man Jr, and Pac-Man Plus but those probably all have rights issues and Pac-Man Plus was sort of in a weird half-official status anyway so it's unlikely it will ever see the light of day again. I hope that the rest of Namco's arcade classics will see such an effort soon, I want a really good, definitive collection of Dig-Dug, Galaga, Bosconian, etc. for Steam soon!
_childDocuments_.name: PAC-MAN MUSEUM+

_childDocuments_.review: Great collection of Pac-Man titles, even some of the more obscure ones are here. There's a nice even spread between both classic and modern titles, so there is definitely something in here for everyone. If you're feeling creative, you can customize your arcade however you see fit with a bunch of collectibles. I do think there were some missed opportunities here though...1) Everything in the arcade feels static. You can't really interact with anything, so any choices you make to your arcade will be strictly aesthetic. Even the ghosts who visit your arcade don't interact with anything, they just float around aimlessly.2) They could've done some interesting multiplayer here. The ability to share and visit other people's arcades to initiate 2-player+ modes would've been really cool, but sadly there is no online multiplayer.Overall, I would say this is worth it strictly for the game collection. The arcade hub and customization are nice touches, but not selling points.

name: Circus Electrique
detailed_description: Named for the greatest show in Victorian steampunk London, Circus Electrique is part story-driven RPG, part tactics, part circus management, and completely enthralling – all with a steampunk twist. When everyday Londoners mysteriously turn into vicious killers, only the circus’ lineup of Strongmen, Fire Blowers, Clowns and other performers possess the unique talents necessary to save the city. Through tactical turn-based battles, these unlikely heroes face Bobbies, British Sailors gone bad, aggressive Posh Girls, and other Victorian-era archetypes stand in their way – not to mention the occasional menacing Mime or Robobear. The game’s innovative Devotion morale system affects characters’ performance not only in battles, but also for actual circus shows, dutifully managed between heroic jaunts through six sprawling districts. Key Features: Electrifying RPG Combat Test the skills of Strongmen, Fire Blowers, Escape Artists, Clowns, and other classic circus performers – 15 playable archetypes total, each with deep tactical options in battle. Assemble the most ideal combination of acrobatic artists to fight against over-the-top enemies. Manage the Greatest Show in Steampunk London Despite the chaos, the show must go on! Rebuild the circus to its former greatness and beyond, recruiting and training the most talented performers coming in from all over the world. Performers’ skill, chemistry with one another, and overall Devotion combine to determine the monetary success of a single show – and you’ll need every single spare Shilling you can get both for Amelia’s quest and to keep everyone paid and happy. A Circus Like No Other Immerse yourself in a striking world based on vintage circus posters, Victorian-era archetypes and classic steampunk charm.

_childDocuments_.review: It is one of those Darkest Dungeon look-a-like games but with a Bioshock-ish/WeHappyFew-ish steampunk coat of paint, which looks very impressive and I considered the artworks alone worth the price. You are basically a reporter lady with her long-dead-circusperforming mother's lion and four circus clowns (literally) dragged behind to protect her exploring a Nightmarish London. It's very Dickensian and your characters will die like flies so very accurate....it's fine. It's a story... it's there. The art's so good that 1st-class plot is not needed. What powers the game up, is the combat. The combat is fun and has depth. It's not a deck-builder but traditional turn-based combat. Each hero/enemy has a health bar and a devotion bar, which is used to perform certain attacks or skills. If any one of the two bars dropped to zero, then the hero/enemy dies or flees. This allows the player to calculate ahead to focus either one of them and is really, really fun.You manage your base by looking after the health of each character, the devotion of them, and the overall financial status of the circus. Performing earns your heroes devotion and earns the circus resources, but lock them out for other tasks and requires skills in a different skill tree. Resting restore health but costs food, training  increases experience but costs other resources. Ideally you want to rotate each hero, or performer I guess, for different tasks each day.There's a crafting system and a pub fight system for you to pokemon famous fighters.Sounds great, right? Surely it's safe to give a recommendation?NO.The campaign mechanism is certainly not for everyone. See, in the campaign map, you move your team of four in a 2d looking-down style traditional map of London, and the key is that you cannot backtrack, thus must select a chosen path and walk to the end of each map. At first I thought this a good feature and added much needed replay value. Yet when I got stuck in the fourth map, I realise that by not allowing backtracking, the game left little room for mistake. You walk a very linear path each time and if you made mistake in levelling up or team building and cannot beat the final boss, well... ...Well, there's no way of fixing things. You cannot change difficulty, you cannot go back to previous locations to level up, or gather resources, you cannot leave the map, you cannot do anything other than fighting that battle again or start over from the beginning (or last save file, if you kept one early enough to make a difference). You can recruit new heroes but your resources will deplete fast finding good ones, once the well went dry, you are done again. The game does allow you to replay a battle again and again, which makes me think this is the recommended way. Since the game relies heavily on chances, it is possible that eventually the enemy will roll bad enough for your team to pass... but it's not fun, it's monkey-typewritering the game. When I got stuck in the fight with Eli Edward, I thought to myself...'Do I monkey-typewriting another 30 minutes or do I start all over again?' In the end, I choose stop playing. The game's fun, but not that fun.I understand that this is like rage-quiting but frustration in Darkest Dungeon served a narrative purpose, why should this game be this irritating? If you want something akin to Darkest Dungeon, I recommend Aria Chronicle instead. It's much much more refined.That being said...This is not a negative rant. Again, I like the game a lot. I just cannot recommend it now. I am sorry that the review system left so little room for a bit of grey. But I do not think my incapability to recommend it now will do much harm to the reputation of this product with clearly so much love put into it. And even though I cannot give it a general, maybe unconditional, recommendation now, I do considered my money very well spent on purchasing this game. If you like the style or don't mind the frustrations in some part of the gameplay, buy it, support the devs, by all means. I will likely buy any DLC if there will ever be one.I think given some time this can become something great, truly. And I hope the devs prove me right.

_childDocuments_.review: One of these days, Steam *really* needs to add a "mixed" rating. I wavered back and forth a lot on this one, thought it was going to be a narrow upvote most of the way through, and then the ending gave me a sufficiently sour note to turn the other way.Yes, it's *kind* of like Darkest Dungeon. I'll use that as a reference point. If you're not familiar with it, go play that instead. :)Darkest Dungeon had two major gameplay pieces: town management and dungeon battles. Circus Electrique adds a third: circus show management. There are a variety of different shows that you can put on, with an expanding list as the game progresses, offering different potential rewards and requirements. Your roster of characters needs to divide their time between fights and performances, as each has statistics that make them ideal for certain show acts. As these shows are a major source of income and XP, this can introduce some interesting tensions: can I manage to leave this character to perform when they'd make a great centerpiece in the next fight's lineup? There's some interesting design here, though it did feel a little underbaked in the end.Town management ended up feeling a little bit more interesting than Darkest Dungeons to me. While there's fewer options and decision points overall, the way resources are calibrated was satisfying. In DD, at some point, you'll have everything and money ceases to be of much concern. In CE, even with a significant amount of grinding, I never got enough resources to fully max everything. The tension of what to improve or which character to train up remained a significant one all the way through to the end. This might be kind of frustrating if you're a true completionist, but I enjoyed the fact that this aspect of gameplay tension never became irrelevant.Then, there's the combat. Ugh.Circus Electrique glows with production values. There's fully animated character models, 15 distinct player classes, and unique voice acting for each. There was a ton of potential here, but a lot of the underlying design behind combat is just... very not good, compared to DD or anything else I've seen in the genre. I'm just going to ramble about my many frustration points here:* Each class has a pool of 10 distinct moves, plus a small number of potential passive talents. Any given character that you recruit possesses 6 of these moves, plus anywhere from 0-2 of the talents. Unlike DD, it is not possible to modify an individual's move or talent set, so if you hire someone that's missing some real lynchpins from the class set, well, sucks to be you. This might be particularly common whenever you're first exposed to a new class, because as far as I could find, there's no "master list" of each classes moves, you only get glimpses through those snapshots of 6.* A lot of class moves are just... not very good. From stances that trigger attacks under circumstances that almost never happen, to status effect inflictions with probabilities that are far too low to be dependable, to some moves just not being usable in good position or able to hit key targets. This varies from class to class, but there are some that as a confluence of these kinds of problems are just nearly useless. I'm looking at you, Ventriloquist...* Many classes, particularly your DPS types, tend towards a squishy "glass cannon" design. Much more so than in DD, *many* enemies can hit your back ranks, with the end result that the game tends increasingly towards rocket tag as the game progresses: will the enemy randomly decide to one-shot one of your strikers or not? Get used to hitting "Restart Fight", because the answer will be yes, aggravatingly often.* On that note, as tense as Death's Door was, it's not half so bad as characters just getting one-shot left and right.* Then, there are Taunts, which force the opposing team to target a unit with them active. IIRC, DD had no such thing, and there were some good reasons for that. A *lot* of enemy types are able to put these up, to a point where you can expect to have to deal with it in a vast majority of fights; having to focus fire on some super tanky dude while the enemies DPS ravages your squishies is certainly annoying. While some player classes are able to inflict Taunt as well, moves that do so seemed very rare; I counted only 3 of the 15 classes able to do so.* Oh, except for one thing... One particular Good Mood (the analog to Virtuous status), "Bold", gives the character a 50% chance to put up a Taunt on their turn. Except, any character can potentially come up Bold when a Good Mood hits. It's kind of infuriating to have your softest targets suddenly tell the enemy team to focus fire on them.* "Devotion" is your stress equivalent, though you want it high rather than low. While many classes are able to boost Devotion temporarily, only a handful are able to permanently restore it. For *all* classes, though, most of their better moves consume Devotion to use. It feels kind of bad to have this be universal, rather than a class-specific gimmick like the Abomination, particularly with everyone making depressed remarks as a result.* Enemies have Devotion too, along with moves to both damage yours and restore/bolster their own. It represents a viable alternative path to knock out some opponents, but I only rarely found it a better option to just punching them to death.* Class themes relevance to their moves sometimes doesn't make too much sense. Why are Clowns one of the best healers AND tanks? I can understand how a Snake Handler's "Belly Dance" might be able to instill some more Devotion into the party, but why on earth is the Stilt Boxer shouting "we can do it!" even better?* One positive thing to add: some fights come with random "environmental effects", such as Night Battles, Rain, Watching Crowd, etc.. Some of these could significantly shake up the effectiveness of certain moves or classes, such that you do at least need to be able to put up a few different team compositions.So yes. The combat, with as much potential as it might have had, was frustrating, sometimes nonsensical, and rarely satisfying. Beating the final boss was a huge relief....or at least it would have been if the story wasn't so bad. While lovingly told, with polish and production values, you'll not only see the twists and turns coming from miles away, but the ending manages to significantly undercut nearly all of your accomplishments. It was rather depressing, and worse, didn't even seem to realize that it was so.If the steampunk circus thing grabs your attention, as it did me, this title might still be worth picking up. It's exceptionally well presented for an indie title, but it does still have some major issues in its writing and game design. If the theme doesn't cry out to you, though, you'll almost certainly have more fun elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Circus Electrique

_childDocuments_.review: I want to be clear that this game has tremendous potential. It is so slick and the core systems are awesome. It's a cool game.However, whether they ran out of time or what I don't know, they made a fatal error that needs to be patched because it honestly ruins the game.This game has almost zero replayability at the moment.Obviously, it's a lot like Darkest Dungeon. Some might even call it a clone, and you're not too far off base. We all expect it to be a similar experience from the start. However, it's got one big difference: there is almost no variation between "runs" in this game.OK, so let's just accept that for what it is. Maybe they'll patch it in later, right? But it becomes a bigger issue than you'd expect. If you run into a wall you can't beat, like a boss, you have to either keep reloading and replaying that boss battle (you can replay any battle infinite times and there's no ironman mode), or you can reload a save to earlier in the map and try a different strategy, or you can... restart the entire game.The cute naive little DD fan that you are, you may think, "That's fine, I'll just try a new run!" But of course, the issue is that you are locked on rails. The maps are always the same. Your initial crew of 6 guys (7 after the first boss) is fixed in stone. You will unlock show templates, buildings, everything in a fixed order. You are railroaded to have a cap of 10 guys in your circus. That leaves 3-4 slots for randomized hires from 4 classes (5 after the first boss). This is the one and only source of variety in a given run.Now, there are tons of classes in this game and tons of slots to unlock in your circus. That's not the issue. The issue is that it railroads you to only have access to 4 (5) classes for a long chunk at the beginning, so every "run" feels the same.And given the total lack of variety on the map, you are left with simply trying to "play better" on almost the exact same content before you hit the boss you couldn't beat before.Honestly, it feels a bit like speedrunning or something.The systems lend themselves to randomization. It really feels like they intended to make things more randomized but ran out of time. If they patch in randomized maps, at the very least, it would do the game a world of good. But as it stands, you're better off waiting til that patch arrives or you're in for a surprisingly on-rails experience that you'd never expect from a "DD clone."

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen some reviews of this game that say things like 'half-baked ideas' and 'slow, frustrating gameplay', but honestly - I kinda like it. If you're a veteran of stats-based, turn-based, deck-building type games then perhaps there are better options - but for me, this was well worth the money.Pros:- It looks great. The Steampunk Circus theme is a great aesthetic, the characters are imaginative, and the different classes of character are distinct enough for you to know what you are dealing with at any moment;- The battles are fun. Turn-based combat is great for old duffers like me, who can't hope to out-smash some kid with an X-Box controller plugged into their PC, but they are sometimes pretty dull. Not so here. Each character in the game has a set of different attacks/moves, which are particular to their class and also their individual character. This means you really do need to pay attention to team composition: are you sure you want to take two strongmen but no clowns?  All attacks and moves are just... great! From the firebreathers whipping a cyclone of flames around an enemy to both damage and de-buff their next turn, to the oh-so-cheerful clowns, playing a song on the trumpet to buff your whole team's attack precision %- The size of the game. I'm not the fastest to play through games, but at 11 hours in I still feel like I'm only just scratching the surface. With each XP level come different buildings and elements to your circus that need careful looking after with each day that passes. There are tiers and tiers of charcater classes, there is a whole crafting system, there's this weird, quirky circus show mechanic where - in between exploring London and fighting weird baddies - you are supposed to use a selected few of your team to put on a show and gather resources from the audience. All of it, of course, stats-based.  There is recruitment and staff management, special ability trees... it goes on.  I spent fifteen minutes figuring out whether to hire Victor (a clown who works well with escape artists but a sub-par laughter and amazement stats) or Shania (a higher-level fire-breather with great combat stats and a desirable special move, but who can't work alongside illusionists).The cons:Well I love the game so far, and so there aren't many, but for the sake of balance:- Some battles seem arbitrarily unbalanced. I've done maybe 30 fights, won 20 of them easily, won 5 of them with a struggle, and got absolutely smashed in the rest. Some of those where I was smashed, I replayed and sailed through. I think maybe there are some maturity tweaks to the combat stats needed. That said, this does not spoil the game - it just leads to occasional unanticipated outcomes.- The game does feel like it is trying to do a lot of things at once: is it a story? (There IS a story! It's cute and quirky and interesting!) or is it a deck-builder? Circus management sim? RPG?  If I am honest, I think maybe this is a criticism for most people, but I don't mind it. IT does mean that you probably need to do a minimum of 3-4 hours in your first session before you're confident to know what you're going to aim to do when you return.I'm going to start finishing my reviews with the CMAG (Casual Middle-Aged Gamer's) Report! In other words, how does this game fit in with the lifestyle of someone with a job, house, and family who doesn't get to game ALL THE DAMN TIME!CMAG Report:- There are a lot of elements to this game, and you can't really pick it up, play for an hour, then come back in a few days to carry on. You'll have forgotten the important things you learned so far, plus there will still be a lot of new stuff to pick up. I'd say it has an initial time-investment requirement of 3-4 hours over the first couple of days, after which you can come back to this when you want.- The story isn't so involving that it's critical to follow it, and so if you did have to neglect the game for a few weeks or longer, you could still drop in where you left off and once the basics come back to you, you're good to go.- You can play this game without having to be immersed in a headset, it's nice and casual, and as it's turn-based you can easily down-tools and go change a nappy, prepare dinner, retrieve the pet llama from next-door's garden or whatever.- The content isn't age-inappropriate for anybody, so there's no issues with playing it if you have an audience.All in all, well worth the money.  Even if you're not sure it's for you - a lot of work has gone into this game, and the devs deserve the £18 or whatever it's priced at locally for you. Even if you play it up to XP level 2 and decide it's crap, you still only paid the equivalent price of a movie ticket for the time it takes.<<<ROOOAAARRR>>>>!

_childDocuments_.review: The Darkest Dungeon comparisons are very appropriate.  This game shamelessly steals most parts of DD and fits them right into my ol timey circus wheelhouse.  I love the art style and the voice acting.  I like that you do one fight, go back to your circus, regroup and go back out.  Its much less stressful than dungeon crawling with no end in sight.  Easy recommendation at full price if you like these type of games.

_childDocuments_.review: The first 4 out of six districts are good, however the balance of resources and lack of any grind to get more in the early middle game can create locks on progress. The difficulty scaling also takes a very sharp turn upward towards the absurd, the punishment for simple ignorance is far to high. I was having fun up to the boss of district four but have hit a lock on my progress to where it feels like starting all over is the only solution. It does not feel as well balanced as Darkest Dungeon or as good at teaching the player different ways to play or presenting it's challenges. I never felt like I had to start over in Darkest Dungeon, this game does not have that feeling that time, learning and stubbornness will lead to victory. I think it would be aided greatly by a mode with which to grind not locked behind a very rare craftable item.What I have seem with the story is interesting and I'm saddened that it is so hard to get more of it.It is a good game and worth it's asking price, but without additional maps for grinding that aren't missable or a massive rebalance (nerf) of many middle game enemies I don't feel like I could recommend it. Or at least play it on Easy NOT Normal to being with. This feels like a game that should have been released in Early Access so these problems could have been caught before a full release.

_childDocuments_.review: I am so torn.I love almost all of the elements of this game but some questionable design decisions and very poor balancing keep this game from being truly great.First off, the most glaring issue for me, is how easy it is to softlock yourself in this game even on the normal difficulty if you're not particularly great at this kind of game (reminiscent of slay the spire, darkest dungeon, etc). You can run into a point where an enemy group can repeatedly wipe your attackers ultimately leaving you with no resources to replace them with strong enough performers to have the slightest chance against the group. Theoretically one could savescum and back up a number of days in the game, but the game itself shouldn't require that for you to progress.That brings me to my next point:This game feels like it was designed as a roguelite experience with a slowly unveiling storyline like Hades. So why did they decide to leave all of those elements in place but then shove it into the skeleton of a linear format? Enemy groups, your own performers, resources, rewards, everything is randomly rolled which means even if you ARE skilled at this game there's no guarantee that the game won't decide to softlock you of its own accord. Other games are designed with this roadblock in mind, hence the circular nature and persistent upgrades of most of the roguelite genre. Instead of frustrating the player by forcing them to fail and start over from scratch with nothing to show for it, they let you carry some progression through. In Circus Electrique, however, you just have to give up on your current playthrough and start a new game, intro sequence and all.And my last point: Some of the classes are COMPLETELY useless. Any space in the game in vulnerable to attack so formation has more to do with what your attackers are able to do from the slot they're placed in rather than any sort of defensive layout. That means squishy characters like healers/debuffers are prone to getting one-shot by enemies. That and, you may run into some enemies with attacks that will simply melt your characters. I had a brand new from the train unique strongman at level 5 with a half bar of devotion who I took into a fight, and he was forced to flee from literally a single attack in the first turn before he even had a chance to act. Against a level 3 trash mob in the middle of the map, not even a boss.I want desperately to love this game but after hitting a sotflock state twice I think I'm going to hold off for a few balancing patches or additional game modes.
_childDocuments_.name: Circus Electrique

_childDocuments_.review: everything about this game is so well made. The battles, the gameplay out of battles, the story, the graphics...And then some level designer thought "hey, wouldn't it be fun if you had no way to undo ANYTHING, and if you end up in a bad fight, you have no way to go back, no way to get stronger, no way to ever get past that fight, aaannnd thats it. you are just stuck there. softlocked into a fight you can't win with no way to get better, so you have to start a new game alll over again.this one desision makes the game extremly demotivating, and ruins the whole game. this game could have been the best followup to darkest dungeon ever, but will not recommend the game until this progression problem is fixed.
_childDocuments_.name: Circus Electrique

_childDocuments_.review: I believe most of the players here are looking for a rogue-lite/like experience and the game does position itself in that way. Once your hero dies/flees you cannot resurrect him and so on.Game is definitely inspired by Darkest Dungeon and for this price it has great production and quality.Unfortunately, I cannot recommend it at the moment.I got stuck on the second boss due to the fact the game does not provide any options than to attack the boss. My party died and all I can do is just take the other party/members to the boss. There are no other battles/areas I can explore. Kill the boss or load up a save file/restart the whole game. Or just load up a save before the boss and pray to RNG. No other options at all.The game is linear in it's completion. You cannot go in to random generated dungeons or any dungeons besides the main story to farm XP/GEAR. If you wish to re-play the game you get exactly the same maps.Game scares you with losing your members, however you can restart any battle as many times as you want. If your member gets killed, just restart the battle. If your party doesn't work in the last fight - just load up an autosave. It really takes away from the whole experience.Great potential. Hopefully it will get patched/improved to make an overall better experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright. I think Circus Electrique has run its course for me. While kinda engaging on one hand, on the other hand, the tedium of some of the requisite gameplay mechanics have me not really wanting to play it any longer.On the surface, Circus Electrique could be called a Darkest Dungeon-like. The combat and presentation is similar. The morale systems are similar. The base camp systems are similar. It's not one for one as Circus Electrique takes a whimsical approach rather than a horror approach, but otherwise, DD is definitely the well from which these devs drank deeply. Which isn't necessarily a bad thing.In Circus Electrique, the narrator isn't a mostly faceless person. Rather, it's a reporter who is also the niece of Circus Electrique's owner, who sends his clowns, strongmen, fire breathers, and so on, to escort and protect his niece while she investigates a madness which has swept across London, turning people psychotic, despite their willingness to fight alongside other psychotic people lol. In the course of your travels, you will fight and recruit more people, constructs, and such to your circus, and thus to your pool of escorts and bodyguards. You can also recruit directly from a train, much like DDs carriage recruiting.The maps are similar to Darkest Dungeon. You make node routing decisions in the form of streets and intersections, leading to treasure, special encounters, interviews, and battles. Each battle ends the current day, after which you go back to the circus, only to head back to the streets the next day. For this, you will assign four of your performers to basically be on active escort duty, who will handle the encounters and battles. They can be swapped out anytime up to the beginning of a battle. The circus itself is functionally your base town, with more services unlocking as you progress. Training, healing, spying, crafting, and so on. Additionally, you are a circus, so you also put on shows daily.And this is really where my issues with the game begin. You have to assign performers (from the pool of aforementioned escorts and bodyguards) to the shows. Each performer has scores in the four circus categories (basically wow factor, audience engagement, etc..) as well as the core aspects of what they can do (such as snake charming, feats of strength, etc...). The first set have points attached. You have to reach minimum thresholds in each category in order for the show to happen. The second set of categories factor into how the performers work with each other. Some performers don't like working with other types of performers, for example. All of this latter stuff creates stars, which form the basis for how well the audience reacts to the show, how much money the circus makes, and how much xp for the shows are earned. This. Is. Not. Fun. At. All.The combat itself is fine, but even there, it's incredibly repetitive, and waffles between very easy and incredibly unfair. The combination of these two things, plus constant resource management for everything, from leveling up abilities to leveling up services to crafting to using your services....it all just became unfun at some point for me. At its core, this isn't specifically a bad game, but the story doesn't carry it and so the tedium just becomes tedium for the sake of tedium. While I can appreciate that a lot of people enjoyed this game throughout the six city areas included in the game, all things considered, I am not one of them.This game is fully Steam Deck compatible, btw. I encountered no technical issues whatsoever.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has really good promise and starts out quite fun.  Unfortunately, the balance of this game is quickly thrown out of proportion.  This is mainly in regard to the growth of enemy stats compared to your own, and the way damage is calculated,  Specifically, shortly after completing the first area of the game, all enemies begin getting "Defence" stats in the 10's.  Unfortunately, because "Defence" is a direct subtraction from damage, almost every fully-upgraded attack available to your performers will have damage reduced to very low single digits, when not reduced completely to zero.  This makes all available class types that do not do large single-hit damage (e.g. the Strongman) useless for doing damage in combat.  Combine this with enemy taunts (which are available in better positions and with better effects than yours,) and enemy heals (which heal for 35-45 when yours heal for 15-25) and the game becomes an extraordinarily pointless slog.  This game's maker has obviously stolen from other similar games, but they seem to not have grasped even the smallest shred of how balance was achieved in those games.  This should not have been released without appropriate playtesting and correction of such a poor battle damage system.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: I'm finally updating my review after the patch the devs pushed out at the end of September. They incorporated feedback and seem to have fixed the glaring issues I cite in this review. I haven't had the time to play much lately, but I look forward to getting back into it when finals are over! Unfortunately, I have to lend my voice to the crowd that has been leaving negative reviews of the game. I kept looking at this page, wondering why it had any negative reviews at all. "These reviews don't make sense," I thought. "This game is hugely stylish, the combat is satisfying, the characters are unique, and the circus management isn't the drag everyone says it is."I was both right and wrong. Personally, I don't find the circus grind as tedious as some people seem to. I enjoy the mechanic well enough and don't mind doing it every day. While I can most certainly understand the general complaints and agree it won't suit everyone, I enjoy making decisions about what resource is most precious to me in the moment and which characters I can afford to leave behind. The biggest problem with the game, as several other users have said, is the combat and some of the cryptic decisions the developer decided to make surrounding it. Firstly, the fact that you can softlock your game and have to start over is completely unacceptable. Under no circumstances should players be forced to quit a game after hours of investment because they were unaware of some system(s) and suddenly find they have no path forward. In all honesty, I was 11 hours in before I realized training on dummies was possible, and that only happened because I checked the sub to see if other folks were running up against the same issues I'd started to experience. I don't recall any sort of tutorial about the daily training, and because there's so much going on in your circus, it's easy to overlook. These systems need better explanation, especially if they're critical to your overall success. Secondly, while combat is a delight to watch and participate in (for me personally), it can also be an agonizing exercise in patience. I had a battle earlier today last until turn 25, due mostly to fight RNG, and I almost quit playing. I realize this genre largely revolves around these RNG mechanics (missing, dodging, random buffs/debuffs, etc.), but a fight that lasts that long just because your characters keep missing or being stunned is simply no fun to watch or participate in. [Reading further will contain boss spoilers.]Still, I wanted to carry on and continue enjoying the game I'd been so excited for, and I managed with relative ease until I came up against the Steam-Man. This boss feels terribly over-tuned, and to be frank, the fight was not fun at all. I generally despise having to save scum in games, and perhaps the argument could be made that I shouldn't play these sorts of games with that in mind, but I now find myself caught in a place from which I cannot progress. Steam-Man starts the battle with three mechanical minions, one of whom is capable of repairing both allies and itself (while it largely tries to stay out of range of the attacks many characters you'll have unlocked at this point in the game have). He's also capable of using a mass Devotion sap every single turn (it strips all of your characters of 16% Devotion per use, which is honestly ludicrous). To top things off, when you manage to destroy a minion or two (or three, if you have some beautiful fight RNG and take out the healer as well), he'll summon more minions to take their place. He can perform team-wide Devotion buffs, damage increases, the minions can perform team-wide damage reduction, all while dishing out huge damage to individuals or two characters at a time. I save scummed multiple times, tried multiple configurations, but every fight ended in failure (generally due to multiple fighters abandoning the fight due to a lack of Devotion). I will add that I'm playing on Normal (between Easy and Hard). I am now stuck with no path forward thanks to some of the confounding design decisions that other players have mentioned in their reviews, like the lack backtracking/trying other battles to grind until you've become strong enough to overcome. I may not be the caliber of player that the developer made the game for, and that's a shame, but there are some glaring issues here that can't be ignored. On the whole, I adore the aesthetic, the spirit, the bones of it... The game is so very interesting and fun to play, until it isn't. I hope to see a patch, or maybe Workshop compatibility so the community can help with the changes, but as it stands, I cannot recommend this game to anyone. I enjoyed myself for hours, longer than some of the other reviewers, and I still desperately want to manage my circus, but the game respects neither my time nor my effort. It won't respect you either.
