_childDocuments_.review: I have a LOT to talk about this game, most of it good. And some of it it's more of a rant from other games released from the company here on Steam.So let's go to the obviously bad:Lack of English dub: That's not a bad thing to me, I always thought the english dub for Cold Steel was lacking at best, horrible at worst. But a lot of people like it, and when we lose content it feels bad. We want improvements both in the technical and in the gameplay values for the game, and removing something that was present for four games in a row is sad. That being said: If having a dub would mean this game would cost MORE than what's costing on launch, then thank god it's not here. I'm not fond of spending 60 bucks on a 2010 game. The PS4 differences: That's more on Falcom than NIS, but then again, Nis was on fault for NOT warning buyers beforehand. Never do that again, Nis. Never.This is a nitpick now, but during certain battle screens, the grass MOVES left to right, and I'm not saying it animates like a normal grass, it litterally changes the position from one point to another, and it feels like a bad simulation that could just be removed. XD It may not be noticeable on PSP or PS Vita but it is on 1080+ resolutions.Now, The good:There's a lot of good stuff here, the game itself is awesome, the OST is amazing and if they ever get the license for the EVO OST I would totally buy it as a DLC. I really like the UI improvements, and the enhancements to the black spots on the edge of the sceens, a thing that plagues the Sky seris and some older YS titles. They did an awesome job, and so far I haven't found a single issue that broke my immersion with the game.The UI improvements are just incredible, there's not a single menu that is pixelated, every artwork looks sharp, the text looks sharp, there's an option for scaling certain things (mostly battle menus) to be bigger, but I do prefer the normal resolution, I love space in the screen. I love that this time, instead of doing a visual and gameplay downgrade from the PS4 version, Durante's team decided not to mes with there's no need, and they left the original High-Speed beautiful icon animating that Falcom puts on their games since Cold Steel 3 (Instead of downgrading it to that small cog from CS1-2), they let the tOGGLE function intact and just added the option for it not to be a toggle, but frankly I have no idea why you would want to keep a button pressed all the time and they left the PS4 prompts Falcom added to the game instead of, for no reason at all, downgrading it to worse looking buttons (I'm still having bad chills whenever I look at the buttons on CS3-Pc version).The Log menu is a god-send, and finally, after at least seven titles of this series, they decided to create the option menus INSIDE the game instead of outside. NOt only those are beautiful menus, I can change everything while in-the-game. And that would be awesome in a more graphically demmanding game such as COLD STEEL III or IV, but I doubt they will ever bring this feature to those games.It's actually ironic that this old game has more modern features than the other ports in that sense.And yes, it annoys me way more when design choices are made that make my life harder or that makes the game uglier, for no reason at all than not having graphics enhancements like the PS4 version suffers from. This game especifically doesn't need these touch-ups, they make the game look cleaner, but these are older games, and I'm fine as long as I can play them.That being said, I don't know what happened, if Durante's team love these games especifially, if the lack of English Dub gave people more time and resources to invest more in other aspects of the game, more technical aspects, or whatever. But looking at it on the technical side and on the UI side of things, this game particularly received a lot more care than Cold Steel III and IV received. I think this is an awesome game. But please, if you wanna buy it, go fro the sky trilogy first. No matter what Nis says, these games NEED to be played in order. You won't lose a lot, but what you lose is taken away from you forever. xD

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best Trails games finally gets the treatment it deserves, with this spectacular PC version.If you’re a fan of the Sky trilogy, continuing directly with Trails from Zero just , and completely explaining why would involve heavy spoilers, so I won’t but…know that when you hear people say “this game is best enjoyed after the Sky series”, they’re not wrong.That said, if you do not care about strong references and plots from the Sky series and want to jump straight into the Crossbell saga (maybe to then continue on to the Cold Steel games), that’s okay too, as a JRPG, Zero is a great game, very complete with a really amazing story that keeps getting more and more intense and interesting with each chapter. When it comes to , this game is pretty easy to run on a wide array of PC setups. Visually speaking, the work done on the textures it’s amazing, compared to the original PC release and other earlier iterations for other consoles.The game looks pretty clean and runs very smoothly at 120 FPS, on my R5 3600 and RTX 3060 Ti, of course, plenty of power for such game, including max MSAA and all.This game does not require a strong computer, so if you prefer to play at locked 60 FPS, a relatively mid-range PC like mine will run at a very low power consumption and very chill, and that’s fine, no need to waste energy, but 120/144 FPS feels quite smoother over 60, if you have a high refresh screen, even when browsing in game menus, so I would recommend that if you can.Gameplay wise, this game follows a similar structure to the Sky series, which is one of the reasons why it feels like the natural saga to jump in afterwards, but if you have already played Cold Steel I and II, the battle menu is also similar there, so your muscle memory will be there at least.One of the greatest features you may love from the Sky or Cold Steel sagas is here too, like the great interactions with NPCs: everyone has something to tell, their stories evolve along our four main characters as well, so doing the rounds talking to everyone we’ve met…it’s quite rewarding. You may even see certain little cameos if you played Cold Steel III, but I won’t spoil that, it’s up to you to find them.  in Falcom games is amazing and Trails from Zero here…is no exception, it has some of the most memorable tracks in the whole franchise, so take your time and enjoy them.The  feature is very useful to go and find that one song you keep remembering in your head.Finally, if you thought that Zero was a great game, you’re in for the journey of your life when Trails to Azure arrives: that game is absolutely incredible, it is all what Zero is, and then more, more and more, and it keeps going on with amazing stuff. Be hyped, because Azure is top JRPG moments, from beginning to end.If you discovered this franchise through the more modern Cold Steel games (like I did with CS I back in the day when it came out), you’ll be happy to notice and see how the Crossbell saga shaped and influenced a lot of the stuff we can see in the Erebonia saga, for sure.Thanks to Nihon Falcom, NISA, Durante and PH3 and Geofront for their hard work in this game and support to the community.Being a Trails fan has never felt this good, and it’s not gonna stop getting better, looking at the release calendar for next year, and obviously I'm looking forward to playing the best Trails To Azure version in 2023, if you thought Zero was epic, your expectations will be greatly surpassed with Azure.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the Geofront fan translation of the game about a year before the official release and I cannot recommend the game enough. It is hands down one of the best JRPG's ever made. That said while you can absolutely jump straight into Trails From Zero and still have a great time it is HIGHLY recommended to play the 3 previous trails games, Trails in the Sky: First Chapter, Trails in the Sky: Second Chapter, and Trails in the Sky: The 3rd. While the previous titles do have a different cast of characters there is some overlap and returning characters in Trails from Zero the games are all set in the same world and share an over arching narrative. Not only that but this game also wraps up one of the most emotionally significant story lines of the Trails in the Sky games which just makes Zero even better if you have that full context. It is a large time investment to play through 3 other 40-60+ hour games before this one but I've yet to hear a single person who has done it say they regretted making that commitment. Fair warning Trails in the Sky: First Chapter starts off slow but absolutely will hook you eventually if you stick with it. Again it is by no means absolutely necessary to play the Sky games first to enjoy Zero but it will make the story even better if you do.If you're reading through other reviews you may run into some people who are review bombing the game and claiming it is a low quality or inaccurate translation. Those reviews are absolutely not an accurate representation of the game and are stemming from a recent controversy that involved a fan translation provider receiving a cease and desist letter for this game as well as other games in the Trails series including 3 other titles which have yet to have official western releases.

_childDocuments_.review: [Note that this review is based on my experiences with the Geofront patch back when it first released in march 2020.]Honestly, I'm gonna keep it as short as I can: Trails from Zero is one of my favourite games in the series, and that's saying something. The first game of Trails's second arc following Trails in the Sky is filled to the brim with *density*. Zero works so well for me because of its smaller setting of Crossbell. You'll encounter many NPC's multiple times and get to know them as a result. The OST is beyond fantastic, the combat system is pretty fun, and puzzling around with orbments is surprisingly engaging when making builds. Combined with a gripping, slow-burn story, one of my favourite main casts of characters ever, and a world that you just learn to love thanks to its locales and inhabitants, Trails from Zero is an all-around fantastic RPG.Trails from Zero... sort of works on its own. You can enter it without having prior knowledge of other games (The Sky trilogy to be more specific) and have an all-around great time, but one of the unresolved plotlines from the Sky trilogy is continued in this game and it actively intertwines with Zero's main plot. Considering this is a Steam review, it means you probably have a device capable of running this game as well as the sky arc. As such, I'd highly, *highly* recommend you check out Trails in the Sky first if you haven't already. But if something about Zero really speaks to you, well, you do you! But if you have played Sky, and are checking this store page out, well, chances are you're already a fan of the series. In which case, I hope you'll be able to enjoy this gem soon if you haven't already!

_childDocuments_.review:
The Crossbell State, located in western Zemlya--

Once the site of fierce territorial battles, it has since developed into one of the continent's leading trade and financial centers.

However, pressure from the Erebonian Empire and the Calvard Republic is steadily increasing. While corrupt officials from both sides remain locked in political disputes, the mafia and underground criminal organizations are preparing to start a war.

In the midst of all this chaos, the Crossbell Police Department has lost the trust of its people.

Among them are Lloyd Bannings, a rookie agent,
Elie MacDowell, granddaughter of Crossbell's mayor,
Tio Plato, a young sorcereress who wields an orbal staff,
and Randy Orlando, a former security guard.

The foursome are assigned to a new department, the Special Support Section, where they are left with no choice but to join forces in the face of adversity.

This is a story about four unlikely heroes fighting to overcome the walls defining their way of life.

name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails to Azure
detailed_description: Following the events of Trails from Zero, the Special Support Section find themselves with new members and new duties. However, rising tensions in Crossbell along with pressure from two neighboring political powers threaten both the safety of their home, as well as the integrity of their team. About The story of aspiring hero Lloyd Bannings continues in Trails to Azure! Set just a few months after the events of Trails from Zero, a temporary peace has settled over Crossbell and the Special Support Section find themselves with newfound fame and status, thanks to their heroic actions. However, the peace is soon broken with the rise of multiple organizations with ulterior motives. Framing these growing tensions is the increasing pressure from the Erebonian Empire and the Republic of Calvard, with Crossbell caught between them. With the safety of their home and the foundations of their team now on the line, Lloyd and his allies must gear themselves for the threats that loom ahead. Little do they know that Crossbell will soon become the stage for a climactic conflict that will determine its future... Key Features The Fate of the City-State: Play through the finale of the Crossbell arc, a key thread within the Trails universe. What lies ahead for Lloyd Bannings and his ragtag squad of allies? Crossbell’s Finest Forces: Experience new combat features introduced by Trails to Azure, including Burst, Back Attack, and even your own customizable car. Also, meet a few familiar faces from the Trails of Cold Steel series! Power from the Past: Import save data from Trails from Zero for a different story experience, including additional event scenes and entirely new scenes! Also, use your save data from Trails to Azure for bonuses in the upcoming release of Trails into Reverie!

_childDocuments_.review: Most of the Trails fans will agree that Trails to Azure is the best entry in the series. And while I disagree (Zero is my fav.), I do understand where this is coming from. Slower pace of Zero, SSS team individual characters growth, all this paved the way for Azure’s glory. There is a lot of “the best” bullet points that can be applied here. Where do I even begin???Best soundtrack in the whole series. Best end boss theme. Best narrative. Best plot twist. Best (kind of) optional boss fight with best boss fight theme music (Unfathomed Force). Best part ways scenes and best characters. And now – best version of the game ever made. The Legend of Durante: Trails to Azure PC is here in full glory. 4k, FULL ultra wide support, 144FPS mode, well received water shader to make water in game look gorgeous. Optional music titles on screen (personally I LOVE this option), and tons of customisation. Support for ALL major gamepads and proper kb+mouse controls. Steam Deck support on D1 with dedicated settings for it. When we’re talking about Deck – I just tested it and the story is similar to Zero (which shouldn’t be a surprise – those games technically are the same), and it runs flawlessly with smooth performance. In 60FPS mode, battery indicator shows over 6 hours of gameplay on one charge. Impressive. There’s plethora of options to use on Deck, heck, you can use trackpads to navigate if you want. UI scales perfectly here and it’s a joy to watch the game. So far I testedPC-wise I didn’t have a time to test it properly, before this review is out, but I can bet on Durante and his team. They are the best after all.Story? Do you even need to be convinced? If you’re coming from Trails from Zero, you know fully well what to expect. For first timers – keep in mind what I said at the beginning. About true meaning of first Crossbell game, Trails from Zero. You will fully get the meaning of it in Azure. It is peak of Falcom storytelling, period and I truly envy you, as I will be playing it probably for 10th time now, so nothing can surprise me, sadly.

_childDocuments_.review: Can you play Trails to Azure first? Absolutely not. You need to at least play Trails from Zero beforehand. It is a direct continuation from that game in terms of cast, location/lore, plotwise, etc.Further, you will enjoy several reveals in this game to a much greater degree if you previously played the Trails in the Sky trilogy and understand the factions/lore etc from there. It's not as strictly necessary as playing Zero though.Whatever your path to get here, you'll find some tweaks/additions to the skill and battle systems that improve and make them more fun, some of which stick with the series from here on out.This game focuses a bit less on the characters than the previous couple games, and the events and politics take center stage. This is greatly to the game's benefit, in my opinion. Prepare yourself for one hell of a rollercoaster, as this thing goes well off the tracks. Especially if you haven't played the Cold Steel games first, you're in for a ride.Highest recommendations for Trails to Azure. Just make sure you play at least Trails from Zero first. Zero + Azure combined is a true masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: After a decade, Zero and now Azure finally gets an official port. Few years back, people thought this game would never get an official release and forever be left in the dust. It is the fans who have spearheaded the English localization and revival of this amazing game, which is still an understatement. Getting an official port on Steam is a phenomenal moment for fans of the Trails games. This port is absolutely terrific, so much work has been done to make it so much better than ever before.Trails to Azure is the 5th installment in the Trails game franchise. This is a direct sequel to Trails from Zero, but I would  recommend to play the previous games (FC, SC & TC) as well as they are all absolutely fantastic in terms of story and characters. Based on timeline, Trails to Azure takes several months after Zero and at the same time as Cold Steel II, so you'll see some overlapping moments in the story. Trails to Azure is simply one of the best Trails game in the series. A must have play before trying the Cold Steel games to truly understand and appreciate the story. The plot twists in this game is beyond mind-blowing. With amazing soundtracks, dialogues & characters, Trails to Azure delivers a truly unforgettable story experience.(Finished this game before so I reviewed early)

_childDocuments_.review: There's not a huge amount to add over my Zero review, so I'll post it here if you're interested, & instead write this review as an extension of that: The slower-paced developments of Zero really pay off in an arc finale that surprises & delights with its twists & turns, & tie in beautifully to other stories in the franchise. The character development on show is extraordinary & Falcom's attention to detail is truly unmatched, creating a city & nearby communities that feel as alive as in any other game I've played, culminating in a finale that had me in tears. If you've played Sky and find yourself wondering if the Crossbell arc is worth it, the answer is an overwhelming YES!Combat feels like a minor step up but a step up nonetheless thanks to the addition of the Burst system, & the larger cast of usable characters also allow for more replayability/variety. The turbo mode again makes playing through the game a pleasure since fights that would perhaps otherwise be a slog become reasonable & the reasonably short but non-interesting fights can be over in just a few seconds.While Zero/Azure fail to usurp Sky for my #1 spot (mostly because Estelle is that brilliant), it absolutely cements Trails as my favourite post-FFIX JRPG experience thanks to its brilliant writing, scope, attention to detail, & above all else, charm.

_childDocuments_.review: Story-wise, the game starts a few weeks after the finale of its predecessor and tries to tie up a few loose ends before the Special Support Section (SSS) resumes its work. The group split up for a short time for various reasons, which is why you spend the first few hours running around with guest characters such as the bracer Arios, as well as the new members of the SSS, Wazy and Noel. Together, they'll face the harsh realities of Crossbell head-on. This is the story of our young heroes, the barriers that stand before them, and the people who live in the light and shadows of Crossbell City. Frustrated with the police's inability to act, Lloyd and the rest of the SSS decided to take matters into their own hands. Hence, almost nothing has changed in the actual gameplay loop, as after the prologue you once again work through support requests from all over Crossbell. This way, you explore all the areas you already visited in the predecessor. In this regard, you could say that it has the same problems as Trails in the Sky SC, but due to the more compact setting, it didn't bother me nearly as much here,even though there are a few quests that were taken over almost 1:1 from the predecessor. Quests should therefore be tackled, and also the ones that are hidden. Many of them are now relevant to the main story, as some scenes give more insight into the current story situation. The gameplay can still seem a bit sluggish due to the battle system and all the optional conversations, which is why I continued to run around with the "Turbo" feature most of the time. Instead of spoiling ourselves with new abilities after a level-up, we learn skills and spells exclusively via previously acquired quartz and sidequests. For example, we can only properly train an effective healer if we equip him with the rare gemstone. This first has to be found and correctly equipped or crafted, whereby the interactions of certain combinations also play a supporting role in order to unlock particularly valuable abilities. Admittedly, you have to get used to this system at first, but since you should've already played Trails from Zero, you'll get used to it rather quickly since it's nearly the same. This method offers a particularly creative and experimental approach to character development.So basically, each party member has an enigma, a device in which crystals are embedded. Slots must be unlocked in the course of the game in order to embed more quartz. The quartz enables various skills, martial arts, attribute bonuses, and art skills. One difference (among some) between the older and newer games is that every party member already has an art skill from the start. This means a full program right from the start and improving on the Trails from Zero foundation almost immediately. We now have "Master Quartz" and additional combat features like the "Burst" in certain climactic storysegments.The other umbrella of combat mechanics I’ve neglected to mention is Crafts, and they are simpler to summarize. They are character-specific skills learned through leveling up and doing sidequests, the most potent of which is S-Crafts. It quickly becomes evident that each character has their own specialized utilities, such as Elie being a prominent healer and Tio being a powerful offensive caster, while her S-Craft can also give us a full invulnerability shield. Recognizing the cast’s strengths from their stats, Crafts, and Orbments is imperative for success.The game is classically turn-based, and various attacks cause the turn order to shuffle around. If our troop is in a certain constellation in the turn order, a group attack can be executed. Smaller challenges offer escort quests where you have to make sure that NPCs do not die or various objects are not destroyed. The NPCs run desperately across the battlefield and are thus also actively attacked by the monsters.The voice acting in this release is entirely Japanese, making this the second localized entry lacking an English dub. Admittedly, this does sadden me as someone who was a massive fan of the Cold Steel saga’s English dub. Still, a significant portion of Azure is voiced, and each character’s line deliveries, both in and out of combat, are stellar. I did find some of the sound mixing to be slightly off, though.As a newcomer to the duology, I found my entry point with The Legend of Heroes: Trails From Zero utterly fascinating, enticing, enjoyable and it continued with Azure. It has some of my favorite mixes of mechanics and tidbits of turn-based combat that I've seen so far. It's a comfortable RPG that you can lose yourself in for a long time. You can get lost in the moving character story, all set in the colorful world of Crossbell. The character models do show their age from time to time, and the menus are a bit clunky. Still, it's easy to forgive and just hang out with Lloyd and friends, saving the better part of humanity. A journey through "The City of Sins" is therefore highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Set only a few months after the ()  (and the  audio-drama),  provides the second half of the story that makes up the Crossbell arc in the long-running  series. As a direct sequel, it should only be played after familiarizing yourself with the story of  first – similar to how  and  previously told one whole story split into two games.In fact, even going beyond that,  shares a surprisingly large amount of similarities with  (SC). As I’ll expand upon in the following review,  actually shares a lot of the criticisms I had to say about  in .For starters, just like , the gameplay of  remains almost unchanged from its predecessor. Apart from the introduction of  new party members, the addition of mastery Quartz and a ”Burst” gauge, which allows the party to dominate the turn order for a bit once built up, everything else should be familiar – from the grid- and turn-based combat system to the “request” quest system and general gameplay loop. Unsurprisingly, you’ll also rarely get to visit actually new locations during , as most of the game takes place in all too familiar places. In short, if you liked the gameplay and world of , you’ll probably enjoy this part of  as well – though I once again recommend using  if you want to make sure you’re not losing out on the (way too many) missable items, events and quests.That said, before moving on to the story, the dungeons of  deserve a special mention, which remain probably the biggest element of the  games that haven’t seen any improvement yet. While they might be straightforward to navigate at least, they’re also playing it safe to the point of just being boring – mostly consisting out of a few hallways, treasure chests and stairs, with almost no gameplay differences between the dungeons such as puzzle solving for example (at most, there’s an occasional lever to pull). This is especially apparent during the lengthy final dungeon, which serves no real purpose but to space apart the last few boss fights and isn’t interesting on its own – a wasted opportunity, to say the least.On a last note regarding the gameplay of , it’s a shame how the game handles fast travelling. After establishing a solid method of quickly getting to the various locations of the Crossbell region during the first chapter of the game, which really helps with the often spread-apart side quests, it’s a shame to see how the game handles fast travel in the later chapters – especially the final chapter, where a new method of fast-travel somehow involves going through even more menus than before.Moving onto the story,  takes another page out of ’s book, with a slower first half once again focusing on world-building before speeding up the pacing during the second half of the story. This is especially apparent during the “Intermission” chapter halfway through the game, which basically serves as the anime-typical “beach episode”. In fact,  unfortunately seems to double down on anime tropes such as these - more examples include protagonist Lloyd simultaneously being a womanizer and incredibly dense when it comes to romance or off-putting “fan-service” through blatantly inappropriate groping by a female character. Considering how well-written large parts of the remaining story are, especially when it comes to the political tensions between Crossbell and its neighbouring nations, it’s sad to see  occasionally slipping into this kind of anime trope territory.Thankfully, spare for the occasional pacing issues and anime tropes,  does a great job at picking up the plot threads that its predecessor deliberately left open. One of my highlights of the game includes a political conference between various Zemurian nations taking place in Crossbell, which is one of the moments where the thorough worldbuilding the  series is known for really gets to pay off. That said, while  gets to close many of the open questions regarding Crossbell and its inhabitants, it’s also far from a finished duology story like the first two  games were: Instead,  is heavily teasing the events simultaneously happening in Erebonia (and thus the next game in the franchise, ). In fact, the ending card of  even says “to be continued … in another land”, which just goes to show how the franchise really doubled down on its multi-game storytelling by this point in time.Setting itself apart from the previous  games however, are the antagonists of , which are way more interesting this time around, as they receive a more thorough build-up and are driven by different motivations instead of just being “evil”. The Special Support Section also receives a fair share of character moments, some of which genuinely brought a tear to my eye. However, it’s important to note that  treats its protagonists quite differently from each other, with some getting a bigger focus and backstory than others. This is especially notable when it comes to the new party members, as one of them barely appears throughout the entire game for example, while the others are significantly more involved in the story proceedings.Still,  provides a great 40+h story overall, with the familiar strengths (world building, characters) and weaknesses (pacing, tropes) fans expected of the franchise by now. Everyone who liked  should enjoy  just as much, maybe even more considering it’s doing a better job of scattering mini-climaxes throughout its story. And if you’re set on continuing with the series through  anyways, the various Erebonia story teasers shouldn’t detract from the overall experience anyway.However,  might prove less satisfactory if you’re either hoping for significant innovations in terms of gameplay or graphics or just want it to be another good drop-off point for the series. The same goes for players who are hoping for the game to focus on the political instead of the supernatural side of Zemuria – while  certainly doesn’t neglect the political conflict between the various nations, it shouldn’t come as a surprise that the (JRPG) franchise doesn’t abandon it’s more fantastical elements in favour of it. As long as you enjoyed the previous  games however, you’ll most likely enjoy  as well.

_childDocuments_.review: The Legend of Heroes: Trails to Azure is an absolute gem in the Trails series, delivering an unforgettable experience. From its rich storytelling to its deep character development, this game excels in every aspect.While the game is quite lengthy, clocking in at around 70 hours (for me at least), it never felt like a slog. The pacing is well-managed, ensuring that the story continually progresses, with new revelations and plot twists keeping you hooked until the very end.If you haven't already guessed it - Azure requires prior knowledge of the series (at least Zero, but would recommend that you play the Sky trilogy beforehand), so newcomers may feel a bit overwhelmed by the extensive lore and references to past events. However, with some effort in reading up on the background or playing the previous games, it becomes a non-issue.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails to Azure

_childDocuments_.review: Trails games are not as popular as, say, Final Fantasy, but they have some features which, in my opinion, put them on an entirely different level from the competition.I'm talking about the unbelievable care for the characters and the world building, in particular.Apart from the excellent shaping of the main cast, there are tons of non-playing characters (NPCs), each one with tons of dialogue lines.Basically, each time the player advances the main story, all the micro-stories of all NPCs advance as well.This makes the game world feel extremely alive and varied: it’s like watching the story progress through the eyes of hundreds of (more or less) active and interested observers.On top of that, the world becomes a character itself, thanks to the incredible care put in its building, be it geographically, politically or economically.And if that’s not enough, there’s a fascinating and mysterious underworld, threatening to change forever the visible one.All the above mentioned features shine particularly bright in the Crossbell arc (Trails from Zero + Trails to Azure), which is also a great entry point to the saga, if you don’t want/have time to play the previous chapters (Trails in the Sky + Trails in the Sky SC + Trails in the Sky the 3rd).Summing it up, I believe this is simply the best JRPG ever.

_childDocuments_.review: Hoo boy, this is probably the first time I’ve ever been scared of writing for something I love so much and being scared of not being able to do it justice with my words.I will say this from the get go, Trails to Azure is my favorite piece of media of all time, one that lives near and dear to my heart, and I will try my best to explain why without spoilers on this absolute mess of a review that is coming.First of all, while Azure IS a direct sequel to Zero, I highly recommend reading the drama CD “Trails to Azure - Road to the Future”, since it will be referenced at early parts of Azure and provides better context for why the characters are where they are now at the start of the story.Azure tells the tale of a small state and its people, one that is not a large on the grand scheme of things by itself, where it inhabitants constantly gets tossed around and trampled over by others agenda and that, despite every odds being against then, each one of its people stands proud as part of Crossbell, trying everything they can to make the most of their situation.And at the middle of this frenetic struggle we once again follow the Special Support Section, now revamped and bigger than ever, having finally won the hearts of Crossbell and gotten over one of the barriers that stood in their way. But now with the political dispute heaten up, new foes emerge to threaten Crossbell existence unlike any that ever came before, now from inside and outside the state borders.Gameplay wise I’d dare say that Azure is the most enjoyable game in the series for me (yes even more then cold steel, tho ive yet to play hajimari).We finally get the introduction of Master Quartz in the series, and ironically enough this is the last comically broken they’ve ever been to my knowledge at least.Battles at the core functions almost the same as Zero, with a feel tweaks where and there, such as the new Burst mechanic, but I’d say where Azure shines on its own is the balance it made to some of Zero’s quite op crafts and how some of the boss themselves where designed, I played the game on the hard difficult for the first time and it stroke a sweet point for me of not being unfairly hard neither braindead easy, just a satisfying and fair challenge, especially the “optional win” fights, getting through those to this day is some of my fondest memories from this series. Or you can ignore all that and build an EVA tank Lloyd.We also got a plethora of minigames this time, this game is packed with side content and has some of my favorite side quests in the series, not to mention the peak of Kiseki fishing (elite 4 my beloved). With Crossbell itself being full of new secrets to discover.As usual this is the part I comment about how this isn't a review but just me rambling about random stuff about the game, but with Azure in special I really just cannot help it, this game means so much to me to a point I still vividly remember going through it for the first time even though it's been more than an year I played it, its themes still motivates me to be better, to try and not be afraid of taking the hard path, to not run way from adversity.I can’t help but feel this is one of the most undercooked reviews I’ve ever written on Steam, I might even edit it later to be a more huh coerent semblance on writing (not like I’ve ever written anything deep here haha), but really nothing I can possibly say will do this game and how much it means to me justice. If this is your first time on this game you are in for a ride, a really really special wild that everyday I wish I could experience for the first time again.Also thank you Geofront and Scott, for allowing me to experience the piece of media of my lifetime, I will be forever grateful for the opportunity to play this game you guys gave me and many others through your hard work and effort. May you rest in peace.

_childDocuments_.review: Trails from Zero, to Azure, is incredible. This is one (or two) of those games that stay with you forever. After spending so much time in crossbell with the SSS and friends I have grown attached in a way I haven't felt since persona 4. This game is so lovingly crafted, packed so densely with details, character and lore. I want to defend crossbell, and all of the inhabitants I have met along my journey.This duology has one of the best stories I have ever encountered in my 34 years of life. The stakes feel real, the WORLD feels real. So many games over telegraph their stories so you can predict what is going to happen 99% of the time, but by the end of azure I couldn't get my jaw off of the table. Betrayals I never saw coming, alliances I would have never guessed I'd make in 1000 years, and a plot that goes back 2000 years; trails to azure astonished and amazed me from beginning to end. Zero made me a fan, azure made me a fanatic. I am excited to keep playing the trails series, and to be honest these games set such an incredibly high bar it's going to be hard for the other games to fill zero/azure shoes. But, after playing these games I now know why you have never heard a trails fan say anything other than praise for this series. Nihon falcon cares about this series and its worlds long interconnected lore. They made a fan out of me and I am excited to be along for the ride. Score 10000000/100

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best JRPG I have ever played. I originally played the Japanese version of it and fell in love with this series forever. I don't think I will ever find a game again that has given me this level of emotion and hype again.This is the fifth installment of the Legend of Heroes franchise, and I highly recommend playing the following games in order:Trail in the Sky FC,Trail in the Sky SC,Trial in the Sky the 3rd,Trails from Zero.Crossbell and the returning characters of the Librel saga blessed this game with an insane level of lore. This game invoked so many emotions that I had to put my controller down and rethink how crazy the plot was getting in the story. Following the intertwining and interaction of all these characters got me watching an avenger ass movie. This ♥♥♥♥ was the first Avenger movie in a crazy form.Master quartz. This one thing introduced following burst mechanics got this gameplay hitting a 10 / 10. While burst mode was something that was pretty busted, master quartz was an amazing introduction to mixing a variety of builds for different characters. I enjoyed this more than (TOCS 1 however that was an experimental period of time which they later cooked harder in later games). _childDocuments_.review: Do not play this game without playing Trails of Zero first!This is part 2 of the Crossbell Arc, and a lot of it won't make sense unless you play Zero, which is part 1.Anyway overall this is one of the best JRPGs in terms of plot and storytelling.If you love plot twists, there's plenty of them here.My only complaint is sometimes the dialogue can be extremely lengthy.This is also much harder than its previous game Trails from Zero. _childDocuments_.review: it's very similar to Zero and every other Trails game so far. New is the introduction of "master quartz" and "burst". Master quartz is the nearest you can get to something like a job system from Square. You can only equip 1 each character and they alter your stats more than any other quartz so far. They also have perks that can you give additional advantages. But they aren't a gamechanger or something, since all roles are still set in stone, so you won't give Tio a strength quartz for example. You can't experiment with them either, because you have to level up each one. So you give every character one that suits them and then only change it once, when you get more or better ones. The burst mechanic can be seen as some kind of limit break, there is a gauge you have to fill up and as soon as it's full you can use some kind of ambush where you are able to use 1 attack for each character and can cast spells without any delay.Both additions are nice to have imo, but both don't change the game and it's mechanics, so it more feels like the desire of putting new mechanics to the game at any costs. Might sounds a bit rough, but the Trails series always was a story focused game, so I personally don't mind. So let's see how it performs there.Oh boy, the story in this game is freaking crazy and carries the game so hard, it's maybe one of the best and most thrilling stories in gaming history. But why is that so? The Trails series now relies on a 5 games long worldbuilding. In Sky, you get an introduction in the political situations, the countries, the fractions and everything else lore wise (quartz, Adios, etc.). But Sky was basically the story of Estelle and her viewpoint on everything. Lloyd has a more neutral viewpoint on everything, yeah he has his opinions and own story and stuff, but it isn't as fleshed out as Estelle. With LLoyd, the worldbuilding from the Trails series comes to shine. And with the knowledge from the previous entries, Falcom managed to pull out the impossible for me. They were able to make a political debate to one of the best moments in the franchise. In other games I normally don't read books or anything not attached to the main plot, because in videogames I'm more a fan of "show, don't tell". But here, any book expands the worldbuilding. And that debate is like the peak in that regard. Any decisions they make there might affect future games storywise and the knowledge from a book might become in handy for a future entry (am I right, gambler Jack?).I know it's a super subjective matter. Not everyone wants a freaking visual novel as a full fledged jrpg. And it's a bit unfair, since this here is a long running series, not a single game story. But this here in that level is something, no other franchise does. And I can totally understand why. In the end, it's a financial matter and if you make a game where you have to play multiple long games beforehand, you'll lose potential customers. But thats why I love this series. Falcom is totally doing their thing here and with Azure, they reached a point where I really don't know how they should improve. And I'm fully aware that not everything is perfect here. The games are super slow paced and later in Cold Steel, they made some decisions I really dislike.Well, I lost myself here, I guess. And I only talked about one single part in the game. But I think everyone should experience this ride on their own. All i can say is that the 2nd half live up to all possible expectations I might have made here. Damn, even some side quests have memorable moments and are highlightsThe port is similar to Zero with all it's new additions. And I have to praise NIS America again for letting the geofront team be an official partner for the western release. This is sadly not common and there might be companies with a slightly different opinion *cough*Like I said earlier, this is the best Trails game so far. As soon as you reach this entry, you are able to excuse the slow pacing from the previous games. It's thrilling, there are some huge twists later on, the music is fantastic. The gameplay is more of the same, but it's still fun. This is one of my favorite games ever and I have a lot of fond memories with this game and the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing, I have yet to complete this version but I've already experienced Azure beforehand thanks to the wonderful and passionate efforts of the Geofront team in 2021, who made a high quality fanpatch that helped make this all possible (RIP Scott 'KillScottKill" Tijerina). With that said, there's so much I love about this game. Zero introduced us to this small city-state that while it looks to be a very prosperous country and thriving nation on the surface, was riddled with various issues and struggles mainly pertaining to it being forced to do the bidding of the 2 powerful nations that surround Crossbell, heavy with tension, corruption, and political intrigue. In Azure, it resolves the unaswered questions coming from Zero, and ramps up the political elements in this game. The pacing of the first 4 chapters was was absolutely unforgettable and I crave more thrills like it. The gameplay and combat system is more refined in Azure, with several new features like the Master Quartz introduced here and allowing for unique builds. Azure also contains one of the best OST's in the series, the composers at Sound Team JDK went all out on this one to close out the arc. As much as a masterpiece this game was, it's not without it's cons. Although I think my only negative things I have to say about Azure is several writing issues that happened in the final chapter, plus one of the explanations for a major plot twist in the story is hidden behind some optional sidequests/NPC dialogue that is easy to miss if you either aren't using a guide, or don't really pay much attention to it. All in all, Trails To Azure is an unforgettable entry in this franchise that is considered by some to be the high point of the franchise. Now that it's finally out in the west, this is one you don't want to miss.

_childDocuments_.review: After Completing Trails to Azure and getting nearly all achievements (which I will go back for), I can confidently say that this game is an absolute must-play for any JRPG fan. The amount of effort put into this game is truly remarkable, and it shows in every aspect of the game. From the captivating story to the charming characters, from the immersive environment to the stunning art, this game truly has it all.One thing that stood out to me the most not only in the game but in literally EVERY Trails game is the attention to detail in the game's world-building. The NPCs are so well-developed that it's easy to get lost in conversations with them, and it really feels like you're a part of the world. The side quests are not just fetch quests, they actually add to the lore of the game and flesh out the world even more. The combat system is also incredibly well-done, with a good balance of strategy and action that keeps you engaged and on your toes.The art style is beautiful, and the attention to detail in the environments is nothing short of impressive. The character designs are also top-notch, with each character having their own unique style and personality that makes them feel like real people.While the game does have some flaws, they are easily overshadowed by the game's many positives. One criticism is that the game can be a bit slow at times, but this is to be expected from a JRPG. Additionally, some players may find the game's length to be a bit daunting, and of course, the obvious critique of having to play 4 other games before you can truly enjoy this game and all it has to offer. But for those who are willing to invest the time, the payoff is well worth it.Overall, The Legend of Heroes: Trails to Azure is one of the best JRPGs I've ever played. It's a game that truly deserves all the praise it's received, and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys the genre.Please consider playing The Legend of Heroes: Trails to Sky FC, SC, The Third, and Trails from Zero before playing this game as it will significantly enhance your enjoyment and help you understand everything that's going on.

_childDocuments_.review: Really the only Trails game I can't recommend so far.On the storytelling side it tries to deal with too many things and people at once, so it kind of lacks a satisfying focus and even main characters that feel like they should be central really only get a handful of appearances. It also becomes much too anime, in that terrible 90's/00's way where sexual assault is a wacky thing to play for boner comedy. Similarly unlike the other Trails games where I largely loved to hate the villains, in this case I just hated them and became very sad that Trails protagonists generally do not kill anyone on purpose, because good Lord I wanted to toss Shirley into a volcano after dealing with her just once.The main cast just also fails to live up to the charisma and writing of the cast of the Trails in the Sky games, and seeing anyone from those games show up was consistently a joy since they were much more fun to have around.And it suffers from far too much talking. Like, I don't need ten paragraphs of text because I *opened a door*. It keeps interrupting the gameplay, taking away control at the wrong points, and generally making the dungeoning unfun.It also does the same thing that Trails from Zero did, which was introducing a gimmick in the very last boss battle(a battlefield slightly more complex than simply a square), revealing that it was something the engine could handle, and then never using it anywhere earlier in the game, which contributes to fights getting very same-y and repetitive.The final dungeon was truly the worst Trails final dungeon, too, it wore out its welcome very early and, for once, I couldn't even be bothered to go cracking all the final chests for special loot, which I don't think any other jRPG has ever managed.Soundtrack's pretty decent, though.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know why the dialog in the Zero and Azure are so funny but it is. They have a lot of good jokes and it's pretty interesting. And making certain bosses with maximum DP gain on nightmare first run is impossible. I feel the pacing on Zero is better, here the game starts with a Blast, then slows down to a point where you get a vacation, then slowly starts heating up again, instead of Zero that starts slow and heats up in a ascending way. To me the biggest flaw is that they added an event in Cold Steel I that has no payoff in Crossbell whatsoever, of course this game was made earlier than the Erebonia arc so that makes sense but they could have inserted some of it here.Lastly, sadly since this game doesn't have a Calendar system it's a little difficult to understand what is happening in Erebonia while you're in crossbell, if the game had some calendar we could overlap dates and know when some sh** will go down in Erebonia or not, so far I'm on chapter 4 and that's the best chapter so far. I think Azure takes the stakes way higher than Cold Steel I and II at least, and I do enjoy most if not all dialogs. I think the dialogs here are peak content compared to the later games, and yes: The change from 2D sprites to 3D models really do makes the game lose some of it's charm in dialogs. I remember Tio on CS3 is not nearly as snappy and sassy as she is on Azure and Zero but she is older so there's that. I really love her more here though.Again: Trails from Azure is one of the best games so far in the series, and it makes me wonder if Falcom ever re-made these games with Cold Steel III levels of quality, how much we would loose. Estelle is also not as fun in CS4 as she is on the Sky games after all.Anyway, if you really want to play these, you NEED to play the Liberl arc. Cold Steel I and II are KIND OF stand alone, you still can see what's happening in crossbell from there but it's not a huge loss. But here, you do interact with people from Liberl so go on, play the trilogy first. Even if XSEED never tried a thing to update the experience from the first three games, sadly. And oh they could.

_childDocuments_.review: Trails to Azure is the perfect game to end the Crossbell duology and lead the series into so much more, and it does it so well that, even after having played it a few times in these past years, I’m still left speechless in front of this incredible display of pure JRPG craftsmanship.As the last game in the series that uses the “chibi” style models, it is such a polished JRPG, a culmination of all the lessons the developers learnt along the way in previous games, with the Sky trilogy, and a step up in every single aspect over Trails From Zero, also an excellent game, of course.Durante and his team at PH3 come back again to deliver us, PC users, one of the best PC ports for a JRPG that we can enjoy in this platform, the attention to detail in the various extra game settings included is a treat, I feel so happy whenever a new game in this series is ported to new, modern platforms, and here we are again.Much like their previous port for Trails From Zero, Azure runs exceptionally well on many different PC setups, I had no issues running the game at 1620p DLDSR and locked at 120 FPS on my R5 3600 and RTX 3060 Ti, overkill for this game, but the positive here is that the PC is barely using any resources, very low power and the GPU fans are not even on, haha, all very silent, so we can listen to the incredible  in this game.And what a : this game has some of my favorite tracks from any Nihon Falcom game, and I like a lot of them from many, many games but…this game has some truly epic ones.If you’re discovering Trails for the first time and this will be your first time with this game and saga, enjoy: what comes next exists thanks to this, because the Crossbell Duology connects many dots from the Sky saga with the Erebonian (Cold Steel) saga so, if you haven’t played any of the Cold Steel games yet…I also envy you, because I have, and you’re all set to go for it, right after Azure.With Trails into Reverie coming July 2023, it is now a very good moment to play this series, either by revisiting it, or playing for the first time.The characters that the Crossbell saga introduces in the series…are some of the best, and you can be sure they’ll have a lot more stories to tell us in the future.If you love the  of the Trails series…this game is incredible in that aspect but it’s up to you to discover all of it, and enjoy it.Thanks to Nihon Falcom, NIS America, Geofront and PH3 for making this series more accessible than ever, so that more people can discover it, because it truly is a series of games that once you get hooked on…there’s nothing like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever since Trails in the Sky 1, I have a soft spot for The Legend of Heroes series. The games are long, some would say too long. There's a lot of dialogue, a lot of lore; a lot of reading in general. If that is something that turns you off, it will negatively affect your enjoyment of this game. There is a skip button to circumvent this, (hold down circle on a playstation controller), but you'll lose most of what makes these games so charming: its world and characters. These games make you feel like you're stepping into an established living world. It constantly changes, every time you do something in the game, you'll find the reactions and dialogue of NPCs changing. The NPCs live their own lives, all have their own little storylines and events, which go from superficial to quite deep, you really get invested in them, it makes you care. There are also loads of hidden events and other easter eggs.If you do choose to play this game, I strongly recommend you look up a walkthrough so as not to miss anything. If you do not, you're going to lose out on a lot of content, which would be a shame.The story is amazing, if you like RPGs, play this series. It has combat that is easy to learn, hard to master. The graphical fidelity isn't off the charts, however, the game has a distinct art style which makes the game enjoyable to look at.If you like JRPGs, and could stand to lose 50 hours or so, try out the Legend of Heroes series. All the games build on each other, the events and characters from one game are referenced and often important in others. This does not mean that you need to have played the previous games, but it will make the game feel much richer. Even as a standalone series, I can still heartily recommend Trails from Zero and Trails to Azure.10/10 will play again.

_childDocuments_.review: Trails to Azure has a lot to offer and if you have played the previous titles this is clearly a no brainer purchase.  It has everything you would expect with rich storytelling and well written characters, as well as an intricate battle system, tons of content, and a fantastic ost.  The only downsides I can think of are that the game is graphically very dated and the dialogue/storytelling is often very dense.  In fact, I would say there is so much story within the game that they could have easily made another entire game out of it.  Either way, the game will give emotional highs and lows and keep you guessing until the end.  If you are a fan of JRPGS and played Zero/Sky then play this game. if you haven't then go buy and play those games and then play this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails to Azure

_childDocuments_.review: Another lovely port by Durante and his team for what is up to date probably the best game in the Trails series. While Trails from Zero felt like mostly setup this is the follow through on all the plot threads that have been set up, either in Zero or in the Sky arc.Crossbell is my favorite Trails setting. There's the downside that you've already explored the city and surrounding areas but it has such a strong sense of location because you can follow the same set of NPCs through multiple games (even more when visiting the city in later games in the series). The old graphics have never looked this sharp and while it clearly shows its age I still find the SD character models charming and the character art I prefer to the first Trails games that used 3D rendered models only. The soundtrack is great just like any Trails games. Added features for this port are great QoL improvements, especially appreciate Auto-Text for voiced lines. All in all just a joy to play again. (I've completed it previously, my Steam playtime does not reflect my real life playtime)

_childDocuments_.review: Another fantastic entry into the game series.  The Legend of Heroes series has ridiculous worldbuilding across their three series that have been released in English.  There are major characters in other games that barely get any mention or show up only once such as Towa, who is a major character in Trails of Cold Steel, appearing in one section of the game as an unnamed NPC and can be missed if you don't speak to her.  You should definitely play Trails from Zero first before this one, but you can play it independent of the other franchises and still follow the story.  The combat is nothing to speak about, but can be made more challenging by raising the difficulty level.  It's more about party/equipment optimization than grinding since the amount of XP gained is reduced at higher levels.The only major drawback to this game (and series) is that it is almost unplayable without a strategy guide because there are so many time-sensitive hidden quests/items in random locations that you wouldn't otherwise visit.

_childDocuments_.review: The 5th game in the Trails series and the sequel & conclusion to Trails from Zero, THE VERY LAST CUTSCENE IN THE GAME CONTAINS GIANT SPOILERS FOR THE COLD STEEL GAMES, avoid watching the final, final cutscene if at all possible.If you've played Zero, you must play Azure, it concludes the story of the SSS, and covers the events that happen in Crossbell during Cold Steel I and II.The story was beautiful, however I did think it had some pacing issues, I thought it was a little bit too fast paced and that we weren't getting enough breathing room inbetween these very massive events that were happening, in this aspect I personally thought Zero did a better job balancing out the very intense moments of the story and the more lighthearted, everyday life kind of moments which I thought were missing a bit from Azure, they're still there, but in smaller amounts.The combat featured another huge improvement! Combat in this game was extremely fun, it took Zero's already excellent combat and bridged the gap between it and Cold Steels combat even further, now introducing Master Quartz, Burst and Masters Arts, your team felt insanely powerful and every character still felt good and useful. And this game had some very epic fights that really forced you to use these new tools, This combat system felt a lot closer to Cold Steel combat than Sky,  while Zero felt much closer to Sky than Cold Steel.Lastly I have to talk about the port! I wish the rest of the Trails games had SUCH good ports like this game and Zero do! A good amount of graphical update settings, excellent QoL settings such as being able to select what kind of controller prompts you want the game to show you, or literally giving you the name of the song that starts playing in game whenever the music changes, full button remapping, this was EXCELLENT! And I didn't encounter any bugs, glitches or crashes.Just like Zero, I'd urge you to buy this game if you played it before it officially came out in the West, they've really gone all out with the excellent port, they have voiced cutscenes with JP audio, and they even added a few relevant characters that were missing from the inital release, before the Cold Steel games came out, worth the support!

_childDocuments_.review: Simply the best turnbased game I've played.Trails to Azure has all the best aspects from Trails From Zero but 10x better. Gameplay wise, it is very similar to Zero but with more party members, mini games, and the introduction of master quartz which adds more depth to your quartz setup. However, the best part of Azure is it continues Zero's story with an explosive second half that dosen't let up the moment it starts. More characters get developed and the politics of Zemuria are extremely engaging. While it still can be a tropey anime jrpg, it covers serious questions of ends justifying the means, how a government should be run, and the ideal of justice and how far one will go to find their justice. While the Trails series will be hard for the majority of people to get into due to each arcs' slow first entries, Azure will more than please those who were patient with Zero.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I give the story of Azure a perfect 10/10 and officially acknowledge the Trails series as The Holy Grail of story-driven video games. It's insanely well written, down to the smallest details, and though its pacing can be slow in the beginning, it never feels watered down and is totally worth it once it picks up the pace. It's such a joy to go through a story, where everyone seems very competent: heroes, villains, neutral parties - a common trait in the Trails series, in fact. Can't wait to finish the whole thing, all the rest of the 12 over-100-hour long games (so far)!Actually, though I loved Liberl & Crossbell arcs, the other games always weren't quite 10/10, namely:*SPOILERS*- Sky 1st was really good for what it was, but what it was was basically a whole-game-long prologue, where two beginner bracers were mostly carried by more expirienced parties. So it was always a bit underwhelming, since almost all of the situations would be probably resolved even without our main heroes. Thus, probably 8/10. That being said, the bit where Capuas were perfectly set up by the Society to be a stepping stone for ID to gain popularity for their later attempt at a coup, and the fact that you don't even realize it on the 1st playthrough, is an absolute stroke of genius. Whoever wrote this, you have my utmost respect! - Sky 2nd improved on everything and had an even better story, probably 9/10, the only problem being that is felt kinda formulaic. New regoin - new experiment - new Society boss - repeat until you run out of regions. But the story and characters totally made up for that, so I still loved the expirience.- Sky 3rd was a weird one, being stuck in a pocket dimension for the duration of the game certainly harmed the expirience a LOT. But still it managed to win me over with its memory doors, a perfect tool to tell any story from anybody's perspective from any point in time. And man, STORIES WERE TOLD! Plus, main plot picks up a lot near the end. So probably 7/10, but please no more pocket dimension adventures..- Zero was really great, handling the inexperience of the main party way better than Sky 1st, plus sidequests were awesome. BUT. A surprise villain, again, after sky 1st and sky 3rd, without ANY hints or foreshadowing beforehand WHATSOEVER? I'm substracting a whole point for that alone, so 9/10 and no higher!- and Azure, especially when stuff starts happenning, will always be a reference point for how to write a perfect story. I mean seriously, so when Zero starts with 4 main heroes going down into sun fort, and in the final chapter 4 main heroes + Sky duo go down into sun fort, all that was not an oversight, but the history being rewritten. Something that is explained in the last scenes of Azure, a full game later. What kind of insane level of planning goes into this series?!
_childDocuments_.name: The Legend of Heroes: Trails to Azure

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the peak of the Trails franchise. Azure takes what was already a very strong foundation from Zero and takes full advantage of the setup its been given.The combat is very good, the characters build off their foundations in Zero in meaningful ways, and the story takes much of what has been looming in the background for the whole of the previous game and brings it to the forefront with results that seem poised to have effects for several games to come.I'm not a fan of most JRPGs. Trails has been one of the few series to genuinely appeal to me, and Azure in particular has done a great job of improving the aspects that I was already the most interested in. I look forward to seeing what the rest of the series has on offer, even if it seems unlikely to top what was accomplished here.

_childDocuments_.review: This game can't decide whether or not it is fantastic or absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  So much of this game is amazing and then it is just ♥♥♥♥ on by terrible decision after terrible decision.  Want max DP?  There are tons of hidden ways that you might not get it, even following a guide, because you can't finish a quest until the chapter end and surprise!  Even though you followed a guide and did everything correctly, you missed a DP.  Go back and play 10 hours if you want it.Want to use all of the awesome customization stuff set up in the first game?  Too bad, it was too good and the developers were too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ lazy to figure out how to balance it so it gets ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nerfed into the ground.Want the characters to act in a way that makes any ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sense?  Alright, well you can have that but with a heavy dose of absolutely not having that.80% of this game is like 9/10 master quality and then 20% of this game is 0/10.  It feels like there were two development teams and one was filled with experts who love this series and game development and one was filled with people who wanted to sabotage the game at every turn.  If ever there was a product ♥♥♥♥ on by C level execs who don't know what the ♥♥♥♥ they are doing, it must be this.  No one actually hates what they're working on enough to ♥♥♥♥ on their own game like this, right!?You should absolutely play this game, because it is worth wading through the stupid ♥♥♥♥ but I'll be damned if I'm giving this a thumbs up for all of the stupid ♥♥♥♥ put into it.Edit: Steam asked if I wanted to update my review since I ended up continuing it for so many hours, so here it is.  I was willing to change my review to positive because I definitely wrote the above while mad, and then I got to the final boss and it is actually the worst final boss I've ever faced in 30+ years of gaming.  It is just absolutely terribly designed.  Hit it too hard with a single attack?  It counters with void.  AoE basic attack it has 2 shots your entire team.  If you use any of the negate-one-attack shields it dispels them at no action cost and then attacks you anyway.  It can also interrupt spellcasting.  If you take too long to kill it, it casts an uninterruptable attack that instant kills everyone with no way to dodge or negate the attack, and with no warning that this attack is coming.  It took me 30 minutes three times to get to this point and then to just die without warning.  This isn't some amazing big brain design decision on the dev's end.  It's bad design.  It's not fun or challenging to fight it.  It's just an awful experience.  I cannot give this game a good review despite it absolutely deserving it.  90% of this game is fantastic and is what all games should hold up as a gold standard.  10% of it is objectively some of the worst design in gaming history.  It is baffling.  If you told me it wasn't made bad on purpose I would not believe you.  There is no way that people intentionally designed some specific elements with any goal other than to make sure the player just stopped having fun.  If it was feasible for me to find out who designed those elements I would do so if only to make sure that no company that hired them, no company, game design or not, ever received any money from me ever, even if those people no longer worked at the company.  It's that bad.  Do I still think you should play this game despite it?  Probably.  But you should absolutely be prepared to slog through some really terrible, unfun content.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very conflicted recommend. The Crossbell setting and the core team is absolutely awesome. There are some truly heartfelt moments. The story ties together all the lose ends of the first game and then some. And the sheer length of the main story, with all the twists and turns, is impressive.However, there are three big drawbacks. The first and smallest is that the combat is essentially unchanged from the first game, but you need to start over from scratch. There is the addition of master quartz, but that's minor. It's basically a copy paste of the entire first game's combat, except with bigger monster with more HP and higher damage. Halfway through the game, I was bored.More importantly, the two remaining issues are in regards to the plot.The first is that the game tackles some truly horrifying themes. War. Murder. Terrorism. Trafficking. Child abuse. Brutal betrayals. And the outcome of each and every one of these things is........ nothing. Lloyd Bannings, or more correctly referred to as Jesus Christ, holds a speech and then forgives people. But here's the thing.... Lloyd is NOT Jesus. He has no right or mandate to forgive anyone of anything done to someone else. But he does. Repeatedly. "Oh, you murdered X people? But you had a rough childhood? It's ok buddy, I forgive you. Just listen to my sermon first." It is SO preachy, and has nothing to do with being a police detective.The second and bigger issue is in regards to the final plot reveals in the end game. As usual with Falcom, there is an endless amount of over the top glorious nonsense. Which only the 18 year old junior detective can fix, of course. Fine. That's alright. And there's endless, repetitive dungeons with like.... 7 final bosses? Myabe 8? OK, fine. Whatever.But the real problem isn't how over the top the game gets in terms of sheer nonsense. The problem is that the game falls into a really, really stupid trap of saying "It is wrong to try to change things. It is wrong to try to prevent war. It is wrong to try to prevent innocent people from dying. Why? Because we are living in the best of worlds, and we can't mess with stuff!" It's an idiotic argument from a group that runs around using super powerful magic spells, routinely sticks their nose inte politics, and tries to impose their own will on the world. It's as if the writers at Falcom never read Voltaire's Candide, where a happy idiot runs around proclaiming we are living in the best of all worlds, even as people die horribly all around him. That idiot is Lloyd.A final note. Spoiler ahead. Anyway. To wrap it up. I love the setting. The characters. The daily life stuff. The political intrigue. The relationships. Combat was OK in the first game, but got boring in this one. But the preaching? The idiotic last quarter of the game? The nonsensical moralizing? The lack of consequences for horrific acts? It really ruins a fantastic series of games.But to be fair.... Falcom does the same in some of the Trails of Cold Steel games, so perhaps they just can't help themselves.

_childDocuments_.review: The 5th game in the Legend of Heroes Trails Series and arguably the best entry so far.  This game is the finale of the second (Crossbell) arc.  Once again the writing and characters are top tier and the music and presentation continues to be exceptional.Not much else to say other than, if you have liked this series thus far.  This game will not disappoint.  Combat remains what you are used to with a couple of new added mechanics that add some new fun to the mix.  The story was probably the best in the series so far as well.  Once again this title supports Ultrawide and has good M/Kb and controller support as well.  This is always appreciated and I hope the next entries continue the good PC ports.

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal game, i can't stress enough how good the story and gameplay is. If you like found family type of stories then this game will catch you by the orbments. The cast feel natural and, although like many other JRPGs it falls into some stereotypes initially, the development of each main cast character truly shines at the end. Also, i love how the team managed to weave into the overarching story the plot of this game, makes you feel like you're watching history unfold from different POVs.The gameplay starts simple but as you get better quartz and upgrade your slots you begin building your characters and creating some nasty combinations.10/10 game i can't wait to play the rest of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: The second part of the Crossbell duology elevates the Trails games to the best it ever was. The Crossbell series delivers an amazing story, both political and supernatural, while having some of the most memorable and interesting characters. Trails to Azures story starts shortly after the end of Zero. Picks up many of the story lines, while further crafting the world of Zemuria. The story, characters and world building are by far the strongest part of the game, while being some of the best in RPG history.  The gameplay mostly stays the same, the only major update is the addition of master quartz and new duo special crafts, that your team members can perform.Only downside is the difficulty spike for the last boss. I would recommend playing the game in normal since you can't change the difficulty once selected.

_childDocuments_.review: As always, I think the Trails game has one of the best story telling among JRPG games. it might not be as well-known and has development budget as big as the likes of Final Fantasy or Persona, but believe me when I said the quality is up there. Not just the story though, but the characterisation, the gameplay loop and the progression system. Even among Trails game, I think Azure is one of the best in terms of story and pacing. It has the right amount of charm, comedy and seriousness. Just perfect.

_childDocuments_.review: Trails to Azure being the second game in the Crossbell arc/series is a curious game, there were many improvements to the system compared to the first game but there were a fair share of flaws too in some regards, overall it's still a fun game and the story is great hence why I'm still suggesting it, frankly it's a satisfying end to this arc and I hope ya'all enjoy it as much as I did dood!Okay onto the main review! So the games much the same as it was originally but with the brand new addition of a new mechanic, that being master quartz, what's the difference between master quartz and normal quartz you ask? For starters they give you a set amount of elements meaning even if you had absolutely no quartz equipped you'd still get a spell or two but even better it means while equipped you can get much more varied and powerful spells due to the extra boost, it also raises various stats which increase over 5 levels and finally! Each one has a unique effect to it from starting with buffs to increased critical rates ect ect, it's a super nice addition especially in the era when what quartz you equipped in combination determined what spells you had dood.Combat is very much the same bar an edition in certain scenarios known as burst, this gives the player free turns to attack at 20% increased damage and even let's you cast spells instantly allowing for a myriad of strategies, otherwise bar one aspect I will talk about later, the games mechanics are pretty much the same dood.The game has additional characters which is a nice change and allows you to make use more often at points of the assist skills for characters not on the field, certain things are more expensive than normal but also have an increased effect due to it which is super nice dood.Mini games! Yeaaaah so they added a mini-game and also made fishing a bit more annoying, they aren't horrible granted and the one only happens once and is easier than it seems at first glance, they are the kind of thing that's fun if you're into them but I feel detracted from the game while kind of forcing you to play them for the ridiculously great rewards at the end that you'll be wanting for the actual gameplay, all in all they both add and take away from the game based on who you are but I'm of the firm belief that mini-games of that nature should never be too hard if they have a reward of that nature to them dood.The music is on point as always and combat is fun but there is a huge gripe I have with it and that's how later on Melee is barely really viable, particularly against bosses, I feel the aim was to get the player to use spells to buff players but even then it wasn't all that viable, the damage was too low, even using S-craft just wasn't really doing it outside of ATS damage attacks and even those seemed rather on the low end, especially with how slowly CP raises in this, it meant the way I played turned from two melee + two casters for a variable team to one tank and three casters meaning the way to play the game changed drastically for any of the fights that were actually a challenge dood.But yeah that's Trails to Azure, it's definitely still fun despite my issues with it on both a personal but also practical level but it was a game that did a lot in it's time and a lot of good at that with a great storyline and characters as is known for the series in general, I hope this helps you decide on whether you wanna buy it or not, thank you for reading and until next we meet dood! *throws a rose*
