_childDocuments_.review: I bounced off of Triumph's prior titles (AOW3 and Planetfall), but AOW4 does so much right. I love it. If you're into fantasy or sci-fi 4x games, it's a must-buy. The world map is just eye-wateringly beautiful. The soundtrack is awesome. Fog of war? Honestly, the best fog of war you will find in a game. Insomnia? The compulsion for one more turn at 3 am is undeniable. Seriously, just stay up and play! AOW4 goes out of its way to not annoy the sh!t out of you with tedious mechanics that add no value. No micro-managing districts. No building wonders -- just go find them! Seize them if you can, and you'll get kick-ass special units. Lose a battle? No need to save-scum -- you'll recover! Feel like switching gears from summoning magic to lightning magic half way through a campaign? Go for it!!!! It's all part of the story you're creating while playing the game. An example: I fired up a campaign playing as wood elves. A few hours into the game, I captured an elephant. I became immensely attached to this elephant. I learned spells to revive the elephant if it should happen to fall in battle as a result of my ill-conceived tactical plans. The elephant -- a not-particularly-special Tier III animal summon, in the big scheme of things -- became the core of my southern armies, as I focused my magical studies on tomes that would make the elephant even more unstoppable. Empires -- literal empires!! -- were crushed by the elephant. It lives in a field now, by the wizard's tower, and we're trying to import another so it will procreate.Is AOW 4 perfect? No. It suffers from the same late-game wars of attrition that other 4x games do. And its tactical battles aren't as visually impressive as they could be -- fire spells are often just orange lines, lightning is purple lines ... the spells and particle effects in particular are a little underwhelming. Maybe AOW5 will give me unreasonably large storms of lightning that demonstrate the extent to which others should not mess with me. Or my elephant.But those are minor issues. AOW4 is simply fun to play, and I command you to buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Short review : It's civ but fantasy, also it brings other things such as Heroes, spells. If there was a Baldur's Gate of turn-based strategy games from a god view this would be it._______________________________________________________________Long Review: Learning the game:Learning the ropes of Age of Wonders 4 is a breeze, especially for those familiar with Civ 6. While there's a slight learning curve due to additional features, it's not overly challenging. The game provides an enjoyable single-player campaign that gradually introduces more complex mechanics, making it an excellent way to grasp the intricacies of the game.Customization in the game:Age of Wonders 4 offers a refreshing departure from the traditional 4X strategy games like Civ. The standout feature here is the remarkable degree of creative freedom right from the start. Unlike Civ's structured approach, players can craft their own faction, choosing the race, special abilities, and technological advancements. Additionally, the customization extends to the hero of your people, whose appearance evolves as you progress, unlocking additional items for personalization. The game's unique maps and the layer beneath them add a layer of depth reminiscent of classics like Baldur's Gate. It's a captivating experience that allows for the creation of immersive scenarios from a god-like perspective in turn-based mode. Despite being underrated, Age of Wonders 4 truly stands out for its unparalleled customization features.Combat and playing the game:The gameplay is incredibly smooth, with a seamless flow that prevents it from ever becoming monotonous. While there may be moments when you wish for more, the game continually surprises you with hidden menus and features. The combat system, akin to Civ but with its unique twists, allows for more strategic depth. Multiple armies can team up against units, and engaging with the world goes beyond just confronting enemy factions. Combat scenarios include battling neutral entities, akin to Civ's barbarians, or even vassalizing free cities, adding an extra layer of complexity. What sets Age of Wonders 4 apart is its dynamic combat system, allowing players to shift between a third-person perspective and a real-time setting, reminiscent of Total War. It's an outstanding game that justifies its cost, making it a highly recommended purchase for strategy enthusiasts.__________________________________________________________________To the developers I wanted to express my immense appreciation for the exceptional work you've done with Age of Wonders 4. Having invested over a hundred hours into the game, it's evident that you've created something truly special. While the overall experience is outstanding, I'd like to highlight a potential area for improvement – the combat and battles. The pacing felt a bit slow, with characters having substantial health, which extended the fights. Streamlining the combat dynamics within battles could elevate the gaming experience. Despite this observation, your efforts in mastering full-scale warfare are commendable. Age of Wonders 4's strategic depth and unique gameplay remind me of classics like Lord of the Rings: Battle for Middle Earth 2, one of the best RTS games ever. I look forward to any future projects from your team and envision the potential for an RTS similar to Age of Wonders 4 but with an even more pronounced real-time approach, capturing the enduring success of Battle for Middle Earth 2.

The game's story is developed primarily through the player's decisions, race choices, and conquest of the world, with the storyline serving as background and the player's actions determining the game's outcome.Although the game's storyline and mechanics are reminiscent of other games in the genre, it has unique and engaging features, such as its advanced character creation and customization, making it stand out. _childDocuments_.review: The game is fantastically fun if you can look past all the flaws. So why am I rating it negatively? Those flaws are extremely prevalent currently in the game. The early game is extremely enjoyable with the battles against equally or a bit higher power foes is very well done, aside from a few issues here and there with the battle AI and its priority system(using any summon/mind control and they'll almost always 100% focus on that). There are even some really fun late game battles against wonders where you're forced to fight with one army, potentially limiting your options. The issues the game has is in its balance, campaign AI, and the late game. There are incredibly blatantly broken things in the game, which is mostly fine for single player, as you can power fantasy your way through the game and still get a reasonable challenge from marauder battles and wonder battles, but the single player AI is horribly broken. They barely interact with the map other than clearing infestations and the occasional wonder, which is extremely noticeable when you attack their lands and see every single resource node uncleared. They're extremely passive to the point of rarely attacking your base. I think I've been sieged three times total, all in close range maps where I started both at war and within 8 provinces of a brutal difficulty AI. Due to this, they pose almost no threat even when on the highest difficulty since they give you all the time in the world to build up. The second major issue is balance, primarily in the broken strategies available. These largely pertain to multiplayer, as using broken nonsense doesn't impact the game as much in singleplayer, but there are certain tome combinations that completely eliminate any form of counterplay. By tome tier 2 you can have 3 full stacks of T1 archers with heroes leading them running seeker arrows(+1 range), high culture for awaken(+1 range and +4 spirit damage), Astral blood(+10% crit EVERY spell cast), and amplified arrows(+4 lightning damage, -2 physical damage, damage bounces to another target in 3 hexes for 30% damage). Throw on another archer enchant tome of roots for an extra 4 blight damage and -2 physical, as well as getting you vine prison to break the AI when you're not fighting the other players, and you've won the game by t2 tomes. If you somehow manage to get past that phase of the game, maybe the other player is playing the same thing, and you get to T5 you can run, with good planning, the T4 tome of the golden realm and the T5 tome of the arch mage to have 100% magic crits as well as have your magic crits gild the enemy(basically a stun) with no chance of resisting it. If you get the T3 lightning orb which bounces damage to other enemies as well, and use summon astral reflections, one hero can lock down 9 enemies permanently with no real counterplay. Even without the lightning orb, lightning evoker allows the same thing every 3 turns, as well as your normal attacks still allowing you to stun one enemy each.My issues with the late game stem from the fact that turns go from extremely quick, to taking ages to rollover as well as calculate combats. Even if you have 18v18 combats in the early game, they're rather quick to auto resolve through, but in the late game, the time for those to complete is incredibly long, and turn times also quickly extend to absurd degrees. Taking 15 turns for a magic or expansion victory feels like it takes as long as all the turns it took to get to that point, despite the AI never making an effort to move their troops your way to stop it. Overall the game needs some large balance overhauls for multiplayer or some serious improvements to the singleplayer AI for this to be a recommendation from me.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR;The game wasn't ready for release, there are many bugs, balancing issues, and AI cheating.  The more you play the game the more you start to realize how flawed it is, and in it's current state it's not fun to play.  Even with mods attempting to fix some of the balance issues, the game has too many issues for it to be enjoyable.  I'd avoid buying this game until these issues are ironed out, but with the developer focusing on DLC more than fixing an already broken game, I doubt this game will recover.  It has a solid fan girl base, so the reviews are very deceiving.More details:Play testing clearly wasn't a priority for this developer as almost all of the issues would have been caught by someone that played the game for at least 30 hours.  Someone that wasn't delusional or ignoring issues within the development team.There is massive lag between turns, and it gets worse as you continue playing.  I played a few games to turn 100, and found I was waiting for around 2 hours for turns to process over a single game.  That's crazy when you consider it only takes me about 5 hours to hit turn 100, this translates to about 40% of game time is waiting for the turn to process.  You don't notice it at first, but late game you'll find you're constantly sitting there waiting for the next turn to finish processing.  If you use the automatic fast movement of units this can be cut down a bit, but not by much.This turn processing time is likely due to how the AI is programmed to move it's armies.  It will break them up into units based on left over movement speed, trying to eek out every last movement, instead of keeping the army whole during movements.  It's likely taking a ton of processing power, and making more calculations than it would if it was forced to keep armies intact during movement.There is also a memory leak somewhere that the developers can't seem to find.  If you play above 1080p you'll find that your card will heat up unlike any other modern AAA graphic intensive title.There are many mechanical bugs, features that don't work, and balancing issues.  Too many to put into a review, but here are two of the major ones that ruin two builds undead, and chaos.The lack of soul resources to maintain a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ undead army that can't really compete against similar tiered units.  You can earn souls by killing units in battle, and from a soul well 3 souls per turn.  It takes 10 souls to make a tier 1 skeleton unit, 30 for a tier two.  So unless you're out there killing everything in site, you'll be unable to maintain units for long.  Spells also cost souls to cast, making them 100% useless to cast if you want an undead army.  Making players choose between undead armies, or using battle spells.  Since the tool-tips don't tell you which battle spells use souls or not during tome research. This means you're basically researching something you'll never use during the game.There are features that simply are 100% resisted (havoc magic), making late game chaos builds useless.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game made by a passionate awesome studio, it has loads of great artwork, I enjoy their previous works, and I am just not a fan of this version of Age of Wonders.  I could talk about the game's over complicated economy that collapses to a few optimal decisions with basic math.  I could talk about the simplifying of movement with abundant teleporters makes army movement trivial and basically results in a blob fight to determine the outcome of a war.  But essentially what makes or breaks the game, and for me it breaks it utterly, is the combination of consistent unit archetypes and a shared tech tree.Now that initially doesn't sound like a bad thing, does it?  What's so wrong with consistent unit archetypes and a shared tech tree?  Well essentially all the units in the game are designed to fit into a set of archetypes that you have access to at the start.  You never unlock a new archetype of unit, the sort of units that you start with are the sort of units that your end with.  Then on top of this all the techs that you unlock impact a certain archetype of unit, so all of your archers do some fire damage if you research a tech.  This essentially makes all the units in these archetypes blend together as the turn count increases.  Any difference between them diminishes as they get upgraded.  Your archers might get more powerful as you upgrade them, you might even unlock a new archer, but it behaves exactly like your starting archers.So what's the big deal?  Well as you click the end turn button, all that happens is the numbers go up.  You unlock a new unit?  It's the same as the unit you were already using except its numbers are higher.  The tactical combat plays out the same way but a unit model changes.  You unlock a new tech?  It causes the numbers to go up.  The tactical combat plays out the same way but now there's more particle effects.  Almost nothing you do in this game gives you a sense of changing direction, everything just causes the numbers to go up.  It's one dimensional.    Furthermore, since the factions you are fighting have the same tech tree, there's no way to prepare for their late game.  You don't pick technologies to counter what your opponent is progressing towards because you don't know what they are progressing towards.  You research and build whatever you think is the most powerful independently of what your opponents are doing.  So the turns go by and the numbers go up but nothing feels different, none of your decisions feel like they have accomplished anything unique other than their particular contribution to the rate at which the numbers increase.  So this makes Age of Wonders 4 feel exactly like other modern strategy games, more of a system of behavioral modification devices than an actual game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Age of Wonders 4 on Steam Deck for a bit, and I can say that this is a great game for those who love strategy games with a touch of magic. This is something that is totally missing from other games in the genre, and it adds a whole new level of depth and personalization to the game.As for the game's performance on the Steam Deck, it runs pretty well. However, I would love to see it officially verified, as there are some key improvements that could be made for Steam Deck users. For example, the UI needs to be scaled for a screen so small, especially text fields. Additionally, the recommended settings need to be better calibrated, as I often experience performance issues with FPS dropping to low 10s, especially during big battles or when I can see someone else's empire.Finally, the control mapping could also be improved. I think that Age of Wonders 4 could take a page from Civilization 6, which mixes joystick and mouse behaviors in a more intuitive way that flows better for the gamer.Overall, Age of Wonders 4 is a great addition to the strategy game genre, especially for those who love magic and personalization in their gameplay. While there are some improvements that could be made for Steam Deck users, the game is still a lot of fun to play and definitely worth checking out.

Endless helper tutorials pop up throughout the game, but are a slog to get through. Unfortunately, they're required because good luck navigating the bad UI for certain features.The tech tree using tomes of magic is great thematically, but implementation-wise there's a lot of illusion of choice. There are very obvious poor picks that don't make the gameplay better or more interesting, or improve your Empire any a very tangible way. It's a feature that should increase replayability, but winds up hurting it instead.The strategic combat is great in theory, but ponderous in practice. You'll find yourself auto-battling more often than not after a few bouts, and grumbling to yourself when your trash AI loses units in battles that should easily be flawless victories.They also went the old lazy developer route of having cheating AI enemies. They probably would have had more time for good AI that could play competently if they didn't waste time implementing useless stuff in the tech trees.Flipped to positive because modding fixes everything.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the third Age of Wonders Game I've played, previously having played AOW 3 and AOW Planetfall. _childDocuments_.review: Great game with some small gripes. Mainly with the AI, which is sort of dumb. Nice update to the AOW formula. Took a little from Planetfall, with districts instead of just tiles to build on, which I like. Streamlines the process. Not entirely sold on the art style, but, that is a personal preference. Not as clear as the old art. Also, I miss the little story excerpts you see from the older games when you examine units. I get the story setup in this game kind of makes it nonsensical due to all these realms being different. Missing some ease of use too, as you have to do more work to see what upgrades your city and units have.All in all, it is pretty great. No crashes on my laptop, and the customization is huge. You can start with many different traits and cultures but can easily morph into others as the game goes. Want dark culture but love the production of a materium culture? Just start as an industrial faction and then get the tomes of the dark. Now my industrious humans are great at production and gets undead perks. It really is a daunting endeavour, but the information is given out in a clear, easy to understand way, that doesn't bog you down.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Had to write a review since some of the reviews I have read that marked down the game completely are baffling to me. TLDR: This is a very strong fun and unique 4x game. It provides loads of replay ability, Multiplayer, and a long tail progression system, and tops it off with a campaign + a new story per DLC. For me strategic depth with strong replay ability is a must. And this hits all the marks. The game allows you to build your race the way you want, you are not locked into a tradition of western mythologies. This means if you want Giant Dwarves that are part Dragon, have at it. Set your Form (aka how you look), your race attributes (aka your base passives) and then choose your culture (base units and more unique passives for your race), Now comes your society traits (foundational passives that dramatically change your game style), lastly choose your upgrades (or Tomes in this game. Provide unique spells, buildings, upgrades and units). The game really appeals to the tinkerer. If you struggle with the amount of choice you can get locked playing your favorite way each and every time and I still enjoy it as both campaign and the random missions provide unique ways to go after each game. But from other 4x games it feels as if you are more limited with this model, mostly because all the unique pieces that builds your games isnt a fixed tree. This means its up to you to differentiate each game run vs other games where your most fundamental choice is "pick race + tech tree". Overall with the options in your hand the breadth of customization that occurs during a game is breath taking until you start to understand how the tome system works. The negatives for the title for me is that the cultures which primarily provide the base units you play need to have stronger differentiation with buildings and unit capabilities. I would say as well that you could provide stronger random world events to make each world that much more unique. Some tomes (order) feel very lacking compared to the other tome trees, especially when you layer on the skill tree. It is almost always more efficient to conquer then gain trust. Lastly AI could use some help, feels it overly cheats and is not as varied in behavioral models. Beyond this the game is a must have for any 4x fan. I play on consoles as well as PC and both provide the same great experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Paradox has really gotten their talons in this one. AOW4 is a cookie cutter 4x game thats lost all of its charm and uniqueness from the last entry. Still, it's a very mechanically solid game, it just feels like every other 4x game out there. In particular, it's a very stereotypical paradox game that loves its "mana" i.e. point values to do stuff; have enough points, click button, do thing. Affinity, imperium, research, gold... all "mana" systems. The whole class system has been scrapped, and just like Stellaris you now have a bunch of options when customizing your faction. It's a nice system that works, but it's a "mana" system too. The classes have been replaced by "tomes" which provide the replability and variation, and again, it works but feels more like a standard tech tree than AOWIII's class system. City building has been turned into CIV 6, which again, is neat and functional, but not really interesting. The best innovation is allowing you to build buildings and units at the same time. Claiming provinces is cool, and building special buildings is also nice, but results in weird things like cities having unclaimed land right next to the city by the end game because the bordering province isn't very good. The single worst part is that, even if the city pop goes down, that land is FOREVER chained to the city. You can't redo borders, or take out a rival to steal their land. You either raze the whole city or watch as they hold on to lands right next to your cities. The worst thing is that this is another game that, rather than balance it's economy, has just thrown a stupid arbitrary limit to make expansion useless after a given point. You now have a city limit, in direct contrast to AOWIII's "this is a game about fantasy war" mentality. Now, you have to turn everything into useless vassal cities that you have no control over. They only send one stack at a time (and only after 5-10 turns), send you limited resources, and worst of all, claim provinces irrationally. I've had so many wonders get cut off from me because my vassal claimed a territory before I could. And there are just a ton of little nice details that were removed. Cities no longer have populations, just a single number from 1-30. Little quotes about each unit are gone. Cities really only add to their tower, but don't change visually as they grow otherwise. It's just another souless paradox game...But despite that, it's balanced, functional, and fun to play for a campaign or two. There are worse games out there, but also plenty of better ones. Overall, it's a solid, soulless 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played all the versions of Age of Wonders through the years and my favorite of all times was AoW: Shadow Magic because it was, up to this day, the most ambitious AoW game made.Even years later, when AoW 3 came out I bought it but I barely played it and went back to replay AoW: SM instead.Now, about AoW 4 ... the game had been in my wishlist until it's release but I was hesitant buying it, fearing a simplified or dumbed down version of the AoW franchise, just like AoW 3 was ... and now I'm happy to say that I was wrong. I enjoy almost everything about AoW 4:The fights are fun, engaging and can be challenging. As I play, I also get better as I learn to master my own units and have better ideas of what to expect from my ennemies. The 4x aspect of the game is not complicated, but it is deep enough that it is possible to build very different empires from one game to the other.The RPG aspects are as fun as ever. It is quite rewarding to see your heros and leader become more and more powerful. In some other games, it is a tedious process that leads to an unrewarding endgame, but this is not the case here for me.Content wise, even without DLCs, there's a lot to play with and enjoy for a long time ... I'm guesstimating that I could play another 55 hours (time played at time of writing this review) before I even think about looking at the DLCs.All-in-all, this is the AoW game I had been waiting for.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get straight to the heart of one point up front: this is a Paradox 4X game. If you've played Stellaris, HoI, etc., you have a pretty good idea of what you're getting into. We'll have multiple DLCs stretched across a few years, we'll have some updates that fundamentally change how some systems work and we'll get a million different Workshop items to fill the voids.Having said that, I've played one game so far and I'm thoroughly impressed with what I've experienced. Let me just summarize my experience from beginning to end by telling you I started off with a race I called "Shadow Orcs" (yeah, I know, the name sucks but I just wanted to jump right in) that were dark/shadow focused orc warriors and ended the game with undead frozen vampiric blight orcs with fire-imbued weapons and enchanted cities constantly spreading ice and snow across a world slowly bowing before my might. I interrupted a dark ritual in an ancient ruin and after killing the beings performing the rite, I completed the summoning they were attempting and summoned the evil creatures from another world: Dire Penguins (this is not a joke, I have screenshots to prove it). The role-play opportunities in this game are endless, there's both a surface map AND an underground/Underdark area ON THE SAME MAP, near endless customization and enhancement of your race and Godir (essentially your avatar in game), custom map creation, and as you continue to play the game you earn points to spend on even more customization/cosmetic options for your race.Three main critiques: First, battles in this game just feel meh. They can be grand, epic affairs with multiple units from different armies on both sides fighting over territory, cities, sites of power, etc. But it essentially equates to selecting your ability, right clicking on the map and watching a small animation as numbers and status indicators pop up over your units. The battlefields look great, but the overall feel of battle kinda leaves you feeling like it could've used some more TLC. The other complaints are QoL gripes, such as requiring RMB to activate ANY abilities in combat or the world map. Wanna launch a special ability? RMB. Wanna cast a spell? RMB. It can throw you off and become easily frustrating in the midst of an already stressful battle. Also, the pop up info screens obscure LMB clicks when selecting things like units, construction options, magic research, etc. The pop ups trigger after holding the cursor over ANYthing for more than 1 second and will block you from clicking on the item you wanted. Then the pop up triggers again a second later. It's mildly infuriating.Overall, I think this game is worth the asking price, especially if you're just wanting the base game. I can already tell I'm going to poor countless hours into this and it'll more than likely become my current obsession for the next little bit. Good game, great presentation, some QoL issues, but an overall great experience!

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game, but I just can't.Let's start with your faction creation - I was really looking forward to that mechanic, and, well...Your race has two traits (in AoW3 it had up to four), nothing prevents you from changing those traits (making each race, essentially, rubber elves).Your civilization has only two available traits, some of the options presented are just bad, some are a must if you don't want to suffer later on.And no, you can't take drawbacks to add more traits.Your culture has a limited roster of units which you, outside of summons, cannot change. Want a 'High' culture with knights, or a 'Dark' one with frontline defenders? Too bad.Speaking of frontline defenders, a unit with spear and shield does not exist - or I have not encountered any.Combat in general is, largely, the same as it was in AoW3 and Planetfall - map is small, whoever lands a good first strike wins, archers suck, AI will always move in a tight group and stay out of you reach for as long as possible, not only ruining immersion, but also needlessly prolonging the fight, while being annoying af and pretending to be a tactical genius, no matter who you fight - feral swines, swamp trolls or ascended angels.On economy, city-building and empire-building side, situation is atrocious. You will pay gold to make anything. And then you have to actually make that thing, by using two different production tracks and capacities - one for units, one for buildings. And no, you can't speed things up. Oh, and you will want gold for diplomacy, since AI always wants to be bribed in order to make a beneficial pact with you. And minor cities will have constant events that will force you to pay with gold or something even more precious, punishing relations or alignment as an alternative.Speaking of making gold. Let's suppose you have a gold vein on map and you just claimed that region. A gold mine will provide you with 15g total. A single T1 unit costs 60 to make (plus production time), around 8 to upkeep. And if you cast any enchantments you will also pay upkeep for them per every unit it affects. And if you want some units from your vassals, they will also cost gold. And building an outpost costs gold and upkeep (and time).Sure, you can cast that one transformation spell to make your entire race into gold golems, or build that astral bridge teleport, but what if you did not want to play king Midas - or go with astral books - in the first place? Seems like the game has other opinions and what you want is sort of irrelevant. Naval combat and exploration are anemic, settlements and races - and dedicated naval units - do not seem to exist. Compared to other games of this genre:Warlock has better map exploration, city development, economy, and is more intuitive.Dominions has better strategic and tactical combat, magic system, economy, and is better explaining what your faction does and how you are supposed to play - and simply is a better game. Also it has water-based races from the start, no dlc required.Civilization Beyond Earth has a better affinity and civ perk system. Economy is, arguably, worse.Hero's Hour is better, even though it is limited to military victory, riddled with balance issues, and it's AI is not good.This all reminds me of Fallen Enchantress - a lot of customization, and not much of an interesting gameplay. tl;dr : pretty visuals, utter mediocrity of strategic, tactical and economic systems, plus some rather unrewarding customisation. Breadth of an ocean, depth of a puddle. Pick something else.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: after giving it a second try I'm going to uninstall this for good as not playable. But I'll write a review. What's wrong with this game? Well, it's a collection of unclear things. First of all we have a map consisting of weird shaped provinces with very different shape, but there's no reason why that shape. Moving on that map is unclear, as you don't really get a good visual clue of how many moving points it takes to go somewhere, producing a feeling your troops are slopping through a morass.All technology is based on "research tomes", which open up additional units, but there is no tech tree, where you'd see what would lead you where, so you're plodding through rng function of "what does this do". If you hate random stuff as I do you'll be constantly annoyed in this unfocused game as it throws stupid quests at you, like go concquer a town on the other side of the map, not one close to your space. Combat is extra badly done. Units are too cartoonish and large, with totally unclar situation of who does what where and who blocks whom and how many strikes who will do. Overall it's confusing interface in confusing concepts and stupid animation. Could had been great, turned out trash.Overall, it's a game that starts really nice, but after some 10h of playtime it feels annoying as hell because of poor design.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I'm not recomending the game it's not because the game is bad. Surely there are some performance issues (it won't slow down the gaem but will cause audio distortions) it will probably be patched soon (tm) and some people were having issues with crashes and not being able to play. I had a few crashes too but that will probably be fixed soon too.The reason why I don't recomend is because while the game has a few good systems, it has some very questionable decisions that actively hinder the game significantly. Things like not being able to remove the underground which is a hinder because it doesn't respects relative player distances and therefore very often causes enemies to spawn right next to the player. Things like not being able to chose the hero limit. Things like not being able to remove the cap of how many cities you can have (this is a hinder if you play domination mode as your only choice is to raise almost every town you come across).The whole game is riddled with some good sterps forward and some steps back too. It's not that the game can't be enjoyed, but as it stands right now it's very hard to recomend until several game start customisation features are added and some balance passes are done, especially considering the price point is 50 Euros which is 10 more than AoW3 was released at (but the same as planetfall).EDIT: The game also has crackling audio issues, these issues have existed for several months but the Devs aren't fixing it, they say they are investigating it but this is not such a hard to fix issue that takes months so in all likelyhood, the Devs aren't even trying.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally, after the new expansion pass's pass sale, I was able to pick this game up at a discount. I absolutely love it. Unlike other games, you can't have 2.4k skeletons in your army because of upkeep costs and 6 single units max per army, up to the max of 3 armies in a fight. (so 18 skeletons though more can be summoned in the fight on the battle screen) This helps prevent me from doing what I would do in Heroes of Might and Magic, load up my main char with everything under the sun and use my other heroes as resource Roombas. The feel and play of this game is just great I really have no complaints other than the learning curve. It probably took me a full day to learn everything but I'm not sure if I did learn everything because there is so much to do.The game seems pretty balanced to me, but some people are saying insanity spells are broken. They basically are if you're lucky, and your opponent doesn't have any healing or resistances. (of which there are a lot) My gravely wounded cannibal midget army and was able to take on waves of enemy troops by just casting insanity spells to make them fight each other.There are stories of multiplayer games being absolutely buggy messes, but I haven't tried it out yet because I don't have any friends. I did come across 1 bug so far on single player when my NPC opponent wouldn't end their turn. After quick saving and reloading, it fixed the issue.Reading through the negative reviews, it seems many of them are negative because of the DLC practices and not because of the actual game. Still, I respect those negative reviews and was very close to giving this game a thumbs down until the developers purchase a subscription to my positive review DLC for $19.99. After thinking it over though, I don't run a game studio or look at these guys' balance sheets. My gut feeling is I got this game at a fair price so I'm giving them a 1 week trial of my positive review DLC for free.
_childDocuments_.name: Age of Wonders 4

_childDocuments_.review: Playing with other people online, this game is unplayable.To be forced to watch every non-auto battle is too much burden. This now kinda forces everyone to do auto battle's instead... In most cases, this turns out into a lot of unnecessary casualties. Losing the most important unit when you clearly have a free win, Losing archers when you have a tanky frontline that didn't even take any damage. etc etc. All battles are easily fixed if you do them personally. I don't recommend buying this game if you are hoping to play it online with or against other humans. Solo games vs AI are fun. But like every AI, when you know how they work you can just win any battle, with a high disadvantage. AI sends half their army after 1 level 1 summon unit, chasing it down while you slaughter the other part of the army. Heal up and slaughter the other half. AI charges in with their hero or strong fast units. Mind control them and send them back to die in their own army. And do it all over again.So, after a couple of games vs AI you probably want to play with or vs humans and then, after watching 2/3 battles with your enemy, you become annoyed because it takes ages. You don't want to do any battles yourself because you don't want to be a burden to your teammates. I understand that they are probably very busy fixing all the out of sync and crashes at the moment. But honestly, until they removed this feature or a mod that allows you to not watch combat , I don't see any point in playing this game online.

_childDocuments_.review: It's still early days, but so far AoW4 is exactly what I wanted it to be! I am a big fan of the first three games, and though I wasn't too enthused by Planetfall, it had some really good ideas that made me wish it was a "proper" Age of Wonders game. AoW4 is basically that game, bringing a lot of what worked in Planetfall back into a much more appropriate fantasy setting. And, as with all the other games, it's not too similar to previous entries and tries some really interesting new ideas.There is a tier 4 dire elephant in the room to mention, which is the state of the game on release. I seem to be having more luck with it than some people, but I did have one crash early on, and encountered a few minor bugs. However, the game has an excellent autosave system and loads quickly, so the crash wasn't too troublesome. But, there is something to be said for yet another Paradox game being pushed out rough around the edges. I have no doubt it will be improved with time, but for those who aren't quite as enthusiastic for the series, it might be best to wait a little while.Update: About 10 months later, I can still safely say this is one of the best 4x games out there, and has felt tragically underrated. Updates have fixed all major issues and vastly improved the game, while DLCs have pretty much all been awesome additions (I own the premium edition so they appear along with major patches for me). There are aspects of AoW3 that I still miss, such as the tighter identity of races with unique units and such, and the modding scene for 4 is undeniably weaker, which really makes me wish the game got more traction. Nevertheless, it's a fantastic game and receiving plenty of ongoing attention from the devs. I'm happy to pick it up again every time they add something new.

Customization capability is unique and limitless but unfortunately also reduced the RPG part of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay. I am sorry to say this, but I will have to go against the mainstream. I am aware that the game has a lot of positive reviews praising some of the new aspects, such as customization and graphics. I will not question that it was an interesting and decent addition to AOW4; however, it does not make the game good in itself. I have played AOW for almost 20 years and had high expectations from this new chapter in its series, and as I said in my review of AOW 3, that game placed the bar very high, which means that Triumph Studios had to work thrice to make a better game.I love the AOW series because of its exciting campaigns, characters, dialogues and music (especially in AOW2 and some in AOW3). I was hoping this game would have a decent drive and compelling story, and, to my surprise, it does not have either! Yes, the game has no exciting stories, characters, or campaigns, and basically, the entire game is just a series of random maps I quickly get tired of. There is no feeling of wanting to play "another turn" before you go to bed, and most of my thoughts while playing were wishing to beat this map as soon as possible in hopes that the following map will be more enjoyable.As for music, the game has yet to have any memorable compositions. I simply do not remember any strong themes after playing several maps of AOW4 (though I admit that I only played some factions and not all maps). The main theme is interesting, but other than this, most of the different compositions do not feel unique. Having said this, I still can easily distinguish between most of the themes from AOW2, even after not playing the game for a long time, because each of its pieces has a soul. I also liked themes of AOW3 from Michel Van Den Boss which could give inspiration in battles and world exploration. It is very unfortunate that I cannot say the same about AOW4.Currently, the game has no handcrafted maps, and the only way to play this game is to enter a random world that often needs to look more attractive. Some of the maps I saw seemed so unrealistic (even by magic standards) that I had to restart the game several times to get immersed in the world. The sea exploration/battles seem incredibly dull and unnecessary (although previous AOW games also had this problem, at least sea exploration was more thrilling and rewarding back then). I also want to question the decisions of Triumph Studios to casual the game by placing harsh restrictions on the number of cities and removing workers/builders units so that the heroes can build new cities. The fun part about the previous game was developing the world on your own, building roads, and eventually migrating your nation to different parts of the world, which is impossible here. This is a massive downturn into more casual gaming, which is a bad sign for TBS games. Look at what happened to HMM series, whose developers decided to take a casual approach.The series of maps they call a story is the worst-written campaign I have seen in a long time. To me, this is just an insult, for I care little about army customization and grinding wheels. The developers clearly spent too much time on the "unnecessary" graphical improvements that they forgot to hire qualified writers. It is funny that I seriously think of sending Triumph Studios my CV/Resume to consider me as their writer. So, if you see a new DLC that adds an exciting campaign, you know what has happened :).I am sorry, Triumph, but you can do better than this. Because of this, I cannot recommend this game in its current state. Notwithstanding, I hope that the game improves, and so will my review.
_childDocuments_.name: Age of Wonders 4

_childDocuments_.review: This seems like a very interesting game created by one of my previously favorite developers of all time. However, while the single player experience is fun and vibrant, the multiplayer section is complete garbage which is a huge let down for someone who has played the previous games to death with my brothers-in-law and put in thousands of hours. I have no idea whether the developers simply don't care that they lied about the viability of MP or if their hands are tied by their publisher but I am quite disappointed and will not support them moving forward after my DLC pass (which I regret purchasing) is complete. TL:DR: Great single player experience, interesting take on 4X. However, MP is a total letdown (desyncs, corrupted files, stupid save file design) coupled with an astounds lack of communication and transparency re: the issue by a company that used to set the standard in that area.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, this is going to be a bit to get into but I'll put the TLDR here first:If you have ever liked any 4X game (Explore, Expand, Exploit, Exterminate) but specifically: Stellaris, Total War: warhammer 3 or Endless LegendIf you have ever liked the old Heroes of Might and Magic GamesIf you like Magic the Gathering TCG deckbuildingIf you like any tactical gameIf you are new to strategy games but love the high fantasy tropes:This game is a I am blown away, I haven't played a videogame in sooooooooo long and felt like I was 10 years old playing my first strategy game for the first time.This game does everything innovative and does it all You expand your cities in a very intuitive way where city placement and growth as choices feel good and important but not huge headaches.The combat system feels like a mixture between Endless Legends and Heroes of Might and Magic and  they did it beautifully. You create your own High Fantasy empire and it is , I'm mulling over a long time what I want to play, so many things to try and I can't get enough of it --- it all leads into what you 'Research' in this game.You research Magical Tomes, NOT Science, the different Magics have their own attribute called affinity. This tells you how much of that magic is influencing your faction and because you can mix and match: It feels like you have lots of funny, cool, or terrifying possibilities to sink your teeth into. It does remind me of thematic magic the gathering deck building and it fits this game soooooo well.Now is this game perfect? No - but damn it is close, honestly I probably won't ever care to download mods as long as the devs put out new content and fix the bugs - which I will maintain. Is very important.It had a semi-rocky launch on bugs and it seems to be only multiplayer ones left, I'm waiting to see how fast they can get fixed and how much the devs are interested in this game long term (past their season pass).I'm interested in this being a permanent upkeep game, in my eyes the game is perfect design wise, give me a longer pantheon tree, more civilization options and more unique map settings. I haven't played games much in the past year, I have played this every day since iv'e found it. I don't plan on stopping anytime soon - I'll update this when Dawn of Dragons releases.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried to give enough time to the game, but I cannot say I really like it. Age of Wonders 4 is not bad game, BUT …1. I love AoW 3, so the game seems to me like a big balance pack. It is probably good for P2P games, because does not matter your starting choices and you have similar chances to win. But it mainly unifies how to play. Result is that the game is not very repeatable. Why to play it again, when it is in 90 % the same?The “balancing” disables some common 4x game tactics. For example expansion, sorry you are limited in number of cities (and heroes). If you want more, use imperium. Finally I found that imperium distribution is one of a few things that could make a difference. Do you want more cities, use imperium; do you want more heroes, use imperium; do you want top ties units, use imperium; do you want some buffs, special abilities, …, use imperium. Otherwise the game is almost the same; only you do not have green units trowing poison, but red trowing fire. In AoW 3 there are OP units, spells, abilities, but each type of ruler have some and usually there exists some contra to eliminate it. And that is the game about know your/opponent strengths, weaknesses and handle it properly. Optional victory could make a sense in P2P. For playing against AI rulers, if you are able to reach one type of victory, you can reach the others, its only your choice what you want.Combat system is balanced too, max 3 sucks that are nearby. Good bye overwhelming defenders, good bye blocking narrow tunnels underground. Improved is also combat AI. On one hand it is good, cause AI is more challenging, on the other hand manual combat does not usually bring significant difference as reward for you time and care. So I stick to autocombat.But AI also behave in strange way. We were ally of 3, rolling over map. The last enemy with the last 2 cities was only thing between us and alliance victory … and war among us was started … and the almost banished ruler won for victory points (Im not proud of it).2. Another issue I have with AoW 4 is “game feeling”. It is not definitely education game, so I expect some fun, some enjoy, some relax. Unfortunately AoW 4 is mostly lacking these for me. What I like at AoW 3:- to develop my empire, build new cities (Sorry # of cities is limited, I reached 8 before game end);- to look for some treasure (Very limited, they are well protected so at beginning of a game you need almost whole army you may need also somewhere else- Protectors level up so later after “epic” battle, you get “basic” shield);- to develop units not only hero (Sorry max rank is limited, tier 1 unit cannot evolve to tier 2, 3 etc., fight are so balanced that your favorite units will die, so do not make favorites);- to make “doom” army at final stage of the game (Sorry, enemy rulers will have the same, … balance over everything);- to use “game changing” abilities, what is very useful at beginning, when each unit means (Sorry these are now available at later research/leveling; yes if you for example convert, stun or banish enemy unit, it could determinate result of a battle, but the difference will be a few units. And at later game it is not the main thing. The main thing are reinforcements that allows you another attack or two in the same turn).Sorry the game is not rewarding me for micromanagement to worth it, it does not make me feel to be creating something extra, does not allow me to have something special I could be proud of. It is like “normal and average” life.3. Third issue is game programming. OMG it is a strategy game not a movie. Nice graphics and effects should be a bonus not the core of the game. I really not appreciate shivering of leaves on trees exploring world map. Actually it is disturbing, I miss some treasure in forests because of it.I have problem with long turns, in later game the opponents turn was even longer then mine. As I find at net it is not rare, but rather often problem. They advice cut down graphics, zoom out, use right button tapping, … to speed up. In one forum a great guy want show off and said we should buy new computer, his 4 year old (top parameter) machine do not have any problem. Cutting graphics to minimum helped a bit.I decided to do something else during opponent turn. I try to read news. Ups… the game was frozen during that time. Opponent could not make their turn without you looking at forests and seas. The game really do not know what is multitasking. You need up-to-date hardware, but software works like in early 90s of last century.I may be, the game is creating local AI center to count NPC actions or it counts 8K graphic effects. But I definitely have not notices that.It is nice that AoW is ready for late 20s, but I play it NOW.The game optimization is the point where programmers did very very poor job.… May be they will release update to fix it...but not for me.ConclusionIf you are keen in P2P competing and you enjoy defending others and use some strategy and game features for it, you can try AoW 4. But you can also play chess or go, what is less energy consuming and has more strategy options.If you want play it for fun, you can several times, but the repetition is not its strong point. Thx Paradox, after Europa Universalis, AoW is another game I loved and you managed to trow it into a shade of average strategy games.
_childDocuments_.name: Age of Wonders 4

_childDocuments_.review: Love the Franchise and The game. The game is beautiful and the region/province system is pretty cool makes you plan out the way to  build out your city. The Wonders can be challenging and custom Faction and races gives you plenty of variety to choose your play style. The AI is pretty smart compared to similar games, and They'll bolster and strengthen themselves before engaging similar to the player. The only thing id be wary of is the game crashing and multiplayer. The crashing is not very consistent and seems to happen for a variety of reason. As for multiplayer its interesting how they did it, you don't need a host to keep playing the game, if someone's game crashing the game continues to go on and they can rejoin without issue. The Multiplayer match can be accessed at any time by players (even if they are the only one) to finish their turn. It is too note your game will not continue until every player turn ends. I had a bug in my multiplayer game after finishing manual combat it was stuck asking me what i wanted to do and wouldn't let me end the turn, simple reload fixed it and it saved the progression automatically. All in all I recommend the game to anyone who likes turn based strategy and/or played AoW3, just be wary of some of the bugs/crashes. I can tell this is a game I will be putting a lot of hours into.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot. Generic fantasy setting (not a movie or book IP) and I love that because the faction builder and world settings are varied and powerful and let me create the faction and setting that fit the mood I want for my playthrough. It has some fun complexity with the diplomacy and espionage systems, which has always been my fav part of a good 4X title. Combat is fun and fights can feel very large without being unwieldy. I really enjoy the immense variety of modifiers available, my units (in different playthroughs using different builds) all became really strong but in such different ways that made for very different gameplay experience each time. Adding a 3rd map layer with the Eldritch DLC plus the great faction editor means lots of replayability so that means good dollars-per-hour value potential. Also I appreciate concurrent turns for multiplayer. Serial turns absolutely ruin the 4X multiplayer experience. Just untenable. This game handles concurrent turns pretty well and I felt like I wasn't waiting too much.

_childDocuments_.review: Good iteration on the series, but it is more of a two step forwards, one step back.The improvements are widely publicized when it comes to how the Minor Factions are handled and the customization of the races etc...The "streamlining" has happened when it comes to trade with other factions. You can't trade item A for item B, or a bunch of items for a territory anymore: You need to trade your items for gold and then the gold for what you want: Thus getting scammed twice by the exchange rates.The other thing they have neglected compared to Planetfall is the sea provinces and zones: Gone are the sea areas to explore and conquer: Water is mostly an obstacle now.This is not a bad game: This is  just a heads up for the features they've removed.

_childDocuments_.review: Seems like latest hotfix has fixed the complaint in my intial review (yay), while it still seems to run max clocks & utility on my GPU, the temperature does not spike dangerously high anymore and I actually feel somewhat safe to play the game now (and I have! And it's great!)TLDNR: I think the best entry to AOW to date. If you're a fan of high customization of races, maps and scenarios in an RNG setting (which grows as you unlock more through the Paragon rank system = win a game, get points and unlock cosmetics,and new map presets/race options), this is the best 4X Fantasy version you will find, and will only get bigger and better with DLCS.Really nice spin on the AOW series, clearing taking lots from Stellaris in terms of customization, but condensed into somewhat of a LITE version of it (or Total War) small maps being able to complete in about 4 hours with lots of toying around) and obviously much longer if you scale it up --- Tome system to modify your race 'as you go' is neat as you don't always follow the plan you first set out to and the results/ending of your race design can be pretty interesting and makes it feel fresh each game.Some people complain the lack of unit upgrades compared to Planetfall, but this isn't really true as it's just been simplified as Unit Enchantments (based on tomes) that run a mana upkeep and apply to your entire army (only to relevant units)... so you cant buff 2-3 units in a group of 10, it'll be 0 or 10, but it honestly saves time and let's you focus more on the other aspects.Personally, the splitting of Draft income (building troops) & production income (constructing buildings) with their own incomes, and own construction timers, is a godsend...I've always hate having to cancel or pause buildings because I needed more troops, or vice versa.The gameplay just feels so much smoother and more satisfying and you can still tech/expand with emphasis on larger armies or stronger infrastructure (or dedicate cities to one or the other).Other complained story is lacking, but there are Story worlds with scripting and such, so it's not like it doesn't exist, personally with all AOW games I generally just played random gen, or custom maps, anyways to keep things fresh/new and unique an experience. I'd only play a story or campaign mission once ever at most.OLD "REVIEW":I think I'd love this game [if it didn't try to immediately melt my GPU in the ...main menu?] ... yeah. :/Don't even think to buy the game yet until at least a week or two when [hopefully] the hundred of bugs in performance, game mechanics, etc. are worked out to justify a fully price game+expansion pass, etc. (clearly not enough, or no QA testing was done, and nothing has got me more depressed after the long wait for this to release).Check the Discussion board / Bugs section and you'll understand immediately -- hope it's resolve soon and hope I can leave a "real" review with more than the 1.6hts of trying to troubleshoot, workaround, tamper and whittle system files, game files and the works in hope I can try to play more than 5s without blowing up my PC.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Civ, but Magical.Also the battles are fought in their own little map based on the area the battle was started. Not directly on the map like civ. I find this more engaging. There is an auto combat to skip these, because it can be tedious to do repeatedly. So when you're sure you can win, you can auto battle to focus on the empire side of things instead of battle. In the event the AI fails to get a favorable outcome in the battle, you can opt to "retry" the battle yourself. This can help you stop certain units from dying by having that manual control.The magic is quite varied and different play styles can be pursued with ease. The major/minor race transformations are pretty freaking cool to see on your citizens, as well as the various effects they can have being quite powerful.World spells and battle spells can really make all the difference in tough situations. The game encourages replayability with various unlocks and meta progression; and the expansions keep adding more and more. Recent updates have improved the UI especially when building provinces that benefit from certain types of neighboring provinces like farms or mines, indicating clearly what is going to provide the adjacent bonus at quick glance. This was pretty easy before if you looked at the border lines and toggling resource icons on and off, but now you can do it much faster and with less mistakes. More time for expansion, conquering or diplomacy when you're not making absolutely sure you're getting the maxium adjacent bonuses. Heros and Forging are awesome and allow even more freedom in your playstyle to spice things up in battle. All in all, would recommend to anyone with a CIv addiction and a hankering for Wizard games.

_childDocuments_.review: This game certainly has some issues. For starters; selecting armies that are on a city tile can be frustrating, especially if the army leader is a flying unit. There is a way around this with the army finder, but the fact that sometimes I have to resort to this is sad. Another problem is that, despite all the choices there are in faction creation and play-styles, the lack of restrictions means that there tends to be a lack of uniqueness.These gripes aside, AoW4 is fun, challenging, and the recent updates help it in bringing creativity to leader and hero builds. The fun factor and replay values far outweigh any and all problems the game has. I definitely recommend to anyone. Also, this game has hotseat: this means that multiplayer games can be played on one machine. Good if you want to test some things out at your own pace, or if you want to play with friend(s) and/or family and not have them commit to something they might not like (or can afford).

_childDocuments_.review: Age of Wonders 4 had the unfortunate start of being a completely competent 4x fantasy TBS that was overshadowed in quality by it's own predecessor, the highly acclaimed Age of Wonders 3. It felt bland in comparison, as if it lacked any real identity of it's own, and after a few games it felt like the game had delivered all that it could. A solid 3 out of 5 in rating, worth the cost but not something I'd necessarily recommend to others.Fortunatly the developers have decided to dedicate themselves to improving their product, smoothing and polishing gameplay, as well as adding more content to the core experience. And as a result I've gone from playing the game for a few dozen hours to hundreds. I feel like I can now recommend AoW4 to anyone who, like me, loves this genre of strategy games. Hopefully it will at the end of it's development stand not just as an equal to the other games in the AoW series, but be remembered as a game that elevated it even further.

_childDocuments_.review: The most amazing civ-like game I have ever played. If you like role-playing, this game have you covered. Races have basic aspects, which you can just use every time, but you can create your own factions with your own idea. Want to make an elven race with focus on magic? Got you! Want the elves to be hunters, with animal companions, and riding wolves? Here you go! The game has many strategic layers, but apart from some (not all) useless magic materials you can harvest in the map, everything you do has an impact. Defeating small monsters along the way with your champion? Congrats, leveling up to face the challenges ahead. Got a new population? Time to decide which province (and its benefits to production of a city) will be added to the city. Made friendship with a city-state? Here is your gold, access to resources, and future possibility of integration. Every single action in a turn can have value. You don't even stop to question if you want another turn. There is so much to do, so much feedback given for your actions in a turn that you just go for the next one, after all, you want to see what happens when your hero invade an ancient ruins to claim it, but you are still six hexes away from it, so, another turn, please!Negative points? This game does not take your hand and teach everything. Also, the game has a story-line, but it is short. The purpose of the story-line is just to teach you how to play the game, and present different world creation templates, so then you will get a better understanding of the worlds you can create. This, allied with the fact that you can create any factions, allows you to create specific worlds with specific factions that fit whatever scenario you can imagine. Want to make a world plagued with the undead, or thriving with wild animals, or abundant with magic resources, you can create it! Want a world with a human feudal faction, an elven mystic (magic) faction, and a dwarven industrial faction? Got you! All the other races just add up the possibilities. Shadow rats with swarm tactics? Right here! Honorable lions Empire? Here you go! In summary, AOW4 is whatever fantasy conquest journey you may want it to be. Now just wait till the dracon faction arrives!

_childDocuments_.review: Age of Wonders 4 is a solid 7 of 10, and could easily reach an 8 with a few fixes.There are major quality-of-life improvements over AoW3 - such as building construction & unit recruitment using separate slots, now - but there are also several drawbacks - for me, the way the UI gets in the way of itself, the "slugfest" AI style, the few but serious bugs/crashes, and the way Auto Resolve Combat is calculated.I was more than a little leery of buying anything with Paradox Interactive's name on it (given the way they've been handling Stellaris and have completely butchered Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines 2 not once but TWICE), but Triumph Studios came through for us, the players. Most of the things we loved about AoW3 are back, like city-building, exploration, and customization - and they padded those aspects a lot. Now you can customize your ruler AND your starting race AND your spell list (through selected tome research). Replayability is still very high, though other reviews are correct when they say it does get samey after a while, and it's easy to min-max a race to get major bonuses early-game. If you start making your own goals or telling your own story, however (such as, "I want to put all minor race transformations on this Godir"), then you can get extra satisfaction out of the game.Certain drawbacks are included, however. The two biggest minuses I see in AoW4 are the way the UI gets in the way of itself, and how pretty much every game turns into a "who's-got-the-bigger-army" slugfest. Often, when I want to click on a specific item in the UI (such as an army stationed inside a city), unless I am very careful, I end up clicking something else in same general area (such as the city). The UI is confusing to navigate, and sometimes unintuitive as to where certain tabs or controls are located (ex: bounties are located under Victory Conditions instead of Diplomacy). If we had a way to customize the UI the same way we customized rulers, that would be golden.In AoW4, there are now several victory conditions & diplomacy has been beefed up - but neither of those matter much, since the AI rulers always create massive armies and prefer to go for the Military Victory above all others. You have to go majorly out of your way - keeping enemies alive on your own sufferance - to score any other kind of victory (like Expansion or Magic). Even if you've had a solid alliance for most of the game, the AI will dislike you enough to declare war if you are the only two rulers left, or if you are trying for any peaceful Victory condition. Thankfully, because of new features like Rally of the Lieges, unit draft, and very common summoning spells, it is easier to create several standing armies than it was in AoW3.On the note of armies, I would give much to see exactly how Auto Resolve Combat is calculated. Often, if an army literally only has a 10-point advantage over the other, they can wipe out the enemy army with few-to-no losses. Alternatively, even if one army is double the size of another, the weaker army can still potentially inflict massive casualties while still losing. The Auto Resolve often defies all expectations. Heroes (including Leaders) and unit Tier seem to have the most impact on the outcome, regardless of unit type or army buffs.My last, and honestly most minor complaint is the few but serious bugs/crashes I've encountered. Mostly these happen when I innocently click on part of the UI (such as one of the dozens of pop-ups you get on a turn, or to end turn), but the game immediately crashes to desktop. When I reload the game (a turn behind) it works fine, even if I click the same UI button again. These crashes have only happened maybe once every few days, but it is worth noting as something for Triumph Studios to address.So overall, Age of Wonders 4 gets a 7 of 10 out of me, which puts it a head above most other games that have come out recently. It seems like Triumph Studios actually play-tested the game for quality control before releasing it, and wanted to improve the series instead of simply make money off the name or recycle the same old gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: AoW4 is all about customization. Customizing your race's appearance, their gameplay features and theme, your leader's appearance gear and play style, you can heavily customize your random maps with various traits and options and you even build your own research tree from a multitude of smaller magic tomes. The idea is to have the ability to make whatever you want, noble knightly frogs, corpse eating barbarian elves, druidic beast summoning orcs, evil, nasty hobitses who kept the One Ring instead of casting it into the pit of fire and have formed an oligarchy based around dark magic. You can stick to traditional fantasy tropes as well of course. Due to all this much less effort was spent on the campaign compared to older games. There are several "story realms" that are loosely connected and continue the story of AoW3 but it's all much smaller in scope. The focus is on the customizable experience, making your own story and the random maps now have a lot of smaller narrative elements, events and quests and, as mentioned before, creating a random map goes far beyond just choosing a size and opponenet makeup and there are choosable "map traits" that can change the aesthetics, climate, difficulty, gameplay and story elements in many ways both big and small. Whether this is good or bad depends on personal taste and priorites but AoW4 does manage to turn itself into a modular kaleodioskope of options (that are too many to adequately describe) and even your basic units can vary greately in terms of appearance and capability.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game for a full year before making my review, bought 5 Major DLC and have gotten many free updates along with just owning the base game. There have been many changes since the release of the game and not all of them have I liked. Some have been good changes like to the astral society and getting 3 different sub traits.Pros =======================================================You can spend a lot of time in the game. Very ImmersiveYou can pick a myriad of options to customise your playstyle, whether they make sense or notBeautiful artwork and graphics - but at this point in gaming history that should be expected imo. We pay big prices for big music and art.Michiel Van Den Bos is a genius and the soundtrack is awesomeCons===============================================================After 400+ hours I can't get over how all my choices eventually feel the same no matter which playthrough. I start with a very interesting race and affinity concept, which plays out through the same similar tome and society choices. Other races can also have the same interesting concept with wildly differing results. It feels chaotic and not in a good way. You can get halfling necromancers and goblin paladins and it just seems if "If everything can be anything than therefore everything is nothing" and the uniqueness that you want to be there, just ultimately isn't. I don't like playing as the Dragon Ruler or the Eldritch Sovereign. I like the mortal champion over the wizard king and personally believe that those 2 options should be the only options. I like the mortal champion much more than wizard king despite until the hero rework the wizard king being the defacto best choice. The ruler DLC for Giant, Dragon and Eldritch Sovereign are just boring. They don't impact your gameplay majorly as you would hope. Despite Giant DLC not being out yet I most likely won't be buying it for the gameplay and my stated reasons for Dragon and ES being boring. My most played races have been the Dwarves, frogs, moles and rats in the early launch of the game, some lizardmen after DD and mostly insects after ER. Because the race traits are not fixed you can still make more tanky/mage-like/hit and run/etcetcetc units. It ends up feeling not special, not unique. Random races and units will specifically start with whatever default traits the game has inherent for them which does lend something to races feeling more unique, but then ruined by the wild other modifiers given them from society and tome traits.To summarise my previous conHaving important choice tied to Tome, Society and traits creates a 6 way problem of each being interchangeable and having an effect on each other, becoming bland and ultimately streamlined.Elemental magic should be their own tomes like tome of PyromancyIce magic should not be tied to shadow affinity. Necromancy has been overhauled and made 10x better but Ice style tomes still make no sense in Shadow Affinity. The AOW2 style of spheres is much better (Life, Death, Water, Earth, Fire, Air)High style Society has effectively been replaced by the new DLC Oathsworn society. Much better implementation of Order society with 3 sub choices of nature, chaos and orderThe way Primal, Astral and Oathsworn is designed should have been how the original Feudal, High, Dark, Astral, Barbarian, Industrial be. Sub specials so the societies change their units and not everything is a carbon copy of another race.The skeleton designs of many models are overused and recycled way too often. Spiders, Dragons, Humanoids. Many flaws in the design show through the cracks after many hours of gameplay. Not to say the 'skins' aren't well designed and good looking but as previously stated when paying big money you expect big art.The game has had visual clipping issues with capes helmets and various other visual aspects, none of which were addressed or fixed when I mentioned them in the discord server.The Devs are split down the middle in the sense of; half of the team are really sweet and great to talk to the game about, the other half are touchy and not able to accept criticism. I was in the discord server many times and ultimately chose to leave permanently because of just how chaotic it is. Again, some devs are really great to talk to and others get super offended at comments being made about their work. I can keep giving more negatives but there are other negative reviews that touch on what I could say.I don't personally like the combat system and I have auto resolved probably 99.9% of my gameplay because it's not like the combat in AOW1. Some like it, I don't.For people who like AOW1/2 This game is a hard pass. At least don't ruin your good memories.For people who haven't played old TBS games like Disciples and AOW, this game is really great. The game tries to cover too many fantasy bases and sometimes you can lose yourself in the immersion and other times you think "Man this is really, really lame.". The company pushes very hard to keep it updated and fresh, the devs are always playing their own game on stream. I hope if the devs see my review they take it with a grain of salt for what it is - 400+ hours playing your game and ENJOYING it.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer, I didn't have performance issue in the short time I played this game so far like some of the others who left a review did. But I seen it often enough that it should be someone one aware of before buying this game.The reason why I don't recommend this game is because the title is misleading. It's more Planetside Fantasy Edition, than Age of Wonders 4. Where most mechanics follows the design of Age of Wonders Planetside with the original Age of Wonder's fantasy skin pasted over. Personally, I liked the mechanics from AoW than Planetside, which is why I feel a bit deceived going into this game blind without doing any proper research (although that's also on me for not doing my due diligence).Overall, this game feels watered down in personality in the name of 'customerization' compared to the older AoW games, even compared to 3rd entry. You get what feels like generic units based on the culture you pick for your faction, rather than unique high tier units based on the race like 2nd installment. It doesn't seem to even have the interesting lore entry for units like the 3rd game did (at least I didn't find it). Maybe I'll have a more positive view on it once I have time to play some more and the Planetside mechanics win me over, but overall, I'm very disappointed in this game, and I certainly won't blindly buy the 5th one if Triumph will make another game in this franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: There are many good things I could say about this game. There are some bad things I could say about this game. None of them matter, and I am not gonna bother. Because it is so bad in one particular area that it will never be worth it    The map AI is painfully passive. Had it been dumb, it could be solved with difficulty settings. But the size of the army standing around their capital doing diddly squat while you are at war and 4 turns away from victory is irrelevant. I have survived overwhelming opponents because they simply did not attack. The only way you can enjoy some challenge is if you are the attacker. If not, you'll enjoy the game for however long it takes you to realise all its admittedly interesting systems are utterly pointless if the opponents refuse to engage. Or you can play online, I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: While Age of Wonders 4 had quite a rough start, I believe Paradox has done an amazing job in making the game a true Age of Wonders game. Many bugs from launch have been fixed including the pesky multiplayer bugs. Additionally, the game has a lot of replayability with many different tomes, cultures, and units. The modding community is also flourishing with many ease-of-life mods and new tomes. Many people have been complaining about crashes due to bugs but I have experienced none of that even though I am playing on an outdated gaming laptop. Overall, I recommend Age of Wonders 4 as a relatively easy to get into 4X strategy game with some challenges for those tougher players. PS: Reviews from early in the game's release do not hold much value anymore as the game has been greatly improved upon.
