_childDocuments_.review: This is an easy stealth game to recommend, especially for anyone who played and enjoyed the first Aragami. Light and shadow are the big power dynamics at work here; you're stealthy and mobile in the dark, literally able to merge into shadows and dart across almost any surfaces. Brightly lit areas keep your character in a corporeal state, putting high stakes on any movement you choose to make while enemies are nearby. This makes navigating the game space a whole lot more interesting, since you can potentially vanish in front of an enemy then reappear behind them, with a bit of care. Aside from this, you gradually unlock a combination of gadgets and shadow powers, and (if you find certain upgrade materials) shadow-powered versions of gadgets. Personal favourites include the shadow mines, which are capable of swallowing multiple enemies into the void, if deployed with the right timing. Being able to blind foes temporarily with Shadow Blind is also nice, enabling you to take on groups of patrolling guards. You can't just use these toys for every encounter, though. Each power and gadget costs resources in the form of scrap parts or shadow dust, which are rare enough to stop players blazing through a mission.Enemies come mostly in the form of security bots, with a few humans added in later. I appreciated that they made the humans... likeable. Irritating at times, but likeable. This, along with the "humans murdered" counter in mission stats, challenges you not to bump off any fellow organics. Without spoilers, being murder-happy will lead to story and gameplay consequences...I think I enjoyed the earlier missions more than the later ones, because the environments got a bit too consistently industrial in the second half of the game. The second and third missions are more open, with big landscapes and locations to explore. The later missions are still good, but there was less focus on the stealth-action elements and more on the puzzle-platforming. Thanks to the "Shadow Merge" mechanics, it held up, but still... I like a good open region with enemies to subvert and take down, and places to explore for loot.The story and humour are probably Ereban: SL's weakest aspects, but the gameplay is consistently on point. I had one bug where I got stuck under the environment; somehow I was able to get myself out again.Overall, this is a great take on the stealth genre. It puts the emphasis on being mobile and aware of your surroundings in a very different way compared to other sneaky games.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by admitting I'm not typically drawn to stealth games, but Ereban managed to captivate me in unexpected ways.The shadow merge mechanic is the star of the show here. _childDocuments_.review: It’s rare for me, a longwinded nitpicker by nature, to emerge from eight hours of anything with nothing to say. After all, my channel has made a meager existence doing the exact opposite: poking and prodding games until they inevitably break, revealing their janky innards upon which whiny critics such as myself love to feast. But when it comes to Ereban: Shadow Legacy—a dystopian stealth platformer that gives you the ability to transform into shadow when... you’re already standing in shadows—well, I am left with surprisingly little to report in the way of either good or bad, which leaves us with the okay.  Though presented in perplexing pieces, Ereban’s story is actually quite simple once you add it all up. You are Ayana, a spunky shadow walker and perhaps the last of the Ereban, a mysterious race that up and disappeared one day for reasons Ayana is still trying to deduce. Now chased for your powerful powers by the well-meaning if wildly unethical Helios corporation, Ayana decides to join forces with a dusty band of domestic terrorists called the Forgotten Suns that live to fight back against the Helios machine. Together, Ayana and the Suns (which is a pretty cool band name) engage in a Helios hacking spree that brings Ayana steadily closer to both unearthing the evil company’s true intentions and the mystery of her people’s disappearance. Meanwhile, the story is fully voice acted, and competently so, but the script suffers from occasionally forced, corny humor. When Ayana isn’t busy shucking corn, she’s probably making use of her handful of gadgets and shadow powers. Ereban gives you a decent assortment of decoys and traps to deploy against Helios’s roaming robot patrols, and if you run out of weapons you can craft more with scrap you gather about the world. While you’re foraging, keep an eye out for shadow orbs, as collecting them allows you to unlock even more shadow powers... that you probably won’t really need to use, because Ayana’s “Shadow Merge” starting power is hilariously overpowered. Really, assuming you monitor your shadow stamina meter and avoid both environmental lighting and the light emitted by Helios forces, you’ll be able to float through most levels undetected. If, despite this, you find yourself struggling against the game’s three robotic enemy types, note that killing Helios's harmless human employees will grant you permanent added Shadow Merge stamina, but kill too much and you’ll unlock the game’s “bad” (read: fun) ending.  During Ereban’s later levels, you’ll begin seeing fewer patrols and more puzzles. For the most part, these puzzles are simple with solutions plastered to the walls in glowing neon blue. After sleepwalking through these, I was surprised by the amount of dexterity required to solve the game’s final few puzzles that make clever use of rotating shadows. It’s a shame the game took seven hours to reach this point, as it's only then that Ereban’s shady central mechanic begins to shine.   Ereban’s in-game visuals are fairly dated-looking and feature a washed-out color palette reminiscent of modern mobile games... which makes the game’s semi-frequent frame stuttering even more disappointing. This said, some of Ereban’s sci-fi set pieces stand out, and there’s a decent variety of biomes to carefully explore. While doing so, however, I can’t say I ever noticed the game’s soundtrack, and the sound design is nothing special. I got to the end of Ereban in about eight hours, but I didn’t come close to finding every collectible, nor did I replay any level to improve my score. Thus, I could see most folks getting closer to 10 hours out of this game. For $25, I consider Ereban: Shadow Legacy reasonably priced, so I’ll leave it with the reasonable score of 3/5 (full scoring breakdown, from “Plot” to “Sound” available in my video review). Let me know if you have any questions about the game, and thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good. The shadow mechanics make for some interesting gameplay through puzzles and platforming. Besides there is plenty of replayability for those who want to get perfect ratings in each level or try different approaches. I liked the character designs and performances a lot. The visuals aren't going for incredibly high fidelity features but the lighting and effects look solid and give the game a unique feel. _childDocuments_.review: Having finished one ghost pacifist playthrough with most side objectives done, Ereban is a decent game that suffers from a lack of smoothness.It initially intrigued me as a fan of Aragami, and the central differences here are enjoyable. Shadow merging and the ability to go on walls opens up a lot of design space, although it could be a little less hand-holding. The controls for said wall-crawling are funky, and the jumping and contextual prompts are often temperamental, leading to frustration, especially since falling deaths are a penalty to your end score. The environments are pretty and nice to figure out, but the open areas tend to be too large and gated awkwardly. The enemies and enemy variety is good, and the non-sniper units could benefit from being a little more threatening. The shadow powers and gadgets are nice, but a tree-reset option feels missing (I can understand it due to it being a shorter game perhaps).Story-wise, the plot didn't grab me personally, and Ayana as a character flip-flopped between trusting - not trusting, friendly - cold for a large part, but the performances were excellent across the board.The visuals were also excellent.The game is brimming with premise, and I await to see what comes next. I recommend the game as the experience it offers is enjoyable and scratches the itch, even with the problems I found.Update: I've since completed all collectibles, S-ranks and merciless. Most of my arguments still hold, with the jumps being less of a sticking point since you get more used to them, and if you are trying to speedrun the missions or get all drone kills, their threat level is usually more important. A merciless run however makes me wish the take down animations were a little faster though.

_childDocuments_.review: Ereban was almost exactly what I wanted: a bunch of meaty, stealth-action levels, tied together with a good-enough sci-fi narrative. I hope the team tackles a sequel and is able to put more work into additional levels and puzzle designs as it felt like there was some potential for the mechanic left on the table.

_childDocuments_.review: A Continuation of the Dishonored & Deus Ex Series.In short, if you're a fan of either or both Dishonored and Deus Ex, you'll definitely want to check out this game. Made by a small studio, they’ve worked on this game for 5 years, and created something memorable  that I wish more people would experience.The gameplay feels comfortably familiar, like slipping into your favorite pair of shoes after some time away—it feels like you never left. I recommend starting on Hard difficulty right away for the best experience.Personally, I always spend my time in Deus Ex crouching and using takedowns on everyone, or Blink + Takedown in Dishonored. This playstyle is easily replicated in Ereban.You’ll also notice similar environmental details, like wall texts throughout Ereban, reminiscent of Dishonored. (I think they even used the same font!) Further references or easter eggs include: 'Karvon Attane,' Mass Effect 3's iconic "Throw it out the airlock" in a lethal playthrough, the Assassin's Creed motto "Nothing is true, everything is permitted" for non-lethal runs, Blade Runner's "Tears in Rain" ending, a Star Wars sand reference, classic WoW Rogue abilities, and probably more that I’ve missed.It’s immediately clear that the developers played—and loved—the same games that I, or we, did. And they’ve drawn a lot of inspiration from them.I mostly opt for the lethal/takedown approach, but the game also accommodates non-lethal playstyles, utilizing gadgets and special powers. These abilities are powerful but limited, though not to the point of frustration, as you get plenty of materials to craft them. I recommend prioritizing the sonar upgrade first, although its duration could have been be a second or two longer. Judging by how quickly you can get caught (on Hard difficulty), a non-lethal Ghost playthrough might even be preferable. Then again, clearing the map opens up more exploration opportunities.The only criticism I have is that I wish more people would buy this game. You often hear YouTubers advocating for indie games or yearning for a return to the way things were—before all the DEI initiatives, microtransactions, and timegating took over. Before games became synonymous with making money rather than creating timeless experiences. Yet, when I look at the number of reviews for this game, it’s pitiful.It makes me lose hope for the future, where all the things I used to love are gone, never to return. Here you have a studio that genuinely deserves our support, offering a game priced the same as a cosmetic or DLC, and too few people are buying it.I wish more people would promote this game.If YouTubers genuinely cared more about games than clicks/views (money), you’d see this game mentioned everywhere.Story: 8/10Evil corporation? Check.Gameplay: 9/10Like a trusted friend whose loyalty never wavers.Powerful, original, and useful abilities: 9/10Due to their strength, you can’t spam the lethal ones constantly, as it would disrupt the balance and difficulty the developers have carefully crafted. Though even if you use them a lot, you will most likely always have a few crafted and ready. You definitely don't feel gimped or short-changed.Cinematics and voice acting: 8/10It doesn’t feel like corners were cut, and this only enhances the experience, making it a very good and memorable game. There’s no pointless text to skip through—just amusing conversations between NPCs, and fairly good main dialogue, especially from Nine, which reminded me a little of the Water Dragon from Jade Empire.(It would have been great if they hired Erica Luttrell as Emily Kaldwin, or Emma Gregory as Minthara, to add a darker tone or make the lethal/darker path feel more justified—or at least somewhat understandable. But hey, I’m definitely biased towards those two. The voice actress of Ayana, Cissy Jones—who also voiced The Absolute in Baldur’s Gate 3—did a fantastic job, no doubt about that.)There’s some platforming, but nothing frustrating and no silly puzzles (looking at you, Immortals of Aveum). Near the end there're two minor puzzles but I watched a walkthrough on YTube for those to get past them quickly. Platforming directions are also provided to help with fluidity—nothing that breaks immersion or hinders your playstyle.Lastly, the absence of a manual save fits the game’s Hard mode. If you get caught, you’ll start a small section over. The game autosaves often, but this adds a small punishment for getting seen. There are ways to force a save, like backtracking or revisiting other save points, so you won’t have to clear out enemies again if you get caught.The AI is fairly agressive —though NPCs follow standard routes, once they spot you (partially or fully), their responses vary. And if you manage to take out several purple repair drones quickly, having a save point would have been helpful, as you probably won’t get that chance again. (or won't be able to repeat the same line of events.)All in all, if you’re a fan of the Dishonored or Deus Ex series, or the Ezio trilogy, I highly recommend this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Most of the game is not bad, but I'm really frustrated about the change-of-domain. It is mostly a quiet stealth gameplay that I enjoy very much, just from time to time there are action sequences that are really killing me. Why do you need to do that?I like the slow play - killing one robot after the other - take my time to watch their walkways and find the best point in time to take them out.What I do not like is the change of this kind of gameplay to completely different set of action sequences like moving in shaddow-form quickly on a complex path.The difficulty of those action sequences may not be that much if you play the game on a controller, but fast moving on a wall following a dynamic path with W A S D keys is above my level. After 50 attempts, my left hand is hurting and my fingers get stiff.If you're looking for a stealth game to be played on a PC - as I do - I cannot recommend this game. Maybe it's better with a controller, but I don't have one (or rather I don't like to use one) to confirm.In this respect it is sharing the same flaw as aragami - why not just stay in the domain of a slow stealth game where you can take as much time as you like to clear a map.I like to play these slow pace games to relax especially after work - like i.e. sniper elite 4/5
_childDocuments_.name: Ereban: Shadow Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: If you love sneaking and hiding in shadows and one-hit stealth kills then Ereban: Shadow Legacy might be the game you’ve been waiting for.  Packed with thrilling action and suspense, you’ll take on the role of Ayana, the last Ereban, a mystical race that has mastered the art of hiding in shadows.  Combining this skill with a nice assortment of upgradable gadgets, prepare for a dark and mysterious adventure that will tax your patience and stealth ability.The core gameplay element in Ereban is shadows and light, and whenever Ayana is in a shadowy area she can blend into the shadows, becoming this sparking fizzle of dark energy, almost like a burning fuse that you can control and move along any flat or vertical surface that remains in shadow.  Obviously, this leads to incredible puzzle potential where you will find yourself crawling along a wall staying in the shadow of some distant item being cast by a distant light source.I had fun with Ereban: Shadow Legacy.  The mix of sneaking and stealth kills reminded me of classics like Hitman, Splinter Cell, and Assassin’s Creed. If you enjoy tension-filled stealth and sneaking around in shadows and even using those shadows for traversal, then you are in for a real treat when you dive into the exotic and dangerous world of Ereban: Shadow Legacy.Read full review at More Steam reviews on our Curator page -
_childDocuments_.name: Ereban: Shadow Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very much a 2010 Xbox 360 game. It's good enough with neat mechanics and it doesn't overstay its welcome or anything. The story is okay, but the stealth gameplay was really fun. It is certainly more forgiving that most others in the genre, but that is a welcome change. I think it might be on the verge of being too expensive but the quality honestly justifies the price tag. A solid 7.5/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Ereban: Shadow Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: Ereban: Shadow Legacy is a beautiful, remarkably competent third person stealther. The art design is excellent with cool character designs and gorgeous environments. The dialogue is solid.  Ereban's headline mechanic, Shadow Merge, is expertly weaved into the environmental design. I highly recommend Ereban for any fans of third person, action-stealth, and adventure games. - Solid dialogue. Love the robots' dialogue especially.- I like Ayana a lot. She's very down to earth. She's a little snippy, sassy, impatient, and very direct. She cuts right to the point and is very single minded in her goal. She's well grounded.- The masks are a cool artistic choice that removes the need to animate mouths. It's a great stylistic choice that's carried by the character designs.- It's like Uncharted 2 without guns, combined with Uncharted 4's open level design. - UI, settings, controls, all great. No notes.
_childDocuments_.name: Ereban: Shadow Legacy

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game with unexploited potentiel. Gameplaywise, movements feel good and your abilities are fun, but there is too little incentive to use them besides the main one (with is a cool one). The level design isn't very complex and always has places for you to hide in: it is too easy for the player to simply sneak past challenges instead of using gadgets and interacting with ennemies. That doesn't mean that the levels aren't engaging to go through, the challenges you face are varied and well deisgned. It is a pleasure to play and its simplicity makes it a good introduction to stealth games with little frustration.The same feeling came to me for the story, with some good elements that don't have time to grow during the 4,5 hours it takes to finish the game, which ends when things start to get interresting. However, the world is intriguing, the art style is really good (with a few striking sceneries) and the story is given life through great voice acting for the protagonist (other performances were good too, it is a nice touch to have every dialogue dubbed). Overall a nice experience, on the chill side of stealth games. I hope the devs will have the opportunity to create a sequel that will truly make use of the strength of their concept.

_childDocuments_.review: There are robots (robotic scum) to slaughter? Then sign me in! But if to speak seriously, I did enjoy playing this game. My real complaints are about how short it is (12 hours while extensively exploring all levels) and about lack of variety when it comes to your enemies (only 4 types). Overall, I rated it 7 out of 10 (on my personal scale). There is a decent story to experience and interesting "shadow merge" gameplay feature to try. I'm a person that needs to kill absolutely every enemy target while been undetected - that's how I'm playing stealth games. So, "shadow merge" made these kills extremely easy. It's a good thing and a bad thing at the same time. Honestly, I had more fun using "shadow merge" as exploration ability rather then for killing. Speaking of exploration, the Radar gadget definitely needs a shorter cool-down and it should highlight items for longer duration. I did miss some precious LOOT since I couldn't determine location of the signal (highlighted item) even after looking for it with several uses of the radar. It just disappearing so fast while you need to check in all 360 degree around you. And then another long wait for the radar to come out of CD. I also hope that devs can do something about inventory capacity: while I understand that they want to limit you in the amount of gadgets you can continuously use (since those are powerful abilities), I also feel irritated when I see there is a scrap to pick but I'm sitting on 20 out of 20 limit. This unpicked loot will be an additional sound signal when I will use my Radar, and sometimes it's just confusing (especially when you have quite a few signals to pick). Last thing to mention about the game itself: it does have replayability. There are more skills there than you can unlock during one playthrough. You can't see the skills you didn't unlock, and different skill set can lead to a different playstyle overall.

name: Somerville
detailed_description: In the wake of catastrophe you must find the means to make your family whole again. Somerville is a Sci-Fi adventure grounded in the intimate repercussions of large scale conflict. FAMILY You embark on a journey to find the whereabouts of your family in the wake of an alien invasion. THE INVASION Live through the personal struggles of a young family separated in the final moments of a global conflict against a hostile alien civilisation. Discover first hand the full impact on others of this catastrophic event. EXPLORE , LEARN , COMMUNICATE Explore the devastation left behind by the invading alien force and those who resisted, learning more about their motives and methods the further you journey. KEY FEATURES Solve the puzzles of an altered landscape drenched in alien sediment Flee, hide from or negotiate dangerous encounters Observe and learn form every alien entity Dig deep and find your way to multiple endings, their meaning and significance JUMPSHIP Jumpship is an independent game studio founded around an original IP by Chris Olsen built in collaboration with ex-CEO and co-founder of Playdead, Dino Patti. Our commitment is to deliver unique experiences that treat people with respect and help expand the definitions of interactive media.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't quite understand why Somerville is reviewed *this* negatively, though I assume it's people going into it with the wrong expectations.Since this game is made by ex-developers that worked on Limbo and Inside, most would assume this also falls into the puzzle-platformer genre and are disappointed when that turns out not to be the case.In fact I would call this much more of a walking simulator with some *very* light puzzling, but with fantastic presentation.If you're fine with mostly just drinking in the atmosphere of a large scale alien invasion for 4-5ish hours, I do recommend Somerville. If you're looking for puzzles akin to Limbo and Inside I suggest you look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Set in the British countryside, Somerville sees an unnamed character and father struggling through a sudden alien invasion to rejoin his family. His journey will bring him about ruined towns and a landscape entirely distorted by the invaders’ incomprehensible, potent weaponry. Despite its low-poly style, an excellent level of detail can be seen in most locales thanks to the care put into polishing their finer details, while a modern lighting and particle effects system gives more eye-candy to each scene. Environments feel interesting and mysterious to traverse, as the alien factor makes the next events unpredictable.There isn’t any writing in the sense of dialogues, files and similar: all actions, reactions and events are narrated purely through visual cues, scenes devoid of any acting or direct narration. While this is a technique already-seen in other titles, most prominently the popular “INSIDE” to name one, it has to be designed and executed well to be effective, which is definitely harder than pulling off a ‘regular’ narrative. In this case the Somerville team missed the mark for two main reasons: first of all, the protagonist feels anonymous and one-sided, as it won’t show any quirks of characters or deeper reactions to the events, thus failing to bind with the player on an emotional and personal level. He will feel like a blank mannequin you have to drive about, while at the same time not having any influence on how he chooses to react to anything. Most actions actually do feel like directionless instruments to further the game’s progression, rather than something someone in his situation would actually do.Secondly, the narrative keeps adding more and more mysterious elements for the sake of keeping attention up, as characters and factions other than the ‘original’ aliens spring up eventually, but fails to properly explain who any of them are or what their purpose is at any point. Even if this narrative style is meant for players to elaborate their own conclusions, it still has to provide some elements to do so… something simply not achieved here. By the end of your adventure, it will feel like the first time you watched Inception at the theater: “what the hell did I just watch?”- that’s not exactly a great feeling.As expected from this kind of game, exploration in Somerville is linear, through different environments that have some degree of interactivity and even a few secondary areas with Easter eggs or optional interactions, that however don’t influence the upcoming events in any way. You’ll usually be free to roam any safe location at will, with environmental cues (lights, graffiti, etc.) marking the way you should go, or anyway be looking at, in order to progress. There are some hazards to account for while exploring even ‘safe’ areas, like heights, water or machinery at times, that can kill you and thus roll you back a short time to one of the frequent checkpoints.Revolve around a mysterious alien power you’ll acquire and evolve through the adventure, capable of influencing the metamorphic alien substance that composes most of their structures present in each area. You’ll eventually be capable of melting and hardening this material through light sources in order to clear the way, create passageways, stop something in place and other uses, each usually tied to a logic-based puzzle you’ll have to solve. These enigmas aren’t very difficult at all, rather repetitive in nature and execution apart from a select few; the variety is just not there, as the game never really builds more upon its basic mechanical foundations, preferring to “play it safe” for the most part in terms of creativity.The chase sequences play out in the expected way for this genre; usually your character will be threatened by either the environment or an enemy, and will have to traverse short sections that involve debris avoidance, some platforming and general obstacle-coursing. These parts are scripted to an extent, however being too slow will lead to death, and have you restarting from the beginning of the “action time”. They are a good change of pace from the usual slow-paced gameplay, and some are genuinely thrilling. Stealth sections are only a few, and generally involve hiding from enemy spotlights that will inevitably lead to your demise should they cross your path. You’ll have to use both solid cover and the shadows they project to stay alive, while also activating machinery to change the environs to your advantage in some cases. They work well enough and have no substantial issues.

_childDocuments_.review: oh man......i want to like this game. it looks and sounds fantastic, just like INSIDE. but the controls are awful. invisible walls everywhere, not just off the beaten path either. its like every object has their collision mesh 150% larger than its visual size, you will constantly be rubbing up against (and slowed down/stopped) by EVERY. LITTLE. PIECE. OF. GEOMETRY.the grab points. they are way too small and precise. you will spend 30% of your playtime wiggling back and forth infront of every obvious yellow colored handle trying to get it to grab the thing an inch from your facethe limited speed. i get that they want you to take it slow and soak in the visuals, but you arent allowed to go faster than a shuffle in wide open areas unless its a scripted chase. even then you will still be limited to slowly, casually, painfully pulling yourself up a half foot rock step with an enemy breathing down your neck. the story is.....ok. i wanted more. there is no conclusion. you will have even more questions than when you started. you could say the journey is the adventure, etc, but look at games like INSIDE for mystery done in a satisfactory waytl:drunlock the walking speed, double the size of the magnetism effect when grabbing interactables, and dont halt momentum when moving towards impassible geometry, and you would have an 8 or 9 out of 10. as it stands, its a frustrating 6

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best examples of a game that is so close to being REALLY FREAKING GOOD. Pros: Breathtaking vistas and design. Actual incredible work. Some of the sound design gives me goosebumps. It's really outstanding work. Cons:1. ReadabilityThe readability of majority of scenes takes a backseat to visuals. It's like they didn't play test their game. I spent 20 minutes in the mines only to realize that I could move to the left through a wall that looked solid from the current camera angle. The bus "puzzle" is another example of that. How was I to know that I could enter the wheel well when it doesn't read that I should? 2. CameraI really get it. The places your artists made are stunning. Downright gorgeous at times. However, I cannot ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ see where my character is and where I need to go. Please push in the camera when it's not time to look at the pretty space. I cannot see my character and I am not getting a magnifying glass out to find where my character is. Many of the opening sections were so bad I had to get inches from my screen. It would be one thing if this game was 2D, but it's 2.5D. Unacceptable. Give the main character a safety vest or something so I can spot him easily. It doesn't help that his color palette blends in with the environment. 3. JankPhysics are cool. But Somverville's are inconsistent and unreliable. Moreover, I had to restart multiple times to ensure that a solution wasn't a bug. Sometimes melting rocks produces a ton of water, sometimes it doesn't? I have no idea whats happening here. Honestly, if you fix these three things this could be an amazing experience. The game is a feast for the eyes, however I cannot recommend this game in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite a disappointing game. While this games comes from some of the creators behind the game INSIDE, it does not share the same qualities that made INSIDE such a great game. Even unmoored from INSIDE, in its current state, Somerville does not stand out as a good game on its own.The visuals and the audio are good (the sound design was actually FANTASTIC and probably the best aspect of the game). It shares a lot of the same visual design language as INSIDE, but that's about the only positive aspect of this game, and even then it comes with some caveats. While the visual elements and environments are striking and memorable, this game oddly seems to suffer from performance hitches. It was unplayable on the steam deck, averaging under 20 fps, but even when playing on a gaming desktop, there were still odd skips and stutters throughout the game. So the visual experience was a bit hindered by less than ideal performance. Another thing to note was that sometimes environments were a bit cluttered, mix in some interesting choices of camera angle, and I was often left confused as to where the player needed to go next to proceed. This persisted even as I was replaying sections of the game.The biggest negative aspect of the game, and frankly, my biggest gripe with it, is the gameplay. The gameplay experience was marred by all sorts of bugs and glitches that ranged from mildly annoying to bugs that downright halted progress (fortunately for me, I didn't encounter any show stopping bugs until after my first playthrough, though my first playthrough still had many minor and moderate bugs.)An example of an annoying bug was the inconsistency of interacting with objects. There'd be a lever that the player needs to pull, but more often than not pressing the interact button will do nothing unless the player positions their character in the EXACT position that the game wants you to be in.This resulted in many puzzles taking more than twice as long to solve, as I often had to mash the interact button while shimmying my character in the hopes that they eventually interact with an object (on average I would try to interact with basic levers & doors about ten times before I would get it right.) This was especially frustrating on my first playthrough as I would enter a new puzzle area, attempt to interact with a lever/door/piece of debris/etc. and after 3 or so attempts to interact with an object, I would assume that I am incorrectly trying to interact with a piece of scenery, only to come back to that object and mash the button until my character would finally grab it.Another negative example of the gameplay was the movement. Moving the character always felt like a chore more than anything. The movement speed of your character is always fluctuating depending on the context of the situation they're in. If they're being chased they will break into a run/sprint. If you're in a puzzle area your character will walk. My big issue isn't the context based movement speed, it's mainly the fine tuning and feel of it. The character's walking speed for most of the game is frustratingly slow. This was compounded by "point-and-click" style puzzles that often involve going back and forth in certain areas (this was exacerbated by the interaction bugs I mentioned above.) I found myself unconsiously straining the thumbstick against the edge of the controller as I was trying to get the character to pick up the pace. I would also hold down the interact button in the desperate hopes that my character will start sprinting like they would in the chase sequence just moments before. Another issue with the movement is that the joystick movement seems to be tied to the camera rather than the character, so even if your character just needs to move from left to right, since the camera will rotate to keep the character in frame, the angle that the joystick needs to be held at will fluctuate from one end of a room to another. I found myself looking down at my controller to see that, in order for my character to walk directly to the left, I had to push the joystick LEFT AND SLIGHTLY DOWN AT AN ANGLE. This is just a few examples of the weird dance I had to do just to get my character to walk in a straight line (and very often I still ran into my fair share of walls and obstacles.)The story was... okay? Again, much like INSIDE (and by extension LIMBO) the story of the game includes no dialogue and is told purely by the actions, environments, and situations that the character finds themselves in. Without going into spoiler territory I will say that there are multiple endings, and by design the game will most likely have the player go with a "bad" ending on their first playthrough, which will leave the player with a lot of questions. In order to get to the "good" ending, you will have to play through the game and look for hints that you couldn't understand the first time around (you'll still probably be left with just as many questions though.)The multiple endings isn't the issue, and neither is having to replay to get the "good" ending. The main problem with the story is that it's really hard to invest in the main character, and often the pacing of the game was so slow and stilted that I was often not thinking about the character's motivations. I think this is due to the middle section being too long, too slow, and too isolated from the main events of the story (avoiding spoilers but for those who've played I'm talking about the underground section.) Credit where it's due: there are a few set piece scenes in the game that were awesome and stunning (mainly the sequences with a lot of action and chaos,) but these didn't tend to pertain to our character's journey, and more or less served as theatrical eye candy.So, to recap, Visuals&Sound were good, Gameplay was buggy and poor, Story was okay with some highs and some lows. The biggest problem is that INSIDE had, at least in my opinion, NAILED (dare I say PERFECTED) all of these criteria already!INSIDE's Visuals&Sound were on par with Somerville (although Somerville often has larger scope than INSIDE.)INSIDE's gameplay was near flawless in almost every aspect! Movement in INSIDE never felt frustrating, and the character handled interactions with puzzles and the environment with ease (the controls in INSIDE did a great job of inferring what the player's intent was rather than just bluntly feeding inputs to the character. ie: The character would often move itself towards objects if the player tried interacting with something that's slightly out of reach.)The story is the most subjective point of comparison between the two games. Some people will like Somerville more for it's world building and high octane action (most of which is happening  the player rather than

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure if I've ever written a review, and if I'm correct that this is my first, I'll keep it brief anyway.First, Somerville is visually quite appealing.  The art style, implementation and tone are superb.  The mechanics around material melting or solidifying is executed well.  The sound design is also excellent, creating really an amazingly atmospheric experience.  Plenty of other reviews have drawn the comparison to Inside in these regards, and they are correct.However, once we get beyond the audio/visuals, the rest of the game is unfortunately a bit of a slog.  The setup of "the story" is quite promising and heavy at first, but the story is barely expanded on: guy is separated from his family due to an alien invasion, and tries to reunite with them.  There's some oddness about three super powers from some (fellow human?) super soldiers, which are used to help you progress, but absolutely nothing is explored in depth.  And then the ending is abstract and vague.  But there is zero elaboration.  I'm not looking for an epic here, but we learn literally *nothing* about the aliens or why they came.  We learn nothing material about these super soldiers (who we *assume* are humans too?), how they know how to use the same alien powers, heck how there is even this apparently technologically advanced resistance in the first place, etc.   Throughout the game, the puzzles, which are all like Inside's: solve some environment situation to progress beyond an obstacle, are brutally simple.  I don't mind some simple puzzles, but it basically started feeling like a walking simulator after about 10 minutes.Which brings me to the last unfortunate aspect: the controls.  I played with a controller (the default, I believe), and everything about this game is sluggish to the point of becoming enraging.  Navigation lacks responsiveness, and your walking speed (there is only one) is so slow that I'm genuinely suspicious it was done on purpose to make the play time longer for the price.  I'm being serious.  It probably took me 5-6 hours to complete this game (some pausing in there due to real life), but it would have been a 2hr game max if the character simply walked faster than a snail.All this being said, I don't *regret* the purchase entirely, as I'd really like to support and see more stuff from Jumpship.  I think the potential is clearly immense.   But unfortunately Somerville, which initially looks incredibly promising, turned out for me to be a pretty boring slog that just happened to be really nice on the eyes and ears.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: Another "wish there was a maybe" button. It's not a bad game but I have a hard time recommending it for the money or time investment, short and bundled though it may be.I normally love me a slow, linear walking simulator with environmental storytelling, but Somerville overdoes it on the "slow" to where it really feels like it's just padding for time for some reason. A lot of the "puzzles" are just figuring out where in the not-quite-linear 3D space you are supposed to stand, or which button they want you to press when. Also, I hate "stealth puzzles". I would compare them to autoscrollers in platformers except sometimes those are still fun. Stealth puzzles are timed things you have 0 agency over and often the longest time waste in any game that has them. There are only a few in here but they still get annoying. I really think the glacial pace of the game is the biggest problem. You could shave 30% of the time off easily and it'd be more enjoyable. The unskippable credits between the final ending scene you have to sit through 4 times if you want to see the endings (and get the achievements) is a pretty good example of the game just trying to waste your time.Another major problem is either the environmental storytelling isn't enough, or the story is so overly simple that it feels underwhelming. It feels like there's a lot more they're trying to convey but it's hard to know because there's nearly nothing beyond the hint that maybe there is. Planet of Lana did this much better (actually a ton of games tell more details and depth with no words than Somerville).Somerville has some good moments but everything else drags it down. I don't hate that I played it but I feel like the time would have been more enjoyable elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: I feel bad writing a negative review because I thought Inside and Limbo were great and this game really shows that Jumpship has potential. But If you buy this game because you enjoyed Inside or Limbo you're going to be pleased with the art style and disappointed in everything else.TL;DR the movement is frustrating, the puzzles are not really even puzzles,  and as great as the art style is, the game has very few moments that allow it to shine. Opting for 3d movement instead of 2d creates plenty of opportunities for jerky immersion-breaking movement and collisions without adding anything really substantial save for being able to move into occasional deep cinematic backdrops. And the movement speed is in almost all circumstances way too slow. There are scenes where you ought to be running for your life to dodge being spotted and the only option you have is a slow shuffle. Matter of fact with the exception of 2 or 3 very short sequences the whole game is spent at a slow shuffle. To make matters worse, in addition to the slow movement speed an overwhelming amount of the environments involve these unnecessarily drawn out paths through them. There are plenty to list but a good example of this is an instance where you walk through a grocery story and are forced to zig zag through every single aisle and do a 5 second animation to move a shelf 3 times, and another 5 second animation to pull open the sliding glass doors. Meanwhile at the end of each aisle is a box blocking your way, but the boxes are the same size as the ones you climb over all throughout the game. I understand that the quality comes from experiencing the environment but when done in this way it seems forced and unnecessary. This is the case for many of the puzzles, they are often as simple as turning on a light to get through somewhere, and all turning the light on requires is climbing a ladder to get to the plug and jumping back down to the switch. I get that this isn't trying to be a high level puzzle game but when the "puzzles" are just walking to the end of the room and back 2x they feel more like inconveniences than gameplay. Which brings me to my third point. Despite the great style of the game and the opportunity to use the 3d movement to move into cinematic depths, an overwhelming amount of the game is spent in a damn claustrophobic mine shaft that does nothing for the story or building the setting. The worlds under alien attack on the surface and you're just crawling (or shuffling) through dark nondescript stone caverns for what felt like at least 50% of the game (not including (spoiler?) the excruciatingly long sections in the late game where you are walking through grey illusory stone walls over and over again). Don't get me wrong, the game is beautiful at times and sets up a couple of great locations and sequences, but Limbo and especially inside had a way of making you feel like you were in this unique environment the whole time, while Somerville puts some significant gaps between those moments.There's more to be said but these are the core issues that jump out after just completing the game. Took 3 hours.So yea, you move noticeably too slow, and spend enormous amounts of time looking at grey story-agnostic stone walls, with the non-walking gameplay mostly being confined to avoiding timed spotlights and moving lamps around. Atmosphere shines at times and when given the opportunity the visuals show great skill, so I am hopeful for the next game.  Giving more attention to gamplay and memorable environments seems like something Jumpship could easily do. If this is paired with the ambition to bring emotional depth and go beyond 2d design then I suspect what is to come will be great.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write reviews, but I'm making an exception.  Did I play the same game as all of these negative reviewers did? First of all, some of my favorite games of all time are Another World, Flashback, and Inside.  This game (despite needing some minor polish) is worthy among those titles.  It's amazing, thought provoking, science fiction.  The "2001" of video games if you will.I don't know if all the negative reviews are due to the fact that we've been force fed a diet of mental baby formula in our pop culture for the last few decades, but I'm sad to live in a world where this is not considered an amazing work of art.  Because that is what it is, an amazing work of art.Jump Ship, you've created a masterpiece.  I've been a game developer for 22 years and these are the types of experiences that I always long for.  ...Wading through the endless handheld / juvenile story telling that permeates this industry to find those rare gems like this one.  I'll be thinking about this one for quite a while.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I really, REALLY liked my experience with Somerville, but I can understand people's frustrations with it. It feels like a game where the director clearly had an IDEA, and then maybe someone left during production, or their design lead or someone just couldn't crack the puzzle of how to put that idea into a solid, polished game, with good conveyance and flawless technical execution. Instead you end up with a bold cinematic adventure, with astonishing audiovisual scope and ambition, incredible sound design, inventive and haunting setpieces, occasionally marred with moments of wandering around an area over and over looking for something to interact with. "... Oh, am I supposed to do something? Do I need to push this?... no? Oh, do I push it the other way? .. wait, did I miss something earlier? ... This doesn't open, does it? Hm, doesn't look like it. Where am I supposed to go? .... "It's not enough to ruin the game, but it is at odds with how amazing everything looks and sounds, enough to snap you out of the magic from time to time. For some people, it'll be too much, and there will be too little to play in terms of pure gameplay.As a journey however, outside the occasional "ok now what do I do?" moment, it moves along quickly, it looks constantly incredible, and will remain with you after you finish it. The endings are very, VERY cryptic, and a lot of people will probably default to one of the "bad" ones through no fault of their own, so there too I can 100% understand someone walking away from the game disappointed.Stick with it tho, if you like cinematic adventures. Once you finish it, read up on the themes of language and communication, maybe even look up a guide to get the other endings if you don't feel like getting deep into it. They're all very memorable and worth experiencing.Somerville is an extremely ambitious attempt at a seamless cinematic adventure, with heavy themes of personal sacrifice, breaking barriers, and learning to understand and communicate. It is blemished by technical stuff like framerate skips, and a few choice moments of "what do you want me to dooo?", but overall I very much enjoyed my journey through it. Buy the bundle with Planet of Lana when it goes on sale, they're both a treat!9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a great atmospheric, cinematographic, sci-fi, puzzle adventure game, in the vein of Another World.  I've read a lot of "It never explains what's happening" or "He walks too slow" reviews and all I can say is, chill out, take in the sights and sounds, and use your damn imagination.  This is a top shelf, artistic set piece, not a run and gun platformer.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: I finished this game wondering what I had just experienced. No words are spoken, nor is there anything to read through the game to  explain what is happening. Somerville is entirely a thematic experience with us to interpret everything in our own way. It's a combination of "Inside" & "War of the Worlds". I recommend playing with a good headset because the sound design in this game is very good. It's also a very short game. I'd place it right up in the ranks of Limbo, Inside, & Journey.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get the cons out of the way first. Also, wait for a sale.Cons:- Interactables are sometimes tricky to activate based on your position.- Game is pretty short for its price.- Narrative is VERY abstract, which based on what you enjoy might ruin your experience with the story.- Final puzzle for the different endings is almost IMPOSSIBLE to understand without paying close attention throughout the whole game. The two guides from  冰河洗剑 help a great deal in not only getting those endings, but understanding how there were hinted and what's going on in the story.Pros:- STELLAR atmosphere and mood from its audio and art direction.- Clever puzzles. No puzzle designs overstays its welcome, and keeps variety and ideas fresh.- Unique gameplay mechanic/gimmick of affecting alien material, with fantastic visuals and animations.- Mostly satisfying pacing. Despite the game being short, the journey you take is well paced, at least until you get to town. But even then, you really feel the journey your character took, which adds to the already emotionally effective story telling.This is why, at least on sale, you should get this game. If you're a fan of what you saw in the trailers, and enjoy 2.5D games, this is a really nice one.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Inside. This is not on the same level. The atmosphere is intriguing but the controls and often lackluster puzzles make this a mediocre experience. Some great but unrefined ideas. Get it on a good sale or ignore as there are better games out there. It's a shame as the visuals are pretty and the sound design is awesome (the sound gave me Inside vibes!)
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: I want to kick myself in the face for listening to the critic reviews before the Steam ones because HO BOY I did NOT enjoy this. The opening scene is fantastic and it does have an interesting central game mechanic but the controls are awful and the gameplay is janky as hell. Interactive objects aren't highlighted properly and sometimes it's hard to even INTERACT with them, puzzles do not feel clever or intuitive (there were a number of times where I was like "what the hell am I supposed to do?"), and I just found the story hollow and meaningless. It just felt super frustrating to play. It's possible that the PC port isn't good (I remember the store page initially saying that a control was required, which implies this was originally meant for consoles), but either way, I feel like any enjoyment I might have gotten out of an otherwise acclaimed game was robbed because of how bad it felt to play. I hope this gets a patch soon so I can give the game a second chance, but for now, I just get no enjoyment out of it, and recommend everyone else to just stick with Limbo and Inside.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fine from a story / progression point of view, it took me 4 hours to finish it (i am a very casual player), the ambiance, music, atmosphere and style are very nice. However, playing it was not a nice experience. - This game is DARK, a lot of the screen space is blacked for no reason, and during some scenes you barely see your character. - You will struggle to find what to climb / where to go. Lots of clipping with the environement, difficulty finding your way around. This is mostly annoying for some "puzzles" where you just have to try and try again before giving up and looking up a walkthrough that shoes you EXACTLY WHAT YOU WHERE DOING except 2pixels to the right. - This game is linear but not really, some scenes take place in a weird fake 3D where you struggle to find your way or to know what you are supposed to interact with. - A lot of the end game is just pressing forward while clicking on the mouse.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: To kick things off, I'll start by saying that I know its not entirely fair to criticise a newly formed studio and their first release but Jumpship took enough top brass and creative talent from Playdead to have been able to make something better.I loved Limbo and Inside so was hoping for so much more.While Somerville is absolutely stunning to look at and even better to listen to, its nothing more than a pretty tech-demo. At just over 4 hours of game-time it represents bad value for money and even if it was cheaper, the game was all potatoes and no meat!Lots of walking around, rubbing up against objects to see if they could be moved or interacted with and when you did manage to find something of interest, you only had a couple of tricks up your sleeve that weren't hard to master or caused you to stop and scratch your head to work out the solution.I know that many here don't like Steams binary 'thumbs up or down' review system but for this game, its a clear thumbs down, at least for the release price.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most awe-inspiring interactive sci-fi stories I have ever experienced! I went into Somerville with pretty low expectations, given the negative reviews, and while I was often frustrated with poor controls and unintuitive gameplay, I mostly was on the edge of my seat and came out wanting more! INSIDE was a revelation for me, and it really changed the way I thought about game design and interactive storytelling. While Somerville is no INSIDE, it is not too far off. The puzzles are MUCH less involved. Somerville feels like it takes the chase/hide mechanisms from INSIDE and pushes them a little bit further, while majorly dialing up the science fiction and supernatural elements. Disappointingly, the supernatural abilities in the game introduce a potential for some really innovative puzzle and level design that never really gets fully realized. However, the engaging story, cinematic visuals and incredible sound design make Somerville a real achievement in visual storytelling. Get it on sale. Play it in the dark. Use the biggest screen, and the highest fidelity sound system you can find!
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: I had such high hopes for this title. It shares a pedigree with Limbo and Inside, two games known for their alluring visual style, puzzles, and atmosphere.  While I appreciate vague storytelling, I do require a modicum of visual narrative. Somerville doesn't feel like a cousin of Inside or Limbo but rather reminiscent of those painfully derivative knock-offs that don't offer enough puzzles or narrative to be recommended. Not a single puzzle had my head scratching for more than 10 seconds, and there weren't enough of them as often I would walk for ten minutes before encountering one. Given my experience in these types of games, I am usually patient. I take my time and try to enjoy the scenery. Given that, I was still able to wrap Somerville in less than 3 hours.  That's insane for a game charging this much. I know it says 3.1 on my record, but that takes account of me sitting through credits, baffled by the game's logic to end when it decided to. Just when you acquire your third ability, the game barely makes use of it before an ending that makes Inside feel straightforward. And let's not ignore the game's polish in that it isn't. You get hung up on terrain, characters vanish and reappear, and navigation can be a real pain as you try to understand where you are supposed to walk to. That ended up being more of a chore than the puzzles. The puzzles were easy. I bet I spent twenty minutes of the game wandering around a room trying to figure out where I can walk to. It's such a damn shame as I was really looking forward to this title. Also, most of the trailers ruin the game's most interesting moments, so if you think there is some great revelation or moments the game is holding back, sorry to disappoint, but that won't happen.Finally, a mild spoiler regarding the ending. It concludes with a puzzle so badly communicated, that you are not even sure that it is a puzzle the first time you play.  In fact, you'll likely have to read discussion groups to discover this. To make matters worse, solving this puzzle requires you to pay attention and interpret moments from the whole game, moments that don't appear important...meaning if you did not pick these up, you have to replay the game. And even if you do pick them up, the final solution still requires a hell of a lot of guesswork. You're likely to default to one of the game's "bad" endings. This results in a slog that could have been solved if the game had a modicum or foresight to have you replay these moments before the end or have a series of flashbacks so you can remember the final solution.  I know people want to feel smart for having to figure this out, but Somerville is a narrative failure. Seriously, I just finished Scorn--that game's a hot mess and it made more sense than this.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: For someone who worked on Limbo and INSIDE and left Playdead, this is really disappointing.- The character controller is floppy and the animations do not blend well.- There are far too many instances of geo clipping when it comes to collisions and there are a lot of bugs.- The frame rate is locked to 60 fps. In this day and age, why??- It does not make use of your entire display, there are black bars at the top and bottom. Simply a waste of real estate.- The ant-aliasing option has ZERO effect, if it's on or off, low or high. It can't be overridden, either.- For what it is, the performance is all over the place.- Sometimes your monitor will flicker black (even with the latest drivers).The one good things I can say about this game is that the idea is compelling, but believe me when I say it is horribly executed. I've only played it for about an hour and I will likely never touch it again, so thank goodness I purchased it on sale. Even at that price, I think it's pretty bad.If you're expecting something like Limbo or INSIDE, stay away! This is a janky mess. It doesn't feel like it even had half of the love or care put into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: Big fan of Inside and the work done by the creatives of this game previously but this one does not hit the mark. From a artistic perspective this game is absolutely incredible. The landscapes are evocative and amazed me. The sound design and music astounded me. But the actual puzzles were extremely underwhelming and the general act of playing the game just didn't land. A lot of this had to do with the endings. Normally when a game has multiple endings you can kind of figure out how to get those naturally. But when some of those endings are a little too arcane to parse that I needed to actually just look up a guide didn't feel great. Overall, I can't really recommend this game. It is an astoundingly beautiful game that had some great artistic direction, but falls short in the mechanical.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard review for me to write as I was so desperately looking forward to this game. Unfortunately, it just didn't live up to any expectations. I was able to reach the ending at three and a half hours, which makes me question the current price tag.The gameplay is aggressively mediocre and is seriously held back by the jank geometry that makes maneuvering incredibly frustrating and confusing. Moving and interacting with things in general is just not well done. The gameplay is fine at first but doesn't really offer much afterwards. For a cinematic story game, I don't feel a lot of emotions. The main character shows no emotion and just seems to be going through the motion which makes me simply not care about what's going on in the game. He shows absolutely no concern when he leaves his only companion, the dog, behind for most of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: Was very excited for Somerville, have had it on my wishlist since last year when it was announced. Unfortunately does not live up to the hype. While the art is beautiful throughout, and the story ideas are interesting at the beginning, the plot and gameplay degrade quickly over the VERY SHORT runtime. This game only takes about 4-5 hours, and half of that is frustration from unintuitive puzzles that are often hampered by the forced perspective of the camera POV. I loved the cinematic visual storytelling, but those techniques often directly interfered with the gameplay. Way too much of the game is spent in underground tunnels with very little significance to the story. In many ways this game is just an inferior remake of Inside, both in structure, the look of the worlds and art style. The character controls are clunky and sluggish. Not being able to run or jump gets frustrating very quickly. I found the last act of the story to be very rushed and confusing. All 5 endings are confusing and unsatisfying, unlike Inside which had two very jarring and thought-provoking endings. I wanted to love this game. The sound design is incredible. The music is great. The graphics, art, and animations are gorgeous. The basic fundamentals of a game like this - interesting story, fun puzzles, and functioning mechanics fell short.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like Somerville but it really isn't a good game.The atmosphere, art style and especially the sound design all are great but the things that actually make a good game are very poor.  The gameplay and level design are both utter garbage, with the early level design in particular being abysmal. The game also seems like it was rushed out, there are numerous technical problems, ranging from the interaction hitboxes being way too much small so you spend a good 10 seconds on some trying to find the perfect pixel the game expects you to stand for the interaction and the character clipping and getting stuck on every single tiny pebble of geometry; up to the game outright breaking if you try to play with a K+M without 1st configuring it and one level just refusing to load for me, forcing a restart.  There also seems to be a small but frequent stutter issue.The story is so-so, you have the overarching alien invasion which is interesting but as the game goes on it just throws new things at the player in an attempt to keep them engaged without any attempt to reason or explain them, things just happen and you go along with it.  The characters also really aren't characters, there's no trace of personality to latch onto, except maybe the dog so there's no investment in anything that happens to them.I give Somerville a 5.5, i'd go as low as a 4 cause I really didn't have a good time but the art style, sound design and surprisingly good opening chapter help keep the game out of true trash tier.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of bugs. From errors popping up reporting missing game assets, to random crashes, glitches that kill you for no apparent reason, and one instance of my entire computer locking up and needing a hard reset. It's an obviously unfinished game and that sucks.There is a lot to like about it otherwise. The art direction is stellar, even if it's not very original considering the pedigree of the developer. The world is at least interesting, and there are a few really cool setpiece moments.But the gameplay itself isn't fantastic, even without the bugs. The mechanics are extremely limited, and nothing very clever is done with them. It gets boring pretty quickly. A much bigger problem though is just how unpolished things are, from janky animations, nonsensical invisible walls, controls that don't quite work half of the time. All of those things break immersion, and they are constant, which makes it really hard to appreciate the good bits. Few and far between as they are.Can't recommend without a plethora of improvements, and a price drop to like $10.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: INSANE art direction and sound design. Great story, heck of a ride. 10/10 from me. An alien invasion story somewhere along the lines of War of the Worlds + Arrival + Close Encounters of the Third Kind + a tiny touch of Interstellar + a tiny TINY touch of Color Out of Space (the vibe, mainly - there is no body horror). I'm placing an emphasis on Arrival due to the theme of communication and its ability to completely change the future of everyone on Earth. You can try to learn the alien language in Somerville, or not. There are 5 possible endings to the game and while you can just stumble into most of them, the ending you get ultimately depends on how much effort you've put into learning to communicate. This is a side-scrolling game with light puzzles and no dialogue, similar to Playdead's games (Limbo, Inside), but technically far less polished. It's got that low budget jank, but this didn't hamper my enjoyment. I felt that the gameplay and controls were pretty intuitive, but it might not be to everyone's standards.

_childDocuments_.review: STONERVILLEIt's a trip. Ok, maybe not the best of the genre but a fairly good one nonetheless. Actually if you can stop comparing it to INSIDE, you will enjoy something different, worth your time. Visually you can screenshot every scenes,  there is this sort of alien corruption that looks like red, blue and purple embers of burning wood and it sounds like ASMR when you interact with it. It's also ASMR for your eyes when it reacts to your light!The story is cryptic, but I like it this way. I don't need to "understand" every painting when I visit a museum. And even tho I didn't get it, I can tell there is something smart and interesting, and if not, I would rather keep this impression over a story badly told. I have the choice to go deeper into it or be satisfied with it. Either way, I had access to a full experience with a beginning and an end. Personnaly it made me wonders for a fews hours and I enjoyed it. I am thankful for the good time.Gameplay wise is not revolutionnary. Yeah pushing crates and opening doors, wouhou, fun ! But every time you interact with the cubical goo its very trippy and quite unique. Plus the game is short so you might finish it before getting bored with it. It's worth the price. Come on peeps, Indie game developers needs to pay their rents too !
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: I can see why the reviews about this game are so divided, but for sure the game's negatives don't outweigh the positives.Despite the fact that the game has some minor technical issues, I think its priority is to immerse the player in its world and atmosphere rather than providing a "classic gaming experience".For those who love to unravel a story through beautiful scenes and mysterious details, Somerville is recommended 100% !Artistically, Somerville is a masterpiece and surely those who admire art in general will deeply appreciate it. Almost every frame is a wallpaper. The story is told silently through the artwork and, although it is quite clear, it leaves room for personal interpretations, which is something I love. Generally, the comparison with Limbo or Inside is inevitable and the fact that both visual and audio assets are so close to those of Inside gave me the nostalgic feeling of "the easter egg" concept, making me look for connecting links for these two worlds.The gameplay is slow and quite similar to the Playdead's games, but Jumpship has added a more active action mechanics through the weapon solutions. The puzzles are decent, most of them really clever but not too hard, while others are pretty simple and do not require further thought. At some points I would like the game to give me a hard time. I think I only stuck one or two times but that doesn't make the puzzles disappointing in any case.The biggest problem I encountered is the controling of the character when he needed to sprint. I don't know if it's my controller's problem but I had to switch to a keyboard to get through this particular action level. That issue threw me out of my immersion but it didn't spoil the overall experience. I would have loved to see Playdead's thoroughness on some of the interaction points or some awkward animations, but these weren't game-breaking issues for me.Overall, Somerville is a beautiful work of art that deserves to be experienced.I can't say it surpasses any game of Playdead, but it's definitely a game you won't regret playing. I really enjoyed it!
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: Begins quite atmospheric in sound and action scape. This is also where you see the first design problems with how the game plays too. It starts off pretty epic, and quickly becomes nothing more than a mild puzzle walking sim. You're given 2 super powers making this less about surviving, and very much more about moving from one dull place to the next completing one answer puzzles (when you manage to find the components to interact with for them).  Many times I thought how easy these obstacles could be solved if I wasn't restricted by invisible walls, or a character with incredibly picky choices where to climb/move. There's a long segment of being underground which was pretty dull, with many seen before puzzles.  As for story, that fell flat the moment you where inside an experiment facility by other people. It gets needlessly pointless (random, and very loose gameplay) from that point on.Totally not worth the time nor money. If you are super curious, just watch someone else play it. You'll get the same experience without having to experience the game's problems first hand. About the only aspect I loved was the start before you get your first super power, mostly because of the sound quality.I'd recommend INSIDE instead which is far better made, or even the Little Nightmares series.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm playing this with a controller, as I believe it is supposed to be played. It's so frustrating to go to every possible door or gateway (or whatever you have to grab), spend five seconds pressing the button there and then getting to conclusion "oh, this is not where I'm supposed to go", then you walk back and spend some time wondering around with no idea where to go. Then you go back and try to adjust your character again to the door etc. and then the character suddenly crabs it... The whole movement of the character is such a tedious task and it's so clumsy. Really awkward to play.I'm really wondering why it is so bad, since the whole game is based on that simple movement and one (1) grabbing mechanic. How did they fail in one mechanic, that requires pressing a one button? It's such a beautiful and atmospheric game and I really want to continue it, but I had to stop playing it for now. Literally half of the stuff that I am supposed to grab it takes like 5-20 tries before I succeed. It started already in the tutorial and I was fearful it would be like that the rest of the game, and so it seems...In a game like this, why they just couldn't "over do" the grabbing mechanic and not the other way around? I'm now comparing this to LIMBO and INSIDE where the mechanics are really similar, and those games really nailed it. It's smooth and effortless, it makes the games enjoyable ride. However, this game is an opposite of that.- if they have fixed it, good, I will continue the game and change my review to positive, because I have a feeling that this COULD be really awesome game- if they haven't fixed it, I will refund the game, keep my review as negative and forget this game and Jumpship (The studio that made this game)

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very glad I ignored the bad reviews - this is 100% not a mixed review game. I am over 1 hour in and I am really enjoying the game play and story. It will be ok on a good desktop PC. Great game to play over Christmas, glad I gave it a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually pleasing, impressive at times, incredible sound design and some great game mechanics, but the tall, clunky, slow-moving character that gets hung up on the terrain and takes forever to get from a to b is a deal breaker. I loved Limbo and Inside, but this fell a bit short. Still worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: Not a game so much as a film where you have to guess what happens in every scene. Is this object interactable? No? Oh, yes, but in a way that you couldn't possibly have guessed? Is this area traversable? No? Well everywhere else that looked like this was- oh I guess you can just climb this ledge nowThere are portions that seem to be signposted (orange paint = interactable)... but only sometimes, and inconsistently. What we see of the narrative is also not great; there is a dog you should care about, and seems to be your companion in the beginning, but then for no reason they remove your ability to comfort the dog, or help it out- it follows you for a bit, and then later in the story the dog is shown explicitly to be trapped and whining to be at your side, but for some reason they prevent you from opening the gate between you and the dog, really for no reason... except that the dog can't be with you in the next scene, where you fall into a pit. Even the main character, it seems, needs to be able to figure out the will of the developer ahead of time. Plus he leaves his front door open and TV running, like a psycho

_childDocuments_.review: Limbo and Inside, to me, are masterpieces...I usually playthrough Inside at least once a year. One of those games that just felt like it was made for me...and then I noticed the development team had split up and there are now two companies making similar games...which is both sad and  a way.Somerville feels like the next logical step for these games to evolve into. Instead of Little Nightmares approach of copying and pasting Somerville actually brings back the special feeling these games offered when they were first released to the masses. The pacing is perfect, the story telling without speech or text is intelligently done as are the puzzle moments. Sound is still amazing and sounds like they are using the same guy who made the sounds for Inside.It is hungry on performance so don't be surprised if you have to run it on Medium or Low settings to get 60fps. I won't spoil by talking about anything else as it is another game that should be experienced. I will just say that it really took me back to the Another World/Flashback days of old. It's so cool...and it had me nearly crying several times!And I understand the criticism that this game received as it's not your usual game. If we split gamers into two groups...let's say "The Do'ers" and "The Dreamers"....then this game would appeal more to "The Dreamers." You will need to think, reflect and contemplate what the game is telling you. Intuition and going with what feels right is how you will succeed. It won't be obvious at first but experiment...and try not to overthink...Warning: There is minor jank due to the ambition of the gameplay and camera. Just reload the checkpoint if you get stuck or are unsure. I got stuck on the environment once.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: My best compliment is that the game feels "adequately competent". The controls feel sluggish throughout, with you getting caught up on the environment often, and about every 5-10 minutes the game decides (mostly arbitrarily) whether to limit your movement speed to a slow walk, normal walk, light jog, or run. As a result, most sections of the game feel poorly paced and take longer than you want.Many of the games' puzzles are not as clever as they first appear and are fairly straight-forward, but despite the pacing issues really limiting your minute-to-minute "fun" there are some good sequences here and there. The ending and wrap-up, however, will have you running to a guide or youtube video to figure out why they don't seem to work and the game serves only a very shallow "bad end". To get the "best" ending you are somehow expected to  I was left feeling very cold on the game by its end.
