_childDocuments_.review: It looks like a duck, but it doesn't quack like a duck.. I was extremely excited to play this, to love this, to support this.. But I can't.Being that it's coming from some of the same people who have worked on LIMBO and INSIDE, games I consider pretty groundbreaking, this was quite the bummer. This is not the ultra polished playdead minimalist perfection - this is something else.  If you appreciated the former games for their very intense atmosphere, open ended-ominous story telling, well paced brooding mood and the brilliantly placed "the fuuuuuu**k?!" moments, etc  - if that is your expectation going into Somerville - it doesn't really do any of ..that. Somerville ditches the whole polished 2D depth/camera tricks and minimalism in favour of adding another axis to play on. And it's wildly unnecessary. It only adds frustration. It's hardly intuitive, it basically completely breaks the flow and immersion to the point where it gets.. chore-y? The "platforming" is BAD - there's hardly any satisfaction from getting from point A to B. The puzzles are frustrating for all the wrong reasons. Some of the curios objects are so hard to interact with, just because of how the space has been laid out. It can feel like a clunky point-and-click adventure game at times.Then there's the optimisation. Random screen tears, FPS drops galore in the most mundane spots. Hopefully this has been patched. TLDR;To all Limbo and Inside fans, If you still wanna try it out, wait for a sale price and lower your expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing through Somerville, I think it can easily be separated into two categories being the Creative/Artistic side of games and the actual Game side of games.Regarding the Creative and Artistic side of Somerville, it gets an A+++ from me. The art style throughout the entire story is always evolving to convey emotions and tones, along with many secrets in the environmental storytelling which is key to the story considering how there is no dialogue between the characters. The sound design too is fantastic, it made me feel the sound, rather than just hear it. I don’t know how else to explain it but it was well thought out. Overall the creatives on the team that worked on Somerville brought so much to the table and just for that alone I think people should try this game out……however……then we come to the gameplay side of the game itself. Overall I was underwhelmed. The puzzles themselves were lacking and I felt like this game became more of a walking simulator than anything else. Even the enemies I never felt threatened by since all I had to do was just keep walking in the correct direction and I knew I would be safe. Regarding the puzzles specifically, this is what disappointed me the most. Whenever you had to learn a new ability or concept, the game did great in setting up a tutorial zone where you would learn the basic ability, and then follow it up with a slightly more complex puzzle to “test what you learned”. But after each of these sections, the remaining puzzles felt like they reverted to the basics of what each ability did. It felt like the puzzles were more so there to be a physical obstacle to get past, rather than something to actually think through and feel accomplished with solving. Not only this, but in general the controls of the game felt clunky. I always found myself getting stuck on flat areas of the ground or not being able to grab something I was right next to. In general, the hardest part of the game was just moving through the environment which was not a great experience. If you are looking for a game and want to focus more on the story and the art, then I would 100% recommend this game, but if you are looking for a good gameplay experience, I would suggest looking elsewhere until you see Somerville on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating as positive but there are several significant issues in this game. It's beautiful and full of style but it's also a mess with an identity crisis. Going in you should expect a spectacle walking simulator with a some  simple puzzle solving here and there. The puzzles are not on the level of Limbo or Inside and there is a lot of just pressing forward and interact to move forward. The only stumbling blocks will be places where you will miss a collision box and the expected interaction will not trigger. Most puzzles are very simple and based on a gimmick mechanic that gets old pretty fast. And a lot of situations which look like puzzles are actually just scripted events where all you need to do is move in the right direction.So gameplay is not great. This game could really use a combat mechanic, even the most basic one. Most of the puzzles feel like an excuse to show off their fancy shader and they are milking it dry. You can't jump or even control when you walk or run so there is also no real platforming in this game. Treat it more like an interactive experience rather than a game. But even then the story is just not that great. It's all over the place and parts of it feel very disconnected from the whole. Emotional beats don't land becuase the story from the player's perspective doesn't make much sense and it's hard to connect with the characters. And the constant vibe of all of this not being real just reinforces that feeling. The ending is particularly atrocious becuase I felt like it was supposed to be some kind of payoff - a moment where you can utilise the skills and abilities you gained through this whole journey. But in reality the outcome of an ending is pretty much random because you have no clue what you're doing and why. Feels like the game is just pretentious artsy nonsense that tries to be profound but falls flat on it's face trying to communicate what it's trying to do. Still it's pretty to look at and it has some cool stuff going on, so get it on a sale and see for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Had no expectations for this game but it was really cool. Definitely worth playing. The story manages to be pretty inventive for an alien invasion plot, and the visual storytelling is really superb. _childDocuments_.review: This game is simple and minimalistic. It is Raw. It manages to tell a story without words, through its emotions. The game centers on the experience of an earth scale invasion from the point of view of one family, one person. The art style is reminiscent of graphic novels and video games from the early 90s like Another World and Flashback.On those games, having a full cinematic experience was probably impractical at the time because of development costs, time restrictions and also technical limitations. So, the developers choose instead to have at least one or two of those special scenes, key moments which were able to transport you emotionally to the adventure, and the rest was just relaying on the gameplay itself.Somerville is what would’ve happened if there weren’t technical limitations or time restrictions (or at least, a lot less of them).The game is not perfect: while having movie like emotional aspirations, and some neat moments, it does miss on a few key scenes in which the action happening on screen, doesn’t meet the expected emotional moment: characters may meet but stay emotionless and in silence. This is noticeable especially towards the later parts of the game where some of the stronger scenes are to be found but also some of the weakest.Nevertheless, Somerville remains an intense and fantastic journey, with some great sci-fi horror moments.

_childDocuments_.review: Somerville may not be as disastrous as some reviews suggest, but it’s clear that expectations were high, especially given the comparisons to classics like Limbo or Inside (co-founder of the studio previously worked on those 2 masterpieces!)✅Positives: The game excels with its meticulously crafted atmosphere and engaging story, particularly for fans of Spielberg's classics such as War of the Worlds and Close Encounters of the Third Kind. The puzzle mechanics, which revolve around the protagonist's powers, are also both intriguing and well-implemented.❌Negatives: However, Somerville does have notable weaknesses. The 3D environments, designed for deep exploration, sometimes make it challenging to identify the correct path. While this doesn't block the player significantly, these moments of wandering can disrupt the game's pace, especially during chase sequences when you might bump into a decor element.Another point of frustration is the lack of clear guidance on how to achieve a satisfying ending. The few logical solutions to the final puzzle often lead to bad conclusions.Additionally, you might find yourself spending a significant amount of time wondering where your dog has gone, rather than focusing on the main story.📝Conclusion: Despite these shortcomings, Somerville is a well-crafted game that deserves recognition for its efforts. While it may not reach the iconic status of Limbo or Inside, it remains a compelling experience worth exploring.Final Note: Where did the dog go?🐕

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved Inside (or Limbo) and think maybe Somerville is only getting mixed reviews because its a niche genre of game (heart of darkness-like puzzle-platformers), don't get this game. The reviews saying Somerville doesn't have game mechanics are only barely exaggerating, as Somerville's gameplay takes a backseat to its story. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, some games do this well, but Somerville's story is so predictable that the trade off is not worth it. Puzzles are few and far between compared to the jam-packed, trial-and-error gameplay of Inside/Limbo, and aren't all that well thought out. What disappointed me most was that this story-driven game emphasizes communication with the alien invaders, to the point the alien spheres scattered throughout the levels speak a seemingly decipherable language of colorful lights emitted in patterns of three, but searching for and studying the spheres and their language has no bearing on the game's events or puzzles, and finding all the hidden alien spheres just earns you a cheap achievement. [SPOILER: example from the final chapter, spoils multiple endings] Given how Jumpship came to be, I was really excited for this game and wanted to like it so much. I at least expect better thought out puzzles than this, and more of them: the opportunities to tie in the underlying story with gameplay were countless and often missed. If you appreciate a strong grasp of visual cues in games, Somerville holds up pretty well to its peers, but it gets a little muddied in some places.Oh, and the game has a huge problem with joystick feedback on Steam controllers. The game does not respond well to diagonal movement, which sucks *** given most chase sequences in the game require frequent diagonal movement, slowing the protagonist significantly (compared to using a keyboard) and causing excess deaths.

_childDocuments_.review: Game elements (objects that can be traversed, moved, or otherwise manipulated) are often difficult to identify within the world. This stems from the (otherwise appealing) visual style, which does not efficiently telegraph which elements can be interacted with and which are simply set dressing. This is exacerbated by the fact that many game elements, such as doors and barriers, function inconsistently through the course of the game. As a result, the player spends an inordinate amount of time probing the game world through trial and error, simply to figure out what elements they are working with, rather than truly solving puzzles. Can I not open this door because it is not meant to be opened, because some other condition needs to be fulfilled before I open it, or because I am not standing quite close enough to open it? Oh, you mean I can actually crawl through this tunnel, contrary to every single previous tunnel I've seen in this game? Once you strip away the issue of the muddy UI, the actual puzzles are quite simple. The core scifi-themed  mechanic does not significantly develop throughout the course of the game, beyond some novelty applications during the endgame. I will not belabor this point, as it has been well trodden by other reviewers.Speaking of the endgame, it goes for the same "mystery box" approach as Inception, Tenet, or Lost, basically by throwing a bunch of worlds-within-worlds/dreams-within-dreams/"what is reality" tropes at the wall to see what sticks. Just a bunch of weirdness presumably to cover up the lack of a coherent narrative. This is distinct from "Inside," which despite not slapping you over the face with its story at least presented an easily discernible sequence of events. I experienced two endings, of which there are apparently five or six. In one of them, I apparently "resigned," and in another I "chose the path of violence." In neither case did my actions suggest these choices, as I was simply button mashing in the hopes of moving the game forward. Reading the forums, it seems the other endings require mastery of some type of esoteric patterns seen earlier in the game, which strikes me as a bit of a tall order given the aforementioned "noisiness" of the game's visual presentation. However, this game is not a disaster, and it is clear that a lot of attention went into its production. It has some bugs and visual glitches, having been released less than a week from when I write these words. Gameplay aside, its visuals and atmosphere are stunning and compelling. It is relatively cheap, at around EUR 20 for around five hours of fairly enjoyable gameplay. I was disappointed that I did not get the "good" ending after all that work, but at least the journey was memorable. So, on balance, I lean towards recommending this one, but with lots of caveats.

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous artstyle with a captivating story and really good sound design. _childDocuments_.review: This game is not perfect. It does have technical issues, such as the missing frame cap which should have been there from launch, confusing controls at times and occasionally bad collisions, awkward camera jumps and occasionally ULTRA slow movement. This game was, without a doubt, brought to the attention of many due to one of the PLAYDEAD Cofounders being part of the team and their fond memories of LIMBO and INSIDE which both were very much perfect games.However (after manually setting an fps cap in my GPU software) I found that the game's strengths by far did outweigh its weaknesses. The beautiful art style, amazing sound design and overall narrative design of the game made me enjoy the whole experience a lot and after finishing it, leaves me with a weirdly satisfying feeling of having lived through an adventure.I can't help but believe that Jumpship needed to keep a tight deadline for Gamepass to get the game out and had to cut a few corners here or there. Surely, 2 more months of polish would have helped the game tremendously, yet I do believe that even in its now released state, it deserves a chance to deliver a compelling narrative experience - and that it does pretty damn well.Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where steam review system needs "Mixed" in between "Yes" and "No" for recommendations, but it's Christmas, so enjoy it, Somerville... The setting of this game is very interesting, visuals are stunning and cinematic setpieces will put to shame even the biggest hollywood blockbusters. Especially the action sequence near the end is an incredible spectacle ride. So why the mixed feelings? Story telling is very lacking, puzzle/exploation sequences are missing visual guidance, resulting in a lot of situations where you get stuck and for a while you don't have a clue what the game wants from you, which ruins the tempo a lot. And the mentioned ending, while praised a lot, seems to be a bit rushed, and could have been stretched a lot more to get more from the entire climax IMHO. It was still a good cinematic experience, but it had big potential to be way better.

_childDocuments_.review: Somerville tells an incredible world-building story that captivates its' audience by grounding the themes and slowly introduces and specifies its' environments and world elements to give a certain survival immersion.It's one of those short but incredibly exhilarating experiences one must participate at least once. From character designs to the sound tracks and to the ever slightly world-building aspects of the game, this game does it top notch.The only two negative criticism this game definitely shows to give its' players, is its' rarest occurrences of visual bugs, and mainly its' short playtime. It would have been a solid game if it had at the very least, twenty hours of game-time with puzzles and even more world building.But seeing as this game is made by an INDIE studio, I will pardon them with how much it cost comparatively to its' playtime. The little details, the innovative yet simple puzzles and in its' entirety, the SCI-FI world they've built, have captivated me. The game is merely a product of the limitations of the Studio in terms of production value, however they did an amazing job overall considering its' their first game (though the co-founder did work from Playdead, worked on Limbo and Inside) a merit worth mentioning.This needs a sequel, a standalone spin-off of the same world, or even further updates onto the story (different perspective on the other characters?). This game accomplished its' ideal goal, I need more of it, I WANT more of it.Support INDIE studios that brings such passion to the gaming industry. I mark this as a MUST buy game!

_childDocuments_.review: i wanted to love this game... i won't compare it to limbo and inside in this review, other than to say that both of those definitely outperform somerville in this genre. by the game's own merits, i found myself intensely frustrated with so many parts of it because of how enrapturing the setting and concept is. i was extremely intrigued by all the trailers leading up to release, and by the opening of the game itself, but rather quickly the experience is so bogged down by...THE FREAKING CONTROLS. my biggest complaint by far.let me start by saying this game is fickle as hell with how it wants you to do certain things - and this is in no way related to the story at all, but the good ending *is* another example of what i mean. but the controls. oh my god. talk about a hand cramp. the amount of time this game has you chasing yourself in circles trying to figure out exactly where you're supposed to be standing, using your abilities, and then shuffling through altered terrain to progress, or where you're supposed to get over something like a fence or ledge, or simply navigating the 2.5d world in tight spaces not knowing how to fit in holes or move backwards in the environment to get to certain places is ridiculous. this game has so much needless overly-precise shimmying and shuffling. you have to do stuff in EXACTLY the right way or it won't work.all of that frustration with the extremely slow movement and janky navigation at least rewards you with....ah... extremely simple, one-note puzzles. puzzles that mostly involve extremely basic movement of objects, flicking various switches, and timing. there's also some halfhearted stealth sections and Bafflingly inconsistent chase sequences that *seem* exciting at first, before you die for a stupid reason, respawn to try again, and *somehow* succeed the second time despite doing exactly the same thing that got you killed the first time.this game is visually magnificent with an intriguing story, but is bogged down by so much jank and awkward stop-and-go pacing that it frustrates me. if it weren't so short (and it feels longer than it actually is) i'm fairly confident i'd have thrown in the towel and watched a youtube playthrough somewhere in the middle.the sluggish navigation leading to overly-simplistic puzzles (which i expected would increase in difficulty eventually, but they didn't) simply isn't a rewarding gameplay loop.you're essentially left with the story, which is an intriguing tale of wandering through a (mid-apocalyptic?) countryside setting and beholding some truly remarkable sights in this rural world. it's really breathtaking, and the intimidating aliens that threaten to rip your idyllic life with your family in the middle of nowhere apart are pretty well done. many simple yet foreboding enemies that remind me of the machines (particularly the watchers) from horizon zero dawn. it's definitely all good in the environmental storytelling front, with GORGEOUS artwork (i'm a huge sucker for wide open countrysides at dusk) and would-be great level design - if you didn't have to fight with the controls every time you tried to climb a ledge.i don't have much to say about the story other than the endings are all pretty good. i like 'em. they're reminiscent of other games in this genre where it's mostly left up to interpretation, and i like what's there - ignoring the ludicrous amount of steps that getting the true ending gets. you're ♥♥♥♥♥♥ without a guide on that one, sorry.i got all the achievements for this game on my own, but having to endure finger cramps while entering 16-18 different inputs in a VERY specific pattern is just the cherry on top of the needlessly soul-sucking tedium of actually *playing* this wonderful-looking and conceptually awesome game.i'm really disappointed with the gameplay, but not so much that i think the game is without merit - it has a lot of merit! i was gifted this game by a friend who knew i was excited about it since the first trailer, and i'm really happy i played it, but for the listed price point on here, i reeeeeally can't recommend it, taking into account all of what i've said. i'm still glad i played it, but i'd only really recommend it to someone with a toooon of patience.

_childDocuments_.review: A good side scrolling puzzle game with great visuals and neat Sci-fi story that will make you want to finish the game in one setting. Good thing the game is short at 2-4 hours. The story is engrossing, and the visuals are great but the game play is lacking. Most of the puzzles involve finding a solution to a blocked passageway. The character can only move as fast as the game chooses. This removes all tension when running away from enemies because you know that as long as you chose the correct path, you will not be caught. Finding the correct path or rock to climb on, or lever to pull is the most frustrating part. Although I only found myself stuck twice without knowing what to do next, those times seemed more frustrating since I did the thing it wanted me to do several times before the game acknowledged. Overall, if you enjoy low key, side scrolling puzzle games, with great visual and an engaging story AND have 2-4 hours to spare I recommend trying out this game. The short length and replayability factor makes me recommend purchasing only if on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Well I started the program. It runs through a set animation. Then a kid hops off the sofa on which his parents remain asleep. Then nothing happens. But nothing happens when I typed A. This program doesn't even tell you to do something. There is nothing, no instructions, no hint, no response.Maybe I'm not smart enough and I'm missing an important puzzle point. If so, could the program let me know.[update] - It turns out that it defaulted to a game controller that does not exist on my PC. _childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed the game despite the technical issues at launch. If you like INSIDE, you'll like this. It's the same type of beautifully crafted, mysterious world where there are more questions than answers. I love this game's world. Excellent music and sound design as well. Somerville has a heavier sci-fi influence than INSIDE, and more focus on individual character development. Gameplay is still very platform-y despite being able to move in 3 dimensions. There are multiple endings, and I recommend getting them all. Most are quite simple to get, but one is very involved, so I recommend just googling how to get it unless you're up for an obscure challenge. You could beat this in 4 hours at a quick pace, but I thoroughly took my time and 100%ed the game, so I ended up with 8 hours. The length felt just right to meMost of my complaints are things that can and will probably be patched. The game is definitely playable in its current form. I didn't come across anything totally game breaking, just...annoying. Here's my list to save you time. I bet most of these will be fixed by the time anyone reads this:- no windowed or borderless windowed modes- you need to manually select gamepad or keyboard mode from the options, it won't auto detect- my logitech gamepad didn't respond at all until I flipped its 'D' input switch to 'X'- big frame dips with a 3060 Ti on 1080 resolution during certain scenes, still playable though- a few spots where the complex camera movements got stuck behind a foreground element, obscuring my view of the player until I blindly wandered around to get out- player collider will sometimes get stuck on tiny pieces of debris during chase sequences- the 'sweet spot' for interacting with things is often very small and easy to miss- I managed to softlock the game when I pressed the use key too many times while attempting to sit on a couch, so I was stuck glitched into it unable to get out (game has a quick restart so it wasnt a big deal)This is worth a play if you liked INSIDE, but don't expect it to be nearly as polished and seamless. The middle of Somerville drags on a bit too long, but the spectacular ending makes up for it!

_childDocuments_.review: The game had an amazing atmosphere and very much felt like a step forward from games like inside. There were a few puzzles I looked up. Walkthrough for and found a solution that didn't really make any sense, making me wonder what the designers were thinking. There were also a few puzzles that automatically solved themselves after a quick death, which felt a little odd to me personally.I would absolutely recommend someone get this game.... In the future. Right now there are a handful of bugs, combined with a myriad of major issues. On PC the audio would stutter and blank out when an abrupt sound was supposed to play, and the game stutterd a lot. On steam deck, I was surprised I was even able to play it at all. Turning the settings down to low and rendering at 480p yielded the exact same 5-25fps results that playing on high upscaled to a 4k tv would. The earlier sections of the game were outright unplayable on the deck. While it did get better later on, it was still a terrible first impression.The game had an amazing direction and was one of the prettiest and most awe inspiring games I've played this year, not to mention it actually had some unique gameplay mechanics. But it's lack of consistency with the quality of the puzzles, and the tech side where it completely dropped the ball, lead me to dislike the execution of the game. I do hope that it can pull a cyberpunk or no man's sky and pull itself up again, but that seems unlikely.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like this type of game, which I do, it's worth it. This is one of those arts-y puzzle type games. It has a great style to it, keep in mind this is not an action game. There are a couple of chase parts in the game, but that's as heart pounding as it gets. I only say that because when I first saw a trailer for this, they focused on those chase scenes, which is a bit misleading if you aren't familiar with the genre.This takes the "silent" approach to story telling, similar to games like "Inside" or "Limbo", so basically stuff is just happening in the background and you have to interpret those glimpses and piece together what is happening. Once again, I think that's a neat approach and I enjoy it, but I know some people do not like that because you don't really get answers to an questions. You mostly are just using your imagination to fill in the story.So I do feel like the puzzles were pretty straight forward, the mechanics were fun, but not a huge amount of variety in how they applied them. Maybe like a handful of "oh, that's neat!" moments of solving the puzzles.Levels were good though, in-game scenes were pretty cool, liked the cutscense. I think the ending was the only thing I was a little annoyed about. I could tell by how it played out that it probably had multiple endings, and luckily they have a checkpoint like right before you do the end part so it's easy to go through all the endings once you hit the credits. The problem was that I had to end up looking up how to get them because I didn't feel there was really much direction to help you figure them out. There was like a little bit of feedback, but not enough for you to really know, especially when you go look up how to do the different endings. Oh and I didn't like that they put scenes after the credits, this is only because there are multiple endings.If you aren't sure about this game type, I'd recommend playing Inside first cause that's a pretty good introduction to these type of games. Also, this is like maybe a 4 hour game tops, so keep that in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: Somerville is a game that had me utterly torn between moments of sheer fascination and episodes of deep frustration. It presents an intriguing idea, but it stumbles in execution, leaving me with mixed feelings about my gaming experience.Let's start with the good. Somerville boasts a captivating story that kept me invested throughout my playthrough. It's a tale filled with mystery and emotional depth, making me genuinely care about the characters and their journey. The game's ability to pique your curiosity and keep you guessing is undoubtedly one of its strongest suits.Visually, Somerville is a feast for the eyes. The minimalist, hand-drawn art style adds a unique touch to the game's atmosphere, creating a world that feels both bleak and beautiful simultaneously. The attention to detail in the environment is commendable and contributes significantly to the game's overall ambiance.However, it's in the gameplay department that Somerville falters. While the core concept is fascinating, it falls flat due to its repetitive nature. You find yourself engaged in similar activities time and time again, which can lead to a sense of monotony. I had hoped for more variety and innovation in the mechanics to keep things fresh and exciting.Additionally, the mission design left much to be desired. Some missions felt like they were designed to artificially extend the game's length, rather than to genuinely challenge the player or advance the narrative. This resulted in moments of frustration and a sense of wasted potential.In conclusion, Somerville is a game that tantalizes with its unique premise, visual charm, and engrossing story. However, it suffers from repetitive gameplay and questionable mission design that may leave players longing for a more diverse and engaging experience. If you're someone who values a captivating narrative and stunning visuals above all else, you may still find it worth your time. Just be prepared for moments of frustration along the way.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: I understand why 90% of the negative reviews talk about the controls and level design being the issue.You can look past both those things very easily, I find that I did not have trouble with the controls very much at all, and the level design was pretty good. To each his own I guess.I was going to thumbs down this game for primarily one reason: Its length.The game is about 3-4 hours total, I finished getting every single achievement and ending at 4.6 hours total. My first ending was about 3.5.If you like limbo or inside, give this game a try because its a wonderfully crafted atmospheric world where there's tons of environmental storytelling. Games like this deserve the support in risk of losing these types of games forever.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: If your looking for an experience that leans more toward telling a visual story, with light puzzle interactions sprinkled throughout, then this might be for you. The visuals are striking, and the sound design is top notch. The downsides...the movement of the main character feels a little off, and doesn't always match the pacing of the story at times. Sometimes your deaths are quite sudden without any kind of telegraphing that you might be in danger. This can happen enough, that you start to lose any real connection to the main character, and don't feel much when he's killed. The ending(s), are interesting, but getting to them all are rather obtuse. It's a bit of a cross between the Close Encounters of the Third Kind, and the 80's game Simon. Some of the ending solutions to the puzzle seem so random, it's a wonder anyone even found them. That said, if you want something interesting and fairly easy to get through in a few hours, and it's on sale, I'd pick it up. If your a fan of the game Inside, you'll appreciate this one, though this one is not quite up to the same level as a total experience. Still fun in its own right.

_childDocuments_.review: This game blows my mind. I have been waiting for it since the first visuals I saw of it a few years ago. I grew up playing old SNES games and Flashback and Out of This World were 2 of my favorite games of all time and they contributed strongly in forging my imagination and my tastes. This game is a tribute to these games and it is an amazing narrative-driven, adventure puzzle game. Every composition in this game is jaw-dropping. The mechanics are super cool and the game keeps surprising me every corner of this adventure. It's just an experience you have to live. It is not perfect, of course, it is the first game of a small studio, but the level of polish and the risks this studio took to bring us such an amazing game, is impressive. Please buy this game if you like narrative-driven adventure puzzle games, I'm just glad that studios like this that love to produce these types of games exist. Congrats to the developers.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a spectacular game. The art was stunning. Although the models for simple they fit the aesthetic of the game perfectly. The story was compelling and kept me interested the whole time. This game appeals to the male fantasy in the best way possible: having a wife and a kid while also being their hero. I think the price ($25) is a little steep for the amount of game play that the game offers. I got the game 50% off and I believe that was a far more appropriate price for this game. The only other complaint I had was that the ending with a satisfying resolve was not accessible to a normal player, I don't think I would have got it without a guide.With that being said, the developers did an amazing job with this game. For a game without any narrative they did a great job conveying what was going on in the story. You were able to feel what the main character was feeling whether that be joy, sadness, worry, or confusion. Amazing game!
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: Somerville is a slow, methodical, and dramatic experience. The game uses wordless narration, which is always a joy, letting the world express itself through music and the visual medium of games.The cinematography is brilliant, with the camera gracefully following our protagonist, framing the journey in a beautiful and dynamic painterly manner, making it more than just a standard platformer.The main gameplay challenge is the light puzzle obstacles. They don't feel particularly difficult; in fact, it's more challenging to see where you're supposed to go. The game does a poor job of guiding the player throughout the levels, making the game feel slightly annoying at times.Some sections feel badly paced, especially the cave section. It's horrendously paced, in fact. I don't understand how a game where all the interesting world-building is happening on the surface is taking place underground. The cave section feels like an easy way to pad out the game without putting many resources into it. Instead of looking forward to playing Somerville again, I feel dread thinking about slogging through the cave.I enjoyed the atmosphere and story. I'm a sucker for alien invasion stories, and I'm quite surprised at how few games use it as a set piece. I do wish the game leaned further into the fantasy of hiding and moving through the ongoing invasion, but the sections that already lean into it make for a great spectacle.I can't exactly point out what Somerville is lacking, but it's lacking some sort of substance. It feels like the game would benefit from a chapter or two. However, Somerville is a solid experience, and I'm very glad I got to play it. It's a game I would recommend to people who are into atmospheric adventure games.

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking for something to follow up the incredible experience I had playing Inside, and Somerville hit my radar. I was not disappointed. While simper in gameplay terms than Playdead's masterpiece, Somerville nonetheless delivers a hauntingly beautiful post-apocalyptic tale full of pathos, atmosphere and excitement. It's a strikingly gorgeous game with audio design to match, and an absolute joy to play throughout its relatively short runtime, typical of something in this genre. If you're into science fiction, and have a taste for indie side scrollers that punch far above their weight, I highly recommend you check our Somerville - and explore its multiple endings.

_childDocuments_.review: Çok fazla sinematik kaygı duyularak yapılmış bir oyun olduğunu hemen anlıyoruz. Görseller, atmosfer ve ses gerçekten başka bir seviyede ve hissiyatı çok iyi veriyor. Bir kavuşma hikayesi oynuyoruz. Uzaylı istilası sonrası yollarımızın ayrıldığı ailemizi bulmaya çalışıyoruz. Bu süreçte bazı güçler elde ediyoruz ve genelde bulmacaları bu güçlerle çözüyoruz. Oyun, sahneyi ve kamerayı hazırlayıp oynamayı bize bırakmış. Devam eden bir filmin içindeki karakter gibi hissediyoruz. Kameranın oyuncu kontrolünde olmamasından dolayı eleştiriler geldiğini gördüm. Ben şahsen fikri sevdim. Kullanılan açılar etkileyiciydi. Eğer biz standart, aynı uzaklıkta bir kamerayla oynasaydık, bu kadar farklı açı ve derinlik yakalayamazdık. Bu fikrin yaratıcı ve yenilikçi olduğunu düşünüyorum. Eksilere gelecek olursam, kamera özelliğinin getirdiği buglar ve takılmalar sinir bozucu tabii, orası ayrı. Bazen 3 boyutta tam olarak nerede olduğumu anlamakta zorlandım. Ama bir süre sonra alıştım. Bunun dışında karakterimizin inanılmaz yavaş hareket etmesi ve sürekli yorulması, karakterden çok beni yordu. Oyundaki bu yavaşlıktan sıkılıp 1 günde bitirilebilecek oyunu 2 güne bölüp bitirdim. Sahneler arası mesafe gereksiz uzun olmuş. Yapımcıların yaratılan dünyayı gösterme ve oyuncuyu doyurma çabasını anlıyorum ama bana biraz fazla geldi. İndirimli fiyatıyla tavsiye ederim.We immediately understand that it is a game made with a lot of cinematic concerns. The visuals, atmosphere and sound are truly on another level and convey the feeling very well. We are playing a reunion story. We are trying to find our family with whom we parted ways after the alien invasion. In this process, we gain some powers and we generally solve puzzles with these powers. The play prepare the stage and the camera and leaves us to play. We feel like a character in an ongoing movie. I saw criticism coming from the camera not being under player control. I personally loved the idea. The angles used were impressive. If we had played with a standard camera at the same distance, we would not have been able to capture so many different angles and depths. I think this idea is creative and innovative. Coming to the minuses, the bugs and hangups brought by the camera feature are annoying, of course. Sometimes I had a hard time understanding exactly where I was in 3 dimensions. But after a while I got used to it. Apart from this, the fact that our character moved incredibly slowly and was constantly tired made me tired more than the character. I got tired of this slowness of the game and finished the game, which could have been completed in 1 day, by dividing it into 2 days. The distance between scenes was unnecessarily long. I understand the gamemakers' effort to show the created world and satisfy the player, but it seemed a bit much to me. I recommend it for its discounted price.

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game. I can tell it was made by individuals that were involved with Inside and this feels very similar with regard to atmosphere, visual and audio style. _childDocuments_.review: The environmental storytelling, both audio-wise and visually, is downright phenomenal. Even in light of what follows, all in all, this was a great experience.So here goes…What holds this game back is the game play.Walking is often too slowly paced.The puzzles are rather simplistic and made tedious by the speed and which the main character moves around.The story beats for the humans are well told, however the “other components” are hidden behind obscurity.This game tells the story of a man going through hell and back for his family.In fact, it does it so well that, unfortunately, it's at the expense of other aspects of the beautifully crafted world/lore.To the extent that this even affects the players (or maybe just my) ability to achieve most of the possible endings (without resorting to guides).I can see why this game has mixed reviews.Even with my complaints above, I still think this game deserves more recognition for its merits.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: Thank you to the developer and publisher of Somerville, Jumpship, for providing a solid good game for me to escape, explore and enjoy.My steam rating Positive*Apparently at launch there were some issues? I had none.An absolutely beautiful 2.5D side scrolling, platforming adventure game that hits all the right marks, Somerville is an easy recommendation but a few negatives could sway your time and money.The story of Somerville is a simple sci-fi story about finding your family after an intense event occurs. There is no voice acting or any sort of lore to read so your take from the story will come from your actions and visuals. This all works like in most of the genres other titles such as Inside, Little Nightmares, Black the Fall to name just a few. The problem though with this title, it comes with 4 endings(There is chapter select so only one play through needed) which IMO was a bad idea and weakens the ending's impact. In addition the last chapter where this choice occurs seems to drag. While the ending was not for me it only slightly lessened the complete journey. As mentioned you will be controlling a man as you wander the above and below grounds of Somerville. You will receive a brief tutorial at the start of the game where you will learn to move, grab and pull objects that are visually identified with a gold/yellow mark. As you venture you will receive the ability to manipulate solid objects into a liquid form and then be able to put it back into a solid form but will require a light source to complete. This ability will be for solving the handful of puzzles which for the most part will open up a path to proceed in the game. All of the above works fine but I wanted to mention the walking speed of the character. I understand for storytelling purposes you want to keep a certain pace but with a slow walking speed It really felt like the whole time I was in quicksand. There is no run option, it's done automatically in sections, and with mud and water making you even slower it for myself was a little annoying and I def would have preferred an ability to run and a bump in walking speed.I don't know how this genre does it but this game easily gets the screenshot simulator stamp of approval. The game uses that abstract, realism painting aesthetic that makes every scene pop in its use of colors and lighting. The lighting really shines in some scripted chase sequences  and when using your abilities. All of this of course is great but becomes even better with the amazing sound work that is included. Truly top tier sound engineering at work here. If you like this genre there is absolutely no reason you should not play Somerville. It’s a simple sci-fi story about finding your family with amazing visuals, sound design and scripted sequences. I would have preferred one ending and a little bump in movement but these are minor issues to my time spent in Somerville and overall it was pretty amazing.PositivesGood sc-fi storySimple controls and puzzlesScreenshot simulator-Looks amazingSound designPerfect game time 4 hrsNegativesMultiple endingsLast chapter seemed to dragMovement speed-No run optionWeak achievement listNo replayability

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: I am surprised at the mixed reviews, because I really enjoyed this. The great things about the game are the sound design, art style, and minimal storytelling. Gameplay is a bit wonky, but not so much as to distract in a major way. At 4 hours the game is very short, so be warned.I think fans of Inside will enjoy this too (I liked it even more than Inside).And yes, you can pet the dog (sometimes).Graphics---------This is one of the games where every single frame could be a wallpaper. It has the right blend between simplistic and detailed, and it knows how to work with colors. Easily one of the most beautiful games I ever played.Surprising to me was that the game seems to be pretty demanding on hardware. I played on the highest setting, and there were noticeable FPS drops. My instincts tell me that it should run better than it actually does, but there is a lot of particle stuff going on; maybe that excuses it. When the frames dropped there was noticeable screen tearing, but enabling Vsync fixed that. Ignoring these small things, it's great.Audio------The sound design is probably the best thing about the game. I can't recall ever playing anything similar to it. It contributes enormously in selling the dark/mysterious atmosphere of the game. Actual music is used rarely, so it stands out at the times when it does appear.Definitely play it with good headphones, if you have some.Story-----I can't say too much about the story without spoilers, but there is also not much to be said. The game has minimal exposition and storytelling. Nothing is explained to the player. There is no dialogue, but characters' intentions are sufficiently indicated by noises or hand motions, so they don't feel lifeless.I really enjoyed this minimal way of storytelling. They succeeded in creating a sense of mystery that feels very similar to games like Limbo or Inside.A pleasant surprise was that the pace/intensity of the story picked up significantly towards the end.Gameplay/Controls--------------------The gameplay is nothing extraordinary, but the puzzles are fitting for this kind of game. They're not too hard; most of them can be solved immediately if you have some practice. Some are harder, but satisfying once you have the solution. There is no puzzle where I felt "cheated" or frustrated. But really, the focus of the game is the atmosphere, not the gameplay.The controls are one of the weaker aspects. It feels a bit wonky, at least when playing with keyboard. This is not a game that needs precise controls, but it still felt off at times. It's sometimes difficult to find the right spot to interact with objects. I also thought it wasn't sufficiently clear which objects could be interacted with, and which couldn't. Often, to avoid missing any secrets, I would just try to touch everything (and rarely was there something to find). The game gives you some visual hints which help significantly, but they are not always present.Some smaller things I noticed: At times the character feels too slow and it takes a while to get where you want to go. I didn't die often so I don't have a big sample size, but sometimes the safepoints were too far apart; I had to walk/swim/climb a considerable distance (which is worse when the character is slow anyways).I only encountered one bug, and that was because the dog was stuck on some random door and prevented a cutscene from being triggered.Other than that my gameplay experience was smooth.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of games like Limbo and Inside (which this game will inevitably be compared to), I was definitely looking forward to Somerville since it was announced. However, my feelings are mixed after a relatively quick playthrough.What it does well:Somerville's visual style is beautiful and had me stopping multiple times just to take in its atmosphere. The game strays from the likes of Inside by using a wider variety of camera angles as you move throughout, giving you a more cinematic and interesting experience. Along with the visuals, the sound design is excellent and punctuates scenes perfectly, adding weight where needed. The premise itself also kept me interested most of the time as I truly wanted to see where the narrative would go right up to the end (I won't talk about the story itself because I don't want to spoil anything). I will say, though, that the narrative style is similar to Inside—don't expect any exposition.What it does badly:The poor gameplay mechanics made me turn off the game more than once. I'm used to minimalist controls in games (i.e. Jump, Walk, Interact) but Somerville's interactions were downright poor throughout the game. Many times while trying to interact with something, I either had to readjust the way the character was facing slightly, tap the joystick to get a bit closer, or have my character let go of a given object, unprompted by me. Sometimes a puzzle would stump me, only for me to find out that the object I previously investigated and dismissed was actually the right thing, I just failed to actually interact with it the first time. The puzzles themselves are mostly pretty easy, but some were so unintuitive to the point of frustration. This was amplified by the decision to use different camera angles throughout the game, sometimes having me walk in random directions to see where I could actually go (rather than just having Left/Right to choose from). Speaking of walking, this game probably took me 4 hours simply because you can only ever walk—slowly—so any fruitless investigations result in even more frustration due to the extra time wasted.I really wanted to like this game going into it. Having finished it, I'd recommend it if only to experience a unique art style and beautiful visuals. Gameplay-wise, it's OK, and will require some patience to get through. I plan to play it again at some point in the future, expecting that I'll have a much better time after knowing how to solve all the puzzles and allowing myself to focus on the visuals more. Maybe they'll fix the clunky mechanics by then too.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for this game for a very long time, and it was by far my most anticipated game of the year. _childDocuments_.review: When Somerville works, it WORKS. The atmosphere is fantastic, the visuals are striking, and the sound design is very impressive. I really liked the tense and well-executed stealth sequences and simple linear platforming segments, and while the puzzles were annoying to get used to during the beginning of the game, I enjoyed the simple but effective puzzle design once the game's tempo picked up.Also, Somerville delivers in spades with a simple but powerful visual narrative, cleverly juxtaposing a simple story about reuniting a family with cool sci-fi elements and massive cinematics. Some of the story elements near the beginning of the game that I initially thought of as meandering and unnecessary serve to further the game's suspense later on, and the story is similarly able to constantly build upon itself with a huge sense of scale while keeping things personal for the main character.Now that I've gotten that praise out of the way...A lot of people are disappointed with the lack of polish in regard to the movement and controls in Somerville, and I get it. A short game that focuses on visuals, atmosphere, and simple, straightforward gameplay needs to be as fine-tuned as possible.Everybody expected a second INSIDE with this game's controls and mechanical polish, and instead, we got something clunky and inconsistent, more reminiscent of Little Nightmares. This game takes a 2.5D approach to movement, which is OK in concept, but here it's wonky in practice: especially during the slower-paced, less linear parts of the game, where the little mechanical annoyances are brought to the forefront. Objects that are just meant for background scenery sometimes seem like they can be interacted with, and vice versa. The character can get stuck on geometry, especially when far away from the camera, when it's hard to tell where to move. Sometimes the main character will run and sometimes he'll walk super slowly, and this speed can't be controlled by the player. Once I had to reload a checkpoint because an AI got stuck doing something it wasn't supposed to do. And out-of-the-way exploration (especially during the introduction of the game) can lead to going into an area where there is nothing to interact with, which made the introductory sequence the most annoying part in the whole game for me.There are also some less annoying but still bizarre creative choices in Somerville, most notably the abrupt camera transitions which took some time to get used to. Also there's the visual approach of having black bars on the top and bottom of the screen for the whole game (when playing on a standard 16:9 monitor). I didn't consciously notice this much because the letterboxing blends into Somerville's dark color palette, but still... why?Performance-wise, I experienced some stuttering that broke my immersion several times near the start of the game. This didn't happen for long, luckily, but it really shouldn't have happened at all - considering I played this game on a high-end PC and medium graphics settings.Overall, I'm disappointed with Somerville's sometimes shoddy execution, but I still think the incredible art and sound direction combined with a powerful visual narrative make this game worth playing. The introductory sequence was undoubtedly my least favorite part of the entire game, but once that was over and the story starting coming together, the atmosphere and narrative had me hooked. If you're not convinced, maybe wait until some of these mechanical issues have been patched (hopefully!) or until the game goes on sale.Also, please add a button to pet the dog. 6/10
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: Although the path to loving this game is fraught with friction, it is a visual stunner with exceptional audio design and its story-telling ambitions are noble.Looking past the lethargic animations, clunky controls, audio & animation glitches, and sub-par puzzle design, Somerville's captivating world is nonetheless as engrossing and oftentimes thrilling as one could desire. It reminds me of Vane, in that the visuals and atmosphere seem to have been prioritized at the expense of flow and agency. Story-wise, it largely left me unaffected due to its disinterest in clearly articulating its intentions or failing to tie a bow on moments that conveyed their importance but left their meaning half-baked.Perhaps my biggest story-related disappointment was the seeming disinterest the game had in developing the father's relationship with his dog. In my opinion, there were a lot of missed opportunities when it came to tightening the game's portrayal of family, which felt so palpable in the first few minutes, but quickly gave way to a focus on spectacle and VFX as opposed to the connection at the heart of this father's journey.

_childDocuments_.review: Longer review: Somerville is one of a lot of recent indie games that has very little to offer besides a good story and presentation.The gameplay is very simplistic - you use a button to interact with orange marked objects or climb things. You eventually get three alien powers that let you manipulate liquid metal and destroy some objects using various different static or carried light sources to solve puzzles or clear a path through each section of the game. There is no dialog or lore exposition here, just environmental storytelling about a family caught in an alien invasion. The soundtrack is very somber and fitting, and the art style looks really cool.That said this is a very short game so anyone looking for extensive replayability should look elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: Comparatively short (about 4.5hrs, plus another half an hour of Achievement cleanup) with a striking visual style.  Not particularly difficult, but engaging.  There are some emotional beats that fail to land with much impact, which is rather surprising given some of the subject matter.There's also an underlying "observational" puzzle that I probably wouldn't have picked up on without at least a few playthroughs, and without which the ending can seem quite bewildering and unsatisfying.It's easy to draw comparisons to games like Limbo and (especially) Inside, but Somerville differs in that here, you walk to the LEFT.All in all, it's not perfect, but I think it's worth a playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: The art team and sound developers did wonders to make this game very atmospheric but for the story I have to say that this is what ruined the experience. I never had any emotional connections or care about the main characters, which the game wanted you to feel.  I already figured out the story later at the end but it was nothing original.  The puzzles were uninspiring and mediocre at best and the slow animated walks of the character had made it less desirable to solve them. What I hated most about the game is that if you ended up getting killed by an enemy a few times whilst experimenting with solutions, the game will punish you by skipping you further ahead, this robs you of any sense of achievement once it's completed and totally immersion breaking. Some of the survival decision-making of the characters as well turned this game into a satirical comedy rather than a gripping emotional thriller like WAR OF THE WORLDS.  I did not care if any of them died. The only character I cared about was the pet Dog and that;s saying something.Do I recommend you to play the game, that's a No from me.  You are better off looking away and just play a game called INSIDE instead, which I've discovered to be more fun and memorable than this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: (No. You cannot pet the dog...For some reason!)Having waited patiently for Somerville, since it was announced in 2017, from Jumpship studios, and Dino Patti of Limbo and Inside fame, I came to the conclusion that, sometimes, good ideas are just that; good ideas. Some things and mechanics that might have worked before, will prove themselves to be outdated, as the years go by. Although nothing majorly wrong with Somerville, nothing majorly outstanding either. A rage-inducing barrage of bugs and a camera that constantly fights the main character, are, in my opinion, the cardinal sins of Jumpship's first game. I have no problem with puzzles, being myself a fan of a genre that more often than not, relies on those to advance the story, with I have a problem is fighting the camera, the lightning, and the game mechanics, while having a split second to react to some cheap death I couldn't see, because, again, the lightning in this game is just atrocious. History wise and with no spoilers ahead, mainly because I couldn't understand what happened, why, and how. And in that state I remained even after finishing the game.Without being judgmental or cynical, I found the game's lack of history to be quite pretentious and bordering on the "cryptic is the way to be".It might be a good game for people far smarter than me. As for my enjoyment, I couldn't wait to finish it, just so I could move on to something else.I can't recommend it. Maybe after a patch or two, but some games, no matter how many patches, simply can't be fixed.You can check my full playthrough on Youtube:
_childDocuments_.name: Somerville

_childDocuments_.review: While it's style is unique and it's atmosphere is good, It is safe to say that this game fails to contest it's previously made counterparts LIMBO and INSIDE as a better game. The character models appear poorly made in contrast to the game map, the movement of the protagonist isn't fluid (at least on PC) and in my opinion, both older games have a better visual aesthetic. This game has been in the making for years, yet it still feels thrown together at the last minute with little to show for. _childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Somerville much more than I expected to based on some of the Steam reviews I had read beforehand. If you have played other games like this and like them then I think you would probably like this one. If you haven't played other games like this then there are probably better introductions (I might recommend Inside or Little Nightmares).Somerville's gameplay mostly consists of puzzles to solve, but these are pretty easy (well, except for figuring out how to get the best ending) and instead are an excuse to experience the world and the story. The levels are generally 2D (but not always), and there is no spoken dialog or written explanation of anything. This is a nice artistic choice in terms of letting you experience events as they unfold (which I liked), but had the drawback in this particular game of making the character that you play feel distant and detached. If you would enjoy being thrust into a situation and having to try and figure out what is going on then I think this game will work for you, but be forewarned that it feels a little bit like Half Life 2 if not only Gordon Freeman didn't talk but none of the people he interacted with did either.Somerville has some of the same weaknesses that other games in this genre seem to: It can be hard to figure out where to walk because of camera angles, and this can be particularly frustrating during timed action sequences when you die because it was difficult to see where you were going. Additionally, this game seemed to have the camera pulled back for much of it, which made it even harder for me to navigate at times. The art style is beautiful, and visually I liked the camera angles that were chosen, but there were lots of times when I wished I could have zoomed in more to where my character was to see a little better. Additionally, I felt like almost all of the events and actions that I was supposed to do as a player were dictated by the choices that the game's designers made; I often didn't actually do things with any intention beyond "well, this is an action that I can do, let's see what happens", and so I didn't feel clever as much as compliant. This isn't unusual for the genre, though, and I should give credit that there were a handful of puzzles that I thought were quite clever and really enjoyed.I think many of the complaints I have seen in reviews and forum posts are because of technical issues. I myself had a really hard time figuring out how to get it to not show a black screen when starting (I had to disable all NVIDIA DSR resolutions and also Windows scaling, if that helps anyone), but once I was able to start it I didn't run into any problems.There was a lot in the story that I didn't understand (and had to look up afterwards), and, as I mentioned, I felt detached from the character I was playing, kind of like I was watching him rather than experiencing things myself, but overall I quite enjoyed this game and thought it was much better than I would have expected based on other reviews. If you would like to experience an interesting story that doesn't explain anything with a strong stylized art style, and wouldn't mind some occasional frustration doing some light puzzles and action then I think there is a reasonable chance that you would like Somerville.

_childDocuments_.review: Those that don't like to read If you love the game Inside, Planet Alpha, Little Nightmares, Limbo, etc then 100% stop what you're doing and buy Somerville right away and thank me later. OMG... what can I say the game is a rush, an experience, pushes your feels, is mind juicing, and you witness an interactive artistic masterpiece. When you play the game start to finish which took me 4 hours just like Inside did in one sitting you will really start to question why so many games feel empty, dead and soulless. The game's experience is priceless and another one of a kind that I will never forget just like Inside(100% play this asap as well if you haven't).Sound: this is incredible and is a large part of the game's whole package. Music, ambient, sound FX basically everything is top tier plus has a purpose. All I can say is hook your game up to your amp and crank it especially if you have a nice 5.1, 7.1 or Atmos system, it's 100% worth it, just make sure you have it cranked. Other than that like I said there is this one spot where you sort of can't see you character but I am not sure if that was an intentional design, everything else you can 100% work out. _childDocuments_.review: A Pretentious Game Designed by Someone with More Ego than TalentAudio: 10/10. The sound effects are amazing. There is no walk button, no crouch button, no jump button.Enjoyment. 2/10. The game can be finished in about 3 hours. I played about 4 hours and made it about 2/3 of the way through then uninstalled the game. I watch the ending on YouTube at 1.5x normal speed.Puzzles: 2/10. None are very interesting. Most are very easy, many are very obtuse and hard to figure out because the game mechanics consistent. I love platform puzzle games like Limbo, Inside, and Shady Part of Me; this game is not even close to those games in quality or enjoyment.

_childDocuments_.review: A thoroughly captivating science fiction mystery, though it definitely won't be everyone's cup of tea.The art direction is impeccable. The modeling, palettes, sound, music, level design, and even camera movement all come together to produce a coherent, enigmatic atmosphere. The inspiration is obviously Stanisław Lem's , and probably more directly Andrei Tarkovsky movie based on it. It's a silent game, but so much is told through environmental storytelling. And yet it is never fully explained. Players have come up with some clever theories, but the mystery endures. This is not a game for those who demand full closure.Also, unfortunately, the gameplay can be grating. It's very slow, and honestly mostly a walking sim most of the time. There are also some puzzles, which are sometimes quite fascinating in that the game silently teaches you the solutions through environmental cues. Some puzzles, however, are obtuse or clunky. There's a bit of stealth, too, and some frustrating chase scenes that I don't think anyone has ever enjoyed in any game ever.All in all, it doesn't hold up as an enjoyable experience throughout, but I think the artistic presentation is so searing that I can easily recommend .

_childDocuments_.review: The settings is interesting and my favourite part of the game, but also a bit weird in the beginning. Is this the future and the character has just been living without current comforts, or why is not phased by some of the things he encounters? It seems like there is a part of the game missing from the beginning. Your character doesn't blink an eye when he discovers a power he has or how the world reacts to certain actions, like that's how things have always been. Maybe it's linked to how you got those powers, not sure.The main gameplay consists of solving puzzles to clear obstacles on your way and hiding from enemies that are after you. The puzzles are confusing occasionally. You can see what you're supposed to do, but the game is very unclear what you can do. However, some solutions are actually pretty clever and I have rarely used similar mechanics.The main obstacles that you are clearing throughout the game work inconsistently story wise. Sometimes you seem to be able to climb on top of it or over it, so why do I have solve some of these puzzles to get rid of them. Why couldn't I climb over it every time?While I like the visual style, the animations are a bit clumsy. Occasionally they seem unnatural or don't fit the action you're doing. It can also be difficult to see if you're standing in the right place, especially if the character is far from the camera. And sometimes the game is just very inconsistent where you need to stand in order to use an object. When you press the action button, your character might walk around a wall to go pet the dog. Some other time he will ignore a switch in front of him, because you need to be a step away from it in order to use it. This inconsistency makes the gameplay annoying.The world and the story were interesting, but because of the gameplay I can't really recommend the game. It's not a difficult game because of these issues, but rather frustrating to play.Minor spoilers for the ending! I think the idea on how the different endings work is neat, but very, very to obtuse. Nowhere in the game a similar mechanic is used. I activated one by accident, but for the rest I had to check a guide.

_childDocuments_.review: this is one of the most unique game experiences I've ever encountered, and this is even after my high expectations coming from being a huge Limbo & Inside fan.  the story is so complex and interesting, and doesn't hold your hand along the way.  I can totally empathize with the negative reviews; yes there isn't much here in terms of gameplay, and sometimes the camera angle or direction of where to go can be confusing or even frustrating.  However, the beautiful camera work and cinematography makes up for this ten fold.  The visual story being told here without a single word is simply a spectacle to be experienced. For such a simply told story to bring me nearly to tears, pump me full of adrenaline, and have me deeply thinking about the ending, was really impressive, and i'm very excited to see what Jumpship does next.  Just know what you're coming into, a four to five hour story with light puzzle work but a mind bending story and breathtaking visuals.  And if you prefer more engaging puzzles with rich visuals but no story at all, Cocoon would be more your thing, however for me, Somerville is definitely more of my thing.  10/10 Bravo to Jumpship

_childDocuments_.review: I will spare this game the disservice of being compared to INSIDE; it's its own game with its own style, merits, and shortcomings, and comparing anything to INSIDE is kinda unfair. Having said that, for certain types of players, this is an amazing game, but I can also see why some people would really dislike it, and there are some small tweaks that future similar games could make to have it be more widely appealing.Those Who Will Love It: If you go into this game looking for a beautiful mildly-interactive storybook with some puzzles, you will enjoy it a lot. The more patient you are, the better. The puzzles are generally good, there are decent visual indicators to guide you without them feeling misplaced in the world; I never found myself stuck for long. The art is stunning, and it's somewhat relaxing to play; other than the puzzles, you're just along for the ride.Those Who Will Hate It: This is largely NOT a fast-paced or action-packed game. If you enjoy storybooks and puzzle games but are impatient or have a short temper you may also not enjoy this game. If your favorite are games where the player has great variety in choices and movement, this is again not the game for you as this game is largely scripted (not that it physically takes control of the player all the time, but pseudo-scripted, it gives almost zero options at any given moment and movement ability is very limited; there are really no choices to make until the very end).To me, a review is both for other players and for the developers, so here's the developer part:Improvements: I'm not much of a game dev, but these are the things I would think could improve a lot with minimal work required to implement. Overall I think it's a great game, and the people who can enjoy it will love it, but a couple of things could make it more widely enjoyable.- Controls: To give even the illusion of control, it'd be better if there was a non-scripted movement speed and sprint option, and then only in key moments did scripted movement speed kick in, rather than the speed always being scripted/triggered. Similarly, jump or crouch options can be given to make the player feel more in control, even if the map is made to still limit the player to only have the designated path to travel on. It wouldn't change much, but would make the player feel more like the're actually in the story and have some control, even if they don't. Making a story be experienced the way it "should" be experienced is tempting, good even, usually, but not if it comes at the cost of immersion.- Secret Ending: I like having a treasure hunt ending, but an indicator at the end of the game of some sort that helps organize it might be good (I'll be cryptic to avoid spoilers). For example, there could be a room that's a sort of docking station where the found ones show up at the end, and missing/empty docking ports can tell the player about where they missed it (such as missed the 4th one), plus each docked one could play their sequence in this room so the player can see it all together and get it there at the end, in case they didn't write or memorize throughout the game.Obviously I don't expect any updates to this game, but it's just something to think about for next time, and I do hope there will be a next time! I'm a big fan of this dev team and can't wait to see what else comes out in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: I *really* wanted to like Somerville. I liked Limbo. I *adored* INSIDE. This should have been a no-brainer. Even the first puzzle sequence puts you in the small shoes of an adorable toddler with the world's least responsible parents, setting an anxious tone that I thought would carry a throughline.But much later, after once again shouting out loud "What the **** do you WANT from me?" at the screen, I had to conclude that no, I cannot in good conscience give Somerville a positive review. Too often the puzzle design is opaque or the mechanism/camera fiddly and frustrating. The plotting and world are obscure without being enigmatic - this isn't the Impressionist cinema of Limbo nor the unsettling nightmare dystopia of INSIDE. There seem to be aliens and destruction and threats and puzzles to do with light and colour but it doesn't hang together as a cohesive whole. I reached one ending without ever really understanding what I was doing nor what I was expected to do. Then there's the insufferable elements. What should be a heart-touching moment was lost on me due to the previous 5 minutes watching the main character limping around AGAIN, making the same "cough cough" sound AGAIN AND AGAIN, collapsing to his knees AGAIN. JFC, I just wanted to smack him.Puzzles happen in this game because it is a game and puzzles need to happen. Story sort of happens but then characters put themselves in danger because video game. Stakes and consequences don't gel adequately enough to make me care. I'm going to look up if there's other endings, then I'm going to uninstall and allow Somerville to rapidly fade from my memory. Such a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: Instinctively you could label this as a Limbo-esque game. True in the sense of atmosphere and the show-don't-tell style of story-telling. However, it's not a platform/puzzler and instead a walking sim/puzzler. Like most similar games, whether paying full price is worth it is something to consider. As much as I like and recommend this one, I'd say it's better to wait for a sale.The setting is built around the invasion of earth by aliens and your character is passed the first of a couple of powers by a dying warrior in advanced armour fighting the threat. Your powers allow you to manipulate the alien tech and that's what creates the puzzles. It's as simple as changing its state back and forth between liquid and solid. The real puzzles are scattered infrequently and are almost all very easy. It would have benefited from a greater number of more intricate puzzles to sway the needle away from its walking sim leanings.The nature of the aliens is indeed very alien. These aliens are so utterly different and their motives are difficult to understand. Some of them are drones, almost childlike and very social and whose job it seems is to clean up the landscape of the alien tech. Others are animal-like and hunt you down. It's great to not see the usual alien threats and having to guess at ambiguous motives.While you do effectively choose from multiple endings, they are a puzzle in of itself and which one you choose comes down to how much attention you are paying to specific encounters throughout the game. In this sense it is great for anyone who likes to replay a game and take in the details. This also applies for making sense of the story overall.Other than the balance of puzzle frequency, my biggest gripe would be the controls. It's not just left-right movement and there is some depth. This get fidgety when moving around obstacles or trying to move to the right spot to grab onto an interactable object. As long as you're aware then this could be a perfect casual game for those who like intriguing sci-fi. It also has the benefit of no dialogue or characters which ruin every other game coming out these days. Great escapism for around four hours.
