_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing Gundam Breaker since the original Vita release. I have two end-game level playthroughs of Gundam Breaker 1, 2 and 3 each. We ignore New Gundam Breaker in this house. I even played Gundam Breaker Mobile for a while. Long story short, I know what I'm talking about.Gundam Breaker 4 is the middest of mid. It doesn't dip to New Gundam Breaker's level, but it doesn't rise above Gundam Breaker 2, let alone 1 or 3. Long story short, I think it was developed in a real hurry after the shutdown of Gundam Breaker Mobile.There are some positives. It looks good, the diorama feature is great, how much you can customise everything cannot be understated. This was also the set of positives attributed to New Gundam Breaker. As per that game, if you can secure a 100% save file, there's tons of enjoyment to be had in building and posing Gunpla, if you're into that sort of thing.The problem is that the gameplay just isn't really there, in a variety of spots. The game holds up for a few hours, there's a bunch of nostalgia drops during the main plot calling back to the previous Gundam Breakers, and it all seems it's going to be fine. Then the cracks start to show...-Enemies never get more aggressive beyond the first mission. Mostly they just stand around and sometimes, rarely, once in a blue moon, take a swing. The semibosses and big bosses are more aggressive, but predictable, and easy to beat (it's much, MUCH too easy to get a semiboss into a permanent stunlock that other semibosses can't interrupt, and big bosses usually have somewhere on their body you can hover around and swing away at their healthbars). The only difficulty comes from how hard they hit; once you max out your HP at the 1.08 million mark (which is so easy to do - elaboration later), you'll never be threatened again even in Newtype difficulty.-Instead of Gundam Breaker 3's difficulty system where you unlock Extreme and Newtype at the end of their previous difficulties, you unlock both by the end of your first run. You also unlock the level cap at the end of your first campaign run, so you can make max level, max rarity parts as soon as that final mission is over, and they give you all the materials you need to do that by finishing a single mission. As a result, your endgame progression goes like this:* Finish final mission.* Level up weapons to 50/max rarity (takes approx 2 missions).* Play a couple of Newtype missions.* Level up the rest of your gear.* You are now unstoppable.There is no such thing as a Gundam Breaker 4 endgame.-Abilities, which Gundam Breaker 3 put such a heavy emphasis on with part fusing, are a lot more streamlined, and entirely for the worse. A bunch of them are always must haves (everything that gives you HP) while others are worthless (OP equipment is so weak that I can't imagine it being better than just swinging weapons, so why would I bother taking the abilities). There's also much fewer of them, some they don't bother explaining (what the hell is Hate) and they even went to the incredibly annoying distance of having some abilities be specific to the hand you wield them in (so you have different abilities for damage increases for Left Hand Twinblade and Right Hand Twinblade). Combine this with the UI that makes it very difficult to tell what you're doing, and your entire process for merging abilities is "select every part you have, also have fun because we prompt you about high rarity parts every time, throw them all into one part and go with the abilities you want" instead of having to make hard choices about what way you want your build to go. It commits the cardinal sin of being BORING. You also can't merge top rarity parts, so if you want to swap your look while keeping your parts, tough. I thought there may have been some relief when they unlocked Ability Cartridges, which is a throwback to Gundam Breaker 1, but again, find two that increase your HP by 400% total and you'll be fine for the entire rest of the game.-And finally, the missions. Story and Quest Missions play exactly the same way, every single time - big open area, one-three waves. Big open area, one-three waves. Boss or slightly - SLIGHTY - different take at the end. No paths to travel down, no choices along the way. I didn't think this would end up mattering as much as it did, but man does it grate after a while. Bounty Hunter is as boring as it's ever been because of the braindead AI. And Survival? The biggest slog imaginable. Over an hour of the same crap - endless waves of identically behaving enemies. I suspect that they really want to push the whole 'time attack' aspect with needing to get S Ranks on both Breaks and Time, but by the time I was at endgame I was S Ranking everything that I tried with no real effort.There's just nothing here, gameplay wise. The simple level design, lack of abilities, completely braindead AI even in comparison to the previous games, it all reeks of being made in a hurry without respecting what made the previous games great - they have the callbacks, but not the soul. Either that, or they just don't have what it takes to get the balance right. I don't hate Gundam Breaker 4, but I find myself thinking I'd rather be playing the original trilogy instead.

_childDocuments_.review: As a Gundam fan and builder of the real models, I was excited for this game. During the preview videos, the game looked like a possible winner. However upon purchase I've found some serious issues with the game that need to be addressed for the amount of money I paid (I bought the deluxe version because I wanted all of the models it came with and the Season Pass). If my number 1 reason is not addressed soon, I will be looking to be refunded.1. With the graphics all set to max using the in-game options, I'm limited to a screen size of 1280x720... and I have a RX 6800 XT with a 4k LG C4 TV. This is absolutely unacceptable when a huge part of Gunpla is the detail of the models. I'm reading the recommended requirements and it says the game can run 3840x2160. The game is as grainy as the videos on the Steam page. It's the year 2024, I seriously expected better.2. The combat does feel very hack/slash with little to no thought regarding tactics for combos or ranged weapons. It's easy to blitz the missions by just rushing the enemy and hacking away with the early OP sabers they give in the missions (Atlas sabers to be specific).3. Camera feels very under-developed. I've played games where the targeting system feels more natural. In this game it's either you lock-on with the camera absolutely nailed to the target with no obvious keys to switch your target, or the camera free floats above you while you turn, either unable to see what you are shooting at or you are hopefully shooting at what is centered on your screen. It's also very strange that you have to switch to a separate "mode" for more accurate targeting when this game obviously is trying to avoid bogging the player down with excess hassles.4. Movement does not feel responsive/tight. I can feel how delayed the jet boosts are when activating/deactivaing. Turning has a bit too much slop. For reference, even though my keyboard and mouse are wireless, I have absolutely no problem playing online multiplayer shooting games where response is critical for success.5. This really doesn't feel like it taps into the true potential it has when you consider how you can combine various parts from unique Gundams (and other machines). Tap into the Gundam universe more, learn what makes each machine unique, and bring that out so that players can really design a Gunpla that speaks to their play style.I'm willing to give positives where they are due as well1. Actual gameplay can be fun (with the caveat that it may become too bland after so many missions of just hack/slash and nothing else)2. The the large library of models (including the rarer ones) make it interesting3. Even though I have a big issue with the graphics quality (as mentioned above), I can tell they are really trying to make the battlefields seem more like you're in a modeled area than a realistic one.Sorry dev team, but I can't really recommend this game right now. This game would be ok if it were the Playstation 3 era, but we are well beyond that. (Note, I AM willing to change the review IF the team addresses the first issue indicated here).

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game with some caveats.First: You have to be willing to put up with a painfully generic storyline with painfully generic characters. The obvious villains turn out to be the villains, through the power of friendship (and this big gun you happen to have) you will triumph over all obstacles with zero issues (even if the cutscenes like to pretend that your team mates do more than they do)...and do A.I. have soooooouls?Second: You have to be prepared to do literally EVERYTHING in a mission. Your teammates are only there to provide commentary if you're playing solo, and are virtually worthless as anything other than cannon fodder and the occasional revive if you somehow miraculously get killed.Third: If you are a fan of the Gundam series, weapons you would think would be highly effective are far less so. The Buster Rifle for instance, a weapon capable of destroying warships and multiple MS in a single shot, is no better than a standard beam rifle. And as another example, your beam sabers are no better than a love tap, you're better off sticking with Zaku II heat axes.Fourth: If you are not using makers parts, you are making a horribly underpowered build. Same for arms, legs, ect that have abilities. Without those your machine will struggle HARD.Fifth: There are quite a few kits missing from the game that, quite frankly, we should have had rather than the space used on SD grade ones. There's a tab for Origin series kits, yet none are in the game. Thunderbolt is missing all but two of its suits. There are a lot of variant kits missing, like GM and Zaku Snipers. Ect ect.It's a solid enough game play loop, if SEVERELY limited by being basically three or four chained arenas that you teleport between beating up enemies that are more speed bumps than real threats. This is on standard difficulty mind you, I haven't done the harder difficulty yet as there is no reward or reason to do so at this point in time that would be worth it. Especially as by the end of the standard difficulty run, along with all the quests on standard and at least one or two survival runs, you will have your personal build at level cap and there won't be any real reason to do anything else with the game (even accounting for switching to the harder to level Master Grade parts you unlock after beating the story).Best advice is buy on sale, not at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, it's solid.Gundam Breaker 4 takes a bit to get into. Honestly, I was a little ambivalent about the game at the start. The basic combat is pretty clunky early on, and the story is pretty poorly paced at the beginning as well, but once you get, like, half-way through the game it starts to open up more.As far as the combat goes: It feels pretty stiff and clunky at the start. The control can feel a bit unresponsive due to recovery times at the end of basic attack actions. This is appears to be intentional. The game really wants you to do a bunch of animation cancelling with your skills. Using EX and OP skills both ignore action recovery animations and dive straight into the skills, and the skills often have extremely short recoveries. This allows you to chain basic attacks into skills back into basic attacks back into more skills, which is pretty fun. The thing is, early on, you're not going to have a lot of parts with a variety of EX and OP skills available, so you're pretty much just stuck with the clunky basic attacks for a while as you farm up parts. The combat certainly feels like departure from the sort of mindless hack & slash that GB3 was (which isn't a knock, I actually enjoyed GB3's combat more, on the whole), and you may or may not particularly like the new direction. One part I don't like as much is that EX skills are exclusively tied to parts - they don't come from weapons. You don't get the bullet bursts, beam blasts, melee tornado launchers, projected blades, etc. from the previous games. Now it's pretty much just powerful rapid melee combos, rail cannon shots, etc. They're pretty much stronger OP skills, that run off the EX gauge rather than on cooldowns. They work well within the game's systems, but I definitely miss the EX skills from the previous Gundam Breaker games.That said, a nice addition is being able to master not just EX skills, but also OP skills. Once you've mastered them, by fully upgrading an associated part's rarity, you can equip them even when you don't have the part on your gunpla. In this game, when you use a skill from a part you don't have, a sort of wireframe version of the part that the skill is pulled from replaces your current part for the duration of the skill. This allows you more freedom to build a unit based on aesthetics, since you don't have to, for example, use the Gouf's right arm to have access to its integrated heat rod.As far as the story goes: It's kind of a mixed bag. If you loved the world built up by Gundam Breaker 3/mobile, you'll be at home here. The new character introductions kind of feel rushed. Kind of feels like you're instant best friends for no reason, rather than having building relationships, and the characters and their conflicts show up and resolve way too quickly. That said, the new cast is likable. Otherwise, the overarching story is very... Gundam Breaker. I won't get into details, because spoilers, but yeah, it's a little silly and melodramatic. It works for the setting and how silly and melodramatic it has been at times in the past, but it certainly could have been better, even by Gundam Breaker standards. Part of the issue is that the entire story happens in an online game setting, so you're somehow helping these characters you've just met solve complex personal problems in their real life just by playing games with them, and not even really having particularly deep discussions. It's kind of weird. This is in contrast to GB3, where a lot of the storytelling happens in the real (game) world, with your characters interacting with each other face to face, and you're allowed to see how characters resolve things with each other and their situations in the real world. In GB4 it's kind of "I feel better after playing games with you and will now instantly solve the interpersonal conflicts I have in real life!"Still, it's a decent enough sequel that respects the setting and characters, so I don't really have any  complaints, and the characters grew on me over time. ... Misa is still the best Gundam Breaker character though. As silly as GB3 was at times, I really loved the story and characters. Anyway, the game definitely grew on me the more I played. It's not GB3, and I still think I like GB3 more, but I still really like GB4.

You can even look at what others are building and you will be amazed by the creativity of the community.- Very big selection of mobile suits from all series including their special powers and unique quirks.Neutral:- Story is meh, it's not bad, it's just the typical thing you could've expected but it could not have had any story at all too, so better than nothing I guess.- Combat is fine, but needs refining,  I could never get used to having jump and boost on same button. If you want to build a default kit to play around with, you will have to google to find out what is their loadout supposed to be. That's insane to me.- MG parts: Why? _childDocuments_.review: 40 hours in, I've completed the main story line on standard difficulty. Pretty fun game if you enjoy making custom gunpla/mechs. Lots of customization options. I haven't counted how many total mobile suits can be unlocked, but it's definitely in the hundreds. Each mobile suit consists of up to 19 parts: Head, Chest, Left Arm, Right Arm, Legs, Back unit, Shield, Two long range weapons, Two short range weapons, and up to eight "builder parts" (basically accent pieces you can add to your mech, and adjust placement, rotation, and scale)Story was pretty cookie cutter anime stuff. Nothing to really write home about, but still enjoyable.Gameplay/combat reminds me a lot of Dynasty Warriors. Waves of enemies, stronger bosses throughout the waves, big boss on the final (3rd) wave. All in all, I'd rank it a solid 7.5/10 fun but nothing spectacular. I'd only recommend full price if you're REALLY itching for a gunpla/mech builder, that has some fun combat, if you don't really care about mech building, I'd say wait to buy it on sale. Also, shoutout to a similar mech building game if you're looking for one: M.A.S.S. Builder. It's a very similar game to this, made by an indie team. That game has even more customization than this game.I do really wish we had more Gundam games that were good like this one, it sucks that most ones are kind of just cashgrabs with super shallow mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game made for Gunpla fans. Please understand that before you buy.In it, you play in a virtual Gunpla battler game where you do arcade like action missions, collect parts and build and customize your own Gunpla. The game has two sides to it: First off, the Gunpla building which is done quite well and provides near limitless combinations of parts and skills. Paint coloring, decals, weathering, and part sizing can all be done in the build mode of the game. You can really unleash your creativity with how deep this side of the game is.The other half of the game is the gameplay. It's features arena based action gameplay of which you will fight a few waves of enemies and occasionally a "big boss". That's... kind of it. The gameplay is highly repetitive, grindy and the story and provided characters for it are not that interesting.Pros: + Visual quality is adequate for the anime inspired aesthetic presented. It's about PS3/PS4 levels of visual fidelity. +++ The Gunpla Building side of the game is done very, very well IMO. This will be the main selling point of this title and will probably be the reason anyone even considers purchasing this title. The sheer variety of kits offered, combined with the painting options, decaling, weathering, and extra add-on parts and the sky is the limit with what you can create here.++ A variety of combat styles for gameplay exist so it's easy to tailor your gunpla to play however you feel fit to play+ Upgrading your gunplas for the most is fairly easy once you unlock it+ Seamless switching between controller and mouse and keyboard+ Mouse and keyboard controls are adequate and usable, but the game is clearly for controller. + In game shop can provide an easy way to acquire parts that would otherwise be a pain to grind for (You will need to progress the main story though to make more kits available)+ Photo mode is pretty basic, but Diorama mode is where the real Photo Mode is and provides much options for your Gunpla photo shots+ Multiplayer modes exist but they are mainly of PvE contentCons:-- Single game save slot. Hope you don't plan on ever starting fresh as you might lose all that progress you worked hard for.- The music is mostly forgettable and doesn't feature any licensed music from the Gundam shows-- The overall story and characters provided is mostly a generic feeling team battle anime and only really gets slightly more interesting past chapter 5. Unfortunately that's too little, too late to save it from the negative. This is not the reason you will be buying this game.- The main villain is unfortunately too clownish to take seriously despite having some noble intentions that are only revealed at the very end of the game.- As great as the build mode is, it does have a few shortcomings; can't change beam effect or frame colors, mastered skills will change the parts on your gunpla to an ugly holographic part when used,  Options were added for these as of the latest version so I'll consider these fixed.- The ability titles in game are at times a bit of an indecipherable mess. I don't if this was a translation issue or something else was going on here but whoever did this needs to redo a LOT of this-- Level design is far too simplistic. Just basic arena after arena with invisible walls as arena edges. Plus there are no space or 0G stages either and is a weird omission for a Gundam game.- The controls take some getting used to. Jumps aren't done naturally for example, you have to boost up first from a standstill, then you can boost in the horizontal plane. If you've played any other 3rd person action game this is going to feel incredibly awkward.- Difficultly increases tend to just increase enemy damage and give them massive HP padding. Their AI doesn't really change much. It's lazy difficulty. --- Speaking of AI, this game has some of the worst AI behavior I've seen in a game.  Your companions for story mode are woefully passive and incompetent most of the time while the enemy AI will often stand around doing nothing as if it's waiting it's turn or something. - The target lock on system in the game can be janky, especially in the big boss fights- Stun locking, for better for worse, exists- The companion audio spam is pretty bad- In the post game, you'll get access to MG parts which are nothing but up-sized regular parts despite their increased cost of acquisition- Bounty mode and the boss level buffs that it gives player Gunplas. This a mode that probably should had been reserved for the late game considered it necessitates having a solid build to make the most of- The Leaderboard, or more the near lack of anti-cheat safeguards against cheaters filling up the top half or so of the rankings. Not a huge problem per se, but some of the special events have flair rewards that require reaching certain ranking threshholds in the leaderboard and this is nigh impossible do fairly due to said cheaters. At the end of this, this game is a double edged sword; it appeals very much to Gunpla fans and it's obviously geared towards that purpose. As a result though, it'll appeal to few others. Gunpla fans may certainly overlook the game's failings in it's gameplay in lieu of it's amazing build mode and for them, this may certainly be worth the asking price.For everyone else, or those with only a passing interest in Gundam, I'd say wait for a sale or even pass if you're looking for a good action game.I still give it a recommend though as there's fun to be had here, even if you just buy it for the building mode.7/10 if you're a Gunpla/Gundam fan, for everyone else it's more like a 5/10Updated: 10/25/24

_childDocuments_.review: I'd heard (mostly) good things about the Gundam Breaker series for years, but didn't get around to actually trying it out until this new installment. I'm glad I did, and had fun with the main campaign. Said campaign's story is in the mold of /: Gunpla enthusiasts playing together, making friends, and confronting challenges. This type of story is well-suited for the game's theme. If you had put Gundam pilots from the main shows in some crossover story, they would doubtless be horrified at the core conceit of mashing together Gundams and other mobile suits into Frankenmecha (though the thought of Char ripping off an RX-78-2's arm and head to slap on his own suit's torso would be pretty funny). Anyway, the story is good, lighthearted fun, with a smattering of typos here and there. It also serves as a decent enough introduction to the world of Gunpla and the concept of kitbashing.Speaking of, I'll get it out of the way right now: there's a roughly 50% chance your favorite mobile suit is in the game. If it's a Gundam piloted by a main character, bump that up to maybe 80 or 90%. Despite that, there's a lot to play around with, including several SD Gundam kits and some oddities like Ball, Fuunsaiki, and Super Fumina (as a mecha musume/MS Girl fan, and a fan of that suit in particular, the inclusion of that last one made me really happy). The customization options are fairly deep, and you can easily spend half your time in the game, or more, tweaking builds to be as pretty or as horrifying as possible. After building, you can pose models for photos or place them in dioramas (and take even more photos). It's all much cheaper and less time-intensive than real-life Gunpla building.Outside of virtual Gunpla assembly, there's a button-mashy action RPG to be played. As long as you keep your parts leveled up to meet the recommendations in the mission descriptions, this portion of the game should be fairly easy. There's a lot of controls to wrap your head around, but if you aren't an idiot like me who chose to play another action RPG at around the same time, said controls should soon become second nature. As in the Front Mission games, the real meat of the gameplay lies in how well you assemble your loadouts.The music is fine, but there is a bug that crops up at times which affects how it loops. The graphics are fine as well, though it was a little odd that lip flaps weren't animated for every variant of every character's static portrait. The sound effects have that Gundam feel, which is the most I could ask for, and though I can't speak for the English dub, the Japanese voice acting is decent. It's fun to play, and very easy to lose track of time in when it comes to the Gunpla customization. Gunpla fans, and mech fans in general, would enjoy this one.

If you give your gundam a backpack with a beam saber then they can pull and use it. If you give them a GN drive from 00 then they can use Trans Am. I've not run into a situation thus far where I'm unable to use an ability or weapon that I felt like I should be able to. No cosmetic weapons.- Fun characters and a simple story line to engage you.- The game's model selection seems very vast from what I've seen thus far.Cons:- The combat is pretty repetitive and is easy to break if you build your mobile suits to be crazy over the top powerful, though the game does try to afford some variety where it can.- Missions stop you for story pretty often even when they don't have much to say. _childDocuments_.review: I see people leaving negative reviews on this game, and I get it, GB3 was more fluid really, and the nerfs to optional parts were not great.That said, more kits, EX-Skills charging faster, so the spread between OP-Parts/Ex-Skills is somewhat better (EX-Skills should also have 2 pages like OP-Parts tho), and one-handed/two-handed options do makes me happy to play this game.No I don't think this is better than GB3, but, it is still a LOT of fun, and I can play with my friends, so all in all an 8/10 for me :)Alright, after a LOT of testing, some of these changes are straight ass, like if you use a mastery skill which has a duration, like a buff or funnels, it stops you from using the original part it's rendered over, so for example, if you use some legs that have beam sabers, and select mastery skill for the leg part that are buffs/funnels, while they mastery skill is in use, you cannot use the original legs OP/EX (which does have  some exceptions, like if you use some buff on the original leg, then pop the mastery from the leg, it doesn't cancel out, but it makes it invisible, making it look like a bug).Also, ranged optional parts using the average damage from ranged weapons L/R is ludicrous, if you want to do a purely melee MS, covering range with OP parts, you're ♥♥♥♥♥♥, since they use damage from ranged weapons, instead of actually averaging the 4 equipable main weapons.Definetly changed my opinion to an 7/10, because I started noticing a bunch of stupidly unbelievable decisions that makes the game worse than GB3 imo, while I still recommend this because it's still incredibly fun.

_childDocuments_.review: As a Mecha enthusiast, I can personally say that this game should satisfy the need for a solid Gundam entry on the PC Market. After the unfortunate disasters that were Gundam Evolution and New Gundam Breaker; Gundam Breaker 4 is a shining gem under a pile of rubbish. So far, I've been enjoying the gameplay quite a bit although do not expect anything in-depth (i.e button combos, strings etc.) it is simplistic and similar to your average hack & slash, albeit with a much larger variety as each weapon type has its own set of unique attack patterns which can be paired with other weapons to create longer strings of attacks and extend the combo meter. The game isn't very restrictive and allows you to cancel out of attacks which can helps players transition to other attacks whether at close or long range and before I forget; yes, there are LOTS OF WEAPONS. Additionally, I'm sure most Gundam fans are looking to see if they are able to find their favorite model kit or create their favorite build from previous games. It's safe to say that there definitely a large variety of Mobile Suits in the game and more are obtainable later in the game. If by some chance you do not find your Mobile Suit of choice; it might just be included in a DLC. Personally, I van safely say that the roster has definitely exceeded my expectations and I hope for the extra to include more of the missing Mobile Suits. Unfortunately, that will cost a dime in the future but worth it if you find yourself loving this game.The grinding isn't tedious and more akin to your average looter shooter yet a bit more rewarding but I do fear that grinding for high rarity parts may be a hassle but the game is quite generous the more you progress and includes features to help further that progression. The story isn't a huge focal point but it is intriguing although the quality of the writing is that of your average anime slop on a Saturday night. Its charming and the characters are likable and the voice acting (this varies depending on language selection) is great, at least when the voices are set to Japanese. TL;DR - It's a niche game meant for fans of the series but its very casual friendly, would rate it gundamslop/10

_childDocuments_.review: My thoughts two weeks after launchFor context regarding my viewpoints here, my history with the franchise is as follows:1: Clear2: Clear3: Clear pre-DLC, need to go back to that at some point and do the DLC after cleaning out my inventory since I literally can't deploy.New: Played for one hour, spent the next two hours filling out the customer survey that came in the package to tell them how offensively bad it was.4: Literally screamed with joy at the reveal in Nintendo Direct half a year ago, been counting the days to launch, played extensively in the Open Network Tests, have it both on Switch and PC, with all told somewhere over 100 hours clocked in as of this writing. Have S Ranked every Story and Quest on every difficulty, cleared Survival, and done a fair bit of Bounty Hunter. To the best of my knowledge, I have "finished" all the contents.To start from my verdict: Absolutely in love with the game, very much worth the wait, a much needed return to form, definitely the best game to come out this year. That said, it's still far from perfect, nor is it a replacement for 2 or 3.Customization has gone three steps forward and one step back from 3 it feels. The ability to mismatch arms, as well as to wield two different weapons for both Close and Long Range is absolutely wonderful, and the interface for customizing your parts has become infinitely more user friendly. On the other hand, as a trade off each part has two fewer Ability slots, "set" Abilities are all but gone, and weapons in particular have had a ridiculous amount of splitting up of Abilities with things like capacity and reload speed on ranged weapons in particular splitting on a per weapon basis, and then all of them getting split based on which hand they're in. It's a ridiculous amount of bloat that exacerbates the problem of "wasting" parts when combining to upgrade, and makes the whole experience a lot less enjoyable than it could be. Ability Cartridges as well are the absolute worst decision in the entire game, though sadly unsurprising considering how common gacha mechanics have become, and how consumers have been Kool-Aided to the point they believe that these somehow "extend the lifespan" of a game rather than killing it.Combat is likewise a plus and minus both. Dual wielding opens up lots of fun possibilities and combos that couldn't be done before, but also makes each individual weapon class's moveset feel less special. Making OPs function like EXs used to while restricting EXs to a special gauge is an interesting balance choice, but overall I find it overly restrictive, which is odd considering how it feels like there are fewer OPs and EXs I even want to use at all now since I haven't found any worth it other than Super Mode/Jigen Haouryuu and the Beam Saber ranbu moves. The combo system adds an interesting level of speed to the combat, but I feel like the costs to the movesets and the stage design to facilitate it aren't really worth it.Story is solid - like previous Breaker titles, it's not the main attraction and certainly not life-changing by any means, but it's good writing with likable characters who are well-acted, with just the right mix of Gundam references and even nods to other properties entirely (I actually burst out laughing at Kurokante going full ダメージを回復してやろう on us.)From what I understand, they're planning to do that thing that newer games do where they use Internet connectivity to update the game and add new contents or fix things, so with that in mind here's what I'm hoping to see:-A fix for Ability Cartridge. This system is the absolute lowest point of the game, and the sooner we get the ability to combine these to improve the Abilities contained within and to mix and match the Abilities within together, the better.-Ability to disable Gousei and selling warnings based on rarity and contained parts. With how many parts flood in and being unable to deploy if a part category is full, this is an absolute must. Increasing the cap would be welcome too - IIRC Breaker 3 was about 1000, so 1500 is a huge improvement, but still not enough, ESPECIALLY with the huge divisions of Abilities into things like Left and Right hand.-Ability to sort and filter by Ability. This ties into the Gousei stuff from earlier, but with how many Abilities have been split into a hundred different ones, it's just a nightmare, especially when trying to tell at a glance whether you're combining for 右 or 左.-BGM. This might be impossible due to Breaker 4 getting a foreign release, since music rights are notoriously annoying to deal with, in which case I can only hope Breaker 5 goes back to being Japan only. BGM is a huge deal for me personally.-More Gunpla. We've gotten great stuff, but there's always a need for more - getting SDs in but none of the original Sangokuden characters was a huge letdown, and I also look forward to seeing some of the other Gaiden characters like Knight Alex and Kenshi Zeta show up too. Gundam X also needs more love, as we still don't have either version of Airmaster or Leopard. I'm also still waiting on Gundam Spiegel from G, and the X2 and X3 from Crossbone, as well as Build Fighters/Try machines like Sengoku Astray and Winning Gundam.-PC version specific problem: they really need to fix the buttons not working right. For some reason the displays keep swapping A with B and X with Y, which is especially frustrating with how the EX and OPs are displayed on screen since it really screws with visual placement. Also the fact that one of the OP slots simply just doesn't work at all. Neither of these problems occur on the Switch version, so unless the PS4/5 version is also bugged, this seems to be a PC port exclusive problem.To conclude, absolutely amazing game, well worth the wait and a triumphant return to form for the franchise after far, FAR too long, though not without shortcomings and potential for growth. Looking forward to see this game improve, and for Gundam Breaker 5 to be even better.

The Story is on the basic side, but this is in parts understandable if you want to appeal to all ages, there are compromises to be made, that said I do miss the CG Cutscenes of GB3. Could it been better? Yes. Could it have been so much worse? See NGB, I rest my case there.  They decided to play it VERY safe this time, while still allowing wiggle room, and also reusing/re-utilizing assets from NGB(Like most if not all of NGB's gunpla is in this game save maybe a couple of the dlc stuff like Zaku III Custom I'm positive was in the game)You can expect more for the game and that's fine really, more power to you, but you also have to take into account that this game is basically one that both young and old can get into without problem, and thus opening the world of Gunpla Customization to them with a simple investment, which I mean as a gunpla owner myself, it's not bad. They admittedly did play this game very safe as a result but still managed to add in new stuff like the arms being left and right parts now.One additional aspect you likely need to consider as well, this game is using the unreal engine, which the first was NGB of the series, that DOES create issues to a degree, because it becomes a little trickier to bring in more of the past gunpla without completely recreating them in unreal, which also explains the content being not as complex, because they wanted to likely create a solid foundation that COULD be improved upon should they make future games now that this is successful product.  As a game itself, it's the gameplay is decent, even if the content of said game is a bit on the basic side in terms of the complexities.   The Building Portion is half the selling point of GB4, but that also could be seen as a con, if you wanting to simply pick up and play, you are not going to get that here.  Now I see some reviews going about how this is not GB3 which is a tad of a half-truth, but mostly ignorant statement.  GB4 is not GB3, this is true, because of the glaring and simple fact that this game is on an entirely different game engine, GB1-3, used I think an engine co developed with ilinx.   Which changed when NGB and onwards being powered by the Unreal Engine.  Which leads into a topic of basically that of course it doesn't have all the kits that past 3 games had, they basically have to be mostly remade in Unreal, which they have made a concentrated effort in doing with some sadly falling through the cracks.   This game has MOST of the roster that was available in NGB, so at least they benefited some from that dumpster fire.It being on Unreal leads to the other topic of naturally that it would feel different from GB3 gameplay wise, you try to replicate the same stuff in GB4 and you will find it's nigh IMPOSSIBLE to get it to be 1to1 system using entirely different power sources.  That said, they did do a decent job at trying to get closer to the style of GB3 combat at the very least, which is impressive and a merit to consider.  The Gundam Breaker series has always been about playing and experimenting to find the build that suits your playstyle most, you are not going to be hand held in that regard, you have to work to find that RIGHT build that suits you the most.
_childDocuments_.name: GUNDAM BREAKER 4

_childDocuments_.review: Gundam Breaker 4 is a single or multiplayer mecha game based around building the perfect Gunpla model. Most of the game will have you taking on various mobile suits from the Gundam universe (from the original series right up to Witch from Mercury, though apparently a suit from Seed Freedom is coming). The 'breaker' part of the name comes from the mechanic of breaking parts off your opponent's Gunpla to add to your own collection.The combat is simple at first glance, but when you add in EX and OP skills it actually becomes very open- you can even air juggle opponents by using different weapon combinations.The Story Mode (which I haven't completed yet) seems a bit of an afterthought, and the mission structures do get very samey (generally you'll do a wave of fighting grunts, then a 2nd area where you fight a miniboss and a final area will usually either be a rival team or a boss fight. Some of the bosses are huge and require you to target specific parts, so it isn't completely mindless.The main reason anyone would play this though is for the Gunpla customisation. There are around 250 mobile suits in the game, each part can have different abilities and you can kitbash pieces together however you want. This means you can make pretty much whatever you want. Seeing what other players come up with can be one of the best (and sometimes, one of the worst) things about the game!If you're a Gundam or general mecha fan, or if you like games with a large amount of customisation you'll probably like this.The only real criticisms I have is that the missions can be samey (as I've mentioned) and the music doesn't vary much. The lobby music in particular will get stuck in your head very quickly, for all the wrong reasons.Overall, I would recommend GB4. With AC6, Mecha Break and this, mecha is back.

_childDocuments_.review: I give this game a strong recommendation with a huge asterisk after it. It's great for putting kitbash ideas together and designing your own gundam, the gameplay is solid, if a little repetitive, and there's a lot of fun to be had if you're the sort of person who enjoys both halves of this game. However, it really is two very separate halves: Building and Combat. The building is very in depth with plenty of customization options that some people have used in very out of the box ways, which is always a blast to see. The combat isn't very deep by any standard, however there are enough options that it almost gains a depth through variety. The story is fairly short at time of writing (DLCs are still being released that include new story missions) and has a bit of a saturday morning cartoon feel to it, but it's enough to get you to feel for the characters and engage with the combat missions. All in all, if you're a fan of Gundam, this is a must have. If you aren't, this game isn't going to make you a fan.

_childDocuments_.review: The story? Idiotic. Chaos did nothing wrong.The presentation? Pretty meh. It's not... completely busted or unplayable, or even unstable (your mileage will, as always, vary) but as with most "primarily for the domestic market" bandai namco games the default mouse and keyboard controls might as well not exist. The absolute nothingburger of the music is disappointing but there'll probably be a music pack DLC at some point because it's a gundam game and they're like that sometimes.The gameplay? Solid, but very, very easy. Juggle guys, combo them til they explode in a shower of colourful pickups, rinse, repeat, occasionally fight a big guy. Absolutely feels like a PS2 game in an alright way.The actual game is all in making and customizing your robots. Hell yeah, the amount you can do and the creativity of the community is amazing. You will see absolutely insane stuff in multiplayer. If they get community events going it'll be a slam dunk on that front. There's always the need for more bits, but there's a very, very solid selection so far with more in DLC eventually.Do I actually recommend this game? Probably on sale if big anime robots appeal at all. To the people who know what the difference between a Dom and Dreissen is, you've probably already bought it. It's not enough to recommend to anyone who's not at least kind of in on painting tiny plastic models so they can slap other tiny plastic models so you can have the cool pointy shoulders.

_childDocuments_.review: I was really disappointed when Gundam Breaker Mobile ended as I really enjoyed the game play and customization and never thought that I'd ever be able to find a game like that again.I'm glad that I was able to come across this game as while I was skeptical at first, I'm glad that I did give this game a chance. The single player story was somewhat predictable if you have watched the Gundam Build series (Gundam Build Fighters, Fighters Tri, Divers, Divers Re:Rise) but still had me guessing with some of the nuance of the story.Fighting had me changed my wants for my main unit from a mid-range fighting style to a Close Quarter Combat fighting style as early range weapons were rather weak compared to the CQC weapons (at least until you’re able to both upgrade and find better weapons) Depending on one’s play style, the combat could be hectic as I often found myself in the enemy’s face more often than not despite my effort not to be on standard difficulty.THe customization I think makes this game really shine as I am able to bring out several designs that I had been creating and been working on for years and even bringing back a few designs that I had created on GB-Mobile. They have an adjust feature where you can move parts around and resize them so that they can actually fit with the design you are going for without making things visibly weird. Then add multiple smaller parts not attached to any of your typical main line parts that you can add to any of your creations. Admittedly I’ve barely touched much of the Diorama feature, but from what I have done, the controles are kind of clucky and a little bit hard to work with, plus I had to constantly readjust the camera for the shot I wanted to get.The game does have its flaws and some things could have done with a little more polish, but overall, I would recommend this game to others, especially Gundam/Gunpla lovers.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that could easily be seen by many as a 5/10 or 6/10; but for the right people it's a flawed but incredibly addictive game. I haven't played a game this much since Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. The potential for this series is higher though. The niche market for the game likely limits the budget for this series.The ideal player (in my opinion) is someone who likes various Gundam shows and likes making Gunpla models. Or the idea of making Gunpla models. I've made a couple of models and liked a few of the shows, so I'm the target audience. A action-brawler with a decent amount of depth in its combat system, with an incredibly detailed building system that spans not only the Gunpla (mobile suits), but also building actual dioramas to display your creations. There's semi-random loot drops, a robust item upgrading system, an ability transfer system (called "Synthesis") and more for 250 Gunpla kits.The combat can often be similar to a "beat-em-up", but some enemies even on Standard difficulty will create and close space, dodge and block attacks and the game can feel like "Devil May Cry" between either side-stepping to cause an attack to whiff (the hit detection feels good most of the time) or boosting, or even dodging the attack.If someone has no interest in Gunpla, you can imagine that you're building actual robots and take this as a fun, easy alternative to Armoured Core. The mission variety is very sparse, and the story is very reminiscent of Sword Art Online games. It takes a while to feel any sort of tension in the game and then the story ends. But beating the story and side-quests took me around 40 hours, building and swapping parts on one mobile suit.The total amount played for the right player could get into the hundreds of hours. Others will get bored after a few quests, as button-mashing can work. But keep in mind that different weapon types/configurations have simple combos that not only offer bonus damage, but also potential utility like AoE damage, or positional advantages. The game is easy to learn, and arguably easy to approach mastery but there's enough here to entertain and be excited about new builds.Grinding for good part drops is its own brand of fun, and then using existing parts to transfer skills makes it easy to begin working at intensely over-powered builds. Or using upgrade materials to simply "level-up" a good part. You can ignore this and beat the game, but if you want to beat all of the difficulties (there are several), grinding for over-powered builds is fun. There are many systems that I'm not describing here, but one is the "attachment" system that has completely randomized stats. Sometimes they're completely awful with no upside. Other times they're incredibly over-powered, like +179% HP.But even at the best of times the player can just keep bumping up the difficulty in order to farm the best possible drops. Then perfect their build(s). Or create fan-service builds. Or other such things. While there's a story mode, side-quests, survival, and bounty (asynchronous PvP against CPU controlled player creations), I think that the game feels lacking in scope in a couple of ways.1) The hub area consists of one, fairly lifeless room. It fills up with people that occupy your lobbies (they remain in your lobby as an CPU-controlled bot), but this game is very niche so finding lobbies isn't going to be easy. Expanding the hub area into more explorable areas with personality, vistas and utlities (shops, mini-games, etc.) would be really nice; similar to Sword Art Online games. Even a huge hangar to display the players mobile suits in their "blue prints" with pilots, mechanics and the like walking around to add flavour.2) The mission structure consists of (usually) very small arenas, making the game feel like a brawler which isn't inherently a bad thing. While the repetition makes it easier to grind, it feels like there should've been an "Adventure" mode where the players explore dungeons/areas to fight mobs and bosses in connected areas.I could imagine dungeons of the scope of Phantasy Star Online 2, (just scaled-up to fit mobile suits). Where they aren't extremely large or visually stunning, but add a back-drop to make grinding more fun and feel more connected to the game's world. While it could be said that there's a lot of content, actually fighting with the Gunpla feels very constrained when it occurs in disconnected arenas.Some of the arenas are cool, where mobile suits can boost between large buildings and on top of them to create "cat and mouse" scenarios mixing ranged and close-range weapons. But most feel like Smash Bros. battles with an added Z-axis. I think for a full-priced game there's a really addictive game that has some good ideas but stopped-short of making a more engrossing game. Not only for its niche audience, but for the potential larger audience it could have drawn in.Despite its niche audience, I think that it could take a page from games like Phantasy Star Portable 2, and Sword Art Online: Hollow Realization where there's just a bit more rooting the players into the game world. For a full-priced game, it feels like they stopped short of the goal. The game doesn't need to have the scale and budget of the best that the industry has to offer, but it should have a larger scale than it does.

_childDocuments_.review: You will love this game if you go into it with the right expectations. This is a Gunpla building sim first and foremost. _childDocuments_.review: I've never played a Gundam Breaker game before, not even New Gundam Breaker which I'm told is markedly different, so this review probably won't say much to people familiar with the series.To the rest, I do definitely recommend this game, but I also suggest you get the game on a sale, unless you're a strong fan of Gundam. The game itself is quite good, which I'll get into, but at $80 Canadian there is a ton of jank and low production value that for most can be really hard to overlook. Things like an extremely repetitive gameplay loop, poor mission structures, bland environment visuals, and very substandard (though serviceable) map design with tonnes of misplaced invisible walls.Anyway, on to the actual review. Gundam Breakers 4 is essentially a Gundam version of Dragon Ball Xenoverse, down to the 3v3-centric combat. The whole game's structure involves you moving about in a (rather small) hub lobby, where you group up with your friends (real or otherwise) to take on missions. Like Xenoverse you have your choice of the Story mode and the Quest mode for extra stages to fight through, as well as a skirmish-like Bounty Hunter mode where you choose from a random pool of opponents to stack up against. Eventually you even unlock a wave Survival mode, but curiously, there doesn't seem to be any sort of PvP offering of any sort. This in itself wouldn't be so jarring, were it not for the fact that the premise of the entire story mode was entirely based around the characters competing in PvP with players in a video game. As a PvE player myself, I'm not super peeved about the lack of a PvP mode, but the context of the whole game really throws me off.It's surprising, because I think the combat in this game really shines. In fact I think it's actually some of the best combat I've seen in a while, just short of something like Devil May Cry. Like Xenoverse, you have a selection of combos followed by a selection of super moves that can be unleashed at the push of a button. Unlike Xenoverse, though, combat in Gundam Breakers 4 isn't methodical, it's chaotic and combo-centric. Gundam Breakers 4 encourages you to shower your enemies in a hail of attacks as fast as you possibly can, and your sheer speed and manoeuvrability really puts the “mobile” in “mobile suit.”There is a staggering variety of moves you can have your character perform depending on your equipment, and both chaining and cancelling them to create new combos is ludicrously addictive, even against the typically braindead AI. Additionally, because the vast majority of the combat takes place on the ground instead of in the air, it means there's a separate set of combos that you can get if you're airborne vs if you're on the floor, which nearly doubles the ways you can already style on your opponents.All your moves are tied specifically to the parts you have equipped, and more so than the combat, the customization for building your own gunpla is a lot more flexible than I would have assumed. There's plenty of ways to attach individual parts to your gunpla, and rotate and scale them to comical degrees. Regrettably, you can't have two separate legs the way you can have two separate arms, but presumably that would have been a whole mess to try and program in for such a liberating customization system already. My only qualm, which probably isn't even a valid criticism, is that since special moves are tied to the part you equip, you will have to sacrifice form for function and there doesn't seem to be a way around that.It’s not easy getting the part you want at all: All the parts in the game have to be acquired by buying them in lootbox style packs (with in game currency, mercifully), or more enjoyably, by running missions and breaking them off your opponent. Naturally, breaking them is a far more fun and satisfying way to go about doing that. This is where Gundam Breaker 4 not only gets its name, but also kind of becomes overwhelming. There is a frankly obscene number of stats available for each individual part; so much so that not one part can ever fit all of them. More than half the experience here, more than playing the game itself, will have you fine tuning your gunpla's stats as you mix, match, and merge your parts for both better performance and balancing it out with aesthetics. You could easily spend hours at a time working on your gunpla, and there’s even a handy practice room to test it out right in the customization menu before you finalize anything, though regrettably it does have a loading screen.While I don't outright dislike the Story mode, it does suffer a lot. Save for the fact the you can play the whole thing with your friends (which is a godsend in these types of games), the story mode is actually kind of a slog to play through. The first half of the game has AI that is far too stupid to fight back, no matter the difficulty. My team cranked things up to Hard mode to have more of a challenge, but we) we had more trouble finishing within a time limit for bonus points than we did trying to survive. Not helping is the fact that every mission in story mode, save for the ones where you have to defend a helpless tower, is exactly the same: you drop in, you fight random gundams that appear, and you get teleported to the next area. Just like Xenoverse, of course, but given that Xenoverse was a PvP fighting game as opposed to a PvE brawler, I'm bummed that there hasn't been some creativity in its mission design to make each mission stick out. None of the other game modes in the game are any different in that regard, either, which makes the whole product feel extremely samey.On the flipside, the story actually brings in bosses, and those are a blast. Bosses might seem like a rescaled regular enemy with more hit points at first, but their movesets are unique and balanced around being large, oppressive forces that you have to take down bit by bit. It's a simple affair; there's no one true way to fight the boss. Simply beat them down with your strongest attacks and combos while dodging their sweeping area of effect attacks. There's no need to memorise enemy patterns and combos. But that combination of styling on giant enemies while carefully avoiding their big attacks has a certain purity to it I don't often see in boss fights as of late. But even then, it isn't like the fights are inherently easy. They are the most challenging part of the game, especially if you play the campaign at a higher difficulty, and are very satisfying to fight, especially in co-op.The story itself, though, is just bad. There’s some good ideas here, really; the idea that this all takes place in an actual video game that the characters play does make the stakes feel very low, but it also does allow for a human element where you get to watch how each character connects through the game to cope with their real life hardships. The idea of people using an MMO to find solace in each other’s company is a pretty real story in itself, so it’s ripe for potential. But with the low production value, you’re never getting to see the world beyond the game, and coupled with the fact that the dialogue is very traditional anime and wholly unnatural, it does cheapen that struggle. It’s a sort of coming of age story where the characters don’t actually grow or mature to deal with their lives’ problems, but instead just become more confident… but mostly just within the confines of the game. It just feels shallow when they find that confidence solely through and exclusively within the video game world, and we never get to see or even hear how it carries through in their real world lives.For all its faults though, it is refreshing to see a game that just works with no caveats. It performs beautifully on the Steam Deck (though for unclear reasons the cutscenes have a massive framerate drop, even tho gun they're real time), and you can play the entirety of the experience both online in co-op AND fully offline with no internet connection.

_childDocuments_.review: As of 65 hours of playing Gundam Breaker 4 I think I can safely give it an 7.5 / 10.- The true spiritual 4th installment of the Gundam Breaker series if you exclude New Gundam Breaker. Combat, customisation and gathering parts follows Gundam Breaker 2 & 3's formulae and I am glad Meister & Crafts returned to the roots where the series shines best.- Large online lobbies and clans.- Playable and customizable SD Gundams make their debut. - Combat rewards you for getting hit and break combos that give certain bonuses like increased drop rates and reduced cooldowns. - Dual wield different close-range and ranged weapons for a combination of different weapon types and situations.- The story starts off good but as it progressed it kind of declined in the second half.- We  have region-locked matchmaking. You can still join online lobbies and clans from other countries though but whenever you try join a mission started by anyone not in your country you get an error message. - A few bugs that hinder your enjoyment. One instance is the name function for your customised gunpla that doesn't stick and ends up reverting to the last name you had or the default one: 'Gundam Breaker'.- You question why you even have 2 AI teammates in the first place. The AI is so terrible they don't hold up well by themselves in the slightest and do the bar minimum damage. There's a common bug where they keep boosting backwards despite hitting the invisible wall.  - New friendly characters keep getting introduced in the story at the wrong time and they don't have much time to flesh out as characters to get invested in. By the time you finish the story and hear their 'tragic' backstories in a heart-to-heart moment, you can't muster a single care for them.- Notification hell. Selecting any high rating or internal part during merging parts to strengthen one or sell unwanted parts will bring up a warning prompt. Every. Single. Time. And there's no way to disable this warning in the options.- Poor weapon balancing. If you played Gundam Breaker 3 you'll notice most ranged weapons have their weapon-type altered (i.e Wing Zero's buster rifle from a continuous firing long rifle to a single shot rifle) and optional equipment (missile pods / funnels) have been nerfed heavily. They do less damage and aren't as effective as they used to be.

_childDocuments_.review: I spent a lot of time with GB3 on the Vita but never ended up picking up NGB due to the bad reviews.  Overall, I'd say this is a fun and addicting successor to GB3 that I recommend.  It runs fast and well and a lot of the time sinks in loading and walking down corridors is gone from GB3.  The boss battles are much better than those in GB3.  Using two different melee weapons in each hand opens up a ton of interesting combinations and there is still a lot of variation even within weapon classes.  I think that adding a way to two-hand one hand weapons with a stat bonus to your EX/OP parts and the 'classic' moveset would be a good option.  I do miss that parts could have unique or rare passive modifiers related to the lore but I think that moving to the current randomized system opens a lot more flexibility to builds.  I liked learning the close weapon EX arts as a separate form of progression rather than upgrading parts.  I've just scratched the surface of the game and I'm itching to get back.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to New Gundam Breaker its a massive improvement. That being said there is room for improvement and refinement.I am pleased that they started separating the parts further than in previous titles , but  they really should have gone further. As a example : head, body, waist, legs, shoulders , arms , backpack and inner frame. The biggest issue I had with the last installment was that the inner frame had set stats. It was a great idea , but poorly implemented by having fixed stats. While this game is a return to form for the main franchise they certainly gone farther with it.Weapon move-sets for melee have seen some improvement, but definitely needs a bit of refinement and more creativity. Particularly in regards to attack strings being the same regardless of series , leaving the only real difference weapon design and beam color in most  cases. I this particular case you have differentiated gundam wing beam saber from the regular beam saber by making its attacks more had hitting playing into the fact in series the gundams in question were more powerful in close quarters than the opposition while leaving  the regular saber to be a quick hitting move-set.  There is also the issue with dual wielding  in that it doesn't change the attack strings very much, that however plays into the lack of variety in attack sets currently. Speaking of that , you have the ability to shield strike but are unable to properly combo with it. I certainly like the Idea of being able to use it  more offensively with its own combo string.To add to this weapons like the Beam Scissor, Beam Trident/ Glaive and Beam Tonfa do not feel appropriate for the weapon in question. A two handed halberd / pole-arm and actual tonfa  move-set would have been more of a improvement. On the subject of  of weapons , there is a distinct lack of generic ex attacks attached to many of the weapons in general. I'm not saying the old ex's should have been kept per say, but at least 4 ex's per weapon type would have been nice to have for those ex slots . Like a full Irradiation shot for the long rifles or a generic combo attack for beam sabers that aren't the original beam saber. That leads me to another minor issue, the appearance of ghost parts when using certain ex's and op skills. I get what they were going for, but its just off putting.Theirs also a distinct lack of builders parts and lack of use of integrated parts. I could have sworn there was more parts in Breaker 3. Like give us more parts to add in general  even if some are just cosmetic and have no real function beyond looking . Even some like the Beam Tonfa  or Wing Zero's Wings. Or some that we can use as integrated parts. I was disappointed that the Blitz Gundams shield arm had zero function outside of Op Skills. It was the same with the Jesta and Gustav Karl's backpack mounted shield, you couldn't really use them.The final thing I want to touch on is the DLC and the limited save slots. Personally I have no interest in the Diorama aspect of the game. Its inclusion in the dlc packs is a moot point for me. Id rather have more units added to be perfectly honest, but as long as they continue to support the game with dlc like this  in the same way they have been doing Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2 I will be content. As for the final part about save slots, its a little self explanatory. We had way more in Gundam Breaker 3 and should have far more than that in this game.Alot of the things I mentioned feel somewhat minor overall, as a long time fan I love the game and would highly recommend it . Id give it 8 out of 10 though admittedly I'm probably being generous. There is alot that was improved on and added to say the least . It has alot lacking as well , but this is a very close return to the Gundam Breaker 3 style of game play and should at least be acknowledged for that fact.* One thing i forgot to mention when I initially wrote this is the inability to change beam colors for integrated parts, ranged and melee weapons. Even if the options were limited it would still let you go with a theme depending on your build or just what suits your fancy. Doesn't have to be wild or out side what we've seen with the kits or the various anime. It would have been a nice addition to the customization options.

_childDocuments_.review: Minecraft Dungeons is a delightful game that offers a fresh take on the classic Minecraft universe. Minecraft plus Action-RPG is greatly harmonized here. From the moment I started playing, I was hooked. Minecraft Dungeons takes a simple yet engaging approach to the action-adventure genre. Unlike the original Minecraft, Minecraft Dungeons focuses on straightforward combat and exploration. The controls are intuitive, making it easy to jump right into the action. When you’re smashing through mobs, the gameplay keeps you entertained and coming back for more.The graphics are a standout feature. They maintain the iconic blocky style of Minecraft but add a layer of polish and detail that makes everything pop. The vibrant colors and varied environments keep things visually interesting. and sound effects complement the visuals perfectly, enhancing the overall atmosphere and making the experience even more immersive. Each biome looks vastly different from the other while following their looks from the original Minecraft. Playing in biomes we played in Minecraft is such a feast. Also, there is a lot of enemy variety in each biome from their respective biomes, making every biome feel fresh.The cooperative multiplayer mode is seamless and adds a whole new dimension of fun. It’s the kind of game that’s perfect for a relaxed evening with friends.The game does a great job of balancing difficulty. It starts easy, making it accessible for new players, but ramps up the challenge as you progress. The different difficulty levels mean there’s always a new challenge waiting, which keeps the game fresh and replayable. I found myself going back to previous levels to try and beat them on harder settings, always aiming for better loot and higher scores.But of course like every game, Minecraft Dungeons has its flaws. The game lacks depth in its combat and progression systems. The customization options for characters and gear are limited, which kind of left me wanting more. Although the game offers different difficulty levels, the lack of varied endgame content can make it less appealing for long-term play. After completing the main story and DLCs, there isn’t much to keep players coming back for more. The music isn't memorable, this game deserved Minecraft's level of music quality.One of the most impressive aspects of Minecraft Dungeons is the sheer amount of content added through its DLCs. Each DLC introduces new levels, enemies, gear, and even story elements, significantly expanding the game. The DLCs do a fantastic job of keeping the game fresh. They add new biomes and mechanics that make each expansion feel unique. If you enjoy the base game, the DLCs are a must-have as they significantly enhance the overall experience.In my opinion, Minecraft Dungeons is a hidden gem that deserves way more recognition. It’s a game that offers pure fun and a sense of adventure, all while staying true to the charm of the Minecraft universe. If you’re looking for a game that’s easy to pick up but hard to put down, this is it. Whether you’re a Minecraft veteran or a newcomer, give Minecraft Dungeons a try. You won’t be disappointed.Follow My

_childDocuments_.review: On the story side, MCD has very minimal narrative; other than a run-of-the-mill villain corrupted by fiddling with powers beyond comprehension, and a brief cutscene at the start of each level, there won’t be any further elaboration on lore, characters or events - that’s alright for an ARPG. The world is built using the original Minecraft as a baseline; many “out of canon” additions have however been made for the sake of variety or gameplay. For instance, Endermen can be hit by arrows and also can walk on water, to name one. These new additions are always made with good criteria and feel well-integrated, rarely out of place. There’s an excellent level of detail in the environment, however interactivity with it is at a bare minimum; you’d expect more of it for a Minecraft-inspired title.The world is divided into self-contained dungeons you can repeat as many times as you want, through four distinct difficulties that become unlocked as you beat the final boss on the previous ones, and get a higher power level from equipment. Each stage is, barring some exceptions, fully explorable without one-way drops, and has many side-areas or, occasionally, hidden sub-dungeons for reaping extra rewards or even unlocking secret levels.Exploration is an integral part of progression, given that enemies very rarely drop any gear, unless they’re bosses; most of the loot is gained either from end-stage rewards or chests found in the levels themselves. The attentive explorer will have massive amounts of loot to scrap for money, use, or gift to a teammate - only one item can be traded between each mission, having you complete another one before trading is enabled again - a pointless decision.There are also puzzles and platforming sections in most levels; some of them are fine, while others prove unclear, frustrating or downright badly designed - they don’t feel like a meaningful addition at any point, and if anything, they’re a waste of time… especially when you’re running some level on repeat to get a specific drop, only to get your time wasted by the same gimmick. Should you want to backtrack because you forgot something, there won’t be teleports or checkpoints: it’s the long haul, with characters having dismal running speed.Combat plays out in a classic ARPG fashion, having Souls in place of Mana, which are gained from slain enemies, a HP bar, and a revive mechanic (in co-op) for fallen companions. About that: if you don’t revive your teammates within 30 seconds, the “night” will start hurting and eventually kill you, while a party wipe will detract one life from the total, and have you repeat the entire dungeon should you run out of them. Enemies are varied in shapes and sizes, often with their own attack patterns and abilities unique to specific biomes and levels. They’re varied enough to not get stale and can become very challenging, especially on higher difficulties where Enchanted foe variants (elites) come by the truckload. The available dodge-roll has a long cooldown and no i-frames unless specific items are equipped, so you won’t actually be able to dodge as frequently as needed to avoid all the various AoE and projectiles.You won’t have a definite build at any point, because MCD doesn’t have classes, skill points, trees and attributes: all of this was completely scrapped for a simplistic, casual gear-based progression system, meaning your equipment, armor and weapons will dictate what your skills and synergies are. This is fine for novices but will downright suck for players that want more depth.On paper, this would mean more variety, but in reality, given that you’ll always need better gear, everything you have will eventually become outdated without any permanent progression outside of equipment. This translates into having to ditch combinations that are enjoyable and work well, simply because the gear enabling them is too outdated. The Blacksmith in your base allows you to scale gear to your current power level, but only after completing three levels, which is a grindy chore.Bosses are interesting enough, multi-phased, and have their own quirks to learn and exploit. Their difficulty is however inconsistent, with some of them clearly being more challenging than others, regardless of how far you find them in the campaign. Other than acquired gear, you’ll be given one enchant point when you level up, usable to unlock enchantments on gear, which trigger passive abilities with three power levels. These traits can make gear pieces significantly more powerful, but are random and can only be changed at a specific trader using Gold, a currency obtainable only in specific level types.

_childDocuments_.review: Minecraft Dungeons is a very simplified take on the formula popularized by Diablo. Skill trees and direct stat customization are out, with most abilities and offensive options being determined by loot to a greater degree than similar games. For those new to the genre or those otherwise looking for a breezier version of it, particularly children, Minecraft Dungeons should be a solid experience, but more experienced players may be left in want by its lack of apparent depth.

_childDocuments_.review: I adore this game. The combination of Minecraft and old school Diablo just does something to my brain that makes me happy. This game is significantly better when you can play with friends, but it would be great if you could play it at all.Suffering from the post-2016 epidemic of AAA practices hitting a massive downhill slide, this game released with very little content and no quality of life on launch. Even today, after a handful of great DLC, lots of QoL, three seasons that brought new weapons and items to the game, it's still hampered by one big thing.This game requires a Microsoft account to play.The offline mode only works when connected to the internet. As of writing, there is an Xbox Life sign-in OUTAGE going on. The game deserved the low player count from its terribly boring release. The game deserved low sales and popularity for its cut and resold content. The game deserves a bad review, because right now, I can't play the game I paid for. Piracy isn't a price issue, it is a service issue. I would not be locked out of this game if I pirated it.Even though it's fun (after years of content and development), Microsoft will still abandon this game despite the gem it was polished into. If I knew how to run community servers for this game, I would. Until then, I'm going back to Java Minecraft. Still riddled with the pain of Mojang accounts being wiped from existence, but at least I can still play the game without a mandatory internet connection.I can't get my refund back. Don't buy this if you care about good consumer treatment. I gotta say, however, that the only people who care are the ones smart enough to read reviews. Lucky you for making it this far.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Diablo, but stylized like Minecraft. It's a bit simple, so a mature audience might not be as captured by it as other ARPGs, but since I enjoy the minecraft universe, I was able to put the simplicity aside and still enjoy it. If you've played many ARPG games, you might find this one a bit pedestrian; it doesn't offer the genre anything new, it's just the minecraft take on it.The soundtrack, audio, and voiceovers are top-notch. The music is very unique and I'm really enjoying the surprise track changes when fighting a certain enemy/boss or when entering rooms/caves. In general, the game is highly stylized towards the minecraft aesthetic, which is the prime factor in elevating this game from a "meh" rating to "this is great!".The combat is fun and challenging. There's a variety of different weapons and they play very differently from each other. The mobs vary from biome to biome, and at harder difficulties modifiers like speed or damage boosts get added to up the challenge. It's not as loot heavy as diablo, so the gear choices you make feel a bit more rewarding, and you can salvage items while in the dungeon, so there's never any contention with inventory space.I'm having fun with it! Recommended.
