_childDocuments_.review: Tbh I really hate writing negative reviews, but XEL has the most terrible controls of all the games I ever played so far.Maybe it's playable with a controller, but don't bother if your plan was to play this with a keyboard and mouse.First of all the keybindings make no sense. Walking with WASD, then K for USE, N for inventory, and several other random buttons.Unless you have 3 hands like the developers, you'll have to remap first. No, you can't bind anything to the mouse. The mouse is apparently only there to click certain things in the menu. The music is kind of annoying and doesn't fit with the art style and gameplay.Another thing that bothers me is that there's no way to disable subtitles?Cut sequences look kinda like 720p and voices are partly out of sync. The game overall feels like it runs at 30FPS for any reason. Another thing I noticed, the lightning in the game switches very abruptly. At one point it's dark, then you take a single step and tadaaa it's bright as day. The transition could have been made much more fluid and natural.Nevertheless, there are some positive things to mention:The voice acting is lovely, not the actors fault that it was so poorly implemented. The world design is very well done, they've created an artsy world with many small detail elements. I think the developers wasted a lot of potential here and at this point I don't even know if they will be able to fix all the problems.

_childDocuments_.review: Xel is essentially a isometric dungeon crawler. It touts that it has puzzles, challenges, and so on, but it is really aimed for kids who just enter the genre. As far as indi titles who tout the same exploration and feel, get HOB. What makes this title lackluster is a hit in all of the following.Story - I'm an amnesiac protagonist that is beckoned to do a journey with all other characters saying, "rather you than me." It's not that original of a premise and none of the supporting cast has anything memorable except for the Village Elder. My problem, and it could be with the English translation, everyone talks like a sassy 16 year old gay teenager. With unnecessary swearing because it sounds "older and tough," the one girl who has to say "ByyyyyyeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeE!" each time you have to interact with her, and there isn't any real stakes. Though the game opens telling you about the mature content like death and suicide, I would let a 6 or 8 year old play. Gameplay: Swing sword, dodge, use specialty items, and always walking. The battle mechanics are simple and I do see where a lot of folks feel they have a hard time hitting enemies as it doesn't track well. Likewise, there isn't really a challenge and when I fought the first boss...it was over as I was thinking it was meant to be a common enemy....which it unfortunately will. The game recycles their bosses and there's (3) types. I'm not spoiling anything here. A lot of times you're reliant on your specialty weapons and some are just painful due to waiting or not completing an animation to trigger the tool.Now wandering and exploration, there isn't much of it and at time, the menu map just acts clucky. Plus, there are these health flowers which you need to grab for an achievement and extending your health bar. They're not marked on the map by default while chests, audio logs, ladders, and warp points are just already on your map. Like I don't understand the choice to just not include it or don't include chests, if it's about exploration. The warp points are somewhat inconsistent and there's even one area that SHOWS a warp point on the map, but it is not in the playable world. Weird bugs.Ok, now onto the bugs, I wish this game had a better autosave because crashes always happen at the worst moments. If you didn't get to that Pylon, you're retracking a lot of steps. I've had a few times where I found locations-consistently, dropping me off the map to a game over. If I don't go back and select a specific location in the map, when I hit start and move, I can hear menu selection beeps while walking. Finally, the character stops moving/ignores your inputs, while the game is somewhat still playing. I think there was some ideas that could have set this game up to something more. Yet, in every aspect, it just does it with mediocrity because it isn't challenging, the story is subpar and brought down with horrific dialogue/no real motivation besides plot device, and lackluster gameplay which bugs out in just the worst places and ways. Unless you're going for an easy 100% or you're looking to find a simple Action RPG for a young kid, there are just better games. Again, I recommend Hob which exceeds in all aspects where this game falls short for mature gamers.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Ok story/combat/exploration, but bad Performance and game breaking bugs.While the game is mostly fun, the bugs bring it down to a negative review.I mostly played on steam deck with proton experimental, but also played a bit on my PCPC specs: Ryzen 5800x, Rx 5600 xt, 32gb ram, m.2 ssd, 1080p 144hrz monitorFirst, the Good:I enjoyed most of the story (couldn't roll credits due to a bug)combat is similar to an isometric dark souls, but only dodge and block cost stamina you get a few gadgets that have both combat and mobility/exploration useSecond, the Bad:Performance, both on PC and Deck. Game will always lag a lot when entering a different area (even on my decently powerful pc) and even worse it does that even when being near an area border.Then there are the graphics, even on Max settings there are often things poping in near the camera and everything looks a bit too pixelated.And the worst of all, The Bugs. Sometimes you cant get on a ladder and you have to move in and out of range to try again.Some areas wont load and you can fall off the world because of that. Also upgrading the last Weapon/Tool/Gadget gets me stuck in the empty upgrade menu and i have to alt+f4 the game (so i can upgrade all, but one item)Finally, the 2 game breaking bugs that stopped me from finishing the game: Near the end of the game after a dialog/cutscene i'll either get stuck in a load screen (if the fps is capped for any reason, like vsync or riva tuner)or if uncapped, i'll load successfully, but the door I have to break doesn't break, so locking me in the small area where I appear after the load screen.From what I red online, the only solution is to start the whole game over, but I don't feel like playing another ~7 hours for the chance to finish the game (starting a new save is not guaranteed to fix these bugs)

_childDocuments_.review: I think there's a decent game hidden somewhere deep inside this mess, but it will take a lot of patches to make it appear. Not only is the game still full of bugs after all the patches already released: you still get stuck in random areas and have to reload from the last save-point; the screen goes black and freezes; even quitting the game sometimes doesn't work properly (twice I've experienced that the game audio continued indefinitely after I quit the game)......but worst of all is the gameplay itself: every area is closed off by hundreds of gates that you can't open, so you wander around aimlessly in the narrow closed off areas, with no clue what to do, fighting off the same enemies that keep respawning again and again.When you finally meet an NPC that gives you an actual mission, and you get a glimmer of hope that the game is finally going somewhere, you don't get any help finding the mission area on the map, so you end up wandering around aimlessly once again in search of that area.And when you  find the right spot - it's full of more gates that you can't open without first finding certain objects. So you once again have to wander around aimlessly in the same old areas trying to find said objects before you can even start the mission.It feels like the developers didn't want people to enjoy this game. They've certainly done everything they could to make it as annoying and frustrating as possible. Why not just let the players move freely? Why all the gates, out of reach ladders, gaps, obstacles and other limitations to stop the players from exploring and experiencing this charming world?There's nothing worse than a game that doesn't respect the players' time. I've invested 4 hours of my life in this game, and so far it's given me absolutely nothing in return. I haven't even been able to complete my first mission because of all the bugs and limiting design choices. The only good thing I have to say about XEL is that I like the art style, which is why I purchased the game in the first place, much to my regret.I hope that the developers will do what it takes to make XEL playable and enjoyable, because I do think that it can become a nice little indie title that many gamers would be happy to endorse. On that day I'll be happy to revise my review. Until then I'll be playing something else, something that works and that's actually fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Xel is as good a "Link to the Past" clone as one can get... Forget about bloody Oceanhorn, this is the real deal. Xel is an action top down platformer that takes you to the land of Xel, a spherical world created then abandonned and now repopulated by humans after they ran away from some sort of cataclysm. Reid, who's your typical GIRL crashing down and instantly getting insomnia, found by the indiginous people only to discover that she's got some sort of amazing power, will have to help the people of Xel against the rampant dingbots and uncover the secret of the world of Xel.Not as shiny nor as peculiar as The Legend of Zelda's plot, huh!! But can Link... ROLL? That's right, much like a Souls-like, Reid can dodge roll out of attack or use her shield, you're going to find yourself using the roll so much that you'll be thinking "huh, those dozens of hours playing Dark Souls really comes in handy here". While Xel retains the simplicity of The Legend of Zelda, it does not retain the spike in difficulty that concerns puzzles. In Xel, the puzzles are very easy to solve, and that's, to me, a good thing! Less puzzles, more combats please.The combat mechanics are simple but very satisfying... The parry works just as intended, the dodge as well; there are some minor bugs that occur, very rarely I might add, but it's okay. The dialogue also seems to hit that gray area between "funny" and "cringe", and it's just the right amount of cringe to keep you interested and looking to find out more. To add to that, just like any Zelda game, you'd have to backtrack into areas previously visited once you find the appropriate upgrades to open up those well hidden treasure chests and bossfights? Well... very easy, but at least they are there (unlike Oceanhorn, where you get ONE bossfight at the end of the game...). Each bossfight has got a pattern, and one reminds me very much of the Ganon fight from the first Zelda game ever made (for the NES) lol... I love how inspired from a beloved franchise the devs were while creating this awesome Indie game called Xel.In my opinion, this should get an , only because some treasure chests eluded me for all the wrong reasons... The time swap powerup is great though, even though at some spots it doesn't seem to work as intended. Plus, Reid's got a very dark sense of humor, need I say more?

_childDocuments_.review: XEL is a perfect example of a game that needed just a few more days of development. There are a few things here missing that hold me back from enjoying the game fully.Steam Curator Page:+ Fully Voice acted+ Interesting story + Intriguing Setting+ Fair enemy variety+ Great music- Character blocked by objects, no see through outline- No sense of direction in missions- Enemies respawn if you move off screen too much- One graphics setting- DOF does not work most of the time- AI is by no means capable- Not enough save points throughout- Items are picked up as new items when game is reloaded (ex. after you die)- No legend in minimap- BuggyXEL is not delivering much in quality of life features but it is also not asking for a lot of money off the bat. I suppose that on a decent sale, this might be a good game to pick up and spend a few hours with.There is A LOT of Breath of The Wild influence here. From the menus, to the way items are explained if you first pick them up, to the sound effects when you pick up items etc. Problem is that every time you die and/ or reload a save, the game forgets that you picked up those items or that you opened those chests, so they will show up as new. The chest icons will also appear as if they have not been opened. Furthermore, some chests will appear closed, confusing the hell out of you. There is a nice variety of environments, a past and present gimmick to solve puzzles, and lots of boss fights. I like the story as well because it seems to be going toward an interesting path. I tend to enjoy settings where humans caused their own demise and destroyed their world.The main issue with the game that I am having however is the fact that you cannot see your character if they go behind any object. _childDocuments_.review: Your adventure of Xel begins with you crashlanding in an unknown place. That is not all, you have lost your memory and cannot remember your own name. However, you’re greeted by Chap, a flying robot who explains that you have crashed landed in The Garden on Xel. You set off with your newly found friend to explore your surroundings and find out where the hell you have found yourself.  After a while you meet up with Desmond, a young lad you gives you some information on where you are and what Xel is. He takes you to meet the Elder at the Needle Eye where most of the folks of Xel live in safety from some of the harsh environments of Xel. Also, at the Needle Eye, there’s a shop where you can buy various items, Desmond has a Dojo where you can beat the hell out of a wooden dummy and then there’s Shirl’s workshop, she’ll upgrade your equipment if you have the right resources. As you progress, you’ll venture in to new areas of Xel, in total there are eleven areas you can explore. Although you may not be able to enter some of them until you acquired the right item or have completed another area. Each area has their own theme, cold and scorching heat, bogs and more and each will have a variety of enemies with in them. The most common enemy you will come across are the Ding Bots, you’ll find them everywhere you go but they are easy to deal with. To help you move through each of the areas and to protect you from enemies you have a sword and shield which you will have to find. You will also gain a Zap-trap, you throw this on the ground and it will shock enemies immobilising them for a small amount of time. The Zap-trap can also be used to power doors or bridges by throwing them near a plug somewhere nearby, this will then open the door or bridge for a short length of time.  Another item in your inventory is the Stickyhook, this allows you to traverse gaps by shooting at a big sticky ball on a post on the other side of a gap. Firing at an enemy will then attach and pull you towards them which can be handy at times. Burnhilde is a flamethrower which can help you move forward when blocks of ice stand in your way of progress, it’s also great against certain enemies when you want to turn up the heat. The last of your equipment is Clobber, a sonic hammer which will not only smash glass barriers but works great against the symbiotic enemy allowing you to deal with the with more ease. There are some puzzles which you have to solve in order to move forward. Sometimes you’re unable to see a way forward but you have this small crystal embedded in your forehead. At times you may see some floating pink crystals (Time Core) they usually span a small area and these crystals interact with the crystal stuck in your forehead. When activated they will open a portal back in time where things may be different, a broken bridge now could be fixed when the time core is activated allowing you to pass over the bridge and reach the other side where as you couldn’t if it wasn’t activated. There are other times where activating the time core will help you progress so keep your minces pies open for those crystals, there may be something of interest close by. You can craft recipes at campsites which are scattered around here and there if you have the recipes. However, I have found only a couple recipes and a part from crafting some gold cables I’m not exactly sure what the point is of the campsite and crafting of recipes. While I have enjoyed playing Xel, it has been extremely frustrating to the point of almost quitting the game. However, I kept at it and at times I could get to enjoy the game but I’ve endured multiple bugs which almost had me at the point of throwing my game pad.  Web Spinner trying to shoot so you can jump over a gap won’t aim at the target on the other side but aims at the one you’re standing next too, manual aiming is a real pain, hit and miss if you can hit the target and then the web spinner stops working. Sometimes it's better to just jump in to the gap and get replaced back on the map on the side where you actually wanted to be.  When you go to throw a Zap-trap and change your mind your character gets stuck in that animation. This mean you think that your character is looking one way but they are not, so just make sure you’re facing the right way otherwise trying to deploy a Zap-trap or anything else and you will come unstuck. This problem only seemed to happen when I had the Zap-trap assigned to “X” on my gamepad. Other bugs I’ve had are falling through the map, getting stuck in the ground after jumping down from an opening. The enemy at times especially if you came up behind them would start to float away and would not attack until it was too late and they died. There are ladders around each area which help you get back to a place instead of running all the way around you came from which is great although, at times I could not activate a ladder to drop down for later use. Then at a later point I’d try to go down a ladder but it would not let me, sometimes the ladder would be shown as being up even though you had activated them to be in the down position.  One other problem was the map which became useless on some of the areas and it could have also done with a Legend so we know what is on the map. There’s a list of areas you can scroll down and then select the map you wish to view. However, it would scroll down so much and that was your lot, you could not pick the map I wanted instead I’d get lost and start running around and around in circles.  A fast travel feature would have been great as I often found myself trying to get back to where I could replenish my health, earlier areas seemed to have a lot more health in boxes and from defeating enemies than when I was hitting the latter stages. A fast travel option does appear but it’s only when you’ve completed about three-quarters of the game, which I found to be a bit silly. It would be a nice game if it wasn’t for the bugs, so I really do hope they can fix the bugs in the near future. In the settings you find options for Screen - Resolution, Window Mode, V Sync and Graphics Quality. Audio - Master, Voices, Music and Sound Effects Volume Adjusters. Controls - Customise Keyboard (Sadly No Game Pad Customisation) and Controller Vibrations. Language - English, German, French, Korean, Japanese, Russian, Brazilian Portuguese.  Positives  + Good graphics + Nice story + Has achievements + Full controller support Negatives  - Some very frustrating bugs - No cards currently After crash landing in a strange garden with no memory, solve puzzles and help the inhabitants to restore Xel to its former glory by unlocking the secrets which have plagued Xel for the past couple decades. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: Story begins when a girl crash-lands in a forest. She has no idea who she is, what happened, or why a rock is lodged into her forehead. The only source of information is a CHAP, a flying sphere that begins to follow you everywhere. The game follows the outdated memory loss plot, which can feel slightly overused. However, it works in games like XEL because you’re learning things about the world alongside the protagonist.If you're anything like me, your first move in this type of game is to jump everywhere and see how far you can travel. Except that's not possible here. Jumping is actually automatic and happens every time you step over the edge. You can turn the character after the jump and still fail to land on the opposite side, proving that it is not some scripted mechanic. It feels odd and doesn't always work. There were far too many circumstances where you may walk off the edge and humiliatingly tumble into a bottomless holeYou do, however, get to roll around and fight a lot. I was concerned by the stamina bar because I assumed this would be yet another stamina-management game. When I realized that I could repeatedly press the attack button, my fear vanished. Nonetheless, rolling and raising a shield deplete your stamina, which could have recharged a little more quickly. I should also point out that a shield is your only defense because you still get hurt while rolling. Projectiles move too fast. Finding unique plants that can permanently boost health or stamina greatly aids in making this feature more tolerable.Enemies don’t pose a huge threat. You can lock on to them for easier targeting and they fall down after a few hits. The majority of your battles involve dumb wildlife and various types of robots. Sometimes they simply remain motionless or become stuck. As a counterweight to their stupidity, they take cheap shots at you that are a pain to block. Defeated enemies regularly drop various material that may also be found by breaking open boxes positioned all throughout the stage.In the main village, this junk is used to upgrade equipment. The other collectible is a circuit board that you can exchange for rare materials in the town store. Because enemies respawn after a while and when you change zones, you can also farm for materials, but I've never felt the need to. By the way, some of the dropped items are so small that it's easy to overlook them; they could use a stronger glow or a better visual hint. The short information that shows up the first time you pick a new item also needs to be fixed; it resets every time you load a game.Another reason why you’re encouraged to smash everything is because hidden food replenishes your health. Saving at the blue pillars only registers your current state, even if you’re left with half a heart. Additionally, there is no autosaving. Another option is to cook food at the campgrounds, although it seems like this concept was added purely for the sake of having an extra function that isn't all that useful. Unless you really want to upgrade everything and don't want to look for rare material; that can be crafted too.The game's globe is one enormous map divided into regions that can be traversed without loading screens. The basic premise is still a technological setting that has become overrun by plants, even though each game has a distinctive environment and group of enemies. Cold, hot and forest biomes are just some generic examples you'll have to go through. The game also loves ladders you drop to make a shortcut. Although the majority of objects of interest are displayed on the minimap, it makes no sense to have a separate icon for a chest that has already been opened. Even more so when you open the chest but the icon doesn't change or resets when you load the game. Additionally, some already opened chests still have their lids on and act as if you haven't opened them in an effort to frustrate the player as much as possible. Naturally, it is impossible to reopen these chests. This broken mechanic is an absolute nightmare for any gamer.Zones make things interesting by incorporating unique mechanics. One enables you to go back in time before the invasion of the plants and influence previous events in a way that immediately affects the present. Waypoints are missing; this means you never get a clear instructions what to do. The main objective is always the same: find the key and the exit by solving problems with your sword or your gadgets. Since no good game misses a chance to include boxes, you’ll have to push them here as well. Gadgets include things like electric mine to power doors and sticky hook to traverse over gaps. Although they have a secondary offensive purpose, you can manage without that except for the boss fights.Finding the key and the exit by using your gadgets or your sword to solve obstacles is always the main goal. Since boxes are a staple of every decent game, you’ll be pushing and pulling them here as well. Gadgets include things like sticky hooks to cross gaps and electric mines to open doors. With the exception of boss battles, you probably won’t be using them in normal battles.Locked camera is problematic. Since there’s no way of moving it, the character and any secrets or resources constantly get hidden behind walls, trees and other objects. I frequently found myself hacking aimlessly while oblivious to my surroundings. It might become problematic during battles as well. Despite the fact that you can't see what you're actually attacking, a lock-on feature that shows a white square around the target is incredibly helpful in this situation.A patch for XEL is urgently needed to address problems that shouldn't have been present in the game in the first place. It's annoying when features don't work properly or you become stuck in the environment, especially when you forget to save. Even though the game isn't perfect, with a little more time spent on development, it could stand together with similar titles.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a strong idea burried behind many bugs and quality of life issues. Do I recommend it? Sure, but with a caveat.TL;DR: Fun game to pick up for a few hours. Cringe dialogue, but at least it's not Neon White. Needs fixes, but probably won't get them at this point. She can play around with time and uses her powers to help the survivors. As a game, it's quite fun! It borrows some interesting ideas from classic top-down adventure RPGs like green-fairy-boy. There are powerups you find as you progress that make combat more interesting, though they're only necessary as a means to continue progressing in the story, not for combat. The controls get some getting used to, but once you do, it flows rather well. The plot is all right, but the dialogue, especially Reid's, takes patience. To be honest, I would hate the in-your-face, let-me-spell-out-the-next-step dialogue on a male protagonist, too. In fact, other than her dialogue, she's a stronger protagonist than many other protagonists out there (regardless of their gender).I didn't finish it. name: Sovereign Syndicate
detailed_description: Explore an open world in this Victorian steampunk cRPG. Play as three characters with branching stories that intertwine. Investigate, interact, and take action to leave your mark on the world and its inhabitants. No random stat points here, use your skills to level them up, and trust your fate to our tarot card chance system. So, how will you solve your problems? Combat, persuasion, magic, explosives? The choice is yours and all your cards are on the table; but be careful, the docklands aren’t for the faint of heart. Tarot Card Chance System – Leave your dice at home as you interact with a variety of characters. NPC’s react to your gender, race, appearance, and choice of dialogue, so you’d better look and act the part if you want the “right” results. But not everything is certain, luck plays a role and it’s all in the cards with our tarot card chance system. Skill and Etiquette System - The skills you use will improve your ability, while ignoring others will cause them to stagnate. Master the skills you choose and learn more about the world and its inhabitants to unlock special dialogue and skill-check options. So go, see, do! And don’t be afraid to try the unconventional. Drown yourself in gin? Sure, provided you’ve got the constitution for it. Smoke that opium? Certainly, but be careful not to doze off— it might not be safe here. Put it all on black? You only live once, as they say. Even in failure you learn something… A Rich Open World to Explore - A steampunk fantasy-inspired Victorian London awaits; filled with interesting characters and locations. Explore the back alleys, opium dens, brothels, and more at your peril, or relax and enjoy their simple pleasures. Investigate, interact, and take action to forge your own path. Three Characters, Three Different Stories – Play as three characters with stories that intertwine through the city’s docklands and unfold based on your choices. Atticus Daley , an orphaned minotaur magician crawling out of the bottom of a bottle to find a sense of belonging, and his next fix. Clara Reed , a corsair with a checkered past, and a cunning woman with a rebellious streak. Follow her on a search for vengeance, and the courtesan killer. Otto , the trusty automaton and companion of engineer Theodore Redgrave. More than just the sum of his parts, Otto wants more to life than servitude and utility. Each character has their own mix of skills, equipment, and expertise, and they might just have to work together to succeed. Will you trust your companions, and should they trust you? Not everyone is a hero after all. Features: A large open world to explore, 20 different locations spread over the city’s east docklands Three playable characters Three intertwined stories to experience Branching narrative and dialogue system Character customization Tarot card chance system Single-player
about_the_game: Explore an open world in this Victorian steampunk cRPG. Play as three characters with branching stories that intertwine. Investigate, interact, and take action to leave your mark on the world and its inhabitants. No random stat points here, use your skills to level them up, and trust your fate to our tarot card chance system. So, how will you solve your problems? Combat, persuasion, magic, explosives? The choice is yours and all your cards are on the table; but be careful, the docklands aren’t for the faint of heart. Tarot Card Chance System – Leave your dice at home as you interact with a variety of characters. NPC’s react to your gender, race, appearance, and choice of dialogue, so you’d better look and act the part if you want the “right” results. But not everything is certain, luck plays a role and it’s all in the cards with our tarot card chance system. Skill and Etiquette System - The skills you use will improve your ability, while ignoring others will cause them to stagnate. Master the skills you choose and learn more about the world and its inhabitants to unlock special dialogue and skill-check options. So go, see, do! And don’t be afraid to try the unconventional. Drown yourself in gin? Sure, provided you’ve got the constitution for it. Smoke that opium? Certainly, but be careful not to doze off— it might not be safe here. Put it all on black? You only live once, as they say. Even in failure you learn something… A Rich Open World to Explore - A steampunk fantasy-inspired Victorian London awaits; filled with interesting characters and locations. Explore the back alleys, opium dens, brothels, and more at your peril, or relax and enjoy their simple pleasures. Investigate, interact, and take action to forge your own path. Three Characters, Three Different Stories – Play as three characters with stories that intertwine through the city’s docklands and unfold based on your choices. Atticus Daley , an orphaned minotaur magician crawling out of the bottom of a bottle to find a sense of belonging, and his next fix. Clara Reed , a corsair with a checkered past, and a cunning woman with a rebellious streak. Follow her on a search for vengeance, and the courtesan killer. Otto , the trusty automaton and companion of engineer Theodore Redgrave. More than just the sum of his parts, Otto wants more to life than servitude and utility. Each character has their own mix of skills, equipment, and expertise, and they might just have to work together to succeed. Will you trust your companions, and should they trust you? Not everyone is a hero after all. Features: A large open world to explore, 20 different locations spread over the city’s east docklands Three playable characters Three intertwined stories to experience Branching narrative and dialogue system Character customization Tarot card chance system Single-player
short_description: A Victorian steampunk RPG with tarot cards instead of dice. Investigate the disappearance of society’s most vulnerable to uncover a mysterious cult. Play as three characters, each with their own skills and motivations. Customize your characters with narrative choices to unlock new tarot cards.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all although I don't know if it was the developers intention or not, but this game was advertised to everyone as the "steampunk disco elysium" and for those who want to buy it just for this, in short, don't. It's not. It is still a good experience just not what you might expect. To summarize a good game for its' price but it leaves many things lacking, although for a 20 euros game you really can not expect more. 6.5/10.  The graphics and the visual direction are generally nice and they have a warm feeling to them, although for a "steampunk" setting I really expected more. Then again, 20 euros. What was really disappointing is that there were no dark or macabre environments in a game where one of the main plot lines is to find a serial killer. The most ominous environment, if it can even be called that, is found in an optional mission in a chapter halfway through the game and it is treated like a big reveal or something... but in the next chapter you casually visit the same place as a different character with cheery music like nothing is wrong. The game suffers from its' budget and consequently from the limited areas/locations. Even though it is a 18 chapters game, it really is like a 7 hour play-through with most of the chapters being less than half an hour long. So, again, I know the resources were limited, but it is still very disappointing for a steampunk game to look this bland and uninteresting. No grim reality of London with rooms full of intrigue or anything of the sort. Just 5 locations for 6 hours and a new final location which is just a house for the final hour.   The music is equally uninteresting which makes it clear that it was not a first thought. This is a shame cause a good soundtrack can really elevate these types of games. I have seen many games that have been visually limited due to budget reasons, but all of them had an interesting soundtrack and good sound design. Here the sound design is good to be fair, but the music is completely missing. I  would like to say that there was one track during the entire game (and one song in a singe chapter, which was nice tbh), but I genuinely do not remember anything other than an inoffensive melody playing constantly. I am not sure if it was one track or two but it doesn't really matter. Overall this was a bigger disappointment than the visuals.  As far as the story goes, if you expect a disco elysium type of open world with countless opportunities and interactions, well you might have guessed it by now, but this is not it. They were clearly influenced by it and you can see that in the dialogues and in the interactions with the environment. You have the inner monologues with your thoughts, so a connection is there, but it is very surface level. It does not feel unique, but more like they tried to implement a system, which they have not really understood. Nothing is bad, but like everything else it feels lacking. Firstly the chapters are very linear, so you can't really "explore the world", and even if you could there are 5 areas to explore as I've said before so not much of a sense of discovery. Everything feels rushed and this defeats the purpose of this interaction system. DE puts you on a hotel room and basically says "you are a disgrace to human nature, now go solve a murder" and you are free to do whatever you like. You can approach if from different angles and generally experiment. This game already can not achieve that based on how linear and short it is, but in my opinion it doesn't even have a great replay-ability. Because out of the 7-8 hours you will spend 5 going around, following an linear objective, which really defeats the purpose of open exploration of a "steampunk London". Also this is a personal gripe, but they did this thing where you put some words highlighted to explain what they mean if you hover your mouse over them. You might have seen that in pathfinder, pillars of eternity, tyrrany, etc etc, but here it is so blatantly pointless. It's like they put random nonsense words in, just to have the feature. For example, the characters say "anyroads" and if you hover the mouse over the word it says : an expression used similar to anyway. It is so pointless, like just say anyway. There are tens of examples like this, which server no purpose other than having the feature for the sake of it.  Finally the story suffers from the budget and the chapter-like system as well. There are 18 chapters in which you play through the adventure of 3 people. After every chapter you change character and you swap between them. It takes around 2-3 chapters for each character to get to the main plot, which basically means at total 7-8, after which there are like 4 or 5 chapters which are 10 minutes long and then for the last 6 they have them very forcefully interject, in a way that feels very rushed, again just for the sake of it, and then the game ends. Overally the game would benefit from 10 extra chapters I would say. In more detail with SPOILERS AHEAD: The Minotaur chapters are honestly fine. They don't really move the overall plot, but they work nicely with their time limit. The dwarf plot line could be scrapped completely, cause there is no point to it. Good character, hunts some monsters, takes a bad contract which he regrets and then at the finale, during the final chapters he just blows up a machine or whatever. Like this could easily be done by the Minotaur. You could have the Minotaur take the bad contract to solve his debts and then blow the machine before going to end his quest-line like it ends now. I was left baffled by how the dwarf story ended. Literally unneeded and with his 2-3 hours of story you could make the other 2 characters more likeable. Finally the human story makes no sense. You basically run around doing errands for the start of the game, which are the longer chapters, and then finally they are like "ah aye another murder eh. how about yeh cop a shiv at it and solve it luv. thanks gov'nor. Hoi what, why ? i dont ♥♥♥♥♥♥ know, just dae it". And then at the end it is like "hoi y did yeh dae it// i think all werewolves r bad or summat so i want to kill em all// but y r yeh fancy killing prostitutes that yeh employ// they r bad because they don't hate em or summat I don't know, my character is obviously not thought out bleedin' well// understandable yeh go to gaol now bye bye// nooooooooo." Very bad writing all round.   In conclusion, I know I seem very negative but all of what I say is understandable problems if you take the budget into account. The game is cheap, but rightly priced for what it offers and honestly I think they bit off more than they could chew. Maybe it is not their fault in the end because of the limited resources, but noone will look back at this game and remember it saying "good for the limited budget". People will just forget it exists. It offers nothing new and although I commend them for trying to make something unique and have a vision, it was clearly not enough. They needed double the budget for what they wanted to achieve and it really shows. 6.5/10 for me

_childDocuments_.review: This starts out pretty charming and fun, but snowballs into a pile of repetitive tasks set in the exact same 5 locations that you grow tired of after the second go. Quests have no branching resolutions so if you failed one dialogue check you either reload or you're done with it forever. QoL stuff is mediocre at best.I really tried to stick with it until the end - the game isn't very long - but realizing you're not completing a 16 hour long quest because of a very random skill check in an optional dialogue from 3 hours ago is a really frustrating last nail to this coffin for me.

_childDocuments_.review: According to the achievements I completed seven of this game's eighteen chapters. I have absolutely no desire to continue, and my recommendation to others is to not start at all. I don't think I've ever played a game with such an interesting premise and potential in world building that was so incredibly boring. One of the characters is a Minotaur illusionist, another is a dwarf with a robot pal verging on sentience, and the other is a lady.... You'd think there would be SOMETHING interesting about this group! Well, it turns out there isn't. They wander the same dull streets at frustratingly slow paces trying to come up with oblique solutions to tedious problems. The same extremely dull music loops far too quickly. The same NPCs stand in their corners. So much of what you do doesn't matter in this game. Mechanically speaking consuming cigarettes and alcohol and laudanum in turn raise your stats and can give you level ups. You can smoke your way to intelligence, and drink your way to happiness with seemingly no downsides to any of it. I avoided smoking and laudanum use until I realized just how easy it was to stay at basically maximum hope all the time.... I had thought there must be some unforseen consequences of my consumption in this gritty, bleak, steampunk city. Surely I'd become an addict or face some consequence for my choice to chain smoke ten cigarettes and down three bottles of laudanum at midday... but I didn't. They are just items that give you numbers. Roleplay wise your choices also don't impact anything. Since it is in the description of the game, it is no spoiler to tell you that the Minotaur is an alcoholic. He has a trait you can invest in called Self-Discipline and his internal monologue expresses a desire to get clean. I made my whole build around that trait, specifically selecting dialogue choices to strengthen it. Imagine my frustration  To me this game doesn't seem to be intended as a dis-empowering experience where, no matter what you try, things are bad. Maybe that is because all three characters had maximum hopefulness for basically the whole time I played. That dissonance between hope being a meter you can fill and the setting trying to be depressing and overbearing just totally ruins the vibe. What does this game WANT to feel like? Who knows.The whole experience was tedious. The tarot card "system" just changes the odds of failure and success slightly. It is still using randomness and modifiers to test outcomes. The traits can be cool, but seem to be achieved at random. TLDR: Sovereign Syndicate literally put me to sleep and was not a good experience. Also, 18 is way too many chapters FFS.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright.  is done and dusted. I've seen this described as a Disco Elysium-like, but I haven't quite gotten around to playing DE yet. It does seem like an accurate comparison best I can tell though. This is a semi open world RPG with zero combat. Everything is resolved via dialogue decisions and skill checks. To that end, it is important to note that this is a dialogue dependent game, so for people unwilling to read and pay attention to what they are reading, this isn't the game for you. There is no voice acting, so you will spend almost all your time exploring and reading. Which for me was !You play as three main characters. A minotaur illusionist, a human prostitute, and a dwarven engineer. How this story works is you play the characters in that order. You will finish a chapter as one, then the next chapter is the next character, rinse and repeat. There is one chapter where you play as a henchman instead of the main characters, but otherwise, the progression stays true to the sequence mentioned. Each chapter focuses on the attendant character's personal story and his/her interaction with the main quest, along with a fair number of very interesting side quests. Most of these side quests span across several chapters. After each chapter, you are treated to an Oscar Wilde quote, and a story set up for the next chapter.An interesting aspect of the progression system is it will happen that one character has to deal with the actions of the other two characters and their actions in previous chapters. So, for example, maybe one character lowers the water level in an area later visited by another character. Or a character picks up an item actually needed by another character. Perhaps something in a shop is unlocked by one character allowing another character access to information they need for their own personal quests. This interactivity between the actions of these characters was very cool. Additionally, the characters will encounter each other at different points in the story, giving you alternate perspectives on each character's lives, personality, and so on. The way in which everything in this game connects to everything else is kind of brilliant IMO.Chapters 1-3 introduce you to each character, and you will choose dominant traits for each, which will impact the rest of your interactions in this game. You might choose wit, tact, grace, animal instincts, and so on. As you progress and use your various traits, they will automatically level up, making skill checks easier when using said traits. You will also unlock tarot cards via dialogue decisions. Each tarot card unlocks a personality trait which are independent of your skill traits and will unlock new dialogue options at various points in the game, thus unlocking more story options. You will also face decisions which make you lose or gain , which is effectively a morale system. I believe this affects dialogue options and possibly skill checks, but I think this is a subtle system, and I wasn't quite sure when it actually came into play.The setting is an alternate timeline version of London, and it is broken up into a handful of districts which you will fast travel back and forth between throughout this game. In each district are several static businesses and NPCs, with a few unlockable places and NPCs depending on where you are in the story. For example, you might unlock and travel to the sewers or an area where werewolves reside when a full moon in coming up, for a few specific quests.The presentation while exploring is isometric and pretty classic CRPG in appearance. But, with a bit more of a favorable camera angle. It's very detailed and very lived in. It very much feels like a living breathing world. The audio is more focused on the sounds of the city and really serves to bring this setting to life. The music itself is more of an enhancement to the adventure rather than a feature in my estimation, Very nice and appropriate, but also more in the background rather than prominent.I thought the way in which the story progressed, the sense of mystery in this alternate Earth setting, the way in which fantasy and steampunk interacted, and the way in which the character stories weaved together until they eventually converged in what I thought was an electric ending was super cool. I really loved this. Additionally, much like the first movie in a movie trilogy, this game, while resolving itself completely, also set up the foundation for what is undoubtedly intended to be an IP with at least a couple more entries. I hope they do in fact make a couple more games in the IP and really explore the idea presented at the end of the game.There was one technical issue that repeated here and there throughout the game: the character pathing would sometimes lead to the character getting stuck on objects. This most frequently happened while entering or leaving staircases or flights of stairs. And, one of the chapter cheevos didn't drop. Otherwise, it handled immaculately for me. I played exclusively with k/m, but there is no doubt you can easily play this with a gamepad or on the Steam Deck.I was gifted this game, but it easily earns the $19.99 retail price tag. This is an evocative experience that will almost definitely hold your attention throughout. It takes some chances, but always remains cohesive and very interesting. It's a must play in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately I found this game to be very disappointing and underwhelming.To address other, minor issues first: the 3D art-style for backgrounds is fairly dull and unimpressive, and I think the game would have benefited significantly by having a more hand-drawn/stylised aesthetic, but I acknowledge that that may have been too ambitious for how small the dev team were. Additionally, the music is fine but nothing noteworthy. And while I have no problem with the game not having any voice-acting (in fact in many RPGs I turn off the voices because I read much faster than they deliver the lines), the game sometimes feels too quiet and lifeless because there isn't much auditory ambience.Still, I gave the game a fair shot, playing four and a half hours of it and sacrificing my ability to refund it, but I just don't care for it, and that's mostly due to the writing. As this game is clearly Disco Elysium-inspired (a polite way of saying it's a wannabe Disco clone), writing is by far the most important aspect of the game, and you NEED good writing to pull off this type of non-combat-style RPG. While I didn't mind the writing in the first chapter.... my goodness, the writing in the second chapter is bad. It's just.... unpleasant. Pretty much put me off playing any more (I finished Chapter 2 but decided to not play any further).The sheer amount of absurdly verbose paragraphs describing every single location, even utterly uninteresting ones, is very excessive and feels unnecessary; the writer/s seem incapable of deciding if they want their dialogue to be period-authentic or modern (the female character is the worst example, she thinks as if she was an arts student from the 2020s); and worst of all there's just no real flavour, flair or charm to the writing, it's very flat, workmanlike and without all that much unique style. It adequately does the job of moving the story forwards but nothing more.While this might be acceptable in a game with other gameplay mechanics, when 95% of the experience is simply reading the writing, this is a huge problem, and not one that can be balanced out by other things. I'm sure the devs put in a lot of time and effort into this game, but ultimately I just don't think they had the writing talent to pull off a Disco Elysium clone - you need to be a REALLY damn good writer to do that, to have the writing be the centre-point of the entire experience.The experience is more in-line with something like Shadowrun (minus the combat) or Gamedec (neither of which I particularly enjoyed), so people should set their expectations accordingly. I do wish the devs good luck in future projects and hope that they can improve, but as it stands, Sovereign Syndicate is a thoroughly mediocre experience.Edit: I'd like to add that I hope this review stays up and is not removed, as the devs seem to have a habit recently of shutting down any thread in the discussions that criticises the game. It is very important that people are able to critically discuss a game so there are multiple viewpoints being presented to potential buyers.

_childDocuments_.review: Many reviewers now are kinda giving the wrong impression of what is this game. They are all comparing it to Disco Elysium when in reality it very much isn't...The more appropriate comparison here one could make on steam would be with the "Pendula Swing" series to be honest as in the same way lack that big budget that would've made it a great experience and it limits itself to be just a knock off shadowrun with a different setting  this case: a steampunk world where you interact with fantasy creatures (we have no voices to read the lines of dialogues to give deep to the different inner voices so it kinda make no difference between them and no real choices that would give a cool animation or choices that would unlock different emotions. So You're pretty much in this just for the story)  As The game in his mechanics have many faults in my opinion (You don't have a reliable way to explore the surrounding as you lack a compass and the perspective don't rotate at all so when you walk you easily get stuck in a frustrating fixed perspective..not that you can explore much as certain points of the map even if they looks like lead somewhere are voids you can't actually reach and pratically you are guiding yourself only by clicking on every orange highlight you can get (kinda reminded me of "Gamedec" for that). The game simply expect you to use the map to "jump" to certain locations at need for check part of the quests you end up getting so you get few views of the steampunk ambience (that is there like Pendula Swing you get the feeling of the city but the exploration is limited and the models only are viewable at a certain hight so they lack any real detail as you can't watch them up close). I think is ok for a indie project but is a mixed feeling as pretty much the gameplay is about read the dialogues and make sure to keep up the spirits/moral bar of your characters (when it reach 0 is over and having a low moral would lead to give certain responses in the dialogue tree) and by the way they get bummed by pretty much everything...You have to click on the most uplifting choice in any situation just for callously get the that +5. The Tarots part of the gameplay is just flair (in reality you have 4 archetypes for each of the 3 characters and for me they translate in: Strength, Dexterity, Wits, Charm. Pick 1 archetype and you are kinda set for the whole game on what kind of approaches you will have success in trying as all the others will have pretty much a low chance of success. as there is no 2nd try what you picking at the begin define how you can use that character.Each "Tarot Card" translate into "Traits" the character can unlock (meaning they get good at doing certain things) and I think each card can be unlocked easily only by certain archetypes of the character. To be clear I truly think this game would've been better with only 1 character as its protagonist as having this many you can't feel pretty much invested in all of their different stories...you get a railroad tale where your perspective systematically jump from one character to another. Starting with the Minotaur (got the orphan backstory, and control his junky/drunkard behind just for the start) and rather quickly you get to play the Harlot and in context she actually feels like the real main character here, it just have that feeling. I mean if the devs just put this girl as the main character it would've been more interesting in my opinion..give her the backstory of being a orphan who escaped the orphanage controlled by the nuns, then grew up in a gang on the streets with her childhood friend with whom she escaped with, at some point left the gang where she acted as a greasy tomboy and developed a interest for build steampunk clockwork robots and then in her adulthood had this 360° apparence change where she become this gorgeous high-maintenance prostitute of this famous Brothel and dress up fancy and put up a fake persona using her sweet talk and fans techniques to milk out sugar daddies, for then behind doors drop the facade just wishing one day to get enough money to leave the town (as she's planning: get new documents and leave town without telling no one but the story with the news of the murders in the street lead to a different development), I think if the story was like this I would've been more captivated by it and the other 2 characters in this could've hit the bench (or become just side characters she met) if they just given this character the main spot you wouldn't have to get dragged around by each one of their troubles and lose tracks because "end chapter you now jump to doofus who have a totally different kind of problem". Could have instead fleshed out the Tarot cards as another of her interests and instead of give it to the dwarf (the only character who pretty much is there just "because") make her have this robot companion/bouncer for the "strength" feats. Heck even keep the "oh because she is a woman can't enter in certain places" part of the story but then allow her in certain part of the game/story to dress up and try to pass up as a guy (with the opportune stealth and charm checks to go undercover without problems). There is a laundry and she's friend with the lady give that possibility.Is just a thought, the game could've been more interesting if the story circled around 1 character with 1 clear objective and that just casually stumbled, while trying to leave, into this mystery (I rather have 1 character done well that I can use than 3 "meh"). I would say 19,50$ (discounted to 17,55 $) feel ok as price for try to help out the dev studio to grow (can still see despite my critics this is a work of love) but the game realistically would've needed more work. Would not recommend for those who are eager to fix their Disco Elysium void but if you loved the Pendula Swing series and don't expect much go ahead.
