_childDocuments_.review: Update (2024-02-02):I tried really hard, but the game refuses to be completed for me. After patch 3 solved the issue with a side quest in chapter 13, I continued playing the game and slowly got back into the story after not having played for two weeks. I admittedly skipped some minor side quests because it no longer seemed possible to complete them for lack of money or ideas on how to continue.Then, in chapter 17, the game starts a very long dialogue with main plot advancements, revelations and a number of skill checks. Unfortunately, my character (Miss Reed) was skilled towards intelligence and speech, leading to fairly abysmal odds on some of those skill checks (< 30%). At some point, many, many, many sentences into the dialogue, an unavoidable skill check appears that, if failed, means game over. Not "character is dead" over, but "retry" game over screen. I literally cannot continue. So I clicked "retry" as I actually preferred to have the character alive anyhow. However, due to the way the skill check system works (by eliminating cards from the deck unless a 0 or a 20 is drawn), the available cards for me to pass the check must have been eliminated quite a lot, so the <30% success rate lowered close to about 3% (for the "critical success" 20 roll).So I literally tried for the last 20 minutes to pass that one check. Continuously pressing "1" for a minute or so to get through the dialogue as fast as possible, only to fail again and getting my bloody skull caved in.At this point I lost interest. I will check out YT for the ending, as I feel my time is wasted trying to bash my head against this wall any longer.---------------------------Quick update (2024-01-28):The recently released patch 3 addressed and fixed the softlock that I mentioned in my review below. I have not yet really continued playing the game, so I will not change my review yet.---------------------------Original review (2024-01-23):This is a tentative non-recommendation. Tentative because I did not fully complete the game (for reasons I will explain below) and because I think that there is a rough gem here that could appeal to the right minds.First of all, I played around 10 hours and 13 of 18 chapters. I did run into a number of minor bugs that were overall not at all concerning, a couple of somewhat strange design decisions (more on that later) and a softlock situation with one of the side quests -- which was discussed in the forums with the very nice and responsive development team, but ultimately hampered my enjoyment of the game to the point I will put it on hold for now, as I do not enjoy being softlocked nor would enjoy having to replay at least a few hours of the game (starting from my last save game before the softlock) to progress back to the same point.The major positive for the game is its rather interesting setting and atmosphere. Clearly inspired by Disco Elysium, the devs opted for a quasi-19th-century London setting with an obvious fantasy touch. It's not bad. In fact, I think it works. The characters are fine and I get to experience (and somewhat steer) the story through overall well-written and interesting dialogue. It is not at the level of Disco Elysium, no, but it is still good, still motivating. The artwork is fitting and the music is often great, setting the mood perfectly for a world that is riddled with dystopian darkness and just few enough slivers of light to not completely lose hope. In fact, the way you play your characters can decide on whether you are ready to jump off a bridge or try to build new ones. It's perfectly acceptable for a point & click adventure visual novel (which is a more apt description than CRPG, but I knew that going in and I didn't mind).On the other side, the game is very opaque about how it wants or needs to be played. To the point where once you get it you say to yourself: "Well, that's certainly a bold choice for a 2024 game".- Forcing a character switch every chapter is the least troubling, although I cannot say that I was a fan at first. It has the feeling of a book or TV series that has to end on a cliffhanger with every chapter/episode before leaving the audience hanging while the next one focusses on a completely different character. It's a choice.- Then having all characters wander the same game world with not many changes other than more or less slightly different dialogue with NPCs, while being incredibly slow even when "running", is another choice.- However, the game does not tell you or prepare you for the fact that the collectible items through which the characters obtain money (i.e. the cogs) not only exist only once in the world, but if you pick them up with one character it will not be available for another, is getting into the "who thought this was a good idea?" department.- Ultimately, it is very likely that many first-time players loot all the available cogs in chapter 2 only to realize that the character you play in chapter 3 needs the cogs in order to progress their personal companion storyline. Cogs are no longer just for getting money, there is actual content locked behind being able to obtain the cogs. Sure, you find ways to get enough, but it's still a curious design choice akin to giving the player a slap in the face while saying "why didn't you see the slap coming?" at the same time.My stowstopper was the aforementioned softlock. If you are interested, look up the discussion in the forums, it's not hard to find with my username. For anyone playing themselves, it might be good idea to postpone a second visit to Sacred Heart until you actually have a questline reason to do so -- and if you do, be sure to save beforehand.Aside from the showstopper, there were however already some other issues that prevent me from "going back two hours" and replaying the part where I softlocked myself. The issue is that the game becomes very, very linear and the city suddenly feels very small. Chapters sometimes end after leaving one or two rooms, which means switching characters again and forcing you to remember how you roleplayed that other character. If there are new quests, they are fetch quests or go-there-and-talk-to-X but reusing the same exact locations that you explored ad nauseum in the first couple of chapters (because you wandered all of them at least three times, once per main character). So you are already getting bored of the same locations and watching your character "run" for what feels like minutes to get from A to B does not help. Yes, you can talk to every NPC again and again (and sometimes dialogue changes), but it gets to be a chore because the world does not change visibly.At circa the eighth or ninth chapter, the story is finally picking up and you start to cross off some of the side quests (unless you played yourself into a corner like I did or the game let you willing dive off a cliff, only to dangle unresolvable plotlines in your journal in front of you to mock you, a matter of perspective I guess). There is probably an interesting section ahead, which also finally changes locations and puts all characters somewhere else than the same 6 main locations in London. Alas, I (currently) do not feel like continuing. A shame. Shame on me, perhaps, and I accept that. Still, my choice, right?Overall, there is huge potential here. Especially for future games. Maybe future patches, if the developer decides to make some available. I don't need voiceover, the written text is just fine -- I played Disco Elysium before its definitive edition as well, where most of the text was not voiced either.Sovereign Syndicate is no Disco Elysium. But it does not have to be. I think it would be perfectly fine as its own thing, if and when the design choices catch up with the year 2024. I have played the Sierra adventure games in the 80s and had my attempt at Dark Seed. I do not enjoy story-telling games that willing allow the player to miss the story not by choice, but by chance.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: We’re enough years on from the critically successful release of “Disco Elysium” that entire dev cycles influenced by its creation have had a chance to pass. We were due for more combatless RPGs and Sovereign Syndicate is a clear descendant of that lineage…maybe a bit too clear to be honest.The first, second, and third things you notice about Sovereign Syndicate are how its constantly kneeling in deference to its inspiration. You’ve got a text-heavy narrative adventure where you spend most of your time looking at a right adjacent dialogue box. You’ve got multiple internal monologues personified by different parts of your psyche. You’ve got this victorian era detective mystery set in a port city with labor sympathetic themes, and you’ve even got at least one amnesiac protagonist among the three you swap between.I’m not normally one to dock points for unoriginality but the striking parallels make unfavorable comparisons far too easy, especially when you consider how many rungs down the production ladder we’re going.Lack of VO is the right call for a game with a budget this thin, but there’s little to no visual flourish or gameplay mechanics to distract from the fact that most of the game is reading a book with the character models awkwardly standing still the whole time.That book does have its moments, particularly when our protagonists converge, but for me its a game whose juice wasn’t worth the squeeze.Part of this game finding its audience, and the question you need to be asking yourself if you think it’s up your alley, is how much this game being an ‘RPG’ was influencing your decision-making. It walks and talks like one: this isometric perspective and all the historical fantasy elements definitely give it that kind of flavor.But it doesn’t really scratch those itches. If this had anime girls we’d all be calling it a visual novel, and I think that’s a much more apt comparison. I’m not trying to gatekeep the genre label, I think we could use an infusion of deep character building systems that manifest in more ways than just swinging pointy sticks differently; but I think what makes Sovereign Syndicate harder pressed to hold that tag compared to something like Disco Elysium, is the relative unimportance of skill checks.When you start the game you can pick an alignment for each of the playable protagonists and they open up different dialogue paths when speaking to NPCs and diceroll your success based on how much you’ve reinforced that alignment type through your choices. Importantly, they’re normally just flavor to how a conversation moves forward rather than a meaningful check. It’s all “RP” no “G”, you can wade your way through the entire story fumbling through every check and you’ll still get to where you need to go. It isn’t until the final act where there’s any meaningful stakes to the options you’re clicking.The few times there are strong requirements for a skill check it will just game over you rather than respond to your failure in the story. There’s a particularly bad sequence towards the end of the game that has a daisy chain of dicerolls you need to succeed in and every failure boots you back to the main menu to retry the sequence again. No opportunity to take your knowledge of the failed check to change strategies nor any cool story consequences to your failed rolls: you either reload an old save or just play diceroll simulator ‘til the gods smile upon you.It doesn’t help that it was a particularly crucial story moment: it’s like the one example of there actually being some semblance of a game here and it takes the wind out of the narratives’ sails rather than aiding them.When you’re not talking to NPCs you’re exploring the world for clues and completing side quests. The three characters typically alternate on a chapter by chapter basis: each having their own distinct motivations but ultimately intertwining on the same story about London’s elite and the needs of the many vs. the needs of the few.The exploration itself is mechanically light: Sovereign Syndicate prioritizes narrative flow over actual detectiving. Your quest log will always point you to where you need to go next, which keeps the pace brisk and the overall runtime of the game somewhere around the 10 hour mark give or take how many extra side things you wanna do.Its greatest virtue is the thoughtfulness of its world and the characters inside of it. Motivations and incentives are a key motif, and you can anticipate a few of the games twists if you’re keeping a keen eye on which parties stand to benefit from some of the murders and events that happen.Dont expect much in the way of mechanical reward for good sleuthing: even if you’re following along closely and observing every clue, structurally the game is still railroading you through a very particular sequence of events and is unwilling to let you leave a handprint until the very end. Its hard not to escape the feeling that you’re just a passenger in this game rather than a player.Those strictly seeking a Victorian era narrative adventure may find what they’re looking for here, but for me that fantasy was too afraid to step out of its inspirations’ shadow, and was underserved by toothless RPG systems.The game does end with a clear setup to either a sequel or another game in the same universe, and I do hope that game comes to pass. As a freshman title from a new studio, Sovereign Syndicate has succeeded in creating a modest “Disco Elysium-lite”, but the only reason its reach didn’t exceed its grasp is because it didn’t reach very far to begin with.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: The comparisons to Disco Elysium, even as reserved as many of them seemed to me, meant that I had to give this a try. I certainly wasn't expecting it to be in the same league, but ultimately even taken purely on its own merits I ended up somewhat disappointed.The pitch and premise here was good and compelling, and a good effort was made. In practice, though:* The game was very linear, and very little in the way of meaningful choice or consequence seemed to be had.* The RPG mechanics were ultimately largely immaterial, largely just affecting your chances at small things like cash rewards that you don't actually need anyway. They didn't meaningfully drive the story, characters, or the gameplay experience.* There are 18 chapters, across 4 different characters, but in truth most of them were only a few minutes long. The vast majority of my playtime was ultimately spent just *painfully* slowly walking about maps, checking to see if there's any new interactions possible in each chapter.* The vast majority of side content ended up without substantive payoff, be it mechanical or narrative.* The main stories likewise just ultimately didn't really satisfy. Only one of the characters felt like they had an arc that properly made sense. Another ends with anticlimax, and the other two... I'm honestly not sure what the point of them was in the first place, save fleshing out the world a bit more, but they didn't actually *do* anything.It was a novel try, but I'd only pick it up if you particularly enjoy steam settings, straight adventure games (as the RPG aspects don't matter much here), are very patient (to cope with the slow movement), and it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: Shouldn't be compared to Disco Elysium much, because it just can never hold against it. Was the ending good? No. Was it an open world? No. Did I enjoy the story and characters? Yes. Did I like the roleplaying aspects? Yeah, somewhat. I wish they would do some QoL improvements. They are desperately needed, but overall I had my fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: It has a promising start and premise, the story itself is interesting enough, but thats unfortunately about all it has going for it. The gameplay is simply, hardly even a game. The dialogue choices are slim and seldom matter much. It would have done much better to have leaned on its comic elements and been a visual novel than whatever this is trying to be. All of this could be looked past if the ending was satisfactory but it is not. It is instead a rushed exposition dump of the authors going a-ha! see! which does not come off as at all fulfilling. One of the three characters honestly need not be in the story at all. All that said, its a valiant effort, and if you need about a ten hour time killer and enjoy the type of story being offered, maybe pick it up in the year 2029 and beyond  when it goes on a sale for about 2$. Otherwise, I would just read a synopsis of the story, it will save you time and money.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: Barely a CRPG. Somewhat competent Point & Click.The RPG mechanics are exceedingly shallow. It's an unfortunate trend that this game, along with Gamedec both took on the concept of Disco Elysium's gameplay, but failed to extrapolate on the RPG depth of the systems. There is a core story that is interesting, but the narrative, albeit verbose, fails to construe anything bar nihilistic characters and a general sense of either extreme cheerfulness or utter depression.Your protagonist's dialogues are inconsistent towards their reactions to other NPCs and the bouncing around between acts feels both pointless and confusing. I can't recommend this game, even for Point & Click fans. The RPG systems aren't there at all and the point & click aspects are menial.I hope the developers grow from this, and I sincerely think there are real chops here and there, but the lack of depth and the inconsistencies in character's personalities make this house of cards fall apart.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: It really breaks my heart to have to give Sovereign Syndicate a negative review; I despise ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the hard work of the talented dev teams of any game, especially a game with such promise. But I can't in good faith recommend this game to my friends, which is why ultimately I have to give this a thumbs down.I'll start off with the good parts of this game. This is a very interesting world! I like the idea of a semi-fantasy steampunk world, and it carries it's premise very well. On that note, I also like the literal environments in the world- they're all very clear and unique, and I never really got lost in where I had to go.The visual design of the game was very nice, the atmosphere was very strong throughout (of course this was helped by the music, which really was a great fit for the game throughout!). The characters were at least visually unmistakable from each other.I actually really enjoyed the Tarot card system, and how it was used to level up skills and help mould your choices by the end of the game. It was a simple and elegant system, and I'd genuinely love to see it again.Unfortunately, anything positive I have to say, though they are numerous, is overshadowed by the game's biggest flaw: it's writing.Now let me be clear! The structure of the plot is actually quite solid. By the end of the game, I could see what they were trying to do, and what they were trying to do was a really great idea. It's just that the script was not strong enough to give the emotional impact they were trying to go for.I understood factually that these characters were struggling in an unfair London, but I didn't feel for them at all. A lot of the time I was being told why I should root for the main characters, I was told what characters were like and what they had done... but I didn't see any of it actually happening. I'm terribly sorry, but the entire time I was playing, I could only think to myself 'This is so shallow.'. I have a feeling that the writers wanted there to be such a level of mystery and intrigue that they obfuscated way too much from the player, which resulted in there being gaps in which they then had to explain to the player why something happened. It made the ending seem so... like, I understood the payoff, but it was incredibly sudden and almost disproportionate.The pacing also leaves a lot to be desired. I actually quite like that the game was split into chapters. But the first act was long to the point of dreariness, and then the final act felt like I blinked and it was over (which was a shame because I liked the final act). Yes, I understand that the world needs to be set up in the first act, but having to start the game from a different perspective for the first three chapters was tedious. Honestly, I only started getting interested in the story from Chapter 13, more than halfway through the game! I almost feel like the game would have been better if it were structured in a way where you played one character's perspective in your first playthrough, and then play another character to get a whole other perspective in your second playthrough, etc.I am disappointed, but honestly? I can see the potential of this game and of it's team. If a sequel popped up, or if this team released anything else in the future, I'd love to check it out. This game was a few steps away from greatness, and I'm excited to see when this team releases that game that really blows everyone out of the water. The ideas and the heart that went into this game shows me that they can make something really incredible. Sovereign Syndicate was just, unfortunately, not that game.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: What makes Disco Elysium good is the engaging world, characters, but mostly, the writing. The writing here has no strong voice, the characters are little better than window dressing, and the world has as much choice in the way you develop said story as you bouncing down a bowling lane with gutter guards.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game, but the positives ultimately outweigh the negatives. I enjoyed the story, the writing is pretty good, and the characters are varied and interesting. I liked the skill system overall, although you mostly end up picking options that give you the most benefits, not thinking about actually roleplaying the character. Arcanum is my favorite game ever, so of course I love the magical steampunk setting and I don’t care about poor graphics. What bothered me though, was the constant backtracking and loading screens every time you switched locations (so every ten seconds or so). I’m also not a fan of swapping characters every chapter. What works in a novel, ended up being jarring in a video game, pulling me out of the experience. Sovereign Syndicate feels like a prologue to a much bigger adventure. It ended exactly when things were picking up. I hope for a sequel as it’s desperately needed.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wanted to play Disco Elysium but it’s set in Steampunk London at the turn of the 20th century where dwarves, centaurs, cyclopses, minotaurs, werewolves, and prostitutes converge in a seedy dance of death and deception? If so, you've come to the right place. Sovereign Syndicate is a non-traditional, combat-free RPG that gives you control of a fascinating quartet of characters, each with a complex backstory and compelling role to play in this wicked Victorian-era nightmare. You’ll kick things off as Atticus Daley, a sexy gin-soaked minotaur seemingly set on drug-induced self-destruction. That is until a mysterious Old Crone telepathically invades your hungover thoughts and starts guiding you on a weird trip down memory lane, back to the orphanage you swore to leave buried in the recesses of your sad subconscious. Maybe a little dance in the opium den will help put your troubled mind at ease... or rip it wide open.  While Atticus trips, let’s check in on Clara Reed: a high-class dollymop to London’s scummy elite, and desperate to buy herself a new life in a faraway land. But when the Courtesan Killer—a Jack the Ripper replica—starts murdering all of Clara’s hooker friends from the Velvet Rose, East End’s favorite fictional brothel, well, it seems like Ms. Reed’s time in London has just begun.  Speaking of time, Sovereign Syndicate rounds out its quirky quartet in an almost abandoned clocktower, where the unlikely duo of Teddy Redgrave and his eager automaton, Otto, plot out bounty-hunting hijinks for the highest bidder, be that the boys in blue down at Scotland Yard or the dockside gang down the street. Together, Teddy and Otto (the latter of whom might go on to accidentally inspire a city-wide robot uprising), find themselves unknowingly intertwined in the drama of Atticus and Clara, thanks in large part to a Masked Stranger who’s for some reason set on bringing everyone together.  In short, Sovereign Syndicate delivers a wonderful narrative-driven experience that sports an intricate, multi-pronged plot, vibrant and memorable characters, and the first non-voice acted 5/5 I’ve ever awarded a game for dialogue (full scoring breakdown available on my profile page). Though technically a shameless recreation of Disco Elysium’s dialogue system whereby parts of your personality compete against each other, Sovereign Syndicate manages to stand out by delivering an unparalleled attention to historical linguistic detail. Really, there's an almost overwhelming amount of Victorian slang on display here, but the game’s handy built-in dictionary means word nerds like me will never have to stop to look something up (for example, did you know the space between your bed and the wall is called a ruelle? Me neither!). It’s a nice touch that earns the game solid marks for User Interface, which brings us to Sovereign Syndicate’s Gameplay and Content.  When you’re not busy reading, and—let's be honest—you always will be, Sovereign Syndicate gives you a wonderfully weird if small slice of Victorian London to explore with six locations excluding the game’s exciting finale. Each location features a fun cast of side characters who will give you dozens of mostly interesting side quests, but the real fun is seeing the same things through the eyes of different playable characters. As Atticus, Clara, Teddy, and Otto interact with the world, you’ll unlock Tarot cards, which open up branching dialogue options and give you more ways to approach RNG encounters. That’s right, as was the case with Disco Elysium’s dice system, Sovereign Syndicate has you draw minor tarot cards to determine whether certain parts of your personality fail or succeed at certain circumstances.  For example, will Atticus’s “Wit” figure out where the heck this Masked Stranger is taking you? Probably not, because I’m roleplaying Atticus as a max Animal Instinct idiot who drinks and/or smashes everything in sight. At least I was, until I started to feel bad about plunging his “Hope” into the gutter, thereby denying me access to happier branching dialogue options, and what can I say? I’m a happy lil’ dude :) So, while nothing about this system impressed me per se, it does a good job of injecting intrigue into the many, many walls of text you’ll read.   Finally, a few words on style. Sovereign Syndicate lacks in high-res textures, quality lighting, and smooth animations, but the overall visual effect is still an enjoyable one thanks to pretty watercolor transitions between menus and hand drawn comic panel style action scenes. And, while the sound effects here are nothing special, the game’s soundtrack stands out thanks to a dedicated song for each area and a full-length oral vocal performance by the lovely Miss Reed herself.  In the end, Sovereign Syndicate is a very enjoyable if non-traditional RPG that, without combat, ends up playing like an interactive point-and-click adventure title. I beat the game in a little over 10 hours but feel like a second playthrough is warranted, so for $20 I think the game presents above-average value.  I’m giving Sovereign Syndicate a solid aggregate MEGA score of 3.75/5 and am happy to answer any questions you have about the game or my review.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: This is a unique game in that it doesn't have any combat, but isn't completely a "point and click" either. You play as a few different characters which I initially was confused about, because I didn't have time to finish my side quests before the switch. The quests stay with your characters, however, so you can finish them when you get thrown back into that character. I really liked the different perspectives offered by looking at the same item (or interacting with a different character) from the other characters' POV. For example, when looking at a building with one character they might observe it to be ugly while a other finds it charming. There aren't too many characters to keep track of, which is nice, because with so much dialogue and story it would be easy to get lost. The body "humours" as a kind of character development is unique, and the characters' mood affects the gameplay in different ways. All in all it's fun to relax and explore the game world, as I'm a kind of player who explores everything. If you don't care for story and nuance then this game isn't for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: I really loved this game and it surprised me.  When it first started and I saw the interface, the voices inside the head, the inebriated, down on his luck main character, I thought – ‘No!  Please don’t try to remake Disco Elysium. Stop!’  But I kept going and although the gameplay mechanics are similar, the story is very different. You play 4 very different characters in a lovely steampunk world.  The art work is beautiful!  Quickly I found the familiar dialogue bar, points and rolls comfortable while embarking in a much different world with likeable characters with their own personalities, skills and motivations.  I found it hard to stop and take breaks as I just wanted to keep playing and see where the story was going.  The change of characters often left on mini cliffhangers which made me want to keep playing even more.  Not giving away the story but there is mystery, murder, magic, and fantastical characters and tech.  I had a great time playing and look forward to playing the sequel when it arrives.  I had 19 hours in my first run and will leave the game in my queue so I can play again with different character setups.  Game play and quality is well worth the price.  Much recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: AAA writing and world building. Honestly, I cannot say enough nice things about both -- better than anything recently released not named Baldur's Gate 3. The three/four main characters you play as each have their own interesting stories and reasons for crossing paths -- this is not a single narrative where you have multiple party members, this is three different narratives of three different characters whose paths cross mainly at the end. The steampunk/fantasy elements and interesting/amusing NPC interactions create a fascinating, believable fictional London. If I could offer two points that I think would have improved the gameplay experience, they would be:1. Dramatically increase the frequency of the comic panels. In the instances they are used, they help illustrate what is going on with the narrative in an art style that perfectly matches the theme, there just aren't enough of them. I'd go so far as to suggest that nearly all important interactions should utilize these panels. And unlike suggesting something outside of the budget available for an indie like this, I think this is actually doable. 2. Unlock the camera. I don't know that this is possible, but if it were, it would certainly add more to the enjoyment of the environments of the game.In any event, I'd love to see a sequel, especially if the sequel addresses my point #1.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: Good  but not great steampunk fantasy RPG in the style of Disco Elysium.  Character driven with a strong central cast but could do more to lean on it's setting. Dialogue is engaging where it matters, though at times it seems the outcome is the same no matter the choices made in conversation. Can become repetitive with retreading the same areas each chapter to ensure nothing is missed.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: Disco elysium type of game.  Don't expect alot of action it's a narrative heavy game. The writing is good. The story is interesting. There are three main characters all pretty different and all well writen. The world is pretty intruiging too a steampunk london filled with creatures like werewolves, cylcopses, minotaurs etc. Story concluded in a satisfactory manner while leaving the path open for sequels. Nice artstyle in pretty much every aspect. Animations weren't great and some textures could be better. Worth a playthrough.  Full Review here :

_childDocuments_.review: So far so good! This game clearly falls into the subgenre of CRPGs that Disco Elysium created and that's perfectly fine with me. The writing is strong and the characters/world are interesting. I'm not a huge fan of using 3D instead of a painted background, but that's just my personal preference so not really a knock against the game.At the moment, I'm only a couple hours in. I'll update this review more once I get further, but for now I recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: This game wants to be compared to Disco Elysium and it loses the comparison heavily. The same mechanics that just don't feel deserved in this one. You feel like traveling on a linear path with a lot of forced decisions. And there is even stronger feeling of choices not meaning anything (biggest offender of this so far is Chapter 7).Most side quests are awkward where you wander around randomly doing random stuff for no good reason. Which doesn't feel justified for the characters most of the time. In each chapter I end up just trying to visit all location to see whether a random NPC or event appears or existing NPC has something randomly new to say. Most of the time there is no logic to it. You might say Disco Elysium was doing the same, but there are crucial differences: in Disco Elysium you are actively investigating and that's natural and also most interactions are much more interesting and deeper than here. Imo that's the issue here: the game is doing things like Disco Elysium, but missing crucial points about what made it good in Disco Elysium.Another big problem for me is that the game is just not engaging. I took a break at Chapter 10 and at this point I don't have much motivation/interest to get back: I don't care for the characters. I will probably still finish it for the sake of completion. But all the plotlines so far are pretty boring.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: It's a Disco Elysium inspired steampunk narrative RPG. But not very similar to Disco Elysium, let me warn you.The playable characters are interesting and fun to play as. The main story made me curious and a little emotional. Overall, I enjoyed playing it without encountering bad-writing which dooms this kind of games. I found dialogue options limited occasionally but it didn't bother me most of the time. To sum up, if you love story-rich games give Sovereign Syndicate a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: Diving into Sovereign Syndicate is an experience I didn't know I needed. The writing captivated me from the get-go. Each character is a window into a different part of this rich world, offering unique reactions and perceptions that kept the narrative fresh and engaging. I found myself eagerly anticipating each new interaction, curious about how the diverse NPCs would respond to the different personas I was playing.I really love the setting.  I quite enjoy the take on steampunk with the petina of Victorian London.  This setting also works extremely well with the Greek mythological creatures; I'd have never come up with a Minotaur in a top hat, but I love it.For me, the game was all about the story, and it delivers brilliantly. It's clear that the developers poured their hearts into this project. The level of detail, the depth of the characters, the way the story unfolded – it is a journey worth taking.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the story. Using tarot cards as the 'dice roll' and for the skill set is clever. The steampunk artwork and concepts are gorgeous. The characters were fun to play and the locations were interesting to explore. The different missions were interesting to solve from different perspectives. I'd buy and play a sequel, for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: A highly enjoyable narrative RPG, though without not its faults. The game takes obvious inspiration from Disco Elysium in the way characters are defined not by a class, but by their inner world, the text crawl resembles a social media feed (much like in Disco), and the main story superficially follows a similar beat. Look deeper, however, and the game is very different. Instead of one protagonist and his inner world, we have three. Instead of an emphasis on that protagonist's psychology, we have an emphasis on action and interacting with the world. Skill checks allow one to progress in a more consequentialist manner (so having high stats across the board is possible and desirable in ways which would have been detrimental in Disco  - as being too logical or too physically weak could be detrimental in that game, but not in this one). The world is made up of discrete hubs, and you will spend a lot of time zipping between loading screens and having three characters visiting the exact same places to inspect the exact same items. In spite of the centaurs, cyclops and minotaurs, the story is far more grounded than in Disco, and far more linear. However, the world and atmosphere that Sovereign Syndicate establishes were so compelling to me that I was left curious for more. I hope the game does well enough to inspire more like it and continue the story of steampunk fantasy London.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: I finished Sovereign Syndicate a while back (on GoG) and I was positively surprised. It's a cRPG set in a fascinating blend of Victorian London and urban fantasy. The three protagonists, each with their own unique motivations, are incredibly compelling. I can't get enough of Otto, the adorable steampunk robot who accompanies Teddy, one of the protagonists. He's more than just a sidekick, he’s a character that adds a touch of humor and heart to the story. I love Otto!What sets Sovereign Syndicate apart is its focus on narrative over combat. Instead of fighting enemies, you resolve conflicts through dialogue. It's a refreshing change of pace and, imho, adds to the flavour of the game.I was reminded of Disco Elysium and Gamedec in terms of their emphasis on character development and world-building. However, Sovereign Syndicate has its own distinct charm with its steampunk setting and intriguing, read “imperfect”,  characters.While the game is relatively short, it's definitely worth the price. The quality of the writing and the unique gameplay experience make it a memorable adventure.If you're looking for a cRPG that's smart, engaging, and full of character, Sovereign Syndicate is a must-play.Played it on GoG first, bought it on Steam, because I liked it that much,
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: A well worthwhile isometric adventure game. Follows the story of three distinct characters operating in the same area and plot. Very much a dialogue-only game, in the skein of Disco Elysium, if not in the scope or achievement.The world is quite interesting, though I'm not too familiar with Steampunk in general to compare it to others. It's not a long game, but is definitely enough to tell its story. The story itself is no mind buster, but put together well enough to compel you to find more. It wraps up a bit too fast and not in a very satisfying way, however overall it's cohesive and well-pacedThe characters themselves are quite fleshed out, though maybe the overall dialogue tries a bit too hard to sound authentic. As a non-native speaker I appreciate all the vernacular explanation pop-ups, even if some of them were rather known or clear from context, but maybe not to all.There's a few RPG elements such as skills levels, unlockable traits, skill checks and branching paths, where the skill checks use a finite deck of playing cards rather than dice, but ultimately the story moves forward either way. Would have liked if the Disco Elysium approach of failure meaning unique progress was implemented here, but alas if you fail some checks, you simply forego extra information or a more favourable outcome.The music is fitting and atmospheric and I quite enjoyed it. Some areas really benefited from it.The game map is not incredibly large or detailed, but gets the job done. The steampunk theme is rather light, but in no way a bad thing. Definitely some padding was achieved having the different characters traverse the same world multiple times, but it doesn't detract from the story. Makes the adventure feel more real, rather than overly grand.Overall it's well worth the cost and the few days spent on the charming world and its characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: There are parts of this game that I love and there are parts that I hate, which ends up creating a very frustrating experience overall. I do love the setting and the writing so far, but the exploration feels tedious. Not only is moving around the map fairly slow, the game also has a lot of backtracking and the fast travel options often put you far away from where you want to go, and since the game has three protagonists you end up having to explore the same locations and talking to the same people three times to make sure you don't miss anything unique to that character. I feel like the game would have benefitted from making each character's chapter a bit more linear to alleviate some of this repetition, or simply just have a single protagonist so you only had to explore the map once. As it is right now every new chapter just makes me feel dread over having to run around all over the city one more time.I'm still giving it a thumbs up because I like what they were going for, but at this point I'm not feeling motivated to actually finish the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Low concept and extremely low frequency imitation of what is clearly supposed to be an ode to Disco Elysium. This here game is what happens when morbidly unexceptional people try to write a storyline with the weak understanding of alt-polit culture only a redditor possesses. Trying to impose the clear conviction and world-view of the writers on a subject matter that is supposedly rooted in conservative times is exactly what Disco Elysium avoided. Ask yourself why Disco Elysium felt so believable and "could-be-rooted-in-reality" and this did not? Hint: it's not the magical aspect. The game would have been better served as a Visual Novel, since the strongest part about the game are the comics and some of the visuals, though the overall world looks very bland and unintentionally colorless. Any aspirations the writer of this game had for being an author, I suggest branching out instead. The game is a drag. Their open world serves no purpose but to waste your time. Every quest is a fetch quest. Characters just don't fit the times the setting is inspired by.Waited so long for this thing, what a shame. Hard pass.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game set in steampunk Victorian London. You begin as Atticus, a minotaur magician, who is battling his personal demons when he's approached by a mysterious stranger. As Atticus, you explore the dark underbelly of the alternate Earth setting, making decisions based on your inner voices and deciding how to approach the different challenges (brute strength, wit, sleight of hand, etc.)When I moved to the second chapter, I was surprised to get a new hero to play! There are three (or four) in all--Atticus the minotaur, Clara the lounge singer, Teddy the inventor, and Teddy's sidekick, Otto the automaton. The way their stories intertwine is the creative heart of the game. I loved seeing the world through each character's eyes and figuring out what was important to each of them.This is a narrative-driven game based on skill checks, with no combat. The writing is stellar; it drew me right into the game and made me care about the people within. The art is gorgeous, too. While the overall play time is short, lots of decision points and ways to tackle challenges means I'll definitely play again after my first game is done.Highly recommended!

For a CRPG, this is a glaring flaw that simply cannot be ignored.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, Sovereign Syndicate is an excellent low-budget indie detective RPG that focuses on narrative-driven gameplay, character development, and dialogue.The game combines Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura (fantasy steampunk setting with the Industrial Revolution and its effect on society) with Disco Elysium (dialogue-focused gameplay with no real combat). While it doesn't live up to the two classics, it does stand out on its own merits, and I recommend it to anyone who loves these kinds of games.The moment you start playing Sovereign Syndicate, you will clearly see that it heavily draws inspiration from Disco Elysium. All RPG elements and stats are focused on dialogue. Each of the three main characters has several central characteristics of their personality, which you can upgrade in order to improve your chances when you pick dialogue options related to that personality trait. Instead of dice-throwing, you draw a random card to determine the success of your dialogue choice (in combination with your stats for that trait). The system is not as intricate and complex as the one in Disco Elysium, but it serves its purpose and allows for player agency and role-play with each of the characters.In addition to talking, you will explore various districts of the East End of Victorian-era London. You will talk with a colourful cast of characters, help them with their problems, find various items, and click on all kinds of clickable things so that your characters can provide commentary.Sovereign Syndicate offers a refreshing take on traditional fantasy RPG settings. Instead of a medieval setting with Tolkien-inspired fantasy creatures, we have Victorian-era London during the height of the fictive Second Industrial Revolution enhanced with steampunk machinery. On top of that, instead of Orcs and Elves, we have creatures from Greek mythology as other intelligent humanoids, including the Minotaurs, the Centaurs, and the Cyclops. The game's overarching lore explores themes of a changing world during the Industrial Revolution and how it affected the poor and downtrodden on the margins of society who were already struggling to meet their basic needs. It follows forgotten war veterans, prostitutes, simple workers, orphans, criminals... and juxtaposes them against the creme de la creme - industrial magnates, landlords, wealthy land owners, corrupted politicians, crime lords, etc. While it doesn't go too deep into any of these topics, it raises a few questions successfully and manages to convey the struggles of people from the bottom of the barrel.The story follows three main characters. Atticus Daley is an ex-orphan turned low-life alcoholic with a miserable outlook on life. Clara Reed is a lady of the night in a prestigious brothel who is trying to leave London for good. Theodore Redgrave, a dwarf, is a battle-hardened monster hunter and inventor, always in the company of his trusty automaton Otto.These characters are written very well, driven by their believable motives, and have multifaceted personalities. They are good people, but none of them are saints, and they will do anything to reach their goals, no matter how ignoble or downright wrong it might be. Life in the East End is not for the faint of heart, and you are either ready to do bad things when push comes to shove, or you might end up as just another rotting corpse at the bottom of the Thames.You play these characters separately, and their paths will eventually intertwine as the story unravels. The main story is written rather ably, and it plays out as a noir murder mystery with a more complex overarching conspiracy, which will be uncovered as you play through the game. The game’s tempo is just perfect, and I’ve never felt like the story is lingering for too long or losing its momentum. I was motivated to finish the story right up until the very end.Similarly to Disco Elysium, the game uses a rather rich vocabulary, with many not-commonly-used words, archaisms, and rare idioms from British vernacular. Luckily, the developers were aware that having too many of these words can obstruct players from following the story, so they have added tooltips for all lesser-known words, idioms, and phrases. You can simply mouse over them, and their meaning will be explained to you in detail. The game is not demanding at all, and you will be able to play it on basically any PC. At first, the visuals were not appealing to me. In fact, I had considered them ugly. But as I played the game, I’ve grown to love the game’s aesthetics. It’s obviously nowhere near modern standards, and it can look relatively low quality at some points. However,  the developers were able to get the maximum out of it. Many areas are rich with details, and I especially like the interiors of several exotic shops you will visit during your playthrough. Hence, I can say that I've enjoyed the game visually more than I originally had expected.However, animations are something I can’t get over it. For starters, there are barely any animations in the game at all, as Sovereign Syndicate is mostly a static experience. And when there are some animations, they are crude, twitchy and often goofy. The main characters all walk awkwardly, usually sliding on the ground or as if they desperately need to go to the bathroom to take number 2. Furthermore, it's not uncommon for them to get stuck somewhere as they walk because path-finding is below expected standards. I understand that this is a low-budget game, but these are still things I need to talk about. Sovereign Syndicate doesn’t feature voice acting. On the one hand, it’s a shame as proper voice acting could possibly significantly enhance the experience. On the other hand, the budgetary restraints of this game would mean sub-optimal solutions. And given how often poor voice acting can absolutely ruin the immersion, their decision to omit it entirely might be for the best. If the game earns enough money, they can always release an "enhanced edition" with proper voice acting added.Sovereign Syndicate doesn't have many sounds in general, save for background sounds and the soundtrack. Each of the locations has its own blend of sounds to help the player better visualise the place. And it does it relatively well, properly conveying the atmosphere and your surroundings. Music is composed in a way that is unintrusive and discreet. It will not be something you will be listening to on YouTube after you finish the game, but you will enjoy it as a part of the overall experience while playing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolute breath of fresh air. I personally fell in love with Disco Elysium and it was easily my GOTY. If you liked Disco Elysium, you're gonna love this. It is all too familiar, even some of the plot points feel similar, but most importantly, it feels fresh. Instead of dice rolls we are drawing tarot cards, and the artwork is awesome. This is a well written, narrative driven game and I would recommend to anyone who enjoys CRPGs and the likeUPDATE after completing the game - I still think the game is good and definitely recommend it for the story, although I will say it has a bit of a slow start. The devs state 8-12hours of gameplay depending on your playstyle, but as someone who explores every nook and cranny and talks to each NPC twice when playing CRPGs, it took me almost 30 hours to get to the credits. Game was awesome nonetheless and it's a damn shame it didn't catch much traction
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: Not a terrible game but hard to recommend.The writing is decent, the environments look pretty good. I appreciate the definitions of Victorian-slang built in to the interface and the characters have personality. The setting reminds me of Arcanum! Great. The Tarot cards representing rolls and abilities is a good idea, and improving your stats through your dialogue choices feels like a very promising mechanic. The first 2 chapters feel a little slow, but promising.There's not really any "gameplay" to speak of, no way to boost or modify or retry your skill checks. Your only moment-to-moment decision is your choice of dialogue, and this would be fine, if there was some agency to exercise in these choices. But the story is ultimately linear and episodic, with choices generally boiling down to "go to the next step cleverly" or "go to the next step violently", etc. Because of this, the Tarot and character advancement mechanics have no teeth. It doesn't really feel like it matters what you DO in the game, on any particularly lasting level.  If you're really just looking for a nice Victorian fantasy story to engage with completely passively, it's a recommend. But if you are looking for a CRPG, or even a Disco-Elysium-Lite, I don't think it gets there.

_childDocuments_.review: London is more fantastical, with Minotaur's and Werewolves and other such mystical beings, it is also decidedly more steampunk with airships and automatons. It’s here we first meet Atticus Daley, an orphaned Minotaur who lived a tough life. We play as two other characters, Clara a dolly as they say who is seeking to leave London, and Teddy a dwarf who has built an automaton. Of these the most interesting is Atticus, having the most fleshed out of the backstories and also the better hook, a mysterious masked figure tasks him with finding his mother who abandoned him as a child, and also potentially solving the case of orphans disappearing from the same orphanage that he grew up in. There are also a great number of other side quests across the three characters to add more to the story. Switching characters is always a risk and unfortunately, it doesn’t work out too well here, I often found myself disinterested in Clara and Teddy's story and it made the whole thing much more disjointed overall. Atticus’ story was entertaining and well done but getting it once every 3 chapters or less in some cases brought the enjoyment down. It does pick up right at the very end but it ends seemingly at the beginning of some other story.There are some very very light RPG elements, you decide how your character should be at the start and get elevated sats in the type of traits you selected this does make the tarot drawings(the game's way of doing dice rolls). These stats can be leveled up by selecting dialogue options that fit with that trait which it does unfortunately tell you what dialogue does what, making it a little less engaging. The traits can all be leveled up by selecting dialogue options and making them easier. Occasionally you’ll get major arcana cards that act as unlocking a specific trait and that unlock some new dialogue options or actions, these are quite minimal though, and don’t impact too much. The dice rolls also don’t seem to be that exciting or eventful and are just there and rather unengaging. A lot of great systems are present and ready they just unfortunately aren’t used in an all too interesting way, I still got a decent amount of enjoyment out of it but it wasn’t as engaging as I’d hoped.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. It wasn't your typical sort of RPG and in a lot of ways felt like a visual novel. But I enjoyed the setting a lot and I liked switching between the perspective of three (technically four) characters' perspectives. The story felt satisfying, but still remained open ended and hinted at a sequel. I'm excited to see what the next chapter could bring.

_childDocuments_.review: The thing you have to understand about this is that its not a CRPG. Instead its a point and click adventure mixed with visual novel. I say this because there doesn't seem to be much in the way of choice and consequence. Sure, there are minor deviations into alternate routes based on using different skills. For example, pick a lock, smash it, find the key, or talk your way past a guard. But they're very minimal and mostly just for flavor. Still, I appreciated that and its one of the strong points of the game. This game also has an interesting story, though at times its a bit too convoluted and verbose. You could also say there are some pacing issues as the first half is very slow. A lot of the early stuff as well as side quests don't seem to matter much to the overall plot, and you can still get a pretty good ending while ignoring several side quests. In fact it seemed kind of weird at one point. I barely looked into the murder mystery that the story revolves around and skipped several leads, only to very easily solve the entire case in a couple of scenes that pretty much give it all away. Because of this, I thought about quitting multiple times early on, but it did eventually end up picking up the pace. In the end I suppose it was worth the effort. I'm sort of mixed on the ending I got, which makes me feel like this game was more of a prequel to set up a future story than anything else, but there is a decent payoff in the climax.   The weak point is in the rest of everything to do with the RPG mechanics. In normal conversations, they really don't do much except change the flavor a bit. Often times, multiple dialogue options are just different ways of phrasing literally the same statement. So what you end up doing is choosing answers based on what skill you want to grind up (as using certain flavored choices levels up the skills associated with them) and not what you actually want to say, so that you can pass story relevant skill checks later and get the outcome you want. Maybe that would be ok if the flavor was good, but its not very flavorable at all as it were. It mostly seems arbitrary how the skills are used. They're different for every character too, so they're hard to conceptualize and keep track of. This is not like the stats in most RPGs like D&D or Fallout. These are more esoteric. For example, one character's stats are intellect (blue), intuition (yellow), grace (red), and tact (green). Another's characters yellow stat might be spryness. What does spryness have to do with intuition? Beats me. And then you have problems like intellect and intuition sounding very similar, so its hard to get a grasp on what exactly they mean. Its a little too abstract and experimental. Having clearer lines drawn between the stats would make more sense and why some stats are certain colors. Additionally, they should be the same for every character. Especially when there are times that you get an option that sounds *witty* but the game calls it *tactful*. Then there is the hope mechanic. It does matter at times, but not much. You might need a certain level (or lack) of hope to make a certain choice. But you aren't punished for having low hope or rewarded for having high hope outside of this. Hope should be something you actively want to keep up if its going to be a game mechanic. And its also very trivial to get your hope maxed out at 100 on every character. Overall, I like the idea, and it could be interesting if it A) had impact other than flavor and B) it was actually hard to maintain hope. Then there's the tarot cards. You get one of these when you pick your starting stats, but you can also earn them during gameplay. I'm not too sure what triggered them to be honest, as they seemed to pop up during random conversations when I didn't do anything impressive or notable. And certain tarot cards are WAY more impactful than others. It seems like they give you alternate routes on rare occasions that bypass skill checks, but its hard to tell. When you put all this together, the RPG mechanics--while very creative and I want to them work well--really just get in the way of the story. It would make more sense to leave most of this stuff up to the player's discretion and just remove them. Let people roleplay however they wish and choose whatever flavor without having to manage a stat system that's muddled and really doesn't matter. Of course, I like the idea of a stat system and if it DID matter more, that would be ideal. Perhaps the developer can find a way to implement them better in their next game. Another thing I didn't like was having to switch characters constantly. Its difficult to keep track of and interest in 3 separate POV story lines at once. Maybe it would have been fine if you stuck with one character till the end of their story, then played through another character's entirely, and so on. Especially when you walk around the exact same locations and see the exact same things and talk to the same exact people the other characters did while doing tedious chores and fetch quests. It gets state very fast.TL;DR: A slow burn narrative that requires a lot of patience and has some half-baked RPG mechanics, but provides an interesting experience for the price if you can tough it out.

_childDocuments_.review: My notes:1) If you're going to have chapters where I can explore the town, people should have something new to say every chapter. Kinda like how Trails in the Sky the NPC dialogs update every time you progress the main quest. Either that or each chapter should have new locations.2) The three character stories was kinda mid.3) It's your first game. Your first RPG. Why are you setting up a future game with the end? Better to tell a good entirely self-contained story (or I guess three in this game's case).4) The tarot card system was a waste. It's mostly acting like dice rolls when really only the Fool should have caused a fail state and every other card you can get leading to a variation. And the variations should lead to very different outcomes on major plot points.I think if the game developers had made a 7 hour instead of 13-15 hour RPG, focused on a single character and his/her/their story, but made it so that the cards could lead to vastly different experiences but a satisfying end, you'd get a much better first RPG.Right now I can't recommend it because it's never interesting enough to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great narrative RPG with a cool setting that has some Arcanum (steampunk + magic/fantasy) vibes! The Magic is fairly muted so far but there might be more in different parts of the setting. I tried two different runs to see how different things get and was happy to see a pretty big change to the personal stories of the characters for me. _childDocuments_.review: While the invitation for comparison with Disco Elysium is very obvious, playing this game felt like a completely different and experience. _childDocuments_.review: Sovereign Syndicate is an interesting game that for the most part, hits the notes that it is trying to accomplish. It has a nice aesthetic, a good build to the story (if frustrating, more on that later), and interesting characters that have distinct capabilities and motivations. This makes for a solid base that does a lot for the overall gameplay. Still, there are two key issues that I have with the game. Story Progression and Quest GoalsFiguring out the various tasks (i.e. – quests) is rather opaque. With no quest markers and a character that moves somewhat slowly (and ungainly, with the minotaur Atticus), you spend a goodly portion of your time traversing a rather limited map to locate the next prompt that will permit you to proceed. Adding to this is the limited utility of the quest log, which often summarizes the end goal without giving too many clues about where to go. Without spoiling anything, there is one quest in Chapter Four that asks you to seek someone with a more specialized knowledge of a more sordid world, and that results in you wandering around trying to find a character that fits the bill. To wit: •	Most NPCs interact with each of your toons differently, and while you of course should be able to retain some level of knowledge of each one’s stories, without a way to cross-check things, you either need to take a few notes or just enjoy speaking to each NPC across the board. •	In this quest in particular, there is also the issue that speaking to someone with knowledge of the seamier side of London has a resolution with a Black character, which, you know, optics. Finally, since there are no quest markers or clues about whether you can complete a quest in a given chapter, you really have no idea whether you missed something that may only be available at a given time. Compound this with a very limited knowledge of gaining money in the world to buy the few things that will complete said quests means that you may be selling items that the other character would find useful. Instead of being strategic, then, this only leaves me feeling frustrated that I sold items in Chapter 1 that a future toon actively uses as part of their build. NarrativeHere, I have no real complaints, even if it is very esoteric and a bit confusing to tie together the myriad events in the early chapters. If anything, possibly building the tale out a little earlier would be nice, especially since each toon has bits of the meta story within their own arcs, and it would make more sense. However, the intent of having strangers unite and giving each other context may be the ultimate goal. I have only just completed the fourth chapter. Controls, Bugs, and GameplayI have only encountered one bug, but since the game has a very aggressive autosave function, I lost little progress that I had to repeat. In the same vein, with this autosave mechanic, SCUMsaving is very viable and means you can re-roll interaction bits to unlock a new path in the solution. The tarot card system is basically a slightly confusing remapping of a normal CRPG method of using dice. Instead, you randomly flip minor arcana tarot cards in the hopes of adding their numerical value to your innate skill with a certain option. Nothing is really novel about this, and failing a check does not seem to impede your progress to any great degree (such as in BG3, wherein a failed check could completely reroute your story; that does not happen here). Controls are straightforward, but as I mentioned earlier, I really feel like you move too slowly and since you have to run all over the map sometimes to find clues (or blindly figure out what will trigger progress, which happens way too often), I have found myself playing this game in bursts because I get frustrated running slowly back and forth to the train station to locate a clue. OverallI do recommend Sovereign Syndicate even with the issues I noted above. It’s a fun game and the story is shaping up to be interesting. With only one bug in 9 hours of gaming, that also means the game is solid in that regard, and controls are simply point and click. Be prepared to run blindly around the map sometimes since there are no markers, but enjoy the story as it develops and see how each character plays into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: Steampunk cRPG MysteriesAt first glance, Sovereign Syndicate promises so much, and with inspirations from Disco Elysium gameplay, it should be a great game, right? Unfortunately, much of my hopes were left in vain. Yes, it's steampunk, set in a fantasy steampunk version of Victorian England. And that's the best part of the game - it's world.Regarding the cRPG definition, the game is far, far from that genre. Yes, the characters (three in total) have some inventory, and they can even use some of the items in it. In terms of gameplay, the game is... well, a visual novel. Walls of text stand before you (often just to enrich the world, without any significance to the plot), and occasionally you're given choices on how to act, but sadly - none of your choices affect the final outcome.As a story, Sovereign Syndicate starts off well, but with each subsequent chapter, it becomes more and more tedious, relying more on the most banal clichés, and by the end, I was simply clicking the "next" button hoping it would end. The game world is intriguing, only if we could do more in it.Graphically, the lack of resources is evident. Although relatively nicely drawn, the game world is small and empty. The movements of the characters are laughably animated, at a level from 20 years ago.There are almost no sounds in the game (including dialogue voicing), yet it manages to be annoying in the sections with Teddy Redgrave and the robot Otto - with each step, Otto emits clicking sounds that become hard to bear after the fifth minute.I didn't encounter any bugs, at least that's good, I suppose. I wish the game were better, I hope the creators make enough to make a sequel (the only possible ending strongly hints at future development), but for now, I just can't recommend it to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes I have only played 2 Hours of this game so far on Steam. But.. I played about 4 hours of the demo for the game during a previous Steam Fest event. Had alot of fun on the demo and said to myself that I would be picking up the full version when it comes out.It is pretty much a Steampunk version of Disco Elysium. The quality of the dialogue and writing is great and the game world is well thought out. Just the type of game I was itching for atm, having just finished BG3, Cyberpunk Expansion & Starfield. _childDocuments_.review: Only on chapter 4, but from what I've played so far: this game is great. Really great, actually. A solid 8/10 kind of great.I went into it...wary, to say the least. The Disco Elysium comparisons were more of a red flag than a green one, if I'm being honest. Lightning rarely strikes the same place twice, and I was afraid that a game that so clearly takes inspiration from one that's considered a masterpiece of it's genre would end up falling flat in comparison. And I still don't think that concern was entirely unfounded - in my opinion, the weakest parts of Sovereign are the ones that feel the most . Of the three characters, it's Atticus who's the most Harrier-esque, and it's Atticus who I feel the least connected to. I'm still enjoying his chapters but the comparisons feel a bit too easy, and not in a good way. The skill portraits, the way they narrate your thoughts, even just how the dialogue panel  - when you're constantly being reminded of another game, you're going to start to compare. Unfortunately for Sovereign, the comparisons aren't in it's favour.With that being said though, all of the things that make the game unique also happen to be the things it does the best. The idea of tarot cards instead of dice is fantastic. It's visually beautiful. The way the three characters have their stories intersect in subtle ways (ones that you often don't even notice until you move onto the next chapter and, oh! That one random thing I did with Teddy is helping me out with Atticus!) is very fun, and super satisfying in action. While having three protagonists makes it harder to  connect with them, they're still interesting enough that it isn't bothering me to much. If you're able to separate it from the game that clearly inspired it, Sovereign holds up really well on it's own. It's more than worth it's price, especially because I can see some replay value in it as well. If that changes by the end I'll update this review to reflect it, but as of right now: more than worth a look.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe the real Sovereign Syndicate was the friends we made along the way. It is not Disco Elysium and that is fine, this game has enough going on its own. My only complain is that the game is designed in a way that forces you to interact with everything each chapter out of fear of missing an important dialogue or item, from time to time it becomes a slog.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty interesting story. If you are confused when it starts, it really started to pick up for me when I got to about chapter 3 and you start to see how the 3 characters' stories will intertwine. There are choices to be made but it felt more like I was reading a book, which can be a good thing. Characters are compelling, once you get to know them a little bit. Ending was slightly anticlimactic IMO, but i think that is a common thing for mysteries, since your imagination runs wild.I will say I'm not totally sure how much your choices impact the game, as I probably won't replay it. But I still found it RPG-adjacent and quite enjoyable.One thing I really liked about this game was that its 3 protagonists' goals aren't always aligned, so it forces you to really role-play whatever character you are playing at that time, possibly making a choice that conflicts with the goals of one of your other characters. This doesn't happen often, but it really made me think.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start off this review by saying I'm not a huge fan of the genre. Up until now there has been only one exception, which was Disco Elysium, this is now the second exception.Sovereign Syndicate is a fantastic plot driven narrative game with multi branching options depending on your decisions. The different characters you control all feel unique, through their personalities, and have their own differing views on the situation and city and allow you to see it through a new light.The dice rolling system has been entirely overhauled into a "Tarot Card" system which is quite refreshing. Also, levelling up certain passive traits as you play unlocks new unique dialogue options and is quite rewarding.The game is incredibly polished and detailed, especially with a price tag of $25. 10/10 worth the money.I haven't completed my first play through as of writing this review so I do plan on updating it soon, but I foresee playing through this game more than a handful of times to see the different ways I can watch it all play out.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: Was trying to find something similar in writing quality to Disco Elysium - this one is not even remotely similar.DE writing was captivating right from the start - quite deep, ironic, somewhat melancholic and at the same time unusual. The writing of this game, however, is bland for my tastes - there's nothing special about it, it's like I'm reading some average D&D campaign in the steampunk setting.Apart from the writing, the graphic is average and music forgettable - so, again, can't really be compared to DE with its unusual graphic and great music.All in all, if you want to find something similar to DE, this is not it (apart from some superficial similarities like dialogue system, etc). If, on other hand, if you just want find something average to play in the steampunk genre, this might do.
_childDocuments_.name: Sovereign Syndicate

_childDocuments_.review: It's a decent little game, but it's has one glaring issue. When you're making a combatless dialogue-centric game your writing is better be EXCEPTIONAL. And this game's writing isn't. Sovereign Syndicate has characters reciting big ideas out loud, but it's just not how people talk. So it's just a game about some characters in steampunk fantasy London, not a philosphical communist paper that Disco Elysium was. But I respect the this game's ideas: the developers are trying to freshen up the Disco-formula with Tarot cards instead of dice and a different take on skills. And It does have poignant moments. But I wouldn't say its commentary on racism or sexism or sex work is any deep. I don't want to bash this game, because clearly this is a passion project of Disco-fans. I say, buy this game, try it for yourself, maybe it'll work for you better. We need to support indie developers.
