_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love walking simulators and adventure games. Any day, I will choose a game with a fantastic story over anything else. The complex story and moral choices in 1000xResist initially drew my attention, but ultimately, it left me with a walking simulator filled with anime tropes and more questions than answers. This game swiftly teaches you that there are no definitive answers or absolutes. The game begins with a reasonable number of questions, but towards the end, only a few remain. What remained for me was a game I will soon forget.You play a character named Watcher. She is one of the Six Sisters, who are part of some sort of post-apocalyptic society or group. The environment is very sterile and too perfect. It almost feels like a starship or something else. The game thrusts you into an unknown part of this timeline. It is up to you to unravel and follow the linear path that the game leads you on. There are a few instances where you have more control over Watcher, specifically when you explore the “center” and engage in conversations with people. This ends up feeling like a chore because you have to do it multiple times, and only yesterday (as of this writing) did the developers patch in a map. There is almost no gameplay. If you consider zipping around the sky on some flying orbs as gameplay, you shouldn’t expect much more. You will likely navigate through thousands of lines of spoken dialogue. The voice-over is decent, if mundane. Even side characters and NPCs speak in every scene.The pacing is the only thing the game has going for it. While the first few chapters feel repetitive, as you commune with various sisters, you go from location to location, simply walking around in small rooms and engaging in dialogue. This will bore anyone who isn’t an adventure game fan. The story is hard enough to follow, and when you try to make sense of it all, you get more characters to trust you. The game advances when you talk to the correct person. At times, the game presents this as a task, while at others, it becomes more evident.This game defies easy description or explanation. At times, the dialogue and story can be quite poignant, touching on topics such as adolescence and parental conflict and separation. Additionally, the game heavily references the COVID-19 pandemic, with characters donning masks and discussing a disease that could potentially wipe out humanity. Honestly. I can’t even tell you if that’s exactly what the story is about, as it’s so vague all the time. We don’t get any true, hard facts on what’s going on in this world. The “Allmother” named Iris serves as the foundation for these Six Sisters, who have the ability to replicate themselves. It’s just a bunch of confusing threads that don’t really lead anywhere.I had a strong desire to enjoy this game. The narrative exhibits promise, featuring numerous characters on the verge of likability or memorability, yet it succumbs to the anime conventions of guiding you through a perpetually perplexing plot, only to leave you feeling let down at the conclusion. At times, the narrative excels, presenting you with a flurry of answers towards the conclusion. This can be satisfying and memorable, but 1000xResist just refuses to give in. I just wanted the game to end, but it goes on for 10–12 hours even if you read all of the dialog and skip most of the voice lines. The choices don’t really matter until the very end of the game, and even then, you aren’t sure if there were choices earlier that mattered. 1000xResist is hard to recommend, even to anime lovers. The animations, visuals, and everything else are fairly generic, forgettable, and mostly dull. The game’s overuse of bloom and lack of lip-syncing during dialog gives it a cheap, low-budget feel, which is normally acceptable if executed well. The game drags the player along for so long that, in the end, you expect a massive pay-off but end up with a fizzle and sputter. I can’t really recommend this game to anyone outside of die-hard adventure game fans.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATEI loved it!I finally managed to make time to finish this game and, wow, that was a rollercoaster of emotions! The comparison with Evangelion and Nier are definitely warranted, although this plays out more like a deep themes narrative adventure game with no action sequences; which was perfect for me, since I like this type of game and it was exactly what I was looking for.There is a lot going on(in a good way). It is definitely the type of game that requires more than one playthrough to fully understand; a lot of "show, don't tell" and many things are left open to each person's interpretation. A lot of the themes explored revolve around asian identiy (diaspora & immigrant), coming of age, family, and mother/daughter relationships, so if those are themes that are interesting to you, this game is definitely for you.I am not asian myself, but my partner is cantonese CBC and he tagged along with me for parts of my playthrough. It felt really special to him that Iris' parents are cantonese and that cantonese voice acting was present within the game. He also really like the representation of each characters, with a soft spot for Iris' dad who reminded him a bit of his own dad in certain aspects.I honestly don't really have much negatives to say about this game. The Orchard's layout required some getting used to navigate more easily, but it didn't take me that long to get accustomed to it. I would probably say for me the one thing I was a bit disappointing in was that dialog choices actually didn't have any impact except for the ones you make in the ending scene at the very end of the game. The game really immersed me and made me feel like a lot of choices would've had consequences on my playthrough, but that was not the case.But all in all, I highly recommend this game: it's a wild emotional ride that can get pretty dark at time and explores deep themes. If that's something you like, give this one a try.Hekki grace, sistersOLD REVIEWI was looking forward to picking up this game ever since I played the demo a while ago. I'm still not done with the content that was already present in the demo, but the game so far is very atmospheric and intriguing. I'm looking forward to what's next! Will be updating my review after getting further.

_childDocuments_.review: What a game!  I liked the trailer and didn't know what to expect.  Just finished chapter 1, and in that you learn how to move around the game and such.  You're plunged into a story with not much explanation of what's going on, but by the end of the chapter, you get a good sense of who you are and what's to come.I'd describe this as a pretty interactive walking sim, that moves along like a visual novel.  The main draw of this game is its story, and I find it very interesting!  I will definitely play this to the end.The voice acting is very nice, and the actors talk slowly, and with feeling.  You can skip forward since the dialogue appears onscreen, but I really enjoy listening to everyone speaking their lines.A great game experience, and I recommend this to anyone who likes a good story with a casual interface - you can take this at your own pace and there's no stress about doing things.  You can explore - it's pretty open-world in that respect, and you can save your game at any time, much like a visual novel.I'm a sucker for time travel movies, and this is the first time I've played a game where you can play with time and it's very well done!Get this game :)

_childDocuments_.review: Normally, the job of a critic is to explain as much as possible. To use language to share a shard of their experience, their perspective, their tastes, and how the piece interacted with them. You can never know art through a critic, but you can occasionally understand a critic very well through their work, and from there it's just an estimation of taste and competence. But good criticism and good critics must always understand their boundaries. Their limits of not just competency but duty. I can do a great deal with words, I can offer the occasional witty insight and play of phrase. At my best I can produce something almost reminiscent of poetry.But sometimes the job of a critic is to shut up. 1000xRESIST speaks for itself.It does not need me waxing poetics, it does not need a humorous remark or comparative parallel. 1000xRESIST is extremely coherent, extremely clear, and extremely upfront about what it is about, what it means, and above all what it wants to say.I have nothing more I could say about it than it says for itself. To filter it through me does no one any good; you will see more of me than you will of it. It deserves to stand on it's own, it earned that. So I will say this:You should purchase and play 1000xRESIST, it is art. It is a supremely well made, well considered, well acted, and well designed piece of digital fiction.And that is all.

Then, it was little quips like 垃圾桶. Between the sci fi lines is a story that, as someone from that cultural diaspora, instantly struck through. _childDocuments_.review: A pretty cool and well written narrative game1000xResist was a pleasant surprise. Presentation does a lot of work here. Though character models and lighting look weird at times (it definitely looks like an indie game), the game's visual identity is striking. The UI has a distinct sci-fi feel, character's clothes are wonderfully weird when they need to be, and the world is odd, misterious and imaginative.Then, on top of that, the game is completely voiced over, and there's a tooon of dialogue. Some of the lines are a bit stilted, sure, but the sheer volume, coupled with consistent editing and direction, does a lot to get you invested in the narrative.And the story is pretty great! It's not groundbreaking, but it has tight pacing and characterization, some nice mistery, and, as all good sci-fi, a whole lot of social commentary. It does especially well in its first rounds of worldbuilding. The way this society operates and the small things characters say to each other are well thought out and really unique. There's also some time manipulation gameplay that interweaves in cool ways with the narrative, which I found pretty interesting.What complaints I have are rather small. Sometimes the "game" portion stands out a bit too much, with game sections that are a tad too long (I'm not a fan of the "flying around" bits. You'll know them when you see them). Navigating the HUB world is more than a bit confusing, which kind of breaks the narrative flow. More importantly, the story can be too heavy handed at times. It would be hard to "fix" this, but I feel like it could have been somewhat less explicit in a few of its ideas and still come across clearly, while avoiding some repetition which does become rote later on. Finally, the last act (from chapter 7 onwards) feels way weaker than what came before, as does the worldbuilding from that point on. The ending is satisfying, though, so I'm giving that a pass.Overall, a great 8-10 hours for people who enjoy narrative games, sci-fi, and want something more than a little bit out there in the story department.

_childDocuments_.review: 1000xRESIST is a solid 8/10 in just about every area; in some areas it excels, like the quality of voice acting (which is easily on par with Disco Elysium) and its soundtrack (perhaps just shy of NieR:Automata's); though in others it's weaker, like the visual style - while the stylised look is striking and, honestly, really pretty, the animations can sometimes feel a little clunky, and the edges a little too soft (particularly on the faces). But overall, most everything about the game sits somewhere between "good" and "great".To start with the good, as I've already mentioned, the auditory aspects of the game are almost perfect - the only scene I believe could be bettered would be when you are prompted to listen to the rain, only for the music to persist rather than fading out. The voice acting is phenomenal, with fantastic nuance to the delivery, and distinct voices for each character; which helps with the writing itself sometimes making characters sound too similar (though perhaps that's intentional, considering).The visual style as well is striking; the colours themselves are beautiful, and many of the levels carry the same love of detail as NieR:Automata (a game 1xR draws clear and significant inspiration from), though the step-down in terms of budget is apparent when the two are compared side-by-side. Where 1xR truly excels in regard to its visuals, however, is the way in which the game uses perspective and medium interchangeably - similar as well to NeiR:Automata, but this time used in less of a "game" way, and more in an "art" way; in terms of individual scenes, 1xR has a number of moments where its use of striking colours and light create some earnestly stunning visual effects.This is where I think 1xR is at its strongest - as a piece of art. A conversation. It carries themes of the Covid-19 pandemic, Sinophobia, generational trauma and abuse, isolation, the Hong Kong protests (and authoritarianism in general), and more still. The sheer number of things the game urges you to think about can be overwhelming by the time the game reaches its conclusion, and all throughout it doesn't feel as though you're given a chance to properly dwell on these themes, or feel them out within the game itself - I can't tell if this choice, to provide a glance at many different aspects of the world the game exists in as opposed to a focused dissection of one or two concepts, is good or not. If nothing else, I feel as though I need to think about it more; and good art makes you think.The game is somewhat weaker in the more... "game" elements, however. To rattle off a few of my biggest frustrations;• The Save/Load system is somewhat buggy. Sometimes loading a file causes characters to disappear if they're scripted to leave after being spoken to (even if you hadn't actually spoken to them on that save yet), and saving during scenes or conversations will load you back to when those scenes or conversations started - which is particularly frustrating during the longer segments of the game.• The "Zip" mechanic feels clunky throughout the game - it's not a big deal as it doesn't come up too often, but it does make the segments where it's implemented feel more frustrating than perhaps they should.• A lack of map for when the player is in the Orchard, alongside a convoluted series of paths and doorways and a waypoint system that poorly represents distance, makes the parts of the game that take place in the Orchard feel like they drag on - going out of your way to speak with every NPC is worth it, but still feels like it could have been streamlined somewhat.• A few smaller things; animations feeling "off", "cluttered" level design that gets in the way just a little too much; subtitles that don't quite match what's being said; a notable lack of actual mechanics. They wouldn't be much on their own, but start to add up little by little, and leave the game feeling "not quite perfect".I think my biggest hangup with 1xR lies in the ending; or, specifically, the endings for the characters. Over a relatively short span of time you meet and talk with so many people, and while they change at points, it doesn't necessarily feel like they... grow. Some simply have key moments that alter them, but they go from being "A" to "G" with no... B, C, D, E, F, and many do not receive even that. There are exceptions; the character you play, Watcher, develops the most of all the cast by far - but it feels more like the rest of the characters simply have more of their facets revealed, rather than seeing them genuinely develop. It feels as though they're all about to grow a great deal, but only after the game concludes - again, art inspiring art, but... Perhaps the most egregious example of this, though not spoiler friendly, is Overall, if 1xR seems like a game you'd enjoy or be interested in, I can say it almost 100% WILL be interesting, and will have specific moments that surpass expectation; but I can't help but feel that it needed just a little more room to explore the themes it wanted to show us.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a true masterpiece. One of the best stories I've ever experienced in a game. One of the most unique and intriguing stories I've ever experienced, and it had me on the edge of my seat from beginning to end. It's the type of story that when you start it, you have no clue what's going on. My literal thoughts during the first scene of the game were "I wonder if any of this means anything or if they're just putting a bunch of random poetic nonsense to make it seem thought provoking". And the main pleasure of this game for me was slowly over time piecing together what's going on and becoming knowledgeable about how this world operates. It's a very unique game, and I say that as a MASSIVE compliment, because in my entire life I've played only a handful of games that had worldbuilding this genuinely unique.I can't recommend this game to everyone. If you play games solely for their gameplay, you're not going to find what you're looking for at literally any point in this games' runtime. But if you enjoy storytelling that invites you to take mental notes and really pay attention to uncover the mystery in front of you, this game is a DEFINITE purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Good stuff. Amazing narrative. Sci-Fi Visual novel (Involves walking around choosing who/who not to interact with and some light platforming. There are no action sequences or puzzles - maybe some riddles)Fully voice acted which makes some of the emotional moments hit hard even if nothing is being shown onscreen.I am finding it kinda hard to express anything about the actual story here at the moment.You'll notice most other reviews of the game follow the same tune. Basically telling you nothing about the actual meat of the game. And after playing the game I understand why it is that way as I can't pick what to write here without feeling like I'm spoiling something or being too vague.If you're intrigued by the trailer and into VNs, I hightly recommend.I'm not a huge sci-fi fan but this trailer and the buzz about this game online still made me try it out and I'm glad I did. My last session of this game started at 9PM and went all the way to 7AM the next day as I was just glued to the screen and wide awake wanting to know what happens next...Even if you're not into VNs, I'd still recommend if you like sci-fi/dystopian genre as it is only 15 hours at max.If you DO pick it up my tip is to try to talk to everyone you can find before beelining objectives(Later on the game even gives you a compass type feature to find all the NPCs that have dialogue). It is a visual novel after all. Every line has something for you. And I think this game does an amazing job with it.Red to Blue.

_childDocuments_.review: 1000xRESIST is a vast game. Not in length, or size, but in how many ideas it contains. It's a rabbit hole that just keeps going. I loved my time with it, and I'm grateful it exists - it's one of those games that pries at the fault line between games and art. We don't get many of these. I'll be thinking about it for a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely gorgeous I can't even.It's incredible a story manages to create so many layers and touch upon so many themes and feelings from nostalgia, parenthood, generational trauma, political protest, death, personal ethics, etc. without feeling tacky and/or pretentious. It's a landmark of game storytelling and you need to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: This ain't really a game.I don't mean that as an insult by any means, I thoroughly enjoyed the story.I'm not even a story kinda guy, I usually am into games with unique mechanics, this game doesn't really scatch that itch.But I sat through the entire story in one 13 hour playthrough.I really enjoyed talking to the NPCs, a rarity in games for me.The world is fascinating and seeing that change and develop as you progress further and further into the story is rather rewarding, even if a lot of the character models feel like they're holding the game's visuals back.My biggest complaint is navigating the main "Hub" area is a nightmare.I'll admit I'm terrible with directions in games and get lost pretty easily but I felt like I was constantly going in loops.The navigation system they gave you isn't very reliable or useful either.I definitely recommend the game, though perhaps not at base price.It has flaws that will likely prevent some from enjoying it, but if you can power through the small faults, the story is well worth it.The music was great too!It wasn't on par with something like NieR's soundtrack, but it was pleasant the entire 13 hours I played so that should mean something!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is weird in both good ways and bad ways and it's a lot to take in. It's practically duality personified. In a lot of senses it's made its own genre of a 3D visual novel where it's not quite a walking simulator but also not quite a narrative game that sometimes has puzzles ala life is strange. It's just narrative only and in 3D with occasional reminders that it's a game that's not into cut scenes. The story itself is awful and a slog to endure but is also really well told, presented, voiced, and expressed. It's seriously on the level with old school final fantasy games in terms of scope. The overall look and aesthetic is a violent insult to the eyes but at the same time has instances of coolness and charm. That being said it's not worth it's time, even if you got it for free. It's hard to say this because the voice acting is great and there are really memorable characters but by the 5th or 6th chapter you'll be begging for the credits to roll and you aren't even halfway there.

_childDocuments_.review: 1000xRESIST has an intricate story with lots of layers, and does a good job blending Sci-Fi with reality. There are lots of relatable themes, the characters have weight and depth to them, and it really makes you think about everything that is going on and what is going to happen next. The writing and visuals are superb. There's some great dialogue that appears throughout the game and I did not realize its importance until it would come up again and again. Playing through different timelines keeps things fresh and also helps push any revelations towards the later part of the game. I also appreciate the ending where This game reminded me a lot of Nier. While I honestly did not like Nier, after completing this game it further solidifies my opinion that this game is much, much better. To all my Sisters: Red to Blue, Six to One, Sphere to Square, Hair to hair. Hekki Allmo.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite my playtime, I have finished the entire game.I'm normally an FPS gamer that doesn't care for story games but this game is easily in my top 5 favorites. Talking to every NPC and slowly having the story and world revealed was really interesting. Filling in the gaps in my own mind and then being blown away when more is revealed later in the game. Definitely a game I will need to replay to pick up on all the subtle hints through out the story.Despite some people not enjoying the visuals, I found them to be one of the games strong points. Some stuff may feel out of place but makes sense once you know the full picture.The music as well is amazing. It made many scenes in the game feel so much more emotional. _childDocuments_.review: 1000xRESIST first appeared on my radar after hearing the studio were influenced by NieR, Satoshi Kon and Wong Kar Wai, which are all touchstones that are very much up my street. The resulting game has blown me away. It's an incredible journey ushering the player across timelines, perspectives and outcomes. It's rare to see a debut game with such narrative ambition and clarity of vision. sunset visitor 斜陽過客 clearly knew the story they wanted to tell, and were laser-focused on achieving it. If you are at all interested in narrative-heavy or story-driven experiences - or are just generally an open-minded gamer - then I urge you to try this game. As long as you know this is a linear, narrative experience and set your gameplay expectations accordingly, I think you'll really like it. Maybe as much as I do!

_childDocuments_.review: First off, don't let the promotional materials mislead you. Despite what the Nier-esque setting and the person being stabbed through the chest in the trailer, there is no combat in this game whatsoever. This is a walking sim. That said, it is the meatiest and most aesthetic walking sim you will ever play. It is the only walking sim that deserves to cost anything close to the 20 dollar price point.The 13 hours you see on my play time are what it took me to get every achievement, which includes seeing every ending. Being a walking sim, there's no actual skill involved in the game, not even the achievements. But you're liable to have some trouble with the "talk to everyone in X chapter" achievements at first, particularly due to the confusing layout of what's effectively the hub.If you want a 10-hour narrative experience using both the "alien entity triggers a cataclysmic disease around the world" elements of Nier Replicant and the existential sci-fi elements of Nier Automata, this is the oddly-specific game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: A truly wonderful story that explores themes of resistance, reconciliation, and the various aspects of self, to name a few. The visuals and framing of scenes are extremely evocative. The Communion scenes especially are playgrounds of symbolism and have a tantalizingly abstract bent. Both music and VO were excellent with only handful of lines that I thought were rough. Took about 15~ hours to beat and was seriously impressed with the storylines cohesion and quality often Sci-Fi/Mystery games lose the plot chasing complexity or channeling "Lost", but 1000x sticks the landing. Thanks was a blast.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent narrative experience with striking art direction and fantastic music. Even though it is primarily a story-based experience, it uses the game medium in some novel ways with effective cinematography and perspective shifts. It's hard to provide a succinct summary of the game here, as it has a huge scope and covers myriad topics over its runtime. At a broad level, I think the more personal stories of the immigrant experience, revolution, and diaspora politics are an effective complement and grounding force for the headier sci-fi philosophical narrative and world-building. The seemingly obtuse, cryptic phrases repeated throughout the game took on a greater meaning by the end - like a secret code so that the story could survive the endless march of time and the manipulations of those who write history.I definitely can't do justice to such a raw and personal story with my review, so I recommend folks play it themselves. Props to the development team for creating such a compelling and truly special experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly its hard to describe how good the narrative to this game is.It plays similarly to a Visual Novel except you are exploring the areas in 3d, the main game play mechanic being the choices you make and questions you ask. Depending on your level of investment there are a multitude of feelings you can take away from this game but it honestly is one of the best sci-fi stories I've experienced in a long time, the exploration of its recursive themes making it very clear what its doing while its prose pulls you along. The look of the game may not look great on the surface but the imagery it uses puts it in the stratosphere.There are so many things I want to say but honestly if the description has you interested then thats all you need, give the game a chance. There are no easy answers, just the you and the you that remains.

_childDocuments_.review: In 2047, a race of aliens called “the Occupants” arrives on Earth. A deadly virus brought by them almost completely wipes out humanity in less than a year. The only person unaffected is Iris, a teenage girl who remains immune to the virus for unknown reasons. When all efforts to communicate with the Occupants fail, the last survivors recruit Iris to experiment on her. Their attempts remain fruitless and the remaining survivors die before they reach their goal. Overwhelmed by her loneliness, Iris perfects the cloning procedure and eventually manages to create five identical clones of her to keep her company.Fast-forward several centuries later to the starting point of the game, the player finds themselves in a bunker filled with Iris’ clones, who multiplied over the years and eventually evolved into a new society. They call each other “sisters” and worship Iris as the “Allmother”, the one who birthed each one of them, the only one who is not only immune to the virus but now also immortal. Six sisters were chosen to have special roles that keep this society together: President - administers and oversees the bunker, Fixer - mechanically fixes broken things, Bang Bang Fire - responsible for military defense against the Occupants, Healer - in charge of cloning, Knower - keeper of historical records and ancient knowledge. You play as the Watcher - the last of the chosen sisters, whose task is to observe the world around her and to commune through feelings with others.The game hooks you right from the first moments with a shocking opening cinematic: we see Watcher stabbing Iris, full of anger for the one who has been her goddess and role model all along. The first part of the game will take you through all the events that lead to this scene, built upon the above synopsis. A floating AI device that follows Watcher wherever she goes also allows Watcher to perform “Communions” with Iris, re-living Iris’ memories. Through these communions, Watcher comes to some surprising revelations about Iris’ true nature and where her immunity and immortality come from. As for what happens in the second part of the game, that’s for you to discover, to avoid any further spoilers. is a game that is hard to fit in any box. It plays like a walking simulator, but the environments are not really created to be explored and despite them being visually appealing, their purpose isn’t to divert the player’s focus from the story, but to support the immersion. Due to the amount of dialogue and the choices you can make during conversations, it also plays as a 3D visual novel. In some ways, it can also be seen as a narrative-driven linear adventure game stripped of any puzzles. Only one type of minigame exists, in which Watcher teleports from node to node (similar to using an invisible zip line) until she reaches a specific location that triggers a memory. This minigame occurs several times throughout the game but only one instance is timed, and it has a very generous timer. If I were to describe the game in a nutshell, I’d say that  is a walk-n-talk adventure with light puzzling, perhaps similar to Telltale games or Life is Strange.The actual strength of the game lies in its unique and innovative storytelling which is bound to blow your mind even from the first few minutes of gameplay. Because of how complex the narrative is, it’s difficult to express it in words. Essentially, the game makes use of all sorts of creative techniques to transform its audience into a Watcher, enabling them to employ mental associations or empathy to understand the story in depth. Playing  is similar to the feeling you have when you look at a piece of art. You can't understand a painting from a logical point of view. You can debate and analyze it logically but you “consume” it, you “take it in” by absorbing it as a whole. And this is exactly where the mastery of ’s storytelling resides. By mixing reality and surrealism, the game gives the player information bits like puzzle pieces. Some things are clearly explained, others are left to the interpretation of the viewer or merely hinted at. Until the very end, you will feel confused about some parts, but deeply fascinated and intrigued at the same time about the whole experience. The title itself gives you the first enigma to solve: with “RESIST” being an anagram of “SISTER”, the title directly points at the clones' society and perhaps also at the time that elapsed since the cataclysm (1000 years).The game also likes to throw at you statements that you won’t initially understand, but which you will learn to interpret or comprehend later in the game based on the game’s world and lore. The most straightforward example of that is the dialogue options that Watcher has in the intro cutscene. Replying to Allmother before stabbing her is a choice between three cryptic options: “red to blue”, “six to one”, or “hair to hair“, the meaning of at least one (if not two) being somewhat deductible from the synopsis - in any case, all being later explained.While the narration is linear (there are no branches), exploring the memory fragments isn’t. Just like in reality, when a memory can trigger another memory, Watcher will scramble through Iris’ memories back and forth, despite them being unlocked in a sequential (ordered) way, one at a time. Navigating the memories also allows in some specific circumstances location navigation (to get past a locked door, you go back one memory, move your character to the target location and then go forward to the desired memory). Like in a Tarantino movie, the memories are not visited in chronological order; they’re scattered over time and space. The game also heavily uses deja vus in two very creative manners. In some dialogue with cryptic choices, these options are actually fragments of what other characters said earlier in the game. Reading them is already enough to trigger a deja vu in the player, who will then try to connect that event to the current dialogue and direct the conversation accordingly. The second one presens scenes already shown to the player, but modified and extended with insights that reflect the realizations that specific characters reached.At deeper layers, the story also has strong cultural and historical references. The Hong Kong Umbrella Movement is a big part of the plot, although not necessarily explicitly stated. Iris’s parents met during one of the protests, several character storylines are suggestive of China’s oppression and express the need to be individualized, to define themselves, while others wear an umbrella. Even the title could hint at the Hong Kong RESISTance. is like a diamond with many facets, it’s a deep philosophical masterpiece that reveals something new, a different perspective every time you turn it towards the light. The game is fully voiced in English, the soundtrack is top-notch and the camerawork is also spot-on. For me,  was a one-of-a-kind experience blending all these together, with a storyline that immersed me so deeply that I couldn’t stop thinking about it even in between my gameplay sessions spread over several days. Even after finishing it and its multiple endings, I had to revisit some bits which allowed me to reach some new realizations. The story is so packed with symbolism that it’s impossible to grasp everything in a single playthrough. All-in-all,  is in all aspects a brilliant game.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a game and it is profound.1000xResist really is an incredible experience and unlike anything I've played.Don't expect combat, or skill trees, or farming or any real mechanic other than moving, selecting dialogue choices, and the occasional time jump.And with that said I do recommend that anyone interested in a unique storytelling experience, this is a must play. I've thought about this game every night now for the past month as I've slowly made my way through it as there is so much emotional depth for multiple characters that by the end you really have to come reckoning with your feelings on them. And as you begin to understand the places and people, the plot stabs you like a Watcher, embracing her AllMother. The many twists, turns and circling back around, it is astounding how they did so much with so little. It is impressive even for an indie title to have so many smart decisions all around by a small team with clearly a limited budget. Each choice from the voice work, to the cinematography, to the scene cuts has such weight and purpose to them. It left me gasping and sighing and teary eyed throughout.I can't say this enough. PLAY THIS GAME.Really looking forward to seeing what is next from this developer. An all timer Story, and world. I won't be forgetting this experience that is for sure.Hekki Grace

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is an interesting game and I'd like to see more from the people behind it, but I think my overall experience tends towards the slightly negative, so I'll begin by summarizing the things I think might have hurt my enjoyment of this game, trying to be spoiler-free: -Playing for extended periods of time made me nauseous for some reason, I figure it might have been the chromatic aberration shader that's on at pretty much all times. This is obviously not something that'll happen to most people, I have experienced this in other games very rarely;-All the running around is unbearable. The main map is huge and mazelike, including some frustrating loops and dead ends. This is the only aspect of the game I've truly hated, especially because I was interested in interacting with every npc I could. By the end of the game I was nearly pulling my hairs out (hehe);-I thought the pacing wasn't great at times, especially in the later half of the game where it felt like it was crawling towards the conclusion;-Lots of reviews on steam seem to be VERY excited about this game being a miraculously perfect life-changing experience, this has obviously colored my expectations, which weren't exactly met. Keep in mind that I do play a lot of plot driven games and read my share of VNs, so that has also helped paint my perspective;-While most main characters were at least somewhat interesting, I didn't find most of them to be very likeable, I ended up not being that invested in any of them; -[MINOR SPOILERS] Not exactly a problem with the game, but I kinda wish the narrative went a bit more in depth in its representation of some real life events, as I think there could be interesting parallels to the main plot (dangers of voluntarism, hijacking of a popular protest). The romantic perspective does feel character-appropriate, though. Now I'll list some things I though were cool, well done and neat:-The setting and aesthetics are very nice. I really enjoyed the mythological aspects of the world and the associated mannerisms didn't feel forced;-I've enjoyed the voice acting, a lot of it is a bit alien and distant which imo helped set the atmosphere. I think this could have something to do with me being unable to connect with most characters, but that's more of a direction thing; -Zipping around was fun, it's a minor gameplay thing but it felt refreshing between the dialogues and the long, long walks;-[VERY MINOR SPOILERS] I thought the last chapter/ending was well done, ASIDE from the forced walking section.Overall I find this a hard game to recommend, but I'd encourage anyone interested to give it a shot. The plot was very unusual and fun, and I even got a bit emotional at times. Do keep in mind that you'll do a loooot of walking around, though.

_childDocuments_.review: What a fantastic story; I didn't expect to get as pulled in or as engaged as I did, but I did.  I want to give this a more thorough review for my friends on why I love this but for now I'm tired and I just want to add onto the Overwhelmingly Positive amount of reviews.---After collecting my thoughts:  You know how some movies or games *feel* like they could have only have been made by the exact crew+director involved with that specific game and no one else?I feel like Sunset Visitor managed to tell a uniquely personal story that only they could have told with 1000xResist.  It touches on so many different topics all at once and manages to weave them together so effortlessly, it's just plain impressive how they all hit the right emotional beats all while spanning the breadth of topics that it does.And this is going to be a bit meta and less specifically about the game and more its context, but in an age where white people seem to lash out at the mere existence of any black or other poc on screen, raging against DEI hire this or that, all while triple A game companies just undergo constant merger after merger only to be followed by layoff after layoff all for the quarterly profits and unsustainable levels of high definition realism graphics for games that don't even feel that fun to play:  1000xresist is just unapologetically a byproduct of a displaced Hong Kong people, be they 1st or 2nd generation, native born or fobs, all of this with the backdrop of an epidemic that people are blaming *you* for...It was just the breathe of fresh air that I didn't know that I needed and I'm eagerly waiting for their next title.  Thank you Sunset Visitor.Fun fact for those who finished the game and are just browsing the reviews to see what other people thought and are saying:  Did you know Jiao's VA is also a singer and is on spotify by the name of Sad China?  Well now you know.

_childDocuments_.review: 1000xRESIST is one of the most impressive displays of storytelling that I've ever seen in video games. You have so many heavy topics touched upon in so many interesting ways. It's also not just how they're touched upon and incorporated, but also how the game reveals these beats to you. Perspectives warp, tonality changes, total camera and means of movement change, emotional shifts (which you also *will* experience, not just the characters). Every question raised may have an answer, but at the cost of creating more questions.To me, this is a work of art that takes the basis and creative format of a game and transcends conventional means of story-telling, giving you a narrative experience that absolutely could not be told in any other kind of medium. I'm only scratching the surface here, intentionally, because left to my own devices I'd write a literal essay about how utterly incredible this game is, and also because I need you to trust me. If there is anything I could ever ask of you, I need you to trust me and go in blind. I promise you that you will not regret it.This is one of those very few games that made me genuinely think "I'm glad everything worked out in such a way, that I was able to be alive and able to experience this in my lifetime"

_childDocuments_.review: Here's a sort of "first impressions" review. I've only played about 3 hours of it so far.I'd seen someone recommend this game on Twitter, saying it's similar to 13 Sentinels: Aegis Rim, which is literally my favorite game of all time. I can see where that idea comes from, but I wouldn't have drawn that comparison if I'd started playing the game without someone mentioning that.But that doesn't mean it's a  game by any means. It's... interesting so far, and, again, not in a bad way. I wish I'd gone in without having read the Steam description, though, because I feel like it gives away too much. Regardless, I'm interested enough to keep playing, I think.The voice acting is surprisingly good for an indie game, too. Every single line so far has been voice acted. It also doesn't sound like the devs just recorded the voices themselves and instead hired actual actors.The graphics are decent, too. They're not , but you can tell the devs are doing the best they can with the tools they have. Many story scenes are artistically framed and not just "camera over this person's shoulder, now over this person's shoulder, now over...", you get the idea. There's intent there, which I appreciate.The story is... I'm not sure yet. It's interesting to follow. I can't go into too much detail without spoiling, obviously, but I'm interested to see where it's going.My only two major gripes about this game so far: There doesn't seem to be a fast-travel function you can use during the game's "free time" (the times between main story bits), and there doesn't seem to be a map. There's a compass-like HUD to find objects and NPCs you can interact with, but there's no map that shows where they are . Though I guess that  make sense. Some of the Steam achievements I got were for finding certain rooms.Overall, I'm interested enough to keep playing. Guess we'll see how the game pans out.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've ever played. I finished it a couple days ago and still go back to watch and listen to the trailer over and over again. I'm not yet ready to let go (oh, the irony...), but this game showed me that everyone feels this way about the things that connect with us deeply. Before playing, I saw other reviews saying that this game beckons a conversation that many survivors may be not ready to have. That it's a lot. That it's about intergenerational trauma, the 2019-2020 Hong Kong protests, COVID (and the anti-Asian racism that accompanied it), British and Chinese colonialism. Most of all: That it is not a game for the white gaze. And immediately, I was awestruck: I need to play this. Then I found out it's by an indie studio local to me in metro Vancouver, which has a strong HK and Taiwanese diaspora. Something I always needed to learn more about as an immigrant myself. Ashamed that I was surviving my own trauma as the protests began in HK, I decided to do my homework before picking up the game. I watched several documentaries about the protests, moved immensely but also reminded of my own trauma as an activist. So as I play 1000xRESIST, the imagery of 'civil unrest' (a paltry term for something so huge and so long-lived in our bodies for generations upon generations, as this game begs to tell us) is especially raw. More raw, still, is how it depicts intergenerational trauma. My mother said the same things Iris' mother did. My boyfriend has heard the things Iris has said, that Jiao experienced. sunset visitor 斜陽過客 does NOT pull punches, and the bloody fearlessness that's not afraid to be ugly at times reminds me a lot of Cathy Park Hong's Minor Feelings. Similarly, the language this game writes with is lofty and had me sometimes looking to a dictionary, but I wouldn't have it any other way. I sometimes wonder if, given the locality of the studio to me, that I had been at protests with some of them. That we know colleagues in common. The writing reminds me of fellow grad students I marched alongside. This game, as such, is practically a thesis. Perhaps more, frankly: A dissertation. On what stays and what goes, on infighting both within ourselves and the social movements we pledge ourselves to, on how to move forward after the unconscionable, on forgiveness (or our inability to offer it).Apart from the game's philosophy, the gameplay is quite accessible and creatively done; I only had a single bug and honestly it was on me lol. I enjoy "zipping" around, communions, and finding new unexpected holes in the Orchard (each of which become story-relevant at appropriate times--so definitely take your Orchard exploration seriously!). The visuals are BEYOND striking. It tastefully pricks your megalophobia and offers up the most awe-inspiring yet horrific visuals. Always in the coolest possible way, no less. This is a game I wish everyone in metro Vancouver would play. I wish everyone ever would play it, too. But I'll start with our city, sunset visitor 斜陽過客. :) Thank you for baring your soul and trusting us with the not-so-pretty parts. I'll never forget this game for my entire life.

_childDocuments_.review: What sold me on giving this a try was some of the inspirations listed on the Steam page: Nier, Perfect Blue and Einstein on the beach are some really interesting stories, and I was intrigued by the premise as described on the Steam page.  "000xRESIST tells a story in ways only a game can while simultaneously bringing fresh ideas to interactive storytelling from theatre, dance, performance art, and cinema." Another influence that came to mind while playing was the world of the 3 body problem novels, which I think has some interesting parallels with the Occupants.  The best complement I can give is that this game made me think a lot.  Nature vs nurture and the kind of world that would exist if everyone was a clone of the same person.  About my understanding of the Hong Kong Protests and the experiences of both the people who fought and on future generations of those who had to flee.  About Protesting and governance in general, and about how the oppressed can/should fight back, while simultaneously telling a sci fi story that kept my attention and made me second guess every step.  The characters were all fascinating, while being believable fully fleshed people who could have come from this sort of world.  I deeply enjoyed the game and easily recommend it if any of that sounds interesting to you and if you like artsy kinds of games that are trying to say something.  The gameplay itself is mostly light puzzles/visual novel like gameplay, but the story and world building more than make it worthwhile and this will be sticking in my head for a long time to come.

_childDocuments_.review: You know that thing where every video game opens with a disclaimer saying “This game is a work of fiction, any characters or events similar to the real world is purely coincidental”? Well 1000x Resist isn’t that game, this is a game that is about generational trauma, authoritarianism, identity, and more specifically the COVID 19 pandemic and 2020 Hong Kong riots all told through the lens of a Nier Automata high concept sci-fi framework. You play as Watcher, one of 5 different colour coded clone sisters who along with her sisters all serve a “function” and hers is to observe her peers. The game opens in media as res with a cutscene where Watcher stabs and kills Allmother, her god and leader who also happen to be her mother, the original. What follows is a seemingly linear but very fragmented sci-fi story that serves to piece together who the Allmother is, who Watcher is, and what the deal is with all the clones, the world having been destroyed and all humans being killed by strange aliens called Occupants who are seemingly non aggressive and there is an ongoing war between the clone sisters and these Occupants to retake the surface (so far so very Nier),What sets it apart is how it also delves into the very real immigrant experience of feeling like you’re a stranger in both your old and new home, of the scars that is imparted on those who escaped oppression and how sometimes those scars gets passed down to the next generation. In spite of its premise feeling particularly 90s sci-fi anime  (Hello Evangelion) with the way a teenage high school girl is handed the keys to humanity’s survival, it does rise above those preconceptions. Iris (the Allmother, high school girl and central figure if the story) is a very multilayered character whose teenage angst feels more real and grounded in its circumstance than the average anime. If stories in vein of Yoko Taro’s games that deal with the nature of conflict, and why video games are always so fixated on violence interests you then 1000x Resist is gonna feel right at home. Although there is no actual combat  to be found in this game there is, however, plenty of ideological conflicts and violence communicated through its several identical yet distinctively different clone sisters that make up the game’s cast all brought to life by an excellent cast with eerie voice performances that feels like they were straight out of Mullholland Drive. It lends itself really well to the use of Dream sequences in the game’s storytelling, and the many sci-fi concepts the game introduces which I’m not gonna delve too much into.While there isn’t much gameplay there is the occasional platforming, and third person action adventure exploration ala Nier. The real meat is the music, art and excellent written dialogue that never gets boring, the characters whom you think are in your corner will do and say things where you can never be sure where the story will go next but always curious to keep playing and find out.1000x Resist is a game much like Disco Elysium that excells beyond most games in its writing, presentation and voice acting while not having much involving gameplay everything that is there makes for a perfect package that is worth experiencing and going through again to see how the story comes together from a new perspective. It’s a reminder that as much as this Industry wants to assure us that video games are a commodity, it’s also a medium that serves for artist to express themselves. And 1000x Resist has a lot to say if you would just hear it out.
_childDocuments_.name: 1000xRESIST

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a fantastic, moving narrative experience that will live in my mind forever, but it is a package deal with some frustrating travel and a mediocre ending. The themes include being an immigrant and trying to assimilate, revolution and violence, protests and the injustice inherent in hierarchical power structures, familial relationships, repetition of human behavior across generations, the pain of loss, cosmic futility, self determination, forgiveness, revenge, and love. I absolutely do recommend it but you should know that it isn't a perfect experience. This is truly a visual novel / walking simulator as game elements only include a frustrating hunt for all the interactable objects and people, one timed course you have to move through, and one meaningful choice. I lied, there is also a time shifting mechanic which serves to make the story reveal non-linear, but that can also be done in other mediums and isn't uniquely gameplay. Frankly, the game would have been better without any of that and released as a show or movie. Here is what I mean: in order to piece together the story, you need to talk to people and find interactable objects. At first it feels investigative, but quickly this begins to feel like a chore. When the main character is 'sprinting' they commit to a certain distance in a fixed direction which often left me running sprinting drills in a hallway, unable to turn until I fully stopped moving. There is a map of the Orchard (the main play area) and a compass that you can use, sometimes. The map does not show objectives, only locations, and the compass shows a little overlay with interactable people and elements but doesn't provide a route to reach them. Unfortunately, the Orchard is a great example of poor level design. Everything looks same-y, the map isn't intuitive, and it is filled with dead ends and little crannies. This was a choice the developers made to make it feel like you are finding secrets, there are even achievements for finding several of the useless and never explained rooms and structures. Functionally all this does is keep players confused and annoyed; I cannot count how many times I tried to reach an object marked by the compass only to find a stairway or ramp going nowhere, a wall, or some other obstacle. From the beginning to the end, I never had an intuitive understanding of where specific landmarks and locations were. Moving doesn't feel good either. Regular speed is slow, and sprinting is clumsy. There is, unfortunately, a TON of walking around to do and it never feels easy or good. The only thing that moving and poor navigation serve to do is force the player to miss out on bits of information or interactions. You have such a great story to tell, why do this? There is another type of moving where you travel between fixed nodes in space. This too isn't really anything special. Visually it is interesting, but it doesn't add much else to the experience. There is a timed course you need to traverse on foot and through nodes, but it is sprung on you as a surprise and doesn't mean anything for the story. There aren't obstacles to traverse or even that many dead ends; it just serves to slightly build tension and give the feeling of a climax.The ending was also a problem for me. The rest of this will be spoiler-y, but shouldn't ruin the substance of the game or the story. It will talk about an event at the end of the game without explaining what is happening in the narrative.  The ending was by far my biggest complaint, but it doesn't RUIN the experience as other video game endings do... it just isn't good or satisfying. I would have gone into even more specifics, but I really don't want to ruin the game for others and, again, I do believe it is worth playing.Everything else is great. At the end of the day, I wish it had been a story rather than a game. A novel or show rather than an interactive experience. I don't feel as though the game elements added anything to the story and that the choice at the end actively detracts from it's ability to draw a conclusion of the various themes that were explored.

_childDocuments_.review: I just wanted to post my Reddit review here, so that y'all see it: Hello u/sunsetvisitor ,I just want to say that I finished your whole game in a whirlwind three days or so, and it has one of the best narratives I have played all year. As far as I can tell, y'all poured your soul - literally - into this game, all for us to see. There's things you do in there that I almost cannot believe you had the metaphorical stones to attempt, and that disturbed and entranced me. I also inadvertently learned a ton about the emotional trauma wrought by the 2014 Hong Kong protests. o__o; And also Chinese parents. XD (Yet it appears to be a thing that is vastly, vastly more than any stereotype, filled with as much love as griping.)The game also plays with the video game medium in some mesmerizing (and yes, very NiER Automata!) ways. It uses perspective (both literal and metaphorical) and player agency in ways I rarely if ever see, not to empower the player but to cause the player to embody and inhabit the story. I talked to as many people throughout as I could find, if only because I have a love of society-focused worldbuilding and there is SO much of that here!Anyway, my hat's off to you. This was something truly special. Hekki ALLMO.-Also, the ending managed to call me out on violating my own values and made me change my mind, which was really impressive and thought-provoking. Like, there were so many punches to the gut, and *so much* thought truly invested in the world and characters. This was a work of art that abjectly *refused* to classify itself as pure escapism, that demanded that its players actually think and perceive and reason with its themes. You can't imagine what a delicacy that is, how *rare* it is, in this day and age.

_childDocuments_.review: I am left with complicated feelings. Emotions that I wasn't expecting to simmer so deeply after experiencing a world I am at once desperate to leave yet also stay.1000xRESIST is a beautiful game that is heavily rooted more in visual novel-style presentation with a cinematic twist. There are some puzzles involving timeline jumping in its "communion" segments, but most of the puzzles are relatively gentle. The game lifts aesthetic ideas from the likes of the NieR franchise, but the story it's trying to tell is much more rooted in parallels to our reality- the presence of a deadly virus that will kill anyone who's not properly equipped or otherwise immune (or immunized), the stress of being an immigrant in a country that seems all too ready to chew you alive, the trauma borne of familial relationships and responsibilities- all wrapped up in time-bending, reality-shifting, revolutionary sci-fi burrito. And that's not even to say the most of it.All dialogue in the game is fully voiced, but I did not fall in love with it for the first hour or two. There is an awkwardness in the delivery that feels very reminiscent of some older PS2-era classics, and while I do feel like some moments could have landed better or hit harder with a more robust delivery, I eventually became accustomed to the flow, sensing it was part of the atmosphere the game was trying to achieve.Aside from some glitchy camera and character movement here and there, and a welcome but slightly out of place  challenge near the end, the overall experience was fantastic. If nothing else I felt the story was solid from beginning to end, with just enough flexibility to allow for some relief between intense moments. It kept me going for the whole play session. And if you're into visual novels, anime style aesthetics, perspective and time shifting, beautiful graphics, and so on, you're bound to have a wonderful time, too.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely brilliant and thought-provoking game that had me mulling it over in my head and chatting with friends for weeks, thinking about my own upbringing as a second-gen Asian immigrant. The Nier and other influences are undeniable but the direct connection to current day society and in turn my own life was something I haven't really experienced before, especially in a sci-fi setting like this. The game is almost like a 3D visual novel and light on gameplay but I will note that some of the sequences running around talking to everyone got to be tedious. They're technically optional but skipping them means missing out on a lot of story and dialogue (though the recent map update should help a bit, or the amazing fan map posted in the guides section). Most importantly though I'll note that this game was very upsetting. I pushed through and couldn't put it down but I felt viscerally upset and almost sick for many parts of it. I love it overall but I think the game's key flaw is that it doesn't really know how to take its foot off the gas and any vaguely happy moments are just steeped in upsetting and otherwise depressing context, while the bulk of the story itself is far from uplifting.That being said I'm really glad I played it and highly recommend it overall.

_childDocuments_.review: I am writing this right after I finished this game and I don't review most games properly because I'm lazy. So for me to be compelled to write a review here is a big deal. Every chapter felt so engaging and the lore had me hooked. I felt like I needed to know everyone's story and so I spent the extra hours conversing with everyone. The team did an amazing job in how they presented this story and I always felt engaged with the diaspora of topics that are discussed in a fictional manner. I loved the HK culture spilled into this game and I can tell it was made with a lot of love and passion. TLDR: Go in for the 10/10 plot and have your heart strings pulled.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, ultimately, does not have the mark of a game, and thats fine. It is more just an interactive visual novel, with an incredible story to tell and mysteries to unravel. I do have gripes with the game that I will mention, but overall it was still a great experience, not too long that it overstays its welcome, the story keeping you pulled in the whole time. Now for the complaints (again, this game is still great, these may be detractors, but they are by no means game ruining).1) The voice acting. This does not account for every actor in the game as some were enjoyable, but for the most part, line delivery was almost always done in a flat or emotionless tone, leaving story moments that were meant to be impactful completely dull/something to laugh at. A large amount of the dialogue sounded like it was being whispered into the microphone, or the post production just did not equalize audio levels at all. This was probably the biggest detractor for me, especially in a primarily story/character based game, I expect the way these characters interact to sound natural and make sense. After a bit I just got over it and stopped hyperanalyzing, but it was still pretty bad.2) Audio Balancing. Mentioned it a bit earlier, but this is mainly the mix of music/voice audio, with the issue of music being too loud to where I couldn't hear a character speaking, even with changing audio levels in settings.3) Minor Bugs. Lots of textures glitching out, what seemed like two objects placed on top of each other and the game not knowing which to show you, not a huge nuisance, just something to see and chuckle at, but did break some meaningful moments.4) Model Staleness. Mostly has to do with the lack of mouth movement when talking (when faces are seeable at least), and the awkward poses characters were left idleing in, especially when in pre rendered cutscenes we can see really good character motion and speech, sad those touches weren't focused on for the majority of the game.5) The way the ending is portrayed to us. Spoilers obviously. This one is more of just a personal gripe, but it would have been nice to see Again, this game is very, very good, I am recommending it, after all. But I wouldn't staple it as a 'must-play' because you enjoyed X or Y in the past.

_childDocuments_.review: The best narrative-based game I have played in a very very long time, if not ever. I cannot believe what the team behind this game achieved. By the end of the first chapter it's already showing just how capable the writers are, how talented the voice actors are, and how unbelievable the art direction is. This game has some of the best visuals ever, and it doesn't come from complex cutting-edge technology. It comes from masterful use of technique. Views that stun, words that touch you, and music that elevates every moment without overpowering them.I've thought for a long time that game narratives were limited and that the medium could be used to achieve much greater heights than it was. This game is what I was imagining. It's everything I wanted and more. There are games with amazing combat. There are games with amazing movement. There are games with amazing realism. There are a select few games with amazing stories, in my opinion. And of those, this is the best I've played. It's original, high-concept, incredibly abstract and politically complex, and at the same time grounded deeply in human emotion. The science-fiction elements quickly reveal themselves to be a conduit for a deeply personal story about deeply flawed people in deeply rooted problems of consciousness. And with that I've officially said too much. Play this game, if you dare. But be warned. It won't leave you.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best story-based experiences in video games ever and easily my GOTY. It will have me thinking back on it for years to come.While those looking for a more gameplay-focused affair will be disappointed here, those looking for a deep and thoughtful story to wrap your head around can't do much better than 1000xRESIST. The gameplay mostly revolves around talking to NPCs, exploring the environments and choosing a few dialogue options. Fans of games like The Beginner's Guide may find some familiarity.The game opens in media-res as you, "Watcher", stab "Iris" through the back in a seeming act of hateful revenge, then flash back to the start. It's a fantastic intro that sets the tone and begins the mystery of "how do we end up there?" The tone of the game is often calming, contemplative and a little confusing as the game has you flashing backward and forward through time, seemingly interacting with past, present and future all at once, creating this beautiful and tragic tapestry which connects the themes throughout. There are themes of bullying, family, generational trauma, diaspora, political resistance, memory and grief all woven into a tight satisfying story. The pacing is well done here, as the game switches from interacting with NPCs in the hub, getting a sense of the place you're living and the population's struggles - to diving into lost memories, which will give you a sense of how everything came to be. The characters here are well written - you get a sense of their personalities pretty early on and they really begin to flourish once things start getting crazy (and trust me - they do).If you're looking to dig deep into an intricate, memorable and unique story game: look no further than 1000xRESIST. It left me in amazement by the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, this game was a journey. I really knew nothing about this game going in aside from it being a sci-fi narrative game with storytelling akin to NieR. That was enough to draw me in, and while that is a simple yet accurate description, it's sooo much more than that. A lot of the praise you'll read about this game goes to its story because this game is essentially a visual novel that you can walk around in and talk to characters. It's pretty light on actual gameplay mechanics which disappointed me at first, but that was my fault for going in with the wrong expectations. Once I got over that initial disappointment, I was able to look past that and see what this game really had to offer. Pros:- Story/Narrative: I wanna start this with what's most likely a controversial opinion: I don't think a lot of video games have really great stories. When you compare video game stories to the narrative depth you might find in a really good novel or TV series, a vast majority of video games can't compare; however, this game has that narrative depth I'm talking about. If the story of this game was translated into a full length novel, it would have a deep enough plot to both be interesting and hold its own as an extremely well-written science fiction story. I honestly don't know how an indie studio wrote a story like this, but this narrative goes layers deeper than anything I was expecting. Not gonna go into any specific examples because it's best experienced with as little knowledge as possible. I remember the game really drawing me in around Chapters 3 and 4, and it never let go after that. This one will definitely stick with you after the credits roll.- Characters & Voice Acting: The voice acting in this game was honestly better than I was expecting. I think the delivery on a lot of lines can feel awkward or forced at times, but for a 10-15 hour, fully voice acted game from an indie studio releasing their debut (!!) game, this was honestly incredible. Not too much else to say.- Soundtrack: I don't think the soundtrack in this game is anything to write home about, but I also don't think it was bad by any means. There's a few standout tracks that I enjoyed a lot, and it kept me immersed the entire time. Every track matched the mood of the scene it played in, and I think that's all a good soundtrack really needs to do. Cons:- Map Design: This is a minor one that bugged me at the start. I found the Orchard very confusing to navigate, and the directional signs didn't help me that much. I would've liked if there was some sort of guiding line to follow and assist with finding NPCs, but I eventually memorized the map layout and got used to it. - Gameplay: Mentioned this earlier, but I was initially disappointed by the lack of actual gameplay mechanics. I understand this game is more of a visual novel/narrative experience, and once I understood that, the game became a lot more enjoyable to me. - Animations: Not gonna mention much here since it's an indie studio obviously, but there's definitely some improvements that could be made to character animations. I don't think the animations in this game are bad necessarily, but there's definitely some improvements that could be made and I fully expect them to improve as this studio become more experienced.Overall, this is an incredible game. It's definitely not an experience everyone is going to enjoy, but if you go in looking for an immersive and deep sci-fi story with minimal gameplay expectations, you're almost certainly going to be satisfied. Cannot recommend enough. Red to Blue. Hair to Hair. Six to One. Hekki ALLMO

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Fantastic story leads to fantastic game. Who knew?-------------------L:RThis is sunset visitor's first game (from what I can tell) but my god did it strike an emotional nerve. It hides an incredibly touching tale of immigration, generational trauma, parenting, and forgiveness in an enthralling sci-fi narrative that evokes NieR: Automata and 13 Sentinels. Those comparisons have come up in other articles I've seen about 1000xRESIST, but really to me the heart of the game is more closely aligned with something like Before Your Eyes, or other Western Visual Novel-esque media than the distinct Japanese style of 13 Sentinels or NieR. This works to the game's advantage, I think, because as a piece that results from a group of Asian-Canadian creators, that backbone is strongly felt throughout some of the deeper themes and aspects of the game. Even from the first Chapter of the game I was struck by how solid the writing, paired with the phenomenal FULL voice acting, really sold both grandiose and unimportant moments. The voice actors all sound a little bit like they're whispering, but in like a really good way (lmao). I guess it's less of a whisper and more of a restraint from the overacting that a lot of indie VA work tends to fall into (e.g. bad Anime dub). The brief, optional character dialogue is incredibly well-used, serving to make memorable characters for later plot happenings AND provide exposition about the world without beating you over the head with it. As for the story, it's almost entirely linear in experience, though nonlinear in presentation of events, told through present-time character interaction and "communions" that give a glimpse into the past. There is "gameplay" and occasional light puzzle solving elements, but it is very much a vehicle for the story, and the developers understand that well. While the story can be confusing in concept, it is very rarely confusing in presentation -- things that are shown to you actually happened, for instance. One problem that I face when looking at other games that involve the general concept of "going into someone's memories" is that too often the dreamlike sequences are too difficult to tell apart with the actual memories and information you're supposed to understand. While at times the storytelling can be very ephemeral and subtextual, it was done in such a way that I never felt lost for very long and overall that served to further the emotions of the scene. It also allows the developers to seamlessly add in parallels relevant to the themes of the story without being overbearing or seeming out of place.The game also has an incredible soundtrack that stuck with me after completing the game and compelled me to buy the soundtrack here so I could listen to it on my phone. I'm listening to it now while writing this review. The OST is firmly in the Sci-Fi soundsphere with lots of moody and ambient songs, but there are also some real bangers and emotional tunes that play when they need to. And, speaking of, I think the USE of the soundtrack is absolutely amazing. The songs don't feel misplaced at all, and listening back to certain tracks puts you right back to where you were when they played in the game.I feel like a lot of times with these grand scale, multi-dimensional stories that involve the fate of the world, they lose a sense of relatability or closeness with the either the characters or the themes. To put it more simply, sometimes it feels like a story tries to do "too much," and as a consequence something is put off to the wayside. But, miraculously, for all the complexities the game has, any one aspect is very tightly connected with everything else. This becomes incredibly clear in the latter half of the game, when several large shifts in the story are perfectly paralleled with things you saw in the past during the earlier sections. Because all of the massive, world-moving events come thematically from somewhere much closer to the chest, it all plays smoothly and smartly despite the large scale. If there is one phrase that really encapsulates everything I think that 1000xRESIST does well, it would be that this game really knows where its heart is. In a very beautiful way. This game is so clearly to me a hallmark of everything that gaming can do well in storytelling. It effortlessly combines despair with hope, sin with forgiveness, and most of all tradition with innovation in a generation-spanning narrative at the end of the world.

Of course the second half has it's moments but it seems as if the writers were to intent on tying up loose ends rather than continuing to give thrills and twists and turns. All in all this is a nice little gem to add to your collection. 8.2/10.

_childDocuments_.review: How does it feel to know you can never go back home...Because your home is gone...I went into this game with pretty high expectations, but I had no idea what I was actually getting into. And while I really want to write about my experience playing this game for the past two days, it wouldn't be fair to deny people the opportunity to experience this game completely blind, as I have. Of thinking you have this game squared off, only to watch it unfold and unfold on itself until it is something so different and so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ beautiful. I had to take a break several times during the final third of this game, because I was sobbing uncontrollably.I pretty much did a full, completionist playthrough of this game, and I'd definitely encourage you to take your time with it. The game pretty much tells you when you've seen everything, and every detail matters, from the names of characters to the dates to what a random girl said about a PIDGEON in the very first chapter of the game. The game is a a masterpiece in non-linear storytelling. You start at the end of the end of the end of the end. You're literally told from the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ store page how this is gonna go, and yet you have no idea what's going on. Just like your character, really. But when this game is over, if you perform your function as Watcher well, you're gonna know all of it, and it's gonna be great.My only complaint is that the way they handled final scene before the ending feels kind of artificial and overly complex, and it just feels wrong. It doesn't ruin the impact of the ending, it's actually pretty great overall, but it's annoying to have a stumbling block like that right at the end.
