_childDocuments_.review: Good aesthetics, kinda moba-esque and an overall fun concept..-- HOWEVER..The experience is massively butchered by terrible PC optimization and snowballing power,A veteran player knows exactly what to do at the beginning of the round to get their "promoted"  build up, which allows them to have a better geared character up, that will have stronger abilities & more HPof course that alone wouldn't be so bad, if it wasn't for the fact that you don't get to choose your build options like your average MOBA, you need to get lucky and find what you want, and then slowly get upgrades to them.This means veteran players have not only experience advantage, but also gear and drops advantage, making them bring a same rank class as you but notably tankier or higher damage.As another rant, you get 5 free character slots, and each character can only be promoted 5 tiers, meaning if you promote your favorite character, you can't use them at start of the game anymore because you need to level up in game to get permission to use higher promoted characters.This means you need to use one of your 4 remaining character slots to make a lower rank version of the class you just promoted in order to be allowed to play early-game with it.Each following promotion makes your character require even more minutes in to the match before you can use them, which means that the more you main a character, the less you get to play them.. what a fun design, huh?Each promotion increases a character's available points for gear and abilities, but if you don't have good gear and abilities, those points will be wasted, meaning you can't even properly benefit from promotions if you don't first get lucky and find enough upgrades.Early game is the only stage of the game that feels even a little balanced, because once the top players get their snowball rolling, they'll come back tankier, doing more damage, having more ability uses, more ammo and shorter cooldowns. Sounds exactly like a MOBA, except you can't do the same without having the options first - in fact, it's so bad, that the game RENTS pre-promoted & geared up characters to you, just so you can keep up a little.The good:+ Cartoon art style+ Variety of skills and classes to play+ decent level design that can be abused by smart playersThe bad:- winning comes down to the skill and gear more than strategy, and strategies are impossible to pull off because map has player dots that reveal you so you can't be sneaky or surprise anyone- Essentially pay to progress, because you can't get better upgrades easily without paying or being lucky- Runs awfully bad on PC despite it's simple graphicsI like the game, and I want to recommend it, but I can't until:1. the game runs better on PC2. the upgrades are chosen in-game, or everyone has access to the same options through progressing and promoting, not luck.For example, all skills should be unlocked at start, and earning promotions would simply unlock higher level variants & allow you to use more game changing abilities / upgrades.I don't see it becoming a competitive E-sports game, but I do want it to become better, more optimized and balanced.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really good overall and they kept the logic simple and detailed, so let's see how it works.The logic is very simple, there are 2 castles in the game and 25 real players in the game, each castle has 5 groups, these groups go as attack, defense, support and progress, you are assigned to one of these groups and you start the game, your goal is to do the tasks that you are assigned to which position in this group, for example, if you are in the attack group, your task is to go and capture the opponent's castle, if your task is defense, repair and improve the items in your castle and also kill the incoming enemies, as I said, it is really simple and fun. There are 3 classes in the game, warrior, healer and mage, using these classes to win the game, that is, you are trying to capture the opponent's castle, the game is simply a 25v25 moba type game. As for the controls, they kept it really simple and beautiful, they took care not to force it too much, my preliminary impressions of the current game are good, and I will continue this review in the future, and in the meantime, there is one more little thing I can say, if the developers can take care of this game and move forward in a good way, they can really do a good job because there are not many games similar to this in terms of logic, even Conqueror's Blade, which is the closest counterpart, does not offer a siege logic as fun as this, I hope the developers will do this job and it will be a nice entertainment for us.

name: Deadlink
detailed_description: Deadlink is a cyberpunk FPS with roguelite elements. You're an elite operative recruited to the experimental Deadlink project. Pilot an autonomous combat shell, fighting your way through cramped slums, twisted labs, grimy warehouses, and sleek office buildings on a mission to thwart the schemes of the most powerful corporations in the world. Wield a deadly arsenal, upgrade your skills and tech, devastate destructible environments, and slash corporate profit margins — all at the same time. You are the Corporate Security Agency’s greatest weapon, and it's your job to make sure the corporations and their shady deals are anything but secure. With the team at HQ backing you up, you're tossed headfirst into the fray, where a military operation with plausible deniability can fix things for a fraction of the cost of a hopeless court case. Every randomized run will be different, but one thing never changes: you will be outnumbered. Get ready to think on your feet as you dash, jump, and use the environment to your advantage. You can't still, not even for a second. Equip your shell with powerful weapon loadouts. Try out various combinations as you blaze a path of destruction. Want to snipe your foes from a distance, debilitate them with status effects, or just go in guns blazing? Whatever your playstyle, you can find the right kit for the job. Your enemies have no shortage of bullets and bodies to throw at you. But you're no slouch either. Sure, you might lose a combat shell here and there, but your next one will be even tougher. Start each new run with amped-up skills and deadlier firepower!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is what i was expecting from Doom Eternal's horde mode.Played GUNFIRE REBORN and beat the game few times with different characters but gunplay felt weak and didn't care for it so much afterwards. ROBOQUEST had better gunplay but it was way too long for what it was to finish a run and having no save system made me quit that even faster. Deadlink on the other hand ticks these two boxes flawlessly.Faster mobility than Doom Eternal which can cause some problems at the beginning for some  people but having only 5 equipment which consist of 2 guns, 2 abilities and 1 grenade for each character/class makes it up for it in a way that you don't need to memorize so many keys and can go between these equipments fairly easily. Which will give you easier time to master the mobility.Like Doom Eternal you can get armor from enemies you kill and you do that by marking your enemies and killing marked enemies before it expires. Grenades that damages enemies marks them for example and almost all abilities of characters also does the same thing. There are no HP recovery by killing enemies though, you only recover HP by purchasing HP from stores or by completing special rooms. Sometimes with perks. But since you can get armor from enemies way more faster and way too easily compared to Doom Eternal, you are not gonna look for HP recovery all that much, thanks to the marking system and how quick and easy you can mark enemies.GAMEPLAY LOOP consist of you entering a room, engaging in combat in arena shooter style with very high mobility for almost all characters which can be even improved further with perks, clearing out the room and then choosing the next room. Before choosing the next room you get to see which type of rewards are you gonna get. Like how it works in HADES basically. You get perks and upgrades for your equipments after completing a room. You do this number of times and eventually enter the boss room, defeat it, and you go to the next stage where there are new enemy types in a new biome if you will. There were 3 stages in early access, now they added the 4th and final one. They also added a new character, making a total of 4 characters to choose.All your characters have 2 weapons. One standart weapon like shotgun for soldier and one special weapon which is rocket launcher for soldier for example. Standart weapons have unlimited ammo, you just reload when magazine is empty, whereas special weapons require you to collect their ammunition in the room if there are any, or by killing enemies which they may drop it or the best and most consistent way, by breaking C-balls. C-balls are energy balls that you can find in every room and you can break them by punching them or with your certain abilities. By breaking them you do get ammo for your secondary weapon.You have perk slots for your characters, 4 of them. Weapon switching, using ability 1, using ability 2 and breaking C-balls. For example soldier has a hook ability that works pretty much like super shotgun's meat hook, you fly towards that enemy and do your thing afterwards. Now if you equip a perk to your hook ability slot that says "Stun enemies that are marked (active) and deal %50 increased damage to marked enemies (passive)" it means you will stun an enemy because hook ability marks an enemy and you will deal %50 increased damage to all enemies whether you used your meat hook on them or not as long as they are marked. Active part of the perk only works when you do that action you assigned it to like using abilities or breaking C-balls. This itself creates fun and interesting builds for your character.Soundtrack is good, it is adrenaline pumping, goes along with the gameplay itself.I recommend this to people who craves for a good FPS roguelike because at the moment, at least for me, this is the best.-----------------------------------------------------------As a sidenote, the game feels at its best when you play it on higher difficulties, highest one to be exact. After getting used to playing at least 50+ runs on hardest difficulty, i chose a different character and started a run with the easiest difficulty by mistake but didn't notice it, and when the game started i thought game was bugged and not spawning enough enemies as it should. Realized later on that i was on easier difficulty. Funny side is that i was not even able to progress through first stage at the easiest difficulty when i first started playing the game but when i got used to the gameplay loop and combat, i was beating the highest difficulty with fresh save and no meta progression whatsoever. It was surely hard to achieve but it was doable. You may feel the difficulty spike at higher ones at first but once you get used to it and learn to use your mobility to your advantage, it will feel like a good and doable challenge.-----------------------------------------------------------[EDIT]Now i needed to do this because it still blews my mind how there are other roguelike FPS games that are doing better than this game, player count wise. Not that i care about the concurrent player base given that this is a single player video game but it feels like this game deserves way more attention than it got. And there are few people i saw were complaining about how difficult the game is. Because of this i wanted to talk about few more things regarding this game. Because this game is not unnecessarily hard, it is just challenging, you just have to know what type of FPS roguelike this game is. And how mobility is way more important than your combat abilities.This is NOT Gunfire Reborn where getting few key items/weapons that you are comfortable with or having alot of meta progression makes you win the game. This game is Doom Eternal on steroids in a roguelike gameplay environment. While how this sounds may scare some people given that there were some who didn't like how Doom Eternal gameplay turned out to be, this game is actually way more managable than Doom Eternal.In Doom Eternal you have 9 weapons. That's 9 keybinds already. There is also a button for switching between weapon's mods. That makes it 10 buttons. A grenade button and grenade switching button, which makes it 12. Chainsaw, flamethrower and punch adds up to 15 buttons. And the last one your sword or warhammer if you are playing the expansions which makes 16 buttons. And of course, dashing. 17 freaking buttons you need to go back and forth when you are dealing with your enemies which if you've played Doom Eternal on higher difficulties, you know as well as i do, you needed almost all of them.Now if we were to check Deadlink, your characters only have 2 weapons, a grenade, 2 abilities, dash. And that's it. All of that adds up to 6 buttons you need to manage. 5, if you just use your scroll button to switch between weapons.This is why this game is way more managable than Doom Eternal. Like in that game, you also need to switch your weapons constantly in here too but switching between just 2 weapons is alot more managable and you don't even need to press 1 or 2 by the way, you can just use your scroll button on your mouse since it is only 2 weapons. Since there aren't so many buttons you need to memorize and go back and forth, you will have easier time to learn combat controls. This will leave you to adjust how to manipulate mobility in this game because compared to Doom Eternal, this game is way more faster in a way that how your enemies come at you, how they fire at you etc. After unlocking few meta progression stuff, plus getting good at how to move, normal difficulty of the game will feel like a joke.Just keep at it, practice your mobility, use C-balls to your advantage. If you think you are still having a hard time, go with soldier! That character has the best mobility in the game than any other character which if you master it, highest difficulty of the game will feel like walk in the park.

_childDocuments_.review: This goes in the category of "good game I don't like".I do recommend checking it out if you like fast arena shooters at all, and I have to give a thumbs-up to any indie dev for finishing a polished project.That said, I was content to finish one run and uninstall.There are plenty of reviews that speak to the game's virtues - and they're right, but I'd like to whine about what didn't do it for me, in case you are similarly snobbish and miserly. Variety is my main issue. There are four classes, each of which has a light and a heavy weapon. Each heavy weapon has four variations (stock, fire, shock and acid) and they can be found at random by other classes. The elemental guns tend to change the nature of the weapon significantly, which I like. Stealth boi's energy gun becomes a railgun when switched to fire, for example. Once you pick your heavy, though, you're probably sticking to it for the rest of the run. Chances to switch are few and far between, and you're usually better off upgrading the one you have.You're also stuck with your light weapon. Like engie turret classes but don't like SMGs? Well, tough.Perks can change the weapons slightly, but not enough to differentiate one run from another. It's usually a linear, unimpactfull change like improved reload speed.Four classes and a total of 20(ish) weapons is already a little slim for a modern roguelite over $20, but unlocking the fourth class is where my enthusiasm started leaking. (Spoilers below are just class 4's loadout)The perk system is cool, actually. You decide what part of your kit the perk is tied to. For example, you could set the perk that resets your dodge cooldown to trigger on weapon swap for maximum CQC jitters, or on grappling hook use to never stop flying around the arena.This game encourages the DOOM Eternal flow of "use everything all the time", though.If you aren't rotating every button you're likely getting mulched in later levels, and few perks are zany enough to greatly impact your playstyle.Speaking of the levels-There are four stages, consisting almost entirely of square arenas with an upper and lower floor, and one main boss each.The bosses also take place in mostly barren square rooms, except for the stage 3 boss, which is honestly a pretty cool fight.This means that if you had a lucky (or very sweaty) first run, you could conceivably see all of the game's playable content in 1 hour, not counting replays with other classes or the cherry-flavored version of your gun.There is a story..I assume.Idunno, I didn't pay attention and can't poo-poo the work that went into world-building just because of my undiagnosed ADD.What did take me out of it a bit, and I admit this is a silly thing to harp on, was some of the lines and delivery.It's hard to pinpoint, maybe it's just me, but it smacks me with feelings of "this was translated". It makes me think of what Civvie 11 called "skin-walker sentences".The words make sense in the order in which they're presented, but they just don't feel like things a human being would say. I get the jokes, but it sometimes comes across as moon person humor.Occasionally the gravelly-voiced man (whose name I will never remember) will totally mispronounce common words and it makes me feel like I'm having a fever dream.As minor note, the shops and first boss made my CPU sweat. Not sure what's up with that - not a big deal.Anyway, that's enough b****ing about what is an actually decent game.Try the demo. It's indicative of what you can expect.The style is cool, the movement is good and the gunshootbang is satisfying.Don't take the word of some fusspot. The only important opinion is your own.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I think the idea is solid: The upgrade system is broad with lots of options, abilities are fun to use, guns have fun gimmicks. But while I can enjoy the game for a bit, there are severe issues that hamper the experience—and the roguelite elements hold it back even more, because the amount of replay value you get from it is nonexistent. The flat colored stages with same cookiecutter enemies flooding you from all angles gets old very quickly. The focus on mobility with dashing, high jumps, and teleportation means nothing when every direction you turn there is some meatsack vying to shoot you. Decisions are split-second and you are punished harshly if you do not capitalize. Some might enjoy this, and I think I would too, but the game fails in other ways that make it more punishing and obnoxious than motivating.When it comes to combat, which I would consider paramount to a shooter, kiting is very difficult unless you put terrain between you and the enemy that they cannot easily path around, and that is just not possible in some stage layouts. The small size of almost every arena is also very restricting, killing a lot of potential momentum. So all that is left is you, backpedaling or strafing around the same 3 or 4 types of enemy per faction, occasionally teleporting/explosion jumping if you've got the ability, every stage, every time. There is no uniqueness in that, no variety, no replayability.Even if you're the kind to enjoy the endless slaughter of faceless mooks as I am, the enemies are the weakest part of the combat. They aren't fun to shoot and aren't fun to be shot by, and there's just not enough of them at once to hit that excessive peak where you feel like an unstoppable killing machine, which would redeem it somewhat. There's also not enough of a focus on individual battles, with every boss continually spawning the same enemies you normally fight—not even trash mobs or creeps like you'd see in other games, just all the usual enemies. And when they can dish out the usual damage too, having to contend with them  the boss is just not fun. What makes the enemies worse is the their sound design, as they have very quiet movement, VO, and guns, that all tend to get lost among other sounds, which makes enemies hard to pinpoint.Really, most every sound in the game is boring and flat, without energy and motivation; there's a lack of punchy SFX, which feels out of place for an action-packed scifi/cyberpunk shooter. All the guns, including your enemies' guns, feel like they're shooting foam darts. The music is good but also lacks fullness and presence, which in other contexts I would praise since I hate the constant ducking and overdriven clipped instruments in most modern electronic music, but when combined with the rest of the game's sound mix holds it back rather than improves it.The thing I dislike the most about the game is a result of the above problems: It's incredibly difficult to interpret taking damage and locating enemies. It would be okay if the sound cues were better, or if the gameplay loop were more engaging, but it isn't. The "you've taken damage" screen effects last way too long; they're not instantaneous and attention-grabbing enough to make it clear you've been hit; the hit sounds lack punch and are overly busy; there is little to no visual feedback on the direction of damage taken; the quiet enemies as I described make it overly difficult to judge damage sources... I could go on. There are frequent moments where I will be getting shot from behind, or backpedal into an enemy, and not know the enemy is there, and if I'm already taking damage from somewhere, it's next to impossible to know I've begun taking more from that. In a shooter, this is very not good, and makes deaths feel unfair or unearned.The levels could save it, but as mentioned, they are small and boring. The design is nice, but they don't do enough to stand out or make them interactable. Explosive barrels, the "C-balls" that only exist to give you ammo that you have enough of anyway, and an unlockable shell in Watts-Rucker are all you'll find while playing. There are shootable objects in the paths between arenas to unlock new items to drop, but they are placed obviously with a sound and visual effect, so there's not a feeling of accomplishment or exploration. They're just kinda there. You know to expect them after the first or second time, and after you unlock everything (which happens fast) they stop showing up. Why not have them give some credits or XP after instead?Speaking of items, most of the upgrades are marginal and do not change your gameplay experience much. And if you really like a particular build, you just have to pray to the entropy gods that you'll get the gear you want, because the swathe of trash upgrades are going to make that difficult. One could argue that picking upgrades is a critical portion of the game, and rolling with the punches to make a build on the spot is the whole point, but forcing users to pick between multiple options that are either marginal at best or unwanted at worst, over and over again, is never good—especially when it happens so frequently (at least with me). Games like Risk of Rain do it right where almost every item is at least  useful or will be in the future. Yet, if you have no use for an item, the money you get for "zapping" them is pitiful, a paltry 30 or so credits, while the cheapest worthwhile mods you can buy at the shop start at 150ish. Sure, you can get 50HP back, but that's also pitiful once you start getting max health upgrades. You can't even buy it twice, so it doesn't scale.Speaking of the player character, the devs went hard on the lore to back up your remote control robot body and to try and make the world interesting. The focus is appreciated but the delivery is not interactive, written very dry, and is lazily gamified—it feels like side content rather than a core part of the experience, which severely limits its entertainment value. Why not get codex notifications and a codex reader ingame, Metroid Prime style? Having the codex right next to the gameplay and the enemy, and making it feel like you're learning and observing as you play, adds a lot of depth and mentally links lore to enemies—it could even be tied into the upgrade system. I honestly want to read the lore and enjoy it, but it's shoved in a submenu outside of the main gameplay, so I am not given any incentive to overcome that inconvenience. The lore doesn't provide any tangible benefit to the main game either, like hints about combat styles or previously unknown weakpoints. Weakpoints are already highlighted ingame anyway, so what good does mentioning those do besides fluff?All that can save the game are abilities and weapons at this point, and I'm pleased to say I think they're... fine. I like the versatility and unique take on the abilities, and each of the combat shells' pair of them work well together. The cooldowns are a bit high but that does tend to force you to vary your approaches. I do feel like they probably had the first two shells' gameplay designed first, and then built the rest of the game around that, because the skills and weapon mixups are clearly the meat of the game. The revolver is especially good and it always feels satisfying to land a slick headshot. All the first person animations are fluid and fun to watch, and the focus on weapon switching as a mechanic is interesting and something you don't see often.So where from here? I don't think more enemy factions/levels will be able to salvage this game, but that's all that seems to be happening in the time I've been playing. A few gameplay tweaks here and there, but nothing to give that spark that really makes me want to pick it up and play another run. The game isn't doing anything new or interesting outside of its few one-note innovations, especially in the current trend of "boomer shooters" that play mostly just like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Gonna be honest, not sure why this is so highly rated, I had to double take to make sure this was full release and not still EA. Figure it's just people playing 2-3 hours(when it's fresh and fun) then just not going back to the game/revising their review later on, because this game has some of the worst replayability and balance.Biggest gripes are the balance and lack of variety(in just about everything). First difficulty level felt like a good intro, nothing felt unfair, bosses weren't complete ass to deal with with mediocre loadouts. Second level you start seeing that some weapons are just completely unusable and you wonder if you're missing something - nope, just bad design. Bosses(the same 4, the only 4, the only 4) start to get a bit stale and gimmicky. Third difficulty is just fishing for an Arc Cannon on loadout select or restarting, because literally everything else is many leagues below it. Bosses and enemies in general getting the 40%(+?) movement speed starts to show just how badly the movement and collision is in the game. Everything takes 3x to kill because of the dogtier armor/shield system the game has. Still all of the same encounters, just mega aids now. The final boss glitches out and gets stuck in place every fight, but it's fine because the fight itself is so trash you're just happy to finish the run. It's like playing melee in a fight where the ai has infinite teleports and no cooldown on them.The way the passive/actives(not class abilities but the nodes or whatever they're called) is actually a neat system, most of the node themselves are super lackluster but some actually change the way you play and at least early on you have to make choices on your limited slots, something that goes away once you start unlocking the progression tree. Speaking of the tree, the economy in this game is so stingy, it's made in a way that it'd take 15+ hours to likely unlock everything, which would actually be on the lower end for a roguelike, thing is this game doesn't have the content to back that up so artificially dragging it is just frustrating. The fact you don't get more experience/currency on stage 4 compared to stage 1 is also bad design, it'd be more efficient to spam the first level on Diff. 3 then do the all 4 stages because the reward per room/boss is the exact same from your first encounter to your final.A lot of the enemies just feel awful to fight against - shield bros(both the Sumo guys and Mr Tower shields) are complete ass design. The exosuit enemies that grab orbs and mega buff/heal/turn on turrets are atrocious in their hitbox and lack of ranged options. The way bigger enemies on the highest difficulty can literally body block you while they have the Flash's speed and just gangbang you.. list goes on. Harder shouldn't equate making bullet sponges or just increasing a slider on the mobs stats. Make more environmental hazards, new mechanics, risk v reward objectives. This game fails in its design of difficulty by turning numbers up for the AI, and down for the player, it's not fun. Outside of the stale encounter design, I was disappointed in how little content the game seemed to offer as a roguelike as well. The stages aren't varied, it's the same tilesets which are all reused, there is zero pro-gen involved and the pool per map is very low, you'll see every tileset within 2-3 visits to the locale and it gets old very quickly. Each class has a single primary, with the primaries and their upgrades in general being fairly lackluster and you'd have to get an insane gambit to even have them be your "primary" through the run. The secondary(what actually does damage) options do actually have some variety, but you'll soon find out the only things worth using are explosives and the arc cannon, with everything else getting severely outclassed. You also can just get the best weapons/upgrades upon starting the run.. so most people will just do that. There is just so little thought put into some of these systems when there are so so so many good roguelikes out there that showcase exactly why this sort of design is trash.The music and art design are both super good and immersive, there just isn't much variety in either. The first few hours/runs as you're unlocking new stuff and things are still fresh are great, but once that honeymoon phase is over you see just how shallow the game is. 10 hours to clear on the hardest difficulty with 2 classes, probably only 5-6 hours of enjoyment from it. For $20 there are worse offenders, but honestly if you're reading reviews to see if you want to try this you care about the cost, and there are many, many better options to spend it on.

_childDocuments_.review: Deadlink is a very fun game that combines fast paced shooting action with rogue elements, all Cyberpunk themed.Add to that the fact that it runs fine, I suspect also on older PCs and you have a game that you can pick up quickly and not let go.Watch my first gameplay here: In Deadlink you have a 'secret agent' who is thrown into battle via the Deadlink Project in a kind of empty avatar.This allows the agent to be tested in combat, but if it is destroyed you will lose everything except your life. zo you are constantly thrown into the action and you feel yourself growing in skills. Pay attention, because where you get stronger and better every time, this also applies to your enemies and that results in an action loop where you are always on the edge of your seat.For example, you have powers that are temporary and powers that are all-session, characteristic of rogue-likes, constantly changing the way you attack your enemies,but you can also partially adjust the environment.You notice that you are always in a kind of chess game, where the rules are always changing, but it is still fun to play. I say chess, but I'm talking about the depth and not the speed, because chess can be boring, while in Deadlink you don't have time to find things boring.

_childDocuments_.review: What is Deadlink? It's Hades... But the combat is DOOM (modern DOOM, not old-school)... With a cartoon-cyberpunk skin… And some Borderlands-style humor, let’s say Borderlands-Lite.That's It. What you get: You get four different characters to play (unlocked as you progress), each with 2 unique weapons, and 2 unique abilities, both on cooldown timers. You have grenades, dodge, and a double-jump. Play through four different areas, each with an average of maybe 7 or 8ish rooms. Pick various upgrades after a room. When you die, spend some of your 2 permanent currencies to upgrade your characters and improve your drops. Combat has a focus on killing “marked” targets. Each character has several ways to mark a target, then when you kill said target they drop shield-refills to help you stay alive. You also get a timed mode, and an endless-wave hoard mode. The Good: - Combat is VERY crisp and polished- Movement and shooting feel great- Room rewards and meta-progression are both addictiveThe Bad: - More repetitive than Hades, but not near as bad as some rogue-likes- Balance of rewards is not great. Many upgrades are downright useless, while others (of the same rarity tier) are OP. (Although this does create more excitement when you get the good stuff)- Humor falls flat most of the time- Could not care less about the storyThe Maybe:- The highest difficulty is quite hard! (there are 3 tiers) You need to get real lucky with your upgrades, and/or spend huge amounts of currencies, which can take hours to acquire. The middle difficulty is appropriate though, far from a guaranteed completion even on a fully upgraded character.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh man, you know that feeling when you find a game that scratches a very particular itch? When you're looking for something oddly specific and start to accept that you won't find it, but then you actually do? That's how I felt for example when I found my now go-to mecha game in M.A.S.S. Builder and this is definitely how I feel now with Deadlink. It's an absolutely stellar game and you should definitely play it.Now what was that particular itch I'm referring to? Well I've been really into roguelikes for several years now and I've been a huge fan of anything cyberpunk for a long long time. I love everything about cyberpunk artistry. As such I played Cyberpunk 2077 and greatly enjoyed it. And the itch that I got is that I wanted a game with similar, perhaps even faster combat than 2077 but on a more casual and on-demand basis, without any of the story weight or expectation of a full RPG. A roguelike would fit perfectly in this bracket. I did find quite a few games that tackle this, kind of, but it was always not exactly what I was imagining. Roboquest, Mothergunship, CyberCorp, Synthetik, GTTOD, I See Red. All of those are amazing games and I recommend them too, but they weren't able to nail the vibe I was looking for. Enter Deadlink, a game that is EXACTLY what I'm looking for.A cyberpunk roguelike first-person shooter with fast-paced gameplay, great mobility, great aesthetics and a banging soundtrack. All the boxes are checked! Now, this game does tend to fall almost too neatly into the stereotypes and cliches of the genre, but honestly, that's completely fine. If you choose a well known aesthetic like this, there is nothing wrong with doubling down and giving people exactly what they expect. The game knows exactly what people are going to expect and is more than happy to deliver. Towering skyscrapers, dirty streets, an overcrowded, massive, neon-drenched metropolis, complete with sex stores and vending machines on every corner, gratuitous advertising and cameras on every wall, pastiches of Japanese culture, cyborg soldiers, gangsters and street thugs, drones, evil laboratories, endless warehouses, references to 3D printing, cryptocurrencies and AI as everyday things, and more. All of the classic elements of cyberpunk culture are present in the visuals and the story. Speaking of which the story itself is quite stereotypical, but quite engaging too. You upload your consciousness into a bio-mechanical body, roam the streets of the massive gigacity, fighting back against cyborg yakuza, ninja geisha robots, cyber sumo wrestlers and robot tanks . Then you can storm the halls of a German biotechnology lab or the warehouses of communist Giga Amazon (yes, really) and face the countless techno-organic monstrosities hidden within. The story tells a classic but still engaging tale of government conspiracy, corporate hegemony, transhumanism and misery in a futuristic world. The soundtrack is also exactly what you need to fit all this and it's an absolute banger. I could go on and on but to put it briefly, if you love the cyberpunk genre, this game is a must play. You will absolutely love it.And my personal story and bias aside, Deadlink is a genuinely awesome game. It's gameplay-wise really similar to Doom Eternal actually, even the armour pickup sound is almost the same. It has great visuals that are stylized and realistic at the same time, the movement and gunplay are both super tight and responsive, there's a decent variety of abilities and weapons and a very unique and varied upgrade system. The roguelike elements as always keep the experience engaging and interesting. The only criticism I can give is that the game is a bit slim on content at the moment, but this is understandable as it's still in early access. The devs have already released quite some stuff post launch, so I know they are dedicated to improving this. There is more than enough content as is and the game is still tons of fun. Come on and go kill some corpo scum!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:- Extremely cohesive and rewarding experience even at this point in early access (17/07/2023).- This is a roguelite FPS with a cyberpunk aesthetic. It burrows its movement from Doom (2016), its roguelite structure from Slay the Spire and its aesthetic from Cyberpunk 2077.Visuals and Sound:- The game is a visual and auditory treat. Every artistic design decision works in service of itself. From the way the game slows itself down when you kill the last enemy, letting you enjoy the flying viscera that used to be someone's face. To the way the music shifts from Deus Ex Human Revolution to Cyberpunk 2077 when you transition from the quite moments to the pure thrill of combat. This game looks, sounds and is - a joy to play. Gameplay:- This game handles build variety really well. It's hard to hone in on a specific preferred playstyle, and more often than not you'll be racking your brain over how to play with the cards you've been dealt. This leaves the game feeling fresh where each subsequent run feels distinct and unique.- The three different classes play vastly different, and there is even more variability coming from the weapon and shell augments.- I really enjoy the way the game handles health management, balance and difficulty. Each run is sufficiently challenging and the implants you get won't offer you anything in the way of lifesteal or healing. In this game, you play around your shield and replenishing it from killing marked enemies. This means that any health damage you take, is a very real and tangible penalty for bad play. You have to either sink a precious end of stage reward or pay for healing from the shop to pay for your mistake. This fact works wonders to help incentivise players into using their brains to overcome stages as opposed to mindlessly running and gunning.- Lastly, the bosses all feel great and pose an appropriate challenge. They all have three distinct phases, with each phase having very specific behavior patterns. The trick is then to figure out how to play your build optimally for each given phase. Again, this design decision promotes the activation of your dusty neurons. Another thing to note is that bosses are not the only challenge, and some stages play very much like a build check, testing if players have been playing their build correctly before allowing them to proceed.Conclusion:- Addictive and fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is sadly very difficult for me to recommend, simply because of the amount of content. You will grind out your upgrade currencies to get further, but your runs will very soon all feel the same. Levels aren't varied enough and mods feel too passive to make different runs stand out from each other.This is a shame, if this game managed to make each run feel more unique with interesting strategies to take, it would hold out much longer. But as it stands, it doesn't matter if your gun shoots blue or red balls, a run with each class will always feel the same.Get it on sale and if you're not put off by repetition. Otherwise look for the plethora of other Boomer Shooters.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played enough to realize that the game was pretty fun for the first 12 hours or so but the longer I played the more I noticed some of the games mechanics felt awful. Here is what I feel should be improved upon.  Power scaling is terrible, at some point I feel that damage drops off for the player far to fast and that even when focusing on more damage you still get lack luster results. Enemies and projectiles are also a pretty huge issue for me. you are constantly being berated with lead and rockets or a melee person chasing you. I get its supposed to be fast pace and on your feet thinking but its ridiculous to put in a dash that has a not so decent cool down mechanic. your almost guaranteed to be hit if not dashing due to the spam of your enemies  who seem to shoot where your moving if not dashing. I'm not entirely considering the temporary upgrades when it comes to this system because one its random and your not always going to get something that improves dashing or even want to allocate your resources to it because well you really want is some more damage if you hope to get through swarms of bullet spongy enemies. I thought the voice acting was great and love the lore introduction, those were nailed! along with the design of the environments and enemies in regards to how they look. The final boss at femto  however is not fun and drastically beings to dampen the mood with a unending torrent of high damage along with the worst combo of lackeys to kill in order to replenish shields. I didn't cover all the issues but im sure someone else will. I see a promising game that was clearly made with love however some design choices killed my enthusiasm for continuing my fight against gangs, corps, and Pmc's.  Ultimately I don't recommend this game till certain things that I discussed  above are worked out. I wish the developers good luck though in any future endeavors!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a competently-made and pretty game, but unfortunately it disappointed me as a roguelite and I feel like while making really cool early impression it doesn't deliver anything as exciting with each new locale.In this game you play as brain in a case that what remains of severely weakened American government is trying to use as template for super-soldiers that would help turn the tide on corporate encroachment. You are stuck in the loop simulating battles against corporate underlings and there's some implied but for me not intriguing plot of who you were before and if you'll ever be free of simulation. The expository character dialogue is nice, though, one of them is real charming and provides fluff explanations on what the heck all the implant upgrades you pick up through runs are.Now, the good thing about gameplay itself is that it's all fast paced with great dynamic feel to it, everything is snappy and dynamic with satisfying motions, mid-gameplay you'll be jumping and dropping abilities and shooting all at same time and it feels natural as long as not overwhelming. The combat is in similar vein to Doom Eternal - it's like an old school arena shooter, except you gotta swap weapons often (not only due to low ammo, some "implants" you unlock can be slotted to activate on weapon swap), apart from guns you gotta use abilities, and those abilities help you turn enemies into health recovery pinatas.The bad thing? Yeah, the roguelike aspect doesn't save from repetitive feel, moreover it's kinda conservative. The slottable implants you pick up are useful but there's rarely ones that truly define your run, more often you'll just rack up a couple that make certain elemental damage more common and handy, but comparing to many other roguelites including FPSes the game-altering wow factor is subdued. The coolest ones I remember are stuff like "you throw extra grenades", except by second half of game only basic fodder enemies are easy to kill with grenades and they exist more to apply effects and mark enemies for resources, or "the action that restores heavy gun ammo does it fully and restores main weapon ammo too", which is useful but that's the creme de la creme here, you'd think they'd allow themselves to get wackier with luck involved but no, everything boils down to core loop using character skills and quick gun swapping and running, which is fine and good until it gets overwhelming. Permanent upgrades are neat but also lack pizzaz you'd wish for, and the risk and reward sort of options mid-run are very hit-or-miss too.Another complaint? First area looks super cool and flavourful, with Japanese corp's gang fielding dollar store tachikomas, sumo guys and geishas, and the streets are colourful and there's a promise of a "Sex club", whatever it entails. But then second area is just industrial futuristic panels and German space marines, and third area is soviet bunker with crazed janitor cyborgs, and fourth is actually for once a fancy upscale office, but then majority of enemies are reskins of previous area ones! And then third area, despite cool ideas like corporation turning hivemind after electing AI as CEO, it's just frustrating and feeling rather phoned in, enemies are Borderlands bandits if they were Russian cyborgs, I can't even tell types apart beyond most annoying one. Bossfights also feel repetitive, wish there was some variation between runs but guess that's out of scope huh.Overall, if you loved playing hero-based shooters like Overwatch or Paladins or whatnot, loved Doom, Eternal, and wished something like those games but as a roguelite, this may very much by for you, it's a flavourful and well-made game, just I feel very disappointingly restrained for a roguelite.

_childDocuments_.review: Fast-paced, action-packed, and disturbingly fun.I enjoy arena games. Quake 3 was my best friend in college. I have been having fun lately with Severed Steel. These games make me realize that after 30 years of playing, I still suck at FPS games. But I also still absolutely adore them.The cyber-enhancements here are a lot of fun. There are a ton of implants and whatnot, so finding the best mix for both your style of play and the shell you're using takes some time and practice. This makes each run is kind of a mystery. Will you get good stuff and breeze through? Will you get trash mixes and have to adapt? It keeps the replay value and the challenge quite high.I don't really have any complaints about this game. Controls are very responsive. The soundtrack is what you'd expect for something like this, but it fits fairly well. Some of the enemies and mini-bosses are an absolute nightmare for bad players like me (looking at you, Laika), but they still keep it fresh and fun. If you are looking for some mindless violence to test your reaction time and everything, this game will deliver.

_childDocuments_.review: This game wakes me up better than coffee in the morning. The combination of roguelite and action shooter elements makes for a really addictive and challenging gameplay loop. Likely just me, but when I have a god tier build and my first thought is "Can't wait to see how I screw this one up," I know the game is challenging. You can have absolute perfection crumble due to poor execution, which may suck, but at the same time, you also have the opportunity to have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ make it through to the final boss due to perfect execution. That's only somewhat true come Neuromancy difficulty, but it's so minimal that it's really only worth mentioning as a sidenote for disclaimer's sake. I would say for 95% of the time, the success of a run comes down to player skill with the randomized elements adding nice little touches/challenges to give you a boost along the way. The levels are limited (4 currently) but the challenges offered the higher you climb in difficulty combined with the soundtrack and variability afforded via randomized upgrades/enemy comps keeps you sufficiently engaged for an arguably bite-sized package. At the highest difficulty (Neuromancy) each run can take anywhere from 30 minutes (we'll get into that) to an hour to complete based on loadout.For those of you that are super into story, there's not a whole lot here. There's some gradual developments that are made following each run a la Hades, but don't expect it to be as in-depth as that game (which I'm not saying it should be considering this is Gruby's first game vs. Supergiant's 4th(?)). Still entertaining though. The more subtle world-building elements are rather creative and lively, and the game actually has a good sense of humor. Never thought I would play an action-cyberpunk-roguelite where one of the enemies is just there to take the piss out of Elizabeth Holmes.  That's my high-level review, anyways. I got some more itemized elements to lay out, though, starting with the good (note a lot of these pertain to Neuromancy difficulty as that's basically the endgame):-Soundtrack, as I said, really tight. Feels like it's in rhythm with the combat in a lot of cases.-Enemies are exceptionally varied in terms of attack patterns and threat priority which keeps combat very dynamic as more enemies spawn in.-No wasted space for combat. You are using everything at your disposal and it rarely ever feels clunky, even at the lower levels where you may have less tools in your arsenal.-Each reward path has its own intrinsic merit where the value of each is able to shift depending upon the state of your run so you rarely have a "Yeah sure fine if there's nothing else," moment.That being said, here are the criticisms:-That 5% where your runs are in the hands of the game? It's Toxic damage. Enemies in Neuromancy all have armor so it's kind of mandatory. The only upside: it's not that had to get on either your light or heavy weapon.-Hunter shell feels off? Lower health, less opportunities to mark, relies on getting the drop on enemies. Should be a highly mobile glass cannon right? Not really. Even with extreme precision, time to kill is either on par or lower than other frames with comparative buffs, its CDs are high, and it doesn't fix the issue where options to mark enemies are limited, which, if you aren't killing marks, you're dying FAST. (Sidenote: I could also really suck at this character.)-The Hammer Bros before the last boss feel supremely overtuned. Unless I am playing the Juggernaut shell, I fear for my life every time I step into that encounter. They can be beaten, yes, but they single-handedly have ended more of my runs than anything else in the game. (Again I could also just suck at these guys.)-Phoenix shielders are legitimately no fun. Fast gunplay screeches to a halt when these losers instant transmission into your pristine headshot and proceed to sit there waiting to poke their head out so you can shoot them, before they duck back behind the shield again. At least the sumos incentivize you outmaneuvering them.-Thoughts are torn on Iskra. I find it interesting that the two most challenging parts of the fight last the longest on Neuromancy and even lead to an overlapping of mechanics. I know I don't like the fact that hitting the weakpoints on the first and third phases basically require you to be in direct line of fire. Otherwise, pretty solid chaos fight.TLDR: Really angry action-shooter-roguelite with an amazingly tight combat system that I pray gets more updates because while what it has now is well worth the price of admission, I will gladly fork over more money for more of this. If you like Ultrakill, the more recent incarnations of Doom, or really just agressive action shooters in general, you will very likely love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun FPS Roguelite!!I knew very little about deadlink before its full launch but after its release I grew interested in it and got it through a bundle recently. Having little knowledge I was curious about what this game would be like and I am honestly really pleased with the outcome. This is a very fun , fast paced and challenging FPS game that will test your skills.- What makes it so fun?I just think this fast paced style of FPS games works well with the roguelite genre. It gives you heavy doom reboot vibes which is a very good thing making you always focus during encounters. With fun gunplay , movement , build variety this makes for an overall great package that I 100% can recommend if it sounds like something you might want to try. I don’t really want to get too in depth with mechanics but there is 1 character to choose from in which you unlock 3 more as you progress and do multiple runs. While the game starts off pretty much unbeatable you quickly will level up your character through a perm skill tree that will make the game tons easier if you learn boss patterns. I have heard people complaining about how hard it is but honestly I did not struggle after a certain point until hitting the hardest difficulty which is pretty damn brutal. I just had so much trying out new classes , weapons , skills because as usual once you stumble across an OP build for a run it truly is an amazing feeling to shred everything. Each character plays vastly differently which makes for a refreshing gameplay loop if you want to try someone else out. A core mechanic across the board is shield regain in which when you use a specific skill on an enemy and by killing them they will drop shields. This is crucial as if you don't utilize this enough you will simply lose runs a lot more so make sure you build around your shield skill and use it at any given moment you can!. After trying each character I landed on Engineer which I found to be very fun / powerful and have beaten multiple playthroughs with him only. I won’t speak on the other characters as I didn’t play them nearly as much but for sure give Engineer a go when you unlock them. There is just something so exhilarating about high action / fast paced FPS games that always stick with me and this game simply hits the spot.- What I didn’t like?I don’t have many complaints about this game past a few. To begin, The bosses do feel pretty basic and lacking; they don’t really try anything too crazy which makes them very easily learnable. This can become a problem because it hits a certain point where the bosses simply pose no challenge and most of the challenging will be within the stage by stage leading up to the bosses. Furthermore, the enemy variety is also lackluster as they just give them different looks in each area past a couple new enemies in the later areas. I didn’t really mind it too much but I do wish they would have created a more vast variety of them.- In the endAn overall great game I enjoyed my time with and probably will return to it as time passes on. This game has made me realize how much I would love even more FPS rougelike/lite games in this fashion because the 2 genres really do blend well with one another. The game imo is worth at full price for how fun it is and its replay value alone but I can recommend it 9439394% on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all I want to say I enjoyed every moment I played this game.The problem is I don't want to start it back up. I have identified why;It's a roguelike with a clear end boss. This makes it impossible to have the funny ridiculous power spikes or really deep runs that you might experience in a game like Risk of Rain 2. After 20ish minutes your run is gone.Another problem is that you get upgrades outside of a run. More grenades or better recharge time for abilties..While that sounds fun, the idea is inherently flawed. Once you beat the game, beating it can only ever be easier as you unlock more upgrades for your classes and thus will never experience the same level of difficulty again.I beat the game for the first after about 4ish hours of play and since then I have done a handful of runs. It was really fun up until that point as I had that doom feeling and wanted to overcome the obstacle. Once I started another run after I realised the only reason to do it again would be to get a better time. Or sure, maybe beat the game on a harder difficulty but I DON'T HAVE ANY MOTIVATION TO.This is because the upgrades or weapon combinations in one specific run arent actually interesting. There isnt anything new to see after just a couple hours, only better times to achieve. I never bought this game to play as a competitive game, I bought it to have fun. Maybe the game will improve as content is being added constantly. But right now.. I can't recommend this game unless you want some good fun for 4 hours and are okay with the pricetag for that amount of playtime.

_childDocuments_.review: Deadlink is a two-hour game that desperately tries to convince you that it has more to deliver.The basic loop is satisfying enough: go into dungeon, shoot mans, dodge their shooting back, tag them with certain abilities that make them loot pinata like in Doom 2016. In fact, the basic loop is very Doom 2016 encouraging you to push forward and explode things so they give you armor and ammo.The problem is that it has a completely unwanted and un-necessary roguelite thing grafted to it where when you die, you go back to start, you pay for a few upgrades with metacurrency, you dive back in again. This is not, fundamentally, a bad idea. I've loved plenty of Roguelites and I enjoy the idea of unlocking more options and coming back again to see what exciting new twists the RNG has thrown on to the table.The problem is that there is a very small amount of arenas, you will see all of them on one run, and the game has no more up its sleeve. The same goes for the enemies, no randomness, you will see the entire pack. Bosses? Yep, one per biome, seen them once, seen them all. What about the loadout, though? Are there surprises there? Yes, and they're all bad. There's exactly one good secondary weapon and if you don't get that, my experience is that you may as well ignore the slot(the basic rocket launcher with the no-self-harm upgrade is what I'm referring to, being able to grapple over to enemies and explode right on top of them is genuinely a bit OP).But what about the classes, or "shells" as Deadlink calls them? Well, a lot of games with this formula start you off with a bad class and it's a relief when you get better ones that can break the game more but... Deadlink just starts you off with the best one. The others may have other mechanics or be more sturdy but... the basic one has the best starting weapons, a balanced durability and the game's best mobility option. No reason to play anything else.So, in one run, you have seen everything. What's the point of more runs, then when you beat that? Higher difficulties. Ah, yes, with new arenas? New mutators? New enemies and challenges? Aside from one really annoying one where you have to punch ammo boxes a lot and a wave survival gimmick event, I didn't see any that did anything other than make the enemies spongier. Which really took away a lot of the fun, it slowed down the game a lot. It should've just dropped more enemies or made them hit harder, maybe given you less options for healing. But making enemies more durable, I feel, was a mistake. It makes your guns feel wimpy and sabotages one of the core joys which was a low time-to-kill for all non-boss enemies.The fourth biome also has a couple of minibosses with mechanics that the game does not deign to explain(the only self-healing and genuinely invincible enemies in the game, any sort of explainer or lower-level enemy using the same sort of behavior would've been a good help in making them not feel kind of puzzling to fight the first time around).So anyway, Deadlink flubbed its core concept on almost every level. If you want the same sort of high mobility, high risk gameplay but shorn of all the pointless parts, I would recommend just playing Ultrakill.The one caveat to this review is that I got bored halfway through the middle difficulty and its possible that the highest difficulty would've totally wowed me, but I feel like there's roughly an 0.0001% chance of that.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a bit rambly, so TL;DR the game is ok, but the second half of each run is more frustrating than fun, the player's damage feels too low most of the time (seriously, even on a good run, the final boss took 10 real life human minutes to beat in a game as fast as this. Plus another 5 for phase 2), and the meta-progression (permanent upgrades bought outside runs) feels unnecessary. If you want an arena fps roguelite/roguelike, BPM: Bullets Per Minute is a ton of fun. If you just want an arena fps... play Doom, Quake, Boltgun, or Ultrakill (especially Ultrakill). I'd rather buy any of those games at full price than buy this game sale, but if you really want to give this a go, wait for at least a 50% off sale. Finally, I apologize if the following is more of a rant than a review. I had more pent up frustration toward this game than I thought, but I stand by my issues with the game, even without the salt. This review would've been positive before the 1.0 changes, but they just had to fix what wasn't broken and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up the enemy armor system and in run progression, ruining the most important part of a game, especially an arena shooter, the gameplay.It's fine for a bit, then you realize there are 2 kinds of runs in this game.1. You basically one shot everything and have little to no issues the entire run2. You tickle fodder enemies, let alone heavy enemies and bosses. If you win runs like this, it's a slog consisting of 20 minute boss fights and running away from enemies because you don't have enough damage to kill them before they kill you.Floors 1 and 2 are good, 1 being the best imo. Floors 3 and 4 are just not fun at all. Honestly, I'd be fine if they went back to runs ending after the second boss just so I don't have to deal with the second half of the game. The C-Ball grabbing enemies on floor 3 are a good idea in concept because it shares a resource with you, forcing you to kill them so you can keep your constant supply of heavy ammo. But they only take one ball at a time, so that part is a non issue, but if they get a single C-Ball, they get full armor immediately then start running away, forcing you to chase them because their C-Ball can only be broken by melee. Soldier and now Juggernaut can deal with them pretty well, Soldier because he can just grapple to them so they can't get away, Juggernaut because his F ability breaks the C-Ball they're carrying and his Q let's him close the distance. Hunter has a hard time with them because his mobility is a swap, so you rely on an enemy being near them to catch up. Engineer can't kill much of anything, so of course he has a hard time, too. It's not like you can just ignore them, either, especially the healer. The non healer does a ton of damage, so you have to chase to get rid of the threat, and the healing ones heal other enemies, forcing you to prioritize them. The boss is also not good. The arena feels like it was designed for a different game. Soldier feels like he's the only one with enough mobility to maybe have fun in the fight because of how vertical the arena gets throughout the fight, but regardless of who you're playing, you have to listen to the same 4 voice lines from the boss on repeat while fighting it, which is the worst part of the boss. The 4th floor is just a series of mini boss encounters with recycled enemies from previous floors leading up to a final boss that is by far the worst part of the game. She's fast and hard to hit, has pretty hard to dodge attacks, and has the health bar of a Destiny strike boss. She's a bullet sponge in the worst way possible. She cycles through the same few attacks while you scramble around the arena for an enemy to kill for shields and deal so little damage to her you can't even see her health bar move. And after spending 10 minutes killing her, she has another phase that's the exact same as the first one, only she's faster, makes clones while going invisible, and her attacks are purple instead of red. You can lower her max HP by doing all the rooms leading up to her fight, but even then she still takes way too long to kill. It's not a challenge, it's an endurance test, and this game is not designed for an endurance test.The combat shells (characters) are hit and miss. Soldier has a grappling hook and a shotgun, giving him a very clear high mobility, high damage playstyle. Juggernaut plays similarly, but has a dash and damage negation instead of the grapple. These are my favorite shells, with Hunter coming in close behind. Hunter's stealth is a very good tool and his revolver doesn't do bad damage. Then there's Engineer. I've never seen a more useless character in any game. His guns do no damage, his Q is both his only CC and his only mobility (not to mention the aoe damage on killing the target), and his turret also doesn't do any damage, but you have to use it because it does more than your weapons do together. The intent of the character is clearly to have a more space control focused playstyle, but the damage numbers make no sense. Other shells can salvage a bad run, this character basically requires a god run just to function.Builds are also much more restrictive than it originally seems. The implant system is a great idea and I love how modular it is. However, the only viable build seems to be toxic damage. Toxic has the best implants that I can find and as far as I can tell not a single enemy is resistant to it, unlike other damage types. After release, it seems that they want all your power to come from the implants. But up until release, you got way more neuralboost upgrades, which boost stats like max hp, damage, skill power etc. This meant that even if you didn't get a great run, you still did damage through sheer force of big numbers. Now, you get far fewer of those upgrades, which means your build rests heavily on the implants you get, but since few of them give stat bonuses, even with good abilities from implants you don't do much damage. This is another reason toxic seems to be the only viable option now because some implants let you apply corrosion, which deals toxic damage over time. Another implant spreads corrosion to nearby enemies with an enemy dies with corrosion on them. Toxic ends up being the best damage type without damage upgrades because it deals damage so often, and toxic is still the best damage type with damage upgrades for the same reason. Finally, the armor system. Before release, enemy armor was basically a shield over their hp you had to get through before touching their actual health bar. Toxic was made to strip this armor, so of course it was also incredibly powerful with this version of armor, too. Now, armor is damage reduction instead. This change makes no sense to me because as it is now, the armor just makes your already low damage feel even lower since your damage is split between the enemy's hp bar and the tiny little strip at the bottom of their hp bar that represents their armor. The old system put all your damage to the armor, then all your damage to the hp once you were through, which meant that even without toxic to quickly deal with armor you still felt like you hit like a bus because you could see all the damage reflected on the enemy's hp very easily. The new armor system also raised the time to kill, to the point that fodder enemies can tank multiple shots from a heavy weapon (i.e. more than 2 shots max), or in the case of beam weapons, it can take multiple full seconds of just holding left click on a fodder enemy before they die. The gameplay can be fixed basically by just reverting the changes from the 1.0 patch. The 3rd floor boss would probably be much more tolerable if the platforms didn't raise up so high and if the voice lines were just removed (seriously, the voice lines are the worst part of the fight. It's so grating). The final boss just needs less hp and a smaller arena so you don't have to walk across a country to get to an enemy for shields mid fight.

_childDocuments_.review: The shooting and movement mechanics are good. Guns and enemy reactions have good player feedback. Feels good to play and runs well so kudos for that. Sadly the positives stop there.The roguelike elements are very barebones. You have a few elemental powers like toxic, fire and electric. That's basically the extent of the interesting builds you can make. The rest are basic meta upgrades like damage, defense etc. Then the upgrades found are tied to the actions you do. If you want that bonus damage on corrosion, then you have to grapple to an orb or use your special and those also have cool-downs, So now in order to get the most out of your build, you have chores and timers to manage. You also have to reload often. So you're constantly reloading, or waiting for something to cool-down. So the game puts you in these hectic arenas, yet strips control away from the player, or leads them away from playing how they want. The game feel is good, but the design decisions hold it back.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game, I can see where the base formula would work to be an amazing, fast-paced shooter. My issues are twofold: inconsistent pacing and grinding for content.There is a lot you need to manage in any firefight, button mashing and holding left click is a recipe for certain failure. The cognitive burden is not too high, there are systems that make it more appealing to mix and match your weapons and tools to be your most effective. The problem comes in when you don't reach a flow early, miss your timings, or fall out of your flow for a moment. The enemies are close, the weapons are slow to reload, and your tools have a timer, so that minor break causes the action to screech to a halt while you slap on another mag like your life doesn't depend on it.The game is a roguelite, so there is a persistent upgrade tree in that sense; however, where other roguelites offer some flexibility to change or adapt builds within or between runs, you enter a run with a set class and are allowed modifiers on what that class brings to the table. No weapon changes and not many movement differences. There are currently only three classes available, one of which is locked behind a certain amount of progress through the areas, thus either of the remaining two are your only options when starting out. I just want to shoot things in a variety of ways and on an increasing power scale, but Deadlink feels like it's holding back for reasons I don't claim to understand.I got the impression that the developers are worried about giving their players too much agency or power, that the fun should be derived from the repetitive and practiced aspects of the gameplay and the sense of progression is a secondary consideration. The feeling I get from a strong run in Roboquest or Hades or Risk of Rain 2 just isn't in this package at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly I'm pretty disappointed by this game. For the most part it ticks the right boxes for me, but some design decisions hold it back. The biggest one is reloading. The game THROWS enemies at you in open arenas, and having to reload feels really bad. Reloading works much better in a corridor FPS and not in arena style FPS. Next is meta upgrades. Meta upgrades are a pretty controversial design decision when it comes to roguelites. You risk making early runs feel pointless due to getting too much power between runs or having upgrades be so small that the game would honestly be better without them. In this case I would it falls into the first category. You get a ton of upgrades between runs.  If this game had more variety in it's gameplay that would make this type of meta upgrade more acceptable.

_childDocuments_.review: Very responsive dev, they have addressed the few little negatives I had about the game. So, is it good? Yes, it's one of the best shooters I've played. Gunplay is impactful, it's a bit on the challenging side, but you have very good and fun tools to deal with that. It's fast, it's smooth, and the more you unlock/find upgrades, the move it opens up. What looks like a simple/boring upgrade turns out to be a game changer when used with the right synergy. Some unique stuff's in this game, and you can make crazy builds. BUT, like in Doom Eternal, YOU have to keep up with the pressure to win, not count on rng - it's a tight shooter first.If you like RoboQuest, Doom, Quake, Shadow Warrior or Titanfall, you might just love Deadlink!
